## Volume front matter

### Series title page

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

A chronological reprint of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, comprising all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; prepared with the greatest care from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with numerous manuscript codices; most diligently corrected; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority, at least, in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers, and in which places of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following matters are considered: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes—consistently alike throughout the entire work—and the low price; above all, this collection, unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but brought together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## Expositions on the Psalms

[Complete Works of St. Augustine]

[Col. 0009]

# Preface to Volume Four

If Augustine had left us those final books of the *Retractations* in which, as he testified in his letter to Quodvultdeus, he intended to review the treatises delivered to the people (*Letter* 224, §2), he would doubtless have illuminated there this immense work on the Psalms of David with observations that might have served in place of a preface—one far more useful than ours. But since death did not permit the blessed man to carry out his plan, we think it our duty here to explain briefly, first, by what considerations he was moved to undertake an exposition of the Psalms; next, what order he followed in it; then, what method he pursued in explaining them; afterward, what rules he prescribed for himself; and finally, which version of the Scriptures he followed.

Augustine was extraordinarily captivated by the Psalms of David. Their singing, when he first began to hear it in the Church at Milan, affected his soul so sweetly that he was stimulated all the more forcefully by these pious emotions toward hastening his conversion (*Confessions* 9.6–7). The holy man also records that during his retreat at Cassiciacum, where he was preparing himself for Baptism, such a love of God was kindled within him by reading those same sacred songs that he burned with the most ardent desire, if it could in any way be done, to recite them throughout the whole world. At the same time he was pierced by an exceedingly bitter feeling of sorrow joined with indignation and compassion, because the Manichaeans, in their pitiable blindness, did not perceive the mysteries and remedies contained there, and therefore rejected the antidote by which health could have been restored to them (*ibid.*, 9.4).

Although, therefore, he understood from his own experience that so much light could be drawn from the Psalms and such abundant nourishment for piety extracted from them, nevertheless, content with his private meditation, he might perhaps never have turned his mind to explaining them publicly, unless causes sought from elsewhere had moved him. For he had formed so lofty an opinion of the excellence of the Psalms that, in his judgment, all those passages which seemed clearest were precisely the most deeply hidden. He himself sufficiently declares that there was no other reason why, after so many delays and postponements, he finally undertook to explain Psalm 118, whose exposition they demanded from him almost with reproaches, than what he says in these words: “For the clearer it seems, the deeper it usually seems to me” (*Prologue to Psalm 118*).

Nevertheless, since the responsibility of the office he held required him to instruct the people entrusted to his care by precepts, correct them by rebukes, form them in piety, and strengthen them in the pursuit and practice of good works and Christian virtues—and although, as the Apostle testifies, all Scripture contributes to this purpose (2 Tim. 3:16)—he nevertheless ought above all to employ the Psalms, since he saw them constantly worn by the hands of the people and repeated on their lips. He judged them especially effective for attaining this goal because they contain within themselves the mysteries and precepts scattered throughout all the sacred pages, of which they offer a kind of compendium.

He therefore labored at this task with the utmost care and diligence. If at times he complied only reluctantly with the troublesome and unreasonable requests of those who demanded commentaries on Psalms that he himself considered excessively difficult, we nevertheless see that on occasion he was unwilling to leave the Psalms he had in hand in order to transfer his pen to other subjects, because he always thought that what would benefit many ought to be given precedence. “Those things press more urgently,” he says, “which we hope will be useful to the greater number” (*Letter* 169, to Evodius, §1).

When Augustine first undertook this work, just as he had no intention of commenting on the entire Psalter of David, so he did not think that the order of arrangement needed much attention. Indeed, a passage in the letter written to Paulinus around the year 414, in which he testifies that he had formerly composed a brief exposition of Psalm 16—“I have revised,” he says, “a certain very brief exposition of that same psalm, which I had dictated long ago” (*Letter* 149, §5)—leads us to suppose that this exposition, together with all the others composed in the same brevity and style, was among the first to be produced in the entire work.

He had also decided to explain in order the Psalms called the Gradual Psalms, as he indicates while discussing Psalm 122 in these words: “I have undertaken, together with Your Holiness, to consider in order the Songs of Ascents.” Likewise, in Psalms 125 and 131 he says that he came to those psalms as the order of each required. Yet he explained Psalm 26 on the feast of Blessed Crispina, whose martyrdom the martyrologies assign to the fifth day before the Ides of December, and Psalm 37 on the feast day of Saint Felix, whose martyrdom is reported on the fifth day before the Ides of November. Various passages make it clear that in all the others he was not bound to order.

For example, in his exposition of Psalm 66 he cites explanations of Psalms 102 and 103; in Psalm 102 he cites an exposition of Psalm 103, which he also seems in some fashion to indicate while explaining Psalm 80. In a letter to Evodius sent toward the end of 415, he states that the expositions of Psalms 67, 71, and 77 had most recently been dictated by him, but that he did not want his labor on the remaining psalms, which he had not yet explained, to be interrupted (*Letter* 169, §1). From this one may infer [Col. 0011] that at that time not very many remained for him to treat. Places, times, circumstances, and persons very often suggested to him the psalm that he was to explain.

We owe the commentaries on Psalms 34 and 139 to the command or requests of bishops whom we may conjecture to have been holding some gathering at that time. The same may be thought of the commentary on Psalm 36, as he himself relates at the beginning of his second sermon on that psalm. He testifies that he undertook to treat Psalm 52 at the urging of a brother, perhaps some bishop. He expounded Psalm 94 to the people in obedience, as he says, to the commands of a father—either Aurelius of Carthage or the aged Valerius, whom Augustine succeeded in the episcopate.

The same is similarly declared concerning Psalm 103 in the second of the four longer sermons in which the holy man explained that psalm at Carthage. He took up Psalm 86 extemporaneously, at the suggestion of a certain man of great authority whom he also calls his father. He even appears to have spoken on Psalm 51 without having previously meditated on what he would say, since he there confesses that he feared he could not accomplish it with the precision required of an address that had to be received not only by the attentive ears of listeners but also by the pen of writers, so that it might become public. “Since it has pleased the brothers,” he says, “that what we say should be received not only by ear and heart but also by the pen, we must consider not only the hearer but also the reader” (*On Psalm 51*, §1).

After Psalm 138 had been recited in place of another shorter one that Augustine had prepared and had ordered to be read before the exposition, as was customary, he turned this circumstance into an argument for divine will and explained that same psalm extemporaneously. On the days sacred to the Lord’s Passion, he delivered a fuller exposition of Psalm 21, since it suited that mystery, just as he did of Psalm 100 during the Paschal feasts, to which its inscription, “Alleluia,” is appropriate.

It is unnecessary here to list the other psalms that he interpreted on various occasions, at so many solemnities and in so many places—Hippo-Regius, Carthage, Utica, and elsewhere. It is enough that we indicate each of these matters in its proper place at the beginning of the respective expositions. We add only this: the holy Bishop placed a finishing touch upon his work by explaining Psalm 118, as he indicates in its prologue. We have decided to reproduce that prologue in full here.

He says:

“I have expounded all the other psalms that we know are contained in the book of Psalms, which by the custom of the Church is now called the Psalter, partly by speaking to the people and partly by dictating, with the Lord’s gift, as I was able. But Psalm 118 I had postponed, not so much because of its well-known length as because of its height, which few can comprehend.

“And when my brothers were greatly distressed that the exposition of this one psalm alone, so far as concerns the psalms belonging to this same body, was lacking from our little works, and when they pressed me vehemently to discharge this obligation, I did not yield for a long time to their requests and commands. For whenever I tried to think about it, it always exceeded the strength of our intention. For the clearer it seems, the deeper it usually seems to me, so that I cannot even show how deep it is.

“In the case of other passages that are difficult to understand, even if the obscurity of their meaning is hidden, the obscurity itself nevertheless appears. But in this one not even that appears, because it presents such a surface that it seems to require a reader and hearer rather than an expositor. And now that at last I approach its treatment, I am entirely unaware of what I can do in it. Nevertheless, I hope that God will be present and help me to accomplish something.

“For I have done this with everything that I have explained adequately, although earlier they seemed difficult and almost impossible for me to understand or explain. I have decided to do this through sermons delivered to the people, which the Greeks call *homilies* (ὁμιλίας). For I think it more fitting that ecclesiastical assemblies should not be deprived of an understanding of this psalm also, whose song, like that of the others, they are accustomed to enjoy.”

These sermons on Psalm 118 were therefore thirty-two in number. They were prepared for the sake of the people but were by no means delivered by Augustine. Possidius may perhaps have intended to indicate this very fact when, after listing the expositions dictated by the holy man alone, he adds: “All the remaining Psalms, except Psalm 118, were discussed before the people” (Possidius, *Index*, chapter 6).

The number of the Psalms delivered from the sacred lectern is, however, far greater. This might easily seem to have happened because the great Bishop, occupied with so many and such varied concerns of the Church, scarcely found any other time that he could devote to this labor. But from what we have reported above concerning the exposition of Psalm 118, it is clear that this method of explaining Scripture was more pleasing to him because of the people, who could be taught the meaning of the divine Scriptures in ecclesiastical preaching by this means alone.

In those treatises addressed to the people, certain observations are inserted, and particular statements of the Psalms are applied to the schisms, errors, and vices of those times; this makes their reading much more agreeable. There one also finds especially notable passages from the Gospel, Acts, and the Epistles of the Apostles, which the holy Doctor explained together with the Psalm because they had been read in the church on the same day.

Finally, there occur vehement exhortations that persuade; fiery expressions that carry the hearer away; figures so full, if one may speak thus, of flames and fires that scarcely anyone can cast his eyes upon them without being kindled by the same ardor that those who experienced it testified when they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

The blessed Fulgentius experienced this when he read the treatise on Psalm 36. Its opening is taken from a consideration of the day of the final judgment because Matthew 24 had been read on that day. For, as Ferrandus, the author of his Life, relates, when Fulgentius had already resolved in his heart to bid farewell [Col. 0013] to the world, he was warned by the discourse of blessed Augustine, who was explaining Psalm 36; he decided to make his vow public, eagerly desiring to change his clothing (chapter 3).

As for the people, whose ears were filled with those sermons, stirred and as though animated by the fervor of their Shepherd, we are readily persuaded that they were often carried away by those emotions, which he sometimes indicates by their applause. To the eagerness of that people we must attribute the many excellent digressions for the formation of morals into which the holy Bishop turned whenever he found an opportunity, as Cassiodorus notes in his prologue to the Psalms:

“When he wishes to satisfy peoples excessively eager for ecclesiastical nourishment,” he says, “he necessarily caused such great streams of preaching to flow forth.”

The same author implies in the same place that this entire commentary of Augustine was divided into groups of ten, in these words: “He wonderfully explained them in fifteen decades.” We have found no trace of this division in the manuscripts, except in three: one Joly manuscript of the Church of Paris, which at the beginning bears the title, “Here begins the book of the decade of the lord Augustine, from Psalm 1, ‘Blessed is the man,’ to Psalm 51”; and two Colbert manuscripts. One of these adds the following at the end of the exposition of Psalm 40: “Here ends the decade from the first book of blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop.”

The other, which contains a summary of the entire work, presents certain verses at the head of the volume that are appropriate to the prefaces and eulogies to be published below and are not unworthy of mention. Among them is this verse:

> Three times five decades: a great work he accomplished.

Nevertheless, since Possidius does not mention such a division, it is not credible that it was made in Augustine’s time or at his command. Perhaps the same thing happened here as with the book of Livy, which, as Petrarch observes in a letter to Giovanni Boccaccio, was divided into parts called decades—not by the author himself, but by the tedious indolence of readers, who cut it apart (*Letters of Various Matters* 22 or 24).

Let us now come to the principal matter, namely, the rules Augustine observed in interpreting. Many things would here require notice, unless the blessed Doctor himself had treated this subject in his books *On Christian Doctrine*.

First, so far as the letter is concerned, he follows in this commentary, to the best of his ability, the precepts he there gives concerning the preservation of the text whole and undefiled. He compares the Latin editions with one another, consults Greek copies, and gathers variant readings. He investigates where the divergence may have entered—whether through the fault of the translators or through an ambiguity in the Greek text. Finally, that diligence of his by which he examined so many passages with such anxious care led him repeatedly to revise and correct the Psalter against the Greek language.

This may be understood from his letter to Audax. After saying that he did not possess the Psalter translated by blessed Jerome from the Hebrew language, he continues in this way:

“We have not translated it, but we have corrected certain errors in the Latin codices from Greek copies. Thus perhaps we have made something more convenient than it was, though not what it ought to have been. For even now, if what perhaps escaped us then should disturb readers, we correct it by collating the codices” (*Letter* 261, §5).

The primary literal sense sometimes contains nothing except what is simple and spiritual; but that same sense is more often extended and figurative. Then we can truly affirm that the expression is compared with its signification—that is, that the literal sense is compared with the spiritual. Just as it is impossible to reach that spiritual sense unless we have first thoroughly examined the literal sense, so knowledge of the literal sense would be superfluous if we neglected to attain the spiritual.

This was why the holy Bishop, whenever he judged the literal sense sufficiently clear and understood in itself, omitted it and proceeded directly toward the spiritual sense. This occurred not only in sermons delivered to the people, in which he was obliged above all to serve their advancement, but also in the expositions that he dictated on certain Psalms, where he was free to indulge the inclination of his mind in writing.

But since many spiritual senses lie hidden in the words of Sacred Scripture, and all of them may appear equally pious and equally true, he was not always content to bring forth only one. From Psalm 3 he drew as many as three: first, by considering Christ the Lord in his own person; then, by considering him joined to the Church, with which he forms, as it were, one body; and finally, by applying the psalm to individual believers.

On the third verse of Psalm 14, after setting forth its first meaning, he adds beautifully and skillfully:

“Let this simple understanding suffice for whoever it satisfies. But some words of Scripture have benefited from their obscurity in this respect: they have produced many understandings. Therefore, if this had been stated plainly, you would hear only one thing; but because it has been said obscurely, you will hear many things.”

In selecting among the various senses that present themselves to the mind, he follows rules that are far from susceptible to error. Apart from the fact that, as we have said, he assigns the greatest importance to the letter, to which the meaning must first of all correspond exactly, he always sets charity before his eyes, teaching that it is the end of all Scripture in his exposition of Psalm 140:

“Whatever is conceived soundly in the mind, whatever is uttered by the mouth, or drawn out from any page, has no end except charity.”

He had taken this teaching both from the Gospel, where Christ generally pronounces the statement, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40), and from the Apostle, who judges that “the end of the commandment is charity” (1 Tim. 1:5).

By the benefit of this rule he banishes far away senses that some passages of the Psalms might seem to present as poorly suited to Christian morals. He teaches that words appearing to arise from a desire for vengeance and to call down destruction upon the wicked are nothing other than prophecies and predictions of the evils with which those wicked people will be overwhelmed unless [Col. 0015] they are corrected. David’s prayers against his enemies are to be taken in a better sense; and in them we are to understand prayers by which holy men commend sinners to God. Those expressions in which he asks that his adversaries be confounded, fall, or be struck down indicate, in a mysterious way, the conversion and repentance of sinners.

Whenever he desires to conquer his enemies or be freed from them, the prayers are in reality prayers that he may not succumb in temptations. Finally, by David’s enemies are designated not only demons or sinners but also vices and the passions of the soul by which we are continually attacked along the way of salvation.

By this same rule he is led to adapt the petitions and promises of the Psalms, which when taken according to the letter signify only temporal goods, to eternal realities. He transfers commands concerning the external practice of virtues to inward piety. Finally, wherever there is mention of the temple, the lifting of the eyes, crying out, a new song, or praise, he leads us from these things to the affections and movements of the mind and heart, to a new life, and to the holiness of the works that God commands to be directed toward his glory.

To prepare a more convenient entrance for us into those meanings so conducive to the inculcation of piety, he could not have chosen a more economical path than to introduce the Lord Jesus speaking through David’s mouth, as both the practice of the ancients and, above all, the interpretation made in the New Testament of certain passages from the Psalms prescribed for him.

Tertullian writes in his book *Against Praxeas*:

“Almost all the Psalms also sustain the person of Christ; they represent the Son speaking to the Father—that is, Christ speaking to God” (chapter 11).

Jerome writes in his letter to Paulinus:

“David, our Simonides, Pindar and Alcaeus, and also Flaccus, Catullus, and Serenus, makes Christ resound upon the lyre” (*Letter* 103).

Hilary, in his own prologue to the Psalms, develops this same point at length. There he argues that all the Psalms are woven together with allegorical and typological virtues belonging to Christ; that his coming, incarnation, passion, resurrection, and finally his judgment provide all the subject matter for these sacred songs; and that faith in these mysteries serves, as it were, as a key, without whose operation access to the understanding of the Psalms is closed.

Augustine likewise never fails to insist on this when explaining them. At times he is even obliged to excuse his repetitions, bringing forward the usefulness of this rule and the necessity of understanding it properly. He adduces arguments drawn from the sacred books, such as Christ’s declaration:

“It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

He frequently repeats that David bears the figure of Christ, who was to be born from his seed; that David’s very name, by its meaning, designates Christ; and that Christ is known to have been announced by many of the Prophets under that name. He observes that there are many things that cannot be applied to David—a point that many very learned writers had already noticed, especially in Psalms 70 and 88—and that the Prince of the Apostles himself does so in Acts 2:25, where he cites a passage from Psalm 15.

Finally, he observes that Christ, hanging upon the cross, used the very words of the Psalms, as though he wished to teach us that they had been written because of him. Yet since many things are read there that are foreign to his holiness, the blessed Doctor repeatedly warns us not to consider Christ as separated from his members—that is, from Christians—but as joined by an indissoluble bond to the whole body of the Church, whose head he is. Hence it follows that he attributes our weaknesses, evils, and sins to himself, as we observe in Psalm 21, whose words he speaks in his Passion.

Augustine’s wonderfully ingenious ways of discovering and uncovering Christ, depicted under various aspects in the Psalms, were suggested by his love for Christ. Yet we will not deny that the ancients, who had already thoroughly examined this same subject, brought to light many excellent meanings hidden beneath the coverings of figures.

But if their commentaries and his are compared with one another, it will be understood that he very often either casts greater light upon those same mysteries or unfolds new ones that they, although following the same general method, had passed over.

Nor should we think that Jerome intended anything else in his letter 92, which is numbered 72 among Augustine’s letters. After stating that, if he said that there might be some who would smear his books with a censor’s mark, since even the Gospel itself is bitten by the impious tooth of the wicked, he did not mean by this, he says, that he already judged certain things in Augustine’s works worthy of reproach, Jerome adds concerning his commentaries on the Psalms that he possessed some of them. These were perhaps the shorter treatises on the first thirty-two Psalms, composed long before the year 414, as we have already observed, and perhaps even before approximately the year 404, when that letter itself was written. Jerome continues:

“If I wished to examine them, I would teach you that they differ—not, I will not say, from me, who am nothing, but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks.”

A certain more recent writer asserts that Jerome here condemns the method by which Augustine, abandoning the method of the other Fathers, interpreted the Psalms. But Jerome explains himself more satisfactorily in his letter 75 among Augustine’s letters, written not long after the preceding one. He sufficiently indicates that the words mentioned were directed to nothing other than dissolving the argument of Augustine, by which, after the version of the Septuagint translators, the version Jerome had published was being declared useless.

Thus he turns the proposed dilemma back in this way:

“Let your wisdom answer me: why, after so many and such interpreters, have you thought differently in explaining the Psalms? If the Psalms are obscure, it must be believed that you too could have been mistaken in them. If they are clear, it is not believed that they could have been mistaken in them. And so, in either case, your interpretation will be superfluous. By this rule, after those who came before, no one will dare to speak; and whatever one person has taken up, another will have no permission to write about.”

And certainly in neither letter is there even a word about the customary method of explaining the Psalms [Col. 0017].

If Jerome had wished to subject Augustine’s labor to examination, he would undoubtedly have encountered meanings in it that he did not find among the earlier writers—not, however, a different method. For in this matter the holy Bishop adhered to the method followed by Hilary, Ambrose, and the others whom Jerome praises.

But if the issue concerns the manner of explaining the divine speech allegorically and morally, who could condemn it in its entirety, since the other Fathers as well as Augustine, and Jerome himself, often employed the same method according to the example and teaching of the Apostles?

Blessed Paul is witness that whatever events are recorded in the Old Testament are figures and were written for our instruction (1 Cor. 10:11). Most of those events, moreover, furnish material for the Psalms; and the Psalms themselves are full of metaphors, enigmas, and prophetic descriptions. Therefore, anyone who wished to confine us within the narrow limits of the simple letter would indeed reduce us to the condition of the Jews, whom God handed over to their own blindness, so that, though seeing, they might not see (Luke 8:10).

Let this much be said by us in defense of Augustine’s method in general. We do not, however, intend to compel everyone to regard even his slightest allusions with the same veneration that we ourselves do. It will be enough if fair-minded judges of such matters do not consider them unworthy of the subject being treated.

Indeed, if the blessed Bishop had not known how to accommodate himself to the spirit of the age and to adapt himself to the understanding of the people, he would have departed from the method that God himself employs in the sacred Scriptures. There the Holy Spirit adopts the customary manner of human speech and does not reject even the humblest forms of expression. There also, in order to instill truths necessary for salvation into human beings, he joins historical variety and poetic charm with the sweetness of musical instruments and the singing of the Psalms.

Let us therefore permit Augustine to use allegories and other observations that he judges not unsuited to his people. Let it be our concern to adhere to the admirable precepts that he conveys to them when occasion permits. We ought likewise to observe this if at times we find that he departs somewhat from the true meaning but nevertheless teaches what is excellent and most suitable for piety.

As for the merit of these commentaries, it must not be judged by comparison with the Hebrew text as it exists today, nor even with Jerome’s text, since Augustine resolved to follow the Septuagint translators, who may have possessed a Hebrew exemplar equally or even more accurately corrected.

No one is unaware how much authority God willed their translation to possess in the Church from the earliest times; how much esteem the Apostles won for it by recording it in the pages of the New Testament; and, finally, how many testimonies they produced for it in the very words that are read in the Psalter of those same translators. Indeed, all the versions that have hitherto held authority in the Church were translated from that Psalter.

But since our discussion has brought us to this point, it will not be outside our purpose to add a few observations about those various Versions. Jerome, in Letter 135 to Sunnias and Fretela, on the occasion of certain passages of the Psalter about which they consulted him, warns that the Greek Version of the Seventy Interpreters circulated in two editions. One of these, and in his judgment the less carefully corrected, was called the Common, the Vulgate, and the edition of Lucian. The other was the one which, to use his own words, “is found in the Hexapla and is preserved incorrupt and undefiled in the books of the learned.” Of this latter edition he had also said shortly before: “It has likewise been faithfully translated by us into the Latin language, and is sung at Jerusalem and in the Churches of the East.” Hincmarus seems to have understood this last part of the sentence, in his letter to Louis, king of Germany, as referring to Jerome’s own translation, whereas it should more properly be understood of the Greek edition of the Hexapla.

Peter Pithoeus, however, held that this was the same as Jerome’s Version and as the Psalter called the Roman Psalter; while our Vulgate, he thought, should be regarded as nothing other than the ancient Version derived from the edition called Lucian’s (*De Latinorum Bibliorum interpretibus*, p. 6). Yet it is scarcely plausible that the Roman Church altered its Psalter so easily—apart from the fact that in that same Psalter certain better and more carefully corrected readings are lacking, readings which Jerome testifies that he found in the Greek Hexapla.

As for the Vulgate edition, we shall here present our conjectures about it in good faith. Jerome himself, in his letter to Paula and Eustochium, indicates that he devoted himself once and again to correcting the Latin Psalter according to the edition of the Seventy Interpreters: first cursorily and for the most part, while he was still living in the city; and secondly with care, after he had withdrawn into his retreat at Bethlehem. He wished copies of this final correction to be transcribed with care and diligence, and to have attached to them the signs he had added: namely, obeli, which enclosed material read in the Seventy but absent from the Hebrew, extending from the obelus to the next two points; and asterisks, by which it would similarly be indicated that the material following up to the next two points had been added to the Seventy from the Hebrew according to Theodotion’s edition.

Such signs, moreover, can still be found in certain ancient manuscripts of the Vulgate, though not in any other Latin Psalter. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis says that he observed them in several codices (*Prologue to the Fivefold Psalter*); and we have before us the ancient tripartite Psalter of the abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres. In its first column it contains Jerome’s Psalter from the Hebrew; in the third, the old Psalter, differing little from the Roman Psalter and from the one used by Augustine; while in the second it presents the Vulgate edition with the aforementioned obeli and asterisks of Jerome.

We are therefore easily persuaded that the Vulgate is that very Version corrected by Jerome in his second undertaking. Our opinion is further confirmed by a manuscript of the Colbert Library, written seven hundred years ago, which contains the Vulgate with the same Jeromean signs and under this heading: “The Book of Psalms from the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, corrected by Saint Jerome anew” [Col. 0019]—perhaps *de novo*, “afresh.” Finally, this is confirmed by the testimony of Walafrid Strabo, whose passage we shall quote below.

It may perhaps be less certain, but in our judgment it is not without plausibility, that this same Vulgate of ours could have been called by Jerome in Letter 135 “the Translation from the Hexapla” which he had published, because he had made it agree with those exemplars; whereas in the letter written to Paula and Eustochium he called it merely a corrected Version, because he had retained, as far as he could, the wording of the ancient one.

Among the reasons that lead us to this conclusion is the following: the passages which Jerome undertakes to defend after mentioning his Version from the Hexapla are found in manuscripts of the Vulgate. For although the printed Bibles of the Vulgate have, for example, in Psalm 5:9, the reading, “Make my way straight in your sight,” which Jerome does not approve, nevertheless the manuscripts preserve the reading which that same Doctor asserts should be read according to the Seventy Interpreters, namely, “Make your way straight in my sight.” Likewise, consider the word *earth*, which Jerome says he deleted from Psalm 47:5 and Psalm 71:11 because it is read neither in the Hebrew nor in the Seventy. That word likewise does not occur in the handwritten codices of the Vulgate. Conversely, they contain the word *his*, which Jerome, having found it added under a dagger in the Hexapla at Psalm 18:6, judged should be retained.

It may also have happened that the Version concerning which Sunnias and Fretela, who lived in Germany, were troubling themselves reached Gaul from that time onward, although, if some authorities are to be trusted, it was not brought there from Rome until more than 150 years later. Walafrid Strabo testifies to this in *Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 25, in these words:

“While the Romans still possess the Psalms according to the Seventy Interpreters, the Gauls and some of the Germans sing the Psalter according to the correction which Father Jerome composed from the edition of the Seventy. Gregory, bishop of Tours, is said to have borrowed this from the Roman regions and introduced it into the Churches of Gaul.”

This Psalter, because the Gauls were the first of all to use it, is called the Gallican Psalter; it was gradually received throughout all the western Churches. Cardinal Bona, a man of exceptional learning and pious memory, judges in *Liturgical Matters*, book 2, chapter 3, that its use was admitted in Italy more than six hundred years ago, except in the Milanese Church, which still retains its ancient Psalter; and except also in the Churches of Rome, where their own Psalter remained in use until the time of Pius V, by whose command they adopted the Vulgate edition, with the exception of the Vatican Church, where the Roman Psalter is still sung.

Once these matters have been explained, someone may perhaps wish to know what place Augustine’s Psalter claims among the other Psalters; whether those various readings in which it differs from our Vulgate rest upon the support of other witnesses; and whether, finally, it agrees more or less with the Greek of the Seventy Interpreters that exists in our own day. These questions led us to compare different copies, both printed and written by hand, and to present to the reader the most significant variants that we discovered.

You will therefore find them below, after we first set down a passage from Book 17 of *The City of God*, in which Augustine expresses his view concerning the Davidic Psalter.

[Col. 0019]

## FROM BOOK XVII OF *THE CITY OF GOD*, CHAPTER XIV: ON THE AUTHOR OF THE PSALMS

David was a man skilled in song, who loved musical harmony not with ordinary pleasure but with faithful devotion; and by it he served his God, who is the true God, through the mystical representation of a great reality. For the rational and measured concord of diverse sounds suggests the unity of the well-ordered city, joined together in harmonious variety.

Almost all his prophecy, in fact, is contained in the Psalms. There are one hundred and fifty of them in the book which we call the Psalms. Some wish only those to have been composed by David which are inscribed with his name. Others think that only those were composed by him which are headed “Of David himself,” while those whose titles read “To David himself” were composed by others and adapted to his person.

This opinion is refuted by the evangelical utterance of the Savior himself, where he says that David, speaking in the Spirit, called Christ his Lord (Matthew 22:43). For Psalm 109 begins in this way: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” Certainly that Psalm does not bear in its title “Of David himself,” but “To David himself,” like many others.

To me those seem more credible who attribute all one hundred and fifty Psalms to his work, while holding that he marked some with the names of others who figuratively represented something relevant to the subject; and that he wished the remaining Psalms to bear in their titles the name of no human being, just as the Lord inspired him to arrange this diversity—hidden, indeed, but not meaningless.

Nor should it prevent belief in this conclusion that the names of certain prophets who lived long after the time of King David are inscribed on some Psalms in that book, and that the things said there appear to be spoken by them. For the prophetic Spirit could certainly have revealed to the prophetic king David even the names of future prophets, so that something appropriate to their persons might be sung prophetically. Thus King Josiah, who would arise and reign more than three hundred years later, was revealed by name to a certain prophet who also foretold his future deeds.

[Col. 0021]

## PASSAGES FROM THE PSALMS

In the passages where Augustine, in the work that follows, differs from the Vulgate edition, there are also certain Latin Psalters which adhere more closely to the Greek interpretation of the Seventy and agree with Augustine here and there. These are the old Psalters, especially those sung from the earliest times in the most celebrated Churches: namely, the Roman Psalter, for the use of the clergy of the Vatican Basilica, printed at Rome in 1663; likewise the Roman Psalter printed in the Fivefold Psalter under the care of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples in the monastery of Saint-Germain at Paris in 1509; the Milanese Psalter, according to the custom of the Ambrosian Church of Milan, printed at Milan in 1555; the handwritten German Psalter, a codex which Blessed Germanus himself, bishop of Paris, is said to have used during his lifetime; the Hilarian and Ambrosian Psalters—that is, the Psalter followed by Hilary and Ambrose in their commentaries; and finally the old Version which, under the heading “According to the Greek,” occupies the third column in the tripartite Psalter of Saint Peter of Chartres. In that Psalter the first column contains the interpretation according to the Hebrew, while the middle column contains the Vulgate.

From these books we have arranged for publication the more notable variants—in fact, all those whose notation seemed likely either to strengthen the authority of Augustine’s Psalter or ultimately to yield some useful result.

In addition, certain variant readings in the Vulgate edition itself are recorded. They have been excerpted from the aforementioned Chartres book, copied seven hundred years ago; from a Colbert manuscript of the same age containing the Vulgate under this title, “The Book of Psalms from the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, corrected by Saint Jerome the presbyter anew”; from another German manuscript nearly seven hundred years old; and from the Gallican Psalter in the Fivefold Psalter printed in 1509, where the Vulgate edition is represented under the name of that Gallican Psalter.

## SIGLA OF THE BOOKS

**Gr.** designates the Greek Psalter according to the Seventy, printed at Paris in 1628 from the exemplar of the Roman edition.

**A.** denotes Augustine’s Psalter.

**R.** denotes the customary Roman Psalter, or that printed in 1663.

**Rom.** denotes the Roman Psalter printed in the Fivefold Psalter in 1508.

**M.** denotes the Milanese Psalter.

**Amb.** denotes the Psalter expounded by Blessed Ambrose.

**G.** denotes the first German Psalter, that is, the one said to have been used by Saint Germanus.

**H.** denotes the Psalter elucidated by Hilary.

**C.** denotes the Chartres Psalter, bearing the inscription “According to the Greek.”

[Col. 0022]

**Hebr.** denotes Jerome’s Psalter from the Hebrew; here it is to be preferred at least in those passages where it supports the ancient Version.

**Vulg.** indicates the Vulgate edition, as now read in the Bibles corrected under the authority of Sixtus V or Clement VIII. The text of this Edition is always presented first here.

**Car.** marks the Chartres Psalter according to the Vulgate.

**Colb.** denotes the Colbert manuscript.

**Ger.** denotes the second German Psalter.

**Gal.** denotes the Gallican Psalter printed in the Fivefold Psalter in 1509.

**Verse 10.** “On the day when.” M., G.: “On whatever day.”

## FROM PSALM XX

**Verse 3.** “The desire of his heart.” A., R., Rom., C.: “The desire of his soul.”

**Verse 3, further.** “And with his will.” The Greek has δέησιν, “petition,” instead of θέλησιν, “will.”

**Verse 3, further.** “You did not defraud him.” A.: “You did not deprive him.”

**Verse 6.** “In your saving power.” A., G., C.: “In your salvation.”

**Verse 7.** “You will give him for a blessing.” A., according to the Greek: “You will give him a blessing.”

**Verse 7, further.** “With joy in your countenance.” G.: “With the joy of your countenance.”

**Verse 10.** “At the time of your countenance.” G.: “At the time of your countenance you will complete them.”

**Verse 13.** “You will prepare.” R., Rom.: “Prepare.”

## FROM PSALM XXI

**Verse 1.** “The words of my offenses.” G.: “The words of my lips.” Hebrew: “The words of my roaring.”

**Verse 11.** “Upon you I was cast.” A. initially has: “Upon you I was made firm”; then, with R., Rom., C.: “I was thrown.”

**Verse 15.** “I have been poured out like water.” R., Rom., M., Amb., G.: “They have been poured out like water.”

**Verse 16.** “And into the dust.” C.: “And into the mire.”

**Verse 16, further.** “You led me down.” Rom., G., C.: “They led me down.”

**Verse 20.** “Your help from me.” C., Colb., Ger. do not have *from me*; instead Jerome, in Letter 135, wishes *with me* to be read. The Greek has “my help.”

**Verse 21.** “Rescue me from the sword, O God.” The word *God* is absent from A., R., Rom., M., G., C., Car., Colb., Ger., Gal., and the Greek.

**Verse 26.** “With you is my praise.” R., Rom., M.: “With you is praise for me.” Amb.: “From you.” Greek: παρὰ σοῦ, “from you.”

**Verse 26, further.** “In the great Church, vows, and so forth.” A., Amb.: “In the great Church I shall confess to you, vows, and so forth.”

**Verse 28.** “Of all the family of the nations.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “All the clans of the nations.”

**Verse 30.** “The fat ones of the earth.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “The rich of the earth.”

**Verse 30, further.** “They will fall.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “They will prostrate themselves.”

**Verse 32.** “And the heavens will proclaim.” The word *heavens* is absent from the Greek, G., Car., Ger., Gal., and Amb., where it reads: “He will proclaim.”

## FROM PSALM XXII

**Verse 1.** “The Lord governs me.” A.: “The Lord feeds me,” according to the Greek ποιμαίνει με, “he shepherds me.” The Hebrew likewise.

**Verse 3.** “Over the paths.” A.: “In the paths.” Hebrew: “Through the paths.”

**Verse 5.** “And my cup.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., according to the Greek: “And your cup.” Jerome disapproves this reading and says in Letter 135 that it came from the Common or Lucian Greek edition.

**Verse 6.** “It will follow me.” R., M.: “May it follow me.” Rom.: “It follows me.”

## FROM PSALM XXIII

[Col. 0027]

**Verse 1.** “The first day of the week.” Greek: τῆς μιᾶς, “of the one,” that is, “of the one day of the Sabbath.”

**Verse 1, further.** “Who dwell in it.” A., R., Rom., G.: “Who dwell in her.” The translator followed the Greek ἐν αὐτῇ, “in her,” which agrees in gender with the preceding noun οἰκουμένη, “inhabited world.”

**Verse 2.** “For he himself.” The word *for* is absent from A., R., Rom., M., G., C., and the Greek.

**Verses 7 and 9.** “Your princes.” A., G.: “Your prince.” Greek: ὑμῶν, “of you.”

## FROM PSALM XXIV

**Verse 1.** “For the end.” This is absent from C., Car., Gal., the Greek, and the Hebrew.

**Verse 3.** “Those who wait for you.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “Those who await you.” Hebrew: “Those who hope in you.”

**Verse 4.** “All who do iniquity needlessly.” A.: “Doing evil things in vain.” R.: “Doing iniquity vainly.” Rom., C.: “The wicked doing vain things.” M.: “Carrying out iniquity needlessly.” The word *all* is absent from A., R., Rom., M., G., C., the Greek, and the Hebrew.

**Verse 5.** “Direct me in your truth.” The Greek reads: “Lead me into your truth.”

**Verse 6.** “And your mercies, which are from eternity.” A., G., according to the Greek: “And because your mercies are from eternity.”

**Verse 7.** “And my ignorances.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “And my ignorance.”

**Verse 7, further.** “According to your mercy.” R., Rom.: “According to your great mercy.”

**Verse 8.** “He will give the law.” A., M.: “He will establish the law.” R., Rom., G., C.: “He established it.”

**Verse 12.** “Who fears the Lord.” A., R., Rom., M., G.: “Who may fear the Lord.”

**Verse 12, further.** “He established the law.” A., M., according to the Greek: “He will establish the law.”

**Verse 17.** “They have multiplied.” R., Rom., G.: “They have been enlarged.”

**Verse 20.** “I have hoped in you.” R., Rom.: “I have called upon you.”

**Verse 21.** “I have waited for you.” A., R., Rom., M., C., according to the Greek: “I have waited for you, Lord.” G.: “I have guarded you.”

**Verse 22.** “Deliver Israel, O God.” A., M., and the Hebrew: “Redeem Israel, O God.” Greek: λύτρωσαι, “redeem.” R., Rom., G., C.: “Redeem me, O God of Israel.”

**Verse 22, further.** “From his tribulations.” R., Rom., G., C.: “From my distresses.” M.: “From his distresses.”

## FROM PSALM XXV

**Verses 1 and 11.** “I have entered.” A.: “I have walked.” Greek: ἐπορεύθην, “I walked.”

**Verse 1, further.** “Hoping, I shall not be weakened.” A.: “Hoping, I shall not be moved.” G.: “Trusting, I shall not be put to shame.” Greek: οὐ μὴ σαλευθῶ, “I shall certainly not be shaken.” Hebrew: “I shall not fail.”

**Verse 5.** “The assembly of the wicked.” A., R., Rom., G.: “The congregation of the wicked.”

**Verse 7.** “The voice of praise.” A., R., Rom., M., C.: “The voice of your praise.”

**Verse 8.** “And the place of habitation.” R., Rom.: “And the place of the tabernacle.” The Hebrew likewise. The Greek has σκηνώματος, “of the tabernacle.”

**Verse 12.** “He stood in a straight place.” A., according to the Greek: “He stood in uprightness.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “In a straight way.”

## FROM PSALM XXVI

**Verse 1.** “And my salvation.” A.: “And my savior.”

**Verse 3.** “In this I shall hope.” A., C., according to the Greek: “In this [feminine form] I shall hope.”

**Verse 4.** “That I may see the delight of the Lord.” A.: “That I may contemplate the pleasure of the Lord.” R., Rom., G., C.: “The will of the Lord.” Hebrew: “The beauty.” Greek: τὴν τερπνότητα, “the delight.”

**Verse 4, further.** “And visit his temple.” A.: “And be protected by his temple.” R., Rom.: “And be protected by his holy temple.” G., C.: “And be protected by his temple.” Greek: καὶ ἐπισκέπτεσθαι τὸν ναὸν αὐτοῦ, “and to visit his temple.” Jerome, from the Hebrew: “And I shall attend to his temple.”

**Verse 5.** “On the day of evils.” A., M., according to the Greek, add: “my evils.”

**Verse 6.** “And now he has exalted.” A., M., according to the Greek: “And now, behold, he has exalted.” R., Rom., G.: “But now he has exalted.”

**Verse 6, further.** “I went around and sacrificed.” R., Rom.: “I shall go around, and I shall sacrifice.”

**Verse 6, further.** “A sacrifice of shouting.” A., R., Rom., M., G. [Col. 0028] C.: “A sacrifice of jubilation.” Hebrew: “Sacrifices of jubilation.” Greek: ἀλαλαγμοῦ, “of joyful shouting.”

**Verse 8.** “My face sought you.” A., R., Rom., C., according to the Greek: “I sought your face.” G.: “I sought your countenance.” M.: “I shall seek the Lord; my countenance sought you.”

**Verse 11.** “On a straight path.” A., G., C., according to the Greek: “On the straight path.” The Vulgate had this in Car., Colb., Ger., and Gal.

**Verse 12.** “Into souls.” G.: “Into hands.” C.: “Into hands.”

## FROM PSALM XXVII

**Verse 1.** “A Psalm to David himself.” A., according to the Greek: “Of David himself.” Car., Gal.: “To this David.”

**Verse 1, further.** “I shall cry.” A., G., C., according to the Greek: “I cried.”

**Verse 1, further.** “Do not be silent toward me.” The Greek reads: “Above me.”

**Verse 1, further.** “Lest you should be silent toward me.” This is omitted in R., Rom., G., and C.

**Verse 2.** “Hear, Lord.” *Lord* is absent from R., Rom., the Greek, the Hebrew, and from A. in the manuscripts.

**Verse 3.** “Do not drag me away together with sinners.” A., according to the Greek: “Do not drag my soul away together with sinners.” R., Rom., M., C.: “Do not hand me over.” The Vulgate likewise had this, though erroneously, in Car., Colb., Ger., and Gal.

**Verse 4.** “And according to the wickedness of their inventions.” A., in the better manuscripts: “And according to the malignity of their affectations.” M., G., C.: “Of their pursuits.” R. and Rom. likewise, but these two books immediately add “repay them,” omitting “according to the works of their hands.”

**Verse 5.** “The works of the Lord.” A., Rom., C., according to the Greek: “In the works of the Lord.” G.: “In the work.”

**Verse 5, further.** “Of his hands.” R., Rom., G., C. add: “They did not consider.”

Item V. 5. “You will destroy them.” R., Rom., G.: “Destroy them.”

Item V. 5. “And you will not build.” G.: “And do not build.”

V. 7. “And I was helped.” M.: “And help was given.”

V. 8. “Of salvations.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., and the Hebrew: “of salvation.”

V. 9. “And rule.” Greek: καὶ ποίμανον, “and shepherd.” So also the Hebrew.

## From Psalm XXVIII

V. 2. “In his holy court.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “in his holy hall.” Greek: ἐν αὐλῇ, “in a court.”

V. 9. “Who prepares the stags.” A., M.: “who completes the stags.” Greek: καταρτιζομένου, “who prepares.” Hebrew: “who assists the stags in giving birth.”

Item V. 9. “Thickets.” A.: “forests.” Greek: δρυμούς, “groves.” Hebrew: “woodlands.”

Item V. 9. “All will say.” A.: “each one says.”

V. 10. “He causes [them] to dwell.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “he dwells.” Greek: κατοικιεῖ, a future-tense form.

## From Psalm XXIX

V. 1. “A psalm of a song.” A., G., C., following the Greek: “For the end: a psalm of a song.”

Item V. 1. “Of the house of David.” A.: “of the house belonging to David.” Greek: τῷ Δαυίδ, “for David.”

V. 4. “You brought [me] up from the underworld.” A.: “you brought [me] back from the lower regions.” Greek: ἀνήγαγες, “you brought up.” R., Rom., C.: “you drew [me] out from the lower regions.” M.: “you drew [me] out from the underworld.”

V. 6. “In the evening he will linger.” A.: “in the evening.” Greek: τὸ ἑσπέρας αὑλισθήσεται, “in the evening he will lodge,” or “in the evening he will prevail.”

V. 8. “In your favor.” R., Rom.: “in your good favor.”

V. 12. “And you surrounded me with gladness.” A., Hebrew: “and you girded me with gladness.” R., Rom., M., G.: “you girded me beforehand.” Greek: περιέζωσάς με, “you girded me.” C.: “you clothed me.”

## From Psalm XXX

V. 1. “For the ecstasy.” This is absent from most books. But in A. and the Greek there is only “Ecstasy.”

V. 2. “Deliver me.” A., following the Greek: “rescue me and bring me out.” R., Rom., M.: “deliver me and rescue me.”

V. 4. “You will lead me.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “you will be a guide for me.” M.: “you will bring me out.”

V. 6. “I commend.” Greek: παραθήσομαι, “I will commend.”

V. 12. “Above all my enemies.” M.: “Before all my enemies.”

V. 13. “I have been given over to oblivion.” R., Rom., G., C.: “I have perished.” M.: “I have gone out.”

V. 16. “My lots.” R., Rom., G., C.: “my times.” So also the Hebrew. But the Greek now has κλῆροι, “lots,” perhaps in place of καιροί, “times.”

[Col. 0029] Item V. 16. “Rescue me.” R., Rom.: “Free me and rescue me.”

V. 19. “And in abuse.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “and in contempt.” Greek: καὶ ἐξουδενώσει, “and in disdain.” Hebrew: “and in scorn.”

V. 22. “To me in a fortified city.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “in a city of refuge” or “in a city of enclosure.” Greek: περιοχῆς, “of a fortified place”; they do not have “to me.”

V. 23. “In the excess of my mind.” Augustine, following the Greek: “in my ecstasy.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “in my fear.”

V. 24. “He will seek truth.” G.: “he seeks truth.” Greek: “he seeks truths.”

Item V. 24. “And he will repay abundantly those who act.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “and he will repay those who act abundantly.”

## From Psalm XXXI

V. 2. “He did not reckon.” C., Colb., Ger.: “he will not reckon.” Greek, here and in the Epistle to the Romans 4:8: λογίσηται, “he will have reckoned.”

Item V. 2. “Nor is there in his spirit.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek: “nor is there in his mouth.”

V. 4. “In my distress.” Rom., following the Greek: “into distress.” A. likewise generally has this in the manuscripts. But M., G., C. have “in distress,” omitting “my.”

Item V. 4. “While the thorn is fastened.” A.: “while it was being fastened.” Rom., G.: “while it is being broken.” M.: “a thorn to me,” following the Greek.

V. 5. “I made [it] known to you.” A.: “I knew.” C.: “I know.” Greek: ἐγνώρισα, “I made known.” Hebrew: “I make [it] known to you.”

Item V. 5. “Of my sin.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek: “of my heart.”

## From Psalm XXXII

Title. “A psalm of David.” Rom., G., Gal.: “For the end: a psalm of David.”

V. 1. “Praise upon praise.” A., G., C., Car., Colb., Gal., following the Greek: “praise.”

V. 3. “Sing praise to him well, with a shout.” G.: “Bless him.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “with jubilation,” following the Hebrew. But the Greek has ἐν ἀλαλαγμῷ, “with a shout.”

V. 7. “As in a wineskin.” A., G., C.: “as into a wineskin.” Greek: “as a wineskin.”

V. 11. “From generation to generation.” A.: “for ages of ages.” R., Rom., G., C.: “for an age of an age.” M.: “from generation and offspring.” Greek: “from generations to generations.”

V. 20. “He sustains the Lord.” A.: “he will be patient for the Lord.” G., C.: “he is patient in the Lord.” Greek: ὑπομένει τῷ κυρίῳ, “he waits for the Lord.” Hebrew: “he will await the Lord.”

## From Psalm XXXIII

V. 1. “Before Achimelech.” A., Rom., C., Car., Gal., Greek: “before Abimelech.” So also the Hebrew.

V. 4. “Together.” R., Rom., M., G.: “with one another.” Many codices, according to Augustine, had “into one.” In the Hebrew it is “equally” or “together.”

V. 19. “Who are broken in heart.” A.: “who have crushed the heart.” Greek: συντετριμμένοις τὴν καρδίαν, “those broken in heart.” Hebrew: “those contrite in heart.”

## From Psalm XXXIV

V. 5. “Constraining them.” A., following the Greek: “troubling them.” R., Rom., M., G.: “afflicting them.” C.: “fighting against them.”

V. 7. “The destruction of his snare.” A.: “the ruin of his trap.” Greek: διαφθοράν, “destruction.” Hebrew: “the ambush of his net.”

V. 8. “Let the snare that he does not know come upon him,” etc. A.: “Let the trap that they do not know come upon them, and let the capture that they have hidden seize them, and let them fall into the trap itself.” Likewise R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek, have the plural: “Let the snare that they do not know come upon them,” etc. R. and Rom. also have: “and let them fall into the snare itself.”

V. 9. “Upon his salvation.” A., R., Rom., M., G.: “upon his salvation.” The Greek favors this, having αὐτοῦ, “his,” not αὐτῆς, “her.”

V. 13. “It will return in my bosom.” A., Rom., M., following the Greek: “into my bosom.” R.: “it was returning.”

V. 15. “Scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know.” R., Rom.: “they gathered scourges against me.” C.: “they were gathered against me.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “and they did not know.”

V. 16. “They were scattered.” A.: “they were torn apart.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “they were dissolved.”

V. 17. “From their wickedness.” A.: “from their cunning.” R. [Col. 0030], Rom., M., G., C.: “from their evil deeds.” Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς κακουργίας αὐτῶν, “from their wrongdoing.”

V. 18. “In the great assembly.” A.: “in the numerous assembly.” Greek: πολλῇ, “great” or “numerous.”

V. 19 and 24. “Let them not exult over me.” A.: “Let them not insult me.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “Let them not insult against me.” The same variations occur generally in Psalm XXXVII, V. 17.

Item V. 19. “And they nod.” A.: “and those nodding.” R., Rom., M.: “and they were nodding.” G., C.: “and they nodded.”

V. 20. “And, speaking deceitfully against the wrath of the earth, they devised.” A., R., Rom., M., C.: “and they deceitfully devised against wrath.” G.: “and they acted deceitfully against wrath.”

V. 24. “According to your righteousness.” A.: “according to my righteousness.” So also the Hebrew. But R., Rom.: “according to your great mercy.” G., C.: “according to your mercy.”

V. 26. “Those who speak great things.” A., C.: “those who speak evil things.” So the Vulgate had it in Car., Colb., Ger., Gal. Nevertheless, the Greek has μεγαλοῤῥημονοῦντες, “speaking grandly”; in the Hebrew: “those who magnify themselves.”

## From Psalm XXXV

V. 2. “Let him sin against himself.” M., G., C.: “let him sin against himself.”

V. 3. “So that his iniquity may be found to hatred.” A., R., Rom., Amb., G.: “so that he might find his iniquity.” A.: “and hate it.” R., Rom., Amb., M., G., C.: “and hatred.”

V. 7. “A great abyss.” A., Amb., G., following the Greek: “like a great abyss.” C.: “as if.”

## From Psalm XXXVI

V. 2. “The vegetables of herbs.” A.: “the vegetables of the meadow.”

V. 8. “So that you may act wickedly.” A.: “so that you may do evil.” R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “so that you may act wickedly.”

V. 9. “Those who act wickedly.” A.: “those who do evil.” R., Rom., M., Amb., C.: “those who act wickedly.” G.: “those who act unjustly.”

V. 17. “He strengthens.” G.: “he supports.” Hebrew: “he raises up.”

V. 18. “The days of the blameless.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “the ways of the blameless.” Greek: τὰς ὁδούς, “the ways.” Hebrew in the manuscripts: “the way.”

V. 20. “They will fail.” The Greek has: “they failed.”

V. 21. “The sinner will borrow and will not repay.” A.: “the sinner lends at interest.” R., Rom., Amb., G.: “he borrows,” etc. R., Rom., Amb.: “and he does not repay.”

Item V. 21. “And he will give.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “and he lends.” Amb.: “and he gave.”

V. 23. “They will be directed.” R., Rom., following the Greek: “they are directed.”

Item V. 23. “He will desire.” M.: “he will desire greatly.”

V. 24. “He will not be struck down.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “he will not be troubled,” namely, with καταραχθήσεται changed to καταταραχθήσεται.

Item V. 24. “He places his hand beneath him.” A., Amb., C., following the Greek: “he strengthens his hand.” R., Rom., M., G.: “he makes firm his hand.” Hebrew: “he sustains his hand.”

V. 26. “And he lends.” A., Amb., G.: “and he lends at interest.”

V. 28. “The unjust will be punished.” The Greek means: “The blameless will be vindicated.”

V. 29. “And they will dwell forever,” etc. Amb.: “and they will honor God for ages of ages.”

V. 32. “To kill him.” R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “to destroy him.” M.: “to slay him.”

V. 33. “Nor will he condemn him when judgment is rendered against him.” Some copies, according to Augustine, had: “and when he judges him, judgment will be rendered against him.”

V. 35. “Like cedars.” A., R., Rom., Amb., M.: “above cedars.”

V. 37. “Guard innocence.” R., Rom., G., C.: “Guard truth.” Greek: ἀκακίαν, “innocence.” Hebrew has: “simplicity.”

Item V. 37. “And see equity.” A.: “and see uprightness.” Hebrew: “what is right.”

V. 38. “They will perish together.” A.: “they will perish together.” Greek: ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, “together.” C.: “they will be punished together.”

## From Psalm XXXVII

V. 5. “They have surpassed.” A.: “they have lifted up.” R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “they have been placed upon.”

V. 6. “And my scars have become corrupt.” A.: “and they have festered,” etc. R., Rom., M., G., C.: “and they have deteriorated.” Hebrew: “and they have wasted away.” A., M.: “my bruises.”

V. 7. “I have become wretched.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “I am afflicted with miseries.”

V. 8. “My loins are filled.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., [Col. 0031] G., C., following the Greek: “my soul is filled.”

V. 9. “I am afflicted.” A.: “I am weakened.” R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “I am bowed down.”

V. 12. “And those who were near me.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “and my neighbors.” Hebrew: “and those near me.”

V. 15. “Reproofs.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “rebukes.”

V. 19. “I will announce.” A., R., Rom., C.: “I announce.”

Item V. 19. “And I will consider.” A.: “and I will take care.” Greek: καὶ μεριμνήσω, “and I will be anxious.” Hebrew: “I will be concerned.”

V. 21. “I pursued goodness.” A., following the Greek: “I pursued righteousness.” R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “I followed righteousness.” M.: “I was following righteousness.”

## From Psalm XXXVIII

V. 1. “To Idithun himself.” A., Amb., C., Car., Gal.: “for Idithun.”

V. 3 and 10. “I became mute.” A.: “I became deaf.”

V. 4. “The fire will burn.” R., Rom., G.: “the fire burns.”

V. 5. “Who is.” A., Amb.: “who is he.”

V. 6. “Behold, measurable [days].” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “Behold, ancient [days].” Greek: ἰδοὺ παλαιάς, “behold, old [things].” Hebrew: “behold, brief [days].”

Item V. 6. “And my substance.” G.: “and my dwelling.” C.: “and my condition.” Hebrew: “and my life.”

V. 7. “Man passes by in an image.” R., Rom., Amb., C.: “man walks in the image of God.”

Item V. 7. “He is troubled.” R., Rom.: “he will be troubled.”

V. 8. “It is with you.” A.: “it is always before you.” Amb., G., C.: “it is before you,” omitting “always.” But R., Rom.: “it is as nothing before you.”

V. 10. “For you made [it].” A., following the Greek: “for you are the one who made me.” R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “for you made me.”

V. 11. “Take your scourges away from me.” A.: “take your lashes away from me.”

V. 12. “You chastised man.” A., M., Amb., G., C.: “you instructed man.” Greek: ἐπαίδευσας, “you instructed.”

Item V. 12. “His soul.” A.: “my soul.”

Item V. 12. “Nevertheless every man is troubled in vain.” A., G., C. add “living.” R., Rom. have: “nevertheless, every living man is altogether vanity.” Hebrew: “nevertheless, every man is vanity.”

V. 13. “And hear my prayer; listen with your ears to my tears; do not be silent.” M.: “And hear my prayer with your ears; do not be silent at my tears.” The Hebrew favors: “at my tear do not become deaf.” But A., R., Rom., Amb., G.: “Do not be silent toward me.”

Item V. 13. “I am with you.” Greek: “I am in the land.” R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “I am with you in the land.”

## From Psalm XXXIX

V. 2. “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” A.: “Sustaining, I sustained the Lord.”

V. 4. “Many will see.” A.: “The righteous will see.”

V. 7. “But you perfected ears for me.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb.: “but you perfected a body for me,” following the Greek here and in the Epistle to the Hebrews 10:5.

V. 9. “In the midst of my heart.” M.: “in the midst of my belly.” So also the Hebrew.

V. 10. “I announced.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “I announced well.” The Greek supports this.

V. 11. “Your righteousness.” A., Amb., G., following the Greek: “my righteousness.”

V. 12. “They have always received me.” M.: “may they always receive me.” Hebrew: “they will continually guard me.”

V. 18. “He is concerned for me.” A., following the Greek: “he will care for me.” Hebrew: “he will be concerned for me.”

## From Psalm XL

V. 3. “And may he make him blessed in the land.” R., Rom.: “and may he make him blessed, and cleanse his soul in the land.” Likewise G. and C., except that G. has “cleanse from the land.” C., after “may he make him,” adds “in the land.”

Item V. 3. “Into the soul of his enemies.” A., R., Rom., G., C., following the Greek: “into the hand of his enemy.” M.: “into the hands of his enemies.”

V. 7. “And if he entered in order to see, he spoke vainly; his heart gathered,” etc. “He went out and spoke,” etc. A., R., Rom., G., C.: “And they entered in order to see; their heart spoke vainly; they gathered,” etc. “They went out and spoke,” etc.

[Col. 0032] V. 8. “Together.” R., Rom., G., C.: “at the same time.”

Item V. 8. “They whispered against me.” R., Rom., G., C.: “They whispered together.”

V. 9. “They established.” A.: “they arranged.” R., Rom.: “they commanded.”

V. 10. “He magnified treachery against me.” A., R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “he enlarged [it].” M.: “he greatly enlarged [it].” A.: “the heel against me.” R., Rom., M., G.: “treachery against me.”

V. 14. “Let it be, let it be.” A.: “and all the people will say, ‘Let it be, let it be.’”

## From Psalm XLI

V. 1. “Understanding for the sons of Korah.” A., following the Greek: “For understanding, for the sons of Korah.”

V. 3. “To the strong, living God.” The word “strong” is absent from A., R., Rom., M., G., C., and from the Greek. But Amb. has “to the fountain.”

V. 4. “Breads.” A., M., Amb., C.: “bread.” So also the Greek and Hebrew.

V. 5. “The sound of one feasting.” A., Amb.: “the sounds of one celebrating a festival.” Greek: ἤχου ἑορταζόντων, “the sound of those celebrating a festival.” Hebrew: “of a multitude celebrating a festival.”

V. 6. “For I will still confess him.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., and the Greek lack the word “still,” which is also absent from most books at V. 12 and in the following Psalm at V. 5.

V. 7. “And my God.” The particle “and” is absent from A., C., and the Greek.

Item V. 7. “To myself.” R., Rom.: “from myself.”

Item V. 7. “I will remember you [lacuna] from a small mountain.” A.: “I remembered you, Lord [lacuna] from a little mountain.” Greek: μικροῦ, “small.”

V. 8. “All your heights.” A.: “All your suspensions.” Greek: μετεωρισμοί σου, “your elevations.” Hebrew: “your whirlpools.”

Item V. 8. “They passed through.” A., G.: “they entered.” Greek: διῆλθον, “they passed through.”

V. 9. “And at night his song.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “and at night he declared.” Greek: δηλώσει, “he will declare.”

V. 10. After “you have forgotten me,” A., R., Rom., Amb., G., C. add: “why have you rejected me?”

V. 11. “While they are crushed.” A., C., with the support of the Greek: “while he crushes.”

Item V. 11. “My enemies.” These words are absent from A., R., Rom., G., C., and the Greek. M. has them, but lacks “those who afflict me.”

V. 12. “Salvation.” A. and the Greek: “salus,” “salvation.”

## From Psalm XLII

V. 1. “And distinguish my cause.” G.: “and distinguish my righteousness.”

V. 2. “God, my strength.” A., R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “my God, my strength.”

## From Psalm XLIII

V. 3. “You afflicted the peoples.” A.: “you weakened the peoples.”

V. 10. “And you will not go forth, O God.” G., C.: “and you will not advance.” But the word “God” is absent from the Greek and Hebrew, and from G., Colb., Ger.

V. 11. “After our enemies.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., following the Greek: “before our enemies.”

V. 13. “In their exchanges.” A.: “in their jubilations.” The Greek favors this: ἐν τοῖς ἀλαλάγμασιν αὐτῶν, “in their shouts.” But some ancient books have ἀλλάγμασιν, “in their exchanges.”

V. 22. “We are put to death.” R., Rom., Amb., G.: “we are subjected to death.” M.: “we are afflicted with death.”

## From Psalm XLIV

V. 1. “Who will be changed.” A., G., C.: “which will be changed.”

V. 6. “Your arrows are sharp.” A.: “your very powerful sharp arrows.” R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek: “very powerful.”

Item V. 6. “Into hearts.” A., R., Rom., G., Colb., following the Greek: “into the heart.” So also the Hebrew.

V. 7. “A rod of direction.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “the straight rod is.”

V. 9. “From ivory houses.” G., C.: “from weighty ivory structures.” R., M.: “from ivory steps,” and so forth—an error arising from another error. For the Greek has ἀπὸ βάρεων, which the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, rendered “from weighty [things],” whereas among the Palestinians βάρεις meant great houses built in the form of towers, as Jerome testifies in Letter 140 and in his commentaries on Jeremiah XVII and Hosea VIII. The same word occurs in Psalms XLVII, 4 and 14.

V. 10. “Surrounded.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “wrapped around.”

V. 12. “And she will desire.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek: “For she desired.”

V. 13. “All the rich women of the people.” The word “all” is absent from A., M., G., C., Car., Colb., Gal., from the Greek, and from the Hebrew.

V. 14. “The king’s daughters.” R., Rom.: “the daughters of kings.”

V. 18. “They will remember.” Car., Ger., Gal., following the Hebrew: “I will remember.” So also Jerome in Letter 140.

## From Psalm XLV

V. 1. “For the sons of Korah.” A., G., C., following the Greek: “for the sons of Korah.”

V. 4. “Their waters.” A., R., Rom., Amb., G., C.: “his water.”

V. 5. “The river’s force makes [her] glad.” A., following the Greek: “The river’s force makes [them] glad.” Hebrew: “The river’s divisions make [them] glad.”

V. 6. “God in the early morning.” A., R., Rom., C.: “God with his countenance.” G.: “God from his countenance.” Greek: τῷ προσώπῳ, “with the countenance,” and it does not add “his.” M.: “God from morning to morning.”

V. 7. “He gave his voice; she was moved,” etc. A., R., Rom., M., Amb., C.: “The Most High gave his voice, and she was moved,” etc. G.: “The Exalted One, and she was moved,” etc.

V. 10. “To the end of the earth.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C., following the Greek: “to the ends of the earth.”

## From Psalm XLVI

V. 1. “For Korah.” A., G., C., Car., following the Greek: “for the sons of Korah.”

V. 3. “The Lord is exalted.” R., Rom.: “God is supreme.”

Item V. 3. “Over all the earth.” R., Rom.: “over all gods.”

V. 6. “With jubilation.” G., C.: “with a clamor.”

V. 8. “Sing praise wisely.” A.: “sing praise intelligently.” Greek: συνετῶς, “wisely” or “with understanding.” Hebrew: “instructively.”

V. 9. “God will reign over the nations.” R., Rom., M., G., C., Colb.: “He reigned.” A., R., Rom., M., C.: “The Lord is over all the nations.”

## From Psalm XLVII

V. 3. “It is founded in exultation.” A., R., Rom., M., C.: “spreading out exultations.” Amb.: “spreading out exultation.” Greek: “well rooted in exultation.”

Item V. 3. “Mount Zion.” A., G., C., following the Greek: “the mountains of Zion.”

V. 4. “In his houses.” R., M.: “in his steps.” Rom., G., C.: “in his weighty structures.” Amb. likewise, as is clear from the method of interpretation. Greek: ἐν ταῖς βάρεσιν. See above, Psalm XLIV, 9.

Item V. 4. “He will be known.” G., and A. in some manuscripts: “he is known,” or “he is recognized,” in the present tense, following the Greek.

V. 5. “The kings of the earth.” The word “earth” is absent from the Vulgate in the Colb. manuscripts and from the Greek. Compare Jerome, Letter 135.

V. 10. “In the midst of your temple.” A., following the Greek: “in the midst of your people.” M., G.: “in the midst of your people.” C.: “in your holy temple.” The variation arises from the similarity of the words ναοῦ, “temple,” and λαοῦ, “people.”

V. 12. “The daughters of Judah.” A. in the manuscripts and Amb., C., following the Greek: “the daughters of Judea.”

V. 14. “His houses.” R., Rom., M., Amb., C.: “his steps.” G.: “his tower.” Greek: τὰς βάρεις, that is, “lofty houses built like towers,” says Ambrose. See Psalm XLIV, 9.

V. 15. “God, our God.” The word “God” is not repeated in A., R., Rom., M., G., C., nor in the Greek.

## From Psalm XLVIII

V. 4. “Prudence.” A.: “understanding.” Greek: σύνεσιν, “understanding.”

V. 9. “And he will labor.” A., R., Rom., G., C., following the Greek: “and he labored.”

V. 10. “And he will still live to the end.” The word “still” is absent from A., R., Rom., M., G., C., and from the Greek.

V. 12. “They called their names in their lands.” A., R., Rom., M.: “They will call upon.” M., Amb.: “They called upon.” G., C.: “he called upon.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “their names in their lands.” Hebrew: “they called their lands by their own names.”

V. 14. “They will be pleasing.” A., R., Rom., G., C.: “they will bless.” M.: “they will prosper well.” Greek: εὐλογήσουσιν, “they will bless.”

V. 15. “Death will pasture them.” A.: “death is a shepherd for them.” Greek: ποιμανεῖ αὐτούς, “he will pasture them.”

[Col. 0034] Item V. 15. “And they will rule over them.” R., Rom., G., C.: “And they will possess them.”

Item V. 15. “In the underworld, away from their glory.” R., Rom., M.: “in the underworld, and they have been driven away from their glory.” G.: “in the underworld, away from their glory, and they have been driven away from their glory.”

V. 18. “When he has perished, he will not take everything.” A., R., Rom., Amb., G., C., following the Greek: “Not when he dies will he receive everything.” M.: “Before he dies, he will receive everything.”

Item V. 18. “His glory.” R., Rom., M., Amb., G., C.: “the glory of his house.”

## From Psalm XLIX

V. 5. “His holy ones.” G.: “his sons.”

Item V. 5. “Who arrange.” R., Rom.: “who arranged.” A.: “who dispose.”

V. 7. “And I will speak.” A., following the Greek: “and I will speak to you.”

V. 17. “You hated discipline.” A.: “you hated instruction.” Greek: παιδείαν, “instruction.”

V. 19. “He composed deceit.” A.: “she embraced deceitfulness.” R., Rom., M., C., Hebrew: “he composed deceit.”

V. 21. “You judged wickedly.” A., following the Greek: “You suspected iniquity.” R., Rom., M., G.: “You judged iniquity.”

Item V. 21. “And I will set [it] before your face.” A.: “I will establish you,” etc. R., Rom.: “and I will establish it,” etc. G., C.: “and I will establish that,” etc. M.: “and I will set your sins before your face.”

V. 22. “Lest he suddenly seize.” A., G.: “lest he seize like a lion.”

## From Psalm L

V. 5. “Is always against me.” A., R., Rom.: “is always before me,” ἐνώπιόν μου, the same expression as in the following verse.

V. 7. “My mother conceived me.” A.: “my mother nourished me in the womb.” R., Rom., M., Amb.: “my mother bore me.” So also the Hebrew. The Greek has ἐκίσσησέ με, “she conceived me.”

V. 10. “You will give joy to my hearing.” The Greek means: “You will make me hear exultation.”

V. 15. “I will teach.” A., Rom., G., C.: “May I teach.”

V. 19. “God, you will not despise.” A., R., Rom., M., Amb., C.: “he does not despise.” G.: “he will not despise.” Greek: ἐξουδενώσει, “he will despise.”

## From Psalm LI

V. 3. “Why do you boast in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity? All day,” etc. A.: “Why does he boast in wickedness, he who is powerful? In iniquity all day,” etc. H.: “Why does he boast in wickedness, powerful in iniquity all day?”

V. 6. “Words of ruin.” A.: “words of drowning.”

Item V. 6. “A deceitful tongue.” A., G., H., following the Greek and Hebrew: “a deceitful tongue.” R., Rom.: “in a deceitful tongue.” C.: “into a deceitful tongue.”

V. 7. “He will destroy you.” The Greek means: “May he destroy you.”

Item V. 7. “He will tear you out and make you emigrate.” G., H.: “May he tear you out and make you emigrate,” following the Greek.

V. 11. “It is good.” A.: “It is pleasant.” Greek: χρηστόν, “good” or “pleasant.”

## From Psalm LII

V. 2. “They have been corrupted.” The Greek means: “They corrupted.”

Item V. 2. “In iniquities.” R., Rom., G., C.: “in their desires.”

V. 5. “As food of bread.” A.: “in the food of bread.” Greek: “food of bread.”

V. 6. “The bones of those who please human beings.” R., Rom., M., G.: “the bones of people pleasing to themselves.” G.: “the plans of people pleasing to themselves.”

V. 7. “When he has turned.” A., C., following the Greek: “in turning away.” M.: “in turning.” R., Rom., G.: “when he turns away.” H.: “when he turns away.”
