V. 3. “Judge me.” R., Rom., M., G., C.: “deliver me.” Hebrew: “avenge me.”

V. 7. “Turn away evils.” G.: “He turns away evils.” Greek: ἀποστρέψει, “he will turn away.” H.: “Turn back evils.” Hebrew: “repay evils.”

V. 9. “He despised.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C.: “he regarded.”

## From Psalm LIV

V. 2. “Hear.” H.: “Give ear.” So also in Psalm CXXXIX, V. 7.

V. 4. “Iniquities have inclined toward me.” A., G., C., following the Greek: “iniquity has inclined toward me.” Hebrew: “they cast iniquity upon me.”

Item V. 4. “They were troublesome to me.” A.: “they overshadowed me,” namely, with ἐνεκότουν changed into ἐπεσκότουν.

[Col. 0035] V. 9. “Who saved me.” A., R., Rom., following the Greek: “who would save me.” C.: “may he save.”

V. 10. “Hurl down.” A.: “Drown.”

V. 13. “Had cursed me.” A.: “had reproached me.” H.: “had reviled me.” Greek: ὠνείδισέ με, “he reproached me.”

V. 16. “Let death come upon them.” G.: “He placed death upon them.”

Item V. 16. “Of wickedness in their dwellings.” A., R., Rom., M., G., H., C., following the Greek: “wickedness in their lodgings.”

V. 17. “He will save me.” A., R., Rom., M., G., C., following the Greek: “he heard me.”

V. 19. “They were with me among many.” A., M., following the Greek: “they were with me in many places.”

Item V. 20. “Who is before the ages.” R., Rom.: “who is before the ages and remains forever.”

V. 22. “From anger.” A.: “because of anger.”

Item V. 22. “His words have been softened.” R., Rom., M.: “They softened their words.” G., H., C.: “They softened his words.”

## From Psalm LV

V. 3 and 4. “All day, because many are fighting against me. I will fear from the height of the day; but I,” etc. A., R., Rom., G., following the Greek: “All day, from the height of the day, because many who fight me will fear; but I,” etc. C. likewise, except that it omits “from the height of the day.” M. has: “All day: from the height of the day I will not fear, because many who fight me—from the height of God I will not fear, because I will hope in you.” H.: “All day. From the height of days I will not fear, because many who fight me will fear.”

V. 5. “My words.” R., Rom., G., H.: “my words all day.”

V. 7. “They will dwell.” A.: “They will sojourn.” Greek: παροικήσουσιν, “they will sojourn.”

V. 8. “You will crush the peoples.” A., H.: “You will lead the peoples down.” Greek: κατάξεις, “you will lead down.”

V. 9. “You have placed.” R., Rom., G.: “I have placed.”

## From Psalm LVI

V. 2. “I will hope.” Rom., G.: “I hope.”

## From Psalm LVII

V. 3. “They compose.” A.: “they join together.” Greek: συμπλέκουσιν, “they intertwine.” H.: “they embrace.”

V. 6. “And the poison of the enchanter who chants wisely.” A., following the Greek: “and the drug of a medicine prepared by a wise person”; H. is nearly the same. R.: “and the poisons that are enchanted by a wise person.” G., C.: “and the poisoners who are enchanted by a wise person.” M. likewise, omitting “and.”

V. 7. “He will crush.” A., G., H., C., following the Greek: “he crushed.”

Item V. 7. “He will break.” A., G., H., following the Greek: “he broke.”

V. 8. “They will come to nothing.” A., H.: “They will be despised.” Greek: ἐξουδενωθήσονται, “they will be despised.”

V. 9. “Wax that flows.” A., R., Rom., G., H., C., following the Greek: “melted wax.”

V. 10. “Before your thorns understand the bramble.” A., R., Rom., H., C.: “Before it produces.” A., H.: “your thorns, the bramble.” R.: “your thorn, the bramble.” Rom.: “your thorn, the bramble.” C.: “your thorns, the bramble.” M., G.: “Before they produce.” M.: “your thorns, the bramble.” G.: “your thorns, the castor plant.” Greek: πρὸ τοῦ συνιέναι τὰς ἀκάνθας ὑμῶν τὴν ῥάμνον, “before your thorns understand the bramble.” Hebrew: “Before your thorns grow into a bramble.”

[Col. 0036] Item V. 10. “Thus in anger he will swallow them.” A.: “as though in anger he drinks them down.” Greek: καταπίεται ὑμᾶς, “he will swallow you.” H.: “he will swallow you.”

V. 11. “When he sees vengeance.” R., Rom., G., C., following the Greek: “when he sees the vengeance of the impious,” etc.

V. 12. “Indeed, God exists.” G.: “and truly God exists.”

## From Psalm LVIII

V. 4. “They seized my soul.” A.: “they hunted my soul.” Greek: ἐθήρευσαν, “they hunted.” R.: “they hunted like birds.” Rom., G., C.: “they occupied.” M.: “they captured.” Hebrew: “they lay in ambush for my soul.”

V. 7. “They will turn back [lacuna] they will suffer.” A.: “May they turn back [lacuna] may they suffer.” The Hebrew supports this.

V. 12. “God will show me over my enemies.” A.: “My God showed me good things among my enemies.” R., Rom.: “My God, show me good things among my enemies.” M.: “My God, show me among my enemies.” G.: “My God showed me among my enemies.”

Item V. 12. “Lest my people forget.” A., R., Rom., M., G., H., C., following the Greek: “lest they forget your law.”

Item V. 12. “And bring down.” A.: “and lead down.” R., Rom., M., G., H.: “and destroy.” So also the Hebrew. But the Greek has καὶ κατάγαγε, “and lead down.”

Item V. 13. “And from the curse.” A.: “and from the malediction.”

V. 5. “I will dwell.” A.: “I will be a sojourner.” Greek: παροικήσω, “I will sojourn.”

V. 8. “He remains.” A., R., Rom., G.: “He will remain,” following the Greek.

V. 2. “My salvation.” C.: “my patience.”

V. 2. “He thirsted for you.” A., H., following the Greek: “He thirsted for you.”

V. 12. “It has been obstructed.” A.: “it has been stopped up.” G.: “it has been blunted.”

## From Psalm LXIII

V. 2. “When I pray.” A., Rom., G., H., C.: “when I am afflicted.”

V. 3. “From the assembly.” M.: “from conversation.”

V. 6. “They announced.” R., Rom., G., H., C.: “They debated.” M.: “They arranged.”

V. 4. “To your name.” A., R., Rom., M., H., G., C. add: “O Most High.”

### From Psalm 67

**Verse 7.** “God, who makes [them] dwell.” Here Augustine notes that the Greek has only: “God makes [them] dwell.”

**Also verse 7.** “Of one disposition in the house.” A: “of one kind in the house.” R, Rom, G, C: “of one mind in the house.”

**Verse 9.** “At the presence of the God of Sinai, at the presence, etc.” A, R, Rom, G, H, C: “at the presence of God. Mount Sinai, at the presence, etc.” M: “at the presence of God who is in Sinai, at the presence, etc.”

**Verse 10.** “You will separate.” A, R, Rom, M: “separating.” G: “separate.”

**Verse 11.** “To the poor.” R, Rom: “the poor.”

**Verse 13.** “Beloved, beloved.” R, Rom, M, G, H, C: “beloved,” only once.

**Verse 14.** “Among the middle divisions.” G: “in the midst of the allotments.”

**Also verse 14.** “And the rearmost parts of his back in the pallor of gold.” A: “and between his shoulders in the greenness of gold.”

**Verse 15.** “Heavenly.” A, following the Greek: “super-heavenly.”

**Verse 16.** “The mountain of God, a rich mountain.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “the mountain of God, a fertile mountain.”

**Also verse 16.** “A curdled mountain, a rich mountain.” A, G: “a mountain made into cheese, a fertile mountain.” H: “a consecrated mountain,” etc.

**Verse 17.** “Why do you suspect?” R, Rom, M, G: “why do you look upon?” C: “why do you reckon?”

**Also verse 17.** “The mountain on which.” A, G: “the mountain on which” [with the accusative, “the mountain”].

**Verse 19.** “You ascended.” R, Rom, following the Greek: “ascending.” G, H: “he ascended.”

**Also verse 19.** “You took captivity; you received gifts among men.” R, Rom, C: “he led captivity captive.” G, H: “he took captivity.” R, Rom, H, C: “he gave gifts to men.” G: “he received gifts in a man.” M: “among men.” The Greek has ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ (“in a man”).

**Also verses 19–20.** “For the Lord God to dwell. Blessed be the Lord, etc.” A, R, Rom, M, C: “the Lord God to dwell, blessed, blessed be the Lord, etc.”

**Also verse 20.** “Our salvations.” A: “our healths.” R, Rom, M: “our Savior.”

**Verse 21.** “And to the Lord, the Lord, belong the issues from death.” A, R, Rom, C, H, and the Greek have “Lord” only once. G: “and the exits of the Lord, the Lord of death.”

**Verse 23.** “I will turn back; I will turn back in,” etc. A, R, Rom, G, H, C: “I will be turned back; I will be turned back in,” etc.

**Verse 24.** “So that it may be dipped.” R, Rom: “until it may be dipped.”

**Verse 25.** “They saw your entrances.” A, R, Rom, M: “your steps were seen.” G, H: “your journeys were seen.” The Vulgate in Car, Colb, Ger: “they saw your entrances.”

**Also verse 25.** “The entrances of my God.” A, M: “the steps of my God.” G, H: “the journeys of my God.”

**Also verse 25.** “Of my king.” The word “my” is absent from A, R, Rom, M, G, H, C, and from the Greek.

**Also verse 25.** “Who is in the sanctuary.” R, Rom add “of him.” G adds “to them.”

**Also verse 25.** “Of young women.” G: “of virgins.”

**Verse 28.** “A young man in ecstasy.” A: “a somewhat older youth in ecstasy.” R, Rom, M, C: “a somewhat older youth in fear.” G: “from youth in fear.” H: “a younger man in fear.”

**Verse 29.** “To your strength.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C, Car, Colb, Ger: “your strength.”

**Verse 31.** “The beasts of the reed.” A, following the Greek: “the beasts of the papyrus.” Hebrew: “the beast of the papyrus.” R, Rom, C: “the beasts of the forests.” M, H: “the beasts of the forest.” G: “the beasts of the forest.”

**Also verse 31.** “Among the cows.” A, R, Rom, M, G, H, C: “between the cows.”

**Also verse 31.** “So that they may exclude them.” A, R, Rom, M: “so that these may be excluded.” G, H, C: “so that they may not be excluded.” The Greek has “may not be excluded,” omitting “so that.”

**Verse 32.** “His hands.” M: “their hands.” The Greek: “his hand.”

**Verse 34.** “To his voice.” A, R, Rom, G, H, C: “his voice.”

**Also verse 34.** After “the voice of strength,” G adds: “I will hear his voice, the voice of strength.”

### From Psalm 68

**Verse 5.** “Then I was paying back.” H: “then I was repeatedly called upon to pay back.”

**Verse 8.** “Confusion covered [me].” A: “irreverence covered [me].” A, R, Rom, M, G, H, C: “reverence covered [me].”

**Verse 9.** “A stranger.” A, following the Greek: “alienated.” H, Hebrew: “foreign.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “an outsider.”

**Also verse 9.** “And a sojourner.” A, R, Rom, M, G, H, C: “and a guest.”

**Verse 13.** “They were speaking.” A: “they were insulting.” R, Rom, M: “they were being occupied.” G, H: “they were slandering.”

**Verse 14.** “My prayer.” A, following the Greek: “with my prayer.”

**Verse 15.** “So that I may not be fixed fast.” A, R, Rom, M, H: “so that I may not cling.”

**Verse 16.** “Nor may it press upon.” A, following the Greek: “nor may it constrict.” G, H: “nor may it contain.” C: “nor may it open.” Hebrew: “and may it not crown.”

**Verse 17.** “Look upon me.” C: “Turn toward me.”

**Verse 21.** “He awaited reproach.” C: “he endured reproach.”

**Verse 28.** “Into your righteousness.” A, G, C, Colb, Ger, Gal: “in your righteousness,” following the Greek.

**Verse 30.** “Your salvation, O God, received me.” A, R, Rom, G, H, C: “and the salvation of your countenance, O God, received me.”

**Verse 31.** “The name of God.” R, Rom, following G, add “my.”

**Verse 34.** “He did not despise.” M: “he did not annul.” The Greek has ἐξουδένωσεν (“he treated as nothing” or “he despised”).

**Verse 35.** “And all the creeping things in them.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “and all that are in them.” H: “and everything creeping in it.” Hebrew: “and everything that moves in them.”

**Verse 36.** “The cities of Judah.” R, Rom, M, C, Car, Colb, Ger, Gal: “the cities of Judea.” G, following the Greek: “the cities of Judea.” A has the same reading in the manuscripts.

### From Psalm 69

**Verse 1.** “Because the Lord saved him.” Rom, C, Car, Gal, following the Greek: “because the Lord saved me.”

**Verse 2.** “God.” Rom, G: “Lord God.” C: “Lord my God.”

**Also verse 2.** “Lord, hasten to help me.” A, G, C, and the Greek omit this part.

### From Psalm 70

**Verse 1.** “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” A, R, Rom, M, C: “God, in you I have hoped, Lord.” G: “Lord God, in you I have hoped.”

**Verse 8.** “My mouth with praise.” R, Rom, M, G, C add “your.” The Hebrew has the same.

**Also verse 8.** “So that I may sing.” A: “so that I may sing hymns.” R, Rom, M, C: “so that I may be able to sing.” G: “so that I may bless.”

**Also verse 8.** “Your greatness.” A, G, following the Greek: “your magnificence.”

**Verse 10.** “My enemies for me.” R, Rom: “the evil of my enemies for me.”

**Verse 13.** “Those who slander my soul.” A: “those who commit my soul.”

**Verse 14.** “I will hope.” A, R, Rom, M, C: “I will hope in you.”

**Verse 15.** “Learning.” A, R, Rom, G, M, C: “commerce,” or “commercial dealings.” The Greek has πραγματείας (“transactions” or “business dealings”).

**Also verse 15.** “In the powers of the Lord.” G: “in your power, Lord.” The Greek has ἐν δυναστείᾳ (“in power”). Hebrew: “in strength.” Car, Colb, Ger, Gal: “into the power of the Lord.”

**Verse 21.** “Your magnificence.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C, following the Greek: “your righteousness.” M adds “over me.”

**Also verse 21.** “You have consoled me.” R, Rom, M, C: “you have encouraged me.” In the Greek it is παρεκάλεσας, an ambiguous verb that produces variation in other passages as well. M further adds: “and you have brought me back again from the depths of the earth.” A similar addition occurs in G and C.

**Verse 24.** “Evil for me.” G, C: “my soul.”

### From Psalm 71

**Verse 2.** “In righteousness.” R, Rom, G: “in your righteousness.”

**Verse 3.** “Peace to the people.” R, Rom, M, G, C, and the Greek add “your.”

**Also verses 3–4.** “And the hills righteousness. He will judge,” etc. R, Rom, C: “and the hills righteousness. In his righteousness he will judge,” etc. G, following the Greek: “and the hills. In righteousness he will judge,” etc. Augustine mentions this reading in *Exposition on Psalm 71*, no. 6.

**Verse 5.** “From generation to generation.” A, following the Greek: “generations of generations,” omitting the preposition “in.” The Vulgate in Car, Colb, Ger also had this reading. R, Rom, G: “for age of age.”

**Verse 7.** “May the moon be taken away.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “may the moon be exalted.”

**Verse 11.** “The kings of the earth.” The Greek now has this, and the Vulgate in Car, Colb, Ger, Gal lacks the word “earth,” which Jerome had deleted as superfluous, according to Letter 135.

**Verse 14.** “And their honorable name before him.” M: “and his illustrious name before them.”

**Verse 15.** “And they will worship because of him.” A, R, Rom, M, C, Car, Ger, following the Greek and Hebrew: “and they will pray.” M: “for him.” G: “for him.”

**Verse 16.** “And they will flourish.” G: “and he will flower.” C: “and they flower.”

**Verse 17.** “His name.” R, Rom, G add: “and before the moon is his throne.” M: “and before the moon his throne is [established] for ages of ages.”

**Also verse 17.** “They will magnify him.” M: “they will bless him.”

**Verse 19.** “Of majesty.” A, G, following the Greek: “of glory.” Likewise below, where the text has “in majesty,” they have “in glory.”

**Also verse 19.** “Forever.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C, and the Greek add: “and for age of age.”

### From Psalm 72

**Verse 4.** “There is no regard for their death.” A in the manuscripts, and R, Rom, M, C: “there is no inclination toward their death.” G: “there is no rest for their death.” Hebrew: “they did not think of their death.” Ambrose: “there is no reclining,” etc.

**Also verse 4.** “In the plague.” A: “in the scourge.” G: “in punishment.”

**Verse 6.** “Pride.” M: “their pride to the end.”

**Verse 7.** “It went forth.” A, following the Greek: “it will go forth.” G: “it will come out.”

**Also verse 7.** “Into affection.” A, R, Rom, M, Ambrose: “into disposition.” G, C: “in disposition.” The Greek has εἰς διάθεσιν (“into disposition”).

**Verse 8.** “Wickedness.” The Greek means “in wickedness.”

**Also verse 8.** “On high.” A, following the Greek: “into the heights.” Rom, G: “into the high place.”

**Verse 9.** “On earth.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “over the earth.”

**Verse 10.** “Therefore this people of mine will turn.” A, R, Rom, M, Ambrose, G, C, following the Greek: “therefore my people will return here.”

**Verse 11.** “God knows.” A, R, Rom, G, C, following the Greek: “God knew.”

**Verse 14.** “And my chastisement.” A: “and my reproach.” Rom, M: “and my judge.” R: “and my witness.” Ambrose: “and my avenger.” Hebrew: “and my rebuke.”

**Verse 15.** “Behold, I rejected the nation.” R, Rom: “behold, a nation.” G: “behold, a progeny.” R, Rom: “for whom I appointed.” M, G, C: “for whom [singular] I appointed.” Ambrose: “Behold, I arranged this for the generation of your sons.” Augustine testifies that certain copies read: “Behold, for the generation … for whom I sang.”

**Verse 16.** “I considered in order to understand this: it is labor,” etc. A, following the Greek: “And he undertook to understand: this is labor,” etc. Moreover, the conjunction “And” at the beginning of the verse is found in all manuscripts of the Vulgate and in the Hebrew.

**Verse 17.** “In their last things.” A, G, following the Greek: “in the last thing,” omitting “their.” R, Rom, C: “in their last thing.”

**Verse 18.** “You placed [things] for them.” R, Rom: “you arranged evils for them.” M, C: “you placed evils for them.” Ambrose: “you placed good things for them.”

**Also verse 18.** “When they were lifted up.” A, M: “when they were exalted.”

**Verse 20.** “Like the dream of those who arise.” A, R, Rom, M, Ambrose, C: “like the dream of one who rises.” G: “like those rising from a dream.”

**Verse 21.** “It was inflamed.” A, R, Rom, Ambrose, C, following the Greek: “it was delighted.” G: “it rejoiced.” M: “it burned.” Hebrew: “it was contracted.”

**Also verse 21.** “They were changed.” R, Rom, C: “they were dissolved.” G: “they were alienated.” Ambrose: “they rested.”

**Verse 22.** “I was reduced to nothing.” G: “I was despised.” Hebrew: “I was foolish.”

**Verse 23.** “With you.” A: “to you.”

**Verse 24.** “My right hand.” A, M: “my right hand’s.” G: “my right hand.”

**Verse 25.** “Is in heaven.” R, Rom, M, Ambrose: “remains in heaven.” G: “survives in heaven.”

**Verse 28.** “In the Lord God.” A, M, C: “in God.” G: “in the Lord God of my salvation.”

**Also verse 28.** “Your proclamations.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “your praises,” or “your hymns of praise.”

**Also verse 28.** “In the gates.” A: “in the courts.”

### From Psalm 73

**Verse 1.** “Your fury.” A, M, C: “your disposition.”

**Also verse 1.** “Your pastures.” A, R, Rom, M, C: “your flock.”

**Verse 2.** “Which you possessed.” G: “which you acquired.” R, Rom, M, C: “which you created”—because the translator took ἐκτήσω as ἐκτίσω.

**Also verse 2.** “Mount Zion, in which you dwelt in it.” A: “Mount Zion, this one which you inhabited in it,” a reading supported by the Greek. R: “Mount Zion, in which you dwell continually.”

**Verse 3.** “Lift up your hands.” A, R, Rom: “Lift up your hand.”

**Also verse 3.** “He acted maliciously.” A: “he acted wickedly.”

**Also verse 3.** “In the sanctuary.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C, following the Greek: “in your sanctuaries.”

**Verse 4.** “In the midst of your solemn assembly.” R, Rom, G, C: “in the midst of your court.” Hebrew: “in the midst of your covenant.”

**Verse 5.** “As at an exit above the summit.” A: “as into an exit from above.” R, Rom: “as on a road above the summit.” M: “as at an exit from above.” The Greek: “as at an entrance from above.” G: “as into their entrance from above.”

**Verse 6.** “With axe and hatchet.” A: “with the adze and the breaking tool.”

**Verse 8.** “Let us cause [it] to cease.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “Come, let us crush [them].”

**Verse 9.** “He will not know any longer.” A: “he will not know yet.” G: “he will not know yet.”

**Verse 11.** “Your hand.” R, Rom: “your face.” G: “your face from us.”

**Also verse 11.** “And your right hand.” G: “and your right hand.”

**Verse 13.** “In the waters.” A, following the Greek: “in the water.” R, Rom, M: “over the waters.” G: “over the water.”

**Verse 14.** “The heads of dragons.” A, M, G: “the head of the dragon.” R, Rom, C: “the head of the great dragon.”

**Verse 16.** “You fashioned the dawn and the sun.” A, G, following the Greek: “you completed the sun and the moon.” R, Rom, C: “you made the sun and the moon.” M: “you prepared the light and the sun.” Hebrew: “you appointed the luminaries and the sun.”

**Verse 18.** “Remember this.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C, and the Greek add: “your creature.”

**Also verse 18.** “He incited.” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “he provoked.” The Greek has παρώξυνε (“he provoked”). Hebrew: “he blasphemed.”

**Verse 20.** “For the dark places of the earth are filled with habitations of iniquity.” A: “because they are filled, those who, etc., with houses of iniquity.” R, Rom, M: “with houses of iniquities.” G: “because the houses of iniquities are filled—perhaps ‘filled’ is feminine—with the darkness of the earth.” The Hebrew supports: “because the unjust dwellings are filled with the darkness of the earth.”

**Verse 23.** “The voices of your enemies.” A, G, following the Greek: “the voice of those who beseech you.” M: “the voice of your suppliants.” R, Rom: “the voices of those who seek you.” C: “the voice of those who seek you.”

**Also verse 23.** “It has always ascended.” A, R, M, following the Greek: “may it always ascend to you.” Rom: “it has always ascended to you.” G: “it has ascended forever.” C: “it has ascended eternally.”

### From Psalm 74

**Verse 2.** “We will recount.” A, following the Greek: “I will recount.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “I will recount.”

**Verse 4.** “It has melted.” A, G: “it has flowed away.”

**Verse 6.** “Do not lift your horn on high.” A: “Therefore do not be lifted up,” unless Augustine said this verse while explaining it.

**Verse 9.** “From this into this.” A: “from this into this one.”

**Verse 10.** “I will announce forever.” A, following the Greek: “I will rejoice forever.” R, Rom, M: “I will rejoice for ages.” G: “I will rejoice in the Lord.”

### From Psalm 75

**Verse 1.** “For the Assyrians.” This is absent from Rom. But Gal, following the Greek: “for the Assyrian.” G: “for the Assyrian.”

**Verse 4.** “The powers of bows.” R, Rom, G, C: “the horns of bows.” M: “powers: the bow.”

**Verse 5.** “You who illumine.” The Greek means: “You illumine.” Hebrew: “You are light.”

**Verse 6.** “In their hands.” The preposition “in” is absent from the Greek, and Jerome wants it deleted in Letter 135.

**Verse 8.** “He will resist you.” M adds: “against your face.”

**Also verse 8.** “From that time your anger.” A, G, C: “then from your anger.” R: “from that time, from your anger.” The Greek has “from your anger,” omitting “from that time.”

**Verse 9.** “You caused [it] to be heard.” A, C: “you hurled.” G: “you cast.” R, Rom: “it was hurled.” The Greek has ἠκούτισας (“you caused to be heard”), for which some manuscripts read ἠκόντισας (“you hurled”).

**Verse 10.** “The meek of the earth.” R, Rom, M, C: “the quiet of the earth.”

**Verse 11.** “They will keep festival for you.” A: “they will celebrate solemn rites for you.”

**Verse 12.** “Who are around it.” In A, M, and the Hebrew, “are” is added.

**Also verse 12.** “You offer.” A, M, with the Hebrew: “they will offer.” C: “they offer.” G, following the Greek: “they will bring.” The Vulgate in Car, Colb, Ger, Gal has the same reading.

### From Psalm 76

**Verse 2.** “With my voice to God.” A, Rom, G, C, following the Greek: “and my voice to God.” R, M: “my voice,” etc., omitting “and.”

**Verse 3.** “Against him.” A, R, Rom, M, G: “before him.” C: “against him always.”

**Also verse 3.** “He refused,” etc. A, M: “he denied.” G: “he refused.” R, Rom, C: “I refused to console my soul.”

**Verse 4.** “And I was exercised.” A, following the Greek: “I chattered,” omitting “and.” Hebrew: “I spoke within myself.” G: “I was alienated.”

**Also verse 4.** “And it failed.” R, Rom, M, C: “and it failed for a little while.”

**Verse 5.** “The watches of my eyes anticipated.” A, C: “all my enemies anticipated the watches.” G: “all my enemies seized the watches in advance,” a reading supported by the Greek.

**Verse 6.** “I considered.” G: “I remembered.”

**Also verse 6.** “And I kept eternal years in mind.” A: “and I remembered eternal years.” G: “and I recalled eternal years.”

**Verse 7.** “And I was exercised.” A, following the Greek: “I chattered.” G: “I considered.” M: “I exercised myself,” omitting “and,” which is also absent from other books.

**Also verse 7.** “And I swept.” A: “and I searched out.” M, G, C: “and I winnowed.” R, Rom: “and I winnowed within myself.” The Greek has καὶ ἔτκαλλον (“and I swept,” or “I searched”).

**Verse 8.** “Surely?” A: “Not.” R, Rom, G: “And I said, Surely?” C: “And I said, Not.”

**Also verse 8.** “Will he cast away?” A: “will he repel?”

**Also verse 8.** “So that he may be more favorable still.” A: “beyond this, so that he may still be well pleased with him.” M: “so that it may still be pleasing.” G: “to do good still.”

**Verse 9.** “Will he cut off from generation to generation?” R, Rom, C: “he will cut off from age and generation.” G: “he will cut off from age and generation unto age.” M: “he will cut off, and he will complete the word from generation to generation.”

**Verse 13.** “And I will exercise myself in your inventions.” A: “and I will chatter about your affections.” R, Rom, M, C: “and I will exercise myself in your observances.” G: “and in your supplications,” etc.

**Verse 14.** “As our God.” G: “apart from our God.”

**Verse 15.** “You who alone do wonders.” A, R, Rom, M, G add “alone.”

**Verse 18.** “A multitude.” M: “from a multitude.”

**Verse 19.** “They pass over.” A, R, Rom, G, C: “they passed through.” M: “they crossed.” Hebrew: “they ran about.”

**Also verse 19.** “Your flashes shone.” A: “your lightning bolts appeared.”

**Also verse 19.** “It was moved.” R, Rom: “he saw.”

**Verse 21.** “And Aaron.” G adds: “of your priests.”

### From Psalm 77

**Verse 2.** “Propositions.” G: “my proposition.”

**Also verse 2.** “From the beginning.” R, Rom, G, C: “from the beginning of the age.”

**Verse 4.** “In another generation.” G, C, following the Greek: “into another generation.”

**Verse 5.** “How great things he commanded … to make them known.” R, Rom, G, C, following the Greek: “which he commanded.” R, Rom: “so that they might make it known.” G, C: “to make it known.”

**Verse 6.** “And they will recount.” A: “and let them recount.” R, Rom: “and they will recount it.”

**Verse 8.** “A crooked and provoking generation.” A: “a crooked and embittering generation.” G: “a crooked and provoking nation.” R, Rom, M: “a crooked and exceedingly bitter race.” C is nearly the same.

**Verse 9.** “Bending and shooting the bow.” R, Rom: “bending the bow and shooting their arrows.” G likewise, omitting only “their.” C: “bending and shooting arrows.”

**Verse 12.** “He did wonders.” A, following the Greek: “which did wonders.”

**Verse 13.** “And he led them through.” A, G: “and he brought them across.” Hebrew: “and he led them over.”

**Also verse 13.** “As in a wineskin.” A: “as in wineskins.” R, Rom, G, C, Car, Colb: “as in a wineskin.” The Greek: “like a wineskin.” Hebrew: “like a heap.”

**Verse 14.** “In the cloud of day.” G, with the Hebrew: “in the cloud by day.” The Greek has ἡμέρας, which there means “by day.”

**Verse 17.** “They provoked [him] to anger … in the waterless place.” A, M, G: “and they provoked [him].” A, R, Rom, M, G, C: “in dryness.”

**Verse 21.** “And he delayed.” R, Rom, G, C: “and he delayed and added.”

**Verse 25.** “He sent provisions,” etc. R, Rom, M, C: “he sent a grain supply,” etc. The Greek has ἐπισιτισμόν (“provision” or “food supply”). G: “he sent them food to satiety.”

**Verse 26.** “He transferred the south wind from heaven.” R, Rom, M: “And he stirred up the south wind from heaven.” G, C likewise, omitting only “and.”

**Also verse 26.** “And he brought in.” G: “and he brought over.”

**Verse 30.** “They were defrauded.” A: “they were deprived.”

**Verse 31.** “Their fat ones.” A: “in the majority of them.” R, Rom, M, G: “the majority of them.” The Greek means “among the fat ones.”

**Also verse 31.** “He hindered.” The Greek means “he fettered.” Hebrew: “he bent down.”

**Verse 34.** “And they returned, and at dawn they came to him.” R: “and they turned back, and before dawn,” etc. Rom, M, C: “and they turned back before dawn,” etc. G: “and they turned back, and they kept watch for him at dawn.” A, R, Car, Ger, following the Greek: “they came to God.” Hebrew: “they rose up toward God.”

**Verse 37.** “Nor were they held faithful,” etc. R, Rom, M: “nor was faith held by them,” etc. G: “nor did they believe in his covenant.”

**Verse 38.** “And he abounded so as to turn away … and he did not kindle.” A, following the Greek: “and he will abound so as to turn away … and he will not kindle.”

**Verse 42.** “On the day when.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “on which day.”

**Verse 44.** “And their rains.” R, Rom, M, G: “and their rainwaters.” C: “their river waters,” etc.

**Verse 45.** “The dog-fly.” R, Rom, M, C: “the dog-fly,” following the Greek κυνόμυιαν. Augustine follows this reading in his exposition. Jerome, however, in Letter 135, wants it written not *cynomyia* but *coenomyia*, in Greek κοινόμυιαν; he himself interprets it from the Hebrew as “every kind of fly.”

**Also verse 45.** “And he destroyed them.” R, Rom, M, G: “and he exterminated them.” G: “and he corrupted them.”

**Verse 46.** “To rust.” A: “to corrosion.” G: “to the dog-star.” Hebrew: “to the locust.”

**Verse 47.** “In hoarfrost.” G: “in ice.”

**Verse 50.** “To their souls.” A, Car, Colb, Ger, following the Greek: “of their souls.”

**Verse 52.** “And he took away.” G: “and he advanced.”

**Verse 54.** “The mountain which.” R, Rom, M, C, following the Greek: “this mountain which.” G and the Hebrew: “this mountain which.”

**Also verse 54.** “Of distribution.” G: “of inheritance.”

**Verse 55.** “And he made [them] dwell.” R, G, C: “and he dwelt.”

**Verse 57.** “And they did not keep the covenant.” Rom: “and they did not observe [it].” G: “and they rejected [it].” The word “covenant” is absent from Rom, C, and G. Hebrew: “and they transgressed.”

**Verse 69.** “On the earth which he founded forever.” R, Rom, C, following the Greek: “on the earth he founded it forever.” G: “and on the earth he founded it eternally.”

**Verse 72.** “And in understandings.” A: “and in understanding.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “and in discernment.” Hebrew: “and in prudence.”

### From Psalm 78

**Verse 1.** “For the keeping of fruit.” R: “like a fruit-orchard watch-house.” G: “like a fruit-orchard hut.” Hebrew: “in heaps of stones.”

**Verse 2.** “Dead bodies.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “mortal remains.” Hebrew: “corpses.”

**Verse 10.** “And let it become known.” R, Rom, G: “and let them become known.”

**Also verse 10.** “Vengeance of blood.” R, Rom, M, G, C: “Avenge the blood.”

## FROM PSALM 101

V. 1. “When he is anxious and … pours out.” A. “When he was troubled, and … he poured out.” G. “When he was afflicted with acedia (listlessness), and … he would pour out.”

Likewise V. 15. “And of its earth.” A. M. G. “And of its dust.” The Greek and Hebrew support this.

V. 17. “He built.” A. R. Car. “He will build.” And so the Greek and Hebrew.

V. 2. “His acts of recompense.” The Greek signifies “his praises.”

## FROM PSALM 103

V. 3 and following. “You cover [them] with waters … you place,” etc. A. “He shelters in the waters.” R. Rom. M. G. C. “He covers in the waters.” A. R. Rom. M. G. C. “He places … he walks … he makes his angels … he founded the earth,” etc.

V. 18. “The houses of the herons,” etc. A. R. Rom. M. G. C. “The houses of the coots.” M. “The house of the starlings provides them a guide.” Hebrew: “The fir tree is the house of the kite.”

[Col. 0049] V. 34. “May my speech be pleasing to him.” A. R. Rom. M. G. C. “May it be sweet to him.” A. M. “My discourse.” R. Rom. G. C. “My praise.”

## FROM PSALM 104

V. 14. “He did not leave.” A. Hebrew: “He dismissed.” R. Rom. M. G. C. “He did not permit.”

V. 18. “It passed through his soul.” G. C. Car., according to the Greek, “His soul passed through.” Hebrew: “His soul entered into iron.”

V. 22. “And that he might teach his elders prudence.” According to Augustine’s interpretation of the Greek, this signifies: “And that he might teach his elders wisdom.”

V. 28. “And he did not embitter his words.” Augustine cites two readings: one found by him in very many manuscripts, namely, “And they embittered his words”; the other in only two books, “And they did not embitter his words.” G. and the Greek have the first reading. R. Rom. M. read, “Because they embittered his words.” C. has, “And he did not pass over his words.” Hebrew: “And they were not disobedient to his words.”

V. 30. “Their land brought forth frogs.” A. “He gave their land frogs.” R. M. “The land sent forth,” etc. Rom. “He sent into the land,” etc. C. “And he sent,” etc. Hebrew: “The land boiled forth,” etc.

V. 31. “And the dog-fly came.” M. “And the dog-fly came.” Likewise V. 31. “And the gnats.” G. “And worms.”

V. 38. “Because he had settled upon them.” R. Rom. M. C. “Because he had fallen.” Hebrew: “Because he had rushed upon them.”

V. 40. “They asked.” R. Rom. “They asked for flesh.” C. “They asked for meat.”

V. 41. “In a dry place.” M. “In dry places.” C. The Greek and Hebrew support this.

V. 44. “And labors.” C. “And cities.”

## FROM PSALM 105

V. 1. “For he is good.” The Greek has *chrēstos*, which some, according to Augustine, translated here and in the following psalm as “sweet.” Hence in V. 5 he himself has “with sweetness” for *chrēstotēti*, where the Vulgate has “with goodness.” The same variation occurs in Psalm 118, V. 65, and in other passages.

V. 5. “To see … to rejoice … that you may be praised.” Augustine observes first that the Greek expression here is one, so that it ought to be rendered “to praise”; then that it could have been translated in two other ways, namely: “That you may see, that you may rejoice, that you may be praised”; or, “That we may see, that we may rejoice, that we may be praised.” Hebrew has: “That I may see, and rejoice, and exult.”

V. 7. “And they provoked.” C. “And they embittered.” Some manuscripts, according to Augustine, read: “And they made bitter.”

Likewise V. 7. “In the sea, the Red Sea.” The word “sea” is not repeated in R. Rom. M. G. C. or in the Greek. *Enarrationes on Psalm* 105, no. 7.

V. 9. “And he led them through the abysses.” A. R. Rom. M. “And he brought them out,” etc. R. Rom. M. G. “In many waters.”

V. 12. “And they praised his praise.” R. Rom. M. “And they sang his praises.”

V. 13. “They acted quickly; they forgot.” G. “They hastened, and forgot.” C. “They quickly forgot.” And so the Hebrew.

V. 17. “Over the assembly of Abiron.” C. “The tent.” A. “Abiron,” with “and it covered over” omitted.

V. 20. “Into a likeness.” A. “In a likeness.”

V. 28. “And they were initiated into Beelphegor.” R. Rom. M. C. “And they were consecrated,” etc. G. “And they were utterly consummated.”

V. 29. “In their inventions.” R. Rom. G. C. Hebrew: “In their pursuits.” M. “In their observances.” R. Rom. likewise later in V. 39, where M. has “pursuits.”

V. 30. “And he made intercession.” R. Rom. M. G. C. “And he entreated.”

V. 38. “And it was defiled.” A. M. G. C. “And it was slain,” according to the Greek *ephonoktonēthē*, “it was murdered.” The Vulgate likewise has this in Car. Ger.

V. 40. “With fury.” R. Rom. G. “With disposition” or “temper.”

V. 44. “And he heard.” A. and Hebrew: “When he heard.” R. Rom. M. G. C. “When he answered.”

## FROM PSALM 106

V. 8. “His mercy.” G. consistently has “his mercies” whenever this verse is repeated; C. usually supports it.

V. 11. “They embittered … they provoked.” A. “They made bitter … they embittered.”

V. 20. “From destructions.” A. G. “From corruption.” R. Rom. Hebrew: “From destruction.” M. “From corruptions.” Greek: *ek tōn diaphthorōn*, “from corruptions.”

V. 29. “And he made its storm stand in a breeze.” A. G., according to the Greek: “And he commanded the storm, and it stood in a breeze.” M. “And he struck the storm, and it stood in a breeze.”

V. 36. “A city.” G. C., according to the Greek, “Cities.”

V. 37. “The fruit of birth.” A. “The fruit of grain.” Greek: “The fruit of produce.” Hebrew: “The produce of growth.”

A few matters remain to be noted concerning the preceding collection. First, the category of discrepancies arising from punctuation within words—which sometimes alters the meaning—has necessarily been omitted here, since it extends too broadly and can scarcely be demonstrated by any other means than by reproducing entire Psalters. Moreover, lest anyone think that the Psalter commonly called the Old has been neglected by us here, it should be pointed out that it differs in no respect from the Augustinian Psalter. Nor do we now doubt that Jacob Faber, the editor of the fivefold Psalter, copied the whole of it from Augustine’s Commentaries: he reproduced the words of the Psalms, sometimes adapted by the preacher to the subject at hand, in no other form than that in which they appeared there, as may be seen in Psalms CXX, “Lift up,” and elsewhere. This was not sufficiently noticed by those who, in their scholia and notes on the Septuagint translators, treat this Old Psalter and the Augustinian one not as one and the same Psalter, but as two Psalters.

Finally, it is worth observing that in certain, although exceedingly rare, passages the Vulgate agrees less closely with the Hebrew than the Old Version does. We believe this is due to the variation in the Greek text of the Hexapla, which Jerome used in correcting the Latin Psalter. For example, in Psalm IV, 8, the Vulgate reads *A fructu* (“From the fruit”), because the Greek exemplar had ἀπὸ καρποῦ (“from fruit”) instead of ἀπὸ καιροῦ (“from the time”), which was the reading of the Old Version and more consistent with the Hebrew.

[Col. 0057]

## CASSIODORUS SENATOR ON THE SUBSEQUENT WORK OF AUGUSTINE

### IN THE PROLOGUE TO HIS COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS

When I had tasted the honey of the heavenly Psalter, I plunged into it as an eager investigator, as those who long for something habitually do, so that after the most bitter pursuits I might sweetly imbibe its saving utterances. But beginners encounter a familiar obscurity, interwoven with various persons and veiled in parables. This obscurity is passed over through a harmful silence in the vital sayings, although what is often found there is ambiguous and bears the secret of a great sacrament. [Col. 0058]

Then I took refuge in the much-renowned reading of Augustine, that most eloquent father [Note: [Col. 0058] Ms. Germ. reads: “most eloquent.”], in which such an abundance of statements had been amassed that what appears to have been fully expounded can scarcely be retained even after rereading. I believe that, when he wished to fill peoples who were exceedingly eager for ecclesiastical nourishment, the streams of so great a preaching necessarily flowed forth [Col. 0059].

Therefore, mindful of my weakness, with divine mercy granting it, I have led the sea poured forth from the sources of certain of his psalms into shallow channels, in a concise abridgment, encompassing in one book what he wonderfully explained in fifteen decades. But, as someone says of Homer, to steal something from his meaning is like taking Hercules’ club from his hand [Note: [Col. 0059] Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 3, chapter 3.].

For he is an outstanding teacher of all letters and, what is rare in one so fertile, an exceedingly cautious disputant. He flows like a most pure spring, polluted by no dregs; while persevering in the integrity of the faith, he does not allow heretics anything by which they might defend themselves in any contest. He is found wholly Catholic, wholly orthodox; and, shining with the sweetest radiance in the Church of the Lord, he is illumined by the brightness of heavenly light.

[Col. 0059]

## VERSES ON THE EPITOME OF AUGUSTINE’S COMMENTARIES ON THE PSALMS, CONTAINED IN THE OLD COLBERTINE MANUSCRIPT

On that manuscript a frontispiece, in the form of a chamber, painted to contain an image of David, may be seen; above the arch it bears these words: “Landulfus, exulting, ordered this little book to be made; for him who reads it, pour forth prayers and songs,” etc. At the feet of the image: “Pray for Anno; this I beg.” (C,S)*

This flowering book contains songs  
That give voice to Christ upon David’s plectrum,  
Set forth in exposition;  
It opens the greatest mysteries in concise words  
And speaks copious meanings with brevity.

Augustine, venerable throughout the whole world,  
An outstanding bishop and apostolic teacher,  
By pouring forth his tongue in a broad stream among the peoples,  
Completed this great work in three sets of five decades,  
While seeking both to grasp the subtle forms of things  
And to move the minds of the people with pious speech.

But because not all seek a marvelous matter,  
Salubrious in every respect, with eager love of heart—  
Indeed, because many are lesser in means and understanding,  
They cannot possess such great treasures at all—  

[Col. 0060]

It pleased us to touch upon everything together in one book  
And to draw modest waves from the sea,  
So that so great a work might often be reviewed briefly  
Without burdening anyone with excessive expense or labor.

Therefore, Reader, move through this work with discerning understanding,  
And receive the heavenly nectar from the sacred mouth:  
It refreshes minds, forms and adorns character;  
From it hope, love, and faith draw their strength.

For here the merciful God presides over the venerable ark  
That holds the heavenly laws on two tablets;  
Soothing the stern rod with the sweetness of manna,  
And covering all things beneath his gracious divinity.

Between the two Cherubim he thunders  
With a trembling voice, and flashes with the fire  
Of swift lightning.

[Col. 0059]

## FRANCESCO PETRARCA TO GIOVANNI BOCCACCIO, ON THE WORK OF AUGUSTINE ON THE PSALMS SENT TO HIM

[Note: [Col. 0059] *Epistles of Various Matters*, 22 or 24.]

You have delighted me with a magnificent and distinguished gift. Now I shall sail more securely across the Davidic sea: I shall avoid the reefs, and I shall fear neither the waves of words nor the collision of broken sentences.

I used to strive into the deep by my own strength, sometimes throwing my arms farther out, sometimes supported by a chance plank, and laboring with an exhausted mind through the obstructing waves. Thus, often beginning to sink with Peter, I would cry out, “Lord, save me” (Matt. XIV, 30); and often I would rise again when Christ stretched out his hand in response to my entreaties.

Amid these storms, you have provided me with a sturdy vessel and a skilled helmsman: Augustine, a man of divine genius. His immense work—contained in many large volumes, divided by common usage into three parts and by some into several divisions—you have sent to me in its entirety, gathered into a single volume [Note: [Col. 0059] This very work is now preserved divided into two volumes in the Royal Library. See the list of manuscripts below, cols. 65–66.]. I received it joyfully and with astonishment. And I said to myself: “There is no place for idleness. If any leisure remains, this book will consume it. A great guest has arrived and must be attended to with great effort. It will not allow me to sleep through whole nights. You lie there in vain with your eyes still closed: one must keep watch, one must work by lamplight. You meditate upon rest in vain: one must labor.”

I shall speak frankly: none of my friends has looked upon it without admiration, and all testify with one voice that they have never seen a book of such magnitude. As for myself, I confess that I am no last investigator of such matters: this is a work greater not in the mass of its writing than in the richness of its meanings.

It is astonishing to consider how great that man was in genius and in devotion; whence came that holy man’s ardor and impulse for writing; that knowledge of divine matters in one first captivated by earthly allurements; that endurance of labor in an old man; that leisure in a bishop; that command of Roman eloquence in an African. Of him one might properly say what he himself, following Terence, said of Marcus Varro: “Varro,” he says, “a most learned man in every respect, read so much that we are amazed he had time to write anything; and he wrote so much that we scarcely believe anyone could read it all” [Note: [Col. 0060] *The City of God*, book VI, chapter 2.].

But to pass over the other monuments of his genius—whether the many that I possess or those of which I am still deprived, and again whether those which he himself recalls in his books of *Revisions*, or those which he perhaps forgot, neglected, or passed over because they had not yet been written, while a human lifetime scarcely suffices even to reread everything—who would not marvel that, even if he had done nothing else, he could have written this one work?

I know of no single work by one author published in Latin letters that can be compared with this in magnitude, unless perhaps it is his other book on the Epistles of Paul, which, unless my judgment deceives me and my memory fails, appears to approach the same mass of writing; or the immense book of Livy on Roman affairs, which was divided into the parts called Decades not by its author but by the tiresome negligence of its readers.

To this gift of your friendship, besides the magnitude I have described, are added the book’s beauty, the majesty of its ancient script, and every sober ornament, so that when I begin to fix my eyes upon it, I cannot draw them away full, like a thirsty leech. Thus many times a day passes without food, and a sleepless night follows. As for the delight I take—now almost my only delight, and one I receive only from reading books—I do not easily think that the common crowd can estimate how much your generosity has added to it, since it has no pleasure beyond bodily senses. You, however, can do so readily, and you will not wonder that I awaited the arrival of this book thirstily and anxiously.

You know how, for desire, even a short interval is long, and haste is slow. If in Ovid there is the mad lover’s phrase:

> “The seventh night is passing; the interval seems longer to me than a year,”

what must you think my experience was, when during my waiting, as the same poet says in another’s voice:

> “The moon four times hid, and four times was renewed throughout her whole circle”?  
> (Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle 2.)

The flame of those who desire honorable things is usually more serene, not less ardent.

Still, I should judge that the delay was intentional—not indeed on your part, since you took great pains in sending it, but rather by some other agency [reading uncertain; Note: [Col. 0061] Perhaps “by another,” or something similar.]—so that the delay might add a spur to my desire [Col. 0062] and increase the favor of your gift. Do not suppose that I can offer you adequate thanks within the limits imposed by the structure of this letter or by a single day: I know no other limit than the end of reading and of life.

Farewell, and remember me.

[Col. 0061]

## PREFACE OF A CERTAIN MORE RECENT WRITER TO AUGUSTINE’S COMMENTARIES, WHICH HE WROTE ON THE PSALMS

Since the truth of both divine and human philosophy teaches that nothing has been made without purpose or cause, whether among the works of God or those of nature, the question of why and for what purpose the human being was created has greatly troubled the minds of those who have attempted to give an account of each created thing.

Although the minds of many philosophers have labored diligently and at great length to solve this question, none of them was able to give a true and complete account. As a result, straying from the straight path of truth, they fell into various and inexcusable errors. Nor is this surprising: for if they did not know the reason for their own existence, how could they know the reason for that of anything else?

But Holy Scripture, inspired by the Creator of humanity, alone brought to light the supreme and perfect reason for humanity’s creation—not only the general reason, according to which the Lord made all things for himself (Prov. XVI, 4), but also the particular purpose of humanity’s function, dignity, and end. For it is written: “God created man from the earth, and made him according to his own image.” And shortly afterward: “He set his eye upon their hearts, to show them the greatness of his works, so that they might praise the name of his holiness and glory in his wonders, and declare the greatness of his works” (Ecclus. XVII, 1, 7–8).

The whole of this may be summed up as follows: God created humanity, and created it in such a way, that there might be one who could understand his works; who could admire inwardly and proclaim and praise aloud his providence in ordering, his reason in making, his power in perfecting, his might in preserving, his wisdom in governing, and his mercy in doing good—that is, so that humanity might worship God as its maker.

Just as the world was made for humanity, to serve it, so humanity was made for God, to serve him. Thus the world was made in order that humanity might come to be; humanity, however, was made so that it might acknowledge God its maker; it was to acknowledge him so that it might love and worship him; it was to love and worship him so that it might receive blessed immortality as the reward of its labor; and it was to receive the reward of blessed immortality so that, made like the angels, it might serve the supreme and immortal God forever and become an eternal kingdom for God himself.

This is the sum of things, this is God’s secret, this is the mystery of the world’s constitution, this is the reason for humanity’s creation, this is the hinge upon which the universe turns. Whoever does not know this does not know whether he himself is human. If the philosophers had held to this, they would not have fallen into so many varied and destructive errors.

Finally, so that humanity might continually retain this understanding of its condition, it was given a command, as the holy lawgiver Moses bears witness when he admonished the Jewish people:

“And now, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances, which I command you today, so that it may be well with you?” And shortly afterward: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. X, 12–13, 20).

Nor should this be passed over: for the same reason not only was humanity created, but the Creator of humanity also became human. Zechariah, the father of the Lord’s forerunner, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied among other things:

“The oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us that, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we might serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” (Luke I, 73–75).

Behold, by the testimony of so great a prophet, God also became human for humanity’s sake—or rather, served humanity—so that humanity in turn might render him a service worthy of him [Col. 0062].

Although the service imposed upon humanity can be interpreted in many ways and can be offered to God the Creator in many different forms, it is nevertheless nothing other than the worship owed to God; and this worship is nothing other than his devoted praise.

“For,” as Lactantius Firmianus bears witness, “the highest rite of worshiping God is praise directed from the mouth of a righteous person to God. Yet, he says, for this praise itself to be acceptable to God, the greatest humility, fear, and devotion are required, lest someone, relying upon his integrity and innocence, incur the charge of pride and arrogance and thereby lose the grace of virtue” [Note: [Col. 0062] Lactantius, book VI, *On True Worship*, chapter 25.]

Therefore holy Moses, after expressing the command mentioned above, added: “You shall cling to him; he is your praise” (Deut. X, 20–21)—that is, he alone is the one whom you ought to praise.

This is true religion, this is upright piety, this is the service owed to God. This is the acceptable and perpetual sacrifice by which God wishes to be worshiped, appeased, honored, and glorified, as he himself testifies through the Prophet:

“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.” And at the end of the same prophecy: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX, 14, 23).

Although all human beings are bound to this service, the Lord nevertheless chose certain people whom he wished to be worshiped and praised especially and more particularly. Thus, in the Old Testament, he chose the people of Israel, to whom Moses spoke:

“The Lord your God chose you to be his special people out of all the peoples who are upon the earth” (Deut. VII, 6).

And again, after much else:

“Behold, the Lord has chosen you today to be his special people, as he spoke to you, and to keep all his commandments. He will make you higher than all the nations which he created, for the praise and glory of his name, so that you may be a holy people of the Lord your God” (Deut. XXVI, 18–19).

Likewise, in the New Testament he specially chose the Christian people for his praise and glory. The Apostle wrote this to the Ephesians, blessing and praising God for it:

“Blessed,” he says, “be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace” (Eph. I, 3–6).

Likewise, in the Old Testament, from the chosen people the Lord selected for himself the sons of Levi, who were to serve him especially in the ministries of the tabernacle, according to what he said to Aaron:

“I have given you your brothers, the Levites, from among the children of Israel, and I have handed them over as a gift to the Lord, that they may serve in the ministries of his tabernacle” (Num. XVIII, 6).

Later King David appointed them to stand in the morning to confess and sing to the Lord (I Chron. XXVI, 4), and likewise in the evening, and so forth.

In the same way, in the New Testament, clerics and priests were selected from the Christian people so that they might serve the Lord especially and, by declaring his virtues, praise and worship him. This is confirmed by the authority of Peter, chief of the apostles, who wrote to them:

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II, 9).

And just as the sons of Levi devoted themselves to divine praises at fixed times and hours, so clerics ought to do. For clerics are called from the word for “lot,” because they belong to the Lord’s lot; together with the sons of Levi, they are to possess him forever as their portion and inheritance, provided that here they serve him with due worship and worthy praise [Col. 0063].

It is also worthy of consideration, and is not without mystery, that although all divinely inspired Scripture has been ordered and written for the praise and glory of God; although all of it has been handed down to humanity for instruction and consolation; and although it is entirely full of divine praises, introducing everything from which due praise of God may be drawn and setting forth every form and manner of praising him, the holy Church nevertheless wished to use certain Scriptures more particularly and more frequently in divine worship.

For just as the Lord specially chose certain people from each of the two Testaments, as explained above, so from the Scriptures of both Testaments he wished certain books to be used more particularly in his worship. From the Old Testament this especially applies to the Book of Psalms, for this reason in particular, as the learned Dionysius holds: the Psalms encompass in the form of praise everything contained in Holy Scripture [Note: [Col. 0063] Dionysius, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3.].

Hence this Book of Psalms is a register of all Holy Scripture and the completion of the whole theological page. The following prologue of our blessed Augustine also commends and exalts it with almost innumerable praises.

The sacred canon urges that this book be learned, among the other things necessary for priests to know. Since one ought to sing psalms to God intelligently, how can someone sing psalms to God properly if he does not know [Col. 0064] what he is singing? Our holy Psalmist commands those who sing to God to sing intelligently:

“God is king of all the earth; sing psalms wisely” (Ps. XLVI, 8)—that is, intelligently, as another text reads.

But because this book is full of so many and such profound mysteries that no one can understand it without revelation or a learned interpreter, our great teacher Augustine, a most devoted worshiper of God and most ardent champion of the salvation of souls, labored over its explanation with vigilant devotion. He unlocked what was closed, revealed what was hidden, disclosed mysteries, clarified obscurities, determined doubtful matters, detested vices, exalted virtues, threatened punishments, promised rewards, strengthened the fainthearted, restrained the presumptuous, and crowned those who persevered, so that no one who reads attentively departs without fruit.

Therefore let all who have been chosen for the Lord’s lot, so that they may praise and glorify him with due service, devote themselves to this work, read it frequently, and retain its meaning. Otherwise, through negligence and ignorance, they may experience the vengeance of that divine threat:

“Because you rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve as priest to me” (Hos. IV, 6).

And also this still more terrible one:

“I said, ‘They are always erring in heart’; but they did not know my ways. So I swore in my anger: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’” (Ps. XCIV, 10–11).

Thus they may come to have their portion with the hypocrites. Rather, let those who understand and retain the reason for which they were created possess their Creator as the portion of their inheritance, and praise and glorify him forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0063]

## PROLOGUE TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS

Attributed in former printed editions to Augustine, but not found in all manuscripts. This is Basil’s preface to his Commentary on the Psalms, from Rufinus’s translation.

“All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching” (II Tim. III, 16). It was written by the Holy Spirit for this very reason: so that, as though from a common fountain of health, we might all draw from it remedies for our particular passions. “Health,” he says, “restrains great sins.”

For the things handed down by the Prophets are one kind, those handed down by historians another [Note: [Col. 0063] Alternatively, “history.”]; the law has its own kind, and the admonition of proverbs another. But the Book of Psalms contains whatever is useful from all of them. It foretells future events, recalls the deeds of earlier times, gives the law to those who live, and establishes the manner in which things should be done. To put it briefly, it is a common treasury of good teaching, supplying each person appropriately with what is necessary.

It knows how to heal the old wounds of souls, but it also knows how to apply the swiftest remedy to recent wounds and to provide perseverance in salvation to those who remain unharmed. It likewise comes to the aid of every passion that troubles human souls under various forms of domination. And it does so with a certain musical rhythm and pleasing melody that summons the human mind [Note: [Col. 0063] Alternatively, “sense.”] to chastity.

For the Holy Spirit, seeing the human mind struggling against and resisting the path of virtue, and inclining more toward the pleasures of life than rising toward the straight path of virtue, mingled the power of his teaching with the pleasing rhythms of song [Note: [Col. 0063] Alternatively: “to be directed; he mingled the pleasing rhythms of song with serious teaching.”]. Thus, while the hearing is soothed by the sweetness of the song, the usefulness of the divine word is implanted at the same time. This is like the wise physicians who, whenever necessity requires them to offer harsher medicines to sick mortals, smear the rims and upper edges of the cup in which they administer the remedy with honey, so that the sick person may not reject its usefulness because of its harshness.

Therefore songs suited to musical rhythms have been provided for us in the Psalms, so that those who are still children in age or adolescents in character may appear to take pleasure in singing them, as in a kind of song. In truth, they illuminate souls and enlighten the mind.

For many of those who attend church can neither easily learn the apostolic commandments nor clearly learn or retain the prophetic teachings once they have learned them. But they sing the responses of the Psalms within their homes and sometimes even in public. And if someone is seized by even the wildest and most savage fury, should he happen to be, so to speak, enchanted by the songs of a Psalm, all the rage of his savagery immediately departs.

The Psalm is tranquility of souls, the standard-bearer of peace. It restrains disturbances and the waves of thought, represses anger, repels luxury, suggests sobriety, gathers friendship, brings those who disagree into harmony, and reconciles enemies. For who could still call someone an enemy when he has raised one voice with him to God in the Psalm?

From this it is understood that the Psalm restores charity, which is the greatest of all good things. It creates a kind of union through the harmony of the voice and joins a diverse people into one choir through concordant melody.

The Psalm puts demons to flight and invites angels to our aid. It is a shield amid nighttime terrors and a rest from the labors of the day; a protection for children, an adornment for young men, a consolation for the old, and a most fitting ornament for women. It causes deserted cities to be inhabited and teaches sobriety. For beginners it becomes the first element; for those making progress, an increase; for the perfect, a firm foundation. It is the single voice of the whole Church.

The Psalm adorns solemn festivals. The Psalm softens sorrow that is according to God. The Psalm also draws tears from a heart of stone. The Psalm is the work of angels and of the heavenly armies; it is spiritual incense.

O truly admirable and wise institution of a master, by which we seem both to sing and to be taught what pertains to the soul’s benefit! Through it the necessary teaching is more deeply formed in our minds. For if something has been implanted in our souls through force and difficulty, it immediately slips away; but what we receive with grace and affection seems, in some inexplicable manner, to remain more firmly in our minds and cling to our memory.

What is there that is not learned in the Psalms? Is there not the whole greatness of virtue, the rule of justice, the beauty of chastity, the perfection of prudence, the discipline of patience—everything that can be called good? From them come perfect knowledge of God, the foretelling of Christ’s coming in the flesh, the hope of the common resurrection, fear of punishments, the promise of glory, and the revelation of mysteries. Absolutely all good things are stored up and gathered together in them, as in one great and common treasury [Col. 0065].

The Prophet adapted this book to the instrument called the Psalter, although there are many musical instruments. It seems to me that by this he teaches the grace of God, inspired from above through the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0065] Alternatively, “to him.”] [Col. 0066]. For this alone among musical instruments is said to produce sounds from above.

The cithara and lyre, having bronze or a drum on their lower side, resound and reverberate when struck by the plectrum. But the Psalter is said to have harmonies fitted from above and to give the causes of its sounds from above. Through this, then, we are also taught to attend to the things that are above and higher, and to avoid what is low—that is, bodily vices.

But I think that a deeper meaning is indicated to us by this prophetic explanation and that, through the form of this instrument, we are taught that those who are diligent, capable, and moderate in character have an easy path to what is above.

But let us finally see what the beginnings of the Psalms themselves indicate.

[Col. 0065]

## ANNOTATION ON THE FIRST PSALM

In older printed editions attributed to Augustine, but not found in all manuscripts; nor does it agree concerning the author of the Psalms with Augustine’s view in *The City of God*, book XVII, chapter 14.

There are different kinds of prophecy. We must therefore inquire whose voice this is, in whose person it was properly spoken, and why it has no title.

There is no doubt that there are one hundred and fifty Psalms, and the inscription of the titles shows which Psalm each one is and by whom it was recited. For not all the Psalms were published by David. David himself chose from the whole people four leaders purified by the Holy Spirit, whose names were Asaph, Heman, Ethan, and Jeduthun, so that whoever the divine Spirit entered might sing a hymn to God.

Thus David alone sang nine Psalms with his own mouth; the others were spoken by those four leaders, according to the inscription of their titles.

But since this Psalm, as I have already said, has no title, we must inquire why, among the others, it alone lacks a title inscription and by whom it was recited. For if the Psalmist was able to number the second, third, fourth, and all the others, or to indicate the reasons for each, why did he not give this one a title and show that it was the first?

[Col. 0066]

But because this Psalm introduces the proper voice of God speaking, it has no title, lest anything be placed before the divine utterance, or lest it be called “first” when it is not first but simply “one.” Therefore it could not and ought not to have a prefatory title. If it had possessed one indicating that it was first, it might have been judged merely superior in the order of numbering, not in authority. Or, as has already been said, the Psalmist might have placed something before the divine utterance by placing a title before it.

Indeed, it could have been understood as superior to the others if it had been called first. For this reason alone it has no title, so that it might be clear how far it stands above the others.

Hence Your Prudence should now recognize how great is the force, authority, and reason contained in this Psalm, before which the scribe did not dare to place a title or indicate a number, so that he might show it to be alone and one rather than first.

Therefore, since, by God’s favor, both the authority of its voice has been demonstrated and the reason for its lack of a title has been explained, it remains for us to discuss the Psalm itself.

[Col. 0065]

## EXPOSITIONS ON THE PSALMS BY SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO (C,S)

### EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST PSALM

**1. [verse 1.]** “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly”: this is to be understood of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, of the Lordly man [Note: [Col. 0067] In *Revisions* I, 19, Augustine disapproves of having called Christ “the Lordly man,” following certain Catholic writers, though not without precedent.].

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly”: unlike the earthly man who consented to the woman deceived by the serpent, so that he might transgress God’s commandments.

“And has not stood in the way of sinners”: for he did indeed come into the way of sinners by being born as sinners are born, but he did not stand there, because worldly allurements did not hold him.

“And has not sat in the seat of pestilence”: he did not desire an earthly kingdom with pride. This is rightly understood as the seat of pestilence because scarcely anyone is free from the love of ruling or does not desire human glory. For pestilence is a disease widely spread and involving all, or nearly all.

Although it may be more appropriately understood as the seat of pestilence, that is, pernicious teaching, whose speech spreads like cancer (II Tim. II, 17).

Next, the order of the words must be considered: “he went,” “he stood,” “he sat.” He went when he withdrew from God; he stood when he took pleasure in sin; he sat when, confirmed in his pride, he could not return except through him who neither went in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence.

## 2. [verse 2]

But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.

The law is not laid down for the righteous, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:9); but it is one thing to be in the law and another to be under the law. Whoever is in the law acts according to the law; whoever is under the law is acted upon according to the law. The former, therefore, is free; the latter is a slave.

Furthermore, one thing is the law that is written and imposed upon a servant; another is the law that is perceived by the mind, by one who has no need of letters.

“He will meditate day and night”: this may be understood either as without interruption, or as by day in joy and by night in tribulations. For it is said, “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56); and concerning tribulation it is said, “Moreover, even unto the night my kidneys chastened me” (Ps. 15:7).

[Note: Nine manuscripts read *increpuerunt* (“rebuked”) instead of *emendaverunt* (“chastened”). Four others also read *increpaverunt*. Nevertheless, below, in Psalm 15, all manuscripts except one have *emendaverunt*.]

## 3. [verse 3]

And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water—that is, either according to Wisdom itself, which deigned to assume humanity for our salvation, so that this man himself is the tree planted beside streams of water. For this too can be understood from what is said in another psalm: “The river of God is filled with water” (Ps. 64:10).

Or it may be understood according to the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the words, “He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3:11), and, “Let whoever thirsts come and drink” (John 7:37), and, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that asks you for water, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water, so that whoever drinks of it will never thirst; rather, it will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life” (John 4:10, 13–14).

Or “beside streams of water” may be understood according to the streams of the sins of peoples, since in the Apocalypse waters are interpreted as peoples (Rev. 17:15), and “streams” may reasonably be understood as a falling, which pertains to sin.

That tree, therefore—that is, our Lord—drawing them from the flowing waters, that is, from sinful peoples, into the way and toward the roots of his discipline, will bear fruit; that is, he will establish churches, “in his season,” namely, after he was glorified by his resurrection and ascension into heaven. For then, when the Holy Spirit had been sent to the Apostles and they had been strengthened and directed among the peoples in confidence in him, he made the churches fruitful.

[Note: Ten manuscripts read *Ecclesia* (“the Church”) rather than *Ecclesias* (“churches”).]

“And his leaf shall not fall”: that is, his word shall not be void, because “all flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of grass: the grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6–8).

“And everything that he does shall prosper”: that is, whatever that tree produces. All these things are to be understood as fruit and leaves, namely, deeds and words.

## 4. [verse 4]

Not so the wicked, not so; but they are like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.

Here “earth” is to be understood as stability itself in God, in accordance with the words, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance; indeed, my inheritance is exceedingly glorious to me” (Ps. 15:5–6). In accordance with this it is said, “Wait for the Lord and observe his ways, and he will exalt you so that you may possess the earth” (Ps. 36:34); and again, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:4).

The comparison is drawn from this: just as this visible earth nourishes and contains the outer human being, so that invisible earth nourishes and contains the inner human being. From the face of this earth the wind drives away the wicked person—that is, pride, because pride puffs him up.

Avoiding this, the one who was intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and given drink from the torrent of his delight says, “Let not the foot of pride come to me” (Ps. 35:9, 12).

Pride drove from the face of this earth the one who said, “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). From the face of this earth it also drove the one who, after consenting to and tasting the forbidden tree so that he might be like God, hid himself from the face of God (Gen. 3:6, 8).

That this earth pertains to the inner human being, and that pride casts a person from it, can be understood especially from what is written: “Why is earth and ashes proud? For in his life he cast away his innermost parts” (Sir. 10:9–10). Since he was cast out from there, he is not unreasonably said to have cast himself out.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *quae* (“which”) instead of *quia* (“because”).]

## 5. [verse 5]

Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment—that is, because they are cast away like dust from the face of the earth.

And rightly is it said that what the proud desire is taken away from them, namely, that they should judge. This is made clearer in the following statement: “Nor sinners in the council of the righteous.” For Scripture commonly repeats more clearly what it has said above, so that “sinners” are understood as “the wicked,” and what was previously said as “in judgment” is here expressed as “in the council of the righteous.”

Or, if the wicked are one thing and sinners another—so that although every wicked person is a sinner, not every sinner is wicked—then “the wicked shall not rise in judgment” means that they will indeed rise, but not in order to be judged, since they have already been assigned to most certain punishments. But “sinners shall not rise in the council of the righteous” means that they will not rise in order to judge, though perhaps in order to be judged. Of such people it is said:

“Each one’s work will become manifest, for the day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work remains, he will receive a reward; but if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:13–15).

## 6. [verse 6]

For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.

Just as one says that medicine knows health but does not know diseases—and yet diseases too are recognized by the art of medicine—so it can be said that the Lord knows the way of the righteous but does not know the way of the wicked. This is not because the Lord is ignorant of anything, although he says to sinners, “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23).

“The way of the wicked shall perish” is put as though it said, “The Lord does not know the way of the wicked.” But it is stated more plainly, so that being unknown by the Lord means perishing, while being known by the Lord means remaining. To belong to God’s knowledge is to exist; to belong to his ignorance is not to exist, because the Lord says, “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

[Note: The same verse 6 is treated below in the First Commentary on Psalm 36, section 9, and Psalm 141, section 6.]

# Commentary on Psalm II

## 1. [verses 1–2]

Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on empty things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.

“Why” is said as if it meant “in vain.” For they did not accomplish what they wanted, namely, that Christ should be destroyed. This is said concerning the Lord’s persecutors, who are also mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4:26).

## 2. [verse 3]

“Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.”

Although this can also be understood otherwise, it is more appropriately taken as spoken by those whom he said had meditated on empty things. Thus, “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us” means: let us take care that the Christian religion neither bind us nor be imposed upon us.

## 3. [verse 4]

“He who dwells in the heavens will mock them, and the Lord will deride them.”

The statement is repeated. For in place of “He who dwells in the heavens” there follows “the Lord,” and in place of “will mock” there follows “will deride.”

Nevertheless, none of this should be understood carnally, as though God mocked with his cheeks or derided with his nose. Rather, we should understand the power that he gives to his saints, so that, seeing what is to come—that is, the name of Christ and his dominion spreading among later generations and prevailing among all nations—they may understand that those people had meditated on empty things. For this power by which these things were foreknown is God’s mockery and derision.

“He who dwells in the heavens will mock them”: if we understand the heavens as holy souls, then through these souls God, foreknowing what would happen, will mock and deride them.

## 4. [verse 5]

“Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will trouble them.”

He shows more plainly how he will speak to them by saying, “He will trouble them,” so that “in his anger” means “in his wrath.”

The anger and wrath of the Lord God should not be understood as mental disturbance, but as the power by which he most justly takes vengeance, with all creation subject to him for service.

Above all, we must clearly see and hold to what is written in Solomon: “But you, Lord of strength, judge with tranquillity, and with great reverence you dispose of us” (Wis. 12:18).

The anger of God, therefore, is the movement that takes place in the soul which knows God’s law when it sees that same law transgressed by a sinner. Through this movement many things are avenged by righteous souls.

Nevertheless, God’s anger can also rightly be understood as the very darkening of mind that follows upon those who transgress God’s law.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “with all creation subjected.”]

## 5. [verse 6]

“But I have been established as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the Lord’s command.”

These words are clearly spoken in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ.
