If Zion signifies “contemplation” (*speculatio*), as some interpret it, we should understand nothing more readily than the Church, where the mind is daily raised to contemplate the glory of God, as the Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face, contemplating the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18).

The meaning, therefore, is this: “I have been established as king by him over his holy Church,” which he calls a mountain because of its eminence and firmness.

“I have been established as king by him”—that is, I, whose bonds they were meditating to break and whose yoke they were meditating to cast away.

“Proclaiming his command”: who does not recognize this, when it is proclaimed every day?

[Note: Thus, at this first occurrence, the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint, have *ipsius* (“his”).]

[Note: On the same verse 6 and the following verses, see Commentary on Psalm 47, section 5.]

## 6. [verse 7]

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

It may also seem that “that day” was spoken prophetically on which Jesus Christ was born according to his humanity. Yet “today,” because it signifies the present, and because in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to be, nor future, as though it did not yet exist, but only present—since whatever is eternal always is—is understood divinely according to the statement, “Today I have begotten you.”

By this the most sincere and catholic faith proclaims the eternal generation of the Power and Wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son.

[Note: The same verse 7 is treated in Commentary on Psalm 60, section 8.]

## 7. [verse 8]

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

This is now temporal, according to the man whom he assumed, who offered himself as a sacrifice in place of all sacrifices and who also intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34). Thus “Ask of me” refers to the whole temporal dispensation that was made for the human race.

The meaning is that the nations should be joined to the Christian name, and thus redeemed from death and possessed by God.

“I will give you the nations as your inheritance”: that you may possess them for their salvation, and that they may bear spiritual fruit for you.

“And your possession to the ends of the earth.” The same idea is repeated: “the ends of the earth” is put in place of “the nations,” but more plainly, so that we understand all nations. “Your possession” is put in place of “your inheritance.”

[Note: Verse 8 is also treated in Commentary on Psalm 21, section 30.]

## 8. [verses 9–10]

“You shall rule them with an iron rod”: with inflexible justice.

“And like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them”—that is, you shall shatter in them earthly desires, the muddy affairs of the old man, and whatever has been acquired and ingrained from the sinner’s clay.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “from the clay of sin.”]

“And now, kings, understand”: “now” means, once renewed, once the clay coverings have been shattered—that is, the bodily vessels of error belonging to the former life.

“Now understand, kings”: that is, now able to rule whatever in you is servile and bestial; now able to fight, not as one striking the air, but disciplining your bodies and bringing them into servitude (1 Cor. 9:26–27).

“Be instructed, all you who judge the earth.” This is repeated: “be instructed” is put in place of “understand,” while “you who judge the earth” is put in place of “kings.”

For he signifies spiritual people who judge the earth. Whatever we judge is beneath us; and whatever is beneath the spiritual person is rightly called earth, because it has been wounded by earthly corruption.

[Note: The same verse 9 is explained in Commentary on Psalm 44, section 18, and Psalm 58, section 1.]

## 9. [verse 11]

“Serve the Lord in fear.”

This was said lest what had been said—“kings who judge the earth”—turn into pride.

“And rejoice in him with trembling.” “Rejoice” has been very appropriately added, lest what was said—“serve the Lord in fear”—seem to lead only to misery. But again, lest this itself proceed into an outpouring of recklessness, “with trembling” was added, so that it might promote cautious and watchful preservation of holiness.

It may also be understood in this way: “And now, kings, understand”—that is, “Now that I have been established as king, do not be sad, kings of the earth, as though your good had been taken away from you; rather, understand and be instructed.”

For it is advantageous for you to be subject to him from whom understanding and instruction are given to you. It is also advantageous for you not to rule recklessly, but to serve the Lord of all with fear and to rejoice in the most certain and sincere blessedness, being cautious and watchful lest you fall from it through pride.

[Note: On the same verse 11, see Commentary on Psalm 65, section 5.]

[Note: The editions read *vertant* (“they may turn”); thirteen manuscripts read *vertat* (“it may turn”); one reads *vertatur* (“it may be turned”).]

## 10. [verse 12]

“Embrace instruction, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way.”

This is what he means by “understand” and “be instructed,” for to understand and be instructed is to embrace instruction. Yet by saying “embrace,” he sufficiently indicates that instruction is a kind of protection and fortification against all things that could harm those who did not grasp it with such care.

“Lest the Lord become angry” is expressed with uncertainty—not according to the vision of the Prophet, for whom it is certain, but according to those who are being admonished. Those to whom God’s anger is not openly revealed commonly think of it with uncertainty.

They ought therefore to say to themselves: “Let us embrace instruction, lest the Lord become angry and we perish from the righteous way.”

What it means for the Lord to become angry has already been explained above.

[Note: Above, section 4.]

“And you perish from the righteous way”: this is a great punishment, feared by those who have tasted something of the sweetness of righteousness. Whoever perishes from the way of righteousness will wander through the ways of iniquity in great misery.

## 11. [verse 13]

“When his anger has burned briefly, blessed are all who trust in him.”

That is, when the vengeance prepared for the wicked and sinners comes, it will not merely fail to touch those who trust in the Lord; it will also contribute to establishing and exalting the kingdom for them.

For he did not say, “When his anger has burned briefly, all who trust in him are secure,” as though they received from it only the fact that they would not be punished. Rather, he said, “blessed,” where the sum and fullness of all good things are found.

I think that “briefly” signifies that the event will be sudden, while sinners consider it distant and far in the future.

# Commentary on Psalm III

*A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Abessalon, his son.*

[Note: Earlier printed editions have *Absalon*. The better manuscripts consistently have *Abessalon*. The Greek Septuagint has *Abesalôm*.]

## 1. [verse 1]

This psalm should be understood as spoken in the person of Christ, as is persuaded by the words, “I slept, and took sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will receive me.”

For this speaks more fittingly of the Lord’s passion and resurrection than of the historical episode in which David is written to have fled from the face of his son, who was waging war against him (2 Sam. 15:17).

And since it is written concerning Christ’s disciples, “As long as the bridegroom is with them, the sons of the bridegroom do not fast” (Matt. 9:15), it is not surprising if his impious son signifies the impious disciple who betrayed him.

[Note: The editions read *jejunabunt* (“will not fast”); the manuscripts read *jejunant* (“do not fast”).]

His having fled from that disciple’s face may indeed be understood historically, when, after Judas departed, Jesus withdrew with the others to the mountain. Yet spiritually, when the Son of God—that is, the Power and Wisdom of God—abandoned the mind of Judas, after the devil had completely invaded him, in accordance with what is written, “And the devil entered into his heart” (John 13:2), it is rightly understood that Christ fled from his face.

This does not mean that Christ yielded to the devil, but that when Christ departed, the devil took possession.

I think that this departure is called flight in this psalm because of its swiftness, as is also signified by the Lord’s saying, “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13:27).

In ordinary speech we also say, “It escaped me,” when something does not come to mind; and of a very learned person we say, “Nothing escapes him.” Thus truth escaped the mind of Judas when it ceased to enlighten him.

Abessalon, however, as some interpret it, is said in Latin to mean “the peace of the Father” (*Patris pax*). This may seem surprising, whether in the history of the Kingdoms, since Abessalon waged war against his father, or in the history of the New Testament, since Judas was the Lord’s betrayer: how can he be understood as “the peace of the Father”?

But there too, those who read carefully see that, in that war, David was at peace with his son. He even mourned his death with profound grief, saying, “Abessalon my son, who will grant me to die for you?” (2 Sam. 18:33).

And in the history of the New Testament, our Lord’s great and astonishing patience is rightly understood as peace shown to his betrayer: he endured him for so long as though he were good, although he was not ignorant of his thoughts; he admitted him to the meal at which he commended and handed over to his disciples the figure of his body and blood (John 13); and finally, at the very betrayal, he received a kiss from him (Matt. 26:49).

[Note: Four manuscripts—namely, Benignianus, Theodericensis, one later Corbie manuscript, and another Remigius manuscript—read *mysterium* (“mystery”) instead of *figuram* (“figure”).]

Thus Christ rightly showed peace to his betrayer, although Judas was being ravaged by the inward warfare of so criminal a thought.

Therefore Abessalon is called “the peace of the Father,” because the father had peace, although Judas did not.

## 2. [verses 2–3]

“Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous?”

They became so numerous, clearly, that even from the number of the disciples there was one who added himself to the number of the persecutors.

“Many rise up against me. Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.”

It is clear that they would not have killed him unless they despaired of his resurrection. To this belong those cries: “Let him come down from the cross, if he is the Son of God,” and, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42).

Thus Judas too would not have betrayed him unless he had belonged to the number of those who despised Christ, saying, “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

## 3. [verse 4]

“But you, Lord, are my protector.”

This is said according to his humanity to God, because the assumption of humanity is the Word made flesh.

“My glory.” He calls God his glory—even he whom the Word of God assumed in such a way that he might become God together with him.

Let the proud learn, those who do not willingly hear it said to them: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

“And you exalt my head.” Here, I think, the human mind is meant, which is not improperly called the head of the soul. It so clung to and, in a certain way, coalesced with the surpassing eminence of the Word who assumed humanity that it was not brought low by the profound humiliation of the passion.

## 4. [verse 5]

“With my voice I cried to the Lord.”

That is, not with the voice of the body, which is produced with the noise of beaten air, but with the voice of the heart, which is silent to human beings but sounds as a cry to God.

By this voice Susanna was heard (Dan. 13:44), and concerning this voice the Lord himself commands that prayer be offered in closed rooms—that is, in the secrets of the heart, without noise (Matt. 6:6).

No one should easily say that one prays less with this voice if no sound of words is produced by the body. For even when we pray silently in our hearts, if thoughts alien to the feeling of the one praying intrude, it cannot yet be said, “With my voice I cried to the Lord.”

Nor is this rightly said unless the soul alone speaks to the Lord, drawing nothing bodily and nothing belonging to carnal concerns into prayer, where he alone hears. Yet this too is called a cry because of the force of the intention itself.

[Note: Several manuscripts read *orationem* (“prayer,” accusative) instead of *oratione* (“in prayer”).]

“And he heard me from his holy mountain.”

We have the Lord himself called a mountain through the Prophet, as it is written that the stone cut without hands grew into the size of a mountain (Dan. 2:35).

But this cannot be understood as spoken from his own person unless perhaps he wished to say: “He heard me from myself, as from his holy mountain, when he dwelled in me, that is, in the mountain itself.”

It is clearer and more straightforward, however, if we understand that God heard from his own justice. For it was just that he should raise from the dead the innocent man who had been killed and to whom evil had been repaid for good, and that he should repay his persecutors with what they deserved. For we read, “Your justice is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7).

[Note: On the same verse 5, see Commentary on Psalm 44, section 33, and Psalm 47, section 2.]

[Note: Five manuscripts read: “But this is to be understood as referring to his person.”]

## 5. [verse 6]

“I slept, and took sleep.”

It may appropriately be observed that the word “I” is used to signify that he endured death by his own will, in accordance with the words:

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:17–18).

Therefore, he says, you did not seize and kill me as though I were unwilling; rather, “I slept, and took sleep.”

Scripture contains innumerable instances in which sleep is used for death, as the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thess. 4:12).

Nor should we ask why “took sleep” was added after “I slept” had already been said. The Scriptures commonly have repetitions of this kind, as we showed many times in the second psalm.

Some manuscripts, however, read, “I slept and was overcome by sleep,” while others have other readings. These variants may reflect the Greek text: *ἐγὼ δὲ ἐκοιμήθην καὶ ὕπνωσα* (“But I slept and took sleep”).

Unless perhaps the sleep of one dying and the sleep of one dead can be distinguished, so that “sleeping” is the transition into sleep, just as awakening is the transition into wakefulness.

We should not suppose that these repetitions exist in the divine books merely as empty ornaments of speech.

Thus “I slept, and took sleep” is rightly understood as: “I submitted myself to the passion, and death followed.”

“And I arose, because the Lord will receive me.”

Here we must especially observe how, in one sentence, he uses both a verb of past time and one of future time. He says “I arose,” which is past, and “he will receive,” which is future, although he could not rise except through that reception.

But in prophecy future things are appropriately mingled with past things, so that both are signified: according to time, the things prophesied are future; according to the knowledge of the prophets, they are already to be regarded as accomplished.

Words of the present tense are also mingled in, and these will be treated in their proper place when they occur.

[Note: The same verse 6 is treated in Commentary on Psalm 40, section 10; Psalm 56, section 11; Psalm 101, section 8; and Psalm 138, section 2.]

## 6. [verse 7]

“I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me.”

The Gospel records how great a multitude surrounded him as he suffered and was crucified (Matt. 27:39 and following).

“Rise, Lord; save me, my God.” The command “rise” is not said to God as though he were sleeping or lying down. Rather, it is customary in the divine Scriptures to attribute to God’s person what he does in us—not everywhere, but wherever it can appropriately be said.

This is the case, for example, when he himself is said to speak, although the Prophets, Apostles, or any messengers of truth speak by his gift. Hence the statement: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

He does not say, “of the one by whose illumination or command I speak,” but attributes the speech itself directly to the one by whose gift he was speaking.

## 7. [verse 8]

“For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.”

The sentence should not be punctuated as though it read: “Rise, Lord; save me, my God, because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause.” For he does not save him because he struck his enemies; rather, after he had saved him, he struck them.

Therefore the words belong with what follows, so that the meaning is: “Because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause, you have broken the teeth of sinners.” That is, you have broken the teeth of sinners because you have struck all those who oppose me.

The punishment of those who oppose him is that their teeth are broken—that is, the words of sinners who tore apart the Son of God with curses have been rendered ineffective, reduced as it were to dust.

Thus “teeth” can be understood as words of cursing. Concerning such teeth the Apostle says, “But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15).

The teeth of sinners may also be understood as the leaders of sinners, by whose authority a person is cut off from the society of a sect in which people live and is, as it were, incorporated into those who live wickedly.

Opposed to these teeth are the teeth of the Church. By their authority believers are cut away from the error of the Gentiles and from various doctrines and are transferred into the Church, which is the body of Christ.

It was with these teeth that Peter was told to eat the slaughtered animals (Acts 10:13)—that is, by killing in the Gentiles what they had been and transforming them into what he himself was.

Concerning these teeth of the Church it is said: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Song 4:2; 6:5).

These are the people who rightly teach and live according to what they teach. They do what was said: “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Moved by the authority of these people, through whom God speaks and acts, human beings believe; separated from the world to which they had been conformed, they pass into the members of the Church.

Therefore those through whom these things are accomplished are rightly called teeth resembling shorn sheep, because they have laid aside the burdens of earthly cares. Ascending from the washing—from the cleansing of the world’s filth through the sacrament of baptism—they all bear twins.

For they carry out the two commandments concerning which it is said, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40): loving God with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind, and loving one’s neighbor as oneself.

Among such people there is no barrenness, because they yield such fruits to God.

According to this interpretation, therefore, “you have broken the teeth of sinners” means: you have rendered the leaders of sinners ineffective, striking all those who oppose me without cause. For according to the Gospel history, the leaders persecuted him, while the lower ranks honored him.

[Note: Five manuscripts read “cleansed from the filth of the world.”]

## 8. [verse 9]

“Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”

In one sentence he both commanded human beings what they should believe and prayed on behalf of believers.

When it is said, “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” the speech is directed toward human beings. It does not then continue, “And his blessing is upon his people,” so that everything would have been addressed to human beings; rather, the prayer turns toward God himself, on behalf of the people to whom it was said, “Salvation belongs to the Lord.”

What does he say, then, except this? Let no one presume upon himself, since it belongs to the Lord to save from the death of sin. For Scripture says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

But you, Lord, bless your people who hope for salvation from you.

[Note: On this same verse 9, see Commentary on Psalm 70, section 16, and Psalm 145, section 9.]

## 9

This psalm can also be understood as spoken in the person of Christ in another way: namely, as spoken by the whole Christ.

I say “the whole,” together with his body, of which he is the head, according to the Apostle who says, “You are the body of Christ and members individually” (1 Cor. 12:27). Therefore he is the head of this body.

For this reason he says elsewhere: “Speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body is joined and fitted together” (Eph. 4:15–16).

The Church, therefore, speaks together with its head through the Prophet, established amid the storms of persecution throughout the whole world—which we know has already happened:

“Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me,” desiring, if they could, to destroy the Christian name.

“Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.” For they would not otherwise have hoped that they could destroy the Church, which was spreading so widely, unless they believed that it did not belong to God’s care.

“But you, Lord, are my protector”—in Christ, certainly. For in that man the Church too was assumed by the Word, which was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). For he also made us sit together with him in the heavenly places (Eph. 2:6).

Since the head goes before, the other members will follow. For “who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35).

The Church therefore rightly also says, “You are my protector, my glory.” It does not attribute its excellence to itself when it understands by whose grace and mercy it is such.

“And you exalt my head”: namely, the one who, firstborn from the dead, ascended into heaven.

“With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.” This is the prayer of all the saints, a fragrance of sweetness that rises before the Lord.

The Church is now heard from that mountain which is also its head, or from that justice of God by which his chosen are delivered and their persecutors punished.

Let God’s people also say: “I slept, and took sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will receive me,” so that they may be joined and united to their head.

For it was said to this people: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will touch you” (Eph. 5:14).

[Note: In place of *epiphausei* (“he will illuminate”), one manuscript read *ephapsetai* (“he will touch”).]

This people was taken from sinners, concerning whom it was said generally: “Those who sleep, sleep at night” (1 Thess. 5:7).

Let it also say: “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me”—that is, nations encamped around it, seeking, if they could, to extinguish the name of the Christian wherever it existed.

But how could they be feared, when the ardor of love was kindled in Christ as though by the oil of the martyrs’ blood?

“Rise, Lord; save me, my God.” The body can say this to its own head. For when he rose, the body was saved—he who ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings (Ps. 67:19).

The Prophet speaks of this in predestination, by which our Lord was brought down even to the earth—that harvest of which it is said in the Gospel, “The harvest is ripe” (Matt. 9:37)—and whose salvation lies in the resurrection of the one who deigned to die for us.

“For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.” Now that the Church reigns, the enemies of the Christian name have been struck with confusion, and whether their words of cursing or their dominion, they have been rendered ineffective.

Believe, therefore, human beings, that salvation belongs to the Lord. And you, Lord, let your blessing be upon your people.

10. Each one of us, too, can say, when a multitude of vices and desires leads the resisting mind into the law of sin: “Lord, why have those who trouble me become so numerous? Many rise up against me.” And since despair of recovery often steals in through the accumulation of vices—as though the vices themselves were taunting the soul, or even the devil and his angels were working through harmful suggestions to make us despair—it is most truly said: “Many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God.’” But you, Lord, are my protector; for this is the hope: that he deigned to assume human nature [Col. 0078] in Christ [Note: [Col. 0078] The editions read *in Christum* (“into Christ”). But some manuscripts read *in Christo* (“in Christ”).]. “My glory”: according to that rule by which no one should attribute anything to himself. “And the one who exalts my head”: either Christ himself, who is the head of us all, or the spirit of each one of us, which is the head of soul and flesh; for “the husband is the head of the woman, and Christ is the head of the man” (1 Cor. 11:3). The mind, moreover, is exalted when one can already say, “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Rom. 7:25), so that the other parts of the human being, having been pacified, may be subject, when, at the resurrection of the flesh, “death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54). “With my voice I cried to the Lord”: with that innermost and most intense voice. “And he heard me from his holy mountain”: from him through whom he comes to our aid, and through whom, as mediator, he hears us. “I slept, and took my sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will receive me”: which believer cannot say this, recalling the death of his sins and the gift of regeneration? “I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me.” Apart from those things which the Church as a whole has endured and endures, each individual also has temptations by which he is surrounded, so that he may say: “Arise, Lord; save me, my God”—that is, “Make me arise.” “For you have struck all those opposing me without cause”: rightly, in the predestination, this is said of the devil and his angels, who rage not only against the whole body of Christ but also privately against each individual. “You have crushed the teeth of sinners”: everyone has those who curse him; everyone also has the authors of vices striving to cut him off from the body of Christ. “But salvation belongs to the Lord”: pride must be avoided, and we must say, “My soul has clung to you” (Ps. 62:9). “And your blessing is upon your people”—that is, upon each one of us.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 4

**For the end. A psalm. A song of David.**

1. **[Verse 1.]** “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Here “end” signifies perfection, not termination. It may be asked whether every song is a psalm, or rather whether every psalm is a song; whether there are certain songs which cannot be called psalms, and certain psalms which cannot be called songs. But attention must be paid to Scripture, lest perhaps “song” indicate joy, while psalms are so called because they are sung to the psaltery—a practice which history reveals the prophet David to have used in a great mystery (1 Chron. 13:8; 16:5). This is not the place to discuss that matter, since it requires prolonged inquiry and extended debate. For the present, we should either expect the words of the Lord’s human nature after the resurrection, or those of the human being in the Church who believes in and hopes in him.

2. **[Verse 2.]** “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me.” “When I called,” he says, “God heard me, from whom my righteousness comes.” “In tribulation you enlarged me”: from the narrowness of sorrow you led me into the breadth of joys; for “tribulation and distress are upon every soul of a human being who works evil” (Rom. 2:9). But the one who says, “We rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance,” continuing to the point where he says, “because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3, 5), does not suffer the heart’s constriction, although it is inflicted externally by persecutors.

The change of person—from the third person, where he says “he heard,” immediately to the second, where he says “you enlarged me”—if it was not made for the sake of variation and sweetness, makes it remarkable that he first seems to have wished to indicate to people that he had been heard, and afterward to address the one who heard him. Unless perhaps, after indicating how he had been heard in that very enlargement of the heart, he preferred to speak with God, so that in this way too he might show what it means for the heart to be enlarged: namely, for God already to have been infused into the heart, so that one may converse inwardly with him.

This is rightly understood of the person who, believing in Christ, has been illumined. But in the person of the Lord’s human nature, which the Wisdom of God assumed, I do not see how it can fit; for he was never at any time deserted by that Wisdom. Yet just as his prayer itself is rather an indication of our weakness, so also the same Lord can speak on behalf of his faithful concerning this sudden enlargement of the heart, since he took their person upon himself even when he said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. 25:35), and so forth. Therefore here too he can say, “You enlarged me,” speaking with God on behalf of one of his least, who has God’s love poured out in his heart through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.

“Have mercy on me, and hear my prayer.” Why does he ask again, when he has already indicated that he was heard and enlarged? Is it on account of us, concerning whom it is said, “If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with endurance” (Rom. 8:25)? Or is it so that what has been begun may be brought to perfection in the one who has believed?

3. **[Verse 3.]** “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” “At least until the coming,” he says, “your error should have lasted”—the coming of the Son of God. Why, then, are you still heavy of heart? When will your deceptions come to an end, if you do not put an end to them while truth is present? “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” Why do you wish to be blessed by things below? Truth alone makes people blessed, since all things are true through it.

“For vanity is the vanity of those who are vain [Note: [Col. 0079] We read this with the sounder manuscripts. See *Retractations* 1.7.3 concerning this reading. M.], and all is vanity. What abundance does a person have in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1:2–3). Why, then, are you held captive by love of temporal things? Why, as though they were first things, do you pursue last things—which is vanity and falsehood? For you desire the things that pass away to remain with you, although they all pass like a shadow.

4. **[Verse 4.]** “And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.” Whom else but the one whom he raised from the dead and placed at his right hand in heaven? The human race is therefore rebuked, so that at last it may turn from love of this world toward him.

But if anyone is troubled by the added conjunction in the words “And know,” it is easy to observe in Scripture that this type of expression is familiar to the language in which the prophets spoke. Often one finds a passage beginning in this way: “And the Lord said to him”; “And the word of the Lord came to him.” This joining of a conjunction, when no preceding sentence exists to which the following one can be attached, perhaps wonderfully suggests that the utterance of truth in the voice is joined to the vision which occurs in the heart.

Nevertheless, it may be said here that the preceding sentence, “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” is phrased as if it said, “Do not love vanity and seek falsehood.” Once this has been stated, it follows with perfectly correct expression: “And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful.”

But the intervening *diapsalma* prevents this from being joined to what precedes. For whether it is a Hebrew word, as some wish, signifying “Let it be”; or a Greek word signifying an interval in psalm-singing—so that a *psalm* is what is sung, while a *diapsalma* is the silence inserted during the singing; and just as *sympsalma* denotes the joining of voices in singing, so *diapsalma* denotes their separation, in which a certain rest within the interrupted continuation is shown—whether, therefore, it is that, or this, or something else, it is certainly probable that the sense is not rightly continued and joined where a *diapsalma* is inserted.

5. “The Lord will hear me when I cry to him.” I believe we are here admonished to implore God’s help with great concentration of heart—that is, with an inward and incorporeal cry—for just as we should rejoice over illumination in this life, so we should pray for rest after this life. Therefore this should be understood either as spoken by the person of the faithful evangelizer, or by the Lord himself, as though it had been said: “The Lord will hear you when you cry to him.”

6. **[Verse 5.]** “Be angry, and do not sin” [Note: [Col. 0080] See also *Exposition 2 on Psalm 25*, no. 3, concerning the same verse 5.]. The question naturally arose: Who is worthy to be heard, or how does the sinner not cry to the Lord in vain? Therefore he says, “Be angry, and do not sin.” This can be understood in two ways.

Either: “Even if you become angry, do not sin”—that is, even if there arises an impulse of the soul which, because of the punishment of sin, is no longer under one’s control, at least let reason and the mind, which has been inwardly regenerated according to God, not consent to it, so that “with the mind we may serve the law of God,” even if “with the flesh we still serve the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

Or: “Do penance”—that is, be angry with yourselves over past sins, and cease to sin thereafter.

“What you say in your hearts”: “say” is understood, so that the complete sentence is: “What you say, say in your hearts”—that is, do not be the people of whom it was said: “With their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

“In your chambers be pierced with compunction”: this is what was already said, “in your hearts.” For these are the chambers concerning which the Lord also instructs us to pray inwardly, with the doors closed (Matt. 6:6). “Be pierced with compunction” refers either to the pain of repentance, so that the soul, punishing itself, may be pierced lest it be condemned and tormented in God’s judgment; or to awakening, so that we may awaken to see the light of Christ, as though goads had been applied.

Some, however, say that *aperimini* (“be opened”) rather than *compungimini* (“be pierced with compunction”) is the better reading [Col. 0081], since the Greek Psalter has κατανύγητε (*katanýgēte*), which they relate to that enlargement of the heart by which the outpouring of love through the Holy Spirit may be received.

7. **[Verses 6–7.]** “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.” He says the same in another psalm: “The sacrifice for God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19). Therefore it is not absurd to understand the sacrifice of righteousness here as that which is made through repentance. For what is more just than for each person to be angry with his own sins rather than with another’s, and, punishing himself, to offer himself as a victim to God?

Or are the works of righteousness performed after repentance the sacrifice of righteousness? For perhaps the intervening *diapsalma* also suggests, not absurdly, a transition from the old life to the new life: when the old person has been put to death or weakened through repentance, the sacrifice of righteousness is offered to God according to the regeneration of the new person, when the soul itself, already cleansed, offers itself and places itself upon the altar of faith, to be seized by the divine fire—that is, by the Holy Spirit.

Thus the sense is: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord”—that is, live rightly and hope for the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that the truth in which you have believed may illumine you.

8. Yet “Hope in the Lord” is still spoken as a separate clause. What is hoped for, if not good things? But since each person wishes to obtain from God the good which he loves, and since those who love interior goods—that is, those pertaining to the inner person, which alone should be loved, while other things should be used for necessity and not enjoyed as objects of delight—are not easily found, he wonderfully adds after saying “Hope in the Lord”: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’”

This saying and question is the daily utterance and inquiry of all foolish and unrighteous people. Some desire the peace and tranquility of secular life but cannot find them because of the perversity of the human race; though blind, they even dare to accuse the order of things, thinking that the times are worse than those which came before, while they are entangled in the consequences of their own merits. Others doubt or despair concerning the future life promised to us, often saying: “Who knows whether these things are true? Or who came from the dead to announce them?”

Therefore, magnificently and briefly—but to those who see inwardly—he shows which good things should be sought, answering the question of those who say, “Who will show us good things?” “The light of your countenance, O Lord,” he says, “has been marked upon us.” This light is the whole and true good of the human being, which is perceived not by the eyes but by the mind.

He said “marked upon us,” as a coin is marked with the image of a king. For the human being was made “in the image and likeness of God” (Gen. 1:26), which he corrupted by sinning. Therefore his good is true and eternal if, by being born again, he is marked with that image.

I believe this also pertains to what some understand wisely: when the Lord, seeing Caesar’s coin, said, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matt. 22:21), it was as if he said: Just as Caesar demands from you the imprint of his image, so does God; and just as the coin is returned to Caesar, so the soul, illumined and marked by the light of God’s countenance, is returned to God.

“You have given gladness to my heart.” Joy, therefore, should not be sought outside by those who are still heavy of heart, love vanity, and seek falsehood, but inwardly, where the light of God’s countenance has been marked. For, as the Apostle says, “Christ dwells in the inner person” (Eph. 3:17). It belongs to him to see the truth, since he said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). And when he spoke in the Apostle, who said, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3), he was speaking not outside him but in his very heart—that is, in the chamber where one must pray (Matt. 6:6).

9. **[Verses 8–9.]** But people who pursue temporal things—and there are certainly many of them—know how to say nothing other than, “Who will show us good things?” since they cannot see within themselves the true and certain goods. Accordingly, it is rightly said of them in what follows: “From the time of their grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied” [Note: [Col. 0082] For ἀπὸ καρποῦ, “from fruit,” he read ἀπὸ καιροῦ, “from time”; Cassiodorus likewise.].

For it is not without significance that he added “their.” There is also God’s grain, since there is the living bread which came down from heaven (John 6:51). There is also God’s wine, for he says, “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house” (Ps. 35:9). There is also God’s oil, concerning which it is said, “You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. 22:5).

But these many people who say, “Who will show us good things?” and do not see that the kingdom of heaven is within them (Luke 17:21), “from the time of their grain, wine, and oil have been multiplied.” For multiplication does not always signify abundance, and often signifies scarcity: when a soul given over to temporal pleasures is continually inflamed by desire and cannot be satisfied, and, stretched out by manifold and sorrowful thought, is prevented from seeing the simple good. Such is the soul of which it is said: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Such a soul, through the departure and succession of temporal goods—that is, “from the time of its grain, wine, and oil”—has been filled with innumerable fantasies and so multiplied that it cannot do what is commanded: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1). For this multiplicity is vehemently opposed to that simplicity.

Therefore, leaving behind those who are many—multiplied, that is, by desire for temporal things, and saying, “Who will show us good things?” which are to be sought not with outward eyes but inwardly through simplicity of heart—the faithful person rejoices and says: “In peace, in unity, I will fall asleep and take sleep.”

For it is rightly hoped by such people that the mind will be wholly detached from mortal things and forget the miseries of this world. This is suitably and prophetically signified by the words “falling asleep” and “sleep,” where supreme peace cannot be interrupted by any disturbance.

But this is not possessed already in this life; it must be hoped for after this life. The words themselves show this, since they are in the future tense. It is not said, “I fell asleep and took sleep,” or “I fall asleep and take sleep,” but “I will fall asleep and take sleep.” Then “this corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality”; then “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54). This is what is meant by: “If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with endurance” (Rom. 8:25).

10. **[Verse 10.]** Accordingly, he appropriately adds the final statement and says: “For you, Lord, have caused me to dwell in hope alone.” Here he did not say, “You will cause me,” but “You have caused me.” Therefore, wherever this hope already exists, what is hoped for will certainly also exist.

And he rightly says “alone.” For this can be understood in contrast to those many who, multiplied by the time of their grain, wine, and oil, say, “Who will show us good things?” This multiplicity perishes, while singleness is preserved among the holy, concerning whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32).

We must therefore be single and simple—that is, set apart from the multitude and crowd of things being born and dying—and lovers of eternity and unity, if we desire to cling to the one God and our Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 5

1. **[Verse 1.]** The title of the psalm is: “For her who receives the inheritance.” This is understood as the Church, which receives eternal life as an inheritance through our Lord Jesus Christ, so that it may possess God himself and, clinging to him, be blessed, according to the words: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance” (Matt. 5:4). What earth, except that of which it is said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6); and, more explicitly: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:5)?

The Church is also called God’s inheritance, according to the words: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8). Therefore God is called our inheritance because he himself nourishes and contains us; and we are called God’s inheritance because he himself administers and rules us. Accordingly, in this psalm the voice is that of the Church, called to the inheritance, so that she herself may also become the Lord’s inheritance.

2. **[Verse 2.]** “Hear my words, O Lord.” She who has been called invokes the Lord, so that, with his help, she may pass through the wickedness of this world and reach him. “Understand my cry.” He clearly shows what sort of cry this is: an inward one, which reaches God from the chamber of the heart without bodily noise; for bodily speech is heard, while spiritual speech is understood. Yet this too is part of God’s hearing—not with a carnal ear, but through the presence of his majesty.

3. **[Verse 3.]** “Attend to the voice of my supplication”—that is, to that voice which she asks God to understand. What sort of voice it is, he has already indicated when he said, “Understand my cry.”

“Attend to the voice of my supplication, my King and my God.” Although the Son is God, and the Father is God, and the Father and Son together are one God; and if we are asked about the Holy Spirit, nothing else should be answered except that he is God; and when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are mentioned together, nothing else should be understood except one God—nevertheless, Scripture commonly calls the Son “King.”

Accordingly, in keeping with the statement, “Through me there is access to the Father” (John 14:6), it is rightly said first, “My King,” and then, “My God.” Yet he did not say, “Attend,” in the plural, but “Attend,” in the singular. For the Catholic faith proclaims not two or three gods, but the Trinity itself as one God—not so that the same Trinity may at some time be called Father, at another time Son, and at another time Holy Spirit, as Sabellius believed, but so that the Father is only Father, the Son only Son, and the Holy Spirit only Holy Spirit, while this Trinity is only one God.

For when the Apostle said, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36), he is believed to have indicated the Trinity itself; yet he did not add, “To them be glory,” but “To him be glory.”

4. **[Verse 4.]** “For to you I will pray, Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice.” What does this mean? Earlier he said “Hear,” as though he desired to be heard in the present; now he says, “In the morning you will hear,” not “Hear.” He says, “To you I will pray,” not “To you I pray”; and afterward, “In the morning I will stand before you and will see,” not “I stand and see.”

Unless perhaps his earlier prayer indicates the invocation itself [Note: [Col. 0084] The editions read *vocationem* (“calling”). But the Colbertine codex and other manuscripts of better quality read *invocationem* (“invocation”).]. Stumbling amid the storms of this world, he realizes that he does not see what he desires, yet he does not cease to hope, for “hope which is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24).

Yet he understands why he does not see: because the night has not yet ended—that is, the darkness deserved by sins. He therefore says, “For to you I will pray, Lord”—that is, “Because you are so great, to you I will pray; in the morning you will hear my voice.” You are not, he says, one who can be seen by those whose eyes have not yet been freed from the night of sins. Therefore, when the night of my error has ended and the darkness which I made for myself through my sins has departed, you will hear my voice.

Why, then, did he earlier not say “You will hear,” but “Hear”? Is it because, after he cried, “Hear,” and was not heard, he understood what must pass away before he could be heard? Or was he heard earlier, but does not yet understand that he was heard because he does not yet see by whom he was heard? And by what he now says, “In the morning you will hear,” did he wish it to be understood: “In the morning I will understand that I have been heard”?

This is like the expression, “Arise, Lord” (Ps. 3:7)—that is, “Make me arise.” But this is understood of Christ’s resurrection [Note: [Col. 0084] The editions read, “But *if* this is understood of Christ’s resurrection.” The particle *if* is absent from the manuscripts.]. Certainly the statement “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3) cannot rightly be understood in any other way than that through him you may know yourselves, and that it may be made manifest to you how far you have advanced in his love.

5. **[Verses 5–8.]** “In the morning I will stand before you, and will see” [Note: [Col. 0084] The same verse 5 is treated in *Exposition 2 on Psalm 26*, no. 8.]. What is “I will stand,” except “I will not lie down”? And what else is it to lie down except to rest upon the earth—that is, to seek blessedness in earthly pleasures?

“I will stand,” he says, “and will see.” We must not, therefore, cling to earthly things if we wish to see God, who is perceived by the pure in heart.

“For you are not a God who wills iniquity. The wicked shall not dwell near you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood. The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.”

Iniquity, wickedness, falsehood, murder, deceit, and everything of this sort are themselves the night. When it passes, morning comes, so that God may be seen. He therefore explained why he will stand in the morning and see: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity.” If God were one who willed iniquity, he could also be seen by the unjust, so that he would be seen not in the morning—that is, once the night of iniquity had passed—but during the night itself.

6. “The wicked shall not dwell near you”—that is, he shall not see in such a way as to cling to you. Therefore it follows: “Nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes.” Their eyes—that is, their minds—are struck back from the light of truth because of the darkness of their sins, whose habit prevents them from enduring the radiance of right understanding.

Thus even those who sometimes see—that is, who understand the truth—yet remain unjust do not remain there, because they love the things that turn them away from the truth. For they carry their own night with them: not merely the habit of sinning, but also the love of sinning. If this night passes—that is, if they cease to sin and that love and habit are driven away—morning comes, so that they not only understand the truth but also cling to it.

7. “You hate all who work iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0085] The printed editions read, “You hate, Lord.” The word “Lord” is absent from the manuscripts.]. God’s hatred is to be understood according to that expression by which every sinner hates the truth. For it appears that the truth also hates those whom it does not permit to remain in it; but they do not remain because they cannot endure it.

“You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” for falsehood is contrary to truth. But lest anyone think that some substance or nature is opposed to truth, let him understand that falsehood belongs to what is not, not to what is. If what is is spoken, the statement is true; but if what is not is spoken, it is falsehood.

Therefore, he says, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood,” because, departing from what is, they turn aside toward what is not [Note: [Col. 0085] The editions read *declinant* (“they turn aside”). The manuscripts read *declinantur* (“they are turned aside”).].

Many falsehoods appear to be told for someone’s safety or advantage, not from malice but from kindness, such as those of the midwives in Exodus, who reported a falsehood to Pharaoh so that the infants of the children of Israel would not be killed (Exod. 1:19). Yet even these are praised not for the act itself but for their disposition, since those who lie only in this way will eventually deserve to be freed from every falsehood.

For among those who are perfect, not even such falsehoods are found. To them it was said: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no’; whatever is more than this is from evil” (Matt. 5:37). Nor is it without reason that it is written elsewhere: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), lest anyone suppose that the perfect and spiritual person ought to lie for the sake of this temporal life, at whose death the soul—whether his own or another’s—is not killed.

But since it is one thing to lie and another to conceal the truth; one thing to say what is false and another to remain silent about what is true—if someone does not wish to betray a person even to visible death, he ought to be prepared to conceal the truth, not to tell a falsehood, so that he may neither betray nor lie, and thus not kill his own soul for another’s body.

But if he cannot yet do this, let his falsehoods be confined to this necessity alone, so that, if these are the only ones remaining, he may deserve to be freed even from them and receive the strength of the Holy Spirit, by which he may despise whatever must be endured for the sake of truth.

There are altogether two kinds of falsehood in which there is no great fault, though they are nevertheless not without fault: when we are joking, and when we lie in order to do good. The first, in joking, is not most harmful because it does not deceive; the person to whom it is spoken knows that it was said as a joke. The second is milder because it retains some benevolence.

But what does not have a double heart should not even be called a lie. For example, if someone entrusts a sword to another and he promises to return it when the person who entrusted it asks for it, but if that person later demands his sword while enraged, it is obvious that it should not then be returned, lest he kill himself or others, until his sanity is restored.

This does not involve a double heart because the person entrusted with the sword, when he promised to return it to the one who asked, did not imagine that the person might demand it while deranged.

The Lord himself concealed the truth when he said to disciples not yet capable of receiving it: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). The Apostle Paul did likewise when he said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1). It is therefore clear that it is not blameworthy to remain silent about the truth on some occasions. But to speak falsely is nowhere found to have been permitted to the perfect.

8. “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.” This may rightly be understood as a repetition of what he said above: “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood.” Thus “the man of blood” may refer to the one who works iniquity, while “the deceitful man” refers to falsehood. For deceit occurs when one thing is done while another is pretended.

He used an appropriate word when he said “will abhor.” Those who are disinherited are commonly said to be abhorred. But this psalm is for her who receives the inheritance, who introduces the exultation of her hope by saying: “But I, in the abundance of your mercy, will enter your house.”

“In the abundance of your mercy” perhaps refers to the multitude of perfect and blessed people of whom that city will consist, which the Church is now bringing forth in labor and gradually giving birth to. Who would deny that many people, regenerated and perfected, may rightly be called the abundance of God’s mercy, when it has been most truly said: “What is a human being, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. 8:5)

“I will enter your house”: this was said, I believe, as of a stone being placed in a building. For what else is the house of God than the temple of God, concerning which it is said: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17)? The cornerstone of this building is he whom the Power and Wisdom of God, coeternal with the Father, assumed (Eph. 2:20).

9. “I will worship toward your holy temple, in fear of you.” We understand “toward the temple” as near the temple. For he did not say, “I will worship in your holy temple,” but “I will worship toward your holy temple.”

It should also be understood that this refers not to perfection but to progress toward perfection, so that “I will enter your house” signifies perfection. But for this to come about, he first says, “I will worship toward your holy temple”; and perhaps for this reason he added, “in your fear,” which is a great protection for those advancing toward salvation.

When each person has arrived, what is said will be fulfilled in him: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). For those to whom it was said, “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15), no longer fear their friend once they have been led to what was promised [Note: [Col. 0087] The Gatian manuscript reads *amici* (“of a friend”).].

10. **[Verses 9–10.]** “Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies.” Here he clearly declared that he is on a journey—that is, advancing toward perfection, not yet in perfection itself—since he desires to be led.

“In your righteousness,” he says, “not in the righteousness that appears so to human beings.” For returning evil for evil appears to be righteousness, but it is not the righteousness of the one concerning whom it was said: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:45).

Even when God punishes sinners, he does not inflict his own evil upon them; rather, he abandons them to their evils. “Behold,” he says, “he conceived injustice, was pregnant with toil, and gave birth to iniquity. He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made. His toil will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown” (Ps. 7:15–17).

When God therefore punishes, he punishes as a judge those who transgress the law. He does not inflict evil upon them from himself, but expels them into what they have chosen, so that the full measure of their miseries may be completed. But when a human being returns evil for evil, he does so with an evil intention; and therefore he himself is evil first, since he wishes to punish evil.

11. “Direct my way in your sight.” Nothing is clearer than that he is commending himself to the time in which he is making progress. For this is a journey accomplished not through earthly places but through the affections of souls.

“In your sight,” he says, “direct my way”—that is, where no human being sees, since those who praise or blame others are not to be trusted. They cannot in any way judge another person’s conscience, in which the journey toward God is directed.

Therefore he added: “For there is no truth in their mouth.” Their judgments are not to be trusted, and therefore one must flee inward, to the conscience and to the sight of God. “Their heart is vain.” How, then, can truth be in the mouth of those whose heart is deceived concerning sin and the punishment of sin? Hence people are recalled by the words: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3)

12. **[Verse 11.]** “Their throat is an open tomb.” This may refer to voracity, on account of which people often lie through flattery. He wonderfully said “an open tomb,” since that voracity is always gaping, unlike tombs, which are secured once they have received corpses.

It may also be understood in this way: through falsehood and flattering speech they draw into themselves those whom they entice to sins, and they devour them, as it were, when they turn them into their own way of life.

Since those to whom this happens die because of sin [Note: [Col. 0088] Four manuscripts read: “having died after their sin has been completed.”], those by whom they are led astray are rightly called open tombs. For they too are, in a certain sense, lifeless, since they do not possess the life of truth; and they receive into themselves the dead whom they turn into themselves after killing them with lying words and a vain heart.

“With their tongues they acted deceitfully”—that is, with evil tongues. For this seems to be signified when he says “their”: the wicked have wicked tongues; that is, they speak evil when they speak deceit. To them the Lord says: “How can you speak good things, since you are evil?” (Matt. 12:34).

13. Judge them, O God; let them fall from their own thoughts. This is prophecy, not a curse: for he does not wish that it should happen, but sees what will happen. It happens to them not because he appears to have wished it, but because they are such that it rightly happens to them. Thus he also says later, “Let all who hope in you rejoice,” prophetically, because he sees that they will rejoice. So too it was said prophetically, “Stir up your power and come” (Ps. LXXIX, 3), because he saw that he would come.

Yet “let them fall from their own thoughts” can also be understood in this way: perhaps it is more rightly believed to have been wished for their good, when they fall from their evil thoughts—that is, when they no longer think evil. But what follows prevents us from understanding it in this way: “Drive them out.” For when someone is driven out by God, this can in no way be taken in a good sense. Therefore it is understood as spoken prophetically, not malevolently, since what is said is something that must necessarily befall those who persist in the sins mentioned. “Let them fall, then, from their own thoughts” means: let them fall under the accusation of their own thoughts, with their conscience bearing witness against them, as the Apostle says: “And of thoughts accusing or defending, at the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II, 15–16).

14. Drive them out according to the multitude of their ungodliness: that is, drive them far away; for this is what “according to the multitude of their ungodliness” means—that they should be driven out exceedingly far. The ungodly are therefore driven out from that inheritance which is possessed by understanding and seeing God, just as diseased eyes are driven away by the brilliance of light, when what is punishment for them is joy for others. They will not, then, stand in the morning and see.

And this expulsion is as great a punishment as the saying, “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28), is a great reward. The contrary of this punishment is: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Its counterpart is: “Cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXV, 21, 30).

15. For they have made you bitter, O Lord. “I am,” he says, “the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 51); and, “Work for the food that does not perish” (ibid., 27); and, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). But for sinners the bread of truth is bitter; therefore they hate the mouth of the one who speaks truth. They, then, have made God bitter, having by sin descended into such a sickness that they cannot endure the food of truth, in which healthy souls rejoice, as though it were gall.

16. [verse 12] And let all who hope in you rejoice: plainly, those for whom the Lord is sweet when they taste him. They will exult forever, and you will dwell in them: their eternal exultation, then, will be this—that the righteous become God’s temple; and their joy will be he himself, their indweller [Note: Col. 0089: The better manuscripts read *incola* (“indweller”); the printed editions, *incolatus* (“indwelling”)]. And all who love your name will glory in you: as though he were present with them for their enjoyment, the one whom they love.

And rightly does it say, “in you,” as though they possessed the inheritance of which the psalm’s title speaks, while they themselves are also his inheritance; this is signified by the words, “You will dwell in them.” From this good those are barred whom God drives out according to the multitude of their ungodliness.

17. [verse 13] For you will bless the righteous: this is the blessing—to glory in God and to be inhabited by God. This sanctification is granted to the righteous; but in order that they may be justified, a calling precedes it, which is not a matter of merits but of God’s grace: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23). “Those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (ibid. VIII, 30).

Because, then, calling is not the result of our merits but of God’s goodwill and mercy, he adds, saying: “Lord, as with the shield of your goodwill you have crowned us.” For God’s goodwill precedes our good will, so that he may call sinners to repentance. And these are the weapons by which the enemy is conquered, against whom it is said: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” and, “If God is for us, who is against us?” He “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (ibid. VIII, 31, 33). “For if, while we were still enemies, Christ died for us, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (ibid. V, 9–10).

This is the unconquerable shield by which the enemy is repelled when he suggests despair of salvation through the multitude of tribulations and temptations.

18. The entire text of the psalm, then, is a prayer that he may be heard, from what is written, “Hear my words, O Lord,” up to “My king and my God.” Next comes an understanding of those things that hinder the vision of God—that is, so that the soul may recognize that it has been heard—from what is written, “For to you I will pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice,” up to “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.”

Third, the soul hopes that it will become God’s household, and that even now it is drawing near to him in fear, before the consummation that drives out fear, from what is written, “But I, in the abundance of your mercy,” up to “I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear.”

Fourth, as it advances and makes progress amid the very things by which it feels itself obstructed, it prays to be helped inwardly, where no human being sees, lest it be turned aside by evil tongues, from what is written, “O Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies,” up to “They dealt deceitfully with their tongues.”

Fifth, it is prophecy concerning the punishment awaiting the ungodly, when the righteous will scarcely be saved, and concerning the reward that the righteous will obtain—those who came when called and bravely endured everything until they were brought to their destination—from what is written, “Judge them, O God,” to the end of the psalm.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM VI

“To the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth, a psalm of David.”

1. [verse 1] The phrase “concerning the eighth” seems obscure; for the other elements of this title are clearer. Some have thought that it signifies the day of judgment, that is, the time of the coming of our Lord, when he will come to judge the living and the dead. This coming is believed to occur, counting the years from Adam, after seven thousand years, so that seven thousand years may pass like seven days, and then that time may arrive as the eighth day.

But since the Lord said, “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I, 7), and, “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the power nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. XXIV, 36), and since what is written—that the day of the Lord will come “like a thief” (I Thess. V, 2)—shows plainly enough that no one ought to claim knowledge of that time by any calculation of years: if that day is to come after seven thousand years, anyone could learn its coming by counting the years. Where, then, would be the truth that even the Son does not know it?

This was said, of course, because human beings do not learn this through the Son—not because he himself does not know it in himself—according to that way of speaking: “The Lord your God is testing you, so that he may know” (Deut. XIII, 3), that is, so that he may make you know; and, “Arise, O Lord” (Ps. III, 7), that is, make us arise.

Since, then, the Son is said not to know this day, not because he is ignorant of it but because he makes those to whom it is not profitable to know it ignorant of it—that is, he does not disclose it to them—what is this presumption, I do not know, which, by counting the years, confidently expects the day of the Lord after seven thousand years?

2. Let us therefore willingly remain ignorant of what the Lord has willed us to be ignorant, and let us seek what this title, written “Concerning the eighth,” means. Even without any rash calculation of years, the day of judgment can indeed be understood as the eighth day, since, after the end of this age, eternal life having been received, the souls of the righteous will then no longer be subject to times. And since all times revolve through the repetition of these seven days, perhaps that day is called the eighth because it will not possess this alternation.

There is another interpretation that may not absurdly be accepted here: why the judgment is called the eighth, since it will occur after two generations, one pertaining to the body and the other to the soul.

For from Adam until Moses the human race lived according to the body, that is, according to the flesh. This is also called the outer and old man (Eph. IV, 22), and to it the Old Testament was given, so that, although to religious people, it might nevertheless foreshadow future spiritual realities through works that were still carnal. Throughout this entire period, during which life was lived according to the body, death reigned, as the Apostle says, even over those who had not sinned. It reigned, however, according to the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as the same Apostle says; for “until Moses” (Rom. V, 14) is to be understood as extending to the time when the works of the Law—that is, those sacraments observed in a carnal manner—kept even those who were subject to the one God under obligation, for the sake of a certain mystery.

From the coming of the Lord, when there was a transition from circumcision of the flesh to circumcision of the heart, a calling was made so that life might be lived according to the soul, that is, according to the inner man, who is also called the new man (Col. III, 10) because of regeneration and the renewal of spiritual conduct.

It is clear that the number four pertains to the body, because of the four universally known elements of which it consists, and the four qualities—dry, moist, hot, and cold. Accordingly, it is also governed by four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These things are widely known. For the number four as it pertains to the body is treated more subtly elsewhere, but also more obscurely; that must be avoided in this discourse, which we want to make suitable even for the less educated.

The number three, however, can be understood to pertain to the soul, from the fact that we are commanded to love God in three ways: with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37). These matters should be discussed not in the Psalter but in the Gospel. For the present, I think what has been said is sufficient as testimony to the number three as it pertains to the soul.

When, therefore, the numbers pertaining to the body, which relate to the old man and the Old Testament, have been completed, and the numbers pertaining to the soul, which relate to the new man and the New Testament, have also been completed—just as the number seven has passed, since everything is enacted temporally, with four distributed to the body and three to the soul—the eighth day of judgment will come. It will assign to each according to what is deserved, transferring the saints now not to temporal works but to eternal life, while condemning the ungodly to eternity.

3. [verse 2] Fearing this condemnation, the Church prays in this psalm, saying: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” The Apostle also speaks of the anger of judgment: “You are storing up for yourself wrath,” he says, “on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. II, 5). Whoever desires to be healed in this life does not wish to be rebuked in that anger.

“Nor correct me in your fury.” “Correct” seems milder, for it serves toward amendment. But when someone is rebuked—that is, accused—we must fear that the end may be condemnation [Note: Col. 0091: The editions read “that he may have condemnation at the end”; the better manuscripts omit *in*].

Yet since fury seems to be more than anger, it may be asked why what is milder, correction, has been placed with what is harsher, fury. I think, however, that one thing is signified by two words. For in Greek, *thymos* (θυμός), which occurs in the first verse, signifies the same as *orgē* (ὀργή), which occurs in the second verse. But when the Latins too wished to use two words [Note: Col. 0091: The manuscripts read “when they wished to use those two words themselves”], they sought what was close to “anger,” and “fury” was chosen.

For this reason manuscripts vary: in some, “anger” is found first and then “fury”; in others, “fury” first and then “anger”; in still others, *indignatio* or *bilis* is used instead of “fury.” Whatever the word may be, it denotes a movement of the soul provoking the infliction of punishment.

That movement, however, must not be attributed to God as though he were a soul subject to passions, since it is said of him: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity” (Wis. XII, 18); and what is tranquil is not disturbed. Disturbance, therefore, does not befall God the judge. But because what happens in his ministers happens through his laws, it is called his anger.

In this anger the soul that now prays does not wish merely to be rebuked, but not even to be corrected—that is, amended or instructed—for in Greek *paideusēs* (παιδεύσῃς) is written, meaning “you may instruct.” All who do not have the foundation, which is Christ, are rebuked on the day of judgment. Those who build wood, hay, and stubble upon this foundation are corrected—that is, purified. They will suffer loss, but they will be saved, as through fire (I Cor. III, 11).

What, then, does this person pray for, who does not wish to be either rebuked or corrected in the Lord’s anger? What else but to be healed? For where there is health, there is no fear either of death or of the hands of a physician who burns or cuts.

4. [verses 3–4] He continues, therefore, and says: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled”—that is, the support or strength of my soul; for this is what bones signify.

The soul therefore says that its strength is troubled when it names “bones”; for we must not believe that it possesses the bones that we see in the body. Accordingly, the explanation is supplied by what follows: “And my soul is greatly troubled,” lest anyone understand “bones” as referring to the body.

“And you, O Lord, how long?” Who would not understand this as signifying a soul struggling with its illnesses, yet long kept waiting by the physician, so that it might be persuaded what evils it had plunged itself into by sinning [Note: Col. 0092: Five manuscripts read “with treatment long deferred by the physician”]. What is easily healed is not guarded with much care; but because healing is difficult, the protection of the health that has been recovered will be more diligent.

God, then, should not be judged cruel when he is asked, “And you, O Lord, how long?” Rather, he is like a good persuader of the soul, showing it what evil it has brought upon itself. For this soul does not yet pray so perfectly [Note: Col. 0092: Several manuscripts read “is not yet so perfect”] that it can be told: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. LXV, 24).

At the same time, it may also recognize how great a punishment is prepared for the ungodly, who refuse to turn to God, if those who do turn suffer such difficulty, as it is written elsewhere: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (I Pet. IV, 18).

5. [verse 5] “Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul.” In turning herself, she prays that God may turn toward her as well, as it is said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you, says the Lord” (Zech. I, 3).

Or should “Turn, O Lord” be understood according to that manner of speaking as meaning, “Make me turn,” since in her very turning she feels difficulty and labor? Our perfect conversion finds God ready, as the Prophet says: “We shall find him ready like the dawn” (Hos. VI, 3, according to the Septuagint).

For it was not the absence of the one who is present everywhere that caused us to lose him, but our turning away: “He was in the world,” he says, “and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I, 10). If he was in the world and the world did not know him, our uncleanness cannot bear the sight of him.

But when we turn—that is, when by changing our former life we reshape our spirit—we find it hard and laborious to turn back from the darkness of earthly desires toward the serenity and tranquillity of the divine light. In such difficulty we say, “Turn, O Lord,” that is, “Help us, so that the conversion in us may be brought to completion”—the conversion that finds you ready and finds you offering yourself to be enjoyed by those who love you.

And therefore, after saying, “Turn, O Lord,” he adds, “and deliver my soul,” as though it were clinging amid the entanglements of this age and, in the very process of conversion, suffering the thorns of desires that tear it apart.

“Save me,” he says, “because of your mercy.” He understands that his healing is not the result of his own merits, since, for one who sinned and passed over the commandment that had been given, just condemnation was deserved. “Heal me, then,” he says, “not because of my merit, but because of your mercy.”

6. [verse 6] “For in death there is no one who remembers you.” He also understands that the present is the time for conversion, because when this life has passed, nothing remains except the repayment of merits.

“But in hell, who will confess to you?” The rich man confessed in hell—the one of whom the Lord says that he saw Lazarus at rest while he himself suffered in torments. He confessed to such an extent that he even wanted his own people to be warned to restrain themselves from sins, because of the punishments believed to exist in the underworld (Luke XVI, 23–31).

Although he confessed in vain, he nevertheless confessed that those torments had justly befallen him, since he wished even his own people to be instructed so that they would not fall into them.

What, then, does “But in hell, who will confess to you?” mean? Does “hell” perhaps refer to the place into which the ungodly will be hurled after judgment, where, because of the deeper darkness, they will no longer see any light of God to whom they might confess?
