For this rich man, although separated by an immense abyss, could still see Lazarus at rest with his eyes raised; and, by comparison with Lazarus, he was compelled to confess his own merits.

It can also be understood in another way, so that “death” is called sin, which is committed in contempt of the divine law; thus we may call the sting of death “death,” because it produces death. For “the sting of death is sin” (I Cor. XV, 56).

In this death, to be forgetful of God means to despise his law and commandments. “Hell,” then, may mean the blindness of the soul, which receives and envelops the sinner—that is, the dying person: “Since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge,” he says, “God gave them over to a depraved mind” (Rom. I, 28).

The soul prays to be kept safe from this death and from this hell while it strives toward conversion to God and experiences its difficulties.

7. [verse 7] Therefore he continues, saying: “I have labored in my groaning.” And as though this had produced little effect, he adds: “Every night I will wash my bed.”

The bed is called here the place where a sick and weak soul rests—that is, in bodily pleasure and every worldly delight. He washes this delight with tears when he tries to withdraw himself from it.

He already sees that he must condemn carnal desires; yet weakness remains held by delight [Note: Col. 0094: Lovaniensis reads “the weakness”; Erasmus and most manuscripts read “weakness”], and willingly lies in it. The soul cannot rise from there unless it has been healed.

When he says “every night,” he may perhaps have wished this to be understood: the person who, being ready in spirit, perceives some light of truth, yet occasionally rests in the delight of this age because of the weakness of the flesh, is compelled to suffer as though through the alternating movement of day and night.

When he says, “With my mind I serve the law of God,” he feels something like day; but when he says again, “With my flesh I serve the law of sin” (Rom. VII, 25), he is bent toward night, until the whole night passes and that one day comes of which it is said: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see” (Ps. V, 5).

Then he will stand; but now he lies down, when he is in the bed that he will wash every night, so that by such abundant tears he may obtain the most effective medicine from God’s mercy.

“I will water my couch with tears” is a repetition. When he says “with tears,” he shows how he meant “I will wash” above. Here we understand “couch” as what he previously called “bed.” Yet “I will water” says somewhat more than “I will wash,” because something can be washed on the surface, whereas watering penetrates inward [Note: Col. 0094: The editions read “flows through”; some manuscripts, “penetrates”; others, “extends”]; this signifies weeping reaching into the inmost recesses of the heart.

The variation of tenses—past when he said, “I have labored in my groaning,” and future when he said, “I will wash my bed every night,” and again future, “I will water my couch with tears”—shows what someone should say after laboring in groaning without effect, as though he were saying: “It did not help when I did this; therefore I will do that.”

8. [verses 8–9] “My eye is troubled because of anger” [Note: On the first part of verse 8, see Exposition of Psalm XXXVI, 9. On the second part of the same verse, see Exposition of Psalm CII, 9.]: whether his own anger or God’s, in which he asks not to be rebuked or corrected?

But if that anger signifies the day of judgment, how can it be understood as present now? Or is its beginning represented by the fact that people here suffer pains and torments, especially the loss of understanding truth, as I have already recalled in the words: “God gave them over to a depraved mind” (Rom. I, 28)?

For this is the blindness of the mind. Whoever is given over to it is shut out from the inner light of God, though not yet completely, since he is still in this life. There is an outer darkness (Matt. XXV, 30), which is understood to belong more properly to the day of judgment, so that whoever refused correction while there was still time may be completely outside God [Note: Col. 0094: Some sound manuscripts read, “But to be completely outside God”; others, with the editions, “For to be completely outside God”].

For what is it to be completely outside God except to be in the utmost blindness? Indeed, God dwells in inaccessible light (I Tim. VI, 16), into which those enter to whom it is said: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 21, 23).

The beginning, then, of this anger is what every sinner suffers in this life. Fearing the day of judgment, he labors and mourns lest he be brought to that state whose beginning he now experiences as so destructive. Therefore he did not say, “My eye has been extinguished,” but, “My eye is troubled because of anger.”

But if he says that his eye has been troubled because of his own anger, this too is not surprising. Perhaps this is why it was said: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 26), because the mind that, through its own disturbance, is prevented from seeing it imagines that the inner sun—that is, the wisdom of God—has undergone a setting within it.

9. “I have grown old among all my enemies.” He had spoken only of anger, if indeed he had spoken of his own anger; but when he considers the remaining vices, he finds himself surrounded by them all.

Since these vices belong to the former life and to the old man, from whom we must strip ourselves in order to put on the new man (Col. III, 9–10), he rightly says, “I have grown old.”

“With all my enemies” may refer either to the vices themselves or to people who refuse to turn to God. For even if they do not know it [Note: Col. 0095: The editions read “are not known”], even if they spare us, even if they use the same banquets, houses, and cities without any dispute intervening, and converse frequently as though in harmony, nevertheless, because their purpose is contrary, they are enemies of those who turn to God.

When some love and desire this world, while others wish to be freed from this world, who does not see that the former are enemies of the latter? For if they can, they drag them with themselves into punishment.

And it is a great gift to move daily among their words and not depart from the path of God’s commandments. Often the mind, striving to proceed toward God, is shaken and trembles on that very path; and frequently it fails to fulfill its good purpose lest it offend those with whom it lives, who love and pursue other good things that are destined to perish and pass away.

Every healthy person is separated from these people—not in place but in mind. Bodies are contained by places, but for the mind its place is its own disposition.

10. Therefore, after labor, groaning, and the most frequent showers of tears—because what is so fervently requested cannot be in vain when it is requested from the one who is the source of all mercies, and because it is most truly said, “The Lord is near to those who are broken in heart” (Ps. XXXIII, 19)—after such great difficulties, the devout soul indicates that it has been heard. The Church may also be understood here. See what it adds:

“Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.”

This may have been said prophetically, because they will depart—that is, the ungodly will be separated from the righteous—when the day of judgment comes. Or it may refer to the present, because even if they are held together and meet in the same assemblies, the grains have already been separated from the chaff on the threshing floor, though they remain hidden among the chaff. They may therefore be together, but they cannot be carried away together by the wind.

11. [verse 10] “For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has accepted my prayer.”

The frequent repetition of the same thought shows not the necessity of someone narrating, but the feeling of one rejoicing. Those who rejoice commonly speak in this way, so that it is not enough for them to state only once what gives them joy.

This is the fruit of that groaning in which one labors, and of those tears with which the bed is washed and the couch watered; for “those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5), and “blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. V, 5).

12. [verse 11] “Let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled.” Above he said, “Depart from me, all of you,” which, as has been explained, can also happen in this life. But when he says, “Let them be ashamed and troubled,” I do not see how this can occur except on that day when the rewards of the righteous and the punishments of sinners will be manifest.

For now the ungodly are so far from being ashamed that they do not cease to insult us. Often their mockery is so powerful that they make weak people ashamed of the name of Christ; hence it was said: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, of him I will be ashamed before my Father” (Luke IX, 26).

Moreover, whoever wishes to fulfill those lofty commandments—to scatter and give to the poor, so that his righteousness may remain forever (Ps. CXI, 9)—and, after selling all his earthly possessions and distributing them to the needy, wishes to follow Christ, saying, “We brought nothing into this world, and plainly we can take nothing out of it; but having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI, 7–8), encounters the sacrilegious mockery of these people. Those who do not wish to be healed call him insane.

Often, lest he be called this by desperate people, he hesitates to do and delays doing what the most faithful and powerful physician has commanded. They cannot, then, be ashamed now—people in relation to whom it must be desired that we not be ashamed, lest we be recalled, hindered, or delayed from the journey we have undertaken.

But the time will come when they will be ashamed, saying, as it is written:

“These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. How have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us. We were filled with the way of iniquity and destruction, and we traveled through difficult wastelands, but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us? All those things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. V, 3–9).

13. When he says, “Let them turn and be confounded,” who would not judge it a most just punishment that those who refused to turn to salvation should have turning as their confusion?

Then he adds, “very swiftly.” For when they have begun to despair of the day of judgment, when they say, “Peace,” sudden destruction will come upon them (I Thess. V, 3). Whenever it comes, what is despaired of as coming arrives very swiftly. The length of this life is made to seem long only by the hope of continuing to live; for nothing seems swifter than whatever part of it has already passed.

When the day of judgment comes, sinners will then realize how short all passing life is. They will not be able to think that what came was late, since it will come not to those desiring it but rather to those who did not believe it.

Yet this may also be understood in another way: since God heard the one who was groaning and weeping so often and for so long, she may be understood to have been freed from sins and to have subdued all the perverse movements of carnal affection, as she says: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Col. 0097). When this has happened to her, it is not surprising if she is already so perfect that she prays for her enemies.

What he said, then, “Let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled,” may refer to this: that they should repent of their sins, which cannot happen without shame and disturbance [Note: Col. 0097: Lovaniensis reads “confession”; Erasmus and almost all our manuscripts read “confusion”].

Nothing therefore prevents us from understanding what follows in the same way: “Let them turn and be ashamed”—that is, let them turn to God and be ashamed that they once gloried in the former darkness of their sins, as the Apostle says: “What glory did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21).

As for the addition, “very swiftly,” it must be referred either to the feeling of one who is praying for this or to the power of Christ, who converted the nations that had persecuted the Church on behalf of their idols to faith in the Gospel with such rapidity.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM VII

“A psalm for David himself, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.”

1. [verse 1] It is easy to learn in the Second Book of Kings (II Kings XVI) the historical event from which this prophecy took its occasion. There Chusi, King David’s friend, went over to the side of Absalom, his son, who was waging war against his father, in order to discover his plans and report what he was plotting against his father under the direction of Achitophel. Achitophel had defected from friendship with David and was equipping his son against his father with whatever counsels he could.

But since it is not the history itself that must be considered in this psalm—the history from which the Prophet took the veil of mysteries—once we have passed over to Christ, “let the veil be removed” (II Cor. III, 16). First, then, let us ask what the meanings of the names themselves signify.

There were interpreters who, investigating these matters not carnally and literally but spiritually, declared that Chusi is interpreted “Silence,” Jemini “Right Hand,” and Achitophel “Brother’s Ruin.”

Through these interpretations Judas the traitor again comes before us, so that Absalom may bear his image, according to the interpretation of his name as “Father’s peace.” For the father remained peaceful toward him, although he himself had war in his heart through his treacheries, as was treated in the third psalm [Note: Col. 0097: Exposition of Psalm III, §1].

Just as the disciples are found in the Gospel to have been called children of our Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. IX, 14), so they are also found in the same Gospel to have been called brothers. For after rising, the Lord says, “Go and tell my brothers” (John XX, 17), and the Apostle calls him “the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII, 29). Therefore, the ruin of his disciple who betrayed him is rightly understood as “Brother’s Ruin,” which we said is the interpretation of Achitophel.

Chusi, however, which is interpreted “Silence,” is rightly understood as indicating that our Lord fought against those treacheries by silence—that is, by the most profound secret through which the blindness that affected part of Israel came about while they were persecuting the Lord, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter and thus all Israel might be saved.

When the Apostle had entered into this profound and lofty secret, he cried out as though struck by awe at its very height: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. XI, 33–34). Thus, rather than opening that great silence by explanation, he commends it through wonder.

By this silence the Lord concealed the sacrament of his venerable passion, and he turned the voluntary ruin of his brother—that is, the unspeakable crime of his betrayer—into the order of his mercy and providence. What the betrayer was doing with a perverse mind toward the destruction of one man, the Lord, by provident governance, directed toward the salvation of all human beings.

The perfect soul, therefore, which is now worthy to know God’s secret sings the psalm to the Lord; it sings concerning the words of Chusi because it has deserved to know the words of that silence.

Among unbelievers and persecutors, that silence and secret remain; but among his own people, to whom it was said, “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing; but I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15), there is not silence but the words of silence—that is, the reason for that silence, explained and made manifest.

This silence, Chusi, is said to be the son of Jemini, that is, of the right hand. For what was accomplished on behalf of the saints was not to be hidden from them. And yet it is said: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3).

The perfect soul therefore sings prophetically, having learned that secret, concerning the words of Chusi—that is, concerning knowledge of the same secret. God, being at the right hand—that is, favourable and gracious—brought about this secret; therefore this silence is called the Son of the Right Hand, that is, Chusi, son of Jemini.

2. [verses 2–3] “O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who persecute me, and deliver me.” As one for whom, now perfected [Note: Col. 0098: Three manuscripts read “the persecutor”], nothing remains but the envious devil, every battle and adversity of the vices having been overcome, he says: “Save me from all who persecute me, and deliver me, lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.”

The Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V, 8).

Thus, when he had said in the plural, “Save me from all who persecute me,” he afterward introduced the singular, saying, “lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion.” For he does not say “lest they seize,” knowing who remains as the enemy and how fiercely he opposes the perfect soul.

“While there is no one who redeems, nor anyone who saves”: that is, lest he seize it while you neither redeem nor save. For if God does not redeem and save, he seizes.

### 3. [verse 4, 5]

And so that it may already be clear that this is spoken by a perfect soul, one that need fear only the devil’s most treacherous snares, see what follows: “O Lord my God, if I have done this.” What does he mean by “this”? Is the universal sin to be understood because he does not name the sin? If that interpretation is unsatisfactory, let us take it as referring to what follows—as though we had asked, “What is this that you say?” He replies: “If there is iniquity in my hands.” It is therefore now clear that the statement concerns every sin: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” No one can truthfully say this except one who is perfect.

For the Lord says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V, 48, 45). Therefore, whoever does not repay those who repay him with evil is perfect.

Since, then, the perfect soul prays “for the words of Chusi, son of Jemini”—that is, for knowledge of that secret and silence which the Lord, gracious and merciful toward us, brought about for our salvation, so that he might tolerate and endure with the greatest patience the deceit of his betrayer—as though he were explaining the reason for that secret to this perfect soul and saying:

“I endured my betrayer for your sake, an ungodly and sinful man, in great silence and with great patience, so that your iniquities might be washed away by the shedding of my blood. Will you not imitate me, so that you too may not repay evil for evil?”

Thus, observing and understanding what the Lord did for him, and advancing toward perfection by the Lord’s example, he says: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil”—that is, if I have not done what you taught by doing it yourself—“then let me fall empty-handed before my enemies.”

And rightly he does not say, “If I have repaid those who have given me evil,” but “those who have repaid me”; for one who repays has already received something. It requires greater patience not to repay evil even to someone who, having received benefits, returns evil for good than if someone had wished to inflict harm without having first received any benefit.

“If, then,” he says, “I have repaid those who repaid me with evil”—that is, if I have not imitated you in that silence, namely, in the patience that you exercised for my sake—“then let me fall empty-handed before my enemies.” For one boasts vainly who, though he himself is also human, desires to avenge himself upon a human being; and while he openly seeks to overcome a human opponent, he is secretly overcome by the devil, becoming empty through the vain and proud joy that he has, as it were, not been defeated.

He therefore understands where the greater victory lies and where the Father gives recompense, who sees in secret. Thus, instead of repaying those who repay evil, he conquers anger rather than the person, instructed also by those words in which it is written: “He who conquers anger is better than he who captures a city” (Prov. XVI, 32, according to the Septuagint).

“If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty-handed before my enemies.” He seems to swear by an imprecation, which is the most serious kind of oath, when a person says: “If I have done that, let me suffer that.” But an oath in the mouth of one who swears is one thing, and its meaning in the mouth of a prophet is another. Here he declares what truly happens to people who repay evil to those who have repaid them with evil; he is not invoking an oath-like curse upon himself or anyone else.

### 4. [verse 6]

“Let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it.” By again naming the enemy in the singular, he makes still clearer the one whom above he called, as it were, a lion. For that enemy pursues the soul; and if he deceives it, he will seize it.

Human beings rage only as far as the killing of the body; after that visible death they cannot retain power over the soul. But the devil will possess those souls whom he has pursued and seized.

“And let him trample my life into the earth” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “on the earth”; the other manuscripts and printed editions, “into the earth,” following the Septuagint, *eis gēn*]: that is, by trampling it, let him make my life earth, namely, his food. For he has been called not only a lion but also a serpent, to whom it was said, “You shall eat earth”; and to sinful man it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. III, 14, 19).

“And let him bring my glory down into the dust.” This is the dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth: the vain and foolish boasting of the proud, inflated rather than solidified [Note: The printed editions read “solid,” while nine manuscripts read “solidified.”], like a globe of dust lifted by the wind. Rightly, therefore, he has placed here “glory,” which he does not wish to be brought into the dust.

He wishes to possess it as something solid in his conscience before God, where there is no boasting: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31). This solidity is brought into the dust if someone, through pride and contempt for the secrets of conscience—where God alone proves a person—wishes to glory before human beings. Hence he says elsewhere: “God will crush the bones of those who please human beings” (Ps. LII, 6).

But whoever has learned well, or experienced, the stages by which vices are overcome understands that this vice of empty glory must be guarded against by the perfect either alone or above all others. For the vice by which the soul first fell is the last one it conquers. “The beginning of every sin is pride”; and “the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Ecclus. X, 15, 14).

### 5. [verse 7]

“Arise, O Lord, in your anger.” Why does this person whom we call perfect still provoke God to anger? Must we not rather consider whether the perfect one is the man who, while being stoned, said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts VII, 59)?

Or is this man also praying not against human beings but against the devil and his angels, whose possession sinful and ungodly human beings are? Whoever prays that this possession may be taken away from him by the Lord who justifies the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5) is not praying in rage but in mercy toward him. For when the ungodly person is justified, he becomes just from being ungodly and passes from being the devil’s possession into the temple of God.

And since it is a punishment for someone to have the possession taken away in which he desires to rule, he calls this punishment God’s anger against the devil: that the devil should cease to possess those whom he possesses.

“Arise, O Lord, in your anger.” By “arise,” he has said, “appear,” using human and hidden language, as though God were sleeping when he lies unknown in his secrets.

“Be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies.” By “boundaries” he means the possession itself, where he wishes God to be exalted—that is, honored and glorified—rather than the devil, while the ungodly are justified and praise God.

“And arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that you commanded.” That is: because you commanded humility, appear humble. And first fulfill what you commanded, so that, by your example, those who conquer pride may not be possessed by the devil, who persuaded pride against your commandments, saying: “Eat, and your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. III, 5).

### 6. [verse 8]

“And the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” There is a twofold interpretation. “The assembly of the peoples” may mean either believers or persecutors, and both came about through the same humility of our Lord.

The multitude of persecutors, despising that humility, surrounded him. Of them it was said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?” (Ps. II, 1). But the multitude of believers, through his humility, surrounded him in such a way that it could most truly be said: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Rom. XI, 25); and: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8).

“And for its sake return on high.” That is: for the sake of this assembly, return on high. This is understood to have occurred when he rose again and ascended into heaven. For when he was glorified in this way, he gave the Holy Spirit, who could not be given before his glorification, as it is written in the Gospel: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39).

Having therefore returned on high for the sake of the assembly of the peoples, he sent the Holy Spirit. Filled with him, the preachers of the Gospel filled the whole world with churches.

### 7

This meaning may also be understood as follows: “Arise, O Lord, in your anger” [Note: Several of the principal manuscripts omit the conjunction *et* (“and”) after *tua* (“your”), and it is absent from the Septuagint: “in your anger, and be exalted.”], “be exalted at the boundaries of my enemies.” That is: arise in your anger, and let my enemies not understand you. In this sense, “be exalted” means “make yourself so high that you are not understood,” which refers to that silence.

For this is how another psalm speaks of such exaltation: “And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew. And he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 11, 12). Through this exaltation—that is, concealment—when those who crucified you failed to understand you on account of their sins, the assembly of believers will surround you.

For he was exalted precisely through that humility: that is, he was not understood. Thus the words “And arise, O Lord my God, in the commandment that you commanded” may refer to this: when you appear humble, be exalted, so that my enemies may not understand you. Sinners are rightly called enemies, and the ungodly enemies of the devout.

“And the assembly of the peoples will surround you.” That is: precisely because those who crucify you do not understand you, the Gentiles will believe in you, and thus the assembly of the peoples will surround you.

But if what follows truly signifies this, it contains more sorrow because it begins to be felt than joy because it is understood. For it continues: “And for its sake return on high.” That is: for the sake of this assembly of the human race, with which the churches are filled, return on high—that is, once again cease to be understood.

What does “for its sake” mean, except that this assembly too will offend you, so that you most truly foretell, saying: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8)? He likewise speaks of the false prophets, who are understood to be heretics: “Because of their iniquity the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12).

When, therefore, even in the churches—that is, in that assembly of peoples and nations where the Christian name has spread most widely—there will be such an abundance of sins, already perceived in large part, is not what is foretold here the famine of the word announced also by another prophet (Amos VIII, 11)?

And because of this assembly, which alienates itself from the light of truth through its sins, does God not return on high, so that sincere faith, either not at all or only among the very few of whom it is said, “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end; this one will be saved” (Matt. X, 22), may be held and received, purified from every stain of corrupt opinions? It is therefore not without reason that it is said: “And for the sake of this assembly return on high.” That is: withdraw again into the heights of your secrets, even because of this assembly of peoples, which bears your name but does not do your works.

### 8

Whether the preceding interpretation or this one is more suitable to the passage, without prejudice to any other better or equally good interpretation, what follows is most appropriate: “The Lord judges the peoples.”

For if he returned on high when, after his resurrection, he ascended into heaven, “The Lord judges the peoples” follows well, since from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. Or if he returns on high when he abandons Christian sinners with respect to their understanding of the truth—for it was said of his coming, “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8)—then also “the Lord judges the peoples.”

Who is the Lord except Jesus Christ? For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John V, 22).

Therefore, observe how this soul, which prays perfectly, does not fear the day of judgment and, with truly secure desire, says in prayer: “Your kingdom come” (Matt. VI, 10). “Judge me,” it says, “O Lord, according to my righteousness.”

In the preceding psalm the weak person pleaded, asking rather for God’s mercy than recalling any merit of his own, because the Son of God came to call sinners to repentance (Luke V, 32). Thus he had said there: “Save me, O Lord, according to your mercy”—that is, not according to my merit.

But now, because the one who was called has held fast and kept the commandments he received, he dares to say: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my innocence that is upon me.”

This is true innocence, which harms not even an enemy. Thus he rightly asks to be judged according to his innocence, since he could truly say: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. VII, 5).

What he added, “that is upon me,” may be understood not only with innocence but also with righteousness, so that the meaning is: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence, which righteousness and innocence are upon me.”

By this addition he shows that the soul’s being just and innocent is not something it possesses from itself, but through God who enlightens and illumines it. Of this he says in another psalm: “You will illumine my lamp, O Lord” (Ps. XVII, 29). And of John it is said that he was not the light but bore witness to the light (John I, 8). “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V, 35).

The light, therefore, from which souls are kindled like lamps shines not with an alien but with its own splendor, and that light is truth itself. Thus the words “according to my righteousness and according to my innocence that is upon me” are spoken as though a burning and shining lamp were saying:

“Judge me according to the flame that is upon me”—that is, not according to what I am [Note: Five manuscripts read, “not according to what I am,” rather than “not by which I am.”], but according to the flame with which I shine, having been kindled by you.

### 9. [verse 10]

“Let the wickedness of sinners be completed.” “Let it be completed,” he says, “let it be brought to perfection,” according to what is written in the Apocalypse: “Let the just person become still more just, and let the filthy person become still filthier” (Apoc. XXII, 11).

The wickedness of the people who crucified the Son of God appears to have been completed; but greater is the wickedness of those who refuse to live rightly and hate the commandments of truth for which the Son of God was crucified.

“Let the wickedness of sinners therefore be completed,” he says—that is, let them reach the summit of wickedness, so that the just judgment may now come.

But since it was said not only, “Let the filthy person become still filthier,” but also, “Let the just person become still more just,” he adds: “And you will direct the just, O God, who searches hearts and kidneys.”

How, then, can the just person be directed except in secret, when even through those things [Note: Lovaniensis reads “when even those things”; the Maurists and Erasmus, “when even that Church,” etc. A little later they read “seemed wondrous to human beings.” Perhaps one should read “even in that Church”; but we preferred to follow the Colbert manuscript, which, in a second but ancient hand, reads “through those things.”] which at the beginning of Christian times, while the saints were still oppressed by the persecution of worldly people, seemed wondrous to human beings, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—has grown after the Christian name began to stand at such a height? This is the hypocrisy of those who, under the Christian name, prefer to please human beings rather than God.

How, then, is the just person directed amid such confusion of pretense, unless God, who searches hearts and kidneys, sees the thoughts of all—signified by the name “heart”—and their pleasures—understood by the name “kidneys”?

The pleasure of temporal and earthly things is rightly attributed to the kidneys, because this too is the lower part of the human being, and because that is the region where the pleasure of carnal generation dwells, through which human nature is transmitted into this wretched life of deceptive joy by the succession of offspring.

Thus God, searching our heart and seeing that our treasure is where our heart is (Matt. VI, 21)—that is, in heaven—and searching the kidneys and seeing that we do not submit to flesh and blood (Gal. I, 16), but take delight in the Lord, directs the just person in that very conscience before him, where no human being sees, but only he who perceives what each person thinks and what gives each person pleasure.

For the end of concern is pleasure, since everyone strives through cares and thoughts to arrive at what gives pleasure. He therefore sees our concerns who searches the heart; and he sees the ends of our concerns—that is, our pleasures—who searches the kidneys.

When he finds that our concerns are not inclined toward the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the ambition of the world—all of which pass away like a shadow (I John II, 16, 17)—but are lifted toward the joys of eternal things, which are violated by no change, then he directs the just person: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys.”

Our works, which we carry out in deeds and words, may be known to human beings; but with what intention they are done, and toward what end we desire to arrive through them, is known only by him who searches hearts and kidneys.

### 10. [verse 11]

“My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

There are two functions of medicine: one by which infirmity is healed, and another by which health is preserved.

With respect to the first, it was said in the preceding psalm: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak.” With respect to the second, it is said in this psalm: “If there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty-handed before my enemies.” There the weak person prays to be freed; here the one who is already healthy prays not to be corrupted.

With respect to the first, it is said: “Save me according to your mercy.” With respect to the second, it is said here: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness.” There he asks for a remedy so that he may escape sickness; here he asks for protection so that he may not fall back into sickness.

With respect to the first, it is said: “Save me, O Lord, according to your mercy.” With respect to the second, it is said: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

Both save; but the former transfers a person from sickness to salvation, while the latter preserves him in salvation itself.

Thus there the help is merciful, because the sinner who still desires to be justified has no merit, believing in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. IV, 5). Here, however, the help is just, because it is granted to one who is already just.

Let the sinner who said, “I am weak,” say there: “Save me, O Lord, according to your mercy.” And let the just person who said, “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil,” say here: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

If he provides the medicine by which we weak people may be healed, how much more will he provide the medicine by which we who are healthy may be preserved? For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, how much more, now that we have been justified, shall we be saved from wrath through him? (Rom. V, 8, 9).

### 11

“My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.”

“God directs the just person, searching hearts and kidneys”; but by just help he saves the upright in heart.

He does not save the upright in heart and kidneys in the same way that he searches hearts and kidneys. For thoughts may be evil in a perverse heart and good in an upright heart. But pleasures that are not good belong to the kidneys because they are lower and earthly; good pleasures belong not to the kidneys but to the heart itself.

For this reason people cannot be called upright in their kidneys in the same way as they are called upright in heart, since wherever thought is, there too is pleasure. This can occur only when divine and eternal things are the objects of thought.

“You have given gladness in my heart,” he says, after having said: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV, 7).

For the images of temporal things that the mind invents when it is carried away by vain and mortal hope may often bring a delirious and insane joy through empty imaginings; yet this pleasure must be attributed not to the heart but to the kidneys, because all those imaginings have been drawn from lower things—that is, from earthly and carnal matters.

Thus God, searching hearts and kidneys and seeing upright thoughts in the heart but no pleasures in the kidneys, grants just help to the upright in heart, where heavenly pleasures are joined to pure thoughts.

Therefore, when another psalm had said, “Even through the night my kidneys have reproved me,” it added, speaking of help: “I set the Lord always before my eyes, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken” (Ps. XV, 7, 8).

Here he shows that he suffered only suggestions from the kidneys, not pleasures. If he had suffered pleasures from them, he would certainly have been shaken.

He said, “The Lord is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken”; then he adds: “Therefore my heart rejoiced” (ibid., 9). Thus the kidneys were able to reprove him but not to delight him.

The pleasure therefore occurred not in the kidneys but there where, against the reproach of the kidneys, he had taken care that God should be at his right hand—that is, in his heart.

### 12. [verse 12]

“God is a just judge, strong and patient.”

Who is God the judge except the Lord who judges the peoples? He is just, and will repay each person according to his works (Matt. XVI, 27).

He is strong, since, although he is all-powerful, he endured even ungodly persecutors for our salvation.

He is patient, since he did not immediately after the resurrection drag even those who had persecuted him away to punishment, but endured them so that at some time they might turn from their ungodliness to salvation. And even now he endures them, reserving the final punishment for the last judgment and continually inviting sinners to repentance.

“He does not bring anger each day.” Perhaps it is expressed more significantly as “bringing anger” than as “being angry,” and this is how we find it in the Greek copies [Note: Greek: *mē orgēn epagōn*, “not bringing anger.”]. Thus the anger by which he punishes is not in God himself but in the minds of those ministers who obey the commandments of truth.

Through them even the lower ministries—those called angels of wrath—are commanded to punish sins. They now take pleasure in human punishment not because of justice, in which they do not rejoice, but because of their malice [Note: Lovaniensis reads *ministris* (“ministers”), but Erasmus and the manuscripts read *ministeriis* (“ministries”). The same expression occurs in *On True Religion*, chapter 40, where evil angels are called “the lower ministries.”].

God therefore does not bring anger each day—that is, he does not gather his ministers for vengeance each day. For now God’s patience invites people to repentance. But at the final time, when human beings have stored up wrath for themselves on account of their hardness and unrepentant heart on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment (Rom. II, 5), he will brandish his sword.

### 13. [verse 13]

“Unless you repent,” he says, “he will brandish his sword.”

The Lord’s man (*homo Dominicus*) may be understood as the two-edged sword of God, that is, the sword which he did not brandish at his first coming but concealed, as it were, in the sheath of humility [Note: *Retractationes*, chapter 19]. He will brandish it when, at his second coming, he comes to judge the living and the dead, flashing forth in the visible splendor of his glory—light to his just ones and terrors to the ungodly [Note: The printed editions read “with light and terror,” but the manuscripts read “light and terrors.”].

For in other copies, in place of “he will brandish his sword,” we find “he will make his sword shine.” By this expression I believe the final coming of the Lord’s glory is most appropriately signified, since from the person of the Lord himself we understand what another psalm says: “Deliver my soul, O Lord, from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand” (Ps. XVI, 13).

“He has bent his bow and prepared it.” We must not casually pass over the tenses of these words: he spoke of the sword in the future—“he will brandish”—but of the bow in the past—“he has bent it.” The words that follow are likewise in the past tense.

### 14. [verse 14]

“And in it he prepared the instruments of death; he made his arrows for those who burn.”

I would readily understand this bow as the Holy Scriptures, in which, through the strength of the New Testament, the harshness of the Old has been bent and subdued, as though by a bowstring.

From this bow the Apostles are shot forth like arrows, or they hurl forth divine proclamations. “He made his arrows for those who burn”—that is, arrows by which those struck might blaze with divine love.

For by what other arrow was she struck who says: “Bring me into the house of wine, place me among the perfumes, press me among the honeycombs” [Note: Perhaps *mala* (“apples”) rather than *mella* (“honeycombs”).], “for I am wounded by love” (Song II, 4, according to the Septuagint)?

By what other arrows is the person kindled who, desiring to return to God and come back from this exile, asks help against deceitful tongues, and is told: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals that lay waste” (Ps. CXIX, 3, 4)?

That is: arrows by which you are struck and inflamed, burning with such love for the heavenly kingdom that you despise the tongues of all who resist and wish to call you back from your purpose, and mock their persecutions, saying:

“Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? For I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor an angel nor a principality, nor things present nor things to come, nor power, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII, 35, 38, 39).

Thus “he made his arrows for those who burn.” For in the Greek copies it is written in this way: “He made his arrows for those who burn”; but most Latin copies have “burning arrows.”

Whether the arrows themselves burn, or whether they make others burn—which they certainly cannot do unless they themselves also burn—the meaning remains complete.

### 15

But since he said that the Lord prepared not only arrows but also instruments of death in the bow, it may be asked what these instruments of death are. Could they perhaps be heretics?

For they too spring from the same bow—that is, from the same Scriptures—not to inflame souls with love but to destroy them with poisons. This does not happen except according to their deserts.

Therefore this arrangement too must be attributed to divine providence—not because providence makes sinners, but because it orders them after they have sinned. For those who read with an evil intention through sin are compelled to understand wrongly, so that this itself becomes the punishment of their sin.

Yet through their death the children of the Catholic Church, as though awakened by certain thorns from sleep, advance toward understanding the divine Scriptures.

For there must also be heresies, so that, as the Apostle says, “those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19)—that is, manifest among human beings, since they are already manifest to God.

Or perhaps he appointed the same arrows and instruments of death for the destruction of unbelievers, while he made them burning, or for those who burn, for the training of believers? For what the Apostle says is not false: “To some we are an aroma of life unto life, and to others an aroma of death unto death; and who is sufficient for these things?” (II Cor. II, 16).

It is therefore not surprising if the same Apostles are both instruments of death among those by whom they suffered persecution and fiery arrows for setting the hearts of believers aflame.

### 16. [verse 15]

After this ordering, the just judgment will come. He speaks of it in such a way that we understand each person’s punishment to arise from his own sin and his iniquity to be turned into punishment.

We must not suppose that the tranquility and ineffable light of God produces from itself something by which sins are punished. Rather, the sins themselves are so ordered that what was a pleasure to the sinner becomes an instrument for the Lord who punishes.

“Behold,” he says, “he was in labor with injustice.” What had he conceived, so that he should be in labor with injustice? “He conceived labor,” he says (Gen. III, 17).

Hence comes the statement: “In labor you shall eat your bread”; and hence also: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28, 30).

For labor cannot come to an end unless each person loves what cannot be taken away from him against his will. When people love things that they can lose against their will, they must labor miserably for them. And in order to obtain them, amid the straits of earthly misery, when each person desires to seize them for himself, forestall another, or extort them from another, we contrive injustices.

Rightly, therefore, and entirely according to the order of things, he “was in labor with injustice” who “conceived labor.”

But what does he give birth to except that with which he was in labor, although he did not give birth to precisely what he conceived? For what is born is not identical with what is conceived: seed is conceived, while what is formed from the seed is born.

Labor, therefore, is the seed of iniquity; sin is the conception of labor—that is, the first sin, apostasy from God (Ecclus. X, 14). Thus “he was in labor with injustice who conceived labor.”

“And he brought forth iniquity.” Iniquity is the same as injustice; therefore he brought forth that with which he had been in labor. What follows next?

### 17. [verse 16]

“He opened a pit and dug it out.”

To open a pit is, amid earthly things—that is, as though in the earth—to prepare a trap into which another may fall, the person whom the unjust man wishes to deceive. This pit is opened when consent is given to the evil suggestion of earthly desires; it is dug out when, after consent has been given, the fraudulent action is pursued.

But how can iniquity first harm the just person against whom it proceeds before harming the unjust heart from which it proceeds?

Thus, for example, while the money-fraudster desires to tear another apart through financial loss, he himself is wounded by the wound of avarice. And who, unless insane, does not see how far apart these two things are, when one suffers the loss of money and the other the loss of innocence?

“He will fall into the pit that he made.” This is said in another psalm: “The Lord is known when he executes judgments; the sinner is caught in the works of his own hands” (Ps. IX, 17).

### 18. [verse 17]

“His labor will return upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his own crown.”

For he did not wish to escape sin; rather, he became subject to sin like a slave, as the Lord says: “Everyone who sins is a slave” (John VIII, 34).

His iniquity will therefore be upon him when he himself is subjected to his iniquity, because he could not say to the Lord what the innocent and upright say: “My glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. III, 4).

Thus he himself will be lower, so that his iniquity is higher and descends upon him, because it weighs him down, burdens him, and does not allow him to fly back to the rest of the saints.

This happens when reason is enslaved in the perverse person and desire rules.

### 19. [verse 18]

“I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness.”

This is not a confession of sins. For the one who says this is the one who above most truthfully said: “If there is iniquity in my hands.” Rather, it is a confession of God’s righteousness, by which we speak in this way:

“Truly, O Lord, you are just, since you protect the just in such a way that through yourself you illumine them, and order sinners in such a way that they are punished not by your but by their own wickedness.”

This confession praises the Lord in such a way that the blasphemies of the ungodly are powerless. Those blasphemers, wishing to excuse their crimes, refuse to attribute their sins to their own fault—that is, they refuse to attribute their own guilt to their own fault.

Thus they either find fortune or fate to accuse; or the devil, whom our Creator willed us to have the power not to obey; or they introduce another nature that does not come from God. Wretched and wandering, they prefer this to confessing to God so that he may forgive them.

For forgiveness is not appropriate except to one who says, “I have sinned.”

Whoever therefore sees God ordering the merits of souls in such a way that, while each person receives what is his own, the beauty of the universe is violated in no part, praises God in everything. And this is not the confession of sinners but of the just.

For it is not a confession of sins when the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Matt. XI, 25).

Likewise, it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “Confess to the Lord in all his works. And you shall say in your confession: All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 19–21). The same may be understood in this psalm if each person, with devout mind and with the Lord’s help, distinguishes between the rewards of the just and the punishments of sinners, and considers how by these two things the whole creation—which God created and governs—is adorned with a wonderful beauty known to few.

Thus he says: “I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness,” as one who has seen that darkness was not made by God but was nevertheless ordered by him.

For God said: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. I, 3). He did not say, “Let there be darkness, and there was darkness”; yet he ordered darkness itself. Therefore it is said: “God divided the light from the darkness, and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night” (ibid., 4, 5).

In this distinction, one thing he made and ordered; another he did not make, but nevertheless ordered.

Now that sins are signified by darkness is found also in the prophet, who said: “Your darkness shall be like midday” (Isa. LVIII, 10); and in the Apostle, who says: “The one who hates his brother is in darkness” (I John II, 11); and especially in the words: “Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light” (Rom. XIII, 12).

This does not mean that there is some nature of darkness. Every nature, insofar as it is nature, is compelled to exist; but existence belongs to light, while nonexistence belongs to darkness.

Whoever therefore abandons him by whom he was made and inclines toward that from which he was made—that is, toward nothingness—is held in darkness by this sin. Yet he does not perish entirely; rather, he is ordered among the lowest things.

After saying, “I will confess to the Lord,” therefore, lest we understand a confession of sins, he adds the final words: “And I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High.”

To sing psalms belongs to joy, whereas the repentance of sinners belongs to sorrow.

### 20

This psalm may also be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord’s man (*homo Dominicus*), provided that the humble words spoken there are referred to our weakness, which he bore.

## Exposition of Psalm VIII

“To the end. For the winepresses. A psalm of David” [Note: On this first verse, see *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm LXXXIII, §§1 ff.].

### Commentary on Psalm VIII

**1. [verse 1.]** He seems to say nothing about winepresses in the text of the psalm whose title this is. Here it becomes evident that one and the same thing is often suggested in Scripture through many different and varied comparisons. We may therefore understand the winepresses as the Churches, by the same reasoning by which we understand the threshing floor as the Church. For whether on a threshing floor or in a winepress, nothing else is being done except that the fruits are stripped of their coverings—coverings that were necessary both for them to be born and to grow, and for them to reach the maturity of either the harvest or the vintage. Thus, from these coverings or supports—that is, from the straw on the threshing floor and the grape-skins in the winepress—the grain and the wine are stripped: just as in the Churches something is done so that, from the multitude of secular people gathered together along with the good—for whom that multitude was necessary in order that they might be born and made fit for the divine word—they may be separated through spiritual love by the ministry of God’s servants. What is being done now is that the good are separated from the wicked, meanwhile not by place but by disposition, although, as far as bodily presence is concerned, they live together in the Churches. Another time will come when either the grain will be separated into granaries or the wine into cellars. “He will gather the grain,” he says, “into the granaries, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Luke 3:17). The same matter can be understood through another comparison in this way: “He will store the wine in storerooms, but he will throw the grape-skins to the animals,” so that the bellies of animals may, by comparison, be understood as the punishments of Gehenna.

**2.** There is another interpretation of the winepresses, provided that we do not depart from their signification of the Churches. For the divine Word too can be understood as a grape: the Lord was even called a cluster of grapes, which those sent ahead by the people of Israel brought from the land of promise, hanging from a piece of wood like one crucified (Num. 13:24). Thus, when the divine Word, out of the necessity of expression, makes use of the sound of the voice so that it may reach the ears of those listening, understanding is enclosed within that same vocal sound as wine within grape-skins. In this way the grape comes into the ears, as though into the pressing-vats of the winepresses [Note: In several manuscripts, though fewer and not the older ones, *torcularium* instead of *torculariorum*.]. There it is separated: the sound is effective in reaching the ears, while the understanding is received in the memory of those who hear, as though in a certain pool; from there it passes into the discipline of conduct and the disposition of the mind, as from a pool into cellars in which, if negligence does not sharpen it, it will be strengthened by age. For among the Jews it became sharp, and with this vinegar they gave the Lord to drink (John 19:29). But the wine that the Lord will drink with his saints in the kingdom of his Father, from the offspring of the vine of the New Testament (Luke 22:18), must necessarily be most sweet and most potent.

**3.** The winepresses are also commonly understood as martyrdoms, as though those who confessed the name of Christ had been trampled under the affliction of persecutions, their mortal bodies remaining on earth like grape-skins, while their souls flowed forth into the rest of a heavenly dwelling. Yet even with this interpretation we do not depart from the fruitfulness of the Churches. Thus the psalm is sung “for the winepresses,” for the establishment of the Church, when our Lord, after rising again, ascended into heaven. For then he sent the Holy Spirit, with whom the disciples were filled and boldly preached the word of God, so that the Churches might be gathered.

**4. [verse 2.]** Accordingly it says: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” I ask: From what does his name become wonderful in all the earth? The answer is: “Because your majesty has been exalted above the heavens.” The meaning is therefore: O Lord, who are our Lord, how greatly are you admired by all who inhabit the earth, because your majesty has been exalted from earthly humility above the heavens! For from this it became apparent who you were in descending, when some saw, and the rest believed, to what heights you had ascended.

**5. [verse 3.]** “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise, because of your enemies.” I cannot understand any other infants and nursing babies than those to whom the Apostle says: “As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2). They were signified by those who went before the Lord praising him; and the Lord himself used this testimony concerning them when the Jews told him to rebuke them, and he replied: “Have you not read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. 21:16). He rightly did not say, “You made praise,” but “you perfected praise.” For there are also people in the Churches who are no longer nourished with milk but eat solid food; the same Apostle signifies them when he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6). Yet the Churches are not perfected from these alone [Note: More manuscripts read: “But they are not perfected from these,” with *solis* omitted.], for if they alone existed, the human race would not be cared for. It is cared for when those also who are not yet capable of knowing spiritual and eternal realities are nourished by faith in the temporal history that, for our salvation, was administered after the Patriarchs and Prophets by the supreme Power and Wisdom of God, through the mystery of the humanity he assumed; in this history there is salvation for everyone who believes. Thus, moved by authority [Note: The African and Erasmus editions, along with more manuscripts, read *commonitus*, “having been admonished,” instead of *commotus*, “having been moved.”], he may obey the commandments, and, once purified and rooted and grounded in love, may run with the saints—no longer a little child on milk, but a young man on solid food—to comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth, and also to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ (Eph. 3:18–19).

**6.** “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise, because of your enemies.” We must generally understand as enemies of this dispensation accomplished through Jesus Christ—and him crucified—all who forbid belief in what they do not know and promise certain knowledge, as all heretics do, as well as those who, among the superstitions of the Gentiles, are called philosophers. This is not because the promise of knowledge is to be criticized, but because they think that the most salutary and necessary step of faith may be neglected—the step by which one must ascend to something certain, which cannot be anything other than eternal. From this it is evident that they do not possess even the knowledge they promise while despising faith, since they are ignorant of so useful and necessary a step toward it.

Thus our Lord perfected praise from the mouth of infants and nursing babies [Note: So the African and Erasmus editions and some manuscripts. A little farther below, most manuscripts and the present text read: “and he himself, being present, saying,” etc. (*perfecisti … ipse per se*, “you perfected … he himself by himself,” etc.)], first commanding through the Prophet: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint), and himself, being present, saying: “Blessed are those who have not seen and will believe” (John 20:29). “Because of the enemies”—against whom this too is said: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). He said “from the wise,” not those who are wise, but those who think they are.

“So that you may destroy the enemy and the defender” [Note: Augustine also treats this part of verse 3 in *Retractions*, chapter 19. There he says that in some manuscripts *ultorem*, “avenger,” is more correctly found instead of *et defensorem*, “and defender.”]. Whom else but the heretic? For he too is both enemy and defender: while attacking the Christian faith, he appears to defend it. Yet the philosophers of this world can also properly be understood as enemies and defenders. For the Son of God is the Power and Wisdom of God, by which everyone who becomes wise through the truth is enlightened. They profess themselves to be lovers of this Wisdom, from which they are also called philosophers; and therefore they seem to defend it while being its enemies, since they do not cease urging that harmful superstitions be observed and that the elements of this world be worshiped and revered.

**7. [verse 4.]** “For I will see your heavens” [Note: Eleven manuscripts omit *tuos*, “your.” This particle was absent from the Septuagint translation, but was later added from Theodotion’s edition under an asterisk, as Jerome explains in Letter 135 to Sunia.], “the works of your fingers.” We read that the Law was written by the finger of God and given through Moses, his holy servant (Exod. 31:18; Deut. 9:10); many understand this finger of God as the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if we rightly understand the fingers of God as those same ministers filled with the Holy Spirit, on account of the Spirit who works in them—for through them all divine Scripture was composed for us—we may suitably understand the heavens mentioned here as the books of both Testaments.

The magicians of King Pharaoh also said about Moses, after they had been defeated by him: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19). And although what is written—“Heaven will be folded up like a book” (Isa. 34:4)—may have been said of this ethereal heaven, nevertheless, by virtue of the same comparison, the books are suitably called “heavens” in allegory. “For I will see,” he says, “your heavens, the works of your fingers”—that is, I will perceive and understand the Scriptures that you composed, with the Holy Spirit working through your ministers.

**8.** The heavens mentioned earlier can therefore also be understood as these same books, where he says: “Because your majesty has been exalted above the heavens.” The whole meaning is: Your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. For your majesty exceeds the utterances of all the Scriptures. “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise,” so that those who desire to arrive at knowledge of your majesty—your majesty which has been exalted above the Scriptures, since it passes beyond and surpasses the proclamations of all words and languages—might begin from faith in the Scriptures.

God therefore bent the Scriptures down to the capacity of infants and nursing babies, as it is sung in another psalm: “He bent heaven and came down” (Ps. 17:10). He did this because of the enemies who, through the pride of loquacity [Note: Lovanius reads: “who, through proud speech.” Other editions and manuscripts read: “who, through the pride of loquacity.”], are enemies of the cross of Christ; even when they say some true things, they cannot benefit little ones and nursing babies. Thus the enemy and defender is destroyed: whether he appears to defend wisdom or even the name of Christ, he nevertheless attacks that truth from the step of faith by which it is approached—the truth he most readily promises. For this reason he is also proved not to possess it: by attacking its step, which is faith, he does not know how one ascends into it.

Thus the rash and blind promiser of truth, who is both enemy and defender, is destroyed when the heavens, the works of God’s fingers—that is, the Scriptures—are seen to have been brought down to the dullness of infants, and when, through the humility of historical faith in events accomplished in time, they nourish and strengthen such people well and raise them toward the exalted understanding of eternal realities that the Scriptures confirm.

These heavens, then—that is, these books—are the works of God’s fingers. For they were composed with the Holy Spirit working in holy people. Those who attended more to their own glory than to the salvation of human beings spoke without the Holy Spirit, in whom are the merciful affections of God.

**9.** “For I will see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you founded.” The moon and stars are founded in the heavens, because both the universal Church—in whose signification the moon is often placed—and the Churches individually in their several locations, which I believe are suggested under the name of stars, have been placed in those same Scriptures that we believe are signified by the name “heavens.”

Why the moon properly signifies the Church will be considered more suitably in another psalm, where it is said: “Sinners have bent the bow, to shoot at the upright in heart in the dark moon” (Ps. 10:2).

**10. [verse 5.]** “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” It may be asked what distinction there is between “man” and “son of man.” For if there were no difference, the words would not be set down in disjunction as “man, or son of man.” If it had been written, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, and the son of man, that you visit him,” the second phrase would seem merely to repeat what had been said about man. But now, when it says “man, or son of man,” a more evident distinction is suggested.

This much must certainly be retained: every son of man is a man, although not every man can be understood as a son of man. Adam was a man, but not a son of man. Accordingly, we may now attend to and discern what distinction this passage makes between man and son of man: those who bear the image of the earthly man, who is not a son of man, are signified by the name “men”; but those who bear the image of the heavenly man (1 Cor. 15:49) are more properly called “sons of men.”

The former is also called the old man, while the latter is the new man (Eph. 4:22, 24). Yet the new man is born from the old, since spiritual regeneration begins through a change from earthly and secular life; and therefore he is called the son of man.

Thus, in this passage, “man” is earthly, while “son of man” is heavenly; the former is far removed from God, while the latter is present to God. Therefore God is mindful of the former, as one placed far away, but visits the latter, whom he enlightens by his immediate presence: “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155), and, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4:6).

In another psalm he says that human beings associated with animals are saved with the animals, not through the inward illumination of God’s presence, but through the multiplication of God’s mercy, by which his goodness extends even to the lowest things—for the salvation of carnal people is carnal, like that of cattle. But separating the sons of men from those whom he joined to beasts under the name “men,” he declares that they become blessed in a far more exalted manner, through the illumination of truth itself and through a kind of inundation from the living fountain. For he says:

“You will save men and animals, O Lord, according to the abundance of your mercy, O God. But the sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings. They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we will see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you” (Ps. 35:7–11).

He is therefore mindful of man, as of animals, through the multiplication of his mercy, because multiplied mercy reaches even those who are far away. But he visits the son of man, to whom, placed under the protection of his wings, he extends mercy, supplies light in his light, gives him drink from his delights, and intoxicates him with the abundance of his house, so that he may forget the hardships and errors of his former way of life.

This son of man—that is, the new man—is brought forth by the repentance of the old man, with pain and groaning. Although he is new, he is nevertheless still called carnal while he is nourished with milk. “I could not speak to you as spiritual people,” the Apostle says, “but as carnal”; and to show that they had already been regenerated, he says: “As little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

When this man falls back into the former life, as often happens, he hears with reproach that he is a man: “Are you not human?” the Apostle says, “and do you not walk according to man?” (1 Cor. 3:1–3).

**11. [verses 6–7.]** The son of man was therefore first visited in the very man of the Lord [Note: *Retractions*, chapter 19.], born from the Virgin Mary. Concerning him, because of the weakness of the flesh that the Wisdom of God deigned to bear, and because of the humility of his passion, it is rightly said: “You made him a little lower than the angels.”

But the glorification by which, rising again, he ascended into heaven is added: “You crowned him,” he says, “with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands.” Since the angels too are works of God’s hands, we understand the only-begotten Son to have been established even over the angels—the one whom we hear and believe to have been made a little lower than the angels through the humility of his bodily generation and passion.

**12. [verses 8–9.]** “You have subjected everything,” he says, “under his feet.” He excludes nothing when he says “everything.” And lest it be understood otherwise, the Apostle commands us to believe this when he says, “except the one who subjected everything to him” (1 Cor. 15:27). He also uses this very testimony of the psalm in the Letter to the Hebrews (Heb. 2:8), wishing everything to be understood as subject to our Lord Jesus Christ, with nothing excepted.

Yet he does not seem to add anything significant when he says: “All sheep and oxen, moreover also the animals of the field; the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea, which travel along the paths of the sea.” For he seems, after leaving out the heavenly Powers and Authorities and all the armies of angels, and after leaving out human beings themselves, to have subjected only animals to him—unless we understand the sheep and oxen as holy souls, either bearing the fruit of innocence or working so that the earth may bear fruit, that is, so that earthly people may be regenerated into spiritual abundance.

We must therefore understand these holy souls as including not only those of human beings but also those of all the angels, if we wish to understand from this passage that everything has been subjected to our Lord Jesus Christ. For no creature will remain unsubjugated to him to whom the highest spirits, so to speak, are subjected.

But how shall we prove that “sheep” can also be understood in a sublime sense as blessed beings—not human beings but spirits of the angelic creation? Perhaps from the fact that the Lord says he left ninety-nine sheep on the mountains, that is, in higher places, and descended because of one (Matt. 18:12). If we understand the one fallen sheep as the human soul in Adam—for Eve too was made from his side (Gen. 2:22), though this is not the time to treat and consider all these matters spiritually—then it remains that the ninety-nine left on the mountains are understood as spirits not human but angelic.

The interpretation of this statement is easy in the case of the oxen [Note: The African and Erasmus editions and some manuscripts read *expositio*, “exposition,” instead of *expeditio*, “interpretation.”], since human beings are called oxen for no other reason than that, in preaching the word of God, they imitate the angels, in reference to which it is said: “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is threshing” (Deut. 25:4).

How much more easily, then, do we understand the angels themselves—messengers of the truth—as oxen, since the Evangelists were called oxen by sharing their name (1 Cor. 9:9; 1 Tim. 5:18)! “You have subjected,” he says, “all sheep and oxen”—that is, every holy spiritual creature. Among these we also understand the holy human beings who are in the Church, in those winepresses that have been suggested under another comparison, that of the moon and stars.

**13.** “Moreover,” he says, “also the animals of the field.” The addition of the word “moreover” is by no means without significance. First, because the animals of the field can be understood as both sheep and oxen: if the animals of rocky and steep places are goats, then sheep may properly be understood as animals of the field. Thus, even if it had been written, “all sheep and oxen and the animals of the field,” it would rightly be asked what the animals of the field meant, since sheep and oxen too can be understood in this way. But the additional word “also,” or “moreover,” compels us to recognize some distinction.

Under this word “moreover,” therefore, we must understand not only the animals of the field but also the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea that travel along the paths of the sea.

What, then, is this distinction? Let the winepresses come to mind, containing grape-skins and wine; the threshing floor, containing chaff and grain (Mark 3:12); the nets, in which good and bad fish are enclosed (Matt. 13:47); and Noah’s ark, in which there were both unclean and clean animals (Gen. 7:8). Then you will see that, during this present time, until the time of the final judgment, the Churches contain not only sheep and oxen—that is, holy laypeople and holy ministers—but also, moreover, the animals of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea that travel along the paths of the sea.

The animals of the field are most suitably understood as people who rejoice in the pleasures of the flesh, ascending toward nothing lofty or laborious. For the field is also the broad way that leads to destruction (Matt. 7:13), and Abel is killed in the field (Gen. 4:8). Therefore it must be feared that someone, descending from the mountains of God’s righteousness—for “your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7)—and choosing the breadths and conveniences of carnal pleasure, may be slaughtered by the devil.

Now consider also the birds of heaven: the proud, of whom it is said, “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. 72:9). See how high they are carried by the wind—those who say: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are with us; who is our lord?” (Ps. 11:5).

Consider also the fish of the sea—that is, the curious, who travel along the paths of the sea, that is, who investigate temporal things in the depths of this world. These things disappear and perish as quickly as paths in the sea are again covered by the water after they have given way to those passing through them, whether ships or whatever else walks or swims.

For he did not merely say, “They walk along the paths of the sea,” but said “they travel throughout them,” showing the most persistent zeal of those who seek empty and passing things.

These three kinds of vice—pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity—embrace all sins. They seem to me to have been enumerated by the Apostle John when he says: “Do not love the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:15–16). For curiosity chiefly prevails through the eyes; the proper reference of the remaining terms is clear.
