The temptation of the Lord’s human nature [Note: *Retractions*, chapter 19.] was also threefold: through food, that is, through the desire of the flesh, when it was suggested, “Tell these stones to become bread” (Matt. 4:3); through empty boasting, when all the kingdoms of this earth were shown from the mountain and promised if he would worship; and through curiosity, when he was urged to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple in order to test whether he would be received by angels.

After the enemy had been unable to prevail against him through any of these temptations, this was said of him: “After the devil had completed every temptation” (Luke 4:13).

Therefore, because of the signification of the winepresses, not only the wine but also the grape-skins have been subjected under his feet—not only, that is, the sheep and oxen, the holy souls of the faithful, whether among the people or among the ministers, but also the animals of pleasure, the birds of pride, and the fish of curiosity. We see all these kinds of sinners now mixed with the good and holy in the Churches.

Let him therefore work in his Churches and separate the wine from the grape-skins. Let us strive to be wine and sheep or oxen—not grape-skins, animals of the field, birds of heaven, or fish of the sea that travel along the paths of the sea.

This is not because these names can be understood and explained in only this one way, but according to the particular passages; elsewhere they signify something else. This rule must be retained in every allegory: what is said by comparison must be considered according to the meaning of the passage at hand. For this is the discipline both of the Lord and of the Apostle.

Let us therefore repeat the final verse, which is also placed at the beginning of the psalm, and praise God, saying: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” For it is fitting, after the body of the discourse, to return to its beginning, to which the whole discourse must be referred.

## Commentary on Psalm IX

**1. [verse 1.]** The inscription of this psalm is: “For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son; a psalm of David.” The hidden things of the Son may be questioned. But since it does not add whose son, we must understand the only-begotten Son of God himself.

When a psalm is inscribed concerning the son of David, it says, “When he fled from the face of Abessalom his son” (Ps. 3:1). Although his name was given and therefore it could not remain uncertain of whom it was speaking, it nevertheless does not say merely “from the face of Abessalom the son,” but adds “his.” Here, however, both the omission of “his” and the fact that the psalm says much about the Gentiles make it impossible to understand Abessalom correctly. For the war that the wicked man waged against his father has no relevance at all to the Gentiles, since only the people of Israel were divided against itself in that conflict.

This psalm, then, is sung concerning the hidden things of the only-begotten Son of God. For when the Lord himself uses the word “Son” without qualification, he wishes himself, the only-begotten, to be understood, as when he says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). He did not say “the Son of God,” but merely “the Son,” thereby indicating whose son he is.

Such an expression is appropriate only to the excellence of the one about whom we speak in such a way that, even if we do not name him, he can be understood. Thus we say, “It is raining,” “It is clearing,” “It is thundering,” and similar expressions, without adding who is doing these things, because the excellence of the agent presents itself spontaneously to everyone’s mind and requires no words.

What, then, are the hidden things of the Son? In this expression we must first understand that there are certain things of the Son that are manifest, from which these called “hidden” are distinguished.

Accordingly, because we believe in two comings of the Lord—one past, which the Jews did not understand, and another future, which we both hope for—and because the coming that the Jews did not understand benefited the Gentiles, it is not improperly understood as referring to this coming when the psalm says “concerning the hidden things of the Son,” in which blindness in part has happened to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Rom. 11:25).

The Scriptures also indicate two judgments, if one pays attention: one hidden and one manifest. The hidden judgment is now taking place, concerning which the Apostle Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (1 Pet. 4:17). The hidden judgment is therefore the punishment by which each human being is now either exercised for purification, admonished to conversion, or, if he has despised God’s calling and discipline, blinded for condemnation.

The manifest judgment is that in which the coming Lord will judge the living and the dead, with everyone confessing that he is the one from whom rewards are given to the good and punishments to the wicked. But then that confession will not benefit the wicked as a remedy; it will increase their condemnation.

It seems to me that the Lord spoke of these two judgments, one hidden and the other manifest, when he said: “Whoever believes in me has passed from death to life, and will not come into judgment” (John 5:24)—that is, into the manifest judgment. For the passing from death to life through a certain affliction, by which he chastises every son whom he receives, is the hidden judgment. “But whoever does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” (John 3:18)—that is, by this hidden judgment he has already been prepared for the manifest one.

We also read of these two judgments in the Book of Wisdom, where it is written: “Therefore, as to senseless children, you gave judgment as a mockery; but those who were not corrected by this judgment experienced a judgment worthy of God” (Wis. 12:25–26). Those, therefore, who are not corrected by this hidden judgment of God will most deservedly be punished by the manifest one.

Accordingly, in this psalm we must observe the hidden things of the Son: both his humble coming, by which he benefited the Gentiles amid the blindness of the Jews, and the punishment now secretly taking place—not yet the condemnation of sinners, but either the exercising of those who are converted, or the admonition of those who should convert, or the blindness by which those who refuse to convert are prepared for condemnation.

**2. [verse 2.]** “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart.” He does not confess to God with his whole heart who doubts anything concerning his providence. Rather, he does so who already perceives the hidden things of God’s wisdom, how great is the invisible reward of the one who says, “We rejoice in tribulations” (Rom. 5:3), and how all the sufferings inflicted bodily either exercise those who have turned to God, admonish them to turn, or prepare the hardened for a just final condemnation. Thus everything is referred to the governance of divine providence, whereas fools think that things happen by chance and accident, without any divine administration.

“I will recount all your wonders.” He recounts all the wonders of God who sees them taking place not only openly in bodies but invisibly—and far more sublimely and excellently—in souls. For earthly people and those devoted to hidden things marvel more that Lazarus rose again in the body than that Paul, a persecutor, rose again in soul. But since the visible miracle calls the soul toward illumination, while the invisible miracle illuminates the soul that has responded to the call, he recounts all the wonders of God who, by believing in visible things, makes the passage toward understanding invisible things.

**3. [verse 3.]** “I will rejoice and exult in you.” No longer in this age; not in the pleasure of touching bodies, nor in the tastes of palate and tongue, nor in the sweetness of scents, nor in the delight of passing sounds, nor in the forms of bodies varied by color, nor in the vanities of human praise, nor in marriage and offspring destined to die, nor in the excesses of temporal riches, nor in the pursuit of this world—whether that pursuit extends through the spaces of places or revolves through the succession of time.

Rather, “I will rejoice and exult in you,” namely, in the hidden things of the Son, where “the light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4:6); for he says: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance” (Ps. 30:21).

He will therefore rejoice and exult in you who recounts all your wonders. And he will recount all your wonders, since it was now prophetically said of him [Note: The printed editions read: “that one was called,” etc. The manuscripts read: “it was said.”] that he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (John 6:38).

**4. [verse 4.]** The person of the Lord speaking in this psalm now begins to appear. For it follows: “I will sing to your name, O Most High, in turning my enemy backward.”

When, then, was this enemy of his turned backward? Was it when he was told: “Go behind me, Satan” (Matt. 4:10)? At that moment the one who, by tempting him, desired to place himself first was put behind—not because he deceived the one tempted, or had any power over him.

Earthly people are behind, while the heavenly man was made first, although he came later: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47). Yet he came from the very line concerning which it was said: “He who comes after me was made before me” (John 1:15). And the Apostle forgets what is behind and stretches forward to what is ahead (Phil. 3:13).

The enemy was therefore turned backward after he was unable to deceive the heavenly man when he tempted him, and turned instead to earthly people, among whom he can exercise dominion. Therefore no human being puts him behind and precedes him except one who, laying aside the image of the earthly man, bears the image of the heavenly man (1 Cor. 15:49).

But if we prefer to understand “my enemy” generally as either a sinner or a Gentile, that too will not be absurd. In that case, “in turning my enemy backward” will not signify punishment but a benefit—and such a benefit that nothing can be compared with it. For what is more blessed than to lay aside pride and not wish to go before Christ, as though someone were healthy who had no need of a physician, but rather to be willing to go behind Christ, who, calling a disciple so that he might be perfected, says: “Follow me” (Matt. 19:21)?

Nevertheless, the statement “in turning my enemy backward” is more suitably understood as referring to the devil. For the devil was also turned backward in the persecution of the righteous, and it is much more beneficial for him to be a persecutor than to go before them as leader and prince.

Therefore we must sing to the name of the Most High while he turns the enemy backward, because we ought rather to flee from him while he persecutes than follow him while he leads. We have somewhere to flee and hide in the hidden things of the Son, because “the Lord has become a refuge for us” (Ps. 89:1).

**5. [verse 5.]** “They will grow weak and perish from your face.” Who will grow weak and perish except the unjust and wicked? They will grow weak because they will have no power, and they will perish because they will no longer be wicked—from the face of God, that is, from the knowledge of God, just as the one who said, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20), perished.

But why will the wicked grow weak and perish from your face? “Because you have made my judgment,” he says, “and my cause”—that is, you made that judgment in which I appeared to be judged my own, and that cause in which human beings condemned me as just and innocent my own.

For these things served him for our liberation, just as sailors call the wind by which they sail well “their own.”

**6.** “You sat upon the throne, judging justice.” Either the Son says this to the Father—the Son who also said, “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11)—referring the same matter to the Father’s justice and to his hidden purposes, since he was judged as judge of human beings for the benefit of human beings;

or a human being says to God, “You sat upon the throne, judging justice,” calling his own soul God’s throne, so that the body may perhaps be the earth which is called his footstool (Isa. 66:1): “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19);

or the soul of the Church, already perfected and without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), worthy, that is, of the hidden things of the Son because “the king brought her into his chamber” (Song 1:3), says to her bridegroom, “You sat upon the throne, judging justice,” because you rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sit at the right hand of the Father.

Whichever of these interpretations one prefers as the reference of the verse, it does not exceed the rule of faith.

7. [verse 6.] “You rebuked the nations, and the impious man perished.” We understand this to be said more appropriately of the Lord Jesus Christ than for Christ himself to say it. For who else rebuked the nations and caused the impious man to perish, except the one who, after ascending into heaven, sent the Holy Spirit? Filled with this Spirit, the Apostles proclaimed the word of God with confidence and freely reproved human sins [Col. 0120]. By this rebuke the impious man perished, because the impious man was justified and became pious.

“You blotted out their name forever and ever.” The name of the impious has been blotted out, for those who believe in the true God are no longer called impious. Their name is blotted out “forever,” that is, for as long as this temporal age revolves.

“And forever and ever.” What is “the age of the age” except that which this age possesses as an image and, so to speak, a shadow? The succession of times following one another—while the moon wanes and is again filled, while the sun returns each year to its place, while spring, summer, autumn, and winter pass in such a way as to return—is a kind of imitation of eternity. But the age of this age is that which endures in unchangeable eternity.

It is like a verse in the mind and a verse in the voice: the former is understood, the latter heard; and the former gives measure to the latter. Therefore the former operates and remains in the art, while the latter sounds in the air and passes away. Thus the form of this mutable age is determined by that immutable age which is called “the age of the age.” Therefore the former remains in God’s art—that is, in Wisdom and Power—whereas the latter is carried out in the administration of creation.

If, however, this is not a repetition—so that after “forever” had been said, “forever and ever” was added lest “forever” be understood as referring to what passes away—then the Greek copies read: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, which most Latin translators rendered not “forever and forever and ever,” but “eternally, and forever and ever.” Thus what is said as “forever and ever” explains what was said as “eternally.” Therefore, “You blotted out the name of the impious eternally,” because from then on they will never be impious. And if their name does not extend into this age, still less does it extend into the age of the age.

8. [verse 7.] [Col. 0121] “The enemy’s swords have failed utterly.” The term “enemy” is not plural, but singular: “of this enemy.” Whose enemy is this, except the devil, whose swords have failed? These swords are understood as the various opinions of error by which he kills souls as though with swords.

Against these swords, to conquer them and bring them to failure, there advances that sword of which it is said in the seventh psalm: “Unless you repent, he will brandish his sword” (Psalm 7:13). Perhaps this is the end toward which the enemy’s swords fail, since they have some power up to that point. This sword now works secretly, but at the last judgment it will be brandished openly.

“[And] you destroyed cities.” By this the cities are destroyed. For the passage continues: “The enemies’ swords have failed utterly, and you destroyed cities.” These are the cities in which the devil reigns, where deceitful and fraudulent counsels occupy the place of a senate-house. Serving that rule as attendants and ministers are the functions of the several members: the eyes for curiosity, the ears for lust—or for anything else willingly heard in an evil sense—the hands for robbery or any other crime or disgrace, and the remaining members serving the tyrannical rule in this way, that is, serving perverse counsels.

All the delicate affections and turbulent movements of the soul, which stir up daily seditions in a person, are like the populace of this city. Therefore, wherever there is a king, a senate, ministers, and a populace, there is a city. Such things would not exist in evil cities unless they first existed in the individual human beings who are, as it were, the elements and seeds of cities.

He destroys these cities when their ruler is expelled—the one of whom it was said, “The ruler of this world has been cast out” (John 12:31). These kingdoms are laid waste by the word of truth; evil counsels are quieted; shameful affections are subdued; and the services of the members and senses are taken captive and transferred to the service of justice and good works. Thus, as the Apostle says, “sin may no longer reign in our mortal body” (Romans 6:12), and so forth in that passage.

Then the soul is pacified, and the human being is ordered toward attaining rest and blessedness.

“Their memory perished with a tumult”—that is, the memory of the impious. “With a tumult” may mean that a tumult occurs when impiety is overthrown. No one passes into perfect peace, where there is perfect silence, unless he has first waged war against his vices with great tumult. Or “with a tumult” may mean that the memory of the impious perishes together with the very tumult in which impiety rages.

9. [verses 8, 9.] “And the Lord remains forever.” Why, then, did the nations rage and the peoples meditate vain things against the Lord and against his Christ (Psalm 2:1)? For “the Lord remains forever.”

“He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in equity.” He prepared his throne when he was judged. Through that patience, the human being acquired heaven, and God, in the human being, benefited believers [Note: [Col. 0121] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “and God benefited human beings.”]; and this is the hidden judgment of the Son.

But because he will also come openly and manifestly to judge the living and the dead, he prepared his throne in the hidden judgment; and likewise he himself will judge the world openly “in equity,” that is, distributing what is appropriate to their merits, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left (Matthew 25:33).

“He will judge the peoples with justice.” This is what was said above: “He will judge the world in equity.” The Lord will not judge as human beings judge, since they do not see hearts and often acquit those who are worse than those whom they condemn. Rather, the Lord will judge in equity and with justice, with the conscience bearing witness and with thoughts accusing or defending (Romans 2:15).

10. [verse 10.] [Note: [Col. 0121] The same verse 10 is expounded in Exposition of Psalm LXXXIII, no. 3.] “And the Lord became a refuge for the poor.” However greatly that enemy who has turned back may persecute them, what harm will he do to those for whom the Lord has become a refuge?

But this will happen if, in this age—whose magistrate he is—they choose to be poor, loving nothing which either abandons the person who lives or loves it here, or is abandoned by the person who is dying. For the Lord has become a refuge for such a poor person, “a helper in times of need, in tribulation.”

Thus he makes them poor, because “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). What it means to be “a helper in times of need” he explained when he added, “in tribulation.” For the soul does not turn toward God unless it turns away from this age; and it does not turn away from this age more opportunely than when its trifling, harmful, and destructive pleasures are mingled with labors and pains.

11. [verse 11.] [Note: [Col. 0122] The printed editions read, “And let all who know your name hope in you.” The word “all” is absent from the manuscripts.] “And let those who know your name hope in you” when they have ceased to hope in riches and in the other blandishments of this age.

When the soul is seeking where to fix its hope as it is torn away from this world, the knowledge of God’s name receives it at the right moment [Note: [Col. 0122] Thus in most manuscripts. The printed editions read: “When the soul is seeking”; and shortly afterward, “receives the knowledge of God’s name.”]. For the name of God is now proclaimed everywhere; but knowledge of the name occurs when he whose name it is is known. A name is not a name on account of itself, but on account of what it signifies.

It is said, “The Lord is his name” (Jeremiah 33:2). Therefore, whoever willingly submits himself as God’s servant has come to know this name.

“And let those who know your name hope in you.” The Lord also says to Moses: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me’” (Exodus 3:14).

Let those who know your name, therefore, hope in you. Let them not hope in those things which pass away with the turning of time, possessing nothing except “will be” and “was.” For what in them is still to come, when it arrives, immediately becomes past; it is awaited with desire and lost with grief.

In God’s nature, however, there is nothing that “will be,” as though it did not yet exist, or that “was,” as though it no longer existed. There is only that which is, and this itself is eternity.

Therefore let those who know the name of the one who said, “I am who I am,” and of whom it was said, “He who is has sent me,” cease to hope in and love temporal things and turn themselves toward eternal hope.

“For you have not forsaken those who seek you, Lord.” Those who seek him no longer seek things that pass away and die, for “no one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

12. [verse 12.] “Sing psalms to the Lord, who dwells in Zion.” This is said to those whom the Lord does not forsake when they seek him.

He dwells in Zion, which is interpreted as “Contemplation,” and which bears the image of the Church that now exists, just as Jerusalem bears the image of the Church that will be—the city of the saints already enjoying angelic life. Jerusalem is interpreted as “Vision of peace.”

Contemplation precedes vision, just as this Church precedes the Church that is promised, the immortal and eternal city. But it precedes it in time, not in dignity, because that toward which we strive to arrive is more honorable than what we do in order to deserve to arrive there. We practice contemplation in order to reach vision.

Yet even the Church that now exists would go astray, however diligent its contemplation, unless the Lord inhabited it. To this Church it was said, “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17), and, “May Christ dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person” (Ephesians 3:16).

We are therefore commanded to sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion, so that in harmony we may praise the Lord who inhabits the Church.

“Declare his wonders among the nations.” This has happened, and it will not cease to happen.

13. [verse 13.] [Col. 0123] “For, seeking their blood, he remembered their blood.”

As though those who were sent to evangelize were responding to the command, “Declare his wonders among the nations,” and were saying, “Lord, who has believed our report?” (Isaiah 53:1), and, “For your sake we are killed all day long” (Psalm 43:22), the following appropriately continues, saying that Christians will not die in persecution without great eternal fruit: “For, seeking their blood, he remembered them.”

But why did he prefer to say “their blood”? Perhaps some less instructed person, or someone of weaker faith, might ask, “How will they proclaim, when the unbelief of the nations will rage against them?” To him the answer is given: “For, seeking their blood, he remembered their blood”—that is, the final judgment will come, when both the glory of those who were killed and the punishment of those who killed them will be made manifest.

“He remembered them”: no one should understand this as though forgetfulness could befall God. Rather, because the judgment will occur after a long time, it is expressed according to the feeling of weak human beings, who suppose that God has forgotten because he does not act as quickly as they wish.

They are also told what follows: “He has not forgotten the cry of the poor.” That is, he has not forgotten it as you suppose. As though they said, after hearing “He remembered them,” “Then he had forgotten,” the answer is: “He has not forgotten the cry of the poor.”

14. [verses 14, 15.] But I ask what the cry of the poor is which God does not forget. Is it this cry whose words are: “Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation by my enemies”?

Why, then, did he not say, “Have mercy on us, Lord; see our humiliation by our enemies,” as though many poor people were crying out, but, as though one person were crying, “Have mercy on me, Lord”?

Or is it because one person intercedes for the saints—the one who first became poor for our sake, though he was rich (2 Corinthians 8:9)—and he himself says, “You lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion”?

The human being is exalted in him—not only the human being whom he bears, who is the head of the Church, but also each one of us who belongs to the other members. He is exalted from all evil desires, which are the gates of death, because through them one goes into death.

Death is itself the joy of enjoyment, when someone acquires what he has desperately desired. For “desire is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10); and therefore it is the gate of death, because “the widow who lives in pleasure is dead” (ibid. 5:6). Through desires, as through the gates of death, one reaches those pleasures.

But the gates of the daughter of Zion are all good pursuits through which one comes to the vision of peace in the holy Church. At these gates, therefore, all the praises of God are rightly proclaimed, so that what is holy may not be given to dogs, nor pearls thrown before swine (Matthew 7:6)—those who prefer to bark obstinately rather than seek diligently, or who prefer neither to bark nor to seek, but to wallow in the filth of their pleasures.

When God’s praises are proclaimed in good pursuits, he gives to those who ask, reveals himself to those who seek, and opens to those who knock.

Or perhaps the gates of death are the bodily senses and the eyes, which were opened to the human being when he tasted from the forbidden tree (Genesis 3:7). Those who are lifted up from these are told to seek not what is seen but what is not seen, because “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

And are the gates of the daughter of Zion the sacraments and beginnings of faith, which are opened to those who knock so that they may reach the hidden things of the Son? For “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Thus far extends the cry of the poor, which the Lord has not forgotten.

15. [verse 16.] [Col. 0124] Then follows: “I will rejoice over your salvation”—that is, I will be held in blessedness by your salvation, which is our Lord Jesus Christ, “the Power and Wisdom of God” (ibid. 1:24).

The Church, which is afflicted here and saved in hope, therefore speaks. While the judgment of the Son remains hidden, it says in hope, “I will rejoice over your salvation,” because now it is battered by the surrounding tumult, whether through the violence or the error of the nations.

“The nations are caught in the destruction which they made.” Observe how punishment is preserved for the sinner from his own works, and how those who wished to persecute the Church have been caught in the destruction which they thought they were inflicting on it. For they wanted to kill bodies while they themselves were dying in soul.

“In this trap, which they concealed, their foot was caught.” The hidden trap is a deceitful thought.

The foot of the soul is rightly understood as love. When it is perverse, it is called desire or lust; when it is rightly ordered, it is called affection or charity. For love moves the soul as though toward the place to which it is headed.

The place of the soul is not in some spatial location occupied by the form of the body, but in the pleasure by which it rejoices that it has arrived through love. Harmful pleasure follows desire; fruitful pleasure follows charity. Hence desire is also called a root (1 Timothy 6:10).

A root is understood as a kind of foot of a tree. Charity too is called a root, when the Lord speaks of the seeds which wither in rocky places under the burning sun because they do not have a deep root (Matthew 13:5). This signifies those who rejoice in receiving the word of truth but yield to persecutions, which are resisted by charity alone. The Apostle says: “That you, being rooted and grounded in charity, may be able to comprehend” (Ephesians 3:17).

The foot of sinners, therefore—that is, love—is caught in the trap which they conceal. For when pleasure follows upon their fraudulent action, when God gives them over to the desire of their heart (Romans 1:24), that pleasure binds them, so that they neither dare to break away from their love nor direct it toward useful things. When they attempt to do so, they suffer inwardly, as though wishing to remove their foot from a fetter; but, overcome by this pain, they refuse to withdraw from their harmful pleasures.

Thus, in the trap which they concealed—that is, in their fraudulent plan—their foot was caught: namely, the love which through fraud arrived at empty pleasure, for which pain is the price.

16. [verse 17.] “The Lord is known as he executes judgments” [Note: [Col. 0124] The printed editions read, “will be known.” But the manuscripts read, “is known,” in agreement with the LXX, γινώσκεται (ginōsketai).]. [Col. 0125] These are the judgments of God: iron, fire, beasts, or anything of that kind by which sinners are tortured do not come forth from the tranquility of his blessedness or from the secrets of wisdom into which blessed souls are received.

But how are they tortured, and how does the Lord execute judgment? “In the works of his hands,” he says, “the sinner is caught.”

17. [verses 18–21.] Here is inserted: “A song of the diapsalma” [Note: Greek LXX, ᾠδὴ διαψάλματος (“song of the diapsalma”).]—as though it were a hidden joy, so far as we can judge, concerning the separation that now occurs, not in places but in the affections of souls, between sinners and the righteous, as grain is separated from chaff while still on the threshing floor.

And it follows: “Let sinners be turned into hell”—that is, let them be handed over to their own hands while they are spared, and let them be ensnared by deadly pleasure.

“All the nations that forget God,” because, “when they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Romans 1:28).

18. “For the poor will not be forgotten forever” [Note: Most manuscripts: “The poor will be in oblivion forever.”]—the poor person who now seems to be forgotten, while sinners are thought to flourish in the happiness of this age and the righteous to suffer.

“But the patience of the poor will not perish” [Note: Five manuscripts: “will not fail.” Others, with the printed editions, read “will not perish”—a faulty form, but perhaps the custom of the singing peoples prevented its correction, just as Augustine discusses the word floriet in Book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 13.] forever.

Therefore patience is now necessary for enduring the wicked, who have already been separated in their wills, until they are also separated at the final judgment.

19. “Arise, Lord; let man not prevail.” The future judgment is invoked. But before it comes: “Let the nations be judged,” he says, “in your sight”—that is, in secret, which is called “before God,” understood by a few holy and righteous persons.

“Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them.” It seems to me that he signifies the Antichrist, of whom the Apostle says, “When the man of sin is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

“Let the nations know” [Note: The printed editions have “so that the nations may know.” The particle “so that” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek LXX.] “that they are human beings.” Those who do not wish to be liberated by the Son of God, to belong to the Son of Man, and to be sons of human beings—that is, new human beings—will serve a human being, that is, the old sinful human being, because they are human beings.

## ON THE SECOND PART OF PSALM IX

20. [verses 1–3.] [Col. 0126] And because he is believed to come to such a height of empty glory, and will be permitted to do so much against all human beings and against God’s saints, that at that time some weak people will truly think that God neglects human affairs, after the insertion of the diapsalma he adds, as though giving voice to those who groan and ask why judgment is delayed:

“Why, Lord,” he says, “have you withdrawn far away?”

Then the one who asked in this way, as though he had suddenly understood, or as though he had asked knowingly in order to teach, adds: “You despise in times of need, in tribulations”—that is, you despise opportunely, and you bring about tribulations in order to kindle souls with desire for your coming. For that fountain of life is sweeter to those who have thirsted greatly.

Thus he intimates the reason for the delay, saying: “While the impious man exalts himself, the poor person is set aflame.”

It is wondrous and true how greatly the little ones of good hope are kindled toward right living by comparison with sinners.

By this mystery it also comes about that heresies are permitted to exist—not because the heretics themselves desire this, but because divine Providence brings this about from their sins. Providence both makes and orders the light, but only orders the darkness (Genesis 1:3–4), so that by comparison with them the light may be more pleasing, just as by comparison with heretics the discovery of truth is more delightful. For by this comparison those who are approved become manifest among human beings who are known to God.

21. “They are caught in the thoughts with which they think.” That is, their evil thoughts become bonds for them.

But why do they become bonds? “Because the sinner is praised,” he says, “in the desires of his soul.” The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. It is pleasing to do things in which one not only does not fear a reprover but even hears a praiser.

“And the one who acts unjustly is blessed.” By this they are caught in the thoughts with which they think.

22. [verse 4.] “The sinner has provoked the Lord.” Let no one congratulate the person who prospers in his way, whose sins lack an avenger and have a praiser. This is the greater wrath of the Lord.

For the sinner has provoked the Lord to suffer these things—that is, not to suffer the scourges of correction.

“The sinner has provoked the Lord: according to the abundance of his anger he will not inquire.” He is greatly angry when he does not inquire, when he seems to forget and pay no attention to sins, and when wealth and honors are gained through frauds and crimes. This will occur above all in that Antichrist, who will appear so blessed to human beings that he will even be thought to be God.

But how great this anger of God is, the following words show.

23. [verse 5.] “God is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times.”

Anyone who knows what the soul rejoices in or delights in knows how great an evil it is to be abandoned by the light of truth [Note: Two manuscripts: “to abandon the light of truth.” Three others: “for the light to be abandoned.”], although human beings consider the blindness of the bodily eyes a great evil, when this light is withdrawn.

What punishment, then, does the person suffer who, through the prosperity of his sins, is brought to the point that God is not before his eyes and that his ways are defiled at all times—that is, that his thoughts and plans are unclean?

“Your judgments are removed from his sight.” A mind conscious of evil, since it seems to itself to suffer no punishment, believes that God does not judge. Thus God’s judgments are removed from his sight, when this very condition is itself a great condemnation.

“And he will rule over all his enemies.” For it is handed down that he will overcome all kings and alone obtain the kingdom, when, as the Apostle says in his prophecy concerning him, “he will sit in the temple of God, exalting himself above everything that is worshiped and called God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

24. [verse 6.] [Col. 0127] And because he has been handed over to the desire of his heart and destined for final condemnation, he will come through wicked arts to that empty and vain height of power and domination. Therefore it follows:

“For he said in his heart: I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil”—that is, “My fame and my name will not pass from this generation to the generations of my descendants unless I acquire through evil arts such an exalted principate that later generations cannot remain silent about it.”

A ruined mind, deprived of good arts and alienated from the light of justice, contrives through evil arts a path to such enduring fame that it may even be celebrated among later generations. Those who cannot become well known desire at least that people speak evil of them, provided that their name may spread as widely as possible.

I think this is what is meant here: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.”

There is another interpretation. If a vain and error-filled mind thinks that it cannot pass from mortal generation to the generation of eternity unless through evil arts—something which was also spread abroad concerning Simon (Acts 8:9–23), when he thought that by criminal arts he had acquired heaven and could pass from human generation into divine generation through magical practices—what wonder is it if that man of sin, who will complete all the wickedness and impiety begun by all the false prophets, and will perform such great signs that, if possible, even the elect will be deceived, says in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil”?

25. [verse 7.] “His mouth is full of his curse” [Note: Thus several manuscripts of good quality, in accordance with the LXX: “his mouth is full.”], “and of bitterness and deceit.”

For it is a great curse to seek heaven through such abominable arts and to acquire such merits as would obtain an eternal dwelling.

But his mouth is full of this curse. This desire will not achieve its object; it will have power only within his mouth, for his destruction—he who has dared to promise these things to himself—with bitterness and deceit, that is, with anger and the snares by which he will turn the multitude to his party.

“Under his tongue are labor and pain.” Nothing is more laborious than iniquity and impiety. Pain follows that labor, because one labors not only without fruit but also toward destruction.

This labor and pain refer to what he said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation without evil.” Therefore it is “under his tongue,” not “in his tongue,” because he will think these things secretly while saying other things to human beings, so that he may appear good, just, and a son of God.

26. [verse 8.] “He sits in ambush with the rich.” With which rich people, except those whom he will heap up with the gifts of this age?

He is therefore said to sit in ambush with them because he will display their false happiness in order to deceive human beings. Those who desire to be such people through perverse will and do not seek eternal goods will fall into his snares.

“In secret, to kill the innocent.” I think “in secret” refers to the place where it is not easily understood what should be sought and what should be avoided. To kill the innocent is to make an innocent person guilty.

27. [verse 9.] [Col. 0128] “His eyes look toward the poor.” For he will chiefly persecute the righteous, of whom it was said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

“He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.” He calls him a lion in his den in whom both force and deceit will operate.

The first persecution of the Church was violent, when through proscriptions, tortures, and killings Christians were forced to sacrifice. The second persecution is deceitful, which is now carried out through various heretics and false brothers. The third remains, destined to come through the Antichrist. Nothing will be more dangerous than it, because it will be both violent and deceitful.

He will possess force in his imperial power and deceit in his miracles. The word “lion” refers to force; the words “in his den” refer to deceit.

And again the same things are repeated in reverse order. “He lies in wait,” he says, “to seize the poor.” This pertains to deceit. But what follows—“seizing the poor as he draws him”—is assigned to violence. For “he draws him” means that he brings him to himself by inflicting whatever tortures he can.

28. [verse 10.] The two things that follow are likewise the same.

“In his trap he will humble him”: this is deceit.

“He will bend down and fall when he has dominion over the poor”: this is force. The trap aptly signifies ambush; domination, however, most clearly conveys terror.

And he says well, “He will humble him in his trap.” When he begins to perform those signs, the more wondrous they appear to human beings, the more those saints who will exist at that time will be despised and regarded as worthless. He will appear to overcome them by marvelous deeds, although they resist him through justice and innocence.

“But he will bend down and fall when he has dominion over the poor”—that is, when he inflicts whatever punishments he can upon the servants of God who resist him.

29. [verses 11, 12.] [Col. 0129] But why will he bend down and fall?

“For he said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so as not to see unto the end.”

This is the most wretched bending and fall: when the human mind seems to prosper in its iniquities and thinks that it is being spared, while it is being blinded and reserved for the final and appropriate vengeance. Concerning this vengeance he now speaks:

“Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted”—that is, let your power be made manifest.

Earlier he had said: “Arise, Lord; let man not prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight”—that is, in secret, where God alone sees.

This occurred when the impious reached the great happiness that appears to human beings. Over them a lawgiver was appointed, such as they deserved to have, concerning whom it is said: “Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are human beings.”

But now, after that hidden punishment and vengeance, it is said: “Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted”—not in secret, but now in the most manifest glory.

“Do not forget the poor forever”—that is, as the impious suppose, who say: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so as not to see unto the end.”

Those who say that God does not see “unto the end” deny that he sees human and earthly affairs. For the earth is, as it were, the end of things, since it is the final element in which human beings labor in an ordered manner, although they cannot see the order of their labors. This order pertains chiefly to the hidden things of the Son.

The Church, therefore, laboring in those times like a ship amid great waves and storms, awakens the Lord as though he were sleeping, so that he may command the winds and tranquility may return. Thus she says: “Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor forever.”

30. [verses 13, 14.] Now, understanding the manifest judgment and rejoicing, they say: “Why has the impious man provoked God?” That is, what did it profit him to do such great evils?

“For he said in his heart: He will not inquire.”

Then follows: “For you see labor and anger” [Note: Lov. adds “and pain,” which is absent from the other books and from the Greek.] “so that you may hand them over into your hands.”

This passage requires careful phrasing; if it is pronounced incorrectly, its meaning becomes obscure. For the impious man said in his heart, “God will not inquire,” as though God considered labor and anger in order to hand them over into his hands—that is, as though God feared to labor and become angry, and therefore spared them lest their punishment prove burdensome to him, or lest he be disturbed by a storm of anger [Note: The printed editions read, “lest he be disturbed by wrath and a storm”; this is absent from the manuscripts.], as human beings often conceal vengeance so that they may not labor or become angry [Note: Thus manuscripts of good quality. The printed editions instead read: “who, concealing vengeance, labor lest they become angry.”].

31. “The poor person is left to you.” For he is poor precisely because he has despised all the temporal goods of this world, so that you alone may be his hope.

“You will be the helper of the orphan”—that is, of the one whose father, this world through which he was begotten carnally, is dying, and who can now say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

For God becomes the father of such orphans. The Lord teaches that his disciples are to become orphans, to whom he says: “Do not call anyone your father on earth” (Matthew 23:9).

He himself first provided an example of this when he said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” (ibid. 12:48). Hence certain most pernicious heretics [Note: The Manichaeans] wish to assert that he had no mother. They do not see that, if they attend to these words, it follows that his disciples also had no fathers. For just as he said, “Who is my mother?” so he taught them when he said: “Do not call anyone your father on earth.”

32. [verses 15, 16.] “Break the arm of the sinner and the evil man”—namely, the one of whom it was said above: “He will rule over all his enemies.”

His arm, therefore, means his power. Opposed to it is the power of Christ, concerning which it is said: “Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted.”

“His sin will be sought, and it will not be found.” Because of that—that is [Note: The printed editions read: “Because of that same thing.” Several manuscripts read: “Because of that, that is.”]—he will be judged for his sin, and he himself will perish because of his sin.

Then what wonder is it if the following comes next? “The Lord will reign forever and ever; you will perish, nations, from his land.” He uses “nations” to mean sinners and impious people.

33. [verse 17.] [Col. 0130] “The Lord heard the desire of the poor”—that desire with which they burned when, amid the distresses and tribulations of this age, they longed for the day of the Lord.

“Your ear heard the preparation of their heart.” This is the preparation of the heart of which it is sung in another psalm: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Psalm 56:8), and of which the Apostle says: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:25).

As for the ear of God, we must understand it according to the rule not as a bodily member, but as the power by which he hears. Likewise, whenever his other members are named—members that are visible and bodily in us—we ought to understand them as powers of operation, lest these expressions continually be repeated. For it is not permissible to think that the Lord God, who hears not a sounding voice but the preparation of the heart, is corporeal.

34. [verse 18.] “To judge for the orphan and the humble”—that is, not for the person who is conformed to this age, nor for the proud person.

For it is one thing to judge the orphan and another to judge for the orphan. Even one who condemns judges the orphan; but one judges for the orphan who pronounces a sentence on his behalf.

“So that man may no longer continue to exalt himself over the earth.” These are the human beings of whom it was said: “Appoint, Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are human beings.”

But even the one who is understood to be appointed over them in that same place will be a human being. Concerning him it is now said: “So that man may no longer continue to exalt himself over the earth”—namely, when the Son of Man comes to judge for the orphan, who has stripped off the old human being and in this way has, as it were, exalted the Father.

35. After the hidden things concerning the Son, of which much has been said in this psalm, there will be revealed things concerning the Son, of which a few have now been said at the end of the same psalm. From the former words, however, the title was formed, since they occupy the greater part here. The very day of the Lord’s coming may also rightly be numbered among the hidden things concerning the Son, although the Lord’s presence itself will be manifest; for of that day it was said that no one knows it—not the angels, nor the Powers, nor the Son of man (Matt. XXIV, 36). What, then, is so hidden as that which is said to have been hidden even from the Judge himself—not for the purpose of knowing it, but of declaring it?

As for the hidden things concerning the Son, even if someone prefers to understand not the Son of God but David himself, whose name is assigned to the whole Psalter—for they are certainly called Davidic psalms—let him hear those words addressed to the Lord: “Have mercy on us, son of David” (ibid. XX, 30); and in this way also let him understand the same Lord Christ, concerning whose hidden things this psalm is inscribed. For thus the angel also says: “God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke I, 32).

Nor is that statement contrary to this interpretation in which the same Lord asks the Jews: “If Christ is the son of David, how does he call him Lord in the Spirit, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet’?” (Matt. XXII, 44). This was said to the unlearned, who, although they hoped that Christ would come, nevertheless expected him according to his humanity, not according to the fact that he is the Power and Wisdom of God. There he therefore teaches the truest and most sincere faith: the Lord is both David’s Lord, insofar as he is the Word who was in the beginning, God with God, through whom all things were made (John I, 1), and his son, insofar as he was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. I, 3). [Col. 0131] For he does not say, “Christ is not the son of David,” but rather: “If you already hold that he is his son, learn how he is his Lord. Do not hold on to what Christ is as son of man—for in that respect he is David’s son—while abandoning what he is as Son of God—for in that respect he is David’s Lord.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM X

*To the end; a psalm for David himself.*

1. [Vers. 1–2.] This title requires no new treatment; for what “to the end” means has already been discussed sufficiently. Let us therefore examine the text of the psalm itself. It seems to me that it should be sung against the heretics [Note: [Col. 0131] Against the Donatists.], who, by recalling and exaggerating the sins of many in the Church—as though either all or most of them were righteous among themselves—attempt to turn us away and tear us from the nourishing breasts of the one true mother, the Church. They assert that Christ is with them and, as though piously and earnestly admonishing us, urge us to cross over to them and so migrate to Christ, whom they falsely claim to possess.

It is well known that Christ, when he was allegorically indicated in prophecy under many names, was also called a mountain. These people must therefore be answered and told: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?” I hold fast to one mountain in which I trust; how do you tell me to cross over to you, as though there were many Christs? Or, if you call yourselves mountains through pride, one must indeed be a winged sparrow through virtues and the commandments of God; but these very things forbid flying to such mountains and placing one’s hope in proud men.

I have a house where I may rest, because I trust in the Lord; for “the sparrow also has found a house for itself” (Ps. LXXXIII, 4), and “the Lord became a refuge for the poor” (Ps. IX, 10). Let us therefore say with complete confidence, lest while seeking Christ among the heretics we lose him: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?”

2. [Vers. 3.] “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot at those who are upright in heart under the darkened moon.” These are the terrors of those who threaten us with sinners, urging us to cross over to them as though they were righteous. “Behold,” they say, “sinners have bent the bow”—I suppose, the Scriptures, from which, by interpreting them carnally, they shoot forth poisoned statements. “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver”: that is, they have prepared in the secrecy of their hearts the very words with which they are going to shoot, relying on the authority of Scripture. “To shoot at those who are upright in heart under the darkened moon”: when they perceive that the light of the Church has been darkened because of the multitude of the ignorant and the carnal, and that they cannot be refuted, they corrupt good morals through evil conversations (1 Cor. XV, 33). But against all these terrors it must be said: “In the Lord I trust.”

3. I remember that I promised to consider in this psalm how fittingly the moon signifies the Church [Note: [Col. 0131] Above, in the Exposition of Psalm VIII, no. 9.]. There are two plausible opinions concerning the moon; which of them is true, or whether either is entirely true, I think a human being can know either not at all or only with the greatest difficulty.

When it is asked where the moon receives its light, some say that it has light of its own, but that half of its sphere is shining and half dark. As it moves in its orbit, they say, it gradually turns toward the earth the same part by which it shines, so that it can be seen by us; and for this reason it first appears, as it were, horned. If you make a ball half white and half dark, and hold the dark part before your eyes, you see no whiteness. When you begin turning the white part toward your eyes, and do so gradually, you first see the horns of whiteness; then the bright portion gradually increases until the whole shining half is turned toward your eyes and none of the darkness of the other half is visible. If you continue turning it gradually, the darkness begins to appear and the whiteness to diminish, until it returns again to the horns and finally is turned entirely away from the eyes, so that the dark half alone can be seen.

They say that this occurs when the moon’s light appears to increase until the fifteenth day and then to diminish again until the thirtieth, returning to the horns until no light at all is visible in it.

According to this opinion, the moon signifies the Church allegorically, because the Church shines in its spiritual part but is dark in its carnal part. At times its spiritual part appears to human beings in good works; at other times it lies hidden in the conscience and is known only to God, while only the body appears to human beings. This happens when we pray in our heart and seem to be doing almost nothing, although we are commanded to have our hearts lifted upward to the Lord rather than toward the earth.

Others say that the moon has no light of its own but is illuminated by the sun. When it is with the sun, they say, it presents to us the part that is not illuminated, and therefore no light is seen in it. When it begins to withdraw from the sun, it is illuminated on the side turned toward the earth, necessarily beginning at the horns, until it becomes full on the fifteenth day opposite the sun. For then it rises at sunset, so that anyone who has been watching the setting sun, once he can no longer see it, may turn toward the east and see the moon rising.

From that point, as the moon again begins to draw near the sun on the other side, it turns toward us the part that is not illuminated, until it returns to the horns and then disappears completely. For at that time the part that is illuminated is above, toward heaven, while toward the earth is the part upon which the sun cannot cast its rays.

According to this opinion also, the moon is understood to signify the Church, because it does not possess its own light but is illuminated by the only-begotten Son of God, who in many places in the holy Scriptures is allegorically called the sun.

Certain heretics, not knowing him and being unable to see him, endeavor to turn the minds of the simple toward this corporeal and visible sun, which is the common light of human flesh and of flies; and they do turn away some who, as long as they cannot contemplate the inner light of truth with the mind, are unwilling to be content with the simple Catholic faith [Col. 0133], which alone is salvation for the little ones and through which alone, by a secure strength, one reaches the firmness of more solid food.

Whichever of these two opinions is true, the moon may appropriately be understood allegorically as the Church. Or, if one neither wishes nor has leisure, or if the mind itself is unable, to exercise itself in these obscurities, which demand more labor than they yield fruit, it is enough to observe the moon with ordinary eyes and not to seek obscure causes, but to experience along with everyone both its waxing, its fullness, and its waning. If it wanes in order to be renewed, it demonstrates even to the unlearned multitude the figure of the Church, in which the resurrection of the dead is believed.

4. Next we must ask what is meant in this psalm by the “darkened moon,” under which sinners prepared to shoot those who are upright in heart. For the darkened moon may be understood in more than one way. When it is ending through its monthly cycles, when its brightness is interrupted by cloud, and when it is eclipsed while full, it may be called a darkened moon.

It may therefore be understood of those who persecuted the martyrs: they wished to shoot at those upright in heart under the darkened moon, either while the Church was still in its infancy, because it had not yet shone more brightly than the earth or overcome the darkness of pagan superstition; or through the tongues of blasphemers and of those who maliciously slandered the Christian name. As though the earth were covered by clouds, the clear moon—that is, the Church—could not be seen.

Or perhaps the infirm were deterred from the Christian name by the slaughter of the martyrs and such a great shedding of blood, as though by that eclipse and darkening in which the moon seems to display a bloodstained face. In that terror the sinners hurled deceitful and sacrilegious words, so that they might pervert even those upright in heart.

It may also be understood of those sinners whom the Church contains: taking advantage of this darkened moon, they committed many offenses [Note: [Col. 0133] He touches on the crime of betrayal committed while the Church was tossed amid the storms of persecution. The Donatists maliciously brought this charge against the Catholics, although certain of their own leaders were rather proved by municipal records to have handed over the sacred books and the Church’s documents to the persecutors, as Augustine writes in Letter LXXVI, no. 2, and in CV, no. 2: “We would certainly show you,” he says, “that those who condemned Caecilian [the bishop of Carthage] and his associates as guilty of betrayal were themselves rather the betrayers.”]. These are the reproaches now cast at us by the heretics, although their own founders are said to have done such things.

But whatever may have happened under the darkened moon, now that the Catholic name has been spread and celebrated throughout the whole world, why should I be disturbed by things unknown to me? For “in the Lord I trust,” and I do not listen to those who say to my soul, “Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow.”

“For behold, sinners have bent the bow, to shoot at those who are upright in heart under the darkened moon.” Or if the moon now appears dark to them because they wish to make uncertain what is Catholic, and attempt to convict it on account of the sins of carnal people, whom it contains in great number, what does that matter to the one who truly says, “In the Lord I trust”? By this utterance each person shows himself to be both wheat and one who patiently endures the chaff until the time of winnowing.

5. “In the Lord, therefore, I trust.” Let those fear who trust in man and cannot deny that they belong to a human faction, by whose gray hairs they swear [Note: [Col. 0134] The Donatists swear by the gray hairs of Donatus.]. When they are asked in conversation whose communion they belong to, they cannot be recognized unless they say that they belong to that man’s faction.

Tell me what these people do when they are reminded of the countless daily sins and crimes with which that society is filled. Can they say, “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?” For they do not trust in the Lord when they say that the holy sacraments exist only if they are administered by holy people.

Accordingly, when they are asked who the holy people are, they are ashamed to say, “We are”; and even if they are not ashamed to say this, those who hear them are ashamed on their behalf. Thus they compel those who receive the sacraments to place their hope in a human being whose heart they cannot see. “And cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII, 5).

For what else does it mean to say, “What I give is holy,” than “Place your hope in me”? What if you are not holy? Or show your heart. If you cannot do that, where shall I see that you are holy? Perhaps you will say what is written: “You will know them by their works” (Matt. VII, 16). I plainly see marvelous works: the daily acts of violence of the Circumcellions, flying about everywhere under bishops and presbyters as their leaders; and I see them calling their dreadful clubs “Israels” [Note: [Col. 0134] Thus several manuscripts of good reputation. The printed editions, however, read: “the clubs of Israel are called.”], things that the people now living see and feel every day.

As for the times of Macarius [Note: [Col. 0134] The “times of Macarius,” during which the Donatists complained that they had suffered harsh persecution from the Catholics, belong approximately to the year 348, when Macarius and Paulus came to Africa, sent there by Constans to relieve the poverty of the needy by distributions and to bring the schismatics back to Catholic unity. Optatus discusses these events in Book III, and Augustine in Letter XLIV, nos. 4–5, and elsewhere.], about which they stir up resentment, many did not see them and no one now sees them. Whoever among the Catholics did see them could say, if he wished to be a servant of God, “In the Lord I trust.” He says the same now, when he sees in the Church many things he does not want to see, because he realizes that he is still swimming within those nets full of good and bad fish (ibid. XIII, 47), until the end of the sea is reached, where the bad will be separated from the good.

But what do these people answer if the person whom one of them baptizes says to him: “How do you command me to presume? For if merit belongs both to the one who gives and to the one who receives, let the merit of the giver be God’s, and that of the recipient my conscience. These two things are not uncertain to me: his goodness and my faith. What about the person placed between them, about whom I can know nothing with certainty? Let me say, ‘In the Lord I trust.’ For if I trust in you, on what grounds can I trust that you did nothing evil last night? Finally, if you want me to believe you, can I do more than believe something about you? How, then, can I trust those with whom you shared communion yesterday, share communion today, and will share communion tomorrow—whether during this three-day period they have committed no evil?”

If what we do not know neither pollutes you nor me, what reason is there for you to rebaptize those who know nothing of the times of the betrayal or of the resentment against Macarius? What reason is there for you to dare to rebaptize Christians coming from Mesopotamia, who have never even heard the names of Caecilian or Donatus, and to deny that they are Christians?

But if the sins of others, unknown to them, pollute them, then whatever is committed each day in your faction without your knowledge holds you guilty, while you bring the emperors’ constitutions against the Catholics in vain [Note: [Col. 0135] Here he refers to constitutions issued in the year 405.]. For in your own camps private clubs and fires rage so violently [Note: [Col. 0135] Thus the manuscripts. Most printed editions instead read: “Does whatever is committed each day in your faction without your knowledge make you guilty? You bring the emperors’ constitutions against the Catholics in vain,” and so forth.].

Behold where those people have fallen who, when they saw sinners in the Catholic Church, could not say, “In the Lord I trust,” and placed their hope in man. They would certainly say this if they themselves—or if they too—were not such as they supposed those to be from whom, in sacrilegious pride, they pretended to wish to separate themselves.

6. [Vers. 5.] Let the Catholic soul therefore say: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?” For “behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot at those who are upright in heart under the darkened moon.” Let it turn its speech from them to the Lord and say: “For they have destroyed what you have perfected.”

Let it say this not only against these people, but against all heretics. For, insofar as it lies within their power, they have all destroyed the praise that God perfected “from the mouths of infants and nursing babies” (Ps. VIII, 3), by harassing little ones with vain and scrupulous questions and not allowing them to be nourished by the milk of faith.

It is as though this soul had been asked: “Why do these people say to you, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’? Why do they terrify you with sinners who have bent the bow in order to shoot at those upright in heart under the darkened moon?” It answers: “They certainly terrify me because they have destroyed what you have perfected.” Where, if not in their conventicles, where they do not nourish little ones ignorant of the inner light with milk, but kill them with poisons?

“But what did the righteous man do?” If Macarius offended you, if Caecilian offended you, what did Christ do to you? He said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27)—the peace that you have violated by your wicked dissension.

What did Christ do to you? He endured his betrayer with such patience that he gave him, as he did the other apostles, the first Eucharist, prepared by his own hands and entrusted through his own mouth (Luke XXII, 19, 21).

What did Christ do to you? He sent the same betrayer, whom he called the devil (John VI, 71), and who, even before the Lord’s betrayal, could not be faithful with the Lord’s money-box (ibid. XII, 6), along with the other disciples to preach the kingdom of heaven (Matt. X, 5), in order to show that God’s gifts reach those who receive them with faith, even if the person through whom they receive them is such as Judas was.

7. [Vers. 4.] “The Lord is in his holy temple.” Indeed, as the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are. Whoever destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. III, 17).

He violates the temple of God who violates unity, for he does not hold fast to the Head (Col. II, 19), from whom the whole body, joined and compacted through every contact [Note: [Col. 0135] Greek: *aphês*.], through the supply of ministry, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, makes the body grow for its building up in love (Eph. IV, 16).

The Lord is in this holy temple of his, which consists of his many members, each carrying out its own functions, built together by love into one edifice. Whoever separates himself from the Catholic fellowship for the sake of his own primacy violates this temple.

“The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven.” If you understand “heaven” as the righteous, just as you understand “earth” as the sinner, to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. III, 19), then when it is said, “The Lord is in his holy temple,” you will understand it as repeated when it is said, “The Lord’s throne is in heaven.”

8. “His eyes look upon the poor.” Certainly, for the poor has been entrusted to him, and he has become a refuge for the poor (Ps. IX, 10). Therefore all the rebellions and disturbances within these nets, until they are brought to shore, about which the heretics taunt us to their own destruction and for our correction, are caused by people who refuse to be Christ’s poor.

But do they turn God’s eyes away from those who wish to be this? For “his eyes look upon the poor.” Should we fear that amid a crowd of rich people he cannot see the few poor whom he protects and nourishes within the bosom of the Catholic Church?

“His eyelids examine the sons of men.” Here I would gladly understand “sons of men” according to that rule as referring to those regenerated from the old through faith. They are exercised by certain obscure passages of Scripture, as though by God’s closed eyes, so that they may seek; and again, by certain clear passages, as though by God’s open eyes, they are illumined so that they may rejoice.

This frequent closing and opening in the holy books is like God’s eyelids, which examine—that is, test—the sons of men. They are neither wearied by the obscurity of things, but exercised by it, nor puffed up by knowledge, but strengthened.

9. [Vers. 6.] “The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked.” Why, then, do we fear that the wicked may harm us if they happen to share the sacraments with us without a sincere heart, when he examines both the righteous and the wicked?

“But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0136] This part of verse 6 is also treated in the Exposition of Psalm XCIII, no. 1, and elsewhere, no. 4.]: that is, the lover of iniquity harms only his own soul, not the person who believes in God and does not place his hope in man.

10. [Vers. 7–8.] “He will rain snares upon sinners.” If clouds are generally understood as the prophets, whether good or evil—for the evil are also called false prophets—then the false prophets are so directed by the Lord God that through them he rains snares upon sinners. No one falls among those who follow them except a sinner, whether for the preparation of the final punishment, if he has preferred to persist in sin, or for the dissuasion of pride, if at some point he seeks God with a more sincere concern [Note: [Col. 0136] Several manuscripts read *desudandam*; some, *dissuadendam*.].

But if only the good and true prophets are understood as clouds, it is equally clear that through them God rains snares upon sinners, although through them he also waters the pious so that they may bear fruit. “To some,” the Apostle says, “we are the aroma of life unto life, and to others the aroma of death unto death” (2 Cor. II, 16).

Not only prophets, but all who water souls with the word of God may be called clouds. When they are wrongly understood, God rains snares upon sinners; but when they are rightly understood, he makes the hearts of the pious and faithful fruitful.

For example, if someone interprets what is written, “The two will be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), in terms of lust, it rains a snare upon the sinner. But if you understand it as the one who says, “I speak of Christ and of the Church” (Eph. V, 32), then he rains upon fertile soil. The same cloud—that is, divine Scripture—has produced both results.

Likewise, the Lord says: “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out” (Matt. XV, 11). The sinner hears this and prepares his throat for gluttony; the righteous person hears it and is protected from superstition concerning the distinction of foods. Here too, from the same cloud of Scripture, according to each person’s merit, both a rain of snares has been poured upon the sinner and a rain of abundance upon the righteous.

11. “Fire and sulphur and the spirit of tempest are the portion of their cup.” This is the punishment and end of those through whom God’s name is blasphemed: first they are ravaged by the fire of their desires; then, through the stench of evil works, they are cast out from the assembly of the blessed; finally, carried away and submerged, they suffer unspeakable punishments.

For this is the portion of their cup, just as the cup of the righteous is: “How excellent is your inebriating cup!” (Ps. XXII, 5). “They will be inebriated by the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV, 9).

I think it is called a cup so that we may not suppose that, through divine providence, anything occurs beyond due measure or proportion, even in the punishments of sinners. Therefore, as though giving the reason why this happens, he adds: “For the Lord is righteous, and he has loved righteousness.”

He does not say “righteousnesses” in the plural without reason, unless because he speaks of human beings, so that “righteousnesses” may be understood as standing for the righteous. For in the many righteous, many righteousnesses seem to exist, although there is one righteousness belonging to God, in which all participate. It is as though one face were reflected in many mirrors: what is singular in the face is represented in the plural by the many mirrors.

For this reason he returns again to the singular when he says: “His face has seen equity.” Perhaps the phrase “His face has seen equity” has been put for the meaning: “Equity has been seen in his face,” that is, in the knowledge of him. For God’s face is the power by which he makes himself known to those who are worthy.

Or certainly, “His face has seen equity,” because he does not offer himself to be known by the wicked but by the good—and this itself is equity.

12. If someone wishes to understand the moon as the synagogue, let him refer the psalm to the Lord’s Passion and say of the Jews: “For they have destroyed what you have perfected”; and of the Lord himself: “But what did the righteous man do?” They accused him as a destroyer of the Law, whose commandments they had destroyed by living perversely, despising them, and establishing their own.

Thus the Lord himself may be understood to speak according to his humanity, as he often does, saying: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountains like a sparrow’?”—because of the terrors of those who wished to seize and crucify him.

The sinners who wished to shoot those upright in heart—that is, those who had believed in Christ—under the darkened moon, that is, the synagogue filled with sinners, may appropriately be understood in this way.

This also corresponds to what is said: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” [Col. 0138]—that is, the Word in man, or the Son of man himself who is in heaven.

“His eyes look upon the poor”: either the one whom he assumed according to God, or the one for whose sake he suffered according to humanity.

“His eyelids examine the sons of men.” We may understand the closing and opening of the eyes—which it is plausible to regard as indicated by the name “eyelids”—as his death and resurrection, where he proved his disciples, the sons of men: terrified by his Passion and made joyful by his resurrection.

“The Lord examines the righteous and the wicked”: now governing the Church from heaven.

“But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.” Why this is so, the following words teach: “For he will rain snares upon sinners,” which must be understood according to the exposition given above, as must everything else through the end of the psalm.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XI

*To the end; for the eighth; a psalm of David.*

1. [Vers. 1.] That the eighth day can be understood as the day of judgment was stated in the sixth psalm. “For the eighth” can also be understood as “for the eternal age,” because after this period, which turns in the cycle of seven days, it will be given to the saints.

2. [Vers. 2.] “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed”—that is, he is not found, just as we say, “The grain has failed,” or “The money has failed.” “For truths have been diminished among the sons of men.” There is one truth by which holy souls are illumined; but because souls are many, many truths can be spoken of in them, just as many images appear in mirrors from one face.

3. [Vers. 3.] “Each person has spoken vanity to his neighbor.” Every human being should be understood as one’s neighbor, because there is no one with whom evil ought to be done, and “love does no evil to one’s neighbor” (Rom. XIII, 10).

“Deceitful lips have spoken evil with a heart and a heart” [Note: [Col. 0138] The printed editions read “vanity.” The manuscripts read “evil.”]. The fact that he says “with a heart and a heart” twice signifies a divided heart.

4. [Vers. 4.] “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips.” He says “all,” so that no one may think himself excepted, as the Apostle says: “Upon every soul of man that works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek” (ibid. II, 9).

“A tongue speaking great things”: a proud tongue.

5. [Vers. 5.] “Those who said: ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips are with us; who is our lord?’” Proud hypocrites are signified, placing their hope in their own speech in order to deceive human beings and refusing submission to God.

6. [Vers. 6.] “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0138] The same verse is explained in the Exposition of Psalm XCIII, no. 7.]. For in the Gospel the Lord himself pitied his people because they had no ruler, although they were capable of obeying well. Hence it is also said in the Gospel: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. IX, 37).
