This must be understood as spoken in the person of God the Father, who, because of the needy [Note: [Col. 0139] Eight manuscripts read “therefore, to the needy.”] and the poor—that is, those lacking and deprived of spiritual goods—deigned to send his Son.

His speech in Matthew begins from this point on the mountain, when he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. V, 3).

“I will place [it] in salvation.” He did not say what he would place; but “in salvation” must be understood as referring to Christ, according to the saying: “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 30). Therefore he is understood to have placed in him what pertains to removing the misery of the needy and comforting the groaning of the poor.

“I will act boldly in him,” according to the Gospel saying: “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes” (Matt. VII, 29).

7. [Vers. 7.] “The words of the Lord are pure words.” This is the person of the prophet himself. “The words of the Lord are pure words”: he calls them pure, without the corruption of pretense. For many preach the truth impurely, because they sell it for the price of this world’s advantages. Of such people the Apostle says that they proclaim Christ “not purely” (Phil. I, 17).

“Silver tested by fire in the earth”: the words of the Lord are tested through tribulations for sinners.

“Purified sevenfold”: through fear of God, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom (Isa. XI, 2).

For there are also seven degrees of blessedness, which the Lord sets forth in the same discourse that he delivered on the mountain, according to Matthew: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the pure in heart; blessed are the peacemakers” (Matt. V, 3–9).

It may be observed that the whole of that lengthy discourse was spoken through these seven statements. For the eighth, where it says, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” signifies the very fire by which the silver is tested sevenfold.

When that discourse had ended, it was said: “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes” (ibid. VII, 29). This pertains to what is said in this psalm: “I will act boldly in him.”

8. [Vers. 8.] “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation and forever” [Note: [Col. 0139] Thus the better manuscripts, following the Septuagint: “from this generation forever.”]: here as needy and poor, there as wealthy and rich.

9. [Vers. 9.] “The wicked walk in a circle” [Note: [Col. 0139] The same verse is treated in the Exposition of Psalm CXXXIX, no. 13.]: that is, in desire for temporal things, which turns like a wheel through the repeated cycle of seven days. Therefore they do not reach the eighth, that is, eternity, for which this psalm is titled.

Thus it is also said through Solomon: “A wise king is a winnower of the wicked and sets the wheel of evils upon them” (Prov. XX, 26, according to the Septuagint).

“According to your exaltation you have multiplied the sons of men.” There is also a multiplication in temporal things that turns people away from the unity of God. Hence “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

But the righteous are multiplied according to the exaltation of God when they go “from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XII

*To the end; a psalm of David.*

1. [Vers. 1.] “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

“How long, Lord, will you forget me forever?” That is: How long will you defer my understanding of Christ spiritually—Christ who is the Wisdom of God and the proper end of every purpose of the soul?

“How long will you turn your face away from me?” Just as God does not forget, so neither does he turn away his face; but Scripture speaks according to our manner of speaking. God is said to turn his face away when he does not grant the soul knowledge of himself, because it does not yet possess a pure eye of the mind.

2. [Vers. 2.] “How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” Counsel is needed only in adversity. Therefore, “How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” means: How long shall I remain in adversity?

Or certainly this is an answer, so that the meaning is: “You will forget me forever, Lord, and you will turn your face away from me for as long as I place counsel in my soul.” Unless each person places counsel in his soul so as to perform mercy perfectly, God will neither direct him to the end nor grant him full knowledge of himself—that is, face to face.

“Grief in my heart by day?” The phrase “how long shall I place” is understood. “By day” signifies continuation, so that “day” is understood as a period of time. Anyone who desires to be freed from that period places grief in his heart, praying to ascend to eternal things and not endure the human day.

3. [Vers. 3.] “How long will my enemy be exalted over me?” Either the devil or carnal habit.

4. [Vers. 4.] “Look upon me and hear me, Lord my God.” “Look upon me” refers to what was said: “How long will you turn your face away from me?” “Hear me” refers to what was said: “How long will you forget me forever?”

“Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” [Note: [Col. 0140] The old Corbie manuscript, following the Septuagint, reads: “lest I ever sleep into death.”]. The eyes of the heart must be understood, lest they be closed by the pleasurable collapse of sin.

5. [Vers. 5.] “Lest my enemy ever say: ‘I have prevailed against him.’” The devil’s taunt must be feared.

“Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved.” The devil and his angels did not rejoice over the righteous man Job when they troubled him, because he was not moved (Job I, 22)—that is, he did not depart from the stability of faith.

6. [Vers. 6.] “But I have hoped in your mercy.” Because the fact that a human being is not moved and remains fixed in the Lord must not be attributed to himself, lest, when he boasts that he has not been moved, he be moved by that very pride.

“My heart will rejoice in your salvation”: in Christ, in the Wisdom of God.

“I will sing to the Lord, who has bestowed good things upon me”: spiritual goods, not things belonging to the human day.

[Col. 0141] “And I will sing psalms to the name of the Most High Lord”—that is, I give thanks with joy and use my body in the most orderly manner; this is the song of the spiritual soul.

But if some distinction is to be considered here: I will sing with the heart; I will sing psalms through works to the Lord, who alone sees this [Note: [Col. 0141] Lov. reads *qui*; Erasmus and the manuscripts read *quod*.]. But I will sing to the name of the Lord, which becomes known among human beings. This is useful not to him but to us.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XIII

*To the end; a psalm for David himself.*
1. **[Verse 1.]** What “for the end” means need not be repeated so often. For “the end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4), as the Apostle says. We believe in him when we begin to enter upon the good way; we shall see him when we have arrived; and therefore he himself is the end.

The fool said in his heart: **“There is no God.”** For not even certain sacrilegious and detestable philosophers who hold perverse and false opinions about God have dared to say, “There is no God.” Therefore it says, “He said in his heart,” because no one dares to say this, even if he has dared to think it.

They are corrupt and have become abominable in their affections—that is, while they love this world and do not love God. These are the affections that corrupt the soul and so blind it that the fool can even say in his heart, “There is no God.” For, because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind (Romans 1:28).

[Note: Most manuscripts here and elsewhere consistently have, “into knowledge.”]

There is no one who does good, not even one. “Not even one” may be understood either together with the one, so that no human being is meant; or as “apart from the one,” so that the Lord Christ is meant. Thus we say, “This field extends as far as the sea,” without counting the sea itself as part of the field. This is the better interpretation: no one is understood to have done good as far as Christ, because no human being can do good unless Christ has shown it. And this is true: until each person comes to know the one God, he cannot do good.

2. **[Verse 2.]** The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God. This may be understood of the Jews, whom he called more honorably “children of men” because of their worship of the one God, in comparison with the Gentiles, of whom I think the preceding statement was made: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God,’” and so forth.

The Lord looks down in order to see through his holy souls. This signifies what was said by “from heaven,” for nothing is hidden from him in himself.

3. **[Verse 3.]** All have turned aside; together they have become useless—that is, the Jews have become such as the Gentiles were, of whom the preceding words were spoken. There is no one who does good, not even one. This is to be understood in the same way as above.

Their throat is an open tomb. Either the voracity of a gaping appetite is signified, or, allegorically, those who kill and, as it were, devour the people whom they have slain by persuading them of the perversity of their own conduct. The contrary is like what was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13), so that he might convert the Gentiles to his faith and good conduct.

They acted deceitfully with their tongues. Flattery accompanies the voracious and all evil people.

The poison of asps is under their lips. He calls deceit “poison”; and “of asps,” because they refuse to hear the commands of the Law, just as asps refuse to hear the words of the enchanter (Psalm 57:5)—something said more plainly in another psalm.

Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. This is the poison of asps.

Their feet are swift to shed blood, through their habitual practice of wrongdoing.

[Note: Thus according to Ambrosianus and the manuscripts. **Here he shows the habitual practice.**]

Destruction and misery are in their ways. For all the ways of evil people are full of toil and misery. Therefore the Lord cries out: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

And they have not known the way of peace—that is, the way that the Lord, as I have said, recalls in the easy yoke and light burden.

There is no fear of God before their eyes. These people do not say, “There is no God,” but nevertheless they do not fear God.

4. **[Verse 4.]** Will not all who work iniquity understand? He threatens judgment.

They devour my people as the food of bread—that is, daily; for bread is daily food.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and seven Gallican manuscripts have, “They devour my people in the food of bread.” The Greek Septuagint supports this.]

They devour the people when they take their own advantages from them, without directing their ministry toward the glory of God and the salvation of those over whom they preside.

5. **[Verse 5.]** They did not call upon the Lord. For the one who desires what displeases him does not truly call upon him.

There they trembled with fear where there was no fear—that is, over the loss of temporal possessions. For they said: “If we leave him like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48).

They feared losing an earthly kingdom where there was no fear, and they lost the kingdom of heaven, which they ought to have feared losing. The same is to be understood of all temporal advantages: when people fear their loss, they do not come to eternal things.

6. **[Verse 6.]** For God is in the righteous generation—that is, he is not in those who love the world. For it is unjust to abandon the Creator of the ages, love the world, and serve the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25).

You have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope. That is, you despised the humble coming of the Son of God because you did not see in him the pomp of the world, so that those whom he called would place their hope in God alone, not in passing things.

7. **[Verse 7.]** Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? The words “except the one whose humility you despised?” are understood. For he will come in glory to judge the living and the dead and to establish the kingdom of the righteous.

Since, through that humble coming, a partial blindness has come upon Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Romans 11:25), what follows will be fulfilled in that other coming, and thus all Israel will be saved. For, concerning the Jews, the Apostle also applies the testimony of Isaiah that says: “A deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isaiah 59:20). So here too it is said: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will exult and Israel will rejoice. This is a repetition, as often happens; for I think “Israel will rejoice” means the same as “Jacob will exult.”

## Exposition of Psalm XIV

[Note: Another exposition of this psalm is added at the end of the volume.]

**“A Psalm of David himself.”**

1. **[Verse 1.]** There is no question concerning this title.

Lord, who will sojourn in your tabernacle? Although “tabernacle” is sometimes used for an eternal dwelling, when it is taken literally it is a military term. Hence soldiers who have their tents together are called *contubernales*, “tent-companions.” This interpretation is supported by the words, “Who will sojourn?” For we fight against the devil for a time, and then a tabernacle is needed in which we may be refreshed. This signifies above all the faith of the temporal dispensation that was enacted for us temporally through the Lord’s incarnation.

And who will rest upon your holy mountain? This perhaps already signifies the eternal dwelling itself, so that we understand the mountain as the surpassing height of Christ’s love in eternal life.

[Note: Six manuscripts have, “into eternal life.”]

2. **[Verse 2.]** The one who enters without blemish and practices righteousness. Here he has proposed the subject; thereafter he develops it.

[Note: The manuscripts have, “Here he proposed.” This may be better.]

3. **[Verse 3.]** The one who speaks truth in his heart. For some have truth on their lips but do not have it in their heart. It is as if someone were deceitfully pointing out a road, knowing that there are robbers on it, and said, “If you go by this road, you will be safe from robbers,” and it happened that no robbers were actually found there. He spoke the truth, but not in his heart: he thought otherwise and, without knowing it, spoke the truth. Therefore it is not enough to speak truth unless it is also true in the heart.

The one who has not practiced deceit with his tongue. Deceit is practiced with the tongue when one thing is brought forth by the mouth and another is concealed in the breast.

Nor has he done evil to his neighbor. It is well known that every human being must be understood as one’s neighbor.

Nor has he accepted reproach against his neighbor—that is, he has not willingly or rashly believed an accuser.

4. **[Verse 4.]** The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight. This is perfection: that the wicked person have no power over anyone, and that this be “in his sight”—that is, that he know with complete certainty that one is wicked only when the mind turns away from the eternal and unchangeable form of its Creator toward the form of the creature, which was made from nothing.

But he glorifies those who fear the Lord—clearly, the Lord himself does so.

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Psalm 110:10; Sirach 1:16). Therefore, just as the preceding statements concern the perfect, so what he is now about to say concerns beginners.

5. **[Verse 5.]** The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive; who has not lent his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent.

[Note: Five manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, have “against the innocent person.” The other manuscripts and editions have “against the innocent,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.]

[Note: The same verse 5 is treated in *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 36, Sermon 3, no. 6.]

These are not great things. But if someone cannot even do these things, much less can he speak truth in his heart and refrain from deceit with his tongue, expressing outwardly what is true in his heart and having in his mouth, “Yes, yes; No, no” (Matthew 5:37); nor can he refrain from doing evil to his neighbor—that is, to any human being—or from accepting reproach against his neighbor. These latter things belong to the perfect, in whose sight the wicked person is brought to nothing.

Nevertheless, he concludes even these lesser matters in this way: The one who does these things will not be shaken forever. That is, he will arrive at those greater things in which there is great and unshaken stability. Perhaps the difference in tense is also not without reason: in the preceding conclusion the past tense was used—“The wicked person is brought to nothing in his sight”—whereas here the future is used—“He will not be shaken forever.”

## Exposition of Psalm XV

**“The inscription of the title, of David himself.”**

1. Our King speaks in this psalm from the standpoint of his assumption of humanity. The royal title inscribed at the time of his Passion stood out prominently.

[Note: The editions have *emicuit*, “shone forth.” The manuscripts have *eminuit*, “stood out prominently.”]

2. **[Verses 1–2.]** He says:

Preserve me, Lord, because I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord, “You are my God,” because you do not need my good things—that is, you do not expect to become blessed through my good things.

[Note: On the same verse 2, see *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 69, no. 7.]

3. **[Verse 3.]** For the saints who are in his land: for the saints who have placed their hope in the land of the living, the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose spiritual way of life is fixed through the anchor of hope in that homeland, which is rightly called God’s land, although they still live in the flesh in these lands.

He has made all my desires wonderful in them.

[Note: The editions have *mirificavi*, “I made wonderful,” and consequently *miras feci*, “I made wonderful.” But Augustine follows the other reading, which we restore here on the authority of the manuscripts, in Letter 149 to Paulinus, where he expounds verses 3 and 4 of this psalm.]

In these saints, therefore, he made all my desires wonderful as they advanced, when they came to understand how the humanity of my divinity benefited them by my dying, and the divinity of my humanity by my rising again.

4. **[Verse 4.]** Their infirmities have been multiplied—not for destruction, but so that they would desire a physician.

[Note: On the same verse 4, see *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 58, Sermon 2, no. 8.]

Afterward they hastened. Thus, after their infirmities had multiplied, they hastened to be healed.

I will not gather their assemblies from blood. Their assemblies will not be carnal, nor, propitiated by the blood of animals, will I gather them.

Nor will I remember their names through my lips. Rather, through a spiritual transformation they will forget what they once were. They will no longer be called by me sinners, enemies, or human beings, but righteous people, my brothers, and children of God through my peace.

5. **[Verse 5.]** The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.

[Note: The same verse 5 is treated in *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 34, Sermon 1, no. 12.]

For they will possess the Lord himself as an inheritance with me. Let others choose for themselves portions in which to take pleasure, earthly and temporal things: the portion of the saints is the eternal Lord.

Let others drink deadly pleasures: the Lord is the portion of my cup.

When I say “my,” I include the Church, because where the head is, there is also the body. For I will gather their assemblies into an inheritance, and through the drunkenness of the cup I will forget their former names.

You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me. Thus the glory that I had with you before the world existed will be known also to those whom I set free (John 17:5). You will not restore to me what I did not lose; rather, you will restore to those who lost the knowledge of that glory. Since I am in them, you will restore it to me.

6. **[Verse 6.]** The measuring lines have fallen to me in splendid places: the boundaries of my possession have fallen by lot in your glory, as though God were the possession of the priests and Levites.

For my inheritance is splendid to me. My inheritance is splendid—not to everyone, but to those who see it. Since I am in them, it is splendid to me.

7. **[Verse 7.]** I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding, by which this inheritance can be seen and possessed.

Moreover, even until night my kidneys have corrected me. Beyond understanding, my lower part—my assumption of flesh—has instructed me even unto death, so that I might experience the darkness of mortality, which that understanding does not possess.

8. **[Verse 8.]** I set the Lord always before me.

[Note: On the same verse 8 above, see column 105, no. 11, near the end.]

But when I came into things that pass away, I did not take my eye away from him who always remains. I did this so that, after temporal matters had been completed, I might return to him.

Because he is at my right hand, I will not be shaken: because he favors me, so that I may remain steadfastly in him.

9. **[Verse 9.]** Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted: therefore there was rejoicing in my thoughts and exultation in my words.

Moreover, my flesh will rest in hope. Moreover, my flesh will not perish into destruction, but will sleep in the hope of resurrection.

10. **[Verse 10.]** For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld.

[Note: Three manuscripts have “into the underworld.” The Greek Septuagint has *eis hadēn*, “into Hades.”]

For you will not give my soul to the underworld to be possessed.

Nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption. You will not permit the sanctified body, through which others also are to be sanctified, to be corrupted.

You have made known to me the paths of life. Through me you have made known the paths of humility, so that human beings might return to life, from which they had fallen through pride. Since I am in them, you have made them known to me.

You will fill me with joy with your countenance. You will fill them with joy, so that they will seek nothing further when they have seen you face to face. Since I am in them, you will fill me.

Pleasures are at your right hand to the end. There is pleasure in your favor and reconciliation along the journey of this life, leading to the end of the glory of your presence.

## Exposition of Psalm XVI

**“A prayer of David himself.”**

1. **[Verses 1–2.]** This is to be attributed to the person of the Lord, together with the Church, which is his body.

2. Hear, O God, my righteousness; attend to my prayer. Give ear to my prayer, not proceeding to you from deceitful lips—that is, not proceeding to you upon deceitful lips.

Let my judgment come forth from your presence. From the illumination of your knowledge, let me judge truly; or certainly, let my judgment not come forth from your presence on deceitful lips, so that I do not pronounce judgment on something other than what I understand in you.

Let my eyes see equity—clearly, the eyes of the heart.

3. **[Verse 3.]** You have tested my heart and visited it by night, because my heart itself was tested by the visitation of tribulation.

You have examined me with fire, and in me no iniquity was found. It is not only night, because it is accustomed to disturb, but also fire, because it burns, that this tribulation must be called. By it I was examined and found righteous.

4. **[Verse 4.]** So that my mouth may not speak of the works of men: so that nothing may proceed from my mouth except what pertains to your glory and praise, not to the works of human beings, which they do contrary to your will.

Because of the words of your lips: because of the words of your peace, or of your prophets.

I have guarded difficult ways: I have guarded the laborious ways of human mortality and suffering.

5. **[Verse 5.]** To perfect my steps in your paths: so that the love of the Church might be perfected on the narrow roads by which one comes to your rest.

So that my footsteps may not be moved: so that the signs of my journey may not be moved—the signs impressed, as it were, through the sacraments and apostolic Scriptures, which those who wish to follow me should contemplate and observe. Or certainly, so that I may also remain steadfast in eternity after I have completed the difficult ways and perfected my steps in your narrow paths.

6. **[Verse 6.]** I cried out, because you heard me, O God. I directed prayers to you with a free and vigorous intention, because you heard me when I was praying in weakness, so that I might be able to possess this strength.

Incline your ear to me and hear my words. May your hearing not abandon my humility.

7. **[Verse 7.]** Make your mercies wonderful. Let your mercies not become cheap, lest they be loved less.

8. **[Verse 8.]** You save those who hope in you from those who resist your right hand—that is, from those who resist the favor with which you favor me.

Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye. It appears very small and insignificant, yet through it the beam of light is directed by which light and darkness are distinguished. So, through Christ’s humanity, divinity distinguishes between the righteous and sinners.

Protect me under the shelter of your wings: protect me within the defense of your love and mercy.

[Note: The editions have “you will protect.” The manuscripts have “protect.”]

From the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me.

9. **[Verses 9–10.]** My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have enclosed themselves in their fat. They have been covered with the fatness of their joy after their desire had been satisfied by their crime.

Their mouth has spoken pride. Therefore their mouth spoke pride, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:29), and other such things.

10. **[Verse 11.]** Now, casting me out, they have surrounded me. After casting me outside the city, they have now surrounded me on the cross.

They have set their eyes to incline toward the earth. They have set the intention of their heart to incline toward earthly things, thinking that the one who was being killed was suffering a great evil, while they themselves, who were killing him, suffered none.

11. **[Verse 12.]** They have seized me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in secret places.

They seized me like that adversary who goes around seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8); and like his cub, the people to whom it was said, “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44), thinking of the ambushes by which they might surround and destroy the righteous.

12. **[Verse 13.]** Arise, Lord; go before them and overthrow them. Arise, Lord, whom they think sleeps and does not care about human iniquities. Let them first be blinded by their own malice, so that retribution may overtake their deed, and thus overthrow them.

13. **[Verse 14.]** Deliver my soul from the ungodly. Deliver my soul by raising me from the death inflicted upon me by the ungodly.

Your sword from the enemies of your hand.

[Note: This part of verse 13 is also treated in *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 34, Sermon 1, no. 4.]

For my soul is your sword, which your hand—that is, your eternal power—assumed, so that through it it might wage war against the kingdoms of iniquity and divide the righteous from the ungodly. Deliver this, then, from the enemies of your hand—that is, of your power; that is, from my enemies.

Lord, destroying them from the earth, scatter them during their lifetime. Lord, destroy them from the earth that they inhabit and scatter them throughout the world during this life, which those who despair of eternity think is their only life.

And their belly has been filled from your hidden things. Not only will a visible punishment overtake them, but their memory has also been filled with sins that are hidden like darkness from the light of your truth, so that they forget God.

They have been filled with swine’s flesh. They have been filled with uncleanness, trampling underfoot the pearls of God’s words.

And they have left their remnants to their little ones, crying out, “This sin is upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

14. **[Verse 15.]** But I will appear in your righteousness in your presence. I, who did not appear to those whose filthy and darkened hearts cannot see the light of wisdom, will appear in your righteousness in your presence.

I will be satisfied when your glory is revealed. While they have been filled with their uncleanness so that they cannot understand me, I will be satisfied when your glory is revealed in those who understand me.

[Note: In the edition of Lovaniensis, “you.” In Erasmus and the manuscripts, “me.”]

It should be noted that in the verse where it says, “They have been filled with swine’s flesh,” some copies have, “They have been filled with sons.”

[Note: The Greek ambiguity gives rise to a twofold interpretation. In some manuscripts the word is *huiōn*, “of sons”; in others *huōn*, “of swine”; or *hueōn*, “of swine’s flesh,” or “swine’s flesh.” Augustine treats the same verse 14 in Letter 149 to Paulinus, written about the year 414, and there, in section 5, he writes: “I have reviewed a very brief exposition of the same psalm, which I dictated long ago.” This exposition, therefore, was dictated long before the year 414.]

We understand “sons” as works. Just as good works are good sons, so evil works are evil sons.

## Exposition of Psalm XVII

1. **[Verse 1.]** “For the end, to the servant of the Lord, to David himself”—that is, to Christ according to the human nature, the strong-handed one.

The words of this song that he spoke to the Lord on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said (2 Samuel 22:1).

“On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul,” that is, from the king of the Jews whom they had asked for themselves. For just as David is said to be interpreted as “Strong-handed,” so Saul is said to be interpreted as “Request.” It is known how that people asked for and received a king for themselves (1 Samuel 8:5), not according to God’s will but according to their own.

2. **[Verse 2.]** Therefore Christ and the Church speak here—that is, the whole Christ, head and body:

I will love you, Lord, my strength. I will love you, Lord, through whom I am strong.

3. **[Verse 3.]** Lord, my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer. Lord, who strengthened me because I fled to you; and I fled because you delivered me.

My God, my helper, and I will hope in him. My God, who first granted me the help of your calling, so that I might be able to hope in you.

My protector, the horn of my salvation, and my redeemer. My protector, because I did not presume upon myself, as though raising up against you the horn of pride; rather, I found you yourself to be the horn—that is, the firm height—of salvation. In order that I might find it, you redeemed me.

[Note: Most manuscripts have, “but the horn itself”; they do not have “you.”]

4. **[Verse 4.]** Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I will be saved from my enemies. Seeking not my own glory but the Lord’s, I will call upon him, and there will be no source from which errors of ungodliness can harm me.

5. **[Verse 5.]** The pains of death surrounded me—that is, of the flesh.

And torrents of iniquity troubled me. Unjust crowds, stirred up for a time like rain-swollen rivers that will soon disappear, acted so as to trouble me.

6. **[Verse 6.]** The pains of the underworld surrounded me. In those who surrounded me in order to destroy me were the pains of envy, which bring about death and lead to the underworld of sin.

The snares of death overtook me. They overtook me because they wanted to do harm first, which would later be repaid to them. Such people capture for destruction those whom they have wickedly persuaded by their display of righteousness, a righteousness of which they boast before the Gentiles in name but not in reality.

[Note: Several manuscripts have “wickedly” in the feminine form.]

7. **[Verse 7.]** And in my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God.

And he heard my voice from his holy temple. He heard my voice from my heart, in which he dwells.

And my cry in his presence. My cry, which I hold inwardly not in the ears of human beings but before him, will enter his ears.

[Note: Thus some manuscripts of good standing, in accordance with the Septuagint. They have *introivit*, “entered,” rather than *introibit*, “will enter.”]

8. **[Verse 8.]** And the earth was shaken and trembled. When the Son of Man was glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled.

And the foundations of the mountains were troubled. The hopes of the proud, which had been placed in this world, were troubled.

And they were shaken because God was angry with them, so that temporal hopes would no longer have a foundation in human hearts.

9. **[Verse 9.]** Smoke rose in his anger. The tearful prayer of penitents rose when they had learned what God threatens the ungodly.

And fire blazed from his face. After repentance, the flame of love kindled from knowledge of him.

Coals were kindled by him. Those who had already died, abandoned by the fire of good desire and the light of righteousness, and had remained cold and dark, were kindled and illuminated again and came back to life.

10. **[Verse 10.]** And he bowed the heavens and descended. He humbled the righteous one so that he might descend to human weakness.

And darkness was under his feet. The ungodly, who savor earthly things, did not know him because of the darkness of their malice. For the earth was under his feet, as the footstool of his feet.

11. **[Verse 11.]** And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew. He was exalted above the fullness of knowledge, so that no one could reach him except through love; for the fullness of the Law is love (Romans 13:10).

And he quickly showed himself to be incomprehensible to those who loved him, lest they suppose that he could be grasped through bodily imaginings.

[Note: Lovaniensis has “images.” The other editions have “imaginings.”]

He flew upon the wings of the winds. This swiftness by which he showed himself incomprehensible is above the virtues of souls, by which they raise themselves like wings from earthly fears into the airs of freedom.

12. **[Verse 12.]** And he made darkness his hiding place. He made the obscurity of the mysteries and the hidden hope in the hearts of believers his hiding place, where he might lie concealed without abandoning them; even in those darknesses in which we still walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7), so long as we hope for what we do not see and await it with patience (Romans 8:25).

His tent was around him. Yet those who believe in him, having turned toward him, surround him, because he is in their midst, favoring all equally—in them as in a tabernacle he dwells at this time.

Dark water in the clouds of the air. Nor, because of this, should anyone who rightly understands the Scriptures suppose that he is already in that light which will exist when we have come from faith to sight. For in the prophets and in all preachers of the divine word the teaching is obscure.

13. **[Verse 13.]** Because of the brightness before his presence—that is, in comparison with the brightness that exists before the manifestation of his presence.

His clouds passed by. The preachers of his word are no longer confined within the boundaries of Judea but have passed over to the Gentiles.

Hail and coals of fire. These are figurative rebukes, by which hard hearts are struck as by hail.

[Note: Several manuscripts have “figurative” as an adjective.]

But if cultivated and gentle soil—that is, a devout soul—receives them, the hardness of the hail dissolves into water, that is, the terror of the rebuke, flashed forth and as though frozen, dissolves into nourishing instruction; and hearts kindled by the fire of love come back to life.

[Note: The editions have: “If the earth receives the hardness of the hail, the same earth changes the flashed-forth and as though frozen rebuke into water—that is, into doctrine,” and so forth. We correct the passage according to the manuscripts, although some have *figuratae*, “figurative,” in place of *fulguratae*, “flashed-forth,” and some have *conligatae*, “bound together,” in place of *congelatae*, “frozen.”]

All these things passed over to the Gentiles in his clouds.

14. **[Verse 14.]** And the Lord thundered from heaven. The Lord sounded forth through the evangelical confidence of the righteous heart.

And the Most High gave his voice, so that we might possess it and hear heavenly things in the depths of human affairs.

15. **[Verse 15.]** And he sent forth his arrows and scattered them. He sent forth the Evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not by their own strength but by the strength of the one who sent them. And he scattered those to whom they were sent, so that to some they might be the fragrance of life unto life, and to others the fragrance of death unto death (2 Corinthians 2:16).

And he multiplied flashes of lightning and troubled them. He multiplied miracles and troubled them.

16. **[Verse 16.]** And the springs of waters appeared. Those who had been made springs of living water welling up into eternal life appeared among the preachers (John 4:14).

And the foundations of the world were revealed. The prophets who were not understood were revealed, upon whom the world believing in the Lord would be built.

[Note: Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and most manuscripts have “believing in the Lord.” The Colbertine manuscript has “in the Lord.”]

At your rebuke, Lord—that is, when the one crying out said, “The kingdom of God has drawn near to you” (Luke 10:9).

At the inspiration of the spirit of your anger—that is, when he said, “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:5).

17. **[Verse 17.]** He sent from on high and took me. Calling me from among the Gentiles into an inheritance, the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).

He took me up from the multitude of waters. He took me up from the multitude of peoples.

18. **[Verse 18.]** He delivered me from my strongest enemies. He delivered me from my enemies, who prevailed in afflicting and corrupting this temporal life of mine.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “destroying.”]

And from those who hated me, because they were strengthened against me—so long as I remain under them, ignorant of God.

[Note: Seven manuscripts have “who are ignorant of God.”]

19. **[Verse 19.]** They overtook me on the day of my tribulation. They harmed me first, at the time when I bear a mortal and laborious body.

And the Lord became my firmament. Since the firmament of earthly pleasure was troubled and shaken by the bitterness of misery, the Lord became my firmament.

20. **[Verse 20.]** And he brought me out into a broad place. Since I was suffering carnal narrowness, he brought me into the spiritual breadth of faith.

He delivered me because he desired me. Before I desired him, he delivered me from my most powerful enemies, who envied me once I desired him, and from those who hated me because I desired him.

21. **[Verse 21.]** And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness. The Lord will repay me according to the righteousness of a good will. He first granted mercy before I possessed a good will.

And according to the purity of my hands he will repay me. He will repay me according to the purity of my deeds, since he granted me the ability to do good by bringing me into the breadth of faith.

22. **[Verse 22.]** For I have guarded the ways of the Lord, so that the breadth of good works, which are through faith, and the long endurance of perseverance may follow.

[Note: Thirteen manuscripts have, “So that I may attain the breadth.”]

23. **[Verse 23.]** Nor have I acted impiously against my God.

For all his judgments are before my eyes. I consider all his judgments—that is, the rewards of the righteous, the punishments of the ungodly, the chastisements of those being corrected, and the trials of those being tested—with persevering contemplation.

[Note: The editions add “are always”; this word, “always,” is absent from the better manuscripts and from the Greek.]

And I have not cast his righteousness away from me, as those do who fail beneath its burden and return to their vomit.

24. And I will be blameless with him, and I will guard myself from my iniquity.

25. **[Verse 25.]** And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness. Therefore the Lord will repay me not only because of the breadth of faith, which works through love (Galatians 5:6), but also because of the length of perseverance.

And according to the purity of my hands in the sight of his eyes—not according to what human beings see, but in the sight of his eyes.

[Note: Lovaniensis has “not according to which.” The other books have “not according to what.”]

For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18). This pertains to the height of hope.

26. **[Verse 26.]** With the holy one you will be holy. There is also a hidden depth by which you are understood to be holy with the holy one, because you sanctify.

And with the innocent man you will be innocent, because you harm no one; rather, each person is bound by the cords of his own sins (Proverbs 5:22).

27. **[Verse 27.]** And with the chosen one you will be chosen, and by the one whom you choose you will be chosen.

And with the perverse you will be perverse.

[Note: The same verse 27 is explained in *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 44, no. 17, and Psalm 72, no. 7.]

[Note: The principal manuscripts have, “And with the perverse you will be overthrown.”]

And with the perverse you will appear perverse, because they say, “The way of the Lord is not right” (Ezekiel 18:25), while their own way is not right.

28. **[Verse 28.]** For you will save the humble people. To the perverse, however, it seems perverse that you will save those who confess their sins.

And you will humble the eyes of the proud: those who do not know God’s righteousness and wish to establish their own (Romans 10:3), you will humble.

29. **[Verse 29.]** For you will illuminate my lamp, Lord. Our light does not come from ourselves; rather, you will illuminate my lamp, Lord.

My God, you will illuminate my darkness. We are darkness because of our sins, but you, my God, will illuminate my darkness.

30. **[Verse 30.]** For by you I will be delivered from temptation. I will be delivered from temptation not by myself but by you.

And in my God I will leap over the wall. I will leap over the wall not in myself but in my God—the wall that sins have raised between human beings and the heavenly Jerusalem.

31. [verse 31.] My God, his way is undefiled: my God does not come to human beings unless they have purified the way of faith by which he comes to them, because his way is undefiled. The sayings of the Lord have been tested by fire: the sayings of the Lord are proved by the fire of tribulation. He is the protector of all who hope in him: and all who hope not in themselves but in him are not consumed by that same tribulation; for hope follows faith.

32. [verse 32.] For who is God besides the Lord? He whom we serve. And who is God besides our God? And who is God besides the Lord, whom, after our good service, we shall possess as the hoped-for inheritance of sons?

33. [verse 33.] God who girded me with strength: God who girded me so that I might be strong, lest the loosened folds of desire impede my works and my steps. And he made my way undefiled: and he made undefiled the way of love by which I shall come to him, just as the way of faith by which he comes to me is undefiled.

34. [verse 34.] Who made my feet like those of a stag: who perfected my love so that it might rise above the thorny and shadowy entanglements of this age. And he will set me upon the heights: and he will fix my intention upon the heavenly dwelling, so that I may be filled unto all the fullness of God (Eph. III, 19).

35. [verse 35.] Who teaches my hands for battle [Note: [Col. 0152] Two manuscripts have *for battle*. Most of the others have *in battle*. The Greek Septuagint has *eis polemon*.]: who teaches me to act so as to overcome the enemies who try to bar the heavenly kingdoms against us. And you made my arms like a bronze bow: and you established the indefatigable resolve of my good works.

36. [verse 36.] And you gave me the protection of my salvation [Note: [Col. 0152] This is the reading of the Louvain edition and the better-quality manuscripts. Erasmus and eight manuscripts have *of your salvation*: Jerome testifies in Letter 353, to Sunia, that this reading corresponds to the Hebrew.], and your right hand received me: and the favor of your grace received me. And your discipline directed me to the end: and your correction, not allowing me to go astray, directed me so that whatever I do I may refer it to that end by which I am joined to you. And your discipline itself will teach me: and that same correction of yours will teach me to reach the place toward which it directed me.

37. [verse 37.] You enlarged my steps beneath me: bodily constraints will not impede me, because you have made my love broad, working cheerfully even with respect to the mortal things and limbs that are beneath me. And my footsteps have not been weakened: neither my journeys nor the signs that I have impressed for those who follow to imitate have been weakened.

38. [verse 38.] I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them [Col. 0153]: I shall pursue my bodily affections and not be overtaken by them; I shall overtake them so that they may be consumed. And I shall not turn back until they fail: and I shall not turn away from this resolve toward rest until those who clamor against me have failed.

39. [verse 39.] I shall break them, and they will not be able to stand: they will not endure against me. They will fall beneath my feet: when they have been cast down, I shall set before me the loves by which I walk forever.

40. [verse 40.] And you girded me with strength for battle: and by your strength you bound the flowing desires of my flesh, so that I would not be hindered in such a struggle. You caused those who rose up against me to stumble beneath me: you caused those who were pursuing me to be deceived, so that those who wished to be above me became subject to me.

41. [verse 41.] And you gave me the backs of my enemies: you turned my enemies around and made them my back, that is, so that they would follow me. And you destroyed those who hated me: you destroyed those among them who persisted in hatred.

42. [verse 42.] They cried out, and there was no one to save them: for who could save those whom you would not save? To the Lord, and he did not answer them: they cried not to just anyone but to the Lord; yet he did not judge those who did not withdraw from their wickedness worthy of being heard.

43. [verse 43.] And I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind [Note: [Col. 0153] Eleven manuscripts have *beside the face of the wind*.]: and I shall crush them, for they are dry, not receiving the rain of God’s mercy; so that, lifted up and inflated by pride, they may be swept away from firm and unshaken hope, as though from the solidity and stability of the earth. Like the mud of the streets I shall destroy them: along the broad ways of destruction on which many walk, I shall destroy them, luxurious and slippery.

44. [verse 44.] You will rescue me from the disputes of the people: you will rescue me from the disputes of those who said, “If we let him go [Note: [Col. 0153] Most manuscripts have, “If we let him go alive, the whole world,” etc.], the whole world will follow him” (John XI, 48).

45. [verse 45.] You will establish me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me: the people of the nations, whom I did not visit in bodily presence, served me. At the hearing of the ear it obeyed me: although it did not see me with its eyes, it received my preachers and obeyed me at the hearing of the ear.

46. [verse 46.] The sons of strangers lied to me: those who should not be called my sons, but rather strangers, to whom it is rightly said, “You are of your father the devil” (ibid. VIII, 44), lied to me. The sons of strangers grew old: the sons of strangers, to whom I brought the New Testament so that they might be renewed, remained in the old man. And they limped from their paths: and, as though weakened in one foot, because they clung to the Old Testament and rejected the New, they became lame even in that very Old Law, following their own traditions rather than God’s; for they complained about unwashed hands (Matt. XV, 2), because such were the paths they themselves had made and worn down through habit, straying from the ways of God’s commandments.

[Col. 0154] 47. [verse 47.] The Lord lives, and blessed is my God: for to think according to the flesh is death (Rom. VIII, 6); indeed, the Lord lives, and blessed is my God. And let the God of my salvation be exalted: let me not think of the God of my salvation according to an earthly habit, nor hope for an earthly salvation itself, but hope in him on high.

48. [verse 48.] God who gives me vengeance and subjects peoples beneath me: God who avenges me by subjecting peoples beneath me. My liberator from enraged enemies [Note: [Col. 0154] This is the reading of several better-quality manuscripts, with *my* omitted; it is also absent from the Greek Septuagint. [*my enemies*, etc.]]: from the Jews shouting, “Crucify, crucify!” (John XIX, 6).

49. [verse 49.] You will exalt me above those rising up against me: above the Jews rising against me in my suffering, you will exalt me in my resurrection. You will rescue me from the unjust man: you will rescue me from their unjust kingdom.

50. [verse 50.] Therefore I will confess you among the nations, O Lord: therefore, through me, the nations will confess you, O Lord. And I will sing psalms to your name: and through my good works you will become known more widely.

51. [verse 51.] Magnifying the salvation of his king: God who magnifies the salvations that his Son grants to believers, making them wonderful. And showing mercy to his Christ: God who shows mercy to his Christ, David, and to his seed forever: to that deliverer, mighty of hand, who conquered this world, and to those whom he begot as believers in the Gospel, unto eternity. Whatever has been said in this psalm that cannot properly apply to the Lord himself, that is, to the head of the Church, must be referred to the Church. For the whole Christ speaks here, in whom all his members are present.

## ON PSALM XVIII

### EXPOSITION I. To the end. A psalm for David himself.

1. [verse 1.] The title is known: it is not the Lord Jesus Christ who says these things, but these things are said about him.

2. [verse 2.] The heavens declare the glory of God: the righteous Evangelists, in whom God dwells as in the heavens, explain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, or the glory with which the Son glorified the Father upon earth. And the firmament announces the works of his hands: and the firmament, made steadfast by confidence in the Holy Spirit and made heaven, which previously was earth through fear, announces the deeds of the Lord’s powers.

3. [verse 3.] Day pours forth the word to day: the Spirit brings forth for spiritual people the fullness of the unchanging wisdom of God, the Word who in the beginning was God with God (John I, 1). And night announces knowledge to night: and the mortality of the flesh, as though to those placed far away in the flesh, announces future knowledge by introducing faith.

4. [verse 4.] There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard: there are none through whom the voices of the Evangelists have not been heard, since the Gospel was preached in every language.

[Col. 0155] 5. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

6. [verse 6.] He placed his tabernacle in the sun [Note: [Col. 0155] On the same verse 6, see Exposition on Psalm XLIV, no. 3.]: but the Lord, in order to wage war against the kingdoms of temporal errors, intending to send not peace but a sword upon the earth (Matt. X, 34), placed his military dwelling in time, or in manifestation—that is, the dispensation of his incarnation. And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber: he himself came forth from the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to his bride. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course: he rejoiced like the strongest of men, surpassing all others in incomparable power, not to dwell in the way but to run it. For he did not stand in the way of sinners (Ps. I, 1).

7. [verse 7.] His going forth is from the highest heaven [Note: [Col. 0155] The same verse 7 is explained in Exposition on Psalm LVIII, sermon 1, no. 10.]: his going forth from the Father is not temporal but eternal, by which he was born from the Father. And his circuit reaches to the summit of heaven [Note: [Col. 0155] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions have, *to his summit*.]. And he reaches, in the fullness of divinity, to equality with the Father. And there is no one who can hide from his heat: when the Word also became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14), assuming our mortality, he did not permit any mortal to excuse himself on account of the shadow of death; for the heat of the Word penetrated even it.

8. [verse 8.] The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls. Therefore the law of the Lord is he himself who came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (Matt. V, 17); and the undefiled law is he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (I Pet. II, 22). He does not press souls beneath the yoke of slavery, but converts them to imitate him through freedom. The testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the little ones: the testimony of the Lord is faithful, because no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him (Matt. XI, 27)—the things hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James IV, 6).

9. [verse 9.] The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening the heart [Note: [Col. 0155] The printed editions have *hearts*. The manuscripts have *heart*, singular, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.]: all the ordinances of the Lord are right in him, who did not teach what he himself did not do, so that those who imitated him might rejoice in their hearts at the things they freely did with love, not slavishly with fear. The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes: the commandment of the Lord is radiant, without the veil of bodily observances, enlightening the perception of the inner person.

10. [verse 10.] The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever: the fear of the Lord is not that penal fear under the law, fearing the loss of temporal goods, through love of which the soul commits fornication; it is the pure fear by which the Church, the more ardently she loves her bridegroom, the more carefully avoids offending him. Therefore perfected love does not cast out this fear (I John IV, 18), but it remains forever and ever.

11. [verse 11.] The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves [Col. 0156]: the judgments of him who judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son (John V, 22) are truly and unchangeably justified. For God deceives no one either by threatening or by promising, nor can anyone take away either his punishment from the wicked or his reward from the godly. More desirable than gold and a very precious stone: whether “much gold and stone,” or “very precious,” or “very desirable,” nevertheless the judgments of God are more desirable than the spectacles of this age. Through desire for these spectacles people cease to desire, and instead fear, despise, or disbelieve the judgments of God. But if someone is himself gold and a precious stone, so that he is not consumed by fire but taken up into God’s treasury, he desires God’s judgments more than himself, preferring God’s will to his own. And sweeter than honey and the honeycomb: whether someone is already honey, already released from the bonds of this life and awaiting the day when he will come to God’s banquets; or whether he is still a honeycomb, enclosed as though in wax by this life—not congealed in it, but filling it, requiring some pressure from the hands of God, not to crush but to press out, so that he may be strained from temporal life into eternal life—God’s judgments are sweeter to him than he is to himself, because they are sweeter to him than honey and the honeycomb.

12. [verse 12.] For your servant also keeps them: for the day of the Lord is not bitter to one who keeps them. In keeping them there is great reward: not in some external advantage, but in the very keeping of God’s judgments there is great reward. It is great because one rejoices in them.

13. [verse 13.] Who understands sins? What sweetness can there be in sins where there is no understanding? For who understands sins, which themselves close the eye that finds truth sweet, to which the judgments of God are desirable and sweet? Just as darkness closes the eyes, so sins close the mind and do not allow it to see either the light or themselves.

14. [verse 14.] Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults: cleanse me, Lord, from the desires hidden within me. And spare your servant from the faults of others [Note: [Col. 0156] The same verse 14 is explained in Exposition on Psalm XXXIX, no. 20.]: let me not be led astray by others; for one who is clean from his own faults is not captured by the faults of others. Therefore spare me from the desires of others—not as one who is proud and wishes to be his own master, but as your servant. If my hidden faults and the sins of others do not rule me, then I shall be undefiled; for there is no third [Note: [Col. 0156] The printed editions have *a more certain origin*. The manuscripts, more correctly, have *a third origin*.] origin of sin besides the hidden sin by which the devil fell and the sin of another by which the human being was deceived, making it his own by consenting. And I shall be cleansed from the great sin: from what else but pride? For there is no greater sin than apostasy from God, which is the beginning of human pride (Ecclus. X, 14). Truly undefiled is the one who is free even from this sin, because for those returning to God this is the last thing, whereas for those departing it was the first.

15. [verse 15.] And the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart will always be pleasing in your sight: the meditation of my heart is not for the boastful purpose of pleasing human beings, because there is now no pride; rather, it is always in your sight, since you examine a pure conscience. Lord, my helper and my redeemer: Lord, my helper as I strive toward you, because you are my redeemer so that I might strive toward you. Let no one, attributing his turning to you to his own wisdom or his reaching you to his own strength, be driven farther from you, who resist the proud; for such a person has not been cleansed from the great sin and has not been pleasing in your sight—you who redeem us so that we may turn and help us so that we may reach you.

### EXPOSITION II. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Since we have entreated the Lord to cleanse us from our hidden faults and to spare his servants from the faults of others, we must understand what this means, so that we may sing with human understanding, not as though with the voices of birds. Blackbirds, parrots, ravens, magpies, and birds of this kind are often taught by human beings to produce sounds they do not understand. But to sing knowingly has been granted to human nature by the divine will. We know and grieve that many wicked and luxurious people sing things worthy of their ears and hearts in this way. They are worse precisely because they cannot be ignorant of what they sing. They know that they are singing obscenities, and yet they sing them all the more willingly the more impurely, because they think themselves happier the more disgraceful they have been.

But we, who have learned to sing God’s sayings in the Church, must also strive to be what is written: “Blessed is the people that understands the shout of joy” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 16). Therefore, dearly beloved, what we have sung with harmonious voices we must also know and perceive with serene hearts. Each one of us, in this song, has entreated the Lord and said to God: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the faults of others. If they do not rule me, then I shall be undefiled, and I shall be cleansed from the great sin.” So that we may know well what this means and what kind of thing it is, let us briefly go through the text of the psalm itself, as far as the Lord grants.

2. For it is sung about Christ, as is evident there, because it is written: “He himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber.” Who is the bridegroom except the one to whom that virgin has been betrothed by the Apostle, the chaste friend of the bridegroom fearing chastely lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so the thoughts of this virgin, the bride of Christ, should be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ (II Cor. XI, 3)?

In this Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ there is established great and complete grace, of which the apostle John says: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14). The heavens declare this glory: the heavens are the saints, raised above the earth and carrying the Lord. Yet even the physical heaven, in a certain way, declared Christ’s glory. When did it declare it? When, at the Lord’s birth, a new star appeared that had never before been seen.

But there are more genuine and higher heavens [Note: [Col. 0157] These words, *more genuine and higher*, are absent from the manuscripts.], of which it is subsequently said: “There are no speeches or conversations whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Whose, if not the heavens’? Whose, then, if not the Apostles’? They declare to us the glory of God established in Christ Jesus through grace for the remission [Note: [Col. 0158] The Gattianus manuscript has *the grace of the remission of sins*. Certain other manuscripts have *grace and remission of sins*.] of sins. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely through his blood” (Rom. III, 23).

Because it is free, it is grace; for it would not be grace if it were not free. Because we had done nothing good beforehand by which we might deserve such gifts—indeed, because [Note: [Col. 0158] Louvain has *because it should not be free*. *Should not be* is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts.] punishment would not have been inflicted freely—therefore the benefit was freely bestowed. Nothing preceded in our merits except that for which we ought to be condemned. Yet he saved us not because of our righteousness but because of his mercy, through the bath of regeneration (Titus III, 5).

This, I say, is the glory of God; the heavens declared it. This, I say, is the glory of God, not yours: you did nothing good, and yet you received so great a good. If, then, you belong to the glory that the heavens declared, say to the Lord your God: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11). It went before you—certainly it went before you—because it found nothing good in you. You went before his punishment by your pride; he went before your punishment by erasing your sins.

As one justified from being a sinner, made godly from being ungodly, taken up into the kingdom from being condemned [Note: [Col. 0158] Erasmus and most manuscripts have *taken up into the kingdom from being condemned*.], say to the Lord your God: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII, second, 1). Let us say, “Not to us”: for to whom, if not to us as though to ourselves? Let us say, I repeat, “Not to us,” because if he acted toward us according to what was ours, he would inflict nothing but punishments upon us. “Not to us, but to his name let him give glory,” because “he has not dealt with us according to our iniquities” (Ps. CII, 10).

Therefore, “Not to us, Lord, not to us”: repetition is confirmation. “Not to us, Lord, but to your name give glory.” The heavens that declared the glory of God knew this.

3. [verse 2.] And the firmament announces the works of his hands: what was said as “the glory of God” is repeated as “the works of his hands.” What are the works of his hands? Not what some think: that God made everything by the Word but made the human being with his own hands, as though making him superior to the rest. This must not be thought. That opinion is weak and insufficiently refined, for he made everything by the Word. Although different works of God are recounted, among them his making the human being in his image (Gen. I), nevertheless all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John I, 3).

As for the hands of God, it is said even of the heavens, “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. CI, 26). And lest you think that “heavens” there means the saints, he adds: “They will perish, but you remain” (ibid., 27). Therefore God made with his hands not only human beings but also the heavens that will perish, since it is said to him, “The heavens are the works of your hands.” The same is said of the earth: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands founded the dry land” (Ps. XCIV, 5).

Therefore, if he made the heavens with his hands and the earth with his hands, he made not only the human being with his hands; and if he made the heavens by the Word and the earth by the Word, he also made the human being by the Word. What he made by the Word, he made by his hand; and what he made by his hand, he made by the Word. God’s stature is not distinguished by human limbs: he is wholly everywhere and contained by no place. Therefore what he made by the Word, he made by wisdom; and what he made by his hand, he made by power.

But Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24). “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” The heavens have declared, declare, and will declare the glory of God. The heavens—that is, the saints suspended above the earth—have declared, I say, and will declare the glory of God: carrying God, thundering his commandments, flashing with wisdom; that glory of God, as I said, by which we, though unworthy, have been saved.

The younger son, constrained by want, acknowledges this unworthiness—that is, the fact that we were not worthy. I repeat, the younger son, far away from his father in a foreign land, a worshiper of demons, like a keeper of pigs, acknowledges this unworthiness. He acknowledges the glory of God, but is constrained by want. And because by that glory of God we have been made what we were not worthy to be, he says to his Father: “I am not worthy to be called your son” (Luke XV, 21). Unhappy, he obtains happiness through humility; and he shows himself worthy precisely by confessing himself unworthy.

The heavens declare this glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands: the firmament is heaven, a firm heart, not a fearful heart. These things were announced among the ungodly, among those hostile to God, among lovers of the world and persecutors of the righteous; they were announced amid a raging world. But what could the raging world do when the firmament was announcing these things? The firmament announces—what? The works of his hands. What are the works of his hands? That glory of God by which we have been saved, by which we have been created for good works; for “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 10). For he made us not only human beings but also righteous, if indeed we are righteous, and “not we ourselves” (Ps. XCIX, 3).

4. [verse 3.] Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night: what does this mean? Perhaps “day pours forth the word to day” is plain and open, clear as day; but “night announces knowledge to night” is obscure, as though spoken through the night.

“Day to day”: the saints to the saints, the Apostles to the faithful, Christ himself to the Apostles, to whom he said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). This seems clear and easy to understand. But how does night announce knowledge to night?

Some have understood these words simply, and perhaps that is correct. They think this statement signifies that what the Apostles heard in the time of our Lord Jesus Christ, while he was present on earth, was transmitted to those who came afterward, as from one time to another: day to day, night to night, the earlier day to the later day and the earlier night to the later night, because this teaching is preached by days and nights. Let this simple interpretation suffice for whoever it satisfies.

But certain words of Scripture have benefited from their obscurity by producing many interpretations. If this passage were clear, you would hear only one thing; but because it was spoken obscurely, you will hear many things. There is another interpretation: “day to day, night to night”—that is, spirit to spirit, flesh to flesh. There is another: “day to day,” the spiritual to the spiritual; and “night to night,” the carnal to the carnal.

Both hear, although both do not understand in the same way. The former hear as a word poured forth; the latter as knowledge announced. What is poured forth is poured forth to those present; what is announced is announced to those who are far away.

Many meanings of the heavens may be found, but moderation must be used because of the limitations of the present time. Let us also state one interpretation that some, as though conjecturing, have disclosed [Note: [Col. 0160] Several manuscripts have *in agreement*.]: when the Lord Christ was speaking to the Apostles, they say, day poured forth the word to day; when Judas betrayed the Lord Christ to the Jews, night announced knowledge to night.

5. [verses 5, 4.] There are no speeches or conversations whose voices are not heard: whose, if not those heavens that declare the glory of God? “There are no speeches or conversations whose voices are not heard.” Read the Acts of the Apostles, how, when the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were all filled with him and spoke in the languages of all the nations, as the Spirit gave them utterance (Acts II, 4).

Behold: there are no speeches or conversations whose voices are not heard. But they did not resound only in the place where they were filled. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” That is why we too speak here: for that sound has reached us, the sound that went out into all the earth, and the heretic does not enter the Church.

That sound went out into all the earth so that you might enter heaven. O pestilential, quarrelsome, wicked person, still wishing to wander in error; proud son, hear the testament of your father. Behold, what could be plainer, what more open? “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Does this require an interpreter? Why do you struggle against yourself? You wish to retain a part in dispute, although you can retain the whole in harmony?

6. [verse 6.] He placed his tabernacle in the sun: in the manifestation he placed his Church, not in concealment, not as one hidden, not as though covered [Note: [Col. 0160] So the manuscripts. Louvain omits the negation, yielding *as though covered*.], lest it should perhaps become like something covered over the flocks of heretics.

It was also said to someone in Holy Scripture, “Because you did it secretly, you will suffer it in the sun” (II Sam. XII, 12): that is, you did evil secretly, but you will suffer punishment in the manifestation of all. Therefore he placed his tabernacle in the sun.

Why do you flee into darkness, heretic? Are you a Christian? Hear Christ. Are you a servant? Hear the Lord. Are you a son? Hear the Father: be corrected, come back to life. Let us also say of you: “He was dead and came to life again; he was lost and was found” (Luke XV, 32).

Do not say to me, “Why do you seek me if I am lost?” Precisely because you are lost, I seek you. “Do not seek me,” he says. Wickedness, by which we have been divided, certainly wants this; but love, by which we are brothers, does not. I would not be wicked if I were seeking my servant; and am I called wicked because I seek my brother? Let the one in whom there is no brotherly love think so; I nevertheless seek my brother. Let him be angry, provided he is sought, for when he is found he is appeased.

I seek my brother, I say, and I appeal not against him but for him to my Lord. Nor will I say in my appeal, “Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me” (Luke XII, 13), but, “Tell my brother to hold the inheritance with me.”

Why, then, do you wander, brother? Why do you flee into corners? Why do you try to lie hidden? “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.” And he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. I think you recognize him. He, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course. He himself placed his tabernacle in the sun: that is, he, like a bridegroom, when the Word became flesh, found a bridal chamber in the virginal womb; and from there, joined to human nature, he came forth from the most chaste chamber, humble in mercy beneath all and strong in majesty above all.

This is what it means that the giant rejoiced to run his course: he was born, grew, taught, suffered, rose again, and ascended; he ran the course and did not linger on the way. Therefore the same bridegroom who did these things himself placed his tabernacle in the sun—that is, in manifestation—namely, his holy Church.

7. [verse 7.] Do you wish to hear how quickly he ran the course? “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his meeting reaches to its summit.” But after he had run forth from there and returned by retracing his path, he sent his Spirit. “There appeared to them tongues divided as though of fire” (Acts II, 3), upon those on whom he came. Like fire the Holy Spirit came, to consume the hay of the flesh and to cook and purify gold. Like fire he came, and therefore it follows: “And there is no one who can hide from his heat.”

8. [verse 8.] The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls. This is the Holy Spirit. The testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to little ones—not to the proud. This is the Holy Spirit.

9. [verse 9.] The ordinances of the Lord are right: not terrifying but gladdening hearts. This is the Holy Spirit. The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes, not dulling them—not the eyes of the flesh but of the heart, not of the outer person but of the inner. This is the Holy Spirit.

10. [verse 10.] The fear of the Lord: not slavish but pure; loving freely, not fearing punishment from the one whom it fears, but separation from the one whom it loves. This is pure fear, not the fear that perfected love casts out (I John IV, 18), but the fear that remains forever and ever.

This is the Holy Spirit; that is, the Holy Spirit gives, confers, and implants this fear. The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves: not for quarrels that produce division, but for the gathering of unity; for this is what “in themselves” means. This is the Holy Spirit.

Therefore he caused those into whom he first came to speak in the languages of all. For he announced that he would gather the languages of all nations into unity. What one person did then, having received the Holy Spirit, so that one person spoke in the languages of all, the unity itself now does: it speaks in all languages.

Even now one person speaks in all languages among all nations: one person, head and body; one person, Christ and the Church; the perfect man, the bridegroom and the bride. “And the two,” he says, “will be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves”: because of unity.

11. [verse 11.] More desirable than gold and a very precious stone [Col. 0162]: whether much gold, or very precious, or very desirable; nevertheless, very much for us, but little for the heretic. They do not love unity with us, though they confess Christ with us. The Christ whom you confess with me, love with me. Whoever does not want unity rejects it, resists it, spurns it; this is not desirable for him above much gold and a precious stone.

Hear another statement: “And sweeter,” he says, “than honey and the honeycomb.” But this is opposed to the one who wanders in error: honey is bitter to one with a fever, yet sweet and acceptable to one who is healed, because it is dear to health. “More desirable than gold and a very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

12. [verse 12.] For your servant also keeps them: your servant proves how sweet these things are by keeping them, not by speaking. Your servant keeps them because they are sweet now and beneficial in the future; for “in keeping them there is great reward.” But the heretic, loving his own contentiousness, neither sees this brightness nor feels this sweetness.

13. [verses 13, 14.] For who understands sins? “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Therefore, he says, this is the servant who keeps this sweetness, the sweetness of love, the love of unity. “I myself,” he says, “who keep it, ask you, since who understands sins? Do not let certain things creep upon me as a human being, or seize me beforehand in some respect as a human being: ‘Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.’”
