This is what we have sung; behold, by speaking we have reached this point. Let us speak with understanding, sing with understanding, and by singing pray, and by praying obtain what we seek. Let us say: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.” For who understands sins?

If darkness is seen, sins are understood. Finally, when we repent of sin, we are in the light. For when someone is entangled in the sin itself, with his eyes as though darkened and covered, he does not see the sin. If the eye of your flesh is covered, you see neither anything else nor the thing by which it is covered.

Therefore let us say to God, who knows how to see what he should cleanse and how to examine what he should heal; let us say to him: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the faults of others.” “My sins,” he says, “defile me; the sins of others afflict me. Cleanse me from the former and spare me from the latter. Take evil thought from my heart; drive away from me the evil counselor.” This is: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from the faults of others.”

These two kinds of sin, both one’s own and another’s, were already made clear at the beginning: the devil fell through his own sin, and Adam was cast down through another’s. This same servant of God, keeping the judgments of God in which there is great reward, prays in another psalm: “Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of sinners move me” (Ps. XXXV, 12).

“Let not,” he says, “the foot of pride come to me”—that is, “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults”—“and let not the hand of sinners move me”—that is, “Spare your servant from the faults of others.”

14. If they do not rule over me: my hidden faults and the sins of others. Then I shall be blameless: he does not dare this on his own strength, but beseeches the Lord to accomplish it, [Col. 0163] to whom it is said in the Psalm: “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133). Do not fear, if you are a Christian, a human master outside you; always fear the Lord your God. Fear the evil within you—that is, your desire—not what God made in you, but what you yourself made for yourself. The Lord made you a good servant; you created a bad master for yourself in your heart. Rightly are you subjected to iniquity; rightly are you subjected to the master whom you yourself made for yourself, because you were unwilling to be subject to the one who made you.

15. But if they do not rule over me, he says, then I shall be blameless; and I shall be cleansed from the great sin. What sin do we suppose this is? What is this great sin? Perhaps it is something other than what I am about to say; nevertheless, I shall not conceal what I think. I consider pride to be the great sin. Perhaps this too is signified in another way by what he says, “And I shall be cleansed from the great sin.” Do you ask how great this sin is—the sin that cast down an angel, that made a devil from an angel, and forever shut him out from the kingdom of heaven? Great indeed is this sin, the head and cause of all sins; for it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride.” And lest you despise it as though it were something trivial, he says: “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Sirach 10:15, 14). This vice is no light evil, my brothers. In the persons whom you see in positions of distinction, it is this vice that finds Christian humility displeasing. Because of this vice they disdain to bend their necks beneath the yoke of Christ, though they are bound more tightly beneath the yoke of sin. For they will not escape serving: they do not wish to serve, but it is advantageous for them to serve. By refusing to serve, they accomplish nothing except that they do not serve a good master—not that they serve no one at all; for whoever is unwilling to serve charity must serve iniquity.

Because of this vice, which is the head of all vices, since the other vices arose from it, apostasy from God took place: the soul went into darkness and misused its free will, and the other sins followed, so that it squandered its substance by living extravagantly with prostitutes and, through poverty, became a keeper of pigs (Luke 15:13), though it had been a companion of angels. Because of this vice, because of this great sin of pride, God came in humility. This cause, this great sin, this immense disease of souls brought the almighty Physician down from heaven; it humbled him even to the form of a servant, subjected him to insults, and hung him upon the wood, so that this swelling might be healed through the salvation provided by so great a remedy. Let human beings at last be ashamed to be proud, for whose sake God became humble. Thus, he says, “I shall be cleansed from the great sin,” because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5).

16. [verse 15] And through this, “may the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart always be pleasing in your sight”: for if I am not cleansed from this great sin, my words will be pleasing in the sight of human beings, not in your sight. A proud soul wishes to please in the sight of human beings; a humble soul wishes to please in secret, where God sees. Thus, if people are pleased by a good work, let the soul rejoice on behalf of those who are pleased by the good work, not on its own behalf, since it ought to be satisfied simply because it has done a good work: “Our glory,” he says, “is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). Therefore let us also say what follows: “Lord, my helper and my redeemer”—helper in good things, redeemer from evil things; helper, so that I may dwell in your charity; redeemer, so that you may free me from my iniquity.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 19

For the end; a Psalm of David.

1. [verse 1] This title is familiar. It is not Christ who speaks, but the Prophet speaks to Christ, singing in the form of a wish about things that are to come.

2. [verse 2] “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation”: may the Lord hear you on the day when you said, “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1). “May the name of the God of Jacob protect you”: for the later-born people belongs to you, because “the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23).

3. [verse 3] “May he send you help from the sanctuary, and protect you from Zion,” making for you a sanctified body—the Church—made secure through contemplation; it awaits your coming from the wedding feast [Note: [Col. 0164] The editions read “to the wedding feast” (*ad nuptias*). The manuscripts, however, read “from the wedding feast” (*a nuptiis*).].

4. [verse 4] “May he remember all your sacrifice”: may he make us mindful of all the injuries and insults that you endured for us. “And may your burnt offering become rich”: may he turn the cross, on which you were wholly offered to God, into the joy of the resurrection.

5. [verse 5] [Note: [Col. 0164] *Diapsalma*.] “May the Lord grant you according to your heart”: may the Lord grant you—not according to the heart of those who thought that by persecuting you they could destroy you, but according to your heart, by which you knew what benefit your suffering would bring. “And may he fulfill all your counsel”: may he fulfill all your counsel, not only that by which you laid down your life for your friends (John 15:13), so that the grain which had died might rise again more abundantly (John 12:25), but also that by which a partial blindness came upon Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. 11:25).

6. [verse 6] “We shall rejoice in your salvation”: we shall rejoice because death will harm you in no way; thus you will show that it cannot harm us either. “And in the name [Note: [Col. 0164] Thus from the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint: “in the name of the Lord God,” etc.] of our God we shall be exalted”: the confession of your name will not only not destroy us, but will also exalt us.

7. [verse 7] “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions”: may the Lord fulfill not only the petitions that you had on earth, but also those by which in heaven you intercede for us. “Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ”: now it has been shown to me through prophecy that the Lord will raise his Christ. “He will hear him from his holy heaven”: he will hear him, not only from earth, where he asked to be glorified (John 17:1), but also from heaven, where he now intercedes for us at the right hand of the Father (Rom. 8:34), and from there has poured out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in him. “In mighty acts is the salvation of his right hand”: our mighty acts are the salvation of his favor, since he also gives help in tribulation, so that when we are weak, then we may be strong (2 Cor. 12:10). For “the salvation of human beings is vain” (Ps. 59:13), since it belongs not to his right hand but to his left; by this salvation all who have been saved temporarily while sinning are lifted up into great pride.

8. [verse 8] “Some trust in chariots and some in horses” [Note: [Col. 0165] The same verse 8 is treated in *Exposition of Psalm 146*, no. 19.]: some are dragged along by the rolling succession of temporal goods, while others are set above others by proud honors [Note: [Col. 0165] The Colbert manuscript reads *feruntur*, “are borne,” rather than *praeferuntur*, “are set above.”], and they exult in these things. “But we shall exult in the name of the Lord our God”: fixing our hope on eternal things and seeking no glory of our own, we shall exult in the name of the Lord our God.

9. [verse 9] “They have been bound, and have fallen”: and therefore they have been bound by desire for temporal things, fearing to spare the Lord lest the Romans destroy their place (John 11:48); and, rushing against the stone of stumbling (Rom. 9:32) and the rock of offense, they have fallen from heavenly hope. For them a partial blindness came upon Israel, since they did not know God’s righteousness and wished to establish their own (Rom. 10:3). “But we have risen” [Note: [Col. 0165] The better manuscripts read “we have risen again.”], “and have been raised upright”: so that the people of the Gentiles might enter, we—raised from stones as children of Abraham (Matt. 3:9), who were not pursuing righteousness but grasped it (Rom. 9:30)—have risen; and, justified not by our own strength but through faith, we have been raised upright.

10. [verse 10] “Lord, save the king”: so that he who showed us an example of fighting through his passion may also offer our sacrifices, the priest raised from the dead and established in heaven. “And hear us on the day when we call upon you”: with him now offering for us [Note: [Col. 0165] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “Because you offer yourself for us.”], hear us on the day when we call upon you.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 20

For the end; a Psalm for David himself.

1. [verse 1] The title is familiar; it is sung concerning Christ.

2. [verse 2] “Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength”: Lord, in your strength [Note: [Col. 0165] The editions read *quod* (“which”); some manuscripts here read *qua* (“by which”), and below *quo* (“by which you give life”).], by which “the Word became flesh,” the man Christ Jesus shall rejoice. “And he shall exult greatly in your salvation”: and in this by which you give life to all, he shall exult greatly.

3. [verse 3] “You gave him the desire of his soul”: he desired to eat the Passover (Luke 22:15), and to lay down his soul when he wished and take it up again when he wished (John 10:18); and you gave it to him. “And you did not deprive him of the desire of his lips” [Note: [Col. 0165] The editions read “you did not defraud him.” The manuscripts, however, read “you did not deprive him.” The Greek has *esterêsas*.]. “My peace,” he says, “I leave you” (John 14:27), and it was done.

4. [verse 4] “For you anticipated him with blessings of sweetness” [Col. 0166]: for he had first drunk deeply of the blessing of your sweetness, and the gall of our sins did not harm him [Note: [Col. 0166] *Diapsalma*.]. “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone”: at the beginning of his preaching, precious stones—his disciples—came to surround him, from whom the beginning of his proclamation would proceed.

5. [verse 5] “He asked for life, and you gave it to him”: he asked for the resurrection, saying, “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1), and you gave it to him. “Length of days for age upon age”: the long periods of this age that the Church would possess, and thereafter eternity for age upon age.

6. [verse 6] “Great is his glory in your salvation”: indeed, great is his glory in the salvation by which you raised him. “You will place glory and great splendor upon him”: but you will still add glory and great splendor to him when you establish him in heaven at your right hand.

7. [verse 7] “For you will grant him blessing for age upon age”: this is the blessing that you will grant him for age upon age: “You will make him joyful with the joy of your countenance.” According to the human condition, you will make him joyful with your countenance, which he raised toward you.

8. [verse 8] “For the king hopes in the Lord”: for the king does not grow proud, but, humble in heart, hopes in the Lord. “And in the mercy of the Most High he shall not be shaken”: in the mercy of the Most High, obedience even unto the death of the cross will not disturb his humility [Note: [Col. 0166] So the manuscripts of the best quality. The editions read, “and his obedience.”].

9. [verse 9] “May your hand be found by all your enemies”: may your power, O king, be found by all your enemies when you come to judge—those who did not understand it in your humility. “May your right hand find all who hate you”: may the splendor by which you reign at the Father’s right hand find, on the day of judgment, all who hate you, to be punished, because now they did not find it.

10. [verse 10] “You will place them like a furnace of fire”: you will establish them burning inwardly with the consciousness of their ungodliness. “At the time of your countenance”: at the time of your manifestation. “The Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them”: then, troubled by the Lord’s vengeance after the accusation of conscience, they will be handed over to be devoured by eternal fire.

11. [verse 11] “You will destroy their fruit from the earth”: you will destroy their fruit from the earth because it is earthly. “And their seed from the children of human beings”: you will not count their works, or those whom they have led astray, among the children of human beings whom you have called to an eternal inheritance.

12. [verse 12] “For they turned evils upon you”: this punishment will be repaid to them because they turned toward killing you the evils that they supposed would threaten them while you reigned. “They devised a plan that they could not establish”: they devised the plan, saying, “It is better that one man should die for all” (John 11:50), but they could not establish it, not knowing what they had said.

[Col. 0167] 13. [verse 13] “For you will make them turn their backs”: you will arrange them among those from whom, once they have been set aside and despised, you turn away. “Among your remnants you will prepare their face”: among the things that you leave behind—that is, the desires of an earthly kingdom—you will prepare their shamelessness for your passion.

14. [verse 14] “Be exalted, Lord, in your strength”: you whom they did not recognize in humility, be exalted, Lord, in the strength that they thought weakness. “We shall sing and chant your mighty works”: with heart and deed we shall celebrate and make known your wonders.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 21

[Note: [Col. 0167] Augustine explains this same Psalm 21 in Letter 140 to Honoratus.]

### EXPOSITION I

For the end, for the morning reception, a Psalm of David.

1. [verse 1] “For the end, for his resurrection”: the Lord Jesus Christ himself speaks. His resurrection was “morning,” the first day of the week, by which he was received into eternal life, over which death will no longer rule (Rom. 6:9). These words are spoken in the person of the crucified one, for the words that he himself cried out while hanging on the cross are from the beginning of this Psalm, while he also retains the person of the old human being, whose mortality he bore. For “our old man was crucified with him” (ibid., 6).

2. [verse 2] “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation” [Note: [Col. 0167] The same verse 2 is treated in *Exposition of Psalm 37*, no. 6; *Psalm 43*, no. 2; *Psalm 58*, sermon 1, no. 2; and *Psalm 87*, no. 14.]?—far removed from my salvation, because “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). “The words of my sins”: for these are the words not of my righteousness but of my sins. The old human being, crucified, speaks; even though he does not know why God has forsaken him. Or certainly: “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.”

3. [verse 3] “My God, I shall cry to you by day, and you will not hear” [Note: [Col. 0167] The same verse 3 is treated in *Exposition of Psalm 53*, no. 5.]: my God, I shall cry to you amid the prosperity of this life, asking that it not be changed, and you will not hear, because I shall cry to you with the words of my sins. “And by night, and not for my foolishness”: I shall likewise cry amid the adversities of this life, asking that they be turned into prosperity, and similarly you will not hear. Nor do you do this for my foolishness, but rather so that I may understand what you want me to cry for—not with the words of sin, out of desire for temporal life, but with words of conversion to you for eternal life.

4. [verse 4] “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel”: you dwell in the holy place, and therefore you do not hear the impure words of sins. You are the praise of the one who sees you, not of the one who sought his own praise by tasting the forbidden food and then, with his bodily eyes opened, attempted to hide himself from your sight (Gen. 3).

5. [verse 5] “In you our fathers hoped”: that is, all the righteous, who did not seek their own praise but yours; they hoped, and you delivered them.

6. [verse 6] “They cried to you, and they were saved”: they cried to you, not with the words of sins, from which salvation is far away, and therefore they were saved. “They hoped in you, and they were not put to shame”: they hoped in you, and their hope did not deceive them; for they did not place it in themselves.

7. [verse 7] “But I am a worm, and not a human being”: now I am no longer speaking in the person of Adam, but I, Jesus Christ himself, was born in the flesh without human seed [Note: [Col. 0168] Several manuscripts read, “I was incarnate without seed.”], so that I might be among human beings beyond human beings; so that even in this way human pride might deign to imitate my humility. “The reproach of human beings and the rejection of the people”: in this I became the reproach of human beings, so that it was said as an insulting curse, “You are his disciple” (John 9:28), and the people despised me.

8. [verse 8] “All who saw me mocked me”: all who saw me ridiculed me. “They spoke with their lips and shook their heads”: they spoke not in their heart but with their lips.

9. [verse 9] For they shook their heads in mockery, saying: “He hoped in the Lord; let him rescue him; let him save him, since he wants him.” These were the words, but they were spoken with the lips.

10. [verse 10] “For you are the one who drew me from the womb”: for you are the one who drew me not only from that virginal womb—for this law of birth applies to all human beings, that they are drawn out from the womb—but also from the womb of the Jewish people. Whoever places salvation in the carnal observance of the Sabbath, circumcision, and the other such practices is covered by that people’s darkness and has not yet been born into the light of Christ. “My hope from my mother’s breasts”: my hope is God, not from the time when I began to nurse at the virgin’s breasts—for certainly I existed even before that—but from the breasts of the Synagogue. As I said concerning the womb, you drew me out so that I would not suck in a carnal custom.

11. [verse 11] “I was strengthened in you from the womb”: this is the womb of the Synagogue, which did not carry me but cast me out; yet I did not fall, because you held me fast. “From the womb of my mother, you are my God.” “From the womb of my mother”: the womb of my mother did not cause me, like a little child, to forget you.

12. [verse 12] “You are my God; do not depart from me”: because tribulation is near. Therefore, you are my God; do not depart from me, because tribulation is beside me; indeed, it is in my body. “For there is no one to help”: for who helps if you do not help?

13. [verse 13] “Many calves surrounded me”: a multitude of a pleasure-seeking people surrounded me. “Fat bulls besieged me”: its leaders, rejoicing in my oppression, besieged me.

14. [verse 14] “They opened their mouths against me”: they opened their mouths against me, not concerning your Scriptures but concerning their own desires. “Like a lion ravening and roaring”: like a lion whose prey consists in my being seized and brought forward [Note: [Col. 0168] So the manuscripts. The editions read “was led away.”], and whose roar was, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6).

15. [verse 15] “I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered”: I was poured out like water when my persecutors fell; and through fear the supports of my body—that is, my Church, my disciples—were scattered from me. “My heart became like melting wax in the midst of my belly” [Col. 0169]: my wisdom, which was written about me in the holy books, was not understood, as though it were hard and sealed; but after the fire of my passion approached, it was manifested as though melted and was received into the memory of my Church.

16. [verse 16] “My strength dried up like a potsherd”: my strength dried up through my passion, not like hay but like a potsherd, which becomes harder through fire. “And my tongue clung to my jaws”: and those through whom I was to speak kept my commandments with themselves. “And you led me into the dust of death”: you led me among the ungodly destined for death, whom the wind casts like dust from the face of the earth.

17. [verse 17] “For many dogs surrounded me”: many surrounded me, barking not for the sake of truth but for the sake of custom. “The assembly of the wicked surrounded me.” “They pierced my hands and feet” [Note: [Col. 0169] On verses 17, 18, and the following, see *Exposition of Psalm 84*, no. 3.]: they pierced my hands and feet with nails.

18. [verse 18] “They counted all my bones”: they counted all my bones stretched out upon the wood of the cross. “But they themselves looked upon me and observed me”: they themselves—that is, unchanged—looked upon me and observed me.

19. [verse 19] “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.”

20. [verse 20] “But you, Lord, do not put your help far from me”: but you, Lord, do not raise me at the end of the age, as you do the others; raise me immediately. “Look upon my defense”: look upon it, lest they harm me.

21. [verse 21] “Deliver my soul from the sword”: deliver my soul from the tongue of division. “And my only one from the hand of the dog”: deliver my Church from the power of the people who bark according to custom.

22. [verse 22] “Save me from the mouth of the lion”: save me from the mouth of the secular kingdom. “And my humility from the horns of unicorns”: save my humility from the exalted positions of the proud, who raise themselves up in isolation and tolerate no companions.

23. [verse 23] “I shall declare your name to my brothers”: I shall declare your name to my brothers, who are humble and love one another just as they have been loved by me. “In the midst of the Church I shall sing to you”: rejoicing in the midst of the Church, I shall proclaim you.

24. [verse 24] “You who fear the Lord, praise him”: you who fear the Lord, do not seek your own praise, but praise him. “All the seed of Jacob, glorify him”: all the seed of the one to whom the elder shall serve, glorify him.

25. [verse 25] “Let all the seed of Israel fear him”: let all those born into new life and restored to the vision of God fear him. “For he did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor”: for he did not despise the prayer—not the prayer of the one who, crying to God with the words of sins, did not wish the vain life to pass away, but the prayer of the poor person who does not swell with passing displays. “Nor did he turn his face away from me”: as from the one who said, “I shall cry to you, and you will not hear.” “And when I cried to him, he heard me.”

26. [verse 26] “My praise is with you”: for I do not seek my own praise, because you are my praise—you who dwell in the holy place and now hear the one who prays to you, the holy one, the praise of Israel. “In the great Church I shall confess to you”: in the Church throughout the world I shall confess you. “I shall fulfill my vows before those who fear him”: I shall offer the sacraments of my body and blood before those who fear him.

27. [verse 27] “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” [Note: [Col. 0170] The same verse 27 is explained in the First Exposition of Psalm 48, sermon 1, no. 3.]: the humble and the despisers of the world shall eat and imitate; for in this way they will neither desire the abundance of this age nor fear its poverty. “And those who seek him shall praise the Lord”: for the praise of the Lord is the overflowing expression of that satisfaction. “Their hearts shall live for age upon age”: for that food is food for the heart.

28. [verse 28] “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord”: they shall remember—for God had slipped from the memory of the Gentiles, born for mortality and reaching toward external things—and then all the ends of the earth shall turn to the Lord. “All the nations’ homelands shall worship in his presence”: all the nations’ homelands shall worship in their consciences.

29. [verse 29] “For the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he himself shall rule the nations”: for the kingdom belongs to the Lord, not to proud human beings; and he himself shall rule the nations.

30. [verse 30] “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped”: even the rich of the earth have eaten the body of the humility of their Lord, and they have not, like the poor, been satisfied unto imitation; nevertheless, they have worshiped. “In his presence all who descend into the earth shall fall”: for he alone sees how all fall who, abandoning a heavenly way of life, choose on earth to appear blessed to human beings who do not see their ruin.

31. [verse 31] “And my soul shall live for him”: my soul, which in contempt of this age appears to human beings to be dying, shall live—not for itself but for him. “And my seed shall serve him”: my works, or those who through me believe in him, shall serve him.

32. [verse 32] “The coming generation shall be proclaimed to the Lord”: the generation of the New Testament shall be proclaimed to the honor of the Lord. “And the heavens shall proclaim his righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0170] Some manuscripts read, “And they shall proclaim his righteousness,” omitting “the heavens,” which is absent from the Septuagint.]: the evangelists shall proclaim his righteousness. “To a people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made”: to a people who shall be born from faith in the Lord.

### EXPOSITION II

A sermon delivered on the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion.

1. What God did not wish to be silent about through his Scriptures must not be silent among us either, and must be heard by you. The Lord’s Passion, as we know, took place once; for Christ died once, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18). We know this, hold it as certain, and retain it with unwavering faith: Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him [Col. 0171] (Rom. 6:9). These are the Apostle’s words. Yet, so that we may not forget what happened once, it is brought into our memory every year. Whenever Easter is celebrated, does Christ die as many times as it is celebrated? Nevertheless, the annual remembrance somehow represents what happened long ago and makes us moved as though we saw the Lord hanging on the cross—not mocking, but believing. For while hanging on the wood he was mocked, but while seated in heaven he is worshiped.

Or is he perhaps still mocked? And should we no longer be angry with the Jews, who mocked him when he was dying, not when he was reigning? And who is there who still mocks Christ? If only there were one; if only there were two; if only they could be counted! The whole chaff of his threshing floor mocks him, and the wheat groans that the Lord is mocked. This is what I wish to groan about with you, for this is a time for mourning. The Lord’s Passion is being celebrated: it is a time for groaning, a time for weeping, a time for confession and supplication. And who among us is fit to pour out tears worthy of so great a sorrow? But what does the prophet say now [Note: [Col. 0171] The Royal manuscript and the Vatican manuscript read, “But how does he say?” Perhaps better.]? “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1). If there truly were a fountain of tears in our eyes, it would not even be sufficient.

Christ is mocked in an open matter, in a matter where no one can say, “I did not understand!” For, while he possesses the whole world, a part is offered to him; and to him seated at the right hand of the Father it is said, “See what you have here,” and Africa alone is shown to him in place of the whole earth [Note: [Col. 0171] Against the Donatists.]!

2. Where shall we place the words we have just heard, brothers? If only they could be written with tears [Note: [Col. 0171] The editions add *deberent*, “they ought to be”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]! What woman was it who entered with the ointment (Matt. 26:7)? Whose type did she bear? Was it not that of the Church? Of what was that ointment a figure? Was it not of the good fragrance of which the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2:14–15)? The Apostle himself was presenting the person of the Church; and when he said “we are,” he spoke to the faithful. And what did he say? “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place.” Paul said that in every place all the faithful are the good fragrance of Christ, and this is contradicted, and it is said: “Africa alone smells good; the whole world stinks.” “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place”—who says this? The Church.

That vessel of ointment, with which the Lord was perfumed, signified this good fragrance. Let us see whether the Lord himself does not bear witness to it. While certain people, seeking what was their own—avaricious men and thieves, namely that Judas—were speaking about the ointment and saying, “Why this waste? This precious substance could have been sold and benefited the poor” [Note: [Col. 0171] Lovaniensis reads: “sold for a large sum and benefited the poor.” We, with the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts, read: “sold and benefited.”], he was trying to sell the good fragrance of Christ. What did the Lord reply? “Why do you trouble the woman? She has performed a good work upon me.” And what more can I say, since he himself said: “Wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told” (Matt. 26:8–10, 13)?

Is there anything to add? Is there anything to subtract? Is there any reason to lend an ear to the slanders of accusers? Either the Lord lied, or he deceived him. Let them choose what they will say: let them say either that the truth lied, or that the truth was deceived [Col. 0172]. “Wherever this Gospel is preached.” And as though you asked him, “Where will it be preached?” he says, “In the whole world.”

Let us hear the Psalm and see whether it says this. Let us hear what is sung with weeping, and truly a matter worthy of mourning when it is sung to the deaf. I wonder, brothers, whether this Psalm is read today even in the party of Donatus. I ask you, my brothers; I confess to you—Christ’s mercy knows it—that I wonder as though they were made of stone there and did not hear. What could be said more openly to the deaf [Note: [Col. 0172] Several manuscripts read “Brothers” instead of “to the deaf.”]? The Passion of Christ is recounted almost as clearly as the Gospel, and it was spoken I do not know how many years before the Lord was born of the Virgin Mary: it was a herald announcing the Judge who was to come.

Let us read as much as the constraint of time permits—not according to the feeling of our grief, but, as I said, as much as the constraint of time permits.

3. [verse 2] “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” We heard this verse first on the cross, where the Lord said, “Eli, Eli,” which means, “My God, my God: Lama sabachthani?” which means, “Why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). The Evangelist interpreted it and said that he spoke in Hebrew: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

What did the Lord wish to say? For God had not forsaken him, since he himself was God; certainly the Son of God was God, certainly the Word of God was God. Hear that Evangelist from the beginning, the one who belched forth what he had drunk from the Lord’s breast (John 13:23); let us see whether Christ is God: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Therefore, the very Word that was God became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1).

And when the Word who was God had become flesh, he hung upon the cross and said: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” Why is this said, unless because we were there, unless because the body of Christ is the Church (Eph. 1:23)? Why did he say, “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” unless to direct our attention in a certain way and say, “This Psalm was written about me”? “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins.” Whose sins? Of him of whom it was said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). How then does he say, “of my sins,” unless because he himself prays on behalf of our sins, and made our sins his own so that he might make his righteousness ours?

4. [verse 3] “My God, I shall cry to you by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for my foolishness”: he certainly spoke concerning me, concerning you, concerning him; for he was bearing his body, that is, the Church.

Unless perhaps you think, brothers, that when the Lord said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), he was afraid to die. A soldier is not stronger than his commander. “It is enough for a servant to be like his master” (Matt. 10:25). Paul speaks as a soldier of Christ the King: “I am constrained by two desires, having the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). He longs for death so that he may be with Christ, and Christ himself fears death?

But what was he doing except bearing our weakness? And on behalf of those who, while still established in the body, fear death [Col. 0173], he spoke these words [Note: [Col. 0173] So Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads “while he was established in the body.”]. Therefore that voice belonged to his members; it was the voice of his members, not of the head. So also here: “By day and by night I cried, and you will not hear.”

For many cry out in tribulation and are not heard—but for salvation, not for foolishness. Paul cried that the thorn of the flesh might be taken away from him, and he was not heard so that it would be taken away; and it was said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). Therefore he was not heard, but not for foolishness—for wisdom. Thus the human being understands that God is the physician and that tribulation is medicine for salvation, not punishment for condemnation. When you are placed under the medicine, you burn, you are cut, you cry out. The physician does not hear according to your desire, but he hears according to your health.

5. [verse 4] “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.” You dwell in those whom you have sanctified and whom you make understand that you do not hear some for their benefit and hear others for their condemnation. Paul was not heard for his benefit; the devil was heard for his condemnation. Job asked to be tested, and it was granted (Job 1:11). The demons asked to go into the pigs, and they were heard (Matt. 8:31). The demons are heard, while the Apostle is not heard; but the demons are heard for condemnation, and the Apostle is not heard for salvation: “not for my foolishness.”

“But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.” Why do you not hear your own people? Why do I say these things? Remember that we are always told, “Thanks be to God.” There is a great multitude here, and those who do not usually come have come. I say to everyone: a Christian is tested when placed in tribulation, to see whether he has abandoned his God. For when things go well for a human being, the Christian is left to himself.

Fire enters a furnace, and the furnace of the goldsmith is a thing of great sacramental significance. There is gold there; there is chaff; there is fire working in a confined space. That fire is not different, yet it produces different results: it turns the chaff into ashes and removes the dirt from the gold. Those in whom God dwells certainly become better in tribulation, like gold tested by fire.

And if the enemy, the devil, should perhaps make a request and it should be granted to him—whether through some bodily pain, some loss, or the loss of loved ones—let the heart remain fixed on the one who does not withdraw himself. Even if he seems to withdraw his ear from the one who weeps, he applies mercy to the one who supplicates. He who made us knows what he is doing; he also knows how to restore us. The builder who constructed the house is good; and if something there should collapse, he knows how to repair it.

6. [verse 5] And see what he says: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them.” We know, and we have read, how many of our fathers who hoped in him God delivered. He delivered the people of Israel from the land of Egypt (Exod. 12:51); he delivered the three youths from the furnace of fire (Dan. 3); he delivered Daniel from the lions’ den (Dan. 14); he delivered Susanna from a false charge (Dan. 13). All called upon him, and they were delivered. Has he failed with regard to his own Son, so that he would not hear him hanging on the cross? Why, then, is he himself not delivered now—the one who said, “In you our fathers hoped, and you delivered them”?

[Col. 0174] **7. [verse 7.]** But I am a worm and not a man. “A worm, and not a man”: for there is also a man who is a worm; but he is *the Worm, and not a man*. Why “not a man”? Because he is God. Why, then, did he abase himself so far as to say, “A worm”? Is it because a worm is born from flesh without intercourse, just as Christ was born from the Virgin Mary? A worm, and yet not a man. Why a worm? Because mortal, because born from flesh, because born without intercourse. Why not a man? Because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

**8.** The reproach of men and the outcast of the people: see how much he suffered! Now, to speak of the Passion and approach it with a greater lament [Note: [Col. 0174] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read: “that we may approach it with that greater lament”], see how much he suffers even now, and then see why. For what is the fruit? “Behold, our fathers hoped, and they were delivered” from the land of Egypt. And as I said, so many called upon God and were immediately delivered for a time—not in the future life, but at once. Job himself was handed over at the devil’s request, rotting with worms; yet in this life he recovered his health and received twice as much as he had lost (Job 42:10). But the Lord was scourged, and no one came to his aid; he was disfigured by spitting, and no one came to his aid; he was struck with blows, and no one came to his aid; he was crowned with thorns, and no one came to his aid; he was raised upon the wood, and no one delivered him. He cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—and no help is given (Matt. 27). Why, my brothers? Why? At what price did he suffer so much?

All these things which he suffered are the price. Let us recount the thing for whose price he suffered so much, and see what he says. First let us ask what he suffered, and then why; and let us see how they are enemies of Christ who confess that he suffered so much but remove the reason why. From this psalm let us hear everything: both what he suffered and why. Hold on to these two things: *what* and *why*. For the moment I shall explain the *what*. Let us not linger there, so that the very words of the psalm may reach you more effectively. See what the Lord suffers; pay attention, Christians: “The reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”

**9. [verses 8–9.]** “All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads. He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he desires him.” But why did they say these things? Because he had become man, they spoke as though he were merely a man.

**10. [verse 10.]** “For you are he who drew me from the womb.” Would they have said such things of that which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”? For that Word through whom all things were made was not drawn from the womb—unless it was because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “For you drew me from the womb”: “my God from my mother’s breasts” [Note: [Col. 0174] In the preceding *Enarratio* he did not read it this way, but, according to the Vulgate translation, read: “My hope from my mother’s breasts,” etc.]. For before the ages he was my Father; from my mother’s breasts he was my God.

**11. [verse 11.]** “Upon you I was cast from the womb”: that is, so that you alone might be my hope—now as man, now as the weak one, now as the Word made flesh. “From my mother’s womb you are my God”: not “my God from you” [Col. 0175]—for “from you, my Father”—but “from my mother’s womb, my God.”

**12. [verse 12.]** “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near, for there is no one to help.” See how deserted he is; and woe to us if he himself abandons us, since there is no one to help.

**13. [verse 13.]** “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me”: the people and the rulers—the people, the many calves; the rulers, the fat bulls.

**14. [verse 14.]** “They opened their mouths against me like a lion that seizes and roars.” Let us hear their roar in the Gospel: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19:6).

**15. [verse 15.]** “I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered.” By his bones he means his steadfast ones, for bones are the firm parts of the body. When did he scatter his bones? When he said to them, “Behold, I am sending you like lambs among wolves” (Matt. 10:16; Luke 10:3). He scattered his steadfast ones, and he was poured out like water. For when water is poured out, it either washes or irrigates. Christ was poured out like water: the filthy were washed, and minds were irrigated [Note: [Col. 0175] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read: “the thirsty were irrigated.”].

“My heart became like melting wax within my belly.” By his belly he means the weak members of his Church. How did his heart become like wax? His heart is his Scripture, that is, his wisdom contained in the Scriptures. For Scripture was closed; no one understood it. The Lord was crucified, and it melted like wax, so that all the weak might understand Scripture. This is also why the veil of the Temple was torn: what had been veiled was revealed.

**16. [verse 16.]** “My strength dried up like a potsherd.” Magnificently spoken: my name became stronger through tribulation. For just as a potsherd is soft before the fire and hard after the fire, so the Lord’s name was despised before the Passion and honored after the Passion.

“And my tongue clung to my jaws.” Just as that member in us is useful only for speaking, so he said that his preachers—his tongue—clung to his jaws, so that they might receive wisdom from his inner depths. “And you brought me down into the dust of death.”

**17. [verse 17.]** “For many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of evildoers surrounded me.” See the Gospel as well. “They pierced my hands and my feet.” Then the wounds were made, the scars of which the doubting disciple touched—the one who said, “Unless I put my fingers into the scars of his wounds, I will not believe.” When he said to him, “Come, put your hand, unbeliever,” he put in his hand and cried out, “My Lord and my God!” And he said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who do not see and believe” (John 20:25, 27–28). “They pierced my hands and my feet.”

**18. [verse 18.]** “They counted all my bones.” This was when he hung stretched out upon the wood. The extension of the body upon the wood could not have been described better than by saying, “They counted all my bones.”

**19. [verse 19.]** “But they themselves looked upon me and saw me” [Col. 0176]—they looked, but did not understand; they saw, but did not perceive. Their eyes reached only to the flesh, while their hearts did not reach the Word.

“They divided my garments among themselves.” His garments are his sacraments. Pay attention, brothers. Heretics were able to divide his garments—his sacraments—among themselves; but there was a garment there which no one divided. “And over my garment they cast lots.” There was a tunic there, the evangelist says, woven from above (John 19:23). Therefore it was from heaven; therefore from the Father; therefore from the Holy Spirit. What is this tunic if not love, which no one can divide? What is this tunic if not unity? The lot is cast for it, but no one divides it.

Heretics were able to divide the sacraments among themselves; they did not divide love. And because they could not divide it, they departed; but it remains whole. By lot it falls to some: whoever possesses it is secure. No one drives him from the Catholic Church; and even if he begins to possess it outside, he is brought in, like the olive branch by the dove (Gen. 8:11).

**20. [verse 20.]** “But you, Lord, do not make your help far from me.” And it happened: after three days he rose again. “Look to my defense.”

**21. [verse 21.]** “Deliver my soul from the sword”—that is, from death. For *framea* is a sword, and by the sword he wished death to be understood. “And my only one from the hand of the dog.” My soul, my only one, the head and the body. By “the only one” he means the Church. “From the hand,” that is, from the power of the dog.

Who are the dogs? Those who bark in a doglike manner [Note: [Col. 0176] The manuscripts read: “in a blind manner”], and do not understand against whom they bark. Nothing is done to them, yet they bark. What has someone passing along his own way done to a dog? Yet it barks. Those who bark with blind eyes, unable to discern against whom or for whom they bark, are dogs.

**22. [verse 22.]** “Save me from the lion’s mouth.” You know who the roaring lion is: he goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8). “And from the horns of unicorns my lowliness.” He would not have said “unicorns” unless he meant the proud; therefore he added, “my lowliness.”

**23. [verse 23.]** You have heard what he suffered and what he prayed, that he might be delivered from these things. Let us now pay attention to why he suffered. Now see, brothers: if someone is not in that lot for the sake of which Christ suffered, why is he a Christian?

Behold, we understand what he suffered: his bones were counted; he was mocked; his garments were divided; moreover, a lot was cast over his garment; raging and savage men surrounded him; all his bones were scattered. We hear these things and read them in the Gospel. Let us see why.

“O Christ, Son of God, if you did not wish to suffer, you would not have suffered. Show us the fruit of your Passion.”

“Listen,” he says, “to the fruit. I am not silent, but people are deaf. Listen to the fruit—to why I suffered all these things. I will declare your name to my brothers.”

Let us see whether he declares the name of God to his brothers in any particular part: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the [Col. 0177] Church I will sing to you.” This is happening now. But let us see what the Church itself is, for he said, “In the midst of the Church I will sing to you.” Let us see the Church, for whose sake he suffered.

**24. [verse 24.]** “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” Wherever God is feared and praised, there is the Church of Christ.

See, my brothers, whether it is without reason that these days, throughout the whole world, people say “Amen” and “Alleluia.” Is God not feared there? Is God not praised there?

Donatus came forth and said, “He is certainly not feared; the whole world has perished.” You say without reason, “The whole world has perished.” Then has only a small part remained in Africa? Does Christ say nothing that might close those mouths, nothing that might uproot the tongues of those who say this?

Let us see whether perhaps we can find something. Again it is said to us, “In the midst of the Church”; he speaks of our Church. “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” Let us see whether they praise the Lord, and understand whether he is speaking of them, and whether he is praised in the midst of their Church.

How do they praise Christ when they say, “The whole world has perished; the devil took everything from him, and he himself remained in one part”? But let us look further. Let him speak more plainly; let him speak more openly. Let there be nothing to interpret, nothing to conjecture: “All the seed of Jacob, magnify him.” Perhaps they will still say, “We are the seed of Jacob.” If they are, let us see.

**25. [verse 25.]** “Let all the seed of Israel fear him.” Let them still say, “We are the seed of Israel”; let us allow them to say it.

“For he did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor.” Which poor? Not those who presume upon themselves. Let us see whether those who say, “We are righteous,” are poor. Christ cries, “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.”

But let them still say whatever they wish: “Nor did he turn his face away from me, and when I cried to him, he heard me.” Why did he hear me? For what purpose?

**26. [verse 26.]** “My praise is with you.” He placed his praise with God; he taught us not to presume upon man.

Let them still say whatever they wish. By now they have begun to burn; the fire has begun to draw near. “There is no one who can hide from its heat” (Ps. 18:7). But let them still say, “We too have placed our praise with him, and we do not presume upon ourselves.”

Let them continue: “In the great Church I will confess to you.” Here, I think, he has begun to touch their inward parts.

What is the great Church, brothers? Is a small part of the world the great Church? The great Church is the whole world.

Now, if someone wishes to contradict Christ: “You said, ‘In the great Church I will confess to you.’ Which great Church? You have remained in a fragment of Africa and lost the whole world [Note: [Col. 0177] The editions read: “That he has remained in a part of Africa is the great Church; the whole world,” etc. We have corrected the passage according to the manuscripts.]. You poured out your blood for the whole world, but you allowed an invader to seize it.”

We said these things to the Lord as though asking, although we knew what he would say. Let us suppose that we do not know what he says: does he not answer us?

“Be silent; I shall continue speaking, from a point about which no one can doubt.” Let us therefore await what he will say. I wanted already to declare it and not allow people to interpret anything else, since Christ says, “In the great Church.” Yet you say that he remained in a remote corner.

And still they dare to say, “Our Church too is great.” What do you say to this, Bagai and Tamugade? If he does not say something [Note: [Col. 0178] The editions read: “What do you say? I now hear it as well. If it is not said,” etc. Lovaniensis reads: “What do you say of Bagai and Tamugade?” The manuscripts, however, read: “What do you say, Bagai and Tamugade?” Perhaps the reading should be “Bagai and Tamugade,” or “Thamugade.” These were evidently the principal towns occupied by the Donatists.] that will silence them, let them continue to say that only Numidia has a great Church.

**27. [verses 27–28.]** Let us see and hear the Lord further: “I will pay my vows before those who fear him.” What are his vows? The sacrifice which he offered to God. Do you know what kind of sacrifice it is? The faithful know the vows which he paid before those who fear him, for it follows: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.”

Blessed are the poor, because they eat in order to be satisfied. The poor eat; but the rich are not satisfied, because they do not hunger.

“The poor shall eat.” The fisherman Peter belonged to them; another fisherman, John, and his brother James belonged to them; the tax collector Matthew also belonged to them. They were among the poor who ate and were satisfied, suffering such things as they ate. He gave his supper; he gave his Passion. The one who imitates him is satisfied.

The poor imitated him, for they suffered in such a way that they followed Christ’s footsteps. “The poor shall eat.” But why poor? “And they shall praise the Lord who seek him.” The rich praise themselves; the poor praise the Lord.

Why are they poor? Because they praise the Lord and seek the Lord. The Lord is the wealth of the poor. Therefore the house is empty, so that the heart may be full of riches. Let the rich seek what they may put into their chest; let the poor seek what they may put into their heart. And when they have filled it, they praise the Lord who seek him.

And see, brothers, in what things those who are truly poor are rich: not in a chest, not in a granary, not in a storeroom, but “their hearts shall live for ever and ever.”

**28.** Therefore pay attention. The Lord suffered; all the things you have heard, the Lord suffered. We ask why he suffered, and he began to tell us: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you.”

But they still say, “This is the Church.” “Let all the seed of Israel fear him.” They say, “We are the seed of Israel.” “For he did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor.” They still say, “We are they.”

“Nor did he turn his face away from me”: Christ the Lord from himself—that is, from his Church, which is his body.

“My praise is with you.” You want to praise yourselves. But they answer, “Certainly we too praise him.”

“I will pay my vows to the Lord before those who fear him.” The faithful know the sacrifice of peace, the sacrifice of love, the sacrifice of his body; this cannot now be disputed.

“I will pay my vows before those who fear him.” Let tax collectors eat; let fishermen eat; let them eat, imitate the Lord, suffer, and be satisfied. The Lord himself died, and the poor also die; the death of the disciples is added to the death of the teacher.

Why? Give me the fruit.

“They shall remember and turn to the Lord, all the ends of the earth.”

Come, brothers! What do you ask us to say in answer to the party of Donatus? Behold the psalm; it is read here today, and it is read there today. Let us write it upon our foreheads; let us go forth with it; let our tongue never rest from saying:

“Behold, Christ suffered. Behold, the merchant has displayed the payment. Behold the price he gave: his blood was poured out.”

He carried our price in a sack. He was pierced by a spear; the sack was opened, and the [Col. 0179] price of the whole world flowed forth.

What do you say to me, heretic? Is this not the price of the whole world? Was Africa alone redeemed? You do not dare to say, “The whole world was redeemed, but it perished.” What invader did Christ suffer, that he should lose what belonged to him?

“Behold, all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

Let it satisfy you still, and let it speak. If it had said “the ends of the earth,” but had not said “all the ends of the earth,” they might say, “Behold, we have the ends of the earth in Mauretania.” But it said, “All the ends of the earth.” O heretic, it said “all.” Where will you go out, so as to escape the question? You have no way out, but you do have a way in.

**29. [verse 29.]** I ask you: I do not wish to argue about this, lest it be said that my speech has any force. Pay attention to the psalm; read the psalm.

Behold, Christ suffered; his blood was poured out. Behold our Redeemer; behold our price. Let someone tell me what he bought.

Why do we ask? What if someone says to me, “Fool, why do you ask? You carry the book; there you have what he bought. Look there to see what he bought.”

There you have it: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” The ends of the earth shall remember.

But the heretics have forgotten, and therefore they hear it every year. Do you suppose they listen when their reader says, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord”?

Perhaps there is one verse: you were thinking of something else, speaking with your brother, when he said it. Pay attention, because he repeats it, and strikes the deaf: “And all the nations’ homelands shall worship in his sight.”

He is still deaf; he does not hear. Let him be struck again: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”

Hold fast to these three verses, brothers. They were sung there today as well—or perhaps they have erased them.

Believe me, my brothers, I burn and suffer such anguish that I marvel at some kind of deafness and hardness of their hearts. At times I even wonder whether they have this in their books.

Today everyone runs to church; today everyone listens attentively; everyone hears the psalm with suspended hearts. But suppose they were not attentive: is “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” only one verse?

You awaken, but you are still rubbing your eyes: “And all the nations’ homelands shall worship in his sight.” Shake off your sleep; you are still weighed down. Listen: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”

**30.** If there is still something they can say, I do not know what it is. Let them quarrel with the Scriptures, not with us. Here is the book itself; let them fight against it.

Where is the claim, “We preserved the Scriptures so that they would not be burned” [Note: [Col. 0179] The Donatists claimed that they had preserved the sacred books, while ours had handed them over]? They were preserved for your burning.

What did you preserve? Open it and read. You preserved it, and you attack it. What did you preserve from the flames which you now seek to erase with your tongue?

I do not believe it—I do not believe that you preserved it. I certainly do not believe it; you did not preserve it. Our people speak most truly when they say that you handed it over.

The traitor is proved to be the one who does not follow the testament once it has been read. It is read, and I follow it; it is read, and you reject it.

Whose hand put it into the flames? [Col. 0180] The hand of the one who believes and follows, or of the one who is distressed because there is something to read?

I do not want to know who preserved it. Wherever the book was found, the testament of our father came out of whatever cave. I do not know which thieves wanted to take it away; I do not know which persecutors wanted to burn it. Wherever it was brought forth, let it be read.

Why do you quarrel? We are brothers; why do we quarrel? Our father did not die intestate. He made a testament and then died; he died and rose again.

A dispute over the inheritance of the dead continues only until the testament is produced in public. Once the testament has been produced in public, everyone is silent so that the tablets may be opened and read aloud. The judge listens attentively; the advocates are silent; the heralds impose silence; the whole people wait expectantly for the words of the dead man to be read, though he himself lies unfeeling in the tomb.

He lies without sensation in the tomb, yet his words have force. Christ sits in heaven, and his testament is contradicted?

Open it; let us read. We are brothers; why do we contend? Let our mind be appeased: our father did not leave us without a testament.

He who made the testament lives forever. He hears our voices and recognizes his own. Let us read; why do we quarrel? Wherever the inheritance itself is found, let us hold to it.

Open the testament; read in the first chapter of its Psalter: “Ask of me” (Ps. 2:8). But who says this? Perhaps it is not Christ. There you have it: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (ibid., 7).

Therefore the Son of God speaks—or the Father speaks to his Son. What, then, does he say to the Son? “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth.”

It is customary, brothers, when possession is at issue, to seek out the adjoining landholders. Between one person and another, one seeks the heir, or the person to whom something is given, or the purchaser. Among which adjoining landholders is the matter sought? Among those possessing this land and that.

He who assigned all the boundaries left no neighboring boundaries. Wherever you turn, Christ is there. You have the ends of the earth as your inheritance; come here and possess it all with me.

Why do you call people to one part by quarreling? Come here: you are overcome to your advantage; you will have everything.

Do you still bring accusations? I have already read the testament, and you bring accusations. Do you still bring accusations because it said “the ends of the earth,” not “all the ends of the earth”?

Let us read, then. How is it written?

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord. And all the nations’ homelands shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”

It belongs to him, not to you. Acknowledge the Lord; acknowledge the Lord’s possession.

**31.** But you also [Note: [Col. 0180] Several manuscripts of good authority have “Sedat vos” (“It quiets you”) instead of “Sed et vos” (“But you also”), because of the following “since you wish to possess your private things,” etc. Some have “Sedete vos” (“Sit yourselves down”).], because you wish to possess your private things and not possess them in the common unity with Christ. For you wish to rule on earth, not reign with him in heaven; you possess your own houses.

At times we come to them saying, “Let us seek the truth; let us find the truth.” And they say, “You keep what you have; you have your sheep, and I have my sheep. Do not trouble my sheep, since I do not trouble yours.”

Thanks be to God! My sheep belong to me, and his sheep belong to him. What did Christ [Col. 0181] buy? Rather, let them belong neither to me nor to you, but to him who bought them; let them belong to him who marked them with his seal.

“Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Why do I have my sheep, and you have yours? If Christ is there, let mine go there, because they are not mine. If Christ is here, let yours come here, because they are not yours.

“Because of possessions, let them kiss our head and hands, and let the children of foreigners perish” [Note: [Col. 0181] Six manuscripts read “let them continue” instead of “let them perish.”].

“It is not my possession,” he says. What is this? Let us see whether it is not your possession; let us see whether you do not claim it for yourself.

I labor in the name of Christ; you labor in the name of Donatus. For if you look to Christ, Christ is everywhere.

You say, “Behold, here is Christ” (Matt. 24:23); I say, “He is throughout the whole.”

“Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord.” From where do they praise him? How far do they praise him? “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 113:1).

Behold what Church I am pointing out; behold what Christ bought; behold what he redeemed; behold for whom he gave his blood.

But what do you say? “I too gather for him.”

“He who does not gather with me,” he says, “scatters” (Matt. 12:30). You divide unity and seek your own possessions. And why do they bear the name of Christ? Because you have placed Christ’s titles over the defense of your possession.

Do not some people do this in their own house? So that no powerful person may invade the house, they place there the titles of the powerful—false titles. He wants to be the possessor himself, but he wants the front of his house to be protected by another’s title, so that when the title has been read, someone terrified by the power of the name may refrain from invading it.

They did this when they condemned the Maximianists. They brought their case before the judges and read out their council [Note: [Col. 0181] The Council of Bagai, in the year 394], displaying their titles as though to appear to be bishops.

Then the judge asked, “Who is this other bishop on Donatus’s side?”

The official replied, “We know no one except Aurelius the Catholic.”

Fearing the laws, they answered with regard to only one bishop. But in order to be heard by the judge, they imposed the name of Christ; they placed his titles upon their possession.

The Lord is good: may he spare them, and wherever he finds his titles, may he vindicate that possession as his own. Great is his mercy: may he cause all whom he finds bearing the name of Christ to be gathered to him.

And see, brothers: when a powerful man finds his titles, does he not rightly claim the property for himself and say, “He would not have placed my titles there unless the property were mine”? He placed my titles there; it is my property. Wherever I find my name, it is mine.

Does he change the titles? The title that was there remains the same; the possessor changes, but the title does not.

So too, if those who possess Christ’s baptism come to unity, we do not change or erase the titles. We recognize the titles of our king, the titles of our emperor.

But what shall we say? O wretched house, let him possess you whose titles you bear. You bear Christ’s titles; do not be Donatus’s possession.

**32.** We have said much, brothers. But let this not depart from your memory, what is read today. Behold, I say it again, and it must often be said: by this very day—that is, by the sacraments of this day—I bind you not to let it depart from your hearts.

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn [Col. 0182] to the Lord. And all the nations’ homelands shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”

Against this possession of Christ, so open and so clearly demonstrated, do not listen to the words of the accuser. Whatever they contradict, human beings say; but this, God says.

## Exposition of Psalm XXII

[Note: [Col. 0182] The editions have “To the end, a psalm,” etc. “To the end” is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.]

*A psalm belonging to David.*

**1. [verse 1.]** The Church speaks to Christ: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing.” The Lord Jesus Christ is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing.

**2. [verse 2.]** “He placed me there in a place of pasture.” Leading me as one beginning in faith [Note: [Col. 0182] The old Corbie manuscript reads: “from faith”], he brought me to a place of pasture and placed me there to be nourished.

“He led me beside the water of refreshment.” He led me beside the water of baptism, by which those who had lost their integrity and strength are refreshed.

**3. [verse 3.]** “He restored my soul. He led me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.” He led me along the narrow paths of his righteousness, which few walk—not because of my merit, but for his name’s sake.

**4. [verse 4.]** “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death”—even if I walk in the midst of this present life, which is the shadow of death—“I will fear no evil, because you are with me.”

I will fear no evil because by faith you dwell in my heart; and now you are with me, so that after the shadow of death I too may be with you.

“Your rod and your staff, they themselves comforted me.” Your discipline, like a rod for a flock of sheep and like a staff for grown sons who are advancing from animal life to spiritual life, did not distress me; rather, it comforted me, because you remember me.

**5. [verse 5.]** “You prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me.” After the rod by which, as a little one and as an animal within the flock, I was trained in the pastures; after I began to be under the staff, you prepared a table before me, so that I would no longer be nourished with milk as a little one (1 Cor. 3:2), but, having grown stronger, would eat solid food [Note: [Col. 0182] The editions read: “but would eat greater food.” Some manuscripts: “greater foods.” Several others: “would eat solid food.”], strengthened against those who trouble me.

“You anointed my head with oil.” You gladdened my mind with spiritual joy.

“And how splendid is your cup that makes drunk” [Note: [Col. 0182] On this part of verse 5, see *Enarratio* on Psalm 35, no. 14]! How splendid is your cup that brings forgetfulness of former empty pleasures!

**6. [verse 6.]** “And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life”—that is, as long as I live in this mortal life, which is mine, not yours.

“And I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.” It shall follow me not only here, but also so that I may dwell in the house of the Lord forever.

## Exposition of Psalm XXIII

*A psalm belonging to David, for the first day of the week.*

[Col. 0183]

**1. [verse 1.]** A psalm belonging to David, concerning the glorification and resurrection of the Lord, which occurred in the morning of the first day of the week, the day now called the Lord’s Day.

**2. [verse 2.]** “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” [Note: [Col. 0183] The editions read “in it” with a masculine pronoun; the manuscripts consistently have the feminine form, “in her”]: when the glorified Lord is proclaimed for the faith of all nations, and the whole world becomes his Church.

“He founded it upon the seas.” He established it most firmly upon all the waves of this present age, so that they might be overcome by it and do it no harm.

“And upon the rivers he prepared it.” Rivers flow into the sea, and greedy people slide into the age; yet the Church overcomes these people as well. Having conquered worldly desires by God’s grace, she is prepared by love to receive immortality [Note: [Col. 0183] Thus the manuscripts read. The editions have: “prepared for the splendor of immortality.”].

**3. [verse 3.]** “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Who shall ascend to the highest righteousness of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” Or who shall remain in that place, founded upon the seas and prepared upon the rivers, to which he will ascend?

**4. [verse 4.]** “The innocent in hands and pure in heart.” Who, then, shall ascend there and remain there except the one who is innocent in deeds and pure in thoughts?

“The one who has not received his soul in vain”: the one who has not assigned his soul to things that do not endure, but, recognizing it as immortal, desired a stable and unchangeable eternity.

“And has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.” Therefore, just as eternal things are simple and incapable of deception, he has presented himself to his neighbor without deceit.

**5. [verse 5.]** “This one shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior.”

**6. [verse 6.]** “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.” For in this way those who seek him are born.

“Of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0183] *Diapsalma*]: they seek the face of God who gave primacy to the one born later.

**7. [verse 7.]** “Lift up your gates, your princes” [Note: [Col. 0183] The editions read “your gates”; the manuscripts consistently read “your princes,” as does Augustine in Letter 237.8].

All you who seek supremacy among human beings, remove the entrances which you have established through desire and fear, lest they impede you.

“And be lifted up, eternal gates.” Be lifted up, entrances of eternal life, through renunciation of the world and conversion to God.

“And the King of glory shall enter.” The King shall enter, in whom we glory without pride; he who, having overcome the gates of mortality and opened the heavenly gates for himself, fulfilled what he said: “Rejoice, for I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

**8. [verse 8.]** “Who is this King of glory?” Mortal nature, trembling in wonder, asks, “Who is this King of glory?”

“The Lord strong and mighty”—the one whom you considered weak and oppressed.

“The Lord mighty in battle.” Touch the scars, and you will perceive that they have been restored and that human weakness has been returned to immortality. The glorification of the Lord, which was owed to the earth where he battled with death, has been paid.

**9. [verse 9.]** “Lift up the gates, your princes.” From here let the journey now proceed into heaven.

Let the prophetic trumpet cry out again: “Lift up the gates”—even you, heavenly princes: lift up the gates which you have in the minds of human beings who worship the host of heaven (2 Kings 17:16).

“And be lifted up, eternal gates.” Be lifted up, eternal gates of righteousness, love, and chastity, through which the soul loves the one true God and does not commit fornication with the many who are called gods.

“And the King of glory shall enter.” The King of glory shall enter, to intercede for us at the right hand of the Father (Rom. 8:34).

**10. [verse 10.]** “Who is this King of glory?” Do you too, prince of the power of the air, marvel and ask, “Who is this King of glory?”

“The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.” Now that his body has been given life, he who was tempted proceeds above you; he rises above all the angels, he who was tempted by the rebellious angel.

Let none of you obstruct or block our way, so that he may be worshiped by us as God. Neither principality, nor angel, nor power separates us from the love of Christ (ibid., 39).

“It is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in a prince” (Ps. 117:9), so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

These powers do indeed exist in the ordering of this world; but the Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.

## Exposition of Psalm XXIV

*To the end, a psalm belonging to David.*

**1. [verse 1.]** Christ speaks, but in the person of the Church; for the things said pertain more particularly to the Christian people converted to God.

**2. [verse 2.]** “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul”—with spiritual desire, though it was being trampled upon the earth by carnal desires.

“My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame.” Because I trusted in myself, I was brought to this weakness of the flesh. When I abandoned God and wished to be like God, I was mocked in my pride, fearing death from the tiniest creature. Now, therefore, I trust in you; I shall not be put to shame.

**3. [verse 3.]** “Nor let my enemies mock me.” Let those who lie in wait through serpent-like and hidden suggestions, and who by saying “Good, good” brought me down to these things, not mock me.

“For all who wait for you shall not be confounded.”

**4. [verse 4.]** “Let those who act unjustly in vain things be confounded.” Let those who act unjustly in acquiring things that pass away be confounded.

“Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths.” Teach me your paths, which are not broad and do not lead the multitude to destruction (Matt. 7:13), but are narrow and known to few.

5. [verse 5.] Guide me in your truth, as I flee errors. And teach me, for by myself I know nothing but falsehood. For you are God my savior, and I have waited for you all day: for, having been dismissed by you from paradise (Gen. 3:23) and having journeyed into a far country (Luke 15:13), I cannot return by myself unless you meet me in my wandering; for throughout the whole course of secular time my return has awaited your mercy.

6. [verse 6.] Remember your mercies, O Lord: remember the works of your mercy, O Lord, since human beings think that you have forgotten. And because your mercies are from eternity: remember this also, because your mercies are from eternity. For you have never been without them; even sinful humanity you subjected to vanity, but in hope, and you did not abandon it amid so many and such great consolations of your creation.

7. [verse 7.] Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance: do not retain for vengeance the sins of my presumptuous boldness and my ignorance, but let them be as though they had slipped from your memory. According to your mercy, remember me, O God: remember me, indeed, not according to the anger I deserve, but according to your mercy, which is worthy of you. For the sake of your goodness, O Lord: not because of my merit, but for the sake of your goodness, O Lord.

8. [verse 8.] The Lord is sweet and upright: the Lord is sweet, since he took pity even on sinners and the ungodly, so as to forgive all their former offenses; but the Lord is also upright, for after the mercy of his call and forgiveness—which possesses grace without merits—he will require merits worthy of the final judgment. Therefore he will establish a law for those who offend on the way, because he first granted mercy in order to lead them onto the way.

9. [verse 9.] He will guide the meek in judgment: he will guide the meek, and in judgment he will not disturb those who follow his will and who do not resist him by placing their own will before his. He will teach the gentle his ways: he will teach his ways, not those who wish to run ahead, as though they could govern themselves better, but those who do not stiffen their necks [Note: In all our manuscripts, *rapiunt* (“tear away,” “snatch”).] nor kick back when a gentle yoke and a light burden are placed upon them (Matt. 11:30).

10. [verse 10.] All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth [Note: The same verse 10 is treated in *Expositions of Psalms* 60, no. 9; 118, sermon 29, no. 8.]. What ways, then, will he teach them, except the mercy by which he is reconciled and the truth by which he is incorruptible? One of these he displayed by forgiving sins, the other by judging merits. And therefore all the ways of the Lord are the two comings of the Son of God: one in mercy, the other in judgment.
