Thus the one who holds fast to his ways reaches him: seeing that he has been freed by no merits of his own, he lays aside pride, and thereafter fears the severity of the examiner, having experienced the clemency of the one who comes to his aid. Those who seek his covenant and his testimonies understand the Lord as merciful in his first coming and as judge in the second. The meek and gentle seek his covenant, by which he redeemed us into new life with his own blood, and his testimonies in the Prophets and Evangelists.

[Col. 0186] 11. [verse 11.] For the sake of your name, O Lord, you will be propitious toward my sin; for it is great: you not only forgave my sins, which I committed before I believed, but you will also be propitious toward my sin, which is great because even on the way offense is not absent, through the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.

12. [verse 12.] Who is the person who fears the Lord? From this he begins to come to wisdom. He will establish a law for him on the way which he has freely embraced [Note: The editions read *statuit* (“he establishes”); the manuscripts, *statuet* (“he will establish”), in accordance with the Septuagint’s *nomothetēsei* (“he will give a law”).], so that he may no longer sin with impunity.

13. [verse 13.] His soul will dwell among good things, and his offspring will possess the land as an inheritance: and his work will possess a firm inheritance, the body restored.

14. [verse 14.] The Lord is the stronghold of those who fear him: fear seems to belong to the weak, but the Lord is the stronghold of those who fear him. And the name of the Lord, which has been glorified throughout the world, strengthens those who fear him. And he makes his covenant manifest to them: and he causes his covenant to be made manifest to them, because the nations and the ends of the earth are Christ’s inheritance.

15. [verse 15.] My eyes are always toward the Lord, because he himself will draw my feet out of the snare [Note: On this verse 15, see *Expositions of Psalm* 31, book 2, no. 21.]: nor will I fear earthly dangers while I do not look upon the earth; for the one upon whom I look will draw my feet out of the snare.

16. [verse 16.] Look upon me and have mercy on me, because I am solitary and poor: because I am the solitary people, preserving the humility of your one Church, which no schisms or heresies possess.

17. [verse 17.] The tribulations of my heart have multiplied: the tribulations of my heart have multiplied as iniquity abounds and charity grows cold. Bring me out of my necessities: for I must endure these things so that, persevering to the end, I may be saved (Matt. 10:22); bring me out of my necessities.

18. [verse 18.] See my humility and my labor: see my humility, by which I never sever myself from unity through a boastful claim to righteousness; and my labor, by which I endure those who have been mingled with me without discipline. And forgive all my sins: and, appeased by these sacrifices, forgive my sins—not only those of my youth and my ignorance, committed before I believed, but also those which, now living by faith, I commit through the weakness or darkness of this life.

19. [verse 19.] Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied: for they are not absent only outside, but also within the very communion of the Church. And they have hated me with unjust hatred: and they have hated me because I love them.

20. [verse 20.] Guard my soul and deliver me: guard my soul, lest I turn toward imitating them [Note: The editions read *declinem*; the manuscripts, *decliner*.]; and deliver me from the perplexity in which they are mixed with me. Let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you: let me not be put to shame if perhaps they rise up against me, for I have hoped not in myself but in you.

21. [verse 21.] The innocent and the upright have adhered to me, because I have waited for you, O Lord: the innocent and the upright are not merely mingled with me through bodily presence, as the wicked are, but adhere to me through the agreement of their hearts in innocence and uprightness; because I have not fallen away so as to imitate the wicked, but have waited for you, awaiting the winnowing of your final harvest.

22. [verse 22.] Redeem Israel, O God, from all his tribulations: redeem your people, O God, whom you have prepared for the vision of yourself, from their tribulations—not only those which they endure outside, but also those which they endure within.

# ON PSALM XXV

## EXPOSITION I. To David himself

1. [verse 1.] “To David himself” can be attributed not to the human mediator Christ Jesus, but to the whole Church, already perfectly established in Christ [Note: Almost all the manuscripts read: “but to the human being … established.”].

2. Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence; judge me, O Lord, because after the mercy you first granted me, I possess some merit of innocence, whose path I have guarded. And hoping in the Lord I shall not be moved [Note: Thus the Louvain edition. Erasmus and seven manuscripts read: “I shall not be weakened.”]: yet even so I shall remain, hoping not in myself but in the Lord.

3. [verses 2–3.] Test me, O Lord, and try me: nevertheless, lest any of my hidden things remain unknown to me, test me, O Lord, and try me—not making me known to you, from whom nothing is hidden, but to myself and to human beings. Burn my kidneys and my heart: apply medicinal purification, as though by fire, to my pleasures and thoughts. For your mercy is before my eyes: so that I may not be consumed by that fire, your mercy—not my merits—by which you have led me to such a life, is before my eyes. And I have been pleasing in your truth: and because my falsehood displeased me while your truth pleased me, I too became pleasing together with it and in it.

4. [verse 4.] I have not sat with the council of vanity: I have not chosen to set my heart on those who try to devise how they might become blessed through the enjoyment of passing things, although this cannot be done [Note: The editions read *perfunctione* (“use,” “enjoyment”). Several manuscripts have the better reading *perfructione* (“enjoyment,” “delight”).]. And I shall not enter in with those who do evil: and since this is the cause of all iniquities, I shall not have a hidden conscience together with those who do evil.

5. [verse 5.] I have hated the assembly of the wicked: in order to reach that very council of vanity, assemblies of the wicked are formed, and I have hated them. And I shall not sit with the ungodly: and therefore I shall not sit with such a council, with the ungodly—that is, I shall not place my approval there. And I shall not sit with the ungodly.

6. [verse 6.] I shall wash my hands among the innocent [Note: The editions read “among the innocent”; the manuscripts, “in the innocent.” The Greek Septuagint has *en athōois* (“among the innocent”).]: I shall make my works clean among the innocent; I shall wash my hands among the innocent, with which I shall embrace your sublime things. And I shall surround your altar, O Lord.

7. [verse 7.] So that I may hear the voice of your praise: so that I may learn how to praise you. And declare all your wonders: and when I have learned, I shall expound all your wonders.

8. [verse 8.] Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house: your Church. And the place of the dwelling of your glory: where you are glorified as you dwell.

9. [verse 9.] Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly: therefore do not destroy my soul together with those who hate you, since it has loved the beauty of your house. And my life with men of blood: and with those who hate their neighbor. For your house is adorned by the two commandments.

10. [verse 10.] In whose hands are iniquities: therefore do not destroy me with the ungodly and with men of blood, whose works are iniquitous. Their right hand is filled with gifts: and what was given to them for obtaining eternal salvation they have turned toward receiving the gifts of this age, thinking that godliness is a means of gain (1 Tim. 6:5).

11. [verse 11.] But I have walked in my innocence: redeem me and have mercy on me: let the price of the blood of my Lord be effective for me toward the perfection of deliverance; and in the dangers of this life, may your mercy not abandon me.

12. [verse 12.] My foot has stood in uprightness: my love has not departed from your justice. In the churches I will bless you, O Lord: I will not conceal your blessing from those whom you have called, O Lord, because I subordinate love of neighbor to your love.

## EXPOSITION II. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. When the Apostle Paul was being read, Your Holiness heard with us: “As the truth is in Jesus, that you put off [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read *deponite* (“put off”). The Amerbach edition and the manuscripts read *deponere* (“to put off”).], with respect to your former way of life, the old man, which is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit; but be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:21–24). And lest anyone suppose that some substance had to be put off, as one strips off a tunic, or that something external had to be taken up, as one takes up a garment—putting down one tunic and taking up another—and lest this carnal understanding prevent people from spiritually doing within themselves what the Apostle commanded, he continued and explained what it meant to strip off the old man and put on the new. For the rest of the reading pertains to the same understanding. He speaks as though someone were saying: “How am I to strip off the old man, or how am I to put on the new? Am I myself some third person who will put off the old man whom I had and take up the new whom I did not have, so that there are understood to be three people, with the one who puts off the old man and takes up the new standing in between?” Therefore, lest anyone hindered by such a carnal thought do less than what is commanded [Note: The editions read *quam* (“than what”); the manuscripts read *quod* (“what”).] and, by failing to do it, excuse himself on the grounds that the reading is obscure, he says in what follows: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another” (Eph. 4:25).

2. But none of you should think in this way, brothers: that truth is to be spoken with a Christian and falsehood with a pagan. Speak with your neighbor. Your neighbor is the one who was born with you from Adam and Eve. By the condition of earthly birth we are all neighbors; but in another way we are brothers through the hope of heavenly inheritance. You must regard every human being as your neighbor, even before he is a Christian. For you do not know what he is before God; you do not know how God has foreknown him. Sometimes the person whom you ridicule for worshiping stones is converted and worships God, perhaps more devoutly than you, who shortly before were ridiculing him. Thus our neighbors are hidden among those people who are not yet in the Church, and they are hidden far from us within the Church. Therefore, since we do not know the future, let us regard each person as our neighbor—not only by the condition of human mortality, through which we have come to this earth by the same lot, but also through the hope of that inheritance, because we do not know what the one who is currently nothing may become.

3. Therefore pay attention to what follows concerning putting on the new man and stripping off the old. “Putting away,” he says, “falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another. Be angry, and do not sin.” If you are angry with your servant because he has sinned, then, so that you yourself do not sin, be angry with yourself. “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4:26): this is indeed understood according to time, brothers; for even if, because of the human condition and the weakness of mortality that we bear, anger steals upon a Christian, it must not be held for long and become a matter of yesterday. Cast it out of your heart before this visible light sets, lest that invisible light abandon you.

But it is also rightly understood in another way, because we have our sun of righteousness, Christ the Truth—not this sun worshiped by pagans and Manichaeans and seen even by sinners, but that other one by whose truth human nature is illumined. The angels rejoice in him, while the eyes of the human heart, weakened though they are [Note: Thus the old Corbie manuscript. The editions read: “the vision of human beings through weakness.”], tremble beneath his rays, yet are purified by the commandments in order to contemplate him. When this sun begins to dwell in a human being through faith, do not let the anger arising within you have such power over you that it sets upon your anger—that is, that Christ abandons your mind, since Christ does not wish to dwell with your anger.

For he seems to set from you when you set from him, because when anger grows old it becomes hatred; and when hatred has come to be, you are already a murderer. “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15), as the Apostle John says. He also says that everyone who hates his brother remains in darkness (1 John 2:9); and it is no wonder that the one from whom the sun has set remains in darkness.

4. Perhaps this also relates to what you heard in the Gospel: “The boat was in danger on the lake, and Jesus was sleeping” (Luke 8:23). We are sailing across a certain lake, and wind and storms are not lacking; our boat is almost swamped by the daily temptations of this age. But why does this happen, unless Jesus is sleeping? If Jesus were not sleeping in you, you would not suffer these storms, but would have inward tranquility, with Jesus keeping watch with you.

What does it mean that Jesus is sleeping? Your faith concerning Jesus has fallen asleep. The storms of this lake arise: you see the wicked prospering and the good suffering. It is a temptation; it bears fruit. And your soul says [Note: Thirteen manuscripts read: “And it doubts.”]: “O God, is this your justice—that the wicked should prosper and the good suffer?” You say to God: “Is this your justice?” And God says to you: “Is this your faith? Did I promise you this? Did you become a Christian in order to prosper in this age? Are you tormented because here the wicked prosper, who will afterward be tormented with the devil?” [Note: Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. The Louvain edition reads: “that you might prosper in this age, and afterward be most wretchedly tormented in hell? Because here the wicked prosper, etc.”]

But why do you say this? Why are you troubled by the waves and storm of the lake? Because Jesus is sleeping—that is, because your faith concerning Jesus is drowsing in your heart. What do you do to be delivered? Awaken Jesus and say, “Teacher, we are perishing!” (Luke 8:24). The uncertainties of the lake are in motion: “We are perishing.” He will awaken—that is, your faith will return to you—and with his help you will consider in your soul that the things now given to the wicked will not remain with them. Either they abandon them while alive, or they are abandoned by them when they die; but what is promised to you will remain forever. What is granted to them temporarily is quickly taken away. “For he flourished like the flower of hay. All flesh is hay: the hay withered and the flower fell; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6, 8).

Therefore turn your back toward what falls and your face toward what remains. When Christ awakens, that storm will no longer shake your heart, nor will the waves swamp your boat, because your faith commands the winds and the waves, and the danger will pass.

To this belongs everything the Apostle says about stripping off the old man: “Be angry, and do not sin; let not the sun go down upon your anger; neither give place to the devil.” The old man therefore gave place; the new must not. “Let the one who stole steal no longer” (Eph. 4:26–28): the old man stole; the new must not steal. It is the same person, one person: he was Adam; let him be Christ. He was old; let him be new—and the rest that follows there.

5. But let us examine the Psalm somewhat more carefully, because when each person has made progress in the Church, it is necessary for him to endure the wicked in the Church. Yet one who is such does not recognize them, although many wicked people murmur against the wicked, just as one healthy person more easily bears two sick people than two sick people bear one another individually.

Therefore this is what we command, brothers: the Church of this time is a threshing floor. We have often said it and often say it: it has both chaff and grain. Let no one seek to remove all the chaff until the time of winnowing. Let no one abandon the threshing floor before the time of winnowing, as though he did not wish to endure sinners, lest, found outside the threshing floor, he be gathered by the birds before he enters the granary.

But attend to how we may say this, brothers. When the grains begin to be threshed, they no longer touch one another among the chaff; thus they seem not to know one another, because chaff lies between them. And whoever looks at the threshing floor from a distance thinks it is nothing but chaff. Unless he looks more carefully, unless he stretches out his hand, unless he separates it by the breath of his mouth—that is, by purifying wind—he scarcely reaches the discernment of the grains.

Thus sometimes the grains themselves are so separated from one another and do not touch one another that each person who has made progress thinks he is alone. This thought tested Elijah, so great a man (1 Kings 19:10), and he said to God, as the Apostle also recalls: “They have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone remain, and they seek my life.” But what divine response was given to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (Rom. 11:3–4).

He did not say to him: “You have two or three others like you.” “Do not,” he says, “think that you are alone. There are another seven thousand, and you think you are alone!”

Therefore this is what we briefly command, as I began to say. Let Your Fraternal Holiness pay attention with me, and may God’s mercy be present in our hearts, so that you may understand this in such a way that it bears fruit and works in you. Listen briefly: whoever is still wicked should not think that no one is good; whoever is good should not think that he alone is good.

Do you understand this? Look, I repeat it; see what I am saying: whoever is wicked, questioning his conscience and receiving a bad report from it, should not suppose that no one is good; whoever is good should not suppose that he alone is good. And let the good person not fear being among the wicked, because the time will come when he will be separated from them.

For this is what we sang today: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, and my life with men of blood.” What does “Do not destroy with the ungodly” mean? Do not destroy together with them. Why does he fear that he may be destroyed together with them? I see that this is said to God: “Since now you endure us together, whom you endure together, do not destroy us together.”

The whole Psalm contains this, and I wish to consider it briefly with Your Holiness, because it is short.

6. [verse 1.] Judge me, O Lord: he desires for himself prayers that are troublesome and seemingly dangerous, that he may be judged [Note: Most manuscripts read *orat* (“he prays”) for *optat* (“he desires”).]. What does the judgment he desires mean? He desires to be distinguished from the wicked. Elsewhere he plainly speaks of this judgment of separation: “Judge me, O Lord, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1).

He shows what he has said by “Judge”: lest, as though without judgment—because now both good and wicked enter the Church—the good and the wicked should go into eternal fire. “Judge me, O Lord.” Why? “For I have walked in my innocence, and hoping in the Lord I shall not be moved.”

What does “hoping in the Lord” mean? The one who does not hope in the Lord staggers among the wicked; from this it happened that schisms arose [Note: Against the Donatists.]. They trembled among the wicked, although they themselves were worse, and as though they did not wish to be good among the wicked. If only they were grains, they would endure the chaff on the threshing floor until the time of winnowing.

But because they were chaff, the wind blew before the very time of winnowing, carried the chaff away from the threshing floor, and threw it into the thorns. The chaff was indeed thrown out from there; but is what remained therefore grain alone? Nothing flies away before the winnowing except chaff; but both grain and chaff remain. The chaff, however, will be winnowed when the time of winnowing comes.

This man said: “I have walked in my innocence, and hoping in the Lord I shall not be moved.” For if I hope in a human being, I may perhaps see that very person at some time living badly and not following the ways that he either learned or teaches as good in the Church, but ways he pursued under the instruction of the devil. And because my hope will be in a human being, when the human being staggers, my hope will stagger, and when the human being falls, my hope will fall. But because I hope in the Lord, I shall not be moved.

7. [verse 2.] It follows: “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart.” What does “Burn my kidneys and my heart” mean? Burn my pleasures; burn my thoughts. He used “heart” for thoughts and “kidneys” for pleasures, so that I may think no evil and no evil may please me.

With what, then, will you burn my kidneys? With the fire of your word. With what will you burn my heart? With the heat of your spirit. Of this heat it is said elsewhere: “And there is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7); and of this fire the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

8. [verse 3.] It follows, then: “For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth.” This means: I have not been pleasing in a human being, but inwardly I have been pleasing to you, where you see; and I do not fear if I displease where human beings see, as the Apostle says: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another” (Gal. 6:4).

9. [verses 4–5.] “I have not sat,” he says, “with the council of vanity.” Your Holiness should pay attention to what this means: “I have not sat.” God sees how he says that he has not sat. Sometimes you are not in the council, yet you sit there. For example, you are not sitting in the theater, but you are thinking theatrical thoughts, against which it was said, “Burn my kidneys.” In your heart you are sitting there, although bodily you are not there.

But suppose that you are detained by someone and are gathered there, or that some pious duty makes you sit there. How can this happen? It may happen as a duty of piety that a servant of God has to be in the amphitheater. He wanted to free some gladiator; it could happen that he sat and waited until the one whom he wished to free came out. Behold, he did not sit in the council of vanity, although he seemed bodily to sit there.

What does it mean to sit? To consent with those who sit there. If you do not do this while present, you have not sat there; if you do it while absent, you have sat there. “And I shall not enter in with those who do evil” [Note: He does not mention what perhaps occurred only later at the Carthaginian conference, where the Donatists refused to sit with the Catholics, saying that this Psalm prohibited sitting with the ungodly. They were answered that they themselves, because they had entered together, had sinned against “And I shall not enter in with those who do evil.” It was shown that the Psalm concerns spiritual entry and sitting together, not bodily entry and sitting. See the book addressed to the Donatists after the Conference, chapter 5.]. “I have hated the assembly of the wicked.” You see that this is within. “And I shall not sit with the ungodly.”

10. [verse 6.] “I shall wash my hands among the innocent”: not with this visible water. You wash your hands when you think piously about your works and act innocently [Note: Erasmus and five manuscripts read *innocens es* (“you are innocent”).] before the eyes of God, because there is also an altar before the eyes of God, into which the priest entered, who first offered himself for us.

There is a heavenly altar, and no one embraces that altar except the one who washes his hands among the innocent. For many unworthy people touch this altar, and God tolerates his sacraments suffering insult for a time. But, my brothers, will the heavenly Jerusalem be as these walls are? Just as you are received with the wicked within these walls of the church, so will you not be received with the wicked into the bosom of Abraham. Therefore do not fear; wash your hands.

“And I shall surround the altar of the Lord”: where you offer vows to the Lord, where you pour out prayers, where your conscience is pure, where you tell God who you are; and if there is perhaps something in you that displeases God, he whom you confess to will cure it. Therefore wash your hands among the innocent and surround the altar of the Lord, so that you may hear the voice of praise.

11. [verse 7.] For this follows: “So that I may hear the voice of praise and declare all your wonders.” What does “So that I may hear the voice of praise” mean? “So that I may understand,” he says. For this is what hearing before God means—not like these sounds, which many hear and many do not hear. How many hear us yet are deaf to God! How many have ears but do not possess those ears of which Jesus says, “Let the one who has ears to hear hear” (Matt. 13:9)!

What, then, does it mean to hear the voice of praise? I shall say, if I can, with the help of the Lord’s mercy and your prayers. To hear the voice of praise means to understand inwardly that whatever evil is in you through sins belongs to you, while whatever good there is in justifications belongs to God.

Hear the voice of praise in such a way that you do not praise yourself even when you are good. For by praising yourself as good, you become bad. Humility had made you good; pride makes you bad.

You had turned so as to be illumined, and by your turning you became luminous, made radiant by conversion. But toward what [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “But by whom? Was it by yourself? If by yourself, etc.”]? Was it toward yourself? If you could be illumined by turning toward yourself, you could never become dark, because you would always be with yourself.

Why were you illumined? Because you turned toward something other than what you were. What is this other than what you were? God is light. You were not light, for you were a sinner. The Apostle says to those whom he wishes to hear the voice of praise: “For you were once darkness, but now light” (Eph. 5:8).

What does “You were once darkness” mean except the old man? “But now light”: you are not light without reason, you who were formerly darkness, unless it is because you have been illumined [Note: The editions read: “why, unless because”; *why* is absent from the manuscripts.]. Do not think that you yourself are the light. The light is the one who illumines every human being coming into this world (John 1:9). But through yourself, through your evil will and your turning away, you were darkened; now you shine.

But he immediately added this so that those to whom it had been said, “Now light,” would not become proud: “in the Lord.” For he says, “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.” Therefore, if you are apart from the Lord, you are not even light; but if you are light because you are in the Lord, what do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?

The Apostle himself said this elsewhere to proud people who wished to attribute to themselves what belongs to God and to boast of the good as though it were their own. He says to them: “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). He who gave to the humble takes away from the proud, because the one who gave can take away.

To this belongs, brothers—if indeed I have explained what I wished to explain, though I have explained as much as I could, even if not as much as I wished—what he says: “I shall wash my hands among the innocent and surround your altar, O Lord, so that I may hear the voice of your praise.” That is, I shall not presume upon myself because of my good, but upon you who gave it; I shall not wish to be praised because of myself and in myself, but because of you and in you.

Therefore it follows: “So that I may hear the voice of your praise and declare all your wonders”: not mine, but yours.

12. [verses 8–9.] And now see, brothers, see that lover of God, trusting in God, placed among the wicked and asking God not to be destroyed with the wicked, because God does not err in judging.

When you see people entering one place together, you think they are of the same merit; but God is not deceived. You distinguish chaff from grain with the wind as judge: you want a wind to blow for you, and you are not a wind, but desire that a wind blow for you; when you have shaken both with a winnowing fan, the wind lifts what is light and what is heavy remains. Thus you seek a wind for judging the threshing floor [Note: The Amerbach edition reads: “When, therefore, one comes to judge the threshing floor; does God, etc.?” Erasmus reads: “When therefore he comes.” The manuscripts, with the Louvain edition, read: “Thus you seek a wind, etc.”]. Does God seek another to judge with him, lest he destroy the good with the wicked? Do not fear. Be secure, good person, even in the midst of the wicked, and say what you hear: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house.”

The house of God is the Church. It still has wicked people, but the beauty of God’s house is in the good, in the holy. “I have loved the beauty of your house.” “And the place of the dwelling of your glory.”

What does this mean? I shall also explain this; it belongs to that somewhat obscure meaning. May the Lord help me, and may he help the attention of your hearts, inspired by that same Lord.

What does he say: “The place of the dwelling of your glory”? First he said, “The beauty of your house,” and he explains what the beauty of God’s house is: “The place,” he says, “of the dwelling of your glory.” It is not enough to say, “The place of the dwelling of God,” but “the place of the dwelling of the glory of God.”

What is the glory of God? It is what I was saying shortly before: that the one who becomes good should glory not in himself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31). “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23).

Therefore those in whom the Lord dwells in such a way that he himself is glorified because of their good works—so that they do not wish to attribute to themselves and claim as their own what they received from him—belong to the beauty of God’s house. Scripture would not wish to distinguish them unless there were some who indeed have God’s gift but do not wish to glory in God, but in themselves. They have God’s gift, but they do not belong to the beauty of God’s house.

For those who belong to the beauty of God’s house, in whom the glory of God dwells, are themselves the place of the dwelling of God’s glory. In whom does the glory of God dwell except in those who glory in such a way that they glory not in themselves but in the Lord?

Therefore, because I have loved the beauty of your house—that is, all who are there and seek your glory—and because I have not presumed upon a human being, nor consented with the ungodly, nor entered in, nor sat in their assembly; because I have thus been in the Church of God, what will you repay me?

What follows is what we answer: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, and my life with men of blood.”

### 13. [verses 10–12]

“In whose hands are iniquities, their right hand is filled with gifts.” Gifts are not only money, not only gold and silver, and not only *exenia* [Note: The editions read *xenia*; all the manuscripts, however, read *exenia*.]. Nor do all who receive such things receive gifts. [Note: [Col. 0195] The manuscripts read *adulare*, “to flatter.”] Sometimes they are received from the Church. What I am saying is this: Peter received them, the Lord received them, he had a money-box, and Judas used to take away what was put into it. But what does it mean to receive gifts? For the sake of gifts, to praise a person, to flatter him, to soothe him with coaxing, to judge against the truth for the sake of gifts. For the sake of what gifts? Not only for the sake of gold and silver and anything of that kind; even for the sake of praise, one who judges badly receives a gift—and a gift more empty than any other. For his hand was opened to receive the judgment of another’s tongue, and he lost the judgment of his own conscience.

Therefore, “in whose hands are iniquities, their right hand is filled with gifts.” You see, brothers, that they are before God; and those in whose hands there are no iniquities, whose right hand is not filled with gifts, are likewise before God. They can say to no one but God, “You know”; they can say to him alone: “Do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood”—he alone can see that they do not receive gifts.

For example, it happens that two men have a case before a servant of God. No one says anything except that his own case is just—for if he thought his case unjust, he would not seek a judge. Each thinks that he has a just case. They come to the judge. Before the judgment is pronounced, both say: “We embrace your judgment; whatever you judge, far be it from us to reject it.” And what do you say? “Judge whatever you wish; only judge. If I should resist you in anything, may I be accursed.” Both love the judge before he judges.

But when the judgment has been pronounced, it will be against one of them; and neither knows against whom it will be. If, then, he wishes to please both, he accepts the gift of human praise. But once he has accepted this gift, see what gift he loses. He accepts what makes a sound and passes away; he loses what is spoken and never passes away. The word of God is always spoken and never passes away; the word of man, as soon as it has been spoken, passes away. He holds on to empty things and lets go of solid ones.

If, however, he looks to God, he will pronounce judgment against one of them, considering God, under whose judgment he delivers it [Note: [Col. 0195] Some manuscripts read *considerante*, “while God considers.”]. But the one against whom it has been pronounced—even if the judgment can no longer be overturned, because he is bound by a law perhaps not ecclesiastical but belonging to the rulers of this age, who have granted such authority to the Church that whatever is judged in it cannot be dissolved [Note: [Col. 0196] On this matter there is a law of Constantine in the Theodosian Code, book 16, title “On Episcopal Judgment,” issued to Ablavius, praetorian prefect. The Emperor decrees: “That sentences delivered by bishops, of whatever kind, shall always be kept inviolate and uncorrupted, and that all cases, whether tried under praetorian or civil law, when concluded by bishops’ sentences, shall be confirmed by the law of perpetual stability.”]—if, then, it cannot be overturned, he no longer wishes to look at himself and directs blind eyes against the judge [Note: [Col. 0196] Several manuscripts read *sed*, “but.”]. He slanders him as much as he can: “He wanted to please him; he favored the rich man; he received something from him; or he was afraid to offend him.” He accuses him as though he had received gifts.

But if a poor man has a case against a rich man and judgment has been given for the poor man, the rich man says likewise, “He received gifts.” What gifts from the poor man? “He saw the poor man,” he says, “and, so as not to be blamed for acting against the poor man, he suppressed justice and delivered a judgment against the truth.”

Since, then, it is necessary that such things be said, see that they cannot be said by those who do not receive gifts—except before the eyes of God, who alone sees who receives and who does not receive: “But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me and have mercy on me. My foot has stood in uprightness.” I have indeed been shaken on every side by scandals and by the temptations of those who criticize judgment through human rashness [Note: Lov. reads, “by the judgment of human rashness.” Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “the judgment of human rashness.” But the reading should undoubtedly be *humana temeritate*, “through human rashness.”]; “but my foot has stood in uprightness.” Why in uprightness? Because above he had said: “And trusting in the Lord, I shall not be moved.”

### 14.

What, then, does he conclude? “In the churches I will bless you, Lord.” That is: in the churches I will not bless myself, as though I were confident in men, but I will bless you in my deeds. For this is what it means to bless God in the churches, brothers: to live in such a way that God is blessed through each person’s conduct. Whoever blesses the Lord with his tongue but curses him by his deeds does not bless the Lord in the churches. Nearly everyone blesses him with the tongue, but not everyone by his deeds. Some bless him with their voice, others by their conduct.

But when what they say is not found in their conduct, they cause God to be blasphemed—like those who have not yet entered the Church. Although they love their sins and therefore do not wish to be Christians, they nevertheless excuse themselves by pointing to the wicked, flattering themselves and deceiving themselves, and say: “Why are you trying to persuade me to become a Christian? I have suffered fraud at the hands of a Christian, and I have never committed fraud. A Christian swore falsely to me, and I have never done so.”

When they say such things, they are hindered from salvation, so that it does them no good—not, indeed, that they are already good, but that they are moderately wicked. For just as it does no good to open one’s eyes if one is in darkness, so it does no good to be in the light if one’s eyes are closed. Thus a pagan—as we may speak of them as though they lived well—is in darkness with open eyes, because he does not acknowledge the Lord as his light. A badly living Christian, however, is indeed in the light—which is God’s alone—but with closed eyes. By living badly he does not wish to see the one in whose name he has been placed, as though blind, in the light; he is not animated by any vision of the true light.

## ON PSALM XXVI

### Exposition I. “Of David himself, before he was anointed.”

#### 1. [verse 1]

The recruit of Christ speaks when he approaches the faith. “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” The Lord will give me both knowledge of himself and salvation; who will take me away from him? “The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” The Lord will repel all the attacks and ambushes of my enemy; I shall tremble before no one.

#### 2. [verse 2]

“When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh”: when evildoers approach to know me and to mock me, so that they may set themselves above me as I change for the better [Note: [Col. 0197] The manuscripts read *mutanti me*; the editions, *mutasti me*, “as you changed me.”]; so that they may not consume me with a cursing tooth, but rather my carnal desires. “My enemies who trouble me”: not only those who trouble me in a friendly spirit, criticizing me and wishing to turn me back from my purpose, but also my enemies. “They themselves were weakened and fell”: while they undertake this in their zeal to defend their own opinion, they became too weak to believe better things, and they began to hate the word of salvation through which I do what displeases them.

#### 3. [verse 3]

“If armies should stand against me, my heart will not fear”: if a conspiring multitude of those who contradict me should stand against me, my heart will not fear, so that I might defect to their side. “If war should rise against me, in this I will hope”: if the persecution of this age should rise against me, in this petition that I am considering I will fix my hope.

#### 4. [verse 4]

“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek”: for I have asked one petition of the Lord; this I will seek. “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life”: that, as long as I am in this life, no adversity may exclude me from the number of those who throughout the world hold to the unity and truth of the Lord’s faith. “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord”: namely, so that, while I persevere in faith, the delightful appearance may be revealed to me, which I shall contemplate face to face. “And may I be protected as his temple”: and when death has been swallowed up in victory, may I be clothed with immortality, having become his temple.

#### 5. [verse 5]

“For he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles”: for he hid me in the dispensation of his incarnate Word, during the time of the temptations to which my mortal life is subject. “He protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle”: he protected me, believing in my heart unto righteousness (Rom. 10:10).

#### 6. [verse 6]

“He exalted me upon a rock”: and, so that what I believed might also be made manifest for salvation, he caused my confession to stand out in his own firmness [Note: Er. and the manuscripts read “in his firmness.” Lov. reads “in weakness.”]. “And now, behold, [Col. 0198] he has exalted my head above my enemies”: what does he reserve for me at the end, when even now, although the body is dead because of sin (Rom. 8:10), I feel my mind serving the law of God and not being led captive under the rebellious law of sin (cf. Rom. 7:22, etc.)?

“I went around and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation”: I considered the world believing in Christ, and, rejoicing in the fact that God was humbled for us for a time, I praised him; for he takes pleasure in such a sacrifice. “I will sing and make melody to the Lord”: with heart and deed I will rejoice in the Lord.

#### 7. [verse 7]

“Hear, Lord, my voice with which I cried to you”: hear, Lord, the inner voice that I have directed to your ears with intense attention. “Have mercy on me and hear me”: have mercy on me and hear me in this voice.

#### 8. [verse 8]

“To you my heart has said: I have sought your face.” I did not display myself to men; but in secret, where you alone hear, my heart said to you: “I have sought”—not some reward outside you from you, but your face. “Your face, Lord, I will seek”: I will persist steadfastly in this search. For I will seek not something worthless, but your face, Lord; I will love you freely, because I find nothing more precious.

#### 9. [verse 9]

“Do not turn your face away from me”: so that I may find what I seek. “Do not turn aside in anger from your servant”: lest, while seeking you, I run into something else. For what punishment could be worse for one who loves and seeks the truth of your face? “Be my helper”: when will I find this, unless you help me? “Do not abandon me, nor despise me, God my Savior”: do not scorn the fact that a mortal being dares to seek what is eternal; for you, God, heal the wound of my sin.

#### 10. [verse 10]

“For my father and my mother abandoned me”: for the kingdom of this age and the city of this age—from which I was born temporarily and mortally—abandoned me when I sought you and despised what they promised, since they could not give what I seek. “But the Lord took me up”: but the Lord, who himself can give me himself, took me up.

#### 11. [verse 11]

“Establish a law for me, Lord, in your way”: therefore, as I strive toward you and, beginning from fear, approach so great a profession of attaining wisdom [Note: The editions and most manuscripts read: “and having attained so great a profession, beginning from fear toward wisdom.” We follow the Colbert manuscript: “and approaching so great a profession of attaining, beginning from fear,” etc.], establish a law for me, Lord, in your way, lest your discipline abandon me when I go astray. “And direct me in the straight path because of my enemies”: direct me in the uprightness of its difficulties; for it is not enough to begin, since the enemies do not cease until one arrives.

#### 12. [verse 12]

“Do not hand me over to the souls of those who trouble me”: do not allow those who trouble me to be satisfied with my misfortunes. “For unjust witnesses have risen against me”: for false witnesses have risen against me, speaking falsely about me in order to remove me from you and turn me back, as though I were seeking glory from men. “And iniquity lied to itself.” [Col. 0199] Thus iniquity took pleasure in its own lie. For it did not move me, since through this a greater reward in heaven was promised to me.

#### 13. [verse 13]

“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living”: and because my Lord first suffered these things; if I too despise the tongues of the dying—for “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11) [Note: [Col. 0199] The Lovaniensian edition reads, “thus I too,” contrary to the other books; and shortly thereafter, with the Erasmian edition, it read “the tongues of the lying.” But the manuscripts’ *morientium*, “of the dying,” is more correct: Augustine’s antithesis with “the living” is clear from the words, “the mouth that lies kills the soul.”]—I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, where there is no place for falsehood.

#### 14. [verse 14]

“Wait for the Lord; act manfully”: let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord. But when will this be? It is arduous for a mortal person and slow for one who loves. But hear the unfailing voice of the one who says: “Wait for the Lord.” Endure bravely the burning of the kidneys and steadfastly the burning of the heart. Do not think that what you have not yet received has been denied you. Do not fail through despair; see that it has been said: “Wait for the Lord.”

## Exposition II. A Sermon to the People

#### 1

Our Lord God, addressing and consoling us—those whom, by his just judgment, he regards as condemned to eat bread in the sweat of our face (Gen. 3:19)—deigns to speak to us through ourselves, to show that he is not only our creator but also our inhabitant. These words of the Psalm, which we have heard and partly sung: if we say that they are ours, we must be concerned about how we can speak truthfully, for they are more the words of God’s Spirit than ours. Again, if we say that they are not ours, we certainly lie.

For there is no groaning except of those who labor; or can this entire voice, which has sounded here, full of pain and tears, belong to one who can never be wretched? The Lord, then, is merciful, and we are wretched. The merciful one has deigned to speak to the wretched, and he also deigns to use, in the wretched themselves, the voice of the wretched. Thus both things are true: that it is our voice and that it is not our voice; that it is the voice of God’s Spirit and that it is not his voice. It is the voice of God’s Spirit because we would not say these things unless he inspired us; but it is not his, because he is neither wretched nor laboring. These are the voices of the wretched and of those who labor.

Again, they are ours because they are voices declaring our wretchedness; and likewise they are not ours, because we merit even the ability to groan through his gift.

#### 2. [verse 1]

“Psalm of David, before he was anointed.” This is what the title of the Psalm contains [Note: The editions omitted the words “we merit even the ability to groan. Psalm of David, before he was anointed. This is what the title of the Psalm contains”; they have been restored on the authority of eleven manuscripts.]: “Psalm of David, before he was anointed”—that is, before he was anointed with oil. For he was anointed as king (1 Kings 16:13). And at that time only a king and a priest were anointed [Note: The Vatican manuscript and five Gallic manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, had: “For he was anointed as king and priest. At that time, then, a king and a priest were anointed,” etc.]. These two anointed persons prefigured the one future [Col. 0200] king and priest, one Christ in both offices; and therefore he is called Christ from *chrism*, that is, anointing.

Not only has our head been anointed, but we ourselves are his body. He is king because he rules and leads us; priest because he intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34). Indeed, he alone was such a priest that he was himself also the sacrifice. He offered to God no other sacrifice than himself. For he would not find, apart from himself, a most pure rational victim—like a spotless lamb redeeming us by the shedding of his blood, incorporating us into himself, making us his members, so that in him we too might be Christ.

Therefore anointing pertains to all Christians; in earlier times of the Old Testament, however, it pertained only to two persons. From this it is evident that we are Christ’s body, because we are all anointed; and in him we are all both of Christ and Christ, because in a certain way the whole Christ is head and body.

This anointing will perfect us spiritually in that life which is promised to us. It is the voice of one who desires that life; it is a kind of voice of one who desires the grace of God, which will be perfected in us at the end. Therefore it was said, “before he was anointed.” For now we are anointed in the sacrament, and by that sacrament itself something is prefigured that we shall be. We ought to desire that ineffable future reality, whatever it is, and groan in the sacrament, so that we may rejoice in the reality represented beforehand by the sacrament.

#### 3

See what he says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” He enlightens me; let darkness depart. He saves me; let weakness depart. Walking firmly in the light, whom shall I fear? For God does not give such salvation as can be wrested away by anyone, nor is this a light that can be darkened by anyone.

The Lord enlightens, and we are enlightened; the Lord saves, and we are saved. If, then, he is the one who enlightens and we are enlightened, and he is the one who saves and we are saved, apart from him we are darkness and weakness. But since we have in him a sure, steadfast, and true hope, whom shall we fear?

The Lord is your light; the Lord is your salvation. Find one more powerful, and fear him. I belong to the most powerful of all, to the Almighty, in such a way that he both enlightens and saves me; and I fear no one apart from him. “The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?”

#### 4. [verse 2]

“When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh: my enemies who trouble me, they themselves were weakened and fell.” What, then, shall I fear, or whom shall I fear? Before whom shall I tremble, or what shall I tremble at? Those who persecute me are themselves weakened and themselves fall.

But why do they persecute me? “To eat my flesh.” What is my flesh? My carnal affections. Let them rage in their persecution; nothing mortal in me dies except what is mortal. There will be something in me to which the persecutor cannot reach, where my God dwells [Note: [Col. 0200] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read *ibi habitat*, “there my God dwells.”].

“Let them eat my flesh”: when my flesh is finished, I shall be spirit and spiritual. Indeed, my Lord promises me such great salvation that even now this mortal flesh—which seems to be handed over [Col. 0201] to the hands of my persecutors [Note: [Col. 0201] Five manuscripts read *perimi*, “to be destroyed.”]—will not perish forever; rather, what was demonstrated in my head when it rose again, all the members should hope for.

Whom should my soul fear, when God inhabits it? Whom should my flesh fear, when this corruptible has put on incorruption? Do you wish to know that those who persecute us eat our flesh, while our flesh itself need not fear? “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise” (1 Cor. 15:44).

How great, then, should be the confidence of one who knows how to say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” An emperor is protected by shield-bearing soldiers and does not fear; a mortal is protected by mortals and is secure. Is a mortal protected by the immortal, and will he fear and tremble?

#### 5. [verse 3]

Hear how great the confidence of one who says these things ought to be: “If armies should stand against me, my heart will not fear.” Armies are fortified, but what is more fortified than God?

“If war should rise against me.” What can war do to me? Can it take away my hope? Can it take away what the Almighty gives? Just as the giver is not conquered, so what he gives is not taken away. If what has been given can be taken away, the giver is conquered.

Therefore no one can take away even the temporal things we receive, my brothers, except the one who gave them. He will not take away the spiritual things he gives unless you let them go [Note: Three manuscripts read “unless you forsake them.” Two others read “unless you cease to have mercy.”]. But temporal and material things he himself takes away; for whoever else takes them away does so by his gift of power.

We know this and read it in the book of Job: even the devil, who seems to have almost the greatest power for a time, can do nothing unless permitted (Job 1). He received power over the lower things and lost the greatest and highest things. Nor is this the power of one who is angry, but the punishment of one who has been condemned. Therefore even he cannot have any power unless he is permitted.

You have this in the book I mentioned, and in the Gospel the Lord says: “This night Satan asked to sift you like wheat, and I prayed for you, Peter, that your faith might not fail” (Luke 22:31). He is permitted either for our punishment or for our testing.

Therefore, since no one can take away from us what God gives, let us fear no one but God. Whatever else may roar, whatever else may grow arrogant against us, let our heart not fear.

#### 6. [verse 4]

“If war should rise against me, in this I will hope.” In what? “One thing,” he says, “I have asked of the Lord.” He used the feminine form for a certain benefit, as though he were saying, “One petition.” And just as we customarily say, for example, “You have two,” rather than “You have two things,” Scripture used this manner of speaking: “One thing,” he says, “I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek.”

Let us see what the one who fears nothing asks. What great security of heart! Do you wish to fear nothing? Ask for this one thing, which the one who fears nothing asks—or which he asks in order to fear nothing? “One thing,” he says, “I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek.”

This is what is being pursued by those who walk well. What is it? What is that one thing? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.”

[Col. 0202] This is the one thing. The place where we shall always remain is called a house. In this pilgrimage it is called a house, but properly it is called a tabernacle: it is the tabernacle of pilgrims and, in a certain sense, of soldiers and of those fighting against an enemy. When, then, it is a tabernacle in this life, it is clear that there is also an enemy; for to have tabernacles together is to be fellow-soldiers, and you know that this is a term used of soldiers.

Here, therefore, there is a tabernacle; there, a house. Yet this tabernacle is sometimes, through a misuse arising from their proximity, called a house, and a house is sometimes called a tabernacle in the same way. Properly, however, that is a house and this is a tabernacle.

#### 7

What we shall do in that house is clearly expressed in another Psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Burning, if I may say so, with this desire and aflame with this love, the speaker longs to dwell all the days of his life in the house of the Lord: in the house of the Lord all the days of his life—not days destined to end, but eternal days.

For days are spoken of in the same way as years, concerning which it is said: “Your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28). The day of eternal life is one day without sunset.

Therefore he said to the Lord, “I desired this”; “One thing I have asked”; “This I will seek” [Note: Two Vatican and Regius manuscripts read, “From the Lord I desired.”].

And as though we were to say to him: “What will you do there? What will your delight be there? What occupation of the heart? What pleasures will supply your joys? For you will not remain there unless you are happy.” From where, then, will that happiness come?

Here we have various kinds of human happiness, and each person is called wretched when what he loves is taken away from him. People love different things; and when each seems to possess what he loves, he is called happy. But a person is truly happy not if he has what he loves, but if he loves what ought to be loved.

For many are more wretched by possessing what they love than by lacking it. By loving harmful things, they are more wretched when they possess them. In his mercy, God denies what we love when we love wrongly; in anger, he gives the lover what he wrongly loves.

You have the Apostle saying this clearly: “God handed them over to the desires of their heart” (Rom. 1:24). He gave them what they loved—but in condemnation. Again, you have him denying a request: “For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might remove it from me”—namely, the thorn of the flesh—“and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:8–9).

Behold: he gave those people over to the desires of their hearts; to the apostle Paul he denied what he prayed for. To them he gave it for condemnation; to him he denied it for healing.

But when we love what God wishes us to love, he will undoubtedly give it to us. This is that one thing which ought to be loved, so that we may dwell in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of our life.

#### 8

And because in these earthly dwellings people take pleasure in various delights and pleasures, and each person wishes to dwell in a house where there is nothing to offend the mind and where there are many things to please it, while, if the things that pleased him are taken away, he wishes to move elsewhere, let us inquire somewhat more curiously, and let the speaker [Col. 0203] tell us what we ourselves will do in that house where he desires, longs, and asks this one thing from the Lord: to dwell there all the days of his life.

“What do you do there, I ask you? What is it that you desire?” Hear what it is: “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.”

Behold what I love; behold why I wish to dwell in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of my life. There he has a great spectacle: to contemplate the delight of the Lord. He wishes, when his night is over, to cling to the Lord’s light.

Then our morning will come, once the night has passed. Therefore the Psalm says elsewhere: “In the morning I will stand before you and contemplate” (Ps. 5:5). Now I do not contemplate because I have fallen; then I will stand and contemplate.

This is a human voice. For man fell, and the one who would raise us would not have been sent unless we had fallen. We fell; he descended. He ascended; we are lifted up, because no one ascends except the one who descended (John 3:13). “The one who fell is lifted up; the one who descended ascends” [Note: These words, “The one who fell is lifted up; the one who descended ascends,” were omitted by Lov. They are found in our manuscripts and in Er.].

And let us not despair because he alone ascended. He lifts us, for whom he descended when we were falling. We shall stand, contemplate, and take great delight.

Behold, I have said this, and you cried out with desire for a certain form not yet seen. Let your heart surpass everything customary, and let your attention surpass all your ordinary thoughts drawn from the flesh by the senses of the flesh, imagining who knows what phantasms [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read this way. The editions have “everything seen,” and shortly afterward “and imagining who knows what phantasm.”].

Reject entirely from your mind whatever may occur; deny it all. Recognize the weakness of your heart, and, because perhaps what you might be able to think has occurred to you [Note: [Col. 0203] The editions read, “and whatever may occur”; the manuscripts, “and because perhaps what may occur,” etc.], say: “It is not that. For if it were that, it would already have occurred to me.” In this way you will desire a certain good.

What kind of good? The good of every good, from which every good comes; the good to which it is not necessary to add what this good itself is. For one says “a good man,” “a good field,” “a good house,” “a good animal,” “a good tree,” “a good body,” and “a good soul.” Each time you say “good,” you have added something.

There is a simple good, the good itself by which all things are good, the good from which all things are good. This is the delight of the Lord; this we shall contemplate.

Now see, brothers: if these good things which are called good delight us, if things delight us which are not good in themselves—for all changeable things are not good in themselves—what will the contemplation of the unchangeable, eternal good be like, which always remains the same?

Indeed, these things that are called good would in no way delight us unless they were good; nor would they be good in any other way unless they came from the one who is simply good.

#### 9

“Behold why I wish to dwell,” he says, “in the house of the Lord throughout all the days of my life.” I have told you why: “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.”

But so that I may contemplate it always, so that no trouble may reach me while I contemplate, no suggestion may turn me away, no power may take it from me, and I may suffer no enemy while contemplating, and so that I may enjoy these delights in security by the Lord God himself, [Col. 0204] what will happen to me? “He will protect me.”

Thus I do not merely wish to contemplate the delight of the Lord, he says, but also “to be protected as his temple.” So that he may protect me as his temple, I will be his temple and will be protected by him.

Is God’s temple like the temples of idols? The idols of the nations are protected by their temples; the Lord our God will protect his temple, and I shall be secure. I will contemplate for delight, and I will be protected for salvation.

As that contemplation will be perfect, so will this protection be perfect; and as that joy of contemplating will be perfect, so also will the incorruption of health be perfect.

The two things he said—“that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord” and “that I may be protected as his temple”—correspond to the two things with which the Psalm began: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” Because I shall contemplate the delight of the Lord, he is my light; because he will protect me as his temple, he is my salvation.

#### 10. [verse 5]

Why, then, does he grant us this at the end? “Because he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles.”

Therefore, I shall have a dwelling in the house throughout all the days of my life, so that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord and be protected as his temple. But how am I to reach there, where I make this promise to myself? “Because he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles.”

Then there will no longer be days of my troubles; but he saw me in the days of my troubles [Note: The better manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “but now he sees me in the days,” etc.]. If, then, he mercifully looked upon me while I was far away, how will he bless me when I am with him [Note: The editions read, “how will he not enlighten me?” Some manuscripts, however, read, “how will he bless me?”]?

Therefore I did not ask for that one thing presumptuously; nor did my heart say to me: “What are you asking, or from whom are you asking?” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “What are you asking? Whom are you asking? From whom are you asking?”] For do you, a sinful and wicked person, dare to ask God for something? Do you, weak and impure in heart, dare to hope that you will have some contemplation of God?

“I dare,” he says—not on the basis of myself, but on the basis of his delight; not through presumption of my own, but through his pledge. Will the one who gave so great a pledge to a pilgrim abandon him when he arrives?

“Because he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles.” Behold, this life is the day of our troubles. The days of troubles are lived differently by the impious and by the faithful.

For even believers, who are still pilgrims away from the Lord—for “as long as we are in this body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6), as the Apostle said—if they do not live days of troubles, why is there the voice of the Lord’s prayer, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13), if we are not in days of troubles?

But those who have not yet believed live the days of troubles in a much different way. Yet he did not despise them either. For “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6).

Let the human soul, then, dare to hope and ask for that one thing. It will possess it securely; it will possess it securely indeed. If what was ugly has been so loved, how will what is beautiful shine!

“Because he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles; he protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle.”

What is the hidden place of his tabernacle? What does this mean? For many parts of the tabernacle appear outwardly. There is also something like an inner chamber, which is called the secret inner sanctuary (*adytum*), “the innermost part [Col. 0205] of the temple” (Heb. 9:3) [Note: The editions read “of the inner temple.” Most manuscripts read “the innermost part of the temple.”].

And what is this? It was the place into which the priest alone entered. Perhaps the priest himself is the hidden place of God’s tabernacle. For he received flesh from this tabernacle and made for us the hidden place of the tabernacle [Note: Some manuscripts read this way. Er. reads “and made us the hidden tabernacle”; Lov. reads “and made for us his hidden tabernacle.”]. Thus the other members of his tabernacle are those who believe in him, while he himself is the hidden place of the tabernacle.

“For you have died,” the Apostle says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

#### 11. [verse 6]

Do you wish to know that he speaks of this? “The rock, of course, is Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Hear what follows: “Because he hid me in his tabernacle on the day of my troubles; he protected me in the hidden place of his tabernacle.”

You were asking what the hidden place of the tabernacle is. Hear what follows: “He exalted me upon a rock.” Therefore, he exalted me in Christ.

Because you humbled yourself in the dust, he exalted you upon a rock. But Christ is above, while you are still below. Hear what follows: “And now he has exalted my head above my enemies.”

“And now”—before I come to that house where I wish to dwell throughout all the days of my life, before I come to that contemplation of the Lord—“and now he has exalted my head above my enemies.”

I still suffer the enemies of Christ’s body; I have not yet been exalted above the enemies. But he has exalted my head above my enemies. Christ our head is already in heaven; our enemies can still rage against us. We have not yet been exalted above them, but our head is already there.

This is why he said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). He said that he was here below in us. Therefore we too are in him above, because “now he has exalted my head above my enemies.”

Behold what a pledge we have: through faith, hope, and love we are with our head in heaven forever, because he himself, through divinity, goodness, and unity, is with us on earth until the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20).

## 12.

“I have gone around, and I sacrificed in his tabernacle an offering of jubilation.” We sacrifice an offering of jubilation; we sacrifice an offering of joy, an offering of rejoicing, an offering of thanksgiving that cannot be expressed in words. But where do we sacrifice it? In his tabernacle itself, in the holy Church. What, then, do we sacrifice? An abundant and indescribable joy, with no words, with an ineffable voice [Note: [Col. 0205] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *sic*. Lovaniensis has *nulla voce effabile*, “expressible with no voice.”].

This is the offering of jubilation. Where was it sought, where was it found? “I have gone around,” he says, “and I sacrificed in his tabernacle an offering of jubilation.” Let your mind go around the whole of creation: everywhere creation will cry out to you, “God made me.” Whatever delights you in a work of art [Note: [Col. 0205] Most manuscripts read *in parte*, “in part”; and shortly afterward: “and especially if you go around, the consideration of the whole universe,” etc.] commends its maker; and especially if you go around the whole universe, contemplation conceives praise of its maker. You see the heavens: they are great works of God. You see the earth: God made the varieties of seeds, the diversity of shoots, the multitude of animals.

[Col. 0206] Go around still further, from the heavens to the earth; leave nothing out. Everything resounds for you with its Creator; and the very forms of created things are, as it were, voices praising their Creator. But who could explain the whole of creation? Who could explain it in praises? Who could worthily praise heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them? And these are visible things. Who could worthily praise Angels, Thrones, Dominations, Principalities, and Powers? Who could worthily praise that very thing which is vigorous within us, giving life to the body, moving the limbs, exercising the senses [Note: [Col. 0206] The manuscripts read *sensu exercens*, “exercising the sense”; the editions have *sensus exercens*, “exercising the senses.”], embracing so many things in memory, distinguishing so many things by understanding? Yet if human speech labors so greatly among these creatures of God, what does it do in the presence of the Creator, unless there remains only jubilation when speech fails?

“I have gone around, and I sacrificed in his tabernacle an offering of jubilation.”

## 13.

There is another meaning, which seems to me to belong more closely to the structure of the psalm. Since he had said that he was exalted in the rock, which is Christ, and that his head was exalted above his enemies, which is Christ, he also wished it to be understood that he, who was exalted in the rock, was exalted in that same head above his enemies. He referred this to the honor of the Church, to which the persecution of the enemies yielded; and because this was accomplished through the faith of the whole world, he says: “I have gone around, and I sacrificed in his tabernacle an offering of jubilation.” That is: I considered the faith of the whole world, in which my head was exalted above those who persecuted me; and in his tabernacle itself—that is, in the Church spread throughout the whole world—I praised the Lord ineffably.

## 14. [Verse 7]

“I shall sing and play psalms to the Lord.” We shall be secure, and we shall sing securely, and we shall play psalms securely, when we contemplate the delight of the Lord and are protected as his temple, in that incorruption when death shall be swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54).

What now? Those joys have already been described, which we shall possess when we have received that one petition. What now? “Hear, O Lord, my voice.” Let us now groan; let us now pray. Groaning belongs only to the miserable; prayer belongs only to those in need. Prayer will pass away, and praise will take its place; weeping will pass away, and joy will take its place. Meanwhile, now, while we are in the days of our evils, let our prayer to God not cease. From him let us ask for that one thing, and let us not desist from that petition until, by his gift and under his guidance, we reach it.

“Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you; have mercy on me, and hear me.” He asks for that one thing; asking, weeping, and groaning for so long, he asks for only one thing. He has brought all desires to an end; that one thing remains which he asks.

## 15. [Verse 8]

Hear that this is what he asks: “My heart said to you, ‘I have sought your face.’” This is therefore what he said shortly before: “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.” “My heart said to you, ‘I have sought your face.’”

If our joy were in this sun, our heart would not say, “I have sought your face,” but the eyes of our body would say it. To whom does our heart say, “I have sought your face,” except to him who pertains to the eye of the heart? The eyes of the flesh seek this light; the eyes of the heart seek that light. But do you wish to see that light which is seen by the eyes of the heart? For that light itself is God. “God is light,” John says, “and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). Do you therefore wish to see that light? Cleanse the eye by which it is seen: “For blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

## 16. [Verse 9]

“My heart said to you, ‘I have sought your face’; ‘Your face, O Lord, I shall seek.’ I asked one thing from the Lord; this I shall seek: your face. Do not turn your face away from me.”

How firmly he has fixed himself upon this one petition! Do you wish to obtain it? Ask for nothing else; be satisfied with the one thing, because the one thing will satisfy you.

“My heart said to you, ‘I have sought your face’; ‘Your face, O Lord, I shall seek.’ Do not turn your face away from me; do not turn away in anger from your servant.” Magnificent words: nothing more divine can be said. Those who truly love feel this.

Another person might wish to be blessed and immortal amid the pleasures of the earthly desires that he loves. Perhaps for this reason he would worship God and pray that he might live here for a long time amid his delights, and that nothing possessed by his earthly desire might perish—not gold, silver, or anything in his estates that delighted his eyes; that his friends might not die, nor his children, nor his wife, nor his dependents. He would wish always to live amid these delights. But because he cannot live forever—for he knows himself to be mortal—perhaps he worships God and prays to God and groans before God for this reason: that all these things may remain available to him until old age [Note: [Col. 0207] The editions read *usque in finem*, “until the end”; the manuscripts have *in senectutem*, “until old age.”].

And if God were to say to him, “Behold, I make you immortal in these things,” he would accept it as a great good, and, rejoicing with exultant joy, would scarcely contain himself.

But this is not what the one who asked one thing from the Lord wants. What does he want? “To contemplate the delight of the Lord throughout all the days of his life.”

Again, another person who worshiped God in this way and for this reason—if those temporal things were present to him—would not fear an angry God except lest he take them away. This man does not fear him because of that, since he even said concerning his enemies, “That they may eat my flesh.” Why, then, does he fear him when angry? Lest he take away what he has loved. What has he loved? “Your face.” Therefore he considers this to be the Lord’s anger: if he turns his face away from him.

“Lord, do not turn away in anger from your servant.” Someone might perhaps answer him in this way: “Why are you afraid that he may turn away from you in anger? Rather, if he turns away from you in anger, he will not punish you; if you run into him while he is angry, he will punish you. So prefer to wish that he turn away from you in anger.”

“No,” he says. He knows what he desires [Note: [Col. 0207] Lovaniensis reads: “that he turn away from you in anger, not approach. What did he vow? What does he desire?” Erasmus has: “that he turn away from you in anger, in anger not approach. What does he know, then?” Some manuscripts read: “that he turn away from you in anger, not in anger. What does he know, then?” Others finally give the reading printed in the text.].

His anger is nothing other than the turning away of his face. What if he were to make you immortal in these delights and pleasures of earthly joys? Such a lover answers: “I do not want it. Whatever I have besides him is not sweet to me. Whatever my Lord wishes to give me, let him take it all away and give himself to me.”

“Do not turn away in anger from your servant.”

Perhaps he turns away from some, but not in anger; for example, from those who say to him, “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11). When he turns his face away from your sins, he does not turn away from you in anger. Let him therefore turn his face away from your sins, but let him not turn his face away from you.

## 17.

“Be my helper; do not abandon me.” For behold, I am on the way. I asked one thing from you: to dwell in your house throughout all the days of my life, to contemplate your delight, to be protected as your temple [Note: [Col. 0208] The editions read *protegi a templo tuo*, “to be protected by your temple.” The manuscripts have *protegi templum tuum*, “to be protected as your temple,” which better corresponds to what precedes.]. This one thing I asked; but in order to reach it, I am on the way.

Perhaps you say to me: “Strive [Note: [Col. 0208] Three manuscripts read *niterе*. Five others have *utere*. The editions read *ut irem*, “that I might go.”]; walk. I have given you free will; you belong to your own will. Pursue the way; seek peace and follow it” (Ps. 33:15). Do not turn aside from the way; do not remain there; do not look back. Persevere in walking, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

Now, having received free will, you seem to presume upon your ability to walk [Note: [Col. 0208] This perhaps refers to the error of Pelagius, introduced into Africa in the year 411.]. Do not presume upon yourself. If he abandons you, you will fail on the very way, fall, go astray, and remain behind.

Say to him, then: “You have indeed given me free will, but without you my effort is nothing: be my helper; do not abandon me; and do not despise me, my God and savior.” For you help the one whom you created; you do not abandon the one whom you made.

## 18. [Verse 10]
