“For my father and my mother have abandoned me.” He has made himself little before God; he has made God his father and his mother. He is the Father because he created, called, commanded, and governs; he is the Mother because he cherishes, nourishes, suckles, and embraces.

“My father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up”—to govern and nourish me. Mortal parents begot me; children succeeded them—mortals succeeded mortals—and those who were born were born for this purpose, that those who begot them might depart. The one who created me will not depart; I shall not withdraw from him.

“My father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up.”

Apart from those two parents from whose flesh we were born—a male father and a female mother, as Adam and Eve—we have here another father and another mother, or rather, we had them. According to this age, the devil is the father, and he was our father when we were unbelievers; for the Lord says to unbelievers, “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

If he is the father of all the ungodly, who works in the sons of disobedience (Eph. 2:2), what is the mother? There is a certain city called Babylon. This city is the society of all the lost, from east to west; it possesses an earthly kingdom. According to this city, a commonwealth is also spoken of [Note: [Col. 0208] The Roman commonwealth is meant, as though growing old and declining from the time of the devastation of Italy in 406 and the capture of the City in 410.], which you now see growing old and diminishing. This was our first mother; in it we were born.

We have come to know another Father, God; we have abandoned the devil. For when does he dare to approach those whom the one who surpasses all things has taken up? We have come to know another mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the holy Church, whose portion is a pilgrim on earth; we have abandoned Babylon.

“My father and my mother have abandoned me.” They no longer have anything that they can provide for me, because even when they seemed to provide for me, you were providing, and I attributed it to them.

[Col. 0209] ## 19.

For from whom, even according to this world, is anything provided to a human being except God? Or what is taken away from a human being unless he who gave it has commanded or permitted it?

But foolish people think that these things are provided by the demons whom they worship. Sometimes they say to themselves: “God is necessary for eternal life, for that spiritual life; but these powers ought to be worshiped by us because of these temporal things.”

O vanity of the human race! You love those things more for the sake of which you wish to worship these beings. Surely, then, you have even more reason to worship them—not to say more reason, at least as much. But God does not wish to be worshiped together with them, not even if he is worshiped much more and they much less.

“What, then,” you will say, “are these beings not necessary for these things either?”

No. But one must fear lest, when angered, they do harm.

They will do no harm unless he permits it. They always have the will to do harm, and neither when appeased nor when entreated do they cease to wish to do harm; for this is characteristic of their malevolence.

What, then, will you accomplish by worshiping them except to offend the one whose offense will deliver you into their power [Note: [Col. 0209] Theoderic’s manuscript has *in istorum potestatem laberis*, “you slip into their power.” Several other manuscripts have *in istorum potestate haberis*, “you will be in their power.”]? Those who could do nothing to you when he was pleased will do whatever they wish when he is angry.

And so that you may know how uselessly you worship them, if you think of doing so for the sake of temporal things: did all who worship Neptune avoid shipwreck? Or did all who blaspheme Neptune fail to reach harbor? Did all women who worshiped Juno give birth safely? Or did all who blasphemed Juno give birth badly?

From this Your Charity may understand that people are empty-headed when they wish to worship these beings even for the sake of earthly things. For if they were to be worshiped on account of these earthly things, only their worshipers would abound in all earthly goods.

Yet even if this were so, we ought to flee such gifts and ask one thing from the Lord. Moreover, these things too are given by the one who is offended when these beings are worshiped.

Let our father, then, and our mother leave us: let the devil leave us; let the city Babylon leave us, together with its ruler. Let the Lord take us up, to console us with temporal things and bless us with eternal things.

“For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up.”

## 20. [Verse 11]

He has therefore now been taken up by the Lord, after that city and its ruler, the devil, have been abandoned; for the devil is the ruler of the ungodly, the ruler of the darkness of this world.

What darkness? The darkness of sins and unbelievers. Hence the Apostle says to those who already believe: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Having therefore now been received by him, what shall we say? “Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way.”

Have you dared to ask for a law? What if he says to you, “You will fulfill the law”? If I give you a law, you will fulfill it. He would not dare to ask unless he had first said, “The Lord has taken me up.” He would not dare to ask unless he had first said, “Be my helper.”

Therefore, if you help, if you take me up, give the law: “Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way.”

Establish the law for me in your Christ. For the Way itself has spoken to us and said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The law in Christ is a law together with mercy. This is the wisdom of which it is written: “He carries law and mercy on his tongue” (Prov. 31:26).

And if you have offended in some matter against the law, he who poured out his blood for you forgives you when you confess. Only do not abandon the way. Say to him: “Be my protector, and direct me on the straight path because of my enemies.”

Give the law, but do not take away mercy; for he who gave the law also said in another psalm, “He will indeed give mercy, who gave the law” (Ps. 83:8).

Therefore, what belongs to the commandment is: “Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way.” What belongs to mercy? “And direct me,” he says, “on the straight path because of my enemies.”

## 21. [Verse 12]

“Do not hand me over to the souls of those who trouble me”—that is, do not let me consent to those who trouble me. For if you consent to the one who troubles you, in accordance with his own purpose, he will somehow not devour your flesh but, through perverse will, eat your soul.

“Do not hand me over to the souls of those who trouble me.” Hand me over, if this pleases you, into the hands of those who trouble me. The martyrs said this to him, and he handed his servants over into the hands of those who troubled them. But what did he hand over? The flesh.

As it is said in the Book of Job, “The earth has been handed over into the hand of the wicked” (Job 9:24): the flesh has been handed over into the hand of the persecutor.

“Do not hand me over”—not my flesh, but me. I speak to you as soul; I speak to you as mind. I do not say, “Do not hand my flesh over into the hands of those who trouble me,” but, “Do not hand me over to the souls of those who trouble me.”

And how are people handed over to the desires of those who trouble them? “Because unjust witnesses have risen up against me.” Since they are unjust witnesses and speak many evils against me and slander me in many ways, if I am handed over to their desires, I too will lie and will become their companion—not a participant in your truth, but a fellow participant in falsehood against you.

“Unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and iniquity has lied to itself.” To itself, not to me: let iniquity always lie to itself, but let it not lie to me.

If you hand me over to the souls of those who trouble me—that is, if I consent to their wills—then iniquity will no longer have lied only to itself, but also to me. But if they rage as much as they wish and try to obstruct my course, do not nevertheless hand me over to their souls. By not consenting to their wills, I shall remain and persevere in your truth, and iniquity will lie not to me but to itself.

## 22. [Verse 13]

After these dangers, labors, and difficulties, amid the hands of persecutors and those who trouble him, he returns to that one thing, burning, panting, laboring, yet firm and confident because the Lord takes him up, helps him, guides him, and rules him.

Nevertheless, after that wandering and jubilation, rejoicing in joy and groaning amid labors, he sighed at last and said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

O good things of the Lord, sweet, immortal, incomparable, eternal, unchangeable! And when shall I see you, good things of the Lord? “I believe that I shall see,” but not in the land of those who die. “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

The Lord will rescue me from the land of those who die—he who for my sake deigned to take upon himself the land of those who die and to die among the hands of those who die. The Lord will rescue me from the land of those who die: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

He spoke while sighing; he spoke while laboring; he spoke while endangered amid a great crowd of temptations. Nevertheless, he hoped everything from his mercy, to whom he had said, “Establish a law for me, O Lord.”

## 23. [Verse 14]

And what does the one who established the law for him say? Let us hear the voice of the Lord from above, exhorting and consoling us—the voice of the one whom we have in place of the father and mother who abandoned us.

Let us hear his voice. For he heard our groans, saw our sighs, and looked upon our desire; and through Christ the Advocate he gladly accepted our one petition, our one request. Until we complete this pilgrimage, during which he will delay rather than withdraw what he promised, he said to us:

“Wait for the Lord.”

You will not be waiting for one who lies, nor for one who can be deceived, nor for one who will not find something to give. The Almighty has promised; he has promised with certainty; he has promised truthfully: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully.”

Do not grow slack. Do not be among those of whom it is said, “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2:16).

“Wait for the Lord” is said to all of us, and it is said to one person. We are one in Christ; we are the body of Christ. We desire that one thing; we ask for that one thing; amid those days of our evils we groan; we believe that we shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

To all of us, who are one in the One, it is said: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully. Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.”

What else could he say to you except repeat what you have heard? “Wait for the Lord; act manfully.”

Therefore, whoever has lost endurance has become effeminate; he has lost strength. Let men and women hear this, because in the one man there are man and woman. In Christ, such a one is neither male nor female (Gal. 3:28).

“Wait for the Lord; act manfully. Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.”

By waiting for the Lord, you will have him; you will have the one for whom you wait. Desire something else, if you find something greater, better, or sweeter.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 27

His, that is, David’s.

## 1. [Verses 1–2]

This is the voice of the Mediator himself, strong-handed in the struggle of his Passion. Whatever he seems to wish for his enemies is not a wish of malevolence but a declaration of their punishment. So in the Gospel, when he had performed miracles in the cities and they had not believed him, he does not malevolently wish what he says, but foretells what threatens them (Matt. 11:20).

## 2.

“To you, O Lord, I cried; my God, do not be silent toward me.” To you, O Lord, I cried; my God, do not separate the unity of your Word from that which I am as a human being.

“Lest at some time I become like those who descend into the pit.” For because the eternity of your Word never ceases to unite itself to me, it happens that I am not such a human being as the others who are born into the profound misery of this age, where your Word is not known, as though you were silent.

“Hear” [Note: [Col. 0211] The better manuscripts omit *Domine* after *Exaudi*, “hear, O Lord”; the word is absent from the Septuagint. The reading is “[Hear, O Lord].”] “the voice of my supplication while I pray to you; while I lift up my hands toward your holy temple”—while I am crucified for the salvation of those who, by believing, become your holy temple.

## 3. [Verse 3]

“Do not drag my soul away together with sinners, and do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity”—with those who speak peace with their neighbor, with those who say to me, “We know that you have come from God as a teacher” (John 3:2), but who speak evil in their hearts.

## 4. [Verse 4]

“Give them according to their works.” Give them according to their works, because this is just.

“And according to the wickedness of their desires” [Note: [Col. 0212] The better manuscripts read *affectationum*; the editions have *affectionum*.]. For since they desire evil, they cannot find good.

“According to the works of their hands, give them.” Although what they have done may benefit others for salvation, give them according to the works of their wills.

“Repay their recompense upon themselves.” For in place of the truth they heard, they wished to repay deceit; may their deceit deceive them.

## 5. [Verse 5]

“Because they did not understand the works of the Lord.” And from what is it evident that this happened to them? Clearly from this: because they did not understand the works of the Lord. This itself was already a recompense: when they tested the human being with a malicious mind, they did not recognize the God according to whose plan the Father sent him incarnate.

“Nor the works of his hands.” Nor were they moved by the visible works themselves, which were extended even to their eyes.

“You will destroy them, and you will not build them up.” Let them do me no harm, and let them have no power to raise up again any devices against my Church.

## 6.

“Blessed is the Lord, because he has heard the voice of my supplication.”

## 7. [Verse 7]

“The Lord is my helper and my protector.” The Lord helps me endure so much and protects me in resurrection through immortality.

“In him my heart hoped, and I was helped. And my flesh blossomed again”—that is, my flesh rose again.

“And by my will I shall confess to him.” Henceforth, when the fear of death has been brought to an end, those who believe in me will confess to him not under the Law through the necessity of fear but under the Law by free will; because I am in them, I shall confess.

## 8. [Verse 8]

“The Lord is the strength of his people”—not of that people which does not know the righteousness of God and wishes to establish its own (Rom. 10:3). For it did not think itself strong by itself, because the Lord is the strength of his people, which fights with the devil amid the difficulties of this life.

“And he is the protector of the salvation of his Christ.” After saving it through his Christ, he will finally protect it with the immortality of peace, following the struggle of warfare.

## 9. [Verse 9]

“Save your people” [Note: [Col. 0212] The editions read *tuum, Domine*, “your people, O Lord.” *Domine* is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.] “and bless your inheritance.”

I therefore make intercession after my flesh has blossomed again, because you said, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:8): “Save your people, and bless your inheritance,” because all that is mine is yours (John 17:10).

“And rule them, and lift them up forever.” Rule them in this temporal life, and from here take them up into eternal life.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 28

A psalm of David himself, concerning the consummation of the tabernacle.

## 1. [Verses 1–2]

A psalm concerning the Mediator himself, strong-handed, concerning the perfection of the Church in this age, in which war is waged temporarily against the devil.

## 2.

The prophet speaks:

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” Bring to the Lord yourselves, whom the Apostles, leaders of the flocks, have begotten through the Gospel.

“Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” Through your works, let the Lord be glorified and honored.

“Bring to the Lord glory for his name.” Let him become known gloriously throughout the world.

“Worship the Lord in his holy court.” Worship the Lord with your enlarged and sanctified heart; for you are his holy royal dwelling.

## 3. [Verse 3]

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters.” The voice of Christ is over the peoples.

“The God of majesty thundered.” The God of majesty, from the cloud of flesh, preached repentance with terror.

“The Lord is over many waters.” After the Lord Jesus sent forth his voice over the peoples and terrified them, he turned them toward himself and dwelt in them.

## 4. [Verse 4]

“The voice of the Lord is in power.” The voice of the Lord is now in them, making them powerful.

“The voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” The voice of the Lord does great things in them.

## 5. [Verse 5]

“The voice of the Lord breaks cedars.” The voice of the Lord humbles the proud through contrition of heart.

“The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.” Through repentance, the Lord will break those exalted by the splendor of earthly nobility, when he chooses the base things of this world to confound them (1 Cor. 1:28), in which he displays his divinity.

## 6. [Verse 6]

“And he will shatter them like the calf of Lebanon.” Having cut down their proud height, he will bring them down to imitate his humility—he who was led to sacrifice like a calf through the very nobility of this age.

“For the kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2:2).

“And the beloved one is like the son of unicorns.” For the beloved and only Son of the Father himself emptied himself of his nobility and became human, like the son of the Jews who did not know the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3) and arrogantly boasted of their righteousness as though it were unique.

## 7. [Verse 7]

“The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire.” The voice of the Lord passes through the intensely burning fury of those persecuting him without suffering any harm, or divides the raging anger of his persecutors, so that some said, “Could this perhaps be the Christ?” and others, “No, but he is deceiving the people” (John 7:12).

Thus he cuts through their insane tumult, transferring some into his love while leaving others in their malice.

## 8. [Verse 8]

“The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness.” The voice of the Lord moves the Gentiles to faith, who had once been without hope and without God in this world (Eph. 2:12), where no prophet or preacher of the word of God had lived, as though no human being had inhabited it.

“And the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh.” Then the Lord will cause the holy word of his Scriptures, which was being abandoned by the Jews who did not understand it, to be celebrated.

## 9. [Verse 9]

“The voice of the Lord brings the stags to maturity.” For the voice of the Lord first perfects those who overcome and repel poisonous tongues.

“And he will reveal the forests.” Then he will reveal to them the shaded depths of the divine books and the leafy shelters of the mysteries, where they may feed in freedom.

“And in his temple everyone says, ‘Glory.’” In his Church, everyone regenerated for eternal hope praises God according to his own gift, which he has received from the Holy Spirit.

## 10. [Verse 10]

“The Lord inhabits the flood.” The Lord therefore first inhabits the flood of this age in his saints, who are guarded in the Church as in an ark.

“And the Lord the King will sit forever.” Then he will sit, reigning in them forever.

## 11. [Verse 11]

“The Lord will give strength to his people.” For the Lord will give strength to his people as they fight against the storms and tempests of this world, because he did not promise them peace in this world.

“The Lord will bless his people with peace.” The same Lord will bless his people, granting them peace in himself; for he says, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 29

## Exposition I

Unto the end: a psalm of a song for the dedication of the house, for David himself.

## 1. [Verse 1]

Unto the end: a psalm concerning the joy of the resurrection, and the transformation and renewal of the body into an immortal state—not only of the Lord but also of the whole Church. For in the preceding psalm the tabernacle was consummated, where we dwell during the time of war; but now the house is dedicated, which will remain in everlasting peace.

## 2. [Verse 2]

The whole Christ therefore speaks:

“I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me.” I shall praise your sublimity, O Lord, because you have received me.

“And you have not made my enemies rejoice over me.” You have not made those who so often tried to oppress me through various persecutions throughout the world rejoice over me.

## 3. [Verse 3]

“O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” O Lord my God, I cried to you, and I no longer bear a body wounded and sick with mortality.

## 4. [Verse 4]

“O Lord, you brought my soul back from the underworld; you saved me from those descending into the pit.” You saved me from the condition of profound blindness and from the lowest mire of corruptible flesh.

## 5. [Verse 5]

“Sing psalms to the Lord, his holy ones; rejoice.” The prophet, seeing these future things, says [Note: [Col. 0214] The manuscripts, with great unanimity, read *Exsultet ... et dicat*, “Let him rejoice ... and let him say.”]: “Sing psalms to the Lord, his holy ones.”

“And confess to the memory of his holiness.” Confess to him that he has not forgotten the holiness with which he sanctified you, although this entire intervening period was long because of your desire.

[Col. 0215] ## 6. [Verse 6]

“For there is anger in his indignation.” For he avenged upon you the first sin, which you paid for with death.

“And life is in his will.” He gave you eternal life, to which you could not return by any strength of your own, because he willed it.

“In the evening weeping will linger” [Note: [Col. 0215] On this part of verse 6, see Exposition II of Psalm 58, no. 10.]. The evening began when the light of wisdom withdrew from sinful humanity, when humanity was condemned to death. From that evening onward, weeping will linger as long as the people of God await the day of the Lord amid labors and temptations.

“And in the morning, rejoicing.” Until the morning in which the rejoicing of the resurrection will take place, which first blossomed in the Lord’s morning resurrection.

## 7. [Verse 7]

“But I said in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever.’” I, that people who was speaking from the beginning, said in my abundance, now suffering no want at all, “I shall not be moved forever.”

## 8. [Verse 8]

“O Lord, in your will you supplied strength to my beauty.” But I learned that this abundance did not come from myself, but that you, in your will, supplied strength to my beauty, from this:

“You turned your face away” [Note: [Col. 0215] Most manuscripts read this way according to the Septuagint: “You turned your face away.”] “from me, and I became troubled.” You once turned your face away from the sinner, and I became troubled when the illumination of knowledge withdrew from me.

## 9. [Verse 9]

“To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and I shall pray to my God.” Recalling that time of my trouble and misery, and as though established in it, I hear the voice of your Firstborn, my head, who was to die for me, saying: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and I shall pray to my God.”

## 10. [Verse 10]

“What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” What profit is there in the pouring out of my blood, when I descend into corruption?

“Will dust confess to you?” For if I do not immediately rise and my body becomes corrupt, will dust—that is, the crowd of the ungodly, whom I shall justify by my resurrection—confess to you?

“Or will it announce your truth?” Or will it announce your truth for the salvation of the others?

## 11. [Verse 11]

“The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.” He did not allow his holy one to see corruption (Ps. 15:10).

## 12. [Verse 12]

“You turned my mourning into joy for me.” The Church, having followed the Firstborn from the dead, now, at the dedication of your house, says: “You turned my mourning into joy for me.”

“You tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.” You tore away the covering of my sins and the sadness of my mortality; and you girded me with the first robe, with immortal joy.

## 13. [Verse 13]

“That my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with grief.” So that now it may not weep but sing to you—not my humility but my glory, because you have exalted me from humility; and so that I may not be pierced by the consciousness of sin, by fear of death, or by fear of judgment.

“O Lord my God, I shall confess to you forever.” And this is my glory, O Lord my God: that I may confess to you forever that nothing comes from myself, but that every good thing comes from you, who are God all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

## Exposition II

A sermon to the people.

1. We have certainly sung this: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me.” If we know from the holy Scriptures who our enemies are, we understand the truth of this song. But if fleshly wisdom deceives us, so that we do not know against whom our struggle is, we find at the very beginning of this psalm a question which we cannot solve. Whose voice, then, do we suppose this to be—that of one praising God, giving thanks, exulting, and saying: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me”?

Let us first consider the Lord himself, who, according to that by which he deigned to become human, could suitably adapt these words to himself through the preceding prophecy. For from the moment he became human, he was also weak; and from the moment he became weak, he also prayed. For we have just heard, when the Gospel was being read, how he withdrew even into the desert from his disciples, who followed him there and found him. While he had withdrawn, he was praying; and the disciples who found him said to him, “Everyone is seeking you.” But he answered, “Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring towns, so that I may preach there also; for this is why I came” (Mark 1:35, 37–38).

If you consider the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is praying? To whom is he praying? Why is he praying? Is God praying? Is he praying to one who is his equal? What reason for prayer could he have, since he is always blessed, always almighty, always unchangeable, eternal, and co-eternal with the Father?

Thus, observing what he himself thundered through John, as through a kind of cloud of his own—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life” [Note: [Col. 0216] The editions read, “In him was life.” The older manuscripts read, “What was made in him was life.”] “and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:1–5)—up to this point, when we speak these words, we find neither a prayer, nor a reason for prayer, nor a place of prayer, nor the disposition of one praying.

But since shortly afterward he says, “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), you have the majesty to whom you may pray, and the humanity that prays for you. For the Apostle said this even after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ: “He sits,” he says, “at the right hand of God, and he also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:34).

Why does he intercede for us? Because he deigned to be mediator. What does it mean to be mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5)? Not between the Father and human beings, but between God and human beings. What is God? The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. What are human beings? Sinners, ungodly, mortal. Between that Trinity and the weakness and iniquity of human beings, the mediator became human—not sinful, but nevertheless weak—so that, by what was not sinful, he might unite you to God, and, by what was weak, he might draw near to you.

[Col. 0217] And thus, in order to exist as mediator between humanity and God, “the Word became flesh,” that is, the Word became human. For human beings are called by the name “flesh.” Hence the saying, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6): “all flesh” means all human beings. The Apostle likewise says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—“but against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Ephesians 6:12). With regard to these, if the Lord helps us, we shall speak in what follows. This distinction belongs to the exposition of the psalm which, in the name of the Lord, we have undertaken to explain to Your Holiness.

I have given these examples, however, so that you may know that human beings are called “flesh,” and understand that when it is said, “The Word became flesh,” it means, “The Word became human.”

2. I have not said this without reason. Let Your Holiness know that there was, or perhaps there still remain some remnants of, a certain heresy whose adherents were called Apollinarists. Some of them said that the human being whom the Wisdom of God assumed—and in whom it expressed its own person, not as in other human beings [Note: [Col. 0217] Thus the Gatian manuscript. Other manuscripts: “not as in other human beings.” Editions: “not as other human beings.”], but as it is said in the psalm, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation above your companions” (Psalm 44:8), that is, more than your companions—should not be thought to have been anointed in the same way as other human beings, other righteous people, or the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and whatever else is great in the human race.

For nothing greater arose in the human race than John the Baptist, “and among those born of women none has arisen greater” (Matthew 11:11). If you seek human excellence, John the Baptist is the one. And to whom John declares that he is unworthy to loosen the strap of his sandal (Mark 1:7), what was he except one greater than other human beings? Even in his humanity he was greater than other human beings.

For according to God, according to divinity, and according to that which was in the beginning—the Word was with God, and the Word was God—he is equal to the Father and above every creature. But we are speaking about the human being. Perhaps some of you, brothers, may think that the human being assumed by the Wisdom of God was equal to other human beings.

If there is a great difference among your members between the head and the other members, certainly all the members together constitute one body; yet there is a great difference between the head and the other members. For in the other members you perceive only by touch: by touching them, you perceive in the other members. But in the head you see, hear, smell, taste, and touch. If there is such excellence of the head over the other members, how great is the excellence of the head of the whole Church—that is, of that human being whom God willed to be mediator between God and human beings?

Therefore those heretics said that the human being whom the Word assumed, when the Word became flesh, did not possess a human mind, but only a soul without human understanding.

You see from what the human being is constituted: from soul and body. But the human soul itself possesses something which the souls of [Col. 0218] animals do not possess. Animals also have souls, and they are called “animals”—for they would not be called animals unless they derived that name from soul—and we see that they themselves live. But what more does the human being possess, by which he was made in the image of God? He understands and possesses wisdom; he distinguishes good from evil. In this he was made in the image and likeness of God.

He therefore possesses something which animals do not. And because he despises in himself that by which he is better than animals, he destroys or wears away [Note: [Col. 0218] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “he destroys or abandons in himself that which is better than animals.”] that quality in himself and, in a certain sense, makes the image of God grow old, so that such people are told: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

Those heretics, then, said that our Lord Jesus Christ did not possess a human mind, and that which the Greeks call λογικόν (*logikon*), which we call “rational”—that by which a human being reasons, and which the other animals do not possess. But what do they say? The Word of God itself took the place of the mind in that human being.

They were excluded; the Catholic faith rejected them, and they formed a heresy. The Catholic faith affirmed that the human being whom the Wisdom of God assumed lacked nothing that other human beings possess, insofar as the integrity of nature is concerned; but, insofar as the excellence of the person is concerned, he was different from other human beings.

For other human beings may be called participants in the Word of God, possessing the Word of God; but none of them can be called the Word of God. That name was given to him when it was said, “The Word became flesh.”

3. There were also certain others who arose from this same error. They said not only that the human being who was mediator, Christ, between God and human beings did not possess a mind, but that he did not possess a soul either. They said only: “There was the Word and flesh”; there was no human soul there, and no human mind there.

This is what they said. But what was there? The Word and flesh. The Catholic Church rejects these people as well and drives them away from the sheep and from the simple and true faith. It has been confirmed, as I said, that that human being, the mediator, possessed everything human except sin.

For if he performed many things according to the body, by which we understand that he possessed a body not falsely but truly—for example, how do we understand that he had a body? He walked, sat, slept, was seized, scourged, struck on the face, crucified, and died. Remove the body, and none of these things could have happened.

How, then, do we recognize from these signs in the Gospel that he possessed a true body, just as he himself said after the resurrection: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39)? Just as from these things, from these actions, we believe, understand, and know that the Lord Jesus possessed a body, so from certain other natural functions we know that he possessed a soul.

Hunger and thirst belong to the soul. Remove the soul, and a lifeless body cannot experience these things. But if they say that these things were false, then those things believed about the body will also be false. If, however, the body was true because the bodily functions were true, then the soul was true because the functions of the soul were true.

4. What, then? Since the Lord became weak [Col. 0219] for your sake, O human being who hears me, do not compare yourself with God. You are a creature; he is your creator. Nor should you compare yourself with that human being, because for your sake your God and the Word, the Son of God, became human.

Rather, place that human being above yourself as mediator, and place God above every creature. Understand in this way that he who became human for your sake could appropriately pray for you.

If, then, he could appropriately pray for you, he could also appropriately speak these words for your sake: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me.”

But if we do not understand who the enemies are, these words will be false when we think of the Lord Jesus Christ himself. For how is it true, if Christ the Lord is speaking, “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me”? How is it true from the person of the human being, from the person of weakness, from the person of flesh? For his enemies did rejoice over him when they crucified him, seized him, scourged him, and struck him, saying, “Prophesy to us, Christ!” (Matthew 26:68 and following).

Their rejoicing seems to force us to think that what was said—“You have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me”—is false. Then, while he was hanging on the cross, they passed by or stood there, watched him, shook their heads, and said: “Behold, he saved others; he cannot save himself. Let him come down from the cross, and we shall believe in him” (Matthew 27:42). When they said these things, were they not rejoicing over him?

Where, then, is this voice: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me”?

5. Perhaps this is not the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ, but [Note: [Col. 0219] The manuscripts read “of that human being”; the editions, “that is, of that human being.”] of that human being, namely, of the whole people of the Christian Church. For every human being in Christ is one human being, and the unity of Christians is one human being.

Perhaps that human being—that is, the unity of Christians itself—says: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me.”

How is this true of them as well? Were the apostles not seized, beaten, scourged, killed, crucified, burned alive, and thrown to the beasts—those whose memories we celebrate? When people did these things to them, were they not rejoicing over them?

How, then, can the Christian people also say: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me”?

6. [Verse 1.] We shall understand this if we first examine the title of the psalm. It reads: “For the end: a psalm, a song at the dedication of the house, for David himself.” In this title lies the whole hope and the entire mystery by which this question is to be resolved.

A house will one day be dedicated which is now being built. For now the house is being built—that is, the Church—and afterward it will be dedicated. At the dedication the glory of the Christian people will appear, though now it is hidden.

Let the enemies rage for now; let them humiliate us; let them do, not whatever they wish, but whatever they are permitted from above. For whatever we suffer from our enemies should not be attributed to the enemies rather than to the Lord our God.

Indeed, in his own example the mediator demonstrated [Col. 0220] [Note: Some manuscripts read: “demonstrated to us that people are permitted from above to harm us”] that, when he permits people from above to harm us, the will to harm is not given from above, but the power. Every wicked person has within himself the will to harm; but he does not have the power to harm at his own disposal.

By willing to harm, he is already guilty. But whether he can do so is permitted by the hidden administration of God’s providence: to one for punishment, to another for testing, and to another for a crown.

For punishment, the ἀλλόφυλοι—that is, foreigners—were permitted to capture the people of Israel, because they had sinned against God (Judges 10:7; 13:1 and following). For testing, the devil was permitted against Job (Job 1:12): Job was tested, and the devil was put to shame. For a crown, persecutors were permitted against the martyrs. The martyrs were killed, and the persecutors thought that they had conquered; the latter triumphed falsely in public, while the former were crowned truly in secret.

Therefore, the one against whom something is permitted is subject to the hidden administration of God’s providence. But the will to harm belongs to the human being himself; for he does not immediately kill everyone whom he wishes to kill.

7. Thus the Lord himself, judge of the living and the dead, standing before a human judge and offering us an example of humility and patience—not defeated, but showing soldiers an example of how to fight—stripped away the arrogance of the judge who threatened him, swollen with pride, and said, “Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to kill you?”

As though returning the breath by which the man might be deflated, he said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:10–11).

And Job—indeed, the devil killed his children, and the devil took away all his possessions—what did Job say? “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Let the enemy not triumph, as though he himself had done it. “I know,” he says, “from whom he was permitted. Let the will to harm be attributed to the devil, but the power to test to my Lord.”

In the very wound of his body, his wife approached him, like Eve—an accomplice of the devil, not a comforter of her husband. She tested him and said, amid many reproaches: “Say some word against God, and die” (Job 2:9).

But that Adam on the dung heap was more cautious than Adam in paradise. Adam in paradise agreed with the woman and was expelled from paradise; Adam on the dung heap rejected the woman and was admitted to paradise.

What, then, did that Adam on the dung heap say to the woman, giving birth inwardly to immortality and streaming outwardly with worms? “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

Again he called it the hand of the Lord when the devil had struck him, because he did not consider who struck him, but who permitted it. Indeed, the devil himself called the same power which he wanted to be given to him the hand of the Lord.

For, bringing an accusation against the righteous man to whom the Lord bore witness, he said to God: “Does Job worship the Lord for nothing? Have you not surrounded him, his house, and all his possessions on every side? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. You have given him so many good things; therefore he worships you. But [Col. 0221] send your hand and touch all that he possesses; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job 1:9–11).

What does “send your hand” mean, when he himself wanted to send it? But because he could not send his own hand, he called the power which he had received from God the hand of God.

8. What, then, brothers? Did the enemies do so many things against Christians, and did they exult and rejoice over them? But when will it become clear that they did not rejoice over them? When they are put to shame and the Christians exult at the coming of the Lord our God, when he comes bearing retribution in his hand: condemnation for the ungodly, a kingdom for the righteous; fellowship with the devil for the wicked, fellowship with Christ for the faithful.

When he reveals this, when the righteous will stand with great confidence—I speak from the Scriptures; remember the reading from the Book of Wisdom: “Then the righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them. But they will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit: ‘What did our pride profit us, and what did the boasting of riches bring us? For all those things passed away like a shadow.’ And what will they say about the righteous? ‘How were they counted among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?’” (Wisdom 5:1 and following)—then will be the dedication of the house which is now being built in tribulations.

[Col. 0221] Then that people will rightly say: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me.”

This voice will therefore be true in the people of God—that people which is now constricted, now afflicted by so many temptations, so many scandals, so many persecutions, and so great an oppression.

The person who does not progress does not feel these torments of the soul in the Church; he thinks that there is peace. But let him begin to progress, and then he will see under what oppression he is, because when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared (Matthew 13:26). “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18).

Let him progress, and he will see where he is. Let fruit appear, and the weeds will become visible. The Apostle’s truthful voice cannot be erased from beginning to end: “Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ suffer persecution. But wicked people and impostors advance toward worse things, deceiving and being deceived” (2 Timothy 3:12–13).

And where are those words of the psalm: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26:14)? It would have been insufficient to say once, “Wait for the Lord,” unless he repeated it. Perhaps someone might wait for two days, three days, or four days, while the oppression and tribulation continued. Therefore he added, “Act manfully”; he added, “and let your heart be strengthened.”

And because this will be so from beginning to end, the conclusion contains what the opening sentence contains: “And wait for the Lord.”

The things that oppress you pass away, and the one whom you await will come and wipe away the sweat. He will dry the tear; you will weep no longer. But for now let us groan in tribulations, as Job says: “Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” (Job 7:1).

9. Nevertheless, brothers, before the day of the dedication of the house comes, let us see that our head has already been dedicated. The dedication of the house has already taken place in the head, as though the dedication of the foundation.

The head is above, the foundation below. But perhaps we have wrongly called Christ the foundation for this reason: he is rather the summit; [Col. 0222] he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Yet I think we have not been mistaken. The Apostle said: “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones”—those who live well, honor and praise God, are patient in tribulations, and long for their homeland build gold, silver, and precious stones.

But those who still love worldly things, are entangled in earthly affairs, and are devoted to certain bonds and attachments of the flesh—to their houses, wives, and possessions—and yet are Christians, so that their hearts do not depart from Christ and they place nothing before Christ: just as nothing is placed before the foundation in building, so they build wood, hay, and straw.

But what follows? “The work of each person will be revealed, for the fire will test it”—the fire of tribulation and temptation.

This fire tested many martyrs here, but it will test the whole human race at the end. Martyrs were found who possessed these worldly things. How many wealthy people and senators suffered! Some of them were nevertheless building wood, hay, and straw in the attachments of carnal and worldly concerns. Yet because they had Christ as the foundation upon which they were building, the hay burned, while they themselves remained upon the foundation.

Thus the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work remains, he will receive a reward,” and he will lose nothing, because he will find what he loved. “But if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:11–15).

But it is one thing not to be harmed by fire, and another to be saved through fire. And why? Because of the foundation.

Therefore let the foundation not depart from your heart. Do not place the foundation upon hay—that is, do not put hay before the foundation, so that hay occupies the first place in your heart and Christ the second. But if hay cannot be absent from that place, let Christ occupy the first place there, and hay the second.

10. Christ, then, is the foundation. How did I say that our head has been dedicated? The head itself is the foundation. But a foundation is usually below, whereas the head is above.

May Your Holiness understand what I am saying; perhaps I shall explain it in the name of Christ.

There are two kinds of weight. Weight is a certain impulse of each thing, as though it were striving toward its own place; that is weight.

You carry a stone in your hand and endure its weight. It presses upon your hand because it seeks its own place. Do you want to see what it seeks? Withdraw your hand: it falls to the earth and comes to rest on the earth. It reaches the place toward which it was striving and finds its own place.

That weight, then, was a kind of movement, spontaneous but without soul and without perception.

There are other things that seek a place above. If you pour water onto oil, the water moves downward by its weight. It seeks its own place; it seeks to be ordered, because water above oil is contrary to order. Until it reaches its proper order, its movement is restless, until it occupies its proper place.

Conversely, pour oil beneath water—for example, if a vessel of oil falls into water, into the depths, into the sea, [Col. 0223] and breaks. The oil does not allow itself to remain underneath. Just as water poured over oil seeks its own place below by its weight, so oil poured beneath water seeks its own place above by its weight.

If this is so, brothers, toward what do fire and water move? Fire rises upward and seeks its own place; water seeks its own place by its weight. A stone seeks the lowest place, as do wood, columns, and earth, from which these houses are built. They therefore belong to the class of things which, by their own weight, are carried downward.

It is therefore clear why the foundation is understood to be below: these things are carried downward by their weight, and unless something supports them, everything falls, because everything tends toward the earth.

Thus, for things tending downward, the foundation is placed below. But the Church of God, placed below, tends toward heaven.

Our foundation, then, has been placed there: our Lord Jesus Christ, seated at the right hand of the Father. If Your Holiness has understood that our foundation has already been dedicated, let us briefly hear the psalm and proceed.

11. [Verse 2.] [Col. 0223] “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, and have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me.”

Which enemies? The Jews? In the dedication of the foundation, let us understand the dedication of the future house. What is now said from the person of the foundation will then be said from the person of the whole house.

Which enemies, then? The Jews, or rather the devil and his angels, who departed in confusion after the Lord rose again? The ruler of death grieved because death had been defeated.

“And you have not given my enemies cause to rejoice over me,” because I could not be held among the dead.

12. [Verse 3.] “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.”

The Lord prayed on the mountain before his passion (Matthew 26:39); he was healed. Whom did he heal—him who had never been sick, the Word who is God, the Word who is divinity? No. He was carrying the death of the flesh; he was carrying your wound, in order to heal you from your wound.

The flesh, however, was healed. When? When he rose again. Hear the Apostle and see the true healing: “Death,” he says, “has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

Therefore that exaltation will then be the voice of us; for now it is the exaltation of Christ.

13. [Verse 4.] “O Lord, you have brought my soul back from the underworld.”

There is no need to explain this.

“You saved me from those who descend into the pit.”

Who are those who descend into the pit? All sinners who sink into the depths. For the pit is the depth of the world.

What is this depth of the world? Abundance of luxury and wickedness. Those, therefore, who immerse themselves in lusts and earthly desires descend into the pit.

Such people persecuted Christ. But what does he say? “You saved me from those who descend into the pit.”

14. [Verse 5.] “Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints.”

For your head has risen again. Hope in your other members what you see in the head; hope in the members what you have believed in the head.

There is an ancient and true proverb: “Where the head is, there also are the other members.” Christ has ascended into heaven, and we shall follow him there. He did not remain among the dead; he rose again and will die no more. When we too have risen, we shall die no more.

Therefore, possessing these [Col. 0224] promises, “Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and give thanks in remembrance of his holiness.”

What does “give thanks in remembrance” mean? You had forgotten him, but he did not forget you.

15. [Verse 6.] “For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his favor.”

There is anger in his indignation against the sinner: “On the day when you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17). They touched it, and they died; they were sent out of paradise, because there is anger in his indignation.

But this was not without hope, because there is life in his favor.

What does “in his favor” mean? Not by our own strength, not by our own merits; but because he willed it, he saved us, not because we were worthy.

For what is a sinner worthy of except punishment? Yet he gave life. And if he gave life even to the ungodly, what does he reserve for the faithful?

16. “In the evening weeping will remain.”

Do not be afraid, because he had said to us, “Sing psalms.” Here too there is groaning: in singing, exultation; in praying, groaning.

Groan over present things; sing about future things. Pray concerning what is real; sing concerning hope.

“In the evening weeping will remain.” What does “in the evening weeping will remain” mean? Evening comes when the sun sets. The sun set for the human being—that is, that light of righteousness, the presence of God.

Therefore, when Adam was expelled, what is said in Genesis? “When God was walking in paradise”—God was walking toward evening. By then that sinner had hidden himself among the trees; he did not want to see the face of God (Genesis 3:8), at which he had been accustomed to rejoice. The sun of righteousness had set for him; he did not rejoice in the presence of God.

From that moment this whole mortal life began.

“In the evening weeping will remain.” You will remain in weeping for a long time, O human race, for you are born from Adam, and this is how it happened. We too are from Adam, and all who have begotten children and all who will beget them are from Adam, from whom they themselves were created.

“In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning exultation”—when the light that had set for sinners begins to rise for the faithful.

For this reason the Lord Jesus Christ also rose from the tomb in the morning (Matthew 28:1): so that what he dedicated in the foundation he might promise to the house.

In our Lord there was evening when he was buried, and morning when he rose again, on the third day. You too were buried in the evening in paradise, and you rose again on the third day.

How on the third day? If you consider the ages of the world, one day is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. What your head displayed in those three days is displayed in you through the three ages of the world.

When will this happen? In the morning we must hope and rejoice; but for now we must endure and groan.

17. [Verse 7.] “But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever.”

In what abundance did the human being say, “I shall not be moved forever”? We understand, brothers, that the person here is that of the humble human being.

Who possesses abundance here? No one. What is human abundance? Misery and calamity.

But do the rich possess abundance? The more they possess, the more they lack. They are wasted by desires, scattered by cravings, tortured by fears, and consumed by sorrow. What abundance is theirs?

There was abundance when the human being was placed in paradise, when he lacked nothing, when he enjoyed God. Yet he said, “I shall not be moved forever.”

How did he say, “I shall not be moved forever”? When he gladly listened to, “Taste, and you will be like gods,” while God had said, “On the day when you eat from it, you shall surely die,” and the devil said, “You shall not surely die” (Genesis 3:4–5).

Believing the one who offered such persuasion, he said: “I shall not be moved forever.”

18. [Verses 8–9.] But because the Lord had spoken the truth—that he would take from the proud man what he had given him while he was humble, when he created him—the psalm continues and says:

“O Lord, in your favor you had granted strength to my beauty.”

That is: “I was not good and strong from myself, but from you I was both beautiful and strong. You had granted strength to my beauty, from your favor by which you had made me.”

“And so that you might show me that I was this by your favor, you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.”

He therefore turned his face away from the one whom he sent out from paradise (Genesis 3:23).

Placed outside, let him cry out and say: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall plead.”

In paradise you did not cry out, but praised; you did not groan, but enjoyed. Placed outside, groan and cry out.

He draws near to the afflicted person who abandoned the proud person. “For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

“To you, O Lord, I shall cry, and to my God I shall plead.”

19. [Verse 10.] What follows is now spoken from the person of the Lord himself, our foundation:

“What profit is there in my [Col. 0225] blood, while I descend into corruption?”

What, then, does he pray for? That he may rise again.

“For if I descend,” he says, “into corruption; if my flesh is corrupted as the flesh of other human beings, so that it may rise again at the end, what profit was there in my shedding blood? For if I do not rise again now, I shall announce wonders to no one and win no one. But in order that I may announce to someone your wonders, your praises, and eternal life, let my flesh rise; let it not go into corruption.

“For if it goes the way of the flesh of other human beings, what profit is there in my blood? Will dust confess to you, or announce your truth?”

There is a twofold confession: either of sin or of praise. When things go badly for us, let us confess our sins in tribulations; when things go well for us, let us confess praise to God in the exultation of righteousness. Nevertheless, let us not be without confession.

20. [Verse 11.] “The Lord heard and had mercy on me.”

How? Attend to the dedication of the house [Note: [Col. 0225] The editions read: “How? Attend to the dedication,” etc.; the manuscripts: “Attend.”]. He heard and had mercy. “The Lord became my helper.”

21. [Verse 12.] Hear now of the resurrection itself:

“You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.”

What is the sackcloth? Mortality.

Sackcloth is made from goats and kids, and goats and kids are placed among sinners (Matthew 25:32). The Lord, from our number, assumed only the sackcloth; he did not assume the merit of the sackcloth.

The merit of the sackcloth is sin; the sackcloth itself [Note: [Col. 0225] Several manuscripts read *illi* (“to/for that one”; uncertain in isolation).] is mortality. He assumed mortality for your sake, although he did not possess the merit of death.

For the person who sins possesses the merit of death; but the person who did not sin did not possess the merit of the sackcloth.

Elsewhere the voice of the same one says: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm 34:13).

What does “I clothed myself in sackcloth” mean? “I presented to my persecutors what I have from sackcloth.” In order that they might think he was a human being, he hid himself from the eyes of his persecutors, because the persecutors were unworthy to see [Col. 0226] him clothed in sackcloth [Note: Perhaps: “unless clothed in sackcloth”].

“Therefore you tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.”

22. [Verse 13.] “That my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced.”

What is in the head is also in the body.

What does “I may not be pierced” mean? “I shall die no more.” For he was pierced while hanging on the cross; he was struck with a spear (John 19:34).

Therefore our head says: “I shall not be pierced; I shall die no more.”

But what do we say, with reference to the dedication of the house? Let the conscience not pierce us with the goads of sins. For everything will be forgiven, and then we shall be free.

“That my glory may sing to you,” he says, “not my humility.”

If it is ours, it is also Christ’s, because we are Christ’s body. Why? Although Christ sits in heaven, he will say to certain people: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:35).

He is there in himself, and here in us.

What, then, does he say? “That my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced.”

“My humility groans to you; my glory will sing to you.”

Now, at the end: “O Lord my God, I shall give thanks to you forever.”

What does “I shall give thanks to you forever” mean? “I shall praise you forever,” because we have said that confession occurs in praise as well, not only in sins.

Confess now what you have done against God, and you will confess what God has done for you. What have you done? Sins. What has God done? To the person who confesses his iniquity, he forgives his sins, so that afterward, confessing his praises to him forever, you may not be pierced by sin.

# ON PSALM 30

## EXPOSITION I

“For the end: a psalm, for David himself; ecstasy.”

1. **[Verse 1.]** “To the end. A psalm of David himself, to the mediator strong-handed in persecutions.” For *ecstasy*, which has been added to the title, signifies an “excess of mind,” arising either from fear or from some revelation. But in this psalm fear chiefly appears: the people of God are disturbed by the persecution of all nations and by the failure of faith throughout the world. [Note: [Col. 0226] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read *et defectus*, “and the failure.”] First, however, the mediator himself speaks; then the people, redeemed by his blood, give thanks; finally, the disturbed people speak at length, which pertains to ecstasy. The person of the Prophet himself is inserted twice, near the end and at the end.

2. **[Verse 2.]** “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever”: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall never be confounded while they insult me as though I were an ordinary man like the rest.” “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me”: “In your righteousness deliver me from the pit of death, and rescue me from their number.”

3. **[Verse 3.]** “Incline your ear to me”: “Hear me in my humility; draw near to me.” “Hasten to rescue me”: “Do not delay until the end of the age my separation from sinners, as you do for all who believe in me.” “Be for me a protecting God”: “Be my protecting God.” “And a house of refuge, that you may save me”: “Be like a house to me, where I may take refuge and be saved.”

4. **[Verse 4.]** “For you are my strength and my refuge”: “You are my strength for enduring my persecutors, and my refuge for abandoning them.” “And for your name’s sake you will be my guide, and you will nourish me”: “So that you may become known through me to all nations, I will follow your will in everything; and, as the saints are gradually gathered to me, you will complete my body and my full stature.”

5. **[Verse 5.]** “You will lead me out of this snare which they concealed for me”: “You will instruct me concerning these ambushes which they concealed for me.” “For you are my protector.”

6. **[Verse 6.]** “Into your hands I commend my spirit”: “I commend my spirit to your power, soon to receive it again.” “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.” Let the people also, redeemed by the Passion of their Lord and rejoicing in the glorification of their Head, say: “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth.”

7. **[Verse 7.]** “You hate those who observe vanity to no purpose”: “You hate those who observe the false happiness of this age.” [Note: [Col. 0227] In several manuscripts: “those who hope.”] “But I have hoped in the Lord.”

8. **[Verse 8.]** “I will exult and rejoice in your mercy”: “Your mercy does not deceive me.” “For you have regarded my humility”: “By which you subjected me in hope to vanity.” “You have saved my soul from distresses”: “You have saved my soul from the distresses of fear, so that, set free by love, it may serve you.”

9. **[Verse 9.]** “And you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy”: “You have not shut me up so that I would have no opening through which to breathe into freedom, and so that I would be handed over to the devil’s everlasting power—the devil who ensnares through desire for this life and terrifies through death.” “You have set my feet in a spacious place”: “With the resurrection of my Lord known and promised to me, my love, drawn out from the narrowness of fear, walks freely and remains in the breadth of liberty.”

10. **[Verse 10.]** “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted.” But what is this unexpected cruelty of my persecutors, striking me with great fear? “Have mercy on me, Lord.” For I am no longer terrified by death, but by tortures and torments. “My eye is troubled in anger”: “I had an eye fixed upon you, by which you would not abandon me; you became angry and troubled it.” “My soul and my belly”: “In that same anger my soul was troubled, as was the memory by which I held what my God had endured for me and what he had promised me.”

11. **[Verse 11.]** “For my life has failed in sorrow”: “For my life is to confess you, but it has failed in sorrow when the enemy said, ‘Let them be tortured until they deny.’” “And my years in groaning”: “The times I spend in this age are not taken from me by death; they remain, and they are in groaning.” “My strength has been weakened in poverty”: “I lack the health of this body, and the tortures are not spared; I lack release from the body, and death is spared. In this poverty my confidence has been weakened.” “And my bones are troubled”: “My firmness has been troubled.”

12. **[Verse 12.]** “I have become a reproach above all my enemies.” My enemies are all the unrighteous; yet they are tortured for their crimes even unto confession. Therefore I have surpassed their reproach, since confession is not followed by death but by continued torment. “And exceedingly so to my neighbors”: This seemed excessive to those who were already drawing near to know you and to hold the faith that I hold. “And a fear to my acquaintances”: I struck even my acquaintances with fear by the dreadful example of my tribulation. “Those who saw me fled outside from me”: Since they did not understand my inward and invisible hope, they fled from me toward external and visible things.

13. **[Verse 13.]** “I have been forgotten like one dead from the heart”: They have forgotten me as though I were dead in their hearts. “I have become like a discarded vessel”: I seemed to myself to have perished for the uses of the Lord, living in this age and gaining no one, since everyone was afraid to join himself to me.

14. **[Verse 14.]** “For I heard the reproach of many who dwell around”: I heard many who were near me reproaching me during their pilgrimage through this land, following the circuit of the ages and refusing to return with me to the eternal homeland. “While they gathered together against me, they took counsel to seize my soul”: So that my soul might consent to them—and could easily escape their power through death—they devised a plan by which they would not even allow me to die.

15. **[Verse 15.]** “But I have hoped in you, Lord; I said, ‘You are my God’”: For you have not changed, so as not to save the one whom you redeem.

16. **[Verse 16.]** “My lots are in your hands”: My lots are in your power. For I see no merit by which, from the whole impiety of the human race, you chose me above all others for salvation. And if there is with you a just and hidden order governing my election, nevertheless I, who do not know it, came by lot to the tunic of my Lord (John 19:24). “Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me.”

17. **[Verse 17.]** “Make your face shine upon your servant”: Make it known to those who do not think that I belong to you that your face is turned toward me and that I serve you. “Save me in your mercy.”

18. **[Verse 18.]** “Lord, let me not be confounded, for I have called upon you”: Lord, let me not be ashamed before those who insult me because I have called upon you. “Let the impious be ashamed and be led down into hell”: Let those rather be ashamed who call upon stones and be joined to shadows.

19. **[Verse 19.]** “Let deceitful lips become mute”: By making your mysteries concerning me known to the peoples, make the lips of those who fabricate falsehoods about me fall silent. “Which speak iniquity against the righteous, in pride and contempt”: Which speak iniquity against Christ, behaving proudly and despising him as a crucified man.

**[Col. 0229] 20. [Verses 20–21.]** “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord!” Here the Prophet, seeing and marveling at this, exclaims how manifold and abundant your sweetness is, Lord. “Which you have hidden for those who fear you”: You love even those whom you correct very greatly; but, so that they may not act more negligently through careless security, you hide from them the sweetness of your love, since it is useful for them to fear you. “You have perfected it for those who hope in you”: You have perfected this sweetness for those who hope in you; for you do not take away from them what they patiently await to the end. [Note: [Col. 0229] Several manuscripts read, “for those who.”] “In the sight of the children of men”: For it is not hidden from the children of men who now live not according to Adam but according to the Son of Man. “You will hide them in the hidden place of your face”: You will reserve for those who hope in you an eternal dwelling in the hidden knowledge of you. “From the disturbance of men”: So that they may no longer suffer any human disturbance.

21. “You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues”: But meanwhile, while slanderous tongues clamor against them, saying, “Who knows this?” or “Who came from there?”, you will protect them in the tabernacle of faith in those things that the Lord temporarily accomplished and endured for us.

22. **[Verse 22.]** “Blessed is the Lord, for he has made his mercy wondrous in the city of the surrounding region”: Blessed is the Lord, for after the correction of the most severe persecutions, he has made his mercy wondrous to all throughout the world, in the city of encirclement, the circuit of human society.

23. **[Verse 23.]** “I said in my ecstasy”: Hence that people, speaking again, says: “I said in my fear, when the nations savagely raged against me.” “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes”: Surely, if you were looking upon me, you would not allow me to suffer these things. “Therefore you heard, Lord, the voice of my prayer when I cried to you”: Therefore, setting a limit to my correction and showing that I belong to your care, you heard, Lord, the voice of my prayer when I intensified it greatly out of tribulation.

24. **[Verse 24.]** “Love the Lord, all his saints”: The Prophet, seeing these things, again exhorts them and says: “Love the Lord, all his saints, for the Lord will require truth.” When “the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the impious appear?” (1 Peter 4:18). “And he will repay those who act with abundant pride”: He will repay those who do not turn even when overcome, because they are exceedingly proud.

25. **[Verse 25.]** “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened”: Work what is good without failing, so that you may reap at the proper time. “All you who hope in the Lord”: That is, all you who rightly fear or worship him, hope in the Lord.

## Exposition II

### Sermon I, delivered shortly after the Feast of the Apostles, from section 3: On the beginning of the psalm

1. **[Verse 1.]** Let us examine, as far as we can, the secrets of this psalm that we have just sung, and then return to your ears and minds a discourse carved out from them. Its title is: “To the end. A psalm of David himself: ecstasy.” [Col. 0230] We know what “to the end” means if we know Christ, for the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). “End” does not mean consuming but perfecting. For we use “end” in two ways: either that by which something ceases to be what it was, or that by which what was begun becomes perfect. Therefore, “to the end” means “to Christ.”

2. “A psalm of David: ecstasy.” The word *ecstasy* is Greek; in Latin, as far as it can be understood, it may be explained by one word if we say *excessus*, “an excess.” An excess of mind is properly called *ecstasy*. In an excess of mind two things are understood: either fear, or attention directed toward heavenly things, so that earthly things somehow slip from the memory. In this ecstasy were all the saints to whom the mysteries of God, surpassing this world, were revealed.

Speaking of this excess of mind, that is, ecstasy, Paul, making himself known, said: “For whether we were beside ourselves for God, or whether we are of sober mind for you, the love of Christ compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:13). This means: If we wished only to do and contemplate those things that we behold in an excess of mind, we would not be with you but would be above, as though despising you. And when you followed us with a weak step [Note: [Col. 0230] Three manuscripts read: “with a strong step.”] toward those higher and inward things, unless the love of Christ again compelled us—he who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6)—we would consider ourselves servants and, not ungrateful to him from whom we received higher things, would not despise lower things on account of the weak. We would accommodate ourselves to those who cannot see sublime things with us.

This, then, is what he says: “Whether we were beside ourselves for God.” For he sees what we see in an excess of mind [Note: [Col. 0230] Thus Erasmus, supported by the manuscripts. But Louvain reads: “For he sees what we see, who grants a human being to enter an excess of mind; he alone,” etc.]; he alone reveals his secrets. Indeed, he is the one who says that he was snatched away and taken up into the third heaven and heard ineffable words that a human being is not permitted to speak. So great was that excess of mind that he said: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12:2).

Therefore, if the title of this psalm signifies this excess of mind, that is, this ecstasy, we ought certainly to expect great and lofty things from the one who composed the psalm—that is, from the Prophet, or rather, through the Prophet, from the Holy Spirit.

3. But if this ecstasy is to be understood as fear, the context of this psalm will not lack that meaning of the word either. For it appears to speak of the Passion, in which there is fear. But whose fear is it? Is it Christ’s, since he said “to the end,” and we understand Christ as the end? Or perhaps it is our fear? For can we properly understand fear in Christ as his Passion approached, when he had come for that very purpose? When he had come to what he came for, was he afraid as he was about to die? If he were wholly human in such a way that he were not God, would he not rejoice more at his resurrection than fear his death?

Nevertheless, because he deigned to assume the form of a servant, and in that form to clothe us with himself—he who did not disdain to assume us into himself did not disdain to transfigure us into himself and to speak in our words, so that we too might speak in his words. For this was a wondrous exchange, and divine transactions were carried out: a transformation of realities was enacted in this world by the heavenly merchant. He came to receive insults and give honors; he came to drain suffering and give salvation; he came to undergo death and give life.

Therefore, as he was about to die because of what he had taken from us, he was afraid—not in himself but in us. For he also said that his soul was sorrowful even unto death (Matthew 26:38), and certainly we ourselves were all with him. For without him, we are nothing; in him, there is Christ himself and us. Why? Because the whole Christ is the Head and the body. He is the Savior of the body, the Head who has already ascended into heaven; the body is the Church, which labors on earth (Ephesians 5:23).

But unless this body adhered to its Head through the bond of love, so that one person might be formed from Head and body, he would not have seized a certain persecutor from heaven and said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). When he was already sitting in heaven and no human being was touching him, how was Saul, raging on earth against Christians, in any way injuring him? He did not say, “Why are you persecuting my saints?” or “my servants?” but, “Why are you persecuting me?” That is, “Why are you persecuting my members?” The Head cried out for the members, and the members transfigured the Head in themselves.

The tongue takes upon itself the voice of the foot. When, perhaps, a foot is crushed in a crowd and hurts, the tongue cries out, “You are treading on me.” It does not say, “You are treading on my foot,” but says that it is being trodden upon, though no one has touched the tongue; yet the foot that is being trodden upon is not separated from the tongue. Thus it is not inappropriate to understand *ecstasy* as fear.

For what shall I say, brothers?
