If there were absolutely no fear for those about to suffer, the Apostle Peter himself would not have been told what we heard on the Feast of the Apostles, when the Lord foretold his future Passion: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and went where you wished; but when you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” “This,” he said, “he spoke to signify by what death he would die” (John 21:18).

Therefore, if the Apostle Peter, with such perfection, went unwillingly where he did not wish to go—he died unwillingly but was crowned willingly [Note: [Col. 0231] Am. and Er. read: “Therefore, if the Apostle Peter, led where he did not wish to go by such persecution, died willingly unwillingly.” Louvain reads: “with such perfection, he was led where he did not wish to go and willingly,” etc. Most manuscripts read: “such perfection that he went willingly where he did not wish.” The Gatian manuscript reads: “he went unwillingly where he did not wish.” But the text should be emended thus: “he went where he did not wish; he died willingly unwillingly, but …”]—what is surprising if there is some fear in the Passion even of the righteous, even of the saints? Fear arises from human weakness; hope from divine promise. What you fear is yours; what you hope for is God’s gift in you. And in your fear you recognize yourself more truly, so that in your deliverance you may glorify the one who made you. Let human weakness fear, but let divine mercy not fail in that fear.

Finally, this fearful man began from that point: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.” You see that he both fears and hopes; you see that this fear is not without hope. Even if there is some disturbance in the human heart, divine consolation does not withdraw.

4. Christ, then, speaks here in the Prophet. I dare to say: Christ speaks. In this psalm he will say certain things that may seem unable to correspond to Christ—to the excellence of our Head, and especially to that Word who in the beginning was God with God. Certain words here may perhaps seem not to correspond even to him in the form of a servant, which he assumed from the Virgin. And yet Christ speaks, because Christ is in the members of Christ.

And so that you may know that the one Christ is said to be Head and his own body, he himself says, speaking about marriage: “The two shall be one flesh; therefore they are no longer two but one flesh” (Matthew 19:5–6). But perhaps he says this about an ordinary marriage? Hear the Apostle Paul: “The two shall be one flesh.” “This mystery is great,” he says, “but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Thus, as it were, one person is formed from two: from Head and body, from bridegroom and bride. The prophet Isaiah also commends the wondrous and sublime unity of this person. For Christ, speaking prophetically through him, says: “As a bridegroom he has bound a turban around me, and as a bride he has adorned me with an ornament” (Isaiah 61:10). He called himself bridegroom and bride. Why bridegroom and bride, unless because “the two shall be one flesh”? If the two are one flesh, why should they not be one voice?

Let Christ therefore speak, because the Church speaks in Christ and Christ speaks in the Church; the body speaks in the Head, and the Head in the body. Hear the Apostle expressing this same point more clearly: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12). Speaking of the members of Christ—that is, of the faithful—he does not say, “So also are the members of Christ”; rather, he called the whole of what he described “Christ.” Just as one body has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ: many members, one body.

Therefore all of us together with our Head, Christ, are nothing without our Head. Why? Because with our Head we are a vine; without our Head—God forbid—we are severed branches, destined not for any work of the gardener but only for the fire. Hence he himself also says in the Gospel: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the gardener”; and, “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Lord, if without you we can do nothing, then everything is in you. For whatever he works through us appears to be worked by us. He can do much, indeed everything, without us; we can do nothing without him.

5. **[Verse 2.]** Therefore, whatever kind of ecstasy he speaks in—whether fear or an excess of mind—the things said are fitting. Let us speak as Christ’s body; let us all speak as one, because we are all one unity. Let us say: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.”

He says: “I dread that confusion which is eternal.” For there is a certain useful temporal shame: a disturbance of the soul that looks upon its sins, shudders at what it sees, blushes from its horror, and corrects itself through its shame. Hence the Apostle also says: “For what glory did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21). Thus he says that those who are already faithful should be ashamed, not of present gifts but of past sins.

A Christian should not fear this shame. Indeed, if he does not have it, he will have eternal shame. What is eternal shame? When what was said comes to pass: “Their iniquities will confront them” (Wisdom 4:20). And when their iniquities confront them, the whole wicked flock will be brought to the left, like goats separated from sheep, and they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” They ask why. “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25:41).

They despised him when they did not give food to Christ who was hungry, drink to him who was thirsty, clothing to him who was naked, welcome to him who was a stranger, or visitation to him who was sick. When these things begin to be enumerated before them, they will be confounded, and this confusion will be eternal.

Fearing this, the one who is afraid—or whose mind is in an excess directed toward God—asks: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever.”

6. “And in your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.” For if you attend to my righteousness, you condemn me. “In your righteousness deliver me.” There is a righteousness of God that becomes ours when it is given to us. It is therefore called God’s righteousness, so that no one may think that he possesses righteousness from himself.

Thus the Apostle Paul says: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly”—what does “who justifies the ungodly” mean? He makes the unjust just—“his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). But the Jews, because they thought they could fulfill righteousness by their own strength, stumbled over the stone of stumbling (Romans 9:32) and the rock of offense, and did not recognize the grace of Christ. They received the Law by which they would become guilty, not by which they would be freed from guilt.

Finally, what does the Apostle say about them? “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” What does he mean by saying that the Jews have zeal for God but not according to knowledge? Hear what “not according to knowledge” means: “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:2–3).

If, then, they have zeal for God but not according to knowledge because they are ignorant of God’s righteousness and wish to establish their own—as though they were made righteous from themselves—for that reason they did not recognize God’s grace, because they did not wish to be saved freely.

Who is saved freely? The one in whom the Savior does not find anything to crown but something to condemn; he does not find merits deserving good things but merits deserving punishment. If he were to act according to the true rule proposed by the Law, the sinner would be condemned. If he acted by this rule, whom would he free? He found everyone a sinner. The one who came alone without sin found us sinners.

This is what the Apostle says: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). What does “they lack the glory of God” mean? It means that he himself must deliver them, not you, because you cannot deliver yourself; you need a deliverer.

Why do you boast? Why do you presume upon the Law and righteousness? Do you not see what is fighting within you, from you, against you? Do you not hear the one who fights, confesses, and desires assistance in the struggle? Do you not hear the Lord’s athlete asking the director of the contest for help in his struggle?

God does not await you as an editor awaits you if you happen to fight in an amphitheater. That man can give you a prize if you win, but he cannot help you when you are in danger. God does not await you in that way.

Consider, then, attend to the one who says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22–25).

Why grace? Because it is given freely. Why is it given freely? Because your merits did not precede it; God’s benefits preceded you. Glory, therefore, belongs to the one who delivers us. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.”

Thus: “In you, Lord, I have hoped,” not in myself. “I shall not be confounded forever,” because I hope in the one who does not confound. [Note: [Col. 0234] Most manuscripts read: “because the one who hopes in him is not confounded.”] “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me”: Since you did not find my righteousness in me, deliver me in yours. That is, let that which justifies me deliver me; that which makes the ungodly godly, the unrighteous righteous, the blind seeing, the fallen rising, and the weeping rejoicing—that delivers me, not I myself. “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.”

7. **[Verse 3.]** “Incline your ear to me.” God did this when he sent Christ himself to us. He sent to us the one who, with his head inclined, was writing on the ground with his finger (John 8:6), when the adulterous woman was brought before him for punishment. He had bent down toward the earth—that is, God toward the human being, to whom it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19).

God does not incline his ear toward us as though toward bodily places, nor is he bounded by these bodily limbs. Let no human fantasies think anything of the kind. God is truth. Truth is neither square nor round nor long. It is present everywhere, if the eye of the heart is open to it.

Yet God inclines his ear toward us by laying his mercy upon us. What mercy is greater than that he should give us his Only-Begotten—not to live with us, but to die for us? “Incline your ear to me.”

8. “Hasten to rescue me.” This is heard when he says, “Hasten.” The word has been placed here so that you may understand that all this which seems long to us while the age revolves is a single moment. What has an end is not long.

From Adam to the present day has already passed, and far more has passed than remains to be completed. If Adam were still alive and were to die today, what would it profit him to have existed and lived so long? Why, then, this haste? Because the ages fly past, and what seems slow to you is brief in God’s eyes.

This man had already understood that haste in his ecstasy: “Hasten to rescue me. Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, that you may save me.” Be my house of refuge, protecting God, house of refuge.

Sometimes I am in danger and wish to flee. Where shall I flee? To what place can I flee safely? To what mountain? To what cave? To what fortified roof? What citadel can I hold? By what walls can I be surrounded? Wherever I go, I follow myself. For, human being, you can flee anything you wish except your conscience.

Enter your house, rest in your bed, go into your inner rooms. You cannot possess anything more inward to which you may flee from your conscience if your sins gnaw at you. But because he said, “Hasten to rescue me,” and “In your righteousness deliver me,” so that you may forgive my sins and build your righteousness in me, you will be my house of refuge; I flee to you.

For where can I flee from you? God is angry with you—where will you flee? Hear what he says in another psalm, fearing God’s anger: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8). Wherever I go, there I find you. If you are angry, I find you as an avenger; if you are appeased, as a helper.

Nothing remains for me, then, except to flee to you, not from you. If you are a servant and wish to escape a human master, you flee to places where your master is not. If you wish to escape God, flee to the Lord. For there is nowhere you can flee from God. All things are present and naked before the eyes of the Almighty.

“You, then,” he says, “be my house of refuge.” For if I am not saved, how can I flee? Heal me, and I will flee to you. If you do not heal me, I cannot walk; how will I be able to flee?

Where could he go or flee if he could not walk—half-alive on the road, wounded by the robbers? The priest passed him by; the Levite passed him by; the Samaritan, passing by, had mercy on him (Luke 10:30)—that is, the Lord himself, who had mercy on the human race.

For *Samaritanus* means “guardian.” And who will guard us if he abandons us? Hence, when the Jews reviled him, saying, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (John 8:48), he rejected one charge and embraced the other: “I do not have a demon.” He did not say, “I am not a Samaritan,” wishing thus to be understood as our guardian.

Having had mercy, he approached, healed him, brought him to the inn, and fulfilled mercy toward him. The man can now walk, and he can also flee. Where could he flee except to God, where he made himself a house of refuge?

9. **[Verse 4.]** “For you are my strength and my refuge, and for your name’s sake you will be my guide and nourish me.” Not for the sake of my merit, but for the sake of your name, so that you may be glorified—not because I am worthy. You will be my guide, so that I do not wander from you; and you will nourish me, so that I may be strong enough to eat the food with which you feed the angels.

Here he nourished us with milk, though he promised us heavenly food; he employed a mother’s mercy. For just as a nursing mother takes the same food that an infant is not yet capable of eating, passes it through her flesh, and pours out milk—what the little child receives is what it will later receive at the table, but what is passed through the flesh is suited to the child—so the Lord came to us clothed in flesh, making his wisdom like milk for us.

Therefore the body of Christ speaks: “And you will nourish me.”

10. **[Verse 5.]** “You will lead me out of this snare which they concealed for me.” The Passion is already signified: “You will lead me out of this snare which they concealed for me.”

Nor is that the only Passion which our Lord Jesus Christ suffered. The devil stretched his snare all the way to the end. And woe to the one who falls into that snare. Everyone falls who does not hope in God, who does not say: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever”; and, “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.”

[Col. 0236] The enemy’s snare has been extended and prepared. He placed error and terror in the snare: error to entice, terror to break and seize. Close the door of desire against error; close the door of fear against terror, and you will be led out of the snare.

Your own Commander, who for your sake also deigned to be tempted, demonstrated this kind of struggle in himself. First he was tempted by enticements, because the door of desire was tested in him when the devil tempted him, saying: “Command these stones to become loaves.” “Worship me, and I will give you these kingdoms.” “Throw yourself down, for it is written: ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will lift you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone’” (Matthew 4:4, 9, 6).

All this enticement tests desire. [Note: [Col. 0236] Thus several manuscripts. Erasmus has: “All these things test desires through enticement.” Lov., “He tests all these things through the enticements of desires.”]

But when he found the door of desire closed in the one who was being tempted for us, he turned to test the door of fear and prepared the Passion for him. Finally, the Evangelist says: “When the devil had finished every temptation, he departed from him until the proper time” (Luke 4:13).

What does “until the proper time” mean? It means that he would return and test the door of fear, because he had found the door of desire closed.

Therefore the whole body of Christ is tempted to the end. My brothers, when some evil order was issued against Christians, this body was struck all at once. The whole body was struck. Hence it had been said in the psalm: “I was pushed hard that I might fall, but the Lord helped me” (Psalm 117:13).

But when those things that struck the whole body so that it would fall had ended, temptation began to occur in its parts. The body of Christ is tempted: one Church does not suffer persecution, another does. One does not suffer the rage of an emperor, but suffers the rage of an evil people.

What devastation has come from the crowds! What evils have been inflicted upon the Church by bad Christians, by those who, caught in that net, became so numerous that they weighed down the boats in that fishing of the Lord before his Passion (Luke 5:7)!

The pressures of temptation, then, do not cease. Let no one say to himself, “This is not a time of temptation.” Whoever says this to himself promises himself peace; whoever promises himself peace is attacked while secure.

Let the whole body of Christ therefore say: “You will lead me out of this snare which they concealed for me.” For our Head too was led out of the snare that they concealed for him—those to whom it was then said in the Gospel that they would say: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” And when questioned, they pronounced judgment against themselves: “What will that householder do to the wicked tenants?” “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly and lease his vineyard to other farmers.”

And have you not read this also? “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” For what is “the builders rejected” but this: “They cast him outside the vineyard and killed him” (Matthew 21:38–42)?

Therefore he too was delivered. Our Head is above; he is free. Let us cling to him through love, so that afterward we may be joined to him more perfectly through immortality. And let us all say:

[Col. 0237] “You will lead me out of this snare which they concealed for me, for you are my protector.”

11. **[Verse 6.]** Let us hear the voice of the Lord, which he spoke on the cross: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” Certainly, when we recognize his words from this psalm in the Gospel, let us not doubt that he himself spoke here.

You have this in the Gospel: He said, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46), and, having inclined his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30). He did not wish the words of this psalm to be his without reason, except to remind you that he spoke in this psalm.

Seek him here himself. Consider how he wished to be sought in that psalm “for the morning reception”: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (Psalm 21:17–19). To remind you that this had been fulfilled in him, he placed the beginning of that psalm in his own voice: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:2).

And yet he transfigured the voice of the body in himself. For the Father never abandoned his Only-Begotten. “You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth”: You have done what you promised; you have not deceived in your promise, God of truth.

12. [verse 7.] You hate those who observe vanity uselessly. Who observes vanity? The one who dies through fear of dying: for, by fearing to die, he lies, and dies before he dies—the one who lied in order to live. You want to lie so that you may not die; and you lie, and you die. While avoiding one death, which you can postpone but cannot remove, you fall into two deaths, so that you die first in soul and afterward in body. How does this happen, except by observing vanity? Because the passing day is sweet to you, because fleeting times are sweet to you—times from which you hold nothing, while you yourself are held by them.

You hate those who observe vanity uselessly. But I, who do not observe vanity, have hoped in the Lord. You hope in money: you observe vanity. You hope in honor and in some lofty position of human power: you observe vanity. You hope in some influential friend: you observe vanity. When you hope in all these things, either you yourself depart and leave them here, or, while you live, everything perishes and you fail in your hope.

Isaiah recalls this vanity when he says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and its flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL, 6–8). But I have hoped in the Lord—not as those who hope in vanity and observe vanity hope—for he is not vanity.

13. [verse 8.] “I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy,” not in my justice. “Because you have regarded my humility, you have saved my soul from distress; nor have you shut me up in the hands of the enemy.”

What are these distresses from which we want our soul to be saved? Who could enumerate them? Who could adequately magnify them? Who could suitably commend their avoidance and flight?

First, there is a harsh distress within the human race: not knowing another’s heart; usually thinking ill of a faithful friend and well of an unfaithful one. O harsh distress! And what can you do to look into hearts? What eye do you bring, frail and lamentable mortality? What can you do to see [Col. 0238] the heart of your brother today? You have no means.

There is another, greater distress: you do not even see what your own condition will be tomorrow. What shall I say now about the distresses belonging to mortality itself? It is necessary to die, and no one wants to. No one wants what is necessary; no one wants what will happen whether he wishes it or not. It is a harsh distress not to want what cannot be avoided.

For if it were possible, we would certainly not want to die; and we would wish to become like the angels, but by some transformation rather than by death, as the Apostle says: “We have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed with our dwelling which is from heaven, if indeed we are found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this dwelling groan under our burden, not wishing to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V, 1–4).

We want to reach the kingdom of God, but we do not want to do so through death; and yet necessity says to you, “By this way you will come.” Do you hesitate to come by this way, human being, when God has come to you by this way?

There are also the distresses involved in overcoming very old desires and long-established evil habits. You know that overcoming habit is a hard struggle. You see how badly you act, how detestably, how miserably; and yet you do it—you have caused it to happen, and you will do it today. If it displeases you so much when I discuss it, how much does it displease you when you think about it? And yet you will do it. Where are you being swept away? Who is dragging you captive? Is it that law in your members which fights against the law of your mind?

Cry out, then: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 23). And what we have just said is fulfilled in you: “But I have hoped in the Lord; I shall exult and rejoice in your mercy, because you have regarded my humility and saved my soul from distress.”

For how has your soul been saved from distress except because your humility was regarded? Unless you had first been humbled, he would not have heard you—he who would deliver you from distress. He was humbled who said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” Were those humbled who, “ignorant of God’s justice and seeking to establish their own, were not subject to the justice of God” (Rom. X, 3)?

14. [verse 9.] “Nor have you shut me up in the hands of the enemy”—not your neighbor, not your fellow possessor, not the one with whom you served as a soldier and whom you injured, or perhaps wronged in your own city. Such people are those for whom we ought to pray.

We have another enemy: the devil, the ancient serpent. All who die, if we die well, are delivered from his hands. For whoever dies badly in his sins is shut up in his hands, so that he may be condemned with him at the end.

Therefore the Lord our God delivers us from the hand of our enemy, for he wants to seize us through our desires. When our desires are strong and we serve them, they are called distresses. But when God delivers our soul from our distresses, what will remain in us for the enemy to hold, so that we may be shut up in his hands?

15. “You have set my feet in a spacious place.” Certainly, the way is narrow (Matt. VII, 14): it is narrow for one who struggles, but broad for one who loves [Col. 0239]. The same way that is narrow becomes broad. “You have set my feet,” he says, “in a spacious place,” so that my feet, being constrained, would not turn inward upon themselves and, stumbling over themselves, cast me down.

What, then, does he mean by “You have set my feet in a spacious place”? Clearly, you have made the justice that was once difficult for me easy: this is, “You have set my feet in a spacious place.”

16. [verses 10–11.] “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am troubled; my eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger. For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groaning.”

Let this suffice for Your Charity. With the Lord’s help, perhaps we shall fulfill our obligation and, having completed the Psalm, depart [Note: [Col. 0239] From this it may be understood that this first discourse and the two following ones on Psalm XXX were delivered in a place outside the church of Hippo.].

## SERMON II. On the middle of the same Psalm

1. Let our attention return to the remaining portions of the Psalm, and let us recognize ourselves in the Prophet’s words. For if we examine ourselves in the time of tribulation, we shall rejoice in the time of reward.

When I was expounding the first parts of this Psalm, I had commended to Your Charity that Christ was speaking; and I had not concealed how the whole Christ, with head and body, must be understood. I had also confirmed this, as it seemed to me, with sufficiently suitable and clear testimonies from Scripture, so that there could be no doubt at all that Christ is head and body, bridegroom and bride, the Son of God and the Church—the Son of God made the son of man for our sake, so that he might make the sons of men sons of God. Thus the two are one flesh in a great sacrament, and in the Prophets they are recognized as two in one voice.

The thanksgiving expressed earlier belongs to the one who says: “You have regarded my humility, you have saved my soul from distress, and you have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place.” It is the thanksgiving of a person delivered from tribulation, of Christ’s members delivered from affliction and ambushes.

And again he says: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am troubled.” In tribulation there is certainly distress. How, then, does he say, “You have set my feet in a spacious place”? If he is still troubled, how are his feet in a spacious place? Perhaps there is one voice because there is one body, but spaciousness is felt in some members and distress in others—that is, some experience the ease of justice, while others labor in tribulation.

For if different members did not suffer different things, the Apostle would not say: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (I Cor. XII, 26). Some churches, for example, have peace; others are in tribulation. In those that have peace, the feet are in a spacious place; those that are in tribulation suffer distress. Yet the tribulation of the latter grieves the former, and the peace of the former consoles the latter.

For the body is one in such a way that there is no division. Nothing produces division except disagreement. Love creates cohesion; cohesion embraces unity; unity preserves love; and love reaches glory [Col. 0240].

Let him therefore speak from certain members: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am troubled; my eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed in anger.”

2. We ask where this tribulation comes from, since shortly before he seemed to rejoice at having been delivered, with a certain justice generously infused into him by the gift of God, and thus space having been made for his feet in the breadth of love.

Where, then, does this tribulation arise, except perhaps from what the Lord says: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12)?

At first, after the small number of the saints had been commended, the Church was multiplied as though nets had been cast, and innumerable people were caught, concerning whom it had been foretold: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). They would even weigh down the boats and break the nets, as happened in that first catch of fish before the Lord’s passion (Luke V, 6).

From these multitudes, then, the churches have been so filled around Easter that the narrowness of their walls cannot contain their crowds. How can this person not be troubled by such a multitude when he sees the very people who shortly before filled the churches filling theaters and amphitheaters? The same people who shortly before were praising God now blaspheming him; the same people who answered “Amen” to God now denying him?

Let him endure; let him persist; let him not fail even amid the great multitude of the wicked, because the grain does not fail amid the multitude of chaff either, until, after winnowing, it is placed in the granary and there joins the company of the saints, so that it may suffer none of the disturbance of dust.

Let him therefore persist. For when the Lord had said, “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold,” lest our feet slip and totter at the prediction of this abundance of iniquity, he immediately added what would raise up, console, and strengthen the faithful: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 13).

3. Consider, then, this person, who, as it seems to me, has been placed in this tribulation. Since, when placed in tribulation, he ought to grieve—for tribulation appropriately produces grief—he says that he is angry in tribulation and declares: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am troubled; my eye is disturbed in anger.”

If you are troubled, why are you angry? He is angry at the sins of others. Who would not be angry on seeing people who confess God with their mouths but deny him by their conduct? Who would not be angry on seeing people renounce the world in words but not in deeds? Who would not be angry on seeing brothers lying in wait for brothers, not keeping faith with the kiss they imprint in [Note: Thus Erasmus and fourteen manuscripts. But in the Louvain text the particle “in” is omitted.] the sacraments of God?

And who could enumerate all the things at which the body of Christ is angry—this body that lives inwardly by [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read “in”; several manuscripts read “from.”] the Spirit of Christ, that groans like a grain among the chaff? Those who groan and are angry in this way scarcely appear, just as grains scarcely appear when the threshing floor is being threshed. One who does not know how much grain was brought in thinks that everything is chaff; yet from what is thought to be entirely chaff, a great mass will be purified.

Among these, then, [Col. 0241] who do not appear but groan, he is angry who says elsewhere: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10). And elsewhere, when he sees many doing evil, he says: “Weariness has seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 53). In another place he says: “I saw the senseless, and I wasted away” (ibid., 158).

4. Yet we must fear lest this anger become so great that it turns into hatred. Anger is not yet hatred. You may be angry with your son without hating your son; you preserve an inheritance for him even though he knows you are angry, and you are angry for this reason: so that he may not lose what you have preserved by living badly [Note: All the manuscripts read “escaping.”] through corrupt conduct.

Anger, therefore, is not yet hatred. We do not yet hate those with whom we are angry. But if this anger remains and is not quickly torn out, it grows and becomes hatred. Therefore, so that fresh anger may be torn out and not turn into hatred, Scripture teaches us, saying: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 26).

Sometimes you find a brother harboring hatred who rebukes someone for being angry. Hatred is in him, yet he condemns anger in another. He has a beam in his own eye and rebukes the splinter in his brother’s eye (Matt. VII, 3). But this splinter and shoot, unless quickly torn out, will become a beam.

He does not therefore say, “My eye has been extinguished because of anger,” but “has been disturbed.” For if it is extinguished, there is already hatred, not anger. And see that it has been extinguished. Hence John says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now” (I John II, 11).

Before one goes into darkness, then, the eye is disturbed in anger. But we must be careful lest anger turn into hatred and the eye be extinguished [Note: [Col. 0241] The editions of Erasmus and Louvain insert after “be extinguished” the following: “Let everyone who has been called into peace—that is, into Christ, who commended the peace of God and at whose birth supreme peace was announced to human beings by the angel—take note of this: if, for some small or great cause, he breaks out into hatred, he can have no fellowship with peace, that is, with Christ, except through worthy correction by repentance.” “Then he continues and says, ‘Disturbed,’ and so on.” We have removed these words because they are absent from all our manuscripts.].

This person therefore says: “My eye, my soul, and my belly are disturbed because of anger”—that is, my inward parts are disturbed. He put “belly” for the inward parts.

Sometimes it is permissible to be angry with the wicked, the perverse, those who deviate from the law, and those who live badly; but it is not permissible to shout. When we are angry and cannot shout, our inward parts are disturbed. For sometimes perversity is so great that it cannot even be rebuked.

5. [verse 11.] “For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groaning.” “My life,” he says, “has failed in sorrow.”

The Apostle says: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (I Thess. III, 8). Whoever is perfect through the Gospel and the grace of God lives here only for the sake of others, for his life in this world is no longer necessary to him. But because their ministry is necessary for others, what the same Apostle says takes place in them: “I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 23–24).

But when a person sees that, through his ministry, his labors, and his preaching, people are not advancing, the vitality of his life grows weak in poverty. Truly miserable are this poverty and hunger. For those whom we win for the Lord, the Church in a certain sense eats. What does [Col. 0242] “eats” mean? It transfers them into its own body. Whatever we eat, we transfer into our body.

The Church does this through the saints. It hungers for those whom it wants to win and, in a certain way, eats those whom it has won. Peter represented the Church when a sheet full of all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles, and birds was sent down to him from heaven; by these kinds all the nations are signified. The Lord prefigured the Church, which was going to devour all nations and transform them into its own body, and he said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13).

O Church—that is, Peter, because “upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18)—kill and eat. First kill, and so eat. Kill what they are, and make them what you are.

When the Gospel is preached and the preacher sees that people are not advancing, why should he not cry out: “For my life has failed in sorrow, and my years in groaning; my strength has grown weak in poverty, and my bones are disturbed”?

These are our years, the years we spend here, and they are in groaning. Why? Because “iniquity has abounded, and the love of many has grown cold.” They are in groaning, not in clear cries. When the Church sees many going astray, it devours its groans within itself, so that it may say to God: “My groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII, 10). Another Psalm says this, but it suits the present passage; and this is what it means: “Although my groaning is hidden from human beings, it is not hidden from you” [Note: [Col. 0242] Erasmus and Louvain read, “but it is appropriate here to say this.” We have corrected the text according to the manuscripts.].

“My strength has grown weak in poverty, and my bones are disturbed.” We have spoken above about this poverty. The bones are understood as the strong members of the Church. Even if they are not disturbed by the persecutions of outsiders, they are nevertheless disturbed by the iniquities of their brothers.

6. [verse 12.] “I have become a reproach among all my enemies, and exceedingly so to my neighbors, and a fear to those who know me.”

“I have become a reproach among all my enemies.” Who are the enemies of the Church? Pagans? Jews? Evil Christians live worse than all of them.

Do you want to see how much worse evil Christians live than all others? The prophet Ezekiel says of such people that they are compared to useless branches (Ezek. XV, 2). Suppose that pagans are wild trees outside the Church. Something can still be made from them. Just as a piece of wood from a forest, even if knotted, crooked, and covered with bark, can be worked, hewn, smoothed, and brought to some use in human craftsmanship, so a carpenter can make something from it.

But from branches cut off, carpenters can make nothing; only the fire awaits them.

Pay attention, brothers. Although a branch remaining on the vine is everywhere preferred to a wild tree, because the branch bears fruit while the tree does not, nevertheless, if a branch cut from the vine is compared with a wild tree, the wild tree is understood to be better, because the carpenter can make something from it, whereas the branch is wanted only by one who supplies the furnace.

Thus, observing the multitude of those who live badly in the Church, he says: “I have become a reproach among all my enemies.” “The wicked,” he says, “live worse within my sacraments than those who have never approached them.”

Why should we not speak plainly in Latin [Col. 0243], or at least when we are expounding the Psalm? And if at other times we perhaps do not dare to say it, let the necessity of exposition at least have the freedom to rebuke.

“I have become a reproach among all my enemies.” The Apostle Peter says of such people: “Their last state has become worse than the first. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.”

When he says, “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of justice,” did he not judge the enemies outside to be better than those living badly within, by whom the Church is oppressed and burdened? “It would have been better for them,” he says, “not to have known the way of justice than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.”

Finally, see to what horrible thing he compared them: “The true proverb has happened to them: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit’” (II Peter II, 20–22).

Since the churches are full of such people, do not the few truly say there—or rather, does not the Church itself speak through the voice of the few: “I have become a reproach among all my enemies, and exceedingly so to my neighbors, and a fear to those who know me”?

“I have become an exceedingly great reproach to my neighbors,” that is, to those who were already drawing near to me in order to believe. My neighbors have been greatly frightened away by the bad life of evil and false Christians.

For how many do you think there are, my brothers, who want to become Christians but are offended by the conduct of Christians? They are the neighbors who were already drawing near, and we appeared to them as an exceedingly great reproach.

7. [also verse 12.] “I have become a fear to those who know me.” What is so fearful? “I have become,” he says, “a fear to those who know me.”

What is so fearful as when a person sees many living badly, and those of whom good things were hoped found involved in many evil deeds? He fears that all those whom he thought good may be like this, and nearly all the good come under evil suspicion.

“What sort of man is he? How he has fallen! How was he found in that disgrace, that crime, that evil deed!” Do you think that all are not like this? This is the fear to those who know me: even those who know us often come to doubt us.

And unless what you are—if you are anything—consoles you, you do not believe that another is like you. Some conscience consoles a person, so that the one who lives well says to himself: “You who now fear that all may be like this—are you like this?” His conscience answers: “I am not.”

“Then if you are not like this, are you alone?” Beware lest this pride be worse than that wickedness. Do not call yourself alone.

Elijah too, at one time, wearied by the multitude of the impious, said: “They have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” But what divine answer was given to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (III Kings XIX, 10; Rom. XI, 3–4).

Therefore, brothers, amid these scandals there is one remedy: do not think badly of your brother. Be humbly what you want him to be, and you will not think him to be what you are not [Note: [Col. 0243] Erasmus and the manuscripts read this way. Louvain has “be humble.”]. Yet let there also be fear among those who know us, even among those who have experience.

8. [verse 13.] “Those who saw me fled outside from me” [Col. 0244].

It might be forgiven if those who did not see me had fled outside from me. But even those who saw me fled outside from me.

If those who did not see me fled outside from me—and one should not say “fled outside,” since they were never inside—for if they had been inside, they would have seen me, that is, they would have recognized the body of Christ, recognized the members of Christ, recognized the unity of Christ.

But this is more grievous, utterly intolerable: that many who saw me fled outside from me. That is, those who knew what the Church was went outside and made heresies and schisms against the Church.

Today, for example, you find a person born among the Donatists. He does not know what the Church is; he holds to the place where he was born. You cannot tear away the habit he absorbed with his nurse’s milk.

Give me instead one who turns daily through the Scriptures, who reads and preaches. Does he not see there: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8)? Does he not see there: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his sight” (Ps. XXI, 28)?

If you see there the unity of the whole world, why do you flee outside, so that you not only suffer blindness yourself but also inflict it upon others?

“Those who saw me”—that is, those who knew what the Church is, who saw it in the Scriptures—“fled outside from me.”

Do you think, my brothers, that all those who created heresies in various places and parties did not know from the Scriptures of God that the Church had been foretold as spread throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0244] The editions read “proclaimed”; some manuscripts read “foretold.”]?

I say this truly to Your Charity: certainly we are all Christians, or are all called Christians, and we are all marked with the sign of Christ. The Prophets spoke more obscurely about Christ than about the Church. I think this was because they saw in the Spirit that people would make factions against the Church, while they would not engage in such great dispute about Christ but would stir up great controversies about the Church.

Therefore, what was going to produce the greater disputes was foretold more plainly and prophesied more openly, so that it might serve as a judgment against those who saw and fled outside.

9. I shall mention one example. Abraham was our father—not on account of descent according to the flesh, but on account of imitation of faith. As a righteous man pleasing to God, through faith he received from Sarah, his barren wife, the son promised to him, Isaac, in his old age (Gen. XXI, 2).

He was commanded to sacrifice this same son to God. He did not hesitate, argue, or dispute God’s command; he did not consider evil what the supremely good God could command. He led his son to be sacrificed, placed the wood of the sacrifice upon him, reached the place, and raised his right hand to strike him. When the one who had commanded him to raise it forbade him, he lowered it (ibid. XXII, 3). He had obeyed in order to strike, and he obeyed in order to spare; obedient everywhere, fearful nowhere.

Yet, so that the sacrifice might be completed and they might not depart without blood, a ram was found caught by its horns in a thorn bush. It was sacrificed, and the sacrifice was completed.

Ask what this means: it is a figure of Christ wrapped in sacramental mysteries. Finally, so that it may be seen, it is examined; so that it may be seen, it is unfolded; so that what is wrapped up may be opened.

Isaac [Col. 0245], like a beloved only son, bearing the figure of the Son of God, carried his own wood, just as Christ carried the cross (John XIX, 17). Finally, that ram itself signified Christ. For what does being caught by the horns mean except, in a certain way, being crucified? This is a figure of Christ.

The Church was immediately to be proclaimed. Once the head had been foretold, the body too had to be foretold. The Spirit of God began—God began—to wish to preach the Church to Abraham, and he introduced a figure.

He preached Christ figuratively; he preached the Church openly. For he said to Abraham: “Because you have obeyed my voice and have not spared your beloved son for my sake, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea; and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your offspring” (Gen. XXII, 16).

Almost everywhere Christ was preached by the Prophets under some covering of sacramental mystery, but the Church was preached openly, so that even those who were going to oppose it might see it, and the wickedness foretold in the Psalm might be fulfilled in them: “Those who saw me fled outside from me.”

“They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II, 19). The Apostle John said this about them.

10. [verse 13.] “I have been forgotten, like one dead from the heart.” I have been forgotten; I have passed into oblivion. Those who saw me have forgotten me. They have forgotten me as though I had been dead in their hearts.

“I have been forgotten, like one dead from the heart. I have become like a discarded vessel.”

What does “I have become like a discarded vessel” mean? This person was laboring and benefiting no one. He saw that he was a vessel and was of benefit to no one, and he says that he had become like a lost vessel.

11. [verse 14.] “For I heard the reproach of many dwelling around.” Many dwell around me and rebuke me every day.

How many evils they say against evil Christians—and those curses reach all Christians! For does the one who curses or rebukes Christians say, “See what bad Christians are doing”? No; he says, “See what Christians are doing.” He does not separate or distinguish.

Yet those who say these things dwell around—that is, they go around but do not enter. Why do they go around and not enter? Because they love the wheel of time. They do not enter into the truth because they do not love eternity. Devoted to temporal things and bound as though to a wheel, they are those of whom it is said elsewhere: “Set their leaders like a wheel” (Ps. LXXXII, 14), and elsewhere: “The wicked walk around” (Ps. XI, 9).

“While they gathered together against me, they conspired to take my soul.” What does “they conspired to take my soul” mean? It means, so that I might consent to their perversities.

For those who curse and do not enter are not content merely to remain outside; by their reproaches they also want to cast others out. If they cast you out of the Church, they have taken your soul—that is, they have secured your consent—and you will be in the circuit, not in the dwelling place.

12. [verse 15.] But amid these reproaches, these scandals, these evils, and these seductions—iniquities outside and perversities within—when I looked for righteous people and sought them, and found none whom I could imitate, what did I do? What counsel did I find [Col. 0246]?

“But I have hoped in you, Lord.” Nothing is more healthful, nothing safer.

You wanted to imitate someone, but you found him to be bad: abandon that imitation. You sought another, and something displeased you; you sought a third, and he too did not please you. Will you perish merely because this one and that one displeased you?

Take hope away from human beings, because “cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. XVII, 5).

If you still look to a human being, and while seeking to imitate him you depend upon him, you still want to be nourished by milk; and you will become *mammothreptus*—as children who suck for a long time are called—which is not fitting.

To use milk, as though wanting food to be transferred into oneself through flesh, is the same as living through a human being. Become capable of the table; take from the source from which he took—or perhaps from which he did not take.

Perhaps you have usefully encountered an evil person whom you thought good, so that you found bitterness at the breast, as from a mother, and were driven away by that offense and invited to stronger food.

Nurses do this for *mammothrepti*: they place something bitter on their breasts, so that the little ones, offended, spring back from the breast and long for the table.

Let him therefore say: “But I have hoped in you, Lord.” He says: “You are my God.”

“You are my God.” Let Donatus depart; let Caecilianus depart. Neither he nor the other is my God. I do not walk under the name of a human being; I hold the name of Christ.

Hear Paul himself saying: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. I, 13). I would perish if I belonged to Paul’s party. How shall I not perish if I belong to Donatus’s party?

Let human names, human crimes, and human inventions depart altogether. “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I said, You are my God.”

No human being, but you are my God. One person fails; one person advances. My God neither fails nor advances. The perfect has nowhere to advance, and the eternal has no source from which to fail. I said to the Lord: “You are my God.”

13. [verse 16.] “My lots are in your hands”—not in human hands, but in your hands.

What are these lots? Why “lots”? When we hear the word “lots,” we should not go looking for sorcerers. A lot is not something evil; rather, it is a matter of human uncertainty that indicates the divine will.

The Apostles also cast lots when Judas, after betraying the Lord, perished and, as it is written of him, “went to his own place.” They began to seek who should be appointed in his place. Two were chosen by human judgment, and one of the two was chosen by divine judgment. God was consulted about which of the two he wished to be appointed, and the lot fell upon Matthias (Acts I, 26).

What, then, is “My lots are in your hands”? He says “lots,” as I understand it, referring to the grace by which we have been saved.

Why does he call God’s grace by the name of “lot”? Because in a lot there is no selection, but the will of God. For when it is said, “This person does it, that person does not,” merits are being considered; and where merits are considered, there is selection, not lot.

But when God found no merits of ours, he saved us by the lot of his will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy. This is the lot.

For good reason, then, when that tunic of the Lord woven from above (John XIX, 23), which signifies the eternity of love, could not be divided by the persecutors, a lot was cast over it. Those to whom it came [Col. 0247] signified those who appear to attain a share in the lot of the saints.

“By grace you have been saved through faith,” the Apostle Paul says. “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves”—look at the lot—“and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works” (as though you had done something beneficial so as to be worthy of approaching this), “not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 8–10).

This is, in a certain way, the hidden lot: the will of God. In the human race there is a lot, a lot proceeding from God’s hidden will, with whom there is no injustice (Rom. IX, 14). For he does not show partiality; rather, his hidden justice is a lot for you.

14. Let Your Charity attend, and see how this very point is confirmed by the Apostle Peter.

When that magician Simon had been baptized by Philip and adhered to him, believing because of the divine miracles performed before his eyes, the Apostles came to Samaria, where the magician himself had also believed and had been baptized. The Apostles laid their hands upon the baptized, and they received the Holy Spirit and began to speak in tongues.

Simon was amazed and astounded at such a great divine miracle: the Holy Spirit came at the laying on of human hands and filled people. He desired this—not grace, but power; not something by which he might be freed, but something by which he might be exalted.

When he desired this, and pride filled his heart, together with diabolical impiety and a height destined to be cast down, he said to the Apostles: “How much money do you want me to give you, so that those upon whom I lay my hands may also receive the Holy Spirit?”

He who sought worldly things, who dwelt around without entering, thought that he could buy God’s gift with money. He who thought he could purchase the Holy Spirit with money also judged the Apostles greedy, because he himself was impious and proud.

Immediately Peter said: “May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be purchased with money. You have neither lot nor share in this faith” (Acts VIII, 13–21). That is, you do not belong to this grace, which we all receive freely, because you think you can buy with money what is given freely.

Because it is given freely, it is called a lot: “You have neither lot nor share in this faith.”

I have said this so that we would not be frightened by the words, “My lots are in your hands.” For what are the lots? The inheritance of the Church.

How far does the inheritance of the Church extend? Among whom are its boundaries [Note: [Col. 0247] The manuscripts of Regius and the Vatican read *affines* (“neighbors” or “adjacent”), rather than *fines* (“boundaries”).]? To all the ends: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8).

Let no human being, then, promise me some little fragment. “My God, my lots are in your hands.”

Let this suffice for Your Charity. What remains we shall render tomorrow, with the Lord himself helping us.

# SERMON III, DELIVERED ON THE DAY AFTER THE PRECEDING SERMON  
## On the End of the Same Psalm

1. What remains of the Psalm—on which we have already delivered two sermons—is somewhat more than a third, and we see that today we must complete what is owed. Therefore I ask Your Charity to be willing that we not linger over its clearer words, so that we may occupy ourselves with those requiring explanation. For many things spontaneously present themselves to the minds of the faithful; many require only a brief admonition; but some—and these are rarer—require labor before they can be understood. Therefore, so that the time may suffice both for our strength and for yours, see how plain these things are; acknowledge them with us, and in them praise God with us. If the Psalm prays, pray; if it groans, groan; if it rejoices, rejoice; if it hopes, hope; and if it fears, fear. For everything written here is our mirror.

2. [Verse 16.] “Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me.” Let us say this, and let each one say it concerning his own enemies; for it is good, and we ought to pray that God deliver us from the hands of our enemies. But we must understand which enemies we should pray for and against which enemies we should pray. Human enemies, whatever they may be, are not to be hated, lest, when an evil person hates the one by whom he suffers evil, there be two evil persons. Let the good person love even the one from whom he suffers evil, so that there may be at least one evil person.

Those enemies against whom we must pray are the devil and his angels. They envy us the kingdom of heaven; they do not want us to ascend from the place from which they were cast down. From them let us pray that our soul may be delivered. For whenever human beings are stirred up against us, they become their vessels. Therefore the apostle Paul, warning us how cautious we must be against our enemies, said to the servants of God who were suffering tribulations—through seditions, wickedness, and human enmities, certainly: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood,” that is, not against human beings, “but against rulers and authorities and the rulers of this world” (Eph. 6:12).

Of what world? Of heaven and earth? Far from it. The ruler of this world is none other than the Creator. But what world does he mean? The lovers of the world. Finally he adds and explains: “What I mean is, of this darkness.” Of what darkness, certainly, except that of unbelievers and the impious? For when the impious and unbelieving had become devout and faithful, the same apostle addressed them in this way: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (ibid. 5:8). “You are fighting,” he says, “against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” against the devil and his angels (ibid. 6:12). You do not see your enemies, and yet you conquer them. “Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me.”

3. [Verse 17.] “Make your face shine upon your servant; save me in your mercy.” We said above [Note: In the preceding sermon, no. 2 and following], if Your Charity remembers yesterday’s discussion—all of you who were present—that those who persecute the Church most fiercely are those who refuse to live good Christian lives. Through them the Church suffers reproach, and from them it endures hostility. When they are corrected, when they are not permitted to live wickedly, when they are addressed even by a word, they meditate evil in their hearts and seek an opportunity to break out.

Among these is this groaning person—and if we wish, we are he—for they are more numerous, while among their multitude the good scarcely appear, like grains on the threshing floor, from which, once cleansed, the Lord’s granaries are nevertheless to be filled (Matt. 3:12; Luke 3:17). Therefore, groaning among them, he says: “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

For it is considered a kind of disgrace when all are called Christians—those who live well and those who live wickedly; all are marked with the same sign, all approach the same altar, all are washed with the same baptism, all recite the same Lord’s Prayer, and all participate in the celebration of the same mysteries. When are those who groan distinguished, and those for whom one should groan, unless he makes his face shine upon his servant? What, then, is “Make your face shine upon your servant”? Let it become evident that I belong to you; and let the impious Christian not likewise say that he belongs to you. Otherwise I would have said to you without cause in another Psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). What he said there—“Distinguish my cause”—he says here: “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

Yet, lest he himself become proud and seem to justify himself, he adds and says: “Save me in your mercy.” That is: not in my justice, not in my merits, but in your mercy; not because I am worthy, but because you are merciful. Do not hear me according to judicial severity, but according to most merciful goodness. “Save me in your mercy.”

4. [Verse 18.] “Lord, let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you.” He has stated a great claim: “Let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you.” Do you want the one who called upon you to be put to shame? Do you want it to be said: “Where is the one in whom he placed his trust?”

But who, even among the impious, does not call upon God? Unless, therefore, he were to say in a particular way, “I have called upon you”—in a way that could not be common to many—he would in no way dare to demand so great a reward for this calling. For God would answer him somehow in his thought and say: “What are you asking of me, that you should not be put to shame? Why? Because you called upon me? Do people not call upon me every day in order to carry out the adulteries they desire? Do people not call upon me every day so that those from whom they expect an inheritance may die? Do people who are plotting fraud not call upon me every day so that they may bring it to a successful conclusion? What, then, is this for which you demand as a great reward that you should say, ‘Let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you’?”

They do indeed call upon him, but they do not call upon you. You call upon God when you call God into yourself. For this is to call upon him: to call him into yourself, in a certain way to invite him into the dwelling of your heart. But you would not dare invite such a head of household unless you knew how to prepare a dwelling for him. For if God said to you, “Behold, you have called upon me; I am coming to you,” where would I enter? Shall I endure such filth in your conscience?

If you were inviting my servant into your house, would you not first take care to clean it? You call me into your heart, and it is full of plunder. The place into which God is called is full of blasphemies, full of adulteries, full of frauds, full of evil desires—and you call upon me!

Finally, what does the Psalm say elsewhere about such people? “They did not call upon the Lord” (Ps. 13:5; 52:6). Certainly they did call upon him, and yet they did not call upon him. I say briefly—for a question has arisen—that when a person demands so great a reward by alleging one merit, saying, “because I have called upon you,” while we see God called upon by so many wicked people, a question has arisen that we must not pass over.

I say, then, briefly to the greedy man: “Do you call upon God?” “Why do you call upon God?” “So that he may give me profit.” Then you are calling upon profit, not upon God. Because you cannot obtain this profit you desire through your servant, your tenant, your client, your friend, or your bodyguard, you call upon God and make God the minister of your profit. God has become cheap in your eyes.

Do you wish to call upon God? Call upon him freely. Greedy man, is it not enough for you if God himself fills you? If God came to you without gold or silver, would you not want him? What, then, of the things God made is sufficient for you, when God himself is not sufficient?

This man therefore rightly asks: “Let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you.” Call upon the Lord, brothers, if you do not wish to be put to shame. For this man fears a certain shame, about which he spoke earlier in the Psalm: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be put to shame forever.” And so that you may know that he fears this shame, what did he add after saying, “Let me not be put to shame forever, because I have called upon you”? “Let the impious be put to shame and led down to hell”—certainly to that eternal shame.

5. [Verse 19.] “Let deceitful lips become mute, which speak iniquity against the just in pride and contempt.” This Just One is Christ. Many lips speak iniquity against him in pride and contempt.

Why “in pride and contempt”? Because he appeared contemptible to the proud, who came in such humility. Do you not want him to be despised by those who love honors—him who received so many insults? Do you not want him to be despised by those who regard this life as something great—him who died? Do you not want him to be despised by those who consider the death of the cross, as though it were a form of condemnation, shameful—him who was crucified? [Note: The word “cross” does not occur in the manuscripts.]

Do you not want him to be despised by the rich—him who lived a poor life in the world, although he was the Creator of the world? All these things that people love, because Christ did not choose to possess them—not because he did not have the power to possess them, but so that by not possessing them he might show that they should be despised—all who love these things despise him.

And whoever among his servants wishes to follow his footsteps, so that he too may walk in that humility in which he learned that his Lord walked, is despised in Christ as a member of Christ. And when the head and members are despised, Christ himself in his entirety is despised, because the whole Christ is the just one, head and body.

Christ himself in his entirety must be despised by the proud and impious, so that what is said may come upon them: “Let deceitful lips become mute, which speak iniquity against the just in pride and contempt.”

When will these lips become mute? In this world? Never. [Note: The Corbie manuscript, by a second hand, has: “in this wicked age.”] Every day they cry out against Christians, especially the humble; every day they blaspheme; every day they bark. They increase by their tongues the punishments by which they will thirst in hell and vainly desire a drop of water.

These lips, therefore, do not become mute now. But when? When their iniquities bring them face to face with them, as it is said in the Book of Wisdom:

“Then the righteous will stand with great confidence before those who oppressed them. Then they will say: ‘These are the ones whom we once held as a laughingstock and as an object of reproach. How have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? We fools regarded their life as madness’” (Wis. 5:1–5).

Then the lips of those who speak iniquity against the just in pride and contempt will become mute. For now they say to us: “Where is your God? What do you worship? What do you see? You believe and labor; it is certain that you labor, but uncertain what you hope for.” When what we hope for becomes certain, the deceitful lips will become mute.

6. [Verse 20.] Therefore see what follows, because the deceitful lips that speak iniquity against the just in pride and contempt will become mute. This man who groans in such a way pays attention; he has seen God’s good things inwardly, in the spirit. He has seen those good things that are perceived in secret but are not seen by the impious.

He saw that they speak iniquity against the just in pride and contempt because they know how to see the good things of this age, but do not even know how to consider the good things of the age to come. But in order to commend those good things of the age to come to people whom he commands to endure the present rather than love it, he cried out and added:

“How abundant is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord!”

If this impious man says, “Where is this multitude of sweetness?” I shall answer: “How can I show you the multitude of this sweetness, when you have lost your palate through the fever of iniquity? If you did not know honey, you would not cry out about how good it tastes unless you had tasted it. You do not have the palate of the heart with which to taste these good things. What shall I do for you? How can I show them to you? There is no one to whom I can say, ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet’” (Ps. 33:9). [Note: The words “to whom I may be able” are understood.]

“How abundant is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!”

What does “you have hidden for them” mean? You have kept it for them; you have not denied it, so that they alone may reach it—for it is good that it cannot be common to the just and the impious—and so that they may reach it through fear. For as long as they still fear, they themselves have not yet arrived; but they believe that they will arrive, and they begin from fear.

Nothing is sweeter than the immortality of wisdom, but “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:7; Ps. 110:10). “Which you have hidden for those who fear you.”

7. “But you have perfected it for those who hope in you in the sight of the sons of men.” It does not say, “You have perfected it in the sight of the sons of men,” but “for those who hope in you in the sight of the sons of men”—that is, you have perfected your sweetness for those who hope in you in the sight of the sons of men.

In the same way the Lord says: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny him before my Father” (Matt. 10:33). Therefore, if you hope in the Lord, hope in him before human beings. Do not perhaps hide this hope of yours in your heart and be afraid to confess it when it is charged against you as a crime that you are a Christian.

But who is now charged with being a Christian? So few non-Christians have remained that people are more likely to be charged with not being Christians than Christians themselves dare to charge others with being Christians. Nevertheless, I say to you, my brothers: begin, whoever you are who hear me, to live as a Christian, and see whether you will not be charged with it even by Christians—but in name, not in life or conduct. No one knows this except one who has experienced it.

Therefore pay attention; observe what you are hearing. Do you wish to live as a Christian? Do you wish to follow the footsteps of your Lord? You are charged with it, you are ashamed, and out of shame you abandon it. You have lost the way. You may think that you have believed in your heart unto righteousness, but you have lost the way; confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10).

If, then, you wish to walk in the Lord’s way, hope in God even in the sight of human beings—that is, do not be ashamed of your hope. Let what lives in your heart also dwell in your mouth, because it was not without reason that Christ wished his sign to be fixed upon our foreheads, as upon the seat of shame, so that a Christian would not be ashamed of Christ’s reproaches.

If you do this in the sight of human beings—if you are not ashamed of it before human beings, if in the sight of the sons of men you deny Christ neither by word nor by deed—hope that God’s sweetness will be perfected for you.

8. [Verse 21.] What follows? “You will hide them in the secrecy of your face.” What kind of place is this? He did not say, “You will hide them in your heaven.” He did not say, “You will hide them in paradise.” He did not say, “You will hide them in Abraham’s bosom.” For many places of the future dwelling of the saints are set forth in the Holy Scriptures for the faithful. Let everything that is other than God become worthless.

The one who protects us in the place of this present life—may he himself, after this life, be our place. For this Psalm also said to him earlier: “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge.” Therefore we shall be hidden in the face of God.

What bosom there is in the face of God—you expect me to tell you? Purify your heart, so that he himself may illuminate it, and so that the one whom you call upon may enter. Be his house, and he will be your house. Let him dwell in you, and you will dwell in him. If you receive him in your heart in this age, he will receive you with his face after this age.

“You will hide them,” he says. Where? “In the secrecy of your face.” “From the disturbance of human beings.” For there they are not disturbed when they are hidden; in the secrecy of your face they are not disturbed.

Do you think anyone can be so happy in this world that, when he begins to hear human reproaches because he serves Christ, he flees to God in his heart, begins to hope in his sweetness, and from the disturbance of the people from whom he hears reproaches enters into the face of God with his conscience?

He enters, certainly—but only if he has something with which to enter; that is, if his conscience is not burdensome and does not make a great load for him at the narrow gate.

Therefore, “you will hide them in the secrecy of your face from the disturbance of human beings.” “You will protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.” At some time you will hide them in the secrecy of your face from the disturbance of human beings, so that human disturbance may no longer be able to exist in them at all. But meanwhile, while they are pilgrims in this age, because those who serve you suffer many contradicting tongues, what do you do for them? “You will protect them in your tabernacle.”

What is the tabernacle? The Church of this present time. It is called a tabernacle because it is still a pilgrim on this earth. For a tabernacle is the dwelling of soldiers stationed on campaign; such dwellings are called tabernacles. A house is not a tabernacle.

Fight as a pilgrim on campaign, so that, saved in the tabernacle, you may be received gloriously into the house. For your eternal house will be in heaven, if you live well in this tabernacle now.

Therefore, “in this tabernacle you will protect them from the contradiction of tongues.” Many tongues contradict; different heresies and different schisms resound. Many tongues contradict true doctrine. Run to God’s tabernacle; hold fast to the Catholic Church; do not depart from the rule of truth; and you will be protected in the tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.

9. [Verse 22.] “Blessed is the Lord, for he has made his mercy wondrous in the city of surrounding.” What is the city of surrounding?

In one Judaea the people of God had been placed, as though in the middle of the world, where praises were offered to God and sacrifices were made to him, where prophecy did not cease to sing of future things that we now see being fulfilled. This people was, as it were, in the midst of the nations.

This prophet paid attention and saw the future Church of God among all the nations. And because all the nations were situated all around, surrounding on every side the one nation of the Jews placed in the middle, he called these nations surrounding on every side “the city of surrounding.”

Indeed, Lord, you made your mercy wondrous in the city of Jerusalem. There Christ suffered; there he rose again; there he ascended into heaven; there he performed many wonders. But your praise is greater because you made your mercy wondrous in the city of surrounding—that is, you spread your mercy among all the nations.

Nor did you keep your ointment in that Jerusalem as though in a vessel; but as though the vessel had been broken, the ointment was spread throughout the world, so that what is said in the Holy Scriptures might be fulfilled: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1:2).

And so you made your mercy wondrous in the city of surrounding. For he ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of the Father, and after ten days sent the Holy Spirit (Acts 1). The disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit; they began to preach the mighty deeds of Christ; they were stoned, killed, and driven away (ibid. 8).

And when they were driven from that place, as though from a single location, like burning logs set aflame by divine fire, they filled the whole forest of the world with the burning heat of the Spirit and the light of truth. Thus the Lord made his mercy wondrous in the city of surrounding.

10. [Verse 23.] “I said in my ecstasy”—remember the title of the Psalm; behold, there is that ecstasy. See what he says: “I said,” he says, “in my ecstasy: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”

“In my fear I said”—that is, I said in my ecstasy. He saw himself inwardly afraid amid some great tribulation, such as are certainly not lacking. He noticed that his heart was fearful and trembling, and he said: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” If I were in your sight, I would not fear in this way; if you were looking upon me, I would not tremble in this way.

But because he says in another Psalm, “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, was helping me” (Ps. 93:18), immediately here too he says: “Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer.”

Because I confessed; because I said, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes”; because I did not become proud, but accused my heart and, staggering in my tribulation, cried out to you—you heard my prayer.

Thus what I commended from that Psalm has been fulfilled. What is there, “I said in my ecstasy, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes,’” is the same as in that Psalm: “If I said, ‘My foot has slipped.’” And what is there, “Your mercy, Lord, was helping me,” is the same as here: “Therefore, Lord, you heard the voice of my prayer.”

Consider this in Peter. He sees the Lord walking on the waters and thinks it is a phantom.
