The Lord cries out: “It is I; do not be afraid.” Peter grows confident and says: “If it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” This is how I shall prove whether it is you: whether, at your word, I can do what you can do.

He says, “Come.” And at the word of the one commanding, the power to obey was created. “Come,” he says. And Peter went down; he began to walk. He walked without fear, as though trusting in him. But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid.

“I said in my ecstasy: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” And when he began to sink, he cried out: “Lord, I am perishing.” And Jesus stretched out his hand to him, lifted him up, and said: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:26–32).

Therefore I said in my fear: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” And as one who was already beginning to perish in the sea, you heard, Lord, the voice of my prayer. You heard when I cried out to you.

A cry to God is not made with the voice but with the heart. Many who were silent with their lips cried out in their hearts; many who made a noise with their mouths, while their hearts were turned away, were unable to obtain anything.

If, then, you cry out, cry out inwardly, where God hears. “When I cried out to you,” he says, “you heard the voice of my prayer.”

11. [Verse 24.] Having experienced this, then, what does he exhort us to do? “Love the Lord, all his saints.” As though he were saying: “Believe me; I have experienced it. I had tribulations; I called upon him and was not deceived. I hoped in God and was not put to shame. He enlightened my thoughts and strengthened my trembling.”

“Love the Lord, all his saints.” That is: you—who do not love the world—love the Lord, all his saints. For to whom should I say, “Love the Lord,” if he still loves the amphitheater? To whom should I say, “Love the Lord,” if he still loves the mime, if he still loves the pantomime, if he still loves drunkenness, if he still loves the spectacles of the world, all its vanities, and its lying madness? [Note: A pantomime was a dancer who expressed any character and emotion through gesture. See Book 2 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 25.]

To whom should I say: “Learn not to love, so that you may learn to love; turn away, so that you may be converted; empty yourself, so that you may be filled”? “Love the Lord, all his saints.”

12. “For the Lord will seek truth.” You know that many evildoers are now to be seen; you know that now they exalt themselves in their vanities. “The Lord will seek truth. And he will repay those who act with abundant pride.”

Endure until you bring them to an end; tolerate until you are free of them. For it is necessary that the Lord, seeking truth, repay those who act with abundant pride.

You are about to say: “When will he repay?” When he wishes. Be certain that he will repay; do not doubt the repayment, but do not presume to advise God about the time. Certainly he will seek truth and repay those who act with abundant pride.

He repays some even here, and we have seen and learned that he does repay. For when those who fear God are humbled—if they had perhaps shone in some dignity of this age—they do not fall when humbled, because they have not excluded God from their hearts. Their height is God.

Job appeared to have been humbled when his property was lost, his children were lost, the things he kept were lost, and those for whom he kept them were lost. He remained without an inheritance and, what is more grievous, without an heir (Job 1). He remained with only his wife—not his comforter, but rather the devil’s helper (ibid. 2:9). He appeared humbled. See whether he became wretched; see whether he was not in the secrecy of God’s face.

“Naked,” he said, “I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid. 1:21).

From where did these jewels of praise of God come? Look at a poor man outwardly and a rich man inwardly. Would these jewels of praise of God have come forth from his mouth unless he had a treasure in his heart?

You who wish to be rich, desire such riches as you cannot lose even in a shipwreck. Therefore, when such people are humbled, do not think them wretched. You are mistaken; you do not know what they possess inwardly. Their ruler is within; their shepherd and comforter is within.

Those are the ones who fall badly who place their hope in this age. What shone outwardly is taken away, and nothing remains within except the smoke of an evil conscience. They have no source of consolation; they have no way to go outward; they have no way to return inward. Abandoned by worldly pomp and empty of spiritual grace, they are truly humbled.

God does these things to many in this present time, but not to everyone. If he did it to no one, divine providence would seem not to be watchful; if he did it to everyone, divine patience would not be preserved.

You, however, Christian, have learned to endure, not to repay with vengeance. Do you wish to be avenged, Christian? Christ has not yet been avenged. Or have you suffered an evil person while he has not suffered? Did the one who had no reason to suffer not suffer first for you?

For in you tribulation is the refiner’s furnace—provided that you are gold and not straw—so that you may be free from filth and not be turned into ashes.

13. [Verse 25.] “Love the Lord, all his saints, for the Lord will seek truth and repay those who act with abundant pride.” But when will he repay? If only he would repay now! I wanted to see them humbled and prostrate now.

Hear what follows: “Act manfully.” Do not let your hands grow weak amid tribulations; do not let your knees waver. “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened.” Let your heart be strengthened to endure and tolerate all the evils of this age.

But to whom does the Prophet say these things: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened”? To those who love the world? No. But to those to whom he says—listen: “All you who hope in the Lord.”

# ON PSALM XXXI

## EXPOSITION I  
### To David Himself, for Understanding

1. [Verse 1.] “To David himself, for understanding”: an understanding by which one understands that a human being is liberated not by the merits of works, but by the grace of God, when he confesses his sins.

2. [Verse 2.] “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered, and whose sins have been consigned to oblivion. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin and in whose mouth there is no deceit”: who does not have in his mouth a display of righteousness while his conscience is full of sins.

3. [Verse 3.] “Because I was silent, my bones grew old”: because I did not bring forth with my mouth a confession unto salvation (Rom. 10:10), all my strength grew old in weakness. “From my crying out all day”: while I was impious and blasphemous, crying out against God, as though defending and excusing my sins.

4. [Verse 4.] “Because day and night your hand was heavy upon me”: because of the continual affliction of your scourges. “I was turned into my misery” [Note: Most manuscripts, omitting “my,” consistently have “into misery,” according to the Septuagint], “while the thorn was being fastened.” I became wretched by recognizing my misery, pierced by an evil conscience.

5. [Verse 5.] [Note: Diapsalma, a musical or liturgical division.] “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not cover my iniquity”—that is, I did not conceal my iniquity. “I said: ‘I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord.’” I said, “I will declare it”—not against God, as in the outcry of impiety when I was silent, but “my iniquity against myself to the Lord.”

“And you forgave the impiety of my heart”: hearing the voice of confession in the heart before it was brought forth in speech.

6. [Verse 6.] “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time”: for this impiety of the heart every holy person will pray to you. For they will not be holy by their own merits, but at the opportune time—that is, at the coming of the one who redeemed us from sins.

“Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not approach him.” Nevertheless, no one should imagine that, when the end suddenly arrives—as in the days of Noah—a place for confession remains by which one may approach God.

7. [Verse 7.] “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me”: you are my refuge from the distress of sins that surrounded my heart. “My joy, redeem me from those surrounding me”: in you I have joy; redeem me from the sorrow that my sins cause me.

8. [Verse 8.] [Note: Diapsalma.] God’s response: “I will give you understanding and establish you in this way in which you will walk” [Note: The manuscripts, here and in the following exposition, have “in which you will enter”]. I will give you understanding after confession, so that you do not depart from the way in which you will enter; do not wish to be your own master.

“I will fix my eyes upon you”: in this way I will make my love firm over you. [Note: The phrase begins on the following column.]

9. [Verse 9.] “Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding.” Therefore they wish to govern themselves. And the Prophet’s voice says: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle.” Therefore let God do to them what is done to a horse and a mule, so that by punishments you compel them to submit to your governance, since they do not draw near to you.

10. [Verse 10.] “Many are the scourges of the sinner”: the one who does not confess his sins to God and wishes to be his own ruler is scourged greatly. “But mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord”: the person who hopes in the Lord and submits himself to be governed by him will be surrounded by mercy.

11. [Verse 11.] “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous”: rejoice and exult, you righteous, not in yourselves but in the Lord. “And glory, all you upright in heart”: glory in him, all of you who have understood that it is right to be subject to him, so that you may be preferred to the others.

# EXPOSITION II  
## SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. The Psalm of God’s grace and of our justification—not by any preceding merits of ours, but by the mercy of our Lord God going before us—commended especially by the apostolic voice, as the reading preceding this Psalm made clear to everyone, has been undertaken by our weakness for discussion with Your Charity.

Therefore, I first commend my weakness to your prayers, as the Apostle says, “that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth” (Eph. 6:19), so that I may speak to you in such a way that what is dangerous for me to say may be beneficial for you to hear.

For the human mind is uncertain and wavering between confessing its weakness and the boldness of presumption. It is often struck from both sides and driven in such a way that falling in either direction becomes a precipice.

If, on the one hand, it gives itself over entirely to its own weakness and inclines to the thought of saying that God’s mercy is prepared for all sinners—even those who persist in any sins—provided only that they believe that God liberates and forgives; if it thinks that, at the end, no believing wicked person is destined to perish—that is, that none of those who say to themselves, “I will do whatever I wish; I will defile myself with whatever crimes and disgraceful acts I wish; however greatly I sin, God’s mercy liberates me because I have believed in him,” is destined to perish—then the person who says that no such people perish is inclined by an evil thought toward impunity for sins.

And that just God, to whom “mercy and judgment” are sung (Ps. 100:1)—not mercy alone, but judgment also—finds a person presuming wrongly about himself and abusing God’s mercy for his own destruction; and it is necessary that he condemn him.

Such a thought therefore casts a person down. Terrified by it, if he raises himself into a kind of bold presumption, presumes upon his own strength and righteousness, and resolves in his mind to fulfill righteousness and to do everything commanded in the Law in such a way that he offend in nothing; if he considers his life to be entirely within his own power, so that he nowhere slips, nowhere fails, nowhere stumbles, nowhere is darkened, and attributes this to himself and to the mastery of his will—even if he should happen to fulfill everything that appears just in the eyes of human beings, so that nothing can be found in his life that people could criticize—God condemns that very presumption and boastful pride.

What, then, happens if a person has justified himself and presumed upon his righteousness? He falls. If, considering and thinking about his weakness and presuming upon God’s mercy, he neglects to cleanse his life from his sins and plunges himself into every flood of disgraceful acts, he too falls.

Presumption concerning righteousness is, as it were, the right hand; the thought that sins will go unpunished is, as it were, the left. Let us hear the voice of God saying to us: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Prov. 4:27). Do not presume upon your own righteousness for attaining the kingdom; do not presume upon God’s mercy for sinning.

The divine command recalls you from both: from that height and from this depth. If you climb there, you will be hurled down; if you fall here, you will be submerged. “Do not,” he says, “turn aside to the right or to the left.”

Again I say what I want all of you to fix briefly in your minds: do not presume upon your own righteousness for attaining the kingdom; do not presume upon God’s mercy for sinning.

You will answer: “What, then, shall I do?” This Psalm teaches us. Once it has been read through and expounded, I think that, with the help of the Lord’s mercy, we shall see the way—either where we are already walking or the way we ought to hold to.

Let each person listen according to his capacity. As each person is conscious of his own state, so let him either grieve because he must be corrected or rejoice because he is approved. If he finds that he has gone astray, let him return so that he may walk on the way. If he finds himself on the way, let him walk so that he may arrive. Let no one be proud outside the way; let no one be sluggish on the way.

## 2.

The Apostle Paul testified that this psalm belongs to that grace by which we are Christians; therefore we wanted to read the passage itself to you. The Apostle said this when he was commending the righteousness that comes from faith against those who boast of the righteousness that comes from works:

“What, then, shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh discovered? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of—but not before God” (Romans 4:1–2).

May God himself turn such boasting away from us, and may we rather hear: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Many boast of their works, and you find many pagans unwilling to become Christians for precisely this reason: they consider their good life sufficient for themselves. “It is necessary to live well,” they say. “What will Christ command me? That I live well? I already live well. Why do I need Christ? I commit no homicide, no theft, no robbery; I do not covet another person’s property; I am stained by no adultery. Let something be found in my life that deserves blame, and let the one who finds fault with me become a Christian.” He has something to boast of—but not before God.

Our father Abraham, however, was not like that. The purpose of this statement of Scripture is to direct our attention to this point. For we confess—and this is also our faith concerning the holy Patriarch, who pleased God—that Abraham has glory before God. Thus the Apostle says: “Certainly it is known and evident to us that Abraham has glory before God; but if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God.” Yet he does have glory before God; therefore he was not justified by works.

If, then, Abraham was not justified by works, by what was he justified? The Apostle continues and tells us: “For what does Scripture say?”—that is, “From where does Scripture say that Abraham was justified?” “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3; Genesis 15:6). Abraham, therefore, was justified by faith.

## 3.

Now let the one who hears that Abraham was justified not by works but by faith beware of that chasm about which I spoke. You see, then, that Abraham was justified by faith, not by works; shall I therefore do whatever I want, because even if I have no good works and merely believe in God, it is reckoned to me as righteousness?

If he says and decides this, he has fallen and been swallowed up. If he is still thinking and wavering, he is in danger. But the Scripture of God, together with its true meaning, not only rescues the one in danger from danger; it also raises the one who has been swallowed up from the depths.

I therefore answer as though speaking against the Apostle, and I say concerning Abraham himself what we also find in the letter of another apostle, who wanted to correct people who had misunderstood this apostle. For James, in his Letter, commended the works of Abraham against those who, presuming on faith alone, were unwilling to do good works, while Paul commended Abraham’s faith. The Apostles are not opposed to one another.

James mentions a work known to everyone: “Abraham offered his son to God to be sacrificed” (James 2:21). A great work—but one arising from faith. I praise the superstructure of the work, but I see the foundation of faith. I praise the fruit of the good work, but in faith I recognize the root.

If Abraham had done this apart from right faith, whatever that work might have been, it would have benefited him nothing. Again, if Abraham had held faith in such a way that, when God commanded him to offer his son for sacrifice, he had said to himself, “I will not do it, and yet I believe that God will rescue me even though I despise his commands,” his faith would have been dead without works, remaining barren and dry like a root without fruit.

## 4.

What, then? Must we place no works before faith—that is, must anyone be said to have done good before faith? Those very works that are called works performed before faith, although they may appear praiseworthy to human beings, are empty. They seem to me like great strength and extremely swift running off the road.

Let no one therefore count his good works as preceding faith. Where faith was absent, there was no good work. For intention makes a work good, and faith directs the intention. Do not pay too much attention to what a person does; observe instead what he is looking toward while doing it, and toward what goal he directs the strength of his excellent steering.

Imagine a man steering a ship extremely well but having lost sight of where he is going. What does it benefit him that he handles the helm expertly, moves it skillfully, presents the bow to the waves, and takes care not to strike the sides? [Note: [Col. 0259] Most manuscripts read “the side” (lateri).] He is so strong that he can turn the ship wherever he wishes and from wherever he wishes. Someone asks him, “Where are you going?” and he replies, “I do not know.” Or he does not say, “I do not know,” but says, “I am going to that harbor,” while rushing not into the harbor but onto the rocks.

Is he not steering the ship toward shipwreck all the more dangerously the more agile and effective he appears to himself in handling it? Such is also the person who runs excellently but off the road.

Would it not therefore have been better and more tolerable for that helmsman to be somewhat weaker, so that he handled the rudder with effort and some difficulty but nevertheless kept to the proper and prescribed course? And would it not likewise have been better for another person, even slower and weaker, to walk on the road rather than run powerfully off it?

The best person, then, is the one who both keeps to the road and walks well upon it. The next best is the one who, although he limps somewhat, does not altogether go astray or remain behind, but advances, even if slowly. [Note: [Col. 0260] Thus several manuscripts. Others read, “does not altogether stick fast.” The editions read, “does not altogether go astray or remain behind.”] For perhaps he may be expected to reach his destination, though later.

## 5.

Therefore, brothers, Abraham was justified by faith. Yet although works did not precede his faith, they followed it. Surely your faith will not be barren? If you are not barren, faith itself is not barren. You have believed something evil, and by the fire of your wickedness you have burned up the root of your faith. Hold fast to faith, then, so that you may act.

But you say, “The Apostle Paul does not say this.” On the contrary, the Apostle Paul does say it: “Faith,” he says, “which works through love” (Galatians 5:6). And elsewhere: “Therefore the fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13:10). And elsewhere: “For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying, namely, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Galatians 5:14).

See whether he does not want you to act when he says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not covet”—and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love of one’s neighbor does no evil; “the fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13:9–10).

Does love permit you to do any evil to the one you love? But perhaps you merely do no evil and do not also do some good. Does love, then, permit you not to provide whatever you can to the one you love? [Note: [Col. 0260] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, “Therefore does not even love permit...?”] Is that not love which even prays for enemies? Does the person who wishes good to an enemy therefore abandon a friend?

Thus, if faith is without love, it will be without works. But so that you may not think too much about the work of faith, add hope and love to it, and do not worry about what you are doing. Love itself cannot be idle. For what is at work, even when someone acts badly toward another person, except love? Give me love that is idle and does nothing. Do not love produce crimes, adulteries, misdeeds, homicides, and every kind of lust?

Cleanse your love, then. Turn the water flowing into a sewer toward a garden. Let the impulses it had toward the world be directed toward the Maker of the world.

Are you being told, “Love nothing”? Far from it. You will be sluggish, dead, detestable, and wretched if you love nothing. Love—but see what you should love. Love of God and love of neighbor are called charity; love of the world and love of this age are called desire. Let desire be restrained; let charity be stirred up.

For charity itself, in one who does good, gives that person the hope of a good conscience. A good conscience carries hope. Just as a bad conscience is wholly in despair, so a good conscience is wholly in hope. And these three will be present, of which the Apostle says: “Faith, hope, and charity” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Elsewhere he names the same three, but in place of hope he puts a good conscience: “The goal of the commandment,” he says, “is” [Note: Perhaps, “of the commandment” should be read.]—what is the goal of the commandment? That by which the commandments are perfected, not that by which they are consumed.

For we say one thing when we say, “The food is finished,” and another when we say, “The tunic being woven is finished.” Food is finished so that it no longer exists; a tunic is finished so that it may be complete. The same word, “finished,” is used in both cases.

He therefore did not mean here the goal of the commandment by which the commandments somehow perish, but the goal by which they are perfected and completed—not consumed. “The goal,” he says, “of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). In place of hope he put a good conscience. For the one who has a good conscience is the one who hopes.

But the person whom a bad conscience pricks withdraws from hope and expects nothing for himself except condemnation. Therefore, if he hopes for the kingdom, let him have a good conscience; and to have a good conscience, let him believe and act. What he believes belongs to faith; what he does belongs to charity.

In one passage, then, the Apostle began with faith: “Faith, hope, charity.” In another he began with charity itself: “Charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.” We have now begun from the middle—from conscience itself and hope. Whoever wants, I say, to have good hope should have a good conscience; and to have a good conscience, let him believe and act. From the middle we proceed to the beginning and the end: let him believe and act. What he believes belongs to faith; what he does belongs to charity.

## 6.

How, then, does the Apostle say that a person is justified by faith without works (Romans 3:28), when elsewhere he says, “Faith which works through love” (Galatians 5:6)?

Let us therefore oppose not the apostle James to Paul, but Paul himself to Paul, and say to him: “By one statement you somehow permit us to sin with impunity, when you say, ‘We consider a person justified by faith without works’; yet by the other you say, ‘Faith which works through love.’ How do I become secure by the first statement if I have not acted, while by the second I seem to have neither good hope nor even genuine faith unless I have acted through love?”

I hear you yourself, Apostle. Here you certainly want to commend faith to me without works. But the work of faith is love; and love cannot be idle, unless it both does no evil and does whatever good it can.

What does love do? “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:37). You commend this faith without works, then, and elsewhere you say: “Even if I have faith so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, it benefits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

If faith without charity benefits nothing, and wherever charity is present it must necessarily act, then faith itself works through love.

How, then, is a person justified by faith without works? The Apostle himself replies: “I said this to you so that you would not appear to presume on your works and think that you received the grace of faith as a reward for your works. Do not therefore presume on works before faith. Know that faith found you a sinner; and although the faith given to you made you righteous, it found an ungodly person whom it would make righteous. ‘To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly,’ he says, ‘his faith is reckoned as righteousness’” (Romans 4:5).

If the ungodly person is justified, he becomes righteous from being ungodly. If an ungodly person becomes righteous, what are the works of the ungodly?

Let the ungodly person also boast of his works and say: “I give to the poor; I take nothing from anyone; I do not covet another man’s wife; I kill no one; I defraud no one; I return a deposit entrusted to me even without a witness.” Let him say all these things. I ask whether he is devout or ungodly.

“How am I ungodly,” he says, “when I do these things?” [Note: [Col. 0262] The editions read, “Behold how you are ungodly.” “Behold” is absent from the manuscripts; two of them instead read: “How are you devout, when concerning all these...?”] Just as those of whom it is said: “They served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Romans 1:25).

“How are you ungodly?” What if, concerning all these good works, you either hope for what should be hoped for, but not from the one from whom it should be hoped, or hope for what should not be hoped for, even from the one from whom eternal life should be hoped?

If, because of your good works, you have hoped for some earthly prosperity, you are ungodly. This is not the reward of faith. Faith is a precious thing, but you have sold it cheaply. [Note: Most manuscripts read “you have led it astray” instead of “you have sold it cheaply.”]

You are therefore ungodly, and these works of yours are nothing. You may exercise your strength in good works and appear to steer a ship excellently, but you are rushing onto the rocks.

What if you hope for what should be hoped for—that is, eternal life—but not from the Lord God through Jesus Christ, through whom alone eternal life is given? What if you think you can reach eternal life through the army of heaven, through the sun and moon, through the powers of the air, sea, and earth, and through the stars? You are ungodly.

Believe in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that your good works too may be good works. For I would not even call them good so long as they do not proceed from a good root.

What does this mean? Either you hope for temporal life from the eternal God, or you hope for eternal life from demons. In either case you are ungodly.

Correct your faith; direct your faith [Note: [Col. 0262] “Direct your faith” is absent from the manuscripts.]; direct your road. If you have good feet, walk now without fear; run—you are keeping to the road. The better you run, the more easily you will arrive.

But perhaps you limp somewhat. At least do not leave the road. Even if slowly, you will arrive. Do not remain behind; do not turn back; do not go astray.

## 7.

What, then? Who are blessed? Are they those in whom God has found no sin? No, for he has found sin in everyone. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

If sins are found in everyone, it remains that only those whose sins have been forgiven are blessed. The Apostle therefore commended this as follows: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

“But to the one who works”—that is, to the one who presumes on works and says that the grace of faith was given to him because of their merit—“the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt” (Romans 4:3–4).

What does this mean except that our reward is called grace? [Note: [Col. 0262] The Vatican, Regius, and Colbert manuscripts read, “What does this mean? Our reward...,” omitting “except that.”] If it is grace, it is given freely. What does “given freely” mean? It is granted without payment.

You have done nothing good, and the forgiveness of sins is given to you. Your works are examined, and they are all found to be evil. If God were to repay what is owed for those works, he would certainly condemn you: “The wages of sin are death” (Romans 6:23).

What is owed to evil works except condemnation? And what is owed to good works? The kingdom of heaven. But you were found among evil works. If what is owed to you were repaid, you would be punished.

What, then, happens? God does not repay the punishment you deserve; instead, he gives an undeserved grace. He owed vengeance; he gives pardon.

You therefore begin to be in faith through pardon. Faith, once joined with hope and love, begins to work well. But even then do not boast or exalt yourself. Remember from whom you were placed on the road. Remember that, although you had sound and swift feet, you were wandering. Remember that, even if you were weak and lying half-dead on the road, you were lifted onto a beast and brought to an inn (Luke 10:30).

“But to the one who works,” he says, “the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt.” If you want to be a stranger to grace, boast of your merits. But he sees what is in you and knows what he owes to whom. [Note: Perhaps, “and to whom,” or “to each one.”]

What about the one who does not work? Imagine an ungodly sinner who does not work. What then? Yet he believes in the one who justifies the ungodly. [Note: [Col. 0263] Perhaps “nevertheless” (tamen) should be read instead of “yet” (autem).] Because he does not work well, he is ungodly; and even if he appears to do good, nevertheless, because he does so without faith, those deeds should not be called good.

“But to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness,” just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God reckons righteousness without works (Romans 4:5–6).

But what righteousness? The righteousness of faith, which good works did not precede, but which good works follow.

## 8.

Pay attention, then. Otherwise, by understanding wrongly, you throw yourselves into that chasm of sinning with impunity. And I am free, just as the Apostle himself was free from all who misunderstood him.

They willingly misunderstood him so that good works would not follow. Do not belong to such people, brothers.

A certain psalm speaks of a certain person of this kind—that is, of this sort of people, as though of one person: “He refused to understand, that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4). It does not say, “He was unable to understand.”

You, therefore, must be willing to understand so that you may do good. For clear understanding will not be lacking to you. What is clear understanding? Let no one boast of his good works before faith; let no one be sluggish in good works after receiving faith.

God therefore grants pardon to all the ungodly and justifies them by faith.

## 9. [Verses 1–2]

[Note: [Col. 0263] In the manuscripts, this second exposition of Psalm 31 immediately follows the preceding preface. In the earlier editions of Erasmus and Louvain, however, Exposition 1—found above, col. 256—had been inserted here.]

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit.”

The psalm now begins, and understanding begins with it. Understanding, or intelligence, is this: you must know that you should neither boast of your merits nor presume upon the impunity of sin.

The title of the psalm is: “For David; understanding.” This psalm is called a psalm of understanding. [Note: All printed editions have the words “For David; understanding” and continue, “It is called understanding,” and so forth. But the manuscripts omit those words and read, “It is called understanding.”]

The first understanding, then, is that you should know yourself to be a sinner. The next understanding is that, once you have begun to do good through faith and love, you should attribute this not to your own strength but to the grace of God.

Then there will be no deceit in your heart—that is, in your inner mouth. You will not have one thing on your lips and another in your thoughts. You will not be one of those Pharisees of whom it was said: “You are like whitewashed tombs; outwardly you appear righteous to human beings, but inwardly you are full of deceit and iniquity” (Matthew 23:27).

When an unrighteous person presents himself as righteous, is he not deceitful?

He is not like Nathanael, of whom the Lord says: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” And how was there no deceit in that Nathanael? “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:47–48).

He was under the fig tree; he was under the condition of the flesh. If he was under the condition of the flesh, because he was held by the ungodliness of his inherited origin, he was under that fig tree over which one laments in another psalm: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquity” (Psalm 50:7).

But the one who came with grace saw him. What does “he saw him” mean? He had mercy on him. Thus he commends the person without deceit in such a way that he commends his own grace in him: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

“I saw you”—what great thing is that, unless you understand that it was spoken in some particular way? What great thing is it to see a man under a fig tree? If Christ had not seen the human race under this fig tree, either we would have withered away altogether, or, like the Pharisees in whom there was deceit—that is, who justified themselves in words but were evil in their deeds—only leaves would have been found in us, not fruit.

For when Christ saw such a fig tree, he cursed it, and it withered. “I see,” he said, “only leaves”—that is, only words, without fruit. “Let it wither,” he said, “so that it may not even have leaves” (Matthew 21:19).

Why does he also take away the words? A dry tree cannot have leaves either. Thus the Jews were: the Pharisees were that tree. They had words but did not have deeds. By the Lord’s judgment they deserved withering.

Let Christ therefore see us under the fig tree. Let him see in our flesh also the fruit of good works, so that we may not wither under his curse.

And because everything is attributed to his grace, not to our merits: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.” It does not say, “Blessed are those in whom sins have not been found,” but “whose sins have been covered.”

Their sins have been covered, concealed, abolished. If God covered sins, he did not wish to turn his attention to them; if he did not wish to turn his attention to them, he did not wish to take punitive notice of them; if he did not wish to take punitive notice of them, he did not wish to punish them; if he did not wish to punish them, he did not wish to acknowledge them; he preferred to forgive them.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.”

Do not understand the statement “their sins have been covered” as though the sins were still there and alive. Why, then, did he say that the sins were covered? So that they would not be seen.

For what did it mean for God to see sins except to punish sins? To know that for God “to see sins” means “to punish sins,” listen to what is said to him: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm 50:11).

Let him therefore not see your sins, so that he may see you. How may he see you? As he saw Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” The shade of the fig tree did not obstruct the eyes of God’s mercy.

## 10.

“And in whose mouth there is no deceit.”

But those who do not want to confess their sins labor without cause in defending their sins. And the more they labor to defend their sins, boasting of their merits and not seeing their iniquities, the more their strength and power fail.

For the strong person is the one who is strong not in himself but in God. Hence the statement: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord that he might take it away from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you.’” He said, “My grace,” not “your strength.” “My grace is sufficient for you,” he said, “for strength is perfected in weakness.” Thus he says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).

The one who wants to be strong, therefore, presuming upon himself and boasting of his merits, whatever they may be, will be like that Pharisee who proudly boasted of what he said he had received from God: “I give you thanks.”

Pay attention, my brothers, to the kind of pride that God condemns: truly, the kind that can enter a righteous person, the kind that can creep even into a person of good hope.

“I give you thanks,” he said. When he said, “I give you thanks,” he confessed that he had received from God what he possessed. “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Thus he said, “I give you thanks; I give you thanks because I am not like the rest of humanity: robbers, unrighteous, adulterers—nor like this tax collector.”

Why, then, was he proud? Not because he gave thanks to God for his good qualities, but because he exalted himself above another on account of those very good qualities.

## 11.

Pay attention, brothers. The Evangelist first indicated the occasion on which the Lord began to give this comparison.

After Christ had said, “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on earth?”—and lest certain heretics should arise who, observing and imagining that the whole world had fallen, since all heretics are found among the few and in a part, would boast that what had perished from the whole world remained in them—the Evangelist immediately added, where the Lord had said, “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith on earth?”:

“He also spoke this parable to some who considered themselves righteous and despised others: ‘A certain Pharisee and a tax collector went up into the temple to pray,’” and the rest, which you know.

That Pharisee therefore said, “I give you thanks.” But why was he proud? Because he despised others.

How do you prove it? In his very words.

How? “That Pharisee,” he says, despised the tax collector who stood at a distance, while God drew near to the one who confessed his sins. [Note: [Col. 0265] Several manuscripts read: “How did that man also despise the tax collector?”]

“The tax collector stood at a distance.” But was God also standing at a distance from him? Why was God not far from him? Because elsewhere it is said: “The Lord is near to those who have crushed their heart” (Psalm 33:19).

See whether this tax collector had crushed his heart, and there you will see that the Lord is near to those who have crushed their heart.

The tax collector stood at a distance and did not even want to lift his eyes toward heaven, but he was striking his breast. The striking of the breast is the crushing of the heart.

What did he say as he struck his breast? “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

And what was the Lord’s judgment? [Note: The printed editions read, “And what was the Lord’s judgment?” The manuscripts read, “And what did the Lord judge?”]

“Amen, I tell you, that tax collector went down from the temple justified more than that Pharisee.”

Why? This is God’s judgment.

“I am not like this tax collector; I am not like the rest of humanity—unrighteous, robbers, adulterers. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

He does not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven; he considers his conscience, stands far off, and is justified more than that Pharisee.

Why? I ask you, Lord: explain this righteousness of yours to us; explain to us the equity of your law.

God explains the rule of his law. [Note: Most manuscripts read, “He explains from the rule of his law.”]

Do you want to hear why? “Because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:8–14).

## 12.

Let Your Charity pay attention. We said that the tax collector did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven. Why did he not look toward heaven? Because he was looking at himself.

He looked at himself so that he might first displease himself and thus please God. But you boast; you stand with your neck held high.

The Lord says to the proud person: “You do not want to look at yourself? I am looking. But do you want me not to look? You look.”

That is why the tax collector did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven: he was looking at himself and punishing his conscience. He was his own judge, so that God might intercede; he punished himself, so that God might free him; he accused himself, so that God might defend him.

Indeed, God defended him so thoroughly that he pronounced judgment in his favor. That tax collector went down justified more than that Pharisee, because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

“He looked at himself,” he says, “and I did not want to look. I heard the one saying, ‘Turn your eyes away from my sins.’” For who said that except the one who also said, “Because I acknowledge my iniquity” (Psalm 50:5, 11)?

Therefore, my brothers, that Pharisee too was a sinner. He was not free from sin merely because he said, “I am not like the rest of humanity: unrighteous, robbers, adulterers”; nor because he fasted twice a week; nor because he gave tithes.

And if he had been without any sins at all, pride itself would have been a great crime. Yet behold, he was saying all those things.

Who, after all, is without sin? “Who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins?” (Proverbs 20:9).

He therefore had sins. But he was perverse and unaware of why he had come. He was like a patient at a doctor’s clinic who needed healing but displayed his healthy limbs and concealed his wounds.

Let God cover the wounds; do not cover them yourself. For if you, out of shame, want to conceal them, the physician will not heal you. Let the physician cover and heal them; he covers them with a dressing.

Under the physician’s covering the wound is healed; under the wounded person’s covering the wound is concealed. From whom are you concealing it? From the one who knows everything.

## 13. [Verses 3–6]

Therefore, brothers, see what he says here: “Because I was silent, my bones grew old from my crying out all day.”

What does this mean? It seems contradictory: “Because I was silent, my bones grew old from crying out.” If he was crying out, how was he silent?

He was silent about one thing and not silent about another. He was silent about what would make him prosper; he was not silent about what would make him fail. He was silent about confession and cried out in presumption.

“I was silent,” he said; “I did not confess.” That was where he ought to have spoken. He should have been silent about his merits and cried out about his sins. But instead he perversely kept silent about his sins and cried out about his merits.

And what happened to him? “His bones grew old.”

Pay attention: if he had cried out about his sins and kept silent about his merits, his bones—that is, his virtues—would have been renewed. He would have been strong in the Lord, because he would have been found weak in himself. [Note: [Col. 0266] Nearly all the manuscripts read, “that is, his strength would have been robust in the Lord.”] But now, because he wanted to be strong in himself, he became weak, and his bones grew old.

He remained in oldness because he did not want, through confession, to love newness. You know, brothers, who become new: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.”

This man did not want his iniquities forgiven. He magnified them, defended them, and boasted of his merits. Therefore, because he was silent about confession, his bones grew old.

“From my crying out all day.” What does “from my crying out all day” mean? Persevering in the defense of his sins.

Yet see what kind of person he is: he recognizes himself. Understanding will now begin. He will look at nothing except himself, and he will displease himself because he recognizes himself. Now you will hear what will heal you.

## 14.

“Blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit. Because I was silent, my bones grew old from my crying out all day. Because day and night your hand was heavy upon me.”

What does “your hand was heavy upon me” mean? It is a great matter, brothers.

Consider the right judgment [Note: [Col. 0267] Perhaps read, “pronounced.”] between the two: the Pharisee and the tax collector.

What was said about the Pharisee? That he would be humbled. What was said about the tax collector? That he would be exalted.

Why was the Pharisee humbled? Because he exalted himself. Why was the tax collector exalted? Because he humbled himself.

Therefore, in order to humble the one who exalts himself, God lays his hand heavily upon him. He did not want to be humbled by confessing his iniquity; he was humbled by the weight of God’s hand.

When could he endure the heavy hand of the one who humbled him? How light was the hand of the one who lifted him up! [Note: Perhaps: “As heavy as the hand of the one who humbles him was, so light was the hand of the one who lifts him up.”]

In each case the hand is strong: strong to press him down, strong to lift him up.

## 15.

“Therefore, because day and night your hand was heavy upon me, I turned in my misery, while the thorn was being fixed.”

Because your hand was made heavy, because I was humbled, I turned in my misery. I became wretched; a thorn was fixed in me; my conscience was pricked.

What happened when the thorn was fixed? He was given a sense of pain, and he discovered his weakness.

The one who had kept silent about confessing his sin, so that by crying out in defense of his sin his strength would grow old—that is, so that his bones would be turned into oldness—what did he do when the thorn was fixed?

“I acknowledged my sin.”

Now he recognizes it. If he recognizes it, God forgives it.

Hear what follows; see whether he himself does not say: “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not cover my iniquity.”

I was saying this earlier: do not cover it yourself, and God will cover it.

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.”

Those who cover their sins are stripped bare; this man stripped himself bare so that he might be covered.

“I did not cover my iniquity.” What does “I did not cover it” mean? Earlier I had been silent; now what? “I spoke”—something contrary to that silence.

“I spoke.” What did you say? “I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart.”

“I spoke.” What did you say? He does not yet declare it; he promises that he will declare it, and God already forgives it.

Pay attention, brothers; this is a great matter. He said, “I will declare it”; he did not say, “I declared it, and you forgave.” He said, “I will declare it, and you forgave.” By saying, “I will declare it,” he shows that he had not yet declared it with his mouth, but had declared it in his heart.

The very act of saying, “I will declare it,” is a declaration. Therefore you also forgave the ungodliness of my heart.

My confession had not yet reached my lips. I had said, “I will declare it against myself.” Nevertheless, God heard the voice of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth, but God’s ear was already in my heart.

“You forgave the ungodliness of my heart,” because I said, “I will declare it.”

16. But that had not been sufficient: he did not say, “I will declare my injustice to the Lord.” He did not say this without reason: “I will declare it against myself.” There is a difference. For many declare their iniquity, but against the Lord God himself. When they are found in sins, they say, “God willed this.” If someone says, “I did not do it,” or, “The act you accuse me of is not a sin,” he declares neither against himself nor against God. But if he says, “Certainly I did it, and it is a sin, but God willed it—what have I done?” this is to declare against God.

Perhaps you will say, “No one says this. Who is there who says, ‘God willed it’?” Many say this. But even those who do not say it—what else are they saying when they say, “Fate did this to me; my stars did this”? Thus they already wish to reach God by a circuitous route. They wish by a circuitous route to arrive at accusing God, because they do not wish to come by the direct route to appeasing God; and they say, “Fate did this to me.” What is fate? “My stars did it.” What are the stars? Surely these which we see in the sky. And who made them? God. Who ordered them? God. Therefore you see that what you wished to say was, “God made me sin.” Thus he is unjust and you are just, because if he had not made it so, you would not have sinned.

Remove these excuses for your sins. Remember that psalm: “Do not incline my heart to evil words, to make excuses for sins, with those who work iniquity.” Yet they are great men who defend their sins; great too are those who count the stars, calculate the constellations and the times, and say when someone will sin or live well, and when Mars makes a murderer and Venus an adulterer. Great, learned men, and in this world they seem distinguished. But what does the psalm say? “Do not incline my heart to evil words with those who work iniquity, and I will not associate with their chosen ones” (Ps. 140:4).

Let them call those who calculate the stars chosen and learned; let them call wise those who, as though sorting out human fates on their fingers, describe human character from the stars. God created me with free will. If I sinned, I sinned. Thus I declare my iniquity not only to the Lord, but against myself, not against him.

“I said, Lord, have mercy on me.” The sick person cries out to the physician, “I said.” Why “I said”? “I said” would have been sufficient. “I” is spoken emphatically: I, I—not fate, not fortune, not the devil; for even he did not compel me, but I consented to his persuasion. “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). Thus he establishes and sets forth the matter here also: “I said, I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.”

17. [Verse 6.] “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.” What time? “For this.” For what? For wickedness. For what? For the forgiveness of sins itself. “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.” It is because you forgave sins that every holy person will pray to you. For if you did not forgive sins, there would be no holy person to pray to you: “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.”

When is the opportune time? When the New Testament would be revealed, when the grace of Christ would be revealed—that is the opportune time. “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman”—that is, born of a female, for the ancients used these words without distinction—“born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4:4–5). From what would he redeem them? From the devil, from destruction, from their sins, from the one to whom they had sold themselves: “to redeem those who were under the Law.”

They were under the Law because the Law pressed upon them. Their condition pressed upon them, convicting them of guilt rather than saving them. It did indeed prohibit evil things; but because they did not possess within themselves the strength to justify themselves, they had to cry out to the one whom the person being led captive under the law of sin cried out to: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:23–24).

All human beings were under the Law, not in the Law: it was already weighing them down and convicting them of guilt. The Law demonstrated sin; it fixed the thorn and caused the heart to be pierced. It itself admonished each person to recognize that he was guilty and to cry out to God for forgiveness.

“For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.” Thus I was speaking of the opportune time: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son.” The Apostle says likewise: “At an acceptable and favorable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” And because this had been foretold by the Prophet concerning all Christians, the Apostle added: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.”

18. “Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not draw near to him.” “To him”—to whom? To God. He is accustomed to change the person, as in: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9). He did not say, “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and his blessing is upon his people”; nor, “Lord, salvation is yours, and your blessing is upon your people.” But when he began with “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” speaking not to him but about him, he then turned to him and said, “And your blessing is upon your people.”

So here also, when you hear first “to you” and then “to him,” do not suppose that someone else is meant: “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time. Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters they will not draw near to him.”

What does “in the flood of many waters” mean? Those who swim in the flood of many waters do not draw near to God. What is this flood of many waters? The multiplicity of various doctrines.

Pay attention, brothers. The many waters are various doctrines. God’s doctrine is one; there are not many waters, but one water—whether the water of the sacrament of baptism or of saving doctrine. Concerning that doctrine by which we are watered through the Holy Spirit, it is said: “Drink water from your own vessels, and from the springs of your own wells” (Prov. 5:15). The impious do not approach these springs, but those who believe in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5), once justified, do approach them.

Other waters—many doctrines—defile human souls, as I was saying shortly before. One doctrine says, “Fate did this to me.” Another doctrine says, “Chance did this to me; fortune did it.” If human beings are governed by chance, then nothing happens through providence—and that itself is a doctrine. Another person said, “There is a hostile race of darkness which rebelled against God; it makes human beings sin.”

In this flood of many waters they will not draw near to God.

What is that water—the true water that flows pure from the innermost spring of the stream of truth? What water is it, brothers, except that which teaches us to confess to the Lord? What water is it, except that which teaches: “It is good to confess to the Lord” (Ps. 91:2)? What water is it, except that which teaches this utterance: “I said, I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord”; and, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you”?

This is the water of confession of sins; this is the water of humility of heart; this is the water of saving life,[2] of casting oneself down, presuming nothing about oneself, and arrogantly attributing nothing to one’s own power.

This water is found in none of the books of outsiders: not among the Epicureans, not among the Stoics, not among the Manichaeans, not among the Platonists. Wherever the finest precepts of morals and discipline are found, this humility is nevertheless not found. The way of this humility flows from elsewhere; it comes from Christ.

This way belongs to him who, although high, came in humility. For what else did he teach by humbling himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8)? What else did he teach by paying what he did not owe, so that he might free us from our debt? What else did he teach by being baptized though he had committed no sin, and crucified though he had no guilt? What else did he teach except this humility?

Not without reason did he say: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6). In this humility, therefore, one draws near to God, because “the Lord is near to those who have crushed their heart” (Ps. 33:19).

But in the flood of many waters—waters lifting themselves up against God and teaching arrogant impieties—they will not draw near to God.

19. [Verse 7.] But what about you, who have also been justified and are among those waters? Everywhere, my brothers, even when we confess our sins, the waters of that flood roar around us. We are not in the flood itself, but we are surrounded by the flood. They press upon us, but they do not crush us; they urge us, but they do not drown us.

What, then, will you do, since you are in the midst of the flood, walking in this world? Does such a person not hear such teachers, not hear such arrogant people, or not suffer daily persecutions in his heart from their words?

What, then, should this person, already justified and presuming upon God, say when he is surrounded by this flood?

“You are my refuge from the distress that surrounds me.”

Let them flee either to their gods, their demons, their own strength, or the defense of their sins. For me, in this flood there is no refuge except you, from the distress that surrounds me.

20. “My joy, redeem me.” If you are already rejoicing, why do you wish to be redeemed? “My joy, redeem me.” I hear a voice of gladness: “My joy”; I hear a groan: “Redeem me.” You rejoice, and you groan.

“Yes,” he says, “I both rejoice and groan: I rejoice in hope, but I still groan in reality.” “My joy, redeem me.”

“Rejoicing in hope,” says the Apostle. Therefore “My joy, redeem me” is rightly said. From what does he redeem me? It follows: “Patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

The Apostle had already been justified. And what does he say? “Not only this,” he says, “but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body.” From what does he redeem me? Because we ourselves groan inwardly, awaiting the redemption of our body.

See, then, from what he redeems me: because we still await, groaning inwardly, the redemption of our body.

From what, then, does my joy come? The same Apostle continues and says: “For by hope we have been saved; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

If you hope, you rejoice; if you await with patience, you still groan. For patience is not needed where you suffer no evil. Endurance, patience, perseverance, and long-suffering exist only amid evils. Where you are pressed, there is distress.

Therefore, if we await with patience, we still say, “Redeem me from the distress that surrounds me.” But because we have been saved by hope, we say both things together: “My joy, redeem me.”

21. [Verse 8.] The response is given: “I will give you understanding.” This is the psalm of understanding. “I will give you understanding, and I will set you in this way, in which you will walk.”

What does “I will set you in this way, in which you will walk” mean? Not that you should remain stuck there, but that you should not stray from it. I will give you understanding so that you may always know yourself and always rejoice in hope toward God, until you reach that homeland where there will no longer be hope, but the reality itself.

“I will fix my eyes upon you.” I will not take my eyes away from you, because you too will not take your eyes away from me.

Now that you have been justified, now after the forgiveness of sins, lift your eyes to God. Your heart had become rotten when it was fixed upon the earth. You do not hear “Lift up your hearts” without reason, lest it decay.

Therefore you too should now always lift your eyes to God, so that he may fix his eyes upon you.

But what are you afraid of? When you have your eyes on God, might you stumble because you are not looking ahead, and perhaps fall into a snare? Do not be afraid. His eyes are there, which he fixes upon you. “Do not be anxious,” he says (Matt. 6:31). And the Apostle Peter says: “Cast all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:7).

“Therefore I will fix my eyes upon you.”

Raise your eyes to him, then, and you will not fear, as I said, that you may fall into a snare. Hear another psalm: “My eyes are always toward the Lord.” And as though someone said to him, “What will you do about your feet when you are not looking before you?” he replies: “For he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15).

“I will fix my eyes upon you.”

22. [Verse 9.] He promised this person both understanding and his protection. He turns to the arrogant who defend their sins and shows us what understanding is:

“Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding.”

The horse and the mule hold their necks stiff. They are not like that ox which recognized its owner, or the donkey the manger of its lord (Isa. 1:3).

“Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding.” What do such people suffer? “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, who do not draw near to you.”

Do you wish to be a horse and a mule? Do you wish to have no rider? Your mouth and your jaws will be constrained with bit and bridle. Your mouth will be constrained—the mouth with which you boast of your merits and commit sins.

“Constrain their jaws,” those who do not draw near to you by humbling themselves.

23. [Verse 10.] “Many are the scourges of the sinner.” It is no wonder that, once the bridle has been applied, scourges follow. The animal wished to be untamed; it is broken by bridle and whip—and would that it may be thoroughly subdued! For there is a danger that, by resisting too much, it may deserve to be left untamed[3] and go off into its own wandering license, so that it may be said of it: “Their iniquity goes forth as from fatness” (Ps. 72:7), as is said of those whose sins presently go unpunished.

Therefore, when it is scourged, let it be corrected and subdued, for this person also said that he had been tamed in this way. He had said that he was a horse and a mule, because he had kept silent. But by what was he subdued? By scourges.

“I turned in my distress, while the thorn was being fixed.” Whether you call them scourges or goads, God tames the beast upon which he sits, because it is good for the beast that it be ridden.

God does not sit upon a beast because he has become tired from walking on foot. Or is it not full of mystery that the little donkey was brought to the Lord (Matt. 21:7)? The gentle and tame people who carry the Lord well are a little donkey, and it is making its way toward Jerusalem.

“For he will guide the gentle in judgment,” as another psalm says; “he will teach the meek his ways” (Ps. 24:9). Which meek? Those who do not raise their necks against their tamer, who endure scourges and bridle—later so tamed that they walk without the scourge and keep to the way without bit or bridle.

If you lose this rider, you will fall, not he.

“Many are the scourges of the sinner; but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.”

How is he a refuge from distress? The one whom distress first surrounds is afterward surrounded by mercy, because he will give mercy who gave the Law (Ps. 83:8): the Law in scourges, mercy in consolations.

“Mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.”

24. [Verse 11.] What, then, is concluded?

“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous.”

O you who rejoice in yourselves—O impious and arrogant people who rejoice in yourselves! Believe now in him who justifies the ungodly, and let your faith be reckoned as righteousness (Rom. 4:5).

“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous.” Understand “exult in the Lord.” Why? Because you are now righteous.

From where are you righteous? Not from your merits, but from his grace.

From where are you righteous? Because you have been justified.

25. “And glory, all you upright of heart.”

What does “upright of heart” mean? Not resisting God.

Let Your Charity pay attention and understand the upright heart. I will say it briefly, but it is nevertheless especially to be commended; and, thanks be to God, may what comes at the end remain fixed in your minds.

The difference between an upright heart and a crooked heart is this: whoever undergoes anything against his will—afflictions, griefs, labors, humiliations—attributes it only to the just will of God, without ascribing folly to him, as though he did not know what he was doing because he scourges one person and spares another. That person is upright of heart.

But those are crooked, perverse, and distorted in heart who say that all the evils they suffer are suffered unjustly, attributing injustice to the one by whose will they suffer; or, because they do not dare to attribute injustice to him, depriving him of governance.

He says: “He cannot do anything unjust. But it is unjust that I should suffer and he should not suffer. I grant that I am a sinner, but surely those who rejoice while I am afflicted are worse. Since, then, it is unjust that those worse than I should rejoice while I am afflicted, I who am either righteous or less sinful than they—and since it is certain to me that this is unjust, and certain to me that God does not do anything unjust—God does not govern human affairs, nor does he care for us.”

Thus those who are crooked in heart—that is, distorted in heart—hold three opinions.

Either: “There is no God.” For “the fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1). This was also mentioned concerning that flood above.[4] Such a doctrine was not absent among philosophers: there were those who said that there is no God who governs and created all things, but that there are many gods, at leisure for themselves beyond the world and taking no care of these matters.

Thus either: “There is no God.” This is what the impious person says when he is displeased by whatever happens to him against his will and does not happen to another whom he places above himself.

Or: “God is unjust,” to whom these things are pleasing and who does these things.

Or: “God does not govern human affairs, nor does he care for everything.”[5]

There is great impiety in these three opinions: either to deny God, or to say that he is unjust, or to remove governance of affairs from him.

Why is this? Because the heart is distorted.

God is upright, and therefore the distorted heart does not submit to him.

In another psalm it says: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright of heart!” And because the psalmist himself had once held such an opinion—“How does God know? Or is there knowledge in the Most High?”—he then added: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. 72:1, 11, 2).

Just as a crooked piece of wood, even if you place it on a level floor, does not settle, fit together, or lie flush, but is always shifting and rocking—not because the place where you put it is uneven, but because what you put there is crooked—so your heart, as long as it is wicked and distorted, cannot be aligned with God’s uprightness. It cannot be placed in him so as to cling to him and become what is said: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

Therefore he said, “Glory, you upright of heart.”

How do the upright of heart glory? Hear their boast. “Not only this,” says the Apostle, “but we also glory in tribulations.” For it is not a great thing to glory in joys and delights. The upright of heart glories even in tribulation.

And hear how he glories in tribulation—not pointlessly or without reason. Look at the upright heart: “Knowing,” he says, “that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

26. Thus, brothers, this is the upright heart. Whatever happens to someone, let him say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.” Behold the upright heart: “As it pleased the Lord, so it happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Who took it away? What did he take away? From whom did he take it away? When did he take it away? “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

He did not say, “The Lord gave; the devil took away.”

Let Your Charity pay attention, lest perhaps you say, “The devil did this to me.” Refer your scourge entirely to your God, because the devil does nothing to you unless the one who possesses power from above permits it, either for punishment or for discipline: for punishment of the impious, for discipline of the son.

“For he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Do not expect to be without a scourge, unless perhaps you are thinking of being disinherited. “He scourges every son whom he receives.”

Every son? Where did you wish to hide? Every one; no one is excepted, no one will be without a scourge.

What? Every one? Do you want to hear how every one? Even the Only-Begotten, though without sin, was not without a scourge.

The Only-Begotten, bearing your weakness and prefiguring your person in himself, carrying as head the person also of his body, when his passion drew near, was saddened in accordance with the human being he bore, so that he might make you joyful; he was saddened so that he might console you.

Certainly the Lord could have gone to his passion without sadness. If a soldier could, could the commander not?

How could a soldier? Consider Paul rejoicing as he approached his passion: “For I am already being poured out,” he says, “and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing” (2 Tim. 4:6–8).

See how he rejoices as he goes toward his passion. Thus he rejoices because he is to be crowned; Christ is saddened because he is to crown.

What, then, was Christ bearing? The weakness of certain people who become sad when tribulation or death approaches.

But see how he leads them toward the uprightness of heart.

You wanted to live; you did not want anything to happen to you. But God willed otherwise. There are two wills; but let your will be corrected to God’s will. Let God’s will not be bent toward yours. For your will is crooked, while his is the rule. Let the rule stand, so that what is crooked may be corrected according to the rule.

See how the Lord Jesus Christ teaches this: “My soul is sorrowful unto death”; and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” Behold, he shows a human will.

But see the upright heart: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:38–39).

Do this, then: rejoice in the things that happen to you. And if that final day comes, rejoice. Or if some frailty of the human will should creep in, let it quickly be directed toward God, so that you may belong among those to whom it is said: “Glory, all you upright of heart.”

# ON PSALM 32

## EXPOSITION I

1. [Verse 1.] “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” Exult, you righteous—not in yourselves, for this is not safe[6]—but in the Lord. Praise befits the upright. Those who submit themselves to the Lord praise him; otherwise they are distorted and crooked.

2. [Verse 2.] “Confess to the Lord on the lyre.” Confess to the Lord, presenting your bodies to him as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12:1).

“Sing praises to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.” Let your members serve the love of God and neighbor, in which the three and the seven commandments are observed.

3. [Verse 3.] “Sing to him a new song.” Sing to him the song of the grace of faith.

“Sing well to him with jubilation.” Sing well to him with joy.

4. [Verse 4.] “For the word of the Lord is upright.” For the word of the Lord is upright, in order to make you what you cannot make yourselves.

“And all his works are in faith.” Let no one think that he has arrived at faith through the merits of works, since all the works that God loves are contained in faith itself.

5. [Verse 5.] “He loves mercy and judgment.” For he loves mercy, which he now bestows in advance, and judgment, by which he demands what he has bestowed in advance.

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” Throughout the world sins are forgiven to human beings through the mercy of the Lord.

6. [Verse 6.] “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” For the righteous were not established by themselves, but by the word of the Lord.

“And by the Spirit of his mouth is all their strength.” By his holy Spirit is all their faith.

7. [Verse 7.] “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin.” He gathers the peoples of the world into confession of deadened sin, so that they may not flow freely through pride.

“Putting the abysses into storehouses.” And in them he preserves his hidden things for riches.[7]

8. [Verse 8.] “Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Let every sinner fear, so that he may cease to sin.

“But let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.” Let them be moved not by the terrors of human beings or of any creature, but by him.

9. [Verse 9.] “For he spoke, and they were made.” It was not someone else who made the things they should fear; he spoke, and they were made.

“He commanded, and they were created.” He commanded by his Word, and they were created.

10. [Verse 10.] “The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations.” Not his own kingdom, but the kingdoms of those who seek their own.

“But he rejects the thoughts of the peoples.” Of those who desire earthly happiness.

“And he rejects the counsels of princes.” Of those who seek to rule such peoples.

11. [Verse 11.] “But the counsel of the Lord remains forever.” The counsel of the Lord, by which he makes no one blessed except the one subject to him, remains forever.

“The thoughts of his heart from generation to generation.” The thoughts of his wisdom are not changeable, but remain for ever and ever.

12. [Verse 12.] “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.” There is one blessed nation, belonging to the heavenly city, which has chosen no one as its Lord except its own God.

“The people whom the Lord chose as an inheritance for himself.” This people too was not chosen by itself, but by God’s gift, so that, by possessing it, he might not allow it to remain uncultivated and miserable.

13. [Verse 13.] “The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the children of human beings.” From the righteous soul the Lord mercifully saw all those who wish to be reborn into a new life.

14. [Verse 14.] “From his prepared dwelling place.” From the dwelling place of human assumption, which he prepared for himself.

“He looked upon all who inhabit the earth”[8]—mercifully he saw all who inhabit the flesh, so that he might preside over them in governing them.

15. [Verse 15.] “He fashioned their hearts individually.” He spiritually bestowed upon their hearts their distinctive gifts, so that the whole body would not be an eye, nor the whole body hearing (1 Cor. 12:17), but that one should be incorporated into Christ in one way and another in another way.

“He understands all their works.” All their works are understood by him.

16. [Verse 16.] “The king is not saved by great strength.” The person who rules his flesh will not be saved if he presumes greatly upon his own strength.

“Nor will the giant be saved by the abundance of his strength.” Nor will anyone who wages war against the habit of his own desire, or against the devil and his angels, be saved if he entrusts himself too greatly to his own strength.

17. [Verse 17.] “A horse is false for salvation.” Anyone is deceived who thinks that he can either obtain salvation through human beings, as accepted among human beings, or be defended from destruction by the force of his own courage.

“By the abundance of his strength he will not be saved.”[9]

18. [Verse 18.] “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him.” If you seek salvation, behold, the Lord’s love is upon those who fear him.

“Upon those who hope in his mercy.” They hope not in their own strength, but in his mercy.

19. [Verse 19.] “To rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine.” To give them the nourishment of the word and of eternal truth, which they had lost while presuming upon their own strength, and therefore did not even possess the strength to hunger for righteousness.

20. [Verse 20.] “Our soul will wait for the Lord.” But in order that it may afterward be fattened with incorruptible food, meanwhile, while it is here, our soul will wait for the Lord.

“For he is our helper and protector.” He is our helper while we strive toward him, and our protector while we resist the adversary.
