21. [Verse 21.] “For our heart will rejoice in him.” For it will not rejoice in ourselves, where there is great poverty without him; rather, our heart will rejoice in him.

“And we have hoped in his holy name.” Therefore we have hoped that we will come to God, because, while we are absent from him, he sent us his name through faith.

22. [Verse 22.] “Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you.” Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us; for hope does not disappoint, because we have hoped in you.

## EXPOSITION II

### SERMON I: On the First Part of the Psalm

1. [Verse 1.] This psalm urges us to exult in the Lord. It is entitled “To David himself.” Therefore those who belong to the most sacred seed of David should hear their own voice, speak their own voice, and exult in the Lord.

It begins in this way: “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord.” Let the unrighteous exult in the world. When the world has ended, the exultation of the unrighteous will end. But let the righteous exult in the Lord, because, while the Lord remains, the exultation of the righteous will remain.

It is fitting to exult in the Lord in such a way that we praise the one alone who has nothing in him that can displease us, although no one has so many things that displease unbelievers.

And there is a brief commandment: “That person pleases God to whom God is pleasing.”

Do not consider this a small matter, beloved. You see how many argue against God and how many are displeased by his works. When he wishes to do something contrary to human will, because he is the Lord and knows what he is doing, and because he pays attention not so much to our will as to our welfare, those who prefer their own will to be fulfilled rather than God’s wish to bend God to their will instead of correcting their will toward God.

For such unbelieving, impious, and unjust people—what I am reluctant to say, yet will say, since you know how true it is—a pantomime more easily pleases than God.[10]

2. Therefore, after he had said, “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord”—since we cannot exult in him except by praising him, and when we praise him, we please him all the more the more he himself has become pleasing to us—he says: “Praise befits the upright.”

Who are the upright? Those who direct their heart according to the will of God. And if human frailty disturbs them, divine equity consoles them. Although, in their mortal heart, they may privately desire something that meanwhile suits their own circumstance, business, or present necessity, once they understand and recognize that God wills something else, they place the will of the better above their own will, the will of the almighty above the will of the weak, and God’s will above human will.

For as far as God is removed from a human being, so far is God’s will removed from human will.

Therefore Christ, bearing the human being, setting before us a rule, teaching us how to live, and granting us life, showed a certain private will belonging to the human being. In this will he represented both his own will and ours, because he is our head and, as you know, we belong to him as members:

“Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

This was a human will, desiring something particular and, as it were, private. But because he wished the human being to be upright in heart, so that whatever in him was somewhat bent might be directed toward the one who is always upright, he said: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

But what evil could Christ have wished? What, finally, could he have wished other than what the Father wished? Since they have one divinity, their wills cannot be different.

But by transforming in himself, in the person of a human being, those whom he transformed in himself—as when he said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35); and when, from above, he cried out to Saul, who was raging and persecuting the saints, though no one was touching him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4)—he showed a certain proper human will. He showed you, and he corrected you.

“Behold,” he says, “see yourself in me. You can desire something of your own, so that God may will something else. This is conceded to human frailty; it is conceded to human weakness. To desire something of your own is difficult not to experience. But immediately consider who is above you: him above you, you beneath him; him the Creator, you the creature; him the Lord, you the servant; him almighty, you weak. Correcting yourself, submitting yourself to his will, say: ‘Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father.’”

How are you separated from God, when you now will what God wills?

You will therefore be upright, and praise will befit you, because praise befits the upright.

Editorial notes from the supplied text:

- §16, col. 268: Perhaps read: “But what he said had not been sufficient.” Some manuscripts read *facta* (“deeds”) for *fata* (“fates”) in the reference to human destinies.
- §17, col. 269: Perhaps read *temporibus* (“times”).
- §18, col. 270: Nearly all manuscripts read *viae* (“way”) for *vitae* (“life”). The manuscripts read, “The way of this humility flows from elsewhere”; the editions read, with a negative particle, “does not flow from elsewhere.”
- §20, col. 271: The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read: “exists only amid evils, where you are pressed, where there is distress.”
- §23, col. 272: Many manuscripts read “by resisting its tamer” rather than “by resisting too much.”
- §25, col. 273: “That flood” refers above to §18. The Vatican manuscript reads “nor does he care for human beings.” The manuscripts omit “heart” in “the distorted heart does not submit to him,” and most read “that distorted [heart] does not submit to him.” The manuscripts read “because he himself once held such an opinion”; the editions read “once expressed such an opinion concerning himself.” The editions add *upright* after “and become”; it is absent from the manuscripts.
- §26, col. 274: Several manuscripts read “leads them in the uprightness of heart.”
- Exposition I, §1, col. 275: Some manuscripts read *justum* (“righteous”) for *tutum* (“safe”).
- Exposition I, §7, col. 275: The manuscripts read “and he preserves his hidden things in them for riches.”
- Exposition I, §14, col. 276: The Louvain edition reads “flesh” instead of “earth”; the manuscripts and Erasmus disagree with it.
- Exposition I, §16, col. 276: The manuscripts consistently spell “giant” as *gigans*.
- Exposition I, §17, col. 276: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “he will not be saved”; the Louvain edition reads “there will be no salvation.”
- Exposition I, §21, col. 277: The manuscripts read “we have hoped” here and in the following verse; the editions read “we shall hope.”
- Exposition II, Sermon I, §1, col. 277: For “pantomimes,” see the Exposition of Psalm 30, Sermon 3, §11.

### 3.

But if you are crooked, you praise God when things go well for you and blaspheme when things go badly. Yet if that “bad” thing is just, it is not bad; and it is just because it is done by him who can do nothing unjust. You will then be a senseless child in your father’s house, loving your father when he flatters you and hating him when he chastises you—as though both his flattering and his chastising did not prepare an inheritance for you.

Consider, then, how praise suits the upright, and hear the voice of an upright person praising from another psalm: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2). What is “at all times” is “always”; and what is “I will bless” is “his praise shall be in my mouth.” At all times and always means both in prosperity and in adversity. For if only in prosperity and not in adversity, how is it “at all times,” how “always”? We have heard many such voices from many people: when some happiness comes to them, they exult, rejoice, sing to God, and praise God. They are not to be condemned; indeed, we should rejoice for them, since many do not praise God even then. But those who have now begun to praise God because of their prosperity must be taught to recognize the Father also when he chastises them, and not to murmur against the hand that corrects them. Otherwise, if they remain crooked forever, they may deserve to be disinherited. Once they have been made upright—for what does “upright” mean? That nothing God has done displeases them—they will be able to praise God even in adversity and to say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Such upright people are suited to praise: not those who praise at first and later blame.

[Col. 0279] **4.** Therefore, “you righteous and upright, exult in the Lord, for praise suits you.” Let no one say, “What righteous person am I, or when will I be righteous?” [Note: [Col. 0279] Thus the manuscripts. The editors instead have: “What righteous person, then, or when will I be righteous?”] Do not cast yourselves down or despair of yourselves. You are human beings; you were made in the image of God. He who made you human also became human for your sake. So that you might be adopted as many sons into an eternal inheritance, the blood of the Only-Begotten was poured out for you.

If, because of your earthly frailty, you have seemed worthless to yourselves, weigh yourselves by your price. Consider worthily what you eat, what you drink, and to what you subscribe your “Amen” [Note: [Col. 0279] The editors have *subscribamini tamen* (“that you may nevertheless be enrolled”). Some manuscripts have *subscribatis tantum* (“that you merely subscribe”); but most of them have *subscribatis Amen* (“that you subscribe ‘Amen’”).]. Surely we are not advising you to be proud and dare to claim some perfection for yourselves? But neither should you think yourselves banished from all righteousness. I do not want to question you about your righteousness, for perhaps none of you would dare answer me, “I am righteous.” But I ask you about your faith. Just as none of you dares say, “I am righteous,” so no one dares say, “I am not faithful.”

I am not yet asking how you live; I am asking what you believe. You will answer that you believe in Christ. Have you not heard the Apostle: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17)? Your faith is your righteousness. For if you believe, you take care; if you take care, you strive; and God knows your striving, sees your intention, considers your struggle with the flesh, urges you to fight, helps you to conquer, watches for you while you fight, lifts you when you falter, and crowns you when you conquer [Note: [Col. 0279] The editors have *inspectat* (“watches over”). The manuscripts have *exspectat* (“waits for”), which Augustine frequently uses in the same sense as *observat* (“observes” or “watches”).].

Therefore, “Exult, you righteous, in the Lord”—that is, “Exult, you faithful, in the Lord,” because “the righteous person lives by faith.” Praise suits the upright. Learn to give thanks to God both in prosperity and in tribulation. Learn to keep in your heart what everyone has on the tongue: “Whatever God wills.” That popular expression is often salutary instruction. Who does not say every day, “May God’s will be done”? Such a person will be upright among those who exult in the Lord and whom praise suits. The Psalm next addresses such people and says: “Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him with the ten-stringed psaltery.”

For we too were singing in this manner, expressing it with a harmonious voice; and in doing so we were teaching your hearts [Note: [Col. 0279] Most manuscripts have *nostra* (“our hearts”); this may be no less correct with the following punctuation: “expressing our hearts with a harmonious voice, we were teaching.”].

### 5. [verse 2]

Did the institution, in the name of Christ, of these Vigils not bring about the removal of lyres from this place? And behold, the lyres themselves are now commanded to sound: “Give thanks,” he says, “to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him with the ten-stringed psaltery.” Let no one turn his heart toward theatrical instruments. What is commanded of him, he has within himself, as it is said elsewhere: “In me are your vows, O God, which I will fulfill in praise of you” (Ps. 55:12).

Those who were present previously remember that we distinguished, as best we could, the difference between the psaltery and the lyre [Note: [Col. 0280] On the distinction between the psaltery and the lyre, see the Exposition on Psalm 42 and Psalm 70, Sermon 11, no. 11.], and meanwhile tried to bring the matter within everyone’s understanding. Let those who heard judge how successful we were. Even now it is not inappropriate to repeat the explanation, so that in this difference between the two musical instruments we may find a difference in human deeds—signified by these instruments, but to be fulfilled in our lives.

The lyre [Note: [Col. 0280] The editors have *Cithara est lignum* (“The lyre is wood”). Delete *est*, since it destroys the sense and is absent from the manuscripts.] has that hollow piece of wood, like a drum, with a tortoise shell hanging beneath it; the strings rest upon the wood so that they resound when touched. I am not referring to the plectrum with which they are struck, but to that hollow piece of wood beneath them, upon which they rest, as it were, so that when they are struck they are shaken by it and, receiving sound from its hollow cavity, become more musical. This piece of wood is beneath the lyre; in the psaltery it is above. That is the distinction.

We are now commanded to give thanks on the lyre and sing on the ten-stringed psaltery. He did not say “on a ten-stringed lyre,” either in this psalm or, if I am not mistaken, anywhere else. Let our sons, the Readers, examine the matter more carefully and at their leisure. Yet, as far as I seem to remember, we find “ten-stringed psaltery” in many places, but nowhere have I encountered “ten-stringed lyre.” Remember that the lyre has its sounding part below, while the psaltery has it above.

From the lower part of life—that is, from earthly existence—we receive prosperity and adversity, from both of which we should praise God, so that his praise may always be in our mouths and we may bless the Lord at all times (Ps. 33:2) [Note: [Col. 0280] Most manuscripts have: “From lower life, from this earth, we have that from which to praise God, and in both, as always…”]. There is an earthly prosperity and an earthly adversity. God is to be praised for both, so that we may play the lyre.

What is earthly prosperity? When we are healthy in the flesh; when everything by which we live is abundant; when our safety is preserved; when the crops grow plentifully; when he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). All these things serve earthly life. Whoever does not praise God for them is ungrateful. Are they not God’s simply because they are earthly? Or should we think that another gives them because they are also given to the wicked? God’s mercy is manifold; he is patient and long-suffering. By showing how much he gives even to the wicked, he reveals all the more what he reserves for the good.

Adversities, likewise belonging to the lower realm, arise from the frailty of the human race: pains, illnesses, pressures, tribulations, and temptations. Let the person who plays the lyre praise God everywhere. Let such a person not attend to the fact that these things are lower, but to the fact that they cannot be ruled and governed except by that Wisdom which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

He does not rule heavenly things and abandon earthly ones. Or is it not said to him: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:7–8)? Where, then, is he absent who is nowhere absent?

Therefore, “give thanks to the Lord on the lyre.” If something earthly abounds for you, give thanks to him who gave it; if you lack something, or if it is perhaps taken away from you by loss, play the lyre without fear. For the one who gave it has not been taken away from you, even though what he gave has been taken away. Even then, I say, play the lyre without fear. Secure in your God, touch the strings in your heart and say, as though on a lyre sounding well in its lower part: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

### 6.

But when you attend to God’s higher gifts—what he has bestowed upon you by way of commandments, with what heavenly teaching he has nourished you, what he has commanded you from above out of the fountain of his truth [Note: [Col. 0281] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts have *prae ceteris dederit* (“what he has given above all else”).]—turn also to the psaltery: sing to the Lord on the ten-stringed psaltery.

The commandments of the Law are ten; in the ten commandments of the Law you have the psaltery. It is a perfect thing. There you have love of God in three commandments and love of neighbor in seven. Surely you know that, as the Lord says, “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

God says to you from above: “The Lord your God is one God.” You have one string. “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” You have another string. “Observe the Sabbath day”—not carnally, not with Jewish pleasures, as those do who misuse leisure for wickedness. It would certainly be better for them to dig all day than to dance all day. But you, contemplating rest in your God and doing everything for the sake of that rest, abstain from servile work. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin (John 8:34)—and would that he were the slave of a human being and not of sin!

These three commandments pertain to love of God: consider his unity, his truth, and his delight [Note: [Col. 0281] So the better manuscripts. The editors have *et voluntatem* (“and his will”), followed shortly by *quaedam voluntas* (“a certain will”).]. There is indeed a certain delight in the Lord, where there is a true Sabbath and true rest. Hence it is said: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. 36:4). For who gives delight in this way except the one who made all the things that delight us?

In these three commandments there is love of God; in the other seven, love of neighbor: you shall not do to another what you do not wish to suffer yourself. “Honor your father and your mother,” because you wish to be honored by your children. “You shall not commit adultery,” because you do not wish your wife to commit adultery against you. “You shall not kill,” because you do not wish to be killed. “You shall not steal,” because you do not wish to suffer theft. “You shall not bear false witness,” because you hate someone who bears false witness against you. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” because you do not wish your own to be coveted by another. “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor” (Exod. 20:1–17; Deut. 5:6–21), because if someone covets what is yours, it displeases you.

Turn the same rule upon yourself when the person who harms you displeases you. All these are God’s commandments; they have been given by the gift of Wisdom, and they sound from above. Touch the psaltery; fulfill the Law, which the Lord your God did not come to abolish but to fulfill (Matt. 5:17).

You will fulfill through love what you could not fulfill through fear. For whoever does not do wrong out of fear would prefer to do it if he were permitted. Thus, even though the opportunity is not given, the will is held guilty [Note: [Col. 0281] The Vatican and Regius manuscripts have *voluntas rea tenetur* (“the will is held guilty”).].

“I do not do it,” he says. “Why?” “Because I am afraid.” You do not yet love righteousness; you are still a slave. Become a son. Yet a good son is made from a good slave. For now, do not do wrong out of fear; you will learn not to do it out of love. There is a certain beauty in righteousness. Let punishment deter you. Righteousness has its own form; it seeks eyes and kindles its lovers.

For this beauty the martyrs, trampling the world underfoot, shed their blood. What did they love when they renounced all these things? Were they not lovers? Or are we telling you not to love? Whoever does not love is cold and frozen. Let there be love—but let it be that beauty which seeks the eyes of the heart. Let there be love—but let it be that beauty which, when righteousness is praised, sets souls on fire.

They bring forth words and utter cries; everywhere they say, “Good! Excellent!” What have they seen? They have seen righteousness, in which a bent old man is beautiful [Note: [Col. 0282] Thus most and better manuscripts. The editors instead have: “but that beauty which, when praised, sets righteousness on fire; kindled by righteousness, they bring forth words and utter cries, everywhere saying, ‘Good! Excellent!’ What did they see? In what is the bent old man beautiful?”].

For if a righteous old man comes forward, there is nothing in his body that ought to be loved, and yet he is loved by everyone. He is loved where he is not seen—or rather, where he is seen by the heart.

Let that beauty therefore delight you, and ask the Lord to make it delight you. “The Lord will indeed give sweetness, and our land will yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:13), so that through love you may fulfill what is difficult to fulfill through fear.

What do I mean by “difficult”? The soul is not yet able. If it is not led to do what is commanded by love but is constrained by fear, it would prefer that the command did not exist. “Do not steal; fear hell.” Such a person would prefer that there were no hell into which thieves might be sent. When does he begin to love righteousness? When he would prefer that theft did not exist even if there were no hell into which thieves would be sent. This is what it means to love righteousness.

### 7.

And what is this righteousness like? Who can paint it? What beauty does the Wisdom of God possess? Through it all things that please the eyes are beautiful. To see it, embrace it, and cleanse their hearts, people must be purified. We profess ourselves its lovers; it shapes us so that we may not displease it.

When people rebuke us in matters by which we please the Wisdom we love, how little we regard our rebukers, how we despise them and count them utterly worthless [Note: [Col. 0282] Thus the manuscripts. The editors have instead: “how we are regarded as bad by our rebukers, how we are despised by them and counted utterly worthless.”]!

Lustful and condemnable lovers of women, when the women they love arrange them according to their own eyes, do not care about those whom they displease, thinking it sufficient for them to please the eyes of those whom they desire. Usually they displease serious people—indeed, they always displease serious people—and are rebuked by better judgment.

“You are not well groomed,” a serious man says to a frivolous young man. “You should not go about with curls like those.” But the young man knows that those hairs please someone or other. He hates you for rebuking him with true judgment and preserves in himself what pleases a perverse opinion. He considers you an enemy because you remove his disgrace [Note: [Col. 0282] Two manuscripts have *diligit* (“loves”); the Benignus manuscript has *damnas* (“condemns”).]. He avoids your eyes and does not care at all by what rule of righteousness he is rebuked.

If, then, such people disregard truthful reprovers in order to appear beautiful to deceitful eyes, should we, in matters by which we please the Wisdom of God, care about unjust mockers who do not possess eyes with which to see what we love? Thinking these things, you who are upright in heart, “give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him with the ten-stringed psaltery.”

### 8. [verse 3]

“Sing to him a new song.” Strip off the oldness; you know the new song. The new person, the New Testament, the new song: the new song does not belong to old people. Only new people learn it—those renewed by grace from their old condition and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven. All our love sighs toward it and sings the new song.

Let him sing a new song—not with the tongue, but with his life. “Sing to him a new song; sing to him well.” Everyone asks how to sing to God. Sing to him, but do not sing badly. He does not wish his ears to be offended. Sing well, brother.

If you were told to sing for the pleasure of some good musical listener, you would hesitate to sing without some instruction in musical art, lest you displease the expert; for what the unskilled person does not recognize in you, the expert rebukes. Who would dare to offer God good singing, since he judges the singer, examines everything, and hears everything? When could you bring such a refined art of singing that you would offend these perfect ears in no respect?

Behold, he gives you, as it were, the manner of singing: do not seek words, as though you could explain what gives God delight. Sing in jubilation. For this is to sing well to God: to sing in jubilation.

What does it mean to sing in jubilation? It means to understand that what is sung by the heart cannot be expressed in words [Note: [Col. 0283] The editors have “what is sung to God by the mouth.” Some manuscripts have “what is sung to God,” omitting *ore* (“by the mouth”). Others have “what is sung by the mouth,” without adding *Deo* (“to God”), or “what is sung by the heart.” Some also have *explicari* (“be expressed”) instead of *explicare* (“to express”).].

Those who sing—whether in the harvest, in the vineyard, or at some labor requiring intense effort—when they begin to exult with joy in the words of their songs, become, as it were, so filled with joy that they cannot express it in words. They turn away from the syllables of the words and proceed into the sound of jubilation.

Jubilation is a certain sound signifying that the heart is giving birth to what it cannot say. And whom does this jubilation suit more than the ineffable God? He is ineffable whom you cannot speak. If you cannot speak him and yet must not remain silent, what remains except that you should exult—so that the heart may rejoice without words, and the immense breadth of its joys may have no limits in syllables?

Sing well to him in jubilation.

### 9. [verse 4]

“For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith.” Even in that wherein he displeases those who are not upright, he himself is upright. “And all his works are in faith.” Let your works be in faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), and “faith works through love” (Gal. 5:6). Let your works be in faith, because by believing in God you become faithful.

How can God’s works be in faith, as though God too lived by faith? We find that God is faithful, and this is not said in our words. Hear the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

You have heard that God is faithful; hear it also elsewhere: “If we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he will also deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2:12–13).

We therefore have a faithful God. Let us rather distinguish the faithful God from the faithful human being. A faithful human being is one who believes God when he promises; a faithful God is one who supplies what he promised to the human being. Let us hold fast to the most faithful debtor, since we hold fast to the most merciful promiser.

We have not lent him anything so as to hold him as a debtor, since we possess from him whatever we offer him, and whatever good we are comes from him. All the good things in which we rejoice [Note: [Col. 0284] Almost all manuscripts have *dona* (“gifts”).] are from him. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:34–36).

Therefore, we have given him nothing, yet we hold him as a debtor. How is he a debtor? Because he is the promiser. We do not say to God, “Lord, repay what you have received”; we say, “Repay what you have promised.”

“For the word of the Lord is upright.” What does “the word of the Lord is upright” mean? It does not deceive you; do not deceive it—or rather, do not deceive yourself. For who deceives the one who knows everything? “But wickedness has lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12). “For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith.”

### 10. [verse 5]

“He loves mercy and judgment.” Do these things, because he does them. Attend to mercy and judgment themselves. The time of mercy is now; the time of judgment will come afterward.

Why is this the time of mercy? He now calls those who have turned away and forgives the sins of those who turn back. He is patient with sinners until they turn. Whenever they turn, he forgets the past and promises the future. He urges the sluggish, consoles the afflicted, teaches the diligent, helps those who struggle. He abandons no one who labors and cries out to him [Note: [Col. 0284] The Vatican manuscript has “and longs for him.”]. He gives what may be sacrificed to him; he himself grants what may please him.

Brothers, let this great time of mercy not pass by; let it not pass us by. Judgment will come. There will also be repentance then, but it will already be fruitless. Those who repent then will say within themselves, groaning in anguish of spirit—these words are certainly written in the Book of Wisdom: “What did our pride profit us, and what did the boasting of riches bring us? All these things have passed like a shadow” (Wis. 5:3, 8–9).

Let us say now, “All things are passing like a shadow.” Let us say “they are passing” fruitfully now, so that then we may not say fruitlessly, “They have passed.” This, then, is the time of mercy; there will also be a time of judgment.

### 11.

Do not think, brothers, that these can in any way be separated from one another in God. They sometimes appear contrary, as though the one who is merciful does not preserve judgment, and the one who is strict in judgment forgets mercy. God is almighty: in mercy he does not lose judgment, nor in judgment does he lose mercy.

He has mercy because he considers his own image, our frailty, our error, and our blindness, and he calls us. To those who turn to him he grants forgiveness; to those who do not turn, he does not grant it. Is he merciful to the unjust? Has he therefore lost judgment, or ought he not to judge between those who turn and those who do not? Does it seem just to you that the one who turns and the one who does not turn should be treated equally; that the person who confesses and the person who lies, the humble and the proud, should be received in the same way? Therefore, he possesses judgment within mercy itself.

Again, in that judgment he will also have mercy—certainly upon those to whom he will say: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35). For it is said in one of the apostolic Letters: “Judgment is without mercy for the one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13). “Blessed are the merciful,” he says, “for they shall receive mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

Therefore, there will also be mercy in that judgment, but not without judgment. For if mercy will not be shown to just anyone, but to the one who has previously shown mercy, then that mercy itself will be just, because it will not be indiscriminate.

It is certainly mercy that sins are forgiven; it is mercy that eternal life is granted. See judgment there: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38). Certainly, “it will be given to you” and “you will be forgiven” are mercy. If judgment had withdrawn from mercy [Note: [Col. 0285] The editors have “if it had withdrawn from judgment.” The manuscripts have “if judgment had withdrawn.”], he would not say: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

### 12.

You have heard how God displays mercy and judgment; display mercy and judgment yourself. Or do these things perhaps pertain to God but not to human beings? If they did not pertain to human beings, the Lord would not say to the Pharisees: “You have neglected the weightier matters of the Law: mercy and judgment” (Matt. 23:23).

Therefore, mercy and judgment concern you. Do not think that mercy concerns you but judgment does not. Sometimes you hear a case between two people, one of whom is rich and the other poor, and it happens that the poor person has a bad case while the rich person has a good one.

If you have not been instructed in the kingdom of God, you may think you are doing well if, out of pity for the poor person, you conceal and cover his injustice and wish to justify him, so that he may appear to have a good case. If you are reproved for having judged badly, you answer as though appealing to mercy: “I know, and I know it well; but he was poor, and mercy was owed to him.”

How did you retain mercy and lose judgment? “And how,” you ask, “if I retained judgment, would I not lose mercy? I would pronounce judgment against a poor man who had nothing with which to repay, or who, if he did have something, would have nothing left to live on after repaying it.”

Your God says to you: “You shall not show partiality to a poor person in judgment” (Exod. 23:3). It is easy, of course, to be warned not to show partiality to the rich. Everyone sees this—and would that everyone acted accordingly! But here is where a person is deceived: he wants to please God by showing partiality to the poor in judgment and saying to God, “I favored the poor man” [Col. 0286].

No: you should have preserved both mercy and judgment. First, what kind of mercy did you show the man whose injustice you washed away? You spared his purse, but struck his heart. This poor man remained unjust, and all the more unjust because he saw you, as though a just person, favoring his injustice.

He left you unjustly assisted, but remained before God justly condemned [Note: [Col. 0286] Thus the manuscripts. The editors instead have: “You remained with him, unjustly assisting him; he departed from God, justly destined for condemnation.”]. What kind of mercy did you show to someone whom you made unjust? Behold, you are found to be more cruel than merciful.

“What, then,” you ask, “should I have done?” You should first have judged according to the case, rebuked the poor man, and softened the rich man. The place for judging is one thing; the place for asking is another. When the rich man saw that you had maintained justice, not stiffened the neck of the unjust poor man, but had justly rebuked him according to the merit of his sin, would he not have been moved to mercy when you asked him—he who had been glad to receive his due because you had judged him?

Although, therefore, brothers, much of the Psalm remains, we must nevertheless take account of the strength of both soul and body because of the variety of our hearers. Just as, from the same wheat, many flavors are made for us to dispel weariness when we are refreshed [Note: [Col. 0286] Many manuscripts have: “because of the variety of what is heard, by which we are refreshed, just as from the same wheat…” They also conclude the sermon with the added clause, “Let us turn to the Lord.”], let this be sufficient for you.

## SERMON II. On the Remaining Part of the Psalm

### 1.

Both proclaiming and hearing the word of truth involve labor. We endure this labor with equanimity if we remember the Lord’s command and our condition. From the very beginning of our race, the human being heard—not from a deceitful human being, nor from a deceiving devil, but from Truth itself, from the mouth of God: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3:19).

Therefore, if our bread is the word of God, let us sweat in hearing it, lest we die of fasting. A few verses from the first part of this Psalm were expounded during the solemnity of the recent Vigils [Note: [Col. 0286] In the church of Saint Cyprian.]. Let us hear what remains.

### 2. [verses 5–6]

Here begins the remaining part, which we have just sung: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” The same thing is meant by: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.”

Earlier he had said, “Sing well to him in jubilation,” that is, sing to him ineffably: “For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith.” He promises nothing and fails to repay it. He has made himself a faithful debtor; be an eager collector.

Then, after saying, “All his works are in faith,” he added the reason: “He loves mercy and judgment.” Therefore, the one who loves mercy shows mercy. But the one who shows mercy—could he promise and not give, when he could give even without promising? [Note: [Col. 0286] The editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis have: “But the one who shows mercy cannot promise and not give, because he could give even if he did not promise.” We follow the manuscripts.]

Therefore, because he loves mercy, he must provide what he promises; and because he loves judgment, he must demand what he has given. Hence the Lord himself says to a certain servant: “You should have given my money, and when I came I would have required it with interest” (Luke 19:23).

We mention this so that we may understand what we have just heard. He himself says elsewhere in the Gospel: “I judge no one; the word that I have spoken to them will judge them on the last day” (John 8:15; 12:48). Let no one who refuses to hear excuse himself, as though there were something that could be demanded from him [Note: [Col. 0287] The editions have “lest there be nothing that can be demanded from him.” The particle *non* (“not”) is absent from the manuscripts.]. What is demanded is demanded precisely because he refused to accept it when it was offered. For it is one thing to be unable to accept and another to be unwilling; in the former there is the excuse of necessity, in the latter the guilt of the will.

Therefore, “all his works are in faith; he loves mercy and judgment.” Receive mercy and fear judgment, lest, when he comes to demand an account from us, he demand it in such a way that he leaves us empty-handed. For he demands an account; once the account has been rendered, he grants eternity.

Receive mercy, then, brothers; let us all receive it. Let none of us sleep while receiving it, lest we be awakened badly when it comes time to render an account [Note: [Col. 0287] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *malum* (“an evil account”). Ambrosianus and the manuscripts have *male* (“badly”).].

Receive mercy. God cries out to us as though, in a time of famine, someone were saying, “Receive grain.” If you heard this during a famine, surely the stimulus of necessity would drive you to run. You would turn this way and that, seeking where you could receive what had been announced: “Receive.” And when you found it, how long would you delay? How much time would you put between yourself and it?

So now too it has been said: “Receive mercy.” For he loves mercy and judgment. When you have received it, use it well, so that you may render a good account when the judgment of the one who now gives you mercy in this famine arrives.

### 3. [verse 5]

Do not say to me, “Where do I receive it? Where should I go?” Remember what you sang: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” Where is the Gospel not preached now? Where is the word of the Lord silent? Where has salvation ceased? You need only be willing to receive; the storehouses are full.

This fullness and abundance itself did not wait for you to come; it came to the one who was sleeping. It was not said, “Let the nations rise and go to one place.” Rather, these things were announced to the nations where they were, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which says: “Everyone shall worship him from his own place” (Zeph. 2:11).

### 4. [verse 6]

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” What of the heavens? Hear what concerns the heavens. They do not need mercy where there is no misery. On earth human misery abounds, while the Lord’s mercy overflows: the earth is full of human misery, and the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy.

What, then, of the heavens, where there is no misery? Do they, because they do not need mercy, not need the Lord? Everything needs the Lord, both miserable things and blessed things. Without him the miserable are not lifted up; without him the blessed are not governed [Note: [Col. 0287] The Regius and Vatican manuscripts have: “without him the blessed are not raised up.” Five others have: “without him the blessed are in need.”].

Therefore, lest you perhaps ask about the heavens when you hear, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” hear that the heavens too need the Lord: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.” They did not provide their own foundation for themselves, nor did the heavens themselves supply their own stability. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.”

They possessed nothing from themselves and received from the Lord something as an addition. For by the Spirit of his mouth—not a part, but all their power exists.

### 5.

Certainly, brothers, observe the same works of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. We must not pass this over carelessly, because of certain wicked dividers and turbulent confusers. Both errors are wrong. Those people, by making improper distinctions, confuse the creature with the Creator; and although the Spirit of God is the Creator, they count him among creatures. They distinguish and confuse. Let them be confounded, so that they may be converted.

Now hear one work of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Certainly the Son is the Word of God, and the Spirit of his mouth is the Holy Spirit. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm.” What does it mean for them to have been made firm except that they possess stable and enduring power? “And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power exists.”

It could also be said: “By the Spirit of his mouth the heavens were made firm, and by the word of the Lord all their power exists.” For “all their power exists” means the same as “they were made firm.” Thus the Son and the Holy Spirit do this work.

Is it without the Father? Who, then, acts through his Word and his Spirit except the one whose Word and whose Spirit they are? Therefore, this Trinity is one God. Whoever knows how to worship worships him; whoever has turned to him has him everywhere [Note: [Col. 0288] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have “wherever he has turned.”]. He is not sought by those who have turned away; rather, he himself calls those who have turned away, so that he may fulfill those who turn to him.

### 6.

Certainly, brothers, apart from those higher heavens unknown to us who labor on earth and seek these matters, however tentatively, through human conjectures—apart, then, from those heavens, concerning how they are arranged above one another, or how many there are, or in what ways they are distinguished, by what inhabitants they are filled, by what ordering they are governed, and how there one unceasing hymn is sung in concert by all, proclaiming God [Note: The Regius and Vatican manuscripts read *praecinetur Deo*, “is sung beforehand to God.”]—it is a great undertaking for us to discover these things, though we strive to reach them. For there is our homeland, which perhaps we have forgotten during a long exile. Our voice is found in that psalm: “Alas for me, for my exile has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5).

Thus, concerning those heavens, it is difficult even for me to speak—though perhaps not impossible—and for you to understand. Certainly, whoever has surpassed me in understanding these matters should enjoy that to which he has gone ahead, and pray for me that I may follow. Meanwhile, apart from those heavens, I have something about which I can speak here, however inadequately: the holy heavens of God nearest to us, the Apostles, preachers of the word of truth, through whom we have been drenched by the heavens,” so that throughout the whole world the harvest of the Church might spring up; although for the present it drinks the same rain as the weeds, it will nevertheless not share their granary.

### 7.

When it had been said, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord,” as though you were asking, “From what has the earth been filled with the mercy of the Lord?”—first the heavens were sent, to scatter the Lord’s mercy over the earth, and over the whole earth. For see what is said elsewhere about these heavens: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” What are called “the heavens” here are called “the firmament” there. “Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night.” There is no cessation and no silence.

But where did they preach, and how far did they reach? “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.” This refers to the fact that they spoke in the languages of all peoples in one place (Acts 2:4). Speaking in all languages, they fulfilled what was said: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.” But I ask how far that very voice, which fulfilled this, reached in all languages. Hear what follows: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. 18:2–5). Whose sound, if not that of the heavens which declare the glory of God?

Therefore, if their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world, let the one who sent them tell us what they proclaimed. He does indeed tell us—faithfully he tells us—for before they came into being he foretold what would happen, he whose works are all in faith. For he rose from the dead, and, recognized by his disciples as they touched his limbs [Note: The manuscripts read “recognized by his disciples.”], said: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name. Where and how far? Among all nations,” he said, “beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

What greater mercy from the Lord do we all await, brothers, than that our sins be forgiven? Since, then, the great mercy of the Lord is the forgiveness of sins, and the Lord foretold that this forgiveness of sins would be preached among all nations: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” From what is the earth full? From the mercy of the Lord. Why? Because everywhere God forgives sins, because he sent the heavens to drench the earth.

### 8.

And how did those heavens dare to go forth with confidence—how could they be made heavens from weak human beings—unless “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established”? From where would sheep among wolves have such strength unless “by the breath of his mouth all their strength” came?

“Behold,” he says, “I am sending you like sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10:16). O most merciful Lord! Certainly you do this so that your mercy may fill the earth. If, then, you are so merciful as to fill the earth with mercy, look at whom you send; look where you send them. Where, I ask, do you send them, and whom do you send?

Sheep among wolves. If one wolf were sent among innumerable sheep, who could resist him? What would he not disturb—unless perhaps he were quickly satisfied? For he would devour everything. Are you sending the weak among the savage? “I am,” he says, “because they become heavens, so that they may drench the earth.”

How do weak human beings become heavens? “By the breath of his mouth all their strength.” “Behold, wolves will seize you, hand you over, and bring you before authorities because of my name. Now arm yourselves.” With your own strength? Far from it. “Do not think about what you will say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (ibid. 19–20), because “by the breath of his mouth is all their strength.”

### 9.

These things happened: the Apostles were sent and endured afflictions. Are we now suffering such great things merely by hearing these words as they suffered in sowing them? No. Will our labor, then, brothers, be fruitless? No. I see your crowded gathering, but you also see our sweat. “If we endure, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12).

Behold, those things have happened. From among those sheep sent among wolves we celebrate the memorials of martyrs. [Col. 0290] This place, when the body of the blessed martyr [Note: Cyprian.] was struck down, was full of wolves. One captured sheep conquered so many wolves and filled the place with sheep when the sheep was killed.

At that time the sea raged with the enormous waves of persecutors; the heaven of God advanced onto thirsty land. But now, through what those who broke through the battle line endured, the name of Christ has been glorified. He has even occupied those very powers, walking upon the heads of the swelling floodwaters.

And since these things have happened, now even those who see them—though they do not yet believe—see our assemblies, celebrations, solemnities, and the praises of our God, now manifest and public. Do you think they do not grieve? Do you think they do not rage? But now what was said about them is being fulfilled: “The sinner will see and be angry.” What follows, then, because he will be angry? Do not fear, sheep, the wolf. Do not now fear their threats and snarling. He is angry—but what follows? “He will gnash with his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111:10).

### 10. [verses 7–9]

Because now the sea’s salty water that remains does not dare to rage against Christians, but hidden murmuring gnaws within itself [Note: The editions read *rugit*, “growls”; the manuscripts read *rodit*, “gnaws.”], and the saltiness enclosed within mortal skin growls—see what follows: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin.”

Previously the sea raged with unrestrained waves; now, enclosed within mortal breasts, it is bitter. He did this who conquered in them, who then set boundaries for the sea, so that its waves, returning upon themselves, would be broken. He gathered the sea’s water as into a wineskin: mortal skin conceals bitter thought. For, fearing for their skin, they hold within what they do not dare to release. The bitterness is the same: this is how they hate, this is how they detest. But what then raged openly now rages secretly. What else can I say but what was said: “He will gnash his teeth and waste away”?

Let the Church therefore proceed and walk. The way has been made; our road has been paved and fortified by the Emperor [Note: A *strata* is a public road strengthened with stones or paving.]. Let us burn with zeal on the paths of good works, for this is our walking.

And if at times there arise pressures from temptations where none were expected, now that the waters of the sea have been gathered as into a wineskin, let us understand that the Lord does this for discipline: to shake from us the security that wrongly relies on temporal things [Note: Several manuscripts read *praefidentem*, “wrongly relying”; the editions read *providentem*, “provident.”], and to direct us toward his kingdom with an ordered desire. This desire is brought forth by tribulations beating upon it from every side, so that we may be melodious in the ears of the Lord, like beaten-out trumpets.

For this too is said in the Psalms, that we should praise God with “beaten-out trumpets” (*tubis ductilibus*) (Ps. 97:6). A beaten-out trumpet is extended by the hammer; so the Christian heart is stretched toward God by the blows of affliction.

### 11.

Let us remember, then, brothers, that even in these times, when the sea’s water has been gathered as into a wineskin, God does not lack the means by which to correct us, whenever correction is needed. For this is why the text continues: “Placing the deeps in his storehouses.”

By God’s storehouses he means God’s secret counsel. He knows the hearts of all: what he should bring forth for a time, from where he should bring it forth, and how much power he should grant the wicked against the good—power by which the wicked are judged and the good are instructed. He knows how to do these things, he who “places the deeps in his storehouses.”

Let what follows therefore be fulfilled: “Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Let it not boast in proud joy and reckless exultation, saying, “Now the sea’s water has been gathered as into a wineskin; who can do anything to me? Who will dare to harm me?” Do you not know that he has placed the deeps in his storehouses? Do you not know from where your Father may bring forth what is necessary to scourge you?

For he has the storehouses of the deep for your discipline, by which he may educate you for the storehouses of heaven. Return, then, to fear, you who were already advancing toward security. Let the earth rejoice, but let it also fear. Let it rejoice—why? Because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” Let it fear—why? Because he has gathered the waters of the sea as into a wineskin in order to place the deeps in his storehouses.

Thus what is said elsewhere in brief is fulfilled in it both ways: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11).

### 12.

“Let all the earth fear the Lord; and let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.” Let them not fear another in his place; let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.

A wild beast rages? Fear God. A serpent lies in wait? Fear God. A human being hates you? Fear God. The devil attacks you? Fear God. For all creation is subject to him whom you are commanded to fear.

“For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” This follows in the Psalm. Since he had said, “Let all who inhabit the world be moved by him,” lest a human being turn to fear something else, and, turned away from the fear of God, fear some creature in his place and worship what was made while abandoning the one who made it, he strengthened us in the fear of God, as though saying and addressing us:

“What are you going to fear from heaven, from earth, or from the sea? He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” He who spoke and they were made, who commanded and they were created—when he commands, they move; when he commands, they are still.

And human wickedness may possess its own desire to do harm [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read: “And human wickedness rests, human desire.” A human being may have a personal desire to do harm. We have here restored the reading of the manuscripts.]; but it does not possess power unless he grants it. “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1): this is the Apostle’s definitive judgment. He did not say, “There is no desire except from God.” For there is an evil desire that is not from God. But because that evil desire harms no one unless he permits it, he says, “There is no power except from God.”

Thus God, as man standing before a human being, said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). He was judging, and he was teaching; while he was being judged, he was teaching, so that he might judge those whom he had taught: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.”

What does this mean? Does a human being have no power except when he has received it from above? What of the devil himself? Did he dare to take even one little sheep from the holy man Job unless he first said, “Stretch out your hand”—that is, “Give me power”? He wanted to, but he was not permitted. When permission was given, he was able. It was therefore not he who could, but the one who permitted him.

Thus Job himself, well instructed, did not say—as we are accustomed to remind you—“The Lord gave and the devil took away,” but “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened” (Job 1:11, 21) [Note: The citation as printed appears to be erroneous; the surrounding wording concerns Job 1:21.].

See, therefore, my brothers, while eating with such labor the wholesome and useful bread, see that you fear no one except the Lord. Scripture tells you: fear no other besides him. Therefore, “let all the earth fear the Lord,” who has placed the deeps in his storehouses. “And let all who inhabit the world be moved by him. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

### 13. [verse 10]

But now the evil kings have ceased and have become good; they themselves have believed [Note: The manuscripts read “have yielded.”]. They now bear on their foreheads the sign of Christ’s cross, a more precious sign than any jewel in a diadem. Those who raged have been destroyed.

But who did this? Perhaps you did, so that you may exalt yourself? “The Lord frustrates the plans of the nations; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the plans of princes.”

When they said, “Let us remove them from the earth. There will be no Christian name if we do this. Let them be killed in this way, tortured in that way; let this and that be inflicted upon them”—these things were said, and amid them the Church grew. “He rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the plans of princes.”

### 14. [verse 11]

“But the plan of the Lord remains forever, the thoughts of his heart unto ages of ages.”

This is a repetition of the statement. What he first called “the plan,” he later calls “the thoughts of his heart”; and what he earlier called “remains forever,” he later calls “unto ages of ages.” The repetition is a confirmation.

But do not think, brothers, that when he says “the thoughts of his heart,” God is sitting and considering what to do, searching out a plan for doing or not doing something. Those delays belong to you, human being; his word runs with utmost swiftness. How could there be delay of thought in that word which is one and embraces all things?

Yet they are called God’s thoughts so that you may understand, so that, in proportion to your own capacity, you may dare to raise your heart toward words resembling your weakness; for the reality itself is far beyond you.

“The thoughts of his heart unto ages of ages.” What are the thoughts of his heart, and what is the plan of the Lord that remains forever? Against this plan, “why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things” (Ps. 2:1)? For the Lord rejects the thoughts of the peoples and rejects the plans of princes.

From where, then, does the plan of the Lord remain forever, unless he foresaw and predestined us beforehand (Eph. 1:4)? Who can overturn God’s predestination? Before the foundation of the world he saw us, made us, corrected us, sent to us, and redeemed us. This is his plan, which remains forever; this is his thought, which remains unto ages of ages.

The nations then raged openly, surging and raging; now let them waste away as though enclosed and gathered into a wineskin. They had free license for their boldness; let them now have fierce and bitter thoughts. When could they destroy what he has thought, and what remains forever?

### 15. [verse 12]

What does this mean? “Blessed is the nation” [Col. 0293]. Who is there who would not lift himself up on hearing this? Everyone loves blessedness. This is why human beings are perverse: they want to be evil, but do not want to be miserable. And although misery is the inseparable companion of wickedness, these perverse people not only want to be evil and do not want to be miserable—something impossible—but they want to be evil precisely so that they will not be miserable.

What do I mean by saying, “They want to be evil so that they will not be miserable”? Consider this for a little while in all the people who do evil: they always want to be blessed. He commits theft; you ask why? Because of hunger, because of necessity. Thus, so that he will not be miserable, he is evil; and therefore he is more miserable, because he is evil.

To drive away misery and acquire blessedness, all people do whatever good or evil they do. They always want to be blessed. Whether living badly or living well, they want to be blessed; but what everyone wants does not happen to everyone. For everyone wants to be blessed, but only those who wish to be just will be blessed.

And behold, someone wants to be blessed while doing evil. How? Through money, silver and gold, estates, farms, houses, slaves, worldly display, and fleeting and perishable honor. By possessing something they want to be blessed. Ask, then, what you should possess in order to be blessed.

When you are blessed, you will certainly be better than when you are miserable. But it cannot happen that something inferior makes you better. You are a human being; whatever you desire in order to be blessed is inferior to you. Gold, silver, any bodily things that you yearn to acquire, possess, and enjoy are inferior to you. You are better; you are superior [Note: Nine manuscripts read *potior*, “superior.” Eight others read *potentior*, “more powerful.” The editions read *fortior*, “stronger.”].

And surely you want to be better than you are when you want to be blessed, because you are miserable. For it is certainly better to be blessed than miserable. You want to be better than yourself; and you seek and pursue the means by which this may happen—things inferior to you. Whatever you seek on earth is worse than you.

Everyone wishes this for his friend and urges him in this way: “May you become better; may we see you better; may we rejoice in you as a better person.” What he wishes for his friend, he also wants for himself.

Receive, then, faithful advice. You want to be better than yourself—I know it, we all know it, we all want it. Seek what is better than you, so that through it you may become better than yourself.

### 16.

Now look upon heaven and earth. Do not be so pleased by their beautiful bodies that you want to become blessed through them. What you seek is in the soul. You want to be blessed; seek through your very soul what is better.

Since there are two things—the soul, that is, and the body—and of these two the thing called the soul is better, your body can be made better through what is better, because the body is subject to the soul. Your body can therefore be made better through your soul, so that when your soul has become just, your body too may afterward become immortal. Through the illumination of the soul, the body merits incorruption, so that what is inferior may be restored through what is better.

If, then, your soul is the good of your body, because it is better than your body, when you seek your good, seek what is better than your soul.

But what is your soul? Take care that, perhaps despising your soul and thinking it something worthless and lowly, you do not seek inferior things by which your soul may be made blessed. In your soul is the image of God; the human mind receives it. It received it, but by bending itself toward sin it discolored it [Note: Several manuscripts read “disgraced it.”].

The one who had first formed it came to restore it, because all things were made through the Word, and through the Word this image was imprinted. The Word itself came, so that we might hear from the Apostle: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12:2).

It remains, then, for you to seek what is better than your soul. What will it be, I ask, unless your God? You find nothing better than your soul. For when your nature has been perfected, it will be equal to the angels. Above that there is nothing but the Creator.

Raise yourself toward him. Do not despair; do not say, “It is too much for me.” It is more difficult for you to possess the gold you seek. Even if you want gold, perhaps you will not have it; but when you want God, you will have him. For before you wanted him, he came to you; when your will was turned away, he called you; when you had turned toward him, he terrified you; and when, terrified, you confessed, he comforted you [Note: Five manuscripts read *conterereris*, “you were crushed,” instead of *confitereris*, “you confessed.”].

He who granted you everything, he who made you exist, who together with those who are with you—even the wicked—gives the sun, gives rain, gives fruits, springs, life, health, and such great consolations, reserves something for you that he gives to no one but you. What does he reserve for you except himself?

Ask for something else, if you find something better. God reserves himself for you. Miser, why do you yearn for heaven and earth? Better is the one who made heaven and earth. You will see him himself; you will possess him himself [Note: Eighteen manuscripts read “you will drink him himself.”].

Why do you seek to make that estate yours, and, passing through it, say, “Blessed is the one who owns this possession”? How many people say this as they pass through it! And yet, after saying it and passing through it, they can shake their heads and sigh. But can they possess it?

Desire speaks; iniquity speaks. “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Deut. 5:21). “Blessed is the one whose estate this is, whose house this is, whose field this is.” Restrain iniquity; hear truth: “Blessed is the nation whose”—what? You already know what I am going to say. Desire, then, to possess him; only then will you be blessed.

You will be blessed in this one way: being made better by what is better than you, you will become better. God, I say, is better than you—he who made you. “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is their God.” Love this; possess this. When you want this, you will have it. You will have it freely.

### 17.

“Blessed is the nation whose Lord is their God.” Our God! Whose God is he not? Certainly not everyone’s in the same way. He is more truly ours—ours who live from him as from our bread. Let him be our inheritance; let him be our possession.

Or do we perhaps speak rashly when we make God our possession, since he is Lord and Creator? This is not rashness; it is the affection of desire and the sweetness of hope. Let the soul speak, entirely secure: “You are my God,” who says to our soul, “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3). Let it speak; let it speak securely. It will not wrong him by saying this; rather, it will wrong him if it does not say it.

Did you want to possess trees through which you might be blessed? Hear Scripture speaking about wisdom: “She is a tree of life to all who possess her.” Behold, it says that wisdom is our possession. But lest you think that this wisdom, since Scripture calls it your possession, is something inferior to you, it continues and adds: “And those who lean upon her as upon the Lord are secure” [Note: The editions read “in a secure house.” But several manuscripts more correctly read “secure in the Lord,” or, as others have it, “secure toward the Lord,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint: *epì Kýrion asphalḗs*.].

Behold, your Lord has become for you like a staff. A secure person leans upon it, because it does not collapse. Say, then, securely: “She is your possession, for those who possess her.” Scripture has spoken; it has filled your doubt with confidence [Note: All manuscripts read “it has filled your doubt with confidence”; the editions read “it has fulfilled confidence and removed doubt.”]. Speak securely, love securely, hope securely.

Let these words from the Psalm also be yours: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5).

### 18.

Therefore we shall be blessed by possessing God. What then? Will we possess him, and will he not possess us? Whence, then, Isaiah’s words: “Lord, possess us” (Isa. 26:13, according to the Septuagint)?

He possesses, then, and is possessed, and all this is for our sake. For he is possessed by us so that we may be blessed from him; but he does not possess us so that he may be blessed. He possesses and is possessed [Note: The editions read: “And all this is for our sake. For he is possessed by us so that we may be blessed from him; but he does not possess us so that he may be blessed. He possesses, and we are possessed by him, not for any other reason,” etc.], for no other reason than that we may be blessed.

We possess him, and he possesses us, because we cultivate him and he cultivates us. We cultivate him as Lord God; he cultivates us as his land.

No one doubts that we cultivate him. Who tells us that he cultivates us? The one who says: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer” (John 15:1, 5).

Behold, in this Psalm too both things are said and both are made known to us. It has already said that we possess him: “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is their God.”

Whose is this estate? His. Whose is that one? His [Note: The manuscripts read: “Whose is that one? His whose this one is.”]. Whose is this one? Let us speak of God; let us say whose it is. And just as we are accustomed to be answered when we ask about large and pleasant estates and farms, “Some senator owns it; this or that is the name of the owner of this property,” and we say, “Blessed is that man”—so, if we ask, “Whose is this God?” there is a blessed nation whose he is, for the Lord is their God.

And he is not like that senator who possesses his estate but is not possessed by his estate. God is not like that with this nation. Therefore, in order that we may belong to him, we must labor; but they possess one another.

You have heard that the nation possesses him: “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is their God.” Hear that he also possesses the nation: “The people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance.” Blessed is the nation in its possession; blessed is the inheritance in its possessor—the people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance.

### 19. [verse 13]

“From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the children of human beings.” Here understand “all” in such a way that you take it to mean all of that nation [Note: The editions read “nations”; the manuscripts more correctly read “nation.”] who hold that inheritance, or who are themselves that inheritance [Note: Several manuscripts read “they are all, and all are his.”]. For they are all God’s inheritance.

And from heaven the Lord looked down upon them all, and he saw them, he who said, “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48). For he saw him because he took pity on him.

Thus, when we often ask for mercy [Note: The manuscripts read “asking for mercy”; the editions read “needing mercy.”], we say to someone, “See me.” And what do you say about someone who despises you? “He does not see me.” There is, then, a kind of seeing that belongs to one who shows mercy [Note: The editions add “of the heart,” absent from the manuscripts.], not to one who punishes.

That other seeing is attention directed toward sins. The one who says, “Turn your face away from my sins” does not want those sins to be seen. “Turn away,” he says, “your face from my sins” (Ps. 50:11). What he wants forgiven, he does not want acknowledged.

When, then, he turns his face away from your sins, will he not see you? And how does he say elsewhere, “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 26:9)? Let him turn it away from your sins, but not away from you. Let him see you, take pity on you, and come to your aid.

“From heaven the Lord looked down; he saw all the children of human beings”—those who belong to the Son of Man.

### 20. [verse 14]

“From his prepared dwelling place”—which he prepared for himself—he saw us through the Apostles, saw us through the preachers of truth, saw us through the angels whom he sent to us. All these are his house; all these are his dwelling place, because all these are the heavens that declare the glory of God.

“He saw all the children of human beings; from his prepared dwelling place he looked upon all who inhabit the earth.” These are his; they belong to him [Note: The manuscripts read: “They are his; they are that blessed nation.”]. This is that blessed nation whose Lord is their God; this is the people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance, because it is spread throughout all lands and is not confined to one part.

“He looked upon all who inhabit the earth.”

### 21. [verse 15]

“He who formed their hearts one by one.” By the hand of his grace, by the hand of his mercy, he formed their hearts; he fashioned our hearts; he formed them one by one, giving us individual hearts that nevertheless do not divide unity.

Just as all the members are formed individually, each has its own function, and yet they live in the unity of the body—the hand does what the eye does not, and the ear has a power that neither the eye nor the hand has—yet all work together in unity, and the hand, eye, and ear perform different functions without opposing one another, so in the body of Christ individual people, like individual members, rejoice in their own gifts, because he who chose the people as his inheritance formed their hearts one by one.

For are all Apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? “To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another faith according to the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healings” (1 Cor. 12:8–9, 29–30).

Why? Because “he formed their hearts one by one.” Just as the functions of our members are different, but their health is one, so in all the members of Christ the ministries are different, but charity is one.

“He who formed their hearts one by one.”

### 22.

“He who understands all their works.” What does “understands” mean? He sees more secretly and inwardly. You have it in the Psalm: “Understand my cry” (Ps. 5:2). For something does not need to reach God through voices, as though his ears required them. Hidden sight is called understanding.

He spoke more precisely than if he had said, “He sees all their works,” lest you think that these works are seen in the way you see a human being’s work. A human being sees a human deed through the movement of the person’s body [Note: The editions read, “A human being sees a human deed through the movement of his body.” Several manuscripts read, “through his moving body.”]; but God sees in the heart.

Because, then, he sees inwardly, it is said, “He understands all their works.” Two people give to the poor. One seeks a heavenly reward for himself; the other seeks human praise. You see one action in the two, but God understands two things. For he understands within and recognizes within; he sees their ends and sees their very intentions.

“He who understands all their works.”

### 23. [verse 16]

“The king is not saved by the multitude of his army.” All belong to the Lord; let all your hope be in God [Note: The old Colbert manuscript reads: “All [belong] to the Lord; all your hope [is] in God. Let God be your strength.”]. Let God be your hope; let God be your strength; let God be your firmness; let him himself be your prayer [Note: Most manuscripts read *exhortatio*, “exhortation,” rather than *exoratio*, “prayer.”]; let him himself be your praise; let him himself be the end in which you rest; let him himself be your help when you labor.

Hear the truth: “The king is not saved by the multitude of his army, nor will the giant be saved by the abundance of his strength.” A giant is some proud person who exalts himself against God, as though he were something in and of himself and through himself. Such a one is not saved by the multitude of his strength.

### 24. [verses 17–18]

But he has a great horse, strong, powerful, and swift. If something should arise, can it quickly free him from danger? Let him not be deceived; let him hear what follows: “A horse is a lie for salvation.”

You understand what is meant by “A horse is a lie for salvation,” do you not? Let your horse not promise you salvation. If it promises it, it will lie to you. If God wills, you will be delivered; if God does not will it, when the horse falls, you will fall more deeply.

Do not think, then, that “A horse is a lie for salvation” means “a lying righteous person is for salvation,” as though the righteous should lie for salvation. It is not written *aequus*, derived from *aequitas*, “a just or equitable thing,” but *equus*, a four-footed animal. The Greek manuscript indicates this: *hippos* [Note: Greek *ἵππος*, “horse.”].

Bad beasts of burden are also rebuked here: people who seek opportunities for lying, while Scripture says, “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7).

What, then, does “A horse is a lie for salvation” mean? The horse lies to you when it promises salvation. Does a horse speak to anyone and promise salvation? No. But when you see a well-formed horse, endowed with good strength and great speed, all these things seem to promise you salvation through it. Yet they deceive you if God does not protect you, because “a horse is a lie for salvation.”

Take “horse” figuratively also as any greatness of this present world, any position of honor upon which you proudly mount. The higher you advance, the more you falsely think yourself not only elevated but also secure. For you do not know how it may cast you down—how much more heavily you will be crushed the higher you were carried.

“A horse is a lie for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved.” From what, then, will it be saved? Not from power, not from strength, not from honor, not from glory, not from a horse. From what, then? Where shall I go? Where shall I find the means of salvation?

Do not search long; do not search far. “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him.” You see that these are the ones whom he looked upon from his dwelling place. “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, who hope in his mercy”—not in their merits, not in strength, not in power, not in a horse, but in his mercy.

### 25. [verse 19]

“To rescue their souls from death.” He promises eternal life. What about in this exile? Does he abandon us? See what follows: “And to feed them in famine.”

Now is the time of famine; afterward will be the time of fullness. He who does not abandon us in the famine of this corruption—how will he satisfy us once we have been made immortal?

But as long as it is the time of famine, we must endure, remain, and persevere to the end. We must now run the whole course, because the road is level and we must consider what we carry.

Perhaps the spectators in the amphitheater are still raging and sitting in the sun. Even if we are standing, we are in the shade, and the things we watch are both more useful and more beautiful [Note: Nearly all manuscripts consistently read forms derived from *exspectare*, “to await”: “let us await,” “let us be awaited,” “awaiting,” “one who awaits,” rather than the forms derived from *spectare*, “to watch,” found in the editions.].

Let us watch beautiful things, and let ourselves be watched by the Beautiful One. Let us watch with the mind those things spoken in the meanings of the divine Scriptures, and rejoice in such a spectacle.
