But who is our spectator? “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, who hope in his mercy,” so that he may rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine.

### 26. [verse 20]

But because of the endurance required by our exile, as long as there is famine, and because we await refreshment on the road lest we fail [Note: Several manuscripts read *reficientes*, “refreshing [ourselves],”], what is imposed upon us, or what must we profess? [Note: The editions read: “as long as there is famine, let us await refreshment on the road lest we fail. What does he impose upon us?”] “Our soul will patiently wait for the Lord.”

It will await securely the one who mercifully promises and mercifully [Note: In several manuscripts this second “mercifully” is absent.] and truthfully fulfills. And until he fulfills his promise, what should we do? “Our soul will patiently wait for the Lord.”

But what if we do not endure in that very patience? On the contrary, we certainly will endure: “For he is our helper and our protector.” He helps in battle; he protects from the heat. He does not abandon you. Endure; persevere. “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

### 27. [verse 21]

And what will happen to you when you have persevered, when you have been patient, when you have reached the end? What will be yours? For what reward do you endure? Why do you suffer so many hardships for so long?

“For our heart will rejoice in him, and in his holy name we have hoped.” Hope here, so that you may rejoice there; hunger and thirst here, so that you may feast there.

28. [verse 22.] He has exhorted us concerning everything, filled us with the joy of hope, and set before us what we should love, and in whom alone and concerning whom alone we should place our confidence. After this comes a brief and saving prayer: “Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us.” And on what merit? “As we have hoped in you.”

I have been burdensome to some—I realize it; and I have also brought my discourse to an end rather quickly for some—and I realize that as well. Let the weak forgive the stronger, and let the stronger pray for the weak. Let us all be members in one body, receiving vitality from our Head; in him is our hope, and in him is our strength.

Let us not hesitate to ask mercy of the Lord our God; he positively wishes to be asked. For he will not be disturbed when he is asked, nor will he be constrained, as one from whom you request what he does not have, or what he has only in small measure and fears to give lest he have less. Do you wish to know how God dispenses mercy to you? Dispense love yourself; let us see whether there is any limit while you dispense it. How great, then, must be the wealth at the summit itself, if it can be so great even in its image?

29. Therefore, brothers, we chiefly exhort you to this love—not only toward yourselves, but also toward those who are outside: whether they are still pagans, not yet believing in Christ, or whether they are separated from us, confessing the Head with us but separated from the body [Note: [Col. 0299] The Donatists.].

Let us grieve for them, brothers, as for our brothers. Whether they wish it or not, they are our brothers. They will cease to be our brothers only if they cease to say, “Our Father” (Matt. 6:9). The prophet said concerning certain people: “To those who say to you, ‘You are not our brothers,’ say, ‘You are our brothers’” (Isa. 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

Consider of whom he could have been speaking. Surely not of the pagans? No; for according to the Scriptures and the customary language of the Church, we do not call them our brothers. Surely not of the Jews who did not believe in Christ? Read the Apostle, and see that when the Apostle says “brother” without any qualification, he wants no one understood except Christians: “But if the brother or sister is not subject in such matters,” he says (1 Cor. 7:15). Speaking of marriage, he called a Christian man or woman “brother” or “sister.” Again he says: “But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother?” (Rom. 14:10). And elsewhere: “But you do injustice and defraud, and this to your brothers” (1 Cor. 6:8).

These people, then, who say, “You are not our brothers,” call us pagans. For this reason they also wish to rebaptize us, saying that we do not possess what they give. From this their error follows: they deny that we are their brothers. But why did the prophet say to us, “You say to them, ‘You are our brothers,’” unless because we recognize in them something that we do not repeat? They, therefore, by not acknowledging our baptism, deny that we are brothers; but we, by not repeating theirs and by acknowledging our own, say to them: “You are our brothers.”

Let them say: “Why do you seek us? What do you want from us?” Let us reply: “You are our brothers.” Let them say: “Go away from us; we have no relationship with you.” We certainly have a relationship with you: we confess one Christ; we must be in one body, under one Head.

“What, then, are you seeking from me?” he says. “If I have perished?” What great absurdity, what great madness! “Why are you seeking me, if I have perished?” Why would I seek you, unless because you have perished? “If, then, I have perished,” he says, “how am I your brother?” So that it may be said of you: “Your brother was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

Therefore we appeal to you, brothers, by the very depths of love, whose milk nourishes us and whose bread strengthens us; by Christ our Lord, by his gentleness, we appeal to you. It is time for us to show them great love and abundant mercy by praying to God for them, so that at some point he may grant them sound understanding [Col. 0300], so that they may recover their senses [Note: [Col. 0300] Most manuscripts read “may look back.”], and see that they have absolutely nothing to say against the truth. Nothing remains to them except the weakness of their hostility, which is all the more feeble the more strength it imagines itself to possess.

For the weak, for those wise according to the flesh, for the merely natural and carnal—for our brothers nevertheless—who celebrate the same sacraments, though not with us, yet the same; who answer the one “Amen,” though not with us, yet the one “Amen”: pour out to God on their behalf the innermost depths of your love [Note: [Col. 0300] This reading is found with almost no difference in most manuscripts. The editions, however, read as follows: “though not with us the same, yet answering one Amen; though not with us one Amen; we exhort you to pour out from the innermost depths of your love prayers to God for them.”].

For we have done something for their salvation [Note: [Col. 0300] Fifteen manuscripts read, “we are doing something in the council.” A smaller number, together with the editions, have “we have done something.” He may be speaking of the conference with the Donatists held at Carthage in the year 411.], in a council whose details there is no longer enough time to explain to you today. Therefore we exhort you to come together tomorrow at the Basilica of the Tricliaria, more eagerly and in greater numbers—for our brothers who are not present now will hear from you [Note: [Col. 0300] Some manuscripts read “Tricilara.” Others read “Tricillara.”].

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 33

## SERMON I, DELIVERED ON SATURDAY

### On the Title of the Psalm

1. This psalm seems to contain nothing obscure in its text, nothing requiring an expositor; but its title makes us attentive and calls for those who knock. Yet, as it is written here, “Blessed is the man who hopes in him,” let us all hope that he will open to those who knock. For he would not exhort us to knock if he did not wish to open to those who knock (Matt. 7:7).

If it sometimes happens that someone who had determined always to keep the door closed, compelled by annoyance, rises and opens to the hand of one knocking contrary to his intention, so that he does not have to endure the person knocking for so long (Luke 11:8), how much more ought we to hope that he will open more quickly who says, “Knock, and it will be opened to you”?

I am now knocking upon the Lord God with the intention of my heart, asking him to deign to reveal this mystery to us. Let Your Charity knock with me through your desire to hear and through your humility in praying for us. For, as must be confessed, this is a secret and great mystery.

2. The title of the psalm reads as follows: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he went away.” We search the Scriptures, according to the events recorded for us concerning David, to discover when this happened, just as we find the title of the psalm, “When David fled from the face of Absalom his son” (Ps. 3:1). For we read in the books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0300] The manuscripts read, “For we read in the books of Kings.” They do not usually add “books.”], and we find when David fled from the face of his son Absalom (2 Sam. 15:14). It is entirely true: the event occurred, and what occurred was written down. Although the title of the psalm has thus been written in a mystical sense, it nevertheless derives from an event that took place.

So I believe that what is written here, “When he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he went away,” was also written in the books of Kings, where everything relating to David’s deeds has been recorded. But we do not find this, although we do find something from which it appears that this was drawn.

For it is written that when David was fleeing from Saul his persecutor, he went to Achish, king of Gath—that is, to the king of a certain people neighboring the kingdom of the Jews. There he hid in order to escape Saul’s persecution. His glory, however, was still recent; because of a good deed he had incurred envy when he killed Goliath and, in a single battle, won glory and security for both the king and the people.

When Saul was in turmoil as Goliath challenged him, after Goliath had been struck down, he began to regard as an enemy the one by whose hand he had killed the enemy, and he envied David’s glory—especially because the people, filled with exultation and already forming a chorus, had sung David’s glory: “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”

Moved by this, because a young man had begun to acquire greater glory through a single battle and was already being preferred to the king in everyone’s praises—as envy’s pestilence and worldly pride dictate—he began to envy David and persecute him.

Then David, as I said, had gone to the king of Gath, whose name was Achish. The king himself was informed that he had with him the man who had begun to enjoy great glory among the Jewish people, and he was told: “Is this not David, for whom the Israelite women formed a chorus, saying, ‘Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

If Saul had begun to envy him because of this glory, was it not to be feared that the king to whom David had fled might also wish to destroy him? If he kept him safe, he could have a nearby enemy in him. David feared him also and, as it is written, “changed his appearance before them, pretended,” and “played the drum at the gates of the city,” and “was carried in his hands,” and “fell down at the doors of the gate,” and “his saliva ran down over his beard.”

That king, in whose territory David was hiding, saw him and said to his men: “Why have you brought this madman to me? Surely he is not going to enter my house?” And so he dismissed him, driving him away. David then departed unharmed through this representation of madness (1 Sam. 17–19; 21:10–15; 22:1).

Thus, because of this representation of madness, what is written here appears to belong to that historical account: “A psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he went away.” But that man was Achish, not Abimelech.

Only the name seems not to correspond; for the event itself is designated in nearly the same words in the Psalms as it is written in the book of Kings. This should move us all the more to seek the mystery, because the name has been changed. For neither was that done without reason, although the event occurred, since it represented something; nor was this written without reason, with the name changed.

3. You certainly see, brothers, the depth of the mysteries. If it is not mystical that Goliath was killed by a boy, then it is not mystical that David changed his appearance, pretended, played the drum at the gates of the city, fell at the doors of the city and at the doors of the gate, and that saliva ran down over his beard. How could this fail to signify something, when the Apostle plainly says: “Now these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come”?

If the manna signifies nothing, of which the Apostle says, “They ate spiritual food”; if it signifies nothing that the sea was divided and the people led through its midst to escape Pharaoh’s persecution, when the Apostle says, “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea”; if it signifies nothing that, when the rock was struck, water flowed forth, when the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:11, 1–4); if, then, those things signify nothing, although they happened; if, finally, the two sons born to Abraham according to the ordinary order of human birth signify nothing, although the Apostle calls those two sons the two Testaments, the Old and the New, and says, “These are the two Testaments, which are in allegory” (Gal. 4:24)—if, then, those things signify nothing, which you see happened by apostolic authority as mysteries of future realities, we ought also to think that what I recently narrated to you from the book of Kings concerning David signifies nothing.

Therefore, it is not meaningless that the name was changed and that it was said, “before Abimelech” [Note: [Col. 0302] Erasmus and Louvain read, “And that what is written here was said before Abimelech (and they add), ‘there before Achish,’” which is absent from the manuscripts.].

4. Attend with me. For everything I have just said belongs, as it were, to the hand of one who knocks; it has not yet been opened. We knocked when we said these things; you also knocked when you listened to them. Let us continue knocking in prayer, so that the Lord may open this to us [Note: [Col. 0302] The manuscripts read, “praying that he may open,” omitting “the Lord” and “to us.”].

We possess interpretations of Hebrew names. There have been learned men who translated the names for us from Hebrew into Greek, and from Greek into Latin. Consulting these names, we find that Abimelech is interpreted as “My father’s kingdom,” while Achish is interpreted as “How is it?”

Let us attend to these names; from this point the matter begins to be opened to us as we knock. If you ask, “What is Achish?” the answer is, “How is it?” “How is it?” is the expression of one who marvels and does not understand.

Abimelech: “My father’s kingdom.” David: “Strong of hand.” David is a figure of Christ, just as Goliath is a figure of the devil; and the fact that David struck down Goliath signifies Christ, who killed the devil.

But what is Christ, who killed the devil? Humility killed pride. Therefore, when I name Christ, my brothers, humility is especially commended to us. He made the way for us through humility. Because we had withdrawn from God through pride, we could not return to him except through humility, and we had no one to set before us for imitation.

For all human mortality had swollen with pride. And if some humble person in spirit appeared, as the prophets and patriarchs were, the human race disdained to imitate humble human beings. So that human beings would not disdain to imitate a humble human being, God became humble, so that even in this way the pride of the human race would not disdain to follow the footsteps of God.

5. Previously, as you know, the sacrifice of the Jews consisted, according to the order of Aaron, in the victims of animals [Col. 0303]—and this too was in mystery. The sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood, known to the faithful and to those who have read the Gospel, had not yet come into being; that sacrifice is now spread throughout the entire world.

Set before your eyes, then, two sacrifices: that according to the order of Aaron, and this according to the order of Melchizedek. For it is written: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 110:4).

Of whom is it said, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”? Of our Lord Jesus Christ. Who was Melchizedek? The king of Salem. Salem was formerly a city, the one that afterward, as learned men have handed down, was called Jerusalem.

Before the Jews reigned there, then, there was the priest Melchizedek, who is written of in Genesis as “priest of God Most High” (Gen. 14:18). He met Abraham when Abraham had rescued Lot from the hands of his pursuers, struck down those by whom Lot was held, and rescued his brother. After the rescue of his brother, Melchizedek met him.

And Melchizedek was so great that Abraham was blessed by him. He brought out bread and wine, blessed Abraham, and Abraham gave him tithes. Observe what he brought forth and whom he blessed [Note: [Col. 0303] So several manuscripts. The editions read: “Observe what he brought forth to the one whom he blessed. And afterward it was said to him.”].

And afterward it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” David spoke this in the Spirit long after Abraham, but Melchizedek lived in the time of Abraham. Of whom else does he say, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” except of the one whose sacrifice you know?

6. Therefore the sacrifice of Aaron was abolished, and the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek began. So someone changed his appearance. Who is this “someone”? Let him not be an unknown someone: he is known, our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0303] Some manuscripts of good authority read: “Who is this ‘someone’? ‘Someone unknown’ is known. For he is …,” and so forth.].

He wished our salvation to be in his body and blood. But how did he commend his body and blood (Matt. 26:26)? Through his humility. For if he had not been humble, he could neither be eaten nor drunk.

Consider his height: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Behold the eternal food. Angels eat it; the heavenly Powers eat it; the celestial Spirits eat it. As they eat, they are nourished, yet what satisfies and gladdens them remains whole.

But what human being could approach that food? What heart would be fit for that food? It was necessary, therefore, for that table to become like milk and reach little ones. But how does food become milk? How is food converted into milk except by passing through flesh? This is what a mother does. What the mother eats, the infant eats; but because the infant is not yet capable of eating bread, the mother makes that very bread flesh and, through the humility of the breast and the substance of milk, feeds the infant with that bread itself.

How, then, did the Wisdom of God feed us with that very bread? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). See, therefore, the humility: “Man ate the bread of angels,” as it is written, “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 78:24).

That is, man ate the Word by which the angels are fed—the eternal Word, which is equal to the Father—because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped. The angels are nourished by him; but he emptied himself so that man might eat the bread of angels, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:6–8), so that from the cross the Lord’s flesh and blood might be commended to us as a new sacrifice.

“For he changed his appearance before Abimelech,” that is, before the kingdom of his father. The father’s kingdom was the kingdom of the Jews. How was it the father’s kingdom? The kingdom of David, the kingdom of Abraham. For the kingdom of God the Father is more truly the Church than the Jewish people; but according to the flesh, the people of Israel was the father’s kingdom.

For it was said: “And God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32). According to the flesh, then, David is shown to be the Lord’s father; according to divinity, however, Christ is not David’s son but David’s Lord.

The Jews know Christ according to the flesh, but according to divinity they do not know him. Therefore he posed this question to them and said: “Whose son do you say that Christ is?” And they answered: “The son of David.” And he said to them: “How, then, does David in the Spirit call him Lord, when he says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place all your enemies under your feet’? If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?” And they could not answer him (Matt. 22:42–46), because in the Lord Christ they knew only what was visible to the eyes, not what was understood by the heart.

But if they had eyes within, just as they had eyes without, they would understand “son of David” from what they saw outwardly, and “Lord of David” from what they understood inwardly.

7. “Therefore he changed his appearance before Abimelech.” What does “before Abimelech” mean? Before the kingdom of his father. What does “before the kingdom of his father” mean? Before the Jews.

“And he dismissed him, and he went away.” Whom did he dismiss? He dismissed that Jewish people itself and went away. You seek Christ among the Jews now, and you do not find him. From where did he dismiss him and go away? Because he changed his appearance.

For they clung to the sacrifice according to the order of Aaron and did not retain the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek (Heb. 7:11). They lost Christ, and the Gentiles began to possess him, although previously he had not sent heralds to them.

He had sent those heralds to the Jews: David himself, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets. A few among them came to know him, though those few were few in comparison with the many who perished—for they were nevertheless numerous. We read that there were thousands. For it is written: “The remnant will be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

But if you now seek Christians among the circumcised, you do not find them. In earlier times, at the beginnings of the faith, there were many thousands of Christians from the circumcision. Now you seek them, and you do not find them. Rightly you do not find them: “For he changed his appearance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he went away.” And before Achish he changed his appearance, dismissed him, and went away.

The names were changed, therefore, to arouse us through the significance of the mystery conveyed by the change of names, lest we think that only what is found as an event in the books of Kings is narrated or commemorated in the books of the Psalms, and fail to seek there figures of future things, receiving them merely as historical events.

When, then, the names are changed, what is being said to you? Something is enclosed here. Knock; do not cling to the letter, because “the letter kills,” but desire the Spirit, “for the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Spiritual understanding makes the believer safe.

8. Now pay attention, brothers, to how King Achish dismissed him. I said that Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” Recall the Gospel. When our Lord Jesus Christ was speaking about his body, he said: “Unless someone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, he will not have life in himself; for my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:54, 56).

And his disciples, who followed him, were terrified and horrified at his words. Not understanding, they thought that our Lord Jesus Christ was saying something harsh: that they were going to eat the flesh they saw him possessing and drink his blood. They could not endure it, as if they were saying, “How is it?”

Error, ignorance, and stupidity are represented in the person of King Achish. For wherever it is said, “How is it?” there is no understanding; and where there is no understanding, there is the darkness of ignorance.

The kingdom of ignorance was therefore in them, as though King Achish were reigning—that is, the kingdom of error dominated them. But he was saying: “Unless someone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood.” Because he had changed his appearance, this seemed like madness and insanity: to give his flesh to human beings to eat and his blood to drink.

Thus David was regarded as a madman when Achish himself said: “You have brought this madman to me.” Does it not seem insane to say, “Eat my flesh and drink my blood”? And when he says, “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood will not have life in himself,” he seems, as it were, to be out of his mind.

But he seems insane to King Achish—that is, to the foolish and ignorant. Therefore he dismissed them and went away: understanding fled from their hearts, so that they could not grasp him.

And what did they say? They said, as it were, “How is it?”—which is what Achish is interpreted to mean. For they said: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:53). They thought the Lord was mad, did not know what he was saying, and was insane.

But he knew what he was saying in that changing of his appearance. Through what seemed like madness and insanity, he was proclaiming the mysteries: he pretended and played the drum at the gates of the city.

9. We must seek what it means that “he pretended” and “beat upon the doors.” It was not said without reason: “He fell at the doors of the gate.” It was not said without reason: “His saliva ran down over his beard.” These things were not said in vain.

A lengthy discourse should not be burdensome when it is rewarded by understanding [Note: [Col. 0305] So the manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “These things were not said in vain, but they require understanding. The lengthy discourse …”].

You know, brothers, that the Jews themselves, before whom he changed his appearance, dismissed them, and went away, are today at leisure. If those who lost Christ, whom he dismissed and from whom he went away, have an empty leisure, we have a fruitful leisure, so that we may understand Christ, who dismissed them and came to us.

Everything was done with a purpose, and in that madness of David, when it is said that he pretended, played the drum at the gates of the city, was carried in his hands, fell at the doors of the gate, and had saliva running down over his beard, nothing was done in vain.

“He pretended.” What does that mean? He had compassion. What does it mean to have compassion? It means that he sympathized with our weaknesses; and for this reason he wished to assume the very flesh in which he would kill death.

Because he sympathized with us, he is said to have had compassion. For this reason the Apostle reproved those who are hard and without compassion. Rebuking certain people, he said: “Without compassion, without mercy” (Rom. 1:31). Where there is compassion, there is mercy. Where is mercy? He pitied us from above.

For if he had not wished to empty himself, remaining in the form in which he was eternal and equal to the Father, we would always have remained in death. But to free us from eternal death, to which the sin of pride had led us, he humbled himself, becoming subject unto death, even death on a cross.

Therefore he had compassion, because he went as far as death on a cross. And because one who is crucified is stretched out upon wood, while a drum is made when leather—flesh, that is—is stretched out upon wood, it was said that “he beat upon the drum,” that is, he was crucified and stretched out upon wood.

“He had compassion,” that is, he had compassion for us, so that he might lay down his life for his sheep (John 10:15).

“He beat upon the drum.” How? “At the doors of the city.” What are the doors of the city except that which opens so that we may believe in God? We had closed the doors against Christ and opened them to the devil; we had a heart closed against eternal life.

But the Lord our God, because we human beings had closed our hearts against eternal life and could not see the Word whom the angels see, opened the hearts of mortals by the cross. This is what it means that he beat upon the doors of the city.

10. “And he was carried in his hands.” But how could this happen in a human being, brothers? Who can understand it? For who is carried in his own hands? A human being can be carried in the hands of others; no one is carried in his own hands.

We do not find how this can be understood literally in David himself, but we do find it in Christ. For Christ was carried in his hands when, commending that very body of his, he said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26). He carried that body in his hands [Note: [Col. 0306] All our manuscripts read: “He carried it in his hands; this is the very humility …”].

This is the humility of our Lord Jesus Christ; it is greatly commended to human beings. He exhorts us to it, brothers, so that we may live—that is, so that we may imitate his humility—in order to strike down Goliath and, by holding fast to Christ, conquer pride.

“For he fell at the doors of the gate.” What does “he fell” mean? He cast himself down into humility. What does “at the doors of the gate” mean? At the beginning of faith, by which we are saved.

For no one begins except from the beginning of faith, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:8, according to the Septuagint).

We shall come face to face. As it is written: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

We shall see him—when? When these things have passed away. Hear also the Apostle Paul: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Before, therefore, we see face to face the Word whom the angels see, we still need the doors of the gate, at which the Lord fell, humbling himself even unto death.

11. What does it mean that saliva ran down over his beard? In this he changed his appearance before Abimelech—or Achish—and dismissed him and went away. He dismissed those who did not understand. To whom did he go? To the Gentiles.

Therefore let us understand what they were unable to understand. Saliva ran down over David’s beard. What is saliva? Something like the speech of infants, for saliva runs from infants. Were these not like childish words: “Eat my flesh and drink my blood”?

But these childish words concealed his power. For power is signified by the beard. What, then, is the saliva running down over his beard except weak words concealing his power?

I think Your Holiness has understood the title of this psalm. If we now wish to expound the psalm itself, there is a danger that what you have heard may slip from your hearts. We have expounded the title of this psalm in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Since tomorrow is the Lord’s Day and we owe you a sermon, let us postpone it until tomorrow, so that you may also listen willingly to the text of the psalm.

## SERMON II, DELIVERED ON SUNDAY

1. Those of you who were present yesterday, I do not doubt that you remember our promise. It is now time, in the name of the Lord, to discharge what we owe. He inspired us to promise; he will grant us the means to fulfill it, while we always remain debtors in love.

For this is the debt that is always repaid and always owed, as the Apostle says: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. 13:8).

Yesterday we expounded the title of this psalm; because its exposition detained us for a longer time, we postponed expounding the text of the same psalm. Let us therefore hear what the Holy Spirit says through the mouth of his holy Prophet in this discourse of the psalm, and how it corresponds to the title that we discussed yesterday.

Those who were not present yesterday make the same request, as though they too were asking for this debt [Note: [Col. 0307] The editions read, “nevertheless”; several manuscripts read, “as though.”]. But lest, by causing still further delays [Note: [Col. 0307] The editions read, “lest, by making such further delays for others, we defraud those to whom what we owe must now be repaid.” Soon afterward Louvain has, “to whom it has already been repaid.” We follow the manuscripts in both places.], we defraud those to whom what we owe must now be repaid, let those who are present today and were absent yesterday recognize, as far as they can, the matter recalled briefly.

If anything troubles them that they ought to ask about more carefully, they will find our ears open in the name of Christ at other times, so that those ears may not be occupied [Note: [Col. 0307] Erasmus and Louvain read, “so that these people may not now be occupied.” But the manuscripts read, “so that these matters may not be occupied.” Ambrose has, “so that these matters may not now be …,” and so forth.].

2. We said that it is written in the book of Kings that, when David was fleeing from Saul, he wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when his glory had been mentioned there, he pretended madness, lest the same king to whom he had fled should plot something against him out of envy. As though seized by madness, he changed his appearance and, as we read, pretended, played the drum at the gates of the city, was carried in his hands, and fell at the doors of the gate.

King Achish said: “Why have you brought this man here to me? Surely I have no need of a madman?” And so he dismissed him, so that what is written here might be fulfilled: “He changed his appearance, and he dismissed him, and he went away.”

He dismissed King Achish; but here it is said that he changed his appearance before Abimelech, dismissed him, and went away. We said that the names were changed so that the mystery might be revealed, lest, if the same name were repeated in the title of the psalm, it should seem that the title had not prophesied something in a mystery but had merely narrated an event.

Both names, therefore, contain a great mystery. For Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” and Abimelech as “My father’s kingdom.” In the expression “How is it?” ignorance is signified, so that you understand it as the word of one who marvels but does not recognize. In the word “Abimelech,” however, the kingdom of the Jews is signified.

From the person of Christ it can be said to be “my father’s kingdom,” because his father according to the flesh was David, and David’s kingdom was among the Jewish people. Before the kingdom of his father, therefore, he changed his appearance, dismissed him, and went away, because there was a sacrifice according to the order of Aaron, and afterward he himself instituted a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek.

He therefore changed his appearance in the priesthood, dismissed the Jewish people, and came to the Gentiles.

What, then, does “he pretended” mean? He was full of compassion. For what is as full of compassion as the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ? Seeing our weakness, he accepted temporal death with such great dishonor and humiliation in order to free us from eternal death.

And “he beat upon the drum,” because a drum is made only when leather is stretched upon wood. David beat upon the drum, signifying that Christ would be crucified.

He beat upon the drum at the doors of the city. What are the doors of the city except our hearts, which we had closed against Christ, who opened the hearts of mortals through the drum of the cross?

And “he was carried in his hands.” How was he carried in his hands? When he commended that very body and blood of his, he took into his hands what the faithful know; and in a certain manner he carried himself when he said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26).

And “he fell at the doors of the gate,” that is, he humbled himself. For this is what it means to fall as far as the beginning of our faith. The door of the gate is the beginning of faith, from which the Church begins and reaches the vision: when, believing what it does not see, it merits to enjoy what it will see when it begins to see face to face.

This, then, is the title of the psalm. We have heard it briefly; now let us hear the very words of the one who had compassion and beat upon the door of the city.

### 3. [verse 2]

“I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.” Christ says this; let the Christian say it too, because the Christian is in the body of Christ. And therefore Christ became man, so that an angel might be able to be a Christian, who says [Note: [Col. 0309] Some manuscripts read, “an angel who now says.” A few others: “an angel. And what does he say?”], “I will bless the Lord.”

When shall I bless the Lord? When he does good to you? When worldly goods abound? When there is a great abundance of grain, oil, wine, gold, silver, slaves, and livestock; when this mortal health remains unharmed and uncorrupted; when everything that is born grows, nothing is taken away by premature death, complete happiness abounds in the household, and everything flows around you—is it then that you will bless the Lord? No: “at all times.” Therefore bless him both then and when these things, according to the times and according to the scourges of the Lord our God, are disturbed and taken away; when fewer things are born and those already born decay. For these things happen, and poverty, want, labor, grief, and temptation follow. But you who have sung, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth,” bless him when he gives these things, and bless him when he takes them away. For he gives, he takes away; but he does not take himself away from the one who blesses him.

### 4.

But who blesses the Lord at all times except the humble in heart? Our Lord taught this very humility in his body and blood: for when he commends his body and blood, he commends his humility, in that which is written in the account itself, in that apparent madness of David which we passed over: “And saliva was running down upon his beard.” When the Apostle was being read, you heard of those very drops of saliva running down upon the beard. Someone says, “What saliva did we hear about?” Was not the Apostle just read, when he said: “The Jews demand signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom”? It was just read: “But we,” he says, “preach Christ crucified” (for then he was beating the drum), “to the Jews a stumbling-block and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:22–26).

Saliva signifies foolishness; saliva signifies weakness. But if what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings, do not be offended as though by saliva; rather, observe that it runs down upon the beard. For just as weakness is shown by saliva, so strength is shown by the beard. He therefore concealed his strength beneath the body of his weakness: what was weak outwardly appeared, as it were, in the saliva; inwardly, however, divine strength was concealed like a beard.

Humility, then, is commended to us. Be humble if you wish to bless the Lord at all times, so that his praise may always be in your mouth. For Job did not bless the Lord only when everything abounded for him—those things in which we read that he was rich and prosperous: livestock, servants, a household, blessed in his children and in all his possessions. Everything was taken away at one time, and he fulfilled what is written in this psalm, saying: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). There you have an example of one who blesses the Lord at all times.

### 5. [verse 3]

Why, then, does a person bless the Lord at all times? Because he is humble. What does it mean to be humble? Not to wish to be praised in oneself. Whoever wishes to be praised in himself is proud. Whoever is not proud is humble.

You do not wish, then, to be proud? To be able to be humble, say what was said: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the gentle hear and rejoice.” Therefore those who do not wish to be praised in the Lord are not gentle but fierce, harsh, haughty, and proud. The Lord wishes to have tame animals: be the Lord’s animal, that is, be gentle. He sits upon you; he himself guides you. Do not fear that you may stumble and fall headlong. Your weakness is indeed present, but observe who presides over you.

You are the foal of a donkey, but you carry Christ. For he himself came into the city on a donkey’s foal, and that animal was gentle. Was that animal praised? Was it said to the animal, “Hosanna, Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9)? The little donkey carried him; but the one who was carried was praised by those going before and following after. Perhaps the animal said: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the gentle hear and rejoice.”

That donkey never said this, brothers. But let the people who imitate that animal say it, if they wish to carry their Lord. Perhaps the people become angry because they are compared with the little donkey on which the Lord sat, and some proud and haughty people will say to me, “Look, he has made donkeys of us.” Let whoever says this be the Lord’s donkey, lest he be a horse or a mule, which have no understanding. For you know the psalm where it says: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

A horse and a mule sometimes raise their necks and, in their fierceness, throw off their rider. They are subdued by reins, bit, and blows until they learn to submit and carry their master. But before your mouth is struck by the bridle, be gentle and carry your Lord. Do not wish to be praised in yourself; let him be praised who sits upon you, and you will say: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the gentle hear and rejoice.”

For when the ungentle hear this, they do not rejoice but become angry; and they are the very ones who say that we have made donkeys of them. But those who are gentle should deign both to hear and to become what they hear.

### 6. [verse 4]

It follows: “Magnify the Lord with me.” Who is this person who exhorts us to magnify the Lord with him? Whoever he is, brothers, if he is in the body of Christ, he ought to work toward this: that the Lord may be magnified with him. For whoever he is loves the Lord.

And how does he love him? So as not to envy his fellow lover. Whoever loves carnally must love with destructive jealousy. If perhaps he has been able to see naked the woman whom he desired with a corrupt love, does he wish anyone else to see her? He must be wounded by jealousy and envy if another also sees her [Note: [Col. 0310] Most manuscripts read, “If another also wishes to see her.” Supply: “to see her.”]. Thus chastity is preserved if either the one to whom it is permitted sees her and another does not, or if not even he sees her.

The Wisdom of God is not like this. We shall see it face to face; we shall all see it, and no one there will be jealous [Note: [Col. 0310] Lovaniensis: “and no one will be jealous of himself there.” Some manuscripts: “of himself.” Others: “will be jealous there,” with *of himself* omitted.]. It presents itself to everyone, whole and chaste to all. They are changed into it, but it is not changed into them. It is truth itself; it is God himself [Col. 0311].

Have you ever heard, brothers, that our God could be changed? He is truth surpassing all things, the Word of God, the Wisdom of God through whom all things were made. He has his lovers. But what does one who loves him say? “Magnify the Lord with me.” I do not wish to magnify the Lord alone; I do not wish to love alone; I do not wish to embrace alone. For if I embrace him, there is not therefore no place for another’s hands. Such breadth is in Wisdom itself that all souls may embrace it and enjoy it.

And what shall I say, brothers? Should those who love God in such a way as to envy others not blush? Ruined men love a charioteer, and whoever loves a charioteer or a hunter wishes the whole people to love him along with him; he urges them and says: “Love that pantomime with me; love that disgrace with me.” He cries out among the people that disgrace should be loved with him; and a Christian does not cry out in the Church that the truth of God should be loved with him!

Stir up love in yourselves, then, brothers, and cry out to each of your fellow people, saying: “Magnify the Lord with me.” Let this fervor be in you. Why are these things recited and explained to you? If you love God, seize for the love of God everyone who is joined to you, and everyone who is in your household. If you love the body of Christ—that is, the unity of the Church—seize them for enjoyment of it and say: “Magnify the Lord with me.”

### 7. [verse 4]

“And let us exalt his name together.” What does “let us exalt his name together” mean? It means, “as one.” For many manuscripts read: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name as one.” Whether it is said “together” or “as one,” the same thing is meant.

Therefore seize as many as you can—by exhorting, carrying [Note: [Col. 0311] Some manuscripts omit “carrying.” A few have in its place, “by working”], asking, arguing, giving a reason, with gentleness and mildness. Seize them for love, so that if they magnify the Lord, they may magnify him as one.

The party of Donatus also seems to itself to magnify the Lord. What does the whole world offend them? Let us say to them, brothers: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name as one.” Why do you wish to magnify the Lord in separation? He is one; why do you wish to make two peoples for God? Why do you wish to scatter the body of Christ?

Certainly he himself was hanging on the cross when he was beating the drum. While he was hanging there, he gave up his spirit. Those who had hanged him came and found that he had given up his spirit, and they did not break his legs; but they broke the legs of the robbers, who were still alive on the cross (John 19:32–33), so that through that pain they might release them from the torture by hastening their death, as was customary with those who had been crucified.

The persecutor therefore came and found that the Lord had peacefully laid down his spirit, because he himself said: “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18). For whom did he lay down his life? For his entire people, for his whole body.

The persecutor came, then, and did not break the legs of Christ; Donatus came and tore apart the Church of Christ. The whole body of Christ was intact on the cross among the hands of persecutors, but the whole body of the Church is not intact among the hands of Christians.

Let us cry out, then, brothers, with as much groaning as we can, saying: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name as one.” For the Church cries out to them; it is the voice of the Church crying out to those who have cut themselves off [Note: [Col. 0312] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions: “those who have thrown themselves headlong.”].

From what were they torn apart? Through pride. But Christ teaches humility when he commends his body and blood—the matter which, as we have said to Your Holiness, is enacted and celebrated in the text of this psalm: where Christ’s body and blood are commended, where Christ’s humility is commended, which he deigned to assume for us.

### 8. [verse 5]

“I sought the Lord, and he answered me.” Where did the Lord answer? Within. Where does he give? Within. There you pray, there you are answered, there you are made blessed.

You prayed [Note: [Col. 0312] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “You prayed within and were answered.” “Within” is absent from the editions of Amerbach and from the manuscripts], you were answered, you were made blessed; and the person standing beside you does not know. Everything happened secretly, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Enter into your room, shut your door, and pray in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:6).

When, therefore, you enter your room, you enter your heart. Blessed are those who rejoice when they enter their heart and find nothing evil there. Let Your Holiness attend: how those who have bad wives do not wish to enter their homes, how they go out to the marketplace and rejoice; when the hour begins to approach at which they must enter their house, they become sad. For they are about to enter into vexations, murmuring, bitterness, and disorder, because a house is not well ordered where there is no peace between husband and wife; and it is better for such a man to wander outside.

If, then, those are wretched who, when they return to their own walls, fear that they may be overturned by some disturbance among their household, how much more wretched are those who do not wish to return to their conscience, lest they be overturned there by the conflicts of sins!

Therefore, so that you may willingly return to your heart, cleanse it. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Remove from it the filth of desires; remove the stain of greed; remove the decay of superstitions; remove sacrileges and evil thoughts; remove hatred—not only hatred against a friend, but even against an enemy. Remove all these things; enter your heart, and you will rejoice there.

When you begin to rejoice there, the purity of your heart itself will delight you and make you pray. It is like coming to a certain place where there is silence, perhaps rest, where the place is clean, and saying, “Let us pray here.” The orderliness of the place delights you, and you believe that God will hear you there.

If, then, the cleanliness of a visible place delights you, why does the uncleanness of your heart not offend you? Enter; cleanse everything; lift your eyes to God, and he will immediately answer you.

Cry out and say: “I sought the Lord, and he answered me; and he delivered me from all my tribulations.” Why? Because when you have been enlightened, when you have begun here to possess a good conscience, tribulations still remain, since something weak remains until death is swallowed up in victory and this mortal puts on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:54). You must be scourged in this world; you must endure certain temptations and suggestions. God will cleanse everything and deliver you from every tribulation. Seek him alone.

[Col. 0313] ### 9.

“I sought the Lord, and he answered me.” Therefore those who are not answered do not seek the Lord.

Let Your Holiness attend: he did not say, “I sought gold from the Lord, and he answered me”; “I sought old age from the Lord, and he answered me”; “I sought this or that from the Lord, and he answered me.” It is one thing to seek something from the Lord, another to seek the Lord himself.

“I sought,” he says, “the Lord, and he answered me.” But when you pray and say, “Kill my enemy,” you are not seeking the Lord. Rather, you make yourself a judge over your enemy and make your God a torturer [Note: [Col. 0313] A *quaestionarius* is the same as an executioner. Thus an old scholiast on Juvenal, Satire 6, at “There are those who provide annual payments for torturers,” notes: “salaries for torturers or executioners.” And in the Acts of the martyr Marciana, section 3, we read: “The angry judge ordered the virgin dedicated to God, struck on the face by the hands of executioners, to be shut up in the gladiatorial school.”].

How do you know that the person whose death you seek may not be better than you? Perhaps precisely because he does not seek yours. Therefore do not seek something external from the Lord; seek the Lord himself, and he will answer you. Indeed, while you are still speaking, he will say: “Behold, I am here” (Isaiah 65:24).

What does “Behold, I am here” mean? “Behold, I am present. What do you want? What do you seek from me? Whatever I give you is less valuable than I am. Possess me myself [Note: [Col. 0313] Almost all manuscripts read, “you possess me”]; enjoy me; embrace me. You cannot yet possess me wholly [Note: [Col. 0313] The editions read “wholly” in the neuter; most manuscripts read “wholly” in the masculine]; touch me through faith, and you will cling to me”—this is God speaking to you—“and I myself will lay down your remaining burdens, so that you may cling wholly to me when I have transformed this mortal nature of yours into immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:54); “so that you may be equal to my angels” (Matthew 22:30), and may always see my face and rejoice, “and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22). For you sought the Lord, and he answered you, and delivered you from all your tribulations.

### 10. [verse 6]

We said [Note: [Col. 0313] Above, section 6] who the exhorter was: that lover who does not wish to embrace alone what he loves, and says: “Come to him, and be enlightened.”

He says what he himself has experienced. What does a certain spiritual person in the body of Christ say—or even our Lord Jesus Christ himself according to the flesh, the head exhorting the remaining members? “Come to him, and be enlightened.” Or rather, some spiritual Christian invites us to come to our Lord Jesus Christ himself.

Let us come to him, then, and be enlightened—not as the Jews came to him, so as to be darkened. They came to him in order to crucify him; let us come to him in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the crucified one; we are enlightened by eating and drinking the crucified one.

“Come to him, and be enlightened”: this is said to the Gentiles. Christ crucified was among the raging Jews who saw him; the Gentiles were absent. Behold, those who were in darkness have come near, and those who did not see have been enlightened.

How do the Gentiles come near? By following in faith, longing with the heart, and running in love. Your feet are your love. Have two feet; do not be lame. What are the two feet? The two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. With these feet run to God; approach him [Col. 0314]. For he himself urged you to run, and he himself spread his light over you in such a way that you may follow him magnificently and divinely [Note: [Col. 0314] The manuscripts, with great agreement, read: “as he followed magnificently and divinely. And your faces …”].

“And your faces shall not be ashamed.” “Come to him,” he says, “and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be ashamed.”

No face will be ashamed except that of the proud. Why? Because he wishes to be exalted, and when he has suffered insult, disgrace, a worldly downfall, or some affliction, he is ashamed.

But do not fear. Come to him, and you will not be ashamed. Whatever your enemy may do to you, he appears superior to you among human beings; but before God you are superior to him.

“I captured him, I bound him, I killed him.” How superior those who say such things seem to themselves! How superior the Jews seemed to themselves when they struck the Lord’s face, when they spat in his face, struck his head with a reed, crowned him with thorns, and clothed him in a disgraceful garment! How superior they were! And he appeared inferior, because he was falling down at the doorway of the gate; but he was not ashamed. For he was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9).

Therefore, just as the light cannot be confounded, so it does not allow the one it has enlightened to be confounded. Come, then, to him and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be ashamed.

### 11. [verses 7–8]

But someone says, “How do I come to him? I am burdened with so many evils and so many sins; such great crimes cry out from my conscience. How do I dare approach God?”

How? If you humble yourself through repentance.

“But I am ashamed,” you say, “to do penance.”

Then come to him, and you will be enlightened, and your face will not be ashamed. For if the fear of shame turns you away from repentance, while repentance makes you approach God, do you not see that you carry punishment on your face? Your face is ashamed for this reason: it has not approached God. And it has not approached him because it does not wish to do penance.

As the prophet testifies: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord answered him.” He teaches you how you are answered. You are not answered because you are rich. Perhaps you cried out and were not answered; hear why [Note: [Col. 0314] Perhaps: “And.” M.]: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord answered him.”

Cry out as a poor person, and the Lord will answer. And how shall I cry out as a poor person? So that, even if you have something, you do not presume upon your own strength; so that you understand that you are needy; so that you understand that you are poor as long as you do not possess him who makes you rich.

And how did the Lord answer him? “And from all his tribulations,” he says, “he saved him.”

And how does he save from all tribulations? “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them.” So it is written, brothers—not as some corrupt manuscripts have it, “The Lord will send an angel around those who fear him, and will deliver them,” but: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them.”

Who is the angel of the Lord whom he says will encamp around those who fear him and deliver them? Our Lord Jesus Christ himself is called in prophecy “the Angel of great counsel,” the messenger of great counsel. Thus the Prophets called him (Isaiah 9:6, according to the Septuagint).

He, then, the Angel of great counsel—that is, the messenger—will encamp around those who fear the Lord and will deliver them [Col. 0315]. Do not fear, then, that you will remain hidden. Wherever you fear the Lord, that Angel who encamps around you knows you and will deliver you.

### 12. [verse 9]

Now he clearly wishes to speak about that sacrament by which he was carried in his hands [Note: [Col. 0315] Thus the manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “by which he was carried.”]: “Taste and see that the Lord is good” [Note: [Col. 0315] The manuscripts consistently have here and elsewhere: “and see how gracious the Lord is.”].

Does the psalm not open itself [Note: [Col. 0315] Some manuscripts: “Does the Psalm itself open?” Others: “Does the Psalm plainly show?”] and show you that apparent madness and enduring frenzy—that healthy madness and sober drunkenness—of that David who, in a figure, was revealing I know not what, when those speaking on behalf of King Achish said to him, “How is this?” [Note: [Col. 0315] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “who figuratively showed the Lord’s sacrament.” A little later the editions and manuscripts read, “he was carried, when those wretches [stood] before the king”; but in two books the reading followed here was rightly restored.] When the Lord was saying, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6:53–54).

And what did those over whom Achish reigned—that is, error and ignorance—say? “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” If you do not understand, taste and see that the Lord is good. But if you do not understand, you are King Achish. David will change his face, withdraw from you, leave you, and depart.

### 13.

“Blessed is the man who hopes in him.” Why does this need a lengthy explanation? Whoever does not hope in the Lord is wretched. Who is the one who does not hope in the Lord? The one who hopes in himself.

Sometimes, what is worse, my brothers, observe this: people do not wish to hope in themselves but in other people. “So long as Gaius Seius is safe, you can do nothing to me.” And perhaps he is speaking of a man who has already died. In this city he says, “So long as that man is safe,” while perhaps that man is dead elsewhere.

How quickly people say this! Yet they do not say, “I trust in God, because he does not allow you to harm me.” They do not say, “I trust in my God, because even if he permits you to take something of mine, he will not permit you to touch my soul.” But when they say, “So long as that man is safe,” they do not even wish to possess salvation themselves, and they burden those through whom they think they possess salvation.

### 14. [verse 10]

“Fear the Lord, all his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing.”

Many do not wish [Note: [Col. 0315] The editions read, “wish.” The manuscripts read more correctly, “do not wish.”] to fear the Lord for this reason: they fear suffering hunger. They are told, “Do not commit fraud.” And they say, “How will I feed myself? A trade cannot exist without deception; business cannot exist without fraud.”

But God punishes fraud. Fear God.

“But if I fear God, I will have no means of living.”

“Fear the Lord, all his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing.” He promises abundance to the one who trembles and doubts lest, if he should fear the Lord, superfluities abandon him. The Lord fed you when you despised him; will he abandon you when you fear him?

Pay attention, and do not say: “He is rich and I am poor. I fear the Lord; he acquired so much by not fearing him, while I am naked because I fear him!”

See what follows: “The rich have become needy and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.”

If you take this literally, it seems to deceive you [Col. 0316]. For you see many wicked rich people die in their wealth, not having become poor while they lived. You see them grow old and reach the end of life amid great abundance of riches; their funeral procession is celebrated with lavish expenditure; they are brought to the tomb rich, having breathed their last on ivory couches, with the household of their own people surrounding them [Note: [Col. 0316] Thus several manuscripts. The editions read *circumfluente*].

And you say in your heart, if you happen to know some of his sins and crimes: “I know how much this man did. Look, he grew old and died in his bed; his family escorts him, and such a great funeral procession is celebrated. I know what he did. Scripture deceived and misled me, where I hear and sing: ‘The rich have become needy and hungry.’ When was this man needy? When did he hunger?”

“Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm 33:11).

“Every day I rise to the basilica; every day I kneel; every day I seek the Lord, and I have no good thing. This man did not seek the Lord, and he died amid such great blessings!”

The snare of scandal chokes the person who thinks this way. He seeks mortal food on earth and does not seek the true reward in heaven; he puts his head into the devil’s snare, his throat is constricted, and the devil holds him for evil-doing, so that he may imitate the rich man whom he sees dying amid such abundance.

### 15.

Do not understand it in this way, then.

“How should I understand it?”

In spiritual goods.

“But where are they?”

They are not seen by the eyes, but by the heart.

“I do not see those goods themselves.”

The one who loves sees them.

“I do not see justice” [Note: [Col. 0316] Some manuscripts read: “The one who loves justice sees it. I do not see it myself.”].

For it is not gold; it is not silver. If it were gold, you would see it. Because it is faith, you do not see it.

And if you do not see faith, why do you love a faithful servant? Ask yourself what kind of servant you love. Perhaps you have one who is handsome, tall, and well-proportioned, but a thief, a scoundrel, and a cheat. You have another who may be short in stature, ugly in face, and of a dark complexion, but faithful, thrifty, sober.

Consider, I ask you, which of these two you love. If you ask the eyes of the flesh, the handsome unjust man wins with you; if you ask the eyes of the heart, the ugly faithful man wins.

You see, then, that what you wish the other to display—that is, faith—you should display to him as well. Why do you rejoice in the one who displays faith to you, and praise him for goods that are seen only by the eye of the heart?

When you have been filled with spiritual riches, will you be poor [Note: [Col. 0316] In most manuscripts: “And do you praise him? When you have been filled with these goods, which are seen only by the eye of the heart, will you be poor?”]? Was that man rich because he had an ivory bed, while you are poor whose chamber of the heart is filled with such jewels of virtue, justice, truth, love, faith, patience, and endurance?

Display your riches, if you have them, and compare them with the riches of the rich. That man found expensive mules at the marketplace and bought them. If you found faith for sale, how much would you give for it—the faith that God wished you to have freely, while you are ungrateful?

The rich are needy, then; they are needy. And what is more serious, they are needy of bread. Do not perhaps think that they are needy of gold and silver, although they are needy of these too. How much did a certain person possess, and what satisfied him? He died needy because he wanted to acquire more than he possessed [Col. 0317].

They are needy of bread too. Why are they needy of bread? If you do not understand what bread means, he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41); and: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

“But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.” We have already said what good that is.

### 16. [verse 12]

“Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

Do you think, brothers, that I am saying this? Think that David is saying it; think that the Apostle is saying it. Rather, think that our Lord Jesus Christ himself is saying it: “Come, children, hear me.”

Let us hear him together; hear him through us. He wishes to teach, that humble one, that one beating the drum, that one full of affection; he wishes to teach us. And what does he say? “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

Let him teach, then; let us offer our ear, let us offer our heart. Let us not open the ears of the flesh while closing the ears of the heart; but, as he himself said in the Gospel, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15).

Who would not wish to hear Christ teaching through the Prophet? [Note: [Col. 0317] The editions read, “Who knows how to hear?” And shortly afterward, “He asks.” But the Regius, Vatican, and other manuscripts read, “Who would not wish to hear? … He asks.”]

### 17. [verse 13]

“Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days?”

He asks. Does not everyone among you answer, “I do”? Is there anyone among you who does not love life—that is, who does not desire life and does not love to see good days?

Do you not murmur this every day and say: “How long shall we endure these things? Every day things grow worse and worse. In the time of our parents there were happier days; there were better days. If only you asked those very parents, they would similarly complain to you about their own days.”

“Our fathers were fortunate; we are wretched; we have evil days. That man ruled; we thought that when he died some relief might be given, but worse things came.”

“O God, show us good days!”

“Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days?”

Let him not seek good days here. He seeks a good thing, but he seeks it in the wrong region. It is as if you were looking for some just man in a country where he did not live, and someone said to you: “You are looking for a good man; you are looking for a great man. Seek him, but not here. You are looking for him here in vain; you will never find him.”

You seek good days; let us seek them together—but not here.

“But our fathers had them.”

You are mistaken. Everyone here has labored. Read the Scriptures. God wished them to be written for this reason: so that we might be comforted.

In the time of Elijah there was famine; our fathers endured it. The heads of dead animals were sold for gold. People killed their own children and ate them. Two women agreed among themselves to kill their sons and eat them; one killed her son, and they both ate him. The other did not wish to kill her son, and the first woman who had killed hers demanded that she do so. Such a quarrel came before the king; they brought themselves before the king, contending over the killing of their children (2 Kings 6:26–30). May God avert from us the kinds of food that we have read about.

There are always evil days in this world, but there are always good days in God.

Abraham had good days, but inwardly, in his heart. He had evil days when, driven by famine, he changed regions and sought food (Genesis 12:10; 26:1). All sought in this way.

Paul had good days—he who says: “In hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27)?

But let servants not become angry: the Lord himself did not have good days in this world. He endured insults, injuries, the cross, and so many evils.

### 18. [verse 14]

Let a Christian not murmur, then; let him consider whose footsteps he is following.

But if he loves good days, let him hear the one who teaches and says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

“What do you want?”

“Life and good days.”

“Listen and do this: Keep your tongue from evil.”

Do it.

“I do not want to,” says the wretched man. “I do not want to keep my tongue from evil, but I do want life and good days.”

If your worker said to you: “I will destroy this vineyard, and I demand wages from you. You brought me to the vineyard to prune it with that pruning hook; I will cut down all the useful trees and cut off the very trunks of the vines, so that you will have nothing to harvest here. And when I have done these things, you will repay me for my labor”—would you not call him insane? Would you not drive him from your house before he laid his hand on the pruning knife?

Such are those who both wish to do evil and to swear falsely, blaspheme against God, murmur, commit fraud, get drunk, quarrel, commit adultery, use magical bindings, go to fortune-tellers, and see good days.

It is said to such a person: “You cannot seek a good reward while doing evil.”

“If you are unjust, will God also be unjust?”

“What, then, shall I do?”

“What do you want?”

“I want life; I want good days.”

“Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit”—that is, commit fraud against no one and tell lies to no one.

### 19. [verse 15]

But what does “Turn away from evil” mean? Is it enough that you harm no one, kill no one, do not rage, do not commit adultery, do not defraud, and do not give false testimony? “Turn away from evil”: once you have turned away, you say, “I am secure; I have accomplished everything; I shall have life; I shall see good days.” Do not merely turn away from evil; “but do good” as well. It is not enough that you do not strip someone; clothe the naked. If you have not stripped anyone, you have turned away from evil; but you do not do good unless you have welcomed a stranger into your house. Thus turn away from evil in such a way that you do good.

“Seek peace, and pursue it.” He did not say to you, “You will have peace here”; seek it, and pursue it. Where should I pursue it? Where it has gone before. For “the Lord is our peace”: he rose again and ascended into heaven. “Seek peace, and pursue it,” because when you too have risen, this mortal condition will be changed, and you will embrace peace, where no one will trouble you. For perfect peace is there, where you will not hunger. Here, bread makes peace for you: take away the bread, and see what kind of war there will be within your entrails.

How the righteous themselves groan here, brothers, so that you may know that here we seek peace, but shall attain it at the end. Yet let us possess it here in part, so that we may deserve to possess it there in full. What does “in part” mean? Let us be at peace here; let us love our neighbor as ourselves. Love your brother as yourself, and be at peace with him.

There can nevertheless be some quarrels, just as there have been quarrels between brothers and saints—between Barnabas and Paul (Acts 15:39)—but not quarrels that destroy harmony or extinguish charity. For you yourself sometimes resist yourself, and yet you do not hate yourself. Everyone who repents of something quarrels with himself. He has sinned, he returns, and he is angry with himself for having done this or committed that [Note: [Col. 0319] Nearly all manuscripts read, “for my having done this, for my having committed that,” if “or” is not read. “He therefore has a quarrel,” etc.].

He therefore has a quarrel with himself, but this quarrel tends toward harmony. See how he quarrels with himself, and how a certain righteous man says: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord, for I shall yet confess him” (Psalm 42:5). When he says to his soul, “Why do you trouble me?”, it was certainly troubling him. Perhaps he himself wanted to suffer for Christ, while his soul was becoming sorrowful. And he who knew this and said, “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”, did not yet have peace with himself; but in his mind he clung to Christ, so that his soul might follow him and not trouble him.

Therefore seek peace, brothers. The Lord said: “I have said these things to you, so that in me you may have peace. I do not promise you peace on earth” (John 16:33). In this life there is neither true peace nor tranquility. The joy of immortality and the fellowship of the angels are promised. But whoever does not seek that peace while he is here will not have it when he comes there.

### 20. [verse 16]

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” Therefore do not be afraid; labor [Note: Some manuscripts read *laboras* (“you labor”); others *laborans* (“laboring”); one has *laborem* (“labor”).]: the eyes of the Lord are upon you. “And his ears are turned to their prayers.” What more do you want?

If the master of a great household did not hear a servant murmuring in the house, would he not complain and say, “How much we suffer here, and no one hears us!” Surely you do not say this about God: “How much I suffer, and no one hears me”? “If he heard me,” you perhaps say, “he would take away my tribulation. I cry out, and I am afflicted.” Only hold fast to his ways, and when you are afflicted, he hears you.

But he is a physician; you still have some sort of putrefying wound. You cry out, but he is still cutting; he does not remove his hand until he has cut away as much as seems necessary. For a physician would be cruel if he listened to a patient and spared the wound and the putrefaction.

How mothers rub their children in the baths for their health! Do the little ones not cry out in their mothers’ hands? Are those mothers therefore cruel, because they do not spare them or heed their tears? Are they not full of affection? And yet the children cry, and they are not spared. So too our God is full of charity; but for this reason he appears not to hear us: in order that he may heal us and spare us forever.

### 21. [verse 17]

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are turned to their prayers.” Perhaps the wicked say: “Then I can safely do evil, because the eyes of the Lord are not upon me. God now attends to the righteous; he does not see me, and whatever I do, I can do without fear.” Immediately the Holy Spirit, seeing the thoughts of human beings, added and said: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.”

### 22. [verse 18]

“The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations.”

The three boys were righteous: from the furnace they cried out to the Lord, and amid their praises the fires grew cold. The flame could neither approach nor harm the innocent and righteous boys praising God, and he delivered them from the fire (Daniel 3:49).

Someone says: “Behold, these truly were righteous, and they were heard, as it is written: ‘The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their tribulations.’ But I cried out, and he did not deliver me. Either I am not righteous, or I do not do what he commands me, or perhaps he does not see me.”

Do not be afraid. Only do what he commands; and if he does not deliver you bodily, he will deliver you spiritually. He who delivered the three boys from the fire—did he not deliver the Maccabees from the fire? Did they not sing hymns in the flames, and did they not breathe their last in the flames (2 Maccabees 6:3)? Is not the God of the three boys also the God of the Maccabees? He delivered the former, and did not deliver the latter; indeed, he delivered both. But he delivered the three boys in such a way that even the carnal-minded were put to shame; whereas he did not deliver the Maccabees in that way, so that those who persecuted them might proceed to greater punishments, since they thought they had overcome the martyrs of God.

He delivered Peter when the angel came to him while he was in chains and said to him, “Rise and go out.” Immediately the chains fell away, and he followed the angel, and the angel delivered him (Acts 12:7). Had Peter lost his righteousness when he was not delivered from the cross? Was he not delivered then? He was delivered then. Did he live long for the purpose of becoming unrighteous? Perhaps he heard Peter more fully afterward than before, when he truly delivered him from all afflictions. For when he first delivered him, how much did Peter suffer afterward! Later he sent him to the place where he could suffer no evil.

### 23. [verses 19–20]

“The Lord is near to those who have a crushed heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.”

God is exalted; let the Christian be humble. If he wants the exalted God to draw near to him, let him be humble. Great are these mysteries, brothers. God is above all things: you raise yourself up, and you do not touch him; you humble yourself, and he descends to you.

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous.” Does he say, “Let them be Christians and righteous for this reason, and hear my word for this reason, so that they may suffer no tribulation”? He does not promise this; rather, he says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous.”

If they are unrighteous, they may have fewer tribulations; if they are righteous, they have many. But after few or no tribulations, the unrighteous will come to everlasting tribulation, from which they will never be delivered. The righteous, however, after many tribulations, will come to everlasting peace, where they will never suffer any evil.
