“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from all of them.”

### 24. [verse 21]

“The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken” [Note: The same verse is treated in Sermon 1 on Psalm 34, no. 14.].

And this, brothers, we must not understand carnally. Bones are the supports of the faithful. Just as bones provide support in our flesh, so faith provides support in a Christian heart. The patience, therefore, that is in faith is the inward bones. These are what cannot be broken.

“The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken.” If he had said this about the Lord our God Jesus Christ—“The Lord keeps all the bones of his Son; not one of them will be broken”—it would be just as when he was prefigured elsewhere, when the lamb was said to be slaughtered [Note: So several manuscripts read. The editions have: “since the lamb was led to be slaughtered.”], and it was said of him, “Do not break its bone” (Exodus 12:46). This was fulfilled in the Lord: when he hung on the cross, he died before they came to him, and they found his body already lifeless; so they did not break his legs, in order that what had been written might be fulfilled (John 19:33).

But he promised this also to other Christians: “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken.” Therefore, brothers, if we see some holy person suffering tribulations, and perhaps a physician cutting him in such a way, or a persecutor beating him in such a way, that his bones are broken, let us not say, “This man was not righteous, for the Lord promised this to his righteous ones, of whom he said, ‘The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken.’”

Do you want to see that he spoke of other bones—the supports of faith that we have mentioned, namely patience and endurance in every tribulation? These are the bones that are not broken. Listen, and observe what I am saying in the very passion of the Lord.

The Lord was crucified in the middle; beside him were two robbers. One insulted him; the other believed. One was condemned; the other was justified. One received his punishment both here and in the future; to the other the Lord said, “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

And yet those who came did not break the Lord’s bones, but they broke the robbers’ bones (John 19:32). The bones of the robber who blasphemed were broken just as the bones of the robber who believed were broken.

Where, then, is what was said: “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken”? Behold, he to whom he said, “Today you will be with me in paradise”—was he unable to keep all his bones? The Lord answers you: “On the contrary, I kept them. For the support of his faith could not be broken by those blows through which his legs were broken.”

### 25. [verses 22–23]

“The death of sinners is most grievous.”

Pay attention, brothers, because of what we were saying [Note: In very many manuscripts: “not because of what we were saying.”]. Truly great is the Lord, and his mercy; truly he gave us his body to eat, in which he suffered so much, and his blood to drink [Note: The American and Erfurt editions have: “and his true mercy, who gave us.” The Regius and Vatican manuscripts have: “truly, to whom he gave.”].

How are we to regard those who think and say, “That man died badly; he was consumed by beasts. He was not righteous; that is why he perished badly. For he would not have perished [Note: Understood: “if he had been righteous.”].”? Is the man righteous, then, who dies in his own house and in his own bed?

“This,” you say, “is precisely what amazes me, because I knew his sins and crimes, yet he died well, in his own house, within his own doors, without the hardship of travel [Note: The editions have: “he had no hardship of travel, no hardship, and so forth.” The words “he had no hardship” are absent from the manuscripts.], and not even at an immature age.”

Listen: “The death of sinners is most grievous.” The death that appears good to you is most grievous, if you see what is within. You see someone lying outwardly on a bed; do you also see him inwardly carried off to Gehenna?

Listen, brothers, and learn from the Gospel what “the death of sinners is most grievous” means. Were there not two men in this world: a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, and another, a poor man, who lay at his gate covered with sores, while dogs came and licked his sores, and he longed to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table?

Now it happened that the poor man died—and he was righteous—and he was carried by angels into the bosom of Abraham. Someone who had seen his body lying at the rich man’s threshold, with no one to bury him, might have said, “May my enemy die like that; may I see the man who persecutes me die like that.” He curses the body with spittle; the wounds rot; yet the man rests in Abraham’s bosom.

If we are Christians, let us believe. If we do not believe, brothers, let no one pretend to be a Christian. Faith leads us onward. Does a mathematician tell you something, and it is true, while Christ tells you something, and it is false?

But by what kind of death did that rich man die? What kind of death could there be amid purple and fine linen—how sumptuous, how pompous? What funeral rites were there? With how many spices was that corpse buried? Yet when he was in torment in the underworld, he desired that a drop of water be dripped from the finger of that despised poor man onto his burning tongue, and he did not obtain it (Luke 16:19–25).

Learn, then, what “the death of sinners is most grievous” means. Do not question beds spread with costly garments, or flesh wrapped in great wealth, presenting a pomp of lamentation, a household mourning, a crowd of attendants preceding and following when the body is carried out, and marble and gilded memorials.

For if you question these things, they answer you falsely: that the death of many who were not merely sinners but altogether criminal was excellent, since they deserved to be mourned, embalmed, covered, carried out, and buried in such a manner.

But question the Gospel, and it will show your faith the rich man’s soul burning in punishments, helped by none of all the honors and services that the vanity of the living had offered to his dead body.

### 26

But since there are many kinds of sins, and it is difficult—or perhaps impossible in this life—not to be a sinner, he immediately added what kind of sinners have a most grievous death.

“And those who hate the righteous,” he says, “shall offend.” Whom does he mean by “the righteous,” except the one who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5)? Whom does he mean by “the righteous,” except the Lord Jesus Christ, who is also the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2)?

Those, therefore, who hate him have a most grievous death, because they die in their sins: they are not reconciled through him to our God. “For the Lord will redeem the souls of his servants.”

Death must be understood as most grievous or most excellent according to the soul, not according to the bodily insults or honors that human beings see. “And all who hope in him shall not offend.”

This is the measure of human righteousness: however much mortal life may progress—and because it cannot be without sin—it does not offend in this respect, namely, that it hopes in him, in whom there is forgiveness of sins. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 34

## SERMON 1 [Note: Delivered at the time of some council.]

### On the first part of the Psalm

#### 1. [verses 1–2]

Let your Charity know that this Psalm was imposed upon me for exposition by my brothers and fellow bishops, who instructed me to treat it [Note: Nearly all manuscripts add: “let your Charity know this also.”]. They wanted all of us to hear something from it. For we all hear from the one from whom we learn together, and in whose school we are fellow disciples.

Its title does not delay us; for it is brief and, especially for those nourished in the Church of God, not difficult to understand. It has, “For David.” The Psalm, then, is for David. “David” is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.”

The Psalm, therefore, is for the one strong of hand and desirable, who conquered our death and promised us life. He is strong of hand because he conquered our death; desirable because he promised eternal life.

For what is stronger than that hand which touched the bier and raised the dead man (Luke 7:14)? What is stronger than that hand which conquered the world, armed not with iron but pierced with wood? And what is more desirable than the one whom the martyrs, though they did not see him, desired to die for, so that they might deserve to reach him?

The Psalm, then, is for him [Note: The Erfurt and Louvain editions read: “Therefore let us sing to him.” The American edition and the manuscripts read: “The Psalm.”]; let our heart and our tongue sing a worthy song to him—if indeed he himself deigns to grant what we are to sing. No one sings anything worthy to him unless he has received from him the ability to sing.

Indeed, what we are singing now was spoken by his Spirit through his Prophet, and in those words we recognize both ourselves and him. We do him no wrong when we say “ourselves and him,” because, while he was in heaven, he cried out, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), although no one was touching him and we were laboring on earth.

Let us therefore hear his voice, now that of the body, now that of the head. This Psalm invokes God against enemies amid the tribulations of this world. And certainly it is Christ himself: at that time the head was in tribulation, and now the body is in tribulation. Yet through tribulations he gives eternal life to all his members, and by promising it he has become desirable.

#### 2

“Judge, O Lord,” he says, “those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me.” If God is for us, who can be against us? (Romans 8:31).

And how does God grant this to us? “Take up,” he says, “arms and shield, and rise up in my help.” It is a great spectacle to see God armed on your behalf. And what is his shield? What are his weapons? “O Lord,” says this man, who speaks here also elsewhere, “with the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Psalm 5:13).

His weapons, by which he not only protects us but also strikes his enemies—if we make good progress—will be ourselves. For just as we have weapons from him with which to arm ourselves, so he is armed with us. He is armed with those whom he made; we are armed with what we received from him who made us.

The Apostle calls these our weapons in one place: “the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:16–17). He armed us with such weapons as you have heard: praiseworthy and unconquered, unconquerable and splendid—spiritual, certainly, and invisible, because we fight invisible enemies.

If you see your enemy, let your weapons be seen. We are armed by faith in things that we do not see, and we overthrow enemies whom we do not see.

Nevertheless, dearly beloved, do not think that these weapons are arranged in such a way that what is a shield is always a shield, what is a helmet always a helmet, or what is a breastplate always a breastplate. In bodily weapons this is so, although even objects made of iron can be changed, as when a sword becomes an axe. Yet we see that the same Apostle says in one place, “the breastplate of faith” (1 Thessalonians 5:8), and in another place, “the shield of faith.”

Thus faith itself can be both a breastplate and a shield. It is a shield because it receives and repels the missiles of the enemies; it is a breastplate because it does not allow your inward parts to be pierced. These are our weapons.

But what are God’s weapons [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The editions have: “These are our weapons, which are God’s”; this is what we read, and so forth.]? We read somewhere: “Deliver my soul from the wicked, your sword from the enemies of your hand” (Psalm 21:21). What he said above, “from the wicked,” he says in the following verse, “from the enemies of your hand”; and what he said above, “my soul,” he says in the following verse, “your sword”—that is, your sword.

Thus he called his own soul God’s sword: “Deliver,” he says, “my soul from the wicked”; that is, “from the enemies of your hand deliver your sword.” For you take hold of my soul and overthrow my enemies.

And what is our soul, however splendid, however extended, however sharp, however anointed, however wielded with the light of wisdom and the flashing of illumination [Note: The editions have: “however struck with the light of wisdom and the flashing of illumination.” The manuscripts have *coruscatione* (“with the flashing”); some of them read: “however splendid with the light of wisdom, and however wielded with flashing illumination.”]? What is our soul itself, or what can it do, unless God holds it and fights through it? For any sword, however well made, lies useless if it has no warrior.

We said concerning our weapons that they should not be understood as something fixed, so that what is one thing could not also be another. We find the same in God’s weapons. Behold, he called the soul of the righteous God’s sword; again, he says that the soul of the righteous is God’s seat: “the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7).

Therefore he does whatever he wishes with our soul. When it is in his hand, let him use it as he wishes.

#### 3

“Let him rise,” for this is how he was invoked: “let him take up arms and rise in our help.” From where he should rise is also said elsewhere to him in these words: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Psalm 43:23).

When he is said to sleep, we sleep; when he is said to rise, we are awakened. The Lord was also sleeping in the boat, and therefore the boat was tossing, because Jesus was sleeping. For if Jesus had been awake there, the boat would not have tossed.

Your boat is your heart; Jesus in the boat is faith in the heart. If you remember your faith, your heart does not toss. If you have forgotten your faith, Christ is sleeping. Take care, lest shipwreck occur.

Nevertheless, do what remains to be done: if he has fallen asleep, awaken him. Say to him, “Lord, rise up; we are perishing,” so that he may rebuke the winds and tranquility may come to your heart (Matthew 8:24).

For all temptations will depart—or at least will have no power—when Christ, that is, your faith, is awake in your heart.

What, then, does “rise up” mean? Become known, appear, be perceived. “Rise up, then, in my help.”

#### 4. [verse 3]

“Draw out your sword, and shut the way against those who persecute me.”

Who are those who persecute you? Perhaps your neighbor, or someone whom you have harmed, or to whom you have done an injustice, or who wants to take away your possessions, or against whom you preach the truth, or whose sin you rebuke, or whom you injure by living well while he lives badly.

These too are certainly our enemies, and they persecute us. But we are taught to recognize other enemies, against whom we fight invisibly. The Apostle warns us about them when he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—“not against those whom you see, but against those whom you do not see, against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Ephesians 6:12).

When he said “the rulers of the world”—for he was speaking of the devil and his angels—it was necessary to guard against people’s misunderstanding and their thinking that the world is ruled by the devil and his demons.

But because “world” refers to this created order that we see [Note: All our manuscripts omit the words “this created order that we see.”], and because the world is also spoken of in relation to sinners and those who love the world, concerning whom it was said, “and the world did not know him” (John 1:10), and, “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19), the Apostle explained what world these rulers belonged to: “of this darkness,” he says.

“The rulers of the world,” I say, “the rulers of this darkness.” Again, this compels us to understand what he meant by “this darkness.” Of what darkness are the devil and his angels the rulers? Of all unbelievers, of all unrighteous people, concerning whom it was said: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

Finally, speaking of many who came to believe from their number, what does the same Apostle say? “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

Do you not want to be ruled by the devil? Move over to the light. And how will you move over to the light unless he draws out his sword, rescues you from your enemies, and rescues you from those who persecute you?

How does he draw out his sword? Since we have already heard what his sword is—for the soul of the righteous is his sword—let the righteous abound, and the sword is drawn out, and the way is shut against the enemies.

Indeed, while warning us through this drawing out of the sword that we should live righteously, the Apostle says in what follows: “So that the adversary may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us” (Titus 2:8). The way is shut against him, because he cannot find anything to say against the saints.

#### 5

And from where will the righteous come? Or what do the enemies who persecute us say—the invisible enemies? Do these enemies say nothing? [Note: Most manuscripts read instead: “What do those invisible enemies who persecute us say? What do these enemies say? Nothing is suggested to the human heart more insistently by the invisible enemies who attack us than that God,” etc.] The invisible enemies who fight against us suggest above all to the human heart that God is not our helper, so that, by seeking other helpers, we may be found weak and captured by those very enemies.

This, then, is what they suggest. We must be especially watchful against these voices, which are shown in another Psalm: “Many rise up against me; many say to my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God’” (Psalm 3:2–3).

What is said here against these voices? “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation.’” When you have said to my soul, “I am your salvation,” it will live righteously, so that I seek no one besides you for help.

#### 6. [verse 4]

And what follows? “Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and made reverent” [Note: The manuscripts have the wording *requirentes animam meam* (“those seeking my soul”) continuing into the next phrase.]: for they seek it in order to destroy it. If only they would seek it rightly!

In another Psalm he rebuked this in human beings, because there was no one who sought his soul: “Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Psalm 141:5).

Who is the one who says, “There is no one who seeks my soul” [Note: Nearly all manuscripts lack the words “Who is the one who says, ‘There is no one who seeks my soul?’” and have in their place: “that is, who seeks. Who is the one who is crucified? There is no one who says, ‘Could he perhaps be the one…?’”]?

Could it perhaps be the one of whom, long beforehand, it was foretold: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves considered and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 21:17–19)?

All these things were already happening before their eyes, and there was no one who sought his soul.

Let us therefore invoke him, brothers, so that he may say to our soul, “I am your salvation,” and open its ears, so that it may hear him saying, “I am your salvation.”

For he does say it, but some become deaf; and therefore, when they are in tribulation, they listen instead to the persecuting enemies. If something is lacking, if the soul is in difficulty, in want of temporal necessities, it often seeks help from demons; it wants to consult those seized by demons, and seeks diviners [Note: In ancient codices, here and elsewhere, *sortilogos* is consistently written; the vowel *e* has been changed to *o*.].

The persecutors—the invisible enemies—have approached it, entered it, attacked it, taken it captive, and conquered it by saying, “There is no salvation for him in his God.” It has become deaf to the voice saying, “I am your salvation.”

Say to my soul, “I am your salvation,” so that those who seek my soul may be put to shame and made reverent, because you say to it, “I am your salvation.” Let me hear him saying to me, “I am your salvation.” I will seek no other salvation besides the Lord my God.

Salvation is suggested to me from creation; it comes from him. And if I lift my eyes to the mountains, from where my help may come, nevertheless my help comes not from the mountains but from the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Psalm 120:1–2).

In temporal difficulties God helps through a human being; he himself is your salvation. God helps through an angel; he himself is your salvation. Everything is subject to him. For this temporal life he helps one person from one source and another from another; but eternal life he gives only from himself.

Behold, when you are in difficulty, what you seek is not present, but the one whom you seek is present. Seek him who can never be absent. Let what he has given be taken away; is the giver himself taken away? Let what he had given be restored; when those things have been restored, are they themselves riches, and not the one who had taken them away to test you and restored them to console you?

For he consoles us when these things are not lacking. He consoles us as though on the road—but only if we understand that we are on the road—because this entire life, and everything you use in this life, ought to be to you like an inn to a traveler, not like a house to a resident.

Remember that you have already traveled some distance and that some remains; that you have turned aside for refreshment, not for abandonment.

#### 7

There are some who say: “The good, great, supreme, invisible, eternal, incorruptible God will give us eternal life and the incorruption that he promised in the resurrection. But these worldly and temporal things belong to demons and to those powers of this darkness.”

By saying this, when they become entangled in love of these things, they abandon God, as though such things did not pertain to him. They seek through wicked sacrifices, through various remedies, or through some unlawful persuasion of human beings, to provide for themselves what is temporal—money, a wife, children, and whatever else either consoles human life as it passes or impedes it as it journeys.

Against this opinion divine providence kept watch, to show that all these things pertain to God and are in his power—not only the eternal things that he promised for the future, but also the temporal things that he gives on earth to whomever he wishes and whenever he wishes, at the appropriate time, knowing to whom he should give and to whom he should not give, like a physician who knows the illness of the patient better than the patient himself knows it.

To show this, God divided the periods of the Old and New Testaments. In the Old Testament there are promises of earthly things; in the New, of the kingdom of heaven. Most of the commands concerning the worship of God and right living are the same there and here. But because the promise appears to be one thing there and another here, the command of the one who orders and the obedience of the servant are the same, but the reward seems not to be the same.

For they were told to receive the promised land, to rule in it, to overcome their enemies, not to be subjected by them, to have all things abound for them in that land, and to beget children (Exodus 23:25–31). These are earthly promises, but they were nevertheless figurative.

Suppose that some people received these promises just as they were made—and many truly did receive them in this way. The land was given to the children of Israel; riches were given; children were given to barren women and to old women who asked God, relying upon him alone and seeking no other helper even for these things.

They heard the Lord’s voice in their heart: “I am your salvation.” If he is salvation for eternal things, why not also for temporal things?

God demonstrated this in the case of that holy man Job: even the devil does not have the power to take these things away unless he receives it from that supreme power. He could envy the holy man; could he harm him? He could accuse him; could he condemn him? Could he take away anything—not even a fingernail, not even a hair—unless he said to God, “Stretch out your hand” (Job 1:11)?

What does “Stretch out your hand” mean? “Grant authority.” He received it. The devil tempted; Job was tempted. Yet the one tempted conquered, and the tempter was conquered.

For God, who had permitted the devil to take those things away, had not abandoned his servant inwardly; and to overcome the devil himself, he had made the soul of his servant into his sword.

How powerful is this? I am speaking of a human being [Note: These words, “I am speaking of a human being,” are absent from most manuscripts.]. He was defeated in paradise (Genesis 3:6), victorious on the dung heap. There he was defeated by the devil through a woman; here he conquered the devil and the woman.

“You have spoken,” he said, “as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

How well he had heard: “I am your salvation”!

#### 8

“Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and made reverent.”

Consider human beings. “Pray,” he says, “for your enemies” (Matthew 5:44). But here it is prophecy. What are expressed in the form of wishes are explained in the prophetic spirit. “Let this happen and let that happen” means nothing other than “this and that will happen.”

Hear the prophecy, then: “Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and dishonored.” What does “let them be put to shame and made reverent” mean? They will be put to shame and will be made reverent.

For it has happened: many have been salutarily put to shame; many, having come to reverence, have passed from persecuting Christ to the fellowship of his members with devoted piety. This would not have happened unless they had been put to shame and had come to reverence.

Thus he wished them well. But because there are two kinds of those who are overcome—for they are overcome in two ways: either so that they may be converted to Christ, or so that they may be condemned by Christ—the two kinds are also set forth here, obscurely indeed, but requiring an interpreter.

Of those who are converted, understand what is said: “Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and dishonored. Let them be turned backward.” Let them not go before, but follow; let them not give counsel, but receive it.

Peter wanted to go before the Lord when the Lord spoke of his future passion. He wanted, as it were, to give him counsel for salvation—a sick man giving the Savior counsel about salvation. And what did he say to the Lord as he confirmed that future passion? “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be favorable to you; this shall not happen.”

He wanted to go before, so that the Lord would follow. And what did the Lord say? “Get behind me, Satan” (Matthew 16:22–23). By going before, you are Satan; by following, you will be a disciple.

This, then, is also said to them: “Let them be turned backward, and let them be put to shame, who think evil against me.” For once they begin to follow behind, they will no longer think evil, but will desire good.

### 9. [verses 5–6]

What of the others? For not all are overcome so as to be converted and believe: many remain in obstinacy, and many keep in their hearts the spirit of wanting to go ahead [Note: In several manuscripts, *renitendi* (“of resisting”). In others, *retinendi* (“of holding back”).]. Even if they do not bring it forth, they nevertheless travail with it, and whenever they find an opportunity, they give birth to it.

What follows concerning such people? “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind.” “Not so are the ungodly, not so, but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4). The wind is temptation; the dust is the wicked person. When temptation comes, the dust is carried away; it neither stands nor resists.

“Let them become like dust before the face of the wind; and let the angel of the Lord afflict them. Let their way become darkness and slipperiness.” A dreadful way. Who would not fear darkness alone? Who would not avoid slipperiness alone? Where are you going in darkness and slipperiness? Where do you set your foot? These are two great evils of human punishment: darkness is ignorance; slipperiness is lust.

“Let their way become darkness and slipperiness; and let the angel of the Lord pursue them,” so that they cannot stand. For when someone is in darkness and slipperiness and sees that, if he moves his foot, he will slip, while there is no light before his feet, perhaps he does at least this much: he waits until it becomes light. But there is the angel of the Lord pursuing them.

He foretold that these things would happen to them; he did not wish them as though they should happen. Yet the Prophet, in the Spirit of God, also speaks of them in the manner in which God brings them about: by a certain judgment—good, just, holy, tranquil—not disturbed by anger, not by bitter jealousy, not with a mind bent on exercising hostility, but with justice punishing vices. Nevertheless, it is prophecy.

### 10. [verses 7–8]

But from what source do these great evils arise? By what merit? Listen to the merit:

“For without cause they secretly hid from me the destruction of their snare.”

Consider this in our very Head: the Jews did this. They secretly hid the destruction of their snare. From whom did they hide the snare? From the one who saw the hearts of those hiding it. Yet he appeared among them as though he were ignorant, as though he could be deceived, while they were deceived in the very matter in which they thought he was being deceived.

For this reason he appeared to be deceived while living among them: because we were going to live among such people in a way that would certainly expose us to deception. He saw his betrayer, and chose him all the more for the necessary work. From that man’s evil he brought about a great good. Yet he was chosen among the Twelve, so that the small number of twelve would not itself be without an evil member.

This was given as an example of our patience, because it was necessary for us to live among the wicked; it was necessary for us to endure the wicked, whether knowingly or unknowingly. He offered an example of patience, so that you would not fail when you began to live among the wicked.

And since that school of Christ did not fail with twelve members, how much more steadfast ought we to be when those things are fulfilled in the great Church that were foretold concerning the mixture of the wicked? For that school itself did not yet see the seed of Abraham receive what had been promised, nor did it yet see the threshing floor from which the mass that will fill the granary is to emerge. Why, then, should the chaff not be rightly tolerated on it while it is being threshed, until it is cleansed by the final winnowing? For this is what will happen to the wicked, as you have heard.

### 11

And yet what must be done? “Without cause they secretly hid from me the destruction of their snare.” What does “without cause” mean? “To whom I did no evil, to whom I did no harm.”

“They falsely reproached my soul.” What does “falsely” mean? They said things that were untrue and proved nothing.

“Let the snare come upon them which they do not know.” A magnificent retribution, nothing more just. They hid the snare so that I would not know it; let the snare which they do not know come upon them. For I know their snare.

But what snare will come upon them? The one they do not know. Let us listen, lest perhaps he should say that snare: “Let the snare come upon them which they do not know.” Perhaps they hid one snare from him, while another is to come upon them? No. But what? “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Proverbs 5:22). They are deceived by the very thing by which they wished to deceive. They are harmed by the very thing by which they attempted to harm.

For it follows: “And let the capture which they concealed seize them.” It is as though someone prepared a cup of poison for another and, forgetting, drank it himself; or as though someone dug a pit into which his enemy might fall in the darkness, and then, forgetting what he had dug, walked along that road and fell into it first.

Brothers, believe this absolutely; be certain of it. If there is in you a more excellent exercise of prudence, observe and understand this clearly: no wicked person fails first to harm himself.

Think of wickedness as being like fire. You want to set something alight: the thing you bring near burns first; unless it burns, it cannot set anything else on fire. A torch is being used; you bring the torch near so that it may ignite something. Does not the very torch that you bring near burn first, so that it can ignite something else?

Thus wickedness proceeds from you, and whom does it devastate first, except you? Wherever it spreads, it damages a branch; does it not damage the place where it has its root? Indeed, I say that it can happen that your wickedness does not harm another; but that it should not harm you cannot happen.

For what harm was done to the holy man Job, about whom we spoke earlier? As it is said in another psalm, “You have practiced deceit like a sharp razor” (Psalm 51:4). What happens to a sharp razor? Superfluous things—hair—are cut away.

What, then, do you do to the one whom you wish to harm? If the person whom you wish to harm, being wicked, consents with you in evil, it is not your wickedness that will harm him, but his own. But if he himself is free from wickedness within and submits a pure heart to that voice which says, “I am your salvation,” then you attack him from outside but do not conquer the inner person. Yet your wickedness proceeds from your own interior and first makes you empty. You are rotten within, and from there this worm has emerged; within, it has left nothing whole.

“And let the capture which they concealed seize them; and let them fall into the snare itself.” Do not suppose, as perhaps you did a little earlier when you heard, “Let the snare come upon them which they do not know,” that this means some other unavoidable thing coming secretly upon them. Into what, then? Into the very wickedness [Note: Manuscripts read: “Into the very wickedness, I say, which they hid from me,” etc.] which they hid from me.

Was this not what happened to the Jews? Their Lord conquered their wickedness; they were conquered by their own wickedness. He rose for our sake; they died in themselves.

### 12. [verse 9]

What, then, does this mean concerning those who wish to harm me? What concerning me?

“But my soul will exult in the Lord”—as though in the one from whom it had heard, “I am your salvation”; as though it were not seeking other riches from outside, as though it were not seeking to overflow with pleasures and earthly goods, but loving the true spouse freely—not wishing to receive from him something that would give delight, but setting before itself only the one from whom it should receive delight.

For what can be given to me that is better than God [Note: Several manuscripts read: “For what is better than God? Someone says to me, ‘He loves me,’” etc.]? God loves me; God loves you. Behold, he has offered himself: ask for whatever you wish (Matthew 7:7).

If an emperor said to you, “Ask for whatever you wish,” what tribunates and official dignities you would demand [Note: Editions read *comitatusve* (“or countships”). Most manuscripts, however, read *comitivasque*, a word denoting the dignity and rank of a *comes*; it is found fairly often in the Theodosian and Justinian Codes and in Cassiodorus’s *Variae*.]! How many things would you propose to receive and to distribute to others!

When God says to you, “Ask for whatever you wish,” what will you ask for? Examine your mind, bring forth your greed, extend it as far as you can, and enlarge your desire. It is not just anyone but almighty God who has said, “Ask for whatever you wish.”

If you are a lover of possessions, you will want the whole earth, so that all who are born may be your tenants or your slaves. And what will you do once you possess the whole earth? You will ask for the sea, although you will still be unable to live in it. In this greed the fish will surpass you.

But perhaps you will possess islands. Go beyond these as well; ask even for the air, although you cannot fly. Extend your desire all the way to heaven. Say that the sun, moon, and stars are yours, because the one who made all things has said, “Ask for whatever you wish.” Yet you will find nothing dearer, nothing better, than the one who made all things.

Ask for the one who made them, and in him and from him you will have all that he made. Everything is dear because everything is beautiful; but what is more beautiful than he? They are strong; but what is stronger than he? And there is nothing he wishes to give more than himself.

If you find something better, ask for it. If you ask for something else, you wrong him and harm yourself, preferring to him what he made, when he wishes to give you himself—the one who made it.

In this love a certain soul said to him: “Are you yourself my portion, Lord?” (Psalm 72:26)—that is, “You are my portion.” Let those who wish choose what they are to possess; let them make portions for themselves out of things. “You are my portion”; I have chosen you for myself.

And again: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” Let him possess you, so that you may possess him; you will be his estate, you will be his house. He possesses in order to benefit; he is possessed in order to benefit.

Not so that you might benefit him in some way? For I said to the Lord: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Psalm 16:5, 2).

“But my soul will exult in the Lord.” It will delight in his salvation. God’s salvation is Christ: “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30).

### 13. [verse 10]

“All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you?”

Who could say anything worthy concerning these words? I think they should simply be pronounced, not explained. Why do you seek this or that? What is like your Lord? You have him himself before you.

“All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you?” “The wicked have told me of their delights, but they are not like your law, Lord” (Psalm 119:85).

There were persecutors who said: “Worship Saturn; worship Mercury.” “I do not worship idols,” he says. “Lord, who is like you?” They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear (Psalm 115:5–6). “Lord, who is like you,” who made the eye for seeing and the ear for hearing?

“But I do not worship idols,” he says, “because a craftsman made them.” “Worship a tree and a mountain.” Did a craftsman make these too? Here also: “Lord, who is like you?” Earthly things are shown to me; you are the creator of the earth.

And perhaps from this they turn their attention to the higher creation and say to me: “Worship the moon; worship this sun, which by its light, like a great lamp, makes day from heaven.” Here too I say plainly: “Lord, who is like you?” You made the moon and the stars; you kindled the sun, as it is called; you arranged the heavens.

There are many invisible things that are better. But perhaps even here someone says to me: “Worship the angels; adore the angels.” Here too I will say: “Lord, who is like you?” You created the angels themselves. The angels are nothing except by seeing you. It is better to possess you with them than, by worshiping them, to fall away from you.

### 14

“All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you?”

O holy Church, body of Christ, let all your bones say: “Lord, who is like you?” And if the flesh gives way under persecution, let the bones say: “Lord, who is like you?”

For it was said of the righteous: “The Lord loves all their bones; not one of them will be broken” (Psalm 34:20) [Note: Fewer manuscripts read *custodit* (“guards”) rather than *diligit* (“loves”).].

How many righteous people had their bones broken in persecution? Finally, “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17), and Christ “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). But how does he justify except the one who believes and confesses? For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Thus that thief, although he was led from robbery to the judge and by the judge to the cross, was nevertheless justified on the cross itself: he believed with his heart and confessed with his mouth. For the Lord would not have said to an unjust man who had not yet been justified, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Yet his bones were broken.

For when the time came to remove the bodies because the approaching Sabbath was at hand, the Lord was found already dead, and his bones were not broken (John 19:33). But those who were still alive, so that they might be removed, had their legs broken, so that they might die from this pain and be buried.

Were the bones broken only of the one thief who remained ungodly on the cross, and not also of the one who believed with his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation?

Where, then, is what was said, “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be crushed” (Psalm 34:20), unless “bones” in the body of the Lord are understood to mean all the righteous—those firm in heart, strong, and not yielding under any persecutions or temptations so as to consent to evil?

And how could they yield to no temptation when persecutors said: “Here is that god; see what sort of god he is. Let him come and bind you. Look, there is some great high priest here on the mountain. Perhaps you are poor because that god does not help you. Pray to him, and he will help you. Perhaps you are sick because you do not pray to him; pray to him, and you will recover. Perhaps you have no children; pray to him, and you will have them.”

But if this person belongs to the bones in the body of the Lord, he rejects all these voices and says: “Lord, who is like you? Give, if you wish to give, even in this life what I seek; but if you do not wish to, be yourself my life, whom I always seek. If I worship another and offend you, with what face shall I come forth to you? Perhaps I shall die tomorrow; with what face shall I see you?”

His mercy is great: he both admonished us to live well and concealed from us the day of our final death, so that we would not make promises to ourselves about the future. “I act today, and I live; tomorrow I will not act.” But what if tomorrow does not find you?

Say, then, among the bones of Christ: “Lord, who is like you?” “All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you?”

### 15

“Rescuing the poor man from the hand of those stronger than he, and the needy and poor man from those who plunder him” [Note: The better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint, read: “from those stronger than he, and the needy and poor man,” etc.].

The Psalm has been read today up to this point, and it should be expounded up to this point, lest what has been said become tedious while we wish to say more. Let what we have said today be sufficient:

“Rescuing the poor man from the hand of those stronger than he.”

Who is the rescuer, except the one who is strong of hand? That David rescues the poor man from the hand of those stronger than he. For the devil had been stronger in holding you, because the one to whom you consented had conquered you.

But what did the strong-handed one do? “No one enters a strong man’s house to plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matthew 12:29). By his most holy and magnificent power he bound the devil, extending the sword to shut him in, so that he might rescue the poor and needy one who had no helper (Psalm 72:12).

For who is your helper except the Lord, to whom you say: “Lord, my helper and my redeemer” (Psalm 19:14)? If you wish to presume on your own strength, you will fall from the very source of your presumption. If you presume on another’s strength, he wishes to rule, not to help.

He alone, therefore, must be sought: the one who redeemed us, set us free, and gave his blood to purchase them, making his servants into brothers.

## SERMON II, DELIVERED ON THE DAY AFTER THE PRECEDING SERMON

### Concerning the remainder of the Psalm

### 1

Let us turn our attention to the remainder of the Psalm, and let us beseech our Lord and God for sound understanding and for the fruit of right action.

I believe Your Charity remembers how far the exposition proceeded yesterday. Let us take up our beginning today from that very point.

For here we understand the voice of Christ—the voice, namely, of Christ the Head and the body. When you hear “Christ,” do not separate the bridegroom from the bride, and understand that great mystery: “The two shall be one flesh” (Ephesians 5:31). If they are two in one flesh, why should they not also be one in voice?

For the Head did not suffer temptations here while the body does not suffer them. Or was there any reason for the Head to suffer except to provide an example for the body? The Lord suffered willingly; we suffer necessarily. He suffered out of mercy; we suffer by condition. Therefore his voluntary suffering is our necessary consolation, so that when we perhaps undergo such things, we may look upon our Head and, instructed by his example, say to ourselves: “If he suffered, what of us?” And: “As he suffered, so do we.”

However fiercely the enemy may rage, he could reach only as far as the death of the body. Yet he could not extinguish even that body in the Lord, because he rose again on the third day. What happened in him on the third day will happen in our case at the end of the age. The hope of our resurrection is delayed, but surely it is not taken away?

Let us therefore recognize here, beloved, the voices of Christ, and separate them from the voices of the ungodly. For they are the voices of the body suffering persecution, distress, and temptations in this age.

But since many suffer here both for their sins and for their crimes, the cause must be distinguished from the punishment with great vigilance. A criminal can have a punishment resembling that of a martyr, yet have a different cause. There were three on the cross (Luke 23:33): one was the Savior, one was to be saved, and one was to be condemned. Their punishment was equal, but their cause was unequal.

### 2. [verses 11–12]

Let our Head, then, say:

“Unjust witnesses rising up against me questioned me about things I did not know.”

But let us say to our Head: “Lord, what did you not know? Did you really not know something? Did you not know the hearts of those questioning you? Had you not foreseen their deceits? Had you not knowingly handed yourself over into their hands? Had you not come so that you might suffer at their hands? What, then, did you not know?”

He did not know sin. And he did not know this sin—not as though he failed to judge it, but because he did not commit it.

There are expressions of this kind in ordinary speech also, when you say of someone, “He does not know how to stand,” meaning that he does not stand; or, “He does not know how to do good,” because he does not do good; or, “He does not know how to do evil,” because he does not do evil.

What is alien to one’s action is alien to one’s conscience; what is alien to one’s conscience appears also to be alien to one’s knowledge. Thus God is said not to know in the same way that an art does not know defects; and yet defects are recognized and judged through the art [Note: Most manuscripts read: “And it is said, ‘He did not know,’ in the same way that an art does not know defects, and yet defects recognized through the art are avoided.”].

Thus our Head responds to us when we question him, on the basis of the truth of his own Gospel. When we say, “Lord, what did you not know? What could you have been questioned about that you did not know?” he replies:

“I did not know iniquities; I was questioned about iniquities.”

You have this in the Gospel, if you do not believe that I did not know iniquities: I also do not know the iniquitous, to whom at the end I will say, “I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:23).

Did he not know those whom he condemned? Or can he justly condemn unless he is a good knower [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read: “unless the wicked person is known,” or, literally, “unless he is known as evil.”]? And yet the good knower did not lie when he said, “I do not know you.” That is: “You do not fit together with my body; you do not cling to my rules. You are vices” [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read: “you have clung to vices.”]. “But I am the art itself, which has no defect, and in which no one learns anything except not to commit defect.”

“Unjust witnesses rising up against me questioned me about things I did not know.”

What did Christ know so little as how to blaspheme? His persecutors questioned him on this account, and because he spoke the truth, he was judged to have blasphemed (Matthew 26:65).

But by whom? The following words tell us:

“They repaid me evil for good and barrenness for my soul.”

I brought fruitfulness; they repaid me with barrenness. I brought life; they brought death. I brought honor; they brought insults. I brought healing; they brought wounds. And in all the things they repaid, there was certainly barrenness.

He cursed this barrenness in the tree when he sought fruit and found none (Matthew 21:19). There were leaves, but there was no fruit; there were words, but there were no deeds.

Observe the abundance in their words and the barrenness in their actions: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” (Romans 2:21–22). Such were those who questioned Christ about things he did not know.

### 3. [verse 13]

“But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth; and I humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer will return into my bosom” [Note: This same verse 13 is treated above, column 225, no. 21.].

We are indeed taught, brothers, because we belong to the body of Christ and are members of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27), and we are admonished in all our tribulation not to think about how we should answer our enemies, but how we should appease God by praying—and especially how we should not be overcome by temptation. Then, too, we should pray that those who persecute us may be converted to the soundness of righteousness.

There is no greater or better work in tribulation than to withdraw from the noise that is outside and enter into the inner chambers of the mind (Matthew 6:6); there to call upon God, where no one sees the one who groans and the one who comes to his aid; to close the door of that room against every trouble imposed from outside; to humble oneself in confessing sin; to magnify and praise God, both when he rebukes and when he consoles [Note: The editions read “advises.” Some manuscripts, however, read “consoles.”]. This must be held to in every way.

Yet let us speak of this in relation to the body, that is, to ourselves. What of our Lord Jesus Christ? What of this do we recognize in him? When we examine and search the Gospel most carefully, we do not find that the Lord put on sackcloth in any suffering or tribulation of his.

We do read that he fasted after he was baptized; but we hear and read nothing there about sackcloth. He fasted, moreover, not while the Jews were persecuting him, but while the devil was tempting him (Matthew 4:1).

I do not say that the Lord fasted at the time when they questioned him about things he did not know, or when they repaid evil for good by attacking, persecuting, seizing, scourging, wounding, and killing him. Yet, brothers, if with a little pious curiosity we lift the veil and examine the inner parts of this Scripture with the attentive eye of the heart, we find that the Lord did this also.

Perhaps “sackcloth” means the mortality of his flesh. Why sackcloth? Because of the likeness of sinful flesh. For the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3). That is, he clothed his Son in sackcloth, so that from the sackcloth he might condemn the goats.

Not because there was sin—not, I say, in the Word of God, nor even in that holy soul and human mind which the Word and Wisdom of God had joined to himself in the unity of person. Nor was there any sin in the body itself. But there was in the Lord the likeness of sinful flesh, because death comes only from sin (Romans 5:12), and that body was certainly mortal.

For unless it were mortal, it would not die; if it did not die, it would not rise again; if it did not rise again, it would not show us an example of eternal life.

Thus death is called sin because it came about through sin, just as one speaks in Greek of the Greek language and in Latin of the Latin language—not meaning the fleshly organ itself, but what is done through that organ.

The tongue among our bodily members is one among the others, like the eyes, nose, ears, and so forth. But “the Greek tongue” means Greek words—not because the words are the tongue, but because they are words spoken through the tongue.

You say of someone, “I recognized his face,” speaking of a bodily member. You also say, “I recognized the hand of someone absent,” meaning not the hand in the body, but the writing produced by the hand that was in the body.

Thus the sin of the Lord is what was made from sin, because he took flesh from that very mass which had merited death through sin.

To put it more briefly: Mary, from Adam, died on account of sin; Adam died on account of sin; and the Lord’s flesh, from Mary, died in order to destroy sins [Note: Thus Lovaniensis and the majority of manuscripts. Erasmus reads: “Mary, from Adam, died on account of Adam’s sin; Adam died on account of sin,” etc. Two Vatican and Colbertine manuscripts read: “Mary from Adam; Adam died on account of sin,” etc. The Florentine manuscript has finally: “Mary, from the first Adam; the second Adam arose from Mary for the destruction of sins.”].

The Lord clothed himself in this sackcloth. And therefore he was not recognized, because he was concealed beneath sackcloth.

“When they troubled me,” he says, “I put on sackcloth”: that is, “They raged; I remained hidden.”

For if he had not wished to remain hidden, he could not have died, since at one moment he displayed a certain drop of his power—if it may be called even a drop—when they wished to seize him, and at his single question, “Whom are you seeking?” they all went backward and fell (John 18:4, 6).

He would not have humbled such power in his passion unless he had been hidden beneath sackcloth.

### 4

“Therefore I put on sackcloth; and I humbled my soul with fasting.”

Again, if we have understood “sackcloth,” how are we to understand “fasting”? Did Christ wish to eat when he sought fruit on the tree, so that he might eat if he found any (Mark 11:13)? Did Christ wish to drink when he said to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink” (John 4:7), and said on the cross, “I thirst” (John 19:28)?

What did Christ hunger and thirst for except our good works? Because he found no good works in those who crucified and persecuted him, he was fasting: they were repaying the barrenness of his soul.

For what sort of fast was his, when he scarcely found one thief whom he could taste on the cross? The apostles had fled and hidden themselves in the crowd. And Peter, who had promised that he would persevere even unto the Lord’s death, had already denied him three times, had already wept, and still hid in the crowd, still afraid that he might be recognized.

Finally, when they saw him dead, they all despaired even of salvation itself. After the resurrection he found them in their despair, and when he spoke with them he found them sorrowful and mourning, no longer hoping for anything.

Some of them spoke to him in this way when he said, “What are you discussing among yourselves?” They were speaking about him:

“Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem,” they said, “and have you not known what the priests and our rulers did to Jesus of Nazareth, who was powerful in deed and word—how they crucified and killed him? But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:18–21).

The Lord would have remained in a great fast unless he refreshed those whom he was to consume. For he refreshed them, consoled them, strengthened them, and converted them into his body. Thus our Lord was in fasting also in this sense.

### 5

“And my prayer,” he says, “will return into my bosom.”

There is a great bosom in this verse; may the Lord grant that it become penetrable to us. In the bosom a secret is understood.

Indeed, brothers, we too are rightly admonished to pray in our bosom, where God sees, where God hears, where no human eye penetrates, where no one sees except the one who comes to our aid. There Susanna prayed, and although her voice was not heard by human beings, it was nevertheless heard by God (Daniel 13:35, 44).

We are rightly admonished to do this. But in our Lord we must understand something more, because he also prayed.

We do not recognize his sackcloth in the Gospel according to the letter. Nor do we recognize his fasting at the time of his passion according to the letter; indeed, we have explained these things as having been spoken allegorically and by way of likeness, as best we could.

But we heard his prayer even from the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46). Yet even there we were [Note: So the manuscripts. The editions read, “we pray.”].

For when did the Father forsake him, from whom he never departed? We also read that Jesus prayed alone on the mountain, and that he spent the night in prayer; and this even at the time of his passion (Matthew 14:23; Luke 6:12).

“Therefore my prayer will return into my bosom.”

I do not know what better meaning to understand concerning the Lord. For the present, whatever occurs to me—perhaps something better will occur later, either to me or to someone better—I understand “my prayer will return into my bosom” to mean that he had the Father in his bosom.

“For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). He had within himself the one whom he was to beseech; he was not far from him, because he himself had said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

But because prayer belongs more properly to the human being—for insofar as Christ is the Word, he does not pray but hears prayer, and he does not seek help for himself but, with the Father, gives help to all—what does “my prayer will return into my bosom” mean except this: “In myself, as human being, I intercede with divinity in myself”?

### 6. [verse 14]

“As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing; as one mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself.”

He turns his attention to his body. Let us now see ourselves here.

When we rejoice in prayer, when our mind is made serene—not by worldly prosperity but by the light of truth—the one who experiences this light knows what I am saying and sees and recognizes here what was said:

“As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing.”

For the soul is then pleasing to God when it is not set far away. “In him,” he says, “we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28), as toward a brother, a close companion, a friend.

But if it is not such that it can rejoice, shine, draw near, and cling in this way, and if it sees itself far from him, let it do what follows:

“As one mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself.”

“As for our brother, so I was pleasing”: the one drawing near spoke this. “As one mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself”: the one who was distant and far away spoke this.

For what does a person mourn except what he desires and does not have? And sometimes both things occur in one person: at one time he draws near, and at another he becomes distant. He draws near to the light of truth; he becomes distant through the cloudiness of the flesh.

For, brothers, we do not draw near to God, who is everywhere and contained by no place, by physical locations, nor are we removed from him by physical locations. To draw near to him is to become like him; to withdraw from him is to become unlike him.

When you see two things that are nearly alike, do you not say, “This approaches that”? And when things unlike one another are shown to you, even though they are held in the same place and often in the same hand, do you not say, “This appearance is far from that one”? You hold both and place both together, yet you say, “This thing is far from that thing”—not in location, certainly, but in unlikeness.

If you wish, then, to draw near, become like him. If you do not wish to be like him, you will become distant. But when you are like him, rejoice; when you are unlike him, groan, so that the groan may stir desire—or rather, so that desire may stir the groan—and through the groan you may draw near, having begun to become distant.

Did Peter not draw near when he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”? And did that same man not again become distant when he said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen”?

Finally, as to one who was near, what did he say to the one drawing near? “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.” As to one who was becoming distant and unlike, what did he say? “Get behind me, Satan.”

To the one drawing near he said: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” His light illumined you; you shine by his light.

But when he became distant and contradicted the future passion of the Lord, which was to be endured for our salvation, he said: “You do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matthew 16:16–17, 22–23).

Rightly, someone placing both things in the Psalm said: “I said in my ecstasy, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes’” (Psalm 31:23).

He would not have said this in ecstasy unless he had drawn near, for ecstasy is an excess or transcendence of the mind. He poured out his soul upon himself and drew near to God. Then, through a certain cloud and the weight of the flesh, he was cast back to earth; recalling where he had been and seeing where he was, he said: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”

Therefore, “As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing”: may this come to be in us. And when it does not, let this at least come to be:

“As one mourning and grieving, so I humbled myself.”

### 7. [verse 15]

“And against me they rejoiced and gathered together in one.”

They rejoiced; I was sad. But we have just heard in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew 5:5). If those who mourn are blessed, those who laugh are wretched.

“Against me they rejoiced and gathered together”: scourges were gathered against me, and they did not understand. For they questioned me about things I did not know, and they did not know whom they were questioning.

### 8. [verse 16]

[Note: Here he omits the first part of verse 16, which he treats later in *Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 57, no. 20.]

“They tested me and mocked me with mockery.”

That is, they ridiculed me and insulted me. This applies to the Head; this applies to the body.

Brothers, consider the glory of the Church as it exists now; look back at its former reproaches. Consider that Christians were once driven away in every direction and, wherever they were found, mocked, beaten, killed, thrown to wild beasts, and burned, while people rejoiced against them.

What happened to the Head happens also to the body. As it happened to the Lord on the cross, so it happened to his body throughout that persecution which has already taken place; nor do their persecutions cease even now.

Wherever they find a Christian, they commonly insult, harass, mock, and call him dull, senseless, without understanding, and without skill.

Let them do whatever they wish. Christ is in heaven. Let them do whatever they wish. He has honored his punishment; he has now fixed his cross upon the foreheads of all. The ungodly are permitted to insult; they are not permitted to rage as they wish. Yet from what the tongue brings forth, what it carries in the heart is understood.

“They gnashed their teeth against me.”

### 9. [verse 17]

“Lord, when will you look upon this? Restore my soul from their deceits, my only one from the lions.”

For it is slow for us, and this is spoken from our perspective: “When will you look upon this?” That is: “When shall we see vengeance upon those who insult us? When will the judge, overcome by the persistence of that widow, hear her?” (Luke 18:3).

Yet our Judge delays our salvation not from weariness but from love; by reason, not from inability—not because he cannot help even now, but so that the number of us all may be completed to the end.

And yet, out of desire, what do we say?

“Lord, when will you look upon this? Restore my soul from their deceits, my only one from the lions”—that is, my Church from the powers that rage.

[Col. 0339] 10. [verse 18.] Finally, do you want to know what that “single one” is? Read what follows: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, in the great assembly; in a mighty people I will praise you.” Clearly, “in the great assembly I will give thanks to you; in a mighty people I will praise you.” Thanksgiving takes place in the whole multitude, but God is not praised in everyone: the whole multitude hears our thanksgiving, but God’s praise is not found in the whole multitude. For in this entire multitude—that is, in the Church spread throughout the whole world—there are chaff and grain: the chaff flies away, the grain remains; therefore, “in a mighty people I will praise you.” In the mighty people, whom the wind of temptation does not carry away, God is praised. For in the chaff he is always blasphemed. When our chaff is noticed, what is said? “See how Christians live; see what Christians do”; and what is written comes to pass: “For the sake of you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (Isa. 52:5; Rom. 2:24). Unjust and envious person, you inspect the threshing floor, although you are wholly chaff; grains do not readily come before you. Seek, and you will find the mighty people in whom you may praise the Lord. Do you want to find them? Become such a person. For if you are not such, it will be difficult for you not to think everyone is like the person you are: “Comparing themselves with themselves,” the Apostle says (2 Cor. 10:12), “they do not understand.” “In a mighty people I will praise you.”

11. [verses 19–21.] “Let those who unjustly oppose me not rejoice over me”: for they rejoice over my chaff. “Those who hate me without cause”: that is, those whom I have injured in nothing. “And who wink with their eyes”: that is, hypocrites and pretenders. “For they spoke peaceably to me.” What does “winking with their eyes” mean? Declaring by their expression what they do not carry in their heart. And who are those who wink with their eyes? “For they spoke peaceably to me”—[Note: [Col. 0339] Several manuscripts read *pacifica*, “peaceful things.”]—“but they secretly plotted anger.” “And they opened their mouth wide against me.” First, those lions, seeking to seize and devour, winking with their eyes, flattering and speaking peaceful words, were secretly plotting anger. What peaceful things were they saying? “Teacher, we know that you show no partiality and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (Matt. 22:16–18.) “They spoke peaceably to me.” What then? Did you not recognize them, and did their winking eyes deceive you? No, he recognized them; therefore he said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” (Matt. 22:18).

Afterward they opened their mouth wide against me, crying: “Crucify him, crucify him!” They said: “Bravo, bravo! Our eyes have seen it.” This was now their mockery: “Bravo, bravo! Prophesy to us, Christ” (Matt. 26:68). Just as their peace was feigned when they questioned him about the coin, so now their praise was insulting. “They said: Bravo, bravo! Our eyes have seen it”—that is, your deeds, your miracles. “This is the Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0339] Four manuscripts read, “This indeed is the Christ.”] “If he is the Christ, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe in him. He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42). “Our eyes have seen it.” This is everything he boasted of, everything he claimed when he called himself the Son of God (John 19:7). But the Lord, suffering, remained hanging on the cross: he had not lost his power, but was displaying his wisdom. What great thing would it have been for him to come down from the cross, when afterward he was able to rise from the tomb? But he would have seemed to yield to those who mocked him. This had to happen, so that when he rose he might show himself to his own, and not to them, in a great mystery; for his resurrection signified a new life, and the new life is known to friends, not to enemies.

12. [verse 22.] “You have seen, Lord; do not be silent.” What does “do not be silent” mean? Judge. For in one place it is said concerning judgment: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. 42:14.) And concerning the delay of judgment it is said to the sinner: “You have done these things, and I was silent; you thought that I was wicked, that I would be like you” (Ps. 49:21). How is he silent, who speaks through the Prophets, who speaks with his own mouth in the Gospel, who speaks through the Evangelists, who speaks through us when we speak the truth? What then? He is silent with respect to judgment, not with respect to commandment, not with respect to teaching.

The Prophet invokes this judgment of his, in a certain sense, and foretells it: “You have seen, Lord; do not be silent”—that is, because you will not be silent, because you must judge. “Lord, do not depart from me.” Until judgment comes, do not depart from me, as you promised: “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

13. [verse 23.] “Rise, Lord, and attend to my judgment.” What judgment? Because you have been afflicted, because you have been tormented by labors and pains? Do not many wicked people also suffer these things? What judgment? Are you righteous merely because you suffer these things? No, but what does he say? “Attend to my judgment.” How does it continue? “Attend to my judgment, my God and my Lord, to my cause.” Not to my punishment, but to my cause; not to what I have in common with the robber, but to what is meant by: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). For this cause is distinct.

The punishment is similar for good and wicked people. Thus it is not punishment that makes martyrs, but their cause. For if punishment made martyrs, all the mines would be full of martyrs, all chains would drag martyrs along, and all who are struck by the sword would be crowned. Therefore, let the cause be distinguished. Let no one say, “Because I suffer, I am righteous.” For he who first suffered suffered for righteousness; therefore he added this important qualification: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

For many who have a good cause inflict persecution, and many who have a bad cause suffer persecution. If persecution could not be inflicted rightly, it would not be said in the psalm: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. 100:5). Furthermore, brothers, does not a good and righteous father persecute his dissolute son? He persecutes his vices, not the son himself; not what he begot, but what the son added.

Does not a physician who is employed for healing often arm himself with iron? But he uses it against the wound, not against the person. He cuts in order to heal; yet when he cuts the sick person, that person suffers, cries out, resists, and, if perhaps he has lost his mind through fever, even strikes the physician. Nevertheless, the physician does not cease seeking the patient’s health [Note: [Col. 0340] Several manuscripts read, “which he knows must be provided.”]; he does what he knows must be done and pays no attention to the patient’s curses and abuse.

Are not all lethargic patients awakened, lest they be overwhelmed by a heavy sleep unto death? They suffer this at the hands of their own children, whom they themselves begot as their dearest ones; and a son is not dear to a sleeping father unless he is troublesome to him. The lethargic are awakened, the delirious are restrained; yet both are loved.

Therefore let no one say, “I suffer persecution.” Let him not parade his punishment, but prove his cause, lest, if he does not prove his cause, he be counted among the wicked. Thus how watchfully and excellently he commends this here: “Lord, attend to my judgment,” not to my punishments; “my God and my Lord, to my cause.”

14. [verses 24–26.] “Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness.” That is, according to my cause. “Not according to my punishment, but according to my righteousness, Lord my God”; that is, judge me according to this.

15. “And let them not rejoice over me: my enemies.” Let them not say in their heart: “Bravo, bravo, to our soul!”—that is, “We have done what we could; we have killed him; we have taken him away.” Let them not say: “Show that they have done nothing.” Let them not say: “We have swallowed him up.” Therefore the martyrs say: “If the Lord had not been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123:1, 3).

What does “they would have swallowed us” mean? They would have transferred us into their own body. For you swallow what you transfer into your body. The world wants to swallow you; you swallow the world, transfer it into your body, slaughter it and eat it. This is what was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13): kill in them what they are, and make them what you are.

But if, on the contrary, they persuade you to impiety, you will be swallowed by them. You are not swallowed by them when they persecute you, but when they persuade you to become what they are. Let them not say: “We have swallowed him.” You swallow the body of the pagans. Why the body of the pagans? It wants to swallow you; do to it what it wants to do to you.

Perhaps that calf, ground into pieces, put into water, and given to drink, was intended to signify that the body of the impious would be swallowed by Israel (Exod. 32:20). Let those who rejoice over my evils be ashamed and confounded together; let them be clothed with confusion and shame, so that we may swallow them while they are ashamed and confounded. Let those who speak maliciously against me be ashamed; let them be confounded.

16. [verses 27–28.] What are you now, the head together with the members? “Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice”—those who have clung to my body. “And let them always say: May the Lord be magnified, who desire the peace of his servant.” “And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, and your praise all day long.”

And whose tongue can endure meditating on God’s praise all day long? Behold, a somewhat longer sermon has now been delivered, and you are growing weary. Who can endure praising God all day? I will suggest a remedy by which you may praise God all day, if you wish. Whatever you do, do it well, and you have praised God. When you sing a hymn, you praise God. What does your tongue do except praise him, while your conscience also praises him? You have stopped singing the hymn and leave to refresh yourself? Do not become drunk, and you have praised God. You leave to sleep? Do not rise to do evil, and you have praised God. Are you conducting business? Do not commit fraud, and you have praised God. Do you cultivate a field? Do not provoke a lawsuit, and you have praised God. In the innocence of your actions, prepare yourself to praise God all day. [Note: [Col. 0341] Several manuscripts read: “The innocence of your actions prepares you,” and so forth.]

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 35. SERMON DELIVERED, PERHAPS, ON A SATURDAY, from no. 19

[Col. 0342]

1. [verse 2.] Let Your Charity attend for a little while to the text and mysteries of this psalm; and let us run through it, since it is clear in many places. But wherever the obscurity of the matter compels us to linger, you will bear with it for the sake of the benefit of learning.

“The unjust person said within himself that he would commit sin: there is no fear of God before his eyes.” He does not speak of one individual, but of a class of unjust people who oppose themselves by refusing to understand how to live well—not because they cannot, but because they do not want to.

For it is one thing when someone tries to understand something but cannot because of the weakness of the flesh, as Scripture says in one place: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). It is another thing when the human heart acts more destructively against itself, so that it does not understand what it could understand if good will were present—not because it is difficult, but because the will is hostile. [Note: [Col. 0342] Eight manuscripts read *aversa*, “turned away.”]

This happens when people love their sins and hate God’s commandments. For the word of God is your adversary if you are a friend of your iniquity; but if you are an adversary of your iniquity, the word of God is your friend and the adversary of your iniquity. If, then, you hate your iniquity, you join yourself to God’s word; and there will be two against it to destroy it—you and God’s word. For by your own strength you can do nothing; he who sent you his word helps you, and iniquity is conquered.

If you hate it, God dismisses it, and you will be free. But if you love it, whatever is said against it is contrary to you understanding it. Suppose someone asks how the Son is equal to the Father: he believes and seeks to understand, but is not yet able. It is a great matter and requires greater strength in order to be grasped; and faith is the beginning that guards the soul until it grows strong. He is nourished with milk so that he may attain the condition and firmness required for solid food, and may understand: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Before he can understand this, he is nourished in faith; and he tries to understand, so far as God grants.

But does he not understand even with effort: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16)—so that, because you do not want to suffer injustice, you do not commit injustice; because you do not want to suffer deceit and ambush, you do not ambush another?
