When you do not want to understand this, the fault is attributed to your will. Therefore he said: “The unjust person said within himself that he would commit sin”; he resolved to commit sin.

2. But does the person who resolves to sin say this publicly, and not within himself? Why “within himself”? Because no human being sees him. What then? Because a human being does not see him, does God not see him in the very heart where he tells himself to sin? God sees him there.

But what follows? “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” The fear of human beings is before his eyes. He does not dare openly to profess his iniquity, lest he be reproved or condemned by people. He withdraws from the sight of human beings—but where? Into himself. He leads himself inward, and no one sees him. No one sees him where he meditates deceit, ambushes, and sins.

He would not even meditate on these things within himself if he considered that God sees him. But because the fear of God is not before his eyes, once he has withdrawn from the sight of people into his heart, whom is he to fear there? Is God not present there? But the fear of God is not before his sight.

3. He therefore meditates deceit; and what follows? (Perhaps it is hidden from him that God sees there? Indeed, what I began to say is also shown: it is hidden from him, but willingly, because he has acted against himself by refusing to understand.) “For he has acted deceitfully in his sight.” In whose sight? In the sight of the one whose fear is not before the eyes of him who acted deceitfully. “So as to discover his iniquity and hate it.” This man acted so as not to discover it.

For there are people who seem to try to seek out their iniquity, yet fear finding it. If they find it, they are told: “Turn away from it. You committed these things before you knew; you committed iniquity while you were ignorant, and God grants forgiveness. Now you have recognized it; abandon it, so that forgiveness may readily be granted for your ignorance, and you may say to God with an open face: ‘Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance’” (Ps. 24:7).

In this way he seeks it, and in this way he fears finding it: for he seeks it deceitfully. When does a person say, “I did not know that it was sin”? When he sees that it is sin and stops committing the sin that he had committed because he was ignorant. Truly he wanted to know his iniquity in order to find it and hate it.

But now many act deceitfully so as to discover their iniquity—that is, they do not sincerely desire to find it and hate it. Because there is deceit in the very search, there will be a defense of iniquity when it is found. For once he has discovered his iniquity, it is already clear to him that it is iniquity. “Do not commit it,” you say. But the man who acted deceitfully in order to discover it has now discovered it, and does not hate it. What does he say? “How many people do this, and who does not do it? Will God really destroy everyone? Or else: if God did not want these things to be done, would the people who commit them be alive?”

You see that you acted deceitfully in discovering your iniquity. For if you had acted sincerely, not deceitfully, you would already have discovered it and hated it. Now you have discovered it and defend it; therefore you acted deceitfully when you sought it.

4. [verse 4.] “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand, so as to act well.” You see that he attributes this to the will: there are people who want to understand and cannot, and there are people who do not want to understand, and therefore do not understand. “He refused to understand, so as to act well.”

5. [verse 5.] “He meditated iniquity upon his bed.” What does “upon his bed” mean? “The unjust person said within himself that he would commit sin”; what he said above, “within himself,” he says here, “upon his bed.” Our bed is our heart. There we suffer the tumult of a bad conscience, and there we rest when our conscience is good. Whoever loves the bed of his heart should do something good there.

This is the bed where the Lord Jesus Christ commands us to pray: “Enter into your room, and shut your door.” What does “shut your door” mean? Do not expect from God things that are external, but those that are internal: “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:6).

Who is it who does not shut his door? The one who asks great things of God and places all his prayers there in order to receive the good things of this age. Your door is open; the crowd sees you when you pray. What does it mean to shut your door? It means to ask God for what God alone knows how to give you.

What is this for which you shut the door and ask? “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). Perhaps it has not entered your own room—that is, your heart. But God knows what he will give you. When will it be? When the Lord is revealed, when the Judge appears. For what is clearer than what he will say to those placed at his right hand? “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

Those who will be at the left hand will hear these words and groan with fruitless repentance (Wis. 5:3), because while they lived in that way, they did not wish to repent fruitfully. How will they groan? Because there is no opportunity for correction for them. They too will hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). This is the evil thing they will hear.

The righteous, however, will rejoice at the good hearing, for it is written: “The righteous will be in everlasting memory; he will not fear an evil report” (Ps. 111:7). What evil report? The one they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire.”

Therefore God, who can do beyond all that we ask or understand (Eph. 3:20), seeks our hidden groaning, so that we may please him in his sight and not boast before human beings as though by our own righteousness. For the one who wishes to please people by his righteousness—not so that the people who see him may praise God, but with the intention that he himself may be praised—does not shut the door against the noise. His door is left open by that noise, and God does not hear him in the way he wishes to be heard.

Let us therefore labor to cleanse our heart, our bed, so that we may be well there. Your Charity knows how much many people suffer in public—in the marketplace, in quarrels, in disputes, and amid the troubles of business. When someone worn out by business outside hurries home to rest there, he makes an effort to finish quickly the affairs outside and withdraw into the rest of his home. For this reason each person has a home: so that he may rest there.

But if he suffers trouble there also, where can he rest? What then? It is good if at least he has rest in his own home. But if he suffers enemies outside and perhaps a bad wife inside, he goes out into public; when he wishes to rest from what is outside, he enters the house. But when he finds rest neither there nor outside, where will his rest be? At least in the bed of his heart, so that he may withdraw into the inner parts of his conscience.

If there you have perhaps found a spouse who does not cause you bitterness—God’s wisdom—join yourself to her, rest within the room of your heart, and let the smoke of an evil conscience not drive you out.

But this man, in order to meditate deceit, withdrew into the place of which this Scripture speaks, where human beings do not see. There he meditated such things that he could not rest even in his own heart. “He meditated iniquity upon his bed.”

6. “He stood upon every path that was not good.” What does “he stood” mean? He sinned perseveringly. Hence it is said of a certain pious and good man: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. 1:1). Just as that man did not stand, so this man stood.

“But he did not hate wickedness.” There is the end; there is the fruit. If he cannot avoid having wickedness, at least let him hate it. For when you hate it, it scarcely creeps upon you so as to make you do something evil.

Sin exists in the mortal body; but what does the Apostle say? “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). When does it begin not to exist? When what is said is fulfilled in us: “When this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53).

Before this happens, there is a delight in iniquity in the body; but greater is the delight of the pleasure found in the word of wisdom and in God’s commandment. Conquer sin and its will. Hate sin and iniquity, so that you may join yourself to God, who hates it together with you.

Once joined in mind to the law of God, you serve the law of God in your mind. And if in the flesh you therefore serve the law of sin (Rom. 7:25), because certain bodily pleasures exist in you, they will then cease when you no longer fight.

It is one thing not to fight and to be in true and perpetual peace; another thing to fight and conquer; another to fight and be conquered; another not to fight, but to be dragged along. For there are people who do not fight at all, such as the one of whom he speaks here. When he says, “He did not hate wickedness,” how does he fight against what he does not hate? This man is dragged along by wickedness and does not fight.

There are others who begin to fight; but because they rely on their own strength, God shows them that he himself conquers when a person submits himself to God. They are defeated while fighting, and when they seem to have begun to possess righteousness, they become proud and are thrown down. These fight, but are conquered.

Who, then, fights and is not conquered? The one who says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind.” See him fighting [Note: [Col. 0345] After the words “the law of my mind,” Ambrosianus has: “See the law fighting against the law of his mind; see it fighting, but not,” and so forth. Erasmus has: “He sees the law fighting against the law of his mind; he sees it fighting.” Lovaniensis has: “See it fighting against the law of his mind; see it fighting,” and so forth. Here we have followed the manuscripts Regius and Vaticanus.]; but this man does not rely on his own strength, and therefore he will be victorious.

For what follows? “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23–25). He relies on the one who commanded him to fight, and, helped by the commander, conquers the enemy [Note: [Col. 0345] Several manuscripts read: “and, helped by the helper, may conquer the enemy.”]. But this man “did not hate wickedness.”

7. [verse 6.] “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds.” I do not know what mercy of his he means by saying that it is in heaven. For the Lord’s mercy is also on earth. You have it written: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5).

Of what mercy, then, does he speak when he says: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven”? God’s gifts are partly temporal and earthly, partly eternal and heavenly. The person who worships God in order to receive these earthly and temporal things, which are available to everyone, is still, as it were, like an animal. He makes use of God’s mercy, but not of that mercy which is set apart [Note: [Col. 0346] The editions read, “which he will await”; the manuscripts, with broad agreement, read, “which is set apart.”], which will be given only to the righteous, holy, and good.

What are the gifts that abound for everyone? “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). Who does not possess this mercy of God—first, simply to exist, to be distinguished from animals, to be a rational creature capable of understanding God; then to enjoy this light, this air, rain, fruits, the succession of seasons, earthly consolations, bodily health, the affection of friends, and the well-being of one’s household?

All these are good things, and they are gifts of God. Do not think, brothers, that anyone can give them except the one God. Therefore there is a great difference between those who expect these things from the Lord alone and those who seek them from demons, fortune-tellers, or astrologers.

These latter are wretched in two ways: they desire only earthly goods, and they do not ask the one who gives every good thing. Those who desire these good things, wish to be happy in these goods, and ask these things from God alone are indeed better, because they ask God; but they are still in danger.

Someone may say: Why are they in danger? At times they consider human affairs and see that the wicked and unjust possess and abound in all the earthly goods they desire. They think that they have lost the reward of worshiping God because they too possess what the wicked possess, although they worship God and those others do not; or sometimes those who worship God do not possess these things, while those who blaspheme possess them. Therefore they are still in danger. [Note: [Col. 0346] The editions read, “or they themselves do not possess them.” The manuscripts, without the negation, read, “and they themselves possess them.”]

8. Here, however, he truly understood what mercy he should ask from God: “Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds.” That is, the mercy that you grant to your saints is heavenly, not earthly; eternal, not temporal.

And how were you able to announce it to human beings? “Because your truth reaches to the clouds.” For who could know the heavenly mercy of God unless God announced it to human beings? How did he announce it? By sending his truth to the clouds.

What are the clouds? The preachers of God’s word. Therefore, in one place, God became angry with a certain vineyard. Your Charity, I think, understands and has heard the prophet Isaiah, where he speaks of a certain vineyard: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns.” And lest anyone think that he was speaking of this visible vineyard, he concluded in this way: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved young plant.”

Therefore he was rebuking the very vineyard that he had expected to produce grapes but that produced thorns. And what does he say? “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it.” God said this in anger: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:4, 6, 7); and it truly came to pass.

For the Apostles, the preachers, were sent. We have this in the Acts of the Apostles: the Apostle Paul wanted to preach to the Jews, and he found there not grapes but thorns. They began to repay good with evil and to persecute him. And he said, as though fulfilling what had been said—“I will command my clouds not to rain upon it”: “We had been sent to you, but because you rejected the word of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Therefore, “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” was fulfilled. Truth came to the clouds; therefore the mercy of God that is in heaven, and not on earth, could be announced to us.

And truly, brothers, the preachers of the word of truth are clouds. When God threatens through the preachers, he thunders through the clouds. When God performs miracles through the preachers, he flashes through the clouds, terrifies through the clouds, and waters through the rain. Therefore these preachers, through whom the Gospel of God is proclaimed, are God’s clouds. [Note: [Col. 0347] With scarcely any exception, the manuscripts read: “Therefore these fleshly persons through whom,” and so forth.] Let us hope, then, for mercy—but for the mercy that is in heaven.

9. [verse 7.] “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like a great abyss.” Who are the mountains of God? Those who were called clouds are also the mountains of God: great preachers, the mountains of God.

And just as, when the sun rises, it first clothes the mountains with light, and from there the light descends to the lowest parts of the earth, so when our Lord Jesus Christ came, he first shone upon the height of the Apostles; he first illumined the mountains, and thus his light descended to the valleys of the earth.

Therefore, in one place, the psalm says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” But do not think that the mountains themselves will give you help. They receive what they give; they do not give from themselves. And if you remain on the mountains, your hope will not be firm. Your hope and confidence must be in the one who illumines the mountains.

Help will come to you from the mountains because the Scriptures were ministered to you through the mountains, through the great preachers of truth. But do not place your hope in them. Hear what follows: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” What then? Do the mountains give you help? No. Hear what follows: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:1–2).

Help comes from the mountains, but not from the mountains. From whom, then? From the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

There were other mountains through which anyone steering his ship would suffer shipwreck. For the leaders of heresies arose, and they were mountains. Arius was a mountain; Donatus was a mountain. Maximianus [Note: [Col. 0347] The editions read *Maximinianus*. The manuscripts Regius and Vaticanus read *Maximus*. But fifteen other manuscripts more correctly read *Maximianus*. He was apparently the deacon from the Donatist schism who, after being made bishop of Carthage against Primianus, became the leader of the Maximianists. See the *Exposition of Psalm 36*, sermon 2.] has now, as it were, become a mountain.

Many who looked toward these mountains and desired earth, when they wished to be freed from the waves, were driven onto the rocks and suffered shipwreck on land. The one who said, “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountains like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:2), was not led astray by such mountains.

I do not want my hope to be in Arius; I do not want it to be in Donatus. “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” Learn how much you should rely on God and how much you should attribute to human beings, because “cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5).

With great modesty and humility, the holy Apostle Paul, truly zealous for the Church but for the bridegroom, not for himself, and horrified when they wished to say, “I belong to Paul,” and “I to Apollos” (1 Cor. 3:4), took up his own person in order to trample it underfoot and despise it, so as to glorify Christ: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13). He drives people away from himself, but in order to send them to Christ. He does not want to be loved by the bride instead of the bridegroom, nor does he want the bridegroom’s friend to be loved in place of the bridegroom [Note: [Col. 0348] The manuscripts read this way. The editions read, “but in place of the bridegroom’s friend.”].

The Apostles are the bridegroom’s friends. The humble John, who was thought to be the Christ, was also zealous for this bridegroom. Hence he says: “I am not the Christ, but he who comes after me is greater than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John 1:20; Mark 1:7). By humbling himself so greatly, he truly showed that he was not the bridegroom, but the bridegroom’s friend. Therefore he says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

And if the bridegroom’s friend is a mountain, the mountain nevertheless does not have light from itself. He hears and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. “We,” he says, “have received from his fullness.” From whose fullness? From the one who was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:16, 9).

The Apostle, then, was zealous for this bridegroom and said: “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. 4:1). That is: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” “Let a person regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.”

But so that your hope may not again be fixed upon the mountains and fail to be in God, hear: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth”; and, “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6–7).

You have now said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” But because neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, say: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” And: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God”—that is, the mountains are filled with your righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0348] Five manuscripts read, “the mountains fulfill your righteousness.” Three others read, “your righteousness fills them.”]

10. “Your judgments are like the great deep.” He calls the depth of sins an abyss, into which each person descends by despising God, just as he says in a certain passage: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is not fitting.” Let Your Charity pay attention. This is a great matter; a great matter is being dealt with. What does this mean? “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is not fitting.” Therefore, if God gave them over to the desires of their hearts so that they might do what is not fitting, is that why they commit such great evils? It is as though someone were to raise the question: If God does this, so that they do what is not fitting, what did they themselves do?

What you heard is hidden: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts.” Therefore, there was a desire which they were unwilling to conquer, so that they might be handed over to it by God’s judgment. But so that they might be considered worthy to be handed over [Note: Erasmus’s edition reads: “which they were unwilling to conquer, not to which they were to be handed over, by God’s judgment; but by which they would be judged worthy to be handed over to the remaining desires.” See what follows, etc. The editions of Louvain and our manuscripts contradict this.], see what he said about them above: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.” Why? Because of pride. “For while claiming to be wise, they became fools.” From this it follows: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts” (Rom. 1:21–22, 24). Therefore, because they were proud and ungrateful, they were judged worthy to be handed over to the desires of their hearts, and they became a great abyss—not merely sinning, but also acting deceitfully, so that they would neither understand nor hate their iniquity. This is the depth of wickedness: that they were unwilling to discover and hate it.

But see how each person reaches this depth: “Your judgments are like the great deep.” Just as God’s mountains are his righteousness—those who become great through his grace—so by his judgments they become a depth, those who are plunged into the lowest places. Let these mountains, then, delight you; by this turn away from the abyss and turn toward what is said: “My help is from the Lord.” But from where? Because “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.”

What does this mean? I shall say it in Latin: In the Church of Christ you find an abyss, and you also find mountains. There you find fewer good people, because the mountains are few, while the abyss is broad; that is [Note: Perhaps “there”], there are many living wickedly under God’s anger, because they acted in such a way that they were handed over to the desires of their hearts. They now defend their sins instead of confessing them, saying: “Why? What have I done? That man did this, and that man did that.” They even want to defend what the divine word condemns: this is the abyss.

Therefore Scripture says in a certain place—listen to the abyss: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). Behold: “Your judgments are like the great deep.” But you are not yet a mountain, nor are you yet an abyss. Flee the abyss; look toward the mountains. But do not remain in the mountains either. For your help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

11. [Verse 8.] “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord; according to the abundance of your mercy, O God.” Because he said, “Your mercy is in heaven,” so that it might also be understood to exist on earth, he says: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord; according to the abundance of your mercy, O God.” Great is your mercy, and manifold is your mercy, O God; and you grant it both to humans and to beasts.

For from whom does human salvation come? From God. Is the salvation of beasts not also from God? He who made the human being also made the beasts; he who made both saves both. But the salvation of beasts is temporal. Yet there are people who ask God as a great favor for what he has given to beasts. “Your mercy is abundant, O God,” so that not only humans but also beasts may receive the carnal and temporal salvation that is given to humans.

12. Therefore, do humans have nothing with God that beasts do not deserve and to which beasts do not attain? They certainly do. And where is what they have? “But the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings.”

Let Your Charity attend to this most sweet sentence: “You will save humans and beasts.” He has already said “humans and beasts”; then he says “the children of men,” as though some were humans and others the children of men. Sometimes Scripture calls human beings generally “children of men”; sometimes, in a particular sense, it calls them “children of men,” so that not all human beings are understood—especially when there is a distinction. For it is not without reason that it says there, “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord; but the children of men,” as though, having separated these others, he preserves the children of men apart.

Separated from whom? Not only from beasts, but also from those humans who seek the salvation of beasts from God and desire it as a great thing. Who, then, are the children of men? Those who hope under the shelter of his wings. Those other humans rejoice with beasts in what is present; the children of men rejoice in hope. The former pursue present goods with beasts; the latter hope for future goods with angels.

Why, then, are the former called “humans” by way of distinction, and the latter “children of men”? Scripture says in another place: “What is a human being, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. 8:5). “What is a human being, that you remember him?” You remember him as one who is absent; but you visit the son of man as one who is present.

What does “you remember a human being” mean? “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord,” because you give salvation even to the wicked, even to those who do not desire the kingdom of heaven. You protect them and do not abandon them according to their own measure, as though they were your cattle; and you do not abandon them, yet you remember them as those who are absent. But the one whom he visits is the son of man, and it is said to him: “But the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings.”

If you wish to distinguish these two kinds of people, first consider two human beings: Adam and Christ. Hear the Apostle: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). We are born from Adam in order to die; we rise again through Christ in order to live forever.

When we bear the image of the earthly human being, we are merely “humans”; when we bear the image of the heavenly human being, we are “children of men,” because Christ was called the Son of Man (Matt. 8:20, etc.). Adam indeed was a human being, but he was not the son of man. Therefore those belong to Adam who desire carnal goods and this temporal salvation.

We urge them to become children of men, those who hope under the shelter of his wings and desire that mercy which is in heaven and which was announced through the clouds. But if they are not yet able to do so, at least for the present let them not desire temporal goods except from the one God. Thus let them serve even in the Old Testament [Note: Some manuscripts read, “thus let them serve also in the Old Testament.” Others read, “thus they are also preserved in the Old Testament”], so that they may reach the New.

13. For that people also desired earthly goods: the kingdom of Jerusalem, the subjection of their enemies, abundance of crops, their own welfare, and the welfare of their children. They desired such things and received such things; they were guarded under the Law [Note: All our manuscripts omit “under the Law.”]. They desired from God the goods that he also gives to beasts, because the Son of Man had not yet come to them, so that they might become children of men. Yet they already had clouds announcing the Son of Man.

The prophets came to them and announced Christ. There were some who understood and possessed future hope, so that they might receive the mercy that is in heaven. But there were others who desired nothing but carnal things and earthly and temporal happiness. Their feet slipped into making or worshiping idols. For whenever God warned them and scourged them in all the things in which they delighted, and took those things away, they suffered famine, wars, pestilences, and diseases—and they turned to idols.

They desired from idols the goods which they ought to have desired from God as a great gift, and they abandoned God. They looked at the very goods they sought, saw them abounding among the impious and criminal, and thought that they were worshiping God in vain because he did not give an earthly reward.

O human being! You are God’s laborer; the time for receiving wages comes afterward. Why are you already demanding your wages before you have worked? If a laborer came to your house, would you give him his wages in advance, before he had completed his work? You would consider him perverse if he said, “First I will receive my wages, and then I will work.” You would be angry.

But why would you be angry? Because he had no trust in a lying human being. How will God not be angry when you do not trust the truth itself? What he promised you, he will give. He does not deceive, because the one who promised is truth.

But do you fear that perhaps he does not have what he can give? He is almighty. Do not fear that there may be no one to give it; he is immortal. Do not fear that he will be succeeded by another; he is everlasting. Be confident.

If you want to rely upon your laborer throughout the whole day, then you too should trust God throughout your whole life, because your life is only a moment of time in relation to God. And what will you be? “But the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings” [Note: Two manuscripts add: “Let your hope be in God, and you will be a child of man. ‘But the children of men …,’” etc.].

14. [Verse 9.] “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house.” He promises us something great. He wants to say it, but does not say it. Is he unable to, or do we fail to grasp it? I dare to say, my brothers, that even from the holy tongues and hearts through which truth was announced to us, what they proclaimed can neither be spoken nor conceived. The reality is great and ineffable. They themselves saw it only partially and in a riddle, as the Apostle says: “Now we see partially and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Behold how, seeing in a riddle, they poured forth what they saw. What will we be when we see face to face what they were bringing forth in their hearts, but could not bring forth with their tongues so that human beings might grasp it?

What necessity was there for him to say, “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house”? He sought a word with which to speak of human realities. Because he saw human beings plunging themselves into drunkenness—receiving wine immoderately and losing their minds—he saw what he should say: when that ineffable joy is received, the human mind somehow perishes, becomes divine, and is intoxicated with the abundance of God’s house.

Hence it is also said in another psalm: “How excellent is your intoxicating cup!” (Ps. 22:5). The martyrs were already intoxicated by this cup when, going to their passion, they did not recognize their own. What is more drunk than not recognizing a weeping wife, children, or parents? They did not recognize them; they did not think that they were before their eyes. Do not be surprised: they were drunk.

With what were they drunk? See: they received the cup with which they would be intoxicated. Hence that man also gives thanks to God, saying: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13).

Therefore, brothers, let us be children of men, let us hope under the shelter of his wings, and let us be intoxicated with the abundance of his house. I have said what I could and as I could see it; what I see, I cannot express.

“They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: Thus the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint: “from the torrent.”]. A torrent is water that comes rushing with force. There will be a rushing force of God’s mercy, to water and intoxicate those who now place their hope under the shelter of his wings.

What is that delight? It is like a torrent intoxicating those who thirst. Therefore, let the one who thirsts now place his hope; let the one who thirsts possess hope; once intoxicated, he will possess the reality. Before he possesses the reality, let him thirst in hope. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

15. [Verse 10.] From what fountain, then, will you be watered, and from where does such a great torrent of his delight flow? “For with you,” he says, “is the fountain of life.” Who is the fountain of life except Christ? He came to you in the flesh to moisten your thirsty throat. He will satisfy the one who hopes—the one who moistened the one who thirsted [Note: Thus most manuscripts. The editions read “watered”].

“For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we will see light” [Note: The editions read: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light …” The words “is” and “and” are absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint.].

Here the fountain is one thing and the light another—but not there. For what is the fountain is also the light; and whatever you wish, you call it that, because it is not contained by the name you give it. Since you cannot find a suitable name, it does not remain within one name.

If you were to say that it is only light, you would be told: “Then I was told without reason to hunger and thirst, for who eats light?” This, however, was rightly said to me: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (ibid., 6, 8). If it is light, let me prepare my eyes. Prepare your throat as well, because what is light is also fountain: fountain, because it satisfies those who thirst; light, because it illuminates the blind.

Here, at times, light is found elsewhere and the fountain elsewhere. For sometimes fountains flow even in darkness, and sometimes in the desert you endure the sun but do not find a fountain. Here, then, these two can be separated; there, they cannot. There you will not be weary, because it is a fountain; you will not be in darkness, because it is light.

16. [Verse 11.] “Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart.” As we have often said, those are upright in heart who follow God’s will in this life.

God’s will is sometimes that you be healthy and sometimes that you be sick. When you are healthy, God’s will is sweet; when you are sick, God’s will is bitter. You are not upright in heart. Why? Because you do not want to direct your will toward God’s will; instead, you want to bend God’s will toward your own. God’s will is straight, but you are crooked. Your will must be corrected toward it; it must not be bent toward you. Then you will have an upright heart.

If things are going well in this world, let God be blessed, who comforts us. If there is hardship in the world, let God be blessed, because he corrects and tests us. Then you will be upright in heart, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2).

17. [Verse 12.] “May the foot of pride not come upon me.” Surely he has already said, “The children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings, and they will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house.” When someone begins to be more abundantly watered by this fountain, let him beware of becoming proud.

For pride was not lacking in the first human being, Adam. But the foot of pride came upon him, and the hand of the sinner moved him—that is, the proud hand of the devil [Note: Some manuscripts read “of the proud man.” Some read “the proud thing.” Others finally read “through pride.”].

Just as the one who deceived him said, “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14:13), so he persuaded him: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Therefore we fell through pride and came into this mortality.

And because pride had wounded us, humility makes us whole. God came in humility to heal the human being from so great a wound of pride. He came because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He was seized by the Jews and mocked. You heard, when the Gospel was read, what they said and to whom they said it: “You have a demon” (ibid. 8:48).

He did not say to them, “You have a demon, because you are in your sins and the devil possesses your hearts.” If he had said this, he would have spoken the truth; but it was not yet the time for him to say it, lest he appear to be returning an insult rather than proclaiming the truth. He disregarded what he heard, as though he had not heard it.

He was a physician, and he had come to heal a madman. A physician does not concern himself with whatever he hears from a madman, but with how the madman may recover and become well. Even if he receives a blow from him, he does not concern himself with it. The madman inflicts new wounds upon him, while he heals the old fever.

So also the Lord came to the sick, came to the mad, so that he might disregard whatever he heard and whatever he suffered. By this very conduct he was teaching them humility, so that, instructed by humility, they might be healed of pride. From this pride the psalmist prays to be freed, saying: “May the foot of pride not come upon me, and may the hand of sinners not move me” [Note: Many manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint, read “of sinners.”].

For if the foot of pride comes, the hand of the sinner moves. What is the hand of the sinner? The action of one who gives evil counsel. Have you become proud? The one who gives evil counsel quickly corrupts you.

Be humble, fixing yourself in God [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Others read “become humble.” The editions read, “Strive to become humble.”], and do not be greatly concerned about what is said to you. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from others’” (Ps. 18:13–14).

What does “from my hidden faults” mean? “May the foot of pride not come upon me.” What does “and spare your servant from others’” mean? “May the hand of sinners not move me.” Preserve what is within, and you will not fear what is outside.

18. [Verse 13.] Why, then, are you so greatly afraid of this? It is as though someone were saying: “There all who practice iniquity fell,” so that they might come to that abyss of which it was said, “Your judgments are like the great deep,” and reach that depth where the despising sinners fell [Note: Many manuscripts read: “where the sinner who despises fell,” singular].

They fell. Where did they first fall? At the foot of pride. Hear the foot of pride: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God.” Therefore the foot of pride came upon them, and from there they came into the depth: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. 1:21, 24).

The one who said, “May the foot of pride not come upon me,” feared the root and head of sin. Why did he call it a foot? Because through pride he abandoned God and departed; he called the person’s affection his foot.

“May the foot of pride not come upon me, and may the hand of sinners not move me”—that is, may the works of sinners not move me away from you, so that I might wish to imitate them.

Why does he say this against pride: “There fell those who practice iniquity”? Because those who are now wicked fell through pride [Note: “Because” is absent from the manuscripts].

Therefore, when the Lord was warning the Church to be cautious, he said: “She will watch your head, and you will watch her heel” (Gen. 3:15). The serpent watches for the moment when the foot of pride may come upon you, when you may slip, so that it may cast you down. But you should watch its head: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sir. 10:15).

“There fell those who practice iniquity”: they were expelled and could not stand. First came the one who did not stand in the truth; then, through him, those whom God expelled from paradise. But that humble man who says that he is not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal was not expelled. He stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice (John 1:27; 3:29), not because of his own voice—lest the foot of pride come upon him, and he be expelled and unable to stand.

19. Even if we have caused some of you weariness through our labor, we have finished the psalm; the weariness has passed, and we shall rejoice because the whole psalm has been expounded.

In the middle of it, fearing that I might burden you, I was going to stop. But I considered that our attention would be cut short, and that we would not return to the halfway point in the same way as if we ran through the whole thing. I preferred to be burdensome to you rather than leave you with the remains of an unfinished work.

For tomorrow’s sermon is also owed to you. Pray for us, so that we may be able to deliver it, and bring hungry throats and devoted hearts.

# Exposition of Psalm 36

[Note: Here it is not permissible to pass over in silence what is related in the Life of Saint Fulgentius, chapter 3: when he had already resolved in his mind to renounce the world, at last, “having been admonished and moved to compunction by blessed Augustine’s exposition of the thirty-sixth Psalm, he decided to make his vow public, eagerly desiring to change his clothing.”]

## Sermon I

[Note: Delivered at Carthage together with the two following sermons.]

### On the first part of the psalm

1. The last day is heard to be coming terrifyingly upon those who do not wish to live well and be secure, but wish to live wickedly for a long time. God wisely wished that day to remain hidden, so that the heart might always be prepared to await what it knows will come, while not knowing when it will come.

Because our Lord Jesus Christ was sent to us as a teacher, he even said that the Son of Man did not know that day (Mark 13:32), because it did not belong to his teaching that we should come to know it through him. For the Father does not know something that the Son does not know, since the Father’s knowledge is itself his wisdom; and his wisdom is his Son, his Word.

But because it was not useful for us to know—although he who had come to teach us did know it—he did not teach only what was useful to us as a teacher; as a teacher, he also did not teach what was not useful. For as a teacher he knew both what was beneficial to teach and what was harmful to teach.

Thus, by a certain manner of speaking, the Son is said not to know what he does not teach. That is, he is said not to know what he makes us not know, in the manner of speech I have mentioned. We call a day joyful because it makes us joyful, and a day sad because it makes us sad, and cold sluggish because it makes us sluggish.

In contrast, how is it said by the Lord, “Now I know”? God said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). God knew this even before that testing. For the testing was carried out so that we might know what God already knew; and it was written down for our instruction, although he already knew it before the demonstration.

Perhaps Abraham himself also did not yet know what strength his faith possessed. Each person recognizes himself through temptation, as though questioned. Peter certainly did not know what strength his faith possessed when he said to the Lord: “I am with you unto death” [Note: The editions read, “I am ready with you unto death.” Most manuscripts omit “I am ready,” while some retain “I am” but omit “ready.”].

But the Lord, who knew him, foretold where he would fail, announcing his weakness to him, as though touching the vein of his heart (Luke 22:33–34). Accordingly, Peter, who before the temptation had presumed upon himself, learned himself in the temptation.

Thus we do not think it absurd that our father Abraham came to know the strength of his faith when, commanded to sacrifice his only son, he did not hesitate or tremble to offer him to the one who had given him. For just as he did not know how God would give him a son who was not yet born, so he believed that God could restore the one sacrificed.

Therefore God said, “Now I know”—which we understand as, “Now I have caused you to know,” according to the expressions we have explained: sluggish cold, because it makes people sluggish; and a joyful day, because it makes people joyful. Thus God is said to know because he makes people know.

Hence there is also this statement: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3). For you would certainly attribute great ignorance to the Lord our God, the supreme and true God, if you understood it in this way: “The Lord is testing you so that he may know,” as though he acquired knowledge from our temptation, when previously he had been ignorant. But what does “he is testing you, to know” mean? “He is testing you so that he may make you know.”

Therefore receive the rule of understanding from the converse. Just as when you hear God say, “I know,” you understand, “I have caused you to know,” so when you hear that the Son of Man—that is, Christ—is said not to know that day, understand it as meaning that he makes it not known.

What does “make it not known” mean? He conceals it, so that what it does not benefit us to have disclosed may remain unknown. This is what I said: the good teacher knows what to reveal and what to conceal, just as we read that he postponed certain things.

From this we understand that not everything should be disclosed to those who cannot bear what is disclosed to them. For he says elsewhere: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). The Apostle also says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able—and indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

What does this sermon accomplish? Since we know that the last day will come, and it is useful for us to know that it will come while also useful for us not to know when it will come, we should keep our hearts prepared by living well. We should not only refrain from fearing that day when it comes, but also love it.

That day increases the labor of unbelievers, but it brings the labor of the faithful to an end. Which of these two you wish to be is now within your power, before it comes; when it has come, it will not be. Choose, then, while there is time, because what God mercifully conceals, he mercifully postpones.

2. Since, in every kind of life that has some profession or vocation, not all are found to be good and not all evil, this is shown by the conclusion concerning certain classes of people whose likenesses we have just heard set forth in the Gospel: “One will be taken, and one will be left” (Matt. 24:40). The good will be taken; the wicked will be left.

Two are seen in a field. Their profession is the same, but their hearts are not. Human beings see the profession; God knows the heart. Whatever the field may signify, “one will be taken, and one will be left.” It does not mean that half will be taken and half left; rather, he speaks of two classes of people. Even if one class is found among a few and the other among many, “one will be taken, and one will be left”—that is, one class will be taken and the other left.

So also with the bed, and so with the mill. Perhaps you are waiting to hear what these things mean. You see that they are veiled and wrapped in certain likenesses. One thing may seem to me and another to someone else. But neither do I impose what I say upon another as the only better understanding, nor does he impose his understanding upon me, provided that both interpretations agree with the faith.

It seems to me that those who labor in the field are the people who preside over the Churches, as the Apostle says: “You are God’s cultivated field, God’s building.” He calls himself an architect when he says, “As a wise architect I laid a foundation,” and a farmer when he says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. 3:9–10).

In the mill, therefore, he spoke of two women, not two men (Matt. 24:41). I believe that this figure refers to the congregations, because leaders govern and congregations are governed.

I think that the mill signifies this world, because it turns upon a certain wheel of times and grinds down its lovers. There are people who do not withdraw from the affairs of the world; yet even there some act well and others badly. Some make friends for themselves from the wealth of iniquity, so that they may be received into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9); to them it is said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” [Note: The editions read “there it will be said.” But the manuscripts more correctly read “there it is said,” that is, in the Gospel which, as he mentioned above, had been read aloud to the congregation]. Others neglect these things, and to them it is said there: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:35, 42).

Therefore, because among those occupied with the business and works of this world some love to do good to the needy while others neglect them, it is as though of two women at the mill, one will be taken and one left.

I think that the bed represents repose. There are people who do not wish either to endure the activities of the world—as married people do, with houses, households, and children—or to do anything in the Church, as those who preside and labor as in agriculture do. Instead, as though weak for such things, they withdraw into leisure and love to be at rest; mindful, as it were, of their weakness, they do not commit themselves to great activities but somehow pray to God upon the bed of their infirmity.

This profession too has good people and hypocrites; therefore, from these also one will be taken and one left.

Whatever profession you turn toward, prepare yourself to encounter hypocrites. Otherwise, if you are not prepared, you will find what you did not expect and will fail or be troubled.

Therefore the one who speaks to you prepares you for everything while there is time—for him to speak, since it is not yet time to judge, and for you to hear, since it is not yet time to repent in vain. For now repentance is not in vain; then it will be in vain. It is not that people will not then regret having lived wickedly, but God’s justice will in no way restore to them what they lost through their own injustice.

For it is just in God that now he bestow mercy, but then exercise judgment. Therefore it is not now kept silent. Is it kept silent? Let anyone object and murmur if this Scripture is not read and sung throughout the whole world, or if it even ceases to be carried publicly for sale.

3. [Verses 1–2.] But truly what disturbs you, a Christian, is that you see wicked people living happily, overflowing with an abundance of these goods, healthy, elevated by proud offices, with their household safe, enjoying the joys of their family and the services of their dependents, possessing outstanding power, with nothing sad interrupting their lives. You see their exceedingly wicked character and perceive their abundant resources, and your heart says that there is no divine judgment, that everything is driven by chance and tossed about by random movements.

“For if God,” you say, “looked upon human affairs, why would his wickedness flourish while my innocence suffers?”

Every illness of the soul has its medicine in Scripture. Therefore, whoever is so sick as to say such things in his heart should drink the potion of this psalm.

What is it? Let us look again at what you were saying. “What was I saying?” you ask. “Only what you see: the wicked flourish, the good suffer. How does God see this?”

Receive and drink. He himself—against whom you murmur about these things—has prepared this potion for you. Only do not refuse the most health-giving cup. Bring the mouth of your heart to your ear, and drink what you hear:

“Do not rival the wicked, nor envy those who practice iniquity. For like grass they will quickly wither, and like the plants of the meadow they will quickly fall.”

What seems long to you is short to God. Submit yourself to God, and it will be short for you as well.

By “grass” we understand the plants of the meadow. They are lowly things covering the surface of the earth [Note: Some manuscripts read “covering.” Others read “they remain,” followed by “for they do not have a deep …”], without a deep root. Therefore they are green during winter; but when the summer sun begins to grow hot, they wither.

Now, then, it is wintertime; your glory has not yet appeared. But if the root of your charity is deep, as with many trees in winter, the cold will pass and summer will come—that is, the day of judgment. Then the greenness of the grass will wither; then the glory of the trees will appear.

“For you have died,” the Apostle says (Col. 3:3). In winter trees appear dry, as though dead. What hope is there, then, if we have died? The root is within. Where our root is, there also is our life, for our charity is there.

“And your life,” he says, “is hidden with Christ in God.” When does one who has such a root wither? When will our spring be? When will our summer come? When will dignity clothe us with leaves and abundance enrich us with fruits? When will this be?

Hear what follows: “When Christ appears, your life, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

What, then, should you do now? “Do not rival the wicked, nor envy those who practice iniquity. For like grass they will quickly wither, and like the plants of the meadow they will quickly fall.”

4. [Verses 3–4.] What about you? “Hope in the Lord.” They do not hope in the Lord. Their hope will be mortal, their hope fleeting, fragile, winged, passing, and empty. “Hope in the Lord.”

“Behold, I hope. What do I do?” “And do good.” Do not practice the wickedness that you observe in those who flourish evilly. Do good, and dwell in the land. Do not perhaps do good outside the dwelling of the land.

For the Lord’s land is his Church. It is this land that the Father, the farmer, waters and cultivates (John 15:1). Many people seem to perform good works, but because they do not dwell in the land, they do not belong to the farmer.

Therefore do good—not outside the land, but dwell in the land. “And what will I have?” “And you will be fed by its riches.” What are the riches of that land? Its riches are its Lord; its riches are its God. He is the one to whom it is said: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26). He is the one of whom it is said: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup” (Ps. 15:5).

In a recent sermon we commended to Your Charity [Note: He certainly commended this above, columns 294–295, in a sermon on Psalm 32 delivered at Carthage in the basilica of Saint Cyprian. From various passages you will understand that these sermons on Psalm 36 were also delivered in that city.] both that God is our possession and that we are God’s possession.

Hear that he himself is the wealth of this land. See what follows: “Delight in the Lord.” It is as though you had asked and said, “Show me the riches of that land in which you command me to dwell.” “Delight,” he says, “in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart.”

5. Pay close attention to “the petitions of your heart.” Distinguish the petitions of your heart from the petitions of the flesh, distinguish them as far as you can. Nor was it said without reason in a certain psalm: “God of my heart.” For it continues and says: “And God, my portion, forever” (Ps. 72:26).

For example, a man is blind in body and asks to be given sight. Let him ask for this [Note: [Col. 0358] Ambrose, Erasmus, and three manuscripts, in place of “let him ask for these things,” read “let him ask for this” (*isto roget*). Other manuscripts read “let him ask for that” (*iste roget*).]—for God also does these things, and God grants these things. But the wicked ask for them as well. This is a petition of the flesh. He falls ill and asks to be restored to health; he is restored to health, only to die. This too is a petition of the flesh, and so are whatever things are like these.

What is the petition of the heart? Just as the petition of the flesh is to want one’s eyes restored, naturally in order to see this light, which can be seen with such eyes, so the petition of the heart concerns another light. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the petitions of your heart.”

6. [Verse 5–6.] “Behold, I desire, I ask, I will: shall I fulfill it myself?” No. Who, then? “Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he himself will act.” Tell him what you suffer; tell him what you want. What do you suffer? “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). What, then, do you want? “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” And because he himself will act when you have committed your way to him, see what follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

What, then, will he do, since it was said, “Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he himself will act”? What will he do? “And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light.” For now your righteousness is hidden: it is a matter of faith, not yet of sight. You believe something in order to do it; you do not yet see what you believe. But when you begin to see what you have believed, your righteousness will be brought forth into the light [Note: [Col. 0359] Five manuscripts read “into light.”], because your righteousness was your faith: “The just person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17).

7. “And he will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday”—that is, like clear light. It was not enough to say, “like the light.” We call it light when the sky grows bright; we call it light when the sun rises. But light is never brighter than at midday. Therefore he will not merely bring forth your righteousness like the light; your judgment will be like midday.

For now you judge that you should follow Christ: this you have proposed, this you have chosen—this is your judgment. No one shows you what he promised; you still hold to the one who made the promise, but you await the one who will fulfill it. In the judgment of your faith, therefore, you have chosen to follow what you do not see.

Your judgment is hidden; it is still criticized and mocked by unbelievers: “What have you believed? What has Christ promised you? That you will be immortal and that he will give you eternal life? Where is this? When will he give it? When can it happen?” Yet you judge that you should follow Christ, who promises what you do not see, rather than the ungodly person who criticizes you for believing what you do not yet see. And this is your judgment.

What kind of judgment yours is does not yet appear: in this age it is, as it were, night. When, then, will he bring forth your judgment like midday? “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

When the day of judgment comes, when Christ comes and gathers all nations to be judged, what will happen then? Where will the ungodly hide his faithlessness, when I see my faith? What, then, is there now? Distresses, tribulations, and temptations. And blessed is the one who endures, “for the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13). Let him not yield to his mockers, lest he choose to flourish here only to become hay from a tree [Note: [Col. 0360] Ambrose and the manuscripts read, “and from a tree,” etc.].

8. [Verse 7–9.] What, then, ought I to do? Hear what you ought to do: “Be subject to the Lord, and beseech him.” Let this be your life: to obey his commands. For this is to be subject to him and to beseech him until he gives what he promised. Let good work continue; let prayer also continue. “For we ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1).

In what way do you appear subject to him? By doing what he commanded. But you do not yet receive the reward, perhaps because you are not yet able to receive it. He is already able to give it, but you are not yet able to receive it. Exercise yourself in good works; labor in the vineyard. When the day is finished, ask for your reward. Faithful is the one who brought you into the vineyard (Matt. 20:8). “Be subject to the Lord, and beseech him.”

9. “Behold, I am doing this; I am subject to the Lord, and I beseech him. But what do you think? That wicked neighbor is doing evil and flourishing. I know his thefts, his adulteries, his robberies. Raised up in every way, proud, exalted through iniquity, he does not deem me worthy of recognition. How shall I endure this?”

That is an illness; drink the remedy against it: “Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way.” He prospers, but in his own way; you labor, but in God’s way. For him, prosperity is on the road and unhappiness at its destination; for you, labor is on the road and happiness at its destination, “for the way of the ungodly will perish.” “The Lord knows the ways of the just, but the way of the ungodly will perish” (Ps. 1:6).

You walk along the ways that the Lord knows; and if you labor in them, they do not deceive you [Note: [Col. 0360] Nearly all manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, have: “Walk along these ways, which the Lord knows; and if you walk in them,” etc.]. But the way of the ungodly is a passing happiness: when the road is over, the happiness is over. Why? Because that road is broad, and its end leads into the depths of hell.

But your way is narrow, and few enter upon it (Matt. 7:13–14). Yet you must consider to what breadth they will arrive [Note: [Col. 0360] The manuscripts read “he may arrive.”]. “Do not be jealous of the one who prospers in his way.”

“Cease from anger against the person who does iniquity, and abandon indignation” [Note: [Col. 0360] Some manuscripts consistently read “resentment.”]. Why are you irritated? Why, through this anger and indignation, do you either blaspheme or nearly blaspheme? “Cease from anger against the person who does iniquity, and abandon indignation.”

Do you not know where this anger is provoking you? You are about to say to God that he is unjust; that is where it is heading. “Look: why is this person happy and that one unhappy?” See what it gives birth to: suffocate the evil conception. Cease from anger and abandon indignation, so that, coming to your senses, you may say: “My eye was troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8).

What eye, if not the eye of faith? I question the eye of your faith: you believed in Christ; why did you believe? What did he promise you? If Christ promised you the happiness of this age, then murmur against Christ—murmur against him when you see an unbeliever happy. What happiness did he promise you? What but the resurrection of the dead?

But what do you suffer in this life? What he himself suffered—what he himself, I say. Or do you disdain, servant and disciple, what the Lord and teacher endured [Note: [Col. 0360] Some manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, have: “But what do you suffer in this life that he himself did not suffer? Why, then, do you disdain it more, servant and disciple, than the Lord and teacher?”]? Do you not hear from him: “A servant is not greater than his master, nor a disciple above his teacher” (John 13:16)?

For you he endured pains, scourges, insults, the cross, and death. And which of these was owed to the righteous man? Which was not owed to you, a sinner?

Therefore keep your eye straight, lest it be troubled by anger: “Cease from anger and abandon indignation.” Do not be jealous so as to do evil, as though imitating the one who flourishes for a time by doing evil. “Do not be jealous so as to do evil. For those who do evil will be exterminated.”

“But I see their happiness.” Believe the one who says, “They will be exterminated,” because he sees better than you, whose eye anger cannot trouble. “For those who do evil will be exterminated. But those who wait for the Lord”—not for someone deceitful, but for truth itself; not for someone lacking power, but for the Almighty—“those who wait for the Lord will possess the land by inheritance.” What land, if not that Jerusalem whose love inflames the person who reaches peace?

10. [Verse 10.] But how long will the sinner flourish? How long shall I endure? You are impatient: what seems long to you will soon be here. Weakness makes what is soon to come seem long.

What are the desires of the sick like? Nothing seems so long as waiting for the cup to be prepared for the thirsty person. Indeed, the attendants hurry, lest the sick person perhaps be offended. “When will it happen? When will it be prepared? When will it be given?” There is speed in those serving you, but your weakness considers what is done quickly to be prolonged.

Therefore see our physician soothing the sick person who says, “How long shall I endure? How long will it be?”: “And yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more.” You groan among sinners; you groan because of the sinner. “A little while, and he will be no more.”

Lest, because I said, “Those who wait for the Lord will possess the land by inheritance,” you think this waiting will be exceedingly long: endure a little, and you will receive without end what you endure for. “Yet a little while”: only a short time.

Recall the years from Adam until the present day; run through the Scriptures. It is almost as though he fell from paradise yesterday. So many ages have passed and rolled away. Where are the times that have gone before? The few that remain will likewise pass away.

If you had lived through all that time, from the day Adam was expelled from paradise until today, you would certainly see that your life had not been long, since it would have flown away so quickly. How long, then, is the life of any one person? Add as many years as you like; extend the longest old age—what is it? Is it not a morning breeze?

Let the day of judgment be far off, when the unjust and the just will receive their recompense. But your own final day certainly cannot be far away. Prepare yourself for it. For whatever sort of person you leave this life, you will be restored to that life in the same condition.

After this brief life you will not yet be where the saints will be, to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). You will not yet be there—who does not know this? But you may already be where that once ulcer-covered poor man was, whom the proud and barren rich man saw from afar, resting amid his own torments (Luke 16:23).

Placed in that rest, you will certainly await the day of judgment in security, when you will receive your body as well, when you will be changed so as to be equal to an angel. How long, then, is it that we hurry and say, “When will it be? Will it be late?”

Our children will say this, and our grandchildren will say this; and as each generation says these things in succession, what is still to be “a little while” passes away just as everything that has already passed has passed away. O weak one! “Yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more.”

11. “And you will seek his place, and you will not find it.” He explains what he meant by “he will be no more”: not that he will not exist at all, but that he will be of no use for any purpose. For if he will not exist at all, he will not be tormented. The sinner would then have been given security, so that he might say: “I shall do whatever I want as long as I live; afterward I will not exist. There will be no one to suffer, no one to be tormented.”

And where, then, is “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41)? But perhaps those sent into that fire will not exist and will be consumed. They would not be told, “Go into the eternal fire,” because if they were not going to exist, it would not be eternal.

Yet the Lord did not leave unspoken what will happen to them there, whether it will be complete annihilation or pain and torment, when he said: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12). How, then, will they weep and gnash their teeth if they will not exist?

How, then, does “Yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more” mean anything except what he explained in the following verse: “And you will seek his place, and you will not find it”? What is “his place”? His use. Does the sinner have any use? He does. In this life God uses him to test the righteous, just as he used the devil to test Job, and just as he used Judas to hand Christ over.

There is, therefore, something to be done with the sinner in this life. This, then, is his place, just as straw has its place in the refiner’s furnace. The straw burns so that the gold may be purified; so the ungodly person rages so that the righteous person may be tested.

But when the time of our testing has passed, when there will no longer be people to be tested, there will no longer be those by whom they are tested. Does our saying, “There will no longer be people to be tested,” mean that those people themselves will no longer exist? No. It means that sinners will no longer be needed as the means by which the righteous are tested: “And you will seek his place, and you will not find it.”

Now seek the sinner’s place, and you will find it. God made the sinner a scourge; he gave him both honor and power. For at times he does this: he gives the sinner power, through which human affairs are scourged and the godly are corrected [Note: [Col. 0362] The word “godly” is absent from the manuscripts. Shortly afterward the editions had “is repaid”; in its place we restore from the manuscripts “will be repaid.”].

What is owed will be repaid to that sinner. Yet something has been made of him by which the godly may advance and the ungodly may fail. “You will seek his place, and you will not find it.”

12. [Verse 11.] “But the meek will possess the land by inheritance.” This is the land of which we have often spoken: holy Jerusalem, which will be freed from this pilgrimage and will live eternally with God and from God.

Therefore they will possess the land by inheritance. What will their delights be? “And they will delight in the abundance of peace.”

Let that ungodly person delight here in an abundance of gold, an abundance of silver, an abundance of slaves, and finally an abundance of villas, roses, drunkenness, and sumptuous and luxurious banquets [Note: [Col. 0362] The editions read “finally, an abundance of various wealth.” Some manuscripts instead read “of perfumes, roses”; some, “of olive trees, roses”; others, “of fragrant roses”; and many, “of villas, roses.” [Col. 0363] “Villas” may derive from the name of Baiae, a beautiful and famous town of Campania; the pleasant places and fertile estates may have been called by this name, as Cicero seems to understand it in his speech Pro Caelio: “Into whose gardens, house, and Baiae, he says, the desires of everyone would freely enter.” Jerome, in Book 2 of Against Jovinianus, chapter 9, testifies that palms or palm leaves were called “baiae.” The word that follows, “roses,” may perhaps have intruded here in place of another neighboring word, such as “tables.”].

Is this the power you envy? Is this the flower that delights you? Even if it always remained so, would it not deserve to be mourned? What, then, will your delights be? “And they will delight in the abundance of peace.”

Your gold will be peace; your silver, peace; your estates, peace; your life, peace; your God, peace. Whatever you desire will be peace for you. For here what is gold cannot be silver for you; what is wine cannot be bread for you; what is light for you cannot be drink. Your God will be everything for you.

You will eat him, so that you do not hunger; you will drink him, so that you do not thirst; you will be illumined by him, so that you are not blind; you will be supported by him, so that you do not fail. He will possess you wholly and perfectly, himself wholly and perfectly. You will suffer no narrowness there with the one with whom you possess everything: you will have everything, and he too will have everything, because you and he will be one; and he who possesses you will possess that one whole thing as well.

These are the remains reserved for the peaceful person. We sang this: the verse is indeed far removed in this psalm from the verses we have been expounding. But since we sang it, we must close with it.

Only be secure: guard innocence, for it is a precious thing. You want to steal something, I suppose, in order to acquire it. See where you put your hand and from where you take. By this you want to acquire, by this you lose: you acquire money, you lose innocence.

Let your heart rather awaken. You who wanted to acquire money and are losing innocence, lose the money instead: “Guard innocence and observe uprightness,” because God will direct you, so that you too may will whatever he wills; for this itself is uprightness.

If you do not will what God wills, you will be crooked, and your perversity will not permit you to be made level [Note: [Col. 0363] Most manuscripts read “to be reconciled.”] with what is straight. Therefore guard innocence and observe uprightness. Do not think that when this life has ended, the human being has ended, because there are remains reserved for the peaceful person.

SERMON II. On the Second Part of the Psalm

1. We have both been commanded to speak to Your Charity about this psalm and have been obliged to obey. For the Lord wished, because of the excessive rains, to delay our departure; and it was commanded that our tongue should not be idle here among you, since you are always the concern of our heart [Note: [Col. 0363] The editions read “you know.” “You are” is better supported by some manuscripts.], just as we are yours.

We had already commended in this psalm the will of God: what he wants to teach us, what he wants to admonish us about, what he wants us to guard against, what he wants us to endure, and what he wants us to hope for.

For two kinds of people—the righteous and the unrighteous—are mingled together in this land and in this life. Each of these kinds has its own intentions of heart. The kind of the righteous strives toward what is above through humility; the kind of the unrighteous inclines toward what is below through pride. The one humbles itself in order to rise; the other exalts itself in order to fall.

The result is that one kind endures while the other is endured. The righteous are determined to win even the unrighteous for eternal life; the unrighteous are determined to repay good with evil and, if possible, to deprive those who desire eternal life even of temporal life.

For the unjust person finds the just person burdensome, and the just person finds the unjust person burdensome: they are burdens to one another. No one doubts that these two are burdens to each other, but with different intentions.

The just person is a burden to the unjust because he does not want him to remain unjust, but wishes him to become just, desires this in prayer, and strives for it in action. The unjust person hates the just in such a way that he does not want him to exist—not in such a way that he wants him to be good. The better he is, the greater a burden he is to that person’s iniquity.

The unjust person works, if possible, to make him unjust; if he cannot do that, he works to remove him from the midst and rid himself of his annoyance and vexation. But even if he makes him unjust, he will still be a burden to him. For it is not only the just person who is a burden to the unjust; even two unjust people scarcely tolerate one another. And when they seem to love one another, they owe each other complicity, not friendship.

They agree with one another when they conspire against the destruction of the just—not because they love each other, but because together they hate the one who ought to be loved.

Against this kind of person our Lord God enjoins upon us endurance and that affection of charity which we know from the Gospel, when the Lord commands us and says: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). Likewise the Apostle says: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12:21). Contend with evil, but by goodness. For this is the true contest—or rather, the salutary struggle: to be good against evil, not for there to be two evil persons.

2. [Verse 12–13.] Therefore look back to the psalm. The first portions have already been expounded; what follows is this: “The sinner will watch the just person and gnash his teeth at him; but the Lord will mock him.” Whom? Certainly the sinner who gnashes his teeth at the just person. Why, then, will the Lord mock him? “Because he sees beforehand that his day will come.”

He seems harsh when he threatens the just person, not knowing the hour of his own tomorrow. But the Lord sees and foresees his day. Which day? The day on which he will repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27). For he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment (Rom. 2:5).

But the Lord foresees; you do not foresee. The one who foresees has revealed it to you [Note: [Col. 0364] The manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “He will reveal to you what he foresees.” Shortly afterward: “You did not know the day on which he would suffer punishment; but the one who knows will not conceal it from you.”].
