You did not know the day of the unjust person, the day on which he will pay the penalty; but the one who knows did not conceal it from you.

It is no small part of knowledge to be joined to the one who knows. He has the eyes of understanding; you should have the eyes of faith. Believe what God sees. The day of the unjust person will come, the day God foresees.

What day? The day of each person’s punishment. For it is necessary that punishment come upon the ungodly and punishment upon the unjust, whether he turns himself or does not turn. If he turns, this very thing is punished in him: the destruction of his iniquity.

Did the Lord not mock when he foresaw the days of the two wicked men—the betrayer Judas and the persecutor Saul (Acts 1 and 9)? [Col. 0365] He foresaw one man’s day for punishment and the other’s for righteousness. Both were punished: one was assigned to the fires of Gehenna; the other was struck down by a heavenly voice.

Therefore you too, when you suffer an unjust person, foresee with God, through the eyes of faith, his day. When you see him raging against you, say to yourself: “If he is corrected, he will be with me; if he perseveres, he will not be with me.”

3. [Verse 14–16.] What then? Does the injustice of the unjust person harm you and not harm him? How can it happen that his iniquity—which proceeds through his anger and hatred to injure you—does not first ravage him inwardly before testing you outwardly?

Adversity presses your body; iniquity corrupts his soul. For whatever he brings forth against you returns upon him. His persecution makes you purified and makes him guilty. Whom, then, does it harm more?

Behold, by raging he has stripped you: who is struck by the more serious loss, the person who loses money or the person who loses faith? Those who possess the inner eye know how to grieve over such losses. Gold shines for many; faith does not shine. They have eyes with which to see gold, but they do not have eyes with which to see faith.

If they had them and saw, they would certainly love faith more. Yet when their faith is broken, they shout, provoke envy, and say, “O faith! Where is faith?” You love it in order to demand it; love it in order to display it.

Therefore, because all who persecute the righteous are struck by a more serious loss and afflicted by a more grievous destruction, when their very spirit is ravaged, the psalm continues and shows this:

“Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow, to overthrow the poor and needy, to slaughter the upright in heart. Let their sword enter their own hearts.”

It is easy for his sword—that is, his blade—to reach your body, just as the sword of persecutors reached the bodies of martyrs. But when the body was struck, the heart remained unharmed. The heart of the one who drew the sword against the body of the just person, however, did not remain unharmed.

This psalm bears witness to it. It does not say, “Let their sword enter their body,” but, “Let their sword enter their own hearts.” They wanted to kill in the body; let them die in the soul.

The Lord made those whose bodies they wanted to kill secure, saying to them: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). What madness is it to rage with a sword, unable to kill anything but the body of one’s enemy, while able to kill one’s own soul?

They are foolish; they rage against themselves; they are insane and do not see themselves. It is as though someone wanted to drive iron through his own body in order to tear another person’s tunic. You pay attention to where you have arrived, but not to what you have pierced: you tore his garment, but your own flesh.

It is clear, then, that the wicked harm themselves more, and injure themselves more, than they seem to harm those whom they hate. Therefore, “Let their sword enter their own hearts.” This is the Lord’s sentence; it cannot happen otherwise.

“And let their bow be broken.” What is “Let their bow be broken”? Let their plots be frustrated. For above he had said: “Sinners have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow.” By drawing the sword he meant open attack; by bending the bow he meant that hidden ambushes should be understood.

Behold, his sword kills him, and the arrangement of his ambushes is frustrated. What does “is frustrated” mean? It harms the righteous person not at all.

How, then, did it not harm him at all—for example, the man whom he stripped and whom he reduced to poverty by taking away his possessions? He has what he may sing: “Better is the little of the just than the great riches of sinners.”

4. [Verse 17.] But the unrighteous are powerful; they accomplish much, and the means for carrying out their affairs are available to them. Their actions proceed rapidly; when they give an order, obedience follows. Will it always be so? “For the arms of sinners will be broken.”

Their arms, then, are their power. What will he do in Gehenna? Or will he do what that rich man did—feasting among the living, tormented among the dead (Luke 16:19, 24)? “The arms of sinners will be broken.”

“But the Lord strengthens the righteous.” How does he strengthen them? What does he say to them? What is said in another psalm: “Wait for the Lord, act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14).

What does “Wait for the Lord” mean? You labor for a time; you will not labor forever. Your trouble is brief; your blessedness will be eternal. You grieve for a little while; you will rejoice without end.

But in the midst of troubles you are beginning to slip? The example of Christ’s sufferings is set before you. See what he endured for you, although he had no reason of his own for enduring it.

However much you suffer, you will not reach those insults, those scourges, that shameful garment, that crown of thorns, or finally that cross, because even that punishment has now been removed from the human race. When criminals were crucified in ancient times, now no one is crucified. It was honored, and it was ended. It has ended as punishment; it remains in glory [Note: [Col. 0366] Fifteen manuscripts read “in grace.”].

From places of punishment it made its way to the foreheads of emperors. He who gave such honor to his punishments—what does he reserve for his faithful?

By these things, these words, these exhortations, and this kind of example, the Lord strengthens the righteous. Let sinners rage as much as they want, and as much as they are permitted: the Lord strengthens the righteous.

Whatever happens to the righteous person, let him attribute it to the divine will, not to the power of the enemy. The enemy can rage; he cannot strike if the Lord does not will it. And if the Lord wills him to strike, he knows how to receive his own: “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

Why, then, does the wicked person boast that my Father has made a scourge for himself out of that man? He employs him in service; he trains me for inheritance. We should not consider how much he permits the unjust, but how much he preserves for the just.

5. But we should also wish for those through whom we are scourged that they may be converted and themselves be scourged. Thus he instructed his faithful servant who had made a scourge for himself out of Saul, but afterward converted Saul as well.

When the Lord told holy Ananias, by whom Saul was baptized, that Saul was to be received because he was a vessel of election, Ananias replied, fearing and trembling at the report he had heard about Saul the persecutor:

“Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how many persecutions he has inflicted on your saints in Jerusalem; and now, having received letters, he is going so that wherever he finds those who invoke your name, he may drag them away, bind them, and bring them to the chief priests.”

And the Lord replied: “Let him be; I will show him what he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:13–16).

“I will repay him,” he said; “I will take vengeance on him, and he will suffer for my name, he who rages against my name. Through him I instruct—or have instructed—others; through others I will also instruct him.”

This happened, and we know how much Saul endured—much more than he had inflicted. Like a greedy tax collector, he received back with interest what he had exacted.

6. But see whether what the psalm now says, “The Lord strengthens the righteous,” was fulfilled in him. “Not only,” Paul himself says, “when we were suffering many evils, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

Good—he is plainly already just, already strengthened. Just as those who persecuted him did no harm to him once he had been strengthened, so neither did he harm those whom he persecuted.

“The Lord strengthens the righteous.” Hear other words of the strengthened righteous person: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or persecution?” (Rom. 8:35). How firmly he remained, since such things did not separate him! “The Lord strengthens the righteous.”

Some prophets had come down from Jerusalem and, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied to Paul that he would suffer many things in Jerusalem. One of them, named Agabus, even untied his belt and bound himself with it—as prophets customarily did in order to demonstrate future events through such signs—and said:

“Thus you see me bound; so must this man be bound in Jerusalem.”

The brothers, having been warned by the prophecy about Saul—now Paul—not to expose himself to such dangers, began to dissuade him, both by admonishing him and by begging him not to go to Jerusalem.

But he, who was already among the number of those of whom it was said, “The Lord strengthens the righteous,” said: “Why are you breaking my heart? I am not holding my life dear to myself.” For he had already said to those whom he had brought forth in the Gospel: “I will gladly spend myself for your souls” (2 Cor. 12:15). “For I am ready,” he said, “not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21:11–13).

7. [Verse 18.] “The Lord therefore strengthens the righteous.” How does he strengthen them? “The Lord knows the ways of the blameless.”

When they suffer evil, those who do not know the ways of the blameless believe that they are walking in evil ways. But the one who knows those ways knows by which straight path he leads his meek ones.

Hence he said in another psalm: “He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways” (Ps. 24:9).

How do you think people regarded the ulcer-covered poor man lying before the rich man’s door? How perhaps they spat at him with their nostrils closed? But the Lord knew how to preserve paradise for him [Note: [Col. 0367] Most manuscripts read “to be preserved for him.”].

How, on the other hand, did he desire the life of the man who wore purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day? But the Lord, who foresaw his day, knew his future torments—torments without end. “The Lord knows the ways of the blameless.”

8. “And their inheritance will be forever.” We have this in faith. Does the Lord possess it merely in faith? The Lord knows these things with such a manifestation as we cannot express, when we shall be made equal to the angels.

For what will be manifest to us will not be as manifest as it is to the one who cannot be changed. Yet what has been said about us? “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

A certain sweet spectacle is therefore being kept for us altogether. Even if it can in some measure be considered in a riddle and through a mirror, the beauty of that sweetness which God keeps for those who fear him and perfects for those who hope in him cannot be expressed at all (Ps. 30:20).

Our hearts are being prepared for that reality amid all the tribulations and temptations of this life. Do not be surprised that you are being prepared through labors: you are being prepared for something great.

Hence the voice of the strengthened righteous person: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

What will our future glory be, if not equality with the angels and the vision of God? How much does a physician benefit a blind man when he heals his eyes so that he can see this light? Once he has been healed, what can that man find worthy to repay his physician? However much he gives him, what could he give comparable to what the physician provided? At most he may give gold, and much gold; but the physician gave him light.

To make him understand that he gives nothing, let him see in the darkness what he gives. What, then, shall we give to that physician who heals our inner eyes so that we may see a certain eternal light—which is himself? What shall we give him?

Let us seek and find, if we can; and amid the distress of our searching, let us cry out: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me?” And what did he find? “I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13).

“Can you,” he says, “drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). Hence he says to Peter: “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17)—the sheep for whom he would drink the Lord’s cup.

“The Lord strengthens the righteous. The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance will be forever.”

9. [Verse 19.] “They will not be put to shame in the evil time.” What does “They will not be put to shame in the evil time” mean? In the day of tribulation, in the day of distress, they will not be put to shame, as the person is put to shame whose hope deceives him.

Who is put to shame? The person who says, “I did not find what I was hoping for.” And rightly so: you were hoping in yourself, or you were hoping in a human friend. “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5).

You are put to shame because your hope deceived you, because the hope placed in falsehood deceived you: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11). But if you place your hope in your God, you will not be put to shame, because the one in whom you have placed your hope cannot be deceived.

Hence the strengthened righteous person whom I mentioned shortly before, placed in an evil time, in a day of tribulation, because he was not put to shame, says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint.”

Why does hope not disappoint? Because it has been placed in God. Therefore it follows: “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

The Holy Spirit has already been given to us. How can the one whose pledge we hold deceive us? “They will not be put to shame in the evil time, and in the days of famine they will be satisfied.”

There is indeed a certain satisfaction for them here. For the days of famine belong to this life: while others hunger, they are satisfied. Where else could the man who said, “We glory in tribulations,” have gloried if he were inwardly suffering want? Distress appeared outwardly, but inwardly there was spaciousness.

### 10. [v. 20]

But what does a wicked person do when he begins to suffer tribulation? Outwardly he has nothing; everything has been taken away, and in his conscience there is no comfort. There is nowhere for him to go out, because things are harsh; there is nowhere for him to go in, because they are evil. Rightly, then, what follows happens to him: “For sinners shall perish.” For those who have no place anywhere, how can they not perish? There is no consolation in external things, and none in internal things. These things are outside us, and from them there is no consolation. All who do not have God serve money, friendships, glory, the resources of the world, and whatever bodily goods there are [Note: Three manuscripts read: “Money, friendship, glory, the resources of the world, servants, and whatever goods,” etc.]; but they cannot be consoled inwardly as that man was consoled who was full of inner abundance and, belching forth from that very abundance, said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Therefore, for those sinners there is no place in the things that are outward, because there they suffer tribulations [Note: Lovaniensis has “where there is conscience.” The word “where” is absent from the manuscripts and from Erasmus.]; their conscience does not console them. They are not at peace with themselves, because it is impossible to be at peace with evil. Whoever is wicked is at odds with himself; he must be tortured by himself as his own torment. He himself is his punishment, for his conscience torments him. He flees from an enemy as best he can; but from himself, where will he flee?

### 11

Thus a certain man from the party of Donatus had come to us, accused and excommunicated by his own people, seeking here what he had lost there. But since he could not be received except in the place where he ought to have been received—for he had not left that party as an upright man among them, so that it might appear that he had acted not from necessity but by choice [Note: Thus the manuscripts of better quality. Erasmus has: “so that it might appear that he had acted not from pleasure but from necessity.” Lovaniensis has: “not from affection but from necessity.”]—because, then, he could not have there what he was seeking, and what he was seeking was vain exaltation and false honor, and because here he did not find what he had lost there, he too perished.

He groaned, wounded, and found no consolation; for there were terrible, silent goads in his conscience. We tried to console him with the word of God, but he was not one of those wise ants that gathered for themselves in summer what they would live on in winter. When circumstances are tranquil, a person ought to gather for himself the word of God and store it in the innermost recesses of his heart, just as the ant hides the labors of summer in secret chambers [Col. 0370] (Prov. 6:6; 30:25). During summer there is leisure for doing this; but winter comes—that is, tribulation overtakes a person—and unless he finds within himself something to eat, he must perish from hunger.

This man, then, had not gathered the word of God for himself. Winter overtook him; here he did not find what he was seeking, and he could not be consoled except from that source, but he had no access to the word of God. Within himself he had nothing; outside himself he did not find what he was seeking. He burned with the flames of indignation and grief; his mind was violently agitated, and remained so secretly for a long time, until it finally broke out in certain groans, so that they sounded among the brothers, although he did not know that he was being heard.

We saw it and grieved intensely—God knows—over such great punishment of the soul, such great crosses, such great hells, such great torments. What more need be said? Impatient of a lowly position—which, if he had been wise, could have been a salutary place for him—he appeared in such a state that he was even expelled.

Nor should we therefore despair, brothers, of others who may have chosen the truth and not followed necessity. Indeed, we must not despair of the others to such an extent that I do not even despair of this man, so long as he lives. For one must despair of no living person.

This, then, brothers, your Charity ought to have learned from this occasion, lest someone perhaps tell you otherwise. Their subdeacon, when no controversy had been raised against him there, chose Catholic peace and unity, left them, and came to us—truly coming as one who chose what is good, not as one rejected by the wicked. He was received in such a way that we rejoice over his conversion and commend him to your prayers. God is powerful enough to make him better and better.

In any case, no judgment should be pronounced about anyone in either direction, whether good or bad. For as long as we live here, the coming day is always unknown.

“They shall not be put to shame in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied; for sinners shall perish.”

### 12

But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they glory and are exalted, shall fail; like smoke they shall fail. Recognize from the comparison itself the matter he has indicated. Smoke rising from the place of fire is lifted upward, and by that very elevation swells into a great globe. But the larger that globe has become, the more insubstantial it is; for its greatness is not founded and solidified, but hanging and inflated, and it passes into the air and disperses, so that you see that its very size has worked against it. The more erect it is, the more extended, the more spread out in every direction into a greater circumference, the thinner it becomes, and it fails and disappears.

“But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they glory and are exalted, shall fail; like smoke they shall fail.” Of such people it has been said: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith. But they shall not make further progress, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:8–9). How do they resist the truth, except through the inflation of their pride, going off into the winds and exalting themselves as though they were righteous and great?

What does he say about them? He speaks as of smoke: “But they shall not make further progress, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:8–9).

“But the enemies of the Lord, as soon as they glory and are exalted, shall fail; like smoke they shall fail.”

### 13. [v. 21]

“The sinner borrows and does not repay.” [Col. 0371] He receives and does not return. What does he not return? Thanksgiving. For what does God want from you, or what does God demand, except what is for your benefit? [Note: The editions read “what he promised”; several manuscripts more correctly read “what is for your benefit.”]

And how much has the sinner received for which he will not repay? He received existence; he received the status of a human being, with a great distinction between himself and an animal; he received the form of the body; he received in the body the differentiation of the senses—eyes for seeing, ears for hearing, nostrils for smelling, the palate for tasting, hands for touching, feet for walking—and bodily health itself.

But so far we share these things with animals. He also received something more: a mind capable of understanding, capable of grasping the truth, capable of distinguishing right from wrong, capable of investigating, desiring, praising, and clinging to the Creator. The sinner received all these things, but by failing to live well he does not return what he owes.

Therefore, “the sinner borrows and does not repay”; he does not return to the one from whom he received, and he does not give thanks. Rather, he repays evil for good: blasphemies, murmuring against God, and indignation. Thus he borrows and does not repay; but “the righteous has compassion and lends.”

The one, then, has nothing; the other has something. See the poverty; see the riches. The one receives and does not repay; the other has compassion and lends. The latter abounds. What if he is poor? Even so, he is rich. Only direct your devout eyes toward his riches. You look at an empty chest, but you do not look at a conscience full of God. He has no resources outwardly, but inwardly he has charity.

How much he dispenses from charity, and it is never exhausted! For if he has resources outwardly, charity itself gives, from what he possesses. But if it finds nothing outwardly to give, it gives goodwill; it offers counsel, if it can; it offers help, if it can. Finally, if it can help neither by counsel nor by assistance, it helps at least by good wishes, or it prays for one suffering together with it—and perhaps he himself is heard more readily than the one who extends bread.

The one whose breast is full of charity always has something from which to give. This is charity, which is also called goodwill. God does not demand more from you than what he has placed within you. Goodwill cannot be idle. For even if you have no coin left over, possessing goodwill does not mean that you fail to stretch out your hand to the poor. The poor themselves provide for one another through goodwill; they are not fruitless toward one another.

You see a sighted person leading a blind man. Because the needy man had no coins to give, he lent his eyes to the one who had none. How did this happen—that he lent his own members to one who did not have them—except because goodwill was present within him, the treasure of the poor? In that treasure there is the sweetest rest and true security. No thief is admitted to steal it, nor is shipwreck feared for it. He keeps with himself what he has within; he escapes naked, yet he is full.

Therefore, “the righteous has compassion and lends.”

### 14. [v. 22]

“For those who bless him shall possess the land as an inheritance”—that is, they shall possess it as that righteous one did, truly the only righteous and the one who justifies. He was poor here, yet he brought great riches with him, by which he might make rich those whom he found poor [Col. 0372].

For he is the one who enriched the hearts of the poor with the Holy Spirit, and filled souls emptied by the confession of sins with the wealth of righteousness. He was able to make a fisherman rich: the fisherman abandoned his nets, despising what he had and drawing up what he did not have (Matt. 4:19). “For God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

He did not win an orator from an orator, but won an orator from a fisherman; he won a senator from a fisherman; he won an emperor from a fisherman.

“For those who bless him shall possess the land as an inheritance”: they shall be his co-heirs in that land of the living, of which it is said in another psalm: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6). “You are yourself my portion,” he says to God, and he did not hesitate to make God his portion.

“They shall possess the land as an inheritance. But those who curse him shall perish.”

That those who bless him should bless was granted to them [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “those who bless.” Lovaniensis has “that they may be blessed,” less suitably.]. For the matter came to those who cursed him, and they became those who bless. Thus those who cursed him have already perished, when by his gift they became those who bless the one whom they had cursed to their own harm, but whom they bless for his good.

### 15. [v. 23]

See what follows: “The steps of a person shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way.” For a person to will the way of the Lord, his steps are directed by the Lord himself. For if the Lord did not direct a person’s steps, they were so crooked that he would always go along crooked paths and, by following winding tracks, could not return.

But he came, called, and redeemed; he shed blood. He paid this price; he did these good things and suffered evils. Consider what he did: he is God. Consider what he suffered: he is human. Who is this God-human? If you, O human being, had not abandoned God, God would not have become human for you.

Was it not enough for you as a reward or gift that he made you human, unless he also became human for you? For he is the one who directed our steps so that we would will his way.

“The steps of a person shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way.”

### 16

Now, when you follow the way of Christ, do not promise yourself the prosperity of the world. He walked through hardship, but he made great promises. Follow him. Do not look only at where you are going to travel, but also at where you will arrive. You will endure temporary hardships, but you will reach eternal joys. If you wish to endure the labor, consider the reward.

A laborer in a vineyard would also collapse unless he considered what he was going to receive. But once you have considered what you are going to receive, everything you suffer will seem worthless to you, and you will not consider it worthy of that for which you receive the reward. You will be amazed that so much is given for such a little labor.

For surely, brothers, eternal labor would have had to be undertaken for eternal rest; and if you were going to receive eternal happiness, you ought to have endured eternal sufferings. But if you endured eternal labor, when would you come to eternal happiness? Thus it necessarily happens that your tribulation is temporary, so that, once it has ended, you may come to happiness without end.

Yet, brothers, tribulation could have been long in comparison with eternal happiness. For example, since our happiness will have no end, our misery, labor, and tribulations might have lasted a very long time. Even if they lasted a thousand years, set a thousand years against eternity: what can you set against the infinite, however finite the amount? Ten thousand years, a hundred thousand, if one may put it so, and thousands upon thousands—all of which have an end—cannot be compared with eternity.

Moreover, God willed not only that your labor be temporary, but also that it be brief. The whole life of a human being consists of few days, even if joyful things were not mixed with hardships—though the joyful are certainly more numerous and longer than the hardships. The hardships are therefore shorter and fewer, so that we may endure.

If, then, throughout his entire life a person were in labors and troubles—in pains, torments, prison, beatings, hunger and thirst, every day and every hour, throughout his whole life up to old age—the whole life of a human being would still be only a few days. When that labor has passed, the eternal kingdom will come; happiness without end will come; equality with the angels will come; the inheritance of Christ will come; Christ will come as co-heir.

For how small a labor do we receive how great a reward!

Veteran soldiers who labor in military service and spend so many years amid wounds begin their service in youth and leave it as old men. In order to have a few quiet days in their old age—when age itself begins to weigh upon them, though wars do not—how many hardships do they endure? What journeys, what cold, what heat, how many necessities, what wounds, what dangers! They endure all these things without considering anything except those few quiet days of old age, although they do not know whether they will reach them.

Therefore, “the steps of a person shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way.”

This is what I had begun to say: if you want the way of Christ, and you are truly a Christian—for a Christian is one who does not reject Christ’s way, but wishes to follow Christ’s way through Christ’s sufferings—do not wish to go by another way than the one by which he himself went.

It appears hard, but it is the safe way. Another way may perhaps have pleasures, but it is full of robbers.

“And he shall will his way.”

### 17. [v. 24]

“When he falls, he shall not be disturbed, because the Lord strengthens his hand.”

See what it means to will the way of Christ. Let it happen that he suffers some tribulation, some dishonor, some insult, some affliction, some losses, and whatever else abounds in this life for the human race. He sets before himself his Lord and considers how many kinds of temptation he endured. “He shall not be disturbed when he falls,” because the Lord strengthens his hand, because Christ suffered first.

What will you fear, O human being, whose steps have been directed so that you would will the way of the Lord? What will you fear? Pains? Christ was scourged (Matt. 27:26). Will you fear insults? He heard, “You have a demon,” though he was casting out demons (John 8:48). Perhaps a faction and conspiracy of wicked people? A conspiracy was formed against him (John 9:22).

You may be unable to show your good conscience in some accusation, and you may suffer violence because false witnesses are heard against you. Against him they first gave false testimony—not only before his death, but also after his resurrection. False witnesses were brought in so that he might be condemned by the judges [Col. 0374] (Matt. 26:60). False witnesses who were guards approached the tomb.

He rose with so great a miracle; the shaken earth revealed the rising Lord. The earth was there too, guarding the earth, but the harder earth could not be changed. It announced the truth, but was deceived by falsehood. For those guards told the Jews what they had seen and what had happened; they received money, and it was said to them: “Say that his disciples came while you were sleeping and stole him away” (Matt. 28:12).

Behold false witnesses, even against the risen one. What blindness there is in false witnesses, brothers—what blindness! False witnesses commonly suffer this: they are blinded and, without knowing where it will appear, speak against themselves, so that it becomes clear that they are false witnesses.

What did they say against themselves? “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away.”

What does this mean? Who is giving the testimony? The one who was sleeping. I would not believe such people even if they were telling me their dreams.

What foolish madness! If you were awake, why did you permit it? If you were asleep, how did you know?

### 18

So too these men are their sons [Note: The Donatists.], as you remember [Note: Here the editions add “up to this point,” but the manuscripts lack it.]; and this should not be passed over on this occasion. We ought all the more to recall their vanity insofar as we seek their salvation.

Behold, the body of Christ suffers false witnesses; the body endures what went before in the head. It is not surprising that even now there are people belonging to Christ’s body, spread throughout the whole world, who say: “The offspring of traitors.”

You are giving false testimony. I convict you there of being a false witness by following a few words. You say to me, “You are a traitor.” I say to you, “You are a liar.” But you nowhere and never prove my alleged betrayal; I, however, now prove your lie by these very words of yours.

Certainly you said there that “we sharpen our swords.” I shall read the records of your Circumcellions.

Certainly [Note: From this point it is clear that Augustine undertook in this sermon to refute that mandate of Primianus which he mentions in the Brief Summary of the Conference with the Donatists, day 3, chapter 8, but more explicitly in Against Cresconius, book 4, chapter 47, in these words: “Why, then, did Primianus, in the records of the Carthaginian magistrate, among the other matters which he ordered to be pursued insultingly against us, say of us: ‘They take away what belongs to others; we leave untouched what has been taken away’?”] you said there that “you pass over what has been taken away.” I shall read the Records, where you made arrangements for exacting it.

Certainly you said there: “We offer only the Gospels.” I shall read the many orders of the judges by which you persecuted those separated from you. I shall read the Petitions to the apostate emperor, to whom you said [Note: This was said in the Petitions presented to Julian the Apostate in the name of the Donatists by Rogatianus and Pontius, according to Letter 105 to the Donatists, no. 9, and Against Petilianus, book 2, chapters 9 [lacuna] and 97.] that only justice has a place with him.

Or does Julian’s apostasy perhaps seem to you to be part of the Gospel? Behold, I have caught you in a lie. What have you said about me that ought to be believed? Even if I could not find a means of showing that you speak falsely, it would be enough to show that you are a liar.

What do you say? “As you are, so are the others” [Note: Eight manuscripts read: “You who say, ‘As you are, so are the others.’” Perhaps this is more correct, in accordance with what is read somewhat later here, in section 20: “This was the rule: Whatever those were like with whom communion had been maintained, all and the whole mass became like them.”]. For this reason you sent such words to everyone: you wanted falsehood to abound through association, so that you alone would not blush at the lie.

### 19

“But,” he says, “let the judgment of our fathers concerning Caecilianus stand.”

Why should it stand? Because bishops judged him. Let what the Maximianists judged in your case stand as well.

First—for I believe you know this—bishops who agreed with Maximianus, then still his deacon, came to Carthage, as the Tractoria states [Note: The Colbert manuscript has Tractoria; the other books, the editions, and the manuscripts disagree.]. They also attached it to the Records while they were litigating over the house with his procurator [Note: Primianus.], the man who “passes over what has been taken away.”

Thus at first they sent a Tractoria concerning him, complaining that he had refused to come out to them. This above all was their complaint.

See how God repaid them with what they had said about Caecilianus. The resemblance is astonishing. God willed, after so many years, to roll before their faces what had happened, so that they could find no way at all to disguise it or escape from it. They might say that they had forgotten what had happened before, but God does not allow them to forget—and would that this might contribute to their salvation! For in his mercy God did this, if they will consider what has happened.

Therefore, brothers, place before your eyes the unity of the whole world that existed then, from which these men separated themselves in opposition to Caecilianus. Now place before your eyes the party of Donatus, from which the Maximianists separated themselves in opposition to Primianus.

What those men then did to Caecilianus, these men have now done to Primianus. For this reason the Maximianists say that they are more genuinely Donatists than the Donatists, because they truly imitated the deeds of their ancestors. They raised up Maximianus against Primianus just as those others raised up Majorinus against Caecilianus; and these men complained about Primianus just as those others complained about Caecilianus.

For, if you remember, those men said that Caecilianus had refused to come out to them because he was mindful of his conscience. But he knew their faction. These men likewise complain that Primianus refused to come out to them.

Why is Primianus allowed to know the faction of the Maximianists, while Caecilianus is not allowed to know the faction of the Donatists?

Maximianus had not yet been ordained; charges were being made against Primianus. The bishops came and wanted him to come out to them. He did not come out, as their Tractoria inserted in the Records indicates.

He did not come out. I do not condemn him; indeed, I praise him. If you saw a faction, you ought not to have approached factional men, but to have preserved your case for the better judgment of your own party. A large part of the Donatists remained, before whom Primianus could clear himself; for that reason he refused to go out to those who had already conspired in faction.

You see how we praise your counsel against the Maximianists. Now pay close attention to Caecilianus’s case. You do not want him treated as a brother; judge him as an outsider.

You refused to come out. What were you saying to yourself? [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read “what was he saying?”]

“These men have conspired in a faction against my safety; they have been corrupted against me. If I entrust myself to them, I prejudice my case. I will not go out to them; let my case be preserved for men of better standing and greater authority.”

Good counsel.

But what if Caecilianus said this? You will work hard to show what other Lucilla corrupted these men against you, and perhaps you will not find it. He knew this so well that it was later revealed in the Records [Note: The Records indicate that these proceedings were conducted before Zenophilus the proconsul in the year 320. Some fragments are cited in Against Cresconius, book 3, chapter 29, where Silvanus of Cirta’s moneychanger-deacon disclosed that bishops and others had been corrupted by the money of Lucilla, a powerful woman, so that Majorinus might become bishop of Carthage against Caecilianus. See Augustine’s Letter 43, no. 17, to Glorius, Eleusius, and others.].

But you saw something hidden—I do not know what—and something alarming was reported to you. I concede this precaution to your fear: you acted rightly by not approaching such men. For there were others who could judge your case.

Now consider Caecilianus: you preserved Numidia for yourself; he preserved the whole world. But if you want the judgments of the Donatists at that time to stand against him, let the judgments of the Maximianists now stand against you. Bishops condemned him; bishops condemned you as well.

Why did you later plead your case and prevail against the Maximianists there, just as he later pleaded his case and prevailed against the Donatists there?

What happened then, therefore, appears to have been rolled before our eyes in a marvelous and manifest example: the Maximianists complain against Primianus in exactly the way all these men complained against Caecilianus.

It is astonishing, brothers, how I am moved and how I give thanks to God, because the mercy of God has truly fashioned an example for these men—if they are wise—in order to enlighten them.

Therefore, brothers, if you please, since God has also placed this in our hands, listen to the council of the Maximianists [Note: Here Augustine recites the letter of the council of the Maximianists at Cabarsussa and briefly explains it in a commentary. For a correct understanding of section 20, it is very important that Augustine’s words be carefully distinguished from the words of the letter. This will certainly be easy for the reader if he observes that the former are printed in Roman type, as they say, and the latter in italics. M.].

## 20.

To the most holy brothers and fellow bishops throughout all Africa—

Their entire unity is in Africa. But here the Catholic Church is with them; in other parts of the world, however, they are not with the Catholic Church.

To the most holy brothers and fellow bishops established throughout all Africa—that is, in the provinces of Proconsular Africa, Numidia, Mauretania, Byzacena, and Tripolitania—and also to the priests and deacons, and to all the congregations who, in the truth of the Gospel, are fighting alongside us: Victorinus, Fortunatus, Victorianus, Migginus,

[Note: Several manuscripts consistently have *Miggin* here and below.]

Saturninus, Constantius, Candorius, Innocentius, Cresconius, Florentius,

[Note: The editions have *Florentinus*. Almost all manuscripts, however, have *Florentius*.]

Salvius, another Salvius, Donatus, Geminius, Praetextatus—

He is the Assuritan whom they later received: the man who had pronounced judgment against himself, they afterward received.

Maximianus, Theodorus, Anastasius, Donatianus, Donatus, another Donatus, Pomponius, Pancratius,

[Note: Five manuscripts have *Prancatius*; nor do they read otherwise at the end of the synodical letter.]

Januarius, Secundinus, Pascasius, Cresconius, Rogatianus, another Maximianus, Benenatus, Gaianus, Victorinus, Guntasius, Quintasius, Felicianus—

This is the Mustitanus who is still alive; but perhaps he is another man from another place.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have *Musticanus*.]

Afterward, those signing add the places from which each man came.

Salvius, Migginus, Proculus, Latinus, and the others who were present at the council at Cabarsussi,

[Note: The Erfurt edition has *Cavernam Susis*; Lovaniensis has *Cavernas Susis*. Four manuscripts have *Cavarnasussis*; three have *Cabarsus*; two, *Cabarsusi*; the Royal manuscript, *Cebarsussi*; and eight others, including the Vatican manuscript, *Cabarsussi*, perhaps in place of *Cabarsussim*. Since Augustine mentions two councils of the Maximianists against Primianus—one held at Carthage and the other at Cabarsussi—some, following Baronius, assign this synodical letter to the former council and therefore wish to read not “at Cabarsussi,” which was situated in Byzacena, but “at Cavernas Susis,” a place which, according to the view they began to establish, was near Carthage. Yet the earlier council at Carthage, as Augustine testifies in *Against Cresconius*, book 4, chapters 6 and 7, was held by only “forty-three bishops, who had not yet dared to carry out a final judgment, but, by way of a certain preliminary decision, determined that, if Primianus trusted his case, an opportunity should be left for him to answer and clear himself at a subsequent and more solemn council. When he refused to come, they then necessarily judged that he should be condemned, without any further suspension of the sentence.” This clearly refers to the council at Cabarsussi, where Primianus was “condemned completely and most fully by a hundred bishops or more.” This synodical letter, as is evident, contains Primianus’s complete and most thorough condemnation; hence, after reading it, Augustine said, “This is your condemnation.” Nor was it issued only by forty-three bishops, or even only by the fifty-three listed at the end. For this is clearly indicated by what we read below, §23: “A hundred—or however many there were—who, on Maximianus’s side, condemned Primianus.” Moreover, the fact that the subscriptions of all who took part in composing the synodical letter were not recited is shown by Anastasius, Constantius, Candorius, and certain other bishops, who are named at its beginning rather than at its end.]

send eternal salvation in the Lord.

No one, most beloved brothers, can be unaware that the priests of God, moved not by their own will but by divine law, must pronounce judgment both against the guilty and, with justice and good reason, remove from the innocent any sentence inflicted upon them. For whoever either spares the guilty or attempts to destroy the innocent will be exposed to no small danger, especially since it is written: “You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous, and you shall not acquit the guilty” (Exodus 23:7).

Warned, therefore, by this ordinance of the Law, it was necessary for us to hear and examine the case of Primianus, whom the holy congregation of the Church of Carthage had received as bishop into the sheepfold of God, at the request of the letters of the elders of that same Church. Our purpose was that, once everything had been explained, we might either clear an innocent man—as we greatly desired—or certainly show that a guilty man had been condemned on the basis of his own merits.

For it was our greatest desire that the holy congregation of the Church of Carthage should rejoice that it had been exalted under a bishop who was holy in every respect and blameworthy in none. For this reason, the priest of the Lord ought indeed to be such that, whatever the people could not obtain from God on their own behalf, he might deserve to obtain for them what they asked, since it is written: “If the people sin, the priest will pray for them; but if the priest sins, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25).

The Apostles also wrote to the congregations asking them to pray for them, and the Apostles, when praying, said: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). The apostle John said: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

But that statement was written concerning that priest whom these people do not understand, so that the people might be warned by the prophecy that they ought to recognize such a priest for whom no one could pray. Who, then, is the one for whom no one prays, except the one who intercedes for everyone? Since at that time the priesthood was Levitical, in which the priest entered the holy places

[Note: The manuscripts have “entered and offered”; they do not contain “into the holy places.”]

and offered sacrifices for the people, he bore an image, not the reality, of a future priest. At that time the priests themselves were sinners, like the rest of humanity. Therefore, wishing through prophecy

[Note: The editions have “through the prophet.” The manuscripts more correctly have “through prophecy.”]

to warn the people that such a priest was now to be desired—a priest who would intercede for everyone and for whom no one would pray—God designated such a one and said: “If the people sin, the priest will pray for them; but if the priest sins, who will pray for him?” Therefore, O people, choose such a priest for whom you will not be compelled to pray, but concerning whose prayer for you you may be secure.

He is our Lord Jesus Christ, the one priest, the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

The scandals of Primianus, therefore, and his singular wickedness, so provoked heavenly judgment against him that it became necessary to cut off entirely the author of these crimes. When he had only recently been ordained—

Now his crimes themselves are being stated—

he urged the presbyters of the aforementioned congregation to enter into an impious conspiracy,

[Note: Several manuscripts have “to participate in an impious conspiracy.”]

and requested from them, as though it were a right granted by favor, that they promise without hesitation to lend their agreement to the condemnation of four deacons, distinguished men approved by their exceptional merits—namely, Maximianus, Rogatianus, Donatus, and also Salgamius.

[Note: The editions have “and also Salgamus, they should agree.” The manuscripts have “and also Salgamius”; most omit “they should agree,” since it was added unnecessarily.]

Among these four was that author of the schism, cutting off piece from piece, yet not grieving that he himself had been cut off from wholeness.

When they refused to promise him this and remained silent, he did not hesitate to carry out by himself the crime he had conceived.

Stunned by his wicked presumption, they rejected his action by their silence; nevertheless, he did not hesitate to carry out by himself the crime he had conceived, to such an extent that he thought a sentence should be pronounced against Maximianus the deacon—a man, as everyone knows, innocent—without cause, without an accuser, without a witness, while he was absent and lying sick in bed.

Behold the crime!

He had previously condemned clergy with no less madness. For when he added incestuous persons to the holy communion contrary to the law and the decrees of all the priests, and when the greater part of the congregation, supported even by letters from the most distinguished elders, summoned him to correct on his own what he had done, he refused to amend it, possessed by his own arrogance.

Moved by these events, therefore, the elders of the aforementioned Church sent letters and messengers to the entire council,

[Note: Three manuscripts have “to the entire clergy.” Two others have “to all the councils,” omitting “to.”]

earnestly pleading, not without tears, that we should come to them more urgently, so that, after weighing everything carefully and examining the accusations,

[Note: Thus several manuscripts. The editions have “intentions.”]

the reputation of the Church might be cleared. Accordingly, when we came to him in response to the letters mentioned, he, inflamed in his familiar manner, entirely avoided our arrival.

You know what is charged against him, because the party of Donatus has now become incestuous. This was the rule:

[Col. 0379]

“Whatever those with whom communion has been shared have been like, all and the entire mass become like them.”

Therefore, if these people speak the truth, the whole party of Donatus is now incestuous. Let the Numidians come forward plainly and say: “It does not concern us if you admitted certain incestuous persons to your communion. Could that harm people situated so far away?” If you who are in Numidia do not wish what happens at Carthage to harm you, could what happens in Africa harm the whole world? They always defend themselves by the very thing by which they accuse us and excuse us.

[Note: The editions have: “They always defend themselves by that very thing, excuse themselves by that very thing, and accuse us.” We have corrected this and other passages according to the manuscripts.]

He entirely avoided our arrival.

What they charged against Caecilianus.

He continued to resist with a rebellious mind and remained in wickedness, so that, having hired a crowd of depraved people—

This goes further. They did not say this about Caecilianus; observe what they did say—

and having obtained the assistance of officials, they blockaded the doors of the basilicas.

So that the bishops could not enter.

They prevented us from entering and from carrying out the solemn rites. If it is fitting for a bishop to do such things, if Christians are permitted to accept them, if the Gospels bear witness to this, let anyone who loves or defends the truth approve or judge it. For this was inflicted upon us by a brother once our own, something a stranger would never have done.

What more is needed?

[Note: “What need is there to say more?” is understood.]

They say many things and condemn the man; but let us now read the condemnation itself.

“We have all decreed, in the presence of the Holy Spirit, that this same Primianus is to be condemned: first, because he appointed other men in the place of living bishops; because he mixed incestuous persons with the communion of the saints; because he attempted to compel the presbyters to enter into a conspiracy; because he had the presbyter Fortunatus thrown into a sewer when he had come to the aid of the sick with baptism; because he denied communion to the presbyter Demetrius in order to compel him to disown his son; because that same presbyter was rebuked for having received bishops as guests; because the aforementioned Primianus sent a crowd to destroy the houses of Christians; because bishops and clergy alike were besieged and afterward stoned by his followers; because elders were beaten in the basilica when they objected to the admission of the Claudianists to communion; because he thought innocent clergy ought to be condemned; because he refused to present himself to be heard by us, having blocked the doors of the basilicas with a crowd and the Office, so that we could not enter;

[Note: The editions have “and the officials.” The manuscripts have “and the Office.”]

because he insultingly rejected the delegates whom we sent to him; because he seized many places, first by force and afterward by judicial authority.”

“One who passes over things taken away”: for the apostle Paul says, “Does any one of you who has a dispute against another dare to be judged before the unrighteous, and not before the saints?” (1 Corinthians 6:1). See what a crime they charged against him: that he did not wish to conduct the case concerning the places before bishops, but before a judge.

“Besides his other unlawful acts,

[Note: Most manuscripts have “his enticement.” Others have “his enticements.”]

which we have suppressed out of respect for the dignity of our style, he is to be condemned perpetually by the priestly council, lest, by flattering him, the Church of God be stained either by contagion or by some crime.

“Paul the apostle also urges and warns us concerning this very matter: ‘We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly’ (2 Thessalonians 3:6).

[Note: The word *brother* is absent from the manuscripts; the Donatists may well have omitted it deliberately.]

“And so, not unmindful of the purity of the Church, we have considered it beneficial to admonish through this Tractatoria all holy fellow priests, all clergy, and all congregations who remember that they are Christians, so that all of them may carefully shun his communion, since he has been condemned. For he himself will give an account of his destruction if, by refusing to hear this decree of ours, he attempts to violate it.

“It has also pleased us and the Holy Spirit that a period should be reserved for those who are slow to turn back. Accordingly, any of our fellow priests or clergy who, forgetful of their salvation, have not withdrawn from the communion of the aforementioned condemned Primianus by the day of his condemnation—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of July

[Note: Lovaniensis omits “the eighth day” here. The Erfurt edition omits the entire phrase, “from the Kalends of July up to the eighth day.” These words are found in most manuscripts; some of them, after “from the Kalends of July,” read: “if even with delay, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January.” The year is not given; it may have been A.D. 393. For the judgment of the later council at Bagai, pronounced in favor of Primianus against Maximianus and the council at Cabarsussi, was issued on April 24, A.D. 394, according to book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 56.]

until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, shall be bound by this sentence.

“Likewise, lay people, unless they separate themselves from his association by the coming Easter Day, reckoned from the aforementioned day of his condemnation, cannot be restored to the Church except through repentance, if indeed they take heed.

“Victorinus, bishop of Munatianum, have subscribed.

“Fortunatus, bishop of Dionysiana,

[Note: Two manuscripts have *Dionysiacensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Victorianus, bishop of Carcabia,

[Note: Lovaniensis has *Carbaniensis*; the Erfurt edition and nine manuscripts have *Carcabinensis*; two manuscripts have *Carcabensis*; others have *Carcabianensis*. The same form occurs in book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 19.]

have subscribed.

“Florentius, bishop of Hadrumetum, have subscribed.

“Migginus, bishop of Elephantaria,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have *Belephantariae*.]

have subscribed.

“Innocentius, bishop of Thebalta,

[Note: Five manuscripts have *Thesbalitensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Migginus, on behalf of my colleague Salvius, bishop of Membressa,

[Note: Thus several manuscripts and book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 19. The editions instead read *Salvianus Pressitanus*.]

have subscribed.

“Salvius, bishop of Ausafa,

[Note: The Erfurt edition has *Ausavensis*; Lovaniensis, *Ausacensis*. Several manuscripts, as in book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 19, have *Ausafensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Sabrata, have subscribed.

“Gemelius, bishop of Tanabae,

[Note: The Erfurt edition has *Anathabeis*. Some manuscripts have *a Tambeis*.]

have subscribed.

“From among the very condemners, Praetextatus, bishop of Assuri, and Felicianus, bishop of Musti, also subscribed.

“Praetextatus, bishop of Assuri, have subscribed.

“Maximianus, bishop of Stabata,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Sabbatensis*; one has *Sabatensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Datianus, bishop of Camiceta,

[Note: Four manuscripts have *Camacetensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Fisciana, have subscribed.

“Theodorus, bishop of Usula, have subscribed.

“Victorianus, at the command of his colleague Agnosius

[Note: Three manuscripts have *Agnasius*.]

the bishop, have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Cebresuta,

[Note: Five manuscripts have *Cebresusitanus*. Some have *Ceberesitanus*.]

have subscribed.

“Natalicus, bishop of Thela, have subscribed.

“Pomponius, bishop of Macriana, have subscribed.

“Pancratius, bishop of Balia,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Basilianensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Januarius, bishop of Aquena,

[Note: More manuscripts have *Aquensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Secundus, bishop of Jacondiana,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Secundinus*; some have *Secundianus*. In certain manuscripts it is *Jocondianensis*, and in others *Jaconnianensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Pascasius, bishop of Vicus Augusti, have subscribed.

“Creso, bishop of Conjustia,

[Note: Four manuscripts have *Cresoconius Titianensis*. Some have *Cresoconius Justicianensis*. Two others have *Cresconius Tacianensis*. The Royal manuscript has *Cresconius Titianus*.]

have subscribed.

“Rogatianus, bishop, have subscribed.

“Maximianus, bishop of Erumminum,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Erumninensis*; one has *Eruminensis*; another, *Erumniacensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Benenatus, bishop of Tuguzza,

[Note: The Vatican and Royal manuscripts have *Benenatus Tigurritanus*; those manuscripts omit below the words “Ritanus, bishop, have subscribed.”]

have subscribed.

“Ritanus, bishop, have subscribed.

“Gaianus, bishop of Tigualis, have subscribed.

“Victorinus, bishop of Leptis Magna,

[Note: Some manuscripts have *Victorianus*. Eleven manuscripts have *Leptimaginensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Guntasius, bishop of Bene, have subscribed.

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Benesensis*; others likewise have *Benefensis*.]

“Quintasius, bishop of Capsa,

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts have this form. The editions have *Capiensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Felicianus, bishop of Musti, have subscribed.

“Victorianus, by delegation of Migginus,

[Note: The editions omit “of Migginus.” Most manuscripts contain it; some instead read *Miggius*, while others have *Migginus*. Some manuscripts omit entirely the words “Miggius, bishop, have subscribed.”]

the bishop, have subscribed.

“Miggius, bishop, have subscribed.

“Latinus, bishop of Muguia, have subscribed.

“Proculus, bishop of Girba,

[Note: Some manuscripts have *Gurbitanus*. Others have *Curbitanus*.]

have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Sabrata, have subscribed on behalf of my brother and colleague Marratio.

“Proculus, bishop of Girba, have subscribed on behalf of my colleague Gallionus.

[Note: The Erfurt edition has *Gallonus*. Eight manuscripts have *Gallonio*.]

“Secundianus, bishop of Prisiana,

[Note: Most manuscripts have *Bissianensis* or *Bisianensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Helpidius, bishop of Thysdrus, have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Samurda, have subscribed.

“Getulicus, bishop of Victorianum, have subscribed.

“Annibonius, bishop of Robautum,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Rabautensis*. Others have *Sabautensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Annibonius, having been requested by my colleague, the bishop of Augendia,

[Note: Several manuscripts have “Annibonius, having been requested by my colleague of Augendia, have subscribed,” omitting the word “bishop.” Perhaps the reading should be “Augendo, or Secundus, bishop of Arus.” For in the *Acts of the Carthaginian Conference*, session 1, chapter 207, a certain Secundus is named as bishop of Arus.]

have subscribed.

“Tertullus, bishop of Abitina, have subscribed.

“Primulianus

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have *Primilianus*.]

the bishop, have subscribed.

“Secundinus, bishop of Arusium,

[Note: Some manuscripts have *Secundianus*. Others have *Arusilianensis* or *Aurisilianensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Maximus, bishop of Pittana,

[Note: In place of *Maximus Pittanensis*, some manuscripts have *Maximianus Bittanensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Crescentianus, bishop of Murra,

[Note: The Royal and Vatican manuscripts and some others have *Crescentianus Narensis*. Four have *Crescentianus Nalensis*. Six others join the two words together as *Crescinarensis*.]

have subscribed.

“Donatus, bishop of Belma,

[Note: Some manuscripts have *Belinensis*. Six others have *Velimensis*. Others have *Belimensis* or *Balmiensis*.]

have subscribed.

[Note: Most manuscripts have *Perserentius* instead of *Perseverantius*. Three others have *Theustinus* instead of *Tebertinus*. More have *Thebestinus* or *Thevestinus*.]

have subscribed.

“Faustinus, bishop of Bina, have subscribed.

“Victor, bishop of Altiburus,

[Note: The editions have *Altiburinanus*. The manuscripts have *Altiburitanus*.]

have subscribed.

“All together, fifty-three.”

## 21.

Deign to pay a little attention. “This is your condemnation.”

We say to him: “What do you want? Does it have weight or does it not? I am on your side. I say plainly that all these men made false accusations against you; and hear why I believe this: because you won your case before other judges, and these men were condemned.

“If, then, I believe you innocent for this reason—that, without going out to the factional men, you demonstrated your innocence elsewhere, so that those who condemned you deserved condemnation—deign to accept Caecilianus as innocent. He refused to go out to your predecessors and thus preserved his case for the whole world, just as you preserved yours for the council of Numidia.

“If the see of Bagai made you innocent,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *Vagaitana* rather than *Bagaitana*, and shortly afterward *Vagai* rather than *Bagai*, consistently changing *B* to *V*.]

how much more did the Apostolic See make him innocent? Or do you want those who condemned him at first to have authority? If they have authority, they have authority against you. For against Caecilianus they neither had nor will have authority. Nevertheless, consider what the judges decided against you.

## 22.

Now they dare to say: “But we who later condemned the Maximianists were more numerous.”

Let your sentence, then, have force against Felicianus, and theirs will have force against Caecilianus. At Bagai they held a council and also condemned Felicianus. Now Felicianus is within your communion: either a guilty man was received, or an innocent man was condemned.

If, then, you receive a guilty man for the sake of Donatus’s peace, yield to all nations for the sake of Christ’s peace. But if you, though innocent, were condemned through your error, could three hundred and ten men who condemned Felicianus have been mistaken, while seventy men who condemned Caecilianus could not have been mistaken?

What, then, do you say? When you are told, “The Maximianists who came before you condemned you,” you retreat and say: “But we who condemned the Maximianists were more numerous.”

A quick answer is given to both points, because your predecessors also condemned Caecilianus. If those who came first have authority, let the Primianists yield to the council of the Maximianists. If the more numerous have authority, let the Donatists yield to the whole world. I think nothing could be more just.

The Maximianists are few, but they came first. One guilty person does not make another guilty. If you think this, how could you, being yourself condemned, have condemned another? For you too were recorded among the condemners, and they did not preserve for him the place of one presenting his case.

[Note: The editions have *causam dicendi* (“the place for presenting a case”). The manuscripts more correctly have *causam dicentis* (“the place of one presenting his case”).]

Caecilianus, however, was treated differently: the place of one presenting his case was preserved for him, as the sentence itself shows, because he was not received into communion until he had been cleared.

This man is found here condemned by judges, but there condemning among the judges.

But let this be the justice of the council of Bagai. We concede everything completely. The Maximianists condemned you wrongly; your predecessors also wrongly condemned Caecilianus. You cleared yourself at Bagai; he cleared himself in the judgment beyond the sea. The whole world consented to that judgment.

What will you say? “We are more numerous than the Maximianists.”

Be more numerous, then. Let us therefore deal with numbers; see how great the difference is.

The Maximianists condemned you in your absence, because you refused to go to them. This is indeed similar: they likewise condemned Caecilianus in his absence, because he avoided their faction. But you in turn caused sentences to be pronounced at the council of Bagai against those who were absent. Caecilianus, however, was cleared while present and while his opponent was present.

There is another major difference. You yourself went to the Numidian judges before whom you were to clear yourself; you yourself appointed them. The Maximianists did not choose those judges. Caecilianus, however, was defeated before judges whom the party of Donatus had requested.

The Maximianists now answer you, and rightly say: “We first came to you from your own province, bishops from the diocese belonging to you, and we wished to hear your case. You despised us and did not come to us. If you feared our judgment, at least we could have chosen judges together; you should not have gone to judges whom you yourself wanted.”

Observe the difference.

At that time the Donatists themselves requested by their letters that the Emperor appoint judges. They rejected the judges before whom they were defeated—the very judges whom they had requested before they were defeated. Others were appointed at their request, and they were defeated there. They appealed to the Emperor and were defeated there also.

The Maximianist was defeated once, in his absence, and remains silent. The Donatist, defeated three times while present, does not remain silent?

## 23.

But you are arguing about numbers with the Maximianists. As I said, I favor your position. Three hundred and ten are more than a hundred—or however many there were who, on Maximianus’s side, condemned Primianus. Do you think that the thousands of bishops throughout the world who, on Caecilianus’s side, condemned Donatus have no weight with you?

But you will say to me: “Did thousands of bishops from the whole world condemn the Donatists?”

Very well: they did not condemn them. Why did they not condemn them? Because they did not take part in the judgment. If they did not take part in the judgment, they did not condemn them because they knew nothing at all about that case.

Why, then, did you separate yourself from the innocent? Someone baptized here from the whole world comes to you, and you want to baptize him again. While you are already carrying out your deadly ministry

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions have *mysterium* (“mystery”) instead of *ministerium* (“ministry”).]

and want to repeat what is given once and is not lost, some Mesopotamian, some Syrian, some Pontic, or someone established even farther away approaches you with a loud cry and a groan and says: “What are you trying to do? Are you going to baptize me again?”

You answer: “Because you do not have baptism.”

“Why?”

“Read the Apostle’s letters sent to me.”

Then someone comes from Galatia, someone from Pontus; someone comes from Philadelphia, to which churches John wrote (Revelation 1:4); someone comes from Colossae, someone from Philippi, someone from Thessalonica:

“Do I not have baptism—I, to whom the Apostle wrote—through whom you have it? You dare to read my letter, though you detest my peace?”

# SERMON III

## On the Third Part of the Psalm

### 1. [verse 25]

The final part of this psalm had remained with you unexplained and untreated. Therefore, as I see it, the Lord has recalled us to discharge our debt—not indeed according to our arrangement, but nevertheless not contrary to his own arrangement. Pay attention, then, brothers, so that, if God helps us, we may now discharge what we recognize that we owe.

Who is the one who says what we have just sung?

“I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.”

If one person speaks as though he were a single human being, how long is the span of one person’s life? And what is so remarkable about a person placed in some one region of the earth, throughout his whole life—brief as human life is, even if he has passed from youth into old age—not seeing the righteous forsaken or his offspring seeking bread?

It is not surprising. It could have happened that, before his lifetime, there had been some righteous person seeking bread. It could have happened that this occurred in another part of the earth, not where he himself was.

Now listen to another point that causes difficulty. Consider each one of you who may already have grown old and, looking back over the stages of life already completed, has reflected in thought upon the people he has known. Perhaps no righteous person seeking bread, or son of a righteous person seeking bread, has come to mind. Yet he turns to the divine Scriptures and finds Abraham, the righteous man, pressed by hunger in his own land and moving to another region (Genesis 12:10). He also finds that his son Isaac, because of the same famine, went into other regions seeking bread (ibid. 26:1).

How, then, can this be true: “I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread”? Even if he found this true within the span of his own life, he finds something different in the divine reading, which is more trustworthy than human life.

### 2.

What, then, are we to do? May your devout attention help us to examine in these verses of the psalm what God’s will is and what he wants us to understand.

There is a danger that someone weak, unable to understand the Scriptures spiritually, may look to human examples and see that God’s good servants are sometimes in need and lacking bread. Above all, he may think of the apostle Paul, who says: “In hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27). He may then be scandalized and say to himself:

“Is what I sang really true? Is what I resounded with such devout voice while standing in church really true: ‘I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread’?”

“Scriptures deceive us,” he may say to himself. Then all his limbs may be relaxed from good work; and, what is more serious, when the limbs of his inner person have been relaxed, he may cease from good work and say to himself:

“Why do I do good? Why do I break my bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, and bring the homeless into my house, while I attend to what is written: ‘I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread,’ when I see so many people living well and often suffering from hunger?”

“But perhaps I am mistaken in thinking that both the one who lives well and the one who lives badly live well; perhaps God knows him differently—that is, knows him to be wicked—whom I think righteous. What, then, shall I do about Abraham, whom Scripture itself commends as righteous? What shall I do about the apostle Paul himself, who says: ‘Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ’ (1 Corinthians 4:16)? Must I too be in such evils as he endured—in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness?”

### 3.

Can we, brothers, take someone who is thinking in this way and, as I said, whose inner limbs have all been relaxed from the ability to perform good works—can we take him up like a paralytic, open the roof of this Scripture, and lower him down to the Lord?

You see that it is obscure. But if it is obscure, it is a roof. And I perceive a certain paralytic in spirit. I see this roof, too, and I recognize that Christ is hidden beneath this roof.

Let me do, insofar as I can, what was praised in those who opened the roof and lowered the paralytic down to Christ, so that he might say to him: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.” For in this way he made the inner person sound from paralysis, forgiving sins and strengthening faith.

But there were people there who had no eyes with which to see that the inner paralytic had already been healed. They thought that the physician who was healing him was blaspheming.

“Who is this,” they said, “who forgives sins? This man is blaspheming. Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

And because he was God, he heard such thoughts from them (Luke 5:18–22). What they were thinking about God was true, but they did not see God present.

Therefore, that physician did something also in the paralytic’s body, so that he might heal the inner paralysis of those who had spoken in this way. He did what they could see and gave them what they could believe.

Come, then, whoever you are, so weak and sick at heart that, looking at human examples, you want to abandon good works and have been dissolved by a kind of inner paralysis: let us act, if we can, and lower you through this roof, once it has been opened, to the Lord.

### 4.

The Lord himself, in his body, which is the Church, was young in its earliest times, and now, behold, it has grown old. You know, recognize, and understand this, because you have been placed in this body and have believed in this way: Christ is our head; we are the body of that head (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 4:15).

Are we alone the body, and not also those who existed before us? All the righteous who have existed from the beginning of the world have Christ as their head. They believed that he would come, whom we now believe has come. They too were healed through faith in him, just as we are healed through faith in him.

Thus he would be the head of the entire city of Jerusalem, with all the faithful counted together from the beginning to the end, and with the legions and armies of angels also joined to them. That one city will come to be under one king, and one province, so to speak, under one emperor, happy in perpetual peace and salvation, praising God without end, blessed without end.

The body of Christ, which is the Church (Colossians 1:18, 24), was, as it were, one human being: at first young, and now, at the end of the age, in a vigorous old age, since it was said of it: “It will still multiply in vigorous old age” (Psalm 91:15).

It has multiplied among all nations, and its voice is that of one human being who observes his earliest age and this final age. It has looked back over everything, because through the Scriptures it knows all the ages. And it speaks exultantly and admonishingly:

“I was young in the earliest times of the world; and now I am old, living also in the final times of the world; and I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.”

### 5.

We have recognized a younger man and an old man, and, as though through a roof opened up, we have reached Christ. But who is the righteous man who has not been seen abandoned, nor his offspring seeking bread? If you understand “bread,” you understand him. For bread is the word of God, which never departs from the mouth of the righteous. This righteous man, when tempted in his Head, gave the same answer. For when the devil said to the Lord himself, who was hungry and suffering hunger, “Tell these stones to become loaves,” he replied: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:3–4).

Furthermore, my brothers, consider when the righteous man does not do the will of God. He always does it, and lives according to his will.
