The will of God does not depart from his heart, because the will of God is itself the law of God. And what is said of such a person? “And on his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

You eat this bread for one hour and then put it aside; but that bread of the word is for day and night. When you hear or read, you eat; when you think about it, you chew it again, so that you may be a clean animal, not an unclean one (Lev. 11). Wisdom also signifies this through Solomon, saying: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it” (Prov. 21:20). For one who swallows it, so that what he has devoured does not appear in him, has forgotten what he heard. But one who has not forgotten thinks about it; by thinking, he chews it again; by chewing it again, he takes delight in it. Hence it is said: “Holy thought will preserve you” (Prov. 2:11). And see: if holy thought preserves you in the chewing again of this bread, you will never see the righteous abandoned, nor his offspring seeking bread.

### 6. [verse 26]

“He is merciful all day long, and lends at interest.” *Feneratur* is indeed said in Latin both of one who lends and of one who receives a loan; but this is expressed more clearly if we say *fenerat*, “he lends at interest.” What does it matter to us what the grammarians want? You understand us better in our barbarism than you would be abandoned by us in our eloquence.

So this righteous man is merciful all day long and lends at interest. But let lenders at interest not rejoice. For we have found a certain lender at interest, just as we found a certain bread, so that everywhere, through a roof opened up, we may reach Christ.

I do not want you to be lenders at interest, and I do not want this because God does not. For if I do not want it but God does, then do it; but if God does not want it, even if I wanted it, whoever acted would act to his own harm. From where is it clear that God does not want this? It is said elsewhere: “The one who has not given his money at interest” (Ps. 15:5).

And how detestable, hateful, and abominable this is, I think the lenders themselves also know. Yet I myself—or rather, our God—who forbids you to be a lender at interest, commands you to be one; and it is said to you, “Lend at interest to God.” If you lend at interest to a human being, you have hope; and if you lend at interest to God, will you have no hope?

If you lend at interest to a human being—that is, if you give your money as a loan and expect to receive from him something more than you gave—not merely money, but something more than you gave, whether it be wheat, wine, oil, or anything else; if you expect to receive more than you gave, you are a lender at interest, and in this you must be condemned, not praised.

“What then,” you ask, “should I do to be a useful lender at interest?” [Note: [Col. 0387] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions have *utilis*, “useful.”]

Consider what a lender at interest does. He certainly wants to give less and receive more: do this yourself; give little, receive great things. See how widely your interest grows. Give temporal things, receive eternal things; give earth, receive heaven.

“And to whom shall I give?” you may perhaps say. The Lord himself comes forward for you to lend to—the one who commanded you not to lend at interest. Hear Scripture, telling you how to lend at interest to the Lord: “The one who has mercy on the poor lends at interest to the Lord” (Prov. 19:17).

For the Lord does not need anything from you; but you have another who needs something from you. You extend it to him, and he receives it. The poor man has nothing with which to repay you; nevertheless, he wants to repay, and finds nothing with which to do so. The sole thing that remains in him is the goodwill of praying for you.

When the poor man prays for you, he speaks, as it were, to God: “Lord, I have received a loan; guarantee me.” [Note: [Col. 0387] Two manuscripts have *fidejussorem dote*, “appoint a guarantor.” Three have *fide mea*, “by my faith,” omitting *dic*. The Corbie manuscript has *fide duc me*; *fidedic* is better, as below, column 599, near the end, no. 24.]

Therefore, even if you do not have the poor man as a reliable debtor, you have a reliable guarantor. See: God says to you from his Scripture, “Give without fear; I repay.” How do guarantors usually speak? What do they say? “I repay; I receive; you give to me.” [Note: [Col. 0387] Most manuscripts have *dicant*, “what do they say?”]

Do we suppose that God also says this: “I receive; you give to me”? Certainly, if Christ is God—which is not doubted—he himself said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food.” And when they said to him, “When did we see you hungry?”—to show that he was the guarantor of the poor, the sponsor of all his members, because he is the Head and they are the members, and when the members receive, the Head receives—he said: “Whenever you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.”

Come now, greedy lender at interest: see what you have given; see what you are going to receive. If you had given a little money, and the one to whom you gave it had given you, in exchange for your small amount of money, a large estate incomparably more valuable than the money you had given, how great would your thanks be, how great your joy!

Hear what possession the one to whom you lent at interest gives: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive.” What? What you gave? Certainly not. You gave earthly things, which, if you had not given them, would have rotted in the earth. What would you have done with what was destined to perish if you had not given it? What was destined to perish on earth has been stored up in heaven.

Therefore, what has been stored up is what we shall receive. Merit has been stored up; your merit has become your treasure. For see what you are going to receive: “Receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

But what will those who were unwilling to lend at interest hear? “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” And what is the kingdom we receive called? Attend to what follows: “These will go away into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:34–36).

Strive for this; purchase this; lend at interest for this. You have Christ seated in heaven and asking on earth. We have found how the righteous man lends at interest: “He is merciful all day long, and lends at interest.”

### 7.

“And his offspring will be in blessing.” Here too, let no carnal thought intrude. We see many children of the righteous dying of hunger; how, then, will his offspring be in blessing?

His offspring are his remains, from which he sows here and later reaps. For the Apostle says: “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow faint. Therefore, while we have opportunity,” he says, “let us do good to all” (Gal. 6:9). This is your offspring, which will be in blessing.

You entrust seed to the earth and gather so much more; do you entrust it to Christ and lose it? See this same offspring named more explicitly by the Apostle when he was speaking about almsgiving. For he says: “The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings” (2 Cor. 9:6).

But perhaps you labor when you sow and grieve when you show mercy, because you see the miserable. For it will be better when someday we shall have no one to whom we can give these things. When all are changed into incorruption, no one will hunger to whom you can extend bread; no one will thirst to whom you can give drink; no one will be naked whom you can clothe; no stranger will exist whom you can receive. Here, amid hardships, temptations, pains, and groans, we cast our seed.

But look back to another psalm: “Going they went, and wept, casting their seeds.” Pay attention, for “his offspring will be in blessing”: “But coming they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6).

### 8. [verse 27]

See, then, what follows, and do not be lazy: “Turn away from evil and do good.” Do not think it is enough for you not to strip the clothed. By not stripping the clothed, you have turned away from evil; but do not wither and become barren. Do not strip the clothed in such a way that you fail to clothe the naked. This is to turn away from evil and do good.

“And what will I have from this?” you will say. The one to whom you lent at interest has already commended to you what he will give: he will give you eternal life; give to him without fear.

Hear also what follows: “Turn away from evil and do good; and dwell forever and ever.” And do not think that when you give no one sees you; or that God abandons you when you perhaps give to a poor man and some loss follows, or some sadness over what has been lost, and you say to yourself: “What benefit was there in my having done good works? I think God does not love people who do good.”

Where do these mutterings of yours come from, where this noise, unless such voices are abundant? Each person now recognizes these voices either in his own mouth, or in the mouth of his neighbor, or in the mouth of his friend. May God erase them and uproot the thorns from his field; may he plant good grain and a fruit-bearing tree.

Why are you saddened, O man, because you gave to a poor person and lost something else? Do you not see that you lost what you did not give? Why do you not look to your God? Where is your faith? Why does it sleep so? Awaken it in your heart.

Consider what the Lord himself told you when he urged you toward such good works: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches” (Luke 12:33).

Remember this, then, when you lament a loss. Why do you weep, foolish man of a small [Note: [Col. 0388] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions have *pravi*, “wicked.”] or unsound heart? Why did you lose it, unless because you did not lend it to me? [Note: [Col. 0388] Seven manuscripts have *commendasti*, “entrusted.”]

Why did you lose it? Who took it from you? You will answer: “A thief.” Had I not warned you beforehand not to place it where a thief could approach? If the one who has lost it grieves, then let him grieve because he did not place it where it could not perish.

### 9. [verse 28]

“Because the Lord loves judgment, and will not abandon his holy ones.” When the holy suffer hardships, do not think that God does not judge, or judges perversely. The one who warns you to judge justly—is he himself going to judge perversely? He loves judgment, and will not abandon his holy ones.

But in what way the life of the holy is hidden with him: [Note: [Col. 0389] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions have: “But how? Thus it is hidden with [him], etc.”] those who now labor on earth are like trees in winter, without fruit and leaves; when he appears like a new sun rising, what was alive in the root will appear in fruits. Therefore he loves judgment and will not abandon his holy ones.

But is the holy man suffering from hunger? God will not abandon him: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). You despise him when he is scourged; you are terrified when he grows rich. From what is he scourged? From temporal pressures. When will he grow rich? When he hears: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Do not, then, be slow to endure scourging, so that you may be among those who deserve to be received. So greatly does he love judgment that he does not abandon the holy ones whom he scourges for a time. [Note: [Col. 0389] The manuscripts have *derelinquit*, “does not abandon.”] And because he scourges every son whom he receives, he did not spare even the Only Son, in whom he found no sin.

“Because the Lord loves judgment, and will not abandon his holy ones.” Since he will not abandon them, perhaps he will give them what you love here: to live many years and grow old? You do not consider that if you desire old age to come, you desire the very old age about which, when it comes, you will complain.

Let your soul not say to you—whether evil, weak, or childish—“How is it true that the Lord loves judgment and will not abandon his holy ones?” Truly, he did not abandon the three youths praising him in the furnace; the fire did not touch them (Dan. 3:50). But were his holy Maccabees not also holy, although they perished in the flames in body, not in faith (2 Macc. 7:7)?

“But this,” you say, “raises a greater question, because although they did not fail in faith, he abandoned them.” Hear what follows: “They will be preserved forever.”

You were wishing for a few years for them—years which, if the Lord gave them, he would not abandon his holy ones. Visibly he did not abandon the three youths; secretly he did not abandon the Maccabees. To the former he also gave temporal life to confound unbelievers; the latter he secretly crowned to judge the persecutor’s impiety. Yet he abandoned neither the one nor the other, who will not abandon his holy ones.

And the three youths received nothing great if they were not preserved forever. “They will be preserved forever.”

### 10.

“But the unrighteous will be punished, and the offspring of the impious will perish.” Just as the offspring of the righteous will be in blessing, so the offspring of the impious will perish. For the offspring of the impious are the works of the impious.

We find again that the son of an impious man flourishes in this world, and sometimes becomes righteous and flourishes in Christ. See, then, how you should understand this, so that you may open the roof and reach Christ: do not understand it carnally, for you will be deceived.

But the offspring of the impious—all the works of the impious—will perish; they will bear no fruit. For a time they have some force; afterward they will seek and will not find what they have done. For the voice of those who lose what they have done will be: “What did pride profit us, or what benefit did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:8).

Therefore, the offspring of the impious will perish.

### 11. [verse 29]

“The righteous will possess the land as an inheritance.” Again, let avarice not creep in and promise you some large estate, lest you hope to have there what you are commanded to despise here.

There is a certain land of the living, the kingdom of the holy. Hence it is said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6). For if that is your life, understand what sort of land you will receive.

That is the land of the living; this is the land of the dying, destined to receive the dead whom it nourished while alive. Therefore, what that land is, such also is that life: if eternal life, eternal land.

And how is the land eternal? “And they will dwell upon it forever and ever.” There will therefore be another land where we shall dwell forever and ever. For of this present land it was said: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

### 12. [verses 30–32]

“The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom.” There is the bread: see how gladly this righteous man eats, how he turns wisdom about in his mouth. “And his tongue will speak judgment.”

“The law of his God is in his heart.” Lest you perhaps think that he has in his mouth what he does not have in his heart; lest you count him among those of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13): “And his tongue will speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart.”

And what benefit does this bring him? “And his steps will not be tripped.” The word of God in the heart frees from the snare; the word of God in the heart frees from the crooked path; the word of God in the heart frees from a *labina*. [Note: [Col. 0390] The editions have *a lapsu*, “from a fall.” But the better manuscripts have *a labina*; some have *a lavina*. Isidore explains this word, and it means a slippery place.]

The one whose word does not depart from you is with you. What evil, then, can befall the one whom God guards? You place a guard in a vineyard and are secure against thieves; but that guard can sleep, fall himself, and admit a thief. Yet “he neither sleeps nor slumbers who guards Israel” (Ps. 120:4).

“The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped.” Let him therefore live securely; let him live securely among the wicked; let him live securely among the impious. For what evil can an impious or unjust person do to the righteous?

See what follows: “The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death.” For he says what was foretold in the Book of Wisdom: “He is grievous to us even to behold, because his life is unlike that of others” (Wis. 2:15).

Therefore he seeks to put him to death. What then? Will the Lord, who guards him, who dwells with him, who does not depart from his mouth or his heart, abandon him? Where is what was said above: “And he will not abandon his holy ones”?

### 13. [verse 33]

Therefore, “the sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death; but the Lord will not abandon him into his hands.”

Why, then, did he abandon the martyrs into the hands of the impious? Why did they do to them whatever they wished? Some they struck with the sword, some they crucified, some they handed over to beasts, [Note: [Col. 0390] The Vatican manuscript has *subrexerunt*; so also the Gallic manuscripts, except one, which has *subjecerunt*.] others they burned in fires, and others, leading them away in chains, they consumed with prolonged decay.

Certainly the Lord will not abandon his holy ones: “The Lord will not abandon him into his hands.” Finally, why did he hand over his own Son into the hands of the Jews?

Here too, open the roof (Luke 5:19), if you want to be bound together with every inner member; reach the Lord. Hear what another Scripture says, foreseeing that the Lord would suffer at the hands of the impious: “The earth has been given into the hands of the impious” (Job 9:24).

What does “The earth has been given into the hands of the impious” mean? The flesh has been given into the hands of the persecutors. But God did not abandon his righteous one there: from the captured flesh he led forth an unconquered soul.

God would have abandoned his righteous one into the hands of the impious if he had made him consent to the impious. Against this evil he prays in another psalm, saying: “Do not hand me over, Lord, to the sinner’s desire” (Ps. 139:9).

It is necessary that you not be handed over to the sinner’s desire, lest, when you desire the present life, you rush upon him and lose the eternal one. From what desire must he not be handed over to the sinner? From that of which it is also said: “I have not desired the day of man; you know it” (Jer. 17:16).

For one who desires and longs for the day of man—when an adversary threatens him that he will take away his human day, because he will kill him and destroy this life—if he does not hope for another life, fails and consents to the enemy.

But whoever hears the Lord saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul”—even if the earth is handed over into the hands of the impious, the soul escapes when the earth is captured; when the soul escapes, the earth will rise again.

The spirit is changed toward the Lord; [Note: [Col. 0391] Most manuscripts have *mutabitur*, “will be changed.”] the earth will be changed into heaven. For nothing of that earth perishes which is handed over for a time into the hands of the impious: “The hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10:28, 30).

There is therefore security—but only if God is within. If the devil is expelled, God is admitted. “The Lord will not abandon him into his hands.”

“Nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed against him.” Some copies have: “And when he judges him, he will be judged against him.” [Note: The phrase “against him” means when judgment is being carried out against him; for we can speak in such a way as to say to a person, “Judge for me,” that is, “Hear my case.”]

When God therefore begins to hear the case of his righteous one—for all must be brought before the tribunal of Christ and stand there, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10)—when that judgment has come, he will not condemn him, even if he appears to be condemned for a time by a human being.

Even if the proconsul pronounced sentence against Cyprian, one is an earthly seat, another the tribunal of heaven: from the lower one he received a sentence, from the higher one a crown.

“Nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed against him.”

### 14. [verses 34, 36]

But when will this be? Do not think it is now. Now is the time of labor, the time of seed, the time of cold. Even amid winds, even amid rains, sow; do not be lazy. Summer will come to gladden you, in which you will rejoice that you have sown.

“What, then, should I do now?” “Wait for the Lord.” “And while I wait, what should I do?” “And keep his ways.” “And if I keep them, what will I receive?” “And he will exalt you, so that you may possess the land as an inheritance.”

What land? Again, let no large estate come to mind: that land of which it is said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

What will become of those who afflicted us, among whom we groaned, whose scandals we endured, and for whom, though they raged, we prayed in vain? What will become of them?

It follows: “When the sinners perish, you will see.” [Note: [Col. 0392] One or two manuscripts have *cum perient*, “when they will perish.” Moreover, the Greek Septuagint has *en tō exolothreuesthai*, “when they are destroyed.”] And how closely you will see them: you will be at the right hand, they at the left. This, however, concerns the eyes of faith.

Those who do not have the eyes of faith grieve over the prosperity of the impious [Note: Erasmus and many manuscripts have *delectantur felicitate impiorum*, “take delight in the prosperity of the impious.”] and think that they are righteous without cause, because they see the impious flourishing here.

But what does the one who has that eye of faith say? “I saw the impious highly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon.” Suppose that he was highly exalted; suppose that he was lifted up. What follows? “And I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.”

Why was he not there, and why was his place not found? Because you passed by. But if you still think carnally, and this earthly prosperity seems to you true prosperity, you have not yet passed by; you are either his equal or beneath him. Advance and pass by. When, by advancing, you have passed by, you will look at him by faith, see his end, and say to yourself: “Behold, this is not the one who had swollen up so greatly”—as if you were passing beside smoke.

For this too was said earlier in this psalm: “They will fail like smoke.” Smoke rises high and advances in a swollen cloud; the higher it is lifted, the more it swells. But when you have passed by, look behind you. Smoke is behind you if God is before you.

Do not look back out of desire, as Lot’s wife looked and remained on the road (Gen. 19:26); rather, look back with contempt, and you will see that the impious person is nowhere, and you will seek his place.

What is his place? The place from which he has power and riches, a certain position in human affairs, so that many obey him, so that he commands and is heard. This place will not remain; it will pass away, so that you may say: “I passed by, and behold, he was not there.” [Note: [Col. 0392] Several manuscripts have: “but pass by yourself, so that you may be able,” etc.]

What does “I passed by” mean? I advanced; I reached spiritual things; I entered into the sanctuary of God, so that I might understand his final destiny (Ps. 72:17). “And behold, he was not there; and I sought him, and his place was not found.”

### 15. [verse 37]

“Keep innocence.” Hold on to it as, when you were greedy, you held your moneybag: as you held your moneybag so that it would not be taken from you by a thief, so keep innocence so that it will not be taken from you by the devil.

Let it be your secure patrimony, of which the rich and the poor alike are possessors. Keep innocence. What benefit is there in a gain of gold and a loss of innocence?

“Keep innocence and behold uprightness.” Have straight eyes, so that you may see uprightness—not crooked eyes with which you see wicked people, nor distorted eyes by which God himself seems distorted and crooked to you, because he favors the impious and persecutes the faithful.

Do you not see how distortedly you see? Correct your eyes and see uprightness. What uprightness? Do not attend to present things. [Note: [Col. 0392] Several manuscripts have *praesentiam*, “the present.”]

And what will you see? “For there are remains for the peaceful man.” What does “there are remains” mean? When you have died, you will not be dead: this is what “there are remains” means. Something will remain for him even after this life; this is the offspring that will be in blessing.

Hence the Lord says: “The one who believes in me, even if he dies, will live” (John 11:25). “For there are remains for the peaceful man.”

### 16. [verse 38]

“But the unrighteous will perish altogether.” What does “altogether” mean? Forever; or, all together as one.

“The remains of the impious will perish.” But “there are remains for the peaceful man”; therefore those who are not peaceful are impious. For “blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

### 17. [verses 39–40]

“But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation; and the Lord will help them, rescue them, and deliver them from sinners.”

Let the righteous therefore endure sinners for the present; let the wheat endure the weeds; let the grain endure the chaff. For the time of separation will come, and the good seed will be removed from what will be consumed by fire: the one will be placed in the granary, the other in eternal conflagration.

For this is why the righteous and the unrighteous were at first together: so that the one might trip up the other [Note: [Col. 0393] Nearly all manuscripts have *supplantaretur*, “might be tripped up.”] and the other be tested; afterward the one would be condemned and the other crowned.

### 18.

Thanks be to God, brothers. In the name of Christ we have paid what was owed; but charity always keeps us in debt. [Note: [Col. 0393] Seven manuscripts have: *nos charitatis debitores semper tenete*, “always keep us debtors of charity.”]

For charity alone is such that, even if it is repaid every day, it is always owed. We have said much against the Donatists; we have read many things to you—many documents, and much material beyond the canon of the Scriptures—because they compelled us to do so.

For even if they criticize this, because we read such things to you, let us be criticized, provided that you are instructed. We can answer them in this respect as well: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor. 12:11).

Nevertheless, brothers, above all guard our inheritance, concerning which we are secure that we are in the testament of our Father—not in some trivial document belonging to a human being, but in the testament of our Father.

From this we are secure, because the one who made the testament lives; the one who made the testament for his heir will himself judge concerning his testament. In human affairs the testator and the judge are different persons; yet the person who holds the testament prevails before another judge, not before a dead judge.

How secure, then, is our victory, since the one who made the testament will be the judge! For even if Christ died for a time, he now lives forever. [Note: [Col. 0393] The editions have *vivit in aeternum*, “he lives forever.” The words *in aeternum*, “forever,” are absent from the manuscripts.]

### 19.

Let them say against us whatever they wish; let us love them even against their will. We know their tongues, brothers; because of them, let us not become angry with them. Bear patiently with us.

They see that they have nothing in their case, so they turn their tongues against us and begin to say many bad things about us—many things they know and many things they do not know.

What they know belongs to our past. For we too were once, as the Apostle says, “foolish and disobedient and unfit for every good work” (Titus 3:3). We were foolish and mad in perverse error; we do not deny it. And the more we do not deny our past, the more we praise God who forgave us.

What then, heretic? You abandon the case and turn to the person. What am I? What am I? Am I the Catholic Church? Am I Christ’s inheritance spread throughout the nations? It is enough for me to be in it.

You reproach my past evils. What great thing are you doing? I am more severe toward my own evils than you are: what you reproached, I condemned. Would that you wished to imitate me, so that your error too might someday become past!

These are the past evils which they know, especially in this city. For here we lived badly [Note: [Col. 0394] At Carthage. See *Confessions* 3.1 and following.], as I confess. And as much as I rejoice in the grace of God, what shall I say about my past? [Note: [Col. 0394] The editions have *tantum de meis praeteritis timeo*, “I fear my past just as much.” The word *timeo* is absent from the manuscripts.] Do I grieve? I would grieve if I were still what I was. But what shall I say? Do I rejoice? I cannot say that either. Would that I had never been!

Whatever I was, however, is past in the name of Christ. But what they now criticize, they do not know. There are things which they could still criticize in me [Note: [Col. 0394] Most manuscripts have *reprehendam*, “which I could criticize.”]; nevertheless, it is already too much for them to know these things.

I do much in my thoughts [Note: [Col. 0394] Two manuscripts have: “For I am greatly distressed.”], fighting against my evil suggestions and engaged in a long, almost continual conflict [Note: [Col. 0394] Ambrose and the manuscripts have *conflictionem*.] [Note: [Col. 0394] The editions have *continuam vim*, “a continual force”; the word *vim* is absent from many manuscripts.] with the temptations of the enemy who wishes to overthrow me.

I groan to God in my weakness, and he knows what my heart is bringing to birth—he who knows my birth. [Note: [Col. 0394] Several manuscripts have *illi*, “to him.”]

“But it is a very small matter to me that I should be judged by you, or by a human day,” says the Apostle; “but I do not even judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3). For I know myself better than they do, but God knows me better than I do.

Therefore, let them not insult you concerning us; may Christ prevent this. For they say: “And who are they? And where are they from? We knew them as wicked here. Where were they baptized?”

If they know us well, they know that we once sailed away; they know that we also traveled abroad; they know that some of us went away and others returned. We were not baptized here. But where we were baptized [Note: [Col. 0394] See *Confessions* 9.6.], the Church is known throughout the entire world.

And there are many of our brothers who know that we were baptized and were baptized together with us. It is easy to know this if any of the brothers there is concerned about it.

Are we going to satisfy these people and produce some testimony from the Church with which they do not share communion? It is no wonder that they do not know that we were baptized across the sea in Christ, because they do not have Christ across the sea either.

For the one who has Christ across the sea is the one who also holds across the sea the communion of the universal Church. How can he know where I was baptized when his communion scarcely crosses the sea? [Note: [Col. 0394] Lovaniensis has *communicationem*, “communication.” The other editions, with the manuscripts, have *communionem*, “communion.”]

Nevertheless, my brothers, what shall I say to them? Suspect whatever you wish about us. If we are good, we are wheat in Christ’s Church; if we are bad, we are chaff in Christ’s Church. Nevertheless, we do not leave the threshing floor.

You who flew outside on the wind of temptation, what are you? The wind does not remove wheat from the threshing floor. Therefore, from the place where you are, recognize what you are.

### 20.

“But who are you,” he says, “to say so much against us?”

Whoever I may be, pay attention to what is said, not to the one by whom it is said.

“But the Lord says to the sinner: ‘Why do you recite my testament through your mouth?’” (Ps. 49:16). Let the Lord say this to a sinner. Perhaps there is a class of sinners to whom the Lord rightly says this; but whoever the Lord says it to, he says it because it does not benefit a sinner when he speaks the law of God.

Does it not benefit those who hear? We have both kinds in the Church, since the Lord speaks of both the good and the bad.

For what do the good say when they preach? “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16). What is said of the good? “Be an example to the faithful.” [Note: [Col. 0395] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions have: “What is said of us? Be an example to the faithful.”]

We work to be this; but what we are, he knows to whom we groan. Yet something else was said about the bad: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2–3).

You see that on Moses’ seat, which was succeeded by Christ’s seat, the bad also sit; nevertheless, by speaking good things they do not harm those who hear.

Why have you abandoned the seat itself because of the bad? Return to peace; return to the harmony which has not offended you.

If I speak good things and do good things, imitate me. But if I do not do what I say, you have the Lord’s command: do what I say, but do not do what I do. Nevertheless, do not depart from the Catholic seat.

We are going to leave in the name of Christ, and they will say many things. What is the conclusion? Quickly disregard our case. Say nothing to them except: “Brothers, answer the matter.”

Augustine is a bishop in the Catholic Church; he carries his own burden and will render an account to God. I know him among the good; if he is bad, he knows it himself; if he is good, even then he is not my hope.

This is what I learned above all in the Catholic Church: that my hope must not be in a human being. Therefore you rightly reproach those people, because you have placed your hope in a human being.

Certainly, when they reproach us, disregard them as well. For we know what place we have in your hearts, because we know what place you have in ours. Do not fight against them on our behalf.

Whatever they say about us, pass over it quickly, lest, while laboring over the case of our defense, [Note: [Col. 0395] The manuscripts have *cura*, “care.”] you abandon your own case. This is what they cunningly do: unwilling and afraid that we should speak about the actual case, they thrust upon us matters by which they may distract us, so that, while we are intent on clearing ourselves, we may be silent about convicting them.

For if you call me altogether bad, I too say that there are countless other things. Quickly remove me from the middle; bring my case to an end; deal with the matter; attend to the case of the Church; see where you are.

Let truth speak to you from wherever it may. Accept it while you hunger, lest bread never reach you because, always seeking something to criticize in the vessel, you are fastidious and slanderous.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 37. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

[Col. 0396]

### 1.

Appropriately, in response to what we sang—“I will declare my iniquity, and I will take care for my sin” [Note: [Col. 0396] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *gero*, “I take care.” Ambrose and many manuscripts have *geram*, “I will take care.”—this woman spoke from the Gospel reading.

Seeing her iniquities, the Lord called her a dog, saying: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15:26). But she, who knew how to declare her iniquity and take care for her sin, did not deny what the Truth had said. Rather, confessing her misery, she obtained mercy, taking care for her sin. [Note: [Col. 0396] Nearly all manuscripts have: “But confessing her misery, she rather obtained mercy.”]

For she had also asked that her daughter be healed, perhaps signifying her own life in her daughter.

Therefore, as we consider and examine the whole psalm, as far as we can, pay attention. May the Lord be present to our hearts, so that here we may find our voices for our healing, and, having found them, may express them—neither with difficulty in finding them nor incompetently in expressing them.

### 2. [Verse 1]

Its title is: “A Psalm for David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.” We look for what has been written for us about the holy prophet David, from whose offspring our Lord Jesus Christ descended according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3). Among the things known to us about him from the Scriptures, however, we do not find that he ever remembered the Sabbath. Why would he remember it according to that observance of the Jews by which they observed the Sabbath? Why would he remember something that necessarily came every seven days? It had to be observed, then, not remembered in this way.

No one remembers anything unless it is not presently before him. For example, in this city you remember Carthage, where you once were; today you remember yesterday, or a day in the preceding year, or any earlier day; and you remember some action you have already performed, or some place where you were, or some event in which you took part. What does this remembrance of the Sabbath mean, my brothers? What soul remembers the Sabbath in this way? What Sabbath is this? It remembers with groaning. When the Psalm was read, you heard—and now, when we go through it again, you will hear—how great the sorrow is, how great the groaning, how great the weeping, how great the misery.

Yet blessed is the one who is miserable in this way. That is why the Lord in the Gospel called certain mourners blessed (Matt. 5:5). How can one be blessed if he is mourning? How can one be blessed if he is miserable? Rather, he would be miserable if he were not mourning. Let us therefore understand this person also as remembering the Sabbath—some unknown mourner—and would that we ourselves were that unknown person! There is someone grieving, groaning, mourning, remembering the Sabbath. The Sabbath is rest. Without doubt, this person was in some kind of unrest, since with groaning he remembered rest.

### 3. [Verse 2]

He therefore tells God about the unrest he was suffering and commends it to him, fearing something more severe than the condition in which he found himself. For since he is in evil [Col. 0397], he says so openly; no interpreter, suspicion, or conjecture is needed. From his words it is clear in what evil he is; we need not search for it, but understand what he says.

And unless he feared something worse than the condition that held him, he would not have begun in this way: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your indignation, nor correct me in your anger.” For it will happen that some will be corrected in God’s anger and rebuked in his indignation. Perhaps not all who are rebuked will be corrected; nevertheless, some who are saved will undergo correction. This will indeed happen, since correction has been mentioned—but as though through fire. There will also be some who are rebuked and will not be corrected.

For he will certainly rebuke those to whom he will say: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” together with the other things he goes on to say, reproving a certain inhumanity and barrenness in those placed on the left, to whom it is said: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41–42).

Fearing these things as more severe, and setting aside this present life—in whose evils he mourns and groans—he asks and says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your indignation.” Let me not be among those to whom you will say: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” “Nor correct me in your anger”: purify me in this life, and make me such a person as will no longer need corrective fire, on account of those who will be saved, yet as through fire.

Why is this? Because here they build with wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation. They should build with gold, silver, and precious stones and be secure from both fires—not only from that eternal fire by which the ungodly will be tortured forever, but also from the fire that will correct those who will be saved through fire. For it is said: “He himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:12, 15).

And because it is said, “he will be saved,” that fire is despised. Certainly, although they will be saved through fire, that fire will nevertheless be more severe than anything a human being can suffer in this life. You know how much the wicked have suffered here, and can suffer; yet they have suffered as much as the good have been able to suffer. What punishment has any criminal, robber, adulterer, wicked person, or sacrilegious person endured under the laws that a martyr has not endured in confessing Christ?

These evils here [Note: [Col. 0397] The word *evils* is absent from the manuscripts], then, are much lighter. Yet observe what people do to avoid suffering them: they do whatever you command. How much better, then, to do what God commands so as not to suffer those more severe punishments?

### 4. [Verse 3]

Why does this person ask not to be rebuked in indignation or corrected in anger? It is as though he were saying to God: “Since the things I am already suffering are many and great, I ask that they be enough.” He begins to enumerate them, satisfying God and offering him what he suffers so that he may not suffer worse things:

“For your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand upon me.”

### 5. [Verse 4]

“There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger.”

He was already speaking of what he was suffering here; yet he attributed it to the Lord’s anger, because it also came from the Lord’s punishment. What punishment was this? The punishment which he received from Adam. He was not left unpunished, nor had God said in vain: “You shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17). Nor do we suffer anything in this life except from that death which we deserved through the first sin.

Indeed, we bear a mortal body—which certainly would not be mortal [Note: [Col. 0398] In the printed editions these words were lacking, “which certainly would not be mortal”; they are found in all our manuscripts]—full of temptations, full of anxieties, subject to bodily pains, subject to need, changeable, weak; and even when it is healthy, it is still weak, because it is certainly not yet completely healthy.

For why did he say, “There is no soundness in my flesh,” unless what is called the health of this life is not truly health to those who understand rightly and remember the Sabbath? If you do not eat, hunger troubles you. This is a kind of natural illness, because our nature has been made a punishment for us through retribution [Note: [Col. 0398] Most manuscripts read: “and through retribution.”].

What was punishment for the first man is nature for us. Hence the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3)—“by nature children of wrath,” that is, bearing the punishment.

But why does he say, “we were”? Because in hope we are no longer so, though in reality we still are. Yet it is better to say what we are in hope, because we are certain of our hope. Our hope is not uncertain, so that we should doubt it.

Hear that very glory in hope. “We ourselves,” he says, “groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body” [Note: [Col. 0398] Four manuscripts read: “waiting for the adoption of sons.”].

What then? Have you not yet been redeemed, O Paul? Has the price not yet been paid for you? Has that blood not already been poured out? Is it not itself the price of us all? Certainly, it is. But observe what he says: “For in hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

What does he await with patience? Salvation. The salvation of what? Of the body itself, because he said: “the redemption of our body.” If he was waiting for the salvation of the body, then the salvation he possessed was not yet complete.

Hunger kills; thirst kills, unless relief is provided. Food is the remedy for hunger, drink the remedy for thirst, sleep the remedy for weariness. Remove these remedies and see whether the conditions they relieve do not kill. If, when these remedies are set aside, there are no illnesses, then there is health. But if you possess something that can kill you unless you eat, do not boast of health; rather, groaning, await the redemption of your body.

Rejoice that you have been redeemed; but not yet in reality: be secure in hope [Note: [Col. 0398] The manuscripts read: “you are.”]. For if you do not groan in hope, you will not reach reality.

Thus he says: “This is not soundness: There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger.” From where, then, are the arrows fixed in him? He means the punishment itself, the very retribution, and perhaps the pains that must be suffered here—of both soul and body. These, he says, are the arrows.

The holy Job also mentioned these arrows. While he was in such pains, he said that the arrows of the Lord were fixed in him (Job 6:4). Yet we are also accustomed to understand God’s words as arrows. But could this person have been in such pain because he was pierced by them? God’s words, like arrows, arouse love, not pain.

Or is it because love itself cannot exist without pain? Whatever we love but do not possess, we must grieve over. The person who has what he loves both loves and does not grieve; but the person who loves, as I have said, and does not yet possess what he loves must groan in pain.

Hence the words spoken in the person of the Church, the bride of Christ, in the Song of Songs: “For I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5; 5:8). She said that she was wounded with love: she loved something but did not yet possess it; she grieved because she did not yet have it. Since she grieved, she was wounded; but this wound was carrying her toward true health [Note: [Col. 0399] Almost all manuscripts read: “was surrounding her,” or “was encompassing her.”].

Whoever has not been wounded by this wound cannot reach true health. Will the wounded person always remain in the wound?

We may therefore understand the fixed arrows in this way also: “Your words are fixed in my heart, and from your words it has come about that I remember the Sabbath. This remembrance of the Sabbath, and the fact that I do not yet possess it, prevent me from rejoicing fully and make me recognize that there is no soundness in this flesh itself. It should not be called soundness when I compare it with the soundness I shall possess in everlasting rest, where ‘this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality’ (1 Cor. 15:53). I see that, in comparison with that soundness, this soundness is illness.”

### 6.

“There is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins.”

It is customary to ask whose voice this is. Some understand it as Christ’s, because certain things said here concern Christ’s passion, to which we shall come shortly, and we shall acknowledge that they are spoken of Christ’s passion.

But how could the one who had no sin say, “There is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins” (1 Pet. 2:22)? Necessity therefore compels us to understand this as referring to Christ in his fullness and entirety—that is, to the head and the body.

When Christ speaks, he sometimes speaks in the person of the head alone, which is the Savior himself, born of the Virgin Mary; at other times he speaks in the person of his body, which is the holy Church spread throughout the whole world.

And we are in his body, provided that our faith in him is sincere, our hope certain, and our love aflame. We are in his body and are his members. We find ourselves speaking there, since the Apostle says: “We are members of his body” (Eph. 5:30); and he says this in many places.

For if we say that the words are not Christ’s, then these words also will not be Christ’s: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” There too you find: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:2). Just as here you have “because of the face of my sins,” so there you have “the words of my sins.”

And if Christ is certainly without sin and without transgression, we shall begin to think that those words do not belong to that Psalm. This is extremely harsh and contradictory, since that Psalm clearly concerns Christ, where we find such an open account of his passion, as though it were being recited from the Gospel. There we have: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 21:19).

Moreover, the Lord himself, hanging on the cross, uttered the first verse of that Psalm with his own mouth and said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). What did he intend us to understand except that the whole Psalm pertained to him, since he himself, its head, proclaimed it?

When it then says, “the words of my sins,” there is no doubt that this is Christ’s voice. Where, then, did the sins come from, except from the body that is the Church? The body of Christ and the head are speaking.

Why does he speak as one person? “The two,” he says, “shall become one flesh.” “This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle; “but I speak in reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

Thus, when he himself was speaking in the Gospel, answering those who had raised the question of dismissing a wife, he said: “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. 19:4–6).

If he himself said, “They are no longer two, but one flesh,” what wonder is it if there is one flesh, one tongue, and the same words—as belonging to one flesh, the head and the body?

Let us hear him as one person, yet understand the head as head and the body as body. The persons are not divided, but their dignity is distinguished, because the head saves and the body is saved. Let the head show mercy; let the body lament its misery. The head is for cleansing sins; the body is for confessing sins. Yet there is one voice, since Scripture does not indicate when the body speaks and when the head speaks. We distinguish this as we listen, but he speaks as one.

Why should he not say, “my sins,” when he said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me”? Certainly the Lord was not in prison.

Why should he not say this, when, after they asked him, “When did we see you hungry or thirsty, or in prison, and did not minister to you?” he replied that he had spoken in the person of his body: “What you did not do for one of the least of mine, you did not do for me” (Matt. 25:42–45)?

Why should he not say, “because of the face of my sins,” when he said to Saul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4)? Certainly, no persecutor was already troubling him in heaven.

But just as the head spoke there on behalf of the body, so here the head speaks the words of the body, while you also hear the words of the head. When you hear the words of the body, do not separate the head from it; and when you hear the words of the head, do not separate the body from it, because they are no longer two, but one flesh.

### 7.

“There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger.”

But perhaps God was angry with you unjustly, O Adam—O human race, God was angry with you unjustly! You have said this while already acknowledging your punishment, while already established in the body of Christ as a human being: “There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger.”

Explain the justice of God’s anger, so that you do not appear to excuse yourself by accusing him [Note: [Col. 0400] Most manuscripts read: “so that you may not appear obliged to accuse him.”]. Continue, and say where the Lord’s anger comes from.

“There is no soundness in my flesh because of the face of your anger; there is no peace in my bones.” He repeated what he had said: “There is no soundness in my flesh”—for this is the meaning of “there is no peace in my bones.” But he did not repeat “because of the face of your anger”; instead, he stated the cause of God’s anger: “There is no peace,” he says, “in my bones because of the face of my sins.”

[Col. 0401]

### 8. [Verse 5]

“For my iniquities have lifted up my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me.”

Here too he placed the cause first and then supplied the effect; he said what resulted from what. “My iniquities have lifted up my head.”

No one is proud unless he is wicked; the head of such a person is lifted up. The one who raises his head against God is lifted upward.

You heard, when the reading from the book of Ecclesiasticus was given: “The beginning of human pride is to apostatize from God” (Ecclus. 10:14). The one who first refused to obey the commandment raised his head against God through his iniquity.

And because his iniquities lifted up his head, what did God do to him? “Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me.”

It belongs to lightness to raise one’s head; the person who raises his head seems to carry nothing. Since what can be raised is light, he receives a weight by which he can be pressed down. His labor is turned back upon his head, and his iniquity descends upon his crown (Ps. 7:17).

“Like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me.”

### 9. [Verse 6]

“My bruises have become putrid and have begun to stink.”

Anyone who has bruises is not healthy. Add that the bruises themselves have become putrid and have begun to stink. Why have they begun to stink? Because they have become putrid.

How this is to be understood in human life—who does not know it [Note: [Col. 0401] The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, and most manuscripts, omit *non* (“not”). One manuscript reads: “Whoever knows this.”]?

Let someone have a sound sense of smell in his soul: he perceives how sins stink. Opposed to the stench of sins is that fragrance of which the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place, among those who are being saved” (2 Cor. 2:15).

But from where does this fragrance come, except from hope? From where, except from remembrance of the Sabbath? In this life we mourn one thing; in that life we anticipate another. What is mourned stinks; what is anticipated gives off fragrance.

If there were not that fragrance inviting us, we would never remember the Sabbath. But because through the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0401] Several manuscripts omit “through the Spirit.”] we possess that fragrance, so that we may say to our bridegroom, “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3), we turn our sense of smell away from our own stench and, turning toward him, breathe for a little while.

But unless our own evils also smell to us, we shall never confess with these groans: “My bruises have become putrid and have begun to stink.” From where? “Because of the face of my foolishness.” Earlier he said, “Because of the face of my sins”; now he says, “Because of the face of my foolishness.”

### 10. [Verse 7]

“I am afflicted and bowed down to the end.”

Why was he bowed down? Because he had been exalted. If you are humble, you will be raised up; if you are exalted, you will be bowed down. God will not lack a weight with which to bend you. That weight will be the burden of your sins; it will be brought back upon your head, and you will be bowed down.

What does it mean to be bowed down? It means being unable to raise oneself up. The Lord found a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years; she could not raise herself upright (Luke 13:11). Such are those whose hearts are fixed on earthly things.

But because that woman found the Lord and he healed her, let her have her heart above. Yet insofar as she is still bowed down, she continues to groan. The one who says this is bowed down: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Let him groan amid these things, so that he may receive the other; let him remember the Sabbath, so that he may deserve to reach the Sabbath.

The Sabbath celebrated by the Jews was a sign. A sign of what? Of what this person remembers when he says: “I am afflicted and bowed down to the end.”

What does “to the end” mean? To death.

“All day long I walked in sorrow.” All day long, without interruption. By “all day long” he means the whole of life. But from what point did he learn this? From the time he began to remember the Sabbath.

As long as he remembers what he does not yet possess, do you not expect him to walk in sorrow? “All day long I walked in sorrow.”

### 11. [Verse 8]

“For my soul is filled with illusions, and there is no soundness in my flesh.”

Where, then, is the whole human being? In soul and flesh. The soul is filled with illusions; the flesh has no soundness. What remains from which there could be joy? Must he not be sorrowful?

“All day long I walked in sorrow.” Let sorrow be ours until our soul is stripped of its illusions and our body is clothed with soundness. For true soundness is immortality.

If I wanted to say how many the illusions of the soul are, when would I have enough time? Whose soul does not suffer from them? I shall briefly indicate how our soul is filled with illusions.

Because of those very illusions, we are sometimes scarcely permitted to pray. We do not know how to think about bodies except through images; and images we do not seek often rush upon us. We want to move from one thought to another and pass from one to the next. Sometimes you want to return to what you were thinking about and abandon the thought you are presently considering, but something else occurs to you. You want to remember what you had forgotten, but it does not come to mind; instead, something you did not want comes to mind.

Where was the thing you had forgotten? Why did it come to mind later, when it was no longer being sought? When it was being sought, countless things that were not being sought came before it.

I have said something brief, brothers. I have sprinkled you with a little of this matter, so that, having received it, you yourselves may reflect on the rest and discover what it means to mourn the illusions of our soul.

The soul received the punishment of illusion and lost truth. For just as illusion is the soul’s punishment, so truth is the soul’s reward.

But while we were established amid these illusions, truth came to us. It found us covered with illusions and took on our flesh—or rather, it took flesh from us, that is, from the human race. It appeared to the eyes of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0402] This is how it reads in the manuscripts. The editions read: “He opened the eyes of the flesh.”] so that through faith it might heal those to whom it was going to reveal the truth, so that truth might become apparent to a healed eye.

For he himself is the truth that he promised us when his flesh was seen, so that faith might be begun, whose reward would be truth. Christ did not reveal himself on earth, but revealed his flesh. If he had revealed himself, the Jews would have seen and recognized him; but if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8).

But perhaps the disciples saw him when they said to him: “Show us the Father, and that is enough for us.” And to demonstrate to them that they had not seen him, he added: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father.”

If they were seeing Christ, how were they still seeking the Father? If they saw Christ, they would also see the Father. They therefore did not yet see Christ, since they desired that the Father be shown to them.

Hear that they did not yet see him. Elsewhere he promised this as a reward, saying: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him.” And as though someone were saying to him, “What will you give to him who loves you?” he replied: “I will show myself to him” (John 14:8–9, 21).

If he promised this as a reward to those who love him—that he would show himself to them—it is clear that the vision of truth promised to us is of such a kind that, once we have seen it, we will no longer say: “My soul is filled with illusions.”

### 12. [Verse 9]

“I am weakened and humbled exceedingly.”

The person who remembers the height of the Sabbath sees how greatly he has been humbled. The one who cannot contemplate the height of that rest does not see where he now is [Note: [Col. 0403] So read Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovanius reads: “does not see where he is not.”].

For this reason another Psalm says: “I said in my ecstasy: I have been cast away from before your eyes” (Ps. 30:23). Having been lifted up in mind, he saw something sublime—something in which he was not yet entirely present. Through a kind of flash, if one may so speak, of eternal light, he perceived that he was not there. Since he had been able to understand something of it, he saw where he was and how he had been weakened and confined by human evils. Thus he said: “I said in my ecstasy: I have been cast away from before your eyes.”

It is something like this that I saw in my ecstasy: from there I realize how far away I am, since I am not yet there.

The one who said that he had been taken up into the third heaven was already there, and he heard ineffable words that it is not permitted a human being to speak. But he was recalled to us, so that he might first groan and be perfected in weakness, and afterward be clothed with power. Yet he was encouraged because, in accordance with the ministry entrusted to him, he had seen something of those realities; therefore he added: “I heard ineffable words, which it is not permitted a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:2–10).

Why, then, should you ask me or anyone else about things that it is not permitted a human being to speak, if it was not permitted him to speak, though it was permitted him to hear?

Let us nevertheless mourn and groan in confession; let us acknowledge where we are; let us remember the Sabbath; and let us patiently await what he promised, who also displayed in himself an example of patience for us.

“I am weakened and humbled exceedingly.”

### 13.

“I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

You often observe the servants of God uttering groans, and the cause is sought. It appears to be nothing except the groaning of some servant of God—if it reaches the ears of the person near him.

There is a hidden groaning that is not heard by human beings. Yet if some thought of desire occupies the heart so fully that the wound of the inner person is expressed in a louder voice, the cause is sought. A person says to himself: “Perhaps this is why he is groaning; perhaps this happened to him.”

Who can understand it except the one before whose eyes and ears he groans? Therefore he says: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

For when people sometimes hear a person’s groaning, they usually hear the groaning of the flesh; they do not hear one groaning from the groaning of the heart.

Someone’s property was taken away; he roared, but not from the groaning of the heart. Another, because he carried his son out for burial [Note: [Col. 0403] The editions read *abstulit filiari*. The manuscripts, more correctly, read *extulit*, that is, “for burial.”]; another, because his wife died; another, because his vineyard was battered by hail, because his cask turned sour, because someone stole his animal; another, because he suffered some loss; another, because he fears an enemy.

All these roar from the groaning of the flesh. But the servant of God, because he roars from remembrance of the Sabbath, where the kingdom of God is, which flesh and blood will not possess (1 Cor. 15:50), says:

“I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”

### 14. [Verse 10]

And who recognized why he was roaring? He added:

“And all my desire is before you.”

Not before human beings, who cannot see the heart, but “all my desire is before you.” Let your desire be before him, and the Father who sees in secret will repay you (Matt. 6:6).

Your desire itself is your prayer; and if your desire is continual, your prayer is continual. The Apostle did not say without reason: “Pray without interruption” (1 Thess. 5:17).

Do we bend the knee without interruption, prostrate the body, or raise our hands, so that he should say, “Pray without interruption”? Or if we say that we pray in this way, I think that we cannot do so without interruption. There is another inward prayer without interruption, which is desire.

Whatever else you may be doing, if you desire that Sabbath, you do not cease praying. If you do not want to cease praying, do not cease desiring. Your continual desire is your continual voice. You will be silent if you cease to love.

Who are the silent ones? Those of whom it is said: “Because iniquity abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). The coldness of love is the silence of the heart; the ardor of love is the cry of the heart. If love remains always, you always cry; if you always cry, you always desire; if you desire, you remember rest.

And you must understand before whom the roar of your heart is made. Consider now what kind of desire should be before God’s eyes.

Is it that our enemy should die, as people almost justly desire? For sometimes we pray for what we ought not. Let us examine what people almost justly pray for. They pray that someone may die and that an inheritance may come to them.

But let those who pray for their enemies to die hear the Lord saying: “Pray for your enemies” (Matt. 5:44; Luke 6:27). Therefore they should not pray that their enemies die; rather, they should pray that they be corrected. Then their enemies will have died, for once corrected they will no longer be enemies.

“And all my desire is before you.” What if the desire is before him, but the groaning is not before him? How could that be, when desire itself has groaning as its voice?

Therefore he continues: “And my groaning is not hidden from you.” It is not hidden from you, though it is hidden from many human beings.

At times the humble servant of God appears to say: “And my groaning is not hidden from you.” At times the servant of God also appears to laugh. Has that desire died in his heart? If desire is present, groaning is present as well. It does not always reach human ears, but it never departs from God’s ears.

[Col. 0405]

### 15. [Verse 11]

“My heart is troubled.”

Why is it troubled?

“And my strength has deserted me.”

Something sudden often rushes upon us, and the heart becomes troubled. The earth trembles; thunder comes from heaven; a terrible rush or noise arises; a lion seems to appear on the road; the heart becomes troubled. Robbers lie in wait; the heart becomes troubled; one is terrified, and anxiety is inflicted from every side.

Why does this happen? “Because my strength has deserted me.” If that strength remained, what would be feared? Whatever might be announced, whatever might gnash its teeth, whatever might sound, whatever might fall, whatever might inspire horror would not terrify.

But from where does that disturbance arise? “My strength has deserted me.”

Why has strength deserted him?

“And the light of my eyes is not with me.”

Adam, therefore, had hidden himself from the light of his eyes [Note: [Col. 0405] Two manuscripts read: “had had.”]. For the light of his eyes was God himself. When Adam offended him, he fled into the shade and hid himself among the trees of paradise (Gen. 3:8). He was afraid before the face of God and sought the shade of the trees. Once among the trees, he no longer had the light of his eyes, in which he had been accustomed to rejoice.

If this was Adam’s condition from his origin, and ours through descent; and these members return to that second, or last, Adam, because “the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15:45), and cry out from his body in this confession, “The light of my eyes is not with me”—how can this person, already confessing, already redeemed, already in the body of Christ, say that the light of his eyes is not with him?

Certainly, it is not with him. But it is present as it is with those who are still remembering the Sabbath [Note: “As it is with those who are still remembering the Sabbath” is found in almost all manuscripts but is omitted by Amerbach.], as it is with those who see in hope. Yet it is not yet that light of which it is said: “I will show myself to him” (John 14:21).

There is a certain light, because we are children of God, and we certainly hold this by faith; but it is not yet the light that we shall see. “What we shall be has not yet appeared; we know that when it appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

For now there is the light of faith and the light of hope. As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). And as long as we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (Rom. 8:25).

These, then, are the voices of those who are away from home and not yet established in their homeland. He rightly and truly says, and if he is not deceitful, he confesses truthfully: “The light of my eyes is not with me.”

This is what a human being suffers inwardly—there within himself, in himself, and concerning himself—without anyone else, from no one to anyone except himself. Whatever he has listed above, he has deserved to suffer as his own punishment.

[Col. 0406]

### 16. [Verses 12–13]

But is this the only thing a human being suffers? Inwardly, he suffers from himself; outwardly, he suffers from those among whom he lives. He suffers his own evils and is compelled to suffer the evils of others.

Hence those two voices: “Cleanse me from my secret faults, Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13–14). He has already confessed his secret faults, from which he desires to be cleansed. Let him also speak of the faults of others, from which he wishes to be spared.

“My friends.”

What shall I say now about enemies?

“My friends and my neighbors [Col. 0406] have drawn near against me, and have stood.”

Understand what he says: “They have stood against me.” For if they stood against me, they fell against themselves.

“My friends and my neighbors have drawn near against me, and have stood.”

Let us now understand the words of the head; let our head begin to shine forth in the passion. But again, when the head begins to speak, do not separate the body from it.

If the head did not wish to separate itself from the words of the body, would the body dare to separate itself from the sufferings of the head? Suffer in Christ, because Christ, as it were, sinned in your weakness.

Just now he was speaking your sins as though from his own mouth, and he called them his. He said: “Because of the face of my sins,” though they were not his. Therefore, just as he wished our sins to be his on account of his body, so let us also be willing to regard his sufferings as ours on account of our head.

For he did not suffer enemies from among his friends while we do not. Rather, let us also prepare ourselves to share the same fellowship, and let us not reject such a cup, so that through his humility we may find the desire for his exaltation.

He answered those who wished to cling to his exaltation but were not yet considering his humility, and said to them: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. 20:22).

Therefore the Lord’s sufferings are also our sufferings. If each person serves God well, keeps the faith faithfully, gives what he owes, and lives justly among human beings, I want to see whether he does not suffer what Christ here enumerates in his passion.

17. My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood firm; and those near me stood at a distance. Who were those who drew near, and who were those who stood at a distance? The Jews were near, because they were related to him: they drew near, even when they crucified him. The Apostles were also near; yet they themselves stood at a distance, lest they suffer with him. This may also be understood as follows: “My friends,” that is, those who pretended to be my friends. They pretended to be his friends when they said, “Teacher, we know that you teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII, 16), when they wanted to test him as to whether tribute should be paid to Caesar. When he convicted them by their own words, they wanted to appear his friends; but he had no need for anyone to testify to him about a human being, for he himself knew what was in a human being (John II, 25). Thus, although they had spoken friendly words, he answered them, “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?” (Matt. XXII, 18).

Therefore: “My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood firm; and those near me stood at a distance.” You know what I said. I called those “near” who drew near [Note: [Col. 0406] Two manuscripts read consistently: “You know that I called the neighbors of God those who drew near.” Six others: “You know that I said ‘near’; I said ‘they drew near.’” Another has *dixit* (“he said”) in both places. Finally, two omit “You know what I said, ‘near.’”], and yet they stood at a distance. They drew near in body, but stood far away in heart. Who were as near in body as those who raised him upon the cross? Who were as far away in heart as those who blasphemed? Hear this distance from the prophet Isaiah; see this nearness and distance: “This people honors me with their lips”—behold, they draw near in body—“but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13). The same people were near and far: near with their lips, far in their hearts.

Nevertheless, because the Apostles stood at a distance out of fear, we understand this more directly and plainly of them, so that we take some to have drawn near and others to have stood at a distance. For even Peter, who had followed more boldly, was still so far away that, when questioned and disturbed, he denied the Lord three times, although he had promised that he would die with him (Matt. XXVI, 70). Later, so that he might become near from afar, he heard after the resurrection, “Do you love me?” and said, “I love you” (John XXI, 17). By saying this he drew near, having become distant through his denial, until with a threefold utterance of love he dissolved his threefold utterance of denial [Note: [Col. 0407] Eight manuscripts read *timoris* (“of fear”).]—“And those near me stood at a distance.”

18. And those who sought my life used force. It is now clear who were seeking his life: those who did not possess his life, because they were not in his body. Those who sought his life were far from his life; but they sought it in order to kill it. His life is rightly sought. For elsewhere he rebukes certain people, saying, “There is no one who seeks my life” (Ps. CXLI, 5). He rebukes some for not seeking his life, and again rebukes others for seeking it.

Who seeks his life rightly? The one who imitates his sufferings. Who are those who sought his life wrongly? Those who used force against him and crucified him.

19. It follows: “Those who sought my harm spoke vanity.” What does “those who sought my harm” mean? They sought many things, but found nothing. Perhaps he means: “They sought my crimes.” For they sought things to say against him, and found none (Matt. XXVI, 59–60). They sought evil in the good; they sought crimes in the innocent. When would they find them in one who had no sin? But because they sought sins in one who had no sin, it remained for them to fabricate what they could not find. Therefore, “Those who sought my harm spoke vanity,” not truth. “And all day long they meditated deceit”: that is, they meditated fraud without ceasing.

You know how many false witnesses were brought forward against the Lord before he suffered. You know how many false testimonies were given even after he had risen. For those soldiers who guarded the tomb, of whom Isaiah said, “I will appoint the wicked for his burial” (Isa. LIII, 9)—they were wicked, and refused to speak the truth, and, having been bribed, sowed a lie—consider what sort of vanity they spoke. They themselves were questioned and said, “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. XXVIII, 13). This is to speak vanity. For if they were sleeping, how did they know what had happened?

20. [Verses 14–15.] Therefore he says: “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear.” One who did not answer what he heard was as though he did not hear. “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute, not opening his mouth.” And he repeats the same thought: “And I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no reproofs in his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0407] Thus here and frequently elsewhere in the Ambrosian, Erfurt, and other manuscripts. The editors and manuscripts more commonly read *redargutiones* (“refutations” or “rebuttals”).] [Col. 0408]—as though he had nothing to say to them, as though he had no grounds on which to rebuke them.

Had he not previously rebuked many things and said many things, including, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. XXIII, 13), and much else of the same kind? Yet when he suffered, he said none of these things—not because he had nothing to say, but because he was waiting for them to complete everything, and for all the prophecies concerning him to be fulfilled. Of him it had been said: “And as a sheep before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

Therefore he had to remain silent in his passion, though he would not remain silent in judgment. He had come to be judged, so that he might later come to judge; and thus he will judge with great power because he was judged with great humility.

21. [Verse 16.] “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.” It is as though someone were saying to him: Why did you not open your mouth? Why did you not say, “Spare me”? Why, hanging upon the cross, did you not rebuke the wicked? He continues and says: “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.”

He has taught you what to do if tribulation should befall you. You seek to defend yourself, and perhaps no one accepts your defense.
