You are already disturbed, as though you had lost your case, because you have no defense or witness. Preserve your innocence within, where no one suppresses your case. False testimony has prevailed against you, but only among human beings. Will it prevail before God, where your case must be pleaded? When God is judge, you will have no other witness than your conscience.

Between the just Judge and your conscience, fear nothing except your own case. If you have no bad case, you will fear no accuser, refute no false witness, and require no true one. Bring only a good conscience, so that you may say: “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.”

22. [Verse 17.] “For I said: Let my enemies never exult over me; and when my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me.” He returns again to the weakness of his body, and again that head attends to its feet. He is not in heaven in such a way as to abandon what he has on earth; he plainly attends to us and sees us.

Sometimes, in the course of this life, our feet are shaken and slip into some sin. Then the most wicked tongues of our enemies rise up. From this we understand what they were seeking even while they were silent. Then they speak harshly and fiercely, rejoicing that they have found what they ought to have grieved over [Note: [Col. 0408] Thus several manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “Those who were then harsh, fierce, rejoice themselves,” etc. Some manuscripts read: “harshly into the gentle.”]. And I said: “Let my enemies never exult over me.” I said this, and yet perhaps you caused them to speak great things against me for my correction, when my feet were shaken—that is, they became exalted and spoke many evil things when I was shaken.

They ought to have shown mercy to the weak, not insulted them, just as the Apostle says: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness.” And he adds why: “Keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1). These were not such people, of whom he says, “And when my feet were shaken, they spoke great things against me”; rather, they were like those of whom he says elsewhere: “Those who oppress me will exult if I am shaken” (Ps. XII, 5).

23. [Verses 18–19.] “For I am ready for scourges.” A magnificent statement, as though he were saying: “For this I was born, that I might endure scourges.” He would not have been born except from Adam, to whom scourges are due [Note: [Col. 0409] Twelve manuscripts read *pateretur* (“would suffer”) instead of *nasceretur* (“would be born”).]

Yet sometimes sinners in this life are scourged either not at all or less severely, because all hope of their amendment has already been abandoned. But those for whom eternal life is prepared must necessarily be scourged here, because this saying is true: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him; for whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III, 11–12).

Therefore, let my enemies not insult me or speak great things. Even if my Father scourges me, I am ready for scourges, because an inheritance is being prepared for me. If you do not want the scourge, no inheritance is given you. For every son must be scourged. So universal is this scourging that he did not even spare him (Rom. VIII, 32) who had no sin (1 Pet. II, 22). “For I am ready for scourges.”

24. “And my sorrow is always before me.” What sorrow? Perhaps the sorrow caused by the scourge. And truly, my brothers, I tell you truly: people grieve over their scourges, but do not grieve over why they are scourged.

He was not like this. Listen, my brothers: if someone suffers a loss, he is more inclined to say, “I have suffered unjustly,” than to consider why he suffered—grieving over the loss of money, but not grieving over righteousness. If you have sinned, grieve over your inner treasure. You have nothing in your house, but perhaps you are even emptier in heart [Note: [Col. 0409] Instead of “you are emptier in heart,” several manuscripts read “in mind and heart.”] If, however, your heart is full of its own good, your God, why do you not say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21)?

What, then, was his sorrow over? The scourge with which he was scourged? Far from it. “And my sorrow,” he says, “is always before me.” And as though we were to ask, “What sorrow? Where does the sorrow come from?”—he answers: “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will take care concerning my sin.” Behold the source of the sorrow. The sorrow is not over the scourge, but over the wound, not over the medicine. For the scourge is medicine against sins.

Listen, brothers: we are Christians, and yet often, if someone’s son dies, the parent mourns him; if he sins, the parent does not mourn him. The parent should mourn and grieve when seeing him sin; then impose limits, then teach him a rule of life and give him discipline. Or, if the parent has done so and he has not listened, then he should have been mourned. Then he was more grievously dead, living luxuriously, than when he ended his luxury by dying. Therefore, when he was doing these things in your house, he was not only dead but also stinking.

These are the things to be grieved over; those are to be endured. Those are to be borne; these are to be mourned. They are to be mourned in the way you heard this man mourn: “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will take care concerning my sin.”

Do not be secure once you have confessed your sin, as though you should always be prepared both to confess and to commit sin. Declare your iniquity in such a way that you take care concerning your sin. What does it mean to take care concerning your sin? It means to take care of your wound. If you said, “I will take care of my wound,” what would be understood except, “I will take pains to have it healed”? To take care concerning an offense means always to strive, always to apply oneself, always to act diligently and earnestly so that you may heal your sin.

Behold, day after day you mourn your sin, but perhaps your tears flow while your hands remain idle. Let alms be given; let sins be redeemed; let the needy person rejoice in what you give, so that you too may rejoice in what God gives. He is in need, and you are in need: he needs you, and you need God [Note: [Col. 0410] Two manuscripts read: “He needs from you, and you need from God.”]

You disregard one who needs you; will God not disregard you who need him? Therefore, fill the needy person’s want, so that God may fill your inward parts. This is what it means: “I will take care concerning my sin.” I will do everything that must be done to abolish and heal my sin. “And I will take care concerning my sin.”

25. [Verse 20.] “But my enemies live.” They prosper; they rejoice in the happiness of this world, while I labor and groan from the anguish of my heart.

How do his enemies live, since he has already said of them that they spoke vanity? Hear also in another psalm: “Whose sons are like newly planted saplings, firmly established.” But earlier he had said: “Whose mouth spoke vanity; their daughters are arranged like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing into another; their oxen are fat; their sheep are fertile, multiplying in their offspring; there is no breach in the hedge, nor outcry in their streets.” Therefore, “my enemies live.” This is life; this is what they praise, this is what they love, and they possess it to their own harm.

For what follows? “They called the people blessed who have these things.” But what of you, who take care concerning your sin? What of you, who declare your iniquity? “Blessed,” he says, “is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. CXLIII, 12–15).

“But my enemies live; and they have been strengthened against me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.” What does “those who hate me unjustly” mean? They hate one who wishes them good. If they returned evil for evil, they would not be good; if they did not return good for good, they would be ungrateful. But those who hate unjustly return evil for good.

Such were the Jews: Christ came to them with good things, and they returned evil for good. Beware of this evil, brothers; it enters quickly. Because we said, “Such were the Jews,” let none of you think that he is far removed from them. If one of your brothers rebukes you, wishing you well, and you hate him, you are such a person. See how quickly and easily this happens, and avoid so great an evil, so swift a sin [Note: [Col. 0410] Thus several manuscripts. Lov. instead reads: “how easily so great an evil runs on,” and so forth.]

26. [Verse 21.] “Those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I pursued righteousness.” Therefore they returned evil for good. What does “I pursued righteousness” mean? I did not abandon it. Lest you understand “pursued” always in an evil sense, he said “pursued” to mean “followed completely”: “Because I pursued righteousness.”

And hear our head lamenting in his passion: “And they cast me away, beloved, like a dead man abhorred.” It was not enough to say “dead”; why “abhorred”? Because he was crucified. For among them this death of the cross was a great abomination, since they did not understand that it had been said in prophecy: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI, 23).

He did not himself bring death; rather, he found it here, propagated from the curse of the first human being (Gal. III, 10). By taking upon himself that same death of ours, he suspended it upon the tree—the death that had come from sin.

Therefore, lest some should think, as certain heretics do [Note: [Col. 0411] Manichaeans.], that our Lord Jesus Christ had false flesh and did not undergo a true death upon the cross, the prophet directs attention to this and says: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” He thus shows that the Son of God also died a true death, the death owed to mortal flesh, so that you would not think that he was not truly dead because he was not accursed.

Since that death was not false but descended from that stock which had come from the curse—when God said, “You shall surely die” (Gen. II, 17)—and since true death reached him in order that true life might reach us, the curse of death also reached him in order that the blessing of life might reach us. “And they cast me away, beloved, like a dead man abhorred.”

27. [Verse 22.] “Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me.” Let us speak in him; let us speak through him, for he intercedes for us (Rom. VIII, 34). And let us say: “Do not abandon me, Lord my God.”

Yet he had said: “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46; Ps. XXI, 2), and he says: “My God, do not depart from me.” If he does not depart from the body, did he depart from the head? Whose voice, then, was it, if not that of the first human being?

Thus, revealing through himself that he truly bore flesh, he says: “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” God did not abandon him. If he does not abandon you who believe in him, would the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the one God—abandon Christ? Rather, he had transformed in himself the person of the first human being.

We know from the Apostle’s words that “our old self was crucified with him” (Rom. VI, 6). But we would not be rid of our old nature unless it were crucified in weakness [Note: [Col. 0411] Thirteen manuscripts read: “unless he crucified us in weakness.” Five others: “unless the old nature were crucified,” and so forth.]

For he came for this purpose: that we might be renewed in him, because we are renewed by desiring him and imitating his passion. Therefore, it was the voice of weakness, it was our voice, in which it was said: “Why have you abandoned me?” Hence it was said there: “The words of my sins” (Ps. XXI, 2), as though he were saying: “These words have been transformed in me as the person of the sinner.” “Do not depart from me.”

28. [Verse 23.] “Attend to my help, Lord of my salvation.” This is the salvation, brothers, which the prophets sought, as the Apostle Peter says. Those who sought it did not receive it; rather, they searched and foretold it, and we have come and found what they sought (1 Pet. I, 10–12).

And behold, we have not yet received it; those who will be born after us will find what they themselves will not receive, and they will pass away. Thus, at the end of the day, all of us together with the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles will receive the denarius of salvation [Col. 0412]. For you know that the laborers hired at different times to work in the vineyard nevertheless received their wage together (Matt. XX, 9).

The prophets, therefore, and the apostles, and the martyrs, and we, and those who will exist after us until the end of the world, will receive eternal salvation at that very end. Then, contemplating the glory of God and gazing upon his face, we shall praise him forever, without weariness, without any punishment for iniquity, without any perversity of sin. We shall praise God and no longer sigh, but cling to him, for whom we have sighed to the end [Note: [Col. 0412] Lov. reads *suspiramus* (“we sigh”), while the other editions and most manuscripts read *suspiravimus* (“we have sighed”).], and in whom we have rejoiced in hope.

For in that city we shall be, where God is our good, God is our light, God is our bread, God is our life. Whatever is our good, from which we labor as exiles, we shall find in him. In him there will be rest, which now, as we remember it, we must grieve over. For we remember that Sabbath about which so much has been said, and about which we must say so much; and in speaking we must never be silent—not with the mouth, but with the heart. For we are silent with the mouth so that we may be able to cry out with the heart.

## Exposition of Psalm XXXVIII. Sermon

[Note: [Col. 0412] Delivered at Carthage at the table of Saint Cyprian. In three manuscripts this sermon is prefaced with “delivered at Carthage at the Mass of Saint Cyprian.” But in other manuscripts the more accurate reading is “at the table,” evidently erected at the very place where Cyprian had suffered. See *Exposition of Psalm LXXX*, no. 4.]

1. [Verse 1.] The psalm that we have just sung and undertaken to expound has this title: “For the end: for Idithun, a song of David himself.” We must therefore expect and hear the words of someone called Idithun; and if each one of us has been able to become Idithun, he finds himself in what he sings and hears himself.

You may see who was called Idithun according to the ancient birth of human beings [Note: [Col. 0412] Thus all our manuscripts. The editions read: “For they will see who were then present, who was called,” and so forth.]; but let us hear what this name means, and in the interpretation of the name itself let us seek an understanding of the truth.

As we have been able to discover by inquiry in those names that have been translated for us from the Hebrew language into Latin by diligent students of sacred literature, Idithun means “one who leaps over them.” Who, then, is this one who leaps over? Or whom has he leapt over? For “one who leaps over” is not given without qualification, but “one who leaps over them.” Does he sing by leaping over, or leap over by singing? Whether he sings by leaping over or leaps over by singing, we have just sung the song of the one who leaps over. Whether we too are among those who leap over, God to whom we have sung will see.

But if someone who leaps over has sung, let him rejoice that he is what he has sung. If someone still clinging to the earth has sung, let him desire to be what he has sung. For this one called “the one who leaps over them” has leapt over certain people clinging to the ground, bent toward the earth, thinking about what is below, and placing their hope in passing things. Whom did he leap over, if not those who remained behind?

2. You know that certain psalms are inscribed “A Song of Ascents.” In Greek, it is quite clear what *ἀναβαθμῶν* means. For *anabathmi* are steps, but steps for those ascending, not descending. Since Latin could not express this precisely, it used a general term; and because it called them “steps,” it left it ambiguous whether they were the steps of those ascending or of those descending.

But because “there are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard” (Ps. XVIII, 4), the preceding language explains the following one, and what was ambiguous in one language becomes certain in another. Just as someone ascends there, so here someone leaps over.

This ascent and this leaping over are not accomplished by feet, ladders, or wings; yet, if you attend to the inner person, they are accomplished by feet, ladders, and wings. For if not by feet, how does the inner person say, “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. XXXV, 12)? If not by ladders, what are the ladders that Jacob saw, where angels were ascending and descending (Gen. XXVIII, 12)? If not by wings, who is the one who says, “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly away and rest” (Ps. LIV, 7)?

In bodily matters, feet, ladders, and wings are different things. Within, however, feet, ladders, and wings are the affections of a good will [Note: [Col. 0413] Thus eleven manuscripts. The editions read: “They are affections and good wills.”] Let us walk with these, ascend with these, and fly with these.

When someone hears this one who leaps over and chooses to imitate him, he should not seek to leap over ditches by bodily lightness or to fly by jumping over something elevated. I speak, of course, of bodily matters, for he does leap over ditches also: “Those that are kindled with fire and dug up shall perish at the rebuke of your face” (Ps. LXXIX, 17).

For what are those that are kindled with fire and dug up, which will perish at the Lord’s rebuke, if not sins? They are kindled with fire when evil desire burns; they are dug up when evil fear lies low. For all sins arise either from desire or from fear.

Let this one, then, leap over everything by which he might be held on earth. Let him raise his ladders and extend his wings. Let him see whether anyone here recognizes himself. Indeed, by the grace of the Lord many recognize themselves—those who, perhaps already holding the world cheap and all the things that delight in the world, choose to live rightly while they live here in certain spiritual joys.

And from where do these joys come to those still walking upon the earth, if not from divine utterances, from the word of God, from some parable of Scripture searched out and investigated, from the sweetness of discovery preceded by the labor of inquiry? There are certain holy and good delights in the books.

For they are not found in gold and silver, in banquets and luxury, in hunting and fishing, in games and amusements, in theatrical frivolities, or in seeking and grasping ruinous honors. There are no true joys in all those things, whereas these books do contain them. On the contrary, let that lowly soul that leaps over them and delights in these books say—for it speaks the truth, and speaks it confidently—“The unjust have told me of their delights, but not as your law, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 83).

Let this Idithun come still further; let him leap over those who delight in low things, and let him delight in these things and rejoice in the word of the Lord, in delight in the law of the Most High.

But what shall we say? Must one leap over this also into something else? Or does the one who desires to leap over have somewhere to leap over as far as this? Rather, let us hear his words. For this one who leaps over seems to me already to have dwelt in the utterances of God, and there to have learned what we are about to hear.

3. [Verse 2.] “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” You may suppose that while he was reading, discussing, preaching, admonishing, rebuking, and exhorting; while he was engaged in practical work and exercised amid certain human difficulties; while he was living as a human being among human beings—although he was already leaping over those who do not delight in these things—for it is difficult for anyone not to slip and sin with the tongue, and “the one who does not sin with the tongue is a perfect man,” as it is written (Jas. III, 2)—he had perhaps said something for which he later repented, and words had slipped from his mouth that he wished he could recall but could not.

For the tongue is not in the mouth for no reason, unless because it slips easily. Seeing, then, how difficult it was for a human being to have the necessity of speaking and, in speaking, not to say something he would wish he had not said, and wearied by these sins, he sought to avoid such things. The one who leaps over suffers this difficulty.

Let no one who has not yet leapt over judge me. Let him leap over and experience what I am saying; then he will be both a witness and a son of the truth.

When these things had happened to him, he had decided not to speak, lest he say something that he would regret having said. His opening words indicate this: “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

Guard your ways, then, O Idithun, and do not sin with your tongue. Weigh what you are about to say; examine it; consult the inner truth; and so bring it forth to the external hearer.

You often seek this amid disturbed circumstances and distracted minds, while the very weakness of the soul—which is weighed down by the corruptible body—wishes both to hear and to speak, to hear within and speak outwardly. Sometimes, disturbed by eagerness to speak, it fails through negligence in recognizing [Note: [Col. 0414] Seventeen manuscripts read *indigentia* (“need”) instead of *indiligentia* (“negligence”).] and in these circumstances says something that perhaps ought not to be said.

Against such things, silence is the better remedy. A sinner stands there, marked by a distinctive sign of the sinner: someone proud and envious. He hears the one who leaps over; he lies in wait for his words; he sets traps. It is difficult for him not to find something said in a way that it ought not to have been said. He does not forgive what he hears, but slanders it out of envy.

Against such people this Idithun, the one who leaps over them, had chosen silence. Hence he sang: “I said: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” As long as I am seized by slanderers—or seize them—and even if I am not seized, “I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

Although I have leapt over earthly delights, although the fleeting affections for temporal things no longer seize me, although I now despise these low things and rise toward better ones, even in these better things the delight of understanding before God is enough for me. Why do I need to speak in order to seek approval and give access to slanderers? “I said, therefore: I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.”

“I set a guard over my mouth.” Why did he do this? For the devout, the studious, the faithful, and the holy? Far from it. They listen in such a way that they praise what they approve; and when they disapprove something among the many things they praise, they grant pardon rather than prepare slander.

For whom, then, do you wish to guard your ways so that you may not sin with your tongue, and set a guard over your mouth? Listen: “While the sinner stands against me.” He does not stand beside me, but stands against me.

What can I say at last? How can I satisfy him? I speak of spiritual things to a carnal person, who sees and hears outwardly but is inwardly deaf and blind. “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. II, 14). If he were not natural, why would he slander?

“Blessed is the one who speaks a word to a listening ear” (Eccli. XXV, 12), not to the ear of a sinner who stands against him. For many such people stood around and howled when he was led like a sheep to be sacrificed; and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. LIII, 7).

What can you say to swollen, agitated, slanderous, quarrelsome, talkative people? What can you say that is holy and devout, and that leaps over them through religion [Note: [Col. 0415] Erasmus reads: “What can you say to a holy and devout person who leaps over them through religion?” Three manuscripts read: “What can a holy and devout person say, who leaps over them through religion?”], when the Lord himself says to those who listen willingly, who desire to learn, who thirst for the food of truth, and eagerly receive it: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI, 12)?

And the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal”—not people to be despaired of, but people to be nourished. For he continues: “As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able” (1 Cor. III, 1–2). Therefore say even now: “Indeed, you are not yet able.”

Do not hasten to hear what you cannot grasp; grow so that you may grasp it. In this way we address a little one who is to be nourished in the bosom of Mother Church with pious milk and made fit for the food of the Lord’s table.

But what of this sort could I say to a sinner standing against me, who thinks or pretends himself capable of what he cannot grasp? When I have told him something and he has not grasped it, might he think not that he failed to understand but that I failed?

Therefore, because of this sinner standing against me, “I set a guard over my mouth.”

4. [Verse 3.] And what followed? “I became deaf, and was humbled, and was silent from good things.” This one who leaps over suffers a difficulty at a certain stage, one that he has already leapt over, and seeks to leap over it from there as well, in order to avoid this difficulty.

I was afraid of sinning [Note: [Col. 0415] Several manuscripts read: “I was afraid of the sinner.”], so that I would not speak, so that I might impose silence upon myself. For I had said: “I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue.” And while I feared speaking lest I sin, “I became deaf, and was humbled, and was silent from good things.”

While I was excessively afraid of saying anything bad, I kept silent about everything good: “I became deaf, and was humbled, and was silent from good things.”

For from where could I say good things, unless I was hearing them? “You will give gladness and joy to my hearing” (Ps. L, 10). And the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of the voice—not his own, but the bridegroom’s (John III, 29). To speak truly, he hears what he is to say. For the one who speaks a lie speaks from his own resources (John VIII, 44).

This man therefore suffered something sad and burdensome; and by this confession of his he warns us to avoid what he suffered, not to imitate it. For, as I said, fearing too much that he might say something not good, he decided to say nothing, not even what was good. And because he had decided to remain silent, he began not to hear.

If you are one who leaps over, you stand and expect to hear from God what you are to say to human beings. Between the rich God and the needy person seeking what he should hear, you intervene as one who leaps over, so that you can hear from one side and speak to the other. If you choose not to speak to the other side, you will not deserve to hear from this side. You disregard the poor person, and the rich person disregards you.

Have you forgotten that you are a servant whom the Lord appointed over his household to give his fellow servants their food (Matt. XXIV, 45)? Why, then, do you seek to receive what you are too lazy to distribute? Rightly, therefore, because you were unwilling to say what you had received, you are prevented from receiving what you desired to receive. You had something; you wanted something. Give what you have, so that you may deserve to receive what you do not have.

Therefore, when I had, as it were, set a guard over my mouth and imposed silence upon myself because I saw speech as dangerous everywhere, what I did not want happened to me, he says: “I became deaf, and was humbled.” I did not humble myself; I was humbled. “I became deaf, and was humbled, and was silent from good things.”

I began not to say what was good because I feared that I might say something bad, and I condemned my decision. For “I was silent from good things.”

“And my sorrow was renewed.” For I had, as it were, rested from a certain sorrow inflicted upon me by slanderers and critics in silence, and that sorrow caused by the slanderers had ceased. But when I was silent from good things, my sorrow was renewed.

I began to grieve more over having kept silent about what I ought to say than I had grieved over saying what I ought not to say. “My sorrow was renewed.”

### 5. [verses 4, 5]

[Note: [Col. 0416] He passes over in silence those words of verse 4: “My heart grew hot within me.”]

“And in my meditation the fire shall blaze.” My heart began to be restless. I saw the senseless and was wasting away (Ps. 118:158), though I did not rebuke them; and while I remained silent, the zeal of your house was consuming me (Ps. 68:10). For I looked back to my Lord saying: “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have given my money to the bankers, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest.” And may God turn away what follows from his stewards: “Let him be cast into the outer darkness, with his hands and feet bound”—a servant, not one who overturned anything so as to destroy it, but one who was lazy in distributing it (Matt. 25:26–27, 30). What should those expect who have squandered everything in luxury, if those who preserved it in laziness are condemned?

“And in my meditation the fire shall blaze.” Placed in this uncertainty between speaking and keeping silent, among those ready to accuse and those eager to be instructed, between the prosperous and the needy, having become “a reproach to those who were at ease, and a contempt to the proud” (Ps. 122:4), while looking upon those as blessed who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. 5:6); struggling on both sides, afflicted on both sides; in danger lest I cast pearls before swine, [Col. 0417] and in danger lest I fail to distribute food to my fellow servants—in this heat he sought another, better place, away from this stewardship in which a person struggles and is endangered in this way. Sighing toward a certain end, where he would not have to suffer these things, toward that end, I say, at which the Lord will say to the good distributor: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21), he says:

“I spoke with my tongue.” Amid these heats, amid these dangers, amid these difficulties—for the law of the Lord is so delightful, yet because of the abundance of scandals the love of many grows cold (Matt. 24:12)—amid these heats, then, he says, “I spoke with my tongue.” To whom? Not to the hearer whom I want to instruct, but to the one who hears me and from whom I want to be instructed. “I spoke with my tongue” to him from whom I hear inwardly, if I hear anything good, if I hear anything true.

What did you say? “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” I have leapt over certain things and have come to certain others; and those to which I have come are better than those over which I leapt. But something still remains to be crossed over. We shall not remain here, where we endure temptations, scandals, hearers, and accusers. “Make my end known to me”—the end that is still lacking to me, not the course that is already before me.

### 6.

He speaks of that end which the Apostle contemplated while running, confessing his own imperfection: he saw one thing in himself and sought another elsewhere. For he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect, brothers; I do not consider myself to have apprehended it.” And lest you should say, “If the Apostle did not apprehend it, have I apprehended it? If the Apostle is not perfect, am I perfect?” see what he is doing; attend to what he says.

What are you doing, Apostle? You have not yet apprehended it; you are not yet perfect? What are you doing? Toward what action are you urging me? What are you setting before me to imitate and follow?

“But one thing,” he says: “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my intention I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:12–14)—according to my intention, not yet according to attainment, not yet according to apprehension.

Let us not fall back from where we have already crossed over, nor remain in what we have already reached. Let us run; let us press forward; we are on the way. Do not be so secure because of what you have crossed over as you are concerned about what you have not yet reached.

“Forgetting what lies behind,” he says, “and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my intention I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.” He himself is the end.

“But one thing”—that is, this one thing: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:9). This one thing is also called “one” in another psalm: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I will seek.” Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” Why? “That I may behold the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4).

There I shall rejoice in my companion and shall not fear my adversary; there the one who beholds with me will be a friend, not an accusing enemy.

This Idithun desired: while he was still here, he desired that his end should be made known to him, so that he might know what was lacking to him; and he might not rejoice so much in what he had reached as desire what he had not yet reached. Having already crossed over certain things, he would not remain on the road but would be carried away by desire toward what is above, until the one who had crossed over certain things should cross over everything, and, from a kind of sprinkling of drops coming from the cloud of the Scriptures, should come like a stag to the fountain of life (Ps. 41:2), and in that light should see light (Ps. 35:10), and should be hidden in the face of God from the disturbance of human beings (Ps. 30:21). There he would say: “All is well; I want nothing further. Here I love everyone; here I fear no one.”

A good desire, a holy desire. Those of you who already possess this, rejoice with us, and pray that we may possess it perseveringly, lest we fail amid scandals. For we also ask the same thing for you. We are not so worthy that we should pray for you while you are unworthy to pray for us. The Apostle commended himself to his hearers, to whom he preached the word of God (Col. 4:3). Pray, therefore, for us, brothers, that we may both see well what must be seen and say well what must be said.

As for this desire, I know that it is found in few; and no one understands me fully except those who have tasted the source from which I speak. Yet we speak to everyone—to those who possess such a desire and to those who do not yet possess it: to those who possess it, so that they may sigh with us for that place; to those who do not possess it, so that they may shake off their laziness, cross over what is below, come to the sweetness of the Lord’s law, and not remain in the pleasures of the wicked.

For many people recount many things, and many people praise many things—wicked people praise wicked things. And truly those wicked things also have their delight, but not like your law, Lord (Ps. 118:85). Let those, then, who believe that we speak these things say with us what Idithun says:

“Make my end known to me, Lord.”

### 7.

“And what is the number of my days.” I seek the number of my days that exists. Thus I can speak, thus I can understand a number without number, just as years can be spoken of without years. For where there are years, there is certainly something like a number; yet still, “You are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

Make the number of my days known to me—but the number that exists. What, then? Does this number in which you exist not exist? Certainly, if I pay close attention, it does not. If I cling to it, it seems to exist; if I cross over it, it does not exist. If, shaking myself free from these things, I contemplate what is above; if I compare passing things with things that remain, I see what is true—and what merely seems to exist more than it does.

Shall I say that these are my days?

[Note: [Col. 0418] Thus most manuscripts. But Lov. reads: “than if he were about to say that you had measured these days of mine?” Er. reads: “that they seem not to exist, unless I should say that these are my days?”]

Shall I, I ask, say that these are my days, and rashly give this great word to this course of fleeting things?

Thus I, myself failing, almost cease to exist, so that I have forgotten the one who said, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

Is there, then, some number of days? There truly is, and it is without end. In speaking of these days, however, I shall say that something exists if I hold fast to the day about which you ask me whether it exists. At least, ask me about it, but hold fast to the point from which you ask me.

Do you hold this day? If you held yesterday, you hold today as well.

“But I do not hold yesterday,” you say, “because it no longer exists. I do hold this day, in which I am and which is with me.”

Has it escaped you, then, how much of this day has already passed since first light? Did this day not begin at the first hour? Give me its first hour; give me its second also, since perhaps that too has flown away.

“I shall give you the third,” you say, “for perhaps we are now in that hour.”

Certainly, then, these days exist, and there is a third day. Yet if you give me the third, you will give me not a day but an hour.

Nevertheless, I do not grant you even this, if you have crossed over these things with me. Give me at least the third hour; give me that very hour in which you are. For if some of it has already passed and some of it still remains, you cannot give me what has passed, because it no longer exists, nor what remains, because it does not yet exist.

What will you give me of this hour that is now passing? What will you give me of that to which I may entrust this word, so that I may say, “It exists”?

When you say “Est” (“is”) itself, it is certainly one syllable and one moment, and the syllable has three letters. In the very utterance, you do not reach the second letter of this word until the first has ended; the third will not sound until the second too has passed.

What will you give me of this one syllable? And do you hold the days, when you do not hold one syllable?

Everything is snatched away as the moments fly past; the torrent of things flows. From this torrent the one who has already lifted up his head drank on the way for our sake (Ps. 109:7).

These days, then, do not exist. They almost depart before they arrive, and when they arrive they cannot stand. They join themselves [Note: [Col. 0419] Seven manuscripts read: “they press upon one another.”], follow one another, and do not hold fast.

Nothing past is recalled. What is future is awaited as something that will pass; it is not possessed while it has not come, and it is not held when it has come.

“What is the number of my days that exists?” Not this number that does not exist—and what disturbs me more difficultly and dangerously, which both exists and does not exist. We cannot say that what does not stand exists, nor that what comes and passes does not exist.

I seek that simple “exists”; I seek the true “exists”; I seek the genuine “exists”; I seek the “exists” that is in that Jerusalem, the bride of my Lord, where there will be no death, no failing, no day that passes, but a day that remains—one that is preceded by no yesterday and driven onward by no tomorrow.

This number of my days that exists, I say: make it known to me.

### 8.

“So that I may know what is lacking to me.”

This is what is lacking to me while I labor here; and as long as it is lacking to me, I do not call myself perfect. As long as I do not receive it, I say: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. 3:12, 14). I shall receive this as the reward of my running.

The end of running will be a kind of dwelling-place; and in that dwelling-place there will be a homeland without wandering, without disturbance, without temptation.

Therefore: “Make known to me this number of my days that exists, so that I may know what is lacking to me,” because I am not yet there. Let me not become proud because of what I already am, so that I may be found in him without possessing my own righteousness.

For when I compare these things, which are not so, with what exists, and see that more is lacking to me than is present, I shall be humbler because of what is lacking than I shall be exalted because of what is present.

Those who think they possess something while they live here do not receive what is lacking because of their pride; they think that what is present is great. “For whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Nor are such people great because of this: inflation and swelling imitate greatness, but do not possess health.

### 9. [verse 6]

Now, then, this man, crossing over and carrying out something hidden in his heart, known only to one who carries it out in the same way—as though, with his end made known to him, he had obtained what he requested, and with the number of his days made known to him, not the number that passes but the number that exists—turns his attention to the things he crossed over and compares them with his superior knowledge.

And as though you were saying to him, “Why did you desire the number of your days that exists? What do you say about these days?”—looking to that other [Note: [Col. 0420] Eleven manuscripts read: “Looking from above at these things.” Seven other manuscripts read: “He, looking from above.”] he says:

“Behold, you have appointed my days as old.”

For these days grow old. I want new days, days that never grow old, so that I may say: “The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (2 Cor. 5:17)—now in hope, then in reality.

For although we have been renewed in faith and hope, how many old things do we still do? We are not so clothed with Christ that we carry nothing of Adam any longer.

See Adam growing old and Christ being renewed in us: “Even if our outer person is being corrupted, our inner person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

Therefore, when we attend to sin, mortality, swiftly passing times, groaning, labor, and sweat [Note: [Col. 0420] The editions add “of Adam”; this is absent from the manuscripts], to successive ages that do not remain, passing without our noticing from infancy to old age, let us see here the old person, the old day, the old song, and the Old Testament.

But when we turn toward the inner person [Note: [Col. 0420] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “toward inward things.”], toward the things that must be renewed in place of those that will be changed, let us find the new person, the new day, the new song, and the New Testament. Let us love this newness in such a way that we do not fear old age there.

Now, therefore, in this course we pass from old things to new. This passage is carried out when outward things are corrupted and inward things are renewed, until even that which is outward and is being corrupted fulfills its debt to nature, comes into death, and is renewed in the resurrection.

Then all things will truly become new; the rest of what now exists is in hope [Note: [Col. 0420] The editions add “exists”; this is absent from the manuscripts].

You are therefore now doing something by stripping off the old things and running toward the new. Running toward the new, then, and stretching forward to what lies ahead, this man says:

“Make known to me, Lord, my end, and the number of my days that exists, so that I may know what is lacking to me.”

Behold, he still drags Adam along, and thus hastens toward Christ.

“Behold,” he says, “you have appointed my days as old.” You have appointed those old days from Adam; they grow old daily, and they grow old in such a way that eventually they are even consumed.

“And my substance is as nothing before you.”

Before you, Lord, my substance is as nothing—before you who see this. And when I see this, I see it before you; before human beings I do not see it.

What shall I say? In what words shall I show that what I am is nothing in comparison with what exists? But this is spoken inwardly [Note: [Col. 0420] Several manuscripts read: “learned inwardly.” And shortly afterward the editions generally read: “both inwardly”; some manuscripts have: “inwardly, in some fashion.”], [Col. 0421] and inwardly it is somehow perceived.

Before you, Lord—where your eyes are, not where human eyes are—what is my substance? It is as nothing.

### 10.

“Nevertheless, utter vanity, every human being who lives.”

“Nevertheless”—for what was he saying? “Behold, I have already crossed over all mortal things, despised what is below, trampled earthly things, ascended to the delight of the Lord’s law, fluctuated amid the stewardship of the number of the Lord’s days [Note: [Col. 0421] Er. and ten manuscripts read: “the number of the Lord’s gifts,” omitting the word “days.” Two manuscripts read: “the number of the Lord’s coins.” Four read: “the number of the Lord’s presents.”], and even desired that end which has no end. I desired the number of my days that exists, because the number of these days does not exist. Behold, I am already such a person; I have crossed over so much; I yearn in this way for the things that stand.”

“Nevertheless”—as I am here, as long as I am here, as long as I am in this world, as long as I carry mortal flesh, as long as human life is temptation upon the earth (Job 7:1), as long as I sigh amid scandals, as long as I fear falling while I stand, as long as both my evils and my goods are uncertain to me—“utter vanity, every human being who lives.”

Every human being, I say, whether clinging to things or crossing over them—even Idithun himself still belongs to universal vanity. For “all is vanity, and vanity of vanities” [Note: [Col. 0421] Thus the better manuscripts. The common editions read: “vanity of vanities.” M.]. “What abundance does a person have from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1:2–3).

Is Idithun still under the sun? He possesses something under the sun; he possesses something beyond the sun.

Under the sun he possesses waking, sleeping, eating, drinking, hunger, thirst, strength, weariness, childhood, youth, old age; he possesses uncertain things that he hopes for and fears. All these things Idithun himself possesses under the sun, even while he is crossing over them.

From where, then, does he cross over them? From that desire: “Make my end known to me, Lord.” For this desire is beyond the sun; it is not under the sun.

All visible things are under the sun. Whatever is not visible is not under the sun. Faith is not visible; hope is not visible; love is not visible; kindness is not visible; finally, that chaste fear which endures forever and ever is not visible (Ps. 18:10).

Finding sweetness and consolation in all these things, and dwelling beyond the sun—for “our citizenship is in heaven”—Idithun groans over the things he still possesses under the sun. He despises and grieves over these things, while he burns with desire for those that he longs for.

He has spoken of the former; let him speak also of the latter. You have heard what is to be desired; hear what is to be despised:

“Nevertheless, utter vanity, every human being who lives.”

### 11. [verse 7]

“Although a human being walks in an image.”

In whose image, unless in the image of the one who said, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)?

“Although a human being walks in an image.” The “although” is used because this image is something great. And this “although” is followed by “nevertheless,” so that the “although” you heard is beyond the sun, while the “nevertheless” that follows is under the sun; the former belongs to truth, the latter to vanity.

“Although, then, a human being walks in an image, nevertheless he is troubled in vain.”

Hear his trouble, and see whether it is not vain, so that you may trample it, cross over it, and dwell in the heights where this vanity does not exist.

What vanity? “He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.”

O insane vanity! “Blessed is the one whose hope is the Lord, who has not turned toward vanities and lying madnesses” (Ps. 39:5).

You may think that I am speaking deliriously to you, miser, when I say these things; these words may seem to you like an old woman’s tales. You, surely, a man of great judgment and great prudence, devise daily ways of acquiring money—from commerce, from agriculture, perhaps even from public speaking, from legal consultation, from military service; and you add interest-bearing loans as well.

As a sensible man, you omit nothing at all by which one coin may be added to another and more carefully disciplined in secret [Note: [Col. 0422] Four or five manuscripts add to “one coin upon another”: “may be placed.” With this omitted, the editions read: “and may be acquired more diligently in secret.” In place of “may be acquired,” four manuscripts have “may be gathered,” one has “may be deposited,” and three have “may be written down.” Nine other manuscripts read “may be disciplined.” A marginal note in the manuscripts of Lyre and Audoen, written about six hundred years ago, apparently by the same hand and at the time the codices were copied, explains the word as follows: “Cartigare is to write something on a carta, that is, on parchment, for the sake of preserving it; the word is more commonly used of usurers.” Finally, this word may have been used here in popular speech for “to shut away,” in which sense Martial metaphorically says, Book 1, epigram 30:

“And whose chest scourges its loose wealth.”

Jurists also speak of “scourging the grain supply,” as in Digest, book 48, title 18, law 6, On Extraordinary Crimes.]

You plunder a human being and beware of being plundered; you fear suffering what you do, and yet you do not correct yourself in what you suffer.

But you do not suffer. You are a prudent man: you preserve well, and not merely gather well. You have somewhere to place it, someone to entrust it to, and a way to ensure that nothing is lost of what you have gathered.

I question your heart; I examine your prudence. Behold, you have gathered; behold, you have preserved it so well that you cannot lose anything you have preserved. Tell me: for whom are you preserving it?

I am not dealing with you about anything else; I do not recall or enlarge upon whatever other evil your vanity’s greed possesses. I present and examine this one point, which gives me occasion for this psalm’s reading.

Certainly, you gather and store up treasure. I do not say: “Perhaps, while gathering, you will be gathered up.” I do not say: “Perhaps, while you wish to be a predator, you will become prey.” Let me put it more plainly, for perhaps you have not heard or understood because greed has blinded you. I do not say: “Perhaps, while you wish to be the predator of a smaller creature, you will become the prey of a larger one.”

You do not perceive that you are at sea, nor do you see smaller fish being devoured by larger ones. I do not say these things; I do not speak of the difficulties and dangers involved in the very acquisition of money, how much those who gather it endure, how they are endangered in everything, and see death almost everywhere. I pass over all these things.

Certainly, you gather without anyone opposing you and preserve without anyone taking it away. Examine your heart and that great prudence with which you mock me, by which you think me foolish for saying these things, and tell me: you store up treasure— for whom will you gather it?

I see what you want to say, as though what you intend to say had not occurred to this person: “I preserve it for my children.”

This is the voice of devotion, an excuse for iniquity: “I preserve it for my children,” you say. You even preserve it for your children.

Did Idithun not know this? He certainly knew these things, but he counted them among the old days and therefore despised them, because he was hastening toward the new days.

### 12.

For behold, I examine you together with your children. You preserve for those who will pass away, while you yourself are passing away—indeed, you are one who passes away preserving for those who pass away.

First I ask you this: do you know whether the one for whom you preserve it will possess it? Or, if he has not yet been born, do you know whether he will be born?

You preserve for children; it is uncertain whether they will come into existence or possess it. And you do not store your treasure where it ought to be stored. For your Lord would not give his servant such advice as would cause him to lose his own funds.

You are a servant possessing private funds under a certain great head of a household. What you love and what you possess, he himself gave you; and he does not want you to lose what he gave you—he who will also give you himself. But, I say, he does not even want you to lose what he gave you temporarily.

It is much; it overflows; it exceeds the needs of your condition; it is already reckoned as surplus. “I do not want you to lose even this,” says your Lord.

“And what shall I do?”

“Move it. The place where you have put it is not safe” [Note: [Col. 0423] The editions read: “Your place is not safe.” The manuscripts’ reading, “the place is not safe,” is better.].

Certainly, you want to serve greed. See whether my advice might not also suit greed itself. You want to keep what you have and not lose it; I show you a place where you may put it.

“Do not store up treasure on earth, not knowing for whom you are gathering it, nor how the one who possesses and holds it will later consume it.” Perhaps the one possessed will become the possessor [Note: [Col. 0423] The editions read: “will possess you.” The manuscripts omit “you.”], and he will not retain what he receives from you. Perhaps, while you preserve it for him, you will lose it before he arrives.

I give advice to your anxiety: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven” (Matt. 6:20).

If you wanted to preserve your wealth here on earth, you would seek a storeroom. Perhaps you would not trust your house because of your household servants; you would entrust it to a money-changer in the neighborhood [Note: [Col. 0423] Four manuscripts read: “to a neighboring money-changer.”]. For loss is difficult there; a thief does not easily approach, and everything is carefully preserved.

Why do you consider these things, unless because you have no better place where you can preserve it? What if I provide a better one? I shall say to you: “Do not entrust it to one who is less reliable; there is a reliable person—entrust it to him. He has great storehouses where wealth cannot perish. He is rich, richer than all the rich.”

Perhaps you will say: “When would I dare to entrust it to such a person?”

What if he himself urges you? Recognize him. He is not only the head of the household; he is also your Lord.

“I do not want you, my servant,” he says, “to lose your funds. Recognize where you should place them. Why do you put them where you may lose them, where, even if you do not lose them, you yourself cannot remain there forever? There is another place to which I shall transfer you.

“Let what you possess go before you. Do not fear losing it: I was the giver; I shall be the keeper.”

Your Lord says this to you. Question your faith [Note: [Col. 0423] Three manuscripts read: “I questioned,” and so forth. One manuscript reads: “I question.”]; see whether you are willing to believe him.

You will say: “I have lost what I cannot see. I want to see it here.”

While you want to see it here, you will see nothing here and will possess nothing there. I do not know what treasures you have hidden in the earth; when you go out, you do not carry them with you.

You have come to hear a sermon, to gather inward riches, and you are thinking about outward things. Did you bring them here with you? Behold, you do not see them even now.

You believe that you have in your house what you know you placed there. Do you also know that you have not lost it? How many people have returned to their houses and have not found what they had placed there?

Perhaps the hearts of the greedy were frightened by this. And because I said that many people have often returned to their house and not found what they had placed there, each one said in his heart: “God forbid, Bishop. Wish us well; pray for us. God forbid that this should happen; God forbid that it should turn out this way. I believe in God, and I shall find what I placed there safe.”

You believe in God, and do not believe God himself?

“I believe in Christ, because what I placed there will be safe; no one will approach it; no one will take it away.”

You want to be secure by believing in Christ, so that you may lose nothing from your house. You will be secure rather by believing Christ, so that you may put it where he advised you to put it.

Are you secure about your servant and anxious about your Lord? Are you secure about your house and anxious about heaven?

“But how do I put it in heaven?” you ask.

I have given you advice: where I tell you, put it. I do not want you to know how it reaches heaven. Put it into the hands of the poor; give it to the needy. What is it to you how it reaches there? Shall I not convey what I receive [Note: [Col. 0424] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “Will he not cause what I receive to be lost?”]?

Or have you forgotten: “Whatever you have done for one of the least of my brothers, you have done for me” (Matt. 25:40)?

If one of your friends had certain reservoirs, cisterns, and various containers constructed for preserving some liquid, whether wine or oil, and you were looking for somewhere to hide or preserve your produce, and he said to you, “I shall preserve it for you,” and if he had hidden channels and passages leading to those containers, so that what was poured out openly might secretly flow through them, and he said to you, “Pour what you have here,” you would see that this was not the place where you had intended to store it and would be afraid to pour it out.

He, knowing the hidden mechanisms of his places, might say to you: “Pour confidently; it reaches from here to there. You do not see by what route, but believe me, who constructed it.”

For the one through whom all things were made constructed mansions for all of us. He wants what we possess to go there ahead of us, so that we do not lose it on earth.

But when you preserve it on earth, tell me: for whom will you gather it?

You have children. Count one more, and give something also to Christ.

“He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” He is troubled in vain.

### 13. [verse 8]

“And now”—when, says this Idithun [Note: [Col. 0424] The earlier editions read: “And now, since this Idithun says,” and shortly afterward: “above himself he has where he stretches forward. What is he like? How great is he?” We have corrected the passage on the authority of several good manuscripts.]—looking down upon a certain vanity and looking up toward a certain truth, placed in the middle, with something beneath him and something above him—beneath him is what he has crossed over; above him is the goal toward which he stretches—“and now,” he says, “when I have crossed over something, when I have trampled many things, when I am no longer held by temporal things, I am not yet perfect; I have not yet received it.”

“For we have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

Therefore, what is my expectation now? Is it not the Lord? He is my expectation, the one who gave me all these things to despise. He will also give me himself, who is above all things, through whom all things were made, and from whom I was made among all things. The Lord himself is my expectation.

You see Idithun, brothers; you see how he awaits. Let no one, then, call himself perfect here. He deceives, cheats, and misleads himself; no one can possess perfection here.

And what does it profit him that he loses humility? “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?”

When he comes, he will no longer be awaited; then there will be perfection. But now, however much Idithun has crossed over, he still awaits.

“And my substance is always before you.”

Already making progress, already stretching toward him, and beginning to exist to some extent: “My substance is always before you.”

This substance is also before human beings. You have gold, silver, slaves, estates, trees, animals, servants; these can be seen by human beings. There is a certain substance that is always before you.

“And my substance is always before you.”

### 14. [verse 9]

“Deliver me from all my iniquities.”

I have crossed over many things—indeed, many. But “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). I have crossed over many things, but I still beat my breast and say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

You, then, are my expectation; you are my end. For “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

“From all”—not merely from those things, lest I fall back into what I have crossed over, but from all iniquities altogether, because of which I now beat my breast and say: “Forgive us our debts.”

“Deliver me from all my iniquities”—while I am wise in this way and hold fast to what the Apostle says: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way.”

For when he said that he was not yet perfect, he immediately continued: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way.”

What does “as many as are perfect” mean? A little earlier you had said: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.” Follow the order of the words [Note: [Col. 0425] Most manuscripts read: “Follow it; say the whole thing.”].

“But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my intention I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:12–15).

He is not yet perfect because he is pursuing the prize of God’s heavenly calling, which he has not yet found and has not yet reached.

But if he is not perfect because he has not reached that place, who among us is perfect? Nevertheless, he continues and says: “As many as are perfect, let us think this way.”

You are not perfect, Apostle, and are we perfect? But have you forgotten that he has just called himself perfect?

For he does not say, “As many as are perfect, think this way,” but rather, “As many as are perfect, let us think this way,” although shortly before he had said: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.”

Therefore, you cannot be perfect here in any other way than by knowing that here you cannot be perfect.

This, then, will be your perfection: to have crossed over certain things in such a way that you hasten toward certain others; to have crossed over certain things in such a way that another thing remains to be crossed over after everything else has been completed.

This is a safe faith [Note: [Col. 0425] The editions read: “This is the whole faith.” Several manuscripts more appropriately read: “This is the safe faith.”]. For whoever thinks he has already arrived places himself on high so that he may fall.

### 15.

Since, then, I think in this way—since I call myself both imperfect and perfect: imperfect because I have not yet received something I desire, but perfect because I know precisely what is lacking to me—since I think in this way, since I despise human things, since I do not want to rejoice in things that perish, since I am mocked by the miser who boasts that he is wise and mocks me for being foolish, since I act in this way, since I travel along this road:

“You have made me a reproach to the foolish.”

You wanted me to live among those who love vanity and to preach the truth among them; and I cannot but be mocked by them, because “we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9): angels praising, human beings reproaching; indeed, both angels praising and blaming, and human beings praising and blaming.

“On the right and on the left we have weapons with which we fight: through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (2 Cor. 6:7–8).

These things occur among angels and among human beings. For among angels there are holy angels, whom we should please by living well, and there are transgressing angels, whom we should displease by living well. Among human beings there are holy men, who are pleased by our life, and there are utterly wicked people who mock our good life.

These are the weapons: those on the right and those on the left. Yet both are weapons. I use both weapons, the right and the left—both those who praise and those who blame, both those who confer honor and those who inflict disgrace. With both kinds of weapons I fight against the devil; with both I strike him: with prosperity, if I am not corrupted; with adversity, if I am not broken.

### 16. [verses 10, 11]

“You have therefore made me a reproach to the foolish.”

“I became deaf and did not open my mouth.”

But I became deaf toward the foolish and did not open my mouth. For to whom should I say what is happening within me?

“For I shall hear what the Lord God speaks within me, because he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84:9). But “there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 48:22).

“I became deaf and did not open my mouth.”

“For you are the one who made me.”

Is this why you did not open your mouth, because God is the one who made you? It is strange. Did God not make your mouth for speaking? “Does the one who planted the ear not hear? Does the one who formed the eye not see?” (Ps. 93:9).

God gave you a mouth for speaking, and you say: “I became deaf and did not open my mouth, because you are the one who made me.”

Or does “because you are the one who made me” belong to the following verse?

“Because you are the one who made me, remove your scourges from me.”

Because you are the one who made me, do not destroy me. Strike me only so that I may progress, not so that I may fail; beat me only so that I may be brought forth, not so that I may be shattered.

“Because you are the one who made me, remove your scourges from me.”

17. [verse 12.] “At the force of your hand I fainted under corrections”—that is, when you corrected me, I fainted. And what is your correction, except what follows? “For iniquity you instructed man, and you made my soul waste away like a spider.” Great is what this Idithun understands—if anyone understands with him, if anyone leaps across with him. For he says that he fainted under God’s corrections, and he wants the scourges removed from him because it is he who made him. Let the one who made him restore him; let the one who created him recreate him. Yet do we suppose, brothers, that he fainted in such a way that he wished both to be recreated and reshaped [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus seven manuscripts. Several others read: “because he fainted in such a way that he wished…”; four, however, read: “who so fainted that he wished both to be recreated and reshaped?” The editions had: “who fainted in such a way that he did not wish,” etc.], without cause? “For iniquity,” he says, “you instructed man.” All that in which I have fainted, in which I am weak, in which I cry out from the depths—all of this is for iniquity; and in this you instructed me, you did not condemn me: “For iniquity you instructed man.”

Hear this more plainly from another psalm: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes” (Ps. 118:71). I have been humbled, and it is good for me; it is both punishment and grace. What does he preserve after punishment who imposes punishment through grace? He is the one of whom it was said, “I was humbled, and he saved me” (Ps. 114:6), and, “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes.” “For iniquity you chastised man.”

And what is written—“You fashion pain through the commandment” (Ps. 93:20)—could have been said of God only by one who leaps across, because it could have been seen only by one who leaps across. “You fashion,” he says, “pain through the commandment”: from pain you make a commandment for me. You shape my pain itself; you do not leave it unformed, but you give it form. And my pain, formed and inflicted by you, will be a commandment for me, so that I may be liberated by you. For “you fashion,” it is said: you form pain, you mold pain; you do not pretend pain—just as an artisan fashions something, whence the potter is also named from fashioning.

Therefore: “For iniquity you instructed man.” I see myself amid evils; I see myself in punishment, and I do not see iniquity with you. If, then, I am in punishment and there is no iniquity with you, does it not remain that you chastise man for iniquity?

18. And how did you chastise him? Tell us of that instruction itself, O Idithun: how were you instructed? “And you made my soul waste away like a spider.” This is the instruction. What is more fragile than a spider? I mean the creature itself. Yet what is more fragile even than the spiders’ webs? Consider how fragile the creature itself is. Place your finger lightly upon it: it is ruined. Nothing at all is more fragile. “Such,” he says, “you made my soul by instructing me for iniquity.”

When instruction made him weak, a certain strength had been a vice. I see some who have flown ahead and understood; but those who are slower must not be abandoned by the swifter, so that they may travel the road of discourse together. This is what I have said; understand it: if the chastisement of the just God produced this weakness, then a certain strength had been vice. Through a certain strength man displeased God, so that he might be chastised through weakness; through a certain pride he displeased God, so that he might be chastised through humility.

All the proud say that they are strong [Note: [Col. 0427] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “All the proud are said to be strong, the humble weak. Therefore they overcame,” etc.]. Therefore many coming from the east and the west prevailed, so that they might recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Why did they prevail? Because they did not wish to be strong. What does “they did not wish to be strong” mean? They feared presuming upon themselves; they did not establish their own righteousness, so that they might be subjected to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

Finally, when the Lord said, “Many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0427] In the editions, “He also said” was added here; it is absent from the manuscripts.], but “the children of the kingdom”—that is, the Jews, who were ignorant of the righteousness of God [Col. 0428] and wished to establish their own—“will go into the outer darkness,” remember the faith of that centurion, one of the gentile people: so weak in himself, so not strong, that he said, “I am not worthy for you to enter under my roof.” He was not worthy to receive Christ into his house, yet he had already received him into his heart. Indeed, that teacher of humility, the Son of Man, had already found in his breast a place to lay his head.

When the Lord regarded this word of the centurion, he said to those who followed him: “Truly I tell you, I have found no such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:8–12). He found this man weak, and the Israelites strong [Note: [Col. 0428] The manuscripts read: “I found this man weak, I found the Israelites strong.”], so that between the two he might say: “It is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (ibid. 9:12).

For this reason, then—that is, because of this humility—“many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness.” Behold, you are mortal; behold, you carry decaying flesh, and “like one of the princes you will fall”; “like men you will die” (Ps. 81:7), and you will fall like the devil. What benefit does the remedy of mortality provide you? The proud devil, as though he did not possess mortal flesh like an angel; but you, who have received mortal flesh, and yet gain no benefit from being humbled by such great weakness—“like one of the princes you will fall.”

This, then, is the first grace of God’s benefaction: to bring us back to a confession of weakness, so that whatever good we can do, whatever power we possess, may be in him; so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). “When I am weak,” he says, “then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). “For iniquity you instructed man, and you made my soul waste away like a spider.”

19. Nevertheless, “every living man is troubled in vain.” He returns to what he mentioned shortly before: although he makes progress here, “every living man is troubled in vain”—living, of course, in uncertainty. For who is secure even concerning his own good? “He is troubled in vain.” Let him cast his care upon the Lord (Ps. 54:23); let him cast upon him whatever causes him anxiety. Let him nourish; let him guard.

For what is certain in this world except death? Consider every good and evil thing of this life, whether in righteousness itself or in iniquity itself: what is certain here except death? You have made progress: you know what you are today; you do not know what you will be tomorrow. You are a sinner: you know what you are today; you do not know what you will be tomorrow. You hope for money: it is uncertain whether it will come. You hope for a wife: it is uncertain whether you will marry, or what sort of wife you will marry. You hope for children: it is uncertain whether they will be born; they are born, and it is uncertain whether they will live; they live, and it is uncertain whether they will prosper or fail.

Whichever way you turn, everything is uncertain; only death is certain. You are poor: it is uncertain whether you will grow rich. You are unlearned: it is uncertain whether you will be educated. You are weak: it is uncertain whether you will recover. You were born: it is certain that you will die; and even in this—that death itself is certain—the day of death is uncertain. Amid these uncertainties, where death alone is certain, though even its hour is uncertain, and where this alone is greatly feared though it cannot in any way be avoided, “every living man is troubled in vain.”

[Col. 0429] 20. [verse 13.] Therefore, having now leapt across these things, having already acted in certain matters above and despised these lower things, placed amid these circumstances, he says: “Hear my prayer.” What should make me rejoice, and what should make me groan? I rejoice over what has passed; I groan over what remains. “Hear my prayer and my supplication; listen with your ears to my tears.”

Because I have leapt across so much, because I have transcended so much, do I no longer weep? Do I not weep all the more? For “whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). [Note: [Col. 0429] Several manuscripts read: “Do I not all the more desire what is absent…?”] Do I not desire what is absent all the more, and groan all the more until it comes, and weep all the more until it comes? Do I not do so all the more as scandals multiply, as iniquity abounds, and as the love of many grows cold (Matt. 24:12) [Note: [Col. 0429] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions read: “Do I not all the more, as scandals increase, as iniquity abounds, so much more does the love of many grow cold,” etc.]?

I say, “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1). “Hear my prayer and my supplication; listen with your ears to my tears. Do not be silent toward me. Do not let me become deaf forever.”

“Do not be silent toward me”: I shall hear you. For God speaks secretly; he speaks to many in the heart. And there is a great sound in the great silence of the heart [Note: [Col. 0429] Eight manuscripts read: “of the body.”], when he says with a loud voice, “I am your salvation.” “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation’” (Ps. 34:3). From this voice, by which God says to the soul, “I am your salvation,” he desires that God not be silent toward him. “Do not be silent toward me.”

21. “For I am a sojourner with you.” But with whom is he a sojourner? When I was with the devil, I was a sojourner, but I had a bad landlord [Note: [Col. 0429] The editions read dominum, “lord.” Several manuscripts read dominium, “dominion.” But the Vatican and Regius manuscripts more correctly read domnaedium. For domnaedius or dominaedius means “lord of a house,” and domnaedius and inquilinus, “tenant,” are set in opposition to one another. Thus Paulinus of Nola calls the martyr Felix his domnaedius, and in Natalis 7 sings of him:

“For what should I undertake to sing, sooner or more fittingly,

than Felix’s work, which he himself performed for me in my own dwelling,

whose lord of the house he likewise is?”]

But now I am indeed with you, yet still a sojourner. What is a sojourner? A place from which I shall depart, not one in which I shall remain forever. Where I shall remain forever, let that be called my home; from where I shall depart, I am a sojourner [Note: [Col. 0429] The editions read: “From where I shall depart—what sort of person is this, now a great sojourner?” But the manuscripts lack the words “what sort of person is this, now a great.”]. Yet I am a sojourner with my God, with whom, once I have received a home, I shall remain.

But what is the home to which one must migrate from this sojourn? Recall that home of which the Apostle says: “We have a dwelling from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1). If this house is eternal in the heavens, when we have come to it we shall not be sojourners. For how will you be a sojourner in an eternal house?

But here, where the Lord of the house will say, “Move away,” and you do not know when he will say it, be ready. By desiring the eternal home, you will be ready. Nor should you be angry with him because, when he wishes, he says, “Move away.” For he has not made a contract with you, nor bound himself by some agreement, and you have not entered as a tenant of a house at a fixed rent for a fixed period.
