When its Lord wishes, you will move away. That is why you remain here for free.

“For I am a sojourner with you, and a pilgrim.” Therefore, there is the homeland; there is the home. “A sojourner with you, and a pilgrim.” Here “with you” is understood as well. For many are pilgrims with the devil; but those who have now believed and are faithful are indeed pilgrims, because they have not yet reached that homeland and home, yet they are with God. “For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; and we make it our aim, whether remaining here or away from home, to be pleasing to him” (2 Cor. 5:6, 9).

“And a pilgrim, like all my fathers.” If, then, I am like all my fathers, shall I say that I will not depart, when they departed? Shall I remain under a different condition from that under which they remained?

22. [verse 14.] What, then, remains for me to ask, since without doubt I shall depart from here? “Forgive me [Note: [Col. 0430] Erasmus reads dimitte me, “dismiss me.” Lovaniensis reads remitte me, “forgive me.” But the manuscripts read dimitte mihi or remitte mihi, “forgive me.”], so that I may be refreshed before I depart.”

See, see, O Idithun, what knots you have that must be loosened for you, once loosened so that you may be refreshed before you depart. For you have certain heats from which you wish to be cooled, and you say, “Let me be refreshed”; and you say, “Forgive me.” What will he forgive you, except perhaps that scruple where you say, and from which you say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12)?

“Forgive me before I depart, and then I shall be no more.” Make me free from sins before I depart, lest I depart with sins. Forgive me, so that I may rest in my conscience, so that it may be relieved of the heat of anxiety—the anxiety with which I am concerned for my sin. Forgive me so that I may be refreshed, above all before I depart, “and then I shall be no more.”

For if you do not forgive me so that I may be refreshed, I shall go, and I shall not be. “Before I depart”: if I depart, I shall no longer be. “Forgive me so that I may be refreshed.”

A question has arisen: how will he no longer be? Is he not already going to rest? May God avert this from Idithun! Idithun will certainly go; he will go to rest. But suppose someone wicked—not Idithun, not one who leaps across—someone who stores up, hoards, is wicked, proud, boastful, haughty, and contemptuous of the poor man lying before his door. Will he not also exist? What, then, does “I shall not be” mean?

For if that rich man did not exist, who was it that burned? Who was it that desired a drop of water to be dripped from Lazarus’s finger onto his tongue? Who was it that said, “Father Abraham, send Lazarus” (Luke 16:24)? Certainly there was one who spoke, and one who burned; one who will rise at the end, and one who will be condemned with the devil in eternal fire.

What, then, does “I shall not be” mean, unless this Idithun is considering what it means to be and not to be? For he saw that end with whatever heart and acuity of mind he possessed; he desired that end to be shown to him when he said, “Make known to me, Lord, my end.” He saw the number of his days, which is what it is; he considered all things below in comparison with that existence to be nonexistence, and he said that he himself was not.

For those things remain; these are changeable, mortal, fragile. And pain itself, eternal and full of corruption, is not brought to an end in order to end without end. He therefore looked toward that blessed region, that blessed homeland, that blessed home, where the saints share in everlasting life and unchangeable truth [Col. 0431]. And he feared going outside, where there is no existence; desiring to be there where supreme Being is.

Placed, then, between the two in this comparison, and still afraid, he says: “Forgive me, so that I may be refreshed before I depart, and then I shall be no more.” For if you do not forgive my sins, I shall go away from you forever. And from whom shall I go away forever? From the one who said, “I am who I am”; from the one who said, “Say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). From him, therefore, who truly is, the one who goes in the opposite direction proceeds toward nonbeing.

23. Therefore, my brothers, although I have been a burden to your bodily labor, bear with it [Note: [Col. 0431] Thus several manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “be certain that”; and shortly afterward: “you cause us labor.”], because I too have labored. And I say truly: you yourselves cause this labor for yourselves. For if I perceived that you were weary of what is being said, I would quickly be silent.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 39. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Everything that our Lord Jesus Christ foretold we know to have happened in part, and in part we hope will happen. Nevertheless, everything will be fulfilled, because this is what the truth says; and as faithfully as it speaks, so faithfully does it require us to be. Whoever believes will rejoice when these things come; whoever does not believe will be confounded when they come. Yet they will come, whether people wish it or not, whether they believe or do not believe, as the Apostle says: “If we deny him, he too will deny us; if we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (2 Tim. 2:12–13).

Above all, brothers, remember this brief saying, and hold fast to what we have all just heard from the Gospel: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

Already our fathers have been handed over to tribunals. They pleaded their cause before enemies whom they loved; they offered them as much correction as they could and as much love as they were able. And righteous blood was shed; from that blood, as though from seed sown throughout the whole world, the harvest of the Church arose.

The succeeding age is one of scandals, pretence, and temptations, through those who say, “Behold, here is the Christ; behold, there” (ibid. 24:23). That enemy of ours was then a lion, when he raged openly; now he is a dragon, when he lies in ambush secretly. But because the one to whom it was said, “You will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13), is one whose body and members we are, just as he trampled under the feet of our fathers the lion raging openly and dragging martyrs to sufferings, so now let him trample the dragon [Note: [Col. 0431] The editions read: “he will trample.” Almost all the manuscripts read: “let him trample.” Two read: “he tramples.”], lest it lie in wait for us.

Making us cautious of this dragon, the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ; but I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 11:2). This serpent, then, that ancient adulterer, seeks to corrupt virginity—not of the flesh, [Col. 0432] but of the heart.

And just as a human adulterer rejoices in his wickedness when he corrupts the flesh, so the devil rejoices when he corrupts the mind. Just as our fathers needed patience against the lion, so we need vigilance against the dragon.

Nevertheless, persecution against the Church never ceases, whether from the lion or from the dragon; and he is more to be feared when he deceives than when he rages. At that time he compelled Christians to deny Christ; in this age he teaches Christians to deny Christ. Then he compelled; now he teaches. Then he inflicted violence; now he employs snares. Then he was seen roaring; now, slippery and wandering, he is difficult to perceive.

How he compelled Christians to deny Christ then is clear. They were dragged forth to deny Christ, and those who confessed Christ were crowned. Now, however, he teaches them to deny Christ; and for this reason he deceives, because the person taught to deny Christ does not seem to himself to be departing from Christ.

For what do heretics say now to the Catholic Christian [Note: [Col. 0432] Donatists.]? “Come, be a Christian.” Is “Be a Christian” said for this purpose, that he may say, “I am not”? It is one thing to say, “Come, be a Christian”; quite another to say, “Come, deny Christ.” Open evil—the roar of a lion—is heard from far away and avoided from far away. The slippery dragon draws near; the serpent, gliding secretly, creeps forward with a gentle movement, murmuring with a crafty hiss, and does not say, “Deny Christ.” For who would listen to him when martyrs are being crowned? Instead he says, “Be a Christian.”

And the other, struck by a marvelous [Note: [Col. 0432] Seven manuscripts read: “miserable.”] voice, if the poison has not yet penetrated him, replies, “Certainly I am a Christian.” But if he is shaken and has been seized by the dragon’s tooth [Note: [Col. 0432] In several manuscripts: “has been approached.” In some: “has been burned.” In others: “has been worn down.”], he replies, “Why do you say to me, ‘Be a Christian’? What—am I not a Christian?” And the other says, “No.” “Then I am not?” “No.” “Then make me a Christian now, if I am not.” “Come. But when you begin to be questioned by the bishop about who you are [Note: [Col. 0432] The manuscripts read: “what.”], do not say, ‘I am a Christian,’ or ‘I am a believer’; say that you are not, so that you may be able to become one.”

For when he hears the confession “Christian believer,” he does not dare to rebaptize [Note: [Col. 0432] Since the penalties established by imperial laws prohibited the repetition of baptism. See Codex Theodosianus, book 16, title “That Holy Baptism Must Not Be Repeated.”]. But when he hears that the person is not one, he gives him what he supposedly did not possess, so that he himself may seem to be free from guilt because he acts according to the other’s statement.

Here I ask you, heretic: why do you think yourself free from guilt? What is this I hear you say [Note: [Col. 0432] Thus several manuscripts of good quality. The editions read: “What are these words I hear—who is the one who teaches denial, who does this by teaching,” etc.]? “It is not you who deny; he denies.” If the one who denies bears guilt, what of the one who teaches the person who denies to deny? Are you really free from guilt because, by teaching, you do to a Christian what the pagan did by threatening?

And what are you doing? Do you take away what he possesses because he has denied what he possesses? You do not make him not have it; you make him have it unto punishment. What he possesses, he possesses. That baptism is like a seal impressed upon him: it adorned the soldier, and it convicts the deserter.

What are you doing? You place Christ upon Christ. If you were simple, you would not duplicate Christ. Moreover, I ask you: have you forgotten that Christ is the stone, and that “the stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22; Matt. 21:42; 1 Pet. 2:4, 7)? If Christ is the stone, and you wish to place Christ upon Christ, have you forgotten what you heard in the Gospel—that “stone upon stone will not be left” (Matt. 24:2)?

So powerful, however, is the bond of love that, although many living stones come together in the structure of God’s temple, one stone is made from them all. But you have torn yourself away: you call people back from the building and summon them to ruin. These snares abound and do not cease. We see them, endure them, and try to restrain them as far as we can—by arguing, proving, meeting, frightening, yet loving in all things [Note: [Col. 0433] Erasmus and several manuscripts read: “yet loving all.”].

And when, as we do these things, they persist in evil; when our heart wastes away over the deaths of our brothers; when we grieve for those who are outside and fear for those who are inside; amid the manifold and unceasing temptations with which this life abounds, what are we to do? For from the abundance of iniquity there arises a certain torpor of love: “because iniquity has abounded, the love of many grows cold.” And what are we to do except what follows, if we can do so with his help? “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. 12–13).

2. [verses 2, 3.] Let us therefore say what this psalm says: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord.” I waited—not for some human promise-maker who can deceive and be deceived; not for some human comforter who can waste away in his own sorrow before refreshing me.

Let a human brother console me when he is sad with me; let us groan together, weep together, pray together, wait together. But whom should we await except the Lord, who does not withdraw his promises but delays them? He will certainly fulfill them; he will fulfill them, because he has already fulfilled many. And we ought to fear nothing concerning God’s truth [Note: [Col. 0433] The Vatican manuscript and some Gallican manuscripts read: “concerning God’s steadfastness.”], even if he had not yet fulfilled anything.

Suppose now that he promised everything but has not yet given anything: he is an able promiser, a faithful giver. You, meanwhile, be a pious claimant; even if you are little, even if you are weak, demand mercy. Do you not see tender lambs butting their heads against their mothers’ breasts so that they may be satisfied with milk? “Waiting,” he says, “I waited for the Lord.”

And what did he do? Did he turn away from you? Did he despise you as you waited? Or perhaps did he not see you? Certainly not. But what? “He also attended to me and heard my supplication.” He attended and heard. Behold, you did not wait in vain: his eyes are upon you, his ears are turned toward you. “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers.”

What, then, when you were doing evil, when you were blaspheming him—did he not see? Did he not hear? And what of what is said in the same psalm: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil”? Why? “To destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:16–17).

Therefore, even when you were evil, he attended to you, but he did not attend for your benefit. Hence this man who “waiting, waited for the Lord” was not content to say, “He attended to me.” “He attended to me,” he says—that is, he attended by consoling me [Note: [Col. 0434] Several manuscripts read: “by caring for me.” Shortly afterward, most have: “so that what he attended to might benefit me.”]. “And he heard my supplication.”

3. And what did he grant you? What did he do for you? “He brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of mud; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps. And he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God.”

He has granted great blessings, and he is still a debtor. But the one who already possesses these things as payments made should believe concerning the rest—the one who ought to have believed even before receiving anything.

Our Lord has persuaded us by the things themselves that he is a faithful promiser and a generous giver. What, then, has he now done? “He brought me out of the pit of misery.” What is the pit of misery? The depth of iniquity arising from carnal desires. This is also “from the mire of mud.”

From where did he bring you out? From a certain depth. Hence in another psalm you cried out: “From the depths I cried to you, Lord” (Ps. 129:1). And those who already cry out from the depths are not entirely in the depths; the cry itself is already lifting them up. There are others deeper in the depths, who do not even perceive that they are in the depths. Such are proud despisers, not pious petitioners, not tearful criers; they are like those whom Scripture describes elsewhere: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

For if it is not enough for someone to be a sinner, but he is not even a confessor of his sins, rather their defender, he is deeper in the depths. But the one who cried out from the depths has already raised his head from the bottom of the depths so that he might cry out. He was heard; he was brought out of the pit of misery and from the mire of mud.

Now he has faith, which he did not have; he has hope, without which he had been; he walks in Christ, who had been wandering in the devil. Therefore he says: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps.” “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Let us be upon the rock; let our steps be directed. Yet we must still walk, so that we may reach something.

For the Apostle Paul, already upon the rock, with his feet already directed, what did he say? “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it.” What, then, has been granted you, if you have not grasped it? From where do you give thanks when you say, “But I have received mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13)? Because his feet have been directed, because he now walks upon the rock.

For what does he say? “But forgetting what lies behind.” What lies behind? The pit of misery. What is “behind”? The mire of mud, carnal desires, the darkness of iniquities. “Forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what lies ahead.” He would not say that he was reaching if he had already arrived. The mind reaches through desire for the object it longs for, not through the joy of possessing it.

“Reaching toward what lies ahead,” he says, “I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:12–13). He was running; he was pursuing the prize. And elsewhere, already near the prize, he says, “I have finished the course.”

When, therefore, he said, “I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling,” because his feet had already been directed upon the rock and he was already walking along the good way, he had grounds for giving thanks and something for which to ask: giving thanks for what he had received, asking for what was still owed [Note: [Col. 0435] Lovaniensis reads: “asking that debts be forgiven.” The word “forgiven” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts.].

For what had he received? Forgiveness of sins, illumination of faith, strength of hope, and the flame of love. For what, then, did he still hold the Lord as debtor? “From now on,” he says, “there remains for me the crown of righteousness.” Something, then, is still owed me. What is owed? “The crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

First he was the gracious Father, rescuing him from the pit of misery, forgiving sins, and freeing him from the mire of mud; afterward he is the just judge, rendering to the one who walks well what he promised—the one to whom he first granted the ability to walk well. Therefore the just judge will render it. But to whom? “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

4. [verse 4.] “And he put a new song into my mouth.” What new song? “A hymn to our God.” Perhaps you were singing old hymns to foreign gods, because the old man was speaking, not the new man. Let the new man speak; let him sing a new song. Let the renewed man love the new things by which he is renewed.

For what is more ancient than God, who is before all things, without end and without beginning? He becomes new to you when you return to him, because by departing you had become old, and you had said: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8).

“Let us sing,” therefore, “a hymn to our God,” and the hymn itself sets us free. “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies” (Ps. 17:4). For a hymn is a song of praise. Call upon him with praise, not with reproach.

When you call upon God to crush your enemy, when you wish to rejoice over another’s evil and call upon God for that evil, you make him a participant in your wickedness. If you make him a participant in your wickedness, you do not call upon him with praise but with reproach. For you imagine God to be what you are.

Hence elsewhere it is said to you: “You have done these things, and I was silent; you thought that I would be like you in wickedness” (Ps. 49:21) [Note: [Col. 0435] The editions read inique, “wickedly.” The manuscripts read iniquitatem, “wickedness”; the same reading is found in the editions of Psalm 49.].

Call upon the Lord, then, with praise. Do not think him like yourself, so that you may become like him. “Be perfect, therefore, as your Father is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:48, 45).

Praise the Lord in such a way that you do not wish evil upon your enemies. “And how much good,” you ask, “should I wish them?” As much as you wish yourself. They will not receive it from what belongs to you, nor will what is given to them diminish what is given to you. Your enemy, because he is evil, is your enemy; if he becomes good, he will be your friend and your companion, so that you may wish together to possess what you loved. He will already be your brother.

Call upon the Lord with praise; sing a hymn to your God. “The sacrifice of praise,” he says, “will glorify me.” What then? Will God’s glory be greater because you glorify him? Do we add glory to God when we say to him, “I glorify you, my God”? Do we make him holier when we say, “I bless you, my God”?

When he blesses us, he makes us holier and happier; when he glorifies us, he makes us more glorious and more honored. When we glorify him, it benefits us, not him. For how do we glorify him? By declaring him glorious, not by making him so.

Accordingly, what does he add after saying, “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me”? Lest you suppose that by offering a sacrifice of praise you contribute something to God, he says: “And there is the way by which I shall show him my salvation” (Ps. 49:23). You see that praising God will benefit you, not God. Do you praise God? You walk along the way. Do you reproach God? You have lost the way.

5. “And he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God.” Perhaps someone asks whose person speaks in this psalm. I shall answer briefly: it is Christ.

But as you know, brothers, and as must often be said, Christ sometimes speaks from himself, that is, from our Head. For he is the Savior of the body, our Head: the Son of God born of a virgin, who suffered for us, rose again to justify us, sits at the right hand of God to intercede for us, and will render all things in judgment—good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

That one who is our Head deigned to become the Head of the body by taking flesh from us, in which he would die for us. He also raised that flesh for our sake, so that in the flesh of the resurrection he might offer us an example, so that we might learn to hope for what we had despaired of, already have our feet upon the rock, and walk in Christ.

Therefore he sometimes speaks from our Head, and sometimes from us—that is, from his members. For even when he said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35), he was speaking from his members, not from himself. And when he said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), the Head was crying out on behalf of the members. Yet he did not say, “Why are you persecuting my members?” but, “Why are you persecuting me?”

If he suffers in us, we shall also be crowned in him. This is the love of Christ. What can be compared with it? He put a hymn of this reality into our mouth, and he says this from his members.

### 6. “The righteous shall see, and fear, and hope in the Lord.”

“The righteous shall see.” Who are the righteous? The faithful, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17). For this is the order in the Church: some go ahead, others follow; and those who go ahead offer themselves as examples to those who follow, while those who follow imitate those who go ahead. But do even those who offer themselves as examples to those who follow follow no one? If they follow no one, they will go astray. Therefore they too follow someone—Christ himself. For the better members of the Church, those who have no human being left to imitate because by progressing they have surpassed them all, Christ himself remains, and him they follow to the end.

And you see these ranks set in order through the Apostle Paul, who says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:16). [Note: The greater part of the manuscripts reads: “And charity orders these ranks.”] Therefore those who already have their steps directed upon the rock should be a model for the faithful: “Be a model,” he says, “to the faithful” (1 Timothy 4:12). These faithful are the righteous, who look attentively upon those who precede them in goodness and follow by imitating them.

How do they follow? “The righteous shall see, and fear.” They will see and fear to follow evil ways when they see the better already choosing good ways; and they say within themselves—as travelers commonly say when they observe others proceeding confidently along a road while they themselves are still uncertain and wavering about which way to go: “Those people are not going this way without reason, since they are going where we wish to go; and why would they go this way with such confidence unless it were dangerous to go that way?” Thus the righteous shall see, and fear.

They see a narrow way here and a broad way there; here they see few, there many (Matthew 7:13–14). But if you are righteous, do not count; weigh. Bring a true, not a deceptive, balance, because you have been called righteous: “The righteous shall see, and fear” was said about you. Do not therefore count the crowds of people traveling the broad ways, filling the circus tomorrow, celebrating the city’s birthday with shouting, and disgracing that very city by their evil living. Do not look to them. They are many—and who can count them? But there are few along the narrow way.

Bring out the balance, I say; weigh them. See how much chaff you lift against a few grains. Let the faithful righteous who follow do this.

What of those who go ahead? [Note: Thus most manuscripts; the editions read: “Let the faithful righteous who follow do what those [who go ahead do],” etc.] Let them not become proud, exalt themselves, or deceive those who follow. How can they deceive those who follow? By promising them salvation in themselves.

What, then, ought those who follow to do? “The righteous shall see, and fear, and hope in the Lord”—not in those whom they follow. They look to those who precede them, and indeed follow and imitate them; but because they consider from whom those leaders received the ability to go ahead, they hope in him. Although they imitate these people, they nevertheless place their hope in the one from whom these too received what makes them such.

“The righteous shall see, and fear, and hope in the Lord.” So also in another psalm: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.” By “mountains” we understand the illustrious and great spiritual men of the Church—great in steadfastness, not in self-exaltation. Through them the whole of Scripture has been dispensed to us: they are the prophets, the evangelists, the good teachers. “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me.” And lest you think that the help is human, he continues and says: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 120:1–2).

“The righteous shall see, and fear, and hope in the Lord.”

### 7. [verse 5]

Come now, you who wish to hope in the Lord, who see and fear: fear to walk along evil ways, the broad ways; choose the narrow way, where the steps of certain people have already been directed upon the rock. Hear now what you ought to do:

“Blessed is the man whose hope is in the name of the Lord, and who has not looked upon vanities and deceitful insanities.”

Look: this is where you wished to go; look: here is the crowd of the broad way. It does not lead to the amphitheater without reason; it does not lead to death without reason. The broad way is deadly: its breadth delights for a time, but its end is narrow forever.

Yet the crowds make a din; the crowds hurry; the crowds rejoice; the crowds rush together. [Note: Thus several manuscripts; the editions read “struggle together.”] Do not imitate them; do not turn aside. They are vanities and deceitful insanities.

Let the Lord your God be your hope. Do not hope for something else from the Lord your God; let the Lord himself be your hope. For many hope from God for money; many hope from God for honors that are fleeting and perishable—for anything whatever from God besides God himself. But you, seek God himself; indeed, rejecting other things, proceed toward him; forgetting other things, remember him; leaving other things behind, stretch yourself toward him.

He himself corrected the one who had turned away; he himself leads the one who is upright; he himself brings him to the destination. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “He corrects the one who has turned away; he himself leads the corrected one.”] Therefore let him himself be your hope, the one who leads and brings you to the end.

Where does earthly greed lead, and where does it bring you? You were seeking estates, wishing to possess land, excluding your neighbors; once they had been excluded, you yearned for other neighbors; and you stretched out your greed for so long, until you reached the shores. [Note: Lovaniensis reads “extended”; several manuscripts, “stretched out”; others, with the editions of Am. and Er., “held.”] Having reached the shores, you desire islands; having possessed the earth, perhaps you wish to seize heaven. Abandon every love: more beautiful is the one who made heaven and earth.

### 8.

“Blessed is the man whose hope is in the name of the Lord, and who has not looked upon vanities and deceitful insanities.”

Whence, then, are deceitful insanities? Insanity is deceitful; health is true. You see things and think them good—but you are deceived. [Note: All the manuscripts lack the word “think.”] You are not healthy; you have become delirious with an excessive fever. What you love is not true.

You praise the charioteer, shout for the charioteer, rave over the charioteer. [Note: An *auriga* was the person who drove and managed racing horses in the Circus. Canons 4 of the First Council of Arles and 20 of the Eleventh Council of Arles concern charioteers, or—what is the same—drivers.] It is vanity; it is a deceitful insanity. “There is nothing better,” he says; “nothing more delightful.” What am I to do with a feverish person? If you have compassion among you, pray for such people.

For even the physician himself, often driven to despair, turns to those who stand around weeping in the house, hanging upon his words to hear his judgment about the sick and endangered person. The physician stands uncertain: he sees no good prospect to promise, yet fears to pronounce the evil lest he terrify them. So he forms a restrained judgment: “God is good; he can do everything. Pray for him.”

Whom, then, shall I reach among these mad people? Who will listen to me? Which of them will not call us miserable? Because when we do not rave with them, they think we have lost the great and varied pleasures in which they themselves rave—and they do not see that these pleasures are deceitful.

When I give him an egg or invite him to eat, or offer a saving cup to a wounded man, how shall I restore him when I find him? So that he may not waste away from hunger and fail to reach health, I urge him to take refreshment. [Note: Er. reads: “When I invite him to an egg, or offer a saving cup to a wounded man, how shall I restore him? What do I find, lest he waste away from hunger and reach health? I urge,” etc. Three manuscripts read: “When I give him an egg or invite him, he wounds himself with a saving cup; how shall I restore him? When I find him,” etc. Vaticanus and Colbertinus read: “When I give him or invite him to a cup of saving *sueci* [uncertain reading], and how shall I restore him,” etc. Some others read: “When I ask or invite him to receive a saving cup.” Some: “How, when I give him wine,” etc.] He prepares his fists and wishes to rage against the physician. Yet if he strikes him, let him be loved; if he commits an outrage, let him not be abandoned: he will return to his senses and give thanks.

How many people here recognize themselves, see one another, and speak about one another in the Church of God? In the womb of the holy Church they observe their own now-good pursuits regarding the word of God, regarding the duties and services of charity, regarding frequenting Christ’s flock and not withdrawing from the Church. They see one another and speak to one another about one another.

Who is this circus-goer? Who is this lover and praiser of that hunter, of that actor? [Note: Here a *venator* is one who fought with beasts in the arena.] One speaks about another, and the other about him. Certainly these things happen; certainly we rejoice over such people. If we rejoice over such people, let us not despair of such people. Let us pray for them, dearest brothers: from the number that was impious, the number of the saints grows.

“And who has not looked upon vanities and deceitful insanities.”

That man has won, has harnessed such a horse, and makes pronouncements, as though he wishes to be divine. [Note: Thus Codex Colbertinus, and several manuscripts come close to this reading. The editions read: “That man defeats such a one, and when he conquers, he makes a pronouncement.”] He strives after divinity by losing the source of divinity; he often announces the result, and often is deceived. Why is this? Because these are deceitful insanities.

Why, then, do the things they say sometimes come to pass? So that they may lead the insane astray: by loving the appearance of truth there, they fall into the snare of falsehood. Let them be left behind; let them be abandoned; let them be cut off. If they were our members, let them be put to death: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5).

Let our hope be our God. He who made all things is better than all; he who made beautiful things is more beautiful than all; he who made strong things is stronger; he who made great things is greater. Whatever you love, he will be that for you. Learn to love the creator in the creature, and the maker in what has been made, lest what was made by him hold you fast and you lose him by whom it too was made.

Therefore:

“Blessed is the man whose hope is in the name of the Lord, and who has not looked upon vanities and deceitful insanities.”

### 9. [verses 6–9]

Perhaps the person who has been struck by this verse and wishes to be corrected, the person whom that fear of the justice of faith has seized and who has begun to wish to walk along the narrow way, will say to us: “I shall not endure walking if I look at nothing.”

What, then, shall we do, brothers? Shall we send him away without a spectacle? He will die; he will not persist; he will not follow us. What shall we do? Let us provide spectacles in place of spectacles.

And what spectacles shall we give to a Christian whom we wish to recall from those spectacles? I give thanks to the Lord our God: the following verse of the psalm shows us what spectacles we ought to provide and display to spectators who wish to watch spectacles.

Look: he has turned away from the circus, the theater, and the amphitheater. He seeks something to watch—he certainly seeks it; we do not leave him without a spectacle. What shall we give him in place of those things? Listen to what follows:

“You have done many things, O Lord my God; your wonders are many.”

He used to gaze upon human marvels; let him attend to God’s wonders. The Lord has done many wonders of his own; let him look upon these.

Why did those other things seem worthless to him? He praises a charioteer who drives four horses running without blemish or mishap. Perhaps the Lord has not performed such spiritual wonders? Let him rule lust, let him rule laziness, let him rule injustice, let him rule folly; let him rule and subject to himself those impulses that, having fallen too far, produce these vices. Let him hold the reins and not be carried away; let him lead where he wills, not be dragged where he does not will.

He praised a charioteer; the charioteer will be praised. He shouted that the charioteer should be covered with a garment; he himself will be clothed with immortality. These are the gifts, these are the spectacles that God stages. [Note: The editions read “gave”; most manuscripts read “stages,” or “has staged.”] He cries out from heaven: “I am watching you; struggle, and I shall help; conquer, and I shall crown.”

“You have done many things, O Lord my God; and there is no one like you in your thoughts.”

Now watch the actor. A man has learned, with great effort, to walk on a rope, and, hanging there, he suspends you in suspense. Attend to the provider of greater spectacles. This man has learned to walk on a rope. Did he walk upon the sea? Forget your theater; attend to our Peter—not a rope-walker but, so to speak, a sea-walker.

You too, walk—not upon those waters on which Peter walked as a sign of something, but upon other waters, because this world is a sea. It has a harmful bitterness; it has waves of tribulations and storms of temptations; it has people like fish, rejoicing in their own misfortune and, as it were, devouring one another. Walk here; tread upon this.

Do you wish to watch? Become a spectacle. Do not falter; look upon the one who goes before you and says: “We have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Corinthians 4:9). Tread upon the sea, lest you be submerged in the sea.

You will not go, you will not tread upon it, unless the one who first walked upon the sea commands it. Thus Peter says: “If it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” And because it was he, he heard the petitioner, granted the desire, called the walker, and raised the one who was sinking (Matthew 14:28–31).

These are the wonders that the Lord has done; look upon them. Let the eye of the spectator be faith. And do such things yourself. For even if the winds disturb you, even if the waves roar, and human frailty brings you to some doubt about your salvation, you can cry out; you say: “Lord, I am perishing.” [Note: Most manuscripts read “a cry.”] He will not allow the one to perish whom he commanded to walk.

Since you are already walking upon the rock, you do not fear the sea. If you are without the rock, you will be submerged in the sea, because one must walk upon such a rock as has not been submerged in the sea.

### 10.

See the wonders of God.

“I announced and spoke; they have multiplied beyond number.”

There is a number, and there are those beyond number. The number is fixed, belonging to that heavenly Jerusalem. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19): Christians who fear, Christians who are faithful, Christians who keep the commandments, who walk in the ways of God, who abstain from sins, and, if they fall, confess them—these belong to the number.

But are they alone? There are also those beyond number. For even if they are few now, they are few in comparison with the crowds of the larger gatherings. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “evil gatherings.”] How large are the crowds that fill the churches, pack the walls, press upon one another, and almost suffocate one another by their multitude! Yet again, when there is a public entertainment, they themselves run to the amphitheater. [Note: The editions read “if it is less”; the manuscripts read “if there is a *munus*,” that is, if games are being staged.] These are beyond number.

But we say these things so that they may be in the number, because they are not present and do not hear us; but when you go out, let them hear from you.

“I announced and spoke,” he says. Christ speaks: he announced from our head; he announced from his members; he sent those who announce; he sent the apostles. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

How many faithful are gathered together; how many crowds run together—many truly converted, many falsely converted. Those truly converted are fewer; those falsely converted are more, because “they have multiplied beyond number.”

### 11.

“I announced and spoke; they have multiplied beyond number.”

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire.”

These are the wonders of God; these are the thoughts of God, to which no one is equal: that the spectator may be led away from curiosity and seek with us better and more fruitful things, [Note: Almost all the manuscripts read “may be led toward curiosity.”] things whose discovery will make him rejoice. And he will rejoice in such a way that he does not fear that the one he loves may be defeated. For he loves the charioteer, and when the charioteer is defeated, he suffers taunts.

When the charioteer wins, he himself is clothed. Is the poor man who shouts for him clothed? The victor himself is clothed, while the defeated man is taunted. Why do you receive reproach on his behalf when you do not share his garment?

There is something different in our spectacles. Everyone runs, the Apostle Paul said, in that race, in that spectacle; yet one receives the prize, while the others depart defeated (1 Corinthians 9:24). They persevered in running, but when one has received the prize, the others who labored in the same way remain behind.

Here it is not so. As many as run, let them run perseveringly; all receive the prize. And the one who arrives first waits to be crowned together with the one who arrives later. For it is not desire, but love, that creates this contest. All who run love one another, and love itself is the running.

### 12.

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,” the psalm says to God.

In ancient times, while the true sacrifice that the faithful know was still being foretold in figures, they celebrated figures of the future reality—many understanding, but more remaining ignorant. For the prophets and holy patriarchs knew what they were celebrating; but the rest of the wicked multitude was so carnal that what would signify the things later to come was brought forth from it.

And he came, once that first sacrifice had been removed—once the holocausts of rams, goats, calves, and the other victims had been taken away; God did not desire those things. [Note: Three manuscripts read: “Behold, truth came, once … had been removed,” etc.]

Why did he not desire them? Why had he desired them at first? Because all those things were, as it were, the words of one making a promise. And when what the words promise has come, the promissory words are no longer spoken. A promisor remains a promisor only until he gives; when he has given, he changes his words. He no longer says, “I shall give,” which he had said he would give; rather, he says, “I have given.” He has changed the word.

Why, then, did that word first please him, and why did he change it? Because it was the word of its own time, and it pleased in accordance with its time. When the promise was being made, that was what was said; but when what had been promised was given, the promissory words were removed and words of fulfillment were given.

Those sacrifices, therefore, were removed like promissory words. What is the thing given in fulfillment? The body that you know—which not all of you know. [Note: By this manner of speaking he indicates the catechumens who were present.] Would that all who know it might not know it unto judgment.

See when this was said. For that Christ is our Lord, now speaking from his members, now speaking in his own person:

“Sacrifice and offering,” he says, “you did not desire.” What, then? Have we at this time been dismissed without a sacrifice? God forbid.

“But you perfected a body for me.” Therefore you did not desire those things in order to perfect this; you desired those things before you perfected this. The fulfillment of the promises removed the words that promised. For if the promissory words still remain, what was promised has not yet been fulfilled.

This was promised through certain signs. The promissory signs were removed because the promised reality had been presented. We are in this body; we are participants in this body, which we know we receive. And those of you who do not know it, learn to know it; and when you have learned, may you not receive it unto judgment. For “whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

The body has been perfected for us; let us be perfected in the body.

### 13.

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you perfected a body for me. You did not even ask for holocausts for sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’” [Note: Some manuscripts read “which you formerly asked for”; others, “and which were formerly asked for.”]

Need it be explained: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you perfected a body for me. You did not even ask for holocausts for sin”—the things you had previously asked for? “Then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’”

The time has come for the things that were promised to arrive, because the things through which they were promised are being removed.

And truly, my brothers, observe: those things have been removed, these have been fulfilled. Let the Jewish people now provide me with a priest. Where are their sacrifices? Surely they have perished; surely they have now been removed.

Would we then have rejected them at that time? We reject them now, because if you wish to perform them now, it is out of season, inappropriate, and unsuitable. You are still making a promise, while I have already received it.

Something has remained for them to celebrate, lest they remain altogether without a sign. For Cain, the elder brother who killed his younger brother, received a sign so that no one would kill him, as it is written in Genesis: “God placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one would kill him.”

Accordingly, the Jewish people also remain with their sign—with the sign of circumcision and the sign of unleavened bread. All nations, subject to Roman law, flowed into Roman jurisdiction and shared their superstitions; afterward they began, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to separate themselves from it. But that people remained thus with its own sign. [Note: The editions read: “remains among all nations, subject to Roman law. Into Roman jurisdiction,” etc. The passage has been corrected from the manuscripts.] Thus they remain. Cain was not killed; he was not killed; he has his sign.

He is accursed by the earth that opened its mouth to receive his brother’s blood from his hand. For he shed the blood; he did not receive it. He shed it, and another earth received it. And by that earth which opened its mouth and received it, he was cursed. That very earth which received the blood with its mouth is the Church.

By this earth, therefore, he was cursed. “And that blood cries out from the earth to me.” For concerning this earth the Lord said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth” (Genesis 4:10).

“It cries out,” he says, “to me from the earth.” It cries out to the Lord; but the one who shed the blood is deaf, because he does not drink it. [Note: Lovaniensis reads “because he does not live.” Er. and several manuscripts read “because he does not drink”; other manuscripts, “which he does not drink.”]

They are therefore like Cain, with his sign. The sacrifices that were performed there have been removed; and what has remained for them as Cain’s sign has already been fulfilled, though they do not know it.

They kill the lamb; they eat unleavened bread. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Behold, I recognize the slaughtered lamb, because Christ has been sacrificed.

What of the unleavened bread? “Therefore,” he says, “let us celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness.” He shows what “old” means: old flour, which has become sour. [Note: The editions read “what old leaven means”; the word “leaven” is absent from the manuscripts.] “But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).

They remained in the shadow; they cannot bear the sun of glory. We are now in the light; we hold the body of Christ; we hold the blood of Christ. If we have new life, let us sing a new song, a hymn to our God.

“You did not ask for holocausts for sin; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’”

### 14.

“At the beginning of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will: my God, I desired it, and your law is in the midst of my heart.”

Behold, he looked to the members; behold, he himself did the will of the Father. But at what beginning of the book was this written concerning him? Perhaps at the beginning of this book of the Psalms. Why should we seek far away, or search other books?

Behold, at the beginning of this book of the Psalms it is written:

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the impious, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence, but whose will was in the law of the Lord”—that is, “My God, I desired it, and your law is in the midst of my heart”—that is, “and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:1–2).

### 15. [verse 10]

“I have well proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church.”

He addresses his members and urges them to do what he has done. He announced; let us announce. He suffered; let us suffer with him. He was glorified; we shall be glorified with him.

“I have well proclaimed your righteousness in the great Church.” How great? Throughout the whole world. How great? Among all nations.

Why among all nations? Because he is the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations will be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). Why among all nations? Because “their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm 18:5).

“In the great Church.”

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips; Lord, you have known.”

My lips speak; I shall not restrain them from speaking. My lips certainly sound in human ears, but you have known my heart.

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips; Lord, you have known.”

A human being hears one thing; God recognizes another. Let the proclamation not be only on our lips, so that it may be said of us: “Do and observe everything they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3). Or let it not be said of the people who praise God with their mouth but not with their heart: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13).

Let what is on the lips sound forth from a heart that is near. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

What sort of man was that thief who was found hanging on the cross with the Lord, recognizing the Lord upon the cross? Others did not recognize him performing miracles; he recognized him hanging upon the wood.

He was fastened with all his limbs: his hands clung to the nails, his feet were pierced, his whole body was attached to the wood. That body was not free for its other members; the tongue and heart were free. With the heart he believed; with the mouth he confessed:

“Remember me,” he said, “Lord, when you come into your kingdom.”

He hoped for his salvation far in the future and was content to receive it after a long time. He hoped for it in the distant future, but the day was not delayed.

He said: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

The Lord replied: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

“Today,” he said, “you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). Paradise has blessed trees: today with me upon the tree of the cross; today with me upon the tree of salvation.

### 16.

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips; Lord, you have known.”

Let no one believe with his heart and, through fear, restrain his lips from announcing what he has believed. For there are Christians who have faith in their hearts, but who, among bitter pagans—wretched townspeople, filthy, faithless, foolish, and insulting—if they begin to be harassed because they are Christians, [Note: The manuscripts read “and if”; shortly afterward, where the editions have “bitterly wretched,” some read “love is to mingle,” and others “love is to mingle oneself.”] have faith in their hearts but fear to confess it with their lips. They restrain their lips from uttering what they know, from uttering what they have within.

But the Lord rebukes such people: “Whoever is ashamed of me before human beings, I shall be ashamed of him before my Father” (Mark 8:38); that is, “I shall not acknowledge him.” Because he was ashamed to confess me before human beings, I shall not confess him before my Father.

Let their lips therefore say what their heart possesses: this is against fear. Let the heart possess what their lips say: this is against hypocrisy. [Note: The editions read: “Let the heart possess, against fear, what the lips say; let the lips possess, against pretence, what the heart believes.” A faulty punctuation and an unsuitable gloss at the end impaired the sense; these have been removed on the authority of the better manuscripts.] Sometimes there is fear, and you do not dare to say what you know and believe. Sometimes there is hypocrisy: you say it, but you do not have it in your heart.

Let your lips agree with your heart. In seeking peace from God, be at peace with yourself; let there be no evil quarrel between your mouth and your heart. [Note: The word “between” is absent from all the manuscripts.]

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips; Lord, you have known.”

How did that man act? What has the Lord known? What is inside, in the heart, where a human being does not see.

Therefore that man too says: “I believed.” Behold, he has a heart; he already possesses what God sees. Let him not restrain his lips. He does not restrain them. What does he say? “Therefore I spoke.”

And because he spoke what he believed, asking what he might render to the Lord for all that he had rendered to him, he adds: “I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.”

Did he shrink from the Lord’s saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:22)? He confesses through his lips what he had in his heart; he reached suffering.

And because he reached suffering, what harm did the enemy do? “Indeed, precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15).

In those deaths at which the pagans raged, we are today refreshed. [Note: Codex Colbertinus reads “we are today perfected.”] We celebrate the birthdays of the martyrs; we set the examples of the martyrs before ourselves. We observe their faith: how they were found, how they were seized, how they stood before judges.

In the Catholic Church, possessing no hypocrisy, joined together by the bond of unity, they confessed Christ. They desired to follow, as members, the head who had gone before them.

But who were those who desired this? [Note: This question is absent in some manuscripts.] Patient in torments, faithful in confession, truthful in speech. For they hurled God’s arrows into the faces of those questioning them and wounded them unto anger; they wounded many unto salvation.

We set all these things before ourselves; we look upon them and desire to imitate them. These are Christian spectacles. God looks down upon them; he exhorts to these contests and helps in them; for these struggles he sets forth and grants rewards.

“Behold, I shall not restrain my lips.”

See that you do not fear and restrain your lips.

“Lord, you have known,” because what sounds forth is also in the heart and on the lips.

### 17. [verse 11]

“I did not hide my righteousness in my heart.”

What is “my righteousness”? My faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17).

Suppose that a persecutor, under threat of punishment—as they were once permitted to do—asks: “What are you? A pagan or a Christian?”

“Christian.”

That is his righteousness: he believed and lives by faith.

He did not hide his righteousness in his heart. He did not say to himself: “I do indeed believe in Christ, but I shall not tell this savage and threatening persecutor what I have believed. My God knows within my heart that I believe; he knows that I do not renounce him.”

Behold, you say that you have this within your heart. What is on your lips? “I am not a Christian.”

Your lips testify against your heart.

“I did not hide my righteousness in my heart.”

### 18.

“I declared your truth and your salvation.”

“I declared your Christ”—that is, “I declared your truth and your salvation.”

How is Christ the truth? “I am the truth” (John 14:6).

How is Christ his salvation? Simeon recognized the infant in his mother’s hands in the temple and said: “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30).

The old man recognized the infant; having become a child in the Child, he was renewed through faith. For he had received a response, and he said this: the Lord had told him that he would not depart from this life before he had seen the salvation of God.

This salvation of God is good so that it may be shown to human beings. But let them cry out: “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Psalm 84:8).

The salvation of God, however, is among all nations. For when he had said in one place, “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he shine his face upon us, so that we may know your way upon earth,” he added: “Your salvation among all nations.”

First he said: “So that we may know your way upon earth”; and he continued: “Your salvation among all nations” (Psalm 66:2–3).

It is as though he were asked: “What is the way that you desire to know?” Human beings come to the way; surely the way does not come to human beings?

Our way came to human beings. It found those who were wandering and called those who were walking outside to itself: [Note: Several manuscripts read: “called to itself. You walk outside; walk in me.”] “Walk in me,” he says, “and you will not go astray. I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Do not say: “Where is the way of God? To what region shall I go? What mountain shall I climb? What plains shall I seek?”

You seek the way of God? The salvation of God is the way of God, and it is everywhere: “Your salvation among all nations.”

“I declared your truth and your salvation.”

### 19.

“I did not conceal your mercy and your truth from the great assembly.”

Let us be there; let us also be counted in this body. Let us not conceal the mercy of the Lord and the truth of the Lord.

Do you wish to hear the mercy of the Lord? Turn away from sins; he will forgive sins.

Do you wish to hear the truth of the Lord? Hold fast to righteousness; righteousness will be crowned.

Now the mercy of God is proclaimed to you; afterward the truth will be manifested. For God is not merciful in such a way that he is unjust, nor just in such a way that he is not merciful.

Is his mercy a small thing to you? He will not reckon your former sins against you. [Note: Several manuscripts read “did not reckon”; and below, instead of “do not conceal,” “you will not conceal.”] You lived badly up to this very day; you are still alive. Live well today; do not conceal this mercy.

If this is mercy, what is truth? “All nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left.”

What will he say to the sheep? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you.”

What to the goats? “Go into eternal fire” (Matthew 25:32, 34, 41).

There is no place for repentance there. Because you despised the mercy of God, you will experience his truth. But if you did not despise his mercy, you will rejoice in his truth.

20. [Verses 12–14.] But you, O Lord, do not withdraw your mercies from me. He looked upon the wounded members [Note: [Col. 0446] The editions read “his wounded members”; “his” is absent from the manuscripts.] Because I did not conceal your mercy and your truth from the great congregation, from the Church of the unity of the whole world: look upon the wounded members; look upon the delinquents and sinners, and do not remove your mercies. Your mercy and your truth have always received me. I would not dare to turn back unless I were confident of forgiveness; I would not endure to persevere unless I were confident of your promise. Your mercy and your truth have always received me.

I consider that you are good; I consider that you are just. I love the good, I fear the just. Love and fear lead me onward, because your mercy and your truth have always received me. Why do they themselves receive me, and why must the eye not be turned away from them? Because evils without number have surrounded me. Who can count sins? Who can count the iniquities of others and of oneself? Beneath what a heap groaned the man who said: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13–14). Our own faults were small; the faults of others are laid upon us. I fear for myself; I fear for the good brother; I tolerate the evil brother. And beneath this heap, what shall become of us if God’s mercy should cease?

But you, O Lord, do not withdraw yourself: be near. To whom is the Lord near? To those who have crushed their heart (Ps. 34:19). He is far from the proud and near to the humble. For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly. But let the proud not suppose that they can hide: “he knows the exalted from afar” (Ps. 138:6). He knew from afar the Pharisee boasting of himself; from nearby he came to the aid of the Publican confessing his sins (Luke 18:11). The one boasted of his merits and concealed his wounds; the other did not boast of merits but offered his wounds. He had come to the physician; he knew that he was sick and knew that he needed healing. He did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven; he beat his breast. He did not spare himself, so that the physician might spare him; he acknowledged himself, so that the physician might forgive him; he punished himself, so that the physician might set him free.

These are the voices heard here. Let us hear them devoutly, and love them devoutly. With heart, tongue, and all the marrow of our being, let us speak these words. Let no one consider himself righteous. The one who speaks is alive—alive, and may he live! He still lives here; he still lives together with death. And although the spirit is life because of righteousness, the body nevertheless is dead because of sin (Rom. 8:10). “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). It therefore belongs to you to cry out, to groan, to confess—not to exalt yourself, not to boast, not to glory in your merits. For even if you have something in which to rejoice, “what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). For evils without number have surrounded me.

21. “My iniquities have seized me, and I was unable to see.” There is something for us to see; what weighs us down so that we cannot see? Is it not iniquity? Perhaps a rushing humor weighed upon your eye, preventing you from seeing that light; perhaps smoke, dust, or something thrown into it pressed upon it, and you could not raise your wounded eye toward that light. What, then, will you raise your wounded heart toward God? Must it not first be healed so that you may see?

Are you not found to be proud when you say, “First I shall see, and then I shall believe”? Who says this? For who, if he is going to see, says, “I shall see, and then I shall believe”? I am going to show you the light—or rather, the light itself wishes to show itself. To whom? It cannot show itself to the blind; he does not see. Why does he not see? Because his eye is weighed down by many sins. What does he say? “My iniquities have seized me, and I was unable to see.”

Let iniquities therefore be removed; let sins be forgiven; let the weight be lifted from the eye; let what is wounded be healed; let a biting commandment be applied like an eye-salve. First do what is commanded you: heal your heart, cleanse your heart, love your enemy (Matt. 5:44; Luke 6:27, 35). And who loves his enemy? The physician commands this. It is bitter, but health-giving. “What shall I do for you?” he says. “You are so afflicted that you may be healed from it.” And he says more: “Once healed, it will not be burdensome; when healed, you will love your enemy with delight. Strive to be healed. In tribulations, hardships, and temptations, be strong; persevere. It is the hand of a physician, not of a robber.”

“Behold,” he says, “having received the commandments and retained faith, first, as you command, I shall heal my heart. When my heart has been healed and cleansed, what shall I see?” “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). “I cannot do this yet,” he says. “My iniquities have seized me, and I was unable to see.”

22. “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” He refers to the hairs of the head to indicate an immense number. Who counts the hairs of his head? Much less can one count sins, which exceed the number of hairs. They seem insignificant, but they are numerous. You have guarded against great sins: you no longer commit adultery, no longer commit murder, do not seize another’s property, do not blaspheme, do not bear false witness. These are the great masses of sin. You have guarded against great sins; what are you doing about the small ones? Do you not fear the small ones? You have thrown off the great mass; take care lest you be buried beneath the sand. “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.”

23. [Verse 14.] “And my heart has forsaken me.” What wonder is it if your heart has been abandoned by your God, when it has abandoned itself? What does “my heart has forsaken me” mean? My heart is not competent to know itself. This is what he said: “My heart has forsaken me.” With my heart I want to see the Lord, and I cannot, because of the multitude of my sins. It is not enough: my heart does not even comprehend itself. For no one comprehends himself; no one should presume upon himself [Note: [Col. 0448] Thus several manuscripts. The editions read: “It is not enough that my heart should comprehend itself. For no one comprehends himself; no one presumes upon himself.”].

Did Peter comprehend his own heart, when he said, “I will remain with you even unto death” (Matt. 26:35)? In his heart there was false presumption; in his heart true fear lay hidden. His heart was not competent to comprehend his heart. The sick heart was hidden, but it was open to the physician. What had been pronounced concerning him was fulfilled. God knew in him what he himself did not know, because his heart had abandoned him; his heart concealed his heart.

“And my heart has forsaken me.” What then? What do we cry out? What do we say? “May it please you, Lord, to rescue me”—as though he were saying, “If you are willing, you can cleanse me” (Matt. 8:2). “May it please you to rescue me, Lord; look upon me to help me.” These are members of repentance [Note: [Col. 0448] The editions read “members of repentance.” Several manuscripts read “repentance”; others, “in repentance.”], members laid in pain, members crying out beneath the physician’s instruments, yet hoping. “Lord, look upon me to help me.”

24. [Verses 15–17.] “Let those who seek my soul to take it away be put to shame and confounded together.” In another place he accuses them and says, “I looked to the right, and I saw, and there was no one who sought my soul” (Ps. 142:5)—that is, there was no one who imitated me. Christ speaks in his Passion: “I looked to the right,” that is, not toward the impious Jews, but toward the right itself, toward the Apostles themselves; “and there was no one who sought my soul.” So completely was there no one who sought his soul that the one who had presumed upon himself denied his soul (Matt. 26:70).

But since a person is sought in two ways—either for one’s enjoyment or for one’s persecution—he therefore speaks here of others whom he wishes to be put to shame and confounded, those who seek his soul. But lest you understand it in the same way as when he complains about some who do not seek his soul [Note: [Col. 0448] The editions read: “as when he complains about some who seek his soul in order to take it away—that is, and so forth.” On the authority of several manuscripts, we restore the particle “not” and the verb “he says.”], he adds, “to take it away,” that is, “they seek my soul for death.” He then adds, “Let them be put to shame and confounded.”

And indeed many sought his soul, and were put to shame and confounded. They sought his soul and, as it seemed to them, took it away. But he had authority to lay down his soul, and authority to take it up again (John 10:18). Therefore they rejoiced when he laid it down; they were confounded when he took it up again. “Let those who seek my soul to take it away be put to shame and confounded together.”

25. “Let those who desire evil for me turn backward and be confounded.” “Let them turn backward”: let us not take this in an evil sense either. He wishes them well; and it is the voice of the one who said from the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Why, then, does he tell them to return backward? Because those who were formerly proud fell backward and became humble, so that they might rise again. When they are in front, they wish to precede the Lord; they wish to be better than the Lord. But if they are behind, they acknowledge him as better and first, themselves as later, so that he may lead and they may follow.

For this reason he rebuked Peter when Peter gave him bad advice. The Lord was about to suffer for our salvation, and he was preaching what was going to happen concerning that Passion [Note: [Col. 0449] Thus some manuscripts. The editions read “was.”]. Peter said, “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be favorable to you; this shall certainly not happen.” He wished to precede the Lord and give advice to his teacher. But the Lord, so as not to make him one who preceded, but one who followed, said, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16:22–23). “Satan,” he says, “because you wish to go before the one whom you ought to follow. But if you remain behind and follow, you will no longer be Satan.” What then? “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (ibid., 18).

26. “Let those who desire evil for me turn backward and be confounded.” They are malevolent who, even when they bless, curse as far as their hearts are concerned. You say to someone, “Be a Christian.” “Be a Christian—but you too” [Note: [Col. 0449] Thus the manuscripts; it is not inappropriate if “and he says” is understood here. The Louvain edition instead reads: “Someone says to another, ‘Be a Christian, and may you too be a Christian.’ Good is what he said, but …”].

He said a good thing, but what he said is not credited to him; rather, the intention with which he said it is credited to him. So it was also charged against the Jews when the man born blind became one who saw. When they pressed him with insults and harassed him, he said to them, “Do you too wish to become his disciples?” And they cursed him. This is what the Evangelist says: “They cursed him, saying, ‘You be his disciple’” (John 9:27–28). While they cursed, the Lord blessed. He did what they said, but repaid them according to the curse they uttered.

“Let those who desire evil for me turn backward and be confounded.” But there are other people who are not good, who wish us good, and they too must be avoided. For just as those people curse and call our things good, but with an evil intention, so many call our things evil with a good intention.

This is what I mean: whoever says to you, “You be a Christian,” calls your good by an evil intention. But whoever says to you, “No one is better than you in evil deeds”—since “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who practices iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 10:3)—calls your evil good by praising it.

Just as the other called your good evil by cursing, so this one calls your evil good by blessing. Flee and beware of both kinds of enemy. The one rages; the other flatters. Both are evil. The one is angry; the other is sly in praise. The one is a critic; the other a praiser. Yet the one is an enemy in his criticism, and the other is sly in his praise. Beware of both; pray against both.

For the one who prayed, “Let those who desire evil for me turn backward and be confounded,” was looking toward another kind of slyly malevolent and falsely blessing person: “Let them immediately bear their confusion who say to me, ‘Good, good.’” They praise falsely [Note: [Col. 0450] Most manuscripts read “falsely” in the feminine form.]: “A great man, a good man, a learned man, an educated man—but why a Christian?” They praise in you what you would not wish to be praised; they criticize the thing in which you rejoice.

But if you should say, “What do you praise in me, O man—that I am a good man, that I am a just man?” If you think this, Christ has made me so; praise him. But he replies, “Far from it; do not do yourself an injustice. You made yourself such.” “Let those who say to me, ‘Good, good,’ be confounded.”

And what follows? “Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad, O Lord.” They do not seek me; they seek you. They do not say “Good, good” to me; they see me glorying in you, if I have anything of which to glory [Note: [Col. 0450] Most manuscripts read: “but in him, and they see me glorifying in you.” Some read: “but they seem to glorify me in you.” Others: “but in him, because they see me glorying in you.”]. For “the one who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

“Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad, O Lord, and let them always say, ‘The Lord be magnified.’” For if a sinner becomes just, let glory be given to the one who calls him to forgiveness; and if someone now walks in the way of righteousness, let glory be given to the one who calls him to the crown. “Let the Lord always be magnified” by those who love your salvation.

27. [Verse 18.] “But I”—the one to whom they desired evil. “But I”—the one whose soul they sought to take away. But turn your attention to another kind of people. “But I,” to whom they said, “Good, good”: “I am needy and poor.” There is nothing of mine that ought to be praised. Let him tear apart my sackcloth and cover me with his robe.

“For I live, yet no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). If Christ lives in you, and everything good that you have belongs to Christ, and everything good that you will have belongs to Christ, what are you by yourself? “I am needy and poor.” I am not rich, because I am not proud.

The rich man was the one who said, “I thank you, Lord, that I am not like the rest of humanity.” But the Publican was poor, saying, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:11, 13). The one belched forth from fullness; the other wept from hunger. “I am needy and poor.”

And what will you do, needy and poor man? Beg before God’s door; knock, and it will be opened to you. “But I am needy and poor: the Lord will care for me.” “Cast your care upon the Lord, hope in him, and he will act” (Ps. 55:23). What are you going to care for yourself? What are you going to provide for yourself? Let the one who made you care for you.

The one who cared for you before you existed—how will he not care for you now that you are what he wished you to be? You are already faithful; you are already walking in the way of righteousness. Will he not care for you, the one who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45)? Will he neglect, abandon, or forsake you, who now live justly by faith (Rom. 1:17)? Certainly not. Even here he cherishes you, here he helps you, here he supplies what is necessary, and cuts away what is harmful. By giving, he consoles you so that you may remain; by taking away, he disciplines you so that you may not perish.

“The Lord cares for you; be secure.” The one who made you carries you [Note: [Col. 0451] The editions read “protects.” Several manuscripts read “will protect.” Four manuscripts read “may he carry.” Three others read “he carries.”]. Do not fall from the hand of your craftsman; if you fall from the craftsman’s hand, you will be broken. But remaining in the craftsman’s hand is brought about by good will. Say, “My God has willed it,” and he himself will carry you; he himself will hold you.

Cast yourself upon him. Do not think that this means nothing, as though you were being thrown headlong; do not see it that way. He said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). He is nowhere absent from you. Do not be absent from him; do not be absent from yourself. “The Lord cares for me.”

28. “You are my helper and my protector; my God, do not delay.” He invokes, entreats, and fears that he may fail: “Do not delay.” What does “Do not delay” mean? “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24:22). We have just read about the days of tribulation.

As though one man were entreating God—the members of Christ, the body of Christ spread everywhere; one beggar, one poor man. For he too was poor who, though rich, became poor. The Apostle says of him: “Though he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). He enriches the truly poor and impoverishes the falsely rich.

He cries out to him: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my soul was growing weary” (Ps. 61:3). Days of tribulation and days of greater tribulation will come [Note: [Col. 0451] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “and evil tribulations will come,” and so forth.]. They will come, as Scripture says; and as the days approach, the tribulations increase.

Let no one promise himself what the Gospel does not promise. My brothers, I beg you, attend to our Scriptures. Have they deceived us in anything? Have they said anything that came about differently from what they said? Everything must necessarily happen to the end just as they said.

Our Scriptures promise us nothing in this age except tribulations, pressures, hardships, increasing sorrows, and an abundance of temptations. Let us prepare ourselves especially for these things, lest we fail when unprepared. “Woe to the pregnant and nursing women” (Matt. 24:19)—you have just heard it.

The pregnant are those who swell with hope. The nursing women, that is, those who suckle, are those who have already obtained what they desired. For a pregnant woman swells with hope of a child, though she does not yet see the child; but the woman who is already nursing embraces what she hoped for.

Let us therefore give an example. “My neighbor’s estate is good. If only it were mine! I would add it to mine and make one property out of this land and that” [Note: [Col. 0451] The manuscripts read: “If only it were mine! If only I could add it!”]. Avarice too loves unity. What it loves is good, but it does not know where it ought to be loved.

Suppose someone has desired his neighbor’s estate. But this neighbor is rich, not needy; he has honor and also power—perhaps a power of which you should be afraid, rather than expecting anything from his property. Expecting nothing, the soul does not conceive; it is not pregnant.
