But if the poor man lives next door—either because he is in such need that he can sell, or because he can be pressured into selling—an eye is cast upon him and the estate is desired. The soul is pregnant: it hopes to obtain the little estate and property of the poor neighbor.

When this poor man suffers want, he comes to his richer neighbor, whom he perhaps usually serves, defers to, rises to greet when he comes, and salutes with bowed head: “Give me something, I beg you; I am suffering want, I am pressed by a creditor.” And the other says, “I do not have anything in hand at present.” If he wanted to sell, he would have it [Note: [Col. 0452] Six manuscripts read: “in hand. Whether he wishes it or not, he has it to sell. We recognize this,” and so forth.].

We recognize this in ourselves. Let it have existed in us; let it no longer exist in us. Did we not live yesterday, and do we not live today? There is still opportunity for correction. That separation has not yet occurred, in which some are placed at the right and others at the left (Matt. 25:33). We are not yet in hell, where that rich man was, thirsting and longing for a drop (Luke 16:22). Let us listen while we live; let us be corrected.

Let us not hope for another’s property, nor swell with pregnancy; and let us not reach those things and, after obtaining them, embrace them as though they were children. For “woe to those pregnant and nursing women in those days.”

The heart must be changed; the heart must be lifted up. The heart must not dwell here; this is an evil region. Let it be enough that for now we must still be here in the flesh. What is not necessary should not be done. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34). Let us dwell with our hearts above.

“If you have risen with Christ”—he says this to the faithful; he says it to those receiving the body and blood of the Lord—“seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; think on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:1–3).

What has been promised to you does not yet appear. It is already prepared, but you do not see it. Do you wish to conceive? Conceive from this source; let this be your hope. Your birth will be certain; it will not be abortive or temporary. You will embrace what you have brought forth forever.

For it is said through Isaiah: “We conceived and gave birth to the spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18). Therefore [Note: [Col. 0452] Perhaps “prepared.”] it is still in the future. It is not given now, but it will be given.

How many things have been given, my brothers—who can count them according to the Scriptures? It is written there concerning the Church, and we see that it exists. It is written there concerning idols that they would not exist, and we see that they do not exist. It is written there that the Jews would lose the kingdom, and we see it. It is written there concerning heretics that they would arise, and we see it. It is written there concerning the day of judgment; it is written there concerning the reward of the good and the punishment of the wicked.

In everything we find God faithful. Will he fail and deceive us at the end? “The Lord will care for me.”

“You are my helper and my protector; my God, do not delay.” “Unless those days were shortened, no flesh would endure; but for the sake of the elect they will be shortened” (Matt. 24:22). Those days will be days of tribulation, but not so long [Note: [Col. 0452] Several manuscripts read: “Those days will be shortened. There will be tribulations, but they will not be so long.” Others read: “but they will not last so long.”] as they are expected to be. They will pass quickly; the rest that is coming will not pass. Although the evil is long, it ought to be endured for the sake of an infinite good.

---

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 40. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE [Note: [Col. 0452] Delivered on the feast of the Martyrs.]

1. Since the solemn day of the Martyrs has dawned—the day of the glory of the Passion of Christ, the commander of the martyrs, who did not spare himself while commanding his soldiers in battle, but fought first and conquered first, so that he might encourage those who fought by his example, help them by his majesty, and crown them by his promise—let us hear in this psalm something that pertains to his Passion.

We often commend this point, and we are not annoyed at repeating what it is useful for you to retain: our Lord Jesus Christ frequently speaks from himself, that is, from the person of himself as our head; frequently from the person of his body, which is us and his Church. Yet he makes the words sound as though from the mouth of one person [Note: [Col. 0453] The word “mouth” is absent from the manuscripts; “person” is to be understood in its place.], so that we may understand that head and body remain in the unity of their integrity and are not separated from one another—like that marriage of which it was said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:31).

If, then, we recognize two in one flesh, let us recognize two in one voice. We sang in response to what was read, although it comes from the middle of the psalm. Nevertheless, let us begin our sermon from here:

“My enemies have spoken evil against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’”

This is the person of our Lord Jesus Christ. But see whether his members are not understood there as well. This was said when our Lord himself was walking here on earth in the flesh.

When the Jews saw the multitude following his authority, and saw divinity and majesty displayed through miracles [Note: [Col. 0453] Six manuscripts read “shining forth” instead.], they said among themselves—those of whom the Lord himself gave the parable, saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21:38). The voice of that high priest Caiaphas arose from among them: “You see that a great crowd follows him, and the world has gone after him. If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation. It is better that one man should die than that the whole nation perish.”

The Evangelist explained to us the words of a man who did not know what he was saying: “He did not say this from himself; but since he was high priest, he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the people and the nation” (John 11:47–51).

Yet when they saw the people going after him, they said, “When will he die, and his name perish?” That is: “When we have killed him, his name will no longer be on earth, nor will he deceive anyone once dead. By his very killing people will understand that they were following a man, that there was no hope of salvation in him; they will abandon his name, and it will be no more.”

He died, and his name did not perish; rather, his name was sown. He died, but he was a grain, and once it had died, a harvest immediately sprang up (John 12:25). After our Lord Jesus Christ had been glorified, people began to believe in him much more greatly and in much greater numbers. His members began to hear what the head had heard.

Thus, with our Lord Jesus Christ established in heaven, while he himself labored in us on earth, his enemies still said, “When will he die, and his name perish?” For the devil stirred up persecutions in the Church in order to destroy the name of Christ.

Unless perhaps you think, brothers, that when the Pagans raged against the Christians, they were not saying to themselves that they would erase the name of Christ from the earth. In order that Christ might die again—not in his head, but in his body—the martyrs too were killed. The holy blood that was shed contributed to the multiplication of the Church; the death of the martyrs was added to its sowing [Note: [Col. 0454] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “the blood that was shed, by its sowing; the death of the martyrs was also added,” and so forth.].

“Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116:15). Christians multiplied more and more, and what the enemies had said was not fulfilled: “When will he die, and his name perish?”

It is still said today. The Pagans sit and calculate the years for themselves [Note: [Col. 0454] “When they saw,” Augustine says in *The City of God* 18.53, “that Christianity could not be destroyed by so many and such great persecutions, but had rather received marvelous growth through them, they devised—I know not what—Greek verses, as though poured forth by a divine oracle to someone consulting it. In them … they add that Peter by magic had caused the name of Christ to be worshiped for three hundred and sixty-five years, after which, when that number of years had been completed, it would immediately come to an end.” But in the year of Christ 399, when the aforementioned number of years—if counted from Peter’s preaching on the day of Pentecost—was shown to have elapsed, the worship of Christ’s name not only did not fail, but grew especially thereafter, when the remaining temples of the gods were overthrown and their images broken, as Augustine relates in the same work, *The City of God* 18.54.], and hear their fanatics saying, “One day there will be no Christians, and those idols will again be worshiped as they were before.” They still say, “When will he die, and his name perish?”

Though twice defeated, be wise at least the third time: Christ died, but his name will not perish; the martyrs died, and the Church has multiplied; the name of Christ grows throughout all nations.

The one who foretold his death and resurrection, who foretold the deaths of his martyrs and their crown, also foretold the future of his Church. If he told the truth twice, did he lie the third time? What you believe against him is therefore vain. It is better for you to believe in him, so that you may understand concerning the poor and needy: for he became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty, he says, you might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9).

But now, because he became poor, he is despised, and people say, “He was a man.” What was he? “He died; he was crucified. You worship a man; you place your hope in a man; you adore one who is dead.” You are deceived. Understand concerning the poor and needy, so that by his poverty you may become rich.

What does “understand concerning the poor and needy” mean? It means that you should recognize Christ himself as poor and needy, saying in another psalm, “But I am needy and poor; the Lord will care for me” (Ps. 40:18).

What does “understand concerning the poor and needy” mean? It means that “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:7): rich with the Father, poor among us; rich in heaven, poor on earth; rich as God, poor as a human being.

Does what troubles you consist in seeing a man, looking upon flesh, considering death, or mocking the cross? Is that what troubles you? Understand concerning the poor and needy. What does this mean? Understand that where weakness is displayed to you, divinity lies hidden.

He is rich because he is so; poor because you were already so. Yet his poverty is our riches; his weakness is our strength; his foolishness is our wisdom; his mortality is our immortality (1 Cor. 1:30).

Consider what it means for him to be poor. Do not measure him in comparison with the poverty of others. He came to fill the poor—the one who became poor. Therefore open the bosom of faith and receive the poor man [Note: [Col. 0455] Five manuscripts read “from the poor man.”], lest you remain poor.

2. [Verse 2.] “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the poor and needy; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him.” For the evil day will come. Whether you wish it or not, it will come: the day of judgment will arrive, an evil day, if you have not understood concerning the poor and needy.

What you do not wish to believe now will be manifest at the end. But you will not escape when it has become manifest, because you do not believe while it is hidden. You are invited to believe what you do not see, lest you blush with shame when you see it.

Understand, then, concerning the poor and needy—that is, concerning Christ. Understand the hidden riches in the one whom you see as poor. For in him “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2:3).

On the evil day he will deliver you by virtue of what he is as God. By virtue of what he is as human, he raised up what was human in him, transformed it for the better, and lifted it into heaven. But the one who is God, who willed to have one person in and together with the human being, could neither decrease nor increase; he could neither die nor rise again. He died according to the weakness of his humanity; otherwise, God does not die.

Do not be surprised that the Word of God does not die, since the soul of a martyr does not die. Did we not just hear the Lord himself saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28)? Therefore, while the martyrs were dying, the souls of the martyrs did not die; and while Christ was dying, was the Word going to die? Certainly, the Word of God is much greater than a human soul. For the human soul was made by God; and if it was made by God, it was made through the Word, because “all things were made through him” (John 1:3). Therefore the Word does not die, just as the soul made through the Word does not die.

But just as we rightly say, “The human being died,” even though his soul does not die [Note: [Col. 0455] All manuscripts read “even though his flesh dies”; some add “alone.”], so we rightly say, “Christ died,” even though his divinity does not die.

From what did he die? Because he was needy and poor. Let his death not overwhelm you and turn you away from contemplating his divinity. “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the poor and needy.”

Look also upon the poor, the needy, the hungry and thirsty, travelers, the naked, the sick, and those held in prison. Understand concerning such a poor person as well, because if you understand concerning such a person, you understand concerning the one who said, “I was hungry, thirsty, naked, a traveler, sick, and in prison” (Matt. 25:35–36). Thus, on the evil day, the Lord will rescue you.

3. [Verse 3.] “And see your blessedness. May the Lord preserve him.” The Prophet rightly wishes good for the one who understands concerning the poor and needy. This wish is a promise; let those who do this await it securely.

“May the Lord preserve him and give him life.” What does “preserve him and give him life” mean? What does “give him life” refer to? To future life. For the one who was dead is given life.

But can a dead person understand concerning the poor and needy? He promises us that life-giving by which the Apostle says: “The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of the one who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, the one who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

This, then, is the life-giving promised to the one who understands concerning the poor and needy.

But because the Apostle says to Timothy, “Having the promise of life, both of the present life and of the future” (1 Tim. 4:8), lest those who understand concerning the poor and needy think that they are indeed to be received into heaven but are to be neglected on earth, and lest they hope only for what will be eternal while thinking that God does not care for what belongs to the present among his saints and faithful people, when he said what we ought especially to expect—“May the Lord preserve him and give him life”—he looked toward this life as well: “And may he make him blessed on earth.”

Raise your eyes, therefore, toward these promises in Christian faith. God does not abandon you on earth, and he promises you something in heaven.

For many evil Christians—observers of almanacs [Note: [Col. 0456] The Colbert manuscript reads “calculators of almanac reckonings.”], investigators and observers of seasons and days—when they begin to be reproved by us or by certain better and more virtuous Christians for doing these things, reply: “These things are necessary for this present time. We are Christians for the sake of eternal life; we believed in Christ so that he might give us eternal life. This temporal life in which we are engaged does not belong to his concern.”

It follows that they are saying, in brief, that God is to be worshiped for eternal life, but the devil for temporal life. Christ himself replies to them: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24).

You worship one for what you hope for in heaven and another for what you hope for on earth. How much better to worship the one who made heaven and earth? The one who cared that the earth should exist—does he neglect his image on earth?

Therefore, “May the Lord preserve him and give him life,” the one who understands concerning the poor and needy. Moreover, although he gives him eternal life, “may he make him blessed on earth.”

4. And do not hand him over to the power of his enemy. That enemy is the devil. Let no one, when he hears these words, think of a human enemy. Perhaps he was already thinking about his neighbor, the man with whom he had a lawsuit in court, the man who wants to take away his property, who wants to pressure him into selling his house to him. Do not think of such things; think instead of that enemy of whom the Lord says, “An enemy has done this” (ibid. XIII, 28). For he is the one who suggests that God should be worshiped for the sake of earthly things. This enemy cannot overthrow the Christian name: for he saw himself defeated by the fame and praises of Christ; he saw that, although he killed Christ’s martyrs, they were crowned and he was vanquished. He therefore began to be unable to persuade people that Christ was nothing. And since he can now scarcely deceive by reviling Christ, he tries to deceive by praising Christ.

What did he say before? “Whom do you worship? A dead Jew, crucified, a man of no importance, who could not drive death away from himself.” But when he saw the human race running in Christ’s name, when he saw that temples were being overthrown, idols broken, and sacrifices extinguished in the name of the Crucified One—and when people observed that all these things had been foretold in the Prophets, were astonished with wonder, and were already closing their hearts against reviling Christ [Note: [Col. 0457] Most manuscripts read this way. But the editions read: “and, by praising [Christ], he now ceased [to attack] by reviling Christ, and clothed himself,” etc. A little later they read: “but who fulfills it? It is fulfilled in the name of our Savior, who tramples the lion,” etc.]—he clothed himself in praises of Christ and began, by another method, to frighten people away from the faith.

“The Christian law is a great law, a powerful law, divine and ineffable. But who fulfills it? In the name of our Savior, trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC, 13). By openly reproving Christ, the lion roared; by cunningly praising Christ, the dragon lies in wait.

Let those who were in doubt come to the faith. Let them not say, “Who fulfills this?” If they rely upon their own strength, they will not fulfill it. Let them believe by relying upon God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0457] Almost all manuscripts omit “by relying upon God’s grace”; a little later they read, “they come to be helped.” The editions, however, read: “let them come to be helped.”]; let them come relying upon that grace, let them come to be helped, not to judge.

All the faithful live in Christ’s name, each fulfilling Christ’s commands according to his own measure—whether married people, or celibates and virgins. They live as much as the Lord grants them to live, and they do not rely upon their own strength; rather, they know that they must glory in him. “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV, 7).

Do not say to me, “Who fulfills that?” He fulfills it in me who came rich to the poor: poor indeed to the poor, but full to the empty. Reflecting on these things, because he understands the one who is needy and poor and does not despise Christ’s poverty, he understands Christ’s riches and becomes blessed on earth. And he is not handed over to the power of his enemy, who wants to persuade him that God should be worshiped for heavenly things and the devil for earthly things. May he not hand him over to the power of his enemy.

5. [verse 4.] May the Lord bring him help. But where? Perhaps in heaven, perhaps in eternal life—so that the devil would still have to be worshiped because of earthly want and the necessities of this life? Far from it. “You have the promise of the present life and of the life to come” (1 Tim. IV, 8). He came to you on earth through whom heaven and earth were made.

Finally, observe what he says: “May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain.” The bed of pain is the infirmity of the flesh. Do not say, “I cannot hold, carry, and restrain my flesh”; you are helped so that you can. May the Lord bring you help upon your bed of pain. The bed carried you; you did not carry the bed. But inwardly you were a paralytic. The one who says to you, “Take up your pallet and go to your house” (Mark II, 11), is present.

“May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain.” And he turns to the Lord himself, as though someone were asking: “Why, then, if God brings us help, do we suffer so many evils in this life—so many scandals, so many hardships, so much unrest of flesh and of the world?” He turns to God and, as though explaining to us the counsel of his healing, says: “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity.”

What does “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity” mean? By “bed” something earthly is understood. Every infirm soul in this life seeks for itself something earthly on which to rest, since it can scarcely endure continuously the strain of labor and of a mind stretched toward God. It acquires for itself something on earth where it may rest and, in a certain kind of pause, recline—such as the things that even innocent people love.

For we need not now speak of the desires of wicked people: many rest in theaters, many in the circus, many in the amphitheater, many in gambling; many in the luxury of taverns, many in the lust of adulteries, many in the violence of robberies, many in deceit and the traps of fraud. People rest in all these things. What does “rest” mean? They take pleasure there.

But let us set all these things aside and come to an innocent person. He rests in his house, in his family, in his wife, in his children, in his poverty, in his little estate, in a new planting cultivated by his own hands, in some building constructed through his own effort. Innocent people rest in these things.

Yet God, wishing us to love nothing except eternal life, mingles bitterness even with these apparently innocent pleasures, so that we may suffer tribulations in them also; and he turns our entire bed in our infirmity. “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity.”

Therefore, let him not complain when, in the things he possesses innocently, he suffers certain tribulations. Through the bitterness of lower things he is taught to love better things, lest the traveler journeying toward his homeland love the inn as his home. “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity.”

6. [verse 5.] But why these things? Because “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). Why these things? Because it was said to sinful humanity: “In the labor of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III, 19).

Therefore, because a person ought to recognize that he suffers on account of his sins these corrections in which our entire bed is turned in our infirmity, let him turn to God and say what follows: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

O Lord, exercise me in tribulations [Note: [Col. 0458] The manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, read: “you exercise me in my tribulations.”]; you judge every son whom you will receive worthy of scourging—you who did not spare even your Only-Begotten. He was scourged without sin; but I say, “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

If he who had no corruption was cut [Note: [Col. 0458] Lov. reads, “if he was burned.” But the manuscripts read, “if he was cut,” or “having been cut” (sectus), and Er. likewise.], if our very medicine did not refuse medicinal fire, should we bear impatiently the physician who burns and cuts—that is, who exercises us through every tribulation and heals us from sin? Certainly, let us entrust ourselves to the physician’s hand. For he does not err and cut what is healthy instead of what is rotten. He knows what he examines; he knows the disease, because he himself made nature. He distinguishes what he himself created from what was added through our desire.

He knows that he gave a healthy person the command not to fall into sickness; he said in paradise: “Eat this, and do not eat that” (ibid. II, 16–17). The healthy person did not heed the physician’s command and so fell; let the sick person at least heed it so that he may rise.

“I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.” In my deeds, in my sins, I do not accuse fortune; I do not say, “Fate did this to me.” I do not say, “Venus made me an adulterer, Mars made me a robber, and Saturn made me greedy.” “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

Was this Christ? Was it that sinless head of ours? Was it he who paid back what he had not stolen (Ps. LXVIII, 5)? Was it he alone who was free among the dead (Ps. LXXXVII, 6)? He was free among the dead because he was without sin; for “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34).

Was it therefore he? Rather, it was he speaking from his members, because the voice of his members is his voice, and the voice of our head is our voice. For we were in him when he said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). He was not afraid to die, since he had come to die; nor did he refuse to die, since he had power to lay down his soul and power to take it up again (John X, 18). But the members were speaking in the head, and the head was speaking for the members.

In him, therefore, we find our voice: “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.” In him we were when he said, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46). For in that very psalm in which this verse occurs at the beginning, it is subsequently said: “The words of my sins” (Ps. XXI, 2). Whose sins are in him, unless because our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin (Rom. VI, 6)?

To him and in him let us say: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

7. [verse 6.] “My enemies spoke evil against me: ‘When will he die, and his name perish?’” We have already discussed these things, and from this point we began. Since we must say other things, there is no need to repeat what has so recently been impressed upon your ears and hearts.

8. [verse 7.] “And they entered in to see.” What Christ suffered, the Church also suffers; what the head suffered, the members also suffer. For “is a servant greater than his lord, or a disciple above his teacher?” “If they persecuted me,” he says, “they will also persecute you. If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (Matt. X, 24; John XV, 20).

“They entered in to see.” That Judas was with our head [Note: [Col. 0459] The manuscripts here omit “with our head.”], entering to see—that is, to investigate—not so that he might find something to believe, but so that he might find something to betray. Behold, he entered to see, and this example was set forth in our head.

What about those members after the assumption of our head? Does not the apostle Paul say: “Because of the false brothers who had slipped in, who entered secretly to spy out our freedom” (Gal. II, 4)? These, too, entered in to see. For they are hypocrites, wicked pretenders who join themselves with feigned charity, watching for every movement and every word of holy people and seeking traps in everything.

And what happens to them? See what follows: “Their heart spoke vanity”—that is, they speak as though with feigned love; what they say is vain, not true, not solid. And because they watch for an opportunity to find an accusation, what does he say? “They gathered iniquity for themselves.” Preparing accusations, the enemies seem great to themselves because they have something to accuse. “They gathered iniquity for themselves” [Col. 0460]. For themselves, he says, not for me. Just as Judas gathered it for himself, not for Christ, so the pretenders in the Church gather it for themselves, not for us, because it is said of them elsewhere: “And iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. XXVI, 12).

“They gathered iniquity for themselves.” And because they entered in to see, “they went out and spoke.” The one who entered in to see went out and spoke. Would that he were inside and spoke the truth! Let him not go outside, where he speaks falsehood. He is a betrayer and persecutor; he goes outside and speaks.

If you belong to Christ’s members, come inside; cling to the head [Note: [Col. 0460] Most manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, read: “come inside to the head.”] “Tolerate the weeds if you are wheat; tolerate the chaff if you are grain” (Matt. XIII, 50); tolerate bad fish within the net if you are a good fish. Why did you fly away before the time of winnowing? Why, before the time of harvest, did you uproot even the grain along with yourself? Why, before reaching the shore, did you tear the nets? “They went out and spoke.”

9. [verse 8.] “All my enemies whispered together against me.” All my enemies were united against me. How much better would it be for them to be united with me! What does “united against me” mean? With one plan, one conspiracy.

Christ therefore says to them: “You agree against me; agree with me. Why against me? Why not with me? If you always had unity, you would not divide yourselves into schisms.” For the apostle says: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you” (1 Cor. I, 10).

“All my enemies whispered together against me; they thought evil against me.” Rather, evil against themselves, because they gathered iniquity for themselves. But it was against me because they are to be judged according to their own intention. For it was not that, because they were unable to do anything, they did not want to do anything. The devil desired to destroy Christ, and Judas wanted to kill Christ; but when Christ was killed and rose again, we were given life. The devil and Judas, however, receive the recompense of their evil will, not of our salvation.

To show that each person will be judged according to his intention, whether for reward or punishment, we find people saying something good to someone, and such a good thing as we ourselves would wish, yet being called slanderers. When the Jews were confounded by that man who had once been blind but was now enlightened in both body and heart [Note: [Col. 0460] The manuscripts read this way. The editions, however, read: “We find a good man saying something to someone, and such a good thing as we ourselves would wish, yet being called a slanderer, when the Jews were reviling that man who had once been blind but had been enlightened in both body and heart,” etc.], they who saw bodily but were blind in heart, that same man who now saw said to them: “Do you also want to become his disciples?” And the Gospel says that they reviled him, saying: “You be his disciple” (John IX, 27–28).

May what they said in reviling come upon all of us! This was called a curse because of the evil intention of those who spoke, not because of any evil in the words themselves. The one who reported that they had cursed him considered the spirit in which they spoke, not what they said.

“They thought evil against me.” And what evil against Christ? What evil against the martyrs? God turned everything to good.

10. [verse 9.] “They devised an iniquitous word against me.” What iniquitous word? Look at the head itself: “Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI, 38). Fools! How will the inheritance be yours because you killed him? Behold, you have killed him, and the inheritance will not be yours.

Will the one who sleeps not add to it that he rise again? When you rejoiced that you had killed him, he slept. For in another psalm he says, “I slept.” They raged and wanted to kill him: “I slept.” For if I had not wished it, I would not have slept. “I slept,” because I have power to lay down my soul and power to take it up again (John X, 18). “I slept, and took sleep, and rose again” (Ps. III, 6).

Let the Jews rage, let the earth be delivered into the hands of the wicked (Job IX, 24), let flesh be given over to the hands of persecutors; let them hang him on the wood, pierce him with nails, and pierce him with a spear. Will the one who sleeps not add to it that he rise again?

Why did he sleep? Because “Adam was a figure of the one to come” (Rom. V, 14), and Adam slept when Eve was made from his side (Gen. II, 21). Adam was a figure of Christ, and Eve a figure of the Church; hence she was called the mother of the living.

When was Eve fashioned? While Adam was sleeping. When did the sacraments of the Church flow from Christ’s side? When he was sleeping on the cross. “Will the one who sleeps not add to it that he rise again?”

11. [verse 10.] And why did he sleep? Because of the one who entered in to see and gathered iniquity for himself. “For the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified his heel against me.” He raised his foot against me; he wanted to trample me.

Who is this man of his peace? Judas. And did Christ trust in him, since he said, “In whom I trusted”? Did he not know him from the beginning? Did he not know, before he was born, what he would become? Had he not said to all his disciples, “I chose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John VI, 71)?

How, then, did he trust in him? Because he is himself present in his members, and what many believers hoped for from Judas, the Lord represented in himself. When many who had believed in Christ saw Judas walking among the twelve disciples, some hoped in him because he was such as the others were. But Christ, because he was in those members who were hoping, was in them as he is in those who hunger and thirst. Just as he said, “I was hungry,” so he said, “I hoped.”

Therefore, if we say to him, “Lord, when did you hope?” it is like the question, “Lord, when were you hungry?” Just as he said to us there, “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 37, 40), so he can say: “When one of the least of mine hoped, I hoped.”

“In whom I trusted? The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread.” How does he identify him in the Passion through these prophetic words? He indicated him by the morsel (John XIII, 26), so that it might be clear that the words “who ate my bread” were spoken of him. Again, when he came to betray him, he gave him a kiss (Matt. XXVI, 49), so that it might be clear that the words “the man of my peace” were spoken of him.

12. [verse 11.] “But you, Lord, have mercy on me.” This is from the form of a servant, this is from the form [Note: [Col. 0461] The editions read “person”; the manuscripts read “form.”] of the needy and poor. For blessed is the one who understands the needy and poor. “Have mercy on me, and raise me up, and I will repay them.”

See when this was said: it has already happened. The Jews killed Christ so that they would not lose their place (John XI, 48); by killing him, they lost their place. They were uprooted from the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0462] Ambrosian manuscripts and other manuscripts read: “when the kingdom was uprooted.”] and scattered.

When he was raised up, he repaid them with tribulation: he repaid them for admonition, not yet for condemnation. For that city in which the people roared like a seizing and roaring lion, crying out, “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke XXIII, 21; John XIX, 6), now has Christians after the Jews were uprooted from it; no Jew inhabits it. The Church of Christ was planted there, where the thorns of the Synagogue were uprooted.

Therefore truly “their fire burned like fire among thorns” (Ps. CXVII, 12); but the Lord was like green wood. He himself said this when certain women were mourning as though Christ were about to die: “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children”—thereby foretelling, “Raise me up, and I will repay them.” “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 28, 31).

When could green wood be consumed by the fire of thorns? For they burned like fire among thorns. Fire consumes thorns, and when it is applied to any green wood, it is difficult to kindle it, because the moisture of the wood resists the slow and feeble flame; yet that flame is sufficient to consume thorns.

“And raise me up, and I will repay them.” But, brothers, do not perhaps suppose from his saying “Raise me up” that the Son is less powerful than the Father and cannot raise himself. What was raised was what could die: the flesh died, and the flesh was raised.

Yet do not suppose that, because God the Father was able to raise Christ—that is, the flesh of his Son—and Christ himself, although he is the Word of God equal to the Father, could not raise his own flesh. Hear this from the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” And the Evangelist, so that we might not doubt even on this account, said: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (John II, 19, 21). “And raise me up, and I will repay them.”

13. [verse 12.] “By this I know that you have desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.” The Jews rejoiced when they saw Christ crucified; they thought they had accomplished their desire to do harm. They saw the outcome and fruit of their savagery: Christ hanging on the cross. They shook their heads and said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 39–40).

He did not come down, though he could have. He demonstrated not power, but taught patience [Note: [Col. 0462] The manuscripts, with great agreement, read: “he was demonstrating not powerlessness.”]. For if he had descended from the cross while they said these things, he would have seemed to yield to their insults, and it would have been thought that, defeated, he could not endure their reproaches. Rather, he remained on the cross while they insulted him, fixed there while they shook their heads.

They shook their heads because they were not clinging to the true head. He certainly taught us patience. For he did what was stronger: he refused to do what the Jews provocatively demanded. It is far more powerful to rise from the tomb than to descend from the cross.

“Because my enemy will not rejoice over me.” So they rejoiced at that time; Christ rose, and Christ was glorified. Now they see the human race converted in his name. Let them insult now; let them shake their heads. Rather, let them now fix their heads—or, if they shake them, let them shake them in astonishment and wonder.

For now they say: “Could this perhaps be the one of whom Moses and the Prophets spoke?” They spoke of him: “Like a sheep he was led to be sacrificed, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth; by his wounds we were healed” (Isa. LIII, 5, 7).

For we see that this crucified man leads the human race after him. And our fathers said without cause, “Let us kill him, lest the world go after him” (John XII, 19). Perhaps it would not have gone after him if he had not been killed.

“By this I know that you have desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.”

14. [verses 13–14.] “But you have received me because of my innocence.” Truly because of innocence: integrity without sin, repayment without debt, scourging without deserving it. “Because of my innocence you have received me, and you have strengthened me in your sight forever.”

You have strengthened me forever; you weakened me for a time. You strengthened me in your sight; you weakened me in the sight of human beings.

What then? Praise to him, glory to him. “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel.” For he is the God of Israel, our God, the God of Jacob, the God of the younger son, the God of the younger people.

Let no one say, “He said this about the Jews; I am not Israel.” Rather, the Jews are not Israel. The elder son is the elder people, rejected; the younger is the beloved people. “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23). This has now been fulfilled. Now, brothers, the Jews serve us; they are like our book-carriers, carrying books for us who are students.

Hear how the Jews serve us, and not without reason. That elder brother Cain, who killed his younger brother, received a sign so that he would not be killed—that is, so that that people might remain (ibid. IV, 15). Among them are the Prophets and the Law, and in that Law and in those Prophets Christ was proclaimed.

When we deal with pagans and show that what was foretold concerning Christ’s name, concerning Christ the head and body, is now taking place in Christ’s Church, lest they think that we invented those prophecies and wrote them after these events had occurred as though they were future, we bring forth the books of the Jews. Indeed, the Jews are our enemies; from the writings of the enemy the adversary is convicted.

Therefore the Lord arranged everything and ordered everything for our salvation. He foretold it before us; he fulfilled it in our time [Note: [Col. 0463] Most manuscripts read: “He foretold it many years ago, he fulfilled it in our time, and what …” One manuscript reads: “many years ago.”]; and what he has not yet fulfilled, he will fulfill.

Thus we hold fast to the one who repays, so that we may believe in the one who owes. For what he has not yet given, he will give, just as he gave what he had not yet given before.

If anyone wishes to prove where these things are written, let him read Moses and the Prophets. If an enemy makes a great uproar and says, “You invented these prophecies for yourselves,” let the books of the Jews be brought forth, because “the elder shall serve the younger.” There let them read the things foretold that we now see fulfilled, and let us all say:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age.” And all the people shall say, “Amen, amen.”

## Exposition of Psalm 41. Sermon to the People

[Col. 0464]

1. [verses 1–3.] It has long been our desire to rejoice with you in the word of God and to greet you in him who is our help and salvation. Therefore, hear through us what the Lord gives, and rejoice with us in his word, in his truth, and in his love.

We have undertaken a psalm about which we must speak to you, one suited to your desire [Note: [Col. 0464] Some manuscripts read “to our desire.” Many more read “our desire.”]. For the psalm itself begins with a holy desire, and the one who sings in this way says: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

Who, then, is the one who says this? If we wish, we are. And why do you seek outside yourself who he is, when it lies within your power to be what you seek? Yet it is not one person, but one body; and the body is Christ’s Church (Col. I, 24).

Nor is such desire found in everyone who enters the Church. Nevertheless, whoever has tasted the sweetness of the Lord and recognizes what is pleasing to him in the Song should not think that he alone possesses it. Let him believe that such seeds have been scattered throughout the Lord’s field, throughout the whole world, and that this is the voice of a certain Christian unity: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

It is not wrongly understood as the voice of those who, while still catechumens, hasten toward the grace of the holy washing. Hence this psalm is solemnly sung, so that they may desire the fountain of the forgiveness of sins as the deer longs for the springs of water. Let this interpretation have its place in the Church, both as a true interpretation and as a solemn one.

Nevertheless, brothers, it seems to me that even in Baptism such desire has not yet been satisfied in the faithful. But perhaps, if they know where they are pilgrims and to where they must journey, they are inflamed even more ardently.

2. Finally, its title is: “For the end, for understanding [Note: [Col. 0464] The manuscripts read this way, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read: “For the end of understanding,”], for the sons of Korah. A psalm.”

We find the sons of Korah in other psalm titles as well (Ps. XLIII–XLVIII), and we remember having already treated the matter and explained what this name means. Yet this title must now be recalled in such a way that what we have already said does not prejudice us, so that we do not say afterward, “We have already discussed this,” for not everyone was present whenever we discussed it.

There may have been a man named Korah, as there was, and he may have had sons who were called the sons of Korah (Num. XXVI, 11). Nevertheless, let us search out the mystery of the sacrament, so that this name may give birth to the mystery with which it is pregnant.

For it is a matter of great sacramental significance that Christians should be called the sons of Korah. Sons of Korah? Sons of the bridegroom, sons of Christ. Christians are called sons of the bridegroom (Matt. IX, 15).

Why, then, is Christ called Korah? Because Korah is interpreted as “Calvary.” This is much more remote. I was asking why Christ is Korah; I ask more intently why Christ appears to be connected with Calvary. Does the one crucified at the place of Calvary not immediately come to mind (Matt. XXVII, 33)? He certainly does.

Therefore the sons of the bridegroom, the sons of that Passion, the sons redeemed by his blood, the sons of that cross, bearing on their forehead what the enemies fixed at the place of Calvary, are called the sons of Korah. This psalm is sung for them for understanding.

Let us therefore be awakened to understanding [Note: [Col. 0465] Some manuscripts read: “Let us therefore search out understanding.”]; and if it is sung for us, let us understand. What are we to understand? For what understanding is this psalm sung?

I dare to say: “His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. I, 20).

Come, brothers, take up my eagerness; share this desire with me. Let us love together, let us burn together in this thirst, let us run together toward the fountain of understanding.

Let us desire the fountain like the deer, apart from that fountain which those being baptized desire for the forgiveness of sins. Let us, already baptized, desire the fountain of which another Scripture says: “For with you is the fountain of life.” It is both fountain and light: “For in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10).

If it is both fountain and light, it is rightly also understanding, because it satisfies the soul eager to know; and everyone who understands is illumined by a certain light—not bodily, not carnal, not external, but internal.

There is therefore, brothers, a certain light within, which those who do not understand do not possess. Hence the Apostle addresses those who desire this fountain of life and draw something from it, beseeching them and saying: “No longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their minds, darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their hearts” (Eph. IV, 17–18).

If, then, they are darkened in understanding—that is, if they are darkened because they do not understand—those who understand are illumined.

Run to the fountains; desire the springs of water. With God is the fountain of life, an unfailing fountain; in his light is an undarkenable light. Desire this light, this kind of fountain, this kind of light unknown to your eyes. For seeing this light the inner eye is prepared; for drawing from this fountain the inner thirst burns.

Run to the fountain; desire the fountain. But do not run just anyhow, like just any animal; run like a deer.

What does “like a deer” mean? Let there be no sluggishness in running. Run eagerly; desire the fountain eagerly. For we find in the deer a notable swiftness.

3. But perhaps Scripture wished us to observe not only this in the deer, but something else as well. Hear what else is found in the deer. Deer are said—and some have even seen it, for nothing of this kind would have been written about them unless it had first been observed—to kill snakes; and after killing the snakes, they burn with a greater thirst and run more eagerly to the fountains once the snakes have been destroyed.

The snakes are your vices. Consume the snakes of iniquity; then you will desire the fountain of truth more greatly.

Perhaps greed hisses something darkly within you, and hisses against the word of God, hisses against God’s command. You are told, “Despise something; do not commit iniquity.” But if you prefer to commit iniquity rather than despise some temporary advantage, you choose to be bitten by the snake rather than kill the snake.

When, then, while you still favor your vice, your desire, your greed—your snake—do I find in you such desire that you run to the fountain of water? When do you long for the fountain of wisdom, while you still struggle in the poison of wickedness?

Kill within yourself whatever is opposed to the truth. And when you see that you are, as it were, free from perverse desires, do not remain as though there were nothing for you to desire. There is something by which you may raise yourself, if you have already acted within yourself so that there is no obstacle opposing you.

For perhaps you will say to me, if you are a deer: “God knows that I am no longer greedy, that I no longer desire anyone’s property, that I do not burn with the desire for adultery, that I am not consumed by hatred and envy of anyone, and so forth.” You will say, “I do not have these things,” and perhaps you will ask where you may find pleasure.

Desire that from which you may find pleasure; desire the springs of water. God has what will refresh you and fill the one who comes to him and thirsts after the destruction of the snakes, like a swift deer.

4. There is something else to observe in the deer. Deer are reported—and some have seen it—for nothing of this kind would have been written about them unless it had first been observed: whether they are walking in a herd or swimming toward other regions of land, they place the burdens of their heads upon one another. One goes first, and those who follow place their heads upon him; others follow above them, and then others, until the herd is complete.

But the one who carried the weight of the heads at the front, when he becomes tired, returns to the rear, so that another may take his place and carry what he had carried, while he refreshes himself from his fatigue by placing his head upon another, just as the others had done. Thus, taking turns in carrying what is heavy, they complete the journey and do not abandon one another.

Does not the Apostle address certain deer when he says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 2)?

5. Such a deer, established in faith, not yet seeing what it believes but desiring to understand what it loves, also suffers from hostile people who are not deer [Note: [Col. 0466] The manuscripts read this way. The editions read: “hostile deer, not only darkened,” etc.], people darkened in understanding, dwelling in inner darkness, blinded by the desire for vices, and, moreover, taunting the believing person who cannot display what he believes: “Where is your God?”

Let us hear what this deer did in response to these words, so that we too may do the same, if we can.

First, he expressed his thirst: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

But what if the deer longs for the springs of water in order to bathe? Do we therefore not know whether it is for drinking or for bathing? Hear what follows, and do not inquire further: “My soul thirsted for the living God.”

What I say by “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God,” I say by this: “My soul thirsted for the living God.”

What did it thirst for? “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” This is what I thirst for: to come and appear. I thirst in pilgrimage; I thirst in my journey. I shall be satisfied at my arrival.

But when shall I come? What is swift for God is slow for desire. “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

This also belongs to that desire from which it is cried elsewhere: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” Why? “To contemplate the delight of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

“When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?”

### 6. [verse 4]

Meanwhile, while I am delayed, while I run, while I am on the way—before I come, before I appear—“My tears have been my bread day and night,” while it is said to me every day, “Where is your God?” “My tears,” he says, “have been my food”—not bitterness, but bread. Those very tears were sweet to me: thirsting for that fountain, because I could not yet drink, I avidly consumed my tears. For he did not say, “My tears became my drink,” lest he seem to have desired the tears themselves as he desires the springs of water. Rather, with that thirst preserved by which I burn and am borne toward the springs of water, my tears became bread for me while I am delayed. And certainly, by eating his tears, he thirsts even more for the springs.

“For day and night my tears have become my bread.” This food, which is called bread, people eat by day, while at night they sleep. But the bread of tears is eaten both day and night—whether you understand “day and night” as the whole of time, or “day” as the prosperity of this age and “night” as its adversity. “Whether,” he says, “in the prosperous circumstances of the age or in its adverse circumstances, I pour out the tears of my longing; I do not abandon the eagerness of my desire. Even when things go well in the world, things go badly for me before I appear before the face of God.”

Why, then, do you compel me to speak as though I were congratulating myself if some prosperity of this age smiles upon me? [Textual note: thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “Why then do you say?,” followed by “as though to congratulate,” etc.] Is it not deceptive? Is it not fleeting, perishable, mortal? Is it not temporary, winged, transitory? Does it not contain more deception than delight? Why, then, should not my tears also become bread for me amid that prosperity? For even when the happiness of the age shines around us, so long as we are in the body we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), and every day it is said to me, “Where is your God?”

If a pagan says this to me, can I not also say to him, “Where is your god?” He points out his god with his finger. He points his finger at some stone and says, “Look, this is my god. Where is your God?” When I have mocked the stone and the person who pointed it out has been put to shame, he lifts his eye from the stone, looks up at heaven, and perhaps, pointing his finger at the sun, says again, “Look, my god. Where is your God?”

He has found something he can point out to the eyes of the flesh. I, however, do not lack someone whom I can point out; rather, he lacks the eyes with which I might point him out. He could point out his god, the sun, to my bodily eyes. With what eyes, then, shall I point out the Creator of the sun?

### 7.

Yet, by hearing every day, “Where is your God?” and being nourished by my daily tears, I meditated day and night on what I had heard: “Where is your God?” I, too, sought my God, so that, if I could, I might not merely believe but also see something.

For I see what my God has made, but I do not see my God himself, who made these things. But since, as a deer, I long for the springs of water, and since with him is the fountain of life, and since this Psalm is inscribed “for the sons of Korah” for understanding, and “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20), what shall I do to find my God?

I shall consider the earth: the earth was made. There is great beauty in the lands, but they have an artificer. There are great marvels in seeds and growing things, but all these have a creator. I point out the vastness of the encircling sea; I am astonished and amazed, and I seek its artificer. I look up at the sky and the beauty of the stars; I admire the splendor of the sun, sufficient to unfold the day, and of the moon, which consoles the darkness of night. [Textual note: the editions read “the day’s exercise”; some manuscripts, “exercendo” (“by exercising”); others, “exserendo” (“unfolding”).]

These things are marvelous, these things are worthy of praise, indeed these things are worthy of wonder. For they are no longer earthly but heavenly. Yet my thirst does not rest there. I marvel at these things and praise them, but I thirst for the one who made them.

I return to myself and investigate what I myself am, since I am seeking such things. I find that I possess a body and a soul: one that I govern, and another by which I am governed; the body serving, the soul commanding. I discern that the soul is something better than the body, and I see that the investigator of such things is not the body but the soul. Yet I recognize that I have examined all these things through the body.

I praised the earth; I had learned of it through my eyes. I praised the sea; I had learned of it through my eyes. I praised the sky, the stars, the sun, and the moon; I had learned of them through my eyes. The eyes are members of the flesh; they are windows of the mind. The one who sees through them is within. When he is absent through thought, they stand open in vain.

My God, who made the things I see with my eyes, is not to be sought with these eyes. Let the soul itself also perceive something through itself [the manuscripts read “perceive”; the editions, “perceives”]: whether there is something that I do not perceive through the eyes, as colors and light; nor through the ears, as song and sound; nor through the nostrils, as the sweetness of scents; nor through the palate and tongue, as taste; nor through the whole body, as I experience hardness and softness, rigidity and heat, roughness and smoothness through touch. Let it perceive whether there is something within that I can see.

What is it that I see within? Something that is neither color, nor sound, nor odor, nor taste, nor heat, nor cold, nor hardness, nor softness. Let someone tell me, then, what color wisdom has. When we think about justice and inwardly enjoy its beauty in the very act of thinking, what sound reaches the ears? What rises to the nostrils like vapor? What is conveyed to the mouth, what is handled by the hand and gives delight?

It is within; it is beautiful; it is praised; it is seen. And if these eyes are in darkness, the mind enjoys its light. What was it that Tobias saw when, though blind, he gave his seeing son counsel for life (Tob. 4:2)?

There is, then, something that the soul itself sees—the soul that is master, ruler, and inhabitant of the body. It does not perceive this through the bodily eyes, ears, nostrils, palate, or bodily touch, but through itself. And certainly what is perceived through itself is better than what is perceived through its servant.

It exists indeed: the soul sees itself through itself, and the soul itself, in order to know itself, sees itself. Nor does it seek the assistance of bodily eyes in order to see itself. Rather, it withdraws itself from all the bodily senses, as though from things that hinder and make a din, toward itself, so that it may see itself within itself and know itself with itself. [Textual note: the manuscripts read “toward itself” (*ad se*); the editions, “from itself” (*a se*).]

But is God himself something of the same kind as the soul? God cannot indeed be seen except by the soul, but he cannot be seen in the same way as the soul can be seen. For this soul seeks something that is God, concerning which those who say, “Where is your God?” should not mock it. It seeks immutable truth, substance without defect.

The soul itself is not such. It fails and advances; it knows and is ignorant; it remembers and forgets; now it wills one thing, now it does not will it. Such mutability does not befit God. If I say, “God is mutable,” those who say, “Where is your God?” will mock me.

### 8. [verse 5]

Seeking my God, then, in visible and bodily things, and not finding him; seeking his substance in myself, as though he were something like what I am, and not finding this either, I perceive that my God is something above the soul.

Therefore, in order to touch him [the Louvain edition inserts “by the intellect of the soul,” absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts], “I meditated on these things, and poured out my soul over myself.” When would my soul touch what is sought above my soul, unless my soul were poured out over itself? For if it remained within itself, it would see nothing other than itself; and when it saw itself, it would certainly not see its God.

Let my mockers now say, “Where is your God?” Let them say it. As long as I do not see him, as long as I am delayed, I eat my tears day and night. Let them continue to say, “Where is your God?” I seek my God in every body, whether earthly or heavenly, and I do not find him. I seek his substance in my soul, and I do not find it.

Yet I meditated on the search for my God, and, desiring to perceive through the things that have been made the invisible things of my God, which are understood and seen (Rom. 1:20), I poured out my soul over myself. And now no one remains for me to touch except my God.

For there is the house of my God, above my soul. There he dwells; from there he looks upon me; from there he created me; from there he governs me; from there he counsels me; from there he awakens me; from there he calls me; from there he directs me; from there he leads me; from there he brings me to the end.

### 9.

For he who has a most exalted house in secret also has a tabernacle on earth. His tabernacle on earth is his Church, still on pilgrimage. But he must be sought here, because in the tabernacle the way is found by which one comes to the house.

Indeed, when I poured out my soul over myself in order to touch my God, why did I do this? “Because I shall enter into the place of the tabernacle.” Outside the place of the tabernacle I shall wander while seeking my God.

“Because I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.” I shall enter into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.

For already I marvel at many things in the tabernacle. See how many things I marvel at in the tabernacle! The tabernacle of God on earth is the faithful human being. I marvel at the obedience of their very members: sin does not reign in them so that they obey its desires, nor do they present their members to sin as weapons of iniquity. Rather, they present them to the living God in good works. I marvel that bodily members serve the soul that serves God (Rom. 6:12–13).

I also look upon the soul itself, obedient to God, distributing the works of its activity, restraining desires, driving away ignorance, extending itself to endure every harsh and difficult thing, and bestowing justice and love upon others. [Two manuscripts read “bestowing justice and truth.”]

I marvel at these virtues in the soul also, but I am still walking in the place of the tabernacle. I pass beyond these things as well. And although the tabernacle is wondrous, I am amazed when I reach the house of God.

Concerning that house he speaks in another psalm, when he had set before himself a certain hard and difficult question: why the wicked are often prosperous in this earth while the good suffer. He says, “I undertook to understand this; it was labor before me, until I entered the sanctuary of God and understood their final destiny” (Ps. 72:16–17).

For there is the fountain of understanding, in the sanctuary of God, in the house of God. There he understood their final destiny and resolved the question concerning the happiness of the wicked and the labor of the righteous.

How did he resolve it? Because when the wicked are delayed here, they are being kept for punishments without end; and when the good labor here, they are being exercised so that in the end they may receive an inheritance. He learned this in the sanctuary of God; he understood their final destiny.

Ascending through the tabernacle, he reached the house of God. Yet while he marvels at the members of the tabernacle, he was led to the house of God by following a certain sweetness—some inward and hidden pleasure, I know not what—as though some instrument were sounding sweetly from the house of God. [Textual note: the editions add “he perceived a certain”; *he perceived* is redundant and absent from the manuscripts.]

As he walked in the tabernacle, he heard a certain inward sound. Led by its sweetness, he followed what was sounding. Withdrawing himself from all the din of flesh and blood, he reached the house of God.

For he himself recalls his way and guidance as though we were saying to him, “You marvel at the tabernacle on this earth; how did you reach the secret place of the house of God?”

“In the voice,” he says, “of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one celebrating a festival.”

When people celebrate their festivals here, often in their luxury, they have the custom of setting up instruments before their houses, or placing musicians there [the editions read “music”; the manuscripts, “musicians”], or arranging whatever musical performances serve and entice luxury. When we hear these things, what do we say as we pass by? “What is happening here?” And we are answered, “There is some festival.” “They are celebrating a birthday,” someone says; “there is a wedding here,” so that those foolish songs may not seem inappropriate, but luxury may be excused on the grounds of celebration. [Nearly all manuscripts read “merriment” rather than “luxury.”]

In the house of God, the festival is everlasting. Nothing there is celebrated and then passes away. The everlasting festival is the choir of angels; the immediate presence of God is joy without decline. That festival is such that it is neither opened at a beginning nor closed at an end.

From that eternal and perpetual festival something tuneful and sweet sounds to the ears of the heart—provided the world does not drown it out. As one walks in this tabernacle [the editions add “the wondrous tabernacle of God,” absent from the manuscripts] and considers the marvels of God for the redemption of the faithful, the sound of that festival delights the ear and carries the deer to the springs of water.

### 10. [verses 6–7]

But since, brothers, so long as we are in this body we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), and since “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15)—even if, as we walk in longing, we somehow disperse the clouds and occasionally reach this sound, so that by striving we grasp something of that house of God—we nevertheless fall back into our accustomed state under a certain burden of our weakness and slip back into these familiar things.

And just as we had found there something in which to rejoice, so here there will be no lack of what causes us to groan. For this deer, eating its tears day and night, carried away by desire toward the springs of water—that is, toward the inward sweetness of God—pouring out its soul over itself in order to touch what is above its soul, walking into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, and led by the delight of an inward and intelligible sound so as to despise all outward things and be carried away into inward things—this deer is nevertheless still a human being.

It still groans here; it still bears fragile flesh; it still faces danger amid the scandals of this world. Thus it looked back upon itself, as though returning from there, and said to itself, placed amid these sorrows and comparing them with what it had entered to see and with what it had seen before leaving:

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? See, we have already rejoiced in a certain inward sweetness. See, with the mind’s eye we have been able, however briefly and fleetingly, to glimpse something immutable. Why do you still trouble me? Why are you still sad?

You do not doubt your God. You are not without something to say to yourself against those who say, ‘Where is your God?’ I have already sensed something immutable; why do you still trouble me? Hope in God.”

And as though its soul were answering it in silence:

“Why do I trouble you, except because I am not yet there where that sweetness is, by which I was so carried away as though in passing? Am I already drinking from that fountain, fearing nothing? Do I already fear no scandal? Am I already secure from all desires, as though they had been subdued and conquered? Is not my enemy, the devil, watching against me? Does he not set traps of deception for me every day?

Do you not want me to be troubled, placed in the world and still on pilgrimage, away from the house of my God?”

But “Hope in God,” it replies to the soul that troubles itself, as though it were giving an account of its disturbance because of the evils with which this world abounds. For now, live in hope. “Hope that is seen is not hope; but if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

### 11.

“Hope in God.” Why hope? “Because I shall confess to him.” What will you confess to him? “The salvation of my countenance, my God.”

Salvation cannot come from myself to myself. This I shall say; this I shall confess: “My God is the salvation of my countenance.”

For, so that it might be cautious amid those things it has come to understand in some fashion, it looked back anxiously lest the enemy should creep in. It does not yet say, “I am saved in every respect.” For “we who have the first fruits of the Spirit groan inwardly, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23).

When that perfect salvation is in us, we shall live without end in the house of God and praise without end the one to whom it was said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

This has not yet happened, because the salvation that is promised has not yet arrived. But I confess to my God in hope, and I say to him, “My God, the salvation of my countenance.” For “we have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24).

Persevere, then, so that you may arrive; persevere until salvation comes. Hear your God himself speaking to you from within: “Wait for the Lord; act bravely, and let your heart be strengthened; and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14). For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

Why, then, are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, because I shall confess to him. This is my confession: “My God is the salvation of my countenance.”

### 12.

“My soul is troubled with respect to myself.” Is it troubled with respect to God? It is troubled with respect to myself. It was refreshed by the immutable; it was disturbed by the mutable.

I know that the justice of my God remains. Whether my own remains, I do not know. For the Apostle terrifies me when he says, “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

Therefore, because there is no firmness in me for myself, and I have no hope in myself, “my soul is troubled with respect to myself.” Do you not want it to be troubled? Do not remain in yourself, but say, “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:1).

Hear this more plainly: do not hope in yourself, but in your God. For if you hope in yourself, your soul is troubled with respect to you, because it has not yet found a basis on which to be secure concerning you.

Therefore, since my soul is troubled with respect to myself, what remains except humility, so that the soul may not presume upon itself? What remains except that it make itself altogether small, that it humble itself, so that it may deserve to be exalted? Let it attribute nothing to itself, so that what is beneficial may be attributed to it by him.

Therefore, because my soul is troubled with respect to myself, and pride causes this disturbance, “I remembered you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and from Mount Hermon, from the little mountain.”

From where did I remember you? From the little mountain and from the land of the Jordan. Perhaps from Baptism, where there is forgiveness of sins. For no one runs to the forgiveness of sins unless he is displeased with himself; no one runs to the forgiveness of sins unless he confesses himself a sinner; and no one confesses himself a sinner without humbling himself before God.

Therefore, “from the land of the Jordan I remembered you, and from the little mountain”—not from the great mountain, so that from the little mountain you may make the great. For “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

But if you also seek the interpretations of the names, Jordan means “their descent.” Descend, then, so that you may be lifted up. Do not exalt yourself, lest you be shattered.

“And from Hermon, from the little mountain.” Hermon is interpreted as “anathema” or “devoting to destruction.” Make yourself an anathema by being displeasing to yourself; for you will be displeasing to God if you are pleasing to yourself.

Therefore, because God grants us every good thing because he himself is good, not because we are worthy; because he is merciful, not because we have deserved anything from him—“from the land of the Jordan and Hermon I remembered God.”

And because he is remembered humbly, he will deserve to be enjoyed when exalted; for the one who glories in the Lord is not exalted in himself.

### 13. [verse 8]

“Deep calls to deep, at the sound of your cataracts.”

Perhaps I can complete the Psalm, helped by your eagerness, whose fervor I see. I am not overly concerned about your labor as you listen, since you see me, who am speaking, sweating in these labors. As you look upon me laboring, you certainly labor with me. For I do not labor for myself but for you.

So listen, because I see that you wish to do so.

“Deep calls to deep, at the sound of your cataracts.” The one who remembered God from the land of the Jordan and Hermon said this to God. In wonder he said, “Deep calls to deep, at the sound of your cataracts.”

What deep calls to what deep? Truly, this understanding is a deep. For a deep is an impenetrable and incomprehensible depth, and the term is especially used of a multitude of waters. There is height there and depth—something that cannot be penetrated to the bottom.

Accordingly, it is said in one place, “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7), by which Scripture wishes to commend the fact that God’s judgments cannot be comprehended.

What deep, then, calls to what deep? If a deep is a depth, do we suppose that the human heart is not a deep? For what is deeper than this deep? Human beings can speak; they can be seen through the activity of their members; they can be heard in speech. But whose thought can be penetrated? Whose heart can be examined? Who can comprehend what someone carries within, what he is capable of within, what he does within, what he arranges within, what he wills within, or what he does not will within?

I think it can properly be understood as referring to the human being of whom it is said elsewhere, “A human being will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Ps. 63:7–8).

If the human being is a deep, then how does deep call to deep? Does a human being call to a human being? Does he call in the way God is invoked? No. But “he calls” means that he calls someone to himself. For it is said of a certain person, “He calls for death” [that is, he lives in such a way that he calls death to himself]. No human being offers a prayer and invokes death; but by living badly, human beings call death upon themselves.

“Deep calls to deep”: human being calls to human being. Thus wisdom is learned; thus faith is learned, when deep calls to deep.

The holy preachers of the word of God call to the deep. Are they not themselves also a deep? To show you that they too are a deep, the Apostle says: “It is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day. Nor do I even judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3).

Do you believe that there is such great depth in a human being that it is hidden even from the human being in whom it exists? How great a depth of weakness was hidden in Peter when he did not know what was taking place within him and rashly promised that he would die with the Lord or for the Lord (John 13:37)! How great was that deep! Yet it was naked before the eyes of God. For Christ foretold to him what he himself did not know within himself.

Therefore every human being, even if holy, even if righteous, even if advancing in many respects, is a deep. He calls to the deep whenever he preaches something of faith or something of truth to a human being for the sake of eternal life.

But a deep is useful to the deep it calls only when it does so “at the sound of your cataracts.” Deep calls to deep; a human being wins a human being—not, however, by his own voice, but at the sound of your cataracts.

### 14.

Receive another interpretation: “Deep calls to deep, at the sound of your cataracts.”

I, who tremble when my soul is troubled with respect to myself, have greatly feared your judgments. For “your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7), and “deep calls to deep.”

For beneath this mortal, laborious, sinful flesh, full of troubles and scandals and subject to desires, there is a certain condemnation arising from your judgment, because you said to the sinner, “You shall surely die,” and, “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 2:17; 3:19). This is the first deep of your judgment.

But if people live badly here, “deep calls to deep,” because they pass from punishment to punishment, from darkness to darkness, from depth to depth, from torment to torment, and from the heat of desire into the flames of Gehenna.
