Perhaps this is what that man feared when he said, “My soul is troubled with respect to myself; therefore I remembered you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and Hermon.” I must be humble. I have shuddered at your judgments; I have greatly feared your judgments. Therefore my soul is troubled with respect to myself.

And what judgments of yours did I fear? Are these judgments of yours small? They are great, harsh, and grievous. But would that they were the only ones! “Deep calls to deep, at the sound of your cataracts.”

For you threaten; you say that after those labors another condemnation remains: “At the sound of your cataracts, deep calls to deep.”

Where, then, shall I go from your presence, and where shall I flee from your spirit (Ps. 138:7), if deep calls to deep, if more grievous things are feared after these labors?

### 15.

“All your suspensions and your waves have passed over me.”

The waves are in the things I experience; the suspensions are in the things you threaten. Every suffering I endure is your wave; every threat of yours is your suspension.

In the waves this deep calls to the deep; in the suspensions it calls to another deep. In what I suffer, there are all your waves; in what you threaten more grievously, all your suspensions have passed over me. For one who threatens does not press down but suspends.

But because you set free, I said this to my soul: “Hope in God, because I shall confess to him, the salvation of my countenance, my God.” Because evils are more frequent, your mercy will be sweeter.

### 16. [verse 9]

Therefore what follows is: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he will declare it.”

No one is free from the need to listen in tribulation. Pay attention when things are going well; listen when things are going well. While you are at peace, learn the discipline of wisdom, and gather the word of God as food. [Textual note: four manuscripts read “and gather the food of God’s word”; three others, “and the word of God as food.”]

For when someone is in tribulation, what he heard while secure ought to benefit him. Indeed, in prosperous circumstances God commands his mercy to you if you serve him faithfully, because he delivers you from tribulation. But he does not reveal to you the mercy he commanded for you by day except through the night.

When tribulation itself comes, he does not abandon you in your need. He shows you that what he commanded you by day was true. For it is written in one place: “The mercy of the Lord is beautiful in the time of tribulation, like a rain cloud in the time of drought” (Sir. 35:26).

“By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he will declare it.” He does not show you that he comes to your aid until tribulation comes upon you, from which you are delivered by the one who promised you help by day.

For this reason we are urged to imitate the ant (Prov. 6:6). Just as the prosperity of the age is signified by day and its adversity by night, so in another way prosperity is signified by summer and adversity by winter.

And what does the ant do? During summer it gathers what will benefit it during winter. Therefore, when it is summer, when things are going well for you, when you are at peace, listen to the word of the Lord.

How could you cross the entire sea of this present age without tribulation? How could you? To whom has this happened among human beings? If it has happened to anyone, that very calm is more to be feared.

“By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he will declare it.”

### 17. [verses 10–12]

What, then, should you do on this pilgrimage? What should you do?

“With me is prayer to the God of my life.”

This is what I do here—the thirsty deer longing for the springs of water, remembering the sweetness of that voice [the manuscripts read “voice”; the editions, “fountain”] by which I was led through the tabernacle to the house of God. So long as this body that is corrupted weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15), “with me is prayer to the God of my life.”

I do not have to purchase a sacrifice for God from overseas places, nor, in order that my God may hear me, do I have to sail away and bring incense and spices from afar, or lead a calf or ram from the flock. “With me is prayer to the God of my life.”

Within myself I have a victim to offer; within myself I have incense to place upon the altar; within myself I have a sacrifice with which to bend my God: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50:19).

That I possess within myself the sacrifice of a troubled spirit, hear this: “I shall say to God, ‘You are my protector; why have you forgotten me?’” For I labor here as though you had forgotten me. Yet you are exercising me; and I know that you are delaying what you promised me, not taking it away from me. Still, “why have you forgotten me?”

As though from our voice, our head, God cried out: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2; Matt. 27:46). “I shall say to God, ‘You are my protector; why have you forgotten me?’”

### 18.

“Why have you rejected me?” [The sacred biblical texts lack these words.] From that height of the fountain of understanding and immutable truth: “Why have you rejected me?” Why, longing for that place, have I been cast down to these things by the weight and burden of my iniquity?

This voice says elsewhere: “I said in my ecstasy”—when he saw I know not what great thing, in an excess of mind [the manuscripts read *excessu*, “in an excess”; the editions, *excessum*]—“I said in my ecstasy, ‘I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes’” (Ps. 30:23).

He compared the things in which he was with those toward which he had been raised [the Erasmus edition and the manuscripts read “raised”; the Louvain edition, “upright”], and saw himself cast far away from the sight of God’s eyes, as here also: “Why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful, while the enemy afflicts me, while he crushes my bones?”

That tempter, the devil, crushes me, while scandals multiply everywhere, and “because of their abundance the love of many grows cold” (Matt. 24:12).

When we see the strong in the Church often yield to scandals, does not the body of Christ say, “The enemy crushes my bones”? For bones are the strong members, and sometimes even the strong yield to temptations.

When someone considers these things from the body of Christ, from the voice of the body of Christ, does he not cry out, “Why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful, while the enemy afflicts me, while he crushes my bones?”

Not merely my flesh but also my bones: so that in those members where some strength was thought to exist, you may see people yielding in temptations, and the other weak members may despair when they see the strong succumb.

How great are these dangers, my brothers!

### 19.

“Those who afflict me reproached me.”

Again that voice: “While they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’”

They say this especially in the Church’s temptations: “Where is your God?” How much the martyrs heard this, strong and patient for the name of Christ; how often it was said to them, “Where is your God? Let him deliver you, if he can.”

People saw their torments outwardly, but they did not see their crowns inwardly.

“Those who afflict me reproached me, while they say to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’”

And because of these things, since my soul is troubled with respect to myself, what else shall I say to it except, “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

And as though it were answering, “Do you not want me to be troubled, placed here amid such great evils? Sighing for good things, thirsting and laboring, do you not want me to be troubled?”

“Hope in God, because I shall still confess to him.” He states the confession itself; he repeats the confirmation of hope: “The salvation of my countenance and my God.” [Most manuscripts read “the salvation”; some also omit “and” in this verse.]

## Exposition of Psalm 42: A Sermon to the People

Delivered on a day of fasting, in the afternoon

### 1.

This Psalm is brief. It satisfies the minds of the listeners without burdening the stomachs of those who are fasting. Let our soul be nourished by it—the soul which the one who sings in this Psalm calls sad. Sad, I believe, because of some fasting of its own, or rather because of some hunger of its own. Fasting is voluntary; hunger is necessary.

The Church hungers; the body of Christ hungers; that human being spread everywhere, whose head is above and whose members are below. [Textual note: the editions read “is spread everywhere”; the word “is” is omitted on the authority of the manuscripts.] We should already recognize his voice in all the Psalms—whether singing, groaning, rejoicing in hope, or sighing in fulfillment—as thoroughly familiar and as our own.

Therefore, there is no need to spend much time explaining to you who is speaking. Let each person be in the body of Christ, and he will speak here.

## 2. [verse 1]

You know, however, all who are making progress and who sigh for that heavenly city, who recognize their pilgrimage, who keep to the way, who have fixed their hope as a most secure anchor in the longing for that steadfast land. You know, then, that this class of people, this good seed, this wheat of Christ, groans among the weeds; and this continues until the time of harvest arrives, that is, until the end of the age, as the truth that cannot deceive explains (Matthew 13:18). [Col. 0477] Groaning, then, among the weeds—that is, among wicked people, among the deceitful and seducers, whether turbulent with anger or poisonous with their plots—this seed looks around and sees itself existing together with them as though in one field throughout the whole world, receiving the same rain, being blown upon alike, and being nourished together with them amid adversities; it sees that it possesses in common with them these gifts of God, granted alike to the wicked and the good by him who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (ibid. 5:45).

Seeing, then, that the seed of Abraham, the holy seed, presently shares so much with the wicked, from whom it will one day be separated—being born under the same conditions, receiving the same lot of human existence, bearing mortal bodies alike, using together the light, springs, and fruits, and the prosperity and adversity of this age, whether famine or abundance, peace or war, health or pestilence—seeing how much it shares with the wicked, although it does not share their cause, it bursts into this cry:

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.” “Judge me,” he says, “O God: I do not fear your judgment, because I know your mercy. Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.”

For the present, during this pilgrimage, you do not yet distinguish my place, since I live together with the weeds until the time of harvest; you do not yet distinguish my rain, nor yet my light: distinguish my cause. Let there be a difference between the one who believes in you and the one who does not believe in you. Their weakness is the same, but their conscience is different; their labor is the same, but their desire is different. The desire of the ungodly will perish; but concerning the desire of the righteous, unless the Promiser were trustworthy, we ought to be in doubt. The end of our desire is the Promiser himself. He will give himself, because he gave himself: he will give himself, immortal, to the immortal, because he gave himself, mortal, to mortals.

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation. Rescue me from an unjust and deceitful man”—that is, from an unholy nation. “From a man,” from a certain kind of human being, because one man and another man exist, and among these two one will be taken and the other left behind (ibid. 24:40).

## 3. [verse 2]

And because patience is necessary to endure until the harvest—a kind of, if one may put it so, undifferentiated distinction, since they are together and therefore have not yet been separated, although the weeds are weeds and the wheat is wheat, and therefore are already distinct—because, then, courage is necessary, it must be sought from him who commanded us to be courageous; unless he himself makes us courageous, we will not be what he commanded. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “we will not be”: “that we may be so, we shall be made by him who said.”] It must be sought from him who said, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. 10:22; 24:13).

So that the soul may not weaken itself by arrogating courage to itself, it immediately adds:

“For you are my God, my strength; why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?”

It asks the cause of its sorrow. “Why,” it says, “do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” I walk sorrowfully; the enemy afflicts me with daily temptations, introducing either something we may love wrongly or something we may fear wrongly. The soul, fighting against both, though not captured, [Col. 0478] is nevertheless in danger; sorrow gathers within it, and it says to God, “Why?” Let it ask him, then, and let it hear the reason.

In the Psalm it asks the cause of its sorrow, saying: “Why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful?” Let it hear from Isaiah; let the reading that has just been recited come to its aid:

“The spirit will go forth from me, and I made every breath; because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I turned my face away from him; and he was grieved, and went away sorrowful in his ways” (Isaiah 57:16–17). [Note: The Louvain edition omitted “sorrowful”; the word is restored from Erasmus and the manuscripts.]

What, then, were you asking: “Why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sorrowful?” You have heard the answer: “Because of sin.” The cause of your sorrow is sin; let the cause of your joy be righteousness. You wanted to sin, but did not want to suffer; it was not enough for you to be unjust unless you also wanted him to be unjust whom you did not want to punish you in yourself.

Consider the better saying in another Psalm: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications” (Psalm 118:71). In my arrogance I had learned my iniquities; humbled, let me learn your justifications.

“Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” You complain about the enemy; he truly afflicts you, but you gave him room. And now you have something to do: choose the counselor, admit the king, exclude the tyrant.

## 4. [verse 3]

But observe what he says, what he pleads, and what he prays, so that he may do this. Pray for what you hear; pray as you hear it. Let this be the voice of all of us:

“Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles.”

For they are your light and your truth [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “For he is your light”]: these two names designate one reality. What else is the light of God but the truth of God? Or what is the truth of God but the light of God? And both are one Christ.

“I am the light of the world; whoever believes in me will not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (ibid. 14:6). He is himself the light; he is himself the truth.

Let him come, then, and rescue us, presently distinguishing our cause from an unholy nation; let him rescue us from an unjust and deceitful man; let him separate the wheat from the weeds. For he himself will send his angels at the time of harvest, so that they may gather from his kingdom all scandals and cast them into the burning fire, while they gather his wheat into the granary (Matthew 13:41–43).

Let him send forth his light and his truth, because they have already led us and brought us to his holy mountain and to his tabernacles. We possess the pledge; we hope for the reward.

His holy mountain is his holy Church. It is that mountain which grew from a very small stone, according to Daniel’s vision, shattering the kingdoms of the earth and growing so greatly that it filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel 2:35). In this mountain he says that he was heard who says: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain” (Psalm 3:5).

Whoever was outside this mountain should not hope to be heard unto eternal life. Many are heard for many things. Let them not applaud themselves because they are heard: the demons were heard, so that they might be sent into the swine (Matthew 8:32). Let us desire to be heard unto eternal life, because of the desire by which we say [Col. 0479] [Note: Three manuscripts read, “because of the desire by which we speak”]:

“Send forth your light and your truth.”

That light seeks the eye of the heart. For he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).

For now we are on his mountain, that is, in his Church, and in his tabernacle. A tabernacle is the dwelling of pilgrims; a house is the dwelling of those who live together. Yet a tabernacle is also the dwelling of pilgrims and soldiers. When you hear “tabernacle,” understand war and beware of the enemy.

But what will the house be [Note: The editions read, “the house of which he said, ‘Blessed,’ etc.” Most manuscripts read, “what will it be?” The Gatian manuscript reads, “which will be”]? “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

## 5. [verse 4]

Now, then, having been brought to the tabernacle and placed upon his holy mountain, what hope do we possess?

“And I will enter the altar of God.”

There is a certain sublime, invisible altar, to which the unjust does not approach. Only the one who approaches this altar with confidence approaches that altar; there he will find his life who here distinguishes his cause.

“And I will enter the altar of God”: from his holy mountain and from his tabernacle, from his holy Church, I will enter the sublime altar of God.

What sacrifice is there? The one who enters is himself taken up as a whole burnt offering.

“I will enter the altar of God.”

What does he mean by saying “to the altar of God”? He means “to God, who makes my youth rejoice.” Youth signifies newness, as though he were saying, “To God, who makes my newness rejoice.” He makes my newness rejoice who grieved my oldness. For now I walk sorrowfully in oldness; then I will stand rejoicing in newness.

“I will confess to you with the lyre, God, my God.”

What does it mean to confess with the lyre and to confess with the psaltery? For one does not always use the lyre, nor always the psaltery. These two musical instruments have between them a distinct and separate significance, worthy of consideration and of being commended to memory.

Both are carried and played with the hands, and both signify certain bodily works of ours. Both are good, if one knows how to play the psaltery and how to play the lyre. But since the psaltery is said to be the instrument that has its sound box above—the drum, that is, and hollow wood upon which the strings rest and resound—whereas the lyre has that same hollow and resonant wood beneath, our works must be distinguished: when they are performed with the psaltery and when with the lyre, although both are pleasing to God and sweet to his hearing.

When, then, we do something according to God’s commandments, obeying and hearkening to his orders in order to fulfill his commandments, when we act without suffering, it is the psaltery. The angels act in this way, for they do not suffer anything.

But when we suffer tribulations, temptations, and scandals in this world—because we suffer only from below, that is, from the fact that we are mortal, from the fact that something of tribulation is owed to our first cause, and because we suffer many things [Note: Five manuscripts read, “is owed”], from those who are not from above—it is the lyre. For a sweet sound comes from below: we suffer and play the psaltery, or rather we sing and play the lyre.

When the Apostle said that he evangelized and preached the Gospel throughout the whole world by God’s command—for he said that he had received that Gospel [Col. 0480] not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:12)—the strings sounded from above.

But when he said, “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance proven character, and proven character hope” (Romans 5:3–4), the lyre sounded from below, yet sweetly. For all endurance is sweet to God.

But if you fail amid those very tribulations, you have broken the lyre.

Why, then, did he say here, “I will confess to you with the lyre”? Because of what he had said: “Why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” He was suffering a certain affliction from below, yet even in this he wished to please God and eagerly desired to give thanks to God, courageous in tribulations. And because he could not exist without tribulation, he owed patience to God:

“I will confess to you with the lyre, God, my God.”

## 6. [verse 5]

And again he speaks to his soul, so that it may draw forth a sound from that resonant wood below:

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul,” he says, “and why do you disturb me?”

I am in tribulations, in distresses [Note: Some manuscripts read “anguishes” instead of “distresses”], in sorrows; why do you disturb me, O soul?

Who is speaking? To whom is he speaking? Everyone knows that he is speaking to the soul; the address is plainly directed to it.

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disturb me?”

The person speaking is being sought. Does the flesh speak to the soul, since the flesh cannot speak without the soul? It is more proper for the soul to address the flesh than for the flesh to address the soul.

But since he did not say, “Why are you sorrowful, my flesh,” but said, “Why are you sorrowful, my soul”—for if he were addressing the flesh, perhaps he would not say, “Why are you sorrowful?” but “Why do you suffer?” The sorrow of the soul is called sadness; the distress that occurs in the body may be called pain, but cannot be called sadness. Nevertheless, the soul is often saddened by bodily pain.

There is a distinction, however, between what suffers and what becomes sad. The flesh suffers; the soul is sad. This saying is therefore clear: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul?”

The soul, then, is not addressing the flesh, since it did not say, “Why are you sorrowful, my flesh?” Nor is the flesh addressing the soul, since it is absurd for the inferior to address the superior.

We understand, therefore, that we possess something in which the image of God resides: namely, the mind and reason. The mind itself was calling upon the light of God and the truth of God. By it we grasp what is just and unjust; by it we distinguish the true from the false. It is called understanding, an understanding that beasts lack. Whoever neglects this understanding within himself, puts it after other things, and casts it aside as though he did not possess it, hears from the Psalm:

“Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

Our understanding, then, addresses our soul. The soul has withered in tribulations, grown weary in anguishes [Note: Some manuscripts read “infirmities” instead of “anguishes”], contracted under temptations, and become sick through labors. The mind, receiving truth from above, raises it up and says:

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disturb me?”

## 7

See whether this is not the address found in the Apostle’s struggle, when he prefigures in himself certain people—and perhaps us—and says:

“I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members” [Col. 0481] [that is, certain carnal movements].

And in a certain struggle and almost despair he invokes the grace of God:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22, 25).

The Lord himself also deigned to prefigure such people fighting in this way when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26:38).

For he knew why he had come. Did he fear the Passion, he who had said:

“I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again” (John 10:17–18).

Yet when he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” he figuratively represented in himself certain of his members.

Often the mind already believes rightly and knows well that the future human being, according to his faith, will be in Abraham’s bosom. It believes this, and yet, when some moment of death arrives, it is disturbed by a certain familiarity with this world. It raises its hearing toward that inward voice of God and hears within a rational melody.

For something sounds from above in silence—not to the ears but to the mind—so that whoever hears that melody becomes wearied by bodily noise, and this whole human life becomes for him a kind of tumult that obstructs his hearing of a certain heavenly sound, exceedingly delightful, incomparable, and ineffable.

And truly, when this happens through some disturbance, the human being suffers violence and addresses his soul:

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disturb me?”

Or is it perhaps because a life purified with difficulty is discovered, when the one who knows how to judge with perfect clarity passes judgment? Even if one’s life is already considered praiseworthy among human beings, so that people have no just grounds for reproving it, the examination proceeds from the eyes of that Judge; the rule that makes no deceitful adjustment proceeds, and God finds in a person certain things to reprove that human beings did not see as deserving reproach—not even the person within who is to be judged.

Fearing this, the soul may perhaps be disturbed. The mind addresses it, as though saying:

“What do you fear concerning sins, since you cannot avoid them all? Hope in the Lord, for I will confess to him.”

The present address heals certain things; faithful confession cleanses what remains. Fear plainly, if you call yourself just; if you do not possess that saying from another Psalm:

“Do not enter into judgment with your servant.”

Why, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant”? Because I need your mercy. For if you bring judgment without mercy, where will I go? “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will stand?” (Psalm 129:3).

“Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

Therefore, if no living person will be justified in your sight, because whoever lives here, however justly he may live, is wretched if God enters into judgment with him.

For elsewhere another prophet repeatedly rebukes the arrogant and proud in this way:

“Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all deserted me, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 2:29).

Do not, then, contend in judgment. Take care to be just; and however just you may be, confess that you are a sinner. Always hope in mercy. In this humble confession [Note: Some manuscripts read “this urgent confession”], address with confidence [Col. 0482] the soul that disturbs and rages against you:

“Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disturb me?”

Perhaps you wanted to hope in yourself: “Hope in the Lord,” not in yourself. For what are you in yourself? What are you from yourself? Let him be your health within you who received wounds on your behalf.

“Hope,” he says, “in the Lord, for I will confess to him.”

What will you confess to him?

“The salvation of my face, my God.”

You are the salvation of my face; you will heal me. Sick, I speak to you; I acknowledge the physician, I do not boast that I am well.

What does “I acknowledge the physician, I do not boast that I am well” mean? It is said in another Psalm:

“I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Psalm 40:5).

## 8

This voice, brothers, is safe [Note: The Vatican and Regius manuscripts read “is yours”]. But be watchful in good works.

Touch the psaltery by obeying the commandments; touch the lyre by enduring sufferings.

“Break your bread for the hungry,” you have heard from Isaiah; do not think that fasting is sufficient. Fasting chastises you; it does not refresh another. Your hardships will be fruitful if you provide another person with relief.

Behold, you have defrauded your soul: to whom will you give what you have taken away from yourself? Where will you put what you have denied yourself? How many poor people could our interrupted meal today feed!

Fast in such a way that, while another eats, you rejoice that you have dined, for the sake of prayers, so that you may be heard.

For Isaiah says there:

“While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am,’ if you break your bread for the hungry from your heart” (Isaiah 58:7, 9–10).

This is because sad and complaining people often give in order to be free of the nuisance of the one who pleads with them, not in order to refresh the needy’s entrails:

“God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If you give bread sadly, you have lost both the bread and the merit. Therefore do it from the heart, so that the one who sees within, while you are still speaking, may say, “Here I am.”

How swiftly the prayers of those who do good are received! And this is the justice of a human being in this life: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer.

Do you want your prayer to fly to God? Give it two wings: fasting and almsgiving.

May the light of God and the truth of God find us such that they find us secure when he comes to free us from death—the one who has already come to undergo death for us.

Amen.

# Exposition of Psalm 43. Sermon to the People

## 1

This Psalm is addressed to the sons of Korah, as its title indicates. Korah is interpreted as “Baldness” or “Calvary,” and in the Gospel we find that the Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary (Matthew 27:33).

It is therefore clear that this Psalm is sung for the sons of his Passion.

We have here, moreover, the clearest and strongest testimony of the Apostle Paul. When the Church was laboring amid the persecutions of the Gentiles, he took from this Psalm a verse to insert into his exhortation and consolation concerning endurance. For here it is said what he placed in his Epistle:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Romans 8:36).

Let us therefore hear the voice [Col. 0483] of the martyrs in the Psalm. And see how good the martyrs’ cause is when it says, “For your sake.”

The Lord also added “for the sake of righteousness” when he said:

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness” (Matthew 5:10),

so that no one who suffers persecution might seek glory from the punishment itself while lacking a good cause.

For this reason he encouraged his own and said:

“You will be blessed when people do such and such things to you or say such and such things against you, for my sake.”

Hence this voice [Note: The editions read, “Hence the voice of the martyrs”; “of the martyrs” is absent from the manuscripts]:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long.”

## 2. [verse 1]

God’s plan is a matter of great reflection and great depth. What was the reason that, after bringing our fathers, the Patriarchs, and that entire people of Israel out of Egypt with a most powerful hand, drowning their pursuing enemies in the sea, leading them through hostile nations, defeating their enemies and placing them in the land of promise, and winning great victories through the small number of his people against the great multitude of their enemies, he later chose, as it were, to turn away from his people, so that his saints would suffer slaughter, killing, and death, while no one resisted, no one defended them, and no one prevented it?

It was as though he had turned his face away from their groanings, as though he had forgotten them, as though he were not the God who, with strong hand and outstretched arm and most evident power, had established our fathers—that people, as I have said—after freeing them from Egypt, defeating and driving out the nations from their land, and establishing them in a kingdom, while everyone marveled that often the many had been defeated by the few.

This, then, begins to be sung in this Psalm amid a groan of confession. These things did not happen without purpose; their purpose must be understood. Since it is clear that they happened, the reason why they happened must be sought more deeply.

For this reason the title says not merely “For the sons of Korah,” but “For understanding, for the sons of Korah” [Note: Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions instead read, “but understanding, for the sons of Korah”].

The same occurs in that Psalm whose first verse the Lord himself spoke from the cross: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”

For, transforming us into what he was saying, and into his body—for we too are his body, and he is our head—he did not speak from the cross in his own voice but in ours.

God never abandoned him, nor did he ever withdraw from the Father. But he said this on our behalf:

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

For there follows:

“Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses.”

And he showed in whose person he had spoken this; for no offense could be found in him.

“I will cry to you,” he says in that same Psalm, “by day, and you will not hear”; and by night is understood, naturally, “and you will not hear.” But he added:

“And not for folly to me” (Psalm 21:2–3),

that is, the fact that you do not hear will not be for my folly, but for my understanding.

What does “you will not hear for understanding” mean? It means: you will not hear me concerning temporal things, so that I may understand that I ought to desire eternal things.

God does not therefore abandon us; when he seems to abandon us, he takes away what we have desired wrongly and teaches us what we ought to desire rightly.

For if God always favored us in these prosperities, so that everything might abound for us, and if in this time of our mortality we suffered no tribulation, no pressures, and no difficulties, [Col. 0484] we would say that only these things are the supreme goods that God grants his servants, and we would not desire anything greater from him.

For this reason he mingles the bitterness of tribulations with this life, which is falsely sweet, so that another life, which is truly and healthfully sweet, may be sought. This is what “for understanding, for the sons of Korah” means.

Let us finally hear the Psalm, and observe this more clearly there.

## 3. [verses 2–3]

“O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers proclaimed to us the work that you performed in their days and in ancient days.”

They marvel [Note: All the manuscripts read the singular, “marveling,” and below, “recalls”] at why he seems in these days to have abandoned those whom he wished to exercise through sufferings, and they recall the past that they heard from their fathers, as though saying:

“Our fathers did not report to us the things we are suffering.”

For in that other Psalm he also said this:

“In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you rescued them. But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:5–7).

They hoped, and you delivered them. Did I hope, and you abandon me? Did I believe in you without cause? Was my name written with you without cause, and your name written in me without cause?

These things, then, our fathers declared to us:

“Your hand destroyed the nations and planted them; you weakened the peoples and drove them out.”

That is, you drove the peoples from their land in order to bring these people in and plant them, and by your mercy you established their kingdom.

“These things we heard from our fathers.”

## 4. [verse 4]

But perhaps they were able to accomplish those things because they were strong, because they were warriors, undefeated, trained, and warlike?

Far be it. Our fathers did not indicate this to us, nor does Scripture contain it. What does it contain, except what follows?

“For they did not take possession of the land by their own sword, and their own arm did not save them, but your right hand, your arm, and the light of your face.”

Your right hand is your power; your arm is your Son himself.

And “the light of your face”—what does this mean? It means that you were present to them through such signs that you were understood to be present.

For when God is present to us through some miracle, do we see his face with our eyes? No. Through the effect of the miracle he makes his presence known to human beings.

Indeed, what do all who marvel at such deeds say?

“I saw God present.”

“But your right hand, your arm, and the light of your face, because you were pleased with them.”

That is, you dealt with them in such a way that you were well pleased in them, so that anyone who observed how he dealt with them would say that God was truly with them and that God was directing them.

## 5. [verse 5]

What then? Was he one person then and another now?

Far be it. What follows?

“You are the same, my king and my God.”

You are the same; you have not changed. I see that the times have changed, but the creator of the times does not change.

“You are the same, my king and my God. You are accustomed to lead me; you are accustomed to govern me; you are accustomed to help me.”

“You who command salvation for Jacob.”

What does “who command” mean? Even if you are hidden in your very substance and nature, by which you are whatever you are, [Col. 0485] and even if you were not present to the fathers in such a way that they saw you face to face, nevertheless, through whatever creature, you command salvation for Jacob.

For that vision face to face is reserved for those liberated in the resurrection.

And although those fathers of the New Testament saw your mysteries revealed [Note: Most manuscripts read, “although they were entrusted with your revealed mystery.” One manuscript of the Fuliensian collection reads, “although they were reporters of your mystery”], although they proclaimed your secrets once revealed, they nevertheless said that they saw in a mirror and in an enigma; the vision, however, is reserved for the future, face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12), when what the Apostle himself says will come to pass:

“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4).

Then, therefore, that vision face to face will be reserved for us, of which John also says:

“Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we will be. We know that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Even if, therefore, our fathers did not see you face to face according to what you are, and even if this vision is reserved for the resurrection, nevertheless, even if angels were present, you command salvation for Jacob.

You are present not only through yourself; whenever you are present through any creature of yours, you command salvation for Jacob. What you yourself do through yourself, you command for the salvation of your servants; and what those whom you command do is done for the salvation of your servants. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “You command that this be done for the salvation of your servants, which is done by those whom you command.”]

Since, then, you are yourself my king and my God, and you command salvation for Jacob, why are we suffering these things now?

## 6. [verse 6]

But perhaps only the past has been related to us, and no such thing is to be hoped for in the future.

On the contrary, it is to be hoped for.

“In you we will winnow our enemies.”

Thus our fathers proclaimed to us the work that you performed in their days and in ancient days: your hand destroyed the nations, you drove out the peoples, and you planted them.

These things belong to the past. What will there be in the future?

“In you we will winnow our enemies.”

The time will come when all the enemies of Christians will be winnowed like chaff, winnowed like dust, and thrown from the earth.

If, then, the past has been related to us in this way and the future has been foretold in such terms, why do we suffer in the intervening present, except for the sake of understanding, for the sons of Korah?

“In you we will winnow our enemies, and in your name we will despise those who rise up against us.”

This concerns the future.

## 7. [verse 7]

“For I will not hope in my bow,” just as the fathers did not hope in their sword.

“And my sword will not save me.”

## 8. [verse 8]

“For you saved us from those who afflicted us.”

This too is spoken in the figure of the past concerning the future. It is said as though it were past because it is so certain that it is as though it had already happened.

Consider why the Prophets so often speak of things as though they were past when they are announcing future events, not things already accomplished.

The future Passion of the Lord himself was foretold, and yet he says:

“They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.”

He did not say, “They will pierce and count.” [Col. 0486]

“They themselves looked upon and observed me.”

He did not say, “They will look upon and observe.”

“They divided my garments among themselves” (Psalm 21:17, 19).

He did not say, “They will divide.”

All these things are spoken as though they were past, although they are future, because future things are as certain to God as past things are to us.

For us, things that have passed are certain; things that are future are uncertain. We know that something happened, and it cannot be that what happened did not happen.

Give me a prophet [Note: One manuscript reads, “for whom it is no less certain”] for whom the future is as certain as the past is for you. Just as what you remember to have happened cannot fail to have happened, so for him who knows the future, what he knows will happen cannot fail to happen.

Therefore, things that are still future are spoken of as though they were past because of their certainty.

This, then, is what we hope for:

“For you saved us from those who afflicted us, and you put to shame those who hated us.”

## 9. [verse 9]

“In God we will glory all day long.”

See how he also mixes in verbs of the future tense, so that you may understand that the past events he has mentioned were foretold concerning the future.

“In God we will glory all day long, and in your name we will confess forever.”

What does “we will glory” mean? What does “we will confess” mean? It means: because you have rescued us from all who afflicted us; because you will give us an everlasting kingdom; because the saying will be fulfilled in us:

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83:5).

## 10. [verse 10]

Since these future things are certain for us, and since we have heard those past things from our fathers, what is the situation now?

“But now you have rejected and put us to shame.”

You have put us to shame, not in our conscience but in the eyes of human beings. There was a time when Christians were afflicted, when they fled everywhere, when everywhere it was said, “He is a Christian,” as though this belonged to insult and reproach.

Where, then, is that God of ours, our king, who commands salvation for Jacob? Where is the one who did all the things our fathers reported to us? Where is the one who is going to do all the things he revealed to us through his Spirit?

Has he changed?

But these things occur for the understanding of the sons of Korah. We must understand why he wished us to suffer all these things in the intervening time.

What things?

“But now you have rejected and put us to shame, and you will not go forth, O God, with our armies.”

We advance against our enemies, and you do not advance with us. We see them; they prevail, and we are weak.

Where is your former strength? Where are your right hand and your power? Where is the sea dried up? Where are the Egyptians who pursued us and were overwhelmed by the waves (Exodus 14:21, 27)? Where is Amalek, who resisted but was defeated by the sign of the cross (ibid. 17:11)?

“And you will not go forth, O God, with our armies.”

## 11. [verse 11]

“But you turned us backward before our enemies,” so that they seemed to be ahead and we behind, they victorious and we considered defeated.

“And those who hated us plundered for themselves”—what, except us?

## 12. [verse 12]

“You gave us like sheep for food, and you scattered us among the nations.”

We were eaten by the nations. Those are signified who suffered in such a way that they were turned into the body [Col. 0487] of the nations.

For the Church mourns them as though her members had been devoured.

## 13. [verse 13]

“You sold your people for no price.”

For we saw those whom you gave away [Note: Several manuscripts read “what” instead of “those”], but we did not see what you received.

“And there was no multitude in their celebrations.”

For when Christians were fleeing from their idolatrous persecutors, were there gatherings and celebrations for God? Were hymns sung from the churches of God, such as are customarily sung in peace and resound in a sweet harmony of brotherhood to God’s ears?

“And there was no multitude in their celebrations.”

14. [verses 14–15.] You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those who are around us. You have made us a byword among the nations. What does “a byword” mean? When people curse, they give a formula concerning the person they detest: “May you die like this; may you be punished like this.” How many such things were said then? “May you be crucified like this.” Even today there are enemies of Christ—those same Jews—who, when we defend Christ against them, say to us: “May you die as he did.” They would not have inflicted that death unless they had greatly dreaded dying in that way—or what mystery it contained, if they had been able to understand it. When a blind man is anointed, he does not see the ointment in the physician’s hand. For the cross itself was also made for those persecutors. By it they were afterward healed and believed in the one whom they had killed.

You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples—a shaking of the head for the purpose of insult. “They spoke with their lips and shook their head” (Psalm 21:8). This happened to the Lord, and also to all his saints, whom they were able to persecute, seize, mock, hand over, afflict, and kill.

15. [verses 16–17.] All day long my disgrace is before me, and the shame of my face has covered me: at the voice of one reproaching and reviling me—that is, at the voice of those insulting me and charging me with a crime because I worship you, because I confess you; charging me with a crime on account of that name by which all my crimes will be erased. At the voice of one reproaching and reviling me—that is, of one speaking against me; at the face of the enemy and persecutor.

And what is the meaning here? The things spoken of as past will not happen among us; the things hoped for as future do not appear. What is past? In your great glory the people were led out of Egypt, delivered from their persecutors, led through the nations, and settled in a kingdom after the nations had been expelled. What is future? The people will be led out of this Egypt of the world, with Christ appearing as their leader in his glory; the saints will be placed at the right hand, the wicked at the left; the wicked will be condemned with the devil to eternal punishment; and the saints will receive the kingdom from Christ forever. These are the future things; those are the past.

What lies between them? Tribulations. Why? So that the disposition of the person who worships God may be revealed—how greatly he worships God—and so that it may be seen whether he worships him freely, from whom he freely received salvation. For if God says to you, “What did you give me in order that I might make you?”—certainly, if you earned my favor after you were made, you had not earned it before I made you. What shall we say to him who first made us freely, because he is good, not because we had earned anything? Then, concerning the restoration itself, concerning the second birth, what shall we say? That our merits caused this everlasting salvation to be sent to us by the Lord? Far from it. If our merits accomplished anything, he would have come for our condemnation. He did not come to examine merits, but to remit sins.

You did not exist, and you were made: what did you give God? You were evil, and you were delivered: what did you give God? What did you not receive freely from him? It is rightly called grace, because it is given freely. It is therefore required of you that you too worship him freely—not because he gives temporal things, but because he grants eternal things.

16. But take care not to think of those eternal things in another way, and, by thinking carnally about eternal things, nevertheless fail to worship God freely. What then? If you worship God because he gives you an estate, will you not worship him because he takes your estate away? But perhaps you say, “I will worship him because he will give me a country estate—not, however, a temporal one.” Even so, you still possess a corrupted mind: you do not worship with chaste love; you still seek a reward. You want to have in the future age the things that you must leave behind here: you want to change carnal pleasure, not cut it off.

A person who keeps his stomach for a luxurious banquet is not praised for fasting. Sometimes people are invited to a great banquet, and, because they want to come to it with an appetite, they fast. Is that fasting to be counted as self-restraint, and not rather as indulgence? Do not therefore hope that God will give you the sort of things that he commands you to despise here.

The Jews were hoping for such things, and that is why they were disturbed by that question. They too hope for a resurrection, but they hope to be resurrected to such bodily pleasures as they love here. Therefore, when the Sadducees, who do not believe in the resurrection, put to them the question about the woman who married seven brothers in succession—“Which of them will she be the wife of in the resurrection?”—they were at a loss and could not answer. [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The editions read: “in the future resurrection, they would be at a loss.”]

But when the question was put to the Lord, because the resurrection promised to us is not one in which such pleasures are recovered, but one in which eternal joys are obtained from God himself, the Lord answered and said: “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage; for they will not begin to die” (Matthew 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36). That is: no successor is sought where there will be no predecessor.

And what will there be? “They will be equal,” he says, “to the angels of God.” Unless you suppose that angels rejoice in daily banquets and in the wine with which you intoxicate yourself, or perhaps imagine that angels have wives. None of these things exists among the angels. From what do the angels rejoice, except from what the Lord says: “Do you not know that their angels always behold the face of my Father?” (Matthew 18:10). If, then, the angels rejoice in the face of the Father, prepare yourself for such joy. Or can you find something better than beholding the face of God? [Note: In the editions, “prepare yourself there” is added here; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

Woe to such love of yours if you even suspect that something more beautiful than he exists—he from whom comes all beauty—which might hold you back from desiring to contemplate him.

The Lord was in the flesh and appeared as a human being to human beings. What sort of person did he appear to be? I have already said: a human being to human beings. What great thing appeared? Flesh to flesh. What great thing appeared of him concerning whom it was said: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2)? Who had neither form nor beauty? The one of whom it is also said: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). As a human being, he had neither form nor beauty; but he was beautiful in form insofar as he was beyond the sons of men.

Therefore, displaying that deformed form of flesh to the eyes of those who looked upon him, what did he say? [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “deformed”; the editions read “of the form.”] “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14:21). He promised that he would show himself to those who saw him. But what does this mean? It is as though he were saying: “You see the form of a servant; the form of God is hidden. Through this form I court you; that form I reserve for you. By this I nourish you as little ones; by that I feed you as adults.”

Therefore, so that this faith of ours, by which we are cleansed, may be prepared for invisible things, all these things were set forth in the understanding of the sons of Korah: so that what the saints possessed might be taken away from them, and temporal life itself might also be taken away, in order that they might not worship the eternal one for the sake of these temporal things, but might endure through chaste love of him all that they would suffer for a time.

17. [verses 18–19.] Finally, because the sons of Korah understood this, what do they say? “All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you.” What does “we have not forgotten you” mean? “We have not acted wickedly against your covenant, and our heart has not turned back; yet you have turned our paths away from your way.”

Here is the meaning: our heart has not turned back; we have not forgotten you; we have not acted wickedly against your covenant, though we have been placed amid great tribulations and persecutions of the nations.

“You have turned our paths away from your way.” For our paths were in the pleasures of the world; our paths were in the prosperity of temporal affairs. You removed our paths from your way and showed us how narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life. “You have turned our paths away from your way.”

What does “you have turned our paths away from your way” mean? It is as though he were saying to us: “You have been placed in tribulation; you suffer many things; you have lost many things that you loved in this world. But I have not abandoned you on the way that I teach you is narrow. You were seeking broad paths; what do I tell you? ‘This is the way to eternal life.’ The way on which you wish to walk leads to death. How broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and how many there are who walk through it! How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and how few there are who walk through it!” (Matthew 7:13–14).

Who are the few? Those who endure tribulations, who endure temptations, who do not fail amid all these troubles; who do not rejoice for a moment at the word and then, when tribulation comes, wither as though the sun had risen (Matthew 13:20–21, 23), but possess the root of love, as we heard in what has just been read in the Gospel (Mark 4:16–17, 20; Luke 8:13, 15).

I say: possess the root of love, so that when the sun has risen, it may not scorch you but nourish you.

“All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you; we have not acted wickedly against your covenant, and our heart has not turned back.” But because we do all these things amid tribulations, now walking on the narrow way, “you have turned our paths away from your way.”

18. [verse 20.] “For you have humbled us in a place of weakness.” Therefore you will exalt us in a place of strength. “And the shadow of death has covered us.” This mortality is indeed the shadow of death. The true death is condemnation with the devil.

19. [verse 21.] “If we have forgotten the name of our God”—this is the understanding of the sons of Korah—“and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god.”

20. [verse 22.] “Will not God search this out?” For he knows the hidden things of the heart. He knows and searches: if he knows the hidden things of the heart, what does he do by searching them out? “Will not God search this out?” He knows in himself; he searches for our sake.

For this is why God sometimes searches and says that he has come to know something: he says that he has done what he makes known to you. He tells you of his action, not of his knowledge. [Note: Two manuscripts read: “not to his knowledge.”] We often say, “A joyful day,” when the weather is clear. Does the day itself rejoice? We call it joyful because it makes us rejoice. We say, “A gloomy sky.” There is no such feeling in the clouds; but because people are saddened when they see such a face of the sky, it is called gloomy because it makes them gloomy.

So God is also said to know when he makes people know. God says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12). Had he not known before? Abraham himself had not known himself; for through that very testing he became known to himself. [Note: In most manuscripts, “had known himself,” with the negation omitted.] Often a person thinks he can do what he cannot, or thinks he cannot do what he can. A question, arising from God’s providential arrangement, comes to him, and through the question he becomes known to himself; and God is said to have known what he caused him to know.

Did Peter know himself when he said to the physician, “I am with you even to death” (Matthew 26:35)? The physician knew, having examined the vein, what was happening within the sick man; the sick man did not know. The attack of temptation came; the physician proved his own diagnosis, and the sick man lost his presumption.

Thus God both knows and searches. He knows. How does he search? For your sake, so that you may discover yourself and give thanks to him who made you. “Will not God search this out?”

21. “For he knows the hidden things of the heart.” What does “he knows the hidden things” mean? What hidden things? “For on your account we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.”

You can see a person being put to death; why he is being put to death, you do not know. God knows this; the matter is hidden. But someone says to me: “Look, he is detained for the name of Christ; he confesses the name of Christ.” Why do heretics also confess the name of Christ, and yet no longer die for him? [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “Why do heretics confess the name of Christ, and yet no longer die for him?” Ambrosianus and several manuscripts read: “Why? Do heretics not also confess the name of Christ, but nevertheless do not die for him?” Other manuscripts read: “Why do heretics also confess the name of Christ,” and so forth.]

Indeed, even within the Catholic Church itself, I say, do you think there have not been, or could not be, people who suffered for the sake of human glory? If there were no such people, the Apostle would not say: “If I deliver my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3). He knew, therefore, that some could do this from ostentation, not from love.

The matter is hidden; God alone sees it, and we cannot. He alone can judge, who knows the hidden things of the heart.

“For on your account we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” I have already said that the apostle Paul also used this testimony to encourage martyrs, so that they would not fail amid the tribulations they undertook for the name of Christ.

22. [verse 23.] “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” To whom does he say this, and who says it? Would it not rather be said that the person who speaks in this way—“Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?”—is the one who is sleeping and bleating? [Note: The editions read “sleeping, bleating, and howling.” The manuscripts omit “howling”; some read “breathing” or “bellowing” in place of “bleating.”] He answers you: “I know what I am saying; I know that he does not sleep who guards Israel” (Psalm 120:4). Nevertheless the martyrs cry out: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?”

O Lord Jesus! You were killed; you slept in your passion; now you have risen for us. For we know that you have risen for us. Why did you rise? The nations that persecute us think you are dead; they do not believe that you have risen. Rise, then, also for them. Why do you sleep—not for us, but for them?

If they already believed that you had risen, could they persecute those who believed in you? But why do they persecute them? “Destroy, kill—I do not know whom—those who have believed in you, some badly dead one.” [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read this way. The editions instead read: “They have destroyed, they have killed those who believed in you—some unknown one,” and so forth.]

You are still asleep for them. Rise, so that they may understand that you have risen and cease.

And so it happened: while the martyrs were dying and saying these things, they slept, and by their own falling asleep awakened Christ, who had truly died. Christ rose, in a certain sense, among the nations—that is, he was believed to have risen. Thus, little by little, even the nations themselves were converted to Christ through believing, and they formed a great number that the persecutors feared, and the persecutions ceased.

Why? Because Christ rose among the nations, among whom he had previously slept because they did not believe in him.

“Rise up, and do not reject us forever.”

23. [verse 24.] “Why do you turn your face away?”—as though you were not present, as though you had forgotten us. “Will you forget our poverty and our tribulation?”

24. [verse 25.] “For our soul has been humbled in the dust.” Where has it been humbled? In the dust—that is, the dust persecutes us. They persecute us of whom you said: “Not so are the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4).

“Our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth.” He seems to have expressed the punishment of excessive humiliation, by which, whenever someone prostrates himself, his belly clings to the earth. For anyone who is humbled in such a way that he fixes his knees still has somewhere to humble himself further; but one who is humbled so that his belly clings to the earth has nowhere further to be humbled. If he wishes to go beyond that, it will no longer be humbling but burying.

Perhaps, then, he said this: “We have been humbled too greatly in this dust; we have nowhere further to be humbled. Humiliation has now reached its highest point; let pity also come.”

25. Or perhaps, brothers, the Church laments those whom the persecutors persuaded to impiety in these words, so that those who endured might say: “Our soul has been humbled in the dust.” That is: amid the hands of this dust, amid the hands of the impious and persecutors, “our soul has been humbled in the dust” in order that we might call upon you, so that you might give help in tribulation.

But “our belly has clung to the earth”—that is, our belly consented to the impiety of this dust; for this is what “has clung” means. If, when you love and burn with charity, you rightly say to God, “My soul has clung after you” (Psalm 62:9), and, “For me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28)—you cling to God when you consent to God—then it was not without reason that it was said of this belly that it “clung to the earth,” since those are signified who, unable to endure persecution, consented to the wicked. Thus they clung to the earth.

But why are they called “the belly”? Because they are carnal: the mouth of the Church is in the saints, in the spiritual; the belly of the Church is in the carnal. Thus the mouth of the Church stands out, while the belly is hidden, as being softer and weaker.

Scripture signifies this somewhere when someone says that he received a book, and that the book was sweet in his mouth but bitter in his belly (Revelation 10:10). What does this mean, except that the highest commands, which spiritual people can grasp, are not grasped by the carnal; [Note: The manuscripts read “grasp” (*capiunt*) here and in the following clause; the editions read “receive” (*accipiunt*).] and that what delights the spiritual makes the carnal sad?

What does this book contain, brothers? “Sell everything you have and give to the poor.” How sweet it is in the mouth of the Church! It has been done by all the spiritual. But if you say this to any carnal person, “Do this,” he more readily goes away from you sad, like that rich man from the Lord (Matthew 19:21–22), than does what was commanded.

Why did he go away sad, except because that book is sweet in the mouth but bitter in the belly?

You have given away some gold and silver. The matter reaches this point: unless you suffer a loss, you may perhaps commit some sin; perhaps you may inflict an injustice upon the Church; you may be forced to blaspheme. When you are placed in difficulties—faced either with the loss of money or the loss of justice—you are told: “Lose your money rather, so that you do not lose justice.”

But you, for whom justice is not sweet in the mouth, who are still weak in those members whom the Church counts as the belly, become sad and sometimes choose to lose something of justice rather than even one coin of money. [Note: Some manuscripts read “the smallest amount.”] You strike yourself with the greater loss, filling your purse and emptying your heart.

Perhaps, then, he said of such people: “Our belly has clung to the earth.”

26. [verse 26.] “Rise up, O Lord; help us.” And truly, beloved, he rose up and helped us. For when he rose—that is, when he rose again—and became known among the nations, the persecutions ceased. Even those who had clung to the earth were drawn out of the earth, and, doing penance, were restored to the body of Christ, although weak and imperfect, so that what was written might be fulfilled in them: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all shall be written” (Psalm 138:16).

“Rise up, O Lord; help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name”—that is, freely; for the sake of your name, not for the sake of my merit, because you deigned to do it, not because I am worthy for you to do it.

For even this—that we have not forgotten you, that our heart has not turned back, and that we have not spread out our hands to a foreign god—if you had not helped us, from where could we have obtained it? If you had not addressed and encouraged us inwardly, and had not abandoned us, from where could we have had strength? [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions instead have: “For if you had abandoned us, from where would we have had strength?”]

Therefore, whether we are patient in tribulations or rejoicing in prosperity, redeem us—not for the sake of our merit, but for the sake of your name.

# Exposition of Psalm 44: Sermon

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript and in the very ancient Remigius book, this psalm bears the following title: “This psalm begins on the fifth day before the Nones of September, on Wednesday; the sermon was delivered in the Basilica Restituta.” In the secretary’s office of this basilica, records of certain councils of Carthage are prefixed, including the general Council of Carthage held in the year 401, on 13 September.]

[Note: Addressed to the people of Carthage.]

1. [verse 1.] Just as we sang this psalm with exultation together with you, so I ask you to consider it attentively together with us. For it is sung about a holy wedding, about bridegroom and bride, about king and people, about the Savior and those who are to be saved.

Whoever comes to the wedding wearing a wedding garment, seeking the glory of the bridegroom and not his own, not only gladly hears what is customary even among people who seek spectacles rather than provide deeds, but also entrusts it to his heart, so that it may not lie idle there, but may germinate, burst forth, grow, be perfected, and be taken up.

For we must be those to whom this is sung: the sons of Korah, as the title of the psalm has it. [Note: Vatican and Regius manuscripts read: “For we must know by whom this is sung: the sons of Korah.”] These were indeed certain human beings; nevertheless, every inscription of the divine Scriptures intimates something to those who understand, and seeks not merely a hearer but also one who knows.

We ask about the force of the Hebrew word: what does “Korah” mean? And, according to the interpretations of all the words placed in Scripture, we are told that “sons of Korah” is interpreted as “sons of the Bald One.” Do not take this name as an insult, lest we be found to possess a childish understanding, like the boys whom we read about in the Book of Kings, who insulted the holy prophet Elisha and shouted after him: “Go up, bald one! Go up, bald one!” Such foolish, chattering boys, cursing to their own destruction, were coming out of the forest when wild beasts devoured them (2 Kings 2:23–24).

This has been written, and we have recalled where it was written. Those who remember it may recognize it; those who do not remember it may read it; those who have not read it may believe it.

Therefore, what that event prefigured for the future should not seize us. For foolish people were signified in those boys, people possessing an ignorant understanding—people whom the Apostle does not want us to be when he says: “Do not be children in your minds” (1 Corinthians 14:20).

And because the Lord had invited us to imitate children when he placed a little child before him and said, “Unless someone becomes like this child, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:2–3), there too the Apostle, careful to call us away from a childish mind, again calls us to imitate children: “Do not become children in your minds,” he says, “but be little ones in wickedness, so that you may be mature in your minds” (1 Corinthians 14:20).

Whoever delights in imitating a child should imitate not ignorance but innocence.

Those boys, however, in their ignorance, insulted the holy Bald One of God and shouted after him: “Bald one, bald one.” It happened that they were consumed by wild beasts; and they prefigured people of the same childish mind, foolishly mocking a certain bald man, because he was crucified at the place of Calvary.

Such people were therefore possessed as though by wild beasts—that is, by demons, by the devil and his angels, who work in the sons of disobedience. Such were the boys who stood before the sacred wood, shaking their heads and saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:33, 39–40).

We are sons of this one, because we are sons of the bridegroom. And this psalm has been inscribed for us, whose title is said to be “For the sons of Korah, concerning the things that will be changed.” [Note: The editions read “concerning those who will be changed,” and somewhat further below “through whom they were changed.” The better manuscripts instead read “concerning the things that will be changed.” In the Septuagint, the Greek expression *hyper tōn alloiōthēsomenōn* is grammatically ambiguous in gender.]

2. What shall I explain about “concerning the things that will be changed”? What shall I say? Every changed person recognizes this. Whoever hears the words “concerning the things that will be changed” should see what he was and what he now is.

First, let him see the world itself changed: formerly worshiping idols, now worshiping God; formerly serving the things it made, now serving the one by whom it was made.

“Concerning the things that will be changed”—see when this was said. Now the remaining pagans are terrified by the changes; those who do not wish to change see churches filled and temples deserted: crowds here, solitude there. They marvel at the changes; let them read what was foretold. Let them lend an ear to the one who promised and believe the one who fulfilled.

But each one of us also, brothers, is changed from the old person into the new: the unbeliever becomes faithful, the plunderer generous, the adulterer chaste, the evildoer beneficent.

Therefore let “concerning the things that will be changed” be sung to us, and let it thus begin to be described through whom they were changed.

3. [The psalm] continues: “Concerning the things that will be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding, a song concerning the beloved.”

That beloved was seen by his persecutors, but not with understanding. For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). He himself was seeking other eyes for this understanding when he said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

Let the psalm now sound forth: let us rejoice at the wedding, and let us ourselves be among those who become the nuptials, who are invited to the wedding; the invited persons themselves are the bride. [Note: Several manuscripts omit “who become the nuptials.”] For the bride is the Church, and the bridegroom is Christ.

Certain songs are customarily recited by the *scholastici* for men taking wives and for those marrying; these are called epithalamia. [Note: The editions read *scholasticis*; the manuscripts read *scolasticis*, perhaps to be restored as *scoliasticis*, from *scolion*, a Greek convivial song customarily sung over cups.] Whatever is sung there is sung to the honor of bridegroom and bride. Or perhaps, in this wedding to which we have been invited, there is no bridal chamber? And from where does another psalm say: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm 18:6)?

The nuptial union is Word and flesh; the bridal chamber of this union is the virgin’s womb. For the flesh itself has been joined to the Word. Hence it is also said: “They are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6; Ephesians 5:32).

The Church was taken from the human race, so that the flesh itself joined to the Word might be the head of the Church, and the other believers might be members of that head.

For do you wish to see who came to the wedding? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Let the bride beloved by God rejoice. When was she loved? While she was still ugly. For “all have sinned,” says the Apostle, “and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). And again: “Christ indeed died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

She was loved while ugly, so that she might not remain ugly. For she was not truly loved as ugly, because ugliness was not loved; if he had loved that, he would have preserved it. He overturned ugliness and fashioned beauty.

To what sort of one did he come, and what sort did he make her? Let the bridegroom himself now come in the words of the prophets; let him come forth to us: let us love him. Or, if we find anything ugly in him, let us not love him. Behold, he found many ugly things in us and loved us. If we find anything ugly in him, let us not love him.

For even the fact that he put on flesh was such that it could be said of him: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2). But if you consider the mercy by which he was made what he was, he is beautiful even there.

The prophet was representing the person of the Jews when he said: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty.” Why? Because they did not understand. But to those who understand, “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14)—and this is great beauty.

“But far be it from me to glory,” said one of the friends of the bridegroom, “except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). It is not enough that you do not blush with shame because of it; you must also glory in it.

Why, then, did he have neither form nor beauty? Because Christ crucified is “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.” But why did he also possess beauty on the cross? Because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Corinthians 1:23, 25).

For us, then, who now believe, let the beautiful bridegroom meet us everywhere.

Beautiful is God, the Word with God; beautiful in the virgin’s womb, where he did not lose divinity but assumed humanity; beautiful as the Word born an infant, for even when he was an infant, when he suckled, when he was carried in hands, the heavens spoke, the angels sang praises, a star guided the Magi, and he was worshiped in the manger—the food of the gentle (Luke 2:8–14; Matthew 2:1).

Beautiful, therefore, in heaven; beautiful on earth; beautiful in the womb; beautiful in the hands of his parents; beautiful in his miracles; beautiful under the scourges; beautiful inviting to life; beautiful unconcerned with death; beautiful in laying down his life; beautiful in receiving it again; beautiful on the wood; beautiful in the tomb; beautiful in heaven.

“For understanding”—listen to the song, and do not let the weakness of the flesh turn your eyes away from the radiance of his beauty. [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions read “beautiful in understanding. Hear the song,” and so forth.]

The highest and true beauty is justice. You will not see him beautiful where you find him unjust; if he is just everywhere, he is beautiful everywhere.

Let him therefore come to be examined by the eyes of our mind, described by one of his prophetic eulogists. Behold, it begins.

4. [verse 2.] “My heart has poured forth a good word.” Who says this—the Father or the prophet? Some have understood it as the person of the Father saying, “My heart has poured forth a good word,” commending to us an ineffable birth.

Lest you imagine that God assumed something from which he might generate the Son, as a human being assumes something from which to beget children—namely, marriage, without which a human being cannot produce offspring—lest, then, you imagine that God needed some marriage by which to generate the Son, he says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.”

Today your heart, O human being, generates a plan, and it does not seek a wife. Through the plan born from your heart you build something; and that structure, before it stands in the work, stands in the plan. [Note: All the manuscripts read: “and that structure, before it stands, the plan stands.”] What you are about to make is already present in that by which you are going to make it. You praise a structure that does not yet exist, that does not yet possess the form of a building, but exists in the expression of the plan; and no one else praises your plan unless you have either disclosed it or he has seen what you made.

Therefore, if all things were made through the Word, and the Word is from God, inspect the structure made through the Word, and from this building admire the plan.
