What sort of Word is it through which heaven and earth were made, and all the adornment of heaven, all the fertility of the earth, the expanse of the sea, the breadth of the air, the splendor of the stars, the brightness of the sun and moon? These things are visible; rise above them also. Consider the angels, principalities, thrones, dominions, powers: all things were made through him.

From where, then, were these good things made? Because that through which they were to be made was poured forth: a good Word.

Therefore, “good Word”; and to that same Word it was said, “Good Teacher.” And the Word itself replied: “Why do you ask me about the good? No one is good except one, God” (Matthew 19:17; Mark 10:18).

It was said, “Good Teacher,” and he says, “Why do you ask me about the good?” He added, “No one is good except one, God.” How, then, is he himself good, except because he is God? And not merely God, but one God with the Father.

For in saying, “No one is good except one, God,” he did not distinguish himself, but united himself.

“My heart has poured forth a good word.” May God the Father have said this concerning his good and beneficent Word, our good, through whom alone we can in any way be good.

### 5

It follows: “I speak of my works to the king.” Is the Father still speaking? If the Father is still speaking, let us also inquire how we are to understand, according to the true and catholic faith, “I speak of my works to the king.” For if the Father says his works to his Son, our king, what works will the Father speak to the Son, since all the Father’s works were made through the Son? Or perhaps “I speak of my works to the king”—the very word “I speak”—signifies the generation of the Son?

I fear that this may at some time be impossible for the slower-minded to understand; nevertheless, I shall speak. Let whoever can follow, so that, if I do not speak, even one who can follow may not fail to follow. [Col. 0497] We read elsewhere in the Psalms: “God has spoken once” (Ps. 61:12). He has spoken so many times through the Prophets, so many times through the Apostles, and even today he speaks through his saints; yet he says, “God has spoken once.” Why has he spoken once, unless because of the one Word? [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions: “unless through his one Word.”] Just as “My heart has uttered a good word” was understood there as referring to the generation of the Son, so the following sentence seems to me to repeat the same thing: what was said, “My heart has uttered a good word,” is repeated in the words, “I speak.”

For what is “I speak”? I bring forth a word. And from where does God bring forth the Word, unless from his own heart, from his inmost being? You speak only what you bring forth from your heart; your word, which sounds and passes away, is brought forth from nowhere else. And you marvel that God speaks in this way? But God’s speaking is eternal. You speak something now because a little earlier you were silent—or look, even now you have not yet brought forth a word; but when you begin to bring it forth, you somehow break the silence and generate a word that previously did not exist.

God did not beget the Word in this way. God’s speaking is without beginning and without end, and yet he speaks one Word. Let him speak another, if what he has spoken has passed away. But when both the one from whom it is spoken remains and that which is spoken remains, when it is spoken once and does not cease, and when that “once” is spoken without beginning and is not spoken twice—for what is spoken once does not pass away—then this is what is meant by “My heart has uttered a good word”: “I speak of my works to the king.”

Why, then, does he say, “I speak of my works”? Because all God’s works are in that Word. Whatever God was going to make in creation already existed in the Word; and it would not exist in reality unless it existed in the Word—just as it would not be in the structure in you unless it existed in your plan [Note: Several manuscripts read, “a structure would not exist,” without the preposition “in.”]. As it is said in the Gospel: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3–4). Therefore what was made existed, but it existed in the Word; and all God’s works were there, though the works themselves did not yet exist. The Word existed, and this Word was God, and was with God, and was the Son of God, and was one God with the Father.

“I speak of my works to the king.” Let the one who understands the Word hear him speaking, and let him see the Word, eternal with the Father, in whom even the things that will be exist, and in whom the things that have passed away have not passed away. These are God’s works in the Word—in the Word, in the Only-Begotten, in the Word of God.

### 6

What follows, then? “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.” What similarity is there, my brothers, between God’s tongue and a scribe’s pen? What similarity is there between the rock and Christ (1 Cor. 10:4)? What similarity is there between the lamb and the Savior (John 1:29)? What similarity is there between the lion and the strength of the Only-Begotten (Rev. 5:5)?

Yet these things were said; and unless they were said, we could not in some way be shaped by visible things toward the invisible. So let us neither compare this humble likeness of a pen with that excellence nor reject it. For I ask why he said that his tongue was the pen of a swiftly writing scribe. However swiftly a scribe may write, it cannot be compared with the swiftness of which another psalm says: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147:15).

But it seems to me, [Col. 0498] insofar as human understanding dares, that this too can be understood as spoken in the person of the Father: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe.” What is called the tongue sounds and passes away; what is written remains. Therefore, when God speaks the Word, and the Word that is spoken does not sound and pass away but is both spoken and remains, God preferred to compare this with writing rather than with sounds.

But when he added, “of one who writes swiftly,” he impelled the mind toward understanding. Yet the mind must not remain sluggish by looking at ancient copyists or at any kind of swift shorthand writers; if it attends to this, it will remain there. Let it consider the “swiftly” as swift, and see why it was said. God’s swiftness is such that nothing is swifter.

In Scripture, one letter is written after another, one syllable after another, one word after another; and one does not pass to the second until the first has been completely written. But there is nothing swifter there where there are not many words, and yet nothing has been omitted, since everything is contained in one.

### 7. [verse 3]

Behold, that Word, thus brought forth, eternal and coeternal from eternity, will come as the bridegroom: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.”

“Beyond the sons of men”: why does he not also say, beyond the angels? What did he wish to say by “beyond the sons of men,” unless that he is man? Lest you should think that Christ, a man, was merely any man, he says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” He is also man beyond the sons of men; even among the sons of men, beyond the sons of men; even from the sons of men, beyond the sons of men.

“Grace has been poured upon your lips.” The Law was given through Moses; “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). “Grace has been poured upon your lips.”

I have rightly been helped, because “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.” But “another law in my members wars against the law of my mind and takes me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

“Grace, therefore, has been poured upon your lips.” He came to us with the word of grace [Note: The Corbie manuscript has *verbum*, “the word,” rather than *verbo*, “with the word.”], with the kiss of grace. What is sweeter than this grace? To what does this grace pertain? “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 32:1).

If the severe Judge had come and had not brought this grace poured upon his lips, who would have hoped for anything concerning salvation? Who would not have feared for himself what was owed to the sinner? He came with grace; he did not demand what was owed, but paid what he did not owe. Did the sinner not owe death? Or, indeed, what was owed to you, a sinner, except punishment? He forgave your debts and paid what he did not owe. Great is grace.

Why is it called grace? Because it is given freely. Therefore you may give thanks to him, but you cannot repay him; you are not able. He was seeking what he might repay and said: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” And he found, as it were, something: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 116:12–13).

Is this what you repay him—that you receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord? Who gave you that very cup of salvation? He remained in the act of giving thanks, but failed in the act of repayment. Find something that you can give to God which [Col. 0499] you have not received from him, and then you will have repaid him. But beware lest, while you seek what you may repay him, you find something that you have not received from him—namely, your sin. You certainly did not receive this from him, but neither ought you to give it to him.

The Jews gave this: they repaid evil for good. They received rain from him, but bore no fruit; instead they produced the thorns of suffering. Therefore, whatever good you wish to give God in yourself, you find that you have received it from God alone.

This is the grace of God poured upon his lips. He made you; he made you freely. Before he made you, there was no one to whom he owed this favor. You had perished; he sought you, and, having found you, brought you back. He did not reckon your past against you; he promised you the future. Truly, grace has been poured upon your lips.

### 8

“Therefore,” he says, “God has blessed you forever.”

There is difficulty in understanding this as still spoken by God the Father: “Therefore God has blessed you forever.” It seems more suitably understood as spoken in the person of the Prophet. Sudden changes of persons, entirely unexpected, are found in the holy books of Scripture; and if anyone observes this, the divine pages are full of them.

“Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue”; and immediately: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” There one person was speaking and here another: there, the one asking; here, the one helping. “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with consuming coals.”

Another person is speaking in “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you?”; and in what follows another appears: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Ps. 120:2–5). Such frequent changes of persons in a few verses admonish the understanding. The text does not indicate the place where the person changes; it does not say, “This was spoken by a human being, this by God.” Rather, from the words themselves we are made to understand what pertains to man and what to God.

The man was saying: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak of my works to the king.” The man was speaking—the one who wrote the psalm—but he was speaking in the person of God. Then he begins to speak also in his own person: “Therefore God has blessed you forever.”

For God had said: “Grace has been poured upon your lips,” to the one whom he had made beautiful beyond the sons of men—indeed, to the man whom God had set before all things [Note: So the manuscripts read. Lovaniensis has: “whom God had preferred before all things.”]—the eternal one coeternal with himself. The Prophet was therefore filled with a kind of ineffable joy, and, observing what God the Father had revealed to man concerning his Son [Note: So the manuscripts. In Lovaniensis, *de* (“concerning”) is absent here, and *qui* (“who”) is omitted shortly afterward], he was able to say this also in the person of God: “Therefore,” he says, “God has blessed you forever.”

Why? Because of grace. To what does that grace pertain? To the kingdom of heaven. For the First Testament had promised the earth; and there was one reward, or promise, for those placed under the Law, and another for those placed under grace: the land of Canaan for the Jews placed under the Law, and the kingdom of heaven for Christians placed under grace.

Thus, what pertained to those who were placed under the Law—the kingdom, that earthly land—has passed away; but the kingdom of heaven, which pertains to those placed under grace, does not pass away. Therefore here he says, “God has blessed you,” not for a time but forever.

### 9

[Col. 0500] There have been those who preferred to understand all the preceding words as spoken in the person of the Prophet. They wished even “My heart has uttered a good word” to be understood as spoken by the Prophet, as though he were singing a hymn. For whoever sings a hymn to God utters from his heart a good word; just as whoever blasphemes against God utters from his heart an evil word.

They also wished “I speak of my works to the king” to signify that man’s supreme work is nothing other than to praise God. His beauty is what pleases you; it is your responsibility to praise him in thanksgiving. If your works are not the praise of God, you begin to love yourself and become one of those of whom the Apostle says: “For men will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2).

Displease yourself, and let the one who made you please you; for you displease yourself in what you yourself have made in yourself. Therefore let your work be the praise of God; let your heart utter a good word. Speak of your works to the king, because the king made you able to speak, and he himself gave you what you might offer.

Return to him what is his own. Do not wish, having received your share of your inheritance, to go off into a distant land and waste it prodigally among prostitutes [Note: Most manuscripts have: “to go off into a distant land and squander it on prostitutes”], and feed pigs. Remember this from the Gospel. But it was also said concerning us: “He was dead and came to life again; he was lost and was found” (Luke 15:32).

### 10

“My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe.”

There have been those who understood the Prophet to have spoken the things he was writing, and therefore to have compared his tongue with a scribe’s pen. By “one who writes swiftly,” they understood him to mean that he was writing things that were soon to come, so that “to write swiftly” meant “to write things that would happen swiftly,” that is, things not destined to be delayed.

For God did not delay in presenting Christ. How quickly is what has been accomplished felt to have unfolded! Recall the generations before you: you will find Adam made, as it were, yesterday. Thus we read that everything was accomplished from the very beginning; therefore it was done swiftly.

The day of judgment will also come swiftly. Anticipate its swiftness: it will come swiftly, so change more swiftly yourself. The face of the Judge will be present, but see what the Prophet says: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Ps. 95:2).

“Grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.”

### 11. [verse 4]

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.”

Your sword—what is it except your word? With that sword he struck down enemies; with that sword he divided son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law.

We read these things in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. And in one household five will be divided against one another, two against three and three against two: son against father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matt. 10:34–35; Luke 12:51–53).

By what sword was this division made, unless by the one Christ brought? [Note: All manuscripts have: “By what sword was this division made? Christ brought it”; they do not have “unless by the one.”]

And indeed, brothers, we see these things even in daily examples. A young man wishes to serve God; his father is displeased. They are divided against one another. The one promises an earthly inheritance; the other loves a heavenly one. One makes one promise; the other chooses something else.

Let the father not think that an injury has been done to him: God alone has been preferred to him. Yet he quarrels with his son who wishes to serve God. But that spiritual sword, which separates, is stronger than [Col. 0501] carnal nature, which joins.

The same happens with daughter against mother, and much more with daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. For sometimes a daughter-in-law and a mother-in-law are found in one household, one a heretic and the other a Catholic. And where this sword is received courageously, we do not fear rebaptism. A daughter could be divided against her mother; surely a daughter-in-law can be divided against her mother-in-law.

### 12

This also happened generally within the human race: son was divided against father. For we were once sons of the devil. To unbelievers it was said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44). And all our unbelief—from where does it come except from the father devil? He was not our father by creating us, but we became his sons by imitating him [Note: In this sentence the manuscripts omit the words “father” and “sons.”].

Now you see a son divided against his father. That sword came; he renounces the devil, finds another father, and finds another mother. The one who offered himself for imitation was generating people for destruction; the two parents whom we find generate us for eternal life.

Son was divided against father. Daughter was divided against her mother: that people from the Jews who believed was divided against the Synagogue. Daughter-in-law was also divided against her mother-in-law: the people coming from the Gentiles is called the daughter-in-law because Christ the bridegroom is the son of the Synagogue.

For from where was the Son of God born according to the flesh? From that Synagogue. He who “left father and mother and clung to his wife, and the two became one flesh” (Gen. 2:24)—this is not our conjecture, but the Apostle bears witness and says: “This is a great mystery, but I am speaking with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32).

In a certain sense he left his father—not that he wholly left him in separation, but in order to assume human flesh. How did he leave him? Because, “being in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

How did he leave his mother? The Jewish people, that Synagogue clinging to the ancient sacraments. The same figure is involved in what he said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48). He was teaching within; they were standing outside.

See whether the Jews are not now in the same condition. Christ teaches in the Church; they stand outside. What, then, is the mother-in-law? The mother of the bridegroom. The mother of the bridegroom of our Lord Jesus Christ is the Synagogue. Therefore his daughter-in-law, the Church, which came from the Gentiles and did not consent to carnal circumcision, was divided against her mother-in-law.

“Gird your sword.” We were speaking about the power of this sword when we said these things.

### 13

“Gird your sword, your word, around your thigh, O most powerful one,” having your sword around your thigh.

What does “around your thigh” mean? What does the thigh signify? The flesh. Hence the saying: “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs” (Gen. 49:10).

Was it not Abraham himself, to whom the seed had been promised in which all nations would be blessed, who, when he sent his servant to seek and bring a wife for his son—the wife from whom that holy seed would come, in which all nations would be blessed—held by faith that in the apparent [Col. 0502] humility of the seed lay the greatness of the name [Note: So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have *numinis*, “of the divine power,” instead of *nominis*, “of the name.”], that is, that the Son of God would come from the sons of men through the seed of Abraham? Did he not make that servant whom he was sending swear to him in this way?

“Place your hand,” he said, “under my thigh, and swear in this way” (Gen. 12:3; 24:2–3; 26:4). It was as though he said: “Place your hand upon the altar, or upon the Gospel, or upon the Prophet, or upon something holy.” “Under my thigh,” he says, “place your hand,” trusting and not shrinking from what is shameful, but understanding the truth.

Therefore: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.” Most powerful even around the thigh, because “what is weak of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). Most powerful.

### 14. [verse 5]

“In your appearance and your beauty.” Understand this as righteousness, by which you are always beautiful and fair. “Attend, and proceed prosperously, and reign.”

Do we not see this? It has certainly already happened. Look upon the world: he has attended, proceeded prosperously, and reigns; all nations have been subjected to him.

What was it to see this in the spirit? It is now to experience it in reality. When these things were being spoken, Christ did not yet reign in this way; he had not yet attended or proceeded. They were being proclaimed; they have been displayed, and now we possess them. In many things we have God as the one who repays; in a few things as the one who is owed.

“Attend, and proceed prosperously, and reign.”

### 15

“For the sake of truth, meekness, and righteousness.”

Truth was restored when “truth sprang up from the earth, and righteousness looked down from heaven” (Ps. 85:12). Christ was presented to the expectation of the human race, so that all nations might be blessed in the seed of Abraham. The Gospel was preached: this is truth.

What is meekness? The martyrs suffered, and from this the kingdom of God advanced and spread greatly through all nations: because the martyrs suffered and did not give way or resist; they declared everything, hiding nothing; they were ready for everything and refused nothing. Great is meekness!

The body of Christ did this; it learned it from its head. He first was led “like a sheep to slaughter,” and “like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7) [Note: The printed editions have “to the sacrifice”; the manuscripts have “to slaughter.”]—so meek that, hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

What does “for the sake of righteousness” mean? He will also come to judge and “repay each one according to his works” (Rom. 2:6). He spoke the truth, endured iniquity [Note: Two manuscripts have “he manifested meekness” instead of “he endured iniquity.”], and will bring equity.

“And your right hand shall lead you wonderfully.” We are his right hand; he is his own right hand. For he is God, and we are human beings. He was led by his own right hand—that is, by his own power. For the power that the Father has, he also has; the Father’s immortality he also has; the Father’s divinity he has; the Father’s eternity he has; the Father’s might he has.

“His right hand shall lead him wonderfully”: doing divine things, enduring human things, and laying low the wickedness of men by his goodness. He is still being led [Col. 0503] where he is not yet present, and his right hand leads him. For that leads him which he himself has bestowed upon his saints.

“Your right hand shall lead you wonderfully.”

### 16. [verse 6]

“Your arrows are sharp, most powerful” [Note: The printed editions have *potentissime*, “O most powerful one,” and this is supported by the Greek Septuagint, *dunate*. Nevertheless, the better manuscripts have *potentissimae*, “most powerful”; and one can easily understand that Augustine read it this way from his very method of interpretation.]: words piercing the heart and arousing love.

Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “For I am wounded by love” (Song 2:5; 5:8). She says that she has been wounded by love—that is, she says that she loves, that she burns, that she sighs for the bridegroom, from whom she received the arrow of the word.

“Your arrows are sharp, most powerful”: both piercing and effective—sharp, most powerful.

“Peoples shall fall beneath you.” Who have fallen? Those who have been struck and fallen. We see peoples subjected to Christ, but we do not see them falling. He explains where they fall: in the heart. There they were rising up against Christ; there they fall before Christ.

Saul was blaspheming Christ; he was standing erect. He supplicates Christ; he fell, he was prostrated. The enemy of Christ was killed so that the disciple of Christ might live.

An arrow sent from heaven struck Saul in the heart—not yet Paul, still Saul, still standing erect, not yet prostrate. He received the arrow and fell in his heart. It was not because he was prostrated face down that he fell there in his heart [Note: The manuscripts here do not have “in his heart.”], but when he said: “Lord, what do you command me to do?” (Acts 9:6).

A moment before, he was going to bind Christians and lead them away to punishment; now he says to Christ: “What do you command me to do?” O sharp, most powerful arrow, by which Saul was struck and fell so as to become Paul!

As with him, so also with the peoples. Look at the nations; see them subjected to Christ. Therefore: “Peoples shall fall beneath you, in the heart of the enemies of the king”—that is, in the heart of your enemies. He himself calls him king; he recognizes him as king.

They were enemies; they received your arrows and fell before you. From enemies they became friends: the enemies died, and the friends live. This is “for the sake of those things that will be changed.” We seek to understand the individual words and the individual verses, but we seek to understand them in such a way that no one doubts that they are spoken concerning Christ.

“Peoples shall fall beneath you, in the heart of the enemies of the king.”

### 17. [verse 7]

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” Because God has blessed you forever, on account of the grace poured upon your lips.

The throne of the Jewish kingdom was temporal, belonging to those who were under the Law, not to those who were under grace. He came to liberate those who were under the Law and establish them under grace.

“His throne is forever and ever.” Why? Because that first throne was a temporal kingdom. From where, then, is the throne now forever and ever? Because it is God’s.

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” O divinity of eternity [Note: Eight manuscripts have *divitias*, “riches,” instead of *divinitas*, “divinity.”]! God could not have a temporal throne.

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.”

The rod of uprightness is the rod that makes people upright. They were crooked and distorted: they wanted to reign for themselves; they loved themselves and loved their evil deeds. [Col. 0504] They did not submit their will to God, but wanted to bend God’s will toward their own desires.

For the sinner and wicked person often becomes angry with God because it does not rain, yet does not want God to be angry with him because he “flows” (*quia fluit*; the sense is uncertain). To this extent, almost every day people sit down to argue against God: “He ought to have done this; he did not do that well.” You, evidently, see what you are doing, while he does not?

You are distorted; he is straight. When can the distorted be joined to the straight? It cannot be aligned. It is as if you placed a crooked piece of wood on an even floor: it does not meet, adhere to, or fit the floor. The floor is even everywhere, but the wood is crooked and does not fit the even surface.

Therefore God’s will is even, while yours is crooked. That is why it seems crooked to you: you cannot fit yourself to it. Direct yourself toward it; do not wish to bend it toward yourself [Note: The printed editions have: “Direct yourself toward it; hold fast to it. For if you wish to bend it toward yourself.” Here we follow the manuscripts.], because you cannot do so; you strive in vain. It is always straight.

Do you wish to cling to it? Be corrected. His rod, which rules you, will be the rod of uprightness. Hence “king” is also derived from “to rule.” But he does not rule who does not correct. For this reason our king is the king of those who are made upright.

Just as a priest is named from sanctifying us, so a king is named from ruling us [Note: Most manuscripts have: “as a priest is named for sanctifying us, so a king is named for ruling us.”].

But what does he say elsewhere? “With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen; and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 18:26–27). This is not because God is perverse, but because the perverse think him perverse. If you approve of what is good, God is good to you; if you disapprove of it, God seems perverse to you. God is crooked toward you because your crookedness causes this; his uprightness always remains.

Hear another psalm: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. 73:1).

### 18. [verse 8]

“The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.”

See the rod of uprightness: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” Approach this rod; let Christ be your king. Let this rod rule you, so that it does not break you. For that rod is an iron rod, inflexible.

And what was said? “You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them” (Ps. 2:9). It rules some and shatters others: it rules the spiritual and shatters the carnal.

Therefore approach this rod. What do you fear in it? This is the whole rod [Note: Six reliable manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have *ruta*, “broken.”]: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” What do you fear? Perhaps you were wicked. You hear that your king hates iniquity, and you are afraid. There is something you can do.

What does he hate? Iniquity—not you. But is there iniquity in you? God hates it; you too should hate it, so that you both hate the same thing. You will be God’s friend if you hate what he hates. In the same way, you will love what he loves.

Let your iniquity displease you in yourself, and let his creature please you. You are an unjust human being. I have said two names: “human being” and “unjust.” In these two names, one refers to nature and the other to guilt; one God made for you, the other you made. Love what God made; hate what you made, because God himself hates it.

See how you now begin to be joined to him, when you hate what he hates.

He will punish sin, because [Col. 0505] the rod of his kingdom is the rod of uprightness. But should he not punish sin? It cannot be otherwise. Sin must be punished; if it did not have to be punished, it would not be sin.

Anticipate him: do you not want him to punish? Punish yourself. This is why he still spares, delays, and holds back his hand; he bends his bow—this means that he threatens [Note: Three manuscripts have “this means that he threatens.” “He would not cry out,” and so forth.]. Would he merely cry out that he was going to strike if he wanted to strike? He therefore holds back his hand from your sins; do not hold back yours.

Turn yourself toward punishing your sins, because sins cannot remain unpunished. They must be punished either by you or by him. Acknowledge them, so that he may forgive.

Consider the example in that penitential psalm: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 51:9). Did he say, “from me”? Elsewhere he plainly says: “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 27:9). Therefore: “Turn your face away from my sins”; I do not want you to see my sins.

For God’s seeing means taking notice. Hence a judge is also said to take notice when he punishes—that is, to turn his mind toward something, to attend to it for the purpose of punishment, because he is a judge. God is likewise a judge.

“Turn your face away from my sins.” You must not turn your face away from them if you want God to turn his face away from them. See how he offers this to God in the same psalm: “I acknowledge my iniquity,” he says, “and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51:5). He does not want that which he wants to be before himself to be before God.

“The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom.” Let no one flatter himself too much concerning God’s mercy: it is the rod of uprightness. Are we saying that God is not merciful? What is more merciful than he, who spares sinners so greatly, who, in all who turn to him, does not take account of the past?

Love him as merciful in such a way that you also wish him to be truthful. For mercy cannot take justice away from him, nor justice mercy. Meanwhile, as long as he delays, do not delay, because it is the rod of uprightness, the rod of his kingdom.

### 19

“You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you.”

He anointed you for this reason: that you might love righteousness and hate iniquity. And see how he says it: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” O you who are God, your God has anointed you. God is anointed by God.

For in Latin the same grammatical case of the noun appears to be repeated; in Greek, however, the distinction is perfectly clear, because one name is being addressed and the other belongs to the one addressing: “God has anointed you.” O you who are God, your God has anointed you—as if he said: “Therefore your God has anointed you, O you who are God.”

Understand it in this way; receive it in this way. In Greek it is perfectly clear.

Who, then, is the God anointed by God? Let the Jews tell us. These Scriptures are common to us all. God has been anointed by God. When you hear “anointed,” understand “Christ.” For *Christus* comes from *chrisma*, “anointing”; the name by which he is called, Christ, derives from anointing.

Nor were kings and priests anointed anywhere else except in that kingdom where Christ was prophesied and anointed, and from which the name “Christ” was destined to come. It exists nowhere else at all—in no nation and in no kingdom.

God, therefore, was anointed by God. With what oil, unless spiritual oil? Visible oil is a sign; invisible oil is a sacrament; spiritual oil is within [Note: Two manuscripts have: “it is a sign of invisible oil; for it is in the sacrament; spiritual oil is within.” The printed editions, after “spiritual oil is within,” add the following words: “visible oil is outward,” which are absent from all our manuscripts.].

[Col. 0506] God was anointed for us and sent to us. And he himself, in order to be anointed, was man. But he was man in such a way that he was God; he was God in such a way that he did not disdain to be man: true man, true God; in no respect deceptive, in no respect false, because everywhere truthful, everywhere truth.

God, therefore, was man; and for this reason God was anointed, because he was man who was God. And he became Christ.

### 20.

This was foreshadowed in what Jacob did when he placed a stone under his head and slept (Gen. 28:11). The patriarch Jacob had placed a stone under his head; while sleeping with that stone beneath his head, he saw, with the heavens opened, a ladder from heaven to earth, and angels ascending and descending. After seeing this, he awoke, anointed the stone, and departed. In that stone he understood Christ; therefore he anointed it.

See from what point onward Christ is proclaimed. What does that anointing of the stone mean, especially among the Patriarchs, who worshiped one God? It was done as a figure, and then the matter was left behind. For he did not anoint the stone and then return there continually to worship and offer sacrifices. The mystery was represented; sacrilege was not begun.

And observe the stone: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22). And because “the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3), therefore the stone was placed under his head. Attend to the great sacrament: the stone is Christ. Peter says, “A living stone, rejected by human beings but chosen by God” (1 Pet. 2:4). And the stone was placed under his head because “the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3). The stone was anointed because Christ is named from *chrisma*, anointing.

And the ladders are seen, with Christ revealing them, from earth to heaven—or from heaven to earth—and angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28:12; John 1:51). We shall see more clearly what this means when we have recalled the evangelical testimony from the Lord himself.

You know that Jacob himself is Israel. For when he wrestled with the angel, prevailed, and was blessed by the one over whom he had prevailed, his name was changed so that he was called Israel (Gen. 32:28). So also the people of Israel prevailed over Christ so as to crucify him; yet, among those who believed in Christ, they were blessed by the one over whom they had prevailed.

But many did not believe; hence Jacob’s lameness. Blessing and lameness: blessing in those who believed—for afterward we know that many from that people believed; but lameness in those who did not believe. And because more did not believe while few believed, therefore, in order that lameness might occur, he touched the breadth of his thigh. What is “the breadth of his thigh”? The multitude of his descendants.

Observe, then, those ladders. When the Lord saw Nathanael in the Gospel, he said, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47). For this is said of Jacob himself: “Jacob was without deceit, dwelling at home” (Gen. 25:27). Recalling this, the Lord, seeing Nathanael—who was without deceit—from that nation and that people, said, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” He called him an Israelite in whom there was no deceit because of Jacob.

And Nathanael said, “From where do you know me?” The Lord replied, “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” That is: when you were established in that people under the Law, which sheltered that people with a carnal shadow, there I saw you. What does “there I saw you” mean? “There I had mercy on you.”

But Nathanael, remembering that he had indeed been under the fig tree, was astonished, because he thought that no one had seen him while he was there. He confessed and said, “You are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.” Who said this? The one who had heard that he was a true Israelite, in whom there was no deceit.

And the Lord said, “Because I told you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believed; you shall see greater things than these.” He speaks with Israel, with Jacob, with the one who had placed a stone under his head: “You shall see greater things than these.”

What greater things? Because now that stone is under the head. “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:48–51).

Let the angels of God ascend and descend by those ladders. Let this take place in the Church. The angels of God are proclaimers of the truth. Let them ascend and see: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Let them descend and see: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Let them ascend, in order to raise up the great; let them descend, in order to nourish the little. See Paul ascending: “Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God.” See him descending: “Whether we are self-controlled, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13). See him ascending: “We speak wisdom among the mature.” See him descending: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 2:6; 3:2).

This happens in the Church: the angels of God ascend and descend upon the Son of Man, because the Son of Man is above, the one to whom they ascend in their hearts—that is, his head—and the Son of Man is below, that is, his body. His members are here; the head is above. One ascends to the head and descends to the members. Christ is there; Christ is here.

For if he were there only and not here, where would that voice come from: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Who was troubling him in heaven? No one—not the Jews, nor Saul, nor the devil the tempter; no one there was troubling him. But just as, when a foot is trodden upon in the structure of the human body, the tongue cries out—

### 21.

“You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you.”

We have spoken of the anointed God, that is, of Christ. The name of Christ could not have been expressed more plainly than by saying “the anointed God.” Just as he is “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” so he is anointed “with the oil of gladness beyond his companions.” Who are his companions? The sons of men, since the Son of Man himself became a participant in their mortality in order to make them participants in his immortality.

### 22. [Verses 9–10.]

“Myrrh and drops and cassia from your garments.”

Good fragrances come from your garments. His garments are his saints, his elect, his whole Church, which he presents to himself as a garment “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27): because of the spot, washing it in blood; because of the wrinkle, stretching it out upon the cross.

Hence comes the good fragrance signified by the naming of certain spices. Hear Paul, that least one, the fringe of the garment which the woman with the flow of blood touched and was healed (Matt. 9:20). Hear him saying, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Cor. 2:15).

He did not say, “We are a good fragrance among those who are being saved and a bad fragrance among those who are perishing”; rather, “As far as we are concerned, we are a good fragrance both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” It is not implausible or incredible that a person should be saved by a good fragrance; but that a person should perish by a good fragrance—what explanation is there for this? Great is the power, great the truth: even if it cannot be grasped, so it is.

To show you that this is difficult to grasp, he immediately added, “And who is sufficient for these things?” Who could understand people dying by a good fragrance?

Nevertheless, I shall say something, brothers. Paul himself was preaching the Gospel. Many loved him as a preacher of the Gospel, and many envied him. Those who loved him were being saved by the good fragrance; those who envied him were perishing by the good fragrance. Therefore, even for those who were perishing, it was not a bad fragrance but a good fragrance.

They envied him all the more because such good grace prevailed in him—for no one envies a wretched person. He was therefore glorious in preaching the word of God and living according to the rule of that rod of uprightness. Those who loved Christ in him loved him; they followed the good fragrance.

The bride herself loved the friend of her bridegroom, the bride who says in the Song of Songs, “We shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3). But the more they saw him in the glory of Gospel preaching and in blameless life, the more they were tortured by envy and were destroyed by the good fragrance.

### 23.

“Myrrh and drops and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses, out of which the daughters of kings have delighted you.”

Understand “ivory houses” spiritually if you wish: great houses and great tabernacles of God, the hearts of the saints; and the kings themselves who rule the flesh, subjecting to themselves the crowds of human emotions, chastising the body and bringing it into servitude. Accept these as the ivory houses, because from them the daughters of kings delighted him.

For all the souls born through those who preach and evangelize are daughters of kings; and the Churches, the daughters of the Apostles, are daughters of kings. He is the King of kings; the kings are those of whom it was said, “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

They preached the word of truth and brought forth Churches—not for themselves but for him. To this mystery belongs what is written in the Law: “If a brother has died, his brother shall take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother” (Deut. 25:5). His brother shall take the wife and raise up offspring—not for himself but for his brother.

Christ said, “Tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). In the psalm he said, “I shall declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23). Christ died, rose again, ascended, and withdrew bodily. His brothers took his wife, in order to produce children through the preaching of the Gospel—not through themselves but through the Gospel, for the sake of their brother’s name.

“For in Christ Jesus,” he says, “through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:15). Thus, all who raised up offspring for their brother, however many they begot, did not call them Paulinians or Petrians, but Christians.

See whether this meaning is not active also in these verses. When he said, “from ivory houses,” he spoke of royal, spacious, beautiful, smooth houses, such as the hearts of the saints are. He added, “Out of which the daughters of kings have delighted you, in your honor.”

They are indeed the daughters of kings, the daughters of your Apostles; but “in your honor,” because they raised up offspring for their brother. Therefore, when Paul saw those whom he had raised up for his brother running after his name, he cried out, “Was Paul crucified for you?” For what does the Law say? “And let the one born bear the name of the deceased” [Note: See *Two Books of Retractions*, book 2, chapter 12, and *Questions on Deuteronomy*, question 46.]. Let a child be born for the deceased and be called by the deceased’s name.

Paul preserves this legal provision: he recalls those who wished to be called by his name: “Was Paul crucified for you?” Look to the deceased: “Was Paul crucified for you?” And then what? When you begot them, did you impose your own name upon them? No. For he says, “Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13).

“The daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” Hold fast to this; preserve it: “in your honor.” This is to possess the wedding garment—to seek his honor, his glory.

Understand also the daughters of kings as the cities that believed in Christ and were founded by kings; and understand the ivory houses as the rich, proud, exalted. The daughters of kings delighted you in your honor because they did not seek the honor of their fathers but sought your honor.

Let the temple of Romulus be shown to me at Rome with as much honor as I show there the memorial of Peter. In Peter, whom is anyone honoring except the one who died for us? We are Christians, not Petrians. Although we were born through the deceased man’s brother, nevertheless we were given the name of the deceased. We were born through the brother, but born for the deceased.

Behold Rome, behold Carthage, behold the other cities: they are daughters of kings, and they have delighted their king in his honor. From them all there comes to be one queen.

### 24.

What a nuptial song! Behold, amid songs full of joy, the bride herself also comes forth. The bridegroom was coming; he himself was being described, and all our attention was directed toward him. Let the bride come forth as well.

“The queen stood at your right hand.” She who stands at the left is not queen. For someone will stand at the left, to whom it will be said, “Go into the eternal fire.” But at the right will stand the one to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

“The queen stood at your right hand, in a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety.” What is the garment of this queen? It is both precious and varied: the mysteries of doctrine in varied languages. One language is African, another Syrian, another Greek, another Hebrew, another this one and that one. These languages make up the variety of this queen’s garment.

And just as every variety in the garment agrees in unity, so all languages agree in one faith. Let there be variety in the garment, but no rending. We have understood variety as the diversity of languages and the garment as signifying unity. But within this variety, what is the gold? Wisdom itself.

Whatever the variety of languages may be, one gold is preached—not different gold, but variety arising from gold. For all languages preach the same wisdom, the same doctrine and discipline. Variety is in the languages; gold is in the meanings.

### 25. [Verse 11.]

The Prophet addresses this queen—gladly does he sing to her—and each one of us, provided that we know where we are, strive to belong to that body, and belong to it in faith and hope, united among the members of Christ.

For he addresses us: “Hear, daughter, and see.” He addresses her as one of the fathers, because she is a daughter of kings. Although it is a prophet who speaks, although it is an apostle who speaks, he speaks as to a daughter. For we say, “Our fathers the Prophets, our fathers the Apostles.” If we regard them as fathers, they regard us as children. One paternal voice addresses the one daughter: “Hear, daughter, and see.”

First hear, then see. The Gospel has come to us, and what we do not yet see has been preached to us. By hearing we believed; by believing we shall see, just as the bridegroom himself says through the Prophet: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45).

What does “at the hearing of the ear” mean? That they did not see. The Jews saw and crucified; the Gentiles did not see and believed.

Let the queen come from the Gentiles, in a golden garment, clothed all around with variety. Let her come from the Gentiles, clothed with all languages in the unity of wisdom. Let it be said to her, “Hear, daughter, and see.” If you do not hear, you will not see.

Hear in order to cleanse your heart by faith, as the Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). For this purpose we hear, so that we may believe before we see; by believing, we cleanse the heart, so that we may be able to see.

“Hear, so that you may believe; cleanse your heart by faith.” And when I have cleansed my heart, what shall I see? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear.” It is not enough to hear: hear humbly. “Incline your ear.”

“And forget your people and your father’s house.” There was a certain people and a certain father’s house in which you were born: the people of Babylon, having the devil as king. From whatever place the Gentiles came, they came from the devil as father; but they renounced the devil as father.

“Forget your people and your father’s house.” He made you foul when he made you a sinner; this one regenerates you beautiful, justifying the ungodly. “Forget your people and your father’s house.”

### 26. [Verses 12, 15.]

“For the king desired your beauty.” What beauty, except the beauty he himself made? He desired beauty. Whose beauty? The beauty of one who had been sinful, unrighteous, ungodly, as she was with the devil as father and among his people?

No; rather, the beauty of the one of whom it is said, “Who is this that ascends, made white?” (Song 8:5). Previously, therefore, she was not white; afterward she was made white. “Though your sins be like scarlet, I shall make them white as snow” (Isa. 1:18).

“The king desired your beauty.” Which king? “For he is the Lord your God” [Note: Better manuscripts read, “For he is your God,” omitting the word “Lord.”]. Now see whether you ought not to abandon that father of yours and that people of yours and come to this king, your God. He is your God; he is your king. Your king is also your bridegroom. You marry God the King, endowed by him, adorned by him, redeemed by him, healed by him. Whatever you have by which you please him, you have from him.

### 27.

“And the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts.”

Your king, your God, they shall worship with gifts. The daughters of Tyre are the daughters of the Gentiles: a part standing for the whole. Tyre, neighboring the land where the prophecy was given, signified the Gentiles who would believe in Christ.

From there was that Canaanite woman, who was first called a dog. To show you that she was from there, the Gospel says: “He withdrew into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, and behold, a Canaanite woman who had come out from those borders was crying out,” followed by the other things narrated there.

At first she was a dog with her father and among her people; but by crying out and coming to this king, she was made beautiful by believing in him [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read, “For at first she was a dog with her father, but by crying out and coming to this king, who made her beautiful, and by believing in him,” etc.]. What did she deserve to hear? “O woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15:21–28).

“The king desired your beauty. And the daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts.” With what gifts? This king wishes people to come to him in this way, and he wishes his treasures to be filled. He himself gave what would fill them, and they are to be filled by you [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and they are filled for you.” Two read, “and they are filled for us.”].

“Come,” he says, “worship him with gifts.” What does “with gifts” mean? “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither thief nor moth corrupts. For where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matt. 6:19–21).

Come with gifts. “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Come with gifts to him who says, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13).

To that temple which was previously a shadow of what was to come, people came with bulls and rams, with goats and all the various animals suitable for sacrifice, so that in that blood one thing might be done and another signified. Now the blood itself, which all those things foreshadowed, has come. The King himself has come, and he himself desires gifts.

What gifts? Alms. For he himself will judge, and he himself will reckon gifts to some [Note: Manuscripts read, “And he himself will reckon gifts to some.” Two of the same manuscripts read, “He will reckon gifts to those to whom he says, ‘Come,’ he says, ‘blessed ones,’” etc.].

“Come,” he says, “blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Why? “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was a stranger, and you took me in; I was sick and in prison, and you visited me.”

These are the gifts with which the daughters of Tyre worship the King. For when they said, “When did we see you?”—he who is both above and below, for the sake of those ascending and descending—said, “When you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:34–40).

### 28.

“The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts.” And who are the daughters of Tyre, and how shall they worship him with gifts? He wished to state this more plainly: “The wealthy among the people shall entreat your face.”

These daughters of Tyre, worshiping with gifts, are the wealthy among the people. The friend of the bridegroom addresses them: “Command the wealthy of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things richly for enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works, generous in giving, sharing.”

Let them worship with gifts, but they do not lose what they give. Let them safely place their treasures where they will always find them. “Let them lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

By worshiping with gifts, “they shall entreat your face.” For they run together to the Church, and there they give alms. Let them not give outside; that is, lest, being placed outside, they give outside. Let them give in the Church.

The face of this bride and queen will benefit those who give. Therefore those who were selling their possessions came, entreating the face of this queen with their gifts; and what they brought they placed at the feet of the Apostles (Acts 4:34).

Love burned fervently in the Church. The face was the queen, the Church; the face of the queen was the service of the daughters of Tyre—that is, of the wealthy worshiping with gifts.

“The wealthy among the people shall entreat your face.” Those who entreat the face, and the one whose face they entreat, are all one bride, all one queen, mother and children together—everything belonging to Christ, belonging to the head.

### 29.

But because these works and these alms are sometimes done for human ostentation, the Lord himself says, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1).

But to show that they should also be done publicly for the sake of the bride’s face, he says, “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). This does not mean that you should seek your own glory in the good works you do publicly, but God’s glory.

And who knows, he says, whether I seek God’s glory or my own? Because I give to the poor, I am seen; but who sees with what intention I give? Let the one who sees be sufficient for you. He sees who will reward.

The one who sees within loves within. Let the one who loves within—and who makes the very beauty interior—be loved within. Do not delight as though in external eyes because you are seen and praised. Pay attention to what follows here: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.”

Externally there is not only a garment of gold and variety; but he who loved her beauty knows her beauty within. What are the inner parts of her beauty? Consciences. There Christ sees; there Christ loves; there Christ addresses; there Christ punishes; there Christ crowns.

Therefore let your alms be in secret, because “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” “In golden borders, clothed all around with variety.” Beauty is within; but in the golden borders there is the variety of languages, the adornment of doctrine.

What do these things benefit us if that inner beauty is absent?

### 30.

“Virgins shall be brought to the King after her.”

It has truly happened. The Church believed, and the Church came to be throughout all the nations. How do virgins now desire to please that King? From where are they encouraged? Because the Church went before.

“Virgins shall be brought to the King after her; her companions shall be brought to you.” For those who are brought are not strangers but her companions, belonging to her. And because he said “to the King,” he turned to him and said, “to you”: “Her companions shall be brought to you.”

### 31. [Verse 16.]

“They shall be brought in joy and exultation; they shall be led into the temple of the King.”

The temple of the King is the Church; the Church itself enters into the temple. From what is the temple built? From the people who enter the temple. Who are the living stones except the faithful of God?

“They shall be led into the temple of the King.” For there are virgins outside the temple of the King: heretical women religious. They are indeed virgins, but what will it profit them unless they are led into the temple of the King?

The temple of the King is in unity. The temple of the King is not ruined, torn apart, or divided. The joining of the living stones is love. “They shall be led into the temple of the King.”

### 32. [Verse 17.]

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”

Nothing could be clearer. Observe now the temple of the King himself, because it speaks from there for the sake of the unity spread throughout the whole world. For those who have wished to be virgins cannot please the bridegroom unless they are led into the temple of the King.

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” The Apostles begot you; they were sent, they preached; they were fathers. But could they always have remained bodily with us? Although one of them said, “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24), how long could he remain here? Surely not until this present time, nor into the future.

Therefore, when they departed, was the Church left desolate? By no means. “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”

What does “instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” mean? The Apostles were sent as fathers; in place of the Apostles, sons were born to you: bishops were appointed.

For the bishops who are throughout the whole world today—from where were they born? The Church herself calls them fathers; she herself begot them, and she herself established them in the seats of the fathers.

Do not think that you have been deserted because you do not see Peter, because you do not see Paul, because you do not see those through whom you were born. From your offspring your fatherhood has increased.

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall establish them as princes over all the earth.” See how widely the temple of the King is spread, so that the virgins who are not led into the temple of the King may know that they do not belong to these nuptials.

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall establish them as princes over all the earth.” This is the Catholic Church: her sons have been established as princes over all the earth; her sons have been appointed in place of the fathers.

Let those who have been cut off recognize this and come to unity; let them be led into the temple of the King. God has established his temple everywhere; everywhere he has made firm the foundations of the Prophets and Apostles. The Church has begotten sons and established them as princes over all the earth in place of her fathers.

### 33. [Verse 18.]

“They shall remember your name throughout every generation and generation. Therefore the peoples shall confess to you.”

What benefit is there in confessing and confessing outside the temple? What benefit is there in praying and not praying on the mountain? “With my voice,” he says, “I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain” (Ps. 3:5).

Which mountain? The one of which it was said, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). Which mountain? The one Daniel saw grow from a small stone, break all the kingdoms of the earth, and fill the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2:35).

Let the one who wishes to receive worship there; let the one who wishes to be heard ask there; let the one who wishes to be forgiven confess there.

“Therefore the peoples shall confess to you forever and unto ages of ages.” For even in that eternal life there will no longer be the groaning of sinners, but in the divine praises of that heavenly and perpetual city there will still be an everlasting confession of such great happiness.

It is to that city of which another psalm sings, “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3); to that bride of Christ, to that queen who is the daughter of the King and the wife of the King. Because her princes remember his name throughout every generation and generation—that is, as long as this age passes, which is conducted through many generations—they care for her in love, so that, freed from this age, she may reign with God forever.

For this reason the peoples will confess to that same city forever, with the hearts of all there made luminous by conspicuous and manifest perfect love, so that she may know herself fully and completely, since here she is hidden from herself in many of her parts.

For this we are admonished by the Apostle to judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, illuminates the hidden things of darkness, manifests the counsels of the heart, and then each person’s praise comes from God (1 Cor. 4:5).

For that holy city will, in a certain sense, confess to itself when its peoples, of whom it consists, confess to that city forever, so that no part of it may remain hidden from it, since there will be no one within it from whom anything is hidden.

# Exposition of Psalm 45. Sermon to the People

### 1. [Verse 1.]

Now we speak to Your Charity about certain matters as though they were very familiar, and we should not linger over them, because things you know should be recalled briefly.

Let us understand ourselves to be the sons of Korah. I remind you, although you know this, that *Korah* is interpreted as “Baldness”; and that our Lord, because he was crucified at the place of Calvary, brought many to himself—like that grain which, unless it had died, would have remained alone (John 12:24). Those who were brought were called the sons of Korah. This is the mystical meaning. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, “and that our Lord signifies him who, crucified at the place of Calvary, brought many.”]

In the historical sense, there were indeed certain sons of Korah at the time when these things were sung (1 Chron. 26:1); but the spirit must give us life, not the letter veil us [Note: Perhaps *pecare*.] (2 Cor. 3:6).

Let us therefore understand ourselves here, and see whether what follows—that is, what the context of the psalm itself contains—fits us. We find ourselves here, provided that we cling to the members of the one whose body has its head in heaven, ascending from that Passion in order to bring with himself those who lay in humility into abundance, bearing fruit in endurance.

It is written: “For the end, for the sons of Korah, for hidden things, a psalm.” It is therefore hidden. But you know that the very one who was crucified at the place of Calvary tore the veil so that the secrets of the temple might be revealed (Matt. 27:51).

Since the cross of our Lord was therefore the key by which closed things would be opened, let us believe that he will be present with us so that these hidden things may be revealed.

Whenever “for the end” occurs, we must always understand Christ. For “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). The end is so called not because it destroys but because it perfects.

We call food “finished” when it has been eaten, and a garment “finished” when it has been woven: the former refers to consumption, the latter to completion. Since, when we have reached Christ, we have nowhere further to go, he is called the end of our course.

Nor should we think that when we have reached him we must strive further in order to reach the Father as well. Philip thought this when he said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” When he says, “It is enough for us,” he seeks the end of satisfaction and perfection.

And the Lord said to him, “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:8–9).

In him, therefore, we have the Father, because he is in the Father, and the Father is in him, and he and the Father are one (John 10:30).

### 2. [Verse 2.]

What, then, does the one who sings here admonish us? Here we must recognize our voice, provided that we possess the disposition expressed by this voice: “Our God is our refuge and strength.”

There are refuges in which there is no strength. When someone flees to them, he becomes weaker rather than stronger. Suppose, for example, that you flee to some powerful person in the world in order to make a powerful friend for yourself; he seems to be a refuge to you.

Yet the uncertainties of this world are so great, and the daily falls of the powerful occur with such increasing frequency, that when you reach such a refuge, you begin to fear more there. Previously you feared only for your own affairs; but when you have fled to such a person, you will also fear on his account.

For many, when they had fled to such refuges, were themselves sought out when those to whom they had fled fell—people whom no one would have sought if they had not fled to such refuges.

Our refuge is not like that; our refuge is strength. When we flee there, we shall be firm.

### 3.

“He is a helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly.”

There are many tribulations, and in every tribulation one must flee to God: whether the tribulation concerns household affairs, bodily health, danger to those most dear to us, or something else necessary for sustaining this life. A Christian should have no other refuge than his Savior, his God. When he flees to him, he is strong.

For he will not be strong in himself, nor will he himself be his own strength; rather, the one who has become his refuge will be his strength.

Nevertheless, beloved, among all the tribulations of the human soul, there is no greater tribulation than the consciousness of sins. For if there is no wound there, and what is within a person—the thing called conscience—is healthy, then wherever else that person suffers tribulation, he will flee there and find God.

But if there is no rest there because of the abundance of iniquity—for God is not there either—what is a person to do? Where will he flee when tribulations begin to afflict him?

He will flee from the countryside to the city, from public places into the house, from the house into the bedroom, and tribulation follows him. Once in the bedroom, he has nowhere else to flee except into his inner chamber.

But if there is tumult there, if there is the smoke of iniquity, if there is the flame of crime, he cannot flee there. He is driven away from there; and when he is driven away from there, he is driven away from himself.

And behold, he finds his enemy where he had fled. Where will he flee from himself? Wherever he flees, he drags himself after him; and wherever he drags such a self, he torments himself by himself.

These are the tribulations that find a person exceedingly; for no tribulations are more bitter. They are not more bitter in proportion as they are not more inward.

Observe, beloved: when timbers are cut down [Note: So the manuscripts read. The editions have *deasciantur*, “are shaped with an adze.”] and tested by carpenters, sometimes they appear on the surface to be damaged and rotten. But the carpenter examines the inner marrow of the wood, as it were; and if he finds that the timber is sound within, he promises that it will last in the building. He is not greatly concerned about damage on the surface when he declares that what is within is sound.

But in a human being the conscience is found within. What benefit is there, then, if what is external is sound while the marrow of the conscience is rotten?

These are indeed severe and altogether violent tribulations, and, as the psalm itself says, exceedingly great tribulations. Yet even in these the Lord has become a helper by forgiving sins.

For the consciences of the wicked are healed only by pardon. If a debtor who has confessed [Note: Fifteen manuscripts read *confossus*, “pierced through.” Two read *confusus*, “confounded.” Three read *compulsus*, “compelled.” A very few have the reading found in the editions, *confessus*, “having confessed,” which is no less suitable.] that he has great tribulations—looking at the distress of his household affairs and seeing that he cannot pay his debts—says that he suffers great tribulations because of the enforcers who come every year to compel payment, and nowhere breathes freely except in the hope of remission of earthly obligations [Note: Thirteen manuscripts read, “the hope of pardon from earthly kings.”], how much more does one suffer who is a debtor to punishment because of the abundance of his sins?

When will he repay what he owes from his evil conscience? When, if he repays it, he himself perishes? For to repay this debt is to undergo punishment.

It remains, therefore, that we may be secure in his pardon—provided that, once pardon has been received, we do not return to contracting debts again.

4. These sons of Korah, then, are perhaps understood to be those to whom Peter spoke in the Acts of the Apostles, when they had been struck with amazement at the wonders accompanying the coming of the Holy Spirit, when all those upon whom he had come were speaking in every language. For he announced Christ to them, the one who had been able to accomplish such great things by sending the Holy Spirit. They had crucified him with their own hands, thinking how contemptible he was when he was killed by them, yet how exalted and lofty he had been made before God—he who filled uneducated people with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0516] Manuscripts: “his own.”] and made the tongues of infants eloquent. Struck to the heart, they said: “What shall we do?” These were the exceedingly great tribulations that had overtaken them. For they themselves did not discover their sins; rather, their sins were discovered in them through the Apostles’ reminder. Therefore tribulations found them; they did not themselves find tribulations.

For when a person, without anyone’s admonition, considers his own deed and asks God, what does he say? “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114:3–4). The tribulation that you find, then, is one thing; the tribulation that finds you is another. Yet in both cases—whether it finds you or you find it—he must be called upon to drive both away who is the helper in tribulations. For even the one who found it said, “And I called upon the name [Col. 0517] of the Lord”; and these people, in the tribulations by which they said they had been found, said this: “Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly.”

But since he became a helper, from what did he become one? “Struck,” he says, “in their heart, they said: What shall we do?” As though in great despair: “He is so great, whom we killed; where shall we be?” And Peter said: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven you” (Acts 2:4, 37–38). They could think of no sin more serious than this. What sin is more serious for a sick person than the killing of the physician? What could a sick person do more grievous than killing his physician? When this is forgiven, what will not be forgiven?

From him, then, to whom it was said, “Refuge and strength,” they received great assurance: “Let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” In the name of the one whom you killed, be baptized, and your sins shall be forgiven you. You have recognized the physician, even afterward; now drink without fear the blood that you shed.

5. [verse 3] Having received such great assurance, what do they say? “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is shaken.” A little earlier they were anxious; suddenly they are secure, placed in great tranquility after exceedingly great tribulations. For Christ was sleeping for them, and therefore they were troubled; Christ was awakened, just as we have now heard in the Gospel: he commanded the winds, and they became still (Matt. 8:24–26). Since Christ is in each person’s heart through faith, it was signified to us that the heart of the one who forgets his faith is troubled as though Christ were sleeping [Note: [Col. 0517] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “Since Christ is not in the heart of anyone through faith, it was signified to us that his heart, like a ship in the tempest of this age, is troubled. He who forgets his faith,” etc.]; but when Christ is awakened, tranquility comes.

Finally, what did the Lord himself say? “Where is your faith?” (Luke 8:25). Christ, once awakened, awakened faith, so that what had happened in the boat might happen in their hearts. “A helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly”: he brought it about that great tranquility should be there.

6. Observe that tranquility itself: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is shaken and mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea.” Then we shall not fear. Let us seek the mountains that have been transferred; and if we are able to find them, it is clear that this is our assurance. For the Lord said to the disciples: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Remove and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matt. 17:19).

Perhaps by “this mountain” he meant himself; for he is called a mountain: “In the last times the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest.” But this mountain has been placed above other mountains, because the Apostles too are mountains, carrying this mountain. Therefore it follows: “In the last times the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared upon the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). Thus it surpasses the summits of all mountains and has been placed upon the summit of all mountains, because those who announce the mountain are mountains.

The sea signifies this world, in comparison with which the Jewish people seemed like land. [Col. 0518] It was not covered by the bitterness of idolatry, but was like dry land surrounded by the bitterness of the Gentiles as by a sea. The earth was destined to be shaken—that is, that very Jewish people—and the mountains were to be transferred into the heart of the sea: that is, first, the great mountain itself, prepared upon the summit of the mountains. For it abandoned the Jewish people and came to exist among the Gentiles; it was transferred from land to sea.

Who transferred it? The Apostles, to whom he had said: “If you have faith in yourselves like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Remove and cast yourself into the sea,’ and it will happen.” That is: through your most faithful preaching it will happen that this mountain—that is, I myself—will be proclaimed among the Gentiles, glorified among the Gentiles, recognized among the Gentiles, and that what was foretold concerning me will come to pass: “A people whom I did not know served me” (Ps. 17:45).

When, then, were those mountains also transferred? Let God’s Scripture indicate this to us. When the Apostle was preaching to the Jews, they rejected the word; and the Apostle Paul said: “We had been sent to you, but since you rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). “The mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea.”

Truly the Gentiles believed in the mountains, so that those mountains might be in the heart of the sea—not like the Jews, of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13; Matt. 15:8).
