For the Lord also promises this concerning the New Testament, saying through the prophet: “I will give my laws in their hearts” (Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10). These laws, these commandments implanted through the Apostles in the faith and belief of all the Gentiles, are called mountains transferred into the heart of the sea.

Then we shall not fear. Who shall not fear? We who were struck in our hearts, lest we become part of the rejected Jews, like broken-off branches. For some of them believed and clung to the Apostles as they preached [Note: [Col. 0518] Four manuscripts: “For they believed and the Apostles came to them.” Almost all the others: “For they believed and came to the Apostles.” They do not have “some of them,” nor the word “preaching.”]. Let those, then, fear whom the mountains abandoned. We did not withdraw from the mountains; and when they were transferred into the heart of the sea, we followed them.

7. [verse 4] What follows now from the fact that the mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea? Pay attention and see the truth. When these things were being said, they were obscure because they had not yet happened; but now, who does not recognize that they have happened? Let the divine page be a book for you, so that you may hear these things; let the whole world be a book for you, so that you may see them. In those books only those who know letters can read them; throughout the whole world, let even the uneducated person read.

What, then, happened when the mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea? “Its waters roared and were troubled.” When the Gospel was being preached [Note: [Col. 0518] Understood: “they said.”], “What is this? He appears to be a proclaimer of foreign demons” (Acts 17:18)—so said the Athenians. And with what tumult did the Ephesians want to kill the Apostles, when they caused such an uproar in the theater on behalf of their Diana that they cried out: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians” (Acts 19:28)?

Amid these waves and sounds of the sea, those who had fled to that [Col. 0519] refuge were not afraid. Finally, the Apostle Paul wanted to enter the theater, but the disciples restrained him, because it was still necessary for him to remain in the flesh for their sake. Yet “its waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his strength.” Whose? Surely not the sea’s, but rather God’s, of whom it was said: “Refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly.”

For the mountains were troubled—that is, the powers of this world. There are mountains of God and mountains of the world: the mountains of the world have the devil as their head; the mountains of God have Christ as their head. But those mountains were troubled through these mountains.

Then they raised their voices [Note: [Col. 0519] Seven manuscripts: “laws.”] against the Christians, when the mountains were troubled by the sounding waves; the mountains were shaken, and there was a great earthquake with the movement of the water. But for whom were these things? For that city founded upon the rock. The waters sound, the mountains are troubled, when the Gospel is announced. What then, city of God? Hear what follows.

8. [verse 5] “The river’s rushing waters make glad the city of God.” [Note: [Col. 0519] Thus the manuscripts, with which the Greek translation of the Septuagint agrees in this verse. Earlier editions read: “The river makes glad the city of God. The mountains are troubled,” etc.] When the mountains are troubled, when the sea rages, God does not abandon his city through the rushing waters of the river. What are these rushing waters of the river? That outpouring of the Holy Spirit of which the Lord said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink; whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Thus these rivers flowed from the belly of Paul, Peter, John, and the other Apostles and the other faithful Evangelists. When these rivers flowed from one river, many rushing waters of the river made glad the city of God.

And so that you may know that this was said concerning the Holy Spirit, the Evangelist says subsequently in the same Gospel: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37–39). When Jesus had been glorified after the resurrection and glorified after the ascension, the Holy Spirit came on the day of Pentecost, filled the believers, and they spoke in tongues (Acts 2:4); they began to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles.

From this the city of God was made glad, while the sea was troubled by the sound of its waters, while the mountains were disturbed, seeking what they should do, how they might drive out the new teaching, and how they might wipe the Christian race from the earth. Against whom? Against the rushing waters of the river that made glad the city of God.

Here too he shows what river he was speaking about, because he signified the Holy Spirit: “The river’s rushing waters make glad the city of God.” And what follows? “The Most High sanctified his tabernacle.” If, then, the name of sanctification follows, it is clear that those rushing waters of the river are to be understood as the Holy Spirit, by whom every devout soul that believes in Christ is sanctified, so that it may become a citizen of the city of God.

9. [verse 6] “God is in [Col. 0520] its midst, and it shall not be shaken.” [Note: [Col. 0519] The editions lack “and.” The manuscripts, and the Septuagint in some Greek codices, have it.] Let the sea rage, let the mountains be troubled: “God is in its midst, and it shall not be shaken.” What does “in its midst” mean? Is it as though God stands in one place, and those who believe in him surround him? Is God therefore enclosed by a place, with the things surrounding him being broad and the one surrounded being confined? Far be such thoughts from you concerning God, who is contained by no place, whose seat is the conscience of the devout.

God’s seat is in human hearts in such a way that, if a person falls away from God, God remains in himself—not as though he falls because he cannot find where to be. Rather, he lifts you up so that you may be in him, than leans upon you so that, if you withdraw yourself, he should fall. If he withdraws himself, you fall; if you withdraw yourself, he does not fall.

What, then, does “God is in its midst” mean? It signifies that God is equal toward all and does not accept persons. Just as what is in the middle has equal distances to all the boundaries, so God is said to be in the midst, caring equally for all.

“God is in its midst, and it shall not be shaken.” From what will it not be shaken? Because God is in its midst. “God will help it with his countenance.” He is the helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly. “God will help it with his countenance.” What does “with his countenance” mean? By his manifestation. How does God manifest himself, so that we may see his countenance? I remind you: you have learned that God is present; we have learned this through his works. When we receive some help from him in such a way that we have no doubt at all that it has been granted to us by the Lord, God’s countenance is with us. “God will help it with his countenance.”

10. [verse 7] “The nations were troubled.” And how were they troubled? Why were they troubled? To cast down the city of God, in whose midst God is? To overthrow the sanctified tabernacle, which God helps with his countenance? No. The nations were already troubled for their salvation.

For what follows? “And kingdoms were bowed down.” “Kingdoms,” he says, “were bowed down”: no longer upright so that they might rage [Note: [Col. 0520] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “might be proud.”], but bowed down so that they might adore. When were kingdoms bowed down? When what was foretold in another psalm came to pass: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11).

What caused kingdoms to bow down? Hear what: “The Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved.” Those possessed by idols croaked like frogs from marshes, all the more noisily because they came more filthily from mud and slime. And what is the racket of frogs compared with the thunder of clouds? For from there “the Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved”: he thundered from his clouds.

What are his clouds? His Apostles, his preachers, from whom he thundered commands and flashed miracles. They are the same ones who are mountains and clouds: mountains because of their height and firmness, clouds because of their rain and abundance. For these clouds watered the earth, of which it was said: “The Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved.”

Concerning these clouds he threatens a certain barren vineyard, from which the mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea: “I will command,” he says, “my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6). This was fulfilled in what we recalled, when the mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea, when it was said: “We had been sent to you, but since you rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). “I will command my clouds not to rain [Col. 0521] rain upon it” was fulfilled.

Indeed, that Jewish people has now remained like a dry fleece upon the threshing floor. You also know that this occurred in a certain miracle. The threshing floor was dry; only the fleece was wet, but rain did not appear upon the fleece (Judg. 6:37–38). So too the sacrament of the New Testament did not appear among the Jewish people. What was the fleece there is the veil here: for the sacrament was veiled in the fleece. But in the threshing floor—that is, among all the Gentiles—the Gospel of Christ is plainly visible; the rain is manifest, the grace of Christ is uncovered [Note: [Col. 0521] Thus in the manuscripts. But the editions have: “because there the fleece was; there this sacrament was veiled in the fleece. But in the threshing floor, that is, among all the Gentiles, where the Gospel of Christ is plainly visible, the rain is manifest, the threshing floor of Christ is uncovered.”].

But in order that the rain might come out from there, the fleece was squeezed. For through oppression they drove Christ out from themselves, and now the Lord pours rain from his clouds upon the threshing floor, while the fleece remains dry. Therefore “the Most High gave his voice” from these clouds, through which voice kingdoms would be bowed down and adore.

11. [verse 8] “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.” Not just any human being, not any power, not even an angel, nor any creature, whether earthly or heavenly, but “the Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.”

He who sent angels came after the angels; he came so that angels might serve him; he came to make human beings equal to angels. Great grace! “If God is for us, who is against us?” The Lord of hosts is with us. Who is the Lord of hosts with us? If God is for us, I say, who is against us? “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things?” (Rom. 8:31–32).

Therefore let us be secure; in the tranquility of our hearts let us nourish a good conscience with the bread of the Lord. “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.” However great your weakness may be, see who receives you. Someone is sick, and a physician is summoned; the physician says that the sick person has been entrusted to him. Who received him? He did. There is great hope of recovery: the great physician has received him.

What physician? Every physician except that one is human; every physician who comes to a sick person can himself become sick on another day, except that one. “The God of Jacob is our protector.”

Make yourself utterly a little child, such as parents receive. For those who are not received are exposed; those who are received are nourished. Do you think that God received you in the same way your mother received you as an infant? Not so, but forever. For your voice is in that psalm: “For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 26:10). “The God of Jacob is our protector.”

12. [verse 9] “Come and see the works of the Lord.” What has the Lord done concerning this reception? Observe the whole world; come and see. For if you do not come, you do not see; if you do not see, you do not believe; if you do not believe, you stand far away. If you believe, you come; if you believe, you see.

How does one come to this mountain? By foot? By ships? By wings? By horses? As far as distances between places are concerned, do not toil, do not be troubled: it has [Col. 0522] itself come to you. For from a small stone it grew and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth.

Why, then, do you wish to come to it across the earth, when it has filled the earth? Look, it has already come; awake! By growing, it strikes even those who are sleeping [Note: [Col. 0522] The editions have: “Awake by believing; it strikes those who are awake.” But eleven manuscripts have: “and it strikes those who are sleeping”; and these, along with the other ancient editions, have *crescendo* (“by growing”), rather than *credendo* (“by believing”), which clearly refers back to the preceding words, “from a small stone it grew.”].

If only there is not such a great sleep in them that they grow hard even against the coming mountain, but that they hear: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illuminate you” (Eph. 5:14).

For it was a great thing for the Jews to see the stone. That stone was still small; deservedly they despised what was small, and by despising they stumbled, and by stumbling they were shaken; what remains is that they should also be crushed. For this was said concerning that stone: “Whoever falls upon that stone will be shattered; and upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Luke 20:18).

To be shattered is one thing, and to be crushed is another. To be shattered is less than to be crushed. But the exalted one who comes does not crush anyone except the one whom the humble one, lying there, has shattered. For now, before our Lord comes, he lay humbly before the Jews; they stumbled over him and were shattered. Later he will come in his judgment, glorious and exalted, great and powerful—not weak, so as to be judged, but strong, so as to judge and crush those who were shattered by stumbling over him.

“For those who do not believe, he himself is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense” (1 Pet. 2:8). Therefore, beloved, it is not surprising that the Jews did not recognize the one whom, like a small stone lying before their feet, they despised. Those are to be marveled at who still refuse to recognize such a great mountain. The Jews stumbled over the small stone because they did not see; heretics stumble over the mountain.

For that stone has already grown. We say to them: “Behold, Daniel’s prophecy has been fulfilled: that stone which was small has become a great mountain and has filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2:35). Why do you stumble over it and not climb upon it? Who is so blind as to stumble over a mountain? As though it had come to you for the purpose of giving you something to stumble over, and not something to climb.

“Come, let us climb the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3). Isaiah says this: “Come, let us climb.” What does “Come, let us climb” mean? “Come” means “believe”; “let us climb” means “let us progress.” But these people neither wish to come nor to climb, neither to believe nor to progress. They bark against the mountain.

By stumbling over it so many times they have already been shattered, yet they do not wish to climb; they continually choose to stumble. Let us say to them: “Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders he has placed upon the earth.” Wonders are called so because they point toward something: those miraculous signs that occurred when the world believed.

And what happened as a result, and what did they point toward?

13. [verse 10] “He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth.” We do not yet see this completed. There are still wars: among nations, for kingdoms; among sects, Jews, pagans, Christians, and heretics. Wars exist and multiply, with some fighting for truth and others for falsehood. [Col. 0523]

Therefore “he makes wars cease to the ends of the earth” has not yet been completed—but perhaps it will be completed. Or has it also been completed now? In some it has been completed: it has been completed in the wheat, but not yet in the weeds.

What, then, does “he makes wars cease to the ends of the earth” mean? Does he mean the wars by which people wage war against God? Who wages war against God? Impiety. And what can impiety do to God? Nothing. What does a clay vessel do when dashed against a rock, however violently it is dashed? It comes with all the greater harm to itself the greater the force with which it comes.

These wars were great and frequent. Impiety fought against God, and clay vessels were shattered, as people presumed upon themselves and relied excessively upon their own strength. Concerning this, Job also said of a certain impious person: “He ran against God with the thick neck of his shield” (Job 15:26). What does “with the thick neck of his shield” mean? Presuming too greatly upon his own protection.

Were such people the ones who said: “Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly”? Or, in another psalm: “For I shall not hope in my bow, and my arm shall not save me” (Ps. 43:7)?

When a person recognizes that he is nothing in himself and has no help from himself, his weapons are broken and his wars are quieted. Such wars, then, were destroyed by that voice of the Most High from the holy clouds, by which the earth was moved and kingdoms were bowed down. He made these wars cease to the ends of the earth.

“He will break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.” Bow, weapons, shields, fire. The bow is ambush; the weapons are public assault; the shield is the empty protection of presumption [Note: [Col. 0523] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “the shields, the empty presumption of its own protection.”]. The fire by which these things are burned is that of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49). Concerning this fire the psalm says: “There is no one who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. 18:7).

When this fire burns fervently, none of the weapons of impiety will remain in us; all must be shattered, crushed, and burned. Remain unarmed, having no help of your own. The weaker you are, possessing none of your own weapons, the more he receives you, of whom it was said: “The God of Jacob is our protector.”

You were strong, as though through yourself, and you were troubled in yourself. Lay down the weapons in which you presumed. Hear the Lord saying: “My grace is sufficient for you.” Say also: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” This is the Apostle’s voice.

He had lost all his weapons, as though they had been his strength, when he said: “I will glory in nothing except my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12:9–10). It is as though he were saying: “I do not run against God with the thick neck of my shield—I who was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an abuser—but for this reason I obtained mercy, so that Christ Jesus might display in me all patience toward those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:13, 16).

“He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth.” But when the Lord receives us, does he send us away unarmed? He arms us, but with other weapons: evangelical weapons, weapons of truth, self-control, salvation, hope, faith, and charity. We shall have these weapons, but not from ourselves. The weapons that we had from ourselves have [Col. 0524] burned—if indeed we have been kindled by that fire of the Holy Spirit concerning which it is said: “He will burn the shields with fire.”

He who wished to be powerful in himself, God made weak, so that he might make him strong through himself, because he had become weak through himself [Note: [Col. 0524] Thus five manuscripts. The editions have: “What next? You wished to be in yourself.”].

14. [verse 11] What follows, then? “Be still.” For what purpose? “And know that I am God.” That is: “Not you, but I am God. I created; I recreate. I formed; I reform. I made; I restore.” If you were unable to make yourself, how can you restore yourself?

The contentious tumult of the human spirit does not see this. To that contentious tumult it is said: “Be still”—that is, restrain your spirits from contradiction. Do not argue and, as though armed, rise up against God; otherwise the weapons not yet burned by that fire will remain alive.

But if they have been burned, “Be still,” because you have nothing with which to fight. If you become still within yourself and ask everything from me—though previously you presumed upon yourselves—“Be still, and you will see that I am God.”

15. [verse 12] “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted in the earth.” A little earlier I said that the name “earth” signified the Jewish people, and the name “sea” the remaining nations. “The mountains were transferred into the heart of the sea; the nations were troubled; kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved. The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector.”

Miracles occurred among the nations; the faith of the nations is being fulfilled; the weapons of human presumption are burning. There is stillness in the tranquility of the heart, so that God, the author of all his gifts, may be recognized.

After this glorification, does he abandon the Jewish people, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For I say to you, lest you be wise in your own sight: blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters”—that is, until the mountains are transferred here, the clouds rain here, and the Lord, by his thunder, bows down kingdoms, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters? “And thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

Therefore here too, preserving the same order, he says: “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted in the earth”—that is, both in the sea and in the earth—so that now all may say what follows: “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector” [Note: [Col. 0524] Thus several manuscripts. The editions have: “Would that all might say,” and so forth.].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 46. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. Our Lord God has spread among us, in many and varied ways, through the holy books and sacred Scriptures, the faith in which we live and from which we live, varying the sacraments of his words but commending one faith. For one and the same thing is said in many ways so that the manner of speech may be varied because of weariness, [Col. 0525] while one faith is held because of harmony [Note: [Col. 0524] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “so that the manner of speaking itself may be varied because of weariness, but one faith may be held because of harmony.”].

And so, in this psalm that we have heard sung and to whose singing we have responded, we shall say things that you know; yet perhaps, with the Lord’s help and gift, we shall bring you some sweetness when, having been reminded, you chew over again what you knew from one place and another.

For even in that act of chewing the cud, by which God signifies clean animals, he wished to suggest this: everyone ought to put what he hears into his heart in such a way that he is not too lazy afterward to think about it. When he hears, he should be like one eating; but when he recalls what he has heard and reviews it in the sweetest reflection, he should become like one chewing the cud.

Thus the same things are said in another way, and they make us think sweetly about what we know and gladly hear the very same things, because the manner of speaking is varied and, through that manner of speaking, an old reality is renewed.

2. [verse 1] The title of the psalm is as follows: “For the end, for the sons of Korah; a psalm of David.” Other psalm titles also contain these sons of Korah, and they indicate a sweet mystery and suggest a great sacrament. Here we may gladly understand ourselves, recognizing in the title those of us who hear and read and, as though a mirror had been set before us, behold who we are.

Who are the sons of Korah? There was a certain man named Korah (Num. 16:1), for that was the name of a certain man. Yet when what has been written is read, and divine speech is found to address certain people who are not clearly understood to be the sons of that one man named Korah, the mind returns to the mystery and seeks what “Korah” signifies.

Since it is a Hebrew word, it is certainly said and interpreted in the Greek language and in the Latin language. This has already been done: many Hebrew names have been interpreted for us. We examine them and find that *Korah* is interpreted as “bald.”

You have paid much more attention now. It was obscure when they said “the sons of Korah”; is it not still more obscure when they say “the sons of the bald man”? Who are these sons of the bald man? Perhaps they are the sons of the bridegroom? For the bridegroom was crucified in the place of the Skull.

Recall the Gospel, where they crucified the Lord, and you will find him crucified in the place of the Skull (Matt. 27:33). Therefore those who mock his cross are devoured by demons as by beasts.

A certain Scripture also signified this. When the prophet of God Elisha was going up, boys mocking him cried out after him: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead!” But he, not so much cruelly as mystically, caused those boys to be devoured by bears coming out (2 Kings 2:23–24).

If those boys had not been devoured, would they still be alive to this day? Or could they not, though born mortal, have been taken by a fever? Yet the mystery would not have been displayed in them, by which later generations might be terrified.

Let no one, therefore, mock the cross of the Lord. The Jews were possessed and devoured by demons. For when they crucified Christ in the place of the Skull and lifted him upon the cross, they were, as it were, saying with childish understanding—without realizing what they were saying: “Go up, baldhead.” For what does “Go up” mean? “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21).

Childhood is presented as something to imitate in humility, and childhood is likewise presented as something against which to guard because of foolishness. Childhood is presented for imitation in humility by the Lord, when he called [Col. 0526] children to himself and, when they were being kept away from him, said: “Let them come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:2; 19:14).

The example of childhood as something against which to guard because of foolishness is presented by the Apostle: “Brothers, do not be children in your thinking.” And again he presents it for imitation: “In malice be infants, so that in your minds you may be perfect” (1 Cor. 14:20).

“For the sons of Korah.” The psalm is sung; therefore it was sung for Christians. Let us hear it as the sons of that bridegroom whom foolish boys crucified in the place of the Skull. They deserved to be devoured by beasts; we deserve to be crowned by angels.

We recognize the humility of our Lord, and we are not ashamed of it. We are not ashamed of him mystically called bald because of the place of the Skull. For the very cross at which they insulted him did not permit our forehead to be bald, because he marked it with his own wood [Note: [Col. 0526] Three manuscripts: “with a sign.”].

Finally, so that you may know that these words are spoken to us, see what is said.

3. [verse 2] “All nations, clap your hands.” Surely the Jewish people were not all nations? But blindness in part happened to Israel, so that foolish boys might cry out, “Baldhead, baldhead,” and thus the Lord might be crucified in the place of the Skull, so that by the shedding of his blood he might redeem the nations and what the Apostle said might be fulfilled: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter” (Rom. 11:25).

Let the empty, dull, and foolish insult and say, “Baldhead, baldhead.” But you, redeemed by his blood, which was shed in the place of the Skull, say: “All nations, clap your hands”; the grace of God has reached you.

“Clap your hands.” What does “clap” mean? Rejoice. But why with your hands? Because of good works. Do not rejoice with your mouth while your hands remain inactive. If you rejoice, clap your hands. Let the hands of the nations be seen by the one who has deigned to give them joys.

What are the hands of the nations? The deeds of those who do good. “All nations, clap your hands; shout joyfully to God with a voice of exultation.” With voice and with hands. If with voice alone, it is not good, because the hands are lazy; if with hands alone, that too is not good, because the tongue is mute. Let hands and tongue agree: let the tongue confess, and let the hands act. “Shout joyfully to God with a voice of exultation.”

4. [verse 3] “For the Lord Most High is terrible.” He who is exalted, having descended as though to be mocked, became terrible by ascending into heaven. “A great king over all the earth.” Not only over the Jews—for he is king even over them. From there the Apostles also believed; from there many thousands of people sold their possessions and placed the proceeds at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 4:34). In them was fulfilled what had been written in the title of the cross: “King of the Jews” (Matt. 27:37).

For he is indeed king of the Jews. But it is too little to say “of the Jews.” “All nations, clap your hands, for God is king of all the earth.” It is not enough for him to have one nation under him. Therefore he gave so great a price from his side, so that he might purchase the whole world. “A great king over all the earth.”

### 5. [Verse 4]

He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet. Whom has he subjected, and to whom? Who are those speaking? Perhaps the Jews? Certainly, if they are the Apostles; certainly, if they are the saints. For God subjected peoples and nations to them, so that today those who deserved to be killed by their fellow citizens might be honored among the nations. Just as their Lord was killed by his fellow citizens and is honored by the nations—crucified by his own people, worshiped by strangers—but by the price [Note: [Col. 0527] So the Erasmian edition, supported by most manuscripts. Lovaniensis has, “but by the price of his blood.” Two manuscripts have, “but by the price of his blood through his deeds.”] of his own deeds. For this reason he bought us, so that we would not be strangers to him.

Do you therefore suppose that these are the voices of the Apostles: “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet”? I do not know. It would be surprising if the Apostles spoke so arrogantly that they rejoiced that the nations had been placed beneath their feet—that is, that Christians had been placed beneath the feet of the Apostles. For they rejoice that we are with them beneath the feet of the one who died for us. Those who wished to belong to Paul were indeed running beneath Paul’s feet; and he said to them: “Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Cor. 1:13). What, then, is meant here? What are we to understand?

“He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet.” All who belong to Christ’s inheritance among all the nations are there, and all who do not belong to Christ’s inheritance among all the nations are there. And you see Christ’s Church exalted in the name of Christ in such a way that all who do not yet believe in Christ lie beneath the feet of Christians. How many people now run to the Church who are not yet Christians and ask the Church’s help! They wish to be assisted in temporal matters, even though they do not yet wish to reign with us eternally. Since everyone seeks the Church’s help, and those who are not yet in the Church do so as well, has he not subjected peoples and nations beneath our feet?

### 6. [Verse 5]

He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved. He chose for us as his inheritance a certain beauty of Jacob.

There were two brothers, Esau and Jacob. Both struggled in their mother’s womb, and their struggle shook their mother’s entrails. There, although there were two, the younger was chosen and placed over the elder; and it was said: “Two peoples are in your womb, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23).

Throughout all the nations there is an elder and a younger: the younger among good Christians, the chosen, devout, and faithful; the elder among the proud, unworthy, sinful, obstinate, and those who defend their sins rather than confess them. Such also was the Jewish people, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own (Rom. 10:3).

But since it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” it is clear that the ungodly will be subjected to the devout, and the proud to the humble. Esau was born first, and Jacob was born afterward; but the one born afterward was placed above the firstborn, who lost his birthright through his appetite.

Thus it is written: “He desired the lentil stew, and his brother said to him, ‘If you want me to give it to you, give me your birthright.’” He loved more what he had carnally desired than what, by being born first, he had spiritually deserved; and he surrendered his birthright in order to eat the lentil stew (Gen. 25:30–34).

We find that lentils are an Egyptian food, for they abound there in Egypt. Hence Alexandrian lentils are highly prized and are brought even to our lands, as though lentils did not grow here. Thus, by desiring Egyptian food, he lost his primacy.

So also the Jewish people, of whom it was said, “They turned back in their hearts to Egypt” (Acts 7:39), desired, as it were, lentils and lost their primacy. “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved.”

### 7. [Verse 6]

God ascended amid jubilation. That very God, our Lord Christ, ascended amid jubilation.

The Lord amid the sound of the trumpet. He ascended—but where, if not to the place we know? To the place the Jews did not follow him, not even with their eyes. For when he was lifted up on the cross, they mocked him; they did not see him ascending into heaven.

“God ascended amid jubilation.” What is jubilation if not an astonishment of joy that cannot be expressed in words? How the disciples rejoiced in amazement when they saw going into heaven the one whom they had mourned as dead (Acts 1:9)! Truly, words were insufficient for that joy; what remained was to exult in a way no one could explain.

There too was the sound of the trumpet, that voice of the angels. For it was said: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1). The angels proclaimed the Lord’s ascension. They saw the disciples clinging to the ascending Lord [Note: [Col. 0528] Nine manuscripts have, “the disciples saw the ascending Lord”], amazed and astonished, saying nothing but exulting in their hearts. Then the voice of the trumpet came in the clear voice of the angels: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand here? This is Jesus.”

It was as though they did not know that he was Jesus. Had they not seen him shortly before? Had they not heard him speaking with them? Indeed, they had not only seen the form of the one present but had also touched his limbs (Luke 24:39). Did they, then, not know that he was Jesus?

But because of their very astonishment, overcome with joy and jubilation as though beside themselves, the angels say: “He is Jesus.” It is as if they were saying: “If you believe in him, he is the one at whose crucifixion your feet faltered, and when he was killed and buried you thought that you had lost your hope. Behold, he is Jesus. He ascended before you; he will come in the same way as you see him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

His body is indeed taken from your eyes, but God is not separated from your hearts. See him ascending; believe in him while absent; hope for him as he comes. Yet through his hidden mercy, also perceive that he is present. For he who ascended into heaven so that he might be taken from your eyes promised you, saying: “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

The Apostle accordingly addressed us in this way: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Phil. 4:5–6). Christ sits above the heavens; the heavens are far away, yet he who sits there is near.

“The Lord amid the sound of the trumpet.” Therefore, sons of Korah, if you have now understood yourselves and recognize yourselves here, you also rejoice, because you see yourselves here.

### 8. [Verse 7]

Sing praise to our God, sing praise. He whom those alienated from God mocked as a human being—sing praise to our God. For he is not only human but also God.

Human from the seed of David (Rom. 1:3), God and Lord of David, possessing flesh from the Jews, whose are the fathers, as the Apostle says, “and from whom is the Christ according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:5). Christ, therefore, is from the Jews according to the flesh. But who is this Christ who is from the Jews according to the flesh? He is “God over all, blessed forever” (ibid. 9:5).

God before the flesh, God in the flesh, God with the flesh. Nor was he God only before the flesh, but God before the earth from which the flesh was made; nor merely God before the earth from which the flesh was made, but also God before heaven, which was made first; God before the day, which was made first; God before all the angels—Christ himself, God.

“For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). He is before all things, through whom all things were made.

Therefore sing praise to our God, sing praise [Note: [Col. 0529] The second part of verse 7, “Sing praise to our king, sing praise,” is omitted.].

### 9. [Verse 8]

For God is king of all the earth. What then? Was he not previously God of all the earth? Is he not God of heaven and earth, since all things were certainly made through him? Who could say that he is not their God?

But not all people acknowledged their God; and wherever he was acknowledged, it was as though he were God only there. “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 75:2). It was not yet said to the sons of Korah, “All nations, clap your hands.” That God who was known in Judah is God, king of all the earth.

Now he is acknowledged by everyone, because what Isaiah says has been fulfilled: “Your God himself, who redeemed you, shall be called the God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:5).

“For God is king of all the earth: sing praise intelligently.” He teaches and admonishes us to sing praise intelligently: let us not seek the sound that reaches the ear, but the light of the heart. “Sing praise,” he says, “intelligently.”

The nations, from whom you were called so that you might become Christians, worshiped gods made by hand and sang praise to them—but not intelligently. If they had sung intelligently, they would not have worshiped stones. When a rational human being sang to an irrational stone, was he singing intelligently?

But now, brothers, although we do not see with our eyes the one whom we worship, we nevertheless worship him, having been corrected [Note: [Col. 0529] The Vatican manuscript has, “correct in heart.”]. God is commended to us all the more [Note: [Col. 0529] Here the editions add, “more powerful”; some manuscripts, “greater”; neither reading occurs in the better manuscripts.] because we do not see him with our eyes. If we saw him with our eyes, perhaps we would despise him. The Jews saw Christ and despised him; the nations, who did not see him, worshiped him.

To the former, then, it was said: “Sing praise intelligently. Do not be like a horse or a mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 32:9).

### 10. [Verse 9]

The Lord will reign over all the nations. He who reigned over one nation, he says, will reign over all nations. When these words were spoken, God reigned over one nation; it was prophecy, and the reality had not yet been manifested.

Thanks be to God: now we see fulfilled what was formerly prophesied. God wrote us a document before the appointed time and, when the time was fulfilled, returned it to us.

“God will reign over all the nations”—this is a promise. “God sits upon his holy throne.” What was then promised as future is now recognized and held as fulfilled.

“God sits upon his holy throne.” What is his holy throne? Perhaps the heavens; and this is rightly understood. For Christ ascended, as we know, with the body in which he was crucified, and sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts 1:2). From there we await him to judge the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4).

“He sits upon his holy throne.” Are the heavens his holy throne? Do you also wish to be his throne? Do not suppose that you cannot be one. Prepare a place for him in your heart; he comes and gladly sits there.

He is certainly the Power of God and the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). And what does Scripture say about Wisdom itself? “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7). If, then, the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, let your soul be righteous, and you will be the royal throne of wisdom.

And truly, brothers, when all people who live well and act well conduct themselves according to devoted charity [Note: [Col. 0530] The Gatian manuscript has, “conduct themselves devoutly according to charity”], does God not sit in them and command? The soul obeys the God seated within it, and itself commands the limbs.

Your soul commands your limb: that the foot move, the hand, the eye, the ear. It commands its limbs as servants; yet it too serves inwardly the Lord who dwells within it. It cannot command what is beneath it well unless it has not disdained to serve what is above it.

“God sits upon his holy throne.”

### 11. [Verse 10]

The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham. “The God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). This is true: God said this, and the Jews grew proud because of it and said, “We are sons of Abraham.”

They were proud of their father’s name, bearing his flesh but not holding his faith; clinging to his seed but degenerating from his way of life. Finally, what did the Lord say to them in their pride? “If you are Abraham’s sons, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:33, 39).

Again, what did John say to those who came to him, when some of them trembled and wished to correct themselves through repentance? “Brood of vipers.” They were unrighteous, lost, sinful, and ungodly. They came to John’s baptism, and what did he say to them? “Brood of vipers.”

They called themselves sons of Abraham, while he called them sons of vipers. Was Abraham a viper? No; but because by living badly they had imitated demons and had become the children of those whom they imitated in their evil living, he said: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore bear fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ as though you should be proud of Abraham’s lineage. For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:7–9).

Abraham will not remain without children if God condemns you. For he is able both to condemn those whom he hates and to give to him those whom he promised.

And from where will he give him children if he condemns the Hebrews descended from his flesh? “From these stones.” He was showing them stones in the wilderness. What were those stones if not the nations, which worshiped stones?

Why were they called stones? Because by worshiping stones they had become like stones; for the psalm had foretold: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8).

Yet from those very stones he raised up children for Abraham. Now all of us who once worshiped stones have turned to the Lord and become children of Abraham—not by deriving flesh from him, but by imitating his faith.

“The princes of the peoples, therefore, have gathered with the God of Abraham.” Princes of the peoples: princes of the nations, not the princes of one people, but the princes of all peoples, have gathered with the God of Abraham.

### 12

Among those princes was also the centurion whom you heard about when the Gospel was read today. He was a centurion possessing honor and authority among men; he was a prince among the princes of the peoples.

When Christ came toward him, he sent his friends to meet him—or rather, he sent his friends to Christ as Christ was truly passing by—and asked him to heal his boy, who was dangerously ill. When the Lord himself wished to come, the centurion sent him this message:

“I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my boy will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me.”

Observe how he maintained the proper order: first he recalled that he was under someone else, and afterward that others were under him. “I am under authority, and I am in authority; I am under someone, and I am over some. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

It was as though he were saying: “If I, who am placed under authority, command those who are under me, can you, who are placed under no one’s authority, not command your own creature? Everything was made through you, and without you nothing was made. Say the word, therefore,” he says, “and my boy will be healed. For I am not worthy that you should enter my house.”

He was afraid to bring Christ inside his walls, yet Christ was already inside his heart. His soul was already Christ’s throne; already there sat the one who sought the humble.

Finally, Christ turned, expressed his wonder, and said to those following him: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Luke 7:6–9).

And as another evangelist relates the same event, the Lord continues and says: “Therefore I say to you, many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

This centurion was not from the people of Israel. Among the people of Israel, the proud drove God away from themselves; among the princes of the nations, a humble man was found who invited God to himself.

In admiring his faith, Jesus condemns the Jews’ unbelief. They seemed healthy to themselves, although they were more dangerously ill, since they did not recognize the physician and killed him.

When, therefore, he rejected and repudiated their pride, what did he say? “Therefore I say to you, many will come from the east and the west,” not belonging to Israel by kinship. Many will come to whom he said, “All nations, clap your hands,” and they will recline with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven.

Abraham did not beget them in his flesh; yet they will come and recline with him in the kingdom of heaven, and they will be his children. Why his children? Not because they were born from his flesh, but because they followed his faith.

“But the children of the kingdom”—that is, the Jews—“will go into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:11–12).

Those born from Abraham’s flesh will be condemned to the outer darkness, while those who imitated Abraham’s faith will recline with him in the kingdom of heaven. Rightly, then, it is said here as well: “The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham.”

### 13

And what of those who belonged to the God of Abraham? “For the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.”

Who were the gods? That people of God, that vineyard of God, of which it is said: “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. 5:3). They will go into the outer darkness; they will not recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; they will not gather with the God of Abraham.

Why? “For the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.” Those who were strong gods of the earth presumed upon the earth. Upon what earth? Upon themselves, because every human being is earth. For it was said to the human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

A human being ought to presume upon God and hope for help from him, not from himself. The earth does not rain upon itself or shine upon itself. Just as the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so a human being ought to await mercy and truth from God.

Those strong gods of the earth, therefore, were greatly exalted—that is, they became very proud. They did not think that they needed a physician; therefore they remained in their sickness, and through that very sickness they were brought to death.

“The natural branches were cut off so that the wild olive might be grafted in” (Rom. 11:17). “For the strong gods of the earth have been greatly exalted.”

Let us therefore hold fast, brothers, to humility, charity, and devotion. We have been called after those others were rejected; or let us fear becoming proud after their example [Note: [Col. 0532] Some editions have “in which”; certain others, “who.” Then, in place of “we have been called,” most have “we have been recalled.” Erasmus likewise has this reading; in that edition, after the word “let us fear,” “having been admonished” is added.].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 47. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [Verse 1]

The title of the psalm is: “A praise-song for the sons of Korah, for the second day of the week.”

Of what the Lord deigns to grant, receive it as sons of the firmament. For on the second day of the week—that is, after the first day, which we call the Lord’s Day and which is also called the second feria—the firmament of heaven was made, or rather, the firmament was made heaven. For God called the firmament “heaven” (Gen. 1:3–8).

On the first day he had made the light and separated it from the darkness; he had called the light “day” and the darkness “night.” As the structure of this psalm indicates, God also foretold something in that work of his which was to be fulfilled in us [Note: [Col. 0532] The editions have, “which was to be fulfilled in us with joy.” “With joy” is absent from the manuscripts.]. And according to the order of this creation, the ages ran their course.

For the Lord would not have said of Moses, “He wrote about me” (John 5:46), unless everything that was written, even when God was creating the creature, could be interpreted as signifying future things. Thus you may understand that God made the light when Christ rose from the dead. For then that light was truly separated from the darkness, when immortality was distinguished from mortality.

What follows, then, except that the body should also be made for the head—the body that is the Church?

Accordingly, there is also a psalm for the first day of the week in which the Lord’s resurrection is most clearly proclaimed. There it says: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter” (Ps. 23:7, 9) [Note: [Col. 0532] The editions have, “your princes”; some manuscripts, “your prince.” See the exposition of Psalm 23.].

What could be clearer than that Christ is the King of glory? Of him it was said: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

We must therefore understand the second day of the week as signifying nothing other than Christ’s Church—but Christ’s Church in the saints, Christ’s Church in those who are written in heaven, Christ’s Church in those who do not yield to the temptations of this world. They are worthy of the name “firmament.”

Therefore Christ’s Church in those who are firm is called the firmament, concerning whom the Apostle says: “We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Rom. 15:1).

This is the firmament of which the psalm is sung. Let us hear, acknowledge, join ourselves to it, glory in it, and reign.

Hear and recognize that it is also called the firmament in the apostolic writings: “which is,” he says, “the Church of the living God, the pillar and firmament of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15).

Of this firmament a song is sung for the sons of Korah, whom you know to be the sons of the bridegroom crucified at the place of the Skull. For Korah is interpreted as “Baldness.”

The psalm continues, the psalm entitled “for the second day of the week.”

### 2. [Verse 2]

“Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.” Behold, the Lord is great and greatly to be praised. But do unbelievers praise the Lord? Do even those who believe and live badly praise the Lord, through whom it happens that God’s name is blasphemed among the nations? Do they praise the Lord (Rom. 2:24)?

Or even if they praise him, is their praise accepted, since it is written: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9)?

You have said, “Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised.” But where? “In the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

Elsewhere it is said of this: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. 23:3–4). In these the Lord is great and greatly to be praised—that is, “in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

This is the city set upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden. This is the lamp that is not concealed beneath a bushel, known and spoken of by everyone (Matt. 5:14–15).

Not all, however, are its citizens, but only those in whom the Lord is great and greatly to be praised.

Let us therefore see what this city is, lest, since it is said, “In the city of our God, on his holy mountain,” we should seek that mountain somewhere from which we too might be heard.

For it is not said without reason in another psalm: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain” (Ps. 3:5). This mountain helped you to be heard. For if you did not ascend it, you could lie below and cry out, but you could not be heard.

What, then, is this mountain, brothers? It must be sought with great care and investigated with great diligence; it must also be occupied and ascended through labor.

But if it is located in some part of the earth, what shall we do? Shall we leave our homeland and travel until we can reach that mountain?

Rather, we are then wandering abroad if we are not in it. For it is our city, if we are members of the king who is himself the head of that city.

Where, then, is this mountain? If it occupies some region, as I said, we must labor to reach it. But why are you anxious? Would that you were not slow to ascend the mountain! The mountain was not slow to come to one who was sleeping.

There was a certain contemptible cornerstone over which the Jews stumbled (Rom. 9:32), cut from a mountain without hands—that is, coming from the kingdom of the Jews without hands, because no human work came to Mary, from whom Christ was born (Matt. 1:16).

But if this stone, where the Jews stumbled over it, had remained there, you would have nowhere to ascend. What happened, then? What does the prophecy of Daniel say? Nothing other than that this stone grew and became a great mountain (Dan. 2:34–35).

How great? So great that it filled the whole face of the earth.

Therefore, as this mountain grew and filled the whole face of the earth, it came to us. Why, then, do we seek the mountain as though it were absent, rather than ascend now into what is present, so that the Lord may be great and greatly to be praised in us?

### 3. [Verse 3]

Finally, lest you fail to recognize this mountain in this psalm and suppose that it must be sought in some region of the earth, see what follows. After saying, “In the city of our God, on his holy mountain,” what did he add?

“Making the rejoicings of the whole earth broad, the mountains of Zion.”

Zion is one mountain. Why, then, “mountains”? Is it because those who came from different directions also belonged to Zion, coming together at the cornerstone and becoming its two walls, like two mountains—one from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision; one from the Jews and the other from the nations? They are no longer opposed; though different because they came from different directions, at the corner they are no longer different [Note: [Col. 0534] Thus several manuscripts. Others have, “no longer different; and although different.” The editions read, “no longer opposed and different.”].

“For he is our peace,” Scripture says, “who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). That very cornerstone, which the builders rejected, “has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22). The mountain joined two mountains in itself.

One house and two houses: two because they came from different directions, one because of the cornerstone in which both are joined.

Hear this also: “The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.”

You had regarded Zion as one place, where Jerusalem was founded, and there you thought of no one but the people from circumcision. That people was indeed gathered by Christ from the remnant, while for the most part it was winnowed like chaff. For it is written: “The remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27).

But pay attention also to the nations; see the wild olive grafted into the richness of the olive tree (Rom. 11:17). Behold the nations: “the sides of the north.” The sides of the north have been joined to the city of the great king.

The north is usually opposed to Zion: Zion is in the south, while the north is opposite the south. Who is this north if not the one who said: “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14)?

The devil had held the kingdom of the ungodly and possessed the nations serving images and worshiping demons. Everything that belonged to the human race throughout the world had become attached to him and had become the north.

But because the one who binds the strong man takes away his vessels and makes them his own vessels (Matt. 12:29), human beings were freed from unbelief and the superstition of demons. Believing in Christ, they were joined to that city; they came together at the corner with the wall that came from circumcision; and the city of the great king was formed from what had been the sides of the north.

For this reason another Scripture also says: “From the north comes a cloud of golden color; in it is great glory and honor of the Almighty” (Job 37:22). The physician’s glory is great when a sick person recovers from a state of despair.

“From the north comes a cloud,” not black clouds, not dark, not gloomy, but golden in color. From where, if not from the grace that enlightens through Christ? [Note: [Col. 0534] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have, “enlightened”; the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts have, “enlightening.”]

Behold, “the sides of the north, the city of the great king.” They are called “sides” because they had clung to the devil. Whoever clings to someone is called that person’s side.

We also commonly speak in this way of certain people: “He is a good man, but he has bad sides”—that is, he himself excels in uprightness, but those associated with him are wicked.

The sides of the north, then, are those who clung to the devil. From them came the son about whom we were just hearing: he was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found.

By departing into a distant region, he had even come to the north, and there, as you heard, he had attached himself to one of the rulers of that region. He became a side of the north by clinging to the ruler of that region.

But because the city of the great king is gathered also from the side of the north [Note: [Col. 0535] Several manuscripts have, “and he gathers the sides of the north,” and so forth], he came to himself and said: “I will arise and go to my father.”

His father met him, saying of him: “He was dead and came to life; he was lost and was found.”

That fattened calf was the cornerstone. Finally, the elder son, who did not wish to feast (Luke 15:11–32), entered after being exhorted by his father. And the two walls, like those two sons arriving at the calf, made the city of the great king.

### 4. [Verse 4]

Let this psalm continue, then, and say: “God shall be known in her houses” [Note: [Col. 0535] An ancient Corbie manuscript has, “God is known”; the Septuagint has *ginōsketai* (“is known”).].

Now there are houses because of the mountains, because of the two walls, because of the two sons. “God shall be known in her houses.”

But he commends grace; therefore he added: “When he receives her.” For what would the city itself be if he had not received her? Would she not immediately fall if she did not have such a foundation?

“For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). Let no one, therefore, glory in his own merits; but “let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

For then she is that great city, and then the Lord is known in her, when he receives her—just as a physician receives a sick person to be cured, not as someone to be loved in the condition in which he is.

The physician hates the fever. The physician loves the sick person, and the physician does not love the sick person. If the physician loved the sick person as sick, he would always wish him to remain sick; yet if he did not love the sick person, he would not come to him. But he loves the sick person in order to make him healthy.

The Lord therefore received this city, and he was known in it—that is, his grace became known in that city—because whatever that city possesses, when it glories in the Lord, it does not possess from itself.

For this reason it is said: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

“God shall be known in her houses, when he receives her.”

### 5–7. [Verses 5–7]

“For behold, the kings of the earth have gathered.” Behold those sides of the north. See how they come; see how they say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord. For he has announced his way to us, so that we may walk in it” (Isa. 2:3).

“Behold, the kings of the earth have gathered and come together as one.” Into what one, if not into that cornerstone (Eph. 2:20)?

Seeing this, they were greatly astonished. After their astonishment at Christ’s miracles and glory, what followed? “They were troubled; they were moved; trembling seized them.”

From where did trembling seize them, if not from the awareness of their sins? Let the kings therefore run after the King; let kings acknowledge the King.

Thus elsewhere he says: “But I have been established as king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the Lord’s command. The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth. You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them’” (Ps. 2:6–9).

The king established in Zion was therefore heard, and possession was handed over to him as far as the ends of the earth.

Must kings fear lest they lose their kingdoms, lest the kingdom be taken away from them, as wretched Herod feared and, because of the child, killed the children (Matt. 2:3, 16)? In fearing to lose his kingdom, he did not deserve to recognize the King.

Would that he too had worshiped the King with the Magi! Then, by seeking the kingdom not wickedly, he would not have destroyed the innocent and perished as a guilty man.

As far as Herod was concerned, he destroyed the innocent; but as far as Christ was concerned, the infant crowned the infants who died for him.

The kings therefore ought to have feared when it was said: “I have been established as king by him, and the one who established me as king will give me an inheritance to the ends of the earth.”

But why are you jealous, kings? See; do not be jealous. This King is of an entirely different kind, for he said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

Do not fear, then, that the kingdom of this world will be taken from you. A kingdom will be given to you—but the kingdom of heaven, where that King is.

What follows there? “And now understand, O kings.” You were already preparing to be jealous; understand. It is said of another king, whose kingdom is not of this world.

Rightly, then, the kings gathered together; they were troubled; trembling seized them. And this is said to them:

“And now understand, O kings; be instructed, all you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:10–11).

And what did they experience? “There were pains like those of a woman in labor.”

What are pains like those of a woman in labor if not the pains of one who repents? Observe the very conception of pain and childbirth. Isaiah says: “From your fear we conceived and gave birth to a spirit of salvation” (Isa. 26:18).

Thus the kings conceived through fear of Christ, so that by giving birth to salvation they might bear it through believing in the one whom they had feared.

“There were pains like those of a woman in labor.” When you hear of a woman in labor, expect the child. The old human being is in labor, but the new human being is born.

“There were pains like those of a woman in labor.”

6. [verse 8.] You will crush the ships of Tarshish with a violent spirit [Note: [Col. 0536] Most manuscripts have *conterens*, “crushing”; and below, *evertens*, “overthrowing.”]. In brief, this is understood to mean: you will overthrow the pride of the nations. But how, from this historical account, is the overthrow of the pride of the nations signified? By the ships of Tarshish.

The learned have sought to identify the city of Tarshish—that is, what city was signified by this name—and some have thought that Cilicia was called Tarshish, because its metropolis is called Tarsus. The Apostle Paul was also from this city, born at Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). Others, however, understood it as Carthage, perhaps because it was once called by that name or signified by it in some usage. [Col. 0537] For in the prophet Isaiah we find: “Howl, ships of Carthage” (Isa. 23:1, according to the Septuagint). In Ezekiel, however, different translators render it variously: some have “Carthage,” others “Tarshish” (Ezek. 38:13, according to the Septuagint); and from this diversity among the translators it may be understood that the place called Carthage was also called Tarsus.

It is clear, moreover, that the beginnings of Carthage’s kingdom flourished through ships, and flourished in such a way that they surpassed the other nations in commerce and navigation. For when Dido, fleeing from her brother, came down to the lands of Africa, where she founded Carthage, she had taken for her flight the ships that had been prepared for trade in her region, with the rulers of that region agreeing to her action; and those same ships did not cease to be used for commerce after Carthage had been founded.

Thus that city became excessively proud, so that by its ships the pride of the nations may rightly be understood—pride that presumes upon uncertainties as upon the blasts of the winds. Let there no longer be presumption upon the sailing and, as it were, prosperity of this age, as upon the sea. Let our foundation be in Zion; there we must be established, not blown about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4:14).

Therefore, let all who had swollen with pride from the uncertainties of this life be overthrown; and let all the pride of the nations be subjected to Christ, who crushes the ships of Tarshish with a violent spirit—not the ships of just any city, but those of Tarshish. How with a violent spirit? With the strongest fear. For all pride feared him who would judge it in such a way that, lest it dread him in his exalted state, it would believe in him in his humility.

7. [verse 9.] “As we have heard, so also we have seen.” O blessed Church! At one time you heard; at another time you saw. You heard in the promises; you see in their fulfillment. You heard in prophecy; you see in the Gospel. For everything that is now being fulfilled was previously prophecy.

Raise your eyes, then, and spread them throughout the world. See now the inheritance extending to the ends of the earth. See now fulfilled what was said: “All the kings of the earth will worship him; all the nations will serve him” (Ps. 71:11). See fulfilled what was said: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Ps. 107:6). See him whose feet and hands were fastened with nails, whose bones, hanging upon the wood, were counted, and over whose clothing lots were cast (Matt. 27:35). See him reigning whom they saw hanging. See him seated in heaven whom they despised as he walked upon the earth.

See thereby fulfilled: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence” (Ps. 21:28). Seeing this, cry out with joy: “As we have heard, so also we have seen.”

Rightly is the Church itself, gathered from the nations, addressed in this way: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11). Your father was the North Wind; come to Mount Zion. Hear and see—not see and hear, but hear and see: hear first, and afterward see. First you hear what you do not see; afterward you will see what you have heard.

“The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45). If they obeyed at the hearing of the ear, then they did not see. And where is this: “Those to whom he was not proclaimed will see him, and those who have not heard will understand” (Isa. 52:15)? Those to whom the Prophets were not sent first heard and understood the Prophets: those who had not heard at first later, when they heard, were astonished.

Those to whom the Prophets had been sent remained behind, carrying the books but not understanding the truth; possessing the tablets of the Testament but not possessing the inheritance. But we have seen as we heard.

“In the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.” There we heard; there also we saw. Whoever is outside it neither hears nor sees; whoever is within it is neither deaf nor blind.

“As we have heard, so also we have seen.” And where do you hear? Where do you see? “In the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.” God founded it forever.

Let heretics, torn apart into factions, not insult it; let those who say, “Here is the Christ,” or, “There he is” (Matt. 24:23), not exalt themselves. Whoever says, “Here he is,” or, “There he is,” introduces divisions. God promised unity: the kings were gathered together into one; they were not scattered through schisms.

But perhaps this city, which has held the world, will one day be overthrown. Far from it! “God founded it forever.” If, then, God founded it forever, why are you afraid that its firmament will fall?

8. [verse 10.] “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your people” [Note: Erasmus and more recent manuscripts have “in the midst of your temple.” But it is clear that Augustine read “in the midst of your people.” Thus some of the ancients read in the Septuagint *laoû sou* (“of your people”) in place of *naoû sou* (“of your temple”).].

Those who received it—where did they receive it? Was it not your own people who received your mercy? If your people received your mercy, how do we say, “We have received your mercy in the midst of your people,” as though some were those who received it and others were those in whose midst they received it?

This is a great mystery, yet one that is nevertheless known. When what you know has been carved out and extracted from these verses, it will not be rougher but sweeter.

For now all who bear God’s sacraments are considered the people of God, but not all belong to his mercy. All who receive the sacrament of Christ’s Baptism are called Christians, but not all live worthily of that sacrament. There are some of whom the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5).

Nevertheless, because of that very appearance of piety, they are named among God’s people—just as, so long as the threshing floor is being threshed, not only the grain but also the chaff belongs to it. Will it also belong to the granary? In the midst of this evil people there is a good people who have received God’s mercy.

He lives worthily of God’s mercy who hears, keeps, and does what the Apostle says: “Therefore, since we exhort you, we beg you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6:1). Whoever therefore does not receive God’s grace in vain receives both God’s sacrament and his mercy.

And what harm does it do him that he lives in the midst of a disobedient people, until this threshing floor is winnowed, until the good are separated from the evil? What harm does it do him to dwell in the midst of such a people?

Let him be among those who are called the firmament, receiving God’s mercy; let him be a lily in the midst of thorns. And since the thorns themselves belong to God’s people, do you wish to hear this? The comparison itself is set forth in this way: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:2). Did he say, “among strangers”? No, but “among daughters.”

There are therefore evil daughters, and among them is a lily in the midst of thorns. Thus those who possess the sacraments but do not possess good conduct are called both God’s and not God’s; they are called both his and strangers’: his because of his sacrament, strangers because of their own vice. So too there are alien daughters: daughters because of the appearance of piety, alien because of the loss of its power.

Let the lily be there; let it receive God’s mercy; let it hold fast the root of the good flower; let it not be ungrateful for the sweet rain coming from heaven. Let the thorns be ungrateful; let them grow from the rains. They grow for the fire, not for the granary.

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your people.” In the midst of your people, who do not receive your mercy, we have received your mercy. “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:11–12).

9. At this point a thought naturally occurs to everyone: What then? How large is this people that receives God’s mercy in the midst of God’s people? How few they are! One can scarcely find anyone. Will God be content with them and destroy so great a multitude?

Those who promise themselves what they have not heard from the God who makes the promise say this. If we live badly, if we enjoy the pleasures of this world, if we serve our own lusts, is God going to destroy us? For how many are there who appear to keep God’s commandments? Scarcely one or two, or very few, can be found. Will God save only these and condemn the rest?

“Far from it,” they say. “When he comes and sees such a great multitude on the left, he will have mercy and grant pardon.” This is precisely what that serpent also promised the first human being. God had threatened death if he tasted the fruit (Gen. 2:17); but the serpent said, “Far from it—you will not die.”

They believed the serpent and found that what God had threatened was true, while what the devil had promised was false.

So now also, brothers, place the Church before your eyes in the likeness and image of paradise. The serpent does not cease to suggest what he suggested then. But the fall of the first human being ought to serve us as an example for avoiding sin, not as an example for imitating it. He fell so that we might rise.

Let us answer such suggestions as Job answered them. For the devil also tested Job through a woman, as through Eve, and Job conquered on the dunghill (Job 2:8–10), whereas the devil had conquered in paradise. Therefore, let us not listen to such voices, nor think that these people are few. They are many, but they lie hidden among the greater number.

For we cannot deny that the evil are more numerous—and so much more numerous that the good do not appear at all among them, just as the grains do not appear on the threshing floor. Anyone who sees a threshing floor may think that it is nothing but chaff. Give it to someone inexperienced, and he thinks it is pointless that oxen are driven there and that people sweat beneath the heat as they crush the chaff. But there is also grain there, to be purified by winnowing.

Then the abundance of grain that was hidden within the abundance of chaff will come forth. And now do you wish to find the good? Be good [Note: [Col. 0539] Thus five manuscripts. The editions, however, have: “And now do you wish to find them? Be good.”], and you will find them.

[Col. 0540] 10. [verse 11.] Against this despair, then, see what follows in this psalm. For when he had said, “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your people,” he indicated that there was a people not receiving God’s mercy, in the midst of which some receive God’s mercy. And lest people think that these are so few as to be almost nonexistent, how did he console them in the words that follow?

“According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth.” What does this mean? “The Lord is great and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.” Nor can his praise exist except in his saints. For those who live badly do not praise him; even if they proclaim him with their tongue, they blaspheme him by their life.

Since, then, his praise exists only in his saints, let heretics not say to themselves: “His praise has remained among us, because we are few and separated from the multitude. We live justly; we praise God not only by speaking but also by our conduct.”

This psalm answers them: What do you mean by saying that you praise God in a faction, when it is said to him, “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth”? That is: just as you are known throughout all lands, so also you are praised throughout all lands; and there are not lacking those who now praise you throughout all lands.

Those praise him who live well. “According to your name, O God, so also is your praise”—not in a part, but “to the ends of the earth.” “Your right hand is full of justice.” That is, many also are those who will stand at the right hand. Not only will there be many who stand at the left, but there will also be a fullness of the mass established at the right: “Your right hand is full of justice.”

11. [verse 12.] “Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult” [Note: [Col. 0540] Here and below in this same section 11, this should be read as it is in the better manuscripts and in the Septuagint: *Judaeae* (“of Judah”).], “because of your judgments, O Lord.”

O Mount Zion, O daughters of Judah, you now labor among weeds, among chaff, among thorns; but exult because of God’s judgments. God does not err in judging.

Live as distinct, even though you were born intermingled. It was not in vain that a voice came forth from your mouth and heart: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood” (Ps. 25:9).
