That great Craftsman will winnow; he will carry a winnowing fan in his hand, so that not one grain of wheat falls into the heap of chaff destined to be burned, nor one ear of chaff passes into the mass to be stored in the granary (Matt. 3:12).

Exult, daughters of Judah, because of the judgments of God, who does not err; and do not now presume to judge rashly. Let gathering belong to you; let separation belong to him.

“Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult, because of your judgments, O Lord.”

But do not think that the daughters of Judah are Jews. Judah means “Confession.” All children of confession are daughters of Judah, because “salvation is from the Jews” means nothing other than that Christ is from the Jews (John 4:22).

The Apostle says this too: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:28–29).

Be such a Jew: glory in circumcision of the heart, even if you do not have circumcision of the flesh. “Let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, O Lord.”

[Col. 0541] 12. [verse 13.] “Surround Zion and embrace her.” Let it be said to those who live badly, in whose midst that people lives which has received God’s mercy: “In your midst there is a people living well. Surround Zion.”

But how? “Embrace her.” Do not surround her with scandals, but surround her with love, so that you may imitate those who live well in your midst and, by imitating them, may be incorporated into Christ, whose members they are [Note: [Col. 0541] Thus most manuscripts. The editions, however, have: “Embrace Christ, whose members they are, in the body.”].

“Surround Zion and embrace her. Tell of her in her towers.” In the height of her fortifications, proclaim her praises.

13. [verse 14.] “Set your hearts upon her strength.” Do not merely possess the appearance of piety while denying its power (2 Tim. 3:5); set your hearts upon her strength.

What is the strength of this city? Whoever wishes to understand the strength of this city should understand the power of love. This is the strength that no one conquers. No waves of this age, no rivers of temptation, extinguish its fire.

Of this love it is said: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). For just as death, when it comes, cannot be resisted by any arts or medicines—whoever was born mortal cannot avoid the violence of death—so the world can do nothing against the violence of love.

The comparison is given by contrast: just as death is most violent in taking away, so love is most violent in saving. Through love many have died to the world so that they might live to God.

Burning with this love, the martyrs—not pretenders, not driven by empty glory, not people of whom it is said, “If I hand over my body to be burned but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3), but people whom the love of Christ and of the truth truly led to suffering—what could the attacks of their persecutors do to them?

The eyes of their weeping loved ones exerted greater violence than the persecutions of those who pursued them. How many children held their fathers back from suffering! How many wives fell at the knees of their husbands so that they would not be left widows! How many parents tried to prevent their children from dying, as we know and read in the passion of blessed Perpetua! These things happened.

Yet however great the tears, and however forcefully they flowed, when could they extinguish the ardor of love?

This is the strength of Zion, to which it is also said elsewhere: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121:7).

“Announce in her towers: set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses.”

14. What do we understand here by “Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses”? That is: distinguish house from house; do not confuse them.

There is a house that has the appearance of piety but does not have piety; and there is a house that has both the appearance and the reality of piety. “Distribute”—do not confuse.

But you distribute and do not confuse them when you set your hearts upon her strength—that is, when you have become spiritual through love. Then you will not judge rashly; then you will see that the evil do no harm to the good so long as we are on this threshing floor. “Distribute her houses.”

There can also be another interpretation. Those two houses—one coming from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision—were to be distributed by the Apostles.

When Saul was called and became the Apostle Paul, he came together in unity with his fellow Apostles and reached this agreement with them: they would go to the circumcision, while he would go to the uncircumcision (Gal. 2:9).

By this arrangement of their apostolate they distributed the houses of the city of the great King. Agreeing at the Cornerstone, they divided the Gospel according to their respective commissions and joined it together in love.

And this is indeed the more appropriate interpretation. For what follows shows that this was said to the preachers: “And distribute her houses,” so that “you may recount it to a future generation”—that is, so that the administration of the Gospel might also reach us, who would come afterward.

For they did not labor only for those with whom they lived on earth; nor did the Lord speak only to those Apostles to whom he graciously showed himself alive even after the resurrection, but also to us.

He was speaking to them and signifying us when he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Were they themselves going to be here until the consummation of the age?

Again he says: “I am not praying for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:20). Therefore he was mindful of us, because he suffered for us.

Rightly, then, it is said: “So that you may recount it to a future generation.”

15. [verse 15.] What are you to recount? “That this is God, our God.”

The earth was visible, but its Creator was not visible. Flesh was held, but God in the flesh was not recognized. They held the flesh that had itself been taken from them—for the Virgin Mary was from the seed of Abraham—but they remained attached to the flesh and did not understand the divinity.

O Apostles, O great city! Proclaim in your towers and say: “This is God, our God.” Just so—as he was despised, as he lay like a stone before the feet of those who stumbled, so that he might humble the hearts of those who confessed him—“this is our God.”

Certainly he was seen, as it is said: “Afterward he appeared upon earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38). “This is our God.” He is also human; and who is the one who will know him? “For this is our God.”

But perhaps he exists only for a time, like the false gods. For although they can be called gods, they cannot be gods in reality; they are called gods only for a time. What does the prophet say to them, or what does he command should be said to them? “Thus you shall say to them: The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from under heaven” (Jer. 10:11).

This God is not like those gods, “for our God is above all gods.” Above which gods? “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5).

He, then, is our God; this is our God. How long? “Forever and unto the age of the age.” He himself will rule us forever.

If he is our God, he is also our King. He protects us, because he is God, so that we may not die; he rules us, because he is King, so that we may not fall.

By ruling us, he does not break us; for those whom he does not rule, he breaks. “You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will crush them” (Ps. 2:9).

But there are those whom he does not rule; he does not spare them, crushing them like a potter’s vessel. Let us therefore desire to be ruled and delivered by him, because “this is our God forever and unto the age of the age; and he himself will rule us forever.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 48

## SERMON I. On the First Part of the Psalm

1. All the divine utterances are salutary to those who understand them well, but dangerous to those who wish to twist them according to the perversity of their own hearts rather than correct their hearts according to the uprightness of those utterances.

This is the great and customary perversity of human beings: although they ought themselves to live according to the will of God, they wish God to live according to their will. Although they themselves refuse to be corrected, they wish him to be corrupted. They do not consider right what he wills, but what they themselves will.

We are accustomed to hear people murmuring against God because the wicked prosper in this life while the good suffer—as though he were perverse and did not know what he was doing, or had altogether turned his eyes away from human affairs; or as though he did not wish his security disturbed and therefore refused to attend to these things, because God either sees or corrects them with difficulty.

People murmur, then, who wish to worship God for the sake of prospering here, when they see those who do not worship God flourishing and prospering in earthly happiness, while they themselves, worshiping God, labor amid straits, necessities, misery, and the other difficulties of human mortality.

Against this voice, and against these blasphemies of the murmurers, the divine word continually sings an incantation, healing the serpent’s bite. This is the corruption of a poisoned heart, belching the stench of blasphemy against God and, what is worse, repelling the hand of the healer rather than repelling the serpent’s bite.

What I have said is this: the human heart repels from itself the severity of God’s word and admits to itself the flatteries of the serpent who gives evil counsel.

Against such people, therefore, the divine word sings, and in this psalm it now speaks to us. Why would I direct your attention to this psalm [Note: [Col. 0543] The editions have: “how I might make Your Holiness attentive.” The word “how” is absent from the manuscripts.] unless it itself made us all attentive—not us alone, but the entire world?

Hear how it begins.

2. [verse 2.] “Hear these things, all nations.” You are not the only ones who are here. For how great is our voice, that we should cry out in such a way that all nations may hear? Our Lord Jesus Christ cried out through the Apostles; he cried out through so many tongues that he sent [Note: [Col. 0543] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts, except the Vatican and Regius manuscripts, which have “as many tongues as he sent.” The reading in Lovaniensis, “into which he sent,” is less suitable.].

And we see this psalm, which previously was recited only among one nation, in the synagogue of the Jews, now recited throughout the whole world, in all the churches. What was said here has been fulfilled: “Hear these things, all nations.”

For this one reason I wish to make your minds attentive: do not, because of bodily weariness, fail to lift up your spirit, frightened by the length of this psalm. If it is possible, it will be completed today; if not, something will remain for us until tomorrow. Nevertheless, always remain attentive. For, if the Lord wills, you will hear as much as will not burden but refresh you.

“Hear these things, all nations”—and you are among them. “Give ear, all you who inhabit the world.” This seems to repeat what he said, as though “Hear” were not enough. What I say, he means, hear; give ear to it—that is, do not hear it in passing.

What does “give ear” mean? It means what the Lord said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:25). All who stood before him certainly had ears; which ears, then, was he seeking, when he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” except the ears of the heart?

This psalm also strikes those ears: “Give ear, all you who inhabit the world.”

Perhaps there is also some distinction here. We ought not to confine the meaning, but there is no harm in explaining this interpretation as well. Perhaps there is a difference between what he said, “all nations,” and what he said, “all who inhabit the world.”

For perhaps he wished us to understand more significantly what he said, “inhabit”—so that we understand all nations as all the wicked, but the inhabitants of the world as all the just.

For the one who is not held captive inhabits; the one who is held captive is inhabited, not an inhabitant. In the same way, a person possesses whatever he has when he is master of his possessions; and he is master when he is not entangled by desire. But whoever is held by desire is possessed, not a possessor.

We find a certain expression marked by the idea of inhabiting in God’s Scripture, where it says: “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). For if you are cast down in the house of the Lord, do you not dwell there?

He did not wish to signify dwelling except among those who rule, hold, govern, and exercise dominion. Those who are despised do not, as it were, dwell; they are subject.

Thus he said: “I wish to be subject in the house of God rather than to reign in the tents of sinners.”

Therefore, if there is some distinction between “all nations” and “the inhabitants of the world,” just as there is a distinction between “hear” and “give ear,” he seems indeed to have repeated himself; nevertheless, he surely wished to signify something else, because these utterances were going to be heard not only by sinners and ungodly people, but also by the just.

For now all hear indiscriminately. But when the time comes to render an account, those who heard without purpose will be separated from those who gave ear.

Let sinners hear, then: “Hear these things, all nations.” Let the just also hear—those who have not heard without purpose, and who rule the earth rather than being ruled by the earth: “Give ear, all you who inhabit the world.”

3. [verse 3.] And again he says: “Both earthborn and children of human beings.” By “earthborn” he referred to sinners; by “children of human beings,” to the faithful and the just.

You see, then, that this distinction is preserved. Who, therefore, are the earthborn? The children of earth. Who are the children of earth? Those who seek earthly inheritances. Who are the children of human beings? Those who belong to the Son of Man.

We have already explained this distinction to Your Holiness on another occasion, and we found that Adam was a human being but was not the Son of Man, whereas Christ was the Son of Man and was God [Note: [Col. 0544] In *Exposition of Psalm 8*, section 10.].

All who belong to Adam are earthborn; all who belong to Christ are children of human beings. Nevertheless, let everyone hear; I withhold my word from no one.

If you are earthborn, hear because of judgment; if you are a child of human beings, hear because of the kingdom.

“Together as one, rich and poor.” Again the same things are repeated. What he says by “rich” pertains to the earthborn; what he says by “poor” pertains to the children of human beings.

Understand “rich” as proud and “poor” as humble. A person may possess many financial resources; if he is not lifted up by them, he is poor. He may possess nothing, yet desire and become inflated; God counts him among the rich and the rejected.

God examines rich and poor in the heart, not in the chest [Note: [Col. 0545] Erasmus and most manuscripts have “in the threshing floor.” The Vatican manuscript has “in the granary.”] and the house.

Are not those poor who receive the Apostle’s command to Timothy: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud” (1 Tim. 6:17)? How did he make those who were rich poor? He took away from them what makes riches desirable.

No one wishes to be rich except in order to become inflated among those with whom he lives and to appear superior to them. But when he said, “not to be proud,” he made them equal to those who do not possess riches. Perhaps a beggar with a few coins is more lifted up than the rich person who hears the Apostle say: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud.”

How are they not to be proud? If they do what follows: “Nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us with all things abundantly for enjoyment” (1 Tim. 6:17).

He did not say, “who provides them with all things,” but “who provides us with all things.” Did Paul himself not possess riches? Certainly he did. What riches? Those of which Scripture says elsewhere: “For the faithful person the whole world is a wealth of riches” (Prov. 17:6, according to the Septuagint).

Hear Paul himself confessing: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10). Whoever wishes to be rich should not cling to a part, and he will possess the whole; let him cling to the one who created the whole.

“Together as one, rich and poor.”

He says in another psalm: “The poor will eat and be satisfied.” How did he commend the poor? “The poor will eat and be satisfied.” What do they eat? The faithful know. How will they be satisfied? By imitating the passion of their Lord and not receiving their price without purpose.

“The poor will eat and be satisfied, and they will praise the Lord who seek him.”

What of the rich? They too eat. But how do they eat? “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped” (Ps. 21:27, 30). He did not say, “They ate and were satisfied,” but, “They ate and worshiped.”

They worship God, certainly, but they do not wish to show brotherly kindness. The one group eats and worships; the other eats and is satisfied. Nevertheless, all eat.

What is required of the one who eats is what he eats. Let the steward not prevent him from eating, but let him warn him to fear the exactor.

Let sinners and the just hear these things; nations and those who inhabit the world; earthborn and children of human beings; rich and poor together as one—not divided, not separated.

The time of the harvest will accomplish this; the hand of the winnower will be able to do it (Matt. 3:12). For now, let rich and poor hear together as one; let goats and lambs be fed together as one, until the one comes who will separate some to the right and others to the left (Matt. 25:32–33).

Let them hear together as one the teacher, lest, separated from one another, they hear the judge.

4. [verse 4.] And what are they now going to hear? “My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart, understanding.”

This is repeated, lest perhaps, when he said “my mouth,” you should understand that the one speaking to you possessed wisdom only on his lips. For many have it on their lips but do not have it in their heart. Scripture says of them: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

What, then, does the one who speaks to you say? After he has said, “My mouth will speak wisdom,” so that you may understand that what flows from his mouth comes forth from the vein of his heart, he adds: “And the meditation of my heart, understanding.”

### 5. [verse 5]

I will incline my ear to a parable; I will disclose my proposition on the psaltery.

Who is this whose heart’s meditation speaks understanding, so that it is not merely on the surface of his lips but possesses the inward parts of the human being? Who is this who hears and then speaks in this way? For many speak what they do not hear.

Who are those who speak what they do not hear? Those who do not do what they say—such as, the Lord says, the Pharisees who sit upon Moses’ seat. He wished to speak to you from Moses’ seat through those who say these things and do not do them, and the Lord wished to give you security. “Do not fear,” he says: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they say things and do not do them” (Matt. 23:2–3). They do not hear what they say.

But those who do what they say, and then speak, hear what they say; and therefore they speak fruitfully, because they hear. Thus, whoever is a speaker but not a hearer benefits another but does not benefit himself.

Therefore this man, who wished to be both a hearer and a speaker, who speaks to you, before saying, “I will disclose my proposition on the psaltery”—which is already to speak through the body, for the soul uses the body as a harpist uses a psaltery—said, “I will incline my ear to a parable.”

“Before I speak to you,” he says, “through the body, before the psaltery sounds, I will first incline my ear to a parable,” that is, I will hear what I am to say to you. And why “to a parable”? Because “now we see through a mirror, in an enigma,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 13:12). “As long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6), because that vision of ours face to face has not yet come—where there are no longer parables, no longer enigmas and likenesses.

Whatever we now understand, we see through enigmas. An enigma is an obscure parable that is difficult to understand. However much a person cultivates his heart and withdraws into the inward regions in order to understand, as long as we see through the corruptibility of this flesh, we see only in part.

But when incorruption has been assumed in the resurrection of the dead, when the Son of Man appears to judge the living and the dead, then the Son of Man will be seen: the one who was first judged will judge, distinguishing the wicked from the good, placing the wicked on the left and the good on the right. Both the good and the wicked will see him, but to the wicked he will say, “Go into eternal fire,” while to the good he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” “The wicked will go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:33–34, 41, 46). And there will be that vision face to face, of which they are not worthy.

Pay attention to what I am saying. For when the Son of Man was here and still had to be judged, [Col. 0547] both the wicked and the good saw him: the Apostles who followed him saw him, and the Jews who crucified him saw him. So when he comes to judge, both the good and the wicked will see him: the good, in order to receive the reward because they followed him; the wicked, in order to receive punishment because they crucified him.

Will only those who crucified him be condemned? I dare to say: only they. “Then we,” say the sinners of this age, “are secure.” If God does not examine the mind, you are secure. What did I mean by that? May Your Charity understand, lest they say this at God’s judgment because they did not understand.

The Jews saw Christ and crucified him; you do not see Christ, yet you resist his word. You who resist his word—would you not crucify his flesh if you saw it? The Jew despised him hanging on the wood; you despise him seated in heaven. Thus both kinds saw him while he was here, and both kinds will see him when he comes. For the Son of Man will come to judge, because the Son of Man came to be judged.

Therefore, since the Father was not incarnate and did not suffer, and judges through the Son of Man—as he himself said in the Gospel, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”—he then adds shortly afterward, “And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:22, 27).

According to the fact that he is the Son of God, the Word is always with the Father; and because he is always with the Father, he always judges with the Father. But according to the fact that he is the Son of Man, he was judged and will judge.

Just as he was seen by those who believed and by those who crucified him when he was judged, so he will be seen when he begins to be judge, both by those whom he will condemn and by those whom he will crown.

But the vision of his divinity, which he promised to those who love him when he said, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14:21), the ungodly will no longer see. This manifestation is, in a certain sense, intimate: he preserves it for his own; he does not show it to the ungodly.

What sort of vision is this? What sort of Christ? Equal to the Father. What sort of Christ? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

For this vision we now sigh and groan as long as we are exiles; to this vision we shall be restored at the end. At present we see this vision in an enigma. Therefore, if we see in an enigma, let us incline our ear to a parable and thus disclose our proposition on the psaltery: let us hear what we say; let us do what we command.

### 6. [verse 6]

And what did he say? “Why should I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.”

He began more obscurely: “Why should I fear,” he says, “on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.” He ought, then, to fear all the more if the iniquity of his heel will surround him.

For, he says, a person ought not to fear what he has no power to avoid. For example, one who fears death—what can he do so as not to die? Let him tell me how he can escape what Adam, who was born from Adam, must undergo.

[Note: [Col. 0547] Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read: “Let him tell me where he is to go. He owes what Adam [Col. 0548] owes, who was born from Adam. But let him consider that he was born from Adam and has followed Christ, that he must,” etc.]

But let him consider that he was born from Adam, followed Christ, and must pay what Adam owes and obtain what Christ promised.

Therefore, the one who fears death has no way to escape it. But [Col. 0548] the one who fears the condemnation that the wicked will hear—“Go into eternal fire”—has a way to escape. Should he not fear, then? Why should he fear? Is the iniquity of his heel going to surround him?

If, therefore, he avoids the iniquity of his heel and walks along God’s paths, he will not come to the evil day. The evil day, the last day, will not be evil for him. For the last day will be evil for some and good for others. Surely it will not be evil for those to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom”? But it will be evil for those to whom it will be said, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

And if the iniquity of his heel will surround him, why then does he fear on the evil day? While they are alive, let them provide for themselves; let them remove iniquity from their heel. Let them walk that way; let them walk along the way of which he himself said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Let them not fear on the evil day, because the one who became the way gives them security.

“Why should I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.” Therefore, let them avoid the iniquity of their heel.

Everyone slips at the heel. Let Your Charity pay attention. What did God say to the serpent? “She shall watch your head, and you shall watch her heel” (Gen. 3:15). The devil watches your heel when you slip, in order to throw you down. He watches your heel; you watch his head.

What is his head? The beginning of an evil suggestion. When he begins to suggest evil, repel it before pleasure arises and consent follows. Then you will avoid his head, and he will not seize your heel.

But why did he say this to Eve? Because a human being slips through the flesh. Eve is our inward flesh. “Whoever loves his wife loves himself.” What does “himself” mean? He continues and says, “For no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:28–29).

Therefore, just as he overthrew that man Adam through Eve (Gen. 3:6), so the devil wishes to overthrow us through the flesh. Eve was commanded to watch the devil’s head, because the devil watches her heel.

If, then, the iniquity of the heel will surround us, why do we fear on the evil day, when, having turned to Christ, we have it in our power not to commit iniquity? Then there will be nothing to surround us, and we shall rejoice on the last day rather than mourn.

### 7. [verse 7]

But who are those whom the iniquity of the heel will surround? “Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the abundance of their riches.”

Therefore, I will avoid these things, and the iniquity of my heel will not surround me. What does it mean to avoid these things? Let us not trust in our own strength; let us not glory in the abundance of our riches. Rather, let us glory in the one who promised exaltation to the humble and threatened condemnation to the proud. Then the iniquity of the heel will not surround us.

“Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the abundance of their riches.”

### 8. [verse 8]

There are those who put their confidence in their friends; others put their confidence in their strength, and others in their riches. This is the presumption of the human race, which does not put its confidence in God.

He has spoken of strength; he has spoken of riches; he now speaks of friends: [Col. 0549] “A brother does not redeem; will a human being redeem?” Do you expect a human being to redeem you from the coming wrath? If a brother does not redeem you, will a human being redeem you?

Who is this brother such that, if he does not redeem, no human being will redeem? The one who said after the resurrection, “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). He wished to be our brother. And when we say to God, “Our Father,” this is made manifest in us. For whoever says to God, “Our Father,” says to Christ, “Brother.”

Therefore, whoever has God as Father and Christ as brother need not fear on the evil day. The iniquity of his heel will not surround him, because he does not presume upon his own strength, nor glory in the abundance of his riches, nor boast of his powerful friends.

Let him therefore put his confidence in the one who died for him, so that he might not die forever; who was humbled for him, so that he might be exalted; who sought the ungodly, so that he might be sought by the faithful.

Therefore, if he himself does not redeem, will a human being redeem? Will some human being redeem if the Son of Man does not redeem? If Christ does not redeem, will Adam redeem?

“A brother does not redeem; will a human being redeem?”

### 9. [verse 9]

“He will not give God his atonement, nor the price of the redemption of his soul.”

[Note: The editions read *de propitiatione sua*, “of his propitiation.” But the manuscripts read *depropitiationem suam*, “his atonement,” in accordance with the Septuagint, *exilasma heautou*.]

The one who trusts in his own strength and glories in the abundance of his riches is the one who “will not give God his atonement”—that is, the appeasement by which he might appease God concerning his sins—nor “the price of the redemption of his soul,” because he presumes upon his strength, his friends, and his riches.

But who are those who give the price of the redemption of their souls? Those to whom the Lord says, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles” (Luke 16:9). Those give the price of the redemption of their souls who do not cease giving alms.

Thus the Apostle did not want those whom he admonished through Timothy to be proud, lest they glory in the abundance of their riches. Indeed, he did not want what they possessed to grow old in their possession, but wanted something to be made from it that would be the price of the redemption of their souls.

For he says: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment.”

And as though they were saying, “What, then, are we to do with our riches?” he replies: “Let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share.” They will not lose that wealth. How do we know? Hear what follows: “Let them lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19). Thus they will give the price of the redemption of their souls.

Our Lord also gives this admonition: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys” (Luke 12:33). God did not want you to lose your riches; he gave you the instruction to change their location.

May Your Charity understand. Suppose your friend entered your house and found that you had placed grain in a damp place. Perhaps he knew the nature of grain’s decay, which you did not know. He would give you this advice, saying: “Brother, you are wasting what you gathered with great labor. [Col. 0550] You have placed it in a damp place; within a few days it will rot.”

“And what should I do, brother?”

“Move it upstairs.”

You would listen to a friend advising you to move your grain from below to above, yet you do not listen to Christ warning you to move your treasure from earth to heaven—where what you store is not returned to you in the same form, but you store up earth and receive heaven; you store up mortal things and receive eternal ones.

“Lend to Christ” [Note: The editions read *fenera Christo*, “lend to Christ.” The manuscripts instead read *feneres Christum*, “you lend Christ.” Martial joins this verb with the accusative in Book 1, Epigram 77: “She alone lends to all the gods.”]; let him receive a little on earth, so that he may return much to you in heaven.

But those whom the iniquity of their heel will surround—because they trust in their own strength, glory in the abundance of their riches, and presume upon human friends who are powerless to provide anything—will not give God their atonement or the price of the redemption of their souls.

[Note: So read the Ambrosian manuscript and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain instead read *qui*, “who.”]

### 10. [verse 10]

And what did he say about such a person? “And he labored forever, and he will live to the end.”

[Note: The editions read *laborabit*, “he will labor.” But the better manuscripts read *laboravit*, “he labored,” in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, *ekopiasen*.]

His labor will be without end; his life will have an end. Why did he say, “He will live to the end”? Such people regard nothing as life except their daily pleasures.

Indeed, many of our needy and poor people, weak in faith and not considering what God promises them in return for these labors, see the rich at daily banquets, in the splendor and brilliance of gold and silver, and say, “These alone are happy; these truly live.” [Note: Erasmus reads “Happy.”]

It is said; let it no longer be said—and we admonish them. Even if it must be said, let it be said by fewer people than would say it if we did not admonish them. For we do not presume that we can speak in such a way that no one will say it; but let it at least be said by fewer people. For it will be said until the end of the age.

It is not enough that he says that the rich man lives; he adds and says—he thunders: “You suppose that he alone lives.” Let him live; his life will end. Since he does not give the price of the redemption of his soul, his life will end, but his labor will not end.

“He labored forever, and he will live to the end.”

How will he live to the end? As the one who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day lived, while he proudly and arrogantly despised the ulcerated man lying at his gate, whose sores the dogs licked, and who desired the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table.

What did those riches profit him? Both exchanged places. The poor man was carried from the rich man’s gate into Abraham’s bosom; the rich man was sent from his splendid banquets into the fire. One rested; the other burned. One was satisfied; the other thirsted. The one had labored to the end and lived forever; the other had lived to the end and labored forever.

And what did it profit the rich man, who, placed in torments in Hades, sought to have a drop of water sprinkled on his tongue from Lazarus’s finger, saying, “For I am burning here in this flame,” and it was not granted to him (Luke 16:19–26)?

He desired a drop from the finger just as the other had desired crumbs from the rich man’s table. But the poor man’s labor ended, and his life ended; the rich man’s labor is eternal, while the poor man’s life is eternal.

We do not have life here, even if we happen to labor here on earth. We shall not be so [Col. 0551] afterward; for our life will be Christ forever. But those who wish to have life here will labor forever and live to the end.

### 11. [verse 11]

“For he will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying.”

This man who labored forever and will live to the end will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying. What does this mean? He will not understand what destruction is when he sees the wise dying.

For he says to himself: “This man was wise, lived with wisdom, and worshiped God with piety. Surely he has died? I shall therefore make good use of myself while I live; for if those who think otherwise could accomplish anything, they would not die.”

He sees the wise man die but does not see what death is. “He will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying.”

Just as the Jews saw Christ hanging on the cross and despised him, saying, “If he were the Son of God, he would come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:42), not seeing what destruction is. If they had seen what destruction is—if only they had seen it! [Note: Thus some manuscripts. The editions instead read, “if they had seen themselves.”]

He was dying temporarily in order to live again eternally; they were living temporarily in order to die eternally. But because they saw him dying, they did not see destruction—that is, they did not understand what true destruction was.

What do they also say in the Book of Wisdom? “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for there will be regard for his words; for if he is truly God’s son, he will deliver him from the hands of his enemies” (Wis. 2:20, 18). He will not permit his son to die, if he is truly his son.

But when they saw him on the cross mocking them, and saw that he did not come down from the cross, they said, “He truly was a man.” It was said. Certainly he could have come down from the cross, who was able to rise from the tomb. But he taught us to endure those who mock us; he taught us to be patient toward human tongues; to drink for now the cup of bitterness and afterward to receive eternal salvation.

Drink, sick person, the bitter cup, so that you may become well—you whose inward parts are not sound. Do not tremble, because, so that you would not tremble, the physician drank first. That is, the Lord first drank the bitterness of suffering.

He drank who had no sin, who had nothing in himself that needed healing. Drink until the bitterness of this age passes and the age comes in which there is no scandal, no anger, no decay, no bitterness, no fever, no deceit, no enmity, no old age, no death, and no contention.

Labor here, since you are coming to the end. Labor, lest, when you are unwilling to labor here, you come to the end of life but never come to the end of labors.

“For he will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying.”

### 12

“Together the foolish and the senseless will perish.”

Who is the foolish person? One who does not provide for himself in the future. Who is the senseless person? One who does not understand what evil he is in.

But understand what evil you are in now, and provide that you may be among good things hereafter. By understanding what evil you are in, you will not be senseless; by providing for yourself in the future, you will not be foolish.

Who is the one who provides for himself? That servant to whom his master gave something to distribute, and afterward said to him, “You cannot continue as my steward; give an account of your stewardship.”

And he said, “What shall I do? I cannot dig, and I am ashamed to beg.” But from his master’s property he made friends for himself [Col. 0552] who would receive him when he was dismissed from his stewardship.

He committed fraud against his master in order to acquire friends who would receive him. You need not fear committing fraud; the Lord himself urges you to do it. He himself says to you, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:1–2).

Perhaps you acquired what you possess through iniquity; or perhaps the very thing is iniquity, because you have something while another does not, you abound while another is in need. From this mammon of iniquity—from these riches that the unjust call riches—make friends for yourself, and you will be prudent. You are acquiring something for yourself; you are not being defrauded.

For now you seem to be losing. Surely you do not lose by placing it in the treasury? [Note: Louvain reads “in Christ’s treasury.” “Christ” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts, most of which here have *thesauro* (“treasure”) for *thesaurario* (“treasury”); Augustine plainly indicates that he borrowed this barbarous word from children.] Children, brothers, somehow find coins with which they can buy something together, and put them in a treasury, and do not open it until later. Surely, because they do not see what they are collecting, have they therefore lost it?

Do not fear. Children put their coins in a treasury and are secure; you put yours in Christ’s hand, and you are afraid!

Be prudent and provide for yourself in the future, in heaven. Therefore, be prudent; imitate the ant, as Scripture says (Prov. 6:6; 30:25). Store up in summer, lest you hunger in winter. Winter is the last day, the day of tribulation; winter is the day of scandals and bitterness. Gather what may benefit you there in the future. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “what may profit you.”]

But if you do not do this, “together the foolish and the senseless will perish.”

### 13

But that rich man died, and such a funeral was held for him. See where human beings have turned their attention: they do not consider how evil his life was while he lived, but what pomp accompanied his death.

O happy man, whom so many mourn! Yet this man [Note: The manuscripts read “so.”] lived in such a way that few mourn him. Everyone ought to mourn one who lived so wickedly.

But there is funeral pomp: he is received into a costly tomb, wrapped in precious garments, and buried with perfumes and spices. Then what kind of memorial does he have—how marble-clad it is! Does one live in that memorial? He died there. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read: “He lives in that memorial, where he died.”]

Thinking these things good, human beings have wandered from God; they have not sought what is true and have been deceived by false things. See what follows.

The one who did not give the price of the redemption of his soul, who did not understand destruction because he saw the wise dying, became foolish and senseless, so that he perished together with them.

“And how will those who leave their riches to others perish?” Together the foolish and the senseless will perish.

### 14

Pay attention, brothers: “And they will leave their riches to others.” It is as though Scripture placed under a curse those whose possessions, when they die, will be owned by others.

So are those happy who leave their possessions to their children, to whom their own succeed? He had children; he has not died. What about his children? They too preserve what their parents left them. It is little that they preserve it; they increase it.

For whom do they preserve it? For their children, and those children for theirs, and the third generation for its children. What about Christ? What about their own souls? Everything is for their children.

Among the children they have on earth, let them count one brother whom they have in heaven, to whom they ought to have given everything—or [Col. 0553] at least to have divided it with him.

But someone may say to me: “Look, Scripture called those accursed whom it said would perish and leave their riches to others. Yet the one who leaves them to his own is blessed.”

I examine this meaning because I incline my ear to a parable, and I see that Scripture does not speak this way without reason. I see many wicked people die whose successors are their children. Scripture could not have spoken in such a way as to separate from misery those whose life it condemns.

What, then, do you suppose I understand, brothers, except that all such people leave their riches to others?

How are their children “others”? The children of the wicked are others. For we find someone who became a stranger’s relative because he did good. If one of your own does nothing for you, he is a stranger to you.

Where do we find someone from outside made a relative because he did good? In the Gospel. A man lay wounded by robbers, but the Lord had said to someone, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” And he had replied, “And who is my neighbor?”

The Lord told this story: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, who wounded him and left him half-dead on the road.” His relatives passed by. For he was a Jew, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest passed by and went on; a Levite passed by and also went on.

Then a certain Samaritan passed by—a Samaritan, I do not know who, a stranger. He approached the man, looked upon his misery, and in mercy treated his wounds. He lifted him onto his beast, brought him to an inn, and entrusted him to the innkeeper.

These matters were spoken in a mystery and now seem too lengthy to discuss. Nevertheless, for the point I have proposed, brothers, the Lord asked, “Which of these was neighbor to the wounded man?”

He replied, “I suppose the one who showed him mercy.”

“Go,” he said, “and do likewise” (Luke 10:27–37).

The one to whom you show mercy is your neighbor. Therefore, if the foreign Samaritan became a neighbor by showing mercy and giving assistance, whoever is unable to help you in tribulation has become a stranger to you.

Now let us consider those rich people who lived wickedly, acted arrogantly, died, and left their riches—not, I will not say, to strangers, but to their children. Their children follow the way of their parents: as the parents were proud, so are the children; as the parents were rapacious, so are the children; as the parents were greedy, so are the children. They are strangers to them.

For you may know that they are strangers by this: would the heirs of that rich man’s wealth have helped him while he was burning in the flame? Perhaps he had no one to succeed him, and strangers possessed his riches?

We find in that very Gospel that he did have heirs, for he says, “I have five brothers” (Luke 16:28). His brothers could not help him while he was burning in the flame.

What would the rich man say to you? “I have five brothers.” [Note: Manuscripts of good quality read: “Would they help him who was burning in the flame? What would the rich man say to you? ‘Which brothers?’ I did not make one brother my friend,” and so forth. Some manuscripts read: “What would the rich man say to you? What brothers? I did not make one brother,” and so forth.]

“I did not make one brother my friend, who lay before my gate. Those who possess my riches cannot help me; they have become strangers to me.”

You see that all who live wickedly leave their riches to strangers.

### 15. [verse 12]

But do those very strangers, [Col. 0554] who are called their own, really benefit them? Hear what they benefit them with; consider how they are mocked:

“Together the foolish and the senseless will perish, and they will leave their riches to others.”

Why did he say “to others”? Because they can benefit them in nothing. Yet in what way do they seem to benefit them?

“And their tombs are their houses forever.”

Since these tombs have been built, the tombs are houses. For you often hear a rich man saying, “I have a marble-clad house that I shall leave behind,” while he does not think about an eternal house where he will always be.

When he thinks about having a marble-clad or sculpted memorial made for himself, he thinks as though he were thinking about an eternal house, as though the rich man would remain there. If he remained there, he would not be burning in Hades.

One must consider where the spirit of the wicked person remains, not where the mortal body is placed. “Their tombs are their houses forever.”

“Their tabernacles are from generation to generation.” Tabernacles are the places in which they remained temporarily; houses, in which they will remain as though forever, are the tombs.

Therefore, they leave their tabernacles to their own, where they lived temporarily, and pass over as though to eternal houses—to the tombs.

What benefit do their tabernacles provide them from generation to generation? Suppose “generation and generation” means children and grandchildren and great-grandchildren. What do they do? What benefit do their tabernacles provide?

What? Hear: “They will invoke their names in their lands.”

What does this mean? They will take bread and wine to the tombs and invoke the names of the dead there. How much do you suppose that rich man’s name was invoked afterward, when people were getting drunk at his memorial, while not one drop descended upon his burning tongue (Luke 16:24)?

People serve their own bellies, not the spirits of their dead. Nothing reaches the spirits of the dead except what the living did with themselves. If the living did not do it with themselves, nothing reaches the dead.

But what do they do? “They will merely invoke their names in their lands.”

### 16. [verse 13]

“And the human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.”

How human beings have been insulted—those who did not understand what they should do with their riches while they lived, and thought they would be blessed if they had a marble-clad memorial, as though it were an eternal house, and if their own, to whom they had left their substance, invoked their names in their lands.

They ought instead to have prepared an eternal house for themselves through good works, prepared immortal life for themselves, sent expenses ahead of themselves, followed their works, paid attention to the needy companion, given to the one with whom they were walking, and not despised Christ, ulcerated before the gate, who said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

Therefore, “the human being did not understand when he was in honor.” What does “when he was in honor” mean? Made according to the image and likeness of God, the human being was placed over the beasts (Gen. 1:26).

For God did not make the human being as he made the beast; rather, God made the human being so that the beasts would serve him. Surely this was not on account of his bodily strength, but on account of his understanding?

But he did not understand. And the one who was made according to the image of God was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.

Thus elsewhere it is said: “Do not be like the horse [Col. 0555] and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

### 17. [verse 14]

“This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves.”

Let it be a stumbling block to them, not to you. When will it also be a stumbling block to you? If you think that such people are blessed. If you understand that they are not blessed, their way will be a stumbling block to them—not to Christ, not to his body, not to his members.

“And afterward they will bless with their mouth.”

What does “afterward they will bless with their mouth” mean? When they have become such that they seek nothing except temporal goods, they become hypocrites. When eternal life is praised to them and they are told that, in Christ’s name, they ought to be despisers of riches, they twist their mouth in their heart. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read, “the contempt of riches ought to exist”; and shortly afterward, “they twist their mouth in their heart,” whereas the editions read, “they are twisted in their heart.”]

If they do not dare to do this openly, lest they be ashamed or reproved by people, they do it in their hearts: they despise it. Thus blessing remains in their mouth, but cursing in their heart.

“And afterward they will bless with their mouth.”

It would take too long to finish the Psalm. Let what Your Charity has heard for now today suffice. Tomorrow you will hear what the Lord wills.

## SERMON II. On the second part of the Psalm

### 1. [verse 14]

Yesterday, as Your Charity remembers, the Psalm that had been begun required a conclusion. We had reached the verse in which the Spirit of God identifies people who pay attention only to present, worldly, earthly matters and think of nothing in the future after this life, supposing that there is no happiness except the riches, honors, and passing power of this age. [Note: Three manuscripts read, “and passing life.” The Ambrosian manuscript reads, “and passing happiness.” Erasmus reads, “and passing power and happiness.”]

After their death they pay attention only to how pompous funerals may be arranged for them, how they may be buried in monuments constructed with marvelous workmanship, and how their names may be invoked in their lands by their households. They do not acquire for themselves a place where the spirit may be after this life. They are fools, not trembling at the voice of Christ, who says, “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

Nor do they pay attention after splendid daily banquets, purple, and fine linen to the rich man condemned to torments in Hades, or after labors, sores, and hunger to the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:19). They do not care about these things, but pay attention to what is present. After this death they provide only that their name—which is rejected in heaven—may be invoked on earth.

Describing such people, therefore, the Holy Spirit says: “This is the way of those who are a stumbling block to themselves, and afterward they will bless with their mouth.”

The Lord Jesus Christ spoke similarly about certain people who at first approach the faith, cleansed by the word of God and by exorcisms in Christ’s name, so that they may receive God’s grace and be baptized, but afterward return to worse evils than those they had previously committed. “Their later condition,” Peter says, “becomes worse than the earlier” (2 Pet. 2:20). This is what the Apostle Peter says. But the Lord [Col. 0556] says, “The later condition of that man will be worse than the earlier” (Luke 11:26).

Why? Because at first he was at least an open pagan, but afterward he is disguised under the Christian name: an evil person concealed beneath the veil of religion. And he will be worse because he is concealed, as it says, “And afterward they will bless with their mouth.” That is, you hear the name of God and the name of Christ on his lips, but you do not find them in his heart.

Of such people it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Thus far, then, the Psalm had been expounded.

2. [verse 15] Then the verses to be examined and expounded today begin as follows:

“Like sheep placed in hell, death is their shepherd.” Whom does he mean? Those whose way is a stumbling-block to them. Whom? Those who attend only to present things, while giving no thought to the future; those who consider no life to be life except this one—which ought rather to be called death. Therefore it is not without reason that, like sheep in hell, they have death as their shepherd.

What does it mean that they have death as their shepherd? Is death some thing, or some power? Death, certainly, is either the separation of the soul from the body—and the death which people fear is indeed the separation of the soul from the body—or true death, which people do not fear, is the separation of the soul from God. And very often, when people fear the death that separates the soul from the body, they fall into that death in which the soul is separated from God.

This, then, is death. But how is death their shepherd? If Christ is life, the devil is death. We find in many places in Scripture that Christ is life. The devil, however, is death—not because he himself is death, but because death comes through him. Whether it was the death into which Adam fell that was offered to humanity through his persuasion, or whether it is the death in which the soul is separated from the body, he is the author of both: he first fell through pride, envied the one who was standing, and cast down the standing man by an invisible death, so that he would also suffer visible death (Genesis 3:2).

[Note: [Col. 0556] Thus in the manuscripts of better quality. Some, however, together with Erasmus, read “would lose him by visible death.” Lovaniensis reads “would lose him by invisible death.”]

Those who belong to him have death as their shepherd. But we who think about future immortality, and who do not carry the sign of Christ’s cross on our foreheads without reason, have no shepherd except life. Death is the shepherd of unbelievers; life is the shepherd of believers. If, then, the sheep whose shepherd is death are in hell, the sheep whose shepherd is life are in heaven.

What then? Are we already in heaven? In heaven according to faith. If we are in heaven, what is meant by “Lift up your hearts”? If we are not in heaven, why does the apostle Paul say, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20)? We walk in the body on earth, but in our hearts we dwell in heaven. We dwell there if we send there something that will hold us there. No one dwells in his heart except where he thinks; and he thinks where he stores his treasure. If he has stored up treasure on earth, his heart does not depart from earth; if he has stored up treasure in heaven, his heart does not descend from heaven, for the Lord plainly says, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

3. These people, then, whose shepherd is death, seem for a time to flourish, while the righteous suffer. But why? Because it is still night.

What does “it is night” mean? The merits of the righteous are not apparent, and the prosperity of the wicked is, as it were, proclaimed.

[Col. 0557]

Grass appears more luxuriant than a tree only as long as winter lasts. Grass flourishes through the winter, while in winter the tree appears almost dry. When the sun emerges more intensely in the summer season, the tree that seemed dry through the winter is filled with leaves and produces fruit; but the grass withers. You will see the tree’s glory, while the grass is dry.

So now the righteous suffer, before summer comes. Life is in the root, but it is not yet visible in the branches. Our root is love. And what does the apostle say? That we ought to have our root above, so that life may be our shepherd; that our dwelling should not depart from heaven; that on this earth we should walk as dead people: so that we may be alive above and dead below—not dead above and alive below.

Since, then, our life and our heart must not depart from above, what does the apostle say? “For you have died”; and, so that you would not be afraid, he adds, “Your life is hidden with Christ in God.” There is our root. But when will our glory appear, as it were in leaves and fruits? He continues: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4).

And it will be morning. For now it is not morning. Let the proud and the rich of this world swell with arrogance; let the wicked insult the good, and unbelievers the faithful, saying: “What benefit is it to you that you have believed? What more do you have because you have Christ?” Let the faithful answer, if they are truly faithful: “It is night; what we hold is not yet visible.”

Let their hands not cease from good works. Hence it is said elsewhere: “In the day of my trouble I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 76:3). Our labor will appear in the morning, and there will be fruit in the morning, so that those who now labor may afterward rule, and those who now boast and are proud may afterward be subjected.

What follows? “Like sheep placed in hell, death is their shepherd. And the upright will rule over them in the morning.”

4. I think this verse is already clear, since we have anticipated its meaning: “The upright will rule over them in the morning.” Endure the night; desire the morning. Do not suppose that night has life while morning does not have life. Does the one who sleeps live, then, while the one who rises does not live? Is not the one who sleeps more like a dead person?

[Note: [Col. 0557] One manuscript reads “like a dead man.”]

And who are those who sleep? Those whom the apostle Paul awakens, if only they are willing to wake up. To some he says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

Those, therefore, who are enlightened by Christ are already awake, but the fruit of their wakefulness is not yet apparent. It will appear in the morning—that is, when the uncertainties of this age have passed. For is this not night? Do these things not seem to you like darkness? He does evil: he lives, flourishes, terrifies, and is honored. He does good: he is criticized, blasphemed, accused, suffers, and is terrified. They are like darkness.

Yet in the root there is vigor, fruitfulness, and abundance. Life is not yet in the branches, but the root has not withered. It resembles something withering, but the time comes when it is clothed in its honor and made fertile with its fruits.

Then those about whom it was said that we should not envy them will appear. What does the psalm say about them? “For like grass they will quickly wither, and like the green herb of the meadow they will quickly fall” (Psalm 36:1–2). They will fall when they see the saints on the right, the very people whom they insulted while they were laboring. Then they will say within themselves, repenting—but with a late and fruitless repentance. They did not wish to practice fruitful repentance now; then they will practice fruitless repentance.

What will they say in that fruitless repentance? “These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made a subject of reproach.” I am quoting the words of the Book of Wisdom; those who are accustomed to hearing them know them. They are the future words of the wicked, when they see the Judge, and all the faithful already at his right hand, and all his saints judging with him. Scripture gives their words:

“These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made a subject of reproach. We fools considered their life madness” (Wisdom 5:3–4).

When someone begins to live for God—to despise the world, to refuse to avenge his injuries, not to seek riches here, not to seek earthly happiness here, to despise everything, to think only of the Lord, and not to abandon the way of Christ—he is called “mad” not only by pagans. More distressingly, because many within are asleep and unwilling to wake up, he hears it from his own people, from Christians: “What are you suffering?”

My brothers, what do we suppose a person living according to the way of Christ means when he says, “What are you suffering?” We shudder at the Jews because they said to the Lord Jesus Christ, “You have a demon” (John 8:48); and when we hear the Gospel read, we beat our breasts. The Jews said a wicked thing to Christ: “You have a demon.”

Now you, Christian: when you see the devil expelled from a person’s heart and Christ dwelling there, and you say, “What are you suffering?”—does it seem to you that he has a demon? It was also said of the Lord himself that he was mad when he spoke words they could not understand. They said, “He is mad; he has a demon.” Yet some were waking from sleep and saying, “These are not the words of one who has a demon” (John 10:20–21).

So also now, brothers, as long as these words are heard by the nations and by those who inhabit the world—by earthborn people and by the children of men, by the rich and the poor, that is, by those who belong to Adam and those who belong to Christ—some say, “He has a demon,” while others say, “These are not the words of one who has a demon.”

Some follow the way of the world and hear these things only for a time. Others do not hear them in vain, but do what was said: “Give ear, you who inhabit the world.” And while they do these things, the fruit is uncertain.

[Note: [Col. 0558] Five manuscripts read “certain.”]

But those who do evil and choose the way of the world have death as their shepherd; those who choose the way of God have life as their shepherd.

[Note: [Col. 0558] Thus Erasmus and most manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads “the name of God.”]

Life itself will come to judge and condemn, together with its shepherd, those to whom it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” But those who were insulted and mocked because they believed will hear from life itself—which they have as their shepherd:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:41, 34).

The upright, then, will rule over them—not now, but in the morning. Let no one say, “Why am I a Christian? I rule over no one; let me rule over the wicked.”

[Note: [Col. 0558] Nearly all manuscripts omit “let me rule over the wicked”; five of them have “an insult to the wicked” in its place. Compare Sermon 72, “To the Brothers in the Desert,” which is copied in its entirety from here.]

Do not hurry: you will rule, but in the morning.

[Col. 0559]

“And their help will grow old in hell, apart from their glory.” Now they have glory; in hell it will grow old. What is their help? Help from money, help from friends, help from their own strength. But when a person dies, “on that day all his thoughts perish” (Psalm 145:4).

However much glory he seemed to have among human beings while he lived, just so much decay and corruption of punishments will he have among the dead when he has died.

5. [verse 16] “But God will redeem my soul.” Observe the voice of one hoping for the future: “But God will redeem my soul.” Perhaps it is still the voice of someone wishing to be delivered from oppression. Someone is in prison, let us suppose, and says, “God will redeem my soul”; someone is in chains: “God will redeem my soul”; someone is suffering danger at sea, tossed by waves and raging storms—what does he say? “God will redeem my soul.”

They want to be delivered into this life. This is not the voice of the person speaking here. Listen to what follows: “God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.” He speaks of the redemption that Christ has already displayed in himself. For he descended into hell and ascended into heaven. What we saw in the head, we find in the body.

What we believe in the head, those who saw it announced to us; and through them we have seen it, because we are all one body (1 Corinthians 12:12; Romans 12:5). But were they better because they saw, and are we worse because it was announced to us? Life itself—our shepherd himself—does not say this. He taunts one of his disciples who doubted and wished to touch the scars. When he had touched the scars and cried out, saying, “My Lord and my God,” the Lord saw the doubting disciple and, looking toward the whole world that would believe, said: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe” (John 20:28–29).

“But God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.” What, then, is found here? Labor, oppression, tribulation, temptation: expect nothing else. Where is joy? In future hope. For the apostle says, “Always rejoicing.” Amid such tribulations, always rejoicing, always sorrowful: always rejoicing because he himself said, “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.”

Our sorrow has an “as though”; our joy has no “as though,” because it rests on certain hope. Why does our sorrow have an “as though”? Because, like sleep, it will pass, and the upright will rule in the morning.

Your Charity knows that someone describing a dream adds “as though”: “As though I were sitting, as though I were speaking, as though I were dining, as though I were riding, as though I were debating.” Everything is “as though,” because when he wakes up he does not find what he was seeing. “As though I had found a treasure,” says the beggar. If it were not “as though,” he would not be a beggar; but because it was “as though,” he is a beggar.

So now, those who open their eyes to worldly pleasures and close their hearts experience their “as though,” and their reality comes afterward. Their worldly happiness is “as though”; their punishment is real.

Our “as though,” however, is sorrow; our joy is not “as though.” The apostle does not say, “As though rejoicing, yet always sorrowful,” or “As though sorrowful and as though rejoicing,” but, “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.”

“As poor,” and there he uses “as” in place of “as though,” “yet making many rich.” When he said this, the apostle had nothing: he had left all his possessions and owned no riches. And what does he say next? “As having nothing”—and that “having nothing” was, for the apostle, an “as though”—“yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10). There he does not say “as though.” He was “as though” poor, but he truly made many rich. He had “as though” nothing, but he truly possessed everything.

How did he truly possess everything? Because he clung to the Creator of everything.

“But,” he says, “God will redeem my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.”

6. [verse 17] What, then, of those who wish to flourish here? You see a wicked person flourishing, and perhaps your feet will stumble. You will say in your soul:

“God, I know this man’s deeds, what crimes this man has committed; and look—he flourishes, he terrifies, he rules, he is exalted, his head does not ache, nothing in his household has diminished.”

And you will be afraid because you have believed; perhaps your heart will say: “Wretched me! I think I believed for no reason. God does not regard human affairs.”

God therefore awakens us. And what does he say? “Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich.” Why were you afraid because a man became rich? You were afraid that you might believe for no reason, that perhaps you had lost the labor of your faith and the hope of your conversion. Perhaps gain came to you through fraud; and if you had pursued that gain through fraud, you could have been rich and free from labor. But, considering what God threatened, you refrained from fraud and despised the profit. Now you see another person gaining through fraud and suffering no harm, and you are afraid to be good.

“Do not be afraid,” the Spirit of God says to you, “when a man becomes rich.” Do you refuse to have eyes except for present things? The one who rose again promised the future; he did not promise peace on this earth or rest in this life. Every person seeks rest; he seeks something good, but he seeks it in the wrong region. There is no peace in this life. What we seek on earth has been promised to us in heaven; what we seek in this age has been promised in the age to come.

7. [verse 18] “Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his household is multiplied.” Why should you not be afraid? Because he will not receive everything when he dies. You see him alive; consider him dying. You observe what he has here; consider what he will take with him.

What does he take with him? Perhaps someone says: “He takes with him what he is wrapped in, and what is provided for him—a costly and marble tomb, to preserve his memory.” I say: Not even that. Such things are displayed for one who cannot perceive them.

If you adorn someone who is asleep and not awake, he has those things with him in bed. Perhaps ornaments are placed on the body of the one lying there, while in his dreams he sees himself in rags. What he perceives is more real to him than what he does not perceive. And even what he perceives will be gone when he wakes; nevertheless, for the sleeper what he saw in his dream was more real than what he did not perceive.

What, then, brothers? Let people say to themselves: “Let something be spent on my death. Why should I leave my heirs rich? They will have much of mine; let me have something of mine as well, for my body.”

What will a dead body have? What will rotting flesh have? What will flesh that does not perceive have? If that rich man had anything—he whose tongue was dry (Luke 16:24)—then a person has something of his own.

Brothers, do we read in the Gospel that the rich man appeared in the fire wearing silken and linen coverings? Was he in hell as he had been at the banquet table? When he thirsted and desired a drop, were all those things there? A person does not take everything with him; nor does the dead man take with him what the burial takes.

Where there is perception, there is a human being; where there is no perception, there is no human being. What lies there is the vessel that contained the human being, the house that had the human being. Let us call the body the house, and the spirit the inhabitant of the house.

The spirit is tormented in hell. What does it profit him that his body lies in cinnamon and spices, wrapped in costly linens? It is as if the master of a house were sent into exile and you adorned his walls. He is in exile, in need, wasting away from hunger, scarcely finding a single room in which to sleep, and you say, “He is fortunate, for his house is decorated.” Who would not think that you were either joking or insane? You adorn the body, while the spirit is tormented.

Give something to the spirit, and you have given something to the dead. But what will you give him when he desired a single drop and did not receive it? Here he despised sending something ahead of himself.

Why did he despise it? Because “this is the way of those people, a stumbling-block to them.” He did not consider any life to exist except the present one; he thought only about how he would be buried wrapped in costly garments. His soul was taken from him, as the Lord says: “Fool! This night your soul will be demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

And what this psalm says was fulfilled in him: “Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his household is multiplied; for he will not receive everything when he dies, nor will his glory descend with him.”

8. [verse 19] “For his soul will be blessed during his life.” Let Your Charity pay attention: “For his soul will be blessed during his life.” As long as he lived, he did well by himself. Everyone says this, but they say it falsely. The blessing comes from the mind of the one who blesses, not from the truth itself.

What are you saying? Because he ate and drank, because he did what he wished, because he feasted splendidly, did he therefore do well by himself? I say: He did evil to himself. It is not I who say this, but Christ: He did evil to himself.

For when that rich man feasted splendidly every day, he was thought to be doing well by himself. But when he began to burn in hell, it was discovered that what had been thought good was evil. What he had eaten among the living, he was digesting in hell. I speak of iniquity, brothers, which he had feasted upon.

[Col. 0562]

He ate costly foods with the mouth of his flesh; with the mouth of his heart he ate iniquity. What he had eaten with the mouth of his heart among the living, he was digesting amid those punishments in hell. He had eaten it temporarily, but he was digesting it eternally to his harm.

Is iniquity, then, eaten? Perhaps someone says, “What is he talking about? Is iniquity eaten?” I am not the one saying it; listen to Scripture: “As a sour grape is a vexation to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who use it” (Proverbs 10:26).

For whoever eats iniquity—that is, whoever willingly embraces iniquity—will not be able to eat righteousness. Righteousness is bread. What bread? “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). He himself is the bread of our hearts.

Just as when someone eats sour grapes with the mouth of the body, his teeth become numb and stiff, and he becomes less able to eat bread, leaving him able only to praise what he sees but unable to eat it, so the person who has used iniquity and fed on sins in his heart begins to be unable to eat bread. He praises the word of God but does not do it.

Why does he not do it? Because when he begins to do it, he suffers. It is like the pain we feel in our teeth after eating sour grapes, when we begin to eat bread.

But what do those whose teeth have become numb do? They abstain for a while from sour grapes; their teeth regain their stability, and they apply themselves to bread. So let us praise righteousness; but if we wish to eat righteousness, let us abstain from iniquities. Then not only the delight of praising righteousness is born in the heart, but also the ease of eating it.

If a Christian says, “God knows that I take delight in it, but I cannot do it,” he has battered teeth: he has eaten iniquity for a long time.

Is righteousness, then, also eaten? If it were not eaten, the Lord would not say, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6). Therefore, “his soul will be blessed during his life”: during life it will be blessed; at death it will be tormented.

9. “He will praise you when you have done well by him.” Pay attention and be nourished; let this cling to your hearts. Eat, observe such people, and do not be such people. Beware of words of this kind.

“He will praise you when you have done well by him.” How many Christians there are, brothers, who give thanks to God only when profit comes to them! This is what is meant by “He will praise you when you have done well by him”: he will praise you and say, “Truly, you are my God. He delivered me from prison; I will give thanks to him.” Profit comes to him, and he gives thanks; an inheritance comes, and he gives thanks. He suffers a loss, and he blasphemes.

What kind of son are you, if you are displeased with your father when he corrects you?

[Note: [Col. 0562] The editions read “because.” The manuscripts, however, read “who.”]

Would he correct you unless you displeased him? Or if you displeased him so greatly that he hated you, would he want to correct you?

[Note: [Col. 0562] The editions read: “He would not correct you unless you displeased him; or if you displeased him so greatly that he hated you, he would not correct you.” The manuscripts, however, have the reading restored in this edition.]

Give thanks, then, to your corrector, so that you may receive an inheritance from God, who corrects you. For you are being instructed when you are corrected. But he corrects you greatly because what you are to receive is great. If you weigh what you are being corrected for against what you will receive, you will find that what you are being corrected for is nothing.
