The apostle Paul says this: “For this momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure.” But when? “While we look not at the things that are seen,” he says, “but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

And again: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

What, then, is it that you suffer? But you suffer continually. I grant it. From the time you were born, through all your ages until your old age, until you die, suppose you suffer what Job suffered; what he suffered for several days, let someone suffer from infancy onward. What you suffer passes and ends; what you will receive will have no end.

I do not want you now to compare punishment with reward; compare periods of time with eternity, if you can.

[Note: [Col. 0563] Erasmus and two manuscripts read: “with a temporal reward, compare periods of time with eternity, if you can.” Amianus reads: “with a reward; compare the temporal thing,” and so forth. Lovaniensis reads: “compare temporal things,” and so forth. But most manuscripts read: “compare periods of time with eternity,” and so forth.]

10. “He will praise you when you have done well by him.” Do not be such people, brothers. See why we say these things, why we sing them, why this discourse is delivered, why we labor: do not do such things.

Your business dealings test you. Sometimes, in your business, you hear the truth and blaspheme; you blaspheme the Church. Why? Because you are Christians. If this is how it is, I will join the party of Donatus; I want to be a pagan.

Why? Because you bit the bread, and your teeth hurt. When you saw the bread itself, you praised it; you began to eat it, and your teeth hurt. That is, when you heard the word of God, you praised it together with us; when you are told, “Do this,” you blaspheme.

Do not wish to act this way. Say: “The bread is good, but I cannot eat it.” But now, if you see it with your eyes, you praise it; when you begin to press it with your teeth, you say, “This bread is bad—and what kind of person is the one who made it?”

Thus it happens that you praise God when God does good to you, but lie when you sing, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2).

The song of your lips is required from your heart. You sang in the Church, “I will bless the Lord at all times.” How is it “at all times”? If there is profit at all times, he is blessed at all times; if there is a loss at some time, he is not blessed but blasphemed.

Surely you bless him at all times; surely his praise is always in your mouth?

[Note: [Col. 0563] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read: “Surely, because you do not bless him at all times; surely, because his praise is not always,” and so forth.]

You will be the kind of person whom the psalm now describes: “He will praise you when you have done well by him.”

11. [verses 20–21] “He will enter into the generation of his fathers”—that is, he will imitate his fathers. For the wicked who exist now have brothers and fathers. The wicked of ancient times are fathers of those who are wicked in the present; and those who are wicked now are fathers of future generations of the wicked. In the same way, the righteous of ancient times, the fathers of the righteous who now exist, are fathers of those who will be righteous in the future.

The Holy Spirit wished to show that there is no injustice when people murmur against it; rather, these people, from the beginning through the generation of their fathers, have their father. Adam begot two sons: in one there was iniquity, in the other righteousness—in Cain, iniquity; in Abel, righteousness.

Iniquity seemed to have prevailed over righteousness, because the unjust Cain killed the righteous Abel at night.

[Note: [Col. 0564] Thus the manuscripts of better quality. The printed editions read “the innocent.”]

Was it morning? But “the upright will rule over them in the morning.” Morning will come, and it will be seen where Abel is and where Cain is.

So it is with all who are like Cain, and with all who are like Abel, until the end of the age.

“He will enter into the generation of his fathers; he will never see light.” For while he was here, he was also in darkness, rejoicing in false goods and not loving true goods. Therefore he will go from here to Tartarus. The darkness of torments will receive him from the darkness of dreams.

Thus he will never see light. But why? What the psalm placed in the middle, it also placed at the end: “A human being, though placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

But you, brothers, consider that you were made human beings according to the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26). The image of God is within, not in the body. It is not in these ears that you see, nor in the eyes, nostrils, palate, hands, or feet. Yet the image has been made wherever there is understanding, wherever there is mind, wherever there is reason for investigating truth, wherever there is your faith, your hope, and your love. There God has his image.

There you understand and see that these things pass away, as he said in another psalm: “Although a human being walks in an image, yet he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Psalm 38:7).

Do not be troubled, because whatever these things may be, they are transitory—provided that you are human beings placed in honor and understand. For if, though placed in honor, you do not understand, you are compared with senseless beasts and become like them.

# Exposition of Psalm 49. Sermon to the People

1. [verse 1] Let each person measure within himself how much the word of God benefits us for the correction of our life, and for hoping for its rewards and fearing its punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0564] The Vatican and Regius manuscripts read “reflect.”]

Let him place his conscience before God’s eyes without deceit and not flatter himself in such great danger, since you see that the Lord our God himself flatters no one. If he consoles us by promising his good things and strengthening our hope, nevertheless he does not spare those who live badly and despise his word.

Let each person question himself while there is time and see where he stands, either persevering in the good or turning away from evil.

For, as this psalm says, it is not just any human being or any angel, but the Lord God of gods who has spoken. And what did he accomplish by speaking? He called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.

The one who called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting is our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0565]

“The Word became flesh, so that he might dwell among us.” Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, is God of gods, because through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made.

If the Word of God is God, then surely he is God of gods. Whether he is God, the Gospel answers: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:14, 1).

And if all things were made through him, as it subsequently says, then any gods who were made were also made through him. For there is one God who was not made, and he alone is truly God. This one God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God.

2. Who, then, are the gods whose God is the true God, or where are they? Another psalm says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among gods.”

We still do not know whether perhaps some gods have gathered in heaven and whether God stood in their assembly—that is, in their congregation—to distinguish among them.

Look at whom he addresses in that same psalm: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall” (Psalm 82:1, 6–7).

It is therefore clear that he called human beings gods, deified by his grace, not born from his substance. For the one who justifies is himself just, not through another; and the one who deifies is God through himself, not through participation in another.

The one who justifies also deifies, because by justifying he makes people children of God. “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). If we have been made children of God, then we have also been made gods. But this comes from the grace of the one who adopts, not from the nature of the one who begets.

For the only-begotten Son of God, God and one God with the Father, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, was in the beginning the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

The others who are made gods become so by his grace. They are not born from his substance so as to be what he is, but so that through his beneficence they may come to him and be coheirs with Christ.

For such is the love in that heir that he wished to have coheirs. What greedy human being would want to have coheirs? Yet even the one who is found willing to have them will divide the inheritance with them, possessing less himself by dividing it than if he possessed it alone.

But the inheritance in which we are coheirs with Christ is not diminished by the number of its possessors or made narrower by the multitude of coheirs. It is as great for many as for few, as great for each as for all.

“See,” says the apostle, “what love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be children of God.” And elsewhere: “Beloved, we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet appeared.” We are therefore children in hope, not yet in reality.

“But we know,” he says, “that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is” (1 John 3:1–2).

The only-begotten Son is like the Father by being born; we are like him by seeing.

[Note: [Col. 0565] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read “by living.”]

We are not like him in such a way as to be what he is, as he is what the one who begot him is. We are like him, but not equal; he is like the Father because he is equal to him.

We have heard who the gods made righteous are, since they are called children of God; and we have heard who the gods that are not gods are, to whom that God of gods is terrible.

For another psalm says: “He is terrible above all gods.” And as though you were asking, “Which gods?” it answers: “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:4–5).

He is terrible to the gods of the nations, the demons; he is lovable to the gods he has made, his sons.

Accordingly, I find both acknowledging the majesty of God: the demons also confessed Christ, and the faithful confessed Christ. “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Peter said (Matthew 16:16). “We know who you are: you are the Son of God,” the demons said (Mark 5:7).

I hear an equal confession, but I do not find an equal love—rather, love here and fear there. Therefore, those to whom he is lovable are sons; those to whom he is terrible are not sons. To those to whom he is lovable he made them gods; to those to whom he is terrible he proves that they are not gods.

For these become gods; those are merely thought to be gods. Truth makes these gods; error considers those gods.

5. The Lord God of gods has spoken. He has spoken in many ways. He himself spoke through the angels; he himself spoke through the prophets; he himself spoke through his own mouth; he himself spoke through his apostles; he speaks through his faithful; when we say something true through our humility, he himself speaks.

Therefore observe what he has done by speaking in many ways, in many forms, through many vessels, through many instruments—yet he himself sounds everywhere, touching, modulating, inspiring.

Observe what he has done. He spoke and called the earth. What earth? Perhaps Africa? This is on account of those who say, “The Church of Christ is the party of Donatus.”

He did not call Africa alone, but he did not exclude Africa either. For the one who called the earth from the rising of the sun to the setting, leaving no regions uncalled, found Africa within his call.

Let it therefore rejoice in unity, not grow proud in division. We rightly say that the voice of the God of gods has come also to Africa; it did not remain in Africa.

For he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. There is no place where the ambushes of heretics can hide; they have no shadow of falsehood in which to conceal themselves. “There is no one who can hide from his heat” (Psalm 19:7).

The one who called the earth called the whole earth. The one who called the earth called as much as he fashioned.

Why do false Christs and false prophets arise against me? Why do they try to ensnare me with deceptive words, saying, “Look, here is the Christ,” or “There he is” (Matthew 24:23)?

I do not listen to those who point out separate parts. The God of gods has shown me the whole: the one who called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting redeemed the whole, while he condemned those who slander the parts.

### 4. [Verse 2]

But we have heard that the earth was called from the rising of the sun to its setting. From where did the one who called begin to call? Hear this also: “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor.” Surely the Psalm agrees with the Gospel, which says: “To all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” Hear: “To all the nations”—he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Hear: “Beginning from Jerusalem”—“From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor.”

Therefore, he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. This agrees with the words of the Lord: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations” (Luke 24:46–47). For all the nations extend from the rising of the sun to its setting.

As for “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor”—that the beauty of his Gospel began there, that there began to be announced the one “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3)—this agrees with the Lord’s words, “Beginning from Jerusalem.” The new harmonizes with the old, and the old with the new. The two seraphim say to one another: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). The two Testaments also sound together and have one voice. Let the voice of the Testaments singing together be heard, not that of the slanderous disinherited.

Thus God, the God of gods, did these things: he called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting, with his beauty proceeding from Zion. For there were the disciples who received the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven on the fiftieth day after his resurrection (Acts 2:4). From there came the Gospel; from there came the preaching; from there the whole world was filled—and this through the grace of faith.

### 5.

For when the Lord himself came, since he came in order to suffer, he came hidden; and although he was strong in himself, he appeared weak in the flesh. It was necessary for him to be seen so that he would not be understood, and to be despised so that he would be killed. There was the appearance of glory in his divinity, but this was concealed in the flesh. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Thus he walked hidden among the Jews, among his enemies, doing wonders and suffering evils, until he was hung upon the wood. When the Jews saw him hanging there, they despised him more and more, and, shaking their heads before the cross, they said: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:38–39).

The God of gods was therefore hidden, and he uttered words arising more from our fellow-feeling than from his majesty. From where else came those words, unless they were taken from us: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:2; Matthew 27:46). When did the Father forsake the Son, or the Son the Father? Are not the Son and the Father one God? Is it not entirely true: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)? Why then, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me,” unless the voice of the sinner was being recognized in the flesh of weakness? For he who assumed “the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3), why would he not also assume the likeness of the voice of sin?

The God of gods was therefore hidden when he walked among human beings, when he hungered and thirsted, when he sat down tired, when he slept with his body exhausted, when he was seized, when he was scourged, when he was placed before the judge, and when he answered the proud man: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11). He was hidden when, led to the sacrifice, he did not open his mouth before the one shearing him (Isaiah 53:7); hidden when he was crucified and when he was buried. Always the God of gods was hidden.

What happened after he rose? The disciples were amazed, and at first they did not believe, until they touched and handled him (Luke 24). [Note: Col. 0567. Colb. Manuscript: “After he rose, the disciples were amazed and at first …,” etc.]

But the flesh had risen, because the flesh had died; the divinity, which could not die, was still concealed in the flesh of the risen one. His form could be seen, his limbs could be held, his scars could be touched. But who sees or holds or touches the Word through whom all things were made? And yet “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Thomas, who was holding the man, understood, as he was able, the God. For when he had touched the scars, he cried out: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Yet the Lord was displaying that same form and that same flesh which they had seen on the cross and which had been placed in the tomb.

He spent forty days with them. [Note: Col. 0568. The editors read: “was”; but all the manuscripts read: “spent,” and not improperly, in the sense of “passed.”] He did not show himself to the impious Jews; he showed himself to those who had believed in him before he was crucified, so that those whom he had left wavering when he was crucified, he might make strong when he rose.

Then, on the fortieth day, commending his Church to them—that is, the earth called from the rising of the sun to its setting—so that those who wish to perish in schism might have no excuse, he ascended into heaven, saying to them: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem” (from which comes the beauty of his splendor), “and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth.”

After he had said these things, a cloud received him. They were looking at the one whom they knew; yet they knew him in humility, not yet in glory. And as he went from them into heaven, they were instructed by an angelic voice saying: “Why do you stand looking, men of Galilee? This Jesus, whom you see going, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”

Thus he ascended. They returned rejoicing and remained in the city, according to his command, until they were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:3–12).

But what had been said to Thomas when he touched him? “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who do not see and believe” [Note: Col. 0568. Editors: “Blessed are those who did not see and believed.” But the manuscripts read: “who do not see and believe.”] (John 20:29).

We were foretold. That earth, called from the rising of the sun to its setting, does not see and believes. The God of gods was therefore hidden from those among whom he walked, from those by whom he was crucified, from those before whose eyes he rose, and from us, who believe that he sits in heaven although we did not see him walking on earth.

But even if we had seen him, would we not have seen what the Jews saw and crucified? It is more that, without seeing Christ, we believe him to be God than that they, seeing him, thought him nothing but a human being. In the end, by thinking wrongly they put him to death; by believing rightly, we are brought to life.

### 6. [Verse 3]

What then, brothers? Is that God of gods, hidden then and hidden now, hidden forever? Certainly not. Hear what follows: “God will come manifestly.” He who came hidden will come manifestly. He came hidden to be judged; he will come manifestly to judge. He came hidden to stand before a judge; he will come manifestly to judge even the judges: “He will come manifestly and will not keep silent.”

What does this mean? Is he silent now? From where, then, are the things we say? From where are these commands, these admonitions, this trumpet of terror? He is not silent, and he is silent: he is not silent in giving admonition, but he is silent in executing vengeance; he is not silent in giving commands, but he is silent in judgment.

For every day he bears with sinners who do evil and do not care about God—not in their conscience, not in heaven, not on earth. None of these things is hidden from him; and he admonishes everyone universally. When he scourges some on earth, it is admonition, not yet condemnation.

He is therefore silent concerning judgment. Hidden in heaven, he still intercedes for us. He is patient toward sinners, not exercising anger but awaiting repentance. Elsewhere he says: “I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever?” (Isaiah 42:14). When, therefore, he will no longer keep silent, God will come manifestly.

Which God? Our God. It is that same God who is our God; for he is not God who is not our God. “The gods of the nations are demons”; the God of Christians is the true God.

He himself will come, but manifestly: no longer to be mocked, no longer to be slapped and scourged; he will come, manifestly, no longer to be struck on the head with a reed, no longer to be crucified, killed, or buried—for the hidden God willed to suffer all these things. He will come manifestly and will not keep silent.

### 7.

Because he will come for judgment, what follows teaches us this: “Fire shall go before him” (Psalm 96:3).

Are we afraid? Let us be changed, and we shall not be afraid. Let straw fear the fire; what does it do to gold? It is now in your power what you do, so that you may not experience, uncorrected, what will come even against your will.

For if we could arrange that the day of judgment would not come, I think that even then we ought not to live badly. If the fire of the day of judgment did not come, and only separation from the face of God threatened sinners, then, however abundant their pleasures might be, since they would not see the one by whom they were created and would be separated from the ineffable sweetness of his countenance, they ought to mourn throughout any eternity and impunity of sin.

But what shall I say, or to whom shall I say it? This punishment is for those who love these things, not for those who despise them. Those who have begun, however faintly, to sense the sweetness of wisdom and truth know what I am saying—how great a punishment it is merely to be separated from the face of God. But those who have not tasted that sweetness, if they do not yet desire the face of God, should at least fear the fire. Let punishments terrify the one whom rewards do not invite.

What God promises seems worthless to you; tremble at what he threatens. The sweetness of his presence will come. You are not changed, not stirred, do not sigh, do not desire it; you embrace your sins and the pleasures of your flesh, and you pile up straw around yourself. The fire will come. “Fire shall burn in his sight.”

That fire will not be like your hearth-fire. Yet if you were compelled to put your hand into it, you would do whatever the one threatening this fire commanded. If he said to you, “Write against your father’s head; write against the heads of your children—for if you do not, I will put your hand into your hearth-fire,” would you do it, so that your hand might not burn, so that your limb might not burn for a time, since it would not suffer forever?

The enemy threatens such a slight evil, and you do evil. God threatens eternal evil, and you do not do good! Threats ought not to compel you to do evil; threats ought not to deter you from doing good. By God’s threats, by the threats of eternal fire, you are restrained from evil and invited to good.

Why are you reluctant, unless you do not believe? Let each person examine his heart and see what faith holds there [Note: Col. 0569. Several manuscripts: “what faith holds there,” with a different grammatical construction.].

If we believe that judgment will come, brothers, let us live well. Now is the time of mercy; then will be the time of judgment. No one will say, “Restore me to my former years.” He will repent then, but he will repent in vain. Let him repent now, while repentance bears fruit. Let a basket of manure—mourning of heart and tears—be applied now to the roots of the tree, lest the wind come and uproot it [Note: Col. 0569. The editors add: “lest the wind come and uproot it.” The word “wind” is absent from the manuscripts.] (Luke 13:8).

For when it has been uprooted, fire is already awaited. Now, even if the branches have been broken, they can be grafted in again. Then every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3:10). “Fire shall burn in his sight.”

### 8.

“And around him a mighty tempest.”

A mighty tempest, winnowing so great a threshing floor. In this tempest there will be that winnowing by which everything unclean will be separated from the holy, every pretense from the faithful, and every despiser and proud person from the devout who tremble at the word of God.

For now there lies a certain mixture from the rising of the sun to its setting. Let us see, then, what the one who is to come will do, what he will do in that tempest, of which it is said: “Around him is a mighty tempest.” Without doubt this tempest will accomplish a certain separation.

This is the separation that those did not await who, before they reached the shore, tore the nets apart (Luke 5:6). In that separation, there is a distinction between the wicked and the good.

Some are now following Christ, with their shoulders free and without the burden of worldly cares. They did not hear in vain: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” To such people it is said: “You shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:21, 28).

Some, then, will judge with the Lord; others will be judged, though not equally, but according to their merits—and will be placed at the right hand. For that some will judge with the Lord, we have the clearest testimony in the words I have just recalled: “You shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

### 9.

But someone says: “The twelve Apostles will sit there, and no more. Where, then, will the apostle Paul be? Will he be excluded from there?” Far be it from us to say this; far be it even to think it silently.

What if he will sit in the place of Judas? But divine Scripture has made clear who was appointed in Judas’s place. Matthias is expressly named in the Acts of the Apostles, so that we could not doubt it (Acts 1:26). When Judas fell, therefore, the number twelve was completed.

When that number twelve has occupied twelve thrones, will the apostle Paul not judge? Or perhaps he will judge while standing? It is not so. That rewarder of justice will not do this; he who labored more than all of them will certainly not judge while standing (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Certainly this one apostle Paul compels us to think and investigate more carefully why twelve thrones were mentioned. For we also find other numbers in Scripture that signify a multitude.

Five virgins are admitted, and five are excluded (Matthew 25:10, 12). Understand “virgins” in whatever way you wish: whether in chastity and integrity of heart, in which the whole Church ought to be a virgin, to whom it is said, “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2); or in those women who also have dedicated the integrity of their flesh to God. Surely among so many thousands there are not only five?

But in the number five, continence from the five senses of the flesh is understood. For many are corrupted through the eyes, many through the ear, many through unlawful smell, many through wicked taste, and many through adulterous embrace. Whoever restrains himself from all these five doors of corruption, and restrains himself in such a way that he has glory in his own conscience and does not await praise from human beings, is among the five wise virgins who have oil with them.

What does it mean to have oil with them? “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

Again, the man who was being tormented in hell says: “I have five brothers” (Luke 16:28). There the people of the Jews under the Law are understood, because Moses the lawgiver wrote five books.

Likewise, after the resurrection, the Lord commands that the nets be cast on the right side, and 153 fish are brought up. Although they were so great in number, the evangelist says, the nets were not torn (John 21:6, 11).

Before his passion, he commanded the nets to be cast without saying whether on the right or on the left. If he had said “on the right,” he would have signified only the good; if “on the left,” only the wicked. But where right and left are not specified, good and wicked are caught together.

They were then caught in such great numbers, as the truth of the Gospel testifies, that the nets were torn (Luke 5:6). That catch signified the present age; the torn nets signified the divisions and ruptures of heretics and schismatics.

But what the Lord did after his resurrection signified what will happen to us after our resurrection, in that number of the kingdom of heaven where no wicked person will be. Therefore the nets cast on the right side represented those on the right, with those on the left removed.

Yet will only 153 righteous people be on that right side? Scripture signifies thousands upon thousands (Daniel 7:10). Read the Apocalypse: perhaps, as it is understood there, twelve times twelve thousand will come from the Jewish people alone (Revelation 7:4).

Consider the multitude of martyrs. The group known nearby as the White Mass [Note: Col. 0571. “White Mass.” See Sermon 306, section 2.] alone has more than 153 martyrs. Finally, those seven thousand about whom the answer is given to Elijah—“I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 19:18)—far exceed that number of fish.

The 153 fish therefore do not signify merely that number of saints. Rather, Scripture signifies the whole number of saints and righteous people by this particular number, so that all may be understood as belonging among those 153 who attain the resurrection of eternal life.

For the Law has ten commandments, while the Spirit of grace, through which alone the Law is fulfilled, is read as sevenfold (Isaiah 11:2–3). The number must therefore be examined: what do ten and seventeen signify? Ten in the commandments, seven in the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which grace the commandments are fulfilled.

All who belong to the resurrection, to the right hand, to the kingdom of heaven, and to eternal life are therefore contained in ten and seventeen—that is, those who fulfill the Law through the grace of the Spirit, not as though through their own work or merit.

If you count from one through seventeen, adding all the numbers successively—adding two to one, then three, then four, making ten; adding five to make fifteen; adding six to make twenty-one; adding seven to make twenty-eight; adding eight to make thirty-six; adding nine to make forty-five; adding ten to make fifty-five; adding eleven to make sixty-six; adding twelve to make seventy-eight; adding thirteen to make ninety-one; adding fourteen to make 105; adding fifteen to make 120; adding sixteen to make 136; and adding seventeen—you arrive at 153.

You will find that the immense number of all the saints belongs to this small number of fish.

As, then, innumerable virgins are contained in the five virgins; as thousands of the Jewish people are contained in the five brothers of the man tormented in hell; and as thousands upon thousands of saints are contained in the number 153 fish—so in the twelve thrones there are not twelve men, but a great number of the perfect.

### 10.

But I see what is consequently required of us. We have explained why many are included in the five virgins, why many Jews are included in those five brothers, and why many perfect people are included in the 153. Show, then, why and how many, rather than twelve men alone, belong to the twelve thrones.

What do the twelve thrones signify? They signify all those everywhere who could be as perfect as those to whom it was said, “You shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

And why do all people everywhere belong to the number twelve? Because when we say “everywhere,” we speak of the whole world. The globe of the earth is contained within its four designated regions: east, west, south, and north. Those called from all these regions in the Trinity, and made perfect in faith and in the commandment of the Trinity—for three times four makes twelve—understand why the saints who will sit on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel belong to the whole world.

For just as those who will judge come from the whole world, so those who will be judged also come from the whole world. When the apostle Paul was rebuking the faithful laity because they were not bringing their cases before the Church but dragging them into the public courts, where they had disputes with one another, he said: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6:3).

See how he made himself a judge—not himself alone, but all who judge rightly in the Church.

### 11.

Since it is therefore clear that many will judge with the Lord, while others will be judged—not equally, but according to their merits—he will come with all his angels, when all the nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 25:31–32). Among all the angels are to be counted those who will have been so perfect that, sitting on twelve thrones, they will judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

For human beings have been called angels. The apostle says of himself: “You received me as an angel of God” (Galatians 4:14). Of John the Baptist it is said: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Malachi 3:1; Matthew 11:10).

Therefore, when he comes with all the angels, he will have the saints with him as well. Isaiah also says this openly: “He will come to judgment with the elders of the people” (Isaiah 3:14).

These elders of the people, these already-called angels, this multitude of perfect people coming from the whole world, are called heaven. But that other reality is earth, fruitful earth.

What earth is fruitful? The earth that is to be placed on the right, to which it will be said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food.” Truly it is fruitful earth—the earth at which the apostle rejoices when they sent what he needed: “Not that I seek the gift,” he says, “but I seek the fruit.” And he gives thanks, saying: “At last you have revived your concern for me” (Philippians 4:17, 10).

He speaks of them as trees that had withered through a certain barrenness and had sprouted again.

The Lord, therefore, coming to judgment—let us now hear, brothers, what he will do in the Psalm—“will summon heaven above”: heaven, all the perfect saints who will judge. He will summon them above, as those who will sit with him and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

But how will he “summon heaven above,” since heaven is always above? He calls those whom he calls heaven here “heavens” elsewhere. Which heavens? Those “that declare the glory of God”: “The heavens declare the glory of God,” of which it is said, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:2, 5).

See how the Lord distinguishes things in judgment: “He will summon heaven above, and the earth to distinguish his people.” From whom, unless from the wicked? They are not mentioned here afterward, as though already judged and assigned to punishment.

Look at these good people and distinguish them: “He will summon heaven above, and the earth to distinguish his people.” He calls the earth also—not to be mingled together, but to be distinguished.

At first he called them while they were mingled together, when the God of gods spoke and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. He had not yet separated them. Those servants had been sent to invite people to the wedding, and they had gathered the good and the wicked [Note: Col. 0573. Thus read several manuscripts. But the editions read: “those servants had not yet distinguished them, who had been sent,” etc.] (Matthew 22:10). [Note: Col. 0573. Thus read most manuscripts. Lov.: “not to be crushed, but to be distinguished. At first, when he called them while mingled together.”]

But when the God of gods comes manifestly and will not keep silent, he will summon heaven above so that it may judge with him. For what is heaven is the heavens; just as what is earth is the earth; just as what is Church is the Churches.

“He will summon heaven above, and the earth to distinguish his people.” Once, together with heaven, he distinguishes the earth—that is, heaven distinguishes the earth with him. How does he distinguish the earth? By placing some at the right and others at the left.

What does he say to the earth once it has been distinguished? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and the rest.

But they say: “When did we see you hungry?” And he says to them: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:34–40).

Heaven shows the earth its least ones, now summoned above and exalted from humility: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Therefore he will summon heaven above and the earth to distinguish his people.

### 12. [Verse 5]

“Gather his righteous to him.”

The divine and prophetic voice, seeing the future as though it were present, exhorts the angels who gather. For he will send his angels, and all the nations will be gathered before him (Matthew 25:32).

“Gather his righteous to him.” Which righteous, unless those who live by faith and do works of mercy? For those works are works of righteousness.

You have the Gospel: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before human beings, in order to be seen by them.” And as though someone asked, “Which righteousness?” he says, “When you give alms” (Matthew 6:1–2). Thus he showed that almsgiving is a work of righteousness.

Gather his righteous to him: gather those who have compassion on the needy, who understand the poor and the pauper. Let the Lord gather and preserve them and give them life (Psalm 40:2–3).

“Gather his righteous to him,” those who arrange his covenant above sacrifices—that is, those who think about his promises above what they do. For these are the sacrifices, since God says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13). Those who arrange his covenant above sacrifices.

### 13. [Verse 6]

“And the heavens shall declare his righteousness.”

Truly the heavens have announced this righteousness of God to us; the evangelists foretold it. Through them we have heard about those who will be at the right hand, to whom the master of the household says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive”—what?—“the kingdom.”

For what reason? “I was hungry, and you gave me food.”

What is as insignificant, what as earthly, as breaking bread for the hungry? Yet it is worth the kingdom of heaven. “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, clothe him” (Isaiah 58:7).

But you have no means to break bread, no house into which to bring him, no clothing with which to cover him. Give a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42); put two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:42).

The widow bought as much with her two small coins as Peter bought by leaving his nets (Matthew 4:20), as Zacchaeus bought by giving half his possessions (Luke 19:8). It is worth as much as you have.

“And the heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God is judge.”

Truly he is judge—not one who mingles together, but one who distinguishes. For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). Even if the grains are hidden in the chaff, they are known to the farmer.

Let no one fear being grain even among the chaff; the eyes of our winnower are not deceived. Do not fear that the tempest which will be around him will mingle you with the chaff. Certainly the tempest will be mighty; nevertheless, it will not take any grain from the portion of wheat to the chaff, because it is not just any farmer with a pitchfork who is judge, but God the Trinity.

“And the heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God is judge.”

Let the heavens go; let the heavens announce it. Let their sound go forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Psalm 18:5). And let that body say: “From the ends of the earth I have cried to you, when my heart was troubled” (Psalm 60:3).

Now, while it is mingled together, it groans; when it has been distinguished, it will rejoice. Let it cry out, then, and say: “Do not destroy my soul with the impious, nor my life with men of blood” (Psalm 25:9). He does not destroy it, because God is judge.

Let it cry to him and say: “Judge me, O Lord, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm 42:1). Let it say; he will do it. “His righteous will be gathered to him” (Psalm 50:5). He called the earth in order to distinguish his people.

### 14. [Verse 7]

“Hear, my people, and I will speak to you.”

The one who will come and will not keep silent—see that even now, if you hear, he is not silent: “Hear, my people, and I will speak to you.” For if you do not hear, I will not speak to you. Hear, and I will speak to you. For if you do not hear, even if I speak, I will not speak to you.

When, then, will I speak to you? If you hear. When do you hear? If you are my people. “Hear, my people”: you do not hear if you are a foreign people.

“Hear, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I will testify to you.” Israel, hear; my people, hear. “Israel” is the name of election: “You shall no longer be called Jacob,” he says, “but you shall be called Israel” (Genesis 32:28).

Hear, then, as Israel, as one who sees God—not yet in appearance, but already in faith. For this is the interpretation of Israel: “Seeing God.” “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 11:15); and whoever has eyes to see, let him see.

“Hear, Israel, and I will testify to you.” What he said above, “my people,” he says here, “Israel”; and what he said above, “I will speak to you,” he says here, “I will testify to you.”

What will the Lord our God speak to his people? What will he testify to his Israel? Let us hear: “I am God, your God.”

“I am God, and I am your God.” How am I God? As it was said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). How am I your God? “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

I am God, and I am your God. And even if I am not your God, I am God. By my goodness I am God; because of your evil I am not your God. For “your God” is properly said of the one whom God holds in a more intimate relationship, as his possession, as his property.

“I am God, your God.” What more do you want? Are you seeking a reward from God, so that God may give you something and what he gives may become yours? Behold, the God who will give is himself yours. What is richer than he? [Note: Col. 0575. Erasmus: “What is sweeter than he?” Better manuscripts: “What is richer than you?”]

You were seeking gifts; you possess the giver himself. “I am God, your God.”

### 15. [Verse 8]

Let us see what he seeks from a human being. Our God, our emperor and our king—what tax does he impose upon us, since he wished to be our king and wished us to be his province? Let us hear his assessments.

Let the poor person not tremble under God’s assessment. What God orders to be given, the one who orders it first gives himself. You need only be devoted.

God does not demand what he has not given, and he has given to everyone what he demands. What does he demand? Let us hear now: “I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices.”

I will not say to you: “Why did you not slaughter a fat bull for me? Why did you not choose the best goat from your flock? Why does that ram walk among your sheep and not appear upon my altar?” I will not say: “Look over your fields, your fold, and your walls, searching for what you can give me.”

“I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices.”

What then? “Do you not accept my sacrifices?” “Your burnt offerings are always before me.”

There are certain burnt offerings of which it is said in another psalm: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.” And again he turns: “The sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.”

What, then, are the burnt offerings he does not despise? What are the burnt offerings that are always before him? “Show favor to Zion,” he says, “in your good will, O Lord, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built. Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and burnt offerings” (Psalm 50:18–21).

He says that God will accept certain burnt offerings.

What is a burnt offering? Something entirely consumed by fire. καῦσις (*kausis*) means “burning,” and ὅλον (*holon*) means “whole”; a holocaust, therefore, is something entirely consumed by fire.

There is a certain fire of the most ardent love. Let the mind be inflamed with love; let that same love seize the limbs for its own use and not allow them to serve desire, so that the whole person who wishes to offer a holocaust to God may burn with the fire of divine love.

Such burnt offerings of yours are always before me.

### 16. [Verse 9]

Perhaps this Israel still does not understand what burnt offerings he has always before him, and is still thinking about oxen, sheep, and goats. Let him not think of these things.

“I will not accept calves from your house.”

I mentioned burnt offerings, and already in mind and thought you were running to earthly herds, choosing something fat from them for me. “I will not accept calves from your house.”

He announces the New Testament, in which all those old sacrifices have ceased. For at that time they were announcing beforehand a certain future sacrifice, by whose blood we would be cleansed.

“I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.”

### 17. [Verse 10]

“For every beast of the forest is mine.”

What shall I ask from you that I myself created? Is it more yours, to whom I gave possession, than mine, who made it?

“For every beast of the forest is mine.”

But perhaps that Israel says: “The beasts belong to God—the wild beasts that I do not enclose in my fold, that I do not tie to my manger. But that ox, that sheep, and that goat are mine.”

“Cattle on the mountains, and oxen.”

Mine are those things which you do not possess; mine are also those which you possess. For if you are my servant, all your property is mine. Surely what the servant acquired for himself is not the Lord’s property, while what the Lord himself created for the servant will not be the Lord’s property?

Therefore, mine are the beasts of the forest that you did not capture; mine also are the cattle on the mountains that belong to you, and the oxen beside your manger. Everything is mine, because I created it.

18. [verse 11.] “I know all the birds of the sky.” How did he know? He weighed them, counted them. Who among us knows all the birds of the sky? But even if God grants someone knowledge of all the birds of the sky, he himself does not know them in the way he grants a human being to know them. God’s knowledge is one thing, human knowledge another; just as God’s possession is one thing, human possession another—that is, possessing as God does is one thing, possessing as a human being does another.

For whatever you possess, you do not have entirely under your control. Whether your ox will live is not in your power, nor whether it will perish, nor whether it will be fed. Where supreme power resides, there also resides supreme and hidden knowledge. Let us attribute this to God, praising God. Let us not dare to say, “How does God know?” Perhaps you expect me, brothers, to explain to you how God knows. I say only this: he does not know in the way a human being knows; he does not know in the way an angel knows. How he knows, I do not dare to say, since I cannot know it either.

Yet I know one thing: even before all the birds of the sky existed, God knew what he was going to create. What sort of knowledge is that? O human being, you began to see the birds only after you were formed, after you received the faculty of sight. These birds came forth from the water at the word of God, who said, “Let the waters produce birds” (Gen. 1:20). Where did God know what he was commanding the water to bring forth? Surely he already knew what he had created—and he knew it before he created it.

God’s knowledge is therefore so great that, in some ineffable manner, things existed with him before they were created. And do you expect him to receive from you what he possessed before he created it? “I know all the birds of the sky,” which you cannot give me. Whatever you are going to slaughter for me, I know it all—not because I made it and then came to know it, but because I knew it in order to make it.

“And the beauty of the field is with me.” “The beauty of the field, the abundance of everything that grows on the earth, is with me,” he says. In what sense is it with him? Were they with him even before they came into being? All future things were with him, and all past things are with him—future things in such a way that the past is not removed from him. Everything is with him, established in a certain ineffable knowledge of God’s Wisdom in the Word, and the Word itself is everything [Note: [Col. 0577] So some manuscripts. Others read, “and in him”; the editions, “and into the Word.”]. Or is the beauty of the field with him in some sense because he himself is everywhere, and he himself said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24)? What is not with him, of whom it is said, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Ps. 138:8)?

Everything is with him; but it is not with him in such a way that he suffers any contamination from the things he created, or suffers any need of them. A column beside which you stand is perhaps with you, and when you grow tired, you lean upon it. You need what is with you; God does not need the field that is with him. The field is with him, the appearance of the earth is with him, the appearance of heaven is with him, all the birds are with him, because he is everywhere. And why is everything with him? Because even before everything existed or was created, everything was known to him.

19. [verse 12.] Who can explain, who can expound what is said to him in another psalm: “For you do not need my goods” (Ps. 15:2)? He said that he does not need anything from us that is necessary. “If I am hungry, I will not tell you.” He will not hunger or thirst, grow weary, or fall asleep—he who guards Israel will not slumber (Ps. 120:4). But let me speak according to your carnal understanding: because when you do not eat, you suffer hunger, perhaps you suppose that God also grows hungry and needs to eat.

Even if he were hungry, he would not tell you: everything is before him; from wherever he wishes, he takes what is necessary for him. These things have been said to refute a childish understanding, not because God declared that he is hungry. Nevertheless, for our sake that God of gods deigned to hunger. He came to hunger and to fill; he came to thirst and to give drink; he came to be clothed with mortality and to clothe us with immortality; he came poor in order to make us rich. For in assuming our poverty he did not lose his riches, because in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3).

“If I am hungry, I will not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine.” Therefore do not trouble yourself about what you should give me. Without effort I possess what I want.

20. [verse 13.] Why, then, do you still think about your herds? “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” You have heard what he does not ask from us—he who wishes to impose something or other upon us. If you were thinking about such things, now remove your thoughts from them; do not think of offering anything of that kind to God.

If you have a fat bull, kill it for the poor. Let them eat the flesh of bulls, even if they will not drink the blood of goats. When you have done this, the one who said, “If I am hungry, I will not tell you,” will reckon it to your account, and will say to you, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35).

“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?”

21. [verse 14.] Say, then, Lord our God, what do you impose upon your people, upon your Israel? “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” Let us also say to him: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will pay them to you as praise” (Ps. 55:12).

I was afraid that you might impose something outside me, something that I considered to be in my fold and that perhaps had already been taken away by a thief. What do you impose upon me? “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” Let me return to myself, where I shall find what I may sacrifice; let me return to myself, and in myself I shall find a sacrifice of praise. “Let my conscience be your altar” [Note: [Col. 0578] So in the manuscripts. In the editions *sit* is omitted, and the text reads: “Your altar, your conscience.”].

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” We are secure: we do not go to Arabia seeking incense; we do not search through the packs of a greedy merchant. God asks for a sacrifice of praise.

Zacchaeus had this sacrifice of praise in his wealth; the widow had it in her little purse; some poor host had it in his cask. Another possessed nothing in his wealth, his purse, or his jar; he possessed everything in his heart. “Salvation has come to this house” of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:8); and “this widow put in more than those rich men” (Mark 12:42). The one who offers a cup of cold water “will not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:42); and there is also “peace on earth among people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” O free sacrifice, given by grace! I did not buy what I was to offer; you gave it to me, for I would not have possessed even this. “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God.” This sacrifice of praise is to give thanks to the one from whom you have whatever good you possess, and by whose mercy whatever evil you possess is forgiven you.

“Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High.” The Lord delights in this fragrance. Pay your vows to the Most High.

22. [verse 15.] “And call upon me on the day of your trouble; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.”

You must not rely upon your own strength; all your aids are false. “Call upon me on the day of your trouble; I will rescue you, and you will glorify me.” For this reason I allowed a day of trouble to come upon you: perhaps, if you were not troubled, you would not call upon me. When you are troubled, you call upon me; when you call upon me, I will deliver you; when I deliver you, you will glorify me, so that you may no longer depart from me.

Someone had become numb and cold, removed from the fervor of prayer, and he said: “I found trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114:3–4). He found trouble as something useful. He had rotted in the decay of his sins and had become insensible; he found trouble as though it were cauterization and surgery. “I found,” he says, “trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.”

And certainly, brothers, there are troubles known to everyone. See the troubles that abound in the human race: one, stricken by loss, mourns; another, struck by bereavement, grieves; another, exiled from his homeland, laments and longs to return, judging his foreign sojourn intolerable; another’s vineyard has been battered by hail, and he considers his labors and how all his effort has been consumed in vain. When can a human being avoid sorrow? He suffers an enemy in place of a friend. What greater misery is there in the human race?

Everyone laments and grieves over these things, and these are troubles. In all these troubles they call upon the Lord, and rightly do so. Let them call upon God: he is able either to teach them to endure what they suffer, or to heal what they have endured. He knows not to allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10:13).

Let us call upon God even in these troubles. But these troubles find us, as it is written in another psalm: “He is our help in the troubles that have found us exceedingly” (Ps. 45:2). There is a certain trouble that we ourselves ought to find.

Let these troubles find us. There is a certain trouble that we ought to seek and find. What is it? That very happiness in this world, that abundance of temporal goods. It is not itself a trouble; it is the comfort of our trouble. Of what trouble? Of our exile. The very fact that we are not yet with God, the very fact that we live amid temptations and vexations and cannot be without fear, is trouble. It is not the security that has been promised to us.

Whoever has not found this trouble of his exile does not think of returning to his homeland. That is the trouble, brothers. Certainly we are now doing good works when we offer bread to the hungry, a gift to the traveler, and the like. This too is trouble. We find the wretched over whom we show mercy, and the misery of the wretched makes us compassionate.

How much better would you already be there, where you find no hungry person to feed, no traveler to welcome, no naked person to clothe, no sick person to visit, no disputant to reconcile! For there everything is complete, true, holy, and eternal. There our bread is righteousness, our drink is wisdom, our clothing is immortality, our house is eternal in the heavens, and our strength is immortality. Does sickness creep in there? Does weariness draw anyone to sleep? No death, no quarrel: there are peace, rest, joy, and righteousness. No enemy enters; no friend falls.

What rest there is! If we reflect and consider where we are, and where the one who cannot lie has promised that we shall be, we discover from his very promise what sort of trouble we are in. No one finds this trouble except the one who seeks it.

You are healthy: see whether you are miserable. It is easy for a sick person to feel that he is miserable. When you are healthy, see whether you are miserable, because you are not yet with God.

“I found trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.” Therefore sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God. Praise the one who promises, praise the one who calls, praise the one who exhorts, praise the one who helps; and understand what trouble you are in. Call upon him, and you will be delivered; you will glorify him [Note: [Col. 0580] So the better manuscripts. The editions have *glorificaberis*, “you will be glorified.”]; you will remain.

23. [verse 16.] Consider what follows, my brothers. Someone or other, since God had said to him, “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God,” and had in a certain sense imposed this tribute upon him, was reflecting and saying to himself: “I shall rise every day, go to church, say one morning hymn and another in the evening, a third or fourth in my house; every day I sacrifice a sacrifice of praise and offer it to my God.”

You do well, if you do this. But take care that you are not already secure simply because you do this, and that perhaps your tongue blesses God while your life curses God.

“O my people,” says the Lord God of gods to you, he who spoke, calling the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Although you are still established among the weeds, sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to your God and pay your vows to him. But take care that you do not live badly and sing well.

Why this warning? “For to the sinner God says: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant upon your mouth?”

You see, brothers, with what trembling we say these things. We take God’s covenant upon our mouth and proclaim to you the teaching and righteousnesses of God. And what does God say to the sinner? “Why do you?”

Does he therefore prohibit sinful preachers? And where is the saying, “Do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3)? Where is the saying, “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. 1:18)?

But these statements were made so that those who hear would not fear, regardless of whom they hear from—not so that those who say good things and do evil might be secure. Therefore, brothers, you are secure: if you hear good things, you hear God [Note: [Col. 0580] More manuscripts read, “They are of God.” Some read, “You hear God.”], regardless of whom you hear.

But God did not wish to leave those who speak without correction, lest, secure merely because they speak, they fall asleep in an evil life and say to themselves: “Surely God will not destroy us, through whose mouth he wished such great good things to be spoken to his people.”

On the contrary, whoever you are who speak, hear what you say; and you who wish to be heard, hear yourself first. Say what someone says in another psalm: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me, for he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84:9).

What sort of person am I, then, if I do not hear what he speaks within me, yet want others to hear what he speaks through me? Let me hear first; let me hear, above all, what the Lord God speaks within me, “for he will speak peace to his people.” Let me hear, and chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27).

“Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” Why do you take for yourself what does not benefit you? He admonishes him to listen—not to lay aside preaching, but to assume obedience.

“But why do you take my covenant upon your mouth?”

24. [verse 17.] “But you hate instruction. You hate discipline.” When I spare you, you sing and praise; when I chastise you, you murmur—as though when I spare you I were your God, but when I chastise you I were not your God. “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19).

“But you hate instruction, and you cast my words behind you.” What is said through you, you cast behind you. “And you cast my words behind you”: where they are not seen by you, but burden you. “And you cast my words behind you.”

25. [verse 18.] “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers.”

Perhaps you would say: “I did not commit theft; I did not commit adultery.” What if you approved of the one who did? By that very approval did you not run with him? By praising the one who did it, did you not place your portion with him?

This is what it means, brothers, to run with a thief and place your portion with an adulterer: even if you do not commit the act, when you praise what is done, you become an accomplice to the deed. For “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who commits iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 9:3).

You do not do evil things, but you praise those who do evil. Is this a small evil? “You placed your portion with adulterers.”

26. [verse 19.] “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue embraced deceitfulness.”

Brothers, he speaks of the malevolence and deceitfulness of certain people who, through flattery, although they know that what they hear is evil, consent—not merely by failing to rebuke those from whom they hear it, but also by remaining silent so as not to offend them.

It is not enough that they do not say, “You have done wrong”; they say, “And you have done well.” They know that it is evil, but their mouth abounds in wickedness, and their tongue embraces deceitfulness.

Deceitfulness is a kind of fraud in words: saying one thing, thinking another. He does not say, “Your tongue admitted deceitfulness,” or “Your tongue perpetrated deceitfulness.” To show you a certain pleasure in the evil itself, he said, “It embraced” it.

It is not enough that you do it; you also take delight in it. You praise it openly and mock it privately. You hurl headlong a person who carelessly exposes his vices and does not know whether they are vices. You, who know it is a vice, do not say [Note: [Col. 0581] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “you do not say that he has fallen.”], “Where are you rushing?”

If you saw him walking heedlessly in darkness, where you knew there was a pit, and you remained silent, what sort of person would you be? Would you not be considered an enemy of his life? And yet, if he fell into the pit, he would die not in soul but in body.

He throws himself into his vices and proclaims his evil deeds to you. You know that they are evil, yet you praise them and mock them privately. If only the one whom you mock, and whom you were unwilling to correct, should at some time turn to God and say: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be confounded” (Ps. 39:16).

“And your tongue embraced deceitfulness.”

27. [verse 20.] “Sitting, you spoke slander against your brother.”

The word “sitting” also pertains to what he said above, “embraced.” For someone who does this standing or passing by does not do it with pleasure; but whoever sits down for this purpose, how much leisure does he seek in order to do it! “Sitting, you spoke slander against your brother”: you carefully practiced that evil slander by sitting; you wanted to occupy yourself with it there; you embraced your evil; you kissed your deceit.

“Sitting, you spoke slander against your brother, and you placed a stumbling block against the son of your mother.”

Who is the son of the mother? Is he not a brother? Therefore he wished to repeat what he had said above, “your brother.” Or did he intend to suggest that we should understand some distinction? Clearly, brothers, I think a distinction should be made.

A brother slanders a brother—for example, someone regarded as a strong and important teacher, already learned, slanders his brother, who perhaps teaches well and walks well. But there is another person who is weak; by slandering the brother, he places a stumbling block before that weak one.

For when good people are slandered by those who appear to be persons of importance and learning, the weak, who do not yet know how to judge, fall into scandal. Therefore that weak person is called “the son of the mother,” not yet of the father: he still needs milk and clings to the breasts. He is still carried in the bosom of Mother Church. He is not able to approach the solid food of his father’s table, but draws nourishment from his mother’s breast, ignorant of judgment, because he is still animal and carnal.

“For the spiritual person judges all things, but the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, because they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:15, 14). The Apostle says to such people: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people. As infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

I was a mother to you. As it is said elsewhere: “I became gentle in your midst, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7). Not a nurse feeding someone else’s children, but a nurse cherishing her own children.

There are mothers who, after giving birth, hand their children over to nurses. Those who gave birth do not cherish their own children, because they gave them to be nursed; those who cherish them do not cherish their own, but someone else’s. But this man himself had given birth and himself cherished; he did not entrust to any nurse the one whom he had given birth to. For he had said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

He therefore cherished and nursed them. But there were certain people who seemed learned and spiritual and who slandered Paul. “His letters,” they say, “are weighty and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Cor. 10:10). He himself says in his Letter that some of his detractors said this.

They sat and slandered their brother, and by slandering him placed a stumbling block before that son of their mother who was still being nursed. They rightly made that mother give birth again.

“And you placed a stumbling block against the son of your mother.”

28. [verse 21.] “You did these things, and I was silent.”

For this reason the Lord our God will come, and he will not be silent. At present: “You did these things, and I was silent.” What does “I was silent” mean? I refrained from vengeance; I postponed my severity; I prolonged my patience toward you; I waited a long time for your repentance.

“You did these things, and I was silent.” But I waited for you to repent, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. 2:5).

“You suspected iniquity, thinking that I would be like you.” It is not enough that your evil deeds please you; you think that they please me also. Because you do not tolerate God as avenger, you wish to have him as your accomplice; you wish to have a corrupt judge as a partner in your plunder.

“You suspected iniquity, thinking that I would be like you,” while you do not wish to be like me. For he says, “Be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:48, 45).

You were unwilling to imitate this one, who gives good things even to the evil, so that you might sit and slander the good. “You suspected iniquity, thinking that I would be like you.”

“I will rebuke you.” When God will come openly—our God—and will not be silent, he will rebuke you. And what will I do to you by rebuking you? What will I do to you?

At present you do not see yourself; I will make you see yourself. For if you saw yourself and found yourself displeasing, you would please me. But because, by not seeing yourself, you pleased yourself, you will displease both me and yourself: me when you are judged, yourself when you burn.

“What will I do to you?” he says. “I will set you before your own face.” Why do you wish to hide from yourself? You are behind your own back, and you do not see yourself. I will make you see yourself. What you placed behind your back I will place before your face. You will see your foulness—not so that you may correct it, but so that you may be ashamed.

Now that he says these things, brothers, should the person to whom they are said despair? Was that city of which it was said, “In three days Nineveh will be overthrown,” not able within three days to convert, pray, mourn, and obtain mercy in place of the punishment that threatened it (Jonah 3:4–10)?

Therefore let those who are such hear while it is possible to hear him who is still silent. For he will come, he will not be silent, and he will rebuke when there will be no opportunity for correction. “I will set you,” he says, “before your own face.”

Now, then, whoever you are who are such, do what God threatens to do to you. Remove yourself from behind yourself, where you do not wish to see yourself, disguising your deeds from yourself, and set yourself before yourself. Ascend the tribunal of your mind; be your own judge. Let fear torment you; let confession burst forth from you, and say to your God: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5).

Let what was behind you become before you, lest later you yourself be placed by God the judge before yourself, with nowhere to flee from yourself.

29. [verse 22.] “Understand this, you who forget God.”

See how he cries out and does not remain silent, does not spare [Note: [Col. 0583] Some manuscripts read, “when.”]. You had forgotten the Lord; you were not thinking about your evil life. Understand that you have forgotten the Lord.

“Lest at some time he seize you like a lion, and there be no one to deliver.”

What does “like a lion” mean? Like one who is strong, powerful, one whom no one can resist. He referred to this in order to say “lion.” The term is used both in praise and in blame. The devil is called a lion: “Your adversary,” he says, “like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

But because that one is called a lion on account of his savage ferocity, is Christ not called a lion on account of his immense strength? And where is the saying, “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5)?

Let Your Charity pay attention for a little while longer to what remains. I beg you to shake off your weariness; he who has given you strength up to this hour will be present.

A little earlier he had said, as you heard, imposing upon us a certain tribute of his praise: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High.” Then: “But to the sinner God said, Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant upon your mouth?”

As if he were saying to him: “Your praise does you no good. I imposed the sacrifice of praise upon those who live well; for them their praise is beneficial. But if you praise, it does you no good. Why do you praise me? ‘Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner’” (Sir. 15:9).

Afterward he concludes, as it were, addressing both groups, and rebuking the wicked who forget God he says: “Understand this, you who forget God, lest at some time he seize you like a lion, and there be no one to deliver.”

30. [verse 23.] “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me.”

How will the sacrifice of praise glorify me? Certainly the sacrifice of praise is of no benefit to the wicked, because they take your covenant upon their mouths and do what deserves condemnation, things that displease your eyes.

“Indeed,” he says, “I say this even to them: ‘The sacrifice of praise will glorify me.’” You had already thought that praise did you no good. Praise, and it will benefit you.

For if you live badly and say good things, you do not yet praise. But again, if you begin to live well and attribute your good life to your own merits, you do not yet praise. I do not want you to be the thief insulting the Lord’s cross (Luke 23:39); but neither do I want you to be the one in the temple boasting of his merits and concealing his wounds (Luke 18:11).

If you are unrighteous and persist in that unrighteousness, I do not say to you, “Praise will not benefit you.” Rather, I say, “You do not praise me; I do not count that as praise.” Again, if you are apparently just—for no one is just except the humble and devout—and walk about inflated by your righteousness, despising others in comparison with yourself and exalting yourself as though boasting of your merits, you do not praise me.

The one who lives badly does not praise me; nor does the one who lives well as though by his own power praise me. But was that Pharisee not such a person, as though he were so by his own power, when he said, “I thank you, because I am not like the other people”?

He was giving thanks to God for what he possessed that was good. Yet even if there is something good in you, even if you now understand that what is good is not from you but that you received it from God, nevertheless, if you exalt yourself above another who does not possess it, you are held to be envious; you are not yet my praiser.

First, then, correct yourself from the worst way; begin to live well. Understand that you are not corrected except by God’s gift, for “the steps of a human being are directed by the Lord” (Ps. 36:23). When you have understood this, favor others also, so that they may become what you are; for you too were once what they are. Favor them as much as you can, and do not despair. God is not rich only as far as you are concerned.

Therefore the one who offends the Lord by living badly does not praise him. The one who, after beginning to live well, thinks that his good life is his own and not something received from God, does not praise him. Nor does the one who knows that he received his good life from God, yet wishes God to be rich only as far as he is concerned, praise him.

That man who said, “I thank you, God, that I am not like the other people—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or like this tax collector”: did he not have something there that he could have said? “Give this tax collector also what you have given me, and supply me with what you have not yet given me.”

But, as though already filled, he belched forth; he did not say, “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. 69:6), as that tax collector said: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Therefore the tax collector went down justified, more than that Pharisee (Luke 18:11–14).

Therefore hear, you who live well; hear, you who live badly: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me.” No one who is evil offers this sacrifice of praise to me. I do not say, “Let the evil person not offer this sacrifice to me”; rather, “No evil person offers this sacrifice to me.”

For the one who praises is good. If he praises, he also lives well; if he praises, he praises not only with his tongue, but his life also agrees with his tongue.

31. “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.”

In the sacrifice of praise there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God. What is the salvation of God? Christ Jesus.

And how is Christ shown to us in the sacrifice of praise? Because Christ came to us with grace. The Apostle says: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20).

Let sinners therefore acknowledge that a physician would not be necessary if they were healthy (Matt. 9:12). For “Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6).

When they acknowledge their ungodliness and first imitate that tax collector who said, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner,” they show their wounds and implore the physician. And because they do not praise themselves but rebuke themselves, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” and not in himself (1 Cor. 1:31), they recognize the reason for Christ’s coming: he came in order to save sinners. “Christ Jesus came into this world,” he says, “to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15).
