Accordingly, the same Apostle rebukes those Jews who gloried in their works, saying that they did not belong to grace because they thought that a reward was owed to them on account of their merits and works (Gal. 5:4).

Therefore whoever knows that he belongs to grace—which is Christ and what belongs to Christ—knows that he needs grace. If it is called grace, it is given freely; if it is given freely, no merits of yours preceded it so that it might be given. For if your merits preceded it, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt (Rom. 4:4).

If, then, you say that your merits came first, you wish yourself, not God, to be praised. For this reason you do not acknowledge Christ, who came with the grace of God.

Turn, therefore, to your merits and see that they were evil, so that nothing was owed to you except punishment, not reward. When you see what is owed to you by merit, you recognize what is given by grace, and by the sacrifice of praise you glorify God.

For there is the way by which you may know Christ, the salvation of God.

**EXPOSITION OF PSALM 50. SERMON** [Note: [Col. 0585] To the people of Carthage. See below, no. 11.]

1. Neither the large number of this congregation should be disappointed nor its weakness burdened. We ask for silence and quiet, so that our voice may be able to continue with some strength after yesterday’s labor.

We must believe that Your Charity has gathered here in greater numbers today for no other reason than to pray for those whom a foreign and perverse desire keeps away. For we are not speaking about pagans, nor about Jews, but about Christians; and not about those who are still catechumens, but about many who have also been baptized, from whose washing you are separated by nothing, yet whose hearts are unlike yours.

How many of our brothers do we think of and lament today—going after vanities and deceitful follies, neglecting the place to which they have been called! If, by chance, they are frightened in the circus itself for some reason, they immediately make the sign [of the cross] and stand there bearing upon their foreheads what they would withdraw from if they bore it in their hearts.

We must entreat the mercy of God, that he may grant understanding to condemn such things, the inclination to flee them, and mercy to forgive them.

Appropriately, therefore, the Psalm sung today concerned repentance. Let us speak also with those who are absent; our voice will reach them through your memory. Do not neglect the wounded and sick, but, so that you may heal them more easily, you must remain healthy yourselves. Correct them by reproving, console them by speaking to them, offer them an example by living well; the one who was present for you will be present for them.

For the fountain of God’s mercy has not been cut off from you now that you have passed beyond these dangers. By the way you came, they will come; by the way you crossed over, they will cross over.

It is indeed troubling, exceedingly dangerous—indeed harmful and certainly fatal—that people sin knowingly. For one person runs after these vanities in one way when he disregards Christ’s voice, and another in another way when he knows what he is avoiding. But this Psalm also shows that we ought not to despair of such people.

2. [verses 1–2.] Its title reads: “A Psalm for David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, when he went in to Bathsheba.” Bathsheba was another man’s wife.

We speak with sorrow and trembling, yet God did not wish to remain silent about what he wished to be written. I shall therefore say not what I want, but what I am compelled to say; I shall speak not to encourage imitation, but to instruct in fear.

King and prophet David, captivated by the beauty of this woman, another man’s wife, from whose seed, according to the flesh, the Lord was to come (Rom. 1:3), committed adultery with her. This is not read in this Psalm, but it appears in its title; in the Book of Kings it is read more fully.

Both Scriptures are canonical, and Christians must give both their faith without any hesitation. The deed was committed and written down. He also arranged for her husband to be killed in battle; he increased adultery by murder. After this deed, the prophet Nathan was sent to him by the Lord, sent to rebuke him for so great a crime (2 Sam. 11–12:1–14).

### 3.

We have said what people should beware of; now let us hear what they should imitate if they have fallen. For many want to fall with David, but do not want to rise with David. The example set before us is therefore not one of falling, but of rising if you have fallen. Take care lest you fall. The fall of the great should not be a delight to the lesser, but the fall of the great should be a trembling for the lesser. This is why it has been set before us, why it has been written, why it has often been read and sung in the church: let those who have not fallen hear, so that they may not fall; let those who have fallen hear, so that they may rise.

The sin of so great a man is not kept silent; it is proclaimed in the church. Those who hear wrongly [Note: [Col. 0586] The editions read *male viventes*, “those living badly.” But the manuscripts, with broad agreement, have *male audientes*, “those hearing wrongly.” Understand this either as those who are corrected by words, or as those who habitually hear this example without deriving benefit from it.] seek for themselves pretexts for sinning. They look for grounds on which to defend what they have resolved to commit, rather than for grounds on which to avoid what they have not committed, and they say to themselves: “If David did it, why should I not?” Thus the soul becomes more wicked, because, having done it for the reason that David did it, it does something worse than David did.

I shall explain this very point more plainly, if I can. David had not set anyone before himself as an example in such a way that you have; he had fallen through the lapse of desire, not through the protection of holiness. You set before yourself, as though he were holy, one whom you may imitate in sinning; you do not imitate his holiness, but imitate his ruin. You love in David what David hated in himself [Note: [Col. 0586] Most manuscripts read: “Love in David what David did not hate in himself.”]. You prepare yourself to sin and arrange to sin; you examine God’s book in order to sin; you listen to God’s Scriptures for the purpose of doing what displeases God. David did not do this: he was rebuked through the Prophet; he did not fall into the prophet.

Others, however, hearing this to their salvation, measure their own weakness by the fall of the strong [Note: [Col. 0587] So the better manuscripts. The editions read: “the strong in the fall.”]. Wishing to avoid what God condemns, they keep their eyes from a careless gaze. They do not fix them on the beauty of another man’s wife, nor do they make themselves secure through perverse simplicity; they do not say, “I looked with a good intention; I looked kindly; I looked for a long time out of affection.” For they set David’s fall before themselves, and see that he, a great man, fell for this reason: so that the small may refuse to see the point from which they themselves could fall.

They restrain their eyes from wantonness; they do not readily associate with women who belong to others; they do not easily lift their eyes toward another’s balconies or rooftops. For David saw from a distance the woman by whom he was captivated. The woman was far away; lust was near. What he saw was elsewhere, but the place from which he fell was within him.

This weakness of the flesh must therefore be watched, and the Apostle’s words must be remembered: “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). He did not say, “Let it not exist,” but “Let it not reign.” Sin is present when you take pleasure; it reigns if you consent. Carnal pleasure, especially when it advances toward what is unlawful and belongs to another, must be restrained, not released; subdued by command, not enthroned in command. Look securely if you have no source of disturbance. But you answer: “I hold firm.” Are you stronger than David?

### 4.

This example also warns that no one should exalt himself in prosperous circumstances. Many fear adversity but do not fear prosperity. Prosperity is more dangerous to the mind than adversity is to the body. Prosperity first corrupts a person, so that adversity may find something to break.

My brothers, we must keep sharper watch against happiness. For this reason, see how God’s utterance removes security from us in our happiness: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psal. II, 11). In rejoicing, so that we may give thanks; in trembling, so that we may not fall.

David did not commit this sin when he was suffering persecution from Saul. When holy David endured Saul as an enemy, when he was harassed by Saul’s persecutions, when he fled from place to place so as not to fall into his hands (I Reg. XXIV, 5, and XXVI, 9), he did not desire another man’s wife, nor did he kill her husband after committing adultery with her. In the weakness of his tribulation he was all the more intent upon God the more wretched he appeared.

Tribulation is useful; it is a useful surgeon’s instrument, rather than a temptation of the devil [Note: [Col. 0587] So the manuscripts. Erasmus has: “as though against a temptation of the devil.” Lovaniensis has: “as a temptation of the devil.”]. Once his enemies had been conquered, he became secure; the pressure was removed, and the swelling grew. This example therefore serves to make us fear prosperity.

“I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Psal. CXIV, 3–4).

### 5.

But it happened. I have said these things to those who have not committed this sin, so that they may watch over and preserve their integrity, and, when they see that a great man fell, the small may fear. But if someone who has already fallen hears these things, and holds some evil in his conscience, let him attend to the words of this psalm: let him recognize the magnitude of his wound, but not despair of the majesty of the physician.

Sin accompanied by despair is certain death. Let no one therefore say: “If I have already done some evil, I am already condemned; God does not forgive such evils. Why should I not add sins to sins? Let me enjoy this age in pleasure, wantonness, and wicked desire. Since I have already lost hope of restoration, let me at least have what I see, if I cannot have what I believe.”

This psalm, then, just as it makes those who have not fallen cautious, does not want those who have fallen to remain in despair [Note: [Col. 0588] Ten manuscripts read: “Thus it raises up those who have fallen.”]. Whoever you are who have sinned and hesitate to repent of your sin, despairing of your salvation, hear David groaning. The prophet Nathan has not been sent to you; David himself has been sent to you. Hear him crying out, and cry out with him; hear him groaning, and groan with him; hear him weeping, and join your tears to his; hear him corrected, and rejoice together with him.

If the sin could not be shut out from you, let the hope of forgiveness not be shut out. The prophet Nathan was sent to that man: observe the king’s humility [Note: [Col. 0588] Most manuscripts read: “Observe the arrogance of the kingdom.” Two read: “Take care lest you grow proud.”]. He did not reject the words of the one giving orders; he did not say, “Do you dare speak to me, a king?” The exalted king listened to the Prophet; let his humble people listen to Christ.

### 6. [verse 3]

Hear these things, then, and say with him:

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

Whoever begs for great mercy confesses great misery. Let those who sinned unknowingly seek your small mercy: “Have mercy on me,” he says, “according to your great mercy.” Help my grievous wound according to your great medicine. What I have is grievous, but I flee to the Almighty. I would despair of my own deadly wound if I had not found so great a physician.

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.”

When he says, “Blot out my iniquity,” this means, “Have mercy on me, O God.” And when he says, “According to the multitude of your mercies,” this means, “According to your great mercy.” Because your mercy is great, your mercies are many; and from your great mercy come your many acts of compassion.

You regard those who despise you, in order to correct them; you regard those who do not know, in order to teach them; you regard those who confess, in order to forgive them.

“Did he do this unknowingly?” Someone had done certain things and had done many evil things: “I obtained mercy,” he says, “because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (I Tim. I, 13). This David could not say: “I acted ignorantly.” For he was not ignorant of how great an evil it was to touch another man’s wife, or how great an evil it was to kill a husband who was unaware of it and had not even shown anger.

Those who acted unknowingly therefore obtain the Lord’s mercy; and those who acted knowingly obtain not merely some mercy, but great mercy.

### 7. [verse 4]

“Wash me more and more from my iniquity.”

What does “Wash me more and more” mean? It means: “I am greatly polluted.” Wash more and more the sins of one who knew, just as you washed away the sins of one who did not know. Yet even so, one must not despair of your mercy.

“And cleanse me from my offense.”

By what merit? He is a physician: offer payment. He is God: offer sacrifice. What will you give in order to be cleansed? Consider whom you are invoking. You invoke the just one: if he is just, he hates sins; if he is just, he punishes sins. You cannot take justice away from the Lord your God.

Implore mercy, but attend to justice. Mercy is that he forgives the sinner; justice is that he punishes sin. What then? You seek mercy; will sin remain unpunished?

David would answer; those who have fallen would answer; they would answer with David, so that they may deserve mercy as David did, and say:

“No, Lord, my sin will not remain unpunished. I know the justice of the one whose mercy I seek. It will not remain unpunished; but for this reason I do not want you to punish me, because I punish my sin. For this reason I ask you to forgive, because I acknowledge it.”

### 8. [verse 5]

“For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my offense is always before me.”

I have not put behind my back what I did. I do not look at others while forgetting myself. I do not try to remove the speck from my brother’s eye when there is a beam in my own eye (Matth. VII, 3). My sin is before me, not behind me.

It was behind me when the Prophet was sent to me and set before me the parable of the poor man’s ewe. For the prophet Nathan said to David:

“There was a certain rich man who had very many sheep. But his poor neighbor had one little ewe, which he nourished in his bosom and from his own food. A guest came to the rich man; he took nothing from his own flock, but coveted the poor neighbor’s ewe and killed it for his guest. What does he deserve?”

Then David, in anger, pronounced the sentence: at that moment the king did not yet know where he had been caught [Note: [Col. 0589] Several manuscripts read: “where he was captive.” Some read: “where he was being held captive.”]. He declared that the rich man was worthy of death and that the sheep must be restored fourfold (II Reg. XII, 2–6).

Most severe and most just! But his sin was not yet before him; what he had done was behind his back. He did not yet acknowledge his own iniquity, and therefore did not forgive another’s. But the Prophet, sent for this purpose, took the sin from behind his back and placed it before his eyes, so that he might see that the severe sentence had been pronounced against himself.

To cut and heal the wound of his heart, the Prophet made a surgical instrument out of his tongue. The Lord did this for the Jews when they brought an adulterous woman to him, setting before him a trap of temptation and falling into the very thing they had proposed.

“This woman,” they said, “was caught in adultery. Moses commanded that such women be stoned; what do you say about her?” They were trying to capture the Wisdom of God with a two-pronged trap, so that, if he ordered her killed, he would lose his reputation for gentleness; but if he ordered her released, he would incur, as one who reproved the Law, the charge [Note: [Col. 0589] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “he would incur blasphemy, being liable to accusation as one who reproved the Law.”].

What did he answer? He did not say, “Kill her”; he did not say, “Release her.” Instead he said: “Let the one who knows himself to be without sin cast the first stone at her.”

The law is just, for it commands that an adulteress be killed; but let this just law have innocent ministers. You attend to the woman whom you bring; attend also to who you are.

When they heard this, they went away one after another [Col. 0590]. The adulterous woman and the Lord remained; the wounded woman and the physician remained; great misery and great mercy remained.

Those who brought her were ashamed, but did not ask for forgiveness; the woman who had been brought was confused, and was healed. The Lord said to her:

“Woman, has no one condemned you?”

And she said:

“No one, Lord.”

And he said:

“Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on do not sin” (Joan. VIII, 4–11).

Did Christ act against his own law? Surely his Father had not given the Law without the Son. If heaven and earth and everything in them were made through him, how was the Law written without the Word of God?

God therefore did not act against his own law, just as an emperor does not act against his own laws when he grants pardon to those who confess. Moses was the minister of the Law; Christ was the promulgator of the Law. Moses stones as judge; Christ forgives as king.

God therefore had mercy on her according to his great mercy, as this man asks, petitions, cries out, and grieves—unlike those who brought the adulteress and refused to do this. When the physician exposed their wounds, they recognized them, but they did not seek medicine from the physician.

There are many people whom it is not shameful to sin, but whom it is shameful to repent. O incredible madness! You are not ashamed of the wound itself, but you are ashamed of the bandage for the wound? Is the naked wound not fouler and more putrid?

Flee, then, to the physician; repent; say:

“I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”

### 9. [verse 6]

“Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.”

What does this mean? Was another man’s wife not adulterated before human beings, and was her husband not killed? Did everyone not know what David had done?

What does “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” mean? It means: because you alone are without sin. He is the just punisher who has nothing in himself that should be punished; he is the just reprover who has nothing in himself that should be reproved.

“Against you alone,” he says, “have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

Brothers, it is difficult to notice to whom he is speaking. He is certainly speaking to God, and it is clear how God the Father was not judged. What does “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” mean?

He sees the future judge being judged—being judged by sinners as the just one—and prevailing in that judgment, because there was nothing in him that could be judged. For among human beings, the man who is God alone could speak the truth:

“If you find sin in me, speak” (Joan. VIII, 46).

But perhaps there was something hidden from human beings, and they did not find what was indeed there because it was not manifest? Elsewhere he says:

“Behold, the prince of this world is coming,” a sharp examiner of all sinners. “Behold,” he says, “the prince of this world is coming”—the one appointed over death, inflicting death upon sinners; for “through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Sap. II, 24). “Behold,” he says, “the prince of this world is coming”—he said this shortly before his Passion—“and he will find nothing in me: no sin, nothing worthy of death, nothing worthy of condemnation” [Col. 0591].

And as though someone were to say to him, “Why then are you dying?” he continues and says:

“But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise; let us go from here” (Joan. XIV, 30–31).

“I suffer,” he says, “undeservedly for the deserving, so that I may make them worthy of life by my life, for whom I undeservedly suffer their death.”

To this one, therefore, who had no sin, the prophet David says in the present passage:

“Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

For you surpass all human beings, all judges; and the one who considers himself just is unjust before you. You alone judge justly, though you were judged unjustly—you who have power to lay down your life and power to take it up again (Id. X, 18).

You therefore prevail when you are judged. You surpass all human beings because you are more than human beings, and human beings were made through you.

### 10. [verse 7]

“Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.”

It is as though someone were to say: “Those who did what you did, David, are defeated. For adultery and murder are not a small evil or a small sin. What about those who, from the time they were born from their mother’s womb, did nothing of this kind? Do you also impute certain sins to them, so that he may prevail over all when he begins to be judged?”

David assumed the person of the human race and considered the bonds of all; he considered the progeny of death and observed the origin of iniquity, and said:

“For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.”

Was David born from adultery—from Jesse, a just man, and his wife (I Reg. XVI, 18)? What does he mean by saying that he was conceived in iniquity, unless it is because iniquity is drawn from Adam? The bond of death itself was formed together with that iniquity [Note: [Col. 0591] Several manuscripts read: “from Adam, from whom the bond itself …”].

No one is born without drawing punishment, without drawing the liability of punishment. The prophet also says elsewhere:

“No one is clean in your sight, not even an infant whose life upon earth is a single day” (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint).

For we know that sins are loosed by Christ’s Baptism and that Christ’s Baptism is effective for the remission of sins. If infants are entirely innocent, why do mothers hurry to the church with sick children? What is removed by that Baptism, and what is forgiven by that remission?

I see the innocent child weeping rather than becoming angry. What does Baptism wash away? What does that grace loose? The transmission of sin is loosed.

For if that infant could speak to you, and if he already possessed the understanding that David possessed, he would answer you:

“Why do you look at me as an infant? You do not see my crimes, certainly; but I was conceived in iniquity, and my mother nourished me in sins in her womb.”

Apart from this bond of carnal desire [Note: [Col. 0591] Nearly all manuscripts read: “mortal.”], Christ was born without a male, conceived from a virgin by the Holy Spirit. He cannot be said to have been conceived in iniquity; it cannot be said of him, “His mother nourished him in sins in her womb,” to whom it was said:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luc. I, 35).

People are therefore not conceived in iniquity and nourished in sins in the womb by their mothers because intercourse between spouses is itself sinful, but because what takes place is certainly produced from mortal flesh. For the punishment of the flesh is death, and mortality itself is certainly present in it.

Thus the Apostle did not call the body one that will die, but one that is dead: “The body is dead because of sin,” he says, “but the spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. VIII, 10).

How, then, is that born without the bond of sin which is conceived [Note: [Col. 0592] Several manuscripts read: “which is conceived” in a different form; others: “which grows together.”] and sown from a body made dead because of sin?

The chaste act between spouses is not guilty, but the origin of sin carries with it the punishment owed. For a husband, merely because he is a husband, is not therefore immortal, nor is he mortal for any other reason than sin.

The Lord too was mortal, but not because of sin. He took upon himself our punishment, and thus removed our guilt. Therefore rightly “all die in Adam, but all will be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV, 22).

“For through one man,” the Apostle says, “sin entered this world, and through sin death; and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

The sentence has been defined: “In Adam,” he says, “all sinned.” The only innocent infant could have been one who was not born from Adam’s work [Note: [Col. 0592] The editions read: “from Adam’s work.” The manuscripts omit “in.”].

### 11. [verse 8]

“For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

“You have loved truth”—that is, you did not leave sins unpunished even in those whom you forgive. “You have loved truth”: you bestowed mercy in such a way that you preserved truth as well. You forgive the one who confesses; you forgive, but the one who punishes himself. Thus mercy and truth are preserved: mercy, because the human being is freed; truth, because the sin is punished.

“For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

What are the hidden and uncertain things? That God forgives even such people. Nothing is so hidden, nothing so uncertain.

Because of this uncertainty, the Ninevites repented. For although the prophet had threatened them, although they had heard that proclamation, “In three days Nineveh will be overthrown,” they said among themselves that mercy should be sought. They reasoned among themselves:

“Who knows whether God may turn his sentence toward the better and have mercy?”

It was uncertain when they said, “Who knows?” From this uncertainty they repented; they earned certain mercy. They prostrated themselves in tears, in fasting, in sackcloth and ashes; they groaned, they wept, and God spared them (Jon. III, 4–10).

Did Nineveh stand, or was Nineveh overthrown? In one way it appears to human beings, and in another way it appeared to God [Note: [Col. 0592] The word “to God” is absent from the manuscripts.].

I think, however, that what the prophet had foretold was fulfilled. Consider what Nineveh was, and see that it was overthrown—overthrown in evil and built up in goodness—just as Saul the persecutor was overthrown and Paul the preacher was built up (Act. IX, 4).

Who would not say that this city in which we now are had been happily overthrown, if all those madmen, abandoning their follies, were to run to the church with contrite hearts and invoke God’s mercy for their past deeds?

Would we not say: “Where is that Carthage?” Because it is not what it was, it has been overthrown. But if it is what it was not, it has been built up.

Thus it is said to Jeremiah:

“Behold, I have appointed you to uproot, to dig up, to overthrow, to destroy, and again to build and to plant” (Jerem. I, 10).

Hence comes that utterance of the Lord:

“I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

He strikes the corruption of the crime and heals the pain of the wound. Physicians do this when they cut: they strike and they heal; they arm themselves so that they may wound, they carry iron, and they come to cure.

But because the sins of the Ninevites were great, they said, “Who knows?” God had revealed this uncertain matter to his servant David. For when the Prophet stood before him and rebuked him, and he had said, “I have sinned,” he immediately heard from the Prophet—that is, from the Spirit of God who was in the Prophet:

“Your sin has been forgiven you” (II Reg. XII, 13).

He made known to him the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom.

### 12. [verse 9]

“You will sprinkle me with hyssop,” he says, “and I shall be cleansed.”

We know hyssop as a lowly but medicinal herb; it is said to cling to rock with its roots. Therefore, as a mystery concerning the cleansing of the heart, its likeness has been adopted.

You too, grasp the root of love, your rock. Be humble in your humble God, so that you may be exalted in your glorified God:

“You will sprinkle me with hyssop”—the humility of Christ will cleanse you.

Do not despise the herb; attend to the power of the medicine.

I shall also say something that we commonly hear from physicians, or observe in the sick. They say that hyssop is suitable for cleansing the lungs. Pride is usually signified in the lungs, for there are swelling and panting there.

It was said of Saul the persecutor, as of a proud Saul, that he went to bind the Christians “breathing out slaughter” (Act. IX, 1). He panted for slaughter; he panted for blood, with his lungs not yet cleansed.

Hear him here also after he has been humbled, because he has been cleansed with hyssop:

“You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me”—that is, you will cleanse me—“and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

“Even if your sins are like scarlet,” he says, “I will make them white as snow” (Isai. I, 18).

From such people Christ presents to himself a garment without spot or wrinkle (Ephes. V, 27). Therefore his garment on the mountain, which shone white like snow (Matth. XVII, 2), signified the Church cleansed from every stain of sin.

### 13. [verse 10]

But where is humility in hyssop? Hear what follows:

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice.”

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing”: I shall rejoice by hearing you, not by speaking against you.

You have sinned; why do you defend yourself? You want to speak: endure, listen, yield to the divine voices, lest you be disturbed and wounded more deeply. What was committed must come into confession, not defense.

You appoint yourself as the defender of your sin and are defeated. You have not appointed an innocent advocate; your defense is of no benefit to you. For who are you to defend yourself? You are competent to accuse yourself.

Do not say either, “I did nothing,” or, “What great thing did I do?” or, “Others did it too.” If, by committing sin, you say that you did nothing, you will be nothing and receive nothing. God is ready to grant pardon; you close the way against yourself. He is ready to give; do not place the obstacle of defense in the way, but open the bosom of confession.

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing.”

May he himself grant me to say what I feel. Those who hear are happier than those who speak. The one who learns is humble; the one who teaches labors not to become proud, lest the desire to please creep in and he displease God while wishing to please human beings.

There is great trembling in the teacher, my brothers; there is great trembling in us in these words of ours. Believe what you cannot see in our hearts. He himself knows how he may make us gentle and be gracious to us, when we speak to you with how great a trembling beneath him.

But when we hear within us the one who suggests and teaches something, we are secure; secure, we rejoice. For we are under the teacher; we seek his glory; we praise him as he teaches. His truth delights us within, where no one creates or hears a disturbance. He said that his joy and gladness are there:

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing.”

And because he is humble, he hears. Whoever hears—whoever truly and rightly hears—hears humbly. For glory belongs to the one from whom he hears what he hears.

After saying, “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing,” he immediately showed what hearing accomplishes:

“And the humbled bones will rejoice.”

The bones are humbled. The bones of the one who hears have neither arrogance nor swelling, which the one who speaks scarcely manages to overcome in himself.

There is also that great humble man than whom no one born of woman has arisen greater (Matth. XI, 11), who humbled himself so greatly that he declared himself unworthy to loosen the strap of his Lord’s sandal (Marc. I, 7): John the Baptist.

He gave glory to his teacher, and therefore to his friend. When John was thought to be Christ, he could have grown proud and exalted himself. For he had not himself declared that he was the Christ, but he could have accepted the error of those who thought this and willingly wished to confer that honor upon him (Luc. III, 15). But he rejected false honor in order to find true glory [Note: [Col. 0594] The manuscripts, except perhaps one or two, read “true grace.”].

Observe his humility arising from hearing. He says:

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him.”

He made himself one who stands and hears, not one who falls and speaks:

“He stands,” he says, “and hears him.”

You have heard about hearing. Where are the joy and gladness? It follows immediately:

“He stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (Joan. III, 29).

“You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice.”

### 14. [verse 11]

“Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.”

The humbled bones are now rejoicing; cleansed with hyssop, I have now become humble.

“Turn your face away”—not from me, but from my sins. Elsewhere, praying, he says:

“Do not turn your face away from me” (Psal. XXVI, 9).

The one who does not want God’s face turned away from him wants God’s face turned away from his sins. For the sin from which God does not turn his face, he regards; and if he regards it, he punishes it.

“Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.”

He is earnestly concerned about that great sin; he presumes to ask that all his iniquities be blotted out. He presumes upon the physician’s hand, upon that great mercy which he invoked at the beginning of the psalm:

“Blot out all my iniquities.”

God turns his face away and thus blots them out; by turning his face away he blots out sins, and by regarding them he writes them down.

You have heard of him blotting out by turning his face away; hear what he does by regarding them:

“The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psal. XXXIII, 17)—not by blotting out their sins.

But what does he ask here?

“Turn your face away from my sins.”

He asks rightly. For he himself does not turn his face away from his sins, saying:

“For I acknowledge my sin.”

You rightly and properly ask God to turn his face away from your sin if you do not turn your face away from it. But if you put your sin behind your back, God turns his face toward it.

Turn your sin before your own face if you want God to turn his face away from it; then you ask securely, and he hears you.

### 15. [verse 12]

“Create a clean heart in me, O God.”

“Create”—he did not mean, “Establish something new” [Note: [Col. 0595] The particle “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]. But because the penitent was praying, and had committed something after which he was less innocent than before committing it, he showed how he had said, “Create.”

“And renew a right spirit within my inward parts.”

“Through my deed,” he says [Note: [Col. 0595] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “Make a perfect spirit in me,” he says. “It had grown old …”], the rightness of my spirit had grown old and become bent. For he says in another psalm:

“They have bent my soul” (Psal. LVI, 7).

When a human being inclines himself toward earthly desires, what is in him is somehow bent; but when he is raised toward heavenly things, his heart becomes upright, so that God is good to him.

“How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (Psal. LXXII, 1).

Therefore, brothers, listen. Sometimes God forgives a person in the age to come, but chastises him for sin in this age. For certain things that God had threatened because of that sin happened even to David, to whom the Prophet had already said, “Your sin has been forgiven.”

His son Absalom waged a bloody war against him and humbled his father in many ways (II Reg. XV, 10). David walked in sorrow and in the tribulation of his humiliation. He was so submissive to God that, attributing everything justly to him, he confessed that he was suffering nothing undeservedly. He already had an upright heart, which was not displeased with God.

He patiently listened to a certain abusive man who hurled harsh curses in his face, one of the opposing side, a soldier who was with his wicked son. When the man was heaping curses upon the king, one of David’s companions became angry and wanted to go and strike him, but David restrained him.

And how did he restrain him? By saying:

“God sent him to curse me” (Id. XVI, 5, 10).

Acknowledging his guilt, he embraced his punishment; seeking not his own glory, he praised the Lord in whatever good he possessed, praised the Lord in what he suffered, blessing the Lord at all times, with his praise always in his mouth (Psal. XXXIII, 2).

Such are all those who are upright in heart—not those perverse people who consider themselves upright and God perverse; who, when they do something evil, rejoice, but when they suffer something evil, blaspheme. Even when placed in tribulation and under the scourge, they say from their distorted heart:

“God, what have I done to you?”

Truly, they have done nothing to God; they have done everything to themselves.

“And renew a right spirit within my inward parts.”

### 16. [verse 13]

“Do not cast me away from your face.”

“Turn your face away from my sins, and do not cast me away from your face.”

He invokes the face of the one whose face he fears.

“Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

For the Holy Spirit is in the one who confesses. It already belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit that you are displeased with what you have done. Sins please an unclean spirit; they displease the Holy Spirit.

Although you are still begging for forgiveness, yet, because the evil you committed displeases you, you are joined to God in another respect: what displeases you also displeases him.

Now there are two of you against your fever—you and the physician.

Since confession of sin and punishment of sin cannot exist in a person from himself, whenever someone is angry with himself and displeased with himself, the gift of the Holy Spirit is present. He does not say, “Give me your Holy Spirit,” but “Do not take him from me.”

“And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

### 17. [verse 14]

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation.”

Restore what I had and lost by sinning:

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation”—that is, of your Christ.

For who could have been healed without him? Even before he was born from Mary, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joan. I, 1). Thus the dispensation of the flesh he was to assume was believed by the holy Fathers as future, just as it is believed by us as having occurred. The times have changed; the faith has not.

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

Some have understood the Trinity here: God himself, apart from the dispensation of the flesh, since it is written, “God is spirit” (Id. IV, 24). For what is not a body, and yet exists, seems to remain as spirit.

Some therefore understand the Trinity to be spoken of here: the Son in the “right spirit,” the Holy Spirit in the “Holy Spirit,” and the Father in the “principal spirit” [Note: [Col. 0596] Jerome, in his Letter to the Galatians, chapter 4, verse 6.].

Whether this is so, or whether he wished “right spirit” to be understood as the spirit of the human being when he said, “Renew a right spirit within my inward parts”—the spirit that I bent and distorted by sinning—so that the Holy Spirit himself is now the “principal spirit,” whom he did not want taken away from him and by whom he wished to be strengthened, neither interpretation is any heretical opinion.

### 18. [verse 15]

But see what he adds: “With a principal spirit strengthen me.” In what respect strengthen me? Because you have forgiven me; because I am secure in the knowledge that what you have pardoned is not counted against me; made secure by this and confirmed by this grace, I shall not be ungrateful. What shall I do? “I will teach transgressors your ways.” “I will teach the wicked as an *ex-iniquus*, one formerly wicked” [Note: [Col. 0596] Several manuscripts read *ex iniquis*, “from transgressors.” Three others read *exiniquus*, with this note added in the margin: “Thus is one called *ex-poenitens* who was penitent and is so no longer, and *ex-consul* who was consul and is so no longer.”]; that is, since I too was once a transgressor and am now no longer a transgressor, since the Holy Spirit has not been taken from me and I have been strengthened by a principal spirit, I will teach transgressors your ways.

Which ways will you teach transgressors? “And the ungodly shall turn back to you.” If David’s sin is reckoned as ungodliness, let the ungodly not despair of themselves, because God spared an ungodly man; but let them turn to him and learn his ways. If, however, David’s deed is not reckoned as ungodliness, but ungodliness is properly called apostasy from God—worshiping not the one God, or never having worshiped him, or abandoning the one whom one had worshiped—then what he says, “And the ungodly shall turn back to you,” adds still greater force. So full are you of the richness of mercy that, for those who turn to you, not only for ordinary sinners but even for the ungodly, there is no reason for despair. “And the ungodly shall turn back to you.” Why? “So that, believing in him who justifies the ungodly, their faith may be reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5).

### 19. [verse 16]

“Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation.” The Latin translator expressed the precise meaning from the Greek by using a word that is less Latin. For we all know that in Latin one does not say *sanguines*, nor *sanguina*; yet because the Greek has used the plural number, not without reason—but because he found this form in the original Hebrew language—the devout translator preferred [Note: [Col. 0597] Most manuscripts read *potius*, “rather.”] to say something less Latin rather than something less exact. Why, then, did he say in the plural, “from bloodguilt” (*de sanguinibus*)?

By “many bloodguilts,” as though in the origin of sinful flesh, he intended many sins to be understood. Referring to those sins that arise from the corruption of flesh and blood, the Apostle says, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Yet, according to the true faith of that same Apostle, this flesh will rise, and it will itself attain incorruption, since he says, “This corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:50, 53).

Because this corruption arises from sin, sins are called by its name. It is as when we say “tongue” both of that piece of flesh and of the member that moves in the mouth when we articulate words, and also of what is done through the tongue, as when we say that one language is Greek and another Latin: the flesh is not different, but the sound is. As, then, the speech produced through the tongue is called “tongue,” so the iniquity produced through blood is called “blood.”

Considering, therefore, his many iniquities, and also the earlier words, “Blot out all my iniquities,” and attributing them to the corruption of flesh and blood, he says, “Deliver me from bloodguilt”—that is, “Deliver me from iniquities; cleanse me from every corruption.” For the one who says, “Deliver me from bloodguilt,” desires incorruption, since “flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” nor shall corruption possess incorruption.

“Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation.” He shows that, when salvation is perfect in this body, there will be no corruption in it—the corruption understood by the terms “flesh and blood.” For this is the body’s perfect health. How can what slips away, what is in need, what has a kind of perpetual sickness of hunger and thirst, be healthy now? These things will not exist then, because “food is for the stomach and the stomach for food”; but “God will bring both it and them to nothing” (1 Cor. 6:13).

The body’s form will then be perfect through God, with death swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54), with no decline creeping in, no change brought by the stages of life, and no weariness requiring it to be sustained by food or restored by nourishment [Note: [Col. 0597] The editions read, “so that it may not be sustained by any food.” The word “any” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Yet we shall not be without food and drink: God himself will be our food, and God himself our drink. He alone is food that restores without failing.

“Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation.” Even now we are already in that salvation. Hear the Apostle: “For by hope we have been saved.” And see that he was speaking of the salvation of the body itself: “Within ourselves,” he says, “we groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body. For by hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

Whoever perseveres to the end—that is the patience—“will be saved” (Matt. 10:21; 24:13). This is the salvation that we do not yet possess, but shall possess. It is not yet the reality, but a certain hope.

“And my tongue shall exult in your righteousness.”

### 20. [verse 17]

“Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” Your praise, because [Note: [Col. 0598] Most manuscripts consistently read *qua*, “by which.”] I was created; your praise, because, though I sinned, I was not abandoned; your praise, because I was admonished to confess; your praise, because I was cleansed so that I might be secure. “You will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

### 21. [verses 18–19]

“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it.” David lived at the time when sacrifices of animal victims were offered to God, and he saw those future times. Do we not recognize ourselves in these words? Those sacrifices were symbolic, announcing the one saving sacrifice.

Nor have we been left without a sacrifice to offer to God. Hear what he says as he takes care for his sin and desires pardon for the evil he has committed: “If you had desired sacrifice,” he says, “I would certainly have given it. You will not delight in burnt offerings.”

Shall we offer nothing, then? Shall we come to God in this way? And by what shall we appease him? Offer something—indeed, you have within yourself what you may offer. Do not purchase incense from outside, but say: “Within me, O God, are your vows, which I shall fulfill as offerings of praise to you” (Ps. 55:12). Do not seek outside yourself an animal to slaughter; you have within yourself what you may kill.

“A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” He certainly despises the bull, the goat, and the ram: the time for offering these things no longer exists. They were offered when they signified something, when they promised something; when the promised realities came, the promises were taken away.

“A broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” You know that God is exalted: if you exalt yourself, he will withdraw from you; if you humble yourself, he will draw near to you.

### 22. [verse 20]

See who this person is. One man seemed to be making supplication—David. See here our image and the type of the Church.

“Deal graciously with Zion, Lord, according to your good will.” Deal graciously with this Zion. What is Zion? The holy city. What is the holy city? The city set upon a mountain that cannot be hidden (Matt. 5:14).

“Zion” means “watchtower,” because it watches for something that it hopes for. For *Zion* is interpreted as “watchtower,” and *Jerusalem* as “vision of peace.” Recognize yourselves, then, in Zion and in Jerusalem, if you confidently await future hope and if you have peace with God.

“And let the walls of Jerusalem be built.” “Deal graciously with Zion, Lord, according to your good will, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built.” Let Zion not attribute any merits to itself: deal graciously with it according to your own will. Let the walls of Jerusalem be built; let the defenses of our immortality be constructed in faith, hope, and love.

### 23. [verse 21]

“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.” But now the sacrifice is for iniquity: a troubled spirit and a humbled heart. Then there will be only the sacrifice of righteousness, for “blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). For this is the sacrifice of righteousness.

“Offerings and burnt offerings.” What are burnt offerings? Something wholly consumed by fire. When an entire animal was placed upon the altar to be consumed by fire, it was called a burnt offering.

May the divine fire consume us wholly, and may that fervor seize us entirely. What fervor? “There is no one who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. 18:7). What fervor? That of which the Apostle says, “Fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11).

Let not only our soul be consumed by that divine fire of wisdom, but also our body, so that it may merit immortality there [Note: [Col. 0599] The manuscripts omit the particle *ut*, “so that,” and some of them consequently read: “may be worthy to be consumed by immortality.”]. Thus let the burnt offering be lifted up, so that “death may be swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54).

“Offerings and burnt offerings.” “Then they will place calves upon your altar.” From where will the calves come? What will he choose there? The innocence of a new age, or necks freed from the yoke of the Law?

### 24

The psalm in the name of Christ has come to an end—perhaps not as we would wish, but nevertheless as we have been able, with the Lord’s help. It remains for me to address you briefly, brothers, because of the many evils among which we live.

For while we live among human affairs, we cannot depart from human affairs. We must live patiently among the wicked, because when we were wicked, the good lived patiently among us. Let us not forget what we once were; then we shall not despair of those who now are what we were.

Nevertheless, dearly beloved, amid such great diversity of character and such detestable corruption, govern your households, govern your children, govern your families [Note: [Col. 0599] Four manuscripts read “your daughters.”]. Just as it belongs to us to speak to you in the Church, so it belongs to you to act in your homes, so that you may give a good account of those subject to you.

God loves discipline. But a perverse and false innocence consists in loosening the reins for sins. It is exceedingly useless, exceedingly harmful, for a son to experience his father’s leniency only to experience the severity of God afterward—and not alone, but together with his dissolute father.

What then? If he himself does not sin and does not do what his son does, should he therefore not restrain his son from that wickedness? Or is it perhaps so that his son may think that his father too would do such things if he had not grown old? The sin that does not displease you in your son pleases you; age has failed, not desire.

Above all, my brothers, take care of your faithful children, whom you have pledged [Note: [Col. 0599] Erasmus and three manuscripts read “whom you have begotten in faith.” Four other manuscripts read “for whom you have stood surety.” [Col. 0600] Lovaniensis has “whom you have pledged,” as do the better manuscripts. The same word was used above, in the exposition of Psalm 36, sermon 3, section 6.] so that they might be baptized.

But perhaps a wicked son disregards either his father’s admonitions, his rebuke, or his severity. You fulfill your role; God will require his from him.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 51. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1

The psalm on which we have undertaken to speak to Your Charity is short [Col. 0600], but its title presents some difficulty. Therefore bear with us patiently until we unravel it as best we can, insofar as the Lord gives assistance.

These matters should not simply be passed over, since it has pleased the brothers that what we say should be received not only by ear and heart but also by writing, so that we must consider not only the hearer but also the reader.

The occasion for this psalm arose from a certain event, which we also had read to you from the Book of Kings. Saul was a king chosen by the Lord not to remain, but given according to the hard and evil heart of the people for their correction, not for their benefit (1 Sam. 8:7), in accordance with that statement of the holy Scriptures concerning God: “Who makes a hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people” (Job 34:30).

Since Saul was such a man, he persecuted David (1 Sam. 18–24). In David, God prefigured the kingdom of eternal salvation, and God had chosen him to remain in his offspring; for he was to be our future king, the king of the ages, with whom we shall reign forever, from the offspring of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3).

Since God had chosen, preferred, and predestined David for kingship, he did not wish David to occupy the throne before first being delivered from his persecutors. In this too he prefigured us—that is, the body of which Christ is the head (Col. 1:18).

For if he did not wish our very Head to reign in heaven without first completing his labor on earth, and did not wish to raise up the body that he had taken below except by way of tribulation, what can the members dare to hope—that they may be more fortunate than their Head? “If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” (Matt. 10:25).

Let us not, then, hope for an easier way. Let us go by the way he went before us; let us follow where he led. For if we stray from his footsteps, we perish.

You see, then, what was prefigured in David; and you also see what was prefigured in Saul: an evil kingdom in Saul, a good kingdom in David; death in Saul, and life in David.

For it is death that persecutes us, and at the end we shall triumph over it, saying: “Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:55). What do I mean by saying that nothing but death persecutes us? If we were not mortal, there would be nothing for the enemy to do to us. Surely he does nothing to angels?

Thus death itself, from which we suffer our greatest persecution, whose contention will be ended at the end when we rise from the dead—as it was ended in our Head—will likewise be ended in us, if we are found righteous. For that dead man was the destroyer of death; in him death itself died more truly than he died in death.

### 2

Finally, if we consider the name itself, it is not without mystery. For *Saul* is interpreted as “request,” that is, “desire.” Why should we doubt that we ourselves brought this death upon ourselves? Death arose from human sin. Rightly, then, a human being desired death for himself, and therefore “request” is the name of death.

For as it is written, “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and he made the nations of the world healable.” And how did death arise, as though you were asking? “But the ungodly,” he says, “summoned it with their hands and words, and, considering it a friend, they melted away” (Wis. 1:13–14, 16).

By desiring death, then, they melted away and rushed into death, considering it their friend—just as the people considered an enemy a friend and asked for a king. For the people forced the Lord to give them a king, and Saul was given to them, as though those who had summoned death with hands and words had been given into their own hands; and death itself was represented in Saul.

Therefore the seventeenth psalm has this title: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.” First he said, “from all his enemies,” and afterward, “from the hand of Saul,” because “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

What does “from the hand of Saul” mean? It means that he removed us from the underworld and delivered us from the hand of death.

### 3

When Saul, then, was persecuting the holy man David, David fled to a place that he thought safe. Passing by a certain priest, Ahimelech, he received loaves from him. There he prefigured not only the person of a king but also that of a priest, because he ate the bread of the Presence, which, as the Lord says in the Gospel, it was not lawful for anyone to eat except the priests (Matt. 12:4).

Afterward Saul began to seek him and became angry with his men because no one wanted to betray David to him. This is how the matter is read in the Book of Kings.

There was a certain Doeg there when he had come to Ahimelech the priest. He was Saul’s chief shepherd, an Idumaean. When Saul was angry with his men because no one wanted to betray David to him, Doeg revealed where he had seen him.

Saul immediately sent for them, brought out the priest and all his people, and ordered them to be killed. None of King Saul’s men dared to lay a hand on the priests of the Lord, even at the king’s command. But the one who had betrayed them, like Judas, who did not turn back from his purpose and persevered to the end in bearing fruit from that root—for what kind of fruit could a bad tree bear?—this Doeg killed the priest and all his people with his own hand, at the king’s command. Then the city of the priests was also destroyed in battle (1 Sam. 21–22).

We find, therefore, that this Doeg was an enemy of King David and of the priest Ahimelech. Doeg is one man, but Doeg is a class of human beings; just as David and the body itself of the king and priest are, as it were, one man and two persons, yet one class of human beings.

Accordingly, in this present time and in this present age, let us look at these two classes, so that what we sing or hear sung may contribute to our benefit. Let us now look at Doeg; let us now look at the body of the king and priest; let us now look at the body of human beings opposed to the king and priest.

### 4

First, consider how mystical the names themselves are. *Doeg* is interpreted as “motion”; *Idumaean* is interpreted as “earthly.”

Now see what class of human beings this moving Doeg signifies: not one who perseveres forever, but one who is to depart. “Earthly”: what fruit do you expect from an earthly human being? The heavenly human being will exist forever [Note: [Col. 0602] Several manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “What fruit do you expect—heavenly fruit? The human being,” etc.].

There is, then, an earthly kingdom—or, to put it briefly and make the point quickly, there is such a kingdom today in this world, where the heavenly kingdom also exists. Both kingdoms have their citizens as strangers here: the earthly kingdom and the heavenly kingdom, the kingdom destined to be uprooted and the kingdom destined to be planted forever.

At present, in this age, the citizens of both kingdoms are mixed together. The body of the earthly kingdom and the body of the heavenly kingdom are mingled. The heavenly kingdom groans among the citizens of the earthly kingdom; and sometimes—for this too must not be left unsaid—the earthly kingdom in a certain sense presses the citizens of the kingdom of heaven into service, while the heavenly kingdom presses the citizens of the earthly kingdom into service.

We shall demonstrate both points to you from the Scripture of God. Daniel and the three youths were placed in charge of the king’s affairs in Babylon (Dan. 2:49). Joseph was placed second after the king in Egypt to administer the state (Gen. 41:40), and from that state the people of God were to be delivered. In that state Joseph, like the three youths and Daniel, was in a certain sense pressed into service.

It is therefore clear that the earthly kingdom had taken citizens of the kingdom of heaven for its own works—that is, for the works of its kingdom, not for its evil deeds.

What about the kingdom of heaven? How does it temporarily press citizens of the earthly kingdom into service in this age? Does the Apostle not say of certain people that they did not preach the Gospel purely, but, desiring earthly things, preached the kingdom of heaven? They sought their own interests, and yet proclaimed Christ.

And so that you may know that they too were taken up for the work of the kingdom of heaven, like hired laborers, the Apostle rejoices concerning them and says: “There are some who proclaim Christ out of envy and rivalry, supposing that they are stirring up trouble for my bonds. What then? So long as Christ is proclaimed in every way, whether as a pretext or in truth, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. 1:17–18).

Christ also speaks of such people when he says: “The Pharisees and scribes have taken their seat on Moses’ chair. Therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they speak and do not act” (Matt. 23:2–3).

What they say belongs to David; what they do belongs to Doeg. Listen to me through them, but do not imitate them.

These two classes of human beings exist today on earth. This psalm sings of these two classes.

### 5. [verses 1–2]

The title of the psalm is: “For the end, an instruction of David, when Doeg the Idumaean came and announced to Saul: David has come to the house of Abimelech” [Note: [Col. 0602] Most manuscripts read: “The title of the psalm says that it was announced to Saul concerning David that David had come to the house of Abimelech.”].

Yet we read that he came to the house of Ahimelech. Perhaps, as we reasonably judge because of the similarity of the names and the difference of one syllable—or rather, of one letter—the titles have been altered.

Nevertheless, when we examined the manuscripts of the Psalms, we found *Abimelech* more often than *Ahimelech*. And since elsewhere we have a very clear psalm indicating not merely a difference in name but an entirely different name—when David changed his appearance before King Achish, not before King Abimelech, and Achish dismissed him and he went away, while the title of the psalm is written, “When he changed his appearance before Abimelech” (Ps. 33:1)—this very alteration of the name makes us attentive to the mystery, lest you pursue the matters as though they were merely historical and disregard the sacred veils [Note: [Col. 0603] Erasmus and the manuscripts read this way. Lovaniensis has “the hidden things.”].

When the name *Abimelech* in that psalm is examined, it is found to be interpreted as “the kingdom of my father.” How, then, did David leave the kingdom of his father and depart, unless it was as Christ left the kingdom of the Jews and passed over to the Gentiles?

Perhaps for this reason the prophetic spirit, writing the title of this psalm, wished it to say not *Ahimelech* but *Abimelech*: when David came to the kingdom of his father, he was then betrayed. That is, when our Lord Jesus Christ came to the kingdom of the Jews, established by his Father, concerning which he says, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits and righteousness” (Matt. 21:43), he was then betrayed to death, which Saul signifies.

But he was not killed [Note: [Col. 0603] The understood subject is David.], just as Isaac was not killed, although he too represented the Lord’s Passion. Nevertheless, the type was not enacted without blood: there, through the blood of the ram (Gen. 22:12), and here, through that of the priest Ahimelech.

For it was not fitting that those whom it was not yet fitting to rise again should be killed. But by preserving their lives from the danger of death, though with blood poured out, Jesus signified resurrection more fully—resurrection that was represented in this way in them, because it was being reserved for the true Lord [Note: [Col. 0603] The better manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “to be delivered from the danger of death. Nevertheless, the deliverance through the shedding of blood signified resurrection more fully, which was represented in this way in them. Since resurrection was reserved for the true Lord, more could be said here,” etc.].

More could be said about this, if we had undertaken in this sermon to treat the mysteries of those historical events.

### 6

Now let us hear these two classes of human beings, since we have reached the end of this title, though with more labor and perhaps more verbosity than usual, as the Lord has permitted.

Consider two classes of human beings: one composed of those who labor, the other of those among whom the labor takes place; one thinking about earthly things, the other about heavenly things; one casting its heart into the depths, the other joining its heart to the angels; one hoping in the earthly things that this world possesses, the other trusting in the heavenly things promised by the God who does not lie [Note: [Col. 0603] In the editions, after “the God who does not lie,” these words were inserted: “We must not despair of good people if something earthly is administered through them; nor, again, should we immediately congratulate people who are known to be conducting heavenly affairs. For often those involved in secular affairs keep their hearts always above, while those who always preach heavenly matters drag their hearts down to earth.” These words are entirely absent from our manuscripts.].

But these classes of human beings are mixed together. At present we find a citizen of Jerusalem, a citizen of the kingdom of heaven, administering something on earth. For example, he wears purple [Note: [Col. 0603] All manuscripts read “he wears purples.”], he is a magistrate, an aedile, a proconsul, or an emperor; he administers an earthly state. But his heart is above, if he is a Christian, if he is faithful, if he is devout, if he despises the things in which he is placed and hopes for what he does not yet possess.

Esther, that holy woman, belonged to this class. When she was the king’s wife and the danger arose that she must plead for her fellow citizens, as she prayed before God, where she could not lie, she said in her prayer that her royal ornaments were, in her eyes, like a menstruous cloth (Esth. 14:16).

Let us not, then, despair of citizens of the kingdom of heaven when we see them conducting some Babylonian affairs or administering something earthly in an earthly state. Nor should we immediately congratulate all the people whom we see conducting heavenly affairs, because the sons of pestilence sometimes sit in Moses’ chair. Of them it is said: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they speak and do not act.”

The former raise their hearts to heaven amid earthly affairs; the latter drag their hearts down to earth amid heavenly words.

But the time of the winnowing fan will come, when the two will be most carefully distinguished: no grain will pass into the heap of straw to be burned, and no single stalk will pass into the mass to be stored in the granary (Matt. 3:12).

As long, then, as the two are now mingled, let us hear from this place our own voice—that is, the voice of the citizens of the kingdom of heaven. For this is what we ought to desire: to tolerate the wicked here rather than to be tolerated by the good. Let us join ourselves to this voice with ear, tongue, heart, and action.

If we do this, we ourselves are speaking here in the things we hear.

Let it therefore first be spoken concerning the evil body of the earthly kingdom.

### 7. [verse 3]

“Why does one who is powerful glory in wickedness?” Consider, my brothers, the glory of wickedness, the glory of evil people. What is this glory? “Why does one who is powerful glory in wickedness?” That is, one who is powerful in wickedness—why does he glory?

It is necessary to be powerful, but in goodness, not in wickedness. Is it something great to glory in wickedness? To build a house is the work of few; anyone ignorant can destroy it. To sow grain, cultivate a field, wait until it ripens, and rejoice in the fruit for which one has labored is the work of few; anyone can set the whole field on fire with a single spark.

To take up an infant, nourish it after birth, educate it, and bring it to youth is a great duty; anyone can kill it in a single moment. Thus the things done for destruction are done most easily.

“Let the one who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31); let the one who glories glory in goodness.

You glory because you are powerful in evil. What are you going to do, powerful one? What will you do, boasting so greatly? You are going to kill a human being. A scorpion can do that; a fever can do that; a poisonous mushroom can do that. Has all your power come down to this—that it is made equal to a poisonous mushroom?

This, then, is what the good citizens of Jerusalem do: they do not glory in wickedness but in goodness. First, they glory not in themselves but in the Lord; then, they diligently do those things that build up, and they do such things as are capable of enduring. Those things they do for destruction, however, they do for the discipline of those who may improve, not for the oppression of the innocent.

Why, then, should that earthly body, compared with this power, not hear these words: “Why does one who is powerful glory in wickedness?”

### 8. [verse 4]

“Your tongue has devised injustice all day long in iniquity.” “All day long in iniquity”—that is, for all time, without weariness, without interruption, without pause. Even when you are not doing evil, you are thinking it, so that when some evil is absent from your hands it is not absent from your heart.

Either you do evil, or, when you cannot do it, you speak evil—that is, you curse—or, when you cannot even do that, you desire and think evil. “All day long,” then, means without interruption.

We expect punishment for this man. Is the punishment too small for him? You threaten him; you threaten to send him where you want to send him—to evil. Leave him to himself. However fiercely you may rage, you will subject him to wild beasts [Note: [Col. 0605] The best manuscripts read: “You will subject him to wild beasts”; this is how we observed the wording in most codices in Psalm 36, sermon 3, section 13. Other manuscripts read: “They subjected others to wild beasts.”].

He is worse to himself than the wild beasts. A beast can tear his body, but he himself cannot leave his heart sound. He rages inwardly against himself, while you seek wounds for him outwardly?

Rather, pray to God for him, that he may be delivered from himself.

Nevertheless, in this psalm, my brothers, there is no prayer for the wicked or against the wicked, but a prophecy of what will happen to the wicked. Do not therefore think that the psalm says anything out of ill will; it is spoken in the spirit of prophecy.

### 9

What follows, then? All your power, all your wicked thinking throughout the day, and your meditation on evil continually upon your tongue—what has it done? What has it accomplished?

“You have practiced deceit like a sharpened razor.”

This is what the wicked do to the saints: they shave their hair.

What do I mean? If there are such citizens of Jerusalem as hear the voice of their Lord and King saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28), and who hear the voice that has just been read from the Gospel, “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of himself?” (Matt. 16:26), they despise all present goods and even life itself.

What, then, can Doeg’s razor do to a person who meditates on the kingdom of heaven in this world, who will be in the kingdom of heaven, who has God with him, and who will remain with God? What can that razor do? It will shave his hair; it will make him bald.

And this pertains to Christ, who was crucified at the place of the Skull. It also produces a son of Korah, whose name is interpreted as “Baldness.”

For these hairs signify the superfluous things of temporal affairs. They were not made superfluously by God on the human body, but for a certain adornment. Yet because they are cut off without sensation, those who cling to the Lord with their hearts regard earthly things as hair.

Sometimes, however, something good must also be done with one’s “hairs”: when you break bread for the hungry, bring the homeless poor into your house, and, if you see someone naked, clothe him (Isa. 58:7).

Finally, the martyrs themselves, imitating the Lord and pouring out their blood for the Church, hearing the words, “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3:16), have in a certain sense done good for us from their own hairs—that is, from those things that the razor can cut off or shave.

That something good can also be done from these hairs was signified by that sinful woman who, after she had wept over the Lord’s feet, wiped them with her hair, which she had wet with her tears (Luke 7:38).

What did she signify? That when you have shown mercy to someone, you ought also to help him if you can. When you show mercy, you are, as it were, pouring out tears; when you help, you wipe with your hair.

And if this is done for just anyone, how much more for the Lord’s feet? What are the Lord’s feet? The holy evangelists, of whom it is said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. 52:7; Rom. 10:15).

Let Doeg sharpen his tongue like a razor; let him sharpen his deceit as much as he can. He will take away superfluous temporal things—but will he take away what is eternally necessary?

### 10. [verse 5]

“You loved wickedness more than goodness.” Goodness lay before you; you should have loved it. You were not going to distribute something, nor were you going to bring back from a distant voyage something you might love. Goodness lay before you, and iniquity lay before you: compare them and choose.

But perhaps you have an eye with which to see wickedness and do not have an eye with which to see goodness. Woe to the iniquitous heart! Worse still, it turns away so that it will not see what it is able to see.

What has been said elsewhere about such people? “He refused to understand, that he might do good.” It does not say, “He was unable,” but, “He refused to understand, that he might do good”; he closed his eyes to the light present. And what follows? “He devised iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. 35:4–5), that is, in the inner secrecy of his heart.

Something of this sort is charged against this Doeg the Idumaean, this evil, earthly, dead body, which does not endure and is not heavenly.

“You loved wickedness more than goodness.” For if you want to know that the wicked person sees both and chooses the former, turning away from the latter, why does he cry out when he suffers something unjust? Why does he then magnify the injustice as much as he can and praise goodness, reproving the one who has acted toward him with wickedness rather than goodness?

Let this therefore be his rule for living: he will be judged by his own standard. If he does what is written, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), and, “Whatever good you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12), he has within himself the means to know that what he does not want done to himself he ought not to do to another (Tob. 4:16).

“You loved wickedness more than goodness.” You want, unjustly, disorderly, perversely, to raise water above oil; the water will sink, and the oil will rise above it. You want to place light beneath darkness; darkness will be driven away, and light will remain. You want to place earth above heaven; by its own weight the earth will fall into its proper place.

You, then, will be submerged because you love wickedness more than goodness. Wickedness will never overcome goodness.

“You loved wickedness more than goodness, and iniquity more than speaking righteousness.” Righteousness lies before you, and iniquity lies before you. You have one tongue; in which direction do you wish to turn it? Why, then, toward iniquity rather than righteousness?

You do not give your stomach food that is bitter, but you give your wicked tongue food that is iniquitous? As you choose what you will eat, so choose what you will say.

You therefore place iniquity above righteousness and wickedness above goodness. You do place them above, but what can be above them except goodness and righteousness? By setting yourself, as it were, above things that must necessarily go downward, you will not make them be above good things; rather, you will sink with them into evil.

### 11. [verse 6]

For this reason the psalm continues: “You loved all the words of submersion.”

Deliver yourself, then, if you can, from submersion. You flee shipwreck and embrace lead! If you do not wish to sink, seize the plank; let the wood carry you; let the cross lead you through.

But now, because you are Doeg the Idumaean, moving and earthly, what are you doing? “You loved all the words of submersion, a deceitful tongue.”

The words of submersion came after the deceitful tongue [Note: [Col. 0607] Erasmus and most manuscripts read: “He expressed the words of submersion, a deceitful tongue.”].

What is a deceitful tongue? A deceitful tongue is the servant of deception: it carries one thing in the heart and brings forth another from the mouth. But in these there is overthrow; in these there is submersion.

12. [verse 7.] Therefore God will destroy you forever—even if now you seem to flourish like grass in the field before the heat of the sun. For “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass: the grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6, 8). See what you should hold fast to: that which remains forever. For if you hold fast to grass and the flower of grass, since the grass will wither and the flower will fall, God will destroy you forever—even if not now, certainly in the end, when that winnowing-fan comes and the heap of chaff has been separated from the grain. Is not the grain for the barns and the chaff for the fire (Matthew 3 and 13:40)? Will not this whole Doeg stand on the left, when the Lord says, “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid. 25:41)?
