God will therefore destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tabernacle. For now this Doeg the Edomite is in the tabernacle; but “a servant does not remain in the house forever” (John 8:35). He performs something good, even if not by his own deeds, at least by the words of God: when he seeks his own interests in the Church (Philippians 2:21), at least he speaks the things that belong to Christ. But he will remove you from your tabernacle. “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2).

“And your root from the land of the living.” Therefore we ought to have our root in the land of the living. Let our root be there. The root is hidden: fruits can be seen, but the root cannot be seen. Our root is our love; our fruits are our works. Your works must proceed from love; then your root is in the land of the living.

This Doeg will be uprooted from the land of the living, and he will not be able to remain there at all, because he did not fix his root deeply there. He is like those seeds on the rock which, although they put out roots, nevertheless, because they have no moisture, with the rising of the sun immediately wither (ibid. 13:5). But what do those who fix their root more deeply hear from the Apostle? “I bend my knees for you before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that you may be rooted and founded in love.” And because the root is already there: “so that,” he says, “you may comprehend what is the height, the breadth, the length, and the depth; and also know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:14, 16–19).

Such fruits are worthy of so great a root—so simple, so budding, so deeply founded in its shoots [Note: [Col. 0607] Some manuscripts read this way. Others have: “so simple, so genuine, so deeply founded.” But Lov.: “so simple, so budding in its shoot, so high, founded, and deep.”]. But this man’s root is uprooted from the land of the living.

13. [verse 8.] “And the righteous will see, and will fear, and will laugh over him.” When will they fear? When will they laugh? [Col. 0608] Let us therefore understand and distinguish two times, highly useful for fearing and laughing. As long as we are in this world, it is not yet time to laugh, lest afterward we weep. We read what is reserved for this Doeg at the end; we read it, and because we understand and believe it, we see—but we fear. This, then, is what is meant: “The righteous will see, and will fear.”

As long as we see what will happen to the wicked in the end, why do we fear? Because the Apostle said, “Work out your own salvation in fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12); because it is said in the Psalm, “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Why “with fear”? Because “whoever thinks that he stands, let him take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). Why “with trembling”? Because elsewhere he says: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

Thus the righteous who exist now, who live by faith, see what will happen to this Doeg, yet they fear for themselves as well. For they know what they are today, but they do not know what they will be tomorrow. Now, therefore, “the righteous will see, and will fear.” But when will they laugh? When iniquity has passed away, when it has flown past—just as the uncertain time has already in large part flown past—when the darkness of this world has been driven away. At present we walk in that darkness only by the lamp of the Scriptures, and therefore we fear as though in the night.

For we walk by prophecy, of which the Apostle Peter says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). As long as we walk by the lamp, then, we must live with fear. But when our day comes—that is, the manifestation of Christ, of which the same Apostle says, “When Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4)—then the righteous will laugh at this Doeg.

For there will no longer be an opportunity for helping him—not as now, when you see a person living unjustly and wish to labor with him so as to correct him. For the unjust person can become just by conversion, just as the just person can become unjust by turning away. Therefore do not presume on yourself, nor despair of him; and, insofar as you can, if you are kind and do not love wickedness more than kindness, make an effort to correct a person walking and wandering along an evil road and bring him back to the good road.

But when the time of judgment comes, there will be no opportunity for correction, only for condemnation. There will be repentance there, but fruitless, because it will be late. Do you want it to be fruitful? Let it not be late: correct yourself today. You are guilty; he is the judge. Correct your guilt, and you will rejoice before the judge. For today he urges you not to let him judge you; and the one who will be your judge is himself your advocate today.

Then, brothers, the time for laughing remains. For the very mockery of the wicked that will belong to the righteous was indicated by that book of Wisdom. For in his own people, into whose souls Wisdom passes, it will do what it said it would do: “I called, and you did not listen; I spoke, and you did not heed my words; [Col. 0609] and I, too, will mock your destruction” (Proverbs 1:24–26). This will then be done by the righteous to this Doeg.

But now let us see and fear, lest we be what we say against him; and if we were such, let us cease to be such, so that, fearing now, we may laugh afterward.

14. [verse 9.] But what will those who laugh say then? “They will laugh over him, and will say: Behold the man who did not set God as his helper.” Look at an earthly body. “As much as you have, so much will you be.” This is the proverb of the greedy, the rapacious, those who oppress the innocent, those who seize what belongs to others, those who deny what has been entrusted to them. What kind of proverb is this? “As much as you have, so much will you be”—that is, the more money you have and the more you acquire, the more powerful you will be.

“Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.” Let no wicked poor man perhaps say, “I do not belong to this body.” He heard the Prophet say, “He trusted in the abundance of his riches.” If he is poor, he immediately looks at his own rags, then perhaps looks beside him at some richly dressed person among the people of God, and says in his heart, “He is speaking of that man, surely not of me?” Do not exempt yourself from this; do not separate yourself from it, unless you see and fear, so that afterward you may laugh.

For what does it benefit you if you lack means but burn with desire? When our Lord Jesus Christ said to that rich man who went away from him sorrowful, “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me,” and had foretold a great despair for the rich, saying that it was easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, did not the disciples immediately become sorrowful and say among themselves, “Who, then, can be saved?” (Matthew 19:21, 24–25)?

Therefore, when they said, “Who, then, can be saved?” were they looking only at the few rich? Did the immense multitude of the poor escape them? Could they not have said to themselves: “If it is difficult—indeed impossible—for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven, just as it is impossible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, let all the poor enter the kingdom of heaven, and let only the rich be excluded”? For how many rich are there? But there are innumerable thousands of poor.

For in the kingdom of heaven we will not be inspecting tunics; rather, each person’s garment will be reckoned as the splendor of righteousness. The poor, therefore, will be equal to the angels of God; clothed in the robes of immortality, they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (ibid. 13:43). Why should we be anxious or troubled about the few rich?

The Apostles did not understand it this way. When the Lord had said, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven,” they said among themselves, “Who, then, can be saved?” What did they consider? Not possessions, but desires. For they saw that even the poor, although they did not possess money, nevertheless possessed greed.

And so that you may know that it is not money in the rich person but greed that is condemned, pay attention to what I am saying. You see that rich man standing beside you; perhaps he has money but no greed. You have no money, but you have greed. The poor man, covered with sores and misery, licked by dogs, without help, without food, perhaps without even clothing, was carried by angels into [Col. 0610] Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22).

Come now, poor man: you rejoice today. Surely you should not therefore desire sores as well? Is not your health your wealth? Lazarus’s merit did not consist in poverty, but in devotion. For you see who was carried away, but you do not see where he was carried. Who was carried away by the angels? A poor, afflicted, ulcerated man. Where was he carried? Into Abraham’s bosom.

Read the Scriptures, and you will find Abraham rich (Genesis 13:2). So that you may know that riches are not blamed [Note: [Col. 0610] The editions read “punished.” The manuscripts, however, read “blamed.”]: Abraham had much gold, silver, livestock, and household; he was rich, and the poor Lazarus was carried into his bosom. A poor man in the bosom of a rich man—or rather, were not both rich in God and both poor in greed?

15. What, then, does Scripture blame in this Doeg? It did not say, “Behold the man who was rich,” but, “Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches.” He is condemned, not because he had riches, but because he trusted in them and did not trust in God. Therefore he is condemned, therefore he is punished, therefore he is moved from the tabernacle like that earthly man, like the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth (Psalm 1:4). Therefore his root is uprooted from the land of the living.

Are the rich like this whom the Apostle Paul speaks of: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, like Doeg, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, as he himself hoped in the abundance of his riches, but in the living God”—not as this man, who did not set God as his helper? Finally, what did he command them? “Let them be rich in good works; let them give readily; let them share” (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

And what if they give readily, if they share with one who has nothing? Will they enter through the eye of the needle? They certainly will, for the camel himself has already entered on their behalf. He entered first: no one would load him like a camel with the burden of suffering unless he himself laid himself down upon the earth. For he himself also said, “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God” (Matthew 19:26).

Let this Doeg, then, be condemned; let the righteous fear him now and laugh over him afterward. He is rightly condemned, for he did not set God as his helper, unlike you—you who perhaps possess money but place your confidence in God, not in money. “And he trusted in the abundance of his riches”: he became like those who, when they said, “Blessed is the people who possess these things”—that is, these earthly things—were immediately answered by the one who mocks this Doeg, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.”

The Psalm enumerates the things by which they called the people blessed. They spoke as sons of strangers, like this Doeg the Edomite, that is, the earthly man: “Their mouth spoke vanity, and their right hand was a right hand of iniquity. Their sons are like young plants, firmly established in their youth; their daughters are adorned and beautified like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing into another; their sheep are fertile, multiplying in their offspring; their oxen are fat; there is no breach in the fence, no going out, and no cry in their streets” (Psalm 143:11–15).

They seem to possess great happiness in earthly peace. But the earthly man is also moved, [Col. 0611] that is, like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Finally, what is reproved in them? Not that they possessed these things, for the good also possess them. But what? Pay attention to this: do not indiscriminately reproach the rich, and again do not presume on poverty and deprivation. If one must not presume on riches, how much more must one not presume on poverty, but on the living God?

In what, then, are these people censured? Because they called blessed the people who possess these things. Therefore they are sons of strangers; therefore their mouth spoke vanity, and their right hand was a right hand of iniquity. But what about you? “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.”

16. Therefore, once he has been condemned who trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity—for what is more vain than one who thinks that a coin is worth more than God?—once he has been condemned who called blessed the people who possess these things, what do you who say, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God,” think about yourself? What do you hope for yourself?

“But I”—now listen to that whole body—“am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” It is not one man who speaks, but that fruitful olive tree from which the proud branches were cut off and the humble wild olive was grafted in (Romans 11:17). “Like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, I have hoped in the mercy of God.”

What about him? “In the abundance of his riches.” Therefore his root will be torn from the land of the living. But because I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, whose root is nourished and not uprooted, “I have hoped in the mercy of God.”

But perhaps only for the present? For people sometimes go astray even in this respect. They do worship God and are no longer like this Doeg; but although they place their hope in God, they do so with regard to temporal things, saying to themselves, “I worship my God, who will make me rich on earth, who will give me children, who will give me a wife.” Such things are indeed given only by God, but God does not wish to be loved for their sake. For this reason he often gives them even to the wicked, so that the good may learn to seek something else from him.

How, then, do you say, “I have hoped in the mercy of God”? Is it perhaps in order to obtain temporal things? No: “forever and unto the age of the age.” By saying “forever,” he wished to repeat the idea by adding “unto the age of the age,” so as to confirm through the repetition how firmly he was grounded in love of the heavenly kingdom and in hope of eternal happiness.

17. [verse 11.] “I will confess to you forever, because you have done it.” What have you done? You condemned Doeg; you crowned David. “I will confess to you forever, because you have done it.” A great confession: “because you have done it.” What have you done except these very things spoken above—that, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, I should hope in the mercy of God forever and unto the age of the age?

You have done it; the impious person cannot justify himself. But who is the one who justifies? “The one who believes,” he says, “in him who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7), as though you possessed it from yourself?

“Far be it from me to boast in this way,” says the one who is set against Doeg, who tolerates Doeg on earth until he departs from the tabernacle and is uprooted from the land of the living. “I do not boast as though I had not received it, but I boast in God. And I will confess to you because you have done it”—that is, because you have done it, not on account of my merits, but on account of your mercy [Col. 0612].

For what have I done? If you recall, I was first a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man. But what have you done? “I received mercy, because I acted in ignorance” (1 Timothy 1:13). “I will confess to you forever, because you have done it.”

18. “And I will wait upon your name, because it is pleasant.” The world is bitter, but your name is pleasant. And if there are certain sweet things in the world, they are digested with bitterness. Your name is preferred not only for its greatness but also for its pleasantness [Note: [Col. 0612] The manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “not only to bitterness, but also to pleasantness.”].

“For the wicked have told me of their delights, but they are not like your law, O Lord” (Psalm 118:85). For if nothing were sweet to the martyrs, they would not endure such bitter tribulations with equanimity. Their bitterness was readily perceived by anyone; their sweetness could not easily be tasted by anyone.

The name of God, then, is pleasant to those who love God above all pleasures. “I will wait upon your name, because it is pleasant.” And to whom do you prove that it is pleasant? Give me a palate to which it is pleasant. Praise honey as much as you can; magnify its sweetness with whatever words you can. A person who does not know what honey is does not know what you are saying unless he has tasted it.

Therefore, inviting you more strongly to experience it, what does the Psalm say? “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). You do not wish to taste, and yet you say, “It is pleasant”? What is pleasant? If you have tasted, let it be found in your fruit, not merely in words, like something existing only in leaves, lest you deserve to wither under the Lord’s curse like that fig tree (Matthew 21:19).

“Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet.” “Taste and see”: then you will see, if you have tasted. But how do you prove it to someone who does not taste? In praising the pleasantness of the name of God, no matter how much you say, there are only words; taste is something else. The wicked hear words praising him, but they do not taste how pleasant he is—only the holy do.

Therefore this man, sensing the sweetness of God’s name and wishing to explain and display it, but finding no means—for there is no need to display it to the holy, since they themselves taste and know it, while the wicked cannot experience what they refuse to taste—what does he do with the pleasantness of God’s name? He immediately withdrew himself from the crowds of the wicked: “And I will wait,” he says, “upon your name, because it is pleasant in the presence of your holy ones.” Your name is pleasant, but not in the presence of the wicked. I know how sweet it is—but only for those who have tasted.

# AN EXPOSITION OF PSALM 52. SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0612] Delivered perhaps at the request of some bishop.]

1. We undertake to discuss this Psalm with you, insofar as the Lord grants us understanding. A brother commands us to be willing, and asks that we may be able. If, perhaps because of haste, I omit something, the one who deigns to give us what we may say will complete it in you.

Its title is: “For the end, for Maeleth, understanding, to David.” “For [Col. 0613] Maeleth,” as we find in Hebrew interpretations of names, seems to mean “for one who is in labor” or “for one who is suffering.” Who in this world labors and suffers, the faithful recognize, because they belong to that one. Christ labors here; Christ suffers here. The head is above, the members below.

For otherwise he would not have said, while laboring and suffering, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The one whom Saul persecuted was in labor; when Saul was converted, he caused him to labor. For afterward Saul himself was enlightened and, having been joined to the members he had persecuted, spoke, pregnant with the same love: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

This Psalm, then, is sung for the members of Christ, for his body, which is the Church (Colossians 1:24), for that one man himself—that is, for the very unity whose head is above. This man groans, labors, and suffers. Why, and among whom, unless because he has received and learned this from his Head, who says, “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold”? But if iniquity will abound and the love of many grow cold, who will remain to labor?

It continues: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:12–13). Why would persevering be a great matter unless one had to persevere amid troubles, temptations, disturbances, and scandals? For no one is commanded to endure good things.

But because this is said for this man, and because it is sung for this man, let us see what it means. Here human beings are rebuked among whom there is groaning and suffering, and at the end of the Psalm the consolation of the one who suffers and labors is brought forth and expressed.

Who, then, are those among whom we labor and groan, if we are in the body of Christ, if we live under that Head, if we are counted among his members? Who are they? Listen.

2. “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” Such is the kind of people among whom the body of Christ suffers and groans. If this is the kind of people they are, we do not labor for many of them. As far as seems to present itself to our thoughts, they are very few; and it is difficult for us to encounter a person who says in his heart, “There is no God” (Psalm 13:1). Yet they are few in such a way that, although they fear to say this among many, they say it in their heart because they do not dare to say it with their mouth.

What we are commanded to endure, then, does not seem very much; such people are scarcely found. It is a rare kind of person who says in his heart, “There is no God.” Or is what we thought existed among the few, the rare, and almost none found, when examined in another sense, found among many?

Let those who live wickedly come forward; let us examine the deeds of disgraceful, criminal, and sinful people, whose crowd is great—those who daily cherish their sins, who, through deeds turned into habit, have even lost their sense of shame. This multitude of people is so great that the body of Christ, placed among them, scarcely dares to rebuke what it is not compelled to commit. It considers it a great achievement to preserve the integrity of innocence, so as not to do what, through habit, it either does not dare to condemn or, if it has dared, the rebuke and outcry of those who live wickedly breaks out more readily than the free voice of those who live well.

Such people say in their heart, “There is no God.” I convict them. On what basis do I convict them? [Col. 0614] They think that their deeds please God. Therefore it does not say, “Some say”; rather, “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” They believe so strongly that God exists that they think God is pleased by what they do.

But if you understand wisely why the fool said in his heart, “There is no God”—if you notice, understand, and examine it—you will see that the person who thinks God is pleased by evil deeds does not think him to be God. For if he is God, he is just; if he is just, injustice displeases him, and iniquity displeases him. But when you think that he is pleased by iniquity, you deny God.

For if God is one whom iniquity displeases, but to you the one whom iniquity displeases does not seem to be God—and there is no God except one whom iniquity displeases—when you say in your heart, “God favors my iniquities,” you say nothing other than, “There is no God.”

3. [verse 2.] Let us also turn to that interpretation which presents itself concerning Christ our Lord, concerning our Head himself. When he appeared on earth in the form of a servant, those who crucified him said, “There is no God.” Since he was the Son of God, he was certainly God. But what did those who were corrupted and became abominable say? “There is no God; let us kill him—there is no God.”

You have their voice in the Book of Wisdom; but first observe them corrupted, so that they could say in their heart, “There is no God.” After the verse, “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God,’” as though causes were being sought by which the fool could say this, it added: “They are corrupted and have become abominable in their iniquities.”

Hear what these corrupted people said. They said among themselves, thinking wrongly: “Short and wearisome is our life.” From this bad faith follows what the Apostle also said: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15:32). Then their luxury is described more extensively: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; everywhere let us leave signs of our joy.” After this more extended description of luxury, what follows? “Let us kill the righteous poor man” (Wisdom 2:1–20). This, then, is what it means to say, “There is no God.”

At first they seemed to be speaking gently: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither.” What could be more delicate, what gentler? Would you have expected crosses and swords from such gentleness? Do not be surprised. The roots of thorns are also gentle; if someone touches them, he is not pricked. Yet from them grows what will prick you.

Thus they were corrupted and became abominable in their iniquities. “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40). There you have them saying openly, “There is no God.”

4. But how does the body of Christ groan among them? The Apostles and the disciples of Christ who were present at that time groaned among them. What do those people have to do with us? How do we labor among such people?

There are still those who say, “Christ is not God.” The remaining pagans say this; the Jews themselves say it, dispersed everywhere as a testimony to their own shame; and many heretics say it. The Arians also said, “There is no God.” The Eunomians said, “There is no God.”

Moreover, brothers, those about whom I spoke shortly before—[Col. 0615] those who live wickedly—say nothing other than, “There is no God.” For when we tell them that Christ will come as judge for judgment, as the unfailing Scriptures say, they instead lend their ear to the serpent who suggests, “You will not surely die” (Genesis 3:4), which he said in paradise against the truth of God, who established and said, “You will surely die” (ibid. 2:17). They do evil in such a way that they say to themselves, “Christ will come and grant pardon to everyone.”

Thus the one who said that he would separate the wicked on the left and the righteous on the right is a liar; that he would say to the righteous, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” and to the wicked, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41). How, then, will he grant pardon to everyone? How will he condemn no one? Therefore, they assert that he is lying. This is to say, “There is no God.”

See, then, whether perhaps you are the one who is lying. You are a human being; he is God. For “God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

But what should you do about these people, O body of Christ? For the present, separate yourself from them in heart and life. Do not imitate them, grow accustomed to them, consent to them, or approve them; rather, rebuke them. Why do you pay attention to those who say such things? “They are corrupted and have become abominable in their iniquities; there is no one who does good.”

5. [verse 3.] “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.”

What does this mean: “They are corrupted and have become abominable, all those who say, ‘There is no God’”? And what of it? Was it hidden from God that they had become such? Or would their inner thought have been disclosed to us unless it had been spoken by him?

If he knew and was aware of it, what does this mean: “He looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God”? The words seem to belong to one who is seeking, not to one who knows: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.”

And as though, by looking and gazing down from heaven, he had found what he sought, he pronounces his judgment: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one.”

Two somewhat difficult questions arise. If God looks down from heaven to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God, an unwise thought intrudes: that God does not know everything. This is one question. What is the other? If there is no one who does good, not even one, who is the person who labors among the wicked?

The first question is resolved in this way: Scripture often speaks so that what the creature does by God’s gift is said to be done by God. For example, when you show mercy to a poor person, because you do so by God’s gift, God is said to show mercy. When you recognize who you are, because you do so with him shining upon you—if you are one who says, “You will light my lamp, Lord my God; you will enlighten my darkness” (Psalm 17:29)—then what you have come to know because he grants and accomplishes it, he is said to know.

For what else is meant by, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy 13:3)? What does “to know” mean? It means that by his gift he makes you know.

So here also: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.” [Col. 0616] May he himself be present and grant us that what he caused our heart to conceive he may also bring it to birth.

The Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God.” By this Spirit, then, through whom we know what has been given to us by God, we distinguish ourselves from those to whom these things have not been given, and we recognize them from among ourselves.

For if we understand that we could not possess any good unless he granted and bestowed it, from whom all good things come, we also see that those to whom God has not given these things cannot possess anything of this kind. This discernment comes to us from the Spirit of God; and by the very one through whom we see this, God sees it, because God causes us to see.

Hence it is also said, “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10, 12)—not because the Spirit searches as one who does not know everything, but because the Spirit has been given to you and makes you search. What you do by his gift is said to be done by him, because without him you would not do it.

Thus God is said to do what you do. By the gift of the Spirit given to the children who have received the Spirit of God, they look upon the children of men to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. But because they do this by God’s gift and by God’s Spirit, God is said to do it—to look down and to see.

Why “from heaven,” if human beings do this? Because the Apostle says, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). From where do you do this, so that you may see? From where do you look, so that you may understand? Is it not with the heart? If you do this with the heart, Christian, see whether you have your heart above. If you have your heart above, you look down from heaven upon the earth. And because you do this by God’s gift, God looks down from heaven upon the children of men.

That question, then, has been resolved according to our limited capacity.

6. [verse 4.] What is it that we recognize when we look down? What is it that God recognizes when he looks down? What does he recognize because he gives it here? Listen to what it is: “Because all have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one.”

What, then, is the other question, except the one I mentioned shortly before? If there is no one who does good, not even one, no one remains who groans among the wicked.

“Wait,” says the Lord. “Do not pass judgment too quickly. I have given human beings the ability to do good—but from me, he says, not from themselves. From themselves they are evil. They are children of men when they do evil; when they do good, they are my children.”

For this is what God does: he makes children of God out of children of men, because from the Son of God he made the Son of Man. See what that participation is. Participation in divinity has been promised to us. The one who promised it is lying if he was not first made a participant in mortality.

For the Son of God became a participant in mortality so that mortal human beings might become participants in divinity. The one who promised to share his good with you first shared your evil with you. The one who promised you divinity showed you love.

Therefore remove what belongs to human beings as children of God, and what remains is that they are children of men: “There is no one who does good, not even one.”

### 7. [verse 5]

“Shall they not all know who work iniquity, who devour my people as they eat bread?” Shall they not know? Shall it not be shown to them? Speak; threaten; speak as one laboring and in travail. For your people are devoured as they eat bread. There is, then, a people of God who is devoured. Certainly, “there is none who does good, not even one.” The answer comes from that principle.

But this people who is devoured, this people who suffers the wicked, this people who groans and labors in travail among the wicked, has already been made from sons of men into sons of God; therefore it is devoured. “You have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope” (Psalm XIII, 6). Often, when the people of God is devoured, this very fact—that it is the people of God—is despised in it. “I will seize and strip him,” someone says; “if he is a Christian, what can he do to me?”

He speaks on behalf of the one who speaks for the woman in labor, and threatens those who devour, saying: “Shall they not all know who work iniquity?” For that man also who saw the thief and ran with him, who shared a portion with adulterers, who sat speaking evil against his brother and placed a stumbling-block against his mother’s son, said in his heart: “There is no God.” Therefore this is said to him: “You did these things, and I was silent; you suspected that I would be like you”—that is, “I would not be God if I were like you.” But what follows? “I will reprove you and set you before your own face” (Psalm XLIX, 18–21).

So here too: “I will reprove you and set you before your own face.” You do not wish to know now, so that you may be displeased with yourself; you will know later, so that you may mourn. For God will certainly reveal their iniquity to the wicked. If he will not reveal it, who will be those who say: “What has our pride profited us, and what has the boasting of our wealth brought us?” (Wisdom V, 8). Then, therefore, those who now refuse to know will know.

“Shall they not all know who work iniquity, who devour my people as they eat bread?” Why did he add, “as they eat bread”? It is as though they eat my people like bread. For the other things we eat may be this at one time and that at another—not always this vegetable, not always this meat, not always these fruits—but bread always. What, then, does it mean, “They devour my people as they eat bread”? It means that they devour them without interruption and without cessation: those who devour my people as they eat bread.

### 8. [verses 6, 7]

“They did not call upon God.” He consoles the one who is groaning, especially by this reminder [Note: Column 0617: Several manuscripts read “by comparison” (*ex comparatione*); some, “by dwelling” (*ex commoratione*)], lest, by imitating the wicked who often prosper, he be pleased to become evil. What has been promised to you is being kept for you: their hope is present, yours is future; theirs is fleeting, yours is certain; theirs is false, yours is true.

For “they did not call upon God.” Do such people not ask God every day? They do not ask God. Attend, if I can say this with God himself assisting me. God wishes to be worshiped freely; God wishes to be loved freely—that is, to be loved chastely. He does not wish to be loved because he gives something apart from himself, but because he gives himself.

Therefore, one who calls upon God in order to become rich does not call upon God; he calls upon that which he wants to come to him. For what is it to call upon, if not to call into oneself? To call into oneself is what “to call upon” means. When you say, “God, give me wealth,” you do not want God himself to come to you; you want wealth to come to you. What you want to come to you, that you call upon.

But if you were calling upon God, he himself would come to you; he himself would be your wealth. Now, however, you want to have a chest full and a conscience empty. God [Col. 0618] does not fill the chest, but the breast. What good do external riches do you if inward poverty weighs upon you? Therefore those who call upon God for worldly advantages, for earthly goods, for the present life and earthly happiness do not call upon God.

### 9

Therefore what follows concerning them? “There they feared with fear where there was no fear.” Is it really fear if someone loses his wealth? There is no fear there, and yet they fear there. But if someone loses wisdom, that truly is fear; and that is not feared.

Listen and recognize such people. Someone is entrusted with a little purse; he does not wish to return it, counts it as his own, does not think it can be reclaimed, and now intends to keep it as his own; he refuses to return it. Let him consider what he fears losing and what he refuses to possess. Money and good faith are at stake; whichever is more precious, there the more serious loss must be feared.

But you, in order to hold on to gold, lose your good faith. You are struck by the greater loss, yet you rejoiced in the gain: there you feared with fear where there was no fear. Return the money. I say too little when I say, “Return it”: lose the money, so that you do not lose your good faith. You feared to return the money and wished to lose your good faith!

The martyrs did not take what belonged to another; but even their own possessions they despised, so that they might not lose their faith. And it was not enough to lose their money when they were proscribed; they also lost their lives when they suffered martyrdom. They lost their lives so that they might find them for eternal life (Matthew X, 39). Therefore they feared where it was necessary to fear.

But those who said of Christ, “There is no God,” feared where there was no fear. For they said: “If we let him go on, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation” (John XI, 48). O folly and lack of understanding, saying in his heart, “There is no God”! You feared losing the earth and lost heaven. You feared that the Romans would come and take away your place and nation; would they have taken God away from you?

What, then, remains? What but that you confess that you wanted to hold on, and by holding on you lost badly? For you lost both the place and the nation by killing Christ. You preferred to kill Christ rather than lose the place, and you lost the place, the nation, and Christ.

They killed Christ through fear. But why did this happen? “Because God scattered the bones of those who pleased men.” Wishing to please men, they feared losing the place. But Christ himself, of whom they said, “There is no God,” preferred to displease men such as they were—sons of men, not sons of God. Therefore their bones were scattered; but no one broke his bones. They were confounded, because God despised them.

Truly, brothers, as far as they are concerned, great confusion came upon them. In the place where they crucified the Lord—whom they crucified for this reason, lest they lose both the place and the kingdom—the Jews are no longer there. God therefore despised them; yet, by despising them, he warned them to turn back. [Note: Column 0618: All our manuscripts read, “yet, by breaking them, he warned them”; most continue: “that they may turn, that they may recognize,” etc.]

Let them now recognize Christ and say, “He is God”—the one of whom they said, “There is no God.” “When God turns back the captivity of his people.” For he would not turn back the captivity of his people unless he had willed to be captive among their hands. But who will understand this?

“Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.” Truly Jacob and truly Israel—the younger, whom the elder served (Genesis XXV, 23)—will rejoice, because he will recognize him.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LIII. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verses 1, 2]

The title of this psalm bears the fruit of its length, if it is understood. Since the psalm itself is short, let us compensate by dwelling on the title for what we shall not spend on the psalm. For every verse that is sung depends upon it.

If, therefore, someone recognizes what has been fixed upon the front of the house, he will enter securely; and once he has entered, he will not go astray. For what is written beforehand upon the very doorpost indicates how one is not to go astray within.

Its title is as follows:

“Unto the end, in hymns, understanding for David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Behold, is not David hidden among us?’”

We know very well that Saul was the persecutor of the holy man David. We also remember having commended to Your Charity that Saul represented the figure of a temporal kingdom, belonging not to life but to death [Note: Above, in the Exposition of Psalm LI, nos. 1 and 2.]. Likewise, you both know and ought to recall—those of you who already know—that David himself represented the figure of Christ, or of the body of Christ.

What, then, were the Ziphites? Ziph was a certain village, whose inhabitants were called Ziphites. David had hidden in their territory when Saul wanted to find and kill him. When these Ziphites learned of this, they betrayed him to the persecuting king, saying: “Behold, is not David hidden among us?” (1 Samuel XXIII, 14, 15, 19).

Their betrayal did them no good, nor did it harm David at all. Their malicious intention was indeed revealed; but Saul, even after their betrayal, was unable to capture David. Rather, in a certain cave of that very region, when Saul had been delivered into David’s hands to be killed, David spared him there and did not do what he had the power to do (ibid. XXIV, 4–8). Saul, however, sought to do what he did not have the power to do.

Let the Ziphites, then, see who they were. Let us see whom the psalm offers us to understand by occasion of them.

### 2

If, then, we ask what “Ziphites” means, we find: “flowering ones.” Some enemies of holy David were therefore flowering ones—flowering while he was hidden.

Let us find them in the human race, if we wish to understand the psalm. Let us first find here David hidden, and then we shall find his adversaries flowering.

Attend to David hidden: “For you have died,” the Apostle says to the members of Christ, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” When, then, will these hidden ones flower? “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III, 3, 4).

When these will flower, then those Ziphites will wither. Consider with what flower their glory may be compared: “All flesh is grass, and all the honor of flesh is like the flower of grass.” What is the end? “The grass withered, and the flower fell.” Where, then, will David be? See what follows: “But the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah XL, 6, 8).

There are therefore two classes of people. You ought both to distinguish them and to choose one of them. For what does it profit you to know, if you are too sluggish to choose? And indeed, the power of choosing is now available to you. The time will come when the power to choose will be taken from you, when God will no longer defer his judgment.

For who are these flowering Ziphites except that body represented by Doeg the Edomite, about whom we spoke to Your Charity a few days ago [Note: See above, Exposition of Psalm LI, no. 13]? Of him it was said: “Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.”

These are the flowering sons of the age, of whom you have just heard from the Gospel that “in their generation they are more prudent” [Note: Good-quality manuscripts read, “more cunning in their own affairs.” Others read, “more prudent in their own kind”] “than the sons of light.” For they appear to look ahead toward the future, although they do not know whether they will reach it.

You heard what that steward did for his master: he made a benefit for himself out of his master’s property and gave to his master’s debtors, so that when he was removed from the stewardship they might receive him. Although he had committed fraud against his master, his master nevertheless praised his prudence, not considering his own loss but the man’s ingenuity.

How much more ought we, admonished by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, to make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “for himself” (*se*)] (Luke XVI, 8, 9)! For *mammon* is interpreted as “riches.” Our riches, however, are where our eternal home is, in the heavens.

Accordingly, those who cannot flower except temporally call temporal money “riches.” They do not wish to make eternal friends for themselves from it, because they do not know true riches. Therefore iniquity alone [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “these things alone”] considers these things riches, flowering for a time like grass.

These are the Ziphites, the enemies of David, flowering in the world.

### 3

The weak sons of light sometimes look upon these people as well, and their feet totter when they see the wicked flourishing in happiness. They say to themselves: “What does my innocence profit me? What does it benefit me that I serve God, that I keep his commandments, that I oppress no one, seize nothing from anyone, harm no one, and do whatever good I can? Behold, I do all these things, and they flourish while I labor.”

What then? Would you also wish to be a Ziphite? They flourish in the world, they will wither in the judgment, and after their withering they will be cast into eternal fire. Would you wish this for yourself?

You do not know what the one who came to you promised you [Note: So Erasmus and most manuscripts. Some, however, read, “came from God.” Lovaniensis: “will come to you”], nor what he displayed in himself. If the flower of the Ziphites were desirable, would your Lord not have flourished in this world as well? Or was he unable to flourish here?

But here he preferred to remain hidden among the Ziphites, and he said to Pontius Pilate, who questioned him as one who was himself a flower of the Ziphites and suspected him of kingship: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII, 36).

Here, therefore, he was hidden; and all good people are hidden here, because their good is within, hidden, in the heart—where their faith, love, hope, and treasure are. Do these goods appear in the world? These goods are hidden, and the reward of these goods is hidden.

But how is worldly dignity white? It shines for a time; will it shine forever? It is winter grass, green until summer. Let what we find in another psalm not come to pass in the soul.

For someone there confesses that he almost fell, tottering, and that his steps nearly slipped as he walked in the way of God, while he looked upon a certain flower and the prosperity of the wicked. Afterward, when he understood what God reserved for the wicked at the end and what the one who cannot deceive promised to the laboring righteous, he gave thanks for this understanding and said:

“How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart!”

Why do you say this? “But my feet,” he says, “were almost moved.” From what cause? “Because I was jealous of the sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.”

His steps, however, were strengthened after he understood the end. For what he says shortly afterward in the same psalm—“This is labor before me”—means: a great question arose in my heart, why people do evil and flourish in the world, while many do good and labor on this earth.

Since this question was great before my eyes and difficult to investigate, he says: “It is labor before me, until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand at the end” (Psalm LXXII, 1–17).

What is this “end”? What but that which we already know was foretold in the Gospel? “When the Son of Man comes, all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left” (Matthew XXV, 31–33).

Behold, then, those Ziphites will be separated. Flame follows the separation. Where is their flower, when they will already be standing at the left? Will they not then groan? Will they not then be tormented by late repentance and say: “What has our pride profited us, and what has the boasting of our riches brought us? All those things passed like a shadow” (Wisdom V, 8, 9)?

O Ziphites standing at the left, too late you regret having flourished in the shadow! Why did you not recognize David, whom you betrayed while he was hidden among you? For if you had been corrected then, this pain would not be fruitless.

There is fruitful pain, and there is fruitless pain. Pain is fruitful now, when you accuse yourself, when you reproach your evil habits in yourself, when you pursue the habits you have reproved, exclude those you have pursued, and, after excluding them, are changed—putting off the old person and putting on the new, choosing the reproach of Christ rather than the flower of the Ziphites.

Moreover, if, while possessing your good in secret and hidden among the Ziphites, and also possessing in secret the promise of your reward, some worldly eminence should come to you, do not become proud [Col. 0622]. For if you are lifted up by it, you will fall into the flower of the Ziphites.

Thus, in that former people of the Jews, a certain holy woman, Esther, when she was the wife of a foreign king and danger came upon her fellow citizens so that she might entreat the king for them, began to pray. In that very prayer she confessed that all her royal insignia seemed to her like a menstruous cloth (Esther XIV, 16).

If women can do this, cannot men? And if a Jewish woman could do it, will the Christian Church not be able to?

This, then, I say to Your Charity: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm LXI, 11). Let them abound, even if worldly prosperity follows you; do not trust the sea, even when it smiles. If riches increase, if they abound, trample upon them and hang upon your God. For when you have them beneath you and hang upon him, when they are taken away, you will not fall.

Otherwise, through an evil and un-Christian thought, what is said in another psalm concerning the flower of those Ziphites may come to pass in you: “Your thoughts,” it says, “have become exceedingly deep.” It says: “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep; the imprudent man will not know, and the fool will not understand these things.”

What will he not understand? “When sinners spring up like grass and all who work iniquity flourish” [Note: So all manuscripts. The printed editions read, “when they have been prolonged”] “in order to perish forever and ever” (Psalm XCI, 6–8).

The flower of evil pleased them. They said to themselves: “Behold, the wicked flourish; I suppose God loves the wicked.” Delighted by the temporal flower of the wicked, they turned toward iniquity, so that they might perish—not for a time, as those people flourish, but forever and ever.

Why did this happen? Because “the imprudent man will not know, and the fool will not understand these things,” since he does not enter the sanctuary of God to understand at the end.

And because this understanding is somewhat difficult, this psalm began from that point: David was to be hidden among the Ziphites and not delighted by the flower of the Ziphites, but was rather to choose humility among them, so that he might possess a hidden brightness with God.

What, then, is attributed to him in this title? “Unto the end, in hymns”—that is, in praises. With what praises? “The Lord has given, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

Did he seem to have withered, having lost all his substance? Far from it. The leaves had fallen, but the root was alive. Therefore: “Unto the end, in hymns.”

What does “understanding for David” mean? Understanding in opposition to this: “The imprudent man will not know, and the fool will not understand these things.”

“Understanding for David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Behold, is not David hidden among us?’” Let him be hidden among you, provided only that he does not flower as you do.

Hear, then, his voice.

### 4. [verse 3]

“O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength.”

Let the Church hidden among the Ziphites say this. Let the Christian body, possessing secretly the good of its conduct and hoping for the reward of its merits from what is hidden, say this:

“O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength.”

You came, O Christ; you appeared in humility; you were despised, scourged, crucified, and killed. But on the third day you rose again; on the fortieth day you ascended into heaven [Col. 0623]. You sit at the right hand of the Father, and no one sees you.

From there you sent your Spirit, whom the worthy received. Filled with your love, they proclaimed throughout the world and among the nations the praise of your very humility. I see your name exalted among the human race, yet you were still preached to us as weak.

For that teacher of the Gentiles said that he knew nothing among us except “Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians II, 2), so that we might choose his reproach rather than the glory of the flourishing Ziphites.

Yet what does he say about him? “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians XIII, 4). He came, therefore, to die through weakness; he will come to judge in the power of God. But through the weakness of the cross his name has been glorified.

Whoever has not believed in the name glorified through weakness will tremble before the judge when he comes in power. Therefore, lest that one who was formerly weak send us to the left by his winnowing-fan when he comes in strength, may he save us by his name and judge us by his power.

For who would be so rash as to say to God, “Judge me”? Is it not ordinarily said to people as a curse, “May God judge you”? It is indeed a curse if he judges you in his power but has not saved you in his name. But when he has first saved you in his name, he will judge you beneficially in his power.

Be confident: that judgment will not be punishment for you, but separation. For in a certain psalm it is said: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy people” (Psalm XLII, 1).

What does “Judge me” mean? Distinguish me from the Ziphites among whom I am hidden. I have endured their flower; let my flower now come. Their flower was temporal and fell as the grass withered. But what will my flower be?

“Those planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm XCI, 14).

A flower therefore remains for us as well, but one that does not fall, like the leaf of that tree planted beside the waters, of which it is said: “Its leaf shall not fall” (Psalm I, 3).

“O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength.”

### 5. [verse 4]

“O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.”

May the words of my mouth reach your ears, because I do not desire from you the flower of the Ziphites. “Give ear to the words of my mouth.” You give ear; for although my prayer sounds to the Ziphites, they do not hear because they do not understand. They rejoice in temporal things and do not know how to desire eternal goods.

May my prayer reach you, shaken loose and hurled forth from the desire for your eternal benefits. I send it to your ears; help it to reach you, lest it fail midway through its journey and, as though collapsing, fall.

But even if the goods I ask for do not come to me now, I am nevertheless secure, because they will come later. For it is said that someone asked God concerning his sins and was not heard for his own good.

Worldly desires had stirred him to pray. Placed amid temporal tribulations, he had wished the temporal tribulations to pass and the flower of grass to return, and he said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” It is Christ’s voice, but spoken for his members.

“The words,” he says, “of my offenses: I cried to you by day, and you did not hear; and by night, and it was not unto folly for me” (Psalm XXI, 2, 3). That is: I cried by night, and you did not hear; yet your not hearing me did not result in folly for me, but rather was for wisdom, so that I might understand what I ought to ask of you.

For I was asking for things that I might perhaps receive to my harm. You ask for riches, O man! How many have been ruined by their riches! How do you know whether riches will benefit you? Did not many poor people lie hidden more safely? Once they became rich, as soon as they began to shine, they became prey to stronger men. How much better they would have remained hidden; how much better they would have remained unknown—those who began to be sought not for what they were, but for what they possessed!

Therefore, brothers, concerning these temporal things, we admonish and exhort you in the Lord not to ask for anything as though it were fixed, but to ask for what God knows is useful for you. For you do not know at all what is useful for you. Sometimes what you think benefits you harms you; and what you think harms you benefits you.

You are sick; do not dictate to the physician what medicines he should apply to you. For if the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, says, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans VIII, 26), how much more do we not know?

Yet when he himself seemed to be praying wisely—that the thorn of the flesh, the angel of Satan who struck him, might be taken away from him, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations—what did he hear from the Lord? Was what he wanted done? No [Note: “No” is absent from the manuscripts]; instead, what was useful was done.

What, then, did he hear from the Lord? “Three times,” he says, “I asked the Lord that he might take it away from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians XII, 7–9).

“I have applied the medicine to the wound. I know when I applied it; I know when it should be removed.” Let the sick person not leave the physician’s hands; let him not give the physician advice.

So are all these temporal things. There are tribulations: if you worship God rightly, know that he knows what is useful for each person. There are prosperities: be even more careful lest they corrupt your soul, so that it withdraws from the one who gave them.

Therefore, understanding this, he says: “O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.”

### 6. [verse 5]

“For strangers have risen up against me.”

Who are the strangers? Was David himself not a Jew from the tribe of Judah? The place Ziph belonged to the tribe of Judah; it was Jewish territory. How, then, were they strangers? Not in city, tribe, or kinship, but in their flower.

Do you wish to know who these strangers are? In another psalm they are called “sons of strangers,” whose mouth spoke vanity and whose right hand was a right hand of iniquity. And it lists the flower of the Ziphites:

“Whose sons are like young plants, firmly established in their youth; their daughters are adorned and embellished like the likeness of a temple; their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing into another; their sheep are fruitful, multiplying in their offspring; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage out, and no outcry in their streets.”

But look at the Ziphites; look at them flourishing for a time. They called the people blessed who possess these things.

Rightly are they sons of strangers. But you, hidden among the Ziphites—what do you say? “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Psalm CXLIII, 7–15).

From this disposition the prayer is sent to the Lord’s ears, when it says: “Give ear to the words of my mouth, for strangers have risen up against me.”

### 7

“And the powerful have sought my life.”

For in a new way, my brothers, all who place their hope in this age wish to destroy the race of the saints and of those who abstain from hope in this age. Certainly they are closely joined; certainly they live together. These two classes are vehemently opposed to each other: one consists of those who place their hope only in worldly things and temporal happiness; the other of those who firmly place their hope in the Lord their God.

And when these Ziphites are in agreement, do not put too much trust in their agreement; temptations are lacking. When some temptation comes, so that someone is tested concerning the flower of the world, I do not say that he will offend the bishop, but he will not even wish to approach the Church, lest some grass fall [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts read, “offend the bishop.”].

Why have I said this, brothers? Because now you all gladly listen in the name of Christ, and as you understand, so you cry out at the word; you would certainly not cry out unless you understood. This understanding of yours ought to be fruitful.

But whether it is fruitful, temptation asks. Take care lest, when you are suddenly called “ours,” you be found through temptation to be strangers, and it be said: “Strangers have risen up against me, and the powerful have sought my life.” Take care lest what follows be said: “They have not set God before their eyes.”

For when will someone set God before his eyes when he has nothing before his eyes but the world? How money may be piled upon money, how flocks may be increased, how storehouses may be filled, how it may be said to the soul, “You have many good things; enjoy yourself, feast, and satisfy yourself”—these are before his eyes.

Does he set before his eyes the one who says to the man boasting in this way and shining with the flower of the Ziphites: “Fool”—that is, one who does not understand, an imprudent man—“this night your soul will be required of you; whose will all these things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII, 20).

“They have not set God before their eyes.”

### 8. [verse 6]

“For behold, God helps me.”

And they themselves do not know among whom I am hidden. But if they too set God before their eyes, they would discover how God helps me.

For all the saints are helped by God, but inwardly, where no one sees. For just as the conscience of the wicked is a great punishment, so the conscience of the godly is a great joy.

“For our glory,” the Apostle says, “is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians I, 12). This man glories inwardly in it, not outwardly in the flower of the Ziphites, when he says: “For behold, God helps me.”

Indeed, although the things he promises are far in the future, his help is sweet and present to me today. Today I find in the joy of my heart that some say without cause: “Who will show us good things?”

“For the light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Psalm IV, 6, 7)—not in my vineyard, not in my flock, not in my wine jar, not at my table, but in my heart.

“For behold, God helps me.” How does he help you? “And the Lord is the sustainer of my soul.”

### 9. [verse 7]

“Turn the evils upon my enemies.”

As they are green, as they flourish, they are being kept for the fire. “In your power destroy them.” Suppose that they flourish now; suppose that they spring up like grass. Do not be an imprudent and foolish man, so as to perish forever and ever by attending to these things (Psalm XCI, 7, 8).

“For turn the evils upon my enemies.” For if you are in the body of that David, he will destroy them in his power. They flourish in worldly prosperity; they perish in the power of God. They do not perish as they flourish: they flourish for a time and perish forever; they flourish through false goods and perish amid true torments.

“In your power destroy them”—those whom you tolerated in your weakness.

### 10. [verse 8]

“I will sacrifice to you willingly.”

Who can even understand this good of the heart when someone else speaks of it, unless he has tasted it in himself? What does “I will sacrifice to you willingly” mean?

I shall nevertheless speak of it. Let whoever can grasp it grasp it as he can; let whoever cannot believe it and pray that he may be able to. Should we pass over this verse, then, without commending it to you? I tell Your Charity: love for it strongly invites me to say something about it, and I thank God that you listen attentively.

If I saw you growing weary of listening, I would unwillingly be silent about this verse. Yet in my heart, insofar as the Lord might grant it, I would not be silent.

Let what has been conceived in the heart therefore come upon the tongue; let what is held in the mind be brought forth in the voice. Let us say, as we can, what “I will sacrifice to you willingly” means.

What sacrifice should I understand here, brothers? Or what could I worthily offer to the Lord for his mercy? Shall I seek victims from a flock of sheep, choose a ram, look for some bull among the herds, or certainly bring incense from the land of the Sabaeans? What shall I do? What shall I offer, except what he says: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Psalm XLIX, 23)?

Why, then, “willingly”? Because I love freely what I praise. I praise God, and in that very praise I rejoice. I rejoice in the praise of the one whom, when praised, I do not blush to praise.

For it is not like the way some charioteer, hunter, or any actor is praised by lovers of theatrical frivolities, while others are invited by his praisers to become praisers as well and are urged to shout together. When all have shouted, they often all blush when he has been defeated.

Our God is not like that. Let him be praised by the will; let him be loved by charity. Let what is loved and praised be gratuitous.

What does “gratuitous” mean? It means loving him for himself, not for something else. For if you praise God so that he may give you something else, you no longer love God freely.

You would blush if your wife loved you for your riches; and perhaps, if poverty came upon you, she would think about adultery. Since, then, you wish to be loved freely by your wife, will you love God for something else?

What reward will you receive from God, you miser? He does not reserve earth for you, but himself—the one who made heaven and earth.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly.” Do not do so out of necessity. For if you praise God for something else, you praise him out of necessity. If what you love were present to you, you would not praise God.

Consider what I am saying. You praise God, for example, so that he may give you abundant money. If you had abundant money from elsewhere, not from God, would you praise God? If, then, you praise God for the sake of money, you do not sacrifice to God willingly, but out of necessity, because you love something else besides him.

Therefore it is said: “I will sacrifice to you willingly.” Despise everything; attend to him alone.

And the things he has given are good because of the giver. He truly gives these temporal things—some for their good, others for their harm, according to the height and depth of his judgments.

In the abyss of these judgments the Apostle cried out in fear: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways! For who has investigated his ways, or who has comprehended his plans?” (Romans XI, 33, 34).

He knows when to give, to whom to give, when to take away, and from whom to take away. Ask in this present time for what will benefit you in the future; ask for what will help you eternally.

But love him freely, because you will not find anything better for him to give than himself. Or, if you find something better, ask for it.

“I will sacrifice to you willingly.” Why willingly? Because freely. What does “freely” mean? “And I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good”—for no other reason than that it is good.

Does he say: “I will confess your name, O Lord, because you give me fertile estates, because you give me gold and silver, because you give me broad riches, abundant money, and the highest rank”? No.

But what does he say? “Because it is good.” I find nothing better than your name; therefore I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good.

### [verse 9]

Because you have rescued me from every tribulation. Therefore I understood that your name is good; for if I had been able to recognize this before the tribulations, perhaps they would not have been necessary for me. But tribulation was applied for admonition, and admonition was given for your praise. For I would not have understood where I was unless I had been admonished by my weakness. From all my tribulations, therefore, you have rescued me.

And my eye looked upon my enemies: my eye looked upon those Ziphites. For I passed beyond their bloom by the height of my heart, came to you, and from there looked down upon them; and I saw that “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). As it is likewise said in another passage: “I saw the impious man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was no more.” Why was he no more? Because you passed by? What does “because you passed by” mean? Because it was not without reason that you heard, “Lift up your heart,” [Note: [Col. 0627] So the manuscripts. But the editions read: “you have lifted up your heart.”] because you did not remain on earth, where you would decay; because you raised your soul to God, transcended the cedars of Lebanon, and looked down from that height. “And behold, he was no more; you sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:35–36).

Now labor is no longer before you, because you entered the sanctuary of God and understood the final things (Ps. 72:16–17). Thus here too he concludes: “And my eye looked upon my enemies.” Do this, then, brothers, with your souls: raise up your hearts, polish the vision of your mind, learn to love God freely, learn to despise the present age, learn voluntarily to sacrifice an offering of praise, so that, transcending the flower of grass, you may look down upon your enemies.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 54. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

[Col. 0628]

### 1. [verse 1]

The title of this psalm is: “For the end, among hymns, understanding, to David.” We shall briefly recall what “the end” is, because you know it. “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Therefore let the intention be directed toward the end, directed toward Christ. Why is he called “the end”? Because whatever we do, we refer to him; and when we have reached him, we shall have nothing further to seek. For “end” is said of that which brings something to completion, and “end” is said of that which perfects it.

We understand one thing when we hear, “The food that was being eaten has been finished,” and another when we hear, “The garment that was being woven has been finished.” In both cases we hear, “It is finished”; but the food is finished so that it may no longer exist, whereas the garment is finished so that it may be perfected. Our end, therefore, ought to be our perfection; and our perfection is Christ. In him we are perfected, because we are members of that head. He is called the end of the Law because no one perfects the Law without him.

Therefore, when you hear in the Psalms, “For the end”—for many psalms are thus inscribed—let your thought be directed not toward termination, but toward completion.

### 2

“Among hymns”: that is, among praises. Whether we are afflicted and distressed, or whether we rejoice and exult, he is to be praised—he who teaches us in tribulations and consoles us in joy. The praise of God ought not to depart from the heart and mouth of a Christian: not so that he praises in prosperity and curses in adversity, but as that psalm prescribes: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:1).

Are you joyful? Recognize the Father as one who is caressing you. Are you afflicted? Recognize the Father as one who is correcting you. Whether he caresses or corrects, he is teaching the one for whom he prepares an inheritance.

### 3

What, then, does “understanding, to David” mean? There was indeed David, as we know, the holy prophet, king of Israel, son of Jesse (1 Sam. 16:18). But because from his offspring came the Lord Jesus Christ, for our salvation according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3), that man is often represented by this name, and David is set forth figuratively for Christ because of the origin of Christ’s flesh.

For in one respect he is David’s son, and in another respect he is David’s Lord: David’s son according to the flesh, David’s Lord according to divinity. For if all things were made through him (John 1:3), then David himself was made through him, from whose offspring he came to human beings.

Accordingly, when the Lord asked the Jews whose son they said Christ was, they answered, “David.” He saw that they had remained in the flesh and lost sight of his divinity, and he corrects them by the question he posed: “How then does David himself, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet’? If, then, he calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22:42–45).

He posed the question; he did not deny that he was the son. You have heard “Lord”; say how he is son. You have heard “son”; say how he is Lord. The catholic faith resolves this question.

How is he Lord? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” How is he son? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Since, therefore, David is Christ in figure, and Christ—as we have often reminded Your Charity—is both head and body, we must neither say that we are alien from Christ, whose members we are, nor reckon ourselves as though we were someone else, because “the two shall be one flesh.” “This mystery is great,” says the Apostle; “but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

Since, then, the whole Christ is head and body, when we hear “understanding, to David,” let us understand that we too are included in David. Let the members of Christ understand, and let Christ understand in his members; let the members of Christ understand in Christ, because head and members are one Christ.

The head was in heaven, and it said, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). We are with him in heaven through hope, and he is with us on earth through love.

Therefore: “understanding, to David.” Let us be admonished when we hear this, and let the Church understand. For it greatly concerns us to understand in what evil we now are, and from what evil we desire to be delivered, remembering the Lord’s Prayer, where at the end we say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

Amid the many tribulations of this age, then, this psalm laments something through understanding. The one who lacks understanding does not weep along with it.

Moreover, dearest brothers, we must remember that we were made in the image of God, and that this image is found nowhere except in understanding. For in many things we are surpassed by beasts [Note: [Col. 0629] So the manuscripts. But the editions read: “we are not distinguished from beasts.”]; but when a human being recognizes that he was made in the image of God, he recognizes in himself something greater than what has been given to animals.

When he considers all the things that a human being possesses, he finds that he is distinguished properly from the animal by this: that he possesses understanding. Therefore the Creator himself rebukes some who despise in themselves what they received as distinctive and pre-eminent from the Creator, saying: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 32:9).

And elsewhere he says: “Man, when he was in honor”—in what honor, unless because he was made in the image of God?—“did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:21).

Let us therefore recognize our honor, and let us understand. If we understand, we see that this is not a region for rejoicing, but for groaning; not yet for exulting, but still for weeping. Yet even if a certain exultation dwells in our hearts, it is not yet in reality but in hope. We rejoice because of the promise, since we know that the one who promises does not deceive us.

But as for the present time, in what evil and in what distress we are, hear now; and if you are following this way, recognize in yourselves what you hear. For whoever does not yet follow the way of piety is astonished that such things are lamented by the members of David; he does not see them in himself. As long as he does not see them in himself, he is not yet there: he does not feel what the body feels, because he is outside the body. Let him be incorporated, and he will feel it.

Let him therefore speak, and let us hear; let us hear, and let us speak:

### 4. [verses 2–5]

“Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my petition; attend to me and hear me.”

These are the words of one who is struggling, anxious, and placed in tribulation. He prays, suffering much and desiring to be delivered from evil. It remains for us to hear what evil he is in; and when he begins to speak, let us recognize that we are there, so that, sharing in the tribulation, we may join in the prayer.

“I was sorrowful in my exercise, and I was troubled.”

Where was he sorrowful? Where was he troubled? “In my exercise,” he says. He is about to mention the evil people whom he suffers [Note: [Col. 0630] So Erasmus and the better manuscripts. But Louvain reads: “he mentioned.”], and he called the suffering inflicted by evil people his exercise.
