Do not think that evil people exist in this world without purpose, and that God does nothing good through them. Every evil person either lives in order to be corrected, or lives so that the good may be exercised through him.

Would that those who now exercise us might be converted and be exercised with us. Nevertheless, as long as they remain such as to exercise us, let us not hate them, because, although one of them is evil, we do not know whether he will persevere in that state to the end. Often, when you think you hate an enemy, you have hated a brother without knowing it.

The devil and his angels have been revealed to us in the holy Scriptures as destined for eternal fire. Only their correction is to be regarded as hopeless. Against them we have an unseen struggle, for which the Apostle arms us, saying: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood”—that is, not against the human beings whom you see—“but against principalities and powers and the rulers of this world, of these darknesses” (Eph. 6:12).

Lest, when he said “of the world,” you should understand that demons are the rulers of heaven and earth, he said, “of this world, of these darknesses.” He said “of the world” meaning the lovers of the world; he said “of the world” meaning the impious and unjust; he said “of the world” of which the Gospel says, “The world did not know him” (John 1:10).

For if the world did not know the light—because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it”—and those very darknesses that did not comprehend the present light are called “the world,” then those rulers are rulers of these darknesses.

Concerning those rulers, therefore, we have a definite judgment of Scripture: no return of any of them is to be hoped for at all. But concerning the darknesses over which they rule, we are not certain; perhaps those who were darkness may become light.

For to those who had already become faithful the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8): darkness in yourselves, light in the Lord.

Therefore, brothers, all evil people, while they are evil, exercise the good. Listen briefly and understand. If you are good, you will have no enemy except an evil person. But this rule of goodness has been established for you: that you imitate the goodness of your Father, who “makes his sun rise over the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45).

For you have an enemy, and God does not? You have as an enemy one who was created with you; he has as an enemy one whom he created. We often read in the Scriptures of the evil and unjust as God’s enemies. Yet he spares them—he who has nothing for which they can accuse him, while every enemy is ungrateful to him; for that person has from him whatever good he has.

From him he has mercy, whatever there is in him that is even the cause of his tribulation. For this purpose he is afflicted: so that he may not become proud; so that in humility he may recognize the Most High.

What, then, have you done for your enemy, whom you endure beyond measure? If God has as an enemy one to whom he has given so much, and makes his sun rise over good and evil and sends rain upon just and unjust, then you, who cannot make the sun rise or send rain upon the earth, cannot preserve one thing for your enemy—that there may be for you “peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Since, then, this rule of love is imposed upon you, that you imitate the Father by loving your enemy—“Love your enemies,” he says (Luke 6:27, 35)—how would you be exercised by this commandment if you suffered no enemy?

You see, then, that something benefits you. The fact that God spares evil people should benefit you by teaching you mercy, because perhaps you too, if you are good, became good from being evil; and if God did not spare evil people, neither would you appear as one who gives thanks.

Let him therefore spare others who spared you. For when you have passed beyond this, the way of piety is not to be closed.

### 5

Why, then, does this man pray, placed among evil people whose enmity exercised him? What does he say? “I was sorrowful in my exercise, and I was troubled.”

When he extended love so as to love his enemies, he was wearied: surrounded by the enmity of many and the fury of many, he sank under a certain human weakness. He saw that he was beginning to be pierced by a wicked persuasion of the devil, so as to introduce hatred against his enemies [Note: [Col. 0631] Some manuscripts read: “put it on.”]. Resisting hatred in order to fulfill love itself, he was troubled in that very battle and struggle.

His voice is heard also in another psalm: “My eye was troubled because of anger.” And what follows there? “I grew old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). He had begun to be submerged, as it were, in storm and waves, like Peter (Matt. 14:30).

For the one who loves his enemies is the one who treads upon the waves of this age. Christ walked upon the sea without fear; the love of his enemy could in no way be removed from his heart. Hanging upon the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

And Peter wished to walk. Christ was like the head, Peter like the body, because he said, “Upon this rock I will build my Church.” Peter was commanded to walk, and he walked by the grace of the one who commanded, not by his own strength.

But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid, and had already begun to sink, troubled in his exercise. From what strong wind? From the voice of the enemy and the tribulation of the sinner.

Thus, just as he cried out amid the waves, “Lord, I am perishing; save me” (Matt. 14:30), so this man’s voice had gone before: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my petition; attend to me and hear me.”

Why? What are you suffering? What are you groaning over? “I was sorrowful in my exercise.” You placed me among evil people to be exercised, but they have risen too far above my strength. Calm the troubled one; extend your hand to the one who is sinking.

“I was sorrowful in my exercise, and I was troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner; for they inclined iniquity against me [Note: [Col. 0631] So the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read: “iniquities.”], and in anger they overshadowed me.” [Col. 0632]

You have heard of waves and winds. As though he had been humbled, they insulted him, and he prayed; all around him they raged with the tumult of insult, while within he invoked the one whom they did not see.

### 6

When a Christian suffers something of this kind, he must not readily turn in hatred against the one from whom he suffers and wish to overcome the wind. Rather, he must turn to prayer, lest he lose love.

For there is no need to fear that an enemy will do something. What will he do? He will say many evil things, hurl insults, rage with abuse. But what does that matter to you? “Rejoice and exult,” he says, “because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:12). He multiplies insults on earth; you multiply gains in heaven.

But let him rage more fiercely; let him be capable of doing something more. What could be safer for you, to whom it was said, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28)?

What, then, is to be feared when you suffer an enemy? That the love by which you love your enemy may be disturbed.

For that human enemy—flesh and blood—desires what he sees in you. But another, hidden enemy, the ruler of these darknesses that you suffer in flesh and blood, seeks your other, hidden self: he attempts to plunder and devastate your inner treasures.

Set two enemies before your eyes, then: one open and the other hidden—the open one, a human being; the hidden one, the devil.

That human being is what you are according to human nature; but according to faith and love he is not yet what you are, although he may become what you are.

Since there are two, see one and understand the other; love one and beware of the other. For even the enemy whom you see wishes to humble in you the very thing by which he is defeated.

For example, if he is defeated by your riches, he wants to make you poor; if he is defeated by your honor, he wants to humble you; if he is defeated by your strength, he wants to make you weak. Thus he seeks either to cast down, take away, or overthrow [Note: [Col. 0632] The editions read: “turn away.”] the things by which he is defeated.

And that hidden enemy wishes to take away from you the thing by which he is defeated. You conquer a human being through human prosperity, but you conquer the devil through love of your enemy.

Therefore, just as a human being seeks to take away from you, cut short, or overturn the prosperity by which he is defeated, so the devil seeks to conquer the human being by taking away the thing by which he is defeated.

Take care, then, to preserve in your heart the love of your enemy, by which you conquer the devil. Let the human being rage as much as he can; let him take away whatever he can. If the one who rages openly is loved, the one who rages secretly has been defeated.

### 7

But this man, troubled and sorrowful, prayed, as though his eye had been troubled by anger. If a brother’s anger grows old, it is already hatred. Anger troubles the eye; hatred extinguishes it. Anger is a splinter; hatred is a beam.

Sometimes you have hated someone and rebuke one who is angry. Hatred is in you, while anger is in the one whom you rebuke. You are rightly told: “First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7:5).

To show you how great the difference is between anger and hatred: people become angry with their children every day; point out those who hate their children.

This man, troubled and sorrowful, prayed, struggling against all the insults of all those who insulted him—not so that he might defeat any of them by returning insult for insult, but so that he might hate none of them.

From this he prays; from this he asks: “From the voice of the enemy and from the tribulation of the sinner; for they inclined iniquity against me, and in anger they overshadowed me.”

“My heart is troubled within me.” This is what is said elsewhere: “My eye was troubled because of anger” (Ps. 6:8). And if the eye was troubled, what follows? “And the fear of death fell upon me.”

Our life is love. If life is love, death is hatred. When a person begins to fear that he may hate someone whom he loved, he fears death—a sharper and more inward death, by which the soul is killed, not the body.

You were looking at a human being raging against you. What could he do against you, when your Lord had given you security by saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28)? By raging, he killed another’s body; by hating, you killed your own soul—and he killed another’s body, while you killed your own soul.

Therefore, “the fear of death fell upon me.”

### 8. [verses 6–8]

“Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said…”

“He who hates his brother is in darkness until now.” If love is light, hatred is darkness (1 John 2:9–11).

And what did he say to himself, placed in that weakness and troubled in that exercise? “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?”

Either he desired death, or he longed for solitude. “As long as this is being done to me, as long as this is commanded of me—that I love my enemies—the increasing insults of these people, overshadowing me, disturb my eye, trouble my light, assail my heart, and kill my soul. I wish I could go away, but I am weak, lest by remaining I add sins to sins; or at least be separated for a little while from the human race, so that my wound may not suffer repeated blows, and may be restored healed to its exercise.”

This happens, brothers, and often a desire for solitude rises in the mind of God’s servant—not for any other reason than because of the crowd of tribulations and scandals—and he says: “Who will give me wings?”

Does he see himself as lacking wings, or rather as having wings tied? If they are lacking, let them be given; if they are tied, let them be released. For even the one who releases a bird’s wings either gives it wings or gives its wings back to it. It did not possess them as its own, since it could not fly with them. Tied wings create a burden.

“Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?”

Where will he rest? I said that there are two possible meanings here. One is as the Apostle says: “To depart and be with Christ is far better.” For he too, although strong, although great, although most robust in heart, although an unconquered soldier in Christ, was troubled in his exercise, as far as we read, and said: “From now on let no one cause me trouble” (Gal. 6:17).

As though he were speaking from that psalm: “Weariness has seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (Ps. 118:53).

Thus a person often attempts to correct distorted and perverse people who indeed belong to his care, but in whom every human effort and vigilance fails. He cannot correct them; he must endure them. And the one who cannot be corrected is yours, either through fellowship in the human race or, very often, through ecclesiastical communion. He is inside. What will you do? Where will you go? Where will you separate yourself so as not to suffer these things?

But be present; speak, exhort, flatter, threaten, rebuke.

“I have done everything. Whatever strength I possessed, I have spent and exhausted. I see that I have accomplished nothing; all my effort has been expended, and the pain remains.”

How, then, will my heart rest from such people, unless I say, “Who will give me wings,” yet “like a dove’s,” not like a raven’s?

The dove seeks flight away from troubles, but does not lose love. The dove is set forth as a sign of love, and in it the groaning is cherished. Nothing is so close to groaning as the dove: by day and by night it groans, as though placed here where there must be groaning.

What, then, does this lover say? “I cannot bear the insults of human beings. They shriek, they rush about in fury, they are inflamed with anger, and in anger they overshadow me. I cannot benefit them. Would that I might rest somewhere, separated from them in body but not in love, so that love itself may not be disturbed within me. I cannot benefit them by my words and conversation; perhaps I may benefit them by praying for them.”

People say such things, but they are often so bound that they cannot fly. Perhaps they are not tied by birdlime, but by duty.

If they are bound by care and duty and cannot abandon them, let them say: “I desired to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24).

The dove [Note: [Col. 0634] The editions read: “The delicate dove, bound,” etc.; “delicate” is absent from the manuscripts.], bound by affection rather than desire, could not fly because of the duty it had to fulfill, not because of any smallness of merit. Nevertheless, the desire must be present in the heart. No one endures this desire unless he has begun to walk that narrow way (Matt. 7:14), so that he may know that the Church’s persecutions do not cease, even in this time when the Church seems tranquil from those persecutions which our martyrs suffered.

Persecutions do not cease, because this is true: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12).

You do not suffer persecution? Then you do not wish to live piously in Christ. Do you wish to prove that what was said is true? Begin to live piously in Christ.

What does it mean to live piously in Christ? It means that the Apostle’s words should belong to your innermost being: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

The weaknesses of others and the scandals of others were persecutions for him. Are these things absent at the present time? They abound more than those who tend to them.

Often a person is seen from a distance, and it is said, “He is doing well.” But the one who says this either tastes only what is his own and cannot taste what belongs to another, or has nothing within himself to taste and does not sympathize with another who is tasting—or rather devouring.

Let him begin, then, to live piously in Christ and prove what is said. He begins to desire wings, to go far away, to flee, and to remain in the desert.

### 9

Why do you think, brothers, that the deserts have been filled with God’s servants? If they had been well off among human beings, would they have withdrawn from human beings?

And yet what do they themselves do? Behold, they go far away in flight and remain in the desert. But do they do so individually? Love holds them, so that they remain with many; and from those many there arise some who exercise them.

For in every gathering of a multitude it is necessary that evil people be found. God, who knows that we must be exercised, mixes in with us those who will not persevere—or at least those who are so hypocritical that they have not even begun what they ought to persevere in.

For he knows that it is necessary for us to endure evil people, so that our goodness may advance. We must love our enemies, rebuke them, chastise them, excommunicate them, and even separate them from us with love.

See what the Apostle says: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him.” But lest anger should steal upon you from this and trouble your eye, he adds: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother, so that he may be ashamed” (2 Thess. 3:14).

From the one of whom he commanded separation, he did not cut off love. That eye lives; your life lives. For when love is lost, your death has occurred.

The man who said, “The fear of death fell upon me,” feared losing this. Therefore, lest I lose the life of love, “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away and rest?”

Where will you go? Where will you fly? Where will you rest?

“Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in the desert.” In what desert? Wherever you are, the others will gather; they will seek the desert with you, they will desire your life, and you cannot reject the fellowship of the brothers. Evil people too will be mixed with you; exercise is still owed to you.

“Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in the desert.” In what desert? Perhaps in your conscience, where no human being enters, where no one is with you, where you and God are.

For if it is a desert in some physical place, what will you do about those who gather together? You cannot be separated from the human race as long as you live among human beings.

Rather, attend to that Lord and king, our commander and creator, who was also created among us. Attend to the fact that he mixed one whom he would suffer among his twelve.

### 10. [verse 9]

He says: “Behold, I have gone far away in flight, and I remained in the desert.”

Perhaps this man, as I said, fled to his conscience and found there for a while a desert in which he could rest. But that love troubled him. He was alone in conscience, but not alone in love; within, his conscience consoled him, but outward tribulations did not leave him.

Therefore, quiet within himself but dependent upon others, while he was still troubled, what did he say? “I was waiting for the one who would save me from faintheartedness [Note: [Col. 0635] So the manuscripts. But the editions have here only: “from a faint heart.”] and storm.”

It is the sea; it is a storm. Nothing remains for you except to cry out, “Lord, I am perishing” (Matt. 14:30). Let the one who treads the waves without fear extend his hand; let him lift up your trembling, establish your security in himself, address you within, and say to you: “Look at me; consider what I endured. Perhaps you suffer an evil brother, or outwardly you suffer an enemy. Who are those whom I did not suffer? The Jews raged outwardly; inwardly a disciple betrayed me.”

The storm therefore rages, but he saves from faintheartedness and storm.

Perhaps your ship is troubled for this reason: because he is asleep in you. The sea raged, and the little boat in which the disciples were sailing was troubled, but Christ was sleeping. At last it seemed to them that the commander and creator of the winds was sleeping among them. They approached and awakened Christ; he commanded the winds, and a great calm arose (Matt. 8:23–26). [Col. 0636]

Perhaps your heart is rightly troubled because you have forgotten in whom you believed. You suffer beyond measure because it has not come to mind what Christ endured for you.

If Christ does not come to your mind, he is asleep. Awaken Christ; recall your faith. Christ is asleep in you when you have forgotten Christ’s sufferings [Note: [Col. 0636] Here the editions add: “if you deny him to be the true Son of God”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]; Christ is awake in you when you remember Christ’s sufferings.

When you have looked with your whole heart upon what he suffered, will you not also endure with an even spirit? Perhaps even rejoicing, because you have been found to share in some likeness of the sufferings of your king.

When, as you ponder these things, you begin to be consoled and to rejoice, he has risen; he has commanded the winds, and therefore a calm has arisen.

“I was waiting for the one who would save me from faintheartedness and storm.”

### 11. [verse 10]

“Sink them, Lord, and divide their tongues.”

He regarded those who afflicted and overshadowed him, and he desired this—not out of anger, brothers. Those who have lifted themselves up wickedly benefit from being sunk; those who have conspired wickedly benefit from having their tongues divided: let them agree for good, and let their tongues be united.

But if they were whispering together against me, as he says, “all my enemies” (Ps. 40:8), let them lose their agreement in evil [Note: [Col. 0636] Some manuscripts read: “let them be lost in their agreement”; Louvain reads: “let them lose their agreement”; Erasmus and some manuscripts read: “let them lose [it] in their agreement.”]; let their tongues be divided; let them not agree among themselves.

“Sink them, Lord, and divide their tongues.” Sink them—why? Because they have lifted themselves up. Divide them—why? Because they have conspired for evil.

Recall that tower of the proud built after the flood. What did the proud say? “Lest we perish in the flood, let us build a high tower” (Gen. 11:4). They imagined that pride had fortified them; they built a high tower, and the Lord divided their tongues.

Then they began not to understand one another. From this arose the origin of the many languages. Previously there had been one language; but one language benefited people who were in agreement, one language benefited human beings. But when that assembly was precipitated into a conspiracy of pride, God spared them by dividing their languages, lest, by understanding one another, they should make a destructive unity.

Through proud people the languages were divided; through humble Apostles the languages were gathered together. The spirit of pride scattered languages; the Holy Spirit gathered languages.

For when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, they spoke in the languages of all and were understood by all (Acts 2:4): the scattered languages were gathered into one.

Therefore, if they still rage and are pagans, it benefits them to have divided languages. Let them desire one language; let them come to the Church. For amid the diversity of the languages of the flesh, there is one language in the faith of the heart.

“Sink them, Lord, and divide their tongues.”

### 12

“Because I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city.”

This man rightly sought the desert, because he saw iniquity and contradiction in the city. There is a certain turbulent city. It was the city that had built the tower; it was confused and was called Babylon; it was scattered among innumerable nations (Gen. 11:9). From there the Church is gathered into the desert of a good conscience. [Col. 0637]

For he saw contradiction in the city.

Christ came. “Who is Christ?” you contradict. “The Son of God.” “And does God have a son?” you contradict. “He was born of a virgin, suffered, and rose again.” “And how can this happen?” you contradict.

At least consider the glory of his cross. Now that cross is fixed upon the foreheads of kings, the very cross at which his enemies insulted him. The result has proved its power [Note: [Col. 0637] Nearly all the manuscripts read: “Prove the power by the results.”]: it conquered the world, not by iron but by wood.

The wood of the cross seemed worthy of insult to his enemies. Standing before that wood, they shook their heads and said: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40).

He extended his hands to the unbelieving and contradicting people. For if “the just person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), the unjust person is the one who does not have faith.

Therefore, by “iniquity” here I understand faithlessness. The Lord saw iniquity and contradiction in the city, and he extended his hands to the unbelieving and contradicting people. Yet, still awaiting them, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Even now remnants of that city rage; even now they contradict. From the foreheads of all, he now extends his hands toward the unbelieving and contradicting remnants.

“Because I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city.”

### 13. [verse 11]

“By day and by night iniquity and labor shall surround her upon her walls.”

Upon her walls, upon her fortifications, seizing, as it were, her heads—her nobles. If that nobleman were a Christian, no pagan would remain.

People often say: “No one would remain a pagan if he were a Christian.” People often say: “And if that man became a Christian, who would remain a pagan?”

Since they do not yet become Christians, they are like the walls of that unbelieving and contradicting city.

How long will these walls stand? They will not stand forever. The ark circles the walls of Jericho; the time will come, at the seventh circuit of the ark, when all the walls of the unbelieving and contradicting city will fall (Josh. 6:5).

Until that happens, this man is troubled in his exercise. Enduring the remnants of those who contradict, he desires wings for flight; he desires the rest of the desert.

Rather, let him remain among those who contradict, endure threats, drink in insults, wait for the one who will save him from faintheartedness and storm. Let him look upon the head, the example of his life [Note: [Col. 0637] Most manuscripts read: “the example of his way.”]; let him be calmed in hope, even if he is troubled in reality.

“By day and by night iniquity shall surround her upon her walls, and labor and injustice in her midst.”

And therefore there is labor there, because there is iniquity there; because there is injustice there, there is also labor there.

But let them hear him who extends his hands: “Come to me, all you who labor.” You cry out, you contradict, you hurl insults; but he, on the contrary, says: “Come to me, all you who labor in your pride, and you shall rest in my humility.”

“Learn from me,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

For why do they labor, unless because they are not gentle and humble in heart? God became humble; let the human being be ashamed to be proud.

### 14. [verse 12]

Usury and deceit have not disappeared from its streets. Usury and deceit are not even concealed because they are evil, but rage openly. For someone who does something evil in his house is at least ashamed of his evil: “In its streets are usury and deceit.” Interest-bearing lending has both a name and a recognized profession; it is called a business, as though it were necessary to the city, and from his profession he pays a tax: so completely is what ought at least to have been hidden out in the street.

There is another, worse kind of usury, when you do not forgive what is owed you; and the eye is troubled at that line of the prayer, “Forgive us our debts.” For what will you do when you are praying and come to that line? You have heard an insulting word: you want to exact the penalty of condemnation. Or you demand only as much as you gave, you lender of injuries. You have been struck with a fist, and you seek murder. Evil usury! How will you proceed into prayer?

If you abandon the prayer, by what path will you go around to the Lord? Look: you will say, “Our Father, who are in heaven: hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” You will say, “Give us today our daily bread.” You will come to, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:9–12).

Let these usuries abound in that evil city, but let them not enter these walls where the breast is beaten. What will you do, since you and that line are there together? The heavenly jurist has composed prayers for you—[Note: See *Tractate 7 on the Gospel of John*, no. 11.] he who knew what was happening there. He says to you, “You will obtain nothing otherwise.” For “Amen, I say to you, if you forgive people’s sins, they will be forgiven you; but if you do not forgive people’s sins, neither will your Father forgive you” (ibid., 14–15).

Who says this? The one who knows what is happening there, what you, standing before him, are asking. See how he wished to be your advocate: he himself, your jurist, your Father’s assessor, your judge, has said, “You will not receive it otherwise.” What will you do? You will not receive it if you do not say this; you will not receive it if you say what is false. Therefore, either do and say it, or you will not obtain what you ask; for those who do not do this are involved in those evil usuries.

Let those who still either worship or seek idols be there; but you, people of God, do not; you, people of Christ, do not; you, body of that head, do not. Consider the bond of your peace; consider the promise of your life. What benefit is it to you that you exact the injuries you have suffered? Does revenge restore you? Then will you rejoice in another’s evil? You have suffered evil: forgive, lest there be two [Note: The words “evils” or “evil persons” are understood.] of you. “And usury and deceit have not disappeared from its streets.”

### 15. [verses 13–15]

Therefore you were seeking solitude and wings; therefore you murmur, because you cannot bear these things—the contradiction and iniquity of this city. Rest among those who are within with you, and do not seek solitude. Hear also what he says about them: “For if an enemy had reproached me.”

Indeed, earlier he was troubled in his exercise by the voice of the enemy and by the tribulation of the sinner, perhaps placed in that city, when that proud tower was raising itself up, the tower that was submerged [Note: The editions read “overthrown,” but the manuscripts read “submerged.” He alludes to verse 10, “Submerge,” etc.] so that their languages might be divided (Genesis 11:4). Consider what he groans over within, because of the dangers caused by false brothers.

“For if an enemy had reproached me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me”—that is, had insulted me through pride, had magnified himself over me, had threatened me with whatever he could—“I would surely have hidden myself from him.” From the one who is outside, where would you hide yourself? Among those who are within.

“But now see whether anything else remains except that you seek solitude. But you,” he says, “a man of one mind, my guide and my acquaintance.” Perhaps at some time you gave good counsel; perhaps at some time you went before me and offered some salutary advice. We were together in the Church of God.

“But you, a man of one mind, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food.” What are the sweet foods? Not all who are present know; but let those who know not embitter those who do not yet know, so that they may be able to say to them, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

“Who together with me used to take sweet food. We walked in the house of God with harmony.” Where, then, did disagreement come from? The one who was within became one who was outside. He walked with me in the house of God in harmony; he set up another house against the house of God. Why was that house abandoned, where we walked together in harmony? Why was that house deserted, where together we used to take sweet food?

### 16. [verse 16]

“Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.” How did he recall this and make us remember that first beginning of schism, when, among that first people of the Jews, certain proud men separated themselves and wished to offer sacrifice outside? A new death came upon them: the earth opened itself and swallowed the living (Numbers 16:1–33).

“Let death,” he says, “come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.” What does “alive” mean? Knowing that they are perishing, and yet perishing. Hear of the living perishing and being swallowed by the opening of the earth—that is, being swallowed by the devouring power of earthly desires.

You say to a man: “What are you suffering, brother? We are brothers; we invoke one God; we believe in one Christ; we hear one Gospel; we sing one Psalm; we answer one Amen; we sound forth one Alleluia; we celebrate one Easter. Why are you outside while I am within?” Often, being distressed and considering how true these words are, he says, “May God repay our ancestors.” Therefore he perishes alive.

Then you add and admonish him: “At least let the evil be only the separation; why do you add rebaptism as well? Recognize in me what you possess; and if you hate me, spare Christ in me.” This evil usually—and especially—displeases them. “It is truly wrong,” they say; “if only it could be avoided! But what are we to do about the decrees of our ancestors?”

“Let them descend alive into hell.” If you descended dead, you would not know what you were doing; but when you know that what you are doing is evil and nevertheless do it, do you not descend alive into hell? And why did the opening of the earth chiefly swallow their leaders alive, while fire rushing down from heaven consumed the people who agreed with them (ibid., 47)?

Therefore, in recalling this punishment, the Psalm began with the people and concluded with the leaders. “Let death come upon them,” he said, referring to those upon whom fire from heaven came; and immediately he added, “Let them descend alive into hell,” referring to the leaders whom the opening of the earth swallowed. For how could those of whom he had said, “Let death come upon them,” descend alive into hell? If death had already come upon them, how were they descending alive into hell? Therefore he began with the lesser and concluded with the greater.

“Let death come upon those who consented and followed.” What of those leaders and princes? “Let them descend alive into hell,” because they themselves handle the Scriptures and know well, by reading them daily, how the Catholic Church has been spread throughout the whole world, so that every contradiction is entirely void and no testimony in support of their schism can be found. They know this well; therefore they descend alive into hell, because they know that the evil they do is evil.

But divine anger consumed the others with fire [Note: All the manuscripts read, “Fire from divine anger consumed them.”]. For, inflamed by the zeal of contention, they were unwilling to withdraw from their evil leaders. Fire came upon fire, and the heat of destruction upon the heat of dissension.

“Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell. For wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.” In their dwellings, where they lodge and pass through. For they will not always be here; and yet, out of temporal passion, they fight in this way. In their dwellings, therefore, there is iniquity; in their midst there is iniquity. Nothing is more truly their midst than their heart.

### 17. [verse 17]

“I cried out to the Lord.” The body of Christ and the unity of Christ are in anguish, weariness, distress, and the disturbance of their exercise. That one man, the unity placed in one body, when his soul was wearied, cried out from the ends of the earth: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you,” he says, “when my heart was troubled” (Psalm 60:3).

He is one, but he is one as unity; and he is one not as one man in one place, but as one who cries from the ends of the earth. How could one man cry from the ends of the earth unless he were one in many?

“I cried out to the Lord.” Rightly so. Cry out to the Lord; do not cry out to Donatus, lest the one who did not wish to be a fellow servant under the Lord become your lord in place of the Lord.

“I cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard me.”

### 18. [verse 18]

“In the evening, and morning, and midday, I will declare, announce, and he will hear my voice.”

Evangelize: do not be silent about what you have received. In the evening, speak of past things; in the morning, of future things; at midday, of eternal things. Therefore, what he says about the evening belongs to what he declares; what he says about the morning belongs to what he announces; what he says about midday belongs to the fact that his voice is heard.

For the end is at midday, but from there there is no decline toward sunset. At midday the light is exalted: the splendor of wisdom, the fervor of love.

“In the evening, and morning, and midday.” In the evening, the Lord was on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at midday, in the ascension. In the evening I declare the patience of the one who dies; in the morning I announce the life of the one who rises; at midday I will pray that he hear me, sitting at the right hand of the Father. He will hear my voice, the one who intercedes for us (Romans 8:34).

How great is the security, how great the consolation, how great the restoration from faintheartedness and storm, against the wicked and the unjust, both outside and within—and among those who are outside, though they had once been within!

### 19. [verse 16]

Therefore, my brothers, those whom you see turbulent within this very gathering of these walls—proud, seeking their own interests, haughty, not possessing a pure, sound, and peaceful zeal for God, but attributing much to themselves; ready for dissension but unable to find an occasion—these are the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor (Matthew 3:12).

The wind of pride has shaken a few of them loose from here. The whole chaff will not fly away until he winnows at the end. But what are we to do except sing with this one, pray with this one, mourn with this one, and confidently say, “He will redeem my soul in peace”?

Against those who do not love peace: “In peace he will redeem my soul,” because “with those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Psalm 119:7).

“He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me.” For the cause of those who are far from me is easy: the one who says to me, “Come, worship an idol,” does not deceive me so quickly; he is very far from me. “Are you a Christian?” “A Christian,” he says. He opposes from nearby; he is close.

“He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, for they were with me in many things.” Why did I say, “They draw near to me”? Because they were with me in many things.

Two interpretations present themselves in this verse. “They were with me in many things”: we both had Baptism—they were with me in that; we both read the Gospel—they were with me in it; we celebrated the feasts of the martyrs—they were with me there; we attended the solemnity of Easter—they were with me there.

But they were not altogether with me: in schism, they were not with me; in heresy, they were not with me. With me in many things, not with me in a few. But those few things in which they are not with me do not benefit them because of the many things in which they are with me [Note: The manuscripts read, “But in the few things in which they are not with me, so that the many things in which they are with me may not benefit them,” etc.].

For, brothers, see how many things the apostle Paul enumerated; he mentioned one thing which, if absent, makes all the others useless. “If I speak in the tongues of men and angels,” he says, “if I have all prophecy and all faith and all knowledge, if I move mountains, if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, if I hand over my body so that it may burn”—how many things he listed! Let one love be absent from all these many things: those are greater in number, but this is greater in weight (1 Corinthians 13). Therefore, they are with me in all the sacraments, but not with me in the one love: “They were with me in many things.”

Again, in another sense: “For they were with me in many things.” Those who separated themselves from me were with me—not in a few things, but in many. For throughout the whole world there are few grains and much chaff. What, then, does he say? They were with me in the chaff; they were not with me in the wheat.

The chaff draws near to the wheat: it comes from the same seed, is rooted in the same field, nourished by the same rain, undergoes the same harvester, endures the same threshing, and awaits the same winnowing—but it does not enter the same granary.

“For they were with me in many things.”

### 20. [verses 20–22]

“God will hear me, and he will humble them, the one who is before the ages.” For they presume upon I know not what leader of theirs who began yesterday. He will humble them who is before the ages.

For even if Christ is, in time, from the Virgin Mary, nevertheless before the ages he was “in the beginning the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1). He will humble them who is before the ages.

“For there is no change in them”—I speak of those for whom there is no change. He knew that some would persevere and die in their perseverance in wickedness. For we see them, and there is no change in them: those who die in that very perversity, in that very schism, have no change.

God will humble them; he will humble them in condemnation, because they have raised themselves up in dissension. There is no change in them because they are not changed for the better but for the worse, neither while they are here nor in the resurrection. For we will all rise, but we will not all be changed (1 Corinthians 15:51).

Why? Because there is no change in them, and they did not fear God.

My brothers, there is one remedy: let them fear God; let them abandon Donatus. You say to him: “You are perishing in heresy, in schism. God must repay these evils; you will come into condemnation. Do not flatter yourself with your own words; do not follow a blind guide. But when the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14).

“What is that to me?” he says. “As I lived yesterday, so I live today. Whatever my parents were, that am I.” You do not fear God. Give him the fear of God. Let him consider that all these things that are read are true, that the faith of Christ cannot be deceived. How will he remain in heresy in the face of such clear evidence of the holy Catholic Church, which God has spread throughout the whole world, which he promised and foretold before spreading it, and fulfilled as he had promised?

Therefore let those who do not fear God be warned and take heed. “He has stretched out his hand in repayment.”

### 21

“They polluted his testament.” Read the testament that they polluted: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3; 26:4).

“They polluted his testament.” What do you say against these words of the testator? “Africa alone deserved this grace of the holy Donatus; in him the Church of Christ remained.” At least say, “The Church of Donatus.” Why do you add “of Christ,” about whom it was said, “In your seed all nations will be blessed”?

Do you wish to go after Donatus? Put Christ first, and then depart.

See, therefore, what follows: “They polluted his testament.” What testament? Promises were made to Abraham and to his seed. The Apostle says: “Brothers, even a human testament, once confirmed, no one annuls or adds provisions to it. Promises were made to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:15–16).

In this Christ, then, what testament was promised? “In your seed all nations will be blessed.” You who have abandoned the unity of all nations and remained in a faction have polluted his testament.

What has happened to you—that you were cut off and separated from the inheritance—comes from the anger of God. Consider what follows: “They polluted his testament; they were divided because of the anger of his face.” What greater mark could you expect by which heretics might be shown? “They were divided because of the anger of his face.”

### 22

“And his heart drew near.” Whose heart do we understand, unless it is the heart of the one whose anger divided them? How did his heart draw near? So that we might understand his will.

Indeed, the Catholic faith was asserted against the heretics, and from those who thought wrongly those who thought rightly were demonstrated. For many things lay hidden in the Scriptures; and when the heretics were cut off, they stirred the Church of God with their questions. What had been hidden was opened, and the will of God was understood.

Hence it is said in another Psalm: “The gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples, so that those approved as silver may be cast out” (Psalm 67:31). For “cast out” means: let them stand forth, let them appear. Hence in the art of the silversmiths those who cast out are also so called—that is, those who draw out forms from a certain confusion of the mass.

Therefore many who could have discerned and expounded the Scriptures most excellently lay hidden among the people of God; nor did they bring forward solutions to difficult questions while no accuser was pressing them. Was the doctrine of the Trinity treated perfectly before the Arians barked against it? Was repentance treated perfectly before the Novatians resisted? In the same way, Baptism was not treated perfectly before the rebaptizers, standing outside, contradicted it. Nor had those things concerning the very unity of Christ been stated with such precision, unless that separation had later begun to oppress the weaker brothers, so that those who knew how to handle and resolve these matters might bring the obscure things of the Law into public discussion through their sermons and debates, lest the weak, troubled by the questions of the impious, should perish.

Therefore, “they were divided because of the anger of his face,” and his heart drew near to us for understanding.

Accordingly, understand what he recalled in another Psalm: “The gathering of bulls”—that is, proud horned men—“among the cows of the peoples.” Whom did he call cows? Souls easily led astray.

Why this? “So that those who are approved as silver may be cast out”—that is, may appear—those who were hidden.

What is “silver”? The utterance of God. “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, approved by the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7).

See how the Apostle brings this obscure meaning into the light: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19).

What does “approved” mean? Approved as silver, approved by the utterance. What does “become manifest” mean? “Let them be cast out.” Why does this happen? Because of the heretics. What does “because of the heretics” mean? Because of “the gathering of bulls among the cows of the peoples.”

Thus they too were divided because of the anger of his face, and his heart drew near.

### 23

“His words were softened above oil, and yet they themselves are arrows.”

Some things in the Scriptures seemed harsh because they were obscure; once expounded, they were softened. For even the first heresy among Christ’s disciples arose, as it were, from the harshness of his words.

When he said, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself,” those who did not understand said to one another, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” Saying, “This saying is hard,” they separated themselves from him; he remained with the other twelve.

When they had told him that those people had been scandalized by his saying, he said, “Do you also wish to go away?” And Peter replied, “You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?” (John 6:54–69).

Pay attention, we beg you, and learn piety, little ones. Did Peter already understand the secret of that saying of the Lord? He did not yet understand it; but he piously believed that the words he did not understand were good.

Therefore, if the saying is hard and has not yet been understood, let it be hard for the impious; but let it be softened for you by piety. For eventually it will be opened, become oil for you, and penetrate even to the bones.

### 24. [verse 23]

Accordingly, as though Peter himself, after those who had been scandalized by what they thought was the harshness of the Lord’s saying, were saying here too, “You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?” he added, “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.”

You are a little one; you do not yet understand the secrets of the words. Perhaps bread is hidden from you, and you still need to be nourished with milk (1 Corinthians 3:2). Do not become angry with the breasts; they themselves will make you fit for the table, for which you are presently less fit.

Look: through the division of the heretics many hard things have been softened. His hard words were softened above oil, and they themselves are arrows. They armed those who preach, and those very words are directed into the breasts of every kind of listener by those who insist, in season and out of season. By those words, by those sayings as by arrows, human hearts are struck for the love of peace.

They were hard, and they became soft. By being softened they did not lose their force, but were turned into arrows. “His words were softened above oil, and they themselves”—the softened words themselves—“are arrows.”

But perhaps you are not yet fit to be armed with these arrows, and what is obscure and hard in the saying has not yet shone upon you: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.”

Cast yourself upon the Lord. Look: you wish to cast yourself upon the Lord, and no one should put himself in the Lord’s place. “Cast your care upon the Lord.”

See how that great soldier of Christ did not wish the care of the little ones to be cast upon himself: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (ibid., 1:13). What else was he saying to them except, “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you”?

But now the little one wishes to cast his care upon the Lord, and some person comes forward and says, “I will receive it.” He comes forward like someone approaching a ship tossed by waves and says, “I will receive it.”

You answer: “I am seeking a harbor, not a rock.”

“Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.” And see that the harbor receives you: “He will not grant the righteous eternal tossing.”

You may seem to toss upon this sea, but the harbor receives you. Only, before you enter the harbor, do not break away from the anchor. The ship tosses at its anchors, but it is not cast far from land; nor will it toss forever, even though it tosses for a time.

Indeed, the preceding words refer to this tossing: “I was sorrowful in my exercise, and I was troubled. I was waiting for the one who would save me from faintheartedness and storm.” The one who tosses speaks, but he will not toss forever; for the anchor is fastened, and his anchor is hope.

“He will not grant the righteous eternal tossing.”

### 25. [verse 24]

But what of those others? “But you, God, will lead them into the pit of corruption.”

The pit of corruption is the darkness of submersion. “You will lead them,” he says, “into the pit of corruption,” because “when the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14).

God leads them into the pit of corruption—not because he is the author of their fault, but because he is the judge of their iniquities. For “God handed them over to the desires of their heart” (Romans 1:24): they loved darkness and not light; they loved blindness and not sight.

For look: the Lord Jesus has shone upon the whole world. Let them sing in unity with the whole world: “There is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Psalm 18:7).

But those who remove themselves from the whole to a part, from the body to a wound, from life to amputation—what will they suffer except to go into the pit of corruption?

### 26

“Men of blood and deceitfulness.”

He calls them men of blood because of their killings—and would that they were only bodily killings, and not spiritual ones! Blood leaving the flesh is seen and causes horror; but who sees the blood of the heart in one who has been rebaptized? Those deaths require other eyes.

Even with regard to those visible deaths, the armed Circumcellions do not cease their activity everywhere. And if we consider these visible deaths, they are men of blood. Look at the armed man and ask whether he is a man of peace and not of blood. If only he carried a club; but he carries a sling, an axe, stones, and spears [Note: The manuscripts read, “If he were a man of peace and not of blood, at least a club,” etc. A little later, for “sling,” all our manuscripts read *fundibalum* rather than *fundibulum*.]. Carrying these things, they roam wherever they can and thirst for the blood of the innocent. Therefore, even with respect to these visible deaths, they are men of blood.

But let us speak also about those other deaths: would that they caused only [Note: “Visible deaths” is understood.] bodily deaths and did not destroy souls!

Those who are men of blood and deceitfulness should not suppose that we understand “men of blood” wrongly when we say that they kill souls; they themselves understood their Maximianists in this way. For when they condemned them, they placed these words in the very sentence of their council [Note: The council of Bagai]: “Their feet are swift to shed the blood of the heralds.” [Note: The word “announced” is omitted in several manuscripts here and is absent from the sentence of the Council of Bagai as reported in *Against Cresconius*, book 4, chapter 4.]. “Affliction and calamity are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Psalm 13:3).

They said this about the Maximianists. But I ask them when the Maximianists shed bodily blood—not because they themselves would not have shed it [Note: The editions read, “would not have shed it.” The manuscript reading, “would have shed it,” is better.] if there had been such a multitude as to shed it, but because, on account of the timidity of their small number, they suffered something at the hands of others more often than they themselves ever did anything of the kind.

Therefore I question a Donatist and say: “In your council you wrote concerning the Maximianists, ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood.’ Show me one person whom the Maximianists wounded with a finger.” What else will he answer me except what I say? Those who separated themselves from unity and kill souls by leading them astray shed blood spiritually, not carnally.

“You have explained it very well; but in your explanation recognize your own deeds.”

“Men of blood and deceitfulness”—deceitfulness in fraud, pretense, and seduction. What, then, of those very people who were divided because of the anger of his face? They are the men of blood and deceitfulness.

### 27

But what does he say about them? “They will not complete half their days.”

What does “They will not complete half their days” mean? They will not advance as far as they think; within the time they hope for, they will perish.

For he is that partridge of whom it was said: “In the middle of his days they will abandon him, and at his end he will be a fool” (Jeremiah 17:11). They make progress, but only for a time.

For what does the Apostle say? “But evil people and deceivers will advance toward worse, deceiving and being deceived.” “When the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14). Rightly do they fall into the pit of corruption.

What, then, does he say? “They will advance toward worse,” but not for long. For shortly before he said, “But they will advance no further”—that is, “They will not complete half their days.”

Let the Apostle continue and say why: “For their madness will be evident to all, as theirs also was” (2 Timothy 3:9, 13).

“Men of blood and deceitfulness will not complete half their days. But I will hope in you, Lord.”

It is rightly that they will not complete half their days, because they have hoped in a human being. But I have passed from temporal days to the eternal day. Why? Because I have hoped in you, Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 55

[Note: In the Royal Manuscript this exposition is preceded by the following title: “Here begins the sermon delivered at Carthage in the Basilica Restituta, on Thursday, on Psalm 55.”]

### SERMON

[Note: To the people of Carthage.]

### 1. [verse 1]

When we are about to enter some house, we look at the inscription to see whose it is and to whom it belongs, lest we rush improperly into a place where we ought not to go, or, on the other hand, be held back by fear from entering where we ought to enter.

Thus, as though we were reading, “This estate belongs to this person or that person,” so on the threshold of this Psalm we find written: “For the end, for the people who have been made far from the holy ones; to David himself, for the inscription of the title, when the Allophyli seized him in Geth.”

Let us therefore recognize in the inscription of the title the people who have been made far from the holy ones. For this pertains to David himself, whom you already know how to understand spiritually. He is not commended to us except the one of whom it was said, “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

Therefore, when you hear “For the end,” direct your attention to Christ, lest, remaining on the way, you fail to reach the end. Whatever there is where you stop below, before you reach Christ, the divine word says nothing else to you except, “Draw near; this is not yet the place where there is security.”

There is a certain place where a most reliable station is established; there is a certain rock upon which a secure house rises, so that it does not fear the rain of the storm. For the rivers beat against that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon the rock (Matthew 7:25). “The rock, however, was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Christ is figured under the name of David [Note: The manuscripts read, “Christ is figured symbolically under the name of David,” omitting the words “Christ.”], because it was said of him that he “was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3).

### 2

Who, then, is the people who have been made far from the holy ones in the inscription of the title? Let the title itself show us this people.

For a certain title was written during the Lord’s Passion, when the Lord was crucified. There was a title inscribed there, in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “King of the Jews.” The title was confirmed in three languages, as though by three witnesses, because “every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).

When the Jews read this title, they became indignant and said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” They said, “Write that he said it; do not write that this is what he is.”

But because the words of another Psalm are true, “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title” (Psalm 56:1), Pilate replied, “What I have written, I have written”—as though saying, “I am not corrupting the truth, although you love falsehood.”

Because, then, in that curse the Jews became indignant, saying, “We have no king except Caesar alone” (John 19:15–22), they were made far from the holy ones because of their offense at the title.

Let those who acknowledge and desire to have Christ as king draw near to the holy ones and cling to the holy one. Let those who rejected the title by contradicting it and rejected God as king, choosing a human being as king, be far from the holy ones.

Therefore every people that delights in a human kingdom and refuses to have the Lord reign over it—though, when he reigns, each person is so subject that he himself also reigns over his own desires—every such people is far from the holy ones.

Do not, therefore, brothers, notice this only among the Jews. They were indeed given as a kind of first example, so that what every person should beware of might shine forth in that people. They openly rejected Christ as king and chose Caesar as king.

Caesar is indeed a human king for human affairs; but there is another king for divine affairs. One king is for temporal life, another for eternal life; one is an earthly king, another a heavenly king. The earthly king is under the heavenly king; the heavenly king is above all.

They did not sin, therefore, because they said they had Caesar as king, but because they did not wish to have Christ as king.

Even now many do not wish to have Christ as king, seated in heaven and reigning everywhere. They are the very people who trouble us. This Psalm strengthens us against such people.

It is necessary that we endure such people to the end; we would not endure them unless it were beneficial for us. For every temptation is a test, and every test has its own fruitful result.

A person is often unknown even to himself: he does not know what he can endure or what he cannot endure. Sometimes he presumes that he can endure what he cannot; sometimes he despairs of being able to endure what he can. Temptation approaches like an interrogation, and a person is discovered by himself, because he was hidden even from himself, though not hidden from his Maker.

Thus Peter presumed, I know not what, which was not yet in him: that he would persevere with the Lord Jesus Christ even unto death. Peter did not know his own strength, but the Lord knew it.

The one who had fashioned him answered one who was not yet capable [Note: All our manuscripts have this reading. The editions read: “He foresaw that he was less capable,” etc. A little later they read: “He knew what he had not yet given.”]. He knew what he had not yet given, though he would give the strength appropriate to the one whom he had fashioned; the one who had not yet received it did not know.

Temptation came: he denied, he wept, he received [restoration] (Luke 22:33–62).

Since, therefore, we do not know what we should ask as though we did not possess it, nor from what we should give thanks as though we were receiving it, we must always be instructed by temptations and tribulations in this world. But we cannot be troubled except by those who make themselves far from the holy ones.

Brothers, understand that this distance is a distance of the heart, not of the body. It often happens that someone who is physically far away from you, traveling abroad, is joined to you because he loves what you love. And it often happens that someone standing beside you is joined to you because he loves what you love. But it also often happens that someone standing beside you, because he loves the world while you love God, is far from you.

### 3

What, then, does it mean—since it still belongs to the title itself—that “the Allophyli seized him in Gath”? Gath was a certain city of the Allophyli, that is, of foreigners, and therefore of a people far from the saints. For by being foreigners they do not approach the saints but are far from the saints.

All who refuse Christ as king become foreigners. Why do they become foreigners? Because even that vine, although planted by him, became bitter. What did it hear? “Why have you been changed into bitterness, a foreign vine?” (Jer. II, 21). It does not say, “My vine,” because if it were mine, it would be sweet; if it is bitter, it is not mine; if it is not mine, it is certainly foreign.

Thus the Allophyli seized him in Gath. [Note: Col. 0648. The manuscripts read: “It is indeed, brothers, because we find David himself,” etc.] We do indeed find, brothers, that David himself, the son of Jesse and king of Israel, stayed among the Allophyli when he was being sought by Saul (I Reg. XXI, 10); he was in this city and with the king of this city, but we do not read that he was detained there.

Therefore our David, the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the seed of that David, was not merely seized by the Allophyli in Gath; he is still held by them there. We have said that Gath is a city. When the meaning of this name is sought, it signifies “press.” Christ, insofar as he is the head of the Savior’s body—that one born of a virgin and crucified, who has already shown us the example of our resurrection in the resurrection of his flesh, who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us—is also here, but in his body, which is the Church.

The body is joined to its head; the head cries out on behalf of the body: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4). And the body is in its head, according to the Apostle’s saying: “And he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II, 6). We too sit there, and he labors here: we sit there according to hope, while he is here with us according to love.

This joining, as though of one person, makes two in one flesh, the bridegroom and the bride. Hence the Lord himself says: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. XIX, 6).

How, then, is he held here in Gath? His body—that is, his Church—is held in the press (Eph. I, 22–23). What does “in the press” mean? In afflictions. But in the press there is a fruitful pressing. A grape on the vine does not feel pressure; it appears whole, but nothing flows from it. It is put into the press, trodden, and squeezed. The grape seems to be suffering injury, but that injury is not fruitless; indeed, if no injury were inflicted, it would remain fruitless.

### 4. [v. 2] [Col. 0649]

[Note: The manuscripts read: “Whatever pressures all the saints suffer.”]

Therefore, all the saints who suffer pressure from those who have become far from the saints should attend to this psalm, recognize themselves here, and say what is said here—those who suffer what is said here.

Certainly, whoever does not suffer should not say it. I do not compel anyone to repeat the words when I see that he is outside suffering. But let him see whether, by wishing to be far from suffering, he may become far from the saints.

Let each person, then, think about his enemy. If he is a Christian, the world itself is his enemy. Let no one think about private enmities, since he is going to hear the words of this psalm: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. VI, 12), that is, against the devil and his angels. For whenever we suffer troublesome people, he provokes them, he inflames them, he moves them as though they were his vessels.

Let us therefore consider two enemies: the one whom we see and the one whom we do not see. We see the human being; we do not see the devil. Let us love the human being and beware of the devil; let us pray for the human being and pray against the devil, and say to God:

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me down.” Do not be afraid because man has trampled you down; have wine in you. You have become a grape in order to be trodden.

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me down; all day long, fighting against me, everyone who has become far from the saints has afflicted me.”

But why should the devil himself not be understood here? [Note: The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.] Perhaps because he was not called “man”? Then the Gospel is mistaken, since it says: “An enemy, a man, has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28). Yet, under a certain figure, he too can be called “man,” though he is not a man.

Whether, then, the one who said these words was looking directly at him, or at the people and at each person who has become far from the saints—through whom the devil afflicts the people clinging to the saints, clinging to the Holy One, clinging to the king whose title provoked them, as though they had been struck back, so that they have become far away—let him say: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me down.”

And let him not fail under this trampling, knowing whom he invokes and by what example he has been made strong. Christ was the first cluster of grapes pressed in the winepress. When that cluster was expressed through suffering, there flowed from it the wine of which it is said: “How splendid is the inebriating cup!” (Ps. XXII, 5).

Therefore let his body also say, looking upon its head: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me down; all day long he has afflicted me while fighting against me.”

“All day long”—throughout all time. Let no one say to himself: “There were tribulations among our fathers, but there are none among us.” If you think you have no tribulations, you have not yet begun to be a Christian.

Where, then, is the Apostle’s saying: “And all who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12)? If, therefore, you suffer no persecution for Christ, beware lest you have not yet begun to live devoutly in Christ.

But when you begin to live devoutly in Christ, you have entered the winepress. Prepare yourself for pressure; but do not be dry, lest nothing come out of the pressure.

### 5. [vv. 3–4]

“My enemies have trampled me down all day long.” [Col. 0650] Those who have become far from the saints are themselves my enemies. “All day long”: this has already been explained.

“From the height of day.” What does “from the height of day” mean? Perhaps it is something difficult to understand. No wonder, since it is the height of day. Perhaps they became far from the saints for this reason: they could not penetrate the height of the day, whose twelve hours are the shining Apostles.

Therefore, those who crucified him as though he were merely a man went astray in the day. But why did they suffer darkness, so that they became far from the saints? Because the day was shining on high, and they did not recognize the one hidden on high. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “was hidden”; another, conversely, has “shining” in place of “hidden.”] For if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II, 8).

Struck back, then, by this height of day and made far from the saints, they became enemies who afflict and trample, as though they were grapes in the winepress.

There is another interpretation: “From the height of day my enemies have trampled me down all day long,” that is, throughout all time. “From the height of day”—that is, from temporal pride. For when they trample, they are exalted; those who are trampled are humble, while those who trample are exalted. But do not fear the height of those who trample you. It is the height of the day; it is temporal, not eternal.

### 6

“For many who fight against me will fear.” When will they fear? When the day on which they are exalted has passed. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “when the days that are exalted have passed.”] For they are exalted only for a time; when the time of their exaltation has ended, they will fear.

“But I will hope in you, Lord.”

He does not say, “But I will not fear”; rather: “Many who fight against me will fear.” When that day of judgment comes, then all the tribes of the earth will mourn (Matt. XXV, 31). When the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven, then all the saints will be secure.

That which they hoped for, desired, and prayed would come will come for them. But no opportunity for repentance will remain for the others, because during the time when repentance could have been fruitful, they hardened their hearts against the Lord who warned them.

Will they perhaps build a wall even against God when he judges? Recognize the piety expressed here, and, if you are in that body [Note: the editions read, “in his body”], imitate it.

After saying, “Many who fight against me will fear,” he did not add, “But I will not fear.” Had he attributed his freedom from fear to his own strength, he too would have been among those exalted in temporal things and, through temporal pride, would not have been worthy to reach everlasting rest. Instead, he made you understand from where he would not fear: “But I will hope in you, Lord.” He did not state his presumption, but the reason for his presumption.

For if I do not fear, I may also not fear through hardness of heart; many people, through excessive pride, fear nothing. Let Your Charity attend: bodily health is one thing, bodily insensibility another, and bodily immortality another.

Perfect health is indeed immortality, but in a certain sense the health we possess in this life is also called health. When no illness affects him, each person is called healthy; when the physician examines him, he is pronounced healthy; and when someone begins to fall ill, that health is disturbed. When he is healed, he returns to that same health.

Consider, then, and distinguish three conditions of the body: health, insensibility, and immortality.

Health has no illness, but when it is touched and troubled, it feels pain. Insensibility, however, does not feel pain: it has lost the sense of pain, and is more insensible in proportion as it is worse. Immortality, again, does not feel pain, because all corruption has been taken away; “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53–54).

There is therefore no pain in an immortal body, and no pain in an insensible body. But let the insensible person not think that he is already immortal. The health of one who feels pain is nearer to immortality than the insensibility of one who feels nothing.

You may find a proud person, with the most arrogant conceit, who has persuaded himself that he fears nothing. Do you think him stronger than the one who says, “Outside were battles, inside fears” (II Cor. VII, 5), or stronger than our very head, the Lord our God, who said, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38)?

He is not stronger. Do not be pleased by his insensibility. He has not been clothed with immortality; he has been deprived of sensation.

You, however, should have a soul that is not without feeling. For those who are without feeling have been condemned. Speak from the sense of health: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not aflame?” (II Cor. XI, 29). [Col. 0651; Note: The editions read “of weakness”; several manuscripts read “of the weak person”; others, “the ruin of one who is weak,” or “the peril of one made weak.”]

If the ruin of every weak person did not concern him, would he appear, as though rigid and without pain, to be better? Far from it: that would be insensibility, not tranquility.

Certainly, brothers, when we come to that place, that seat, that blessedness, that heavenly homeland where our soul will be filled with security, rest, and everlasting happiness, there will be no pain, because there will be nothing from which pain can arise.

“Many,” he says, “who fight against me will fear.” Even those who are now insensible and fear nothing will one day fear. For a terror will come so great that it will shatter and crush all hardness.

“Many who fight against me will fear. But I will hope in you, Lord.”

### 7. [v. 5]

“In God I will praise my words; in God I hoped” [several manuscripts read, “I will hope”]. “I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

Why? Because I will hope in God. Why? Because in God I will praise my words.

If you praise your words in yourself, I will not say that you should not fear; it is impossible for you not to fear. For either you will have lying words, and they will be yours precisely because they are lies; or, if your words are true and you think that you possess them not from God but speak them from yourself, they will be true, but you will be a liar.

But if you recognize that you can say nothing true in God’s wisdom and in the faith of truth except what you have received from him of whom it is said, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7), then “in God you praise your words,” so that you may be praised in God’s words.

For if what belongs to God in you is honored by you, then you, having been made by God, will be honored in God. But if you honor what belongs to God in you as though it were yours and not God’s, how will you not be far from the Holy One, just as that people became far from the saints?

Therefore: “In God I will praise my words.” If they are in God, why are they mine? They are both in God and mine. They are in God because they come from him; they are mine because I received them.

He who gave them wished them to be mine, since I love the one whose they are. Because they are from him, they have become mine.

Why, then, do we say, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. VI, 11)? In what sense is it “ours”? In what sense do we say “give”? By asking him, you will not be empty; by confessing that it is yours, you will not be ungrateful.

For if you do not call it yours, you have not received it. But if you call it yours in such a way that what you call yours seems to come from you, you lose what you had received, because you are ungrateful to him from whom you had received it.

Therefore, “in God I will praise my words,” because there he is himself the source of true words; “mine,” because I came thirsty and drank.

“In God I will praise my words; in God I hoped. I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

Were you not the one who shortly before said: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for man has trampled me down; all day long, fighting against me, he has afflicted me”? How, then, do you now say: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me”?

What will it do to you? You yourself said a moment ago: “He has trampled me down; he has afflicted me.” Will it do nothing when it does these things?

He looked toward the wine flowing from the pressing and answered: “Certainly he has trampled me; certainly he has afflicted me. But what will he do to me? I was a grape; I will be wine. In God I hoped; I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

### 8. [v. 6]

“All day long they abominated my words.”

That is how they are; you know it. Speak the truth, preach the truth, announce Christ to the pagans, announce the Church to heretics, announce salvation to everyone: they contradict and abominate my words.

But when they abominate my words, whom do we think they abominate, if not the one in whom I will praise my words?
