“All day long they abominated my words.” Let it at least be enough for them to abominate the words; let them go no further. Let them criticize and reject them. Far from it.

Why do I say this? When they reject and abominate the words that flow from the fountain of truth, what will they do to the one through whom those words are spoken? What, except what follows: “All their designs against me are for evil”?

If they abominate the bread itself, how will they spare the vessel in which it is served? “All their designs against me are for evil.”

If they treated the Lord himself in this way, let the body that follows its head not disdain to suffer what preceded in the head, so that the body may cling to the head.

Your Lord was despised, and you want to be honored by those who have become far from the saints? Do not claim for yourself what did not first occur in him. “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master” (Matt. X, 24–25).

“If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household?” “All their designs against me are for evil.”

### 9. [v. 7]

“They will sojourn and hide themselves.”

To sojourn is to live as a foreigner. Those who inhabit a homeland that is not theirs are called sojourners.

Every human being is a stranger in this life. In this life, as you see, we are clothed with flesh, and through this flesh the heart cannot be seen. Therefore the Apostle says: “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes; he will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts, and then each one will receive praise from God” (I Cor. IV, 5).

Before this happens, in this pilgrimage of bodily life, each person carries his own heart, and every heart is closed to every other heart.

Therefore these people, whose designs against him are for evil, “will sojourn and hide themselves,” because they are still in this pilgrimage and carry flesh. They conceal deceit in their hearts; whatever evil they think, they hide.

Why? Because this life is still a pilgrimage. Let them hide: what they hide will appear, and they themselves will not remain hidden.

There is another interpretation of this hiddenness, which perhaps will be more pleasing. For among those who have become far from the saints, certain hypocrites enter secretly and inflict worse tribulations on Christ’s body, because they are not avoided as completely alien.

The Apostle recalls the more serious dangers that came from them when, listing his many sufferings, he said: “In dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea”—and then: “dangers among false brothers” (II Cor. XI, 26).

These are exceedingly dangerous people, of whom it is said in another psalm: “And they entered in to see” (Ps. XL, 7). They entered in to see, and no one says, “Do not enter in to see.” [Note: Some manuscripts read, “you enter.”]

For he enters as though he were your own; he is not guarded against as a stranger. Therefore these people “will sojourn and hide themselves.”

Because they enter the great house in this manner, without intending to remain there, they will sojourn. The Lord wished such sinners to be understood as servants, according to the Gospel interpretation in which everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. He says: “A slave does not remain in the house forever, but a son remains forever” (John VIII, 34–35).

Whoever enters as a son will not be a sojourner, because he will persevere to the end (Matt. X, 22; XXIV, 13). Whoever enters as a servant—deceitful, sinful, attentive only to appearances, looking for what he may seize, or what he may accuse or blame—enters as a sojourner, not to dwell and persevere.

Yet let us not fear these people, brothers: “In God I hoped; I will not fear what flesh can do to me.” Even if they sojourn, even if they enter, even if they pretend, even if they hide, they are flesh. You hope in the Lord; flesh will do nothing to you.

But it brings tribulation; it brings trampling. The wine comes forth because the grape is pressed. Your tribulation will not be fruitless. Another person sees you and imitates you, because you too, in order to learn to endure such things, looked upon your head: that first cluster, into whom the betrayer Judas entered in to see, sojourned, and hid.

Therefore do not fear all those who enter with a false heart, sojourn, and hide. Their father Judas was with your Lord, and he knew him. Although Judas the betrayer sojourned and hid, his heart lay open to the Lord of all things. Knowing him, the Lord chose one from whom he could provide consolation for you, who do not know whom to avoid.

He could have not chosen Judas, because he knew Judas. For he said to the disciples: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John VI, 71).

Was the devil, then, also chosen? Or, if he was not chosen, how did he choose twelve rather than eleven? He too was chosen, but for another purpose. Eleven were chosen for the work of testing; one was chosen for the work of temptation.

How could he give you an example, since you did not know which evil people to avoid, which false and hypocritical people—those who sojourn and hide—to beware of? He could say to you: “Behold, I had one of them with me.” He went before you as an example; I endured him and was willing to bear what I knew, so that I might provide consolation for you, who did not know.

“What he did to me, he will also do to you,” insofar as he has power and rages greatly. He will accuse you and bring false charges. “Will falsehoods prevail?” [Most manuscripts read, “false witnesses.”] Will they prevail against you, when they did not prevail against me?

They certainly prevailed against me, but they did not take heaven away from me. His flesh, already buried, endured false witnesses. It was not enough for him to endure them in the judgment; he endured them even in the tomb.

They accepted money in order to lie, and said: “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. XXVIII, 13).

Yet the Jews were so blind that they believed an entirely unbelievable statement: they believed sleeping witnesses! Either it was false that they had slept, in which case they ought not to have believed liars; or it was true that they had slept, in which case they did not know what had happened.

“They will sojourn and hide.” Let them sojourn and hide. What will they do? “In God I hoped; I will not fear what flesh can do to me.”

### 10 [Col. 0654]

“They will watch my heel.”

Indeed, they will sojourn and hide in such a way as to watch where a person slips. They are intent upon the heel, waiting for a fall, so that they may seize the foot for ruin or place their foot in the way as a stumbling block—in any case, so that they may find something to accuse.

And who walks in such a way that he never slips? Certainly a person slips quickly, if nowhere else, in speech. For it is written: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James III, 2).

Who, then, would dare to say or think that he is perfect? It is therefore necessary that someone slip in speech.

But those who sojourn and hide snare every word, looking everywhere for traps and twisting accusations. By these they become entangled before those whom they attempt to entangle, so that they are caught and perish before they can catch and destroy others.

For a person returns to his own heart, and from there returns to God, and knows how to say: “In God I will praise my words.”

Whatever good I have said, whatever true thing I have said, I have said from God [the editions read, “I have said to God.” But the manuscripts read, “I have said from God”; a similar manner of expression is found above in *Expositions on the Psalms* 49.23 in some manuscripts: “If you hear good things, you hear God’s things.]. Whatever else I may have said that I ought not to have said, I said as a human being, but I said it under God.

He strengthens the one who walks, threatens the one who strays, forgives the one who acknowledges his fault, recalls the tongue, and recalls the one who has fallen. “The righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked will be weakened by evils” (Prov. XXIV, 16).

Therefore none of us should fear cunning pursuers, word-snare hunters, people who count almost every syllable, and transgressors of commandments. He watches for what he may accuse in you; he does not watch in order to believe Christ through you.

Attend to the words of the person whom you criticize, lest he perhaps teach you something salutary. “And what salutary thing,” he says, “could he teach me, since he has slipped so badly in speech?” Perhaps this very thing is what he teaches you for your salvation: not to be a hunter of words, but a gatherer of commandments.

“They will watch my heel.”

### 11

“As my soul has endured.”

I say what I have endured. He was speaking as one who had experienced it: “As my soul has endured.”

“They will sojourn and hide.” Let my soul endure them all: those barking outside [Note: Am. and some manuscripts read, “robbers”] and those hiding within.

The temptation that comes from outside approaches like a river. [Note: The manuscripts read, “Coming from outside”; the editions read, “let it endure those coming from outside.”] Let it find you on a rock; let it strike against you but not cast you down. “The house was founded upon the rock” (Matt. VII, 25).

There is also one within: let him sojourn and hide. Let the chaff come near you; let the threshing oxen enter; let the threshing instrument of temptations enter. You are purified, while the chaff is crushed.

### 12. [v. 8]

“As my soul has endured, for nothing you will save them.” [Col. 0655]

He also taught us to pray for them. They will indeed sojourn and hide; they are deceitful, hypocritical, and treacherous. You should pray for them, and do not say: “Will God correct such a person—so evil and so perverse?”

Do not despair. Consider whom you are asking, not for whom you are asking. You see the magnitude of the disease, but you do not see the physician’s power.

“They will sojourn and hide: as my soul has endured.” Endure and pray. And what happens? “For nothing you will save them.”

You will save them in such a way that it will be nothing for you, that is, no labor for you. They are desperate in human eyes, but you heal by your word. You will not labor in healing them, although we may be astonished when we look upon them.

There is another meaning in the verse, “For nothing you will save them”: you will save them without any preceding merits of theirs.

“I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer and a persecutor and an insolent man” (I Tim. I, 13). He received letters from the priests so that wherever he found Christians, he might bind and bring them in (Acts IX, 2). Certainly, in order to bind and bring them in, he first sojourned and hid.

No good merits, therefore, had preceded him. Rather, such things had preceded him that he deserved condemnation. He brought nothing good, and yet he was saved.

“For nothing you will save them.” They will not bring goats, rams, or bulls to you; they will not bring gifts and spices [most manuscripts read, “ornaments”] into your temple; they will not pour over you some offering from a good conscience. Everything in them is rough, foul, and detestable. And when they bring nothing to you by which they may be saved, “for nothing you will save them”—that is, by your grace freely given.

What had the thief brought to the cross? From the place of his robberies (*de fauce*) to judgment, from judgment to the wood, from the wood to paradise (Luke XXIII, 43). [Note: Some manuscripts read *de falce* (“from the sickle”); *de fauce* is better attested, referring to the place where he practiced robbery. Thus also in *Homilies on the Gospel of John*, Tractate [lacuna], no. 12: “The thief who comes out to the haunt to kill a man.”] “He believed, and therefore he spoke” (Ps. CXV, 10). But who gave him that very faith, except the one who hung beside him?

“For nothing you will save them.”

### 13

“In anger you will lead the peoples.”

You are angry and you lead them; you rage and you save; you terrify and you call.

What does “In anger you will lead the peoples” mean? You fill all things with tribulations, so that people placed amid tribulations may return to you, lest they be led astray by pleasures and perverted security.

Your anger appears, but it is paternal anger. A father becomes angry with a son who despises his instructions: in his anger he slaps him, beats him, pulls his ear, takes him by the hand, and leads him to school.

“In anger you will lead the peoples.” How many have entered, how many have filled the house of the Lord, led in his anger—that is, terrified by tribulations and filled with faith!

For tribulation agitates for this purpose: to empty the vessel that is full of wickedness, so that it may be filled with grace.

“In anger you will lead the peoples.”

### 14. [v. 9]

[Col. 0656]

“God, I have declared my life to you.”

You made me live, and for this reason I declare my life to you. Did God truly not know what he had given? What does it mean that you declare it to him? Do you wish to teach God? Far from it.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “I have declared it to you”? Perhaps it means: “Because what I have declared about my life benefits you.” And what benefit does it bring God? It benefits God in his gains.

“I have declared my life to God,” because God made me live. How did the Apostle Paul declare his life when he said, “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor and an insolent man”? Let him declare his life: “But I received mercy” (I Tim. I, 13).

He declared his life not to himself but to him, because he declared it in such a way that God would be believed—not for his own gain, but for God’s gain.

For what does Paul himself say? “Christ died and rose again for this reason: so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for all” (II Cor. V, 15).

If, therefore, you live and do not live from yourself, because he enabled you to live, declare your life not to yourself but to him. Do not seek your own interests or live for yourself, but for him who died for all.

For what does the same Apostle say about certain reprobates? “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II, 21).

If you declare your life so that it may benefit you and not benefit others, you declare it to yourself, not to God. But if you declare your life in such a way that you invite others also to receive the life that you received, you declare your life to him from whom you received it, and you will have a greater reward, because you have not proved ungrateful for what you received.

“God, I have declared my life to you. You have placed my tears in your sight. You heard me when I prayed to you, just as in your promise.”

Because you had promised this, you did it. You said that you would hear the one who wept; I believed, I wept, and I was heard. I found you merciful in promising and truthful in fulfilling.

“Just as in your promise.”

### 15. [v. 10]

“Let my enemies be turned backward.”

This benefits them; he does not wish them evil. For they wish to go ahead, and for this reason they do not wish to be corrected.

You warn your enemy to live well and correct himself. He despises and rejects your word: “Look at the person admonishing me! From whom am I going to hear the commandments by which I should live?” He wants to go ahead of you, and by going ahead he is not corrected.

He does not attend to the fact that your words are not yours. He does not attend to the fact that you declare your life to God, not to yourself.

By going ahead, therefore, he is not corrected. It is good for him to be turned backward and to follow the one whom he wished to precede.

The Lord was speaking to his disciples about his future passion. Peter was horrified and said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this will not happen.” Shortly before, he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Having confessed him as God, he feared that he would die as a man.

But the Lord had come in order to suffer; indeed, we could not otherwise be saved unless we were redeemed by his blood. Shortly before Peter’s confession [the editions read, “Peter”], he had praised it and said:

“Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

Observe how he followed up the true, devout, and confident confession, since Peter had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

But immediately, when the Lord began to speak about his passion, Peter feared that he would perish by dying, although we would perish unless he died. He said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this will not happen.”

And the Lord said to the one to whom he had shortly before said, “Blessed are you, and upon this rock I will build my Church”: “Go behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me.”

Why, then, was he called Satan, when shortly before he had been called blessed and the rock?

“For you do not think the things that are mine,” he said, “but those that are human” (Matt. XVI, 16–23).

Shortly before, Peter had thought the things of God, because it was not flesh and blood that had revealed them to him, but the Father in heaven. When he praised the word in God, he was not Satan but Peter, from the rock. But when he spoke from himself and from human weakness, through a carnal human affection that would impede his own salvation and that of others, he was called Satan.

Why? Because he wanted to go ahead of the Lord and give earthly advice to the heavenly Leader.

“Far be it from you, Lord; this will not happen.”

You say, “Far be it,” and you say, “Lord.” Certainly, if he is Lord, he acts with authority; if he is teacher, he knows what he is doing and knows what he is teaching.

But you want to lead the leader, teach the teacher, command the Lord, and make requests of God [Note: the editions read “give orders”; the manuscripts read “make requests”]. You are going far ahead; go behind.

Was this not also beneficial for those enemies? “Let my enemies be turned backward”—but let them not remain backward. Let them be turned backward for this reason: not to go ahead, but to follow, not to remain behind.

“Let my enemies be turned backward.”

### 16

[Col. 0657]

“On whatever day I call upon you, behold, I know that you are my God.”

Great knowledge! He does not say, “I know that you are God,” but, “I know that you are my God.”

He is yours when he helps you; he is yours when you are not alienated from him. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God.”

Why say, “whose”? Whose is he not? He is indeed the God of all, but he is properly called the God of those who love him, hold fast to him, possess him, and worship him—as though they were members of his household, his great family, redeemed by the great blood of his only Son.

How much God has given us, so that we might belong to him and he might be ours!

But the foreigners who have become far from the saints are foreign sons. See what is said about them in another psalm:

“Lord, deliver me,” he says, “from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.”

And observe their height—but the height of the day, that is, temporal pride:

“Whose sons are like young plants firmly established; their daughters adorned like the likeness of a temple. Their storerooms are full, overflowing from one thing to another; their oxen are fat; their sheep are fertile, multiplying in their offspring; there is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no cry in their streets.”

And what follows? “They called that people blessed which possesses these things.”

But who called them blessed? The foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity.

What do you say? “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. CXLIII, 11–15).

He removed all the other things that God gives and gave God himself.

For all those things, brothers, that the foreign sons mentioned, God gives. He gives them also to foreigners; he gives them also to the wicked; he gives them also to blasphemers. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and he sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V, 45). [Col. 0658]

Sometimes he gives these things to the good, and sometimes he does not give them. Sometimes he gives them to the wicked, and sometimes he does not give them. Yet to the good he reserves himself, while for the wicked he reserves everlasting fire.

There is therefore an evil that he does not give to the good, and there is a good that he does not give to the wicked. There are certain intermediate things, both good and bad, which he gives to both the good and the wicked.

17. Let us therefore love God, brothers, purely and chastely. The heart is not chaste if it worships God for a reward. What, then? Shall we have no reward from the worship of God? Certainly we shall—but God himself, whom we worship. He himself will be our reward, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Observe [Note: [Col. 0658] Some manuscripts read, “how great.”] that you will obtain a reward. What does our Lord Jesus Christ say to those who love him? “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him.” What, then, will you give him? “And I will show myself to him” (John 14:23).

If you do not love, it is little enough; but if you love, if you sigh for him, if you worship freely the one by whom you were freely bought—for you had done nothing to merit his redeeming you—if, considering his benefits toward you, you sigh for him and keep your heart restless with desire for him, seek nothing from him apart from himself: he himself is sufficient for you.

However greedy you may be, God is sufficient for you. Greed was seeking to possess the whole earth; add heaven as well: greater is the one who made heaven and earth. I shall say, brothers: in these human marriages, consider what a chaste heart toward God is like. They are certainly human marriages: a man does not love his wife if he loves her because of her dowry; nor does a wife love her husband chastely if she loves him for that reason, because he has given her something, or because he has given her much. The husband who was rich may become poor, yet he remains a husband [Note: [Col. 0658] So the better manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “he gave much, and the rich husband gave, and he became a poor husband,” etc.]. How many men, proscribed and dispossessed, have been loved even more by their chaste wives? Many chaste marriages have been tested by the husbands’ misfortunes: lest they be thought to love anything other than their husbands, the wives not only did not abandon them but served them all the more devotedly.

If, then, a human husband is loved freely, if he is loved chastely; and if a human wife is loved freely, if she is loved chastely—how ought God to be loved, the true and truthful husband of the soul, making it fruitful for offspring of eternal life and not allowing us to remain barren? Let us therefore love him in such a way that nothing besides him is loved; and let what we have said, what we have sung, come to pass in us, since here too our voice is heard: “On whatever day I call upon you, behold, I know that you are my God.” This is to call upon God: to call upon him freely.

Accordingly, what has been said about certain people? “They did not call upon the Lord.” They seemed to themselves to be calling upon the Lord; and they asked him for inheritances, for an increase of wealth, for the prolongation of this life, and for other temporal things. And what does Scripture say about them? “They did not call upon the Lord.” Therefore what follows? “There they feared with fear, where there was no fear” (Psalm 13:5). What does “where there was no fear” mean? They feared lest their money be taken from them, lest something in their household become less, and finally lest they have fewer years in this life than they hoped for themselves. Thus they trembled with fear where there was no fear.

Such were those Jews: “If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). There they feared with fear where there was no fear. “Behold, I know that you are my God.” Great are the riches of the heart, great the light of the inner eye, great the confidence of security! “Behold, I know that you are my God.”

18. [verse 11.] “In God I shall praise the word; in the Lord I shall praise the utterance. In God I hoped” [Note: [Col. 0659] Several manuscripts read, “I shall hope.”]; “I shall not fear what man can do to me.” This is now the same meaning that was repeated above.

19. [verse 12.] “In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall repay as praise to you.” “Make vows, and repay them to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75:12). What vows are you to make, what are you to repay? Perhaps those animals that were once offered at the altars? Offer nothing of that kind: in you is what you should vow and repay. From the treasury of your heart bring forth the incense of praise; from the storehouse of a good conscience bring forth the sacrifice of faith. Whatever you bring forth, set it ablaze with love. Let the vows that you repay in praise to God be within you.

Praise of what kind? What has he bestowed upon you? “Because you have delivered my soul from death.” This is that life which he declares to him: “O God, I have declared my life to you.” For what was I? Dead. By myself I was dead; through you, what am I? Alive. Therefore, “in me, O God, are your vows, which I shall repay as praise to you.”

Behold, I love my God; no one takes him from me. What I give him no one takes from me, because it is enclosed in my heart. With good reason it is said in that earlier confidence: “What can man do to me?” Let man rage; let him be permitted to rage; let him be permitted to accomplish what he attempts. What can he take away? Gold, silver, cattle, male servants, female servants, estates, houses—let him take everything. Can he take away the vows that are within me, which I shall repay as praise to God?

The tempter was permitted to test the holy man Job. In a single moment he took away everything; he stripped him of whatever possessions he had, took away his inheritance, and killed his heirs—not little by little, but all together, in one blow, in one assault, so that everything was reported suddenly. After everything had been taken away, Job alone remained. But within him were vows of praise that he could repay to God; indeed, they were within him. The thief, the devil, had not invaded the treasury of his holy breast: he was full of what he could offer in sacrifice.

Hear what he possessed; hear what he brought forth: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:12–21). O inner riches, where no thief can enter! God himself had given what he received; God himself had enriched him with what he offered to the one he loved.

God seeks your praise; God seeks your confession. Are you going to give something from your field? He himself sent the rain so that you might have it. Are you going to give something from your treasury? He himself established what you are going to give. What are you going to give that you did not receive from him? “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). Will you give from your heart? He himself gave faith, hope, and love. This is what you are going to bring forth; this is what you are going to sacrifice.

But the enemy can take all those other things from you against your will; this he cannot take away unless you are willing. You will lose those things even unwillingly: if you want to possess gold, you will lose your gold; if you want to possess a house, you will lose your house. No one loses faith except the one who has despised it.

[Col. 0660] 20. [verse 13.] “In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall repay as praise to you, because you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from slipping, so that I may please before God in the light of the living.”

With good reason he does not please the alien sons, who are far removed from the holy, because they do not possess the light of the living, by which they may see what pleases God. The light of the living is the light of the immortal, the light of the holy. Whoever is not in darkness pleases in the light of the living.

A person and the things that belong to him are observed, but no one knows what he is like; God sees what he is like. Sometimes even the devil himself does not know it: unless he tests a person, he does not discover it, as happened with the man whom I have just mentioned. God knew him and bore witness concerning him; the devil did not know him, and therefore said, “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

See what the enemy is challenging: there is perfection there. See what the enemy alleges. He saw a man serving God, obeying him in everything, doing everything well; and because he was rich and his household was exceedingly prosperous, he alleges that the man worships God for this reason, because God had given him all these things: “Does Job worship God for nothing?”

For him to worship God freely—this was the true light, this was the light of the living. God saw in the heart of his servant that his worship was freely offered. That heart pleased in the sight of the Lord, in the light of the living; it was hidden from the devil, because he was in darkness.

God admitted the tempter, not so that he might learn what God already knew, but so that he might provide us with something to know and imitate. For if the tempter had not been admitted, would we ourselves have seen in Job what we ought and wished to imitate? The tempter was admitted; he took everything away. Job remained alone—without possessions, alone without his household, alone without his children, but full of God.

His wife, to be sure, was left behind. Do you think the devil was merciful because he left him his wife? He knew the means by which he had deceived Adam. He had left him his own helper—not a comforter of her husband.

He, therefore, full of God, in whom were vows that he would repay as praise, so that he might show that he worshipped God freely and not because he had received so many things, was such a man after losing everything because he had not lost the one who had given him everything: “The Lord gave,” he says, “and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Even when struck with a wound from head to foot, he remained whole within. He answered the tempter from the light of the living, from the light of his heart: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks” (Job 2:10)—that is, as one who does not possess the light of the living. For the light of the living is wisdom, and the darkness of the foolish is folly.

“You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks”: you see my flesh, but you do not see the light of my heart. She could then have loved her husband more, if she had known the inner beauty and looked to see where he was beautiful before the eyes of God, because within him were vows that he would repay as praise to God.

How had the enemy not invaded that inheritance! How whole was what he possessed, and for the fuller possession of which he hoped as he went from virtue to virtue!

Therefore, brothers, let all these things serve this purpose for us: that we may love God freely, hope always in him, and fear neither man nor the devil. Neither the one nor the other does anything unless permitted; and nothing can be permitted against us except what benefits us.

Let us endure the wicked and be good, because we too were once wicked. “God will freely save all those of whom we dare to despair” [Note: [Col. 0661] The editions read, “of whom we ought not to despair.” The manuscripts, however, read, “of whom we dare to despair.”]. Therefore let us despair of no one; let us pray for all whom we endure; let us never depart from God.

Let he himself be our inheritance; let he himself be our hope; let he himself be our salvation. Here let him be our comforter, there our giver of rewards, everywhere our giver of life and the giver of life—not of another life, but of that life of which it was said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)—so that here, in the light of faith, and there, in the light of vision, as in the light of the living, we may please in the sight of the Lord.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 56. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. We have just heard in the Gospel, brothers, how greatly our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ loves us—God with the Father, man among us, from among us ourselves, now at the right hand of the Father. You have heard how greatly he loves us. For he himself both stated the measure of his love and imposed it upon us, saying that his commandment is that we love one another (John 13:34).

And lest we should inquire, doubting and agitated, how greatly we ought to love one another, and what that perfect measure of love is which pleases God—for that measure is perfect beyond which nothing greater can be—the Lord himself expressed and taught it, saying: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:12).

He himself did what he taught; the Apostles did what they learned from him, and proclaimed that we too should do it. Let us do so as well; for although, according to what he created us to be, we are not what he is, yet according to what he became for us, we are what he is. And if he alone had done this, perhaps none of us ought to dare imitate him; for he was man in such a way that he was also God. But in what he was as man, servants imitated the Lord, disciples the Master, and those who preceded us in his household did so—our fathers, indeed, but nevertheless our fellow servants. God would not command us to do this if he judged that it was impossible for a human being to accomplish it.

But, considering your weakness, do you fail beneath the command? Take strength from the example. Yet is the example itself too great for you? The one who provided the example is present also to provide help.

Let us therefore hear in this psalm—for it has happened opportunely, and through his providence, that the Gospel should harmonize with it—an affirmation of Christ’s love. He laid down his life for us, so that we too might lay down our lives for our brothers (1 John 4:16).

This psalm agrees and harmonizes with the Gospel, so that we may see how our Lord himself laid down his life for us; for this psalm sings of his Passion. And since the whole Christ is the head and the body, as I do not doubt you know well—the head is our Savior himself, who suffered under Pontius Pilate and now, after rising from the dead, sits at the right hand of the Father; his body is the Church—not this or that church, but the Church spread throughout the whole world; and not only the Church now present in human beings living the present life, but also those belonging to it who lived before us and those who will come after us until the end of the age.

The whole Church, consisting of all the faithful—for all the faithful are members of Christ—has that head placed in heaven, governing his body. Although separated from it in sight, it is joined to it by love.

Therefore, since the whole Christ is the head and his body, let us hear in all the Psalms the voices of the head in such a way that we also hear the voices of the body. He did not wish to speak separately, because he did not wish to be separated, saying: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). If he is with us, he speaks in us, he speaks about us, he speaks through us; and we too speak in him. Therefore we speak the truth, because we speak in him. For whenever we wish to speak in and from ourselves, we shall remain in falsehood.

2. [verse 1.] Since this psalm sings of the Lord’s Passion, see what title it bears: “For the end.” Christ is the end (Romans 10:4). Why is he called the end? Not one who brings to an end by destroying, but one who brings to completion. To consume is to destroy; to complete is to perfect.

Whatever we call finished, we call so from its end. But we say one thing when we say, “The bread is finished,” and another when we say, “The tunic is finished.” The bread is finished because it was eaten; the tunic is finished because it was woven. The bread, therefore, is finished so that it may be consumed; the tunic is finished so that it may be completed.

Christ, then, is the end of our purpose, because however much we strive, we are perfected in him and by him. Our perfection is to reach him. But when you have reached him, you seek no further: he is your end.

Just as the end of your journey is the place toward which you are traveling, and when you reach it you will remain there, so the end of your pursuit, your purpose, your effort, and your intention is the one toward whom you are traveling. When you have reached him, you will desire nothing further, because you will have nothing better. Thus, in this life he has set before us an example of how to live, and in the future life he will give the reward of living.

3. “For the end; do not corrupt; for David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.”

When we refer ourselves to Holy Scripture, we find that holy David, that king of Israel from whom the Psalter of David also received its name, suffered persecution from Saul, king of that same people (1 Samuel 24:1–4), as many of you know, who have either read or heard the Scriptures.

David the king, then, had Saul as his persecutor. One was exceedingly gentle, the other exceedingly ferocious; one mild, the other envious; one patient, the other cruel; one beneficent, the other ungrateful. David endured him with such gentleness that, when Saul had fallen into his hands, David did not touch or harm him.

For the Lord God had given David the power, if he wished, to kill Saul; but he chose to spare rather than to kill. Saul, however, was not overcome even by such a benefit, so as to cease persecuting him.

We therefore find that at that time, when Saul was persecuting David, the future and predestined king fled from the face of Saul—the king already rejected—into the cave.

What does this have to do with Christ? If everything that happened then was a figure of things to come, we find Christ there, and all the more clearly. For the words, “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title,” do not seem to me to refer to that David. No title had been inscribed upon David himself which Saul wished to corrupt.

But in the Lord’s Passion we see that a title was written: “King of the Jews,” so that this title might reproach their foreheads, because they did not spare their king. Saul was in them; David was in Christ.

For Christ, as the apostolic Gospel says—and as we know and confess—is “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3; Matthew 1:1). According to his divinity, however, he is above David, above all human beings, above heaven and earth, above the angels, above all visible and invisible things, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

Yet he deigned to become man and came to us from the seed of David, because he was born from the tribe of David, from which came the virgin Mary who bore Christ (Luke 1:27; 2:4).

That title, then, was inscribed: “King of the Jews.” Saul, as we have said, was the Jewish people; David was Christ. The title there was: “King of the Jews.”

The Jews were indignant because the title “King of the Jews” had been inscribed. They were ashamed to have as king the one whom they had been able to crucify. For they did not see that the very cross on which they fixed him would one day be on the foreheads of kings.

When they were therefore indignant at that title, they approached Pilate the judge, to whom they had brought Christ to be killed, and said to him: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but write that he himself said, ‘I am king of the Jews.’”

And because it had already been sung through the Holy Spirit, “For the end; do not corrupt the inscription of the title,” Pilate answered them: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:19–22). Why do you suggest falsehood to me? I do not corrupt the truth.

4. We have heard, then, what is meant by “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title.” What, then, does “when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave” mean?

That David too did this; but because we do not find an inscription of a title in his case, let us find in this one the flight into the cave. That cave in which David concealed himself signified something. Why did he conceal himself? So that he might be hidden and not found.

What does it mean to be covered by a cave? To be covered by earth. For one who flees into a cave is covered by earth so that he may not be seen.

Jesus, however, was carrying earth—the flesh that he had received from earth—and in it he was concealing himself, so that God would not be found by the Jews. For “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had hidden himself in a cave—that is, he presented the weakness of his flesh to their eyes, while he concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as though hidden in the earth.

Not recognizing God, they therefore crucified a man. He could neither die nor be crucified except in his humanity; for he could not be held except in his humanity. To those who wickedly sought him he presented earth; to those who sought life rightly he preserved it.

According to the flesh, therefore, he fled into the cave from the face of Saul. If you wish to understand this also as the Lord’s fleeing into a cave from the face of Saul because he suffered, he concealed himself from the Jews to such an extent that he even died.

However fiercely the Jews raged against him until he died, they still thought that he might be delivered and might show by some miracle that he was the Son of God. This had been foretold in the Book of Wisdom: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death; for there will be regard for him because of his words. For if he is truly the son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies” (Wisdom 2:20, 18).

Because he was crucified and not delivered, they believed that he was not the Son of God. Therefore, mocking him as he hung upon the wood and shaking their heads, they said to him: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:40, 42).

By saying these things, they “thought these things and went astray; for their malice blinded them” (Wisdom 2:21).

For what great thing was it to come down from the cross for one to whom it was easy to rise from the tomb? But why [Note: [Col. 0664] The editions read, “Why? Because he wished,” etc. The word “because” is absent from the manuscripts.] did he wish to remain patient even unto death? “So that he might flee from the face of Saul into the cave.”

The cave can indeed be understood as the lower part of the earth. And certainly it is evident and certain to all that his body was placed in a tomb cut out of rock. That tomb, then, was a cave; there he fled from the face of Saul.

The Jews persecuted him until he was placed in the cave. How do we prove that they persecuted him until he was placed there? They pierced him with a lance even after he was dead and hanging on the cross (John 19:34). But once he had been wrapped and placed in the cave after the burial rites had been completed, they had nothing more they could do to his flesh.

The Lord therefore rose unharmed and incorrupt from that cave into which he had fled from the face of Saul, concealing himself from the impious whom Saul prefigured, but revealing himself to his members.

For the members of his body touched the members of the risen one: his Apostles touched him when he had risen and believed (Luke 24:39). And behold, Saul’s persecution achieved nothing.

Let us now hear the Psalm, since we have spoken sufficiently about its title, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it.

5. [verse 2.] “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, because my soul has trusted in you.”

Christ, in his Passion, says, “Have mercy on me, O God.” God says to God, “Have mercy on me.” The one who, together with the Father, has mercy on you cries out in you, “Have mercy on me.”

For the fact that he cries out to him, “Have mercy on me,” belongs to you: he received this from you, because for your deliverance he put on flesh.

The flesh itself cries out, “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me”: the man himself, soul and flesh [Note: [Col. 0664] The editions read, “the man himself is soul and flesh.” Delete “is,” in accordance with the manuscripts, and understand “cries out” in its place.].

For the Word assumed the whole human being, and the whole human being became the Word. Let no one therefore suppose that the soul was not there because the Evangelist says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

For “flesh” is used to mean “human being,” as Scripture says elsewhere: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:5; Luke 3:6). Will flesh alone see, and will the soul not be there?

Again, the Lord himself says concerning human beings: “As you gave him power over all flesh” (John 17:2). Did he receive power over flesh alone, and not especially over the souls whom he first delivered?

The soul, therefore, was there; the flesh was there; the whole human being was there. The whole human being was with the Word, and the Word with the human being; and the human being and the Word were one human being, and the Word and the human being one God.

Let him therefore say, “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me.” Let us not be frightened by the voice of one asking for mercy and displaying mercy. He asks for this reason: because he displays it. He became man for this reason: because he is merciful—not so that he might be born by the necessity of his condition, but so that he might free us from the condition of necessity.

“Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, because my soul has trusted in you.”

You hear the Master praying; learn to pray. He prayed for this purpose: to teach us to pray. He suffered for this purpose: to teach us to suffer. He rose for this purpose: to teach us to hope for the resurrection.

6. “And in the shadow of your wings I shall hope, until iniquity passes away.”

The whole Christ has already said this; here it is also our voice. For iniquity has not yet passed away; iniquity is still burning. At the end the Lord himself foretold that iniquity would abound: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:12).

Who, then, will persevere to the end, until iniquity passes away? The one who is in the body of Christ, who is among the members of Christ, and who has learned from the head the patience of perseverance.

You pass away, and behold, your temptations have passed away; and you go into another life, into which the saints have gone, if you have been holy. The martyrs went into another life; if you are a martyr, you too go into another life.

Does iniquity therefore pass away simply because you have passed from here? Other wicked people are born, just as other wicked people die. Just as some wicked people die and others are born, so some righteous people depart and others are born.

Until the end of the age there will be neither a lack of iniquity pressing upon us nor a lack of righteousness enduring. “And in the shadow of your wings I shall hope, until iniquity passes away”: that is, you will protect me, and so that I may not wither from the heat of iniquity, you will provide me with shade.

7. [verse 3.] “I shall cry out to God Most High.”

If he is Most High, how does he hear you crying out? Confidence was born from experience: “The God,” he says, “who has done good to me.”

If he did good to me before I sought him, will he not hear me when I cry out? The Lord our God did good to us by sending us our Savior Jesus Christ, so that he might die for our sins and rise for our justification (Romans 4:25).

For what kind of people did he wish his Son to die? For the ungodly. The ungodly were not seeking God, and they were sought by God.

He is therefore so Most High that our misery and our groaning are not far from him, because “the Lord is near to those who have crushed hearts” (Psalm 33:19).

“I shall cry out to God Most High, to God who has done good to me.”

8. [verses 4–5.] “He sent from heaven and saved me.”

Now the man himself, now the flesh itself, now the Son of God—according to our participation in him—it is manifest that he was saved, and that the Father sent from heaven and saved him. He sent from heaven and raised him up.

But so that you may know that the Lord himself also raised himself up, both things are stated in Scripture: that the Father raised him up, and that he raised himself up.

Hear that the Father raised him up. The Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9).

You have heard of the Father raising and exalting the Son; hear that he himself also raised his flesh. Speaking of the temple, he says to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Evangelist explained what he meant to us: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21).

Now, therefore, in the person of one praying, in the person of a man, in the person of the flesh, he says: “He sent from heaven and saved me.”

9. “He gave those who trample me over to reproach.”

Those who trampled upon him, who mocked him after his death, who crucified him as though he were a man because they did not understand God—he gave them over to reproach.

See whether this has not happened. We do not believe it is still to come; we recognize that it has been fulfilled. The Jews raged against Christ; they grew proud against Christ. Where? In the city of Jerusalem. Where they reigned, there they swelled with pride; there they raised their necks.

After the Lord’s Passion they were uprooted from there, and they lost the kingdom in which they refused to acknowledge Christ as king.

See how they were given over to reproach: they were scattered among all nations, possessing stability nowhere and no secure dwelling anywhere.

But the reason the Jews still exist is so that they may carry our books for their own confusion. When we wish to show the pagans that Christ was prophesied, we produce these Scriptures. And lest those who are slow to believe should perhaps say that we Christians composed them, inventing the Prophets together with the Gospel we preach so that what we preach might appear to have been foretold, we refute them on this point: all the Scriptures in which Christ was prophesied are in the possession of the Jews; the Jews possess all those very Scriptures.

We bring forth books from our enemies in order to confound other enemies. In what kind of reproach, then, are the Jews? A Jew carries the book from which a Christian believes. They have become our librarians, just as slaves are accustomed to carry books behind their masters: the slaves become exhausted from carrying them, while the masters advance by reading them.

The Jews were given over to such reproach, and what had been foretold so long before was fulfilled: “He gave those who trample me over to reproach.”

What a reproach it is, brothers, that they read this verse and yet, blind themselves, look upon their own reflection! The Jews appear in relation to the Holy Scripture they carry just as the face of a blind man appears in a mirror: it is seen by others, but not by him.

“He gave those who trample me over to reproach.”

10. Perhaps when he said, “He sent from heaven and saved me,” you were asking: What did he send from heaven? Whom did he send from heaven?

Did he send an angel to save Christ, so that the Lord would be saved through a servant? For every angel is a serving creature subject to Christ. Angels could be sent to attend upon him; they could be sent to serve him, but not to assist him. It is written that angels ministered to him (Matthew 4:11), not as merciful beings helping one in need, but as subjects of the Almighty.

What, then, did he send from heaven and save me? In another verse we now hear [Note: [Col. 0667] The editions read, “we shall hear.” Most manuscripts read, “we have heard”; some, “we hear.”] what he sent from heaven: “He sent from heaven his mercy and his truth.”

For what purpose? “And he delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs.”

“He sent,” he says, “his mercy and his truth from heaven.” And Christ himself says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6).

Truth, then, was sent to deliver my soul from here, from the midst of lion cubs; mercy was sent. We find Christ himself to be both mercy and truth: mercy, in his compassion toward us; truth, in his recompense to us [Note: [Col. 0667] The editions read, “granting”; in its place we restore “recompensing” from the manuscripts.].

This is therefore what I said shortly before: that he also raised himself up. For if truth raised Christ, and if truth delivered Christ’s soul from the midst of lion cubs, then just as he was merciful in dying for us, so he was truthful in rising for our justification.

He had said that he would rise, and truth could not lie. And because he is truth and truthful, he therefore showed true scars, because he endured true wounds. The disciples held these scars, touched them, and made them known to one another. The one who placed his fingers into the pierced side cried out and said, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

In mercy he had died for him; in truth he had risen for him.

“He sent from heaven his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs.”

Who are the lion cubs? That diminished people, badly deceived and badly led astray by the rulers [Note: [Col. 0667] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “by the chief priests.” The word “priests” is absent from Ambrosianus and the manuscripts.]. The rulers were the lions, and the people the lion cubs. All roared; all killed.

For in the following verses of this psalm we are going to hear also of their slaughter.

11. “And he delivered,” he says, “my soul from the midst of lion cubs.”

Why do you say, “And he delivered my soul”? What had you suffered [Note: [Col. 0667] The editions read, “were you about to suffer?” The manuscripts read, “had you suffered.”], so that your soul needed to be delivered?

“I slept, troubled.”

Christ expressed his death. We certainly read that the other David fled into a cave, but not that he slept in the cave. Another David is in the cave; another David is the one who says, “I slept, troubled.”

We see his disturbance—not because he himself was disturbed, but because they were disturbing him. He said that he was troubled according to the opinion of those who roared, not according to the conscience of one who was yielding.

They thought they had troubled him; they thought they had conquered. But he slept, troubled.

He was so tranquil in his disturbance that he slept whenever he wished. No one who is troubled sleeps: all who are disturbed are either roused from sleep or prevented from falling asleep. But he was troubled and slept.

Great was the humility of the troubled one; great the power of the one sleeping. From what power did it come that he slept? From the power of which he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me; rather, I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:18).

They disturbed him, and he slept.

Adam prefigured him when God cast a deep sleep upon him in order to make a wife for him from his side (Genesis 2:21). Could he not have made a wife for the first man from the side of one who was awake? Or did he wish him to sleep for this reason, so that he would not feel the rib being removed?

Finally, who sleeps in such a way that he does not awaken when a bone is torn from him? He who could remove a rib from a sleeping man without pain could also remove it from one who was awake.

But why did he wish to do it while he slept? Because the Church was made a wife from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross. The side of the one hanging there was pierced by a lance (John 19:34), and the sacraments of the Church flowed forth.

“I slept,” he says, “troubled.”

In another psalm he makes this clear, where he says: “I slept and took sleep.” There he expressed his power. There too he could have said, “I slept,” just as he says here.

What does “I slept” mean? It means: because I wished to, I slept. They did not force me unwillingly into sleep; I slept of my own will, in accordance with this: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.”

Therefore he continues there and says: “I slept and took sleep; and I rose, because the Lord will receive me” (Psalm 3:6).

12. “I slept, troubled.” Why troubled? By whom troubled? Let us see how he brands the Jews’ evil conscience, since they wished to excuse themselves from the killing of the Lord. For, as the Gospel says, they handed him over to the judge so that they themselves might not appear to have killed him. When the judge at that time, Pilate, had said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law,” they replied, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18:31). It is not lawful to kill, but lawful to hand someone over to be killed?

Who, then, killed him? The one who, on hearing the shouting, yielded, or those who by shouting extorted his death? Let the Lord himself testify by whom he was killed—whether by that Pilate who killed him unwillingly. For this reason he even scourged him, clothed him in a garment of disgrace, and brought him out scourged before their eyes, so that, satisfied at least with the punishment of his scourging, they might not extort his death. Therefore, when he saw that they persisted, as we read, he washed his hands and said, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. 27:24).

You may judge whether he was innocent who at least yielded to those shouting; but much more guilty were those who by shouting wished to kill him. But let us question and hear from the Lord to whom he attributes his death, since he said, “I slept, troubled.” Let us question him and say: Since you slept troubled, who persecuted you? Who killed you? Was it perhaps Pilate, who handed you over to soldiers to be hung on the wood and pierced with nails?

Hear whom: “The sons of men.” He certainly means those whom he endured as persecutors. But how did they kill him, since they carried no iron? They did not draw a sword; they did not rush upon him to kill him. How, then, did they kill him? “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” [Col. 0669]. [Note: Col. 0668. Seven manuscripts read *inurat* (“brands,” “burns into”); the editions read *indurat* (“hardens”), incorrectly.]

Do not look at their unarmed hands, but at their armed mouth: from there proceeded the sword by which Christ was killed—just as from Christ’s mouth came the sword by which the Jews would be killed. For he has a two-edged sword (Rev. 1:16) [Note: Col. 0669. Here the editions add “of the one who kills and of the one who rises again,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]. When he rose again, he struck them and separated them from those whom he would make his faithful ones.

They had an evil sword; he a good one. They had evil arrows; he good ones. For he too has good arrows—good words—with which he shoots the faithful heart so that it may love. Thus they have evil arrows and an evil sword, while he has arrows and a sword of another kind. “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” The tongue of the sons of men is a sharp sword, and their teeth are weapons and arrows.

When, then, did they strike him, if not when they shouted, “Crucify, crucify” (Matt. 27:4; John 19:6)?

13. [Verse 6.] And what did they do to you, O Lord? Let the Prophet rejoice here. Above, the Lord was speaking all those verses—indeed, the Prophet was speaking, but in the person of the Lord, because the Lord is in the Prophet. And when the Prophet speaks in his own person, the Lord himself speaks through him, for he dictates to him the truth that he is to speak.

Now, therefore, hear in the person of the Prophet, my brothers. This prophet saw in the Spirit the Lord humbled, beaten, scourged, struck with blows, slapped with the hands, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, hung upon the wood. He saw them raging and him enduring; them rejoicing and him, as though defeated. After all that humiliation and their fury, he saw him rise again, and all that the raging Jews had done become futile. And, lifted up [Note: Col. 0669. The manuscripts read *elatus*; the editions, *elevatus*.] with joy, as though he were seeing it happen, he said, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God.” A man on the cross, and God above the heavens.

Let those who rage remain on earth; be you in heaven as judge. Where are those who were raging? Where are their teeth, weapons and arrows? Have not the arrows of infants become their wounds? For elsewhere the psalm says this, wishing to show that they raged in vain and were driven into frenzies in vain: because they could do nothing against Christ, crucified for a time and afterward rising again and seated in heaven, “the arrows of infants became their wounds” (Ps. 63:8).

How do infants make arrows for themselves? From reeds [Note: Col. 0669. The manuscripts read *canniciis* (“reeds”); the form in the text is *cannis*.]. But what arrows? What strength? What bow? What blows? What wound?

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.”

Why are you exalted above the heavens, O God? Brothers, we do not see God exalted above the heavens, but we believe it. Yet his glory over all the earth we not only believe but also see.

I ask you to observe what true madness the heretics suffer. Cut off from the structure of Christ’s Church, holding a part and losing the whole, they do not wish to share communion with the whole world, throughout which Christ’s glory has been spread. We Catholics, however, are throughout the whole earth, because we share communion with the whole earth wherever Christ’s glory has been spread.

For we see that what was then sung has now been fulfilled: “Our God has been exalted above the heavens, and his glory over all the earth.” [Col. 0670] O heretical madness! What you do not see, you believe with me; what you see, you deny. You believe with me that Christ has been exalted above the heavens, which we do not see; and you deny his glory over all the earth, which we do see.

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.”

14. [Verse 7.] He returns to the words of the Lord; and the Lord himself begins to tell us, as though addressing us, while the Prophet also rejoices and says, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.” He too confirms us, as though saying to us: What could those who persecuted me do to me? Why does he address us? Because they do the same things to us. Yet those who persecute us in the same way accomplish nothing.

Let Your Charity observe the Lord addressing and encouraging us by his example: “They prepared a snare for my feet and bent down my soul.” They wished to bring it down, as though from heaven, and depress it to lower things: “They bent down my soul.” “They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it.” Did they harm me, or themselves?

Behold, God has been exalted above the heavens, and behold, his glory is over all the earth. We see the kingdom of Christ; where is the kingdom of the Jews? Therefore, because they did what they ought not to have done, what they deserved to suffer happened to them: they dug the pit, and they themselves fell into it. For their persecution of Christ did not harm Christ; it harmed them.

And do not think, brothers, that this happened only to them. Everyone who prepares a pit for his brother must himself fall into it.

Pay attention, my brothers; have Christian eyes. Do not be deceived by visible things. Perhaps, because I have said this, one of you has just thought of someone who wished to defraud his brother, plotted some ambush against him, carried it out, and succeeded; and the brother fell into his trap and was stripped of his possessions, or was oppressed—whether by imprisonment, false testimony, or some wicked accusation. It seems that the one was oppressed and the other oppressed him; the one was defeated and the other won. What we said is therefore thought false: that whoever prepares a pit for his brother himself falls into it.

I ask you as Christians to take an example from things we already know. The pagans persecuted the martyrs, and the martyrs were captured, bound, sent to prison, exposed to the beasts, while others were struck down by the sword and others burned by fire [Note: Col. 0670. The editions read *bestiis subjecti* (“subjected to the beasts”); the manuscripts read *bestiis subrecti* (“put before/exposed to the beasts”; reading uncertain). See above, col. 605, line 10, with the note.]. Did the persecutors win and the martyrs lose? Far from it.

Seek the glory of the martyrs with God; seek the pit of the pagans in their wounded conscience. For that is the pit into which the wicked person falls—in an evil conscience. Do you think that he did not fall into the pit who lost the light of Christ and was struck with blindness? If he had not fallen into the pit, he would see what lay before him. He does not know where he is going; just as one walking along a road, when he falls into a pit, has lost the road.

You see, then, that all evildoers have lost the way, entangled in crime. But now perhaps he has handed you over into the hands of a robber, or into the hands of some unjust judge whom he has suborned; you are in distress [Col. 0671], while he rejoices and exults. Do not, as I have already said, have pagan eyes; have Christian eyes.

You see him rejoicing: that very rejoicing is his pit. For the sorrow of one suffering injustice is better than the unjust joy of the one committing it. That unjust joy itself is the pit; when someone falls into it, he loses his eyes.

You grieve because you have lost your garment, but do you not grieve for him because he has lost his faith? Which of you has suffered the greater loss? Behold, he kills, and you are killed: he lives, and you are dead? Far from it. Where is the faith of Christians? Where is the one who dies for a time? Let him hear his Lord: “Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live” (John 11:25). Therefore whoever does not believe, even though he lives, is dead.

“They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it.” This must happen to all evildoers.

15. [Verse 8.] [Col. 0671] But the patience of the good, through the preparation of the heart, receives the will of God and glories in tribulations, saying what follows:

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody.”

What has he done to me? He prepared a pit; my heart is ready. He prepared a pit in order to deceive; shall I not prepare my heart to endure? He prepared a pit in order to oppress; shall I not prepare my heart to bear it? Therefore he will fall into it, while I will sing and make melody.

Hear the heart prepared in the Apostle, because he imitated his Lord: “We glory,” he says, “in tribulations, because tribulation produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

He was in hardships, in chains, in prisons, in blows, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, amid every devastation of labors and sufferings (2 Cor. 11:27), and he said, “We glory in tribulations.” Why, unless because his heart was ready? Therefore he sang and made melody:

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody.”

16. [Verse 9.] “Awake, my glory.” He who had fled from Saul’s presence into a cave says, “Awake, my glory”: let Jesus be glorified after his Passion.

“Awake, psaltery and lyre.” What does he call upon to arise? I see two instruments, but I see one body of Christ. One flesh rose again, and two instruments arose. One instrument, then, is the psaltery, the other the lyre.

All musical instruments are called instruments. It is not only that large instrument called an organ, which is inflated by bellows; whatever is adapted for song and is bodily, whatever instrument the singer uses, is called an instrument.

These instruments are distinct from each other. I wish, insofar as the Lord grants, to point out to you how they are distinct, why they are distinct, and why both are told, “Awake.”

We have already said that the Lord’s one flesh rose again; and it is said, “Awake, psaltery and lyre.” The psaltery is an instrument carried in the hands of the player and possessing stretched strings. But the place from which the strings receive their sound—the hollow piece of wood that hangs down and resounds when touched, because it takes in air—the psaltery has in its upper part. The lyre, however, has this kind of hollow and resonant wood in its lower part [Col. 0672]. Thus, in the psaltery the strings receive their sound from above; in the lyre the strings receive their sound from below. This is the difference between the psaltery and the lyre.

What, then, do these two instruments signify for us? Christ the Lord, our God, awakens his psaltery and his lyre and says, “I will rise at dawn.” I think that by now you recognize here the Lord rising again.

We read in the Gospel; observe the hour of the resurrection. How long was Christ sought among the shadows? “It dawned”—let him be recognized; he rose at dawn (Mark 16:2) [Note: Some editions read *quaeretur Christus?* (“Will Christ be sought?”). Later editions read *Lux itaque* (“Therefore, light”); the manuscripts read *Luxit* (“It dawned”).].

But what is the psaltery? What is the lyre? Through his flesh the Lord performed two kinds of deeds: miracles and sufferings. The miracles were from above; the sufferings were from below. For the miracles he performed were divine, but he performed them through the body, through the flesh.

The flesh, therefore, performing divine works, is the psaltery; the human flesh suffering is the lyre.

Let the psaltery sound: let the blind be enlightened, the deaf hear, the paralytics be strengthened, the lame walk, the sick rise, and the dead rise again. This is the sound of the psaltery.

Let the lyre also sound: let him hunger, thirst, sleep, be seized, scourged, mocked, crucified, and buried.

When, therefore, you see certain things sounding from above in that flesh, and others from below, one flesh rose again; and in one flesh we recognize both psaltery and lyre. These two kinds of deeds fulfilled the Gospel, and it is preached among the nations: both the Lord’s miracles and his sufferings are preached.

17. [Verses 10–12.] Therefore the psaltery and the lyre rose at dawn and give thanks to the Lord. And what does it say?

“I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and I will make melody to you among the nations; for your mercy has been magnified to the heavens, and your truth to the clouds.”

The heavens are above the clouds, and the clouds below the heavens; yet the clouds belong to this nearby heaven. Sometimes, indeed, clouds rest upon the mountains, so densely do they gather in the lower air. But heaven above is the dwelling place of Angels, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers.

It might therefore seem that it ought rather to have been said, “Your truth has been magnified to the heavens, and your mercy to the clouds.” For in heaven the angels praise God, seeing the very appearance of truth without any obscurity of vision and without any admixture [Note: Most manuscripts read *interpellatione* (“interruption”); the text of the editions has *interpolatione*.] of falsehood. They see, love, and praise, and are not wearied. There is truth there; here, in our misery, there is surely mercy. Mercy must be shown to the miserable. Mercy is not needed above, where there is no miserable person.

I have said this because it seems more fitting that it could have been said: “Your truth has been magnified to the heavens, and your mercy to the clouds.”

For by clouds we understand the preachers of truth, human beings bearing this flesh, dark, so to speak, through which God both flashes with miracles and thunders with commandments. These are the clouds of which Isaiah speaks in the person of the Lord, rebuking a certain evil, barren, thorny vineyard: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6) [Col. 0673]—that is, “I will command my Apostles to abandon the Jews and not evangelize them, but to evangelize in the good soil of the Gentiles, from which not thorns but grapes may come forth.”

We know, then, that God’s clouds are the preachers of truth: the Prophets, the Apostles, and all who rightly bring forth the word of truth and possess within themselves a hidden light, just as clouds possess the source from which they flash. Human beings, therefore, are clouds.

What, then, does this mean, Lord: “For your mercy has been magnified to the heavens, and your truth to the clouds”?

Truth prevails in the angels; but you have also given it to human beings and brought it down to the clouds. Above [Note: Col. 0673. All manuscripts read *Rursus* (“Again”).], the angels seem not to need mercy; but because you have mercy on human beings in their misery, and by granting them mercy through participation in the resurrection you make them angels, your mercy extends to the heavens.

Glory to our Lord, to his mercy, and to his truth, because in his mercy he has not ceased to make us blessed by his grace, nor in his truth has he defrauded us. For first truth came to us hidden in flesh, and through his flesh healed the inner eye of our heart, so that afterward we might see it face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

Therefore, giving him thanks, let us say with the psalm itself the final verses, which it said earlier as well:

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth.”

The Prophet said this to him so many years ago; we now see it. Let us therefore say this also.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 57. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [Verses 1–2.] The voice we have sung is more for us to hear than to shout. For truth cries out to all, as though in an assembly of the human race:

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

For what unjust person finds it difficult to speak of justice? Or who, when questioned about justice, if he has no personal case at stake, would not readily answer what is just? For the hand of our Maker has written truth in our very hearts:

“What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16; Matt. 7:12).

Even before the Law was given, no one was permitted to be ignorant of this, so that there might be a basis for judging those to whom the Law had not been given. But lest people complain that something had been lacking to them, what they did not read in their hearts was also written on tablets.

They did not lack the written text; they were unwilling to read it. What they were compelled to see in their conscience was placed before their eyes; and, as though by a voice of God brought from outside, the human being was driven inward, since Scripture says: “For the interrogation of the wicked will be in their thoughts” (Wis. 1:9). Where there is interrogation, there is law.

But because human beings, desiring the things that are outside, had become exiles even from themselves, a written law was also given—not because it was not written in their hearts, but because you were a fugitive from your own heart. You have been seized by the one who is everywhere and recalled within to yourself.

Therefore, what does the written law cry out to those who have abandoned the law written in their hearts (Rom. 2:15)? “Return, transgressors, to your heart” [Col. 0674] (Isa. 46:8).

Who taught you not to want another man to approach your wife? Who taught you not to want to be robbed? Who taught you not to want to suffer injury, and all the other things that can be stated either universally or individually? There are many matters about which, when questioned one by one, people answer in a clear voice that they do not wish to suffer them.

Come now: if you do not wish to suffer these things, are you the only human being? Do you not live in the society of the human race? The one who was made together with you is your companion; and all were made in the image of God, unless they destroy by earthly desires what he formed.

Therefore, what you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. For you judge that something is evil in another when you do not wish to suffer it; and the inner law, written in your own heart, compels you to know this.

You were doing it, and it was being cried out amid your hands. How will you be compelled to return to your heart when you suffer this amid the hands of another?

Is theft good? No. I ask: Is adultery good? Everyone cries out: No. Is murder good? Everyone cries out that he detests it. Is it good to desire your neighbor’s property? No; this is everyone’s voice.

Or if you still do not confess it, let someone who desires your property come along. Let it please you, and answer as you wish. Everyone, then, when questioned about these matters, cries out that they are not good.

Again, consider benefits—not merely refraining from harming, but also doing and giving. Every hungry soul is asked: You are suffering hunger; another person has bread, and has more than enough; he knows that you are in need, but does not give. It displeases you while you are hungry; let it also displease the one who is full when he learns that another is hungry.

A traveler in need of a roof comes into your homeland, but is not received. He then cries out that the city is inhuman and that he could more easily have found refuge among barbarians. He perceives the injustice because he suffers it; perhaps you do not perceive it. But you ought to imagine yourself a traveler as well, and see how you could be displeased with someone who did not provide you with what you do not wish to provide to a traveler in your own homeland.

I ask everyone: Are these things true? True. Are these things just? Just.

2. But hear the psalm:

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

Let justice be not merely of the lips, but also of deeds. For if you act otherwise than you speak, you speak good things but judge badly.
