If you act, how do you judge? When asked what is better, gold or faith, you are not so perverse and estranged from all truth that you would answer that gold is better. When asked, then, you put faith before gold; you have spoken justice.

Have you heard the psalm? “If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.” And where will I prove that you do not judge as you have spoken? I already have your answer, which puts faith before gold.

Behold, I do not know where a friend has come from and entrusted gold without witnesses. Only he and you know this, as far as human beings are concerned. There is another witness present who is not seen but sees. He entrusted the gold to you in secret, perhaps in your bedroom, with all observers removed. The witness who is present is not present in the bedroom of your walls, but in the bedrooms of your consciences.

He entrusted it and departed. He told none of his people, hoping to return and receive back from his friend what he had given. But, as human affairs go, he died; [Col. 0675] he has an heir, he left a son. The son does not know what his father possessed or what he entrusted to you.

Come, return—return, transgressor, to your heart. There the law is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

Imagine that you had entrusted something, told none of your people, died, and left a son. What would you want your friend to provide for him? Answer; judge the case. The tribunal of the judge is in your mind; God sits there, accusing conscience is present, and fear is the torturer.

You are among human affairs; you are held within human society. Consider what you would want your friend to provide for your son. I know what your thought replies to you: judge as you hear.

“Judge”—it will be a voice [Note: Col. 0675. This is the reading of Erasmus and nearly all the manuscripts. Some omit *vox erit* (“it will be a voice”). The Lovaniensis edition reads *Juridica vox erit* (“it will be a juridical voice”).].

The voice of truth is not silent. It does not cry out with the lips, but it cries aloud from the heart. Lend your ear; be there with your friend’s son.

Perhaps you see him also wandering [Note: Col. 0675. Erasmus and the manuscripts read *vagari* (“wandering”); the Lovaniensis edition reads *vacare*.] in need, not knowing what his father possessed, where he placed it, or to whom he entrusted it. Think also of your own son. Make the one whom you despise as dead live; consider yourself dead so that you may live.

But avarice commands something else; it commands against God. God says one thing, avarice another; our Creator in paradise said one thing, the serpent that seduces from aside another.

Let your former condition come to mind: for that reason you are mortal, for that reason you labor, for that reason you eat bread in the sweat of your face, for that reason the earth produces thorns and thistles for you (Gen. 3:17–18). Learn by experience what you were unwilling to learn by command.

But desire prevails. Why not rather truth? And where is what you were saying? Behold, you are thinking of denying the gold; behold, you are thinking of hiding it entirely from your friend’s heir.

A little earlier I had asked what is dearer and what is better, gold or faith. Why do you say one thing and do another? Do you not fear this voice: “If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men”?

Behold, you told me that faith is better, yet in your judgment you considered gold better. You did not judge as you spoke. You spoke truth and judged falsely.

Therefore, even when you were speaking justice, you were not speaking it truly:

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

When you answered me about justice, you spoke with shame, not with confession.

3. But now let us come, if it pleases you, to the present case. For that is a sweet and familiar voice to the ears of the Church: the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ and the voice of his body; the voice of the Church laboring, traveling as a pilgrim on earth, living amid the dangers of those who curse and those who flatter.

You will not fear the threatener if you do not love the flatterer.

He whose voice this is therefore paid attention and saw everyone speaking justice. For who dares not speak it, lest he be called unjust? Thus, as though he heard everyone’s voices and observed everyone’s lips, he cried out to them:

“If you truly speak justice, if you do not speak justice falsely, if one thing does not resound on your lips while another is concealed in your hearts, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

Hear from the Gospel his own voice, the very same voice that is in this psalm. “Hypocrites,” the Lord said to the Pharisees, “how can you speak good things [Col. 0676], since you are evil? Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:34, 33).

Why do you wish to whitewash yourself, mud-plastered wall? I know your interior; your plaster does not deceive me. I know what you pretend; I know what you conceal.

For, as the evangelist says, he did not need anyone to testify to him about a human being, because he himself knew what was in a human being (John 2:25). He knew what was in a human being who had made the human being and had become human in order to seek the human being.

See, then, whether these voices do not follow one another:

“Hypocrites, how can you speak good things, since you are evil?”

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

Did you not speak justice when you said, “Teacher, we know that you are just and show no partiality” (Matt. 22:16)? Why were you concealing deceit in your heart? Why were you showing the image of Caesar to your Creator, while erasing his image from your hearts?

Was it not heard what you spoke, and was it not tested how you judged? Did you not crucify the one whom you had said was just?

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

Why do I hear your words, “We know that you are just,” when I foresee your judgment, “Crucify, crucify”?

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

For what did you do when you raged against God who was human and killed your king? He was not for that reason not destined to be king, because you killed him and he was to rise again.

In the inscription placed above the Lord’s cross, where it was written “King of the Jews” in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (Luke 23:38)—the human judge knew how to say, “What I have written, I have written.” Did God not know how to say, “What I have written, I have written”?

He is truly your king. Alive, he is your king; killed, he is your king. Behold, he has risen, and in heaven he is your king. Behold, he is coming; woe to you, because he is your king.

Go now, speak justice, and do not judge rightly, O sons of men. You do not wish to judge rightly; you will be judged rightly.

For your king lives, and he no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9). Behold, he is coming. “Return, transgressors, to your heart” [Col. 0674] (Isa. 46:8). Behold, he will come; reform yourselves before he comes. “Go before his face in confession” (Ps. 94:2).

Behold, he will come; he is your king. Remember the inscription above the cross. If you do not see it written, it nevertheless remains. It is not read on earth, but it is preserved in heaven.

Do you think that inscription was corrupted? And what does the title of this psalm say?

“To the end; do not corrupt; for David, concerning the inscription of the title.”

That inscription of the title is therefore not corrupted. Christ is your king, because Christ is king of all, since “the kingdom is his, and he will rule the nations” (Ps. 21:29).

If, then, he is king, behold, before he comes he says to you: “I am still speaking,” he says, “I am not yet judging.” I who cry out in warning in this way do not wish to strike in judgment.

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

4. [Verse 3.] But what are you doing now? Why am I saying these things to you? “For in your heart you work iniquities on the earth.”

Perhaps you work iniquities only in your heart? Hear what follows: [Col. 0677] your hands follow your heart, and your hands serve your heart. Something is thought and done—or it is not done, not because we do not wish it, but because we cannot.

Whatever you wish but cannot do, God counts as done.

“For in your heart you work iniquities on the earth.” What next? “Your hands weave together iniquities.”

What does “weave together” mean? Sin from sin, and sin onto sin, because of sin.

What does this mean? He committed theft; it is a sin. He was seen and seeks to kill the one who saw him: sin has been joined to sin. God, by a hidden judgment, may permit him to kill the one he wished to kill. He realizes that he is known and seeks to kill another: he has joined a third sin.

While contriving these things, perhaps so that he will not be found, or because he committed the act and wishes not to be convicted, he consults an astrologer; a fourth has been added. Perhaps the astrologer gives a harsh and evil answer. He runs to a soothsayer so that the matter may be expiated. The soothsayer replies that he cannot expiate it; a sorcerer is sought.

And who could count all the sins that are joined to sins?

“Your hands weave together iniquities.”

As long as you weave together, you bind sin to sin. Free yourself from sins.

“But I cannot,” you say. Cry out to him: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

For the grace of God will come, so that righteousness may delight you as iniquity delighted you. And you, a human being released from bonds, will cry out to God: “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. 115:16).

What is “You have broken my bonds” other than “You have forgiven my sins”?

Hear that they are bonds. Scripture replies: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. 5:22). They are not only bonds, but also cords. Cords are made by twisting; this is what you were doing when you joined sins to sins.

“Woe to those who drag sins like a long rope,” Isaiah cries out. “Woe to those who drag sins like a long garment” (Isa. 5:18). What else does this mean than, “Woe to those whose hands weave together iniquity”?

And because each person is bound by his sins, just as each person is struck by his sins, the Lord drove the evil-doers from the temple with a whip made of cords (John 2:15).

But you do not now wish your bonds to be broken, because you do not feel your bonds. They even delight you and give you pleasure. You will feel them at the end, when it will be said: “Bind his hands and feet, and throw him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13).

You shudder, you fear, you beat your breast; you say that sins are evil and justice good.

“If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, O sons of men.”

Let your words be found in your life; let your lips be recognized in your deeds. Do not, therefore, weave together iniquity, because whatever you weave together will be used to bind you.

They do not listen—not everyone, however. And those who do not listen have been foreknown.

5. [Verse 4.] “Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.”

When they speak iniquity, they speak falsehood, because iniquity is deceitful. And when they speak justice, they speak falsehood, because they bring one thing forth from their mouth and conceal another in their heart.

“Sinners have been estranged from the womb.” What does this mean? Let us inquire more carefully. Perhaps he means that God foreknew sinful human beings even in their mothers’ wombs [Col. 0678].

For why, while Rebecca was still pregnant and carrying twins in her womb, was it said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Gen. 25:23; Mal. 1:2–3; Rom. 9:13)? For it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger.” There is a hidden judgment of God there; nevertheless, sinners were estranged from the womb—that is, from their very origin.

From what were they estranged? From truth. From what were they estranged? From the blessed homeland, from blessed life.

Or were they perhaps estranged from the womb itself? And which sinners were estranged from the womb? For who would be born if they were not held there? Or who would live today to hear these words without purpose, unless he had been born?

Perhaps, then, sinners were estranged from a certain womb in which charity suffered the pains of childbirth, saying through the Apostle: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

Wait, then; form [reading uncertain; Note: The editions read *formari* (“to be formed”); the manuscripts read *formulare* (“to form, to shape”).].

Do not claim for yourself a judgment that perhaps you do not yet know. You are still carnal; you have been conceived. By the very fact that you have received the name of Christ, you have been born in a sacramental way in the mother’s womb.

For a human being is not born only from the womb, but also in the womb. First he is born in the womb, so that he may be born from the womb. Therefore it was said of Mary: “For that which is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). It had not yet been born from her, but it had already been born in her.

Therefore certain little ones are born within the womb of the Church; and it is good that they emerge formed, lest they slip away through miscarriage.

Let the mother give birth to you; let her not miscarry you. If you are patient until you are formed, until the doctrine of truth is secure in you, the mother’s womb ought to contain you. But if through impatience you shake the mother’s sides, she does indeed cast you out with pain, but more to your harm than to hers.

### 6. “Sinners have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods.”

Did they therefore go astray from the belly because they spoke falsehoods? Or rather, did they speak falsehoods because they went astray from the belly? For in the womb of the Church truth remains. Whoever has been separated from this womb of the Church must necessarily speak falsehoods—must, I say, speak falsehoods—whether he has refused to be conceived or whether, after being conceived, his mother has cast him out.

Hence heretics cry out against the Gospel; let us speak instead of those whom we grieve to have been cast out. We read to them: “Behold, Christ said, ‘It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.’” There I recognize our Head; there I recognize our Bridegroom. Recognize with me also the Bride: see what follows—“and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

“Come here, come here!” [Note: [Col. 0678] A cry of the Donatists.] Behold, the Church is among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. I do not say, “Come here”; she herself has come to you.

But they, growing deaf against the Gospel and not allowing us to read the words of God—which they boast that they have preserved from the flame and wish to erase with their tongue—speak their own words, speak empty things: “That man betrayed; and that man betrayed.” Indeed, I too say, “That man betrayed, and that man betrayed”—and I speak the truth. But what does that have to do with me? You do not read from the Gospel the men whom you name, nor do I read from the Gospel those whom I name. Let our papers be removed from the midst; let the Book of God be brought forth into the midst.

Hear Christ speaking; hear the truth speaking: “‘Repentance and the forgiveness of sins,’ he says, ‘are to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.’”

“No,” they say; “but hear what we say. We do not wish to hear what the Gospel says.”

“They have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods.”

Let us speak what is true, because we have heard what is true—what the Lord says, not what a human being says. A human being may lie; the truth cannot lie. From the mouth of truth I recognize Christ, who is himself the truth; from the mouth of truth I recognize the Church, which shares in the truth.

Let no one who has gone astray from the womb in the inner parts of the Church speak falsehoods to me. First I would see what he wished to teach me. I see that he has been alienated from the womb; I see that he has gone astray from the belly; and what will I hear from him except falsehoods? “They have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods.”

### 7. [Verses 5–6]

“Their indignation is according to the likeness of a serpent.”

You are about to hear something great: “Their indignation is according to the likeness of a serpent.” As though we had asked, “What is this that you have said?” the text continues: “Like a deaf asp.” Why deaf? “And one that stops its ears.” It is deaf because it stops its ears—“and one that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of a drug prepared by a wise man.”

As we have heard—and people say this who have learned these matters as far as they could through such knowledge—yet the Spirit of God knows them much better than all human beings. He did not say this without reason, unless what we have heard about the asp may also be true.

When an asp begins to suffer the incantation of a Marsian, who summons it by certain special spells—as there are also many magical practices—listen to what it does.

But meanwhile attend to this, brothers; it must first be said, lest anyone listen with hesitation: whenever Scripture draws a likeness from something, it does not thereby praise the thing itself; it merely derives a likeness from it. The Lord did not praise the unjust judge who did not wish to hear the widow and neither feared God nor respected human beings; yet he drew a likeness from him (Luke 18:2). Nor did he praise the lazy man who gave the asker three loaves, not because of friendship but because he was overcome by annoyance; yet he too supplied a likeness from him (Luke 11:8).

Thus, from things that are not themselves to be praised, certain likenesses are drawn in a particular manner. Or, if you think that one ought to go to the Marsians because you have heard this in the Scripture of God, then one ought also to go to theatrical spectacles, because the Apostle says: “I do not box as though beating the air”; for boxing means practicing the pancratium. Since a likeness has been drawn from this, ought these spectacles therefore to delight us? Or because he said, “Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything” (1 Corinthians 9:26, 28), ought a Christian for that reason to desire these vain and playful athletic contests?

Attend to what is being presented to you as a likeness and what is being urged upon you as a prohibition.

Thus here too a certain likeness is given from the Marsian who chants an incantation in order to draw the asp out of its dark cavern. Certainly he wishes to bring it out into the light. But because it loves its darkness, in which it wraps and conceals itself, it is said that, when it refuses to come out while nevertheless unwilling to hear those voices by which it feels itself compelled, it presses one ear against the earth and blocks the other with its tail. In this way, avoiding those voices as much as it can, it does not come out to the enchanter.

The Spirit of God said that certain people are like this: they do not hear the word of God and not only fail to do it, but altogether refuse to hear it lest they do it. [Note: [Col. 0680] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “and not only fail to hear, but altogether make it impossible for them to hear.”]

### 8.

This also happened in the earliest times of the faith. The martyr Stephen was preaching the truth and, as though chanting an incantation over darkened minds in order to bring them into the light, was drawing them out. When he came to mention Christ, whom they absolutely refused to hear, what does Scripture say about them? What does it relate concerning them? “They stopped up their ears,” it says.

But what they did afterward is made clear by the account of Stephen’s passion. They were not deaf, but made themselves deaf. Because they did not have ears open in their hearts, the violence of the word nevertheless burst in through the ears of their flesh and forced its way even upon the ears of their hearts. They closed the ears of their bodies as well and went for stones (Acts 7:56–57).

Behold deaf asps, harder than the stones with which they stoned their enchanter: they did not hear the voice of the enchanter, nor the drug prepared by a wise man.

What is “the drug prepared by a wise man”? Perhaps “a compounded drug”; let “drug prepared” mean a drug compounded. Or are we looking for something here—how, if it is already a drug, it can also be prepared as a drug?

There were drugs in the Prophets; there were drugs in the Law. All those commandments themselves were drugs. Yet this drug had not previously been prepared. At the coming of the Lord, the drug was prepared; they could not bear it. Since they were not being healed by the drug, the drug itself was prepared at the Lord’s coming.

Stephen was already chanting the prepared drug; they refused to hear it. They stopped their ears against the source from which the drug had been prepared. For they did this when Christ was named.

Their indignation was like the indignation of a serpent. Why do you close your ears? Wait, listen; and, if you can, rage. Since they wanted nothing but to rage, they refused to listen. If they had listened, perhaps they would have ceased raging. Their indignation was like the indignation of a serpent.

### 9.

We also endure such people here. [Note: [Col. 0680] The Donatists.] At first they seemed to themselves to possess the truth. But God did not cease; he did not rest. The truth was preached in his Church [Note: [Col. 0680] The particle “in,” absent from the editions, is restored here from the manuscripts.]; within the womb of the mother their falsehoods were opened up.

What shines was disclosed; the city established upon a mountain, which cannot be hidden, was demonstrated, and the lamp was placed upon the lampstand, shining for all who are in the house (Matthew 5:14–15).

Where, then, is the Church of Christ hidden? Where is the truth of Christ hidden? Is he not the mountain that grew from the smallest stone and filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel 2:35)?

By this they are convicted; they have nothing to say against the Church. And what remains for them? “Why do you seek us? What do you want from us?” they say. “Withdraw from us.”

They say also to their own people: “Let no one speak with them; let no one join himself to them; let no one listen to them.”

Their indignation is the indignation of serpents—like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers and the drug, that is, the voice of the drug prepared by a wise man.

Is it not already clear from this what sort of drug it is, when he speaks of its voice? Does a drug have a voice? There is a certain drug that has a voice. We carry the drug; hear its voice, unlike deaf asps.

“If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, children of men.” This is the voice of the drug, and of the drug prepared by a wise man. For Christ has now come to fulfill the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17), to establish the truth itself: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:40).

### 10.

Or perhaps we should seek some meaning also in the statement that the asp closes its ears in such a way that it presses one of them against the earth and blocks the other with its tail?

What does this signify? By the tail, the things behind are surely understood; therefore the past—[Note: [Col. 0681] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “therefore not the past.”] the past, upon which we ought now to turn our back, so that we may direct our attention to what is promised to us. Therefore we ought to take delight neither in our past life nor in the present.

The Apostle gives this admonition: “What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:21). He recalls us from remembering the past with delight and with a certain desire to enjoy it [Note: [Col. 0681] So the manuscripts; the editions read: “to enjoy them.”], lest we return in heart to Egypt.

What of the present? How does he command us to despise that also? “Not looking,” he says, “at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

Again, concerning the present life, he says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all human beings the most pitiable” (1 Corinthians 15:19).

Forget, then, the past in which you lived wickedly; despise the present in which you live temporally, lest, by binding yourself to it, the present prevent you from reaching the future.

If the present life delights you, you have placed your ear upon the earth. If you take delight even in your past, which is continually slipping away behind you, you have blocked your ear with your tail.

You must therefore go into the light, come out of the darkness, and hear the voice of the drug prepared by a wise man, so that, now walking in the light and rejoicing, you may say: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13).

He did not say, “Forgetting what lies behind and taking delight in the present.” When he says, “Forgetting what lies behind,” he did not block his ear with his tail; when he says, “Stretching forward to what lies ahead,” he did not become deaf to these present things either. Rightly hearing, rightly preaching, rightly does his tongue rejoice as it proclaims the truth in new light, having put off the old garment.

For this too the serpent’s cunning is useful—the cunning that the Lord urges us to imitate. He says: “Be shrewd as serpents” (Matthew 10:16).

What does “shrewd as serpents” mean? Offer all your limbs to the one striking you, provided that you preserve your head unharmed. “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

But something like the weight of a hide and something like the old age of the old human being weighs you down. Hear the Apostle saying: “Stripping off the old human being and putting on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10).

“And how,” you ask, “do I strip off the old human being?” Imitate the serpent’s cunning. What does the serpent do in order to strip off its old garment? It compresses itself through a narrow opening.

“And where,” you ask, “do I find this narrow opening?” Hear: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it” (Matthew 7:14).

Do you shrink from it and refuse to walk because there are few? The old garment must be left there; it cannot be left elsewhere. Or, if you wish to be hindered, burdened, and weighed down by old age, do not go through the narrow way.

But if you are weighed down by a certain oldness of your sin and past life, you cannot pass through. Since “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15), either bodily desires must not press you down, or the desires of the flesh must be stripped away.

From where are they stripped away, unless you go through the narrow way, unless you are shrewd like the serpent? [Note: [Col. 0682] So the manuscripts. The editions read here: “through the narrow passage.”]

### 11. [Verse 7]

“God has crushed their teeth in their own mouths.”

Whose teeth? Those whose indignation is like the likeness of a serpent and of an asp that stops its ears so as not to hear the voice of charmers and the drug prepared by a wise man.

What did the Lord do to them? “He crushed their teeth in their own mouths.”

It happened; this happened first, and it still happens. But, my brothers, it would have been enough to say, “God has crushed their teeth.” Why add, “in their own mouths”?

The Pharisees did not wish to hear the Law; they did not wish to hear the commandments of truth from Christ. They were like that serpent and asp. They took delight in their past sins and did not wish to lose their present life—that is, earthly joys for the sake of eternal joys.

They closed one ear out of delight in the past and the other out of delight in the present. [Note: [Col. 0682] The manuscripts read: “that is, earthly joys. They closed one ear because of earthly joys, the other because of delight in the past; therefore, etc.”] For this reason they did not wish to hear.

Where else does that saying come from: “If we let him go on, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation” (John 11:48)? Clearly, they did not wish to lose their place; they had struck their ear against the earth, and for this reason they refused to hear those words prepared by a wise man.

It is also said of them that they were greedy and lovers of money. Their whole life, including their past, has been described by the Lord in the Gospel. Whoever reads the Gospel carefully finds the reason why they blocked both ears.

Let Your Charity attend: what did the Lord do? “He crushed their teeth in their own mouths.”

What does “in their own mouths” mean? So that with their own mouths they might pronounce judgment against themselves; he compelled them to speak the sentence against themselves with their own mouths.

They wished to slander him concerning the tribute. He did not say, “It is lawful to pay tribute,” or, “It is not lawful to pay tribute.” He wanted to crush the teeth with which they gaped to bite, but he wanted to crush them in their own mouths.

If he had said, “Let tribute be paid to Caesar,” they would have slandered him, claiming that he had cursed the nation of the Jews by making it tributary. For, humbled by sin, they were paying tribute, just as had been foretold to them in the Law.

“We have him,” they said, “as a reviler of our nation if he orders us to pay tribute. But if he says, ‘Do not pay,’ we have him as one who contradicts our duty to Caesar.”

They set such a two-headed snare, as though they were about to catch the Lord. But to whom had they come? To the one who knew how to crush their teeth in their own mouths.

“Show me a coin,” he said. [Col. 0683] “Why do you test me, hypocrites? Are you thinking about paying tribute? Do you wish to practice justice? [Note: [Col. 0683] So the manuscripts; the editions read: “Do you not wish to practice justice?”] Are you seeking the counsel of justice? If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, children of men.”

But since you speak one thing and judge another, you are hypocrites. “Why do you test me? Now I will crush your teeth in your own mouths. Show me a coin.”

And they showed him one. He did not say, “It belongs to Caesar,” but asked, “Whose is this?” so that their teeth might be crushed in their own mouths.

For when he asked whose image and inscription it bore, they said, “Caesar’s.” Now the Lord would crush their teeth in their own mouths. You have already answered; your teeth have already been crushed in your own mouths.

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:17–21).

Caesar seeks his image: render it to him. God seeks his image: render it to him. Let Caesar not lose his coin in you; let God not lose his coin in you.

They found nothing to answer. They had been sent to slander him and returned saying that no one could answer him. Why? Because their teeth had been crushed in their own mouths.

### 12.

The same is true of the saying: “By what authority do you do these things? And I will ask you one question; answer me.”

He asked them about John—whether John’s baptism was from heaven or from human beings—so that whatever they answered would be against them.

They did not wish to say, “From human beings,” fearing the people, lest they be stoned by them because they regarded John as a prophet. But they feared even more to say, “From heaven,” lest they acknowledge Christ himself, because John had preached Christ.

Hemmed in on both sides, from this side and from that, those who were preparing to bring an accusation answered with ignorance; they said, “We do not know” (Mark 11:28–33).

They were preparing a slander [Note: [Col. 0683] Erasmus and the manuscripts read: “to slander.”] when they said, “By what authority do you do these things?” If he had said, “I am the Christ,” they would have attacked him as arrogant, proud, and sacrilegious.

He did not say, “I am the Christ,” but asked about John, who had said that he himself was the Christ. They did not dare criticize John, fearing that they would be killed by the people. They did not dare say, “John spoke the truth,” lest they be told, “Believe him.”

They fell silent and said that they did not know. They were no longer able to bite. Why were they unable? It has already occurred to you: their teeth had been crushed in their own mouths.

### 13.

A Pharisee was displeased with the Lord, who had invited him to dinner, because a sinful woman had approached his feet. He murmured against him, saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman this is who has approached his feet.”

O you who are not a prophet, how do you know that he did not know what sort of woman had approached his feet?

Because she did not observe, as he supposed, the Jewish purity that was guarded outwardly in the flesh but absent from the heart [Note: [Col. 0683] So the manuscripts; the editions read: “and was not cultivated from the heart.”], he formed this suspicion about the Lord.

But the Lord, who knew the woman’s sins, also heard the thoughts of his host and answered as you know. And, not to speak at length about this, he nevertheless wished to crush his teeth in his own mouth.

For he proposed: “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since neither had anything with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them loved him more?”

He asks this so that the man may answer; the man answers so that his teeth may be crushed in his own mouth.

He answered in confusion and was shut out. She was admitted to receive mercy—she who had burst into another person’s dwelling, but had not approached a foreign God (Luke 7:39–50).

“The Lord crushed their teeth in their own mouths.”

### 14.

“The Lord has broken the molars of lions.”

Not merely those of asps. What about the asps? Asps lie in wait, wishing to inject, scatter, and hiss their poisons.

The nations raged openly and roared like lions. “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise empty things?” (Psalm 2:1).

When they lay in wait for the Lord—“Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?”—they were asps; they were serpents. Their teeth were crushed in their own mouths.

Afterward they cried out, “Crucify, crucify!” (Matthew 27:23; John 19:6). Now it was no longer the tongue of an asp but the roar of a lion.

But “the Lord has also broken the molars of lions.” Perhaps it is not without significance that he did not add, “in their mouths.” Those who lay in wait with crafty questions were compelled to be defeated by their own answer. But those who raged openly—were they to be convicted by questions?

Nevertheless, their molars too have been crushed. The crucified one rose again; he ascended into heaven; Christ was glorified; he is worshiped by all nations; he is worshiped by all kings.

Let the Jews rage now, if they can. They do not rage. The Lord has broken the molars of lions.

### 15.

We have this proof and experience also among heretics, because we find them to be serpents deafened by indignation, unwilling to hear the drug prepared by a wise man. In their own mouths the Lord has crushed their teeth.

How they raged against us, criticizing us as though we were persecutors because we excluded them from the basilicas! Ask them now: “Ought heretics to be excluded from the basilicas, or ought they not?” Let them answer now.

If they say that they ought not, the Maximianists reclaim the basilicas. But if they say that the Maximianists ought not to reclaim the basilicas, they say that heretics ought to be excluded.

What, then, was the meaning of what you were saying against us? Have your teeth been crushed in your own mouths?

“What have we to do with kings?” they say. “What have we to do with emperors? You rely upon the emperors.”

And I ask in turn: What have you to do with the proconsuls whom the emperors sent? What have you to do with the laws that the emperors issued against you?

The emperors of our communion issued laws against all heretics. They call those people heretics who are not of their communion; and among these, clearly, are you.

If the laws are true, let them apply also to you as heretics. If the laws are false, why do they apply against your heretics?

Brothers, attend for a little while and understand what we have said. When they pursued their cases against the Maximianists, intending to expel from their places those whom they had condemned as schismatics—places which the Maximianists had held from ancient times and had inherited from their predecessor bishops—they sought to exclude them by the public laws. They came before judges and called themselves Catholics, so that they might exclude heretics.

Why do you call yourself Catholic so that a heretic may be excluded, rather than be Catholic so that you may not be excluded as a heretic? Now you are Catholic so that you may be able to exclude a heretic.

For a judge could judge only according to his own laws. They called themselves Catholics and were admitted to bring their case. They called the others heretics; the judge asked how this could be proved.

The Council of Bagai was read, where the Maximianists had been condemned. It was inserted into the proconsular records; it was proved that those who had been condemned ought not to hold the basilicas; and the proconsul pronounced judgment according to the law.

According to what law? The law enacted against heretics.

“If it is against heretics, then it is against you too.”

“Why,” he says, “against me? I am not a heretic.”

If you are not a heretic, those laws are false. For they were issued by emperors who are not of your communion; and all who are not of their communion are called heretics by their laws.

I am not asking for now whether the laws are true or false; let that question be set aside, if it is still a question. For the moment I ask you according to your own position: Are the laws true or false?

If they are true, let them be believed. If they are false, why do you use them?

You said to the proconsul: “I am Catholic; exclude the heretic.” He asked how the man could be proved a heretic. You produced your council and showed that you had condemned him.

The proconsul, either winking at the matter [Note: [Col. 0685] In many manuscripts, “conhibens”; in others and in Erasmus, “cohibens.”] or not understanding it, nevertheless used the law as a judge. And you made the judge do what you do not wish to be done to you.

For if the judge used the emperor’s law at your suggestion, why do you not use it for your correction? Behold, he expelled your heretic according to the law of his emperor. Why do you not wish him to expel you according to the same law?

We bring back before you what you did. Behold, the basilicas were held by the Maximianists; now they are held by you. The Maximianists were expelled from them. The proconsuls’ orders exist; the records of the proceedings exist. Court officials are engaged; cities are stirred up; people are driven from their places.

Why? Because they are heretics.

By what law are they driven out? Answer. Let us see whether your teeth have not yet been crushed in your own mouths.

Is the law false? Let it not apply to your heretic.

Is the law true? Let it apply also to you.

They have nothing to answer. God has crushed their teeth in their own mouths.

Therefore, wherever they cannot creep through slippery deceit like asps, they roar with open violence like lions. Armed bands of Circumcellions spring forth and rage; they inflict as much slaughter as they can—as much as they possibly can.

But the Lord has also broken the molars of lions.

### 16. [Verse 8]

“They will be despised like running water.”

Do not be frightened, brothers, by certain rivers called torrents. They are filled with winter waters. Do not fear; after a little while it passes; the water runs down; for a time it roars, and soon it will cease. They cannot stand for long.

Many heresies have already died out. They ran through their channels as far as they could; they flowed away; their channels dried up; scarcely any memory of them remains, or even of the fact that they existed.

“They will be despised like running water.”

But not only they: this entire age roars for a time and seeks someone to carry away. All the impious, all the proud, roaring against the rocks of their pride like rushing and gathering waters—do not fear them. They are winter waters; they cannot flow forever. They must run down to their own place, to their own end.

And yet the Lord drinks from this torrent of the world. He suffered here; he drank the torrent itself. But he drank it on the way, in passing, because he did not stand in the way of sinners (Psalm 1:1).

But what does Scripture say about him? “He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Psalm 109:7). That is, he was glorified because he died; he rose again because he suffered.

If he had not wished to drink from the torrent on the way, he would not have died. If he had not died, he would not have risen again. If he had not risen again, he would not have been glorified.

Therefore: “He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.”

Our Head has already been lifted up; let his members follow him.

“They will be despised like running water.”

“He has drawn his bow until they are weakened.”

God’s threats do not cease. The bow of God is the threats of God. The bow is drawn; it has not yet struck.

“He has drawn his bow until they are weakened.”

And many have been weakened [Note: [Col. 0686] Some manuscripts add: “and converted.”], terrified by the drawing of his bow. For this is how the one who said, “What do you command me to do?” was weakened: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute,” he said (Acts 9:6, 5).

When he cried out from heaven, he was drawing the bow. Many, therefore, who had been enemies were weakened and converted; they refused to raise their necks for long against the perseverance of the drawn bow.

For this is how the one who said, “When I am weak, then I am strong,” was also weakened—so that we should not fear being weakened. And when he prayed that the thorn of the flesh be taken from him, what was said to him? “Power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:10, 9).

“He has drawn his bow until they are weakened.”

### 17. [Verse 9]

“Like wax melted, they will be taken away.”

You were about to say: “Not everyone is weakened as I was, so that they may believe. Many persist in their evil and wickedness.”

Do not fear anything from them either: “Like wax melted, they will be taken away.” They will not stand against you; they will not endure. By a certain fire of their desires they will perish.

There is here a certain hidden punishment; the Psalm is about to speak of it from this point to the end. There are few verses; pay close attention.

There is a future punishment: the fire of Gehenna, eternal fire. For future punishment has two forms. One is the punishment of the underworld, where that rich man was burning, who wished a drop of water to be dropped upon his tongue from the finger of the poor man whom he had previously despised at his gate, when he said: “For I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

The other is that punishment at the end, concerning which those placed on the left will hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

Those punishments will be manifest at the time when one departs from this life or, when the age has ended, reaches the resurrection of the dead.

Is there, then, no punishment now? Does God leave sins altogether unpunished until that day? There is also a certain hidden punishment here; it is this that is now being discussed.

The Spirit of God wishes to commend this punishment to us. Let us understand it, beware of it, avoid it, and we shall not fall into those much more fearful punishments.

Perhaps someone will say to me: “There are punishments here too—prisons, exiles, tortures, deaths, various kinds of pain and tribulation.”

There certainly are such things, and they are distributed according to God’s judgment—some for testing, others for condemnation. Yet we sometimes see the righteous afflicted by these punishments while the wicked are free from them.

This caused the feet of the one who later rejoiced to totter, saying: “How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.”

He had seen the prosperity of the wicked and had taken pleasure in being wicked, seeing the wicked reign, seeing them prosper and abound in every abundance of temporal things—things that, while still a little one, he himself desired from the Lord.

His feet tottered until he saw what should be hoped for or feared at the end. For in the same Psalm he says: “This is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand concerning the last things” (Psalm 72:1–3, 16–17).

The Spirit of God, then, does not wish to commend the punishments of the underworld, nor the punishments of that eternal fire after the resurrection, nor those punishments that are still common in this age to the just and the unjust and are often heavier for the just than for the unjust.

Rather, I do not know what punishment of the present life the Spirit of God wishes to commend. Attend and listen to me speaking of something you already knew. Yet it is sweeter when it is shown in the Psalm—something that, before it was shown, was thought obscure.

For behold, I bring forth things you already knew. But because they are brought forth from a place where you did not yet see them, even familiar things become delightful as though new.

Hear the punishment of the impious: “Like wax,” he says, “melted, they will be taken away.”

I said that this happens to them through their desires. Evil desire is like heat and fire [Note: [Col. 0687] The particle “and” is absent from the editions.]. Fire consumes clothing; does the lust of adultery not consume the soul?

When Scripture spoke of contemplated adultery, it said: “Can someone carry fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned? Can someone carry coals and his tunic not be scorched? Can he carry adultery in his thought and his soul remain intact?” (Proverbs 6:27–29). [Note: [Col. 0687] So all the manuscripts. The editions read: “in the heart.”]

### 18.

But few people see these punishments; therefore the Spirit of God especially commends them. Hear the Apostle saying: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts.”

Behold the fire, before whose face they melt like wax. They are dissolved from a certain steadfastness of chastity; therefore, as they go into their lusts, they are said to be loosened and flowing away.

From what do they flow away? From what are they loosened? From the fire of desires.

“God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might do what is improper,” filled with every iniquity.

He lists many things that are sins, and yet calls them the punishments of sins. For he says that the first punishment is pride—or rather, not the punishment but the first sin: pride.

The first sin is pride; the final punishment is eternal fire, or the fire of the underworld—for it already belongs to the condemned.

Between that first sin and this final punishment, the things in the middle are both sins and punishments. For the Apostle says that they commit many detestable sins, and yet calls them punishments.

“For this reason,” he says, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might do what is improper.”

And lest anyone think that he is afflicted only by those punishments in which he now takes delight, and fail to fear what will come at the end, he mentioned the final punishment:

“Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand,” he says, “that those who do such things are worthy of death—and not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them.”

Those who do such things are worthy of death. What things? The things he listed above as punishments. For he said, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, so that they might do what is improper.”

To be an adulterer is already a punishment; to be a liar, a greedy person, a fraudster, or a murderer—these are already punishments.

The punishments of what sin are they? Of the earlier apostasy, of that pride: “The beginning of human sin is apostasy from God, and the beginning of every sin is pride” (Sirach 10:14–15).

For this reason he first mentioned that sin: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.”

Already this darkening of the heart is a punishment. But how did it happen? “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:21–29).

They said that they possessed from themselves what they had received from God. Or, if they knew from whom they had received it, they did not glorify the one from whom they knew they had received it. This is what is meant by “claiming to be wise.”

And immediately the punishment followed: “They became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened.” “Claiming to be wise, they became fools.”

Is this a small punishment? To speak only of this one thing: is the darkening of the heart, the blinding of the mind, a small punishment?

If someone had lost an eye immediately after committing a theft, everyone would say that God had inflicted a present punishment. He has lost the eye of his heart, and God is thought to have spared him!

“Like wax melted, they will be taken away.”

### 19

“Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.” You see how he speaks of a certain punishment of darkness. Fire fell upon them: the fire of pride, the smoky fire, the fire of desire, the fire of anger. What a great fire it is! Whoever it falls upon will not see the sun. Hence it is said: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 26).

Therefore, brothers, fear the fire of evil desire, if you do not wish to be melted like wax and perish from the presence of God. For this fire falls upon you, and you will not see the sun. Which sun? Not this one that cattle, flies, good people, and wicked people see with you—for “he makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked” (Matt. V, 45). There is another sun, of which those people will say: “The sun did not rise for us; all those things passed away like a shadow. Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. V, 6, 9). Why, unless because fire fell upon them and they did not see the sun?

The desire of the flesh overcame them. And where does this desire come from? Pay attention. You were born from the stock of humanity together with that which you must conquer: do not add enemies to yourself; conquer the one with whom you were born. You came with him to the arena of this life; engage in combat with the one who came forth together with you. If you have not conquered him, why do you provoke whole battalions of desires?

For carnal pleasure, brothers, is born together with the human being. But one who is well instructed quickly sees his enemy, attacks and wrestles with him, and quickly conquers him—for he is capable of this while his enemies are not yet growing. But one who refuses to conquer that desire with which he was born from the propagation of sin, and arouses and unleashes many further lusts, overcomes them only with difficulty; divided against himself, he is burned up by his own fire.

Do not therefore suppose that only those future punishments will exist; see the present ones. “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun.”

### 20. [verse 10]

“Before the thorn-bush produces your thorns, as though they were living, as though in anger, he will consume them.”

What is the thorn-bush (*rhamnus*)? It is a kind of thorny plant; it is said to have extremely dense thorns. At first it is a plant, and when it is still a plant it is soft and beautiful; yet the thorns that will later emerge are already there. Thus sins now give pleasure and seem not to prick. It is a plant, yet it is already a thorn.

“Before the thorn-bush produces its thorns”: before the manifest torments of wretched pleasures and delights emerge. Let those who love something and cannot attain it question themselves; let them see whether they are not tormented by desire. And when they have attained what they unlawfully desire, let them consider whether they are not tormented by fear.

Let them therefore see their punishments here, before that resurrection comes when, rising again in the flesh, they will not be changed. “For we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV, 51). They will have the corruption of the flesh in which they suffer, though not in which they die; otherwise those sufferings too would come to an end.

Then the thorns of that thorn-bush—that is, all the pains and pricks of torments—will be brought forth. What thorns will those people suffer who will say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision” (Wis. V, 3)? Thorns of the pricking of repentance, but late and fruitless, like the sterility of thorns.

Repentance in this age is medicinal pain; repentance in that age is penal pain. You do not wish to suffer those thorns? Here, let yourself be pricked by the thorns of repentance, so that you may do what was said: “I was turned in my anguish when the thorn was fixed in me. I acknowledged my sin, and I did not conceal my iniquity. I said: ‘I will confess my transgression against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the iniquity of my heart” (Ps. XXXI, 4–6).

Do it now; let yourself be pricked now. Let what was said of certain detestable people not happen to you: “They were torn apart, and they were not pricked” (Ps. XXXIV, 16). Consider those who were torn apart and were not pricked. You see that they are torn apart, but you do not see them repent. Behold, they are outside the Church, and they do not repent, so that they may laugh at the place from which they were torn away.

Later the thorn-bush will produce their thorns. They do not wish to have medicinal repentance now; later they will have penal repentance. But even now, before the thorn-bush produces its thorns, fire has fallen upon them, a fire that does not allow them to see the sun and that, while they are still alive, consumes them in the anger of God: the fire of evil desires, empty honors, pride, and their own avarice; and whatever presses upon them [Note: [Col. 0689] “And for whatever presses upon them” (*et probae notae Mss.*), rather than “in order that it may press upon them” (*in quid eos premit*).] so that they may not recognize the truth, so that they may not appear to have been defeated, so that even the truth itself may not subject them.

For what is more glorious, brothers, than to be subjected to and conquered by the truth? Let the truth overcome you willingly; for even if you are unwilling, it will overcome you.

Therefore that fire of evil desires, which fell upon them so that they would not see the sun, consumes the thorn-bush before it produces their thorns. That is, it conceals their evil life before that same life brings forth manifest torments at the end; but in the anger of God this fire conceals the thorn-bush.

For it is no small punishment that they do not see the sun now, nor believe that the thorns of punishments will later arise for them from this evil life. “For you,” he says, “are the thorn-bush”; that is, you yourselves, while living—that is, while you still remain in this life—before at the future judgment you produce the manifest thorns of your punishments, are now, in anger, consumed; that is, as though by being swallowed up, you are prevented from appearing.

The order of the words, as I think, can therefore be set out more clearly as follows: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun”: the fire, as though in anger, consumes you, the thorn-bush, as though you were living, before you produce your thorns. That is, it consumes you yourselves, whom the thorn-bush represents, before death, before that same thorn-bush produces your thorns after death, in that punitive resurrection.

Why did he not say “while living,” but “as though living,” unless because this life of the wicked is false? For they do not live, but seem to themselves to live. And why did he not say “in anger,” but “as though in anger,” unless because God does this calmly? For it is also written: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity” (Wis. XII, 18).

When he threatens, therefore, he is not angry. For he is not disturbed, but acts as though he were angry, because he punishes and avenges. And those who refuse correction seem to live, but do not live. The punishment of the first sin, and of the sins they have added, remains upon them; and it is called the anger of God because it comes from the judgment of God.

Hence the Lord says of the unbeliever: “But the anger of God remains upon him” (John III, 36). In the anger of God we are born as mortals. Hence the Apostle says: “We too were once by nature children of anger, as were the rest” (Eph. II, 3). What does “by nature children of anger” mean, unless that we carry with us the punishment of the first sin?

But if we turn back, the anger is removed and grace is granted. If you do not wish to turn back, you add further to what you were born with: you will be consumed, as though in anger, in the present age.

### 21. [verse 11]

Recognize this punishment, therefore, and rejoice that you are not all subject to it—you who are making progress, all of you who understand and love the truth, all of you who desire the victory of the truth in yourselves more than your own victory, who do not close your ears against the truth because of present pleasure or the memory of past things, lest you become “a dog returning to its own vomit” (2 Pet. II, 22).

All of you who are such, see the punishments of those who are not such, and rejoice. The punishments of hell have not yet come; the eternal fire has not yet come. Let the person who is making progress in God now compare himself with the wicked, the blind heart with the enlightened heart; compare the two, the one who sees and the one who does not see in the flesh.

And what great thing is bodily sight? Did Tobias have bodily eyes? His son had them, but he did not; and the blind man showed the one who could see the way of life (Tob. IV, 1).

Therefore, when you see this punishment, rejoice because you are not in it. For this reason Scripture says: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” It does not mean future vengeance; see what follows: “He will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”

What does this mean? Let Your Charity attend. When murderers are punished, should innocent people go there and wash their hands? What, then, does it mean that “he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner”? When the righteous person sees the punishment of the sinner, he himself makes progress; the death of one becomes useful for the life of another.

For if blood flows spiritually from those who are dying inwardly, then, when you see such vengeance, wash your hands there; from then on live more purely. And how will he wash his hands if he is righteous? What does he have on his hands that could be washed, if he is righteous?

But “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17). By “the righteous,” therefore, he meant the faithful; and from the moment you have believed, you begin already to be called righteous. The forgiveness of sins has taken place.

Even if, in this remaining life, you still have certain sins that cannot help but flow in like water from the sea into a cesspool, nevertheless, because you have believed, when you see one who is wholly turned away from God being killed in that blindness—when, as fire falls upon him, he does not see the sun—you who already see Christ through faith, in order to see him by sight, because “the righteous lives by faith,” observe the wicked person dying and cleanse yourself from sins.

In this way you will, so to speak, wash your hands in the blood of the sinner. “He will therefore wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”

### 22. [verse 12]

“And the human being will say: ‘Then there is fruit for the righteous.’”

Behold: before what is promised comes, before eternal life is given, before the wicked are cast into eternal fire, there is fruit for the righteous here in this life.

What fruit? “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII, 12). What fruit is there for the righteous? “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces tested character, tested character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint; because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 3–5).

Does the drunkard rejoice, and does the righteous not rejoice? In love there is fruit for the righteous. The wretched man is miserable even when he makes himself drunk; the blessed man is blessed even when he hungers and thirsts. Drunkenness stuffs the former; hope feeds the latter.

Let him therefore see the punishment of the former, his own joy, and consider God. If God has now given such joy through faith, hope, love, and the truth of his Scriptures, what does he prepare for the end! If he feeds us in the way, how will he fatten us in our homeland!

“And the human being will say: ‘Then there is fruit for the righteous.’” Let those who see believe, and let them see and understand.

“The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” But if he does not have eyes with which to see vengeance, he will be saddened by it and will not be corrected through it. But if he sees it, he sees the difference between the darkened eye of the heart [Note: [Col. 0691] So the manuscripts. The editions have “the eye of the body” (*corporis*) here.] and the enlightened eye of the heart; between the security of hope and the enlightened eye of the heart; between the refreshment of chastity and the flame of lust; between the security of hope and the fear of crime.

When he sees this, let him distinguish himself and wash his hands in the blood of that man. Let him make progress through the comparison and say: “Then there is fruit for the righteous; then there is a God judging them on earth”—not yet in that life, not yet in eternal fire, not yet among the dead, but here on earth.

Behold, that rich man is still clothed in purple and fine linen, and still feasts splendidly every day. The thorn-bush has not yet produced its thorns; he does not yet say, “I am tormented in this flame” (Luke XVI, 19, 24). But there is already blindness of mind; the eye of the mind has already been extinguished.

If a man blind in his bodily eyes were reclining at his table, however sumptuous it might be, you would call him wretched. Yet a man blind inwardly, who does not see Christ the bread, is blessed? No one says this except one who is equally blind.

“Then there is fruit for the righteous; then there is a God judging them on earth.”

### 23

If we have been somewhat more lengthy, grant us pardon. We exhort you in the name of Christ to consider for your benefit the things you have heard. For it is useless to preach the truth if the heart disagrees with the tongue; and it is of no benefit to hear the truth if a person does not build upon the rock.

The one who builds upon the rock is the one who hears and does. But the one who hears and does not do builds upon sand (Matt. VII, 24, 26). The one who neither hears nor does builds nothing.

But just as the person who builds upon sand builds a ruin for himself, so the one who does not build upon the rock, when the river comes, is swept away without a house. There is nothing to do except both build and build upon the rock—that is, both hear and do.

Let no one else say: “Why should I come to the church? Behold, those who come to church every day do not do what they hear.” They do, however, come in order to hear; in this way they can come to hear and do. But how far you are from doing, when you flee so far from hearing!

“But I,” he says, “do not build upon sand.” The river will find you naked; does that mean it will not carry you away? Does that mean the rain will not destroy you? Will the winds therefore not snatch you away?

“Then I will come and hear.” But when you have heard, do. For if you hear and do not do, you have indeed built, but upon sand. Since, then, without a building we are naked, while in a building placed upon sand we are beneath a ruin, it remains for us to build upon the rock and do what we have heard.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 58

### SERMON I [Note: [Col. 0692] Delivered after Pelagius’s error had been discovered, as appears from no. 19.]

#### On the First Part of the Psalm

### 1. [verse 1]

As Scripture is accustomed to place mysteries in the titles of the Psalms and to adorn the front of a Psalm with the sublimity of its sacrament, so that we may know what we are about to enter when, as though upon a doorway, we have read what is taking place inside, or whose house it is, or who is the owner of that property, so in this Psalm a title has been written upon a title.

For it has: “For the end; do not corrupt; for David; in the inscription of the title.” This is what I called a title upon a title. What the inscription of this title is—which he forbids to be corrupted—the Gospel indicates to us.

For when the Lord was crucified, a title was written by Pilate and placed there: “King of the Jews,” in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (Luke XXIII, 38)—languages that are especially prominent throughout the world.

Therefore, if the King of the Jews was crucified, and the Jews crucified their king, by crucifying him they also made him King of the Gentiles, more than they killed him. Indeed, insofar as it lay with them, they lost Christ—but for themselves, not for us. He died for us and redeemed us with his blood.

And now the title has not been corrupted, because he is king not only of the Gentiles but also of the Jews themselves. What then? Because they contradicted him, were they able to overthrow the dominion of their king? He is king even over them. For that king carries an iron rod, with which he both rules and breaks.

“I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the Lord’s decree. The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth. You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them’” (Ps. II, 6–9).

Whom will he rule? Whom will he shatter? He will rule those who obey; he will shatter those who resist.

Therefore, “Do not corrupt” is most fitting and prophetic. For at that time those Jews also made a suggestion to Pilate and said: “Do not write ‘King of the Jews,’ but write that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews’”; for, they said, “this title has made him our king.” And Pilate said: “What I have written, I have written” (John XIX, 21). Thus “Do not corrupt” was fulfilled.

### 2

This is not the only Psalm to have such an inscription, so that the title should not be corrupted. Several Psalms are marked in this way (Ps. LVI–LVIII), but in all of them the Lord’s passion is foretold.

Therefore here too let us understand the Lord’s passion, and let Christ, the head and the body, speak to us. Thus let us always—or almost always—hear the voices of Christ in the Psalm, so that we may not contemplate only that one head, “the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II, 5), who also according to his divinity “was in the beginning the Word, God with God,” and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 1, 14), flesh from the seed of Abraham, from the seed of David, from the Virgin Mary (Matt. I, 1).

When we hear Christ speaking, therefore, let us not think only of him who is our head; let us think of Christ the head and the body, a whole and complete human being. For the Apostle Paul says to us: “You are the body of Christ and members” (1 Cor. XII, 27). And the same Apostle says of him that he is “the head of the Church” (Eph. I, 22; Col. I, 18).

If he is the head and we are the body, then the whole is Christ, head and body. Sometimes you find words that do not fit the head, and unless you adapt them to the body your understanding will falter. Again, you find words that do not fit the body, and yet Christ is speaking. Here one need not fear that anyone will go astray; he quickly proceeds to adapt to the head what he sees does not fit the body.

Finally, while hanging on the cross, he spoke from the person of the body: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI, 2; Matt. XXVII, 46). For God had not forsaken Christ, by whom he had not been forsaken. Did he come to us in such a way as to abandon him? Or did he send him in such a way as to depart from him?

But because the human being was abandoned by God—that Adam who sinned and, although he had been accustomed to rejoice in the presence of God, frightened by the consciousness of sin, fled from his joy (Gen. III, 8)—God truly abandoned him, because he himself abandoned God.

From that Adam, once Christ had assumed flesh, he said this from the person of that flesh, because then “our old human being was crucified together with him” (Rom. VI, 6).

### 3

Let us therefore hear what follows: “When Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him.”

This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless it pertains to the Lord’s passion. Christ was crucified, died, and was buried. That burial was therefore like a house, which the kingdom of the Jews sent guards to protect when guards were placed at Christ’s tomb (Matt. XXVII, 66).

There is indeed a history in the Book of Kings, when Saul sent to guard the house in order to kill David (1 Kings XIX, 11). But when we discuss the title of the Psalm, we must examine how much the Psalmist drew from that account.

Did he merely intend to signify that someone was sent to the house so that it might be guarded and he might be killed? How, then, was the house guarded for this purpose, if David represented Christ and Christ was to be killed, when Christ was placed in the tomb only after he had been killed on the cross?

Refer this, therefore, to the body of Christ. For to kill Christ meant to remove the name of Christ, so that people would not believe in Christ, while the lie of the guards prevailed—guards who were bribed to say that, while they were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away (Matt. XXVIII, 13).

This is truly to wish to kill Christ: to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that a lie might be preferred to the Gospel. But just as Saul did not accomplish his purpose of killing David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not make the testimony of sleeping guards prevail over that of the watchful Apostles.

What were the guards taught to say? “We will give you,” they said, “as much money as you want; and say that while you were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away.”

Behold the sort of witnesses of falsehood against the truth and the resurrection of Christ that his enemies, represented by Saul, produced. Question the sleeping witnesses, O unbelief; let them answer you what happened in the tomb. If they were sleeping, how did they know? If they were awake, why did they not seize the thieves?

Let him therefore say what follows.

### 4. [verse 2]

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and redeem me from those who rise up against me.”

This happened in the flesh of Christ, and it also happens in us. For our enemies—the devil and his angels—do not cease to rise up against us daily, wishing to mock our weakness and frailty, to entangle us in deceptions, suggestions, temptations, and every kind of snare while we still live on earth.

But let our voice remain watchful toward God, and let it cry out in the members of Christ, beneath the head established in heaven: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and redeem me from those who rise up against me.”

### 5. [verse 3]

“Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood.”

They were indeed men of blood, those who killed the righteous one in whom they found no fault. They were men of blood because, when the foreigner wished to release Christ after washing his hands, they cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” They were men of blood because, when the charge of Christ’s blood was already being laid before them, they replied, offering it as a drink to their descendants: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 23, 25).

Nor did men of blood cease to rise up against his body. For even after Christ’s resurrection and ascension, the Church suffered persecutions—and first that Church which blossomed forth from the Jewish people, from whom our Apostles also came.

There Stephen was first stoned (Acts VII, 58), and he received what his name signified. For Stephen means “Crown.” He was humbly stoned, but sublimely crowned.

Then the kingdoms of the Gentiles rose up among the nations, before what had been foretold concerning them was fulfilled: “All the kings of the earth will adore him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 11). The force of that kingdom raged against Christ’s witnesses; a great and abundant blood of martyrs was poured out. Once poured out, like seed sown, the harvest of the Church sprang up more fruitfully and occupied the whole world, as we now see.

Christ, therefore, is delivered from these men of blood—not only the head, but also the body. Christ is delivered from men of blood, both from those who were, those who are, and those who will be; Christ is delivered, whether he is the one who preceded, the one who is, or the one who is to come.

For Christ is the whole body of Christ. All good Christians who now exist, those who existed before us, and those who will exist after us: the whole Christ is delivered from men of blood. Nor is this voice without meaning: “Save me from men of blood.”

### 6. [verse 4]

“For behold, they hunted my soul.”

They were able to seize it; they were able to kill it; they hunted my soul. But where is: “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. CXV, 16)? Where is: “The trap has been broken, and we have been delivered”? Where is that for which we bless God, who did not give us as prey to their teeth (Ps. CXXIII, 7, 6)?

They hunted, indeed, but the one who guards Israel does not abandon him into the hands of those who hunt.

“For behold, they hunted my soul; the strong rushed upon me.” We must not pass casually over these “strong” men; we must carefully explain who these strong men are who rise up.

Strong men—over whom, if not over the weak, the feeble, and those who are not strong? Yet the weak are praised and the strong are condemned.

If we understand who the strong are, the Lord first called the devil himself strong: “No one,” he says, “can enter the house of the strong man and seize his possessions unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. XII, 29).

He therefore bound the strong man with the bonds of his domination, seized his vessels, and made them his own vessels. For all the wicked were vessels of the devil; those who believed became vessels of Christ. To them the Apostle says: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8); he “makes known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy” (Rom. IX, 23).

These people, therefore, may be understood as the strong. But among human beings there are also certain strong men whose strength is blameworthy and condemnable: they presume upon themselves, but upon temporal prosperity.

Do you not think that the rich man whose story has just been read from the Gospel was strong, since his land yielded abundantly? Disturbed, he devised a plan for storage: he would destroy his old storehouses, build larger ones, fill them, and say to his soul: “You have many good things, soul; feast, rejoice, and be satisfied” (Luke XII, 16–19).

What sort of strong man do you see? Behold a man who did not set God as his helper but trusted in the abundance of his riches. See how strong he is: “He prevailed,” it says, “in his vanity” (Ps. LI, 9).

### 7

There are also other strong men—not strong through riches, bodily strength, or some eminent power of rank in this age, but presuming upon their own righteousness.

This class of strong men must be avoided, feared, and shunned, not imitated: those, I say, who presume not upon the body, wealth, ancestry, or honor—for who does not see that all these things are temporal, fleeting, perishable, and flying away?—but presume upon their own righteousness.

Such strength prevented the Jews from entering through the eye of a needle (Matt. XIX, 24). For when they presumed upon themselves that they were righteous and seemed to themselves to be healthy, they refused medicine and killed the physician himself.

He who said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,” did not come to call such strong people, but the weak.

These were the strong men who insulted Christ’s disciples because their teacher entered in to the weak and ate with the weak. “Why,” they asked, “does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” (Matt. IX, 11–13).

O strong men who have no need of a physician! This strength is not health but madness. For nothing is stronger than the frenzied; they have greater physical power than the healthy. But the greater their strength, the nearer their death.

Therefore may God turn these strong men away from our imitation. For we must fear that anyone may wish to imitate them.

The teacher of humility, sharing in our weakness and granting us a share in his divinity, descended in order to teach the way and to become the way (John XIV, 6). He especially deigned to commend his humility to us, and for that reason did not disdain to be baptized by a servant (Matt. III, 13), so that he might teach us to confess our sins and become weak in order that we might be strong, possessing rather the Apostle’s saying: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. XII, 10).

How, then, did he refuse to be strong? But those who wished to be strong—that is, those who wished to presume upon their own virtue as though they were righteous—“stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (Rom. IX, 32). The Lamb seemed to them to be a kid; and because they killed him as though he were a kid, they did not deserve to be redeemed by the Lamb.

These, then, are the strong men who rushed upon Christ, commending their own righteousness.
