Hear these strong men. When certain inhabitants of Jerusalem, sent by their leaders to seize Christ, said that they had not dared to seize him—for he was truly strong and was seized only when he wished to be seized—those leaders asked them: “Why were you not able to seize him?” They answered: “No one has ever spoken as this man speaks.”

And those strong men replied: “Has any one of the Pharisees believed in him, or any of the scribes, except this crowd that does not know the Law?” (John VII, 45–49).

They set themselves above the weak crowd running to the physician. Why, unless because they themselves were strong? And by their strength—what is worse—they led the whole crowd over to themselves and killed the physician of all.

Yet by being killed he made medicine for the sick from his blood.

“The strong rushed upon me.” Pay particular attention to these strong men and see whether a human being should presume upon anything, when he ought not even to presume upon his own righteousness.

Now see where those who presume upon riches, bodily strength, noble ancestry, and worldly rank lie, if the one who presumes upon righteousness as though it were his own falls.

“The strong rushed upon me.”

Among those strong men was the one boasting of his strength: “I thank you,” he said, “that I am not like the rest of humanity—unjust, rapacious, adulterous—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

See the strong man boasting of his strength. In contrast, observe the weak man standing far away and drawing near through humility.

“But the tax collector,” it says, “stood at a distance and did not dare even to raise his eyes toward heaven, but beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ Amen I say to you, that tax collector went down justified rather than the Pharisee.”

And see the righteousness: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII, 11–14).

These strong men—those proud people—rushed upon Christ. “They were ignorant of God’s righteousness and wished to establish their own righteousness; they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3).

### 8. [verse 5]

What follows? “Neither is there iniquity in me, nor is there sin, Lord.”

The strong men who presumed upon their own righteousness did rush upon him; they rushed upon him, but they found no sin in me. For indeed, why could those strong men—that is, those who seemed righteous—persecute Christ unless as though he were a sinner?

But let them see how strong they are: strong through the violence of fever, not through the firmness of health. Let them see how strong they are; and, as though they were righteous, they raged against the unrighteous.

“Neither is there iniquity in me, nor is there sin, Lord. I ran without iniquity, and I was directed” [Note: [Col. 0697] Most manuscripts read “I directed” (*dirigebam*) and below, instead of “he was directed” (*dirigebatur*), they have “he directed” (*dirigebat*); shortly afterward they read “I direct” (*dirigo*) instead of “I am directed” (*dirigor*).].

Those strong men therefore could not follow me as I ran. For this reason they thought me a sinner: they did not see my footsteps.

### 9. [verse 6]

“I ran without iniquity, and I was directed; rise up to meet me, and see.”

This is said to God: “I ran without iniquity, and I was directed; rise up to meet me, and see.” What then? If he does not come to meet him, can he not see?

It is as if you were walking along a road and could not be recognized by someone at a distance; you would call out to him and say: “Come to meet me and see how I am walking. For when you look at me from a distance, you cannot see my steps.”

Is it therefore the case that unless God came to meet him, he would not see how he was directed without iniquity and how he ran without sin?

We can indeed understand “Rise up to meet me” as “Help me.” But what he added—“and see”—should be understood as: “Make it visible that I run; make it visible that I am being directed.” This follows the figure in which it was also said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII, 12).

God says, “Now I know.” How, unless because he now caused Abraham to be known? For before the testing of temptation each person is unknown even to himself. Thus Peter, through presumption, did not know himself; by denying, he learned what strength he possessed. In his own wavering he understood that he had presumed falsely. He wept (Matt. XXVI, 35, 69, 75), and by weeping deserved to know fruitfully what he had been and to become what he had not been.

Abraham, therefore, having been tested, became known to himself; and God said, “Now I know”—that is, “Now I have caused you to know.”

As a joyful day is that which makes people joyful, and bitter bitterness is that which saddens the one who tastes it, so God, by seeing, causes one to see.

“Rise up,” therefore, he says, “to meet me, and see.” What does “and see” mean? “Help me”; that is, do this among them [Note: [Col. 0698] So the manuscripts. Lov. reads: “And see? Help me; that is, cause it to be done among them,” etc.], so that they may see my course and follow me; so that what is straight may not seem crooked to them, and what keeps to the rule [Note: [Col. 0698] Several manuscripts read “the rule” (*regula*).] of truth may not seem distorted to them:

“For I ran without iniquity, and I was directed; rise up to meet me, and see.”

### 10.

Something also prompts me to say here concerning the sublimity of our very Head, since he was weakened even unto death and took upon himself the flesh of weakness, in order to gather the young of Jerusalem beneath his wings, like a hen weakened together with her chicks. For we have never observed this in any other bird—not even in those that build nests before our eyes: sparrows on the walls, swallows as our annual guests, storks, and the many other birds that nest before our eyes, sit on their eggs, and feed their young, such as the very doves we see every day. We have not known, observed, or seen any bird becoming weak with its young.

How does a hen behave in this way? Certainly I am speaking of a familiar sight, one that occurs before our eyes every day: how her voice grows hoarse, how her whole body becomes rough; her wings droop, her feathers loosen, and you see around her chicks something sickly—yet that weakness is maternal affection. Why, then, did the Lord wish to be called a hen in Holy Scripture, unless for this reason, when he said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (the same, XXIII, 37)?

He gathered all the nations like a hen gathering her chicks: he who was weakened for our sake, taking flesh from us, that is, from the human race; crucified, despised, struck with blows, scourged, hung upon the wood, and wounded with a lance. This, therefore, is the weakness of a mother, not the loss of majesty.

Since Christ was such—and therefore despised, and therefore a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, and therefore many stumbled over him (Rom. IX, 32, and I Pet. II, 8)—since he was such, yet had assumed flesh without sin, he became a participant in our weakness, not in our iniquity, so that by sharing weakness with us he might destroy our iniquity. Therefore: “I ran without iniquity, and I was directed.”

What, then? Is he not to be acknowledged according to what he is as God, and is only that in him to be considered which he became for our sake, and not that by which he made us? Certainly that too must be considered, because it is a great proof of piety to know who endured something for you. It was not some insignificant person for you who were great, but the Most High for you who were weak.

What happened? He was made little: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.” Who was this? Hear above: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped.” Therefore, equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II, 6–8). Thus he emptied himself by taking upon himself what he was not, not by losing what he was.

How, then, did he empty himself? Because he appeared such to you; because he did not display to you the dignity that he possesses with the Father; because he then offered you weakness, while reserving glory for you after you had been purified. He who was equal to the Father was made such—and yet, in that very weakness, he must be acknowledged, not by sight but by faith, so that what we cannot yet see we may at least believe, and by believing what we do not see may also deserve to see it.

Appropriately, after he had risen, he said to Mary Magdalene, to whom he graciously chose first to appear: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John XX, 17). What does this mean? A little later the women touched him. For, returning from the tomb, they worshiped him when he came to meet them and held his feet (Matt. XXVIII, 9); the disciples also touched his scars (Luke XXIV, 39).

What, then, does “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” mean, unless: Do not believe that I am only what you see, lest your sight remain here like your touch? I appear humble to you; I have not yet ascended to the Father—from whom I also descended to you, and from whom I have not departed. I have not yet ascended there, because I have not abandoned you. He came without departing; he ascended without abandoning [Note: [Col. 0699] So the manuscripts. The editors instead have: “I came without departing; I ascended without abandoning.”].

But what does it mean that he ascended to the Father? It means that he becomes known to us as equal to the Father. For we ascend by making progress, so that we may be able to see this, understand this, and in some fashion grasp this. Therefore he delayed the touch; he did not take it away, repel it, or refuse it. “For I have not yet,” he says, “ascended to the Father.”

“His going forth is from the summit of heaven,” says another Psalm, “and his meeting is unto the summit of heaven” (Ps. XVIII, 7). The summit of heaven—that is, the Father is supreme in all spiritual things. From there is his going forth, and his meeting extends unto the summit of heaven. It is said that his meeting reaches the summit only of one who is equal. Indeed, when we compare unequal things and apply something small to something great, in order to see how much one is in relation to the other, if we find them unequal we commonly say, “It does not meet.” But if they are equal, we say, “It meets.” Therefore, “his meeting is unto the summit of heaven,” because he is equal to the Father.

He wished to make himself known as such to his faithful, when he said: “Do not touch me.” This is what he wished the Father to grant to his faithful when he said: “Rise to meet me, and see”—make it known that I am equal to you. “And see”: what does this mean? Make it possible to see that I am equal to you.

How long will Philip say to me, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”? How long will I say, “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known the Father? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 8–11). And perhaps he still does not believe that I am equal.

“Rise to meet me, and see.” Make me visible; make yourself visible; make our equality known to human beings. Let the Jews not think that they crucified merely a human being. Although nothing in him was crucified except insofar as he was human, they did not know whom they crucified. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II, 8). So that my faithful may know this Lord of glory: “Rise to meet me, and see.”

### 11.

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel.” You are the God of Israel, who might be thought to be the God only of Israel, the God only of that one nation which worships you, while all the nations worship idols. You, God of Israel, attend to visiting all the nations.

Let this prophecy be fulfilled in which Isaiah, speaking in your person, addresses your Church, your holy city, that barren woman whose children are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband. To her it was said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband”—more numerous than those of the Jewish nation that has a husband, that received the Law; more numerous than those of that nation which had a visible king. For your King is hidden, and you have more children from a hidden bridegroom.

Therefore it is said to her: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.” Then the Prophet adds: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out your curtains; do not spare. Lengthen your cords farther, and make your stakes strong; extend them again and again to the right and to the left.” Hold the good on the right and the wicked on the left (Matt. XXV, 33), until the winnowing fan comes (the same, III, 12); nevertheless, possess all the nations.

Let good and wicked alike be invited to the wedding; let the wedding feast of those reclining at table be filled (the same, XXII, 9–10). It is the servants’ task to invite; it is the Lord’s task to separate. Extend yourself again and again to the right and to the left. “For your offspring shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit cities that had been deserted”: deserted by God, deserted by the Prophets, deserted by the Apostles, deserted by the Gospel, and full of demons.

You shall inhabit cities that had been deserted. There is no reason for you to fear, for you will prevail; nor should you be ashamed that you were detested. Therefore, because the strong rose up against me [Note: [Col. 0700] So most manuscripts. The editions have “against you”; and shortly afterward, “when it was disgrace and blasphemy,” etc.], do not be ashamed—when laws were enacted against the Christian name, when it was a disgrace and an infamy to be a Christian. “Do not be ashamed that you were detested, for you shall forget your shame forever; you shall remember no more the reproach of your widowhood. For I am the Lord who made you; the Lord is his name, and he who redeemed you shall be called the Lord God of Israel of all the earth” (Isa. LIV, 1–5).

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visiting all the nations”—attend, I say, to visiting all the nations.

### 12.

“Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.” Here he plainly caused fear. Whom would this not frighten? Who, returning to his own conscience, would not tremble? Even if it is conscious of piety, it would be astonishing if it were not also conscious of some iniquity. “For whoever commits sin also commits iniquity” (1 John III, 4). “If you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Ps. CXXIX, 3).

And yet this is true; it was not said without purpose, nor can or will it be wholly without effect: “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.” But look: he had mercy on Paul, who was first Saul and was working iniquity. What good had he done by which he might deserve God? Was he not dragging his saints to death? Was he not carrying letters from the chief priests, so that wherever he found Christians he might seize them for punishment? Was he not doing this, hastening toward it, breathing and panting slaughter, as Scripture bears witness concerning him? From heaven he was summoned by a sublime voice; he was cast down, raised up, blinded, enlightened, killed, brought to life, lost, and restored (Acts IX).

By what merit? Let us say nothing; let us rather hear him himself: “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. I, 13).

Certainly, “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity” can be understood in two ways: either because God leaves no sins altogether unpunished, or because there is a certain iniquity whose perpetrators God does not pity at all. According to these two interpretations, let us say briefly as much as the time permits to Your Charity.

### 13.

Every iniquity, whether small or great, must necessarily be punished, either by the repentant person himself or by God as avenger. For the one who repents also punishes himself. Therefore, brothers, let us punish our sins if we seek God’s mercy.

God cannot have mercy on all who work iniquity as though he were flattering sins or failing to eradicate them. Either you punish, or he punishes. Do you want him not to punish? Then punish yourself. For you have done something that cannot remain unpunished; but let it rather be punished by you, so that you may do what is written in that Psalm: “Let us anticipate his face in confession” (Ps. XCIV, 2).

What does “Let us anticipate his face” mean? Before he himself attends to punishing, anticipate him by confessing and punishing. Let him not find something to punish. For when you punish iniquity, you perform righteousness. And therefore God will have mercy on you, because God now finds you performing righteousness.

What does “performing righteousness” mean? It means that you hate in yourself what he also hates, so that you begin to please God while punishing in yourself what displeases God. For sin cannot be left unpunished, since this is true: “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.”

### 14.

But let us now examine another way in which this sentence can be understood. There is a certain iniquity whose perpetrator God cannot possibly pity. Perhaps you ask what that iniquity is. It is the defense of sins.

Whenever someone defends his sins, he commits great iniquity: he defends what God hates. And see how perversely and unjustly he does so. If he has done something good, he wants it credited to himself; if something evil, to God. In this way people defend their sins by invoking God’s person—which is worse.

What does this mean? There is no one who would dare to say, “Adultery is good; murder is good; fraud is good; perjury is good”—no human being at all. For even those who commit such acts cry out when they suffer. Therefore you will never find a soul so perverse, so estranged from the fellowship of the human race and from participation in the common blood of Adam, that adultery—as I said—fraud, robbery, or perjury seems good to it.

How, then, do they defend these things? “If God had not wished it, I would not have done it. What do you want me to do with my fate?” Now you ask what fate is: you run to the stars. You ask who made and ordered the stars: it is God. Thus you defend your sin in order to accuse God. The guilty person is excused so that the judge may be blamed.

God certainly does not pity those who commit such iniquity. “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.” “Pursue,” he says, “their sins; punish them; pierce them; turn back to themselves those who put themselves behind themselves. Let them be ashamed of themselves, so that they may rejoice in you. Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.”

### 15. [verse 7]

“Let them return in the evening.” I do not know which former workers of iniquity, formerly darkness, he says are to return in the evening. What does “in the evening” mean? Later. What does “in the evening” mean? Too late.

They ought to have done so earlier, before they crucified Christ, recognizing the physician. Why, after he had already been crucified, risen, and ascended into heaven, and after he had sent his Holy Spirit, with which those who were in one house were filled and began to speak in the languages of all nations, did Christ’s crucifiers become terrified? They were pierced in their conscience and sought from the Apostles a plan of salvation. They heard: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven you” (Acts II, 38).

After Christ was killed, after Christ’s blood was poured out, your sins are forgiven. He wished to die in such a way that by his blood he might also redeem those who shed that blood. You shed it in your fury; drink it in confession.

Appropriately, “let them return in the evening, and let them suffer hunger like dogs.” The Jews called the Gentiles dogs, as though they were unclean. For this reason also the Lord himself, when a certain Canaanite woman—not a Jewish woman—followed him, crying out after him and seeking to turn his mercy toward the healing of her daughter, delayed granting the benefit. He foresaw and knew everything, but wished to display her faith, and therefore kept her waiting.

How did he delay? “I was not sent,” he said, “except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” Israel are sheep; what are the Gentiles? “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” Thus he called the Gentiles dogs, because of their uncleanness.

But what did that hungry woman do? This did not repel her. She humbly accepted the insult and deserved the benefit. Indeed, it ought not to be called an insult when it was spoken by the Lord. If a servant said something of that sort to his master, it would be an insult; but when a master says such a thing to a servant, it may rather be called condescension.

“Yes, Lord,” she said. What does “yes” mean? You speak the truth; you speak entirely the truth; I am indeed a dog. “But even the dogs,” she said, “eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters.” And immediately the Lord said: “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matt. XV, 24–28).

A dog a moment ago, now a woman. From where did she become a woman, who shortly before was a dog? By humbly confessing, by not rejecting what had been said by the Lord.

Thus the Gentiles are dogs, and for that reason hungry. It is also good for the Jews to recognize that they are sinners; and, even if late, to return and suffer hunger like dogs.

For he who said, “I fast twice in the week,” was badly satiated. But the publican was a dog, suffering hunger; and therefore he hungered for the Lord’s benefit, saying: “Be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII, 12–13).

Let them, therefore, return in the evening and suffer hunger like dogs. Let them desire God’s grace; let them understand that they are sinners. Let those who were strong become weak; let those who were rich become poor; let those who were righteous recognize that they are sinners; let those who were lions become dogs.

“Let them return in the evening, and let them suffer hunger like dogs, and they shall go around the city.” What city? This world, which Scripture calls in certain places “the city of the surrounding region” (Ps. XXX, 22; LIX, 11; and CVII, 11, according to the Septuagint), that is, because the world had surrounded on every side, among all the nations, that one nation of the Jews where such things were said [Note: [Col. 0703] The editions have *quaerebantur* (“were sought”). The manuscripts have *dicebantur* (“were said”).], and which was called “the city of the surrounding region.”

They, now made hungry dogs, shall go around this city. How shall they go around it? By evangelizing. Saul became a dog from a wolf in the evening—that is, converted late—ran in his Lord’s grace from the crumbs of his master’s table, and went around the city.

### 16. [verse 8]

“Behold, they shall speak with their own mouth, and a sword is in their lips.” It is that two-edged sword of which the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17).

Why two-edged? Why, except because it strikes from both Testaments? By this sword those of whom it was said to Peter, “Kill and eat,” were slaughtered (Acts X, 13).

“And a sword is in their lips,” because—who has heard? “They shall speak with their own mouth.” Who has heard? That is, they shall grow angry against those who are slow to believe. Those who shortly before were themselves unwilling to believe become weary of those who do not believe.

And truly, brothers, this happens. You see a person slow to become a Christian; you call out to him every day, and he scarcely converts. Once converted, he wants everyone to be Christian and is astonished that they are not yet. He has forgotten that he was converted in the evening; but because he has become hungry like a dog, he also has a sword in his lips. He says, “Who has heard?”

What does “Who has heard?” mean? “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). “For who has heard?” The Jews do not believe; they turned to the Gentiles and announced the gospel. The Jews did not believe; nevertheless, through believing Jews the Gospel went around the city, and they said: “For who has heard?”

### 17. [verse 9]

“And you, Lord, shall laugh at them.” “Who has heard?” All the nations will become Christian, and you say, “Who has heard?” What does “you shall laugh at them” mean? You will regard all the nations as nothing. They will be nothing before you, because it will be exceedingly easy for all the nations to believe in you.

### 18. [verse 10]

“I shall keep my strength for you.” Those strong ones fell because they did not keep their strength for you; that is, those who rose up from above and attacked presumed upon themselves.

But I shall keep my strength for you, because if I depart, I fall; if I draw near, I become stronger. See, brothers, what occurs in the human soul. It does not possess light from itself; it does not possess strength from itself. Everything beautiful in the soul is virtue and wisdom, but the soul neither has wisdom for itself nor strength for itself; it is neither its own light nor its own virtue.

There is a certain source and fountain of virtue, a certain root of wisdom, and, so to speak—if it is proper to say this—a certain unchangeable realm of truth. When the soul departs from this, it is darkened; when it draws near, it is illuminated. “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6), because by departing you are darkened.

Therefore: “I shall keep my strength for you.” I shall not depart from you; I shall not presume upon myself. “I shall keep my strength for you, because you, God, are my protector.” For where was I, and where am I? From where did you take me up? What iniquities of mine did you forgive? Where was I lying? To where was I raised?

Therefore I ought to remember what is said in another Psalm: “For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. XXVI, 10). “I shall keep my strength for you, because you, God, are my protector.”

### 19. [verse 11]

“My God, his mercy shall go before me.” Behold what it means: “I shall keep my strength for you”—I shall presume absolutely nothing upon myself. For what good did I bring you, so that you might have mercy on me and justify me? What did you find in me except sins alone? Nothing is yours in me except the nature that you created; everything else is my evil, which you destroyed.

I did not first rise up to you; you came to awaken me. For “his mercy shall go before me.” Before I do anything good, his mercy shall go before me. What will wretched Pelagius say to this?

### 20. [verses 12–14]

“My God has shown me in my enemies.” What does he say? He has shown me in my enemies how great a mercy he has displayed toward me. Let the one who has been gathered compare himself with those who have been left behind; let the chosen compare himself with those who have been rejected; let the vessel of mercy compare itself with the vessels of wrath; and let it see that from one mass God made one vessel for honor and another for dishonor.

What does “he has shown me in my enemies” mean? “If God, wishing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath that were prepared for destruction—and for what purpose?—in order to make known his riches to the vessels of mercy” (Rom. IX, 21–23), then, if he brought forth vessels of wrath in which he might make known his riches to the vessels of mercy, it was most rightly said: “His mercy shall go before me.”

“My God has shown me in my enemies”—that is, he has shown me in those toward whom he did not have mercy how much mercy he had toward me. For unless a debtor is held back, the one whose debt is forgiven gives less thanks. “My God has shown me in my enemies.”

### 21.

But what does he say concerning those very enemies? “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law.” He prays for his enemies and fulfills the commandment.

What, then, do “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity” and “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law” mean? How does he not have mercy on all who work iniquity, and how does he not kill them, lest they forget his law?

But here he spoke of his enemies. What, then? Do his enemies perform righteousness? If those who are hostile to him perform righteousness, then he himself performs iniquity. But because he performs righteousness, and whoever performs righteousness certainly suffers iniquity from his enemies, it remains that those who are hostile to the righteous perform iniquity.

How, then, did he say shortly before, “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity,” and now, concerning his enemies, “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law”? Do not, therefore, have mercy on them; kill their sins. Do not kill those whose sins you kill.

What does it mean to be killed? It means to forget the law of the Lord. That is the true death: to descend into the depth of sin.

This can also be understood concerning the Jews. What does “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law” mean concerning the Jews? Do not kill these enemies of mine, those very people who killed me.

Let the Jewish nation remain. Certainly it was conquered by the Romans; certainly their city was destroyed; Jews are not admitted to their own city, and yet they remain Jews. For all these provinces were subjected to the Romans. Who now recognizes what nations once were under the Roman empire, when all became Roman and all are called Romans? Yet the Jews remain with their sign; they were not conquered in such a way that they were absorbed by the victors.

Not without reason is that man Cain, who had killed his brother, for whom God placed a sign upon him so that no one would kill him (Gen. IV, 15). This is the sign that the Jews possess: they retain all the remnants of their law. They are circumcised, observe Sabbaths, sacrifice the Passover, and eat unleavened bread.

Thus they are Jews; they have not been killed. They are necessary for the believing Gentiles. Why is this so? So that he may show us his mercy in our enemies. “My God has shown me in my enemies.” In branches cut off because of pride, he shows his mercy to the wild olive into which we have been grafted. Behold where those who were proud lie; behold where you have been grafted, though you were lying low. Do not become proud, lest you deserve to be cut off.

“My God, do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law.”

### 22.

“Scatter them by your strength.” It has already happened: the Jews have been scattered throughout all the nations, witnesses to their own iniquity and to our truth. They possess the books in which Christ was prophesied, while we possess Christ.

If a pagan should ever doubt, and when we tell him the prophecies concerning Christ, whose clarity astonishes him, he should suppose that they were written by us, we prove from the books of the Jews that this was foretold long beforehand. See how, from our enemies, we confound other enemies.

“Scatter them by your strength”: take away their strength; take away their power. “And lead them, my protector, Lord.”

“The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride. And from cursing and lying they shall proclaim consummations, in the anger of consummation, and they shall not be.”

These things are obscure, and I fear that they have not been adequately explained. You are already weary from listening; therefore, if it pleases Your Charity, let us defer what remains until tomorrow. The Lord will help us to pay what we owe you, since we make our promise concerning him more than concerning ourselves.

## SERMON II. On the second part of the same Psalm

### 1.

Yesterday’s sermon, having been prolonged, left me a debtor for today. Since the Lord has willed it, the time for repayment has arrived. Just as devoted repay­ers we are, so eager must you be as collectors—not that what he gives and we return (for he is the Lord and we are servants) should be received by you in such a way that there is fruit in your hearing for your life.

For cultivated soil that does not return fruit, and that brings thorns to the farmer instead of crops, seeks not a granary but fire. Our Lord God, however, just as you see him visit this earth with regular rains, so he graciously visits our heart with his word as with his own field. He seeks fruit from our heart, because he knows both what he sows there and how much he rains upon it.

And because, in truth, we are nothing without him—for before we existed we were nothing, and whoever is now a human being and wishes to be without him will be nothing other than a sinful human being—the statement made here is true: “I shall keep my strength for you.” Whatever we can do, unless we preserve it with him and toward him, we lose by departing.

Our mind must always be watchful, not to depart from him, but, if it was far away, to draw nearer and approach more and more—not by the movement of feet, not by conveyance in vehicles, not by the speed of animals, not by the lifting of wings, but by purity of affection and uprightness of holy conduct [Note: [Col. 0706] So six manuscripts. Others, with the editions, have *probabilitate* (“probability” or “credibility”).].

### 2. [verses 12–14]

Let us see, then, what remains of this Psalm. We had stopped at the point where he began to speak of his enemies, saying to God: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law.”

Although he called them his enemies, he nevertheless asked God that they not be killed and forget his law. Yet merely to hold the law—that is, not to forget the law—is not already perfection, a kind of security concerning the reward, and freedom from all concern about punishment.

For there are people who hold the law in memory but do not fulfill it in life. Those who fulfill it in life, however, cannot fail to hold it in memory. Therefore the person who makes God’s commandments his way of life and, by living, continually acts in his heart so that what he holds may not be erased—who, by living, reminds himself what has been written in his heart concerning God’s law—this person holds God’s law fruitfully; he will not be reckoned an enemy [Note: [Col. 0706] So the manuscripts. The editions have: “and by living continually recalls it.”].

For behold, the Jewish enemies whom this Psalm appears to signify hold God’s law, and therefore it was said concerning them: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law,” so that the Jewish nation might remain and, while it remained, the multitude of Christians might increase.

They certainly remain throughout all the nations, and they are Jews; they have not ceased to be what they were. That is, this nation did not submit to Roman authority in such a way that it lost the form of the Jews; rather, it was subjected to the Romans while still retaining its laws—and those laws are God’s laws.

But what happened among them? “You tithe mint and cumin, and you have left aside the weightier matters of the Law: mercy and judgment; straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel” (Matt. XXIII, 23–24). The Lord says this to them.

And indeed, this is how they are: they hold the Law; they hold the Prophets; they read everything and sing everything, but they do not see there the light of the Prophets, who is Christ Jesus. They do not see him now, when he sits in heaven; but neither did they see him then, when he walked humbly among them, and they became guilty by shedding his blood—but not all of them.

We commend this also today to Your Charity: not all of them. For many of them turned to the one whom they had killed, and by believing in him obtained forgiveness and mercy even for the blood they had shed; and they offered human beings an example of how they ought not to despair of being forgiven for any sin whatsoever, since even the killing of Christ was forgiven to those who confessed.

Therefore it was said: “Because you, God, are my protector”; “my God, his mercy shall go before me”—that is, his mercy went before all my good merits. Even if he found nothing good in me, he himself makes me good; he himself justifies the one who turns; and he himself urges the one who has turned away to turn back.

“My God,” he says again, “has shown me in my enemies”—that is, he has shown me by comparison with my enemies how much he loves me and how greatly he grants me from his goodness. For since vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy are from one mass (Rom. IX, 21), through the vessels of wrath the vessels of mercy learn how much good God grants them.

Then: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law.” This was said concerning the Jews.

But what will you do to them? “Scatter them by your strength.” Show them that you are strong, not they, who by presuming upon their own strength did not know your truth—not strong in the way those strong men were of whom it was said, “The strong rose up against me,” but strong in the way you are strong to scatter them.

“And lead them, my protector, Lord”—that is, scatter them in such a way that you do not abandon them, lest they at some time forget your law; and in this very matter protect me, so that from their dispersion I may possess testimony to your mercy.

### 3.

And it follows: “The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips.” To what is this sentence joined and connected? “The sins,” he says, “of their mouth, the word of their lips.” The following words are not connected in such a way as to teach us with what this sentence should be joined.

“The sins,” he says, “of their mouth, the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride. And from cursing and lying they shall proclaim consummations, in the anger of consummation, and they shall not be.”

Yesterday we also said that this was obscure, and for that reason postponed its explanation until your minds were fresher. Now, therefore, since you are not yet weary of listening, lift up your hearts so that you may assist me with your attention, lest perhaps in the obscurity and difficulty our discourse should prove insufficient for your understanding. You too ought to bring something of your own, so that what we have not completed by speaking you may complete by understanding.

This sentence has therefore been placed in the middle in such a way that we cannot easily see to what it is joined: “The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips.”

Let us return, then, to what came before. Since he had said, “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law,” although he had called them enemies, he added two verses: “Scatter them by your strength, and lead them, my protector, Lord.” Immediately he introduced: “The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips”—that is, kill that, not them.

Therefore: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law.” But there is something in them that you should kill, so that you may fulfill what was said above: “Have no mercy on all who work iniquity.”

Scatter them, then, and lead them—that is, do not abandon them when you scatter them. By not abandoning them, you have something to do in them, while you do not kill them themselves.

What, then, will you kill? “The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips.” What will you kill in them? “Crucify, crucify!” (John XIX, 6)—what they shouted, not those who shouted it.

For they wished to destroy, kill, and annihilate Christ. But by raising Christ from the dead, whom they wished to destroy, you kill the sins of their mouth, the word of their lips. The one whose destruction they shouted now causes them fear by living; and the one whom they despised on earth they marvel to see worshiped by all the nations in heaven.

Thus the sins of their mouth and the word of their lips are killed.

4. And let them be caught in their pride. What does “let them be caught in their pride” mean? Because they rushed upon him in vain, as strong men, and it seemed almost as though they had succeeded in doing something and had prevailed against the Lord. They were able to crucify a human being; weakness was able to prevail, and strength to be killed. They thought themselves something—strong, powerful, victorious—like a lion ready for prey, like fat bulls, as he recalls them elsewhere: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Psalm 21:13).

But what did they accomplish against Christ? They killed not life but death. For when death had been extinguished in the one who was dying, and life arose from death in [Note: [Col. 0708] Three manuscripts of better quality read “in the living one.”] the living one—for he himself also raised himself, since there was in him that which could not die—what did they accomplish? Hear what they accomplished: “They destroyed the temple.” And what did he himself do? “In three days he raised it up” (John 2:19).

Thus, therefore, “the sins of their mouth and the word of their lips” were killed. And what has now happened in those who were converted? “Let them be caught in their pride.” For it was announced to them that the one whom they had killed had risen. They believed that he had risen because they saw him placed in heaven, sending the Holy Spirit from there and filling those who believed in him (Acts 1:9; 2:4). And they discovered that they had condemned nothing and accomplished nothing. Their deed came to nothing; their sin remained. Since their deed had been nullified but the sin remained upon those who had committed it, they were caught in their pride: they saw themselves under their own iniquity.

It remained, therefore, for them to confess their sin, and for him to forgive who had yielded to sinners, giving his death when he was killed by the dead and giving life to the dead. Thus they were caught in their pride.

5. “And from cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced, in the wrath of consummation, and they shall not be.” This too is difficult to understand: with what should “and they shall not be” be joined? What shall not be? Let us therefore examine the preceding text: “When they have been caught in their pride, consummations shall be announced from cursing and deceit.” What are these consummations? Perfections; for to be consummated means to be perfected.

To be consummated is one thing, and to be consumed another. Something is consummated when it is brought to an end in such a way that it is perfected; something is consumed when it is brought to an end in such a way that it no longer exists. Pride did not permit a human being to be perfected; nothing so obstructs perfection.

Let Your Charity attend for a little to what I am saying, and see a very grievous evil, one that must be greatly avoided. What sort of evil do you think it is? How long must I enlarge upon the evil that lies in pride? The devil is to be punished for this alone. Certainly he is the prince of all sins; certainly he is the seducer toward sin. Adultery is not charged to him, nor drunkenness, fornication, or the robbery of another’s property: he fell through pride alone.

And since envy accompanies pride, it is impossible for a proud person not to be envious. Through this vice, which necessarily follows pride, the one who had fallen also envied the one who stood, and took pains to seduce the human being, lest that person be raised to the place from which he himself had been cast down.

For this reason he strives to persuade people to commit actual sins, since we have such a Judge that he cannot bring false accusations against us. If our case were being tried before a human judge whom he could deceive with false charges, he would not need to work very hard to make us sin: by deceiving the judge, he could oppress the innocent, draw the deceived over to himself, and make them condemned along with him. But now, because he knows that the Judge cannot be deceived, and knows that, being just, he cannot show partiality, he wants to bring before him as guilty those whom it is necessary for him to condemn, because he is just.

He therefore strives to make us sin through envy alone, and envy necessarily accompanies pride. Such, then, is the evil of pride: it obstructs perfection.

Let someone boast about wealth, beauty, or bodily strength. All these things are mortal; those who boast of mortal things deserve to be laughed at, since such things usually abandon them while they are alive, or they must abandon them when they die. But there is a capital vice which, when someone has made good progress, tempts him through pride so that he loses everything he has gained. Thus all vices must be feared in evil deeds, but pride must be feared even more in good deeds.

It is therefore no wonder that the Apostle is so humble that he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” To prevent himself from being tempted by this vice, what medicine does he say was applied against his swelling by the physician who knew what he was treating? “So that I might not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations,” he says, “there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that it might depart from me; and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

See what the consummations are. The Apostle, teacher of the nations and father of believers through the Gospel, received a thorn in the flesh by which he was buffeted. Who among us would dare to say such a thing, unless he were not ashamed to confess it? For if we say that Paul did not suffer this, while supposedly honoring him, we make him a liar. But because he is truthful and spoke the truth, we must believe that an angel of Satan was given to him so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of the revelations.

Behold how greatly the serpent of pride must be feared! What, then, happened to these people? They were caught in their sin because they killed Christ; and through the very greatness of their sin they were more deeply humbled, and by greater humility they deserved to be raised up. This is: “Let them be caught in their pride.”

“And from cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced”—that is, they shall be perfected all the more because they were caught in cursing and deceit. Pride did not permit them to be perfected; their crime removed their pride through their confession; forgiveness erased the crime through God’s mercy. Thus “from cursing and deceit consummations were announced.” That is, the following was said to the human being: “You have seen what you are; you have experienced what you are. You have gone astray, you have been blinded, you have sinned and fallen, and you have recognized your weakness. Beg the physician; do not imagine that you are well. Where is your madness? Behold, you killed the physician, whom you could not destroy by killing him. Yet, as far as you were concerned, you killed him.”

“From cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced.” You did what belonged to cursing, O Jews: “For accursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). You crucified Christ; you regarded him as accursed. Add deceit to the cursing: you placed guards at the tomb and gave them money so that they might lie (Matthew 28:12). Behold, Christ has risen: where is the curse of the cross that you effected? Where is the lie of the guards whom you bribed?

6. “From cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced, in the wrath of consummation, and they shall not be.” What does “in the wrath of consummation consummations shall be announced” mean?

There is a wrath of consummation, and there is a wrath of consumption. Every divine punishment is called wrath. But sometimes God punishes in order to perfect, and sometimes he punishes in order to condemn.

How does he punish in order to perfect? “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). How does he punish in order to condemn? When he places the wicked on his left and says to them: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). That is the wrath of consumption, not of consummation.

But “consummations shall be announced in the wrath of consummation”—that is, the Apostles will preach that “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20), and that human weakness served as a medicine of humiliation. Thinking upon this, and discovering and confessing their iniquities, “they shall not be.” What shall they not be? They shall not be in their pride. For above he had said: “Let them be caught in their pride.”

“And from cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced in the wrath of consummation, and they shall not be”—namely, they shall not be in the pride in which they were caught.

7. “And they shall know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” Previously they seemed righteous to themselves because the Jewish people had received the Law and had kept God’s commandments. It is shown to them that they did not keep it, since they did not understand Christ within those very commandments of God, because “a partial blindness has happened in Israel” (Romans 9:25).

The Jews themselves also see that they ought not to despise the nations, whom they regarded as dogs and sinners. For just as both were found alike in iniquity, so they will alike attain salvation. “Not from the Jews only,” says the Apostle, “but also from the nations” (Romans 9:24).

For this reason, “the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Psalm 117:22), so that it might join the two in itself; for a corner unites two walls. The Jews seemed exalted and great to themselves; the nations seemed weak, sinful, servants of demons, and worshipers of idols. Yet in both there was iniquity.

The Jews too were shown to be sinners, because “there is none who does good, not even one” (Romans 3:12). They laid aside their pride and did not envy the salvation of the nations, because they recognized that their weakness and that of the nations were alike; and, joined together in the cornerstone, they worshiped the Lord together.

“And they shall know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” He will not rule the Jews alone, but also the ends of the earth. They would not know this if they still remained in their pride; and they would remain in their pride if they still seemed righteous to themselves. But so that they would not seem righteous to themselves, consummations were announced to them from cursing and deceit, in the wrath of consummation, because they had been caught in their pride through the cursing they committed when they killed Christ.

Behold what our Lord Jesus Christ did. He died in the hands of the Jews and redeemed a multitude of the nations. For this reason his blood was poured out; for this reason it was beneficial—but beneficial to all who were converted. For those who had killed him recognized him, and from him they merited forgiveness for the very act of killing him and for their great sin.

8. [verse 15] What, then, about these very people? The same as above: “They shall return toward evening”—that is, even if late, that is, after the killing of our Lord Jesus Christ. “They shall return toward evening, and they shall suffer hunger like dogs.” Like dogs, not like sheep or calves: like dogs, like the nations, like sinners, because those who had seemed righteous to themselves also recognized their sin.

Of them it is said in another psalm: “Afterward they hastened.” Here this is expressed as “toward evening.” For there it reads: “Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Psalm 15:4). Why did they hasten afterward? Because their infirmities had been multiplied. For if they still seemed healthy to themselves, they would never hasten.

What is said there—“Their infirmities have been multiplied”—is said here as: “Let them be caught in their pride, and from cursing and deceit consummations shall be announced in the wrath of consummation.” And what is said there—“Afterward they hastened”—is said here as: “And they shall not be,” namely, in their pride.

“And they shall know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth; and they shall return toward evening.” It is therefore good for a sinner to be humbled, and no one is more incurable than one who seems well to himself.

“And they shall go around the city.” Yesterday too we explained the city: namely, all the nations surrounding the city.

9. [verse 16] “They shall be scattered in order to eat”—that is, in order to gain others and transform believers into their own body. “But if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.” For above he had also mentioned their murmuring, when they said: “For who has heard?” And you, Lord, he says, will laugh at them when they say: “Who has heard?” Why? “Because you will regard all the nations as nothing.” So also here: “But if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.”

10. [verses 17–18] Let the Psalm be brought to a conclusion. See the rejoicing corner, already glad because of both walls (Ephesians 2), rejoicing in both walls. The Jews were proud; they have been humbled. The nations were despairing; they have been raised up. Let them come to the corner; let them meet there, come together there, and find there the kiss of peace. Let them come from different directions, but let them not come against one another: the one from circumcision, the other from uncircumcision.

The walls were far apart before they came to the corner. But at the corner let them hold fast to one another. And what does the whole Church, formed from both walls, now say?

“But I shall sing of your power, and I shall exult in your mercy in the morning.” In the morning, after the temptations have passed; in the morning, when the night of this age has passed; in the morning, when we are no longer afraid of the ambushes of robbers, or of the devil and his angels; in the morning, when we no longer walk by the lamp of prophecy, but contemplate the very Word of God as the sun.

“And I shall exult in your mercy in the morning.” Rightly it is said in another psalm: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall contemplate” (Psalm 5:5). Rightly also the Lord’s resurrection took place at dawn, so that what is said in another psalm might be fulfilled: “In the evening weeping will linger, and in the morning rejoicing” (Psalm 29:6).

In the evening the disciples mourned our Lord Jesus Christ as dead; at dawn they rejoiced in him as risen. “I shall exult in your mercy in the morning.”

11. “Because you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation. To you, my helper, I shall sing psalms, because you, God, are my protector.”

What would I have been, unless you had come to my aid? How desperate would I have been, unless you had cared for me? Where would I have lain, unless you had come? Certainly I was in peril from a great wound, but my wound required an all-powerful physician.

For the all-powerful physician nothing is incurable. He gives up on no one [Note: [Col. 0712] The printed editions read *renuntiat alicui*; the manuscripts, *renuntiat ad aliquem*.]. It is necessary that you wish to be healed; it is necessary that you not shrink from his hand. But even if you do not wish to be healed, your wound urges you to be healed: it calls back the one who has turned away, somehow compels the one who flees to return to it, and draws him.

In all things he fulfills what is said: “His mercy will anticipate me.” Consider what is meant by “will anticipate me.” If you brought forward something of your own first, and by some good of yours first merited God’s mercy, then it did not anticipate you. But when do you understand that you have been anticipated, unless you understand what the Apostle says: “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

This is: “His mercy will anticipate me.” Finally, considering all the good things we may possess—whether in our nature, in our formation, in our very way of life [Note: [Col. 0712] The manuscripts read “conversion.”], in faith, hope, charity, good conduct, justice, and fear of God—and recognizing that everything comes only from his gifts, he concluded in this way: “My God is my mercy.”

When filled with God’s good things, he found nothing by which to call his God except “my mercy.” O name under which no one need despair! “My God,” he says, “is my mercy.”

What does “my mercy” mean? If you say, “My salvation,” I understand that he gives salvation. If you say, “My refuge,” I understand that you flee to him. If you say, “My strength,” I understand that he gives you strength. But “my mercy”—what does that mean? Everything that I am comes from your mercy.

“But I deserved you by calling upon you!” What did I do in order to exist? What did I do in order to exist as one who would call upon you? For if I did something in order to exist, I already existed before I existed. But if I was altogether nothing before I existed, I did nothing to deserve you so that I might exist.

You made me exist, and did you not make me good? You gave me existence, and could someone else give me goodness? If you gave me existence and another gave me goodness, the one who gave me goodness would be better than the one who gave me existence.

But because no one is better than you, no one more powerful than you, and no one more generous than you in mercy, from the one from whom I received existence, from him I also received goodness. “My God is my mercy.”

# Exposition of Psalm 59: Sermon to the People

[Note: [Col. 0713] Delivered some time after the exposition of the preceding Psalm; see no. 11.]

1. [verses 1–2] The title of this psalm is somewhat lengthy, but it should not frighten us, because the Psalm itself is short. Let us therefore listen as though we had heard a somewhat longer psalm. Since we speak in the Church of God in the name of Christ to those who are nourished and are still to be nourished, and since you are not strangers to the flavor of these Scriptures, from which the world is estranged, these things should not always be new to you.

For if you have chewed over with delight in the mouth of your mind things you have heard very often, and have not buried them through forgetfulness as though in your stomach, that same recollection and memory of yours will greatly help us, so that we need not speak at such length to explain to you, as though you were beginners, what we know you already understand.

Certainly you often remember hearing us say this: it is scarcely possible to find voices in the Psalms except those of Christ and the Church, or of Christ alone, or of the Church alone—which, in any case, we are in part. And therefore, when we recognize our own voices, we cannot recognize them without feeling; and we take all the greater delight when we sense that we are from the same source [Note: [Col. 0713] Thus several manuscripts; some read *in iisdem* (“in the same things”), while the printed editions read *in idem* (“into the same thing”).].

David the king was one man, but he did not represent only one man. When he represented the Church, he represented one consisting of many and spread to the ends of the earth; when, however, he represented one man, he represented the one who is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

In this psalm, or rather in the title of this psalm, certain victories of David are mentioned: that he acted bravely in waging war against certain enemies and making them tributary, when, after the death of Saul his persecutor, he openly received his kingdom in Israel.

For even before he suffered persecution he was king, but he was known only to God. Later, after his kingdom had become manifest and had been received openly and conspicuously, he defeated those who are mentioned in this title. The title of the Psalm is recorded [Note: [Col. 0714] Thus the royal manuscript; the others, with the printed editions, read *natus est* (“was born”) rather than *notatus est* (“was recorded”).] as follows:

“To the end, for those who shall be changed, for the inscription of the title, for David, for instruction, when he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab turned back and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

We read in the Books of Kings that all those whom he has named were defeated by David: Mesopotamia of Syria, Syria of Zobah, Joab, and Edom (2 Samuel 8). These events happened, and just as they happened they were written down there and are read there; let whoever wishes read them.

Nevertheless, as the prophetic Spirit is accustomed in the titles of the Psalms to depart somewhat from the exact expression of historical events, and to say something that is not found in the historical account, thereby warning us rather that such titles were inscribed not for the purpose of learning historical events but for prefiguring future things—as it is said that David changed his appearance before Abimelech, dismissed him, and departed (Psalm 33:1), although the Book of Kings indicates that he did not do this before Abimelech but before Achish the king (1 Samuel 21:13)—so in this title too we find something by which we are reminded of something.

For in that account of the wars and brave deeds of King David, in which all those whom we have mentioned were defeated, we do not read that he set anything on fire. Here, however, this is especially inserted, although it is not written there: that he set fire to Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah.

Let us therefore now begin to examine these matters according to their significance for future things, and to bring the obscurity of the shadows back into the light of the Word.

2. You know what “to the end” means: “For Christ is the end of the Law” (Romans 10:4). You know who those are who are changed. Who are they, if not those who pass from an old life into a new one? Far be it from us to understand this change as something blameworthy. It is not the change by which Adam passed from righteousness to iniquity and from pleasure to toil, but the change by which those are changed to whom it was said: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

They are changed “for the inscription of the title.” You know the inscription of the title. A title was fixed above the Lord’s cross, written: “This is the King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:37). Those who pass from the kingdom of the devil into the kingdom of Christ are changed into the inscription of this title.

They are rightly changed into the inscription of this title. They are changed, as follows, “for instruction.” For after saying, “For those who shall be changed into the inscription of the title,” he added, “for David himself, for instruction.” That is, they are changed not for themselves but for David himself, and they are changed for instruction.

Christ is not king in such a way that he will reign over this age, since he plainly said: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Therefore let us pass into his instruction [Note: [Col. 0714] The manuscripts read “into his grace and instruction”; the printed editions, “into his instruction.”], if we wish to be changed into the inscription of the title—not for ourselves but for David himself—so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them (2 Corinthians 5:15).

When would Christ change us unless he had done what he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)? If Christ came to cast fire upon the earth, certainly he did so beneficially and profitably—not in the sense in which he will cast the world into fire.

But how did he cast fire upon the earth? Since he came to cast fire upon the earth, let us now ask what Mesopotamia is that was set on fire, and what Syria of Zobah is.

Let us therefore inquire into the interpretations of the names according to the Hebrew language in which this Scripture was first spoken. They say that Mesopotamia means “Elevated Calling.” Now the whole world has been elevated through calling. Syria means “Sublime.” But that which had been sublime was set on fire and humbled; and just as what had been exalted was humbled, so let what had been humbled be exalted.

Zobah means “Vain Old Age.” Thanks be to Christ, who set it on fire. When old brushwood is burned, green growth takes its place; new things arise more vigorously, more abundantly, and more verdantly when fire has first preceded them in the burning of the old.

Let Christ’s fire not be feared, then: it consumes hay. For “all flesh is hay, and all the glory of human beings is like the flower of hay” (Isaiah 40:6). He set these things on fire with that fire.

“And he turned back Joab.” Joab means “Enemy.” The enemy was turned back. Understand this as you wish. If he was turned back in flight, he is the devil; if he was turned toward faith, he is a Christian.

How is he turned back in flight? From the heart of the Christian: “The prince of this world,” he says, “has now been cast out” (John 12:31). But if the Christian, who had been an enemy, is turned toward the Lord, why is the enemy turned? Because the one who had been an enemy has become faithful.

“He struck Edom.” Edom means “Earthly.” This earthly person had to be struck. Why should the earthly person live, when the heavenly person ought to live? The earthly life, therefore, has been killed; let the heavenly life live.

“For just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49). See him being killed: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5).

When he had struck Edom, he struck twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt. Twelve thousand is a perfect number, and to this perfect number the number twelve of the Apostles also belongs. For it was not without reason that there were twelve: the word was to be sent throughout the whole world.

The Word of God, however, is Christ, in the clouds—that is, in preachers of the truth. The world consists of four parts. Its four parts are well known to everyone and are often mentioned in Scripture; they are also called the four winds (Ezekiel 37:9): east, west, north, and south.

The word was sent to all four parts, so that all might be called in the Trinity. Three times four makes the number twelve. Rightly, therefore, twelve thousand earthly people were struck: the whole world was struck. For from the whole world the Church was chosen, put to death with respect to earthly life.

Why “in the Valley of Salt”? A valley signifies humility; saltworks signify flavor. For many people are humbled, but vainly and foolishly: they are humbled in vain old age.

Someone suffers tribulation for money; someone suffers tribulation for temporal honor; someone suffers tribulation for the advantages of this life. He will suffer tribulation and be humbled—why not for God? Why not for Christ? Why not for the flavor of salt?

Do you not know that it was said to you: “You are the salt of the earth”; and, “If salt has lost its savor, it is good for nothing except to be thrown outside” (Matthew 5:13)? It is therefore good to be humbled wisely.

Do we not see the heretics being humbled now? Have not laws been enacted against them even by human beings, against whom the divine laws reign—laws that had already condemned them? Behold, they are humbled; behold, they are driven out; behold, they suffer persecution—but without flavor, for foolishness and vanity. The salt has already lost its savor; therefore it has been thrown outside, to be trampled by human beings.

We have heard the title of the Psalm; let us hear also the words of the Psalm.

3. [verse 3] “O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us.” Is it David who speaks—the one who struck, who set fire, who conquered—or are these the ones to whom he did these things, so that those who were evil might be struck and rejected, and then brought back to life and return in order to become good?

That David, strong of hand, our Christ, carried out this slaughter, while that man bore his figure. He did these things; he brought this slaughter with his sword and his fire. For he brought both into this world. “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), you have in the Gospel; and, “I have come to bring a sword upon the earth” (Matthew 10:34), you have in the Gospel.

He brought fire by which Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah would be set ablaze; he brought the sword by which Edom would be struck.

This slaughter, then, was carried out for those who are changed into the inscription of the title, for David himself. Let us therefore hear their voice. They were struck for their salvation; let them speak when raised up.

Let those who have been changed for the better, changed into the inscription of the title, changed for instruction, for David himself, speak:

“O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us; you were angry, and you have shown us mercy.”

You destroyed us in order to build us; you destroyed us who had been badly built; you destroyed vain old age so that there might be a building in the new human being, a building that would remain forever.

Rightly you were angry and showed us mercy. You would not show mercy unless you were angry. You destroyed us in your anger; but your anger was directed against our old age, so that old age might be destroyed. But you showed us mercy because of the newness, because of those who are changed into the inscription of the title; for “although our outward person is being corrupted, our inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

4. [verse 4] “You have shaken the earth and troubled it.” How has the earth been troubled? Through the conscience of sinners. Where shall we go? Where shall we flee when that sword has been brandished: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2)?

“You have shaken the earth and troubled it. Heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.” It is not worthy to be healed if it has not been shaken.

But you speak, preach, threaten in the name of God, do not remain silent about the coming judgment, and remind people of God’s commandment. If the one who hears does not fear and is not shaken, that person is not worthy to be healed.

Another hears, is shaken, is goaded, beats his breast, and pours out tears: “Heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.”

5. [verse 5] After this—the earthly person having been struck, old age having been set on fire, the human being having been changed for the better, and light having been made for those who were darkness—there follows what is written elsewhere: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1).

The first labor is to become displeasing to yourself, to conquer your sins [Note: [Col. 0717] The manuscripts read *expugnes* (“conquer”); the printed editions, *expurges* (“purge”).], and to be changed for the better. The second labor is, because you have been changed, to endure the tribulations and temptations of this age, and to persevere amid them to the end.

While he was speaking of these things and signifying them, what does he add? “You have shown your people hard things”—now your people, made tributary after David’s victory. “You have shown your people hard things.”

In what things? In the persecutions endured by the Church of Christ, when so much martyr blood was shed. “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of piercing.” What does “of piercing” mean? Not of destruction. For it was not a destruction that ruined, but a medicine that burned. “You have given us wine of piercing.”

6. [verse 6] Why this? “You have given those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

Through temporal tribulations, he says, you have signified to your people that they should flee from the wrath of eternal fire. For the Apostle Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God.”

And when he was exhorting the martyrs to endurance—while the world raged, while slaughter was being carried out by persecutors, while the blood of the faithful was being poured out far and wide, while Christians endured many hard things in chains, prisons, and torments—so that they would not fail amid these hardships, Peter addressed them:

“It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Peter 4:17–18).

What, then, will happen in the judgment? The bow has been stretched; it is still at the stage of threat, not yet at that of fulfillment.

And consider what is in a bow. Must not the arrow be sent forward? Yet the bowstring is drawn backward, in the opposite direction from that in which the arrow is to be sent. And the farther backward the drawing extends, the greater the force with which the arrow moves forward.

What did I mean? The longer judgment is delayed, the greater the force with which it will come.

Therefore let us also give thanks to God for temporal tribulations, because he has given his people a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow. Thus, trained through temporal tribulations, his faithful may be worthy to escape the condemnation of eternal fire, which will overtake all who do not believe these things.

“You have given those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

7. [verse 7] “So that your beloved may be delivered. Save me with your right hand, and hear me.”

“Save me with your right hand, O Lord”: save me in such a way that I may stand at your right hand. “Save me with your right hand.” I am not asking for temporal salvation; let your will be done concerning this.

We do not at all know what may benefit us for the present time, for “we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should” (Romans 8:26). But “save me with your right hand,” so that even if I suffer some tribulations in this present time, when the night of all tribulations has passed I may be found at your right hand among the sheep, not on the left among the goats.

“Save me with your right hand, and hear me.” For now I ask for what you wish to give. I do not cry out throughout the day because of the words of my sins, so that you may not hear me, and at night [Note: [Col. 0717] The phrase “so that you may not hear me” is absent from the printed editions; it is repeated in the manuscripts.], so that you may not hear me, and not for my foolishness [Col. 0718] (Psalm 21:2–3). Rather, this is certainly for my admonition, adding the flavor of the Valley of Salt, so that in tribulation I may know what to ask.

I ask for eternal life; therefore hear me, because I ask for your right hand.

Let Your Charity understand that every faithful person who has the word of God in his heart, who fears with reverence the coming judgment, and who lives honorably, so that the holy name of his Lord may not be blasphemed because of him, asks for many things according to this age and is not heard; but in regard to eternal life he is always heard.

Who would not ask for health when he is sick? And yet perhaps it is still useful for him to remain sick. It may happen that you are not heard concerning this matter. Yet you are not heard according to your wish in order that you may be heard according to your benefit.

But when you ask that God give you eternal life, that God give you the kingdom of heaven, that God grant you to stand at the right hand of his Son when he comes to judge the earth, be confident: you will receive it, though you do not receive it now—for the time to receive it has not yet come.

You are heard, and you do not know it. What you ask is being accomplished, even though you do not know in what way it is being accomplished. The matter is in the root, not yet in the fruit.

“Save me with your right hand, and hear me.”

8. [verse 8.] God has spoken in his sanctuary. Why are you afraid that what God has spoken will not come to pass? If you had some grave and wise friend, how would you speak? “He has spoken these things; what he has spoken must necessarily happen. He is a serious man; he does not act frivolously; he is not easily moved from his decision; what he has promised is fixed.” Yet he is still a human being, who sometimes wants to do what he has promised but cannot. There is nothing for you to fear from God: that he is truthful is certain; that he is almighty is certain; he cannot deceive you, and he has the means to accomplish what he has said. Why, then, are you afraid that you will be deceived? You must ensure that you do not deceive yourself, and persevere to the end, when he will give what he has promised.

God has spoken in his sanctuary. In which sanctuary of his? “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. 5:19). In that sanctuary of which you heard elsewhere: “O God, your way is in the sanctuary” (Ps. 76:14).

God has spoken in his sanctuary. “I shall rejoice, and I shall divide Shechem.” Because God has spoken this, it will happen: it is the voice of the Church—“God has spoken in his sanctuary.” It does not repeat the words that God spoke; but because God has spoken in his sanctuary, and nothing can happen except as God has spoken, these events consequently follow: “I shall rejoice, and I shall divide Shechem, and I shall measure out the valley of tents.”

“Shechem” is interpreted as “Shoulders.” According to the historical account, Jacob, returning from Laban his father-in-law with all his people, concealed in Shechem the idols that he had brought from Syria, where he had long sojourned, and from which he was finally returning (Gen. 35:4). He made tents there for his sheep and herds, and called that place “Tents” (ibid. 33:17). “And these,” says the Church, “I shall divide.”

What does “I shall divide Shechem” mean? If it is referred to the historical place where the idols were hidden, it signifies the Gentiles: I divide the Gentiles. What does “I divide” mean? “For not all have faith” (II Thess. 3:2). What does “I divide” mean? Some will believe, others will not believe; yet those who believe should not fear among those who do not believe. For they are now divided by faith; afterward they will be divided in judgment, the sheep on the right and the goats on the left (Matt. 25:33). Behold, we have found how the Church divides Shechem.

How does she divide the shoulders, according to the interpretation of the name? Shoulders are divided so that their sins weigh down some, while others lift Christ’s burden. For he was seeking pious shoulders when he said: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (ibid. 11:30). Another burden presses and weighs you down; Christ’s burden, however, lifts you up.
