Another burden has weight; Christ’s burden has wings. If you take away a bird’s wings, you seem to remove a burden; yet the more burden you have removed, the more it will remain on the ground. The bird you wished to unburden lies there: it does not fly, because you have taken away its burden. Let the burden return, and it flies. Such is Christ’s burden. Let people carry it; let them not be lazy. Do not look to those who refuse to bear it; let those who wish bear it, and they will discover how light, how pleasant, how delightful it is—how it carries them up into heaven and snatches them away from the earth [Note: [Col. 0719] Gatian. reads “lifting up” (erigens) instead of “snatching away” (rapiens).].

“I shall divide Shechem, and I shall measure out the valley of tents.” Perhaps, because of Jacob’s sheep, the valley of tents is understood as the Jewish people, and it too is divided: those who believed passed out from it; the rest remained outside.

9. [verse 9.] Gilead is mine. These are names read in the Scriptures of God. Gilead has a meaning that conveys its own interpretation and a great mystery: it is interpreted as “Heap of Testimony.” How great a heap of testimony there is in the martyrs! “Gilead is mine”: my heap of testimony is mine; the true martyrs are mine.

Let others die [Note: [Col. 0719] The printed editions read “let the wicked die” (moriantur mali); the manuscripts, however, read “let others die” (moriantur alii), where the pseudo-martyrs of the Donatists seem to be indicated.] for their ancient vanity without salt; do they perhaps belong to the heap of testimony? For “even if I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. 13:3). But when the Lord warned in a certain passage that peace must be maintained, he prefaced it with salt: “Have salt in yourselves,” he said, “and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49).

Therefore, “Gilead is mine”; but Gilead, that is, the heap of testimony, was clearly formed amid great tribulation. At that time the Church was held in disgrace among human beings; reproach was cast upon that widow because she belonged to Christ, because she bore the sign of the cross on her forehead. There was not yet honor; at that time it was a crime. When, therefore, it was not honor but a crime, then the heap of testimony was formed. Through the heap of testimony the charity of Christ was spread abroad, and through the spreading of Christ’s charity the nations were won over.

It follows: “And Manasseh is mine,” which is interpreted as “Forgotten.” For to her it had been said: “You shall forget your confusion forever, and you shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood” (Isa. 54:4). There was therefore once confusion for the Church, which she has now forgotten; she no longer remembers the confusion and disgrace of her widowhood. When there was a certain confusion among human beings, the heap of testimony was formed. Now no one even remembers that confusion, when it was a disgrace to be a Christian; no one remembers it now, everyone has forgotten it; now “Manasseh is mine.”

“And Ephraim is the strength of my head.” Ephraim is interpreted as “Fruitfulness.” “My fruitfulness,” he says, “and this fruitfulness is the strength of my head.” For Christ is my head. And from where is fruitfulness his strength? Because unless the grain fell into the earth, it would not multiply but would remain alone. Christ therefore fell into the earth in his passion, and fruitfulness followed in his resurrection.

“And Ephraim is the strength of my head.” He hung there and was despised; within, he was a grain, possessing the power to draw all things after himself (John 12:24, 32). As the number of seeds lies hidden in a grain, while some insignificant thing cast into the earth appears to the eyes, but the power that transforms matter into itself and brings forth fruit remains hidden, so in Christ’s cross his power was hidden while weakness appeared.

O great grain! Certainly he is weak as he hangs there; certainly that crowd shook its head before him; certainly they said: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40). Hear his strength: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. 1:25). Rightly, then, such great fruitfulness followed. “This is mine,” says the Church.

10. [verse 10.] Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope. “Judah is my king.” Who is Judah? He who is from the tribe of Judah. Who is Judah, except the one to whom Jacob himself said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. 49:8)? “Judah is my king.” Why, then, should I fear, when Judah my king says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28)?

“Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope.” Why a pot? Because of tribulation. Why “of my hope”? Because Judah my king went before me. Along the way by which he went before, why are you afraid to follow? [Note: [Col. 0720] Several manuscripts read thus. The printed editions have: “Since your king went before you, you ought to follow. Why are you afraid?”]

By what way did he go before? Through tribulations, through hardships, through reproaches. The way was enclosed before he passed through; after he passed through, follow: the way is already open by his passage.

“I am solitary,” he says, “but until I pass through” (Ps. 140:10): a solitary grain, but only until it passes through; when it has passed through, fruitfulness will follow. “Judah is my king.” Therefore, because Judah is my king, “Moab is the pot of my hope.”

Moab is understood among the Gentiles. This people was born from sin: it was born from the daughters of Lot, who slept with their drunken father, treating their father wrongly (Gen. 19:31–38). It would have been better for them to remain barren than to become mothers in this way. That event was a certain figure of those who use the law wrongly.

Do not pay attention to the fact that in Latin the word “law” (lex) is feminine, while in Greek it is masculine. Whether it is feminine in speech or masculine, language does not prescribe to the truth. The law has rather masculine force, because it rules and is not ruled. What does the apostle Paul say? “The law is good, if someone uses it lawfully” (I Tim. 1:8). Those daughters of Lot, however, did not use their father lawfully.

As good works are born when someone uses the law well, so evil works are born when someone uses the law badly. Thus, by using their father wrongly—that is, by using the law wrongly—they produced the Moabites, through whom evil works are signified. Hence the Church’s tribulation; hence the boiling pot.

Concerning this pot, prophecy says in a certain passage: “A pot kindled from the north” (Jer. 1:13). From where, unless from the regions of the devil, who said: “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14:13)? The greatest tribulations therefore arise against the Church only from those who use the law wrongly.

What then? Will the Church fail here, and, because of the pot—that is, the abundance of scandals—will she not persevere to the end? Did not her king Judah foretell this to her? Did he not say to her: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12)? When the pot boils, charity grows cold.

Why, O charity, do you not rather grow hot against the pot? Or do you not know that this was said to you, when your king was speaking about that abundance of scandals: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (ibid. 24:13)? Persevere, then, to the end against the pot of scandals. The pot of iniquity burns, but the flame of charity is greater. Do not be overcome; persevere to the end.

Why do you fear the Moabites, the evil works of those who use the law wrongly? For did not Judah your king, who went before you, endure such people? Do you not know that the Jews, by using the law wrongly, killed Christ? Therefore hope [Note: [Col. 0721] The manuscripts read “hope” (spera); the printed editions have “hasten” (propera).], and follow wherever your king went before you. Say: “Judah is my king.”

And because Judah is my king, what has Moab become? “The pot of my hope,” not of my destruction. See the pot of hope amid tribulations; hear the apostle: “But we glory,” he says, “in tribulations.” The pot is already present; but see whether he explains the pot of hope. “Knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope.” If tribulation produces endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope, while tribulation is the pot that produces hope, then rightly “Moab is the pot of my hope.”

“And hope does not disappoint.” And what follows? Do you grow hot against the pot? Certainly, because “the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

11. Into Edom I shall extend my sandal. The Church speaks: “I shall reach as far as Edom.” Let tribulations rage; let the world boil with scandals; “I shall extend my sandal into Edom,” even to those who live an earthly life—for Edom is interpreted as “Earthly”—even to those very people, “into Edom I shall extend my sandal.”

Whose sandal is it, if not that of the Gospel? “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (ibid. 10:15); and, “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:15).

Certainly, because tribulation produces endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope, the pot will not consume me: “For the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” Let us not cease preaching the Gospel; let us not cease announcing the Lord.

“Into Edom I shall extend my sandal.” Do earthly people not also serve? Although they are bound by earthly desires, they nevertheless adore Christ. Today we see, brothers, how many earthly people commit fraud for profit, perjury because of their fraud, and consult fortune-tellers and astrologers because of their fears. All these are Edomites, earthly people; and yet all of them adore Christ, they are beneath his sandal. Already he has extended his sandal into Edom.

The Allophyli are subject to me. Who are the Allophyli? Foreigners, those who do not belong to my race. They are subject because many adore Christ but will not reign with Christ. “The Allophyli are subject to me.”

12. [verse 11.] Who will lead me into the city of the surrounding region? What is the city of the surrounding region? If you remember, I already mentioned it in another psalm, where it says: “And they will go around the city” [Note: [Col. 0722] Above, in Ps. 58, Sermon 1, no. 15.].

The city of the surrounding region is the encircling multitude of the Gentiles. This surrounding multitude of the Gentiles had in its midst one Jewish people worshiping one God; the rest of the surrounding Gentiles offered worship to idols and served demons. It was mystically called “the city of the surrounding region,” because the Gentiles had surrounded it on every side and stood around the people who worshiped one God.

“Who will lead me into the city of the surrounding region?” Who, except God? He means: How will he lead me through those clouds of which it is said: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76:19)? The wheel itself is the city of the surrounding region, which is called a wheel—that is, the circle of the earth.

“Who will lead me into the city of the surrounding region? Who will lead me as far as Edom?” That is, so that I may reign even over earthly people [Note: [Col. 0722] Several manuscripts read: “that is, into an earthly kingdom also”], so that even those who are not of me, who do not wish to make progress through me, may honor me.

13. [verse 12.] “Who will lead me as far as Edom? Will it not be you, O God, who have rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, in our powers?”

Will you not lead us, you who rejected us? But why did you reject us? Because you destroyed us. Why did you destroy us? Because you were angry and had mercy on us. You, then, will lead us—you who rejected us, who will not go forth, O God, in our powers; you will lead us.

What does “you will not go forth in our powers” mean? The world will rage; the world will trample us; a heap of testimony will be formed through the outpouring of the martyrs’ blood, and the raging pagans will say: “Where is their God?” (Ps. 78:10). Then you will not go forth, O God, in our powers: you will not appear against them; you will not display your power as you displayed it in David, in Moses, and in Joshua, when the nations yielded to their strength, and after slaughter had taken place and great devastation had been inflicted, you led your people into the land that you had promised.

You will not do this then; you will not go forth, O God, in our powers, but you will work within. What does “you will not go forth” mean? You will not appear. For surely, when the martyrs were led away in chains, when they were shut up in prison, when they were brought out to be mocked, when they were exposed to beasts [Note: [Col. 0722] Erasmus reads “subjected” (subjiciebantur); Lovaniensis, “subdued” (subigebantur); the manuscripts, “raised up” (subrigebantur).], when they were struck with iron, when they were burned with fire, were they not despised as though abandoned, as though without a helper?

How was God working within? How was he comforting them within? How was he making the hope of eternal life sweet to them? How was he not abandoning their hearts, where the human being dwelt in silence—well, if he was good; badly, if he was evil? Did he therefore abandon them because he did not go forth in their powers? Rather, by not going forth in their powers, did he not lead the Church as far as Edom, did he not lead the Church into the city of the surrounding region?

For if the Church had wished to wage war and use the sword, she would have seemed to be fighting for the present life. But because she despised the present life, a heap of testimony concerning the future life was formed.

14. [verse 13.] “You, therefore, O God, who will not go forth in our powers, give us help from tribulation; and the salvation of man is vain.”

Let those who do not have salt go now and wish temporal salvation for their own people, which is the vain oldness of age. “Give us help”: give it from where you were thought to abandon us; come to our aid from there. “Give us help from tribulation; and the salvation of man is vain” [Note: [Col. 0723] The printed editions read “salvation” (salutem); several manuscripts read “salt” (salem), alluding to Mark 9:49, “Have salt in yourselves,” as above, no. 9. See also nos. 2 and 7.].

15. [verse 14.] In God we shall perform our strength, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing [Note: [Col. 0723] Some manuscripts read “those who trouble us.”].

We shall not perform our strength with the sword, nor with horses, breastplates, shields, or the power of an army—not outwardly. But where? Within, where we lie hidden. Where within? “In God we shall perform our strength.” We shall be like the rejected, the trampled, and the insignificant—people of no account; but he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.

In the end, this happened to our enemies. The martyrs were trampled; by suffering, enduring, and persevering to the end, they performed their strength in God. He also accomplished what follows: he brought their enemies to nothing. Where are the martyrs’ enemies now, except perhaps that drunkards now persecute them with cups, whereas the enraged once persecuted them with stones?

## Exposition of Psalm 60. Sermon to the People

1. [verse 1.] With Your Charity we have undertaken this psalm for consideration. It is brief; the Lord will be present so that we may speak about it sufficiently and briefly. Insofar as he himself assists us who commands us to speak, I shall be obliging to those who wish to listen, so that I am not troublesome to the sluggish, excessive to the few, or burdensome to those who are occupied.

Its title does not detain us. It is: “To the end, in hymns, for David himself.” “In hymns,” certainly means “in praises.” “To the end,” certainly means “to Christ.” For “Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). And “for David”: we must understand no other than him, who came from the seed of David, so that he might be human among human beings and make human beings equal to the angels.

As for the voice in this psalm, if we are in his members and in his body—as we dare to presume, since he exhorts us—we must recognize it as our voice, not the voice of some outsider. By “our” I do not mean only those who are now present here, but our voice because we exist throughout the whole world, from east to west.

And so that you may know that this is our voice, he speaks here as though one person. Yet it is not one person; rather, unity speaks as one. In Christ we are all one person, because the head of this one person is in heaven, while the members still labor on earth. And because they labor, see what he says [Note: [Col. 0724] Several manuscripts read “they say.”].

2. [verses 2–4.] “Hear my prayer, O God; attend to my prayer.” Who speaks? As though one person. See whether it is one: “From the ends of the earth I have cried out to you, when my heart was troubled.” It is therefore no longer one person; but it is one because Christ is one, whose members we all are.

For what one person cries out from the ends of the earth? No one cries out from the ends of the earth except that inheritance concerning which it was said to the Son himself: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

This, then, is Christ’s possession; this is Christ’s inheritance; this is Christ’s body; this is Christ’s one Church; this unity, which we are, cries out from the ends of the earth. What does it cry out? What I said above: “Hear my prayer, O God; attend to my prayer: from the ends of the earth I have cried out to you.” That is, this is what I have cried out to you—from the ends of the earth, that is, from everywhere.

3. But why did I cry out this? “When my heart was troubled.” He shows himself to be throughout all the nations, throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0724] The printed editions read “not in great glory.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.] in great glory, but in great temptation. For our life in this pilgrimage cannot be without temptation, because our progress is made through our temptation. No one comes to know himself except by being tested; no one can be crowned unless he has conquered; no one can conquer unless he has fought; no one can fight unless he has an enemy and temptations.

This person, then, is troubled, crying out from the ends of the earth, yet he is not abandoned. For he wished to prefigure us ourselves, who are his body, in that body of his in which he has already died, risen, and ascended into heaven, so that the members might confidently expect to follow where the head has gone before.

Therefore he transfigured us into himself when he wished to be tempted by Satan (Matt. 4:1). The Gospel was read just now, saying that the Lord Jesus Christ was tempted by the devil in the wilderness. Christ was truly tempted by the devil. For in Christ you were tempted, because Christ had flesh from you and salvation from himself; death from you and life from himself; insults from you and honors from himself. Therefore he had temptation from you and victory from himself.

If we were tempted in him, in him we overcome the devil. You notice that Christ was tempted, but do you not notice that he conquered? Recognize yourself as tempted in him, and recognize yourself as conquering in him.

He could have kept the devil away from himself; but if he had not been tempted, he would not have provided you, through his temptation, the instruction in how to conquer. It is therefore not surprising that, placed among temptations, this person cries out from the ends of the earth.

But why is he not conquered? “You exalted me upon a rock.” Here, then, we recognize who cries out from the ends of the earth. Let us recall the Gospel: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid. 16:18). Therefore she cries out from the ends of the earth whom he wished to be built upon a rock.

But in order that the Church might be built upon a rock, who was made the rock? Hear Paul saying: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. 10:4). In him, therefore, we have been built. For this reason, the rock upon which we were built was first struck by winds, storm, and rain (Matt. 7:24–25), when Christ was tempted by the devil.

Behold the firmness in which he wished to establish you. Rightly our voice is not empty, but is heard, because we have been placed in great hope: “You exalted me upon a rock.”

4. “You led me, because you became my hope.” If he had not become our hope, he would not lead us. He leads us like a guide; he leads us into himself like a way; and he brings us to himself like our homeland. Therefore he leads us.

From where? Because he became our hope. From what did he become our hope? Behold: as you heard, because he was tempted, because he suffered, because he rose again, he became our hope.

For what do we say to ourselves when we read these things? God will not destroy us, for whose sake he sent his Son to be tempted, crucified, to die, and to rise again. God surely does not despise us, for whose sake he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. 8:32).

Thus he became our hope. In him you see both your labor and your reward: labor in his passion, reward in his resurrection. Thus he became our hope.

For we have two lives: one in which we are, and another which we hope for. The one in which we are is known to us; the one for which we hope is unknown to us. Endure the life in which you are, and you will have the one you do not yet have.

How do you endure? So that you are not conquered by the tempter. Through his labors, temptations, sufferings, and death, Christ showed you the life in which you are; through his resurrection he showed you the life in which you will be.

We knew only that a human being is born and dies; we did not know that a human being rises again and lives eternally. He took upon himself what you knew and demonstrated what you did not know. Therefore he became our hope in tribulations and temptations.

Hear the apostle saying: “And not only this, but we glory,” he says, “in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid. 5:3–5).

He himself, therefore, became our hope, he who gave us the Holy Spirit; and now we walk toward hope, for we would not walk unless we hoped. What does the apostle himself say? “For what a person sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.” And again: “For by hope we have been saved” (ibid. 8:24–25).

5. “You led me, because you became my hope: a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.” “My heart is troubled,” says this unity, “from the ends of the earth, and I labor amid temptations and scandals. The pagans are envious because they have been conquered; heretics, cloaked in the appearance of the Christian name, lie in wait; within the Church itself the wheat suffers violence from the chaff. Amid all these things, when my heart is troubled, I shall cry out from the ends of the earth.”

But he himself does not abandon me—the one who exalted me upon the rock so that he might lead me to himself. For although I labor, while the devil lies in wait against me through so many places, times, and opportunities, he is my tower of strength. When I have fled there, I shall not only escape the enemy’s arrows, but, secure, I shall hurl against him whatever I wish.

Christ himself is the tower; he became for us a tower against the face of the enemy, and he is also the rock upon which the Church has been built. Are you afraid of being struck by the devil? Flee to the tower. The devil’s arrows will never follow you to that tower; there you will stand fortified and fixed.

But how will you flee to the tower? Perhaps someone placed in temptation may seek this tower bodily; and when he does not find it, he may grow weary or fail in temptation. The tower is before you: remember Christ and enter the tower.

How do you remember Christ so as to enter the tower? Whatever you suffer, consider that he suffered it first, and consider the outcome for which he suffered: that he might die and rise again. Hope for an end such as came first in him, and you have entered the tower by refusing consent to the enemy.

For if you consent to the enemy, then the arrow of the attacker reaches you. Rather, hurl at him the arrows by which he may be struck and overcome. What are these arrows? The words of God, your faith, your hope itself, and good works.

I do not say: “Remain in this tower so that you are idle there, and it is enough for you that the enemy’s arrows do not reach you.” Do something there; let your hands not cease. Your good works are swords that destroy the enemy.

6. [verse 5.] “I shall be an inhabitant in your tent forever.” You see that the one about whom we have spoken is the one who cries out. Who among us is an inhabitant forever? We live here for a few days and pass on; for here we are inhabitants, but in heaven we shall be dwellers.

Here you are an inhabitant, from which place you will hear the voice of the Lord your God: “Move away.” For from that eternal house in heaven no one will command you to move away. Here, then, you are an inhabitant.

Thus it is also said in another psalm: “I am an inhabitant with you and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38:13). Here, then, we are inhabitants; there the Lord will give us eternal dwelling places: “There are many dwelling places,” he says, “in my Father’s house” (John 14:2). He will give those dwelling places not as to inhabitants but as to citizens who will remain forever.

Yet here, brothers, because the Church was not destined to exist on this earth for a short time, but will remain here until the end of the age, for this reason he said here: “I shall be an inhabitant in your tent forever.”

Let the enemy rage as much as he wishes; let him attack me, prepare ambushes for me, increase scandals, and cause my heart to be troubled: “I shall be an inhabitant in your tent forever.” The Church will not be conquered or uprooted, nor will she yield to any temptations, until the end of this age comes and that eternal dwelling receives us from this temporal one—the dwelling to which he will lead us who became our hope.

“I shall be an inhabitant in your tent forever.”

If you will be an inhabitant for a long time—as though we were saying this to him—then you will have to labor on earth amid so many temptations. For if the Church were here only a few days, the tempter’s ambushes would soon end.

Very well: you would like the temptations to last only a few days. But how would he gather all those who are born, unless he remained here for a long time, unless he extended to the end? Do not begrudge those who will come afterward; do not, because you have already crossed it, wish to cut off the bridge of mercy [Note: [Col. 0726] The words “of mercy” are absent from most manuscripts.]. Let him remain here forever.

And what of the temptations, which must increase as scandals increase? For he himself says: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.” But that Church which cries out from the ends of the earth is among those of whom he continues by saying: “But he who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13).

But how will you persevere? What are your powers amid so many scandals, so many temptations, and so many battles? By what powers do you overcome an enemy whom you do not see? Surely not by your own. Therefore, because this inhabitant will remain here forever, what hope does he have of enduring?

“I shall be covered by the shelter of your wings.” Behold why we are secure amid so many temptations, until the end of the age comes and the eternal ages receive us: because we are covered by his wings’ shelter. The age is hot, but there is great shade beneath God’s wings: “I shall be covered by the shelter of your wings.”

7. [verse 6.] “For you, O God” [Note: [Col. 0727] Lovaniensis reads “my God.” “My” is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts, and it is not present in the Septuagint.], “have heard my prayer.” Which prayer? The one with which he began: “Hear my prayer, O God; attend to my prayer: from the ends of the earth I have cried out to you.” This is what I cried out to you from the ends of the earth.

Therefore I shall be covered by the shelter of your wings, because you have heard my prayer. We are thus admonished, brothers, not to cease praying as long as the time of temptations lasts.

“You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” Let us therefore persevere in fear of the name of God. The eternal Father does not deceive us. Do children labor to receive the inheritance of their parents, whom they will succeed after their death? Shall we not labor to receive an inheritance from that Father whom we will not succeed as one who has died, but with whom we shall live eternally in the inheritance itself?

“You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.”

8. [verse 7.] “You will add days upon days to the king; you will increase his years.” This, then, is the king whose members we are. Christ is the king, our head, our king.

“You have given him days upon days”: not only these days in this temporal age, with its end, but days upon these days without end. “I shall dwell,” he says, “in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Ps. 22:6). Why “for length of days,” unless because now the days are short? For every thing that has an end is short.

But the days of this king are added upon days, so that Christ may not reign in his Church only during these passing days, but that the saints may reign with him in those days that have no end.

There is one day there, and there are many days. Because there are many days, I have already said, “for length of days.” Because there is one day, it is understood in the words: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). He said “today,” one day; but this day is not placed in the middle between yesterday and tomorrow. Its beginning is not the end of yesterday, nor is its end the beginning of tomorrow.

For God’s years are also mentioned: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28). As years, so days; as days, so one day. You may say whatever you wish about eternity. You may say whatever you wish because whatever you say, you say less than the reality. But for this reason you must say something: so that there may be a starting point from which you may contemplate what cannot be said.

“You will add days upon days to the king; you will increase his years, unto the day of generation and generation.” Of this generation and of the future generation. I understand “this generation” as the one compared with the moon, because the moon is born, grows, reaches fullness, ages, and sets; so are these mortal generations. And I understand “the generation” by which we are regenerated through rising again, and shall remain eternally with God, when we shall no longer be like the moon, but, as the Lord says, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

For the moon is figuratively placed in the Scriptures to signify the mutability of this mortality. Therefore that man who fell among robbers was descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, because Jericho is a Hebrew word and is interpreted in Latin as “Moon.” He was descending, as it were, from immortality to mortality; and rightly, on the way, after being wounded by robbers, that Adam from whom the whole human race comes was left half-dead (Luke 10:30).

Therefore, “you will add days upon days to the king; you will increase his years, unto the day of generation.” I understand this as the generation of mortality. Which other generation did you mention? Whose? Listen:

9. [v. 8.] He will remain forever in the presence of God. According to what, or on account of what? Who will seek his mercy and truth for him? He says elsewhere also: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies” (Psalm 24:10). A great subject is truth and mercy, but we promised brevity. Briefly understand what truth and mercy are, since what has been said is no small matter: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” It is called mercy because God does not consider our merits but his own goodness, so that he might forgive us all our sins and promise us eternal life; it is called truth because he does not fail to grant what he has promised.

Let us acknowledge it here and practice it ourselves, so that just as God has shown us his mercy and his truth—mercy by forgiving our sins, truth by fulfilling his promises—so we too may practice mercy and truth here: mercy toward the weak, toward the needy, even toward our enemies; truth by not sinning and not adding sin to sin. For whoever presumes greatly upon the mercy of God secretly persuades himself to make God unjust, thinking that if he remains a sinner and refuses to turn away from his iniquities, God will come and place him where he places his servants who obey him. And would it be just for him to place you, persisting in sins, where he will place those who have turned away from sins? Do you want to be so unjust that you make God unjust as well? Why, then, do you want to bend God to your will? Bend yourself to the will of God.

Who, then, does this, except one of those few of whom it is said: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13)? Rightly, then, does he say here also: “Who will seek his mercy and his truth?” What does “to him” mean? “Who will seek” would have been sufficient. Why did he add “to him,” unless because many seek his mercy and learn his truth in his books, and once they have learned them, live for themselves, not for him; seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21); preach mercy and truth, but do not practice mercy and truth? By preaching them, they know them—for they would not preach them unless they knew them. But whoever loves God and Christ, in preaching his mercy and truth, seeks them for him, not for himself—that is, not so that he may gain temporal advantages from this preaching, but so that it may benefit his members, that is, his faithful people, by ministering with truth what he knows; so that he who lives may no longer live for himself but for him who died for all (2 Corinthians 5:15). “Who will seek his mercy and truth for him?”

10. [v. 9.] “So I will sing praise to your name forever and ever, to fulfill my vows from day to day.” If you sing praise to the name of God, do not sing for a time only. Do you wish to sing forever and ever? Do you wish to sing eternally? Fulfill your vows to him from day to day. What does “fulfill your vows to him from day to day” mean? From this day to that day. Persevere in fulfilling your vows on this day until you come to that day. This is: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

# Exposition of Psalm 61. Sermon to the People

1. [v. 1.] The delight of the divine utterances and the sweetness of understanding the word of God—he himself assisting, who gives us delight so that our land may yield its fruit (Psalm 84:13)—encourage us both to speak and you to listen. I see that you listen without weariness, and I rejoice in the palate of your hearts, which does not reject what is health-giving but receives it eagerly and retains it profitably. Let us therefore speak to you today also, insofar as the Lord grants it, about this psalm that we have just sung.

Its title is: “For the end; for Idithun; a Psalm of David.” I recall that I have already explained to you what Idithun means [Note: [Col. 0729] In Psalm 38, no. 1.]. According to the interpretation of the Hebrew language as it has come down to us, Idithun is rendered in Latin as “Transcending them” (*Transiliens eos*). Thus the one who sings transcends certain people, whom he looks down upon from above. Let us see how far he has transcended, whom he has transcended, and where he has been placed, although he has transcended certain people: from what kind of spiritual and secure place he looks down upon what is below—not looking down in such a way as to fall, but so as to stir those whom he has transcended, namely the sluggish, to follow him, and to praise the place to which he has arrived by transcending.

For this one who transcends is above something in such a way that he is beneath something. Therefore he first wished to make clear to us beneath what he is secure, so that what he has transcended may be not pride but advancement.

2. [vv. 2–4.] Placed, then, in a certain fortified place, he says: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” For he had heard: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). And, fearing that he might become proud by transcending, he was not elated by those who were below but humble because of the one who was above. As though those envious of him, who were grieved that he had transcended them, were threatening him with ruin, he replied: “Will not my soul be subject to God?”

Why, as though I were transcending, do you seek snares for me? Do you want to cast me down by insult or deceive me by seduction? Can I be so mindful of what is above me that I have forgotten beneath whom I am? Will not my soul be subject to God? However much I approach, however much I ascend, however much I transcend, I will be beneath God, not against God. I therefore pass beyond other things securely, since the one who is above all holds me beneath himself.

“Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” Indeed, he is my God and my Savior, my protector; I will not be moved any longer. I know who is above me; I know who extends his mercy over those who know him; I know beneath whose wings I hope. I will not be moved any longer.

“You are indeed acting,” he says to certain people, transcending those very people to whom he speaks. “You are indeed acting so as to move me—but may the foot of pride not come to me.” For this is what follows in that same psalm: “May the hand of sinners not move me” (Psalm 35:12), which corresponds to “I will not be moved any longer.” To what is said there, “May the hand of sinners not move me,” he responds here, “I will not be moved any longer”; and to what is said there, “May the foot of pride not come to me,” he responds here, “Will not my soul be subject to God?”

3. Thus, fortified and secure in a higher place, where the Lord has become his refuge and God himself is his fortified place, he looks upon those whom he has transcended and, looking down upon them, speaks as though from a lofty tower. For this too was said of him: “A tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Psalm 60:4).

He therefore attends to them and says: “How long will you attack a man?” By insulting, hurling reproaches, lying in wait, and persecuting, you place burdens upon a man; you impose upon a man as much as a human being can bear [Note: [Col. 0730] Three manuscripts: “as much as he cannot bear.”]. But so that a human being may bear it, he is beneath the one who made the human being.

“How long will you attack a man? If you look to the man, kill all of them.” Behold, attack, rage, kill them all. “Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence”: press on, push, as though you were about to throw it down. And where is “I will not be moved any longer”? Why, then, “I will not be moved any longer”? Because he is my God and Savior, my protector.

Thus you can impose burdens upon a man—can you impose them upon God, who protects the man?

4. “Kill them all.” What bodily space is there in one man where everyone could kill him? But we must understand our own person, the person of our Church, the person of the body of Christ. For one man, Jesus Christ, with his head and his body, is the Savior of the body and the members of the body; “the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24 and Ephesians 5:31), in one voice and in one suffering, and, when iniquity has passed away, in one rest.

The sufferings of Christ, therefore, are not in Christ alone; rather, the sufferings of Christ are only in Christ. For if by Christ you understand the head and the body, the sufferings of Christ are only in Christ. But if by Christ you understand the head alone, the sufferings of Christ are not in Christ alone. For if the sufferings of Christ were in Christ alone—indeed, in the head alone—why does the apostle Paul, one of his members, say: “That I may complete what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ in my flesh” (Colossians 1:24)?

If, then, you are in the members of Christ—whoever you are, whoever hears these things, whoever does not now hear these things but nevertheless hears them if you are in the members of Christ—whatever you suffer from those who are not in the members of Christ was lacking from the sufferings of Christ. Therefore it is added because it was lacking: you fill up the measure, but do not overflow it; you suffer only as much as, from your own sufferings [Note: [Col. 0731] The editions read: “filling up the measure, not overflowing it. Therefore you suffer only as much as, from his sufferings,” and shortly afterward: “that is, in ourselves, for this commonwealth, as it were. For each one …” Then below: “and according to the capacity of our strength we bring in, as it were, a canon of sufferings; the full payment of all sufferings will not come until …” The passage is emended according to the manuscripts and Bede’s collection on Paul. That collection, in the Corbie manuscript, where it is attributed to Florus, has *pro portione virium* (“according to the proportion of strength”); other manuscripts here have *possessione*. Either reading is equally suitable, since Augustine alludes to the manner of paying a canon after taking possessions into account. Moreover, the word *finis* (“end”) is absent from the manuscripts, which instead of *parat[or]ia* some prefer *pariatoria*, others *paritoria*—perhaps the name of some measure or tax. In its place, perhaps one should read *parata vero*, as the distinguished Cangius reads in the *Glossary*, under the word *Plenaria*.], had to be contributed to the whole suffering of Christ, who suffered in our head and suffers in his members, that is, in us ourselves.

For this commonwealth of ours, as it were, each of us pays what we owe according to our measure; and according to the resources of our strength we contribute, as it were, a fixed assessment of sufferings. The full payment of all sufferings will not come until the age has ended.

“How long will you attack a man?” Whatever the prophets suffered—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matthew 23:35)—was imposed upon the man, because certain members of Christ preceded the advent of Christ’s incarnation. As in the case of a child being born, a hand came forth before the head had yet emerged (Genesis 38:27), but the hand was nevertheless connected to the head.

Do not think, therefore, brothers, that all the righteous who suffered persecution from the wicked—including those who were sent before the Lord’s coming to announce the Lord’s coming—did not belong to the members of Christ. Far be it that one should not belong to the members of Christ who belongs to the city whose king is Christ.

That city is the one heavenly Jerusalem, the holy city; this one city has one king. Christ is the king of this city. For he says to it: “A man will say, Mother Zion.” He says “Mother” to it, but “a man.” “A man will say, Mother Zion; and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5). Therefore its king is he who founded it as the Most High; he himself became a most humble man in it.

Before the advent of his incarnation, then, he sent ahead certain members of himself. After these members had announced that he would come, he himself came, joined to them. Apply the likeness of that newborn child [Note: [Col. 0731] So most manuscripts. Erasmus has: “joined to them; apply it to the likeness,” while Louvain has: “joined to them; apply the likeness.” The Royal manuscript reads: “apply it to …”]: the hand comes forth before the head, yet is with the head and beneath the head.

For it was said of Christ, when the excellence of the first people was praised and the broken natural branches were mourned (Romans 11:21): “Their adoption, and the covenants, and the giving of the Law; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Romans 9:4–5).

“From them is Christ according to the flesh,” as from Zion, because he became man in her; “who is over all, God blessed forever,” because the Most High himself founded her. “From them is Christ according to the flesh,” the son of David; “who is over all, God blessed forever,” the Lord of David.

That entire city, then, speaks from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah. From that point onward—from the blood of John, through the blood of the apostles, through the blood of the martyrs, through the blood of Christ’s faithful—the one city speaks, and one man says: “How long will you attack a man? Kill them all.”

Let us see whether you can erase them; let us see whether you can extinguish them; let us see whether you can remove his name from the earth; let us see whether you are not meditating on vain things among the peoples (Psalm 2:1), saying: “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Psalm 40:6). “Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence,” lean upon him and push him. Hear what was said above: “My protector, I will not be moved any longer,” because “I was pushed so as to fall, like a heap of sand, and the Lord received me” (Psalm 117:13).

5. [v. 5.] “Nevertheless they planned to drive away my honor.” They were defeated while they killed those who were yielding, multiplying the faithful by the blood of those they killed; those who had yielded to them and were no longer able to kill.

“Nevertheless they planned to drive away my honor.” Now that a Christian cannot be killed, efforts are made to dishonor the Christian. For now the hearts of the impious are tormented by the honor of Christians. That spiritual Joseph—after being sold by his brothers, after being transferred from his homeland to the nations, as though into Egypt, after the humiliation of prison, after the fabrication of false testimony, after what was said of him had come to pass, “Iron passed through his soul” (Psalm 104:18)—has now been honored. He is no longer subject to the brothers who sold him, but distributes grain to the hungry (Genesis 37; 39; 41).

Defeated by his humility and chastity, by his incorruptibility, temptations, and sufferings, they now see him honored and plan to drive away his honor. For this is in their thoughts: “The sinner will see.” Indeed, he will see, since “a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14). The sinner, therefore, will see and become angry; “he will gnash with his teeth and waste away” (Psalm 111:10).

Poison lies hidden in the heart and is covered by the brow of those who rage and are indignant. Therefore here too he speaks of their thoughts: “They planned,” he says, “to drive away my honor.” They do not dare to bring into words what they think.

Let us wish them good, even if they wish evil [Note: [Col. 0732] Most manuscripts: “Let us wish them well, even if they think evil.”]. “Judge them, O God; let them fall from their own thoughts” (Psalm 5:11). For what is better or more useful for them than to fall from where they stand badly, so that, corrected, they may themselves say: “You have set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm 39:3)?

[Col. 0733] 6. “Nevertheless they planned to drive away my honor.” Are all against one, or one against all; or all against all, or one against one? For meanwhile, when he says, “You attack a man,” it is as though they are attacking one; and when he says, “Kill them all,” it is as though all are against one. Yet they are also all against all, because all Christians are in one.

But are those various errors of the enemies of Christ to be called only “all”? Is there not also “one”? I dare plainly to call it one, because there is one city and one city, one people and one people, king and king.

What does “one city and one city” mean? Babylon is one; Jerusalem is one. Whatever other mystical names may be given them, there is nevertheless one city and one city: one ruled by the devil as king, the other ruled by Christ as king.

I am considering a passage in the Gospel, and it moves me; I think it moves you as well. After many good and evil people had been invited to the wedding and the wedding hall was filled with those reclining—for the servants who were sent, as they had been commanded, invited both good and evil—and the king entered to inspect those reclining, he found a man who did not have a wedding garment. He said to him what you know: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” But he was speechless. And he ordered his hands and feet to be bound and him to be thrown into the outer darkness.

Someone was taken from the banquet and sent to the deserved punishments amid so great a crowd of those reclining. Yet the Lord, wishing to show that that one man represented one body composed of many, after commanding that he be thrown outside and sending him to the punishments he deserved, immediately added: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:10–14).

What does this mean? You summoned crowds; a vast multitude came; you announced and spoke, and they multiplied beyond number (Psalm 39:6); the wedding hall was filled with those reclining. One solitary man was thrown out, and you say: “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Why not rather: “All are called, many are chosen, and one is thrown out”? If he had said, “For many are called, and more are chosen, but few are rejected,” we might perhaps more plausibly have understood that one man to be among the few.

But now he says that one was thrown out, and adds: “For many are called, but few are chosen.” Who are the chosen, except those who remained? Once one had been thrown out, the chosen remained. How, when one has been thrown out from many, are few chosen, unless because many are in that one?

All who think earthly things, all who prefer earthly happiness to God, all who seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), belong to that one city which is mystically called Babylon and has the devil as its king.

But all who think of the things above, who meditate on heavenly things, who live in the world attentively so as not to offend God, who take care not to sin, and who are not ashamed to confess their sins when they do sin—humble, meek, holy, just, devout, and good—all belong to that one city whose king is Christ.

That city is, as far as time is concerned, older on earth—not in sublimity or honor. That city was born first; this city was born later. The former began with Cain; the latter with Abel. These two bodies, living under two kings and belonging to their respective cities, oppose one another until the end of the age, until separation is made from their commingling and some are placed at the right hand, others at the left, and it is said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; but to the others: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

For Christ says this: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.” He is the king of his city, victorious over all. But to those placed at the left, as though to the city of the wicked, he says: “Go into the eternal fire.” Does he separate the king from them? No; for he adds: “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

7. Pay attention, brothers; pay attention, I beg you. I am pleased to speak a little more to you about this beloved city. “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86:3). And: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me” (Psalm 136:5).

There is one homeland, and it is truly one homeland, the only homeland; apart from it, whatever we have is exile. I shall say something that you recognize and approve; I shall recall what you know, not teach what you do not know.

The apostle says: “The spiritual was not first, but the natural; afterward the spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15:46). Therefore that city is older in age, because Cain was born first and afterward Abel (Genesis 4:1–2); but in these, “the elder will serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). The former is older in age; the latter greater in dignity.

Why is the former older in age? Because “the spiritual was not first, but the natural.” Why is the latter greater in dignity? Because “the elder will serve the younger.”

Cain built a city, as we read (Genesis 4:17). Before there was any city, at the beginning of human affairs, Cain built a city. Without doubt, understand that many people had already been born from those two and from those whom they had begotten, so that there could be a suitable and appropriate number to which the name “city” might be given.

Cain therefore built a city where there was no city. Jerusalem too was later built: the kingdom of God, the holy city, the city of God, set forth in a certain form as a shadow signifying what was to come.

Understand, then, the great mystery, and hold fast what I said earlier: “The spiritual was not first, but the natural; afterward the spiritual.” Thus Cain built a city first, and built it where there was no city.

But when Jerusalem was to be built, it was not built where there was no city. There was already a city called Jebus, whence came the Jebusites. After it had been captured, defeated, and subjected, a new city was built as though the old one had been destroyed, and it was called Jerusalem, “Vision of peace,” the city of God (Joshua 18:28).

Therefore everyone born from Adam does not yet belong to Jerusalem. He carries with him the inheritance of iniquity and the punishment of sin, appointed to death, and in a certain sense belongs to an old city. But if he is destined to be among the people of God, the old will be destroyed and the new will be built.

Thus Cain built a city where there was no city. Everyone begins from mortality and wickedness, in order afterward to become good. For just as “through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

“And all die in Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and each one of us is born from Adam. Let him pass over to Jerusalem; the old will be destroyed and the new will be built. As the Jebusites are defeated so that Jerusalem may be built, it is said: “Put off the old man and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10).

And to those already built into Jerusalem and shining with the light of grace it is said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). Thus the evil city runs from beginning to end, while the good city is founded through the transformation of the wicked.

8. These two cities are meanwhile mingled together and are to be separated at the end. They fight against one another: one for iniquity, the other for justice; one for vanity, the other for truth.

Sometimes this temporal commingling causes certain people belonging to the city of Babylon to administer affairs belonging to Jerusalem, and, conversely, certain people belonging to Jerusalem to administer affairs belonging to Babylon.

I seem to have promised something difficult. Be patient until it is demonstrated by examples. For everything in the former people, as the apostle writes, “happened to them in a figurative way,” and “was written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Look, then, at that first people, also set forth to signify the later people, and see there what I am saying. There were great kings in Jerusalem; this is known: they are counted and named. All the wicked, therefore, were citizens of Babylon, and administered the affairs of Jerusalem; in the end they will all be separated from there and belong only to the devil.

Conversely, we find citizens of Jerusalem administering certain affairs belonging to Babylon. For after the three boys had been tested by the miracle, Nebuchadnezzar made them administrators of his kingdom and set them over his satraps; and citizens of Jerusalem administered the affairs of Babylon (Daniel 3:97).

Consider now that this is fulfilled and enacted in the Church and in our own times. All those of whom it was said, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do,” are citizens of Babylon administering the commonwealth of the city of Jerusalem. For if they administered nothing belonging to the city of Jerusalem, how could it be said, “Do what they say”? How could it be said that they “sit upon the chair of Moses”?

Conversely, if those who will reign forever with Christ are citizens of Jerusalem itself, how could it be said, “Do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:2–3), unless they will also hear: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27)?

It is therefore known to you that citizens of the evil city administer certain affairs of the good city. Let us see whether citizens of the good city also administer certain affairs of the evil city.

Every earthly commonwealth will eventually perish; its kingdom will pass away [Note: [Col. 0735] The editions read: “whose kingdom is transitory”; the manuscripts: “whose kingdom will pass away.], when that kingdom comes for which we pray, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), and of which it was foretold: “There will be no end of his kingdom” (Luke 1:33).

The earthly commonwealth, then, has our citizens administering its affairs. How many faithful and good people are magistrates in their cities, judges, commanders, counts, and kings? All the just and good, having in their hearts only those most glorious things that were said of you, “city of God” (Psalm 86:3).

And as though performing forced labor in a city that will pass away, they are commanded by the teachers of the holy city to remain faithful to those set over them: whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of the wicked and the praise of the good; whether they are servants, so that they may be subject to their masters (1 Peter 2:13, 18), and Christians to pagans; and so that the better may for a time remain faithful to the worse, destined to serve for a time and to rule forever.

These things happen until iniquity passes away (Psalm 56:2). Servants are commanded to endure wicked and difficult masters. Citizens of Babylon are commanded to be tolerated by citizens of Jerusalem, who render even greater service than they would if they were citizens of Babylon itself—as though fulfilling the command: “Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two” (Matthew 5:41).

To this whole city, scattered, spread out, and mingled together, he speaks these words and says: “How long will you attack a man? Kill them all.” And those outside, like thorns in hedges or like unfruitful wood in forests; and those inside, like weeds or chaff: all of you, however many you are—separated, mingled, to be tolerated, to be separated—“kill them all,” like a leaning wall and a tottering fence.

“Nevertheless they planned to drive away my honor.” They did not say it, but they nevertheless thought it. They planned to drive away my honor.

9. “I ran in thirst.” For they were repaying evil for good (Psalm 34:12). They were killing; they were driving away; I thirsted for them. They planned to drive away my honor; I thirsted to transfer them into my body.

For what do we do by drinking except send liquid that was outside into our members and draw it into our body? Moses did this with the head of that calf. The head of the calf is a great sacrament. For the head of the calf represented the body of the wicked, in the likeness of a calf eating grass (Psalm 105:20), that is, of those seeking earthly things, because “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

It was, then, as I said, the body of the wicked. Moses, angry, put it into the fire, crushed it, scattered it in water, and gave it to the people to drink (Exodus 32:20); and the prophet’s anger became an instrument of prophecy.

For that body is cast into the fire of tribulations and crushed by the word of God. Gradually they cease to belong to the unity of his body. For just as a garment, it is consumed over time. And each person who becomes a Christian is separated from that people and, as it were, crushed away from the mass.

Those who had conspired hated; once crushed, they believe [Note: [Col. 0736] Most manuscripts: “they believe little by little.”]. And what is clearer than this: people were to be transferred through baptism into the body of that city of Jerusalem whose image was the people of Israel? Therefore it was scattered in water so that it might be given as drink [Note: [Col. 0736] Several manuscripts: “so that it might be given as drink.” Some: “so that it might be given as a beverage.”].

This one thirsts for this until the end; he runs and thirsts. For he has drunk many, but he will never be without thirst. Hence: “I thirst. Woman, give me to drink” (John 4:7). The Samaritan woman perceived the Lord thirsty at the well, and she was satisfied by the thirsty one; she first perceived him thirsty so that he might drink the believer [Col. 0737]. And when he was hanging on the cross, he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28), although they did not give him what he thirsted for.

For he thirsted for them, but they gave him vinegar—not the new wine with which new wineskins are filled (Matthew 9:17), but old wine, badly old. For old vinegar is also mentioned [Note: [Col. 0737] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “and bad old wine. Old wine is also mentioned.”], the old people of whom it was said: “There is no change in them” (Psalm 54:20), so that, after the Jebusites had been overthrown, Jerusalem might be built (2 Samuel 5:6).

10. Thus the body of this head runs in thirst from the beginning to the end. And as though someone were saying to it: “Why are you thirsty? What is lacking to you, O body of Christ, O Church of Christ? Established in such honor, such sublimity, and such exaltation, even in this age, what is lacking to you? What was foretold about you is being fulfilled: ‘All the kings of the earth will adore him; all nations will serve him’ (Psalm 71:11). Why, then, are you thirsty? Why are you thirsty? Are you not satisfied with such multitudes?”

What multitudes do you mean? “With their mouths they were blessing, but with their hearts they were cursing.” “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14).

A woman suffering from a flow of blood touched the fringe of his garment and was healed. When the Lord was surprised by the one who touched him because he had perceived power go forth from him, namely, to heal the woman, he said: “Who touched me?” And the disciples, astonished, said: “The crowds press around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And he said: “Someone touched me” (Mark 5:25–31).

It was as though he were saying: “One touched me; crowds press around me.” Those who fill the churches on the festivals of Jerusalem fill the theaters on the festivals of Babylon. Yet they serve, honor, and pay homage—not only those who bear the sacraments of Christ and hate the commandments of Christ, but even those who bear neither the sacraments themselves, whether they are pagans or Jews. They honor, praise, and proclaim, but “with their mouths they were blessing.”

I do not attend to the mouth; he who instructed me knows that “with their hearts they were cursing.” They cursed there where they planned to drive away my honor.

11. [v. 6.] What of you, O Idithun, body of Christ, transcending them? What of you amid all this? What of you? Will you fail? Will you not persevere to the end? Will you not hear: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved,” even though, “because iniquity abounds, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:13, 12)?

And where is the fact that you transcended them? Where is the fact that “your citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20)? They cling to earthly things; like earthborn creatures, they think of earth, and they are earth, food for the serpent.

What of you amid all this? Nevertheless, although they do these things, although they think these things, although they push, although they press upon what is leaning, although they now perceive it standing upright and plan to drive away my honor; although they bless with their mouths and curse with their hearts; although they lie in wait wherever they can and slander wherever they can:

“Nevertheless, my soul will be subject to God.” And who can endure so much—whether open wars or hidden snares? Who can endure so much among open enemies, among false brothers? Who can endure so much? A human being? And if a human being, is he a human being from himself?

I did not transcend in such a way as to become exalted and fall: “My soul will be subject to God, for from him comes my patience.” What patience amid such scandals, unless because “if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:25)?

My pain has come; my rest will also come. My tribulation has come; my purification will also come. Does gold shine in the furnace of the goldsmith? It will shine in the necklace; it will shine in the ornament. Yet let it endure the furnace, so that, purified from its dross, it may come into the light.

This is the furnace: there is chaff, there is gold, there is fire; the goldsmith blows upon it. In the furnace the chaff burns and the gold is purified; the former is turned to ash, while the latter is stripped of its impurities.

The furnace is the world; the chaff is the wicked; the gold is the righteous; the fire is tribulation; the goldsmith is God. Therefore I do what the goldsmith wants; wherever the craftsman places me, I endure. I am commanded to endure; he knows how to purify.

Let the chaff burn, even if it burns me and seems to consume me; it is turned to ash, while I am freed from my impurities. Why? Because “my soul will be subject to God, for from him comes my patience.”

12. [v. 7.] Who is this from whom your patience comes? “For he is my God and my Savior, my protector; I will not depart.” For he is my God—therefore he calls me; and my Savior—therefore he justifies me; and my protector—therefore he glorifies me.

Here I am called and justified; there I am glorified. And from there, where I am glorified, I will not depart. For I will not remain in my pilgrimage: here there is a place from which I may depart, but I will come to a place from which I will not depart.

“For I am a sojourner with you on earth, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 38:13). Therefore I will migrate from my sojourning; from the heavenly dwelling I will not depart.

### 13. [verse 8]

“In God is my salvation and my glory.” I shall be saved in God; I shall be glorified in God. For I shall not merely be saved, but also glorified: saved because, from being ungodly, I have become righteous, justified by him (Rom. 4:5); glorified, however, because I have not only been justified but also honored. “For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (ibid. 8:30). Justification, then, pertains to salvation; glorification, to honor.

There is no need to argue that glorification pertains to honor. Since justification pertains to salvation, let us seek some proof. Look: an example presents itself from the Gospel. There were people who seemed righteous to themselves and criticized the Lord because he admitted sinners to the banquet and ate with tax collectors and sinners. To such proud men—men greatly exalted in their earthly strength and boasting much of the health they imagined they possessed, not of what they actually possessed—what did the Lord reply? “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” Whom does he call “those who are well”? Whom does he call “those who are sick”? He continues and says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:12–13).

He therefore called the righteous “those who are well,” not because the Pharisees were this, but because they considered themselves to be so. For that reason they were proud, begrudged the sick their physician, and, being more seriously ill, killed the physician. Yet he called the righteous “those who are well,” and sinners “those who are sick.”

Thus, in order that I might be justified, this man says, leaping across, it is from him; and in order that I might be glorified, it is from him: “In God is my salvation and my glory.” “My salvation,” so that I may be saved; “my glory,” so that I may be honored.

That was then; what is it now? “God is my help, and my hope is in God”—until I arrive at perfect justification and salvation. “For in hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24). Until I come to that glorification where “the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun” (Matt. 13:43), for the present, amid temptations, amid iniquities, amid scandals, amid open attacks and cunning words, amid those who bless with their mouths but curse in their hearts, amid those who plan to repel my honor—what is here? “God is my help,” for he gives help to those who struggle.

Against whom do they struggle? “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12). “God, therefore, is my help, and my hope is in God.” Hope exists as long as what has been promised is not yet present and what is not yet seen is believed. When it comes, there will be salvation and glorification. Yet while these things are delayed, we are not abandoned: “God is my help, and my hope is in God.”

### 14. [verse 9]

“Hope in him, all the assembly of the people.” Imitate Idithun; leap across your enemies. Leap across those who oppose you, resist your journey, and hate you. “Hope in him, all the assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him.”

Do not yield [Note: [Col. 0739] The editions read *credere* (“believe”); the manuscripts read *cedere* (“yield”).] to those who say to you, “Where is your God?” “My tears,” he says, “have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” But what does he say there? “I have meditated on these things and poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41:4–5). I remembered what I hear—“Where is your God?” I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me. Seeking my God, I poured out my soul in order to reach him; I did not remain within myself.

Therefore: “Hope in him, all the assembly of the people. Pour out your hearts before him”—by entreating, confessing, and hoping. Do not hold your hearts back within your hearts: “Pour out your hearts before him.” What you pour out is not lost. For he is my receiver. If he receives it, why are you afraid to pour it out? “Cast your care upon the Lord” (Ps. 54:23), and hope in him.

“Pour out your hearts before him: God is our helper.” What are you afraid of among whisperers, slanderers hateful to God (Rom. 1:29–30)—those who attack openly where they can, and lie in ambush secretly where they cannot; those who praise falsely and are truly hostile? What are you afraid of among them? “God is our helper.” Are they jealous rivals of God? Are they stronger than he? “God is our helper.” Be secure. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (ibid. 8:31).

“Pour out your hearts before him,” leaping across toward him and lifting up your souls: “God is our helper.”

### 15. [verse 10]

And now, established in a fortified place, in a tower of strength, away from the face of the enemy, have pity on those whom you feared—for you ought to run in thirst. Look down, then, upon them, now that you have been established in that place, and say:

“Yet the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars. Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Sons of men are vain, sons of men are liars; sons of men, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

Say these things with compassion, and understand them. If you have leapt across, if you love your enemies, if you desire to destroy in order to build, if you love him who judges among the nations and fills the ruins (Ps. 109:6), speak these words to them in this way—not hating them, not repaying evil for evil (Rom. 12:17).

“The sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they deceive, together, from vanity.” Certainly they are many. Look: there is that one—the one who was cast out from the company of the banqueters (Matt. 22:13). They conspire; they all seek temporal things: the carnal seek carnal things, and whoever hopes, hopes in the future. Although they differ from one another in the variety of their opinions, they are nevertheless one in vanity. Their errors are diverse and manifold, and “a kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (ibid. 12:25). Yet all have a similar vain and lying will, belonging to one king, with whom they are to be hurled into eternal fire (ibid. 25:41): “They are one in vanity.”

### 16. [verse 11]

And see that he thirsts; see that he runs in thirst. He therefore turns toward them, thirsting for them:

“Do not hope upon iniquity.” For my hope is in God. “Do not hope upon iniquity.” You who do not wish to approach and leap across, do not hope upon iniquity. For I who have leapt across have my hope in God. And is there iniquity with God? “Certainly not!” (Rom. 9:14).

“Do not hope upon iniquity.” Let us do this; let us do that; let us devise that; let us arrange our ambushes in this way—one in vanity. You thirst: those who think these things against you are betrayed by those whom you drink.

[Note: [Col. 0740] Most manuscripts read: “You thirst, for those who think these things against you …”]

“Do not hope upon iniquity.” Iniquity is vain; iniquity is nothing. Only righteousness has power. Truth can be concealed for a time; it cannot be conquered. Iniquity can flourish for a time; it cannot endure.

“And do not desire plunder.” You are poor, and you wish to rob? What do you gain? What do you lose? O destructive profit! You gain money; you lose righteousness. “Do not desire plunder.” “I am poor; I have nothing.” Is that why you wish to rob? You see what you may rob; you do not see from whom you may be robbed. Do you not know that the enemy circles about “like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8)? The prey you wish to seize is in a trap: you hold it, and you are held.

Therefore, poor man, do not desire plunder; desire God, who provides all things richly for us to enjoy (1 Tim. 6:17). He who made you will feed you. Will he who feeds the robber not feed the innocent? He will feed you who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). If he feeds those destined for condemnation, will he not feed those destined for deliverance? Therefore do not desire plunder.

This was said to the poor man, perhaps about to steal something out of necessity. Let the rich man come forward: “I,” he says, “have no need to steal. I lack nothing; everything is abundant.” And you also hear: “If riches increase” [Note: [Col. 0740] Several manuscripts read *affluant* (“if they abound”).] “do not set your heart upon them.”

The one has nothing; the other has something. Let the one not seek to steal what he does not have; let the other not set his heart upon what he has. “If riches increase”—that is, if they overflow, running as if from a fountain—“do not set your heart upon them.” Do not presume upon yourself; do not fix yourself there. At least fear this: “If riches increase.” Do you not see that, if you place your heart there, you too will flow away?

You are rich, and because you possess much you no longer desire to have more. Hear: “Command those who are rich in this present world not to be high-minded.” And what does “Do not set your heart upon them” mean? “Nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6:17).

Therefore: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.” Do not trust in riches; do not presume upon them; do not hope in them. Otherwise it may be said: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. 51:9).

Therefore, vain sons of men, lying sons of men, neither steal nor, if riches increase, set your heart upon them. Do not love vanity any longer or seek falsehood. For “blessed is the one whose hope is the Lord his God, who has not looked to vanities and lying insanities” (Ps. 39:5).

You wish to deceive; you wish to commit fraud. What do you bring forward in order to deceive? Dishonest balances. For “the sons of men are liars in the balances,” bringing forward dishonest scales in order to deceive. By a false standard you cheat those who look on. Do you not know that there is one who weighs and another who judges the weight? The one to whom you weigh does not see; but he who weighs both you and that person sees.

Therefore do not desire fraud or plunder; do not place your hope in what you possess. “I have warned; I have foretold,” says this Idithun.

### 17. [verses 12–13]

What follows?

“God has spoken once; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy; for you will repay each one according to his works.”

Idithun spoke; he sounded forth from the height to which he had leapt. There he heard something and told us. But I am somewhat troubled by what he told us, brothers; and until I share with you either my disturbance or some relief from it, I want you to remain attentive.

For, with the Lord’s help, we have brought the psalm to its conclusion. After what we are about to say, nothing further remains for us to explain about it. Therefore, strive with me to see whether we can understand this. And if I cannot, but one of you understands what I cannot, I shall rejoice rather than be jealous.

It is exceedingly difficult to investigate how the words were arranged: “God has spoken once”; then, when he had spoken once, “I heard these two things.” If he had said, “God has spoken once; I heard this one thing,” he would seem to have cut off part of the question, so that we would ask only what “God has spoken once” means. But now we must ask both what “God has spoken once” means and what “I heard these two things” means, since he spoke only once.

### 18. “God has spoken once”

What do you say, Idithun? If you are speaking—the one who has leapt across them—“He has spoken once”? I consult another Scripture, and it says to me: “In many parts and in many ways, God spoke formerly to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. 1:1).

What does “God has spoken once” mean? Is he not the God who, at the beginning of the human race, spoke to Adam?
