Is it not the same one who spoke to Cain, to Noah, to Abraham, to Isaac, to Jacob, to all the prophets, and to Moses? Moses was one man; and how many times did God speak to him? Look: even to one man God spoke not once but often.

Then God spoke to the Son who was present here: “You are my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17). God spoke to the apostles; he spoke to all the saints, even if not with a voice resounding through a cloud, nevertheless in the heart, where he himself is the teacher. Hence the psalm says: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me, for he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84:9).

What, then, does “God has spoken once” mean? This man had leapt across a great distance in order to arrive there, where God spoke once.

I have said this briefly to Your Charity. Here among human beings, to human beings, God has often spoken, in many ways and in many parts, through manifold creation. With himself, God spoke once, because God brought forth one Word.

This Idithun, then, leaping across them, had crossed over by the strong, powerful, and confident vision of his mind. He had crossed over the earth and everything that is on the earth; the air; all the clouds from which God spoke many things, often, and in many ways. He had also crossed over all the angels by the vision of faith.

For he was one who leapt across—not content with earthly things, but, like an eagle in flight, carried beyond every cloud by which the whole earth is covered. For Wisdom says: “And I covered the whole earth with mist” (Sir. 24:6).

He arrived at something clear, crossing over the whole of creation, seeking God, and pouring out his soul within himself. He arrived at the Beginning, and at the Word who was God with God. He found the one Word of the one Father, and he saw that God had spoken once. He saw the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3), and in whom all things exist together—not diverse, not separate, not unequal.

For God did not fail to know what he was making through the Word. If he knew what he was making, then what was being made was in him before it was made. If what was being made was not in him before it was made, where did he know what he was making? You cannot say that God made things he did not know.

God therefore knew what he made. And where did he know it before he made it, if things cannot be known except once they have been made? They cannot be known from the things made except after they have been made—by you, that is, by a human being made and placed in the lowest realm. But before all these things were made, they were known by him from whom they were made, and what he knew, he made.

Therefore, in that Word through whom he made all things, all things existed before they were made; and when they were made, they are all there. But they are there in one way here and in another way there: here in their proper nature, in which they were made; there in the art through which they were made.

Who can explain this? We can attempt it: go with Idithun and see.

### 19. “These two things I heard”

Now, as we have been able, we have explained how “God has spoken once.” Let us see how he heard these two things: “I heard these two things.”

Perhaps it does not follow that he heard only these two things. But he says, “I heard these two things”—certain two things which it is necessary for us to hear. Perhaps he heard many other things, but it is not necessary for them to be told to us. For the Lord also says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

What, then, does “I heard these two things” mean? “These two things that I am about to tell you I do not tell you from myself; I tell you what I heard.”

“God has spoken once”: God has one only-begotten Word. In that Word are all things, because all things were made through the Word. He has one Word “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). He has one Word: “God has spoken once.”

“These two things that I am about to tell you I heard there.” I do not speak from myself; I do not say this from myself. This is what “I heard” refers to. “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him” (John 3:29), so that he may speak the truth. For he hears him so that, by speaking, he may not speak a lie from himself (ibid. 8:44).

Otherwise you might say: “Who are you to tell me this? From where do you get this to tell me?” I heard these two things, and I speak them to you because I heard these two things, and because I also came to know that God has spoken once.

[Note: [Col. 0743] The manuscripts read *ille*; the editions read *illa* (“those things”).]

Do not despise the hearer who tells you two things necessary for you: he who, by leaping across the whole of creation, arrived at the only-begotten Word of God, where he learned that God has spoken once.

### 20. The power and mercy of God

Let him now tell us these two things. For these two things greatly concern us:

“That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy.”

Are these the two things: power and mercy? Certainly. Understand the power of God; understand the mercy of God.

Nearly all the Scriptures are contained in these two things. Because of these two, the prophets; because of these two, the patriarchs; because of these, the Law; because of these, our Lord Jesus Christ himself; because of these, the apostles; because of these, every proclamation and celebration of the word of God in the Church: because of these two things, the power of God and the mercy of God.

Fear his power; love his mercy. Do not presume upon his mercy in such a way that you despise his power; nor fear his power in such a way that you despair of his mercy. With him there is power; with him there is mercy. “He humbles this one and exalts that one” (Ps. 74:8): he humbles one by his power; he exalts another by his mercy.

“For if God, wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath, which are prepared for destruction”—you have heard about power; seek mercy—“in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy” (Rom. 9:22–23).

It therefore pertains to his power to condemn the wicked. And who could say to him, “What have you done?” For, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (ibid. 9:20).

Fear and tremble, therefore, before his power, but hope in his mercy.

The devil is a certain power. Yet he often wishes to harm and cannot, because this power is under another power. For if the devil could harm as much as he wished, no righteous person would remain and there would be no believer on earth.

Through his vessels he pushes, as against a leaning wall; but he pushes only as much as he is granted power. In order that the wall may not fall, the Lord will uphold it, because the one who gives power to the tempter himself provides mercy to the tempted.

The devil is permitted to tempt within a measure [Note: [Col. 0743] The manuscripts read *admittitur* (“is admitted” or “is allowed”).]: “And you will give us drink in tears by measure,” he says (Ps. 79:6).

Therefore do not fear the tempter, who has been permitted to do something. You have a most merciful Savior. He is permitted to tempt only as much as benefits you: so that you may be exercised, so that you may be tested, so that you who did not know yourself may be discovered by yourself.

For where and from what source, except from this power and mercy of God, should we be secure, in accordance with that apostolic saying: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10:13)?

### 21. God’s power and justice

Therefore: “Power belongs to God.” For “there is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1).

Do not say, “Why does he give him such great power?” And why should he not give power? The one who gives power possesses justice.

[Note: [Col. 0744] Thus the manuscripts. The editions instead read: “And why does he give such great power, and does he not have justice from power?”]

You can murmur unjustly; he cannot lose his justice. Is there injustice with God? “Certainly not!” (ibid. 9:14). Fix this in your heart; let the enemy not shake it from your thoughts.

God may do something while you do not know why he does it; nevertheless, he cannot act unjustly, since there is no injustice in him. For look: you criticize God as though on account of injustice. I am making a point with you; pay attention for a little while. You would not criticize injustice unless you saw justice. One who does not discern justice, by comparison with which to criticize injustice, cannot be a critic of injustice.

How do you know that this is unjust unless you know what is just? What if this too is just, which you call unjust? “Certainly not,” you say; “it is unjust.” And you cry out as though with eyes that see, seeing that this is unjust by reference to some rule of justice. Comparing what you see to that rule, and perceiving that it does not conform to the straightness of your rule, you criticize it—as though an expert distinguishing the just from the unjust.

Therefore I ask you: From where do you see that this is just? Where, I ask, do you see the just, so that, having seen it, you criticize what is unjust? From where comes this something with which your soul, standing in darkness on many sides, is sprinkled—this something that flashes before your mind? From where comes this justice? Does it really have no source of its own?

Is what is just given to you by yourself? Can you give justice to yourself? No one gives himself what he does not possess. Therefore, since you are unjust, you cannot become just except by turning toward a certain abiding justice. If you withdraw from it, you are unjust; if you approach it, you are just. When you withdraw, it does not fail; when you approach, it does not increase.

Where, then, is this justice? Will you seek it on earth? Certainly not. For in seeking justice you are not seeking gold or precious stones. Seek it in the sea; seek it in the clouds; seek it in the stars. Seek it among the angels: you find it in them, but they too drink from the fountain.

The justice of the angels exists in all of them, but it is received from one source. Look back, transcend, go to the place where God has spoken once. There you will find the fountain of justice, where there is the fountain of life: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10).

If you wish to judge what is just and what is unjust from a small drop of dew, is there injustice with God, from whom justice flows to you as from a fountain, insofar as you understand what is just, while in many respects you understand unjustly?

God therefore has the fountain of justice. Do not seek injustice where there is light without shadow.

But the reason may indeed be hidden from you. If the reason is hidden from you, look back at your ignorance; see who you are. Consider these two things: “That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy.”

Do not seek what is too difficult for you, and do not investigate what is higher than you; but “always consider what the Lord has commanded you” (Sir. 3:22). For these two things belong to what God has commanded you: “That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy.”

Do not fear the enemy: he does only as much as he has received power to do. Fear the one who possesses supreme power; fear the one who does as much as he wills, who does nothing unjustly, and whatever he does is just.

We thought something was unjust; because God has done it, believe that it is just.

### 22. God’s permission and Christ’s passion

“But then,” you say, “if someone kills an innocent person, does he act justly or unjustly?”

Unjustly, certainly.

“Why, then, does God permit this?”

First see whether you ought to do this: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; if you see someone naked, clothe him” (Isa. 58:7). For this is your justice. The Lord commanded you this:

“Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove wickedness from your hearts and from before my eyes. Learn to do good; judge for the orphan and the widow. And come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (ibid. 1:16–18).

You wish to reason before you have done what makes you worthy to reason about why God permitted this. I cannot tell you the counsel of God, O man. Yet I say this: the man who killed an innocent person acted unjustly, and it would not have happened unless God had permitted it. But although that man acted unjustly, God did not permit it unjustly.

Let the reason remain hidden in this unknown matter that disturbs you, whose innocence moves you. For I could quickly answer you, “He would not have been killed unless he were guilty,” but you consider him innocent. I could say this to you quickly. You did not examine his heart, investigate his deeds, or scrutinize his thoughts so that you could say to me, “He was unjustly killed.”

I could therefore answer easily. But a certain righteous man is set before me—unquestionably righteous, without any doubt righteous—who had no sin and was killed by sinners, handed over by a sinner: Christ the Lord himself. We cannot say of him that he had any iniquity, because “he paid what he had not taken” (Ps. 68:5). He is set before me.

“And what will you say about Christ?”

“You are speaking with me,” you say.

“And I am speaking with you. You raise the question about him; I resolve the question from him.”

For there we know the counsel of God, which we could know only because he revealed it: so that, when you have discovered God’s counsel by which he permitted his innocent Son to be killed by the unjust—and a counsel such as pleases you, and which, if you are just, you cannot disapprove—you may believe that God acts by counsel in other matters also, though it is hidden from you.

Come, brothers: the blood of the righteous man was necessary to erase the record of sins; an example of patience was necessary; an example of humility was necessary; the sign of the cross was necessary for the overthrow of the devil and his angels (Col. 2:14–15); the passion of our Lord was necessary for us. For through the Lord’s passion the world was redeemed.

How many good things the Lord’s passion accomplished! Yet this righteous man’s passion would not have occurred unless the unjust had killed the Lord.

What, then? Is this good that has been granted to us through the Lord’s passion to be attributed to the unjust killers of Christ?

Certainly not. They wished it; God permitted it. They would have been guilty even if they had merely wished it. God, however, would not have permitted it unless it were just.

They wished to kill him. Suppose that they were unable to do so: they would still have been unjust and murderers. Who would doubt this? For “the Lord examines the righteous and the ungodly” (Ps. 10:6), and “there will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. 1:9).

God examines what each person wished, not what he was able to do. Therefore, if they had wished to kill him but had been unable to do so and had not killed him, they would still have remained unjust, while the passion of Christ would not have been granted to you.

The ungodly man therefore wished to do what would condemn him; he was permitted to do it so that it might be granted to you. What he wished is charged to the iniquity of the ungodly man; the fact that he was permitted is charged to the power of God.

He therefore wished unjustly; God permitted justly. Thus, my brothers, Judas, the wicked betrayer of Christ, and Christ’s persecutors—all wicked, all ungodly, all unjust, all deserving condemnation—and yet the Father “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

Arrange the matter, if you can; distinguish it, if you can. “Offer to God the vows that your lips have distinguished” (Ps. 65:13). See what the unjust man did there and what the just man did. One wished; the other permitted. One wished unjustly; the other permitted justly. Let the unjust will be condemned; let the just permission be glorified.

What evil happened to Christ because Christ died? Those who wished to do evil are evil; the one to whom they did it suffered no evil. Mortal flesh was killed, killing death by death, offering an example of patience, and presenting beforehand an example of resurrection.

How many good things were accomplished through the evil of the unjust by the righteousness of the just! This is the great work of God: the good that you do, he himself gave you; and from your evil he himself brings about good.

Therefore do not be surprised. God permits, and he permits by judgment; he permits, and he permits by measure, number, and weight. With him there is no injustice.

Only belong to him; place your hope in him. Let him be your helper and your salvation. In him let there be a fortified place, a tower of strength. Let him himself be your refuge, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure (1 Cor. 10:13).

The fact that he permits you to suffer temptation is his power; the fact that he does not allow more to happen to you than you can bear is his mercy:

“That power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy, for you will repay each one according to his works.”

After the discourse on the psalm, when an astrologer was pointed out among the people, he himself added the following concerning him.

### 23. The conversion of the astrologer

The thirst of the Church wishes to drink even this man whom you see. At the same time, so that you may know how many among the Christians bless with their mouths but curse in their hearts, this man returns as a penitent from being a Christian and faithful man, and, terrified by the Lord’s power, turns toward the Lord’s mercy.

Although he was a believer, he was led astray by the enemy and was an astrologer for a long time: led astray while leading others astray, deceived while deceiving others, he enticed and cheated them, uttering many lies against God, who gave human beings the power to do what is good and not to do what is evil.

This man used to say that adultery was not committed by one’s own will but by Venus; that murder was not committed by one’s own will but by Mars; and that justice was not made by God but by Jupiter. He said many other sacrilegious things, and not insignificant ones. [Note: [Col. 0747] Most manuscripts read *mala* (“evil things”) in place of *multa* (“many things”).]

How many Christians do you think he deprived of their money? How many bought a lie from him—people to whom we said: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

Now, as we must believe about him, he has recoiled from falsehood. He has realized that he, who enticed many people, was himself once enticed by the devil, and he turns to God as a penitent. [Note: [Col. 0747] The editions read *hominum interitum, se, etc.* (“the destruction of men, himself, etc.”).]

We believe, brothers, that this has happened because of great fear in his heart. For what shall we say? If an astrologer were converted from paganism, there would indeed be great joy; yet it might seem that, if he were converted, he would seek clerical office in the Church.

He is a penitent; he seeks nothing except mercy alone. He must therefore be commended both to your eyes and to your hearts. Love in your hearts the man whom you see; guard him with your eyes. Look at him, recognize him, and wherever he passes, show him to the other brothers who are not here now.

This diligence is mercy, lest that deceiver draw his heart back [Note: [Col. 0747] Three manuscripts read: “lest he return to his heart.”] and attack him. Guard yourselves; do not let his conduct and his way be hidden from you, so that by your testimony it may be confirmed to us that he has truly been converted to the Lord.

For his reputation will not be silent about his life, when he is presented to you in this way, both to be seen and to be pitied.

You know that it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that many who had been ruined—that is, people involved in such arts and followers of wicked teachings—brought all their books to the apostles. So many books were burned that it was necessary for the author to assess their value and record the total price (Acts 19:19).

This happened, certainly, for the glory of God, so that such ruined people would not despair of him who knows how to seek what was lost (Luke 15:32).

This man had been lost; now, having been sought, found, and brought back, he carries with him books to be burned—books through which he himself had been destined to burn—so that, when they have been thrown into the fire, he himself may pass into refreshment.

Nevertheless, know this about him, brothers: for a long time he had been knocking at the Church before Easter. Before Easter he began to ask the Church of Christ for medicine. But because his profession was one in which he had been trained, and which was suspect on account of falsehood and deceit [Note: [Col. 0747] Several manuscripts read *suscepta* (“undertaken” or “received”).], he was delayed, lest he be tempted; nevertheless, he was eventually admitted, lest he be tempted more dangerously.

Pray for him through Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0747] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads: “Pray to Christ for him.”]

Pour out today’s prayer for him to the Lord our God. For we know and are certain that your prayer wipes away all his impieties.

The Lord be with you.

## Exposition of Psalm 62: Sermon to the People

### 1.

For the sake of those who perhaps are still inexperienced in the name of Christ—for he who gave his blood for all gathers from every quarter—it is necessary to say briefly what those who know will gladly hear and those who do not know will learn.

These psalms that we sing were spoken and written under the direction of the Spirit of God before our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the virgin Mary.

There was a king named David among the Jewish people. That people worshiped the one God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, whether visible or invisible.

Other peoples, however, either worshiped idols that they had made with their own hands, or worshiped God’s creature rather than the Creator himself—that is, either the sun, the moon, the stars, the sea, the mountains, or the trees.

God made all these things, and he wishes to be praised in them, not for them to be worshiped in his place.

Therefore, among that Jewish people there was King David, from whose seed our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the virgin Mary (Rom. 1:3), because the virgin Mary, who bore Christ (Luke 2:7), traced her lineage from him.

These psalms were spoken, and Christ was prophesied in them as coming many years later. The prophets who lived before our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the virgin Mary declared in them whatever was destined to occur in our own times—what we now read and see.

We rejoice greatly because our hope was foretold by the saints, who did not see it fulfilled but saw in the Spirit that it was going to happen. We now read and hear it from the readers; we discuss it; and, just as it is written in the Scriptures, so we see it fulfilled throughout the whole world.

Who would not rejoice at this? Who would not hope that what has not yet come will come, because of those many things that have already been fulfilled?

For now, brothers, you see that the whole world, the entire earth, all peoples, and all regions are rushing to the name of Christ and believing in Christ. Certainly you see this: how the vanities of the pagans are overturned everywhere. You see it; it is evident to you.

Are we reading this to you from a book, rather than seeing it happen before your eyes? All this that you see happening before your eyes was written, many immense volumes of years ago, by those whom we are now reading, at the time when we now see these things being fulfilled.

But since those things also have been written that have not yet come—namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ will come to judge, he who first came to be judged—for he came first in humility, but afterward he will come in exaltation; he came to display an example of patience, but afterward he will come to judge all according to their merits, both the good and the evil—because, then, what we hope for has not yet come, namely Christ the judge of the living and the dead, we must believe that it will come.

Let us believe that the little that remains is still to come, since we already see so many things fulfilled that were then going to happen. For he is foolish who does not wish to believe the few things that remain, when he sees so many things fulfilled that did not yet exist when they were foretold.

2. This psalm, then, is spoken in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, both the Head and the members. For that one man who was born of Mary, suffered, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, and [Col. 0749] now sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us—he is our Head. If he is the Head, we are the members. His whole Church, spread throughout the world, is his body, of which he himself is the Head. Not only the faithful who are now living, but also those who lived before us and those who will come after us, all the way to the end of the age—all belong to his body, whose Head is he who ascended into heaven (Col. 1:18).

Since, then, we already know the Head and the body—he is the Head, and we are the body—when we hear his voice, we must hear it both from the Head and from the body. For whatever he suffered, we suffered in him; and whatever we suffer, he himself suffers in us. If the head suffers some injury, can the hand say that it does not suffer? Or if the hand suffers something, can the head say that it does not suffer? Or if the foot suffers something, can the head say that it does not suffer? When one of our members suffers, all the members hasten to help the suffering member.

If, then, when he suffered, we suffered in him, and he has now ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, whatever his Church suffers amid the tribulations, temptations, necessities, and afflictions of this age—for it must be instructed in this way, so that it may be purified by fire like gold—he himself suffers. We prove that we suffered in him by the Apostle’s words: “But if you died with Christ, why, as though you were still living in the world, do you make judgments?” (Col. 2:20). He says again: “Our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing” (Rom. 6:6).

If, then, we died in him, we also rose in him. For the same Apostle said: “But if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1). If, then, we died in him and rose in him, he also dies in us and rises in us—for he is the unity of the Head and the body. It is therefore not without reason that his voice is also ours, and our voice is also his. Let us therefore hear the psalm and understand Christ speaking in it.

3. [Verse 1.] This psalm has the title: “For David, when he was in the wilderness of Idumaea.” By the name Idumaea, this present age is understood. Idumaea was a certain nation of wandering people, where idols were worshiped. This Idumaea is not presented in a favorable sense. If it is not presented favorably, we must understand that this life, in which we endure such great labors and are subjected to such great necessities, is signified by the name Idumaea.

This is also the wilderness where there is much thirst, and you are about to hear the voice of one who thirsts in the wilderness. But if we recognize that we are thirsty, we will also recognize that we are drinking. For whoever thirsts in this age will be satisfied in the age to come, as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

In this age, therefore, we must not love fullness as though it were our true nourishment. Here we must thirst; elsewhere we shall be filled. But now, so that we do not fail in this wilderness, he sprinkles us with the dew of his word [Note: [Col. 0749] Three manuscripts read, “sprinkles us with dew”] and does not allow us to dry out completely, [Col. 0750] so that there may not be, as it were, a repetition concerning us [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, “so that now there may be desire in us”], but so that we may thirst in such a way that we drink. In order that we may drink, we are sprinkled with some grace of his; nevertheless, we thirst. And what does our soul say to God?

4. [Verse 2.] “God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn.” What is it to keep watch? Certainly, it is not to sleep. What is it to sleep? There is a sleep of the soul, and there is a sleep of the body. We must all have bodily sleep; for if the body does not sleep, the human being fails, and the body itself fails. Our fragile body cannot long sustain a soul that remains awake and intent upon its activities. If the soul remains intent upon its activities for a long time, the fragile and earthly body cannot contain it or support it in perpetual action; it gives way and collapses.

For this reason God gave sleep to the body, by which the body’s members are restored, so that they may support the watchful soul. We must take care, however, that our soul itself does not sleep; for the soul’s sleep is evil. Bodily sleep is good, because it restores bodily health. But the soul’s sleep is to forget its God. Whatever soul forgets its God is asleep.

Thus the Apostle says to certain people who had forgotten their God and, as though in sleep, were practicing the madness of idol worship: “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). Was the Apostle awakening someone who was asleep in body? No; he was awakening a sleeping soul, awakening it for the purpose of being enlightened by Christ.

Accordingly, in reference to this very watchfulness, the psalm says: “God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn.” You would not keep watch in him unless his light had risen, the light that would awaken you from sleep. Christ enlightens souls and makes them watchful; but if he withdraws his light, they fall asleep.

That is why it is said to him in another psalm: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4). Or, if souls turned away from him fall asleep, the light is present to them, but they cannot see because they are asleep. So it is with someone who sleeps during the day: the sun has already risen, the day is already warm, but he is as though in night, because he is not awake to see that the day has already dawned.

Likewise, for some people Christ is already present and the truth has already been proclaimed, yet the soul’s sleep still remains in them. Therefore, if you are watchful, you will say to them every day: “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.” Your life and your conduct must keep watch in Christ, so that other people—sleeping pagans—may perceive this and be awakened by the sound of your watchfulness; then they too may shake off their sleep and begin to say with you in Christ: “God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn.”

5. “My soul has thirsted for you.” Behold the wilderness of Idumaea. See how it thirsts here; but see what is good here: “for you.” There are indeed people who thirst, but not for God. Everyone who wants something to be provided for him is burning with desire; desire itself is the soul’s thirst.

And see how many desires there are in human hearts. One desires gold, another silver; one desires [Col. 0751] estates, another inheritances; one desires abundant money, another many cattle; one desires a large house, another a wife, another honors, another children. You see how these desires exist in human hearts. All people burn with desire, and scarcely anyone is found who says: “My soul has thirsted for you.”

People thirst for the world and do not understand that they are in the wilderness of Idumaea, where their souls ought to thirst for God. Let us therefore say this ourselves: “My soul has thirsted for you.” Let us all say it, because in the harmony of Christ we are all one soul. Let that soul thirst in Idumaea.

6. “My soul,” he says, “has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsts for you.” It is not enough that my soul has thirsted; my flesh too has thirsted. But if the soul thirsts for God, how does the flesh also thirst for God? When the flesh thirsts, it thirsts for water; when the soul thirsts, it thirsts for the fountain of wisdom.

From that fountain our souls will be intoxicated, as another psalm says: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Ps. 35:9). Wisdom, then, must be thirsted for; righteousness must be thirsted for. We shall not be satisfied or filled with them until this life has ended and we have come to what God has promised.

For God has promised us equality with the angels (Luke 20:36). Even now the angels do not thirst as we do or hunger as we do; they possess the fullness of truth, light, and immortal wisdom. That is why they are blessed. And from that great blessedness, because they are in the heavenly city of Jerusalem from which we are now pilgrims, they look upon us pilgrims and pity us. At the Lord’s command they assist us, so that we may someday return to that common homeland and there, with them, be filled at the Lord’s fountain of truth and eternity.

For now, then, let our soul thirst. Hence our flesh also thirsts—and how greatly? “How greatly,” he says, “my flesh also thirsts for you.” For resurrection is promised to our flesh. Just as blessedness is promised to our souls, so resurrection is promised to our flesh.

This is the resurrection of the flesh promised to us: listen, learn, and hold fast to the hope of Christians—to why we are Christians. We are not Christians in order to seek for ourselves an earthly happiness, which even robbers and criminals often possess. We are Christians for another happiness, which we shall receive when this whole life of the present age has passed away.

The resurrection of the flesh, then, is promised to us; and such a resurrection of the flesh is promised that this flesh which we now carry will rise at the end. Do not consider this incredible. If God made us when we did not exist, is it a great thing for him to restore us when we did exist?

Do not consider this incredible because you see the dead apparently decaying, turning into ashes and dust. Or if someone’s corpse is burned, or dogs tear it apart, do you think that he will not rise from it? Everything that is torn apart and decays into various ashes is whole before God. These things pass into the elements of the world from which they first came when we were made. We do not see them, but God nevertheless knows from where he will produce them, just as he produced us from what he knew before we existed.

Such, then, is the [Col. 0752] resurrection of the flesh promised to us: although it is the very flesh that we now carry which will rise, it will not possess the corruption that it now possesses. Now, because of the corruption of our frailty, if we do not eat, we fail and grow hungry; if we do not drink, we fail and grow thirsty; if we stay awake for a long time, we fail and sleep; if we sleep for a long time, we fail, and therefore we keep watch. If we eat and drink for a long time—even though we eat and drink for refreshment—that prolonged refreshment becomes exhaustion. If we stand for a long time, we grow tired; therefore we sit. And if we sit for a long time, we grow tired even there, and therefore we rise.

Consider also that our flesh has no stable condition. Infancy flies into childhood; you look for infancy, and infancy is no more, because childhood has taken its place. Then childhood itself passes into adolescence; you look for childhood, and you do not find it. The adolescent becomes a young man; you look for the adolescent, and he is no more. The young man becomes an old man; you look for the young man, and you do not find him. The old man dies; you look for the old man, and you do not find him.

Our age, then, does not stand still. Everywhere there is fatigue, everywhere weariness, everywhere corruption. In all these manifold failures of ours, as we attend to the kind of hope of resurrection God promises us, we thirst for that incorruption. Thus our flesh thirsts for God in many ways. In this Idumaea, in this wilderness, as it labors in many ways, so it thirsts in many ways; as it grows weary in many ways, so it thirsts in many ways for that incorruption which cannot grow weary.

7. [Verse 3.] Yet, my brothers, the flesh of a good and faithful Christian thirsts for God even in this age. If this flesh needs bread, water, wine, money, or an animal for its use, it ought to ask these things from God, not from demons, idols, or I know not what powers of this age.

There are people who, when they suffer hunger in this age, abandon God and ask Mercury, or ask Jupiter to give them what they need, or ask the one whom they call the Heavenly One [Note: The editions read, “or the one whom they call the heavenly Pan.” “Pan” is absent from the manuscripts; two of them read, “or the one whom they call Ceres,” while the others have “the Heavenly One.” This deity was clearly a goddess held in particular honor by the pagan Africans. See Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapters 23–24, and Augustine, *City of God*, book 2, chapter 4.], or similar demons. Their flesh does not thirst for God.

Those who thirst for God ought to thirst for him in every way—in soul and in flesh. For God gives the soul its bread, that is, the word of truth; and God gives the flesh what it needs, because God made both soul and flesh.

You ask demons for the sake of your flesh. Did God make the soul, while demons made your flesh? He who made the soul also made the flesh; he who made both nourishes both. Let both aspects of our being thirst for God, and let us be simply satisfied after our manifold labor.

8. When our soul thirsts and our flesh thirsts in many ways, it is not for just anyone but for you, Lord—that is, for our God. Where does it thirst? “In a desert land, without a road and without water.” We have said that this signifies the present age; it is Idumaea, that is, the wilderness of Idumaea, from which the psalm received its title.

“In a desert land.” It is not enough that it is deserted, where no human being lives; it is also without a road and without water. If only [Col. 0753] the wilderness itself had a road! If only a person who entered it might at least know how to get out! He sees no human being for consolation; he sees no road by which he might leave the wilderness.

So there he turns aside. If only there were water from which the person who cannot get out might be refreshed! An evil wilderness, dreadful and fearsome! And yet God took pity on us and made a road for us in the wilderness: our Lord Jesus Christ himself (John 14:6). He made consolation for us in the wilderness by sending preachers of his word to us. And he gave us water in the wilderness, filling his preachers with the Holy Spirit, so that in them there might be “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

And behold, we have all these things here—but they do not come from the wilderness. The psalm therefore first emphasized the character of the wilderness, so that when you heard what an evil condition you were in, whatever consolations you might have here—whether of companions, a road, or water—you would not attribute them to the wilderness, but to the one who deigned to visit you in the wilderness.

9. “Thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory.” First my soul thirsted, and my flesh thirsted for you in many ways, in a wilderness and in a land without a road and without water; “and thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory.”

Unless someone first thirsts in this wilderness—that is, in the evil condition in which he is [Note: Most manuscripts read, “in this evil condition in which he is”; they do not have “in the wilderness, that is.”]—he will never reach the good that is God.

“But I appeared to you,” he says, “in the sanctuary.” Already there is great consolation in the sanctuary. What does “I appeared to you” mean? “So that you might see me”; and you saw me for this purpose, “so that I might see you.” “I appeared to you, so that I might see.”

He did not say, “I appeared to you so that you might see,” but, “I appeared to you so that I might see your power and your glory.” Hence the Apostle also says: “Now, knowing God—or rather, being known by God” (Gal. 4:9). You first appeared to God, so that God might be able to appear to you.

“To see your power and your glory.” Truly, in this wilderness—that is, in this desert—if a person demands from the desert, as though from the desert itself, whatever is useful for his salvation, he will never see the power of the Lord and the glory of the Lord. He will remain there, dying of thirst; he will find neither a road, nor consolation [Note: Several manuscripts read, “a consoler”], nor water by which he might endure in the desert.

But when he raises himself toward God, so that he may say to him from the depths of his whole being, “My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsts for you”—lest he seek the necessities of the flesh from others rather than from God, or fail to desire the resurrection of the flesh that God promises us—when, then, he raises himself up, he will have no small consolations.

10. Behold, brothers, as long as our flesh is mortal and fragile, before that resurrection it has these consolations by which we live: bread, water, fruits, wine, and oil. If all these consolations and supports were to abandon us, we certainly could not continue to live. Yet this flesh has not received that perfect health in which it will suffer no affliction and experience no want.

So also our soul, while it is here in this flesh, amid the temptations and dangers of this age, is still weak. It too has the consolations of the word, the consolations of prayer, and the consolations of discussion. These are [Col. 0754] to our soul what those things are to our flesh.

But when our flesh has risen, so that we no longer need these things, it will possess a certain place and condition of incorruption. So also our soul will have its food: the Word of God himself, through whom all things were made (John 1:3).

Nevertheless, thanks be to God, who does not abandon us now in this desert—whether by giving us what the flesh needs or by giving us what the soul needs. And when he trains us through certain necessities, he wants us to love him more, lest we be corrupted by fullness and forget him.

Sometimes he withdraws from us the things we need and wears us down, so that we may know that he is Father and Lord, not only flattering us but also chastising us. For he prepares us for a certain great and incorruptible inheritance.

If you are thinking of leaving your son one cup, or one room, or anything else you possess in your house, and, lest he lose it, you train him and correct him with disciplinary blows so that he may not lose anything of yours—something which he too will leave here, just as you will—do you not want our Father to train us also through the chastisements of necessities and tribulations, since he is going to give us an inheritance that cannot pass away?

God will give us himself as our inheritance, so that we may possess him and be possessed by him forever.

11. Let us therefore appear to God in the sanctuary, so that he may appear to us. Let us appear to him in holy desire, so that he may appear to us in the power and glory of the Son of God.

For he has not appeared to many. Let them be in the sanctuary, so that he may appear to them as well. Many think that he was merely a human being because he is proclaimed as having been born from a human being, crucified and killed, having walked upon the earth, eaten and drunk, and performed the other things that are human. They think that he was such as other human beings are.

But you heard just now, when the Gospel was being read, how he made his majesty known: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Behold what majesty, and what equality with the Father, descended into the flesh because of our weakness!

Behold how greatly we were loved before we loved God! If, before we loved God, we were loved by him to such an extent that for our sake he made his Son, who is equal to himself, a human being, what does he reserve for us now that we love him?

Many therefore consider it a small and insignificant thing that the Son of God appeared on earth. Because they are not in the sanctuary, his power and glory do not appear to them. That is, their hearts have not yet been sanctified sufficiently for them to understand the greatness of his power and to give thanks to God that one so great came for their sake, to what birth and to what passion he came. They cannot see his glory and his power.

12. [Verse 4.] “For your mercy is better than lives.” There are many human lives, but God promises one life. He does not give it to us as though on account of our merits, but on account of his mercy.

For what good have we done to deserve it? Or what good works of ours preceded it, so that God might give us his grace? Did he find righteous deeds to crown, and not sins to forgive? If he had wished to punish the sins he forgave, that would not have been unjust. For what is more [Col. 0755] just than that the sinner should be punished?

Although it is just that the sinner be punished, it belonged to his mercy not to punish the sinner, but to justify him—to make the sinner righteous and the ungodly godly. Therefore his mercy is better than lives.

Which lives? The lives people have chosen for themselves. One has chosen for himself the life of conducting business, another the life of farming, another the life of lending at interest, another the life of soldiering. One chooses this life, another that. There are different lives, but “your mercy is better than our lives.”

What you give to those whom you have corrected is better than what the perverse choose. You give one life, which is to be preferred to all the lives we might choose in the world.

“For your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you.” My lips would not praise you unless your mercy went before me. By your gift I praise you; through your mercy I praise you. I could not praise God unless he granted me the ability to praise him.

“For your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you.”

13. [Verse 5.] “Thus I will bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands.” “Thus I will bless you in my life”—now, in the life you have given me; not in the life that I chose according to the world along with others, among the many lives, but in the life you gave me through your mercy, so that I might praise you.

“Thus I will bless you in my life.” What does “thus” mean? That I should attribute to your mercy the life in which I praise you, not to my merits.

“And in your name I will lift up my hands.” Lift up your hands, then, in prayer. Our Lord lifted up his hands for us upon the cross, and his hands were extended for us. His hands were extended upon the cross so that our hands might be extended in good works, because his cross provided us with mercy.

Behold, he lifted up his hands and offered himself as a sacrifice to God for us; and through that sacrifice all our sins were blotted out. Let us also lift up our hands to God in prayer. Our hands lifted up to God will not be put to shame if they are exercised in good works.

For what does someone do who lifts up his hands? Why were we commanded to pray to God with raised hands? The Apostle says: “Lifting up holy hands, without anger or disputation” (1 Tim. 2:8). When you lift your hands to God, let your works come to mind. Since these hands are lifted in order to obtain what you seek, think of exercising those very hands in good works, so that they may not be ashamed to be lifted up to God.

“In your name I will lift up my hands.” These are our prayers in this Idumaea, in this wilderness, in a land without water and without a road, where Christ is our road (John 14:6)—but not a road belonging to this earth.

“In your name I will lift up my hands.”

14. [Verse 6.] And what shall I say when I lift up my hands in your name? What shall I ask? Come, brothers: when you lift your hands, consider what you are asking, for you are asking the Almighty. Ask for something great; not for the kinds of things those who have not yet believed ask for.

You see what is given even to the ungodly. Are you going to ask your God for money? Does he not also give it to criminals who do not believe in him? What great thing, then, are you going to ask for that he gives even to the wicked?

But do not be displeased that the things he gives even to the wicked are so trivial that they are suitable to be given even to the wicked. Do not regard as great [Col. 0756] the things that can be given even to the wicked.

All earthly gifts are indeed God’s; but see that the things he gives even to the wicked are not to be considered great. He reserves something else for us. Let us consider what he gives even to the wicked, and from this understand what he reserves for the good.

See what he gives to the wicked: he gives them this light. See that good and evil alike see it. He gives the rain that descends upon the earth—and what great blessings arise from it! It is provided both for the wicked and for the good, as the Gospel says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45).

These gifts, then, which arise either from rain or from the sun, we ought indeed to ask from our Lord when they are necessary; but not these alone, since they are given to both good and evil.

What, then, ought we to ask when we lift our hands? For the psalm expressed it as best it could. What do I mean by “as best it could”? As a human mouth could express it to human ears. These things were spoken through human mouths and through certain comparisons, in the way that all the weak and all the little ones could understand.

What did it say? What did it ask for? “In your name,” it says, “I will lift up my hands.” What will I receive? “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness.”

Do you think this soul desired some bodily fatness, my brothers? Did it consider it a great thing that we should be slaughtered as fat rams or fat pigs, or that it should come to some tavern where it would find rich dishes with which it could be filled?

If we believe this, we are worthy [Note: Several manuscripts read, “unworthy”] to hear such things. We must therefore understand something spiritual.

Our soul has a certain fatness. There is a certain rich fullness of wisdom. Souls that lack this wisdom wither away; they become so utterly thin that they quickly fail in every good work.

Why do they quickly fail in every good work? Because they do not possess the fatness of their fullness. Hear the Apostle speaking of a fat soul, commanding each person to act well. What does he say? “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

How would the soul be fat unless it were filled by the Lord? Yet however fat it may be here, what will it be in that future age in which God will feed us? Meanwhile, during this pilgrimage, what we shall be then cannot even be expressed.

Perhaps we desire that very fullness here, when we lift our hands—there we shall be filled with such richness that all our want will utterly perish and we shall desire nothing. Everything we desire here, everything we love here as something great, will be present to us in its entirety.

Our fathers are already dead, but God lives. Here we could not always have our fathers; there we shall always have one living Father, while possessing our homeland. In whatever homeland is earthly, we cannot remain there forever; others must be born, and the children of those citizens are born for the purpose of excluding their parents from that place.

For a child is born in order to say to an older person: “What are you doing here?” Those who succeed and those who are born must exclude those who came before them. There we shall all live together; there will be no [Col. 0757] successor, because there will be no predecessor.

What a homeland that will be!

But do you love riches here? God himself will be your riches. Do you love a good spring? What is more splendid than that wisdom? What is brighter? Whatever can be loved here will be yours in place of everything, because the one who made all things will be that for you.

“Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and lips of rejoicing shall praise your name.” In this wilderness, in your name I will lift up my hands. Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and lips of rejoicing shall praise your name.

For now there is prayer, as long as there is thirst. When the thirst has passed, prayer passes, and praise takes its place: “And lips of rejoicing shall praise your name.”

15. [Verses 7–8.] “If I remembered you upon my bed, at dawn I meditated upon you” [Note: Several manuscripts read, “I shall meditate upon you”], “because you became my helper.”

He calls his bed his repose. When someone is at rest, let him remember God. When someone is at rest, let him not be dissolved by rest and forget God. If he remembers God when he is at rest, he meditates upon God in his activities.

For he called dawn “activities,” because every person begins to do something at dawn. What, then, did he say? “If I remembered you upon my bed, and at dawn I meditated upon you.” If, then, I did not remember you upon my bed, I did not meditate upon you at dawn.

Can someone who does not think of God when he is idle think of God in his activities? But whoever remembers him when he is at rest meditates upon him while he acts, so that he does not fail in action.

That is why he added: “And at dawn I meditated upon you, because you became my helper.” For unless God helps our good works, we cannot complete them.

We must perform works that are worthy—that is, as though in the light, when we work with Christ showing us the way. Whoever does evil works in night, not at dawn, as the Apostle says: “Those who are drunk are drunk at night, and those who sleep sleep at night; but since we belong to the day, let us be sober.”

He urges us to walk honorably as in the day: “Let us walk honorably,” he says, “as in the day” (Rom. 13:13). And again: “You are sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of night or of darkness” (1 Thess. 5:5–8).

Who are the sons of night and the sons of darkness? Those who do every evil work. They are so much the sons of night that they are afraid of what they do being seen. They perform in public the evils that many people perform; those that few perform, they do in secret.

Those who perform such things publicly are indeed in the light of the sun, but in the darkness of their hearts. No one, then, works at dawn except the one who works in Christ.

But whoever remembers Christ when he is idle meditates upon him in all his activities; and Christ is his helper in the good work, so that he does not fail through his own weakness.

“If I remembered you upon my bed, at dawn I meditated upon you, because you became my helper.”

16. “And in the shelter of your wings I will rejoice.” I rejoice in good works because the shelter of your wings is over me. If you do not protect me, because I am a chick, the hawk will carry me away.

In a certain passage our Lord himself says to Jerusalem, that city where he was crucified: “Jerusalem, [Col. 0758] Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

We are little ones. Therefore may God protect us beneath the shelter of his wings. What will happen when we have grown greater? It is good for us that he protect us then as well, so that beneath him we may always remain chicks. For he is always greater, however much we may grow.

Let no one say, “Let him protect me while I am little,” as though he could ever attain such greatness as to be sufficient for himself. Without God’s protection, you are nothing. Let us always desire to be protected by him. We shall then always be able to be great in him if we are always little beneath him.

“And in the shelter of your wings I will rejoice.”

17. [Verse 9.] “My soul has clung close after you.” See the one who desires; see the one who thirsts; see how he clings to God. Let this affection arise in you. If it is already budding, let it be watered and grow. Let it reach such strength that you too may say with your whole heart: “My soul has clung close after you.”

Where is this very glue? Love is the glue itself. Have love, the glue by which your soul may cling to God. Not alongside God, but after God, so that he goes before and you follow.

For whoever wants to go ahead of God wants to live by his own counsel and does not want to follow God’s commands. For this reason Peter too was rebuked when he wanted to give advice to Christ, who was about to suffer for us.

Peter was still weak and did not know how great a benefit for the human race lay in Christ’s blood. But the Lord, who had come to redeem us and give his blood as the price for us, began to proclaim his passion.

Peter was horrified that the Lord he wanted always to live here, as he saw him, should die. He was governed by carnal sight and held fast to the Lord with carnal affection. He said to him: “Far be it from you, Lord; be merciful to yourself.”

And the Lord said: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matt. 16:22–23).

Why “the things of human beings”? “Because you want to go before me. Get behind me, so that you may follow me.” Then, following Christ, he could say: “My soul has clung close after you.”

He rightly adds: “Your right hand has upheld me.” “My soul has clung close after you; your right hand has upheld me.”

Christ said this in us—that is, in the human being whom he bore for us and offered for us, he said this. The Church also says this in Christ; she says it in her Head. For she too has suffered great persecutions here, and even now suffers them individually.

Who among those who belong to Christ is not shaken by various temptations? Every day the devil and his angels strive with him to corrupt him through some desire, some suggestion, some promise of profit, or fear of loss, some promise of life, or fear of death, or through the hostility of someone powerful, or the friendship of someone powerful.

The devil presses in from every side, seeking how to overthrow him. We live amid persecutions and have perpetual enemies—the devil and his angels—but let us not be afraid.

The devil and his angels are like hawks; we are beneath the wings of that hen, and he cannot touch us. The hen who protects us is strong. He is weak for our sake, but in himself our Lord Jesus [Col. 0759] Christ, the very Wisdom of God, is strong.

Thus the Church also says this: “My soul has clung close after you; your right hand has upheld me.”

### 18. [verse 10]

But they sought my life in vain. What did those who sought to destroy my life accomplish? Would that they had sought my life in order to believe with me! But they sought my life in order to destroy me. What were they going to do? For they could not tear away the bond by which my soul was attached to you. “Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or the sword?” (Rom. VII, 35). Your right hand received me. Therefore, because of that bond and because of your most powerful right hand, they sought my life in vain.

This can be understood of all who have persecuted, or desire to persecute, the Church. Yet let us understand it especially of the Jews, who sought to destroy Christ’s life—both in our Head, whom they crucified, and in his disciples, whom they afterward persecuted. “They sought my life.” “They shall enter into the depths of the earth.” They did not wish to lose the land, and so they crucified Christ; they entered into the depths of the earth.

What are “the depths of the earth”? Earthly desires. It is better to walk upon the earth in the flesh than to descend beneath the earth through desire. For everyone who desires earthly things against his own salvation is beneath the earth: he has placed the earth before himself, placed the earth above himself, and made himself beneath it.

Therefore, fearing to lose the land, what did they say about the Lord Jesus Christ when they saw many crowds following him because he was performing miracles? “If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation” (John XI, 48). They feared losing the land, and they went beneath the earth; what they feared happened to them as well. For this reason they wished to kill Christ, lest they lose the land; and for this reason they lost the land, because they killed Christ.

After Christ had been killed—for the Lord himself had said to them, “The kingdom shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing righteousness” (Matt. XXI, 43)—great disasters of persecution followed them. The Roman emperors and the kings of the nations conquered them. They were expelled from the very place where they had crucified Christ; and now that place is full of Christian worshipers and contains no Jew. It was rid of the enemies of Christ and filled with worshipers of Christ.

Behold, they lost the place to the Romans because they killed Christ—the one whom they had killed precisely so that they would not lose the place to the Romans. Therefore, “they shall enter into the depths of the earth.”

### 19. [verse 11]

“They shall be handed over to the hands of the sword.” In visible fact this happened to them: they were overcome when enemies attacked them. “They shall be the portions of foxes.” By “foxes” he means the kings of this world who existed at the time when Judaea was conquered. Listen, so that you may know and understand that he calls those men foxes. The Lord himself called King Herod a fox: “Go,” he said, “and tell that fox” (Luke XIII, 32).

See and observe, my brothers: they refused to have Christ as king, and they became portions of foxes.

[Note: [Col. 0759] At this point all the manuscripts read *secuti sunt*.]

For when Pilate, the governor and Roman legate in Judaea, killed Christ at the insistence of the Jews, he said to the Jews themselves: “Shall I crucify your king?” For he was called the King of the Jews, and he truly was king. But they rejected Christ and said: “We have no king except Caesar” (John XIX, 15). They rejected the lamb and chose the fox; deservedly they became portions of foxes.

### 20. [verse 12]

“But the king”: this is placed in this way because they chose the fox but refused the king. “But the king”—that is, the true king, whose title was inscribed when he suffered. For Pilate placed this title inscribed above his head: “King of the Jews,” in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so that all who passed by might read the glory of the king and the disgrace of those Jews who, rejecting the true king, chose Caesar the fox.

“But the king shall rejoice in God.” They became portions of foxes; “but the king shall rejoice in God.” The one whom they seemed to have overcome when they crucified him then, though crucified, poured out the price by which he purchased the whole world.

“But the king shall rejoice in God; everyone who swears by him shall be praised.” Why shall everyone who swears by him be praised? Because he chose Christ for himself, not the fox; because when those Jews insulted him, he then provided the means by which we might be redeemed. Therefore we belong to the one who redeemed us, who conquered the world for us—not with armed soldiers, but through the cross, which they mocked.

“But the king shall rejoice in God; everyone who swears by him shall be praised.” Who swears by him? The one who promises him his life, who makes a vow to him and fulfills it, who becomes a Christian. This is what is meant by: “Everyone who swears by him shall be praised.”

“For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” How much iniquity did the Jews speak? How many evils did they utter—not only the Jews, but also all who persecuted Christians because of the idols? When they raged against Christians, they thought they could put an end to Christians. When they thought they could put an end to them, the Christians multiplied and their persecutors themselves came to an end.

“The mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” No one now dares to speak publicly against Christ; everyone now fears Christ. “For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” When the Lamb was in weakness, even the foxes dared to rage against the Lamb. The Lion from the tribe of Judah conquered (Rev. V, 5), and the foxes fell silent: “For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 63. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1

Since today we are celebrating the feast of the passion of the holy martyrs, let us rejoice in their memory, recalling what they suffered and understanding what they contemplated. For they would never have endured such great tribulations in the flesh unless they had conceived great repose in their minds.

Let us therefore proceed through this psalm for the sake of this solemnity. Yesterday Your Charity heard much, and yet today we could not refuse this festival our service. Since the Lord’s passion is especially commended in this psalm, the martyrs could not have been strong unless they had looked upon the one who first suffered; nor would they have endured such things in their passion as he did unless they had hoped for such things in the resurrection as he himself demonstrated.

Your Holiness knows that our Head is our Lord Jesus Christ, and that all who adhere to him are members of that Head. You already know his voice very well, because he speaks not only from the Head but also from the body. His words not only signify or proclaim the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who has already ascended into heaven, but also his members, who are to follow their own Head. Let us recognize here not only his voice but also ours.

And let no one say that today we are not in the tribulation of sufferings. You have always heard this: in those times the Church was as though attacked all at once, whereas now she is tested one person at a time.

[Note: [Col. 0761] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read *supra* (“above”).]

The devil has indeed been bound, so that he cannot do as much as he can or as much as he wishes; nevertheless, he is permitted to tempt us as much as is useful for those who are making progress. It is not beneficial for us to be without temptations. Nor should we ask God not to be tempted, but rather not to be led into temptation.

### 2. [verse 2]

Let us therefore also say: “Hear my prayer, O God, while I am afflicted” [Note: [Col. 0761] The editions read *cum deprecor* (“when I beseech”); all the manuscripts read *dum tribulor* (“while I am afflicted”), and Hilary also read this.] “From the fear of the enemy deliver my soul.”

The enemies raged against the martyrs. What did this voice of Christ’s body pray? It prayed that they might be delivered from their enemies, and that their enemies might not be able to kill them. Were they therefore not heard, because they were killed? Did God abandon his servants who were brokenhearted, and despise those who hoped in him? Far from it. “Who ever called upon the Lord and was abandoned? Who ever hoped in him and was forsaken by him?” (Ecclus. II, 11–12).

They were therefore heard, and they were killed; yet they were delivered from their enemies. Others, through fear, consented and remained alive; yet they themselves were swallowed up by their enemies. Those who were killed were delivered; those who remained alive were swallowed up.

Hence also that voice of thanksgiving: “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. CXXIII, 3). Many were swallowed up, and many were swallowed up alive; many dead were swallowed up. Those who thought the Christian faith empty were swallowed up dead. But those who knew that the Gospel’s preaching was the truth, who knew that Christ was the Son of God, and who believed this and held it inwardly, yet yielded to their pains and sacrificed to idols—those were swallowed up alive.

The former were swallowed up because they were dead; the latter, because they were swallowed up, became dead. For they could not live after being swallowed up, although they were swallowed up alive.

Therefore the voice of the martyrs prays this: “From the fear of the enemy deliver my soul”—not so that the enemy may not kill me, but so that I may not fear the enemy who kills me. The servant prays in the psalm that what the Lord commanded in the Gospel may be fulfilled. What did the Lord command just now? “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who has power to destroy both soul and body in the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28). And he repeated: “I say to you, fear him” (Luke XII, 5).

Who are those who kill the body? The enemies. What did the Lord command? That they should not be feared. Let us therefore pray that he may grant what he commands: “From the fear of the enemy deliver my soul.” Deliver me from the fear of the enemy, and subject me to your fear. I will not fear the one who kills the body, but I will fear the one who has the power to kill both body and soul in the fire of Gehenna.

For I do not wish to be free from all fear; rather, let me be free from the fear of the enemy and a servant under the fear of the Lord.

### 3. [verse 3]

“You protected me from the assembly of the malicious, from the multitude of those working iniquity.”

Let us now contemplate our Head himself. Many martyrs suffered such things, but nothing shines forth as does the Head of the martyrs. In him we see more clearly what they experienced.

He was protected from the multitude of the malicious, God protecting him, and the Son himself protecting his flesh—that is, the man whom he bore. For he is the Son of man and the Son of God: the Son of God according to the form of God, and the Son of man according to the form of a servant (Phil. II, 6–7), possessing the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John X, 18).

What could his enemies do to him? They killed the body; they did not kill the soul. Pay attention. It would therefore have been little for the Lord to exhort the martyrs by word unless he strengthened them by example.

You know what an assembly of malicious Jews there was, and what a multitude of those working iniquity there was. What iniquity? The iniquity by which they wished to kill the Lord Jesus Christ. “I have shown you many good works,” he said; “for which of these do you wish to kill me?” (John X, 32).

He endured all their weaknesses, healed all their sick, preached the kingdom of heaven, and did not conceal their vices, so that it was their vices themselves that ought to displease them, not the physician by whom they were being healed. Ungrateful for all these cures, like people delirious with a high fever, they raged madly against the physician who had come to heal them and devised a plan to destroy him—as though they wished to test whether he was truly a man who could die, or something greater than human beings who would not allow himself to die.

We recognize their words in the Wisdom of Solomon: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death,” they say. “Let us question him, for there will be regard for his words; for if he is truly the Son of God, let him deliver him” (Wis. II, 18–20). Let us therefore see what happened.

### 4. [verses 4–5]

“For they sharpened their tongues like a sword.” “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI, 5), as another psalm also says. So here too: “They sharpened their tongues like a sword.”

Let the Jews not say: “We did not kill Christ.” For this very reason they handed him over to the judge, Pilate, so that they might appear, as it were, free from responsibility for his death. For when Pilate said to them, “You kill him,” they replied: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John XVIII, 31).

They wished to shift the guilt of their crime onto a human judge. But did they deceive God, the judge? In what Pilate did, he was to some extent a participant simply because he did it; but in comparison with them he was much more innocent. For he persisted as far as he could in trying to free him from their hands.

For this reason he brought him out to them after having him scourged. He did not scourge the Lord in order to persecute him, but wishing to satisfy their fury, so that perhaps they might then become gentler and cease wishing to kill him when they saw him scourged (John XIX, 1–5). He did this as well.

But when they persisted, you know that he washed his hands and said that he himself had not done it and was innocent of his death (Matt. XXVII, 24). Yet he did it. But if he was guilty because he did it, even unwillingly, were those who forced him to do it innocent? Certainly not.

But he pronounced the sentence against him and ordered him to be crucified, and thus, as it were, he himself killed him; and you, O Jews, killed him. How did you kill him? By the sword of the tongue: for you sharpened your tongues. And when did you strike him, except when you cried out, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke XXIII, 21)?

### 5

This should not be passed over, since it has come to mind, lest the reading of the divine Books perhaps trouble anyone. One evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour (John XIX, 14), and another at the third hour (Mark XV, 25). Unless we understand this, we are disturbed.

It is said that, as the sixth hour was beginning, Pilate sat upon the tribunal; and in fact, when the Lord was lifted up upon the wood, it was the sixth hour. But another evangelist, considering the attitude of the Jews—for they wanted to appear free from responsibility for the Lord’s death—shows them to be guilty by saying that the Lord was crucified at the third hour.

When we consider the whole context of the reading and how many things could have occurred while the Lord was being accused before Pilate in order to be crucified, we find that the third hour could have been the time when they cried out, “Crucify, crucify.” Therefore they truly killed him at the time when they cried out.

The officials of the authorities crucified him at the sixth hour; the transgressors of the Law cried out at the third hour. What the former did with their hands at the sixth hour, the latter did with their tongues at the third hour. These were more guilty, raging as they cried out, than those who carried out the order by obedience.

This was the whole subtlety of the Jews; this was what they sought as a great achievement: “Let us kill him, and yet not kill him; let us kill him in such a way that we ourselves will not be judged to have killed him.” “They sharpened their tongues like a sword.”

### 6

“They bent the bow—a bitter matter.” By “bow” he means ambushes. For one who fights at close quarters with a sword fights openly; one who shoots an arrow deceives in order to strike. The arrow wounds before its approach to the wound can be foreseen.

But from whom could the ambushes of the human heart be hidden? Could they be hidden from our Lord Jesus Christ, who had no need for anyone to bear witness to him about man? For he himself knew what was in man, as the evangelist testifies (John II, 25).

Nevertheless, let us listen to them and observe them as though the Lord did not know what they were plotting. “They bent the bow, a bitter matter, to shoot in secret at the blameless.” What he said—“They bent the bow”—means “in secret,” as though they were deceiving through ambushes.

You know by what deceptions they did this: how they corrupted with money a disciple who adhered to him, so that he might be handed over to them (Matt. XXVI, 14–15); how they arranged for false witnesses; by what ambushes and deceptions they acted “to shoot in secret at the blameless.”

Great iniquity! Behold, from concealment comes the arrow that strikes the blameless one, who did not possess even as much stain as could be pierced by an arrow. For he was a blameless lamb, wholly blameless, always blameless—not one from whom stains had been removed, but one who had contracted no stains at all.

For he made many blameless by granting forgiveness of sins; he himself was blameless because he had no sins. “To shoot in secret at the blameless.”

### 7. [verse 6]

“Suddenly they will shoot him, and they will not fear.”

O hard heart, wishing to kill a man who raised the dead! “Suddenly”—that is, treacherously, as though unexpectedly, as though not foreseen. The Lord appeared among them like one who did not know, while they themselves did not know what he did not know and what he knew—or rather, they did not know that he knew nothing imperfectly and knew everything, and that he had come for them to do what they thought they could do by their own power.

“Suddenly they will shoot him, and they will not fear.”

### 8

“They confirmed for themselves an evil word.”

“They confirmed”: so many miracles had been performed, yet they were not moved; they persisted in the plan of their evil word.

He was handed over to the judge; the judge trembled, but those who had handed him over to the judge did not tremble. Authority quaked, but brutality did not quake. He wished to wash his hands, while they stained their tongues.

But why was this? They confirmed for themselves an evil word. How much did Pilate do? How much did he do to restrain them? What did he say? What did he undertake? But they confirmed for themselves an evil word: “Crucify, crucify!” Repetition is confirmation of the evil word.

Let us see how they confirmed for themselves an evil word. “Shall I crucify your king?” They said: “We have no king except Caesar alone” (John XIX, 15). They confirmed the evil word.

He was offering them the king, the Son of God; they turned back to a human being—worthy to have him, and not to have him. Listen further to how they confirmed the evil word. “I find no case against this man,” said the judge, “by which he deserves death” (Luke XXIII, 14, 22). And those who had confirmed the evil word said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25)!

They confirmed the evil word. They confirmed the evil word not for the Lord, but for themselves. How could it not be for themselves, when they said, “Upon us and upon our children”? What they confirmed, they confirmed for themselves. For there is also that word elsewhere: “They dug a pit before my face, and they fell into it.”

Death did not kill the Lord; he killed death. But iniquity killed them, because they did not wish to kill iniquity.

### 9

Indeed, brothers, it is certain: either you kill iniquity, or you are killed by iniquity. But do not seek to kill iniquity as though it were something outside you. Look to yourself; see what within you is fighting against you.
