Take care lest your iniquity, your enemy, overcome you if it is not killed; for it comes from you, and your soul rebels against you—not something else.

In one respect you adhere to God; in another respect you take pleasure in the world. That in which you take pleasure in the world fights against the mind that adheres to God. Let it adhere, let it adhere; let it not fall away or abandon itself. It has great help. What rebels against it is conquered if it perseveres in the struggle.

There is sin in your body, but let it not reign. “Therefore,” he says, “let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI, 12). But if you do not obey it—even though there is something that persuades and delights you toward evil—by refusing to obey, you cause that which exists not to reign; and afterward it will happen that what was will no longer be.

When? When “death will be swallowed up in victory,” when “this corruptible will have put on incorruption” (I Cor. XV, 54). There will be nothing there to oppose you; there will be nothing else to delight you except God.

Thus these Jews also envied the Lord; domination delighted them. Some saw that their authority was being taken away by him, and out of their delight in it they rebelled against the Lord. If they had rebelled against their own evil delight, they would have conquered that envy and would not have been conquered by it; and the Lord who had come to heal them would have been their savior.

But now they favored the fever and resisted the physician. Whatever the fever suggested, they did; whatever the physician commanded against it, they neglected. Therefore they were killed rather than the Lord. For in the Lord, death was killed; in them, iniquity lived, and while iniquity lived within them, they were dead.

### 10

“They recounted their plans in order to conceal the traps; they said: ‘Who will see them?’”

They thought that the one whom they were killing could be concealed from, and that God could be concealed from. Suppose Christ was a man, like other men, and did not know what was being plotted against him. But does God not know?

O human heart, why did you say to yourself, “Who sees me?” when the one who made you sees you? They said: “Who will see them?” God saw, and Christ also saw, because Christ is God.

But why did it seem to them that he did not see? Listen to what follows.

### 11. [verse 7]

“They searched out iniquity; they failed while searching out their schemes”—that is, their bitter and sharp plans.

“Let him not be handed over by us, but by his disciple; let him not be killed by us, but by the judge. Let us do everything, and appear to have done nothing.” And where is the cry of the tongue: “Crucify, crucify”? You are so blind that you are also deaf.

Pretended innocence is not innocence. Pretended justice is not justice, but double iniquity, because it is both iniquity and pretense. Here, then, they failed while searching out their schemes. The more cleverly they seemed to devise their plans, the more they failed, because they were sinking from the light of truth and justice into the depths of evil counsels.

Justice possesses a certain light of its own; it bathes and illuminates the soul that clings to it. But when the soul turns away from the light of justice, the more it seeks to discover something against justice, the more it is driven from the light and sunk into darkness.

Therefore these men, rightly, while investigating what they were plotting against the just man, were withdrawing from justice; and the farther they withdrew from justice, the more they failed while searching out their schemes.

There was a great plan of innocence when Judas himself repented that he had handed over Christ and threw back at them the money they had given him. They refused to put it into the treasury and said: “It is the price of blood; we must not put it into the treasury” (Matt. XXVII, 6).

What is the treasury? The chest of God, where the things sent for the needs of God’s servants were collected. O man, let your heart rather be the chest of God, where God’s riches dwell, where God’s coin is found, your mind bearing the image of your Emperor.

Since these things are so, what kind of pretense of innocence was it not to put the price of blood into the treasury, while putting the blood itself into their conscience?

### 12

But what happened to them? “They failed while searching out their schemes.” Why? Because he says, “Who will see them?”—that is, because they thought that no one saw them.

This is what they said and thought among themselves: that no one saw them. See what happens to an evil soul. It withdraws from the light of truth, and because it itself does not see God, it thinks that it is not seen by God.

So these men, by withdrawing, went into darkness, so that they themselves did not see God, and said: “Who sees us?” The one whom they were crucifying also saw. By failing, they saw neither the Son nor the Father.

If he saw, then, why did he allow himself to be seized and killed by them? Why, if he saw, did he wish their plans to prevail against him? Why? Because he was man for the sake of man, and God hidden in man; he had come to give the ignorant an example of courage. Therefore, knowing everything, he endured these things.

### 13. [verse 8]

“For man shall approach, and the deep heart” [Note: [Col. 0766] Thus most and the better manuscripts read, in accordance with the Septuagint. The editions read *ad cor altum* (“to the deep heart”).]

“And God shall be exalted.”

They said: “Who will see us?” They failed while searching out their schemes, their evil plans. Man approached these very plans and allowed himself to be seized as man.

For he would not have been seized unless he were man; he would not have been seen unless he were man; he would not have been beaten unless he were man; he would not have been crucified or died unless he were man. Man therefore approached all those sufferings, which had no power over him unless he were man.

But if he were not man, man would not be delivered.

“Man approached, and the deep heart”—that is, the secret heart. He presented man to human eyes, while preserving God within; concealing the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, and offering the form of a servant, in which he is less than the Father.

For he himself said both things, but one statement belongs to the form of God and the other to the form of a servant. In the form of God he said: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). In the form of a servant he said: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

Why, according to the form of God, did he say, “I and the Father are one”? Because, “being in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped” [or: a thing to be seized] (Phil. II, 6). Why, according to the form of a servant, did he say, “The Father is greater than I”? Because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6–7).

“Man therefore approached, and the deep heart; and God was exalted.” Man was killed, and God was exalted. The fact that he was killed was from human weakness; the fact that he rose and ascended was from divine power (II Cor. XIII, 4).

Man approached—the deep heart, the secret heart, the hidden heart—not revealing what he knew, not revealing what he was. Those who thought that he was wholly what he appeared to be killed the man in the deep heart, and God was exalted in the divine heart. For he was exalted by the power of his majesty.

And where did he go when exalted? To the place from which he had not departed when humbled.

### 14

“Man shall approach, and the deep heart; and God shall be exalted.”

Therefore, my brothers, pay attention now to the deep heart of man. Of what man? “Mother Zion,” the man will say; “and man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5).

In that city man was made which the Most High himself founded—the same one who was made man in it. Therefore man approached, and the deep heart.

Look upon the man in the deep heart. See as much as you can, if you can, and see God in the deep heart.

Man approached. And because he was God, because he was willingly going to suffer, because he was going to provide an example for the weak, and because those who raged against him could do nothing to him as God about to suffer, but only to him in man and in flesh—what follows?

“The arrows of infants became their wounds” [Note: [Col. 0767] This part of verse 8 is treated above in the exposition of Psalm 56, no. 13.]

Where is that savagery? Where is that roaring—the roar of the people roaring like a lion and saying, “Crucify, crucify”? Where are the ambushes of those bending the bow?

Have not “the arrows of infants become their wounds”? You know how infants make arrows out of reeds. What do they strike, or from what do they strike? What hand, or what weapon? What arms, or what limbs?

“The arrows of infants became their wounds.”

### 15. [verse 9]

“And their tongues were weakened against them.”

Let them now sharpen their tongues like a sword; let them confirm an evil word for themselves. They rightly confirmed it for themselves, because their tongues were weakened against them.

Could this have been firm against God? “Iniquity,” he says, “lied to itself” (Ps. XXVI, 12): “Their tongues were weakened against them.”

Behold, the Lord who had been killed has risen. They passed before the cross, or stood there, and looked upon him, as the psalm had long before foretold: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and gazed upon me” (Ps. XXI, 17–18).

Then they shook their heads, saying: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross.” They tested, in a way, whether he was the Son of God, and seemed to have discovered that he was not, because when they insulted him he did not come down from the cross. If he had come down from the cross, he would have been the Son of God (Matt. XXVII, 40–43).

What do you think of the one who did not come down from the cross but rose from the tomb? What did they accomplish? Even if the Lord had not risen, what would they have accomplished except what the persecutors of the martyrs accomplished? For the martyrs have not yet risen, and yet their persecutors accomplished nothing. We already celebrate the birthdays of those who have not yet risen.

Where is the fury of those who raged? “The arrows of infants became their wounds, and their tongues were weakened against them.”

To what lengths did they carry their schemes, in which they failed while searching them out, that even after the Lord had died and been buried they placed guards at the tomb?

For they said to Pilate: “That deceiver”—this is the name by which the Lord Jesus Christ was called, for the consolation of his servants when they are called deceivers—“that deceiver,” they said to Pilate, “while he was still alive, said: ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Therefore order the tomb to be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the last error will be worse than the first.”

Pilate said to them: “You have a guard; go, guard it as you know how.” But they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards (Matt. XXVII, 63–66).

They placed soldiers as guards at the tomb. The earth was shaken, and the Lord rose. Such miracles occurred around the tomb that the soldiers who had come as guards themselves became witnesses, if they had wished to report the truth.

But that avarice which had taken captive the disciple, the companion of Christ, also took captive the soldier guarding the tomb. “We will give you money,” they said, “and say that his disciples came while you were sleeping and stole him” (Matt. XXVIII, 12–13).

Truly, “they failed while searching out their schemes.” What is this that you have said, O wretched cunning? Do you abandon the light of a pious plan so completely and sink into the depths of deceit [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts read *versutia* (“cunning”).] to such an extent that you say: “Say that his disciples came while you were sleeping and stole him”?

You call upon sleeping witnesses. Truly you yourself have fallen asleep, since you failed while devising such things. If they were sleeping, what could they have seen? If they saw nothing, how are they witnesses?

But “they failed while searching out their schemes.” They failed by turning away from the light of God; they failed in the very execution of their plans. When they could accomplish nothing of what they wished, they certainly failed.

Why was this? Because “man approached, and the deep heart; and God was exalted.”

Therefore, later, when Christ’s resurrection had become known and the Holy Spirit had filled certain fearful disciples with confidence, so that they dared, no longer fearing death, to preach what they had seen, God was exalted in his majesty—the one who had been judged humble for the sake of our weakness.

And when the heavenly trumpets began to sound, proclaiming the Judge who was to come, the one whom they had first seen judged, “all who saw them were troubled.” With God exalted, as I have said, and Christ preached, some Jews saw that Jews were failing in their schemes.

For they saw that, in the name of the crucified one whom they themselves had killed, such great miracles were being performed. They withdrew in their hearts from those who remained in impiety; their hardness displeased them; they sought counsel for their salvation and said to the apostles: “What shall we do?”

“Then all who saw them were troubled” (Acts II, 1–37)—that is, those who understood that their tongues had been weakened against them, who understood that in all their evil and searching schemes they had everywhere failed.

These men were troubled.

### 16. [verse 10]

“And every man was afraid.” Those who were not afraid were not even men. “Every man was afraid,” that is, everyone who used reason to understand what had happened. Those who were not afraid are rather to be called cattle, or savage and fierce beasts. That people was still like a lion, seizing and roaring. But every man was afraid: that is, those who wished to believe, who trembled at the coming judgment.

“And every man was afraid, and they proclaimed the works of God.” He who said, “From the fear of the enemy deliver my soul,” caused every man to fear. He was delivered from the fear of the enemy, but subjected to the fear of God. He did not fear those who kill the body, but him who has power to cast both body and soul into Gehenna (Matt. X, 28).

They preached the Lord. For at first Peter was afraid, and he feared the enemy; his soul had not yet been delivered from the enemy. When a maidservant asked whether he was among his disciples, he denied the Lord three times (Matt. XXVI, 69). The Lord rose and strengthened the pillar. Now Peter preaches without fear, and with fear: without fear of those who kill the body, with fear of him who has power to kill both body and soul in the fire of Gehenna.

“Every man was afraid, and they proclaimed the works of God.” For when these apostles proclaimed the works of God, the chief priests brought them before themselves and threatened them, commanding them not to preach in the name of Jesus. But they said: “Tell us to whom we ought rather to obey, God or men?” (Acts V, 27–29). What could those priests say? “Men rather than God”? Undoubtedly they would not answer except, “God rather.” But the apostles knew what God commanded, and they despised the threatening priests. Therefore, because every man feared, man did not terrify them; and they proclaimed the works of God.

If man fears, let him not terrify man: for man ought to fear him by whom man was made. Fear what is above human beings, and human beings will not terrify you. Fear everlasting death, and you will not care for present death. Desire that incorruptible delight and rest without blemish; and you will mock the one who promises these temporal gifts and the whole world. Therefore love and fear: love what God promises, fear what God threatens. Then you will neither be corrupted by what man promises nor terrified by what man threatens.

“And every man was afraid, and they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds.” What does “they understood his deeds” mean? Was this, O Lord Jesus Christ, what you concealed when you were silent and were led like a sheep to slaughter, and did not open your mouth before the shearer, while we thought you were stricken and set in pain, and knew how to bear weakness? Was this why you hid your form, you who are beautiful in form beyond the children of men (Ps. XLIV, 3)? Was this why you seemed to have neither form nor beauty (Isa. LIII, 2–7)? You endured on the cross those who mocked and said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

What servant of yours, perhaps knowing your power, what one beloved by you, did not cry out in his heart and say: “O, if only he would come down now, and all those who mock him would be confounded”? But it was not so: he had to die for those who were to die, and rise again for those who would live forever. Those who wanted him to come down from the cross did not understand this; but when he rose and ascended glorified into heaven, they understood the works of the Lord. They proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds.

### 17. [verse 11]

The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord. The righteous man is no longer sad. For the disciples were sad when the Lord had been crucified; sorrowful and mourning, they went away and thought that they had lost their hope. He rose again; yet even when he appeared, he found them sad. He restrained the eyes of the two who were walking along the road, so that they would not recognize him, and he found them groaning and sighing. He kept them in this state until he had explained the Scriptures and, through those very Scriptures, shown that it had to happen as it had happened. For he showed from the Scriptures that the Lord had to rise on the third day.

And how would he rise on the third day if he had come down from the cross? Now you who are sad along the way, if you had seen the Lord come down from the cross while the Jews were insulting him, how greatly would you have exulted! You would have rejoiced that he had thus silenced the mouths of the Jews. Await the physician’s plan: by not coming down, by willing to be killed, he is preparing the antidote. Behold, he has already risen; behold, he is already speaking. He is not yet recognized, so that he may be recognized with greater joy. Later he opened their eyes in the breaking of the bread: they recognize him, rejoice, and cry out (Luke 24:16–46). The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord.

Word is brought to one who was rather hard-hearted: “The Lord has been seen; the Lord has risen.” Yet he is still sad; he does not believe. “Unless,” he says, “I put my hand there and touch the scars of the nails, I will not believe.” The body is also offered for touching; he puts in his hand, he handles it, and cries out: “My Lord and my God!” The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord.

Those righteous men, then, rejoiced in the Lord who saw, touched, and believed. What of the righteous who exist now [Note: [Col. 0770] Most manuscripts read, “who have now wished to be.”], since they do not see, since they do not touch? Do they not rejoice in the Lord? And where is that saying of the Lord addressed to Thomas himself: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:25–29)?

Therefore let us all rejoice in the Lord. In accordance with faith, let us all be one righteous man; and let us all have one head in one body, and rejoice in the Lord, not in ourselves, because our good is not ourselves for ourselves, but he who made us. He is our good, to make us rejoice. Let no one rejoice in himself; let no one presume; let no one despair of himself, nor of any person whom he ought to bring along so that he may be a companion of his hope, not the giver of hope.

### 18

The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord and will hope in him; and all who are upright in heart will be praised. Now that the Lord has risen, now that he has ascended into heaven, now that he has shown that there is another life, now that it is clear that his counsels—which were hidden in the depth of his heart—were not empty, because that blood was poured out so that it might be the price of the redeemed; now that everything has been made manifest, because everything has been preached, because everything has been believed, under every heaven the righteous man will rejoice in the Lord and will hope in him; and all who are upright in heart will be praised.

Who are the upright in heart? Come, my brothers, we are always saying this, and it is good for you to know it. Who are the upright in heart? Those who attribute everything they suffer in this life not to foolishness, but to God’s plan for their healing; nor do they presume upon their own righteousness, thinking that they suffer unjustly what they suffer, or that God is unjust because the one who sins more does not suffer more.

See, brothers: we often say these things. You are experiencing something, whether in your body, or through the loss of your property, or through the bereavement of some of your dearest ones. Do not look at those whom you know to be more wicked than yourself—for perhaps you do not dare to call yourself righteous, but you know them to be worse than you—and see them prospering in these things and not being scourged, so that God’s plan displeases you and you say: “Suppose that I am a sinner, and for that reason I am scourged; why is that man not scourged, though I know his crimes to be so great? However much evil I may have done, surely I have not done as much as he?”

Your heart is distorted. “How good is the God of Israel”—but only “to those who are upright in heart”! Yet your feet slip, because you are jealous of sinners when you observe the peace of sinners (Psalm 72:1–3). Let him take care of it; he who knows the wound knows what he is doing. Another person is not being cut. What if he is being despaired of? What if you are being cut precisely because you are not being despaired of?

Therefore, with an upright heart, endure whatever you suffer. God knows what he gives you and what he takes away from you. [Col. 0771] May what he gives you serve for consolation, not for corruption; and may what he takes away from you serve for endurance, not for blasphemy.

But if you blaspheme, and God displeases you while you please yourself, you are of a perverse and distorted heart. And this is worse, because you want to correct God’s heart according to your own heart, so that he may do what you want, whereas you ought to do what he wants. What, then? Do you wish to twist the heart of God, which is always upright, toward the perversity of your heart? How much better to correct your heart according to God’s uprightness!

Did not your Lord teach you this—the Lord of whose passion we were just speaking? Was he not carrying your weakness when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death”? Was he not representing yourself in himself when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”? For the Father and the Son did not have two different hearts; rather, in the form of a servant he carried your heart, so that he might teach it by his example.

Now, behold, tribulation has found in you a kind of different heart, wishing that what threatened you might pass away; but God did not will this. God does not agree with your heart; you agree with the heart of God. Hear his own voice: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matthew 26:38–39).

### 19

All the upright in heart, therefore, will be praised. What follows? If all the upright in heart will be praised, those of perverse heart will be condemned. Two things have now been set before you; choose while there is time. If you are upright in heart, you will be on the right, and you will be praised. How? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

But if you are of perverse heart; if you mock God; if you laugh at his providence; if you say in your heart, “Truly, God does not care about human affairs. If he cared about human affairs, why would that thief have so much while I, an innocent man, am in need?”—then you have become perverse in heart.

That judgment will come. Everything for which God does all these things will appear. And you, who did not wish in this life to correct your heart according to God’s uprightness and to prepare yourself for the right, where all the upright in heart will be praised, will be on the left, where you will then hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

Will there then be time to correct the heart? Correct it now, brothers; correct it now. Who prevents you? The Psalm is sung, the Gospel is read, the reader’s voice rings out, the preacher’s voice rings out. The Lord is patient: you sin, and he spares you; you sin again, and he still spares you, and you continue adding to your sins. How long is God patient? You will also experience the just God.

We frighten you because we are afraid. Teach us not to be afraid, and we will not frighten you. But God teaches us better to fear than any human being teaches us not to fear. For every human being was afraid. And they proclaimed the works of God. May God count us among those who feared and proclaimed them.

Because we are afraid, we proclaim these things to you, brothers. We see your eagerness to hear the word, and we see your desires pressing for it; we see your affections. The earth is being well watered: may it produce grain, not thorns. A granary is prepared for the grain; fire for the thorns.

You know what you do with your field; and does God not know what to do with [Col. 0772] his servant [Note: [Col. 0772] Some manuscripts read, “with his servant-field”; others, “with the field of his servant.”]? What rains upon a fertile field is sweet; and what rains upon a thorny field is sweet. Does the one who has produced thorns accuse the rain? Will not that rain be a witness in God’s judgment, and say: “I came sweetly upon all” [Note: [Col. 0772] Thus our manuscripts. The editions read, “I came sweet upon all things.”]?”

Therefore see what you produce, so that you may attend to what is being prepared for you. You produce grain: hope for the granary. You produce thorns: hope for the fire. But the time of the granary or the time of the fire has not yet arrived. Let preparation be made now, then, so that it will not be feared.

In the name of Christ, both we who speak live and you to whom we speak live. Is there no opportunity, no time, to correct one’s purpose and change an evil life into a good one? If you wish, does it not happen today? If you wish, does it not happen now? What will you have to buy in order to do it? What *symplasia* [Note: [Col. 0772] The editions read *emplastra* (“plasters”). The manuscripts have *symplasia*, or *simplasia*; with a few exceptions, some of which read *templasia*, others *templa Asiae* (“the temples of Asia”).] will you have to seek? To which Indians will you sail? What ship will you prepare?

Behold, while I am speaking, change your heart. And what has so often and for so long been cried out to happen has happened—and what, if it does not happen, gives birth to eternal punishment.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 64. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verse 1]

The voice of holy prophecy must be recognized from the title itself of this psalm. It is entitled: “For the end: A Psalm of David, a Song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel from the people of the captivity, when they began to go out.”

How this event took place among our ancestors at the time of the Babylonian captivity is not known to everyone, but it is known to those who carefully attend to the holy Scriptures, whether by hearing or by reading. For when the people of Israel had been taken captive, they were led from the city of Jerusalem into servitude in Babylon (2 Kings 24:25). The holy Jeremiah prophesied that after seventy years the people would return from captivity and restore the city of Jerusalem itself, which he had mourned after it had been conquered by its enemies (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10).

At that time there were prophets in Babylon, established there during the captivity of the people; among them was the prophet Ezekiel. That people waited until the period of seventy years had been completed, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy. When the seventy years had been completed, the temple that had been thrown down was restored, and a large part of that people returned from captivity.

But since the Apostle says, “These things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11), we too must first know our captivity and then our liberation. We must know the Babylon in which we are captives, and the Jerusalem for whose return we sigh.

These two cities are, in the literal sense, truly two cities. That Jerusalem, however, is not now inhabited by the Jews. After the Lord had been crucified, a great scourge was exacted upon them; and they were uprooted from that place where, in impious freedom, they had raged madly against the physician. They were scattered among all the nations, and that land was given to Christians. What the Lord had said to them was fulfilled: “Therefore the kingdom will be taken away from you and given to a nation doing righteousness” (Matthew 21:43).

When they saw many crowds then following the Lord, who was preaching the kingdom of heaven and performing miracles, the rulers of that city said: “If we let him go on, everyone will follow him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). To avoid losing their place, they killed the Lord; and therefore they lost it, because they killed him.

That earthly city, then, bore the shadow of a certain eternal city in heaven. But when the city that was signified began to be preached more clearly, the shadow by which it was signified was thrown down. Therefore there is now no temple there that had been built as an image of the Lord’s future body. We possess the light; the shadow has passed away. Yet we are still in a certain captivity: “As long as we are in the body,” he says, “we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6).

### 2

And consider the names of these two cities, Babylon and Jerusalem. Babylon is interpreted as “Confusion”; Jerusalem as “Vision of Peace.” Attend now to the city of confusion, so that you may understand the vision of peace. Endure this one; sigh for that one.

How can these two cities be recognized? Can we separate them from one another now? They are mixed together, and from the very beginning of the human race they have run mixed together until the end of the age. Jerusalem received its beginning through Abel; Babylon through Cain. The actual buildings of the cities were made later.

That Jerusalem was in the land of the Jebusites, for at first it was called Jebus (2 Samuel 5:6; Joshua 18:28). The nation of the Jebusites was driven out when the people of God were freed from Egypt and brought into the promised land. Babylon, however, was founded in the inner regions of Persia, and for a long time raised its head above the other nations.

These two cities, then, were founded at particular times, so that the figure of the two cities—which had begun long ago and would remain in this age until the end, but would be separated at the end—might be made manifest.

How, then, can we point them out now, since they are mixed together? The Lord will show them then, when he places some at the right and others at the left. Jerusalem will be at the right; Babylon at the left. Jerusalem will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Babylon will hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

Yet we can also offer something, insofar as the Lord grants it, by which the faithful who are devout may even now be distinguished: the citizens of Jerusalem from the citizens of Babylon. Two loves make these two cities: love of God makes Jerusalem; love of the world makes Babylon. Let each person therefore ask what he loves, and he will discover whose citizen he is.

If he finds himself to be a citizen of Babylon, let him uproot desire and plant charity. But if he finds himself to be a citizen of Jerusalem, let him endure captivity and hope for freedom.

For many citizens of holy mother Jerusalem were held by Babylonian desires and, through the corruption of those desires, had become as if citizens of that city. Many are still like this, and many after us will likewise be in this land. But the Lord, the founder of Jerusalem, knows which people he has predestined to be its citizens; he knows those whom he sees as still to be redeemed from the devil’s dominion by the blood of Christ. He himself knows them before they know themselves.

This psalm, then, is sung under this figure. In its title two prophets are also mentioned, who were in captivity at that time—Jeremiah and Ezekiel—and who sang certain things when they began to go out.

The person who begins to love begins to go out. Many go out secretly, and the feet of those going out are the affections of the heart. They go out from Babylon.

What does “from Babylon” mean? From confusion. How does one go out from Babylon, that is, from confusion? Those who were previously confused by similar desires begin to be distinguished by charity. Once distinguished, they are no longer confused. Although they are still mixed together bodily, they are distinguished by holy desire. Because of their bodily mixture they have not yet gone out; because of the affection of their hearts they have begun to go out.

Let us now listen, brothers; let us listen, sing, and desire the place whose citizens we are. And what joys are sung to us? How is the love of our city restored in us, the city we had forgotten through our prolonged pilgrimage?

But our Father sent us letters from there. God supplied us with the Scriptures, through which the desire to return might be produced in us, because by loving our pilgrimage we had turned our face toward our enemies and our back toward our homeland.

What, then, is sung here?

### 3. [verse 2]

“Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” That homeland is Zion. It is Jerusalem, which is Zion; and you ought to know the interpretation of this name. Just as Jerusalem is interpreted as “Vision of Peace,” so Zion means “Watchtower” or “Contemplation,” that is, vision and contemplation.

I do not know what great spectacle is promised to us. And it is God himself who founded the city. What a beautiful and splendid city, whose founder is more beautiful still!

“Praise is fitting for you, O God,” he says. But where? In Zion; in Babylon it is not fitting. For when anyone begins to be renewed, he already sings in his heart in Jerusalem, as the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

“Though we walk in the flesh,” he says, “we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:3). Already we are there in desire; already we have sent our hope ahead to that land like an anchor, so that we may not be tossed about and shipwrecked in this sea.

Just as we rightly say of a ship that is at anchor that it is already on land—for it still rises and falls on the waves, but in a certain sense has been drawn toward land against the winds and storms—so, against the temptations of this pilgrimage of ours, our hope, founded in that city of Jerusalem, keeps us from being carried onto the rocks.

Therefore the person who sings according to this hope sings there. Let him say: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” In Zion, not in Babylon.

But are you still there in Babylon? “I am there,” he says—this lover and this citizen: “I am there, but in the flesh, not in the heart.” Yet when I have said two things, that I am there in the flesh but not in the heart, where do I sing? Not there. For I do not sing in the flesh, but in the heart.

The citizens of Babylon hear the sound of the flesh singing; the founder of Jerusalem hears the sound of the heart. Therefore the Apostle, exhorting those citizens to songs of love and to the desire to return to that most beautiful city, the vision of peace, says: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19).

What does “singing in your hearts” mean? Do not sing from the place where you are in Babylon; sing from the place where you dwell above.

Therefore: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.” In Zion praise is fitting for you, not in Babylon. Those who sing in Babylon—the citizens of Babylon—even when they sing a hymn of God, do not sing it fittingly.

Hear the voice of Scripture: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15:9). “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion.”

### 4

“And to you the vow will be paid in Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0775] Several manuscripts read, “and there the vow will be paid.” Indeed, when the basis for interpretation is considered, we may readily believe that Augustine read it this way.].

Here we make vows, and it is good that we pay them there. Who are those who make vows here but do not pay them? Those who do not persevere to the end in what they have vowed. Therefore another psalm says: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 76:12).

“And to you the vow will be paid in Jerusalem.” For there we shall be wholly complete, that is, entire in the resurrection of the righteous. There our entire vow will be paid—not the soul alone, but also the flesh itself, now no longer corruptible, because it will no longer be in Babylon, but will have been changed into a heavenly body.

What kind of change is promised? “We shall all rise,” says the Apostle, “but we shall not all be changed.” He himself said how those who are changed will be changed: “In an instant, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, that is, entire, and we shall be changed” [Note: [Col. 0775] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “in what manner.”].

What kind of change it will be, he goes on to say: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality. But when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption, and this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?’” (1 Corinthians 15:51–55).

For now, while the first fruits of the mind are beginning in us—the first fruits from which we desire Jerusalem—many things from corruptible flesh contend against us. They will not contend when death has been swallowed up in victory.

Peace will conquer, and the war will end. When peace conquers, that city which is called “Vision of Peace” will conquer. Therefore there will be no conflict with death. But now, how much we contend with death! From it come carnal delights, which suggest many things to us, even things that are unlawful. We do not consent to them, but by not consenting we nevertheless contend.

At first, then, following it, the desire of the flesh led us; later, while resisting, it dragged us; then, after grace had been received, it began neither to lead nor to drag us, but it still contended with us. After the contention there will be victory.

Now, even if it attacks you, let it not defeat you. Later, when death has been swallowed up in victory, it will cease to fight. What has been said? “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).

“I will pay my vow.” What vow? Something like a whole burnt offering. A sacrifice is called a whole burnt offering when fire consumes it entirely. A whole burnt offering is a sacrifice in which everything is consumed. For *holon* means “whole,” and *kausis* means “burning” or “kindling.” A whole burnt offering: wholly burned.

Therefore let the fire seize us—the divine fire in Jerusalem. Let us begin to burn with charity until everything mortal is consumed, and whatever has been against us passes into a sacrifice to the Lord.

Hence it is said elsewhere: “Deal graciously, O Lord, with Zion according to your good pleasure, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built. Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and whole burnt offerings” (Psalm 50:20–21).

“Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion; and to you the vow will be paid in Jerusalem.”

We are seeking here whether perhaps the King of that very city, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, is being commended to us. Let us continue singing until we reach clearer evidence. For I could already say that he is the one to whom this is said: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion; and to you the vow will be paid in Jerusalem.”

But if I said this, belief would be given to me rather than to Scripture—and for that reason perhaps it would not be given to me at all. Let us hear what follows.

### 5. [verse 3]

“Hear my prayer,” he says; “to you all flesh will come.”

And we have the Lord saying that authority over all flesh was given to him (John 17:2). That King, then, began already to appear when it was said: “To you all flesh will come.”

“To you,” he says, “all flesh will come.” Why will all flesh come to him? Because he assumed flesh. Where will all flesh come? From there he took the first fruits from a virgin’s womb. Once the first fruits have been assumed, the rest will follow, so that the whole burnt offering may be completed.

What, then, is “all flesh”? Every human being. And what is “every human being”? Were all people foretold as believers in Christ? Are there not many ungodly people who will also be condemned? Do not many unbelievers die daily in their unbelief?

In what sense, then, do we understand “to you all flesh will come”? He said “all flesh,” meaning flesh from every kind: from every kind of flesh people will come to you.

What does “from every kind of flesh” mean? Have the poor come, but not the rich? Have the humble come, but not the exalted? Have the uneducated come, but not the educated? Have men come, but not women? Have masters come, but not slaves? Have the old come, but not the young? Or have the young come, but not adolescents? Or have adolescents come, but not boys? Or have boys come, but were infants not brought?

Finally, have Jews come—for the Apostles were from them, and from them came many thousands who first handed him over and later believed—and have Greeks not come? Or have Greeks come, but Romans not come? Or have Romans come, but barbarians not come?

Who could count all the nations coming to him to whom it was said: “To you all flesh will come”? “Hear my prayer: to you all flesh will come.”

### 6. [verse 4]

“The words of the wicked have prevailed against us; and you will be propitious toward our iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0776] All the books here read *propitiaberis* (“you will be propitious”); but below most have *propitiabis* (“you will propitiate”).].

What does “The words of the wicked have prevailed against us; and you will be propitious toward our iniquities” mean?

Because we were born in this world, we found wicked people and heard them speaking. [Col. 0777] If I could explain what I feel, may the attention of Your Charity assist me.

Every person, wherever he is born, learns the language of that land, region, or city; he is imbued with its customs and way of life. What could a child born among pagans do so as not to worship a stone, when his parents introduced him to that worship? From them he heard his first words; he drank that error in with his milk. And because those who spoke were adults while the child learning to speak was an infant, how could the little one do anything but follow the authority of his elders and regard as good what they praised?

Thus, when nations were later converted to Christ, they remembered the impieties of their parents and said what the prophet Jeremiah himself said: “Truly our fathers possessed a lie, vanity that did not profit them” (Jeremiah 16:19). When they say this, they renounce the opinions and sacrileges of their wicked parents.

But because those who had persuaded them into such opinions and sacrileges were thought to possess greater authority in proportion as they were older, the person who now wishes to return from Babylon to Jerusalem confesses and says: “The words of the wicked have prevailed against us.” They led us while teaching evil; they made us citizens of Babylon. We abandoned the Creator and worshiped the creature; we abandoned him by whom we were made and worshiped what we ourselves had made.

“For the words of the wicked have prevailed against us.” Yet they did not overpower us. Why? “You will be propitious toward our iniquities.”

Let Your Charity attend. “You will be propitious toward our iniquities” is said only to a certain priest offering something by which iniquity may be expiated and propitiation made. Iniquity is said to be propitiated when God is made propitious toward iniquity.

What does it mean for God to be propitious toward iniquity? It means that he forgives and grants pardon. But for God’s pardon to be obtained, propitiation is made through a sacrifice.

Therefore a certain priest of ours was sent by God the Lord. He took from us what he would offer to the Lord: as we have said, the holy first fruits of flesh from a virgin’s womb. He offered this whole burnt offering to God. He stretched out his hands on the cross, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140:2).

As you know, the Lord hung on the cross toward evening (Matthew 27:46). And our iniquities were propitiated; otherwise they would have swallowed us up. The words of the wicked had prevailed against us; the preachers of Jupiter, Saturn, and Mercury had led us. “The words of the wicked have prevailed against us.”

But what will you do? “You will be propitious toward our iniquities.” You are the priest; you are the victim. You are the one who offers; you are the offering.

He is the priest who, having now entered within the veil, alone among those who have borne flesh, intercedes for us there (Hebrews 6:19–20). This was prefigured in that first people and in that first temple: one priest entered the Holy of Holies, while the whole people stood outside; and the one who alone entered within the veil offered sacrifice for the people standing outside (Hebrews 9:7).

“If it is understood rightly, the spirit gives life; if it is not understood, the letter kills.” Just now, when the Apostle was being read, you heard: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

The Jews did not understand what was being enacted among that people; nor do they understand it now. For it was said of them: “As long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts.” There the veil is a figure; but the figure will be removed, and the truth will appear in those very people.

But when will the veil be removed? Hear the Apostle: “But when you turn to the Lord, the veil will be taken away” [Note: [Col. 0778] The editions read, “when they turn.” The manuscripts have, “when you turn”; and, as we have already observed elsewhere, Augustine commonly reads in this way, so that the Greek *epistrepsē* is taken as the second person of a middle verb.].

Therefore, as long as they do not turn to the Lord, as long as they read Moses, they have a veil over their hearts.

For this sacrament Moses’ face then shone, so that the children of Israel could not look upon his face—you heard this just now when it was read—and there was a veil between the face of Moses as he spoke and the people hearing his words. Through the veil they heard the words; they did not see the face.

And what does the Apostle say? “So that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses.” They did not look, he says, “until the end” (2 Corinthians 3:6–16).

What does “until the end” mean? Until they understood Christ. For the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

There is indeed a splendor on Moses’ face, as on a fleshly and mortal face. Could it have been lasting or eternal? Since death would follow, it would certainly be taken away. But the splendor of the glory of our blessed Lord Jesus Christ is everlasting.

That, however, was a temporal figure; what was signified by that figure is the truth. They read, therefore, and do not understand Christ. They do not carry their attention through to the end, because the veil placed before them denies them a view of the inner splendor.

And see Christ there beneath the veil. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

But once our sins and iniquities have been propitiated through that evening sacrifice, we turn to the Lord and the veil is removed. Therefore, when the Lord was crucified, the veil of the temple was also torn (Matthew 27:51).

“Hear my prayer: to you all flesh will come. The words of the wicked have prevailed against us; and you will be propitious toward our iniquities.”

### 7. [verses 5–6]

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up.”

Who is chosen and taken up by him? Is someone chosen by our Savior Jesus Christ? Or was he himself, according to the flesh, insofar as he is human, chosen and taken up? Is it said to him as the Word of God, of whom the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; because he himself is also the Son of God, the Word of God, of whom he further says, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3)?

Is it said to that Son of God—because he is our priest, and afterward assumed flesh—“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up”? That is, is it said of the human being with whom you clothed yourself, who began in time, born of a woman, a kind of temple of him who always exists and always existed eternally?

Or rather, did Christ himself take up a certain blessed person, and is the one whom he took up not spoken of as plural but as singular? For he takes up one, because he takes up unity. He does not take up schisms; he does not take up heresies. They have made a multitude out of themselves; the one who is taken up is not there.

Those who remain in the structure of Christ and are his members form, in a certain sense, one man, of whom the Apostle says: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).

Therefore one man is taken up, whose head is Christ, because “Christ is the head of man” (1 Corinthians 11:3). He is the blessed man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and the rest that is said there (Psalm 1:1). He is the one who is taken up.

He is not outside us. We are in his members; we are governed under one head; we all live by one Spirit; we all desire one homeland.

Let us therefore see whether what is said to Christ pertains to us and is said about us. Let us question our consciences; let us examine that love. If it is still small and this love has only just been born—for perhaps it has just begun to sprout in someone—let it diligently uproot the thorns growing alongside it, that is, worldly cares, lest as they grow they choke the holy seed.

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up.” Let us be in him, and we will be taken up; let us be in him, and we will be chosen.

8. And what will he give us? “He will dwell,” he says, “in your courts.” That Jerusalem is the one to which those who begin to depart from Babylon sing: “He will dwell in your courts.” “We shall be filled with the good things of your house.” What are the good things of God’s house? Brothers, let us imagine for ourselves some wealthy house: how full of good things it is, how abundant; how many vessels of gold there are there, and also of silver; how large the household, how many beasts of burden and animals; finally, how pleasing the house itself is with paintings, marble, ceilings, columns, open spaces, and rooms. Such things are desired, but still from the confusion of Babylon. Cut off all these desires, citizen of Jerusalem—cut them off! If you wish to return, do not let captivity delight you. You have already begun to depart: do not look back; do not remain on the road. There are still enemies who persuade you to remain in captivity and exile: let the words of the wicked no longer prevail over you.

Desire the house of God, and desire the good things of his house; but do not desire things such as you are accustomed to desire in your own house, or in your neighbor’s house, or in your patron’s house. The good of that house is something else. Why should we say what the good things of that house are? Let him who sings while departing from Babylon declare it: “We shall be filled,” he says, “with the good things of your house.” What are these good things? Perhaps we had lifted our hearts toward gold, silver, and other precious things: do not seek such things; they weigh down rather than lift up.

Let us therefore now contemplate those good things of Jerusalem, those good things of the Lord’s house, those good things of the Lord’s temple—for the Lord’s house is itself the Lord’s temple. “We shall be filled with the good things of your house: your holy temple, marvelous in righteousness.” These are the good things of that house. He did not say, “Your holy temple, marvelous in its columns, marvelous in its marbles, marvelous in its gilded roofs,” but “marvelous in righteousness.”

You have eyes in your flesh with which to see marble and gold; inwardly there is an eye with which the beauty of righteousness may be seen. Inwardly, I say, there is an eye with which the beauty of righteousness may be seen. If there were no beauty in righteousness, why is a righteous old man loved? What does he offer in his body that delights the eyes? Limbs bent with age, a wrinkled brow, a head whitened with gray hair, weakness everywhere, full of complaints. But perhaps, although this decrepit old man does not delight your eyes, he delights your ears. With what words? With what singing? Even if perhaps he sang well as a young man, everything has failed with age. Or perhaps the sound of his words delights your ears, although he can scarcely utter complete words through fallen teeth.

Yet if he is righteous, if he does not covet what belongs to another, if he distributes to the needy what he possesses, if he gives good counsel and has sound judgment, if he believes with integrity [Note: [Col. 0780] Several manuscripts read, “and has sound judgment, practices integrity.” Others read, “believes with integrity.”], if he is prepared, for the faith of the truth, to offer even his shattered limbs—for many martyrs were old men—why do we love him? What good do we see in him with the eyes of the flesh? Nothing.

There is therefore a certain beauty of righteousness that we see with the eye of the heart, love, and burn with desire for—a beauty that people loved greatly in the martyrs themselves while beasts were tearing their limbs apart. When blood defiled everything, when their entrails were poured out by the bites of beasts, did their eyes have anything except what they might dread? What was there to love, unless, amid the foulness of those mangled limbs, there was the unimpaired beauty of righteousness?

These are the good things of God’s house; prepare yourself to be filled with them. But in order that you may be satisfied with them when you arrive, you must hunger and thirst for them while you are on pilgrimage: thirst for this, hunger for this, because these themselves will be the good things of God.

Hear the King to whom these words are addressed, who came to lead you back and made himself the way for you (John XIV, 6). What does he say? “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V, 6). “Your holy temple, marvelous in righteousness.”

And do not think of that temple, brothers, as something outside yourselves. Love righteousness, and you are the temple of God.

9. “Hear us, O God, our Savior.” He has now made clear which God he means. The Lord Jesus Christ is properly the Savior. It has now become clearer of whom he was speaking when he said, “To you all flesh shall come”: “Hear us, O God, our Savior.”

That one man who is assumed into the temple of God is both many and one. Speaking in the person of one, he said, “Hear, O God, my prayer”; and because that one consists of many, he now says, “Hear us, O God, our Savior.”

Hear him now proclaimed more openly: “Hear us, O God, our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far away at sea.” Behold the meaning of “To you all flesh shall come.” They come from every direction. “The hope of all the ends of the earth”: not the hope of one corner, not of Judea alone, not of Africa alone, not of Pannonia, not of the East or the West alone, but “the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far away at sea”—of those very ends of the earth. “And of those far away at sea”: and because they are at sea, they are far away.

For the sea is a figure of this present age, bitter with saltiness and turbulent with storms, where human beings, made vicious and perverse by their desires, have become like fish devouring one another. Consider the evil sea, the bitter sea, savage with waves; consider what sort of people fill it. Who desires an inheritance except through another’s death? Who desires profit except through another’s loss? How many desire to be exalted by the downfall of others! How many, in order to buy, desire that others sell their possessions! How they oppress one another, and those who can devour one another! And when one larger fish has devoured a smaller, it too is devoured by a larger one.

O evil fish, you seek prey from the small; you will become prey for the great. These things happen every day; they are before our eyes; we see them [Note: [Col. 0781] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, “let us avoid them.”]. Let us dread them. Let us not do such things, brothers, because he is the hope of the ends of the earth.

If he were not the hope “of those far away at sea,” he would not have said to his disciples, “I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew IV, 19). Now that we have been caught in the sea by the nets of faith, let us rejoice that we still swim within the nets; for this sea still rages with storms, but the nets that have caught us will be brought to shore. The shore is the end of the sea; therefore it signifies arrival at the end of the age.

Meanwhile, let us live well within the nets themselves, brothers; let us not tear the nets and go out. For many have torn the nets, made schisms, and gone out because they claimed that they could not tolerate the bad fish caught within the nets. They themselves became bad rather than those whom they said they had been unable to tolerate [Note: [Col. 0781] Several manuscripts read, “whom they imagined they could not tolerate.”].

For those nets caught both good and bad fish. The Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out, and sitting beside the shore they selected the good into vessels, but threw the bad outside. So it will be,” he says, “at the consummation of the age.” He showed the shore; he showed the end of the sea. “The angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid. XIII, 47–50).

Come, citizens of Jerusalem, you who are within the nets and are good fish: tolerate the bad; do not tear the nets. You are with them in the sea; you will not be with them in the vessels. For he is the hope of the ends of the earth; he himself is the hope, even of those far away at sea. Far away, because they are also at sea.

10. [verse 7.] “Preparing the mountains by his strength,” not by their strength. For he prepared great preachers and called them mountains: humble in themselves, exalted in him. “Preparing the mountains by his strength.” What does one of those mountains say? “We had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead” (II Corinthians I, 9).

Whoever trusts in himself and does not trust in Christ does not belong to those mountains whom he prepares by his strength. “Preparing the mountains by his strength, girded with power.” I understand the power; but what does “girded” mean? Those who place Christ in the midst make him girded, that is, surrounded on every side. We all possess him in common; therefore he is in the midst. All of us who believe in him surround him; and because our faith comes not from our own strength but from his power, therefore he is “girded with his power,” not with our strength.

11. [verses 8, 9.] “You who trouble the depths of the sea.” He did this; it is evident what he did. He prepared the mountains by his strength and sent them to preach; he is surrounded by believers in his power; and the sea was shaken—the age was shaken—and it began to persecute his saints.

“Girded with power: you who trouble the depths of the sea.” He did not say, “You who trouble the sea,” but “the depths of the sea.” The depths of the sea are the heart of the wicked. For just as everything is moved more violently from the depths, and the depths contain everything, so whatever proceeded through the tongue, through hands, and through the various powers for the persecution of the Church proceeded from the depths.

If the root of iniquity had not been in the heart, all those things would not have proceeded against Christ. He troubled the depths, perhaps in order also to drain them; for in certain wicked people he drained the sea from its depths and made the sea desolate. Another psalm says: “He turned the sea into dry land” (Psalm LXV, 6). All the wicked and pagans who believed were the sea; they became land: at first barren with salty waves, afterward made fruitful by the fruit of righteousness.

“You who trouble the depths of the sea: who could endure the sound of its waves?” What does “who could endure” mean? What human being could endure the sound of the waves of the sea—the commands of the exalted powers of the age? But how are they endured? Because he prepares the mountains by his strength.

Therefore, when he said, “Who could endure?” he meant: We ourselves, by ourselves, could not endure those persecutions unless he gave us strength. “You who trouble the depths of the sea: who could endure the sound of its waves?”

12. “The nations will be troubled.” At first they will be troubled. But were those mountains, prepared in the strength of Christ, themselves troubled? The sea was troubled; it was dashed against the mountains. The sea was broken; the mountains remained unshaken.

“The nations will be troubled, and all who dwell at the ends of the earth will fear.” Behold, now all fear. Those who were previously troubled now all fear. Christians did not fear [Note: [Col. 0782] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. But the Louvain edition reads, “and they feared.”], and now Christians are feared. All who were persecuting now fear.

For he who is girded with power has prevailed; all flesh has come to him, so that the others now fear because of their very small number. “And all who dwell at the ends of the earth will fear because of your signs.” For the Apostles performed miracles; and through them all the ends of the earth feared and believed.

13. “You will make the exits of morning and evening delightful”—that is, you make them delightful. What is promised to us already in this life? “You will make the exits of morning and evening delightful.” There are exits at morning; there are exits at evening. Morning signifies the prosperity of the age; evening signifies the tribulation of the age.

Let Your Charity pay attention, for the human soul is tested in both: lest it be corrupted by prosperity, and lest it be broken by adversity. Morning signifies prosperity because morning is joyful, as though the sadness of night had passed. Darkness is sad when evening comes; therefore, when the evening of the world came, he offered the evening sacrifice.

Let no one therefore fear evening, and let no one be corrupted by morning [Note: [Col. 0782] Thus the manuscripts, except for a few that, with Erasmus, read, “lest he be corrupted by morning.”]. Behold, someone has promised you profit in order that you may do something evil. It is morning: abundant money smiles upon you; morning has dawned for you. Do not be corrupted, and you will have an exit at morning. For if you have an exit, you will not be caught.

The promise of profit is like bait in a trap: you are constricted, and there is no way out; you are caught in the trap. But the Lord your God has given you an exit, so that you may not be caught by profit, when he says to you in your heart: “I am your riches.”

Do not pay attention to what the world promises, but to what the Creator of the world promises. Pay attention to what God has promised you if you practice righteousness, and despise what a human being promises you in order to lead you away from righteousness and bring you to iniquity. Do not therefore pay attention to what the world promises, but to what the Creator of the world promises; and you will have an exit at morning, through the word of the Lord who says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew XVI, 26).

But the one who could not corrupt you with promised profit or lead you into iniquity will threaten punishments, turn to hostility, and begin to say to you: “If you do not do this, I will show you; I will act; you will have me as an enemy.” At first, when he was promising profit, it was morning for you; now evening is coming, and you have become sad.

But he who gave you an exit at morning will also give you one at evening. Just as you despised the morning of the age through the light of the Lord, so despise its evening through the sufferings of the Lord, so that you may say to your soul: “What more can this man do to me than my Lord has suffered for me? Let me hold fast to righteousness; let me not consent to iniquity.”

Let him rage against the flesh: the trap will be broken, and I will fly to my Lord, who says to me: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (ibid. X, 28). And concerning the body itself he gave assurance, saying: “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke XXI, 18).

Magnificently he placed here: “You will make the exits of morning and evening delightful.” For if the exit itself does not delight you, you will not labor to escape from there. You plunge your head into promised profit if the Savior’s promise does not delight you. And again, you yield to the one who tempts and terrifies you if the one who first suffered in order to make an exit for you does not delight you.

“You will make the exits of morning and evening delightful.”

14. [verse 10.] “You visited the earth and intoxicated it.” From where did he intoxicate the earth? “Your cup, intoxicating—how splendid it is!” (Psalm XXII, 5). “You visited the earth and intoxicated it”: you sent your clouds; they rained the preaching of truth, and the earth was intoxicated.

“You multiplied it to enrich it.” From where did you multiply it to enrich it? “The river of God is filled with water.” What is the river of God? The people of God. The first people were filled so that the rest of the earth might be watered from them.

Hear him promising water: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 37–38). If there are rivers, there is also one river, because through unity the many are one. Many churches, and one Church; many believers, and one bride of Christ: so there are many rivers, and one river.

Many Israelites believed and were filled with the Holy Spirit; from there they spread among the nations. They began to preach the truth, and from the river of God, which was filled with water, the whole earth was watered.

“You prepared their food; for such is your preparation.” Not because those to whom you forgave sins had deserved you: their merits were evil. But you did so because of your mercy, because such is your preparation; thus you prepared their food.

15. [verse 11.] “Intoxicate its furrows.” Let furrows therefore first be made, to be intoxicated: let the hardness of our heart be opened by the plowshare of God’s word. “Intoxicate its furrows; multiply its generations.”

We see it: they believe, and from those who believe others believe, and from them still others believe. Nor is it enough for one person, once he himself has become a believer, to gain one other [Note: [Col. 0784] Thus all the manuscripts. But the editions read, “once he himself has become a believer, unless he also gains another.”]. Thus the seed is multiplied as well: a few grains are sown, and crops rise up.

“Intoxicate its furrows; multiply its generations: in its drops it will rejoice when it rises.” That is, before it is perhaps capable of receiving the river, when it rises it will rejoice in its drops—that is, in those appropriate to it. For certain things are dripped upon the little ones, who are still weak, from the mysteries, because they cannot contain the fullness of truth.

Hear how he drips upon the little ones as they rise—that is, upon those who, in their recent birth, have little capacity. The Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ” (I Corinthians III, 1). When he says “little ones in Christ,” he declares that they have already arisen, but are not yet capable of receiving that abundant wisdom of which he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (ibid. II, 6).

Let it rejoice in its drops as it rises and grows; once strengthened [Note: [Col. 0784] Thus several manuscripts. But the editions read, “when it rises, grows, and is strengthened.”], it will receive wisdom. Just as an infant is nourished with milk and becomes capable of solid food, so at first the food of which it was less capable was made into milk for it. “In its drops it will rejoice when it rises.”

16. [verse 12.] “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” What is sown now grows; what is sown will also be harvested. And now the enemy has sown weeds over the seed, and evil people have arisen among the good—false Christians, having grass that looks similar but does not produce an equal fruit.

For weeds are properly so called because they grow in the likeness of grain, such as darnel, oats, and other plants of this kind that initially have grass entirely resembling grain. Therefore, concerning the sowing of weeds, the Lord says: “An enemy came and sowed weeds over it. But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared.”

Therefore the enemy came and sowed weeds. But what did he do to the wheat? The wheat is not crushed by the weeds; rather, through tolerating the weeds, the fruit of the wheat grows. For the Lord himself said to certain workers who wished to uproot the weeds: “Allow both to grow until the harvest, lest while you wish to uproot the weeds you also uproot the wheat with them. But at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to burn; but store the wheat in the barn” (Matthew XIII, 25–30).

That is the end of the year, the harvest of the age. “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” When you hear “crown,” understand the glory of victory. Conquer the Devil, and you will have a crown. “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” Again he commends the goodness of God, so that no one may glory in his own merits.

17. [verse 13.] “And your fields will be filled with abundance.” “The boundaries of the wilderness will grow rich, and the hills will gird themselves with rejoicing.” The fields, the hills, and the boundaries of the wilderness are the same people.

They are called fields because of their equality: on account of their equality, therefore, the righteous peoples are called fields. They are called hills because of their elevation, since God raises up those who humble themselves before him. They are called the boundaries of the wilderness—meaning all the nations.

Why “the boundaries of the wilderness”? They were wilderness; no prophet had been sent to them. They were like a desert through which no person passes. No word of God had been sent to the nations; the prophets preached only to the people of Israel.

The Lord came; the grains in the Jewish people believed in him. For he said then to his disciples: “You say that the harvest is still far away; lift up your eyes and see that the fields are white for harvest.” There was therefore a first harvest; there will be a second at the end of the age.

The first harvest was from the Jews, because the prophets were sent to them announcing the coming Savior. Therefore the Lord said to his disciples: “See that the fields are white for harvest”—namely, the fields of Judea. “Others,” he says, “have labored, and you have entered into their labor” (John IV, 35, 38).

The prophets labored to sow, and you entered with the sickle into their labor. Thus the first harvest took place; and from that very grain which was then cleansed, the whole world was sown, so that another harvest might arise, to be reaped at the end.

In the second harvest the weeds were sown over the wheat; now the work is being done here. Just as the prophets labored in that first harvest until the Lord came, so in this second harvest the Apostles labored, and all preachers of the truth labor, until at the end the Lord sends his angels into the harvest.

Previously, therefore, it was wilderness; but “the boundaries of the wilderness will grow rich.” Behold, where the prophets had not sounded forth, the Lord of the prophets has been received. “The boundaries of the wilderness will grow rich, and the hills will gird themselves with rejoicing.”

18. [verse 14.] “The rams of the sheep are clothed”—the phrase “with rejoicing” being understood. With the rejoicing with which the hills will gird themselves, the rams of the sheep are clothed. The rams themselves are the hills. They are hills because of their more eminent grace; they are rams because they are leaders of the flocks.

The Apostles, then, the rams, are clothed with rejoicing: they rejoice in their fruits; they did not labor in vain, nor did they preach in vain. “The rams of the sheep are clothed with rejoicing; and the valleys will abound with grain.” The humble peoples will bear much fruit.

“They will cry out.” Therefore they will abound with grain, because they will cry out. What will they cry out? They will sing a hymn. For it is one thing to cry out against God, and another to sing a hymn; it is one thing to cry out sacrilege, and another to cry out the praises of God. If you cry out in blasphemy, you have produced thorns; if you cry out in a hymn, you abound with grain.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXV. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

1. [verse 1.] This psalm is inscribed in its title: “For the end, a song of the Psalm of resurrection.” When you hear “for the end” as the psalms are proclaimed, understand it as referring to Christ, since the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans X, 4).

How, then, this resurrection is to be sung, and whose resurrection it is, you will hear insofar as he himself deigns to grant and reveal it. We know that the resurrection of Christians has already taken place in our Head and will take place in the members. Christ is the Head of the Church, and the Church is the members of Christ (Colossians I, 18). What preceded in the Head will follow in the body.

This is our hope. For this we believe; for this we endure and persevere amid the great wickedness of this age, hope consoling us before hope becomes reality. It will become reality when we too have risen and, changed into a heavenly form [Note: [Col. 0786] Most manuscripts read, “of heavenly beings.”], have become equal to the angels. Who would dare to hope for this unless the truth promised it?

The Jews, however, held this hope as promised to them; and they gloried greatly in their good and seemingly righteous works, because they had received the Law. By living according to it, they had both bodily goods here and hoped for such things in the resurrection as they rejoiced in here.

Therefore the Jews could not answer the Sadducees, who denied the future resurrection, when those Sadducees proposed to the Lord the question that follows. We understand from this that they were unable to solve the question, since they marveled when the Lord solved it.

The Sadducees therefore proposed a question concerning a certain woman who had had seven husbands—not simultaneously, but in succession. This was prescribed by the Law for the propagation of the people: if someone happened to die without children, his brother, if he had one, was to take his wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother (Deuteronomy XXV, 5).

They therefore proposed the case of a woman who had had seven husbands, all of whom died without children, and who successively took her as wife in order to fulfill this duty. They asked: “In the resurrection, whose wife will she be?”

Without doubt, the Jews would not have been troubled or confounded by this question if they had not hoped for themselves in the resurrection the sort of things they practiced in this life.

But the Lord, promising equality with the angels rather than human carnal corruption, said to them: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage; nor do they begin to die, but they will be equal to the angels of God” (Matthew XXII, 23–30; Luke XX, 27–36).

He showed that succession is necessary where departure is mourned [Note: [Col. 0786] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read, “there succession is not necessary, where departure is abolished.”]. Since there will be no one departing, no successors will be sought. For this reason he added: “They do not begin to die.”

Nevertheless, because the Jews held—though in a carnal way—the hope of a future resurrection, they rejoiced that the Sadducees had been answered, since they had a dispute with them over this difficult and obscure question.

The Jews therefore held the hope of the resurrection of the dead, and believed that they alone would rise to blessed life because of the work of the Law and the justifications of the Scriptures, which the Jews alone possessed and the nations did not.

Christ was crucified; “a partial blindness has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters” (Romans XI, 25), as the Apostle says. The resurrection of the dead also began to be promised to the nations, to those who believed in Jesus Christ and that he had risen.
