This psalm, then, is directed against the presumption and pride of the Jews, and on behalf of the faith of the nations, which have been called to the same hope of resurrection.

2. In a certain sense, my brothers, you have heard the mind of the psalm [Note: [Col. 0787] Nearly all manuscripts read “aninam” (as printed)]. Let your entire attention hang upon what I have said and what I have set forth; let no thought turn you away from it. It is spoken against the presumption of the Jews, who hoped for resurrection through the justifications of the Law and crucified Christ, who was the first to rise—not to have as future members of his resurrection Jews alone [Note: [Col. 0787] Thus several manuscripts. But the editions read, “not to have Jews alone as those who would rise.”], but all who would believe in him, that is, all the nations.

It began: “Shout joyfully to God.” Who? “All the earth.” Therefore not Judea alone.

See, brothers, how the universality of the Church spread throughout the whole world is commended. And do not merely grieve for the Jews who begrudged this grace to the nations; grieve still more for heretics. For if those who were not gathered together are to be mourned, how much more those who, after being gathered together, were divided?

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.” What does “shout joyfully” mean? Break forth into a voice of joy, if you cannot do so in words. For one does not shout joyfully with words; rather, only the sound of those who rejoice is produced, like the joy of a woman in labor and giving birth, expressing in a voice what has been conceived in the heart but cannot be explained in words [Note: [Col. 0787] The manuscripts read, “in the voice of the joy (or joy) of the thing conceived.”].

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth”: let no one shout joyfully in a faction. Let no one, I say, shout joyfully in a faction: let the whole earth shout joyfully; let the Catholic Church shout joyfully. The Catholic Church holds the whole; whoever holds only a part, and has been cut off from the whole, wishes to howl, not to shout joyfully.

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.”

3. [verse 2.] “Sing praises to his name.” What does he mean? May his name be blessed as you sing praises. What it means to sing praises, I explained yesterday, and I believe Your Charity remembers.

To sing praises is also to take up the instrument called the psaltery, and to make the voice agree with the striking and work of the hands. If, therefore, you shout joyfully in a way that God hears, sing praises also in a way that human beings both see and hear—but not to your own name.

“Beware of practicing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew VI, 1). And for whose name, you will say, should I sing praises, so that my works may not be seen by people [Note: [Col. 0787] The word “not” is absent from most manuscripts.]? Listen elsewhere: “Let your works shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid. V, 16).

Let them see your good works and glorify not you but God. For if you do good works in order that you may be glorified, the response is what he said concerning certain people of this kind: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.” And again: “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (ibid. VI, 2, 1).

“Therefore,” you will say, “I ought to hide my works, lest I do them before people?” No. But what does he say? “Let your works shine before people.” I am left uncertain, then: on the one hand you say to me, “Beware of practicing your righteousness before people”; on the other you say to me, “Let your good works shine before people.” What shall I observe? What shall I do? What shall I leave undone?

As a human being cannot serve two masters giving different commands, so neither can he serve one master giving different commands. “No,” says the Lord, “I do not give different commands.” Pay attention to the end; sing with reference to the end; consider the purpose for which you act. If you act so that you may be glorified, that is what I prohibited; but if you act so that God may be glorified, that is what I commanded.

Therefore sing praises, not to your own name, but to the name of the Lord your God. You sing praises; let him be praised. You live well; let him be glorified. For from where do you have the ability to live well? If you possessed it eternally, you would never have lived badly; if you possessed it from yourselves, you would never have failed to live well [Note: [Col. 0788] The editions and manuscripts read, “you would never have lived well,” omitting the negation, which could not be absent without destroying the sense.].

“Sing praises to his name.”

4. “Give glory to his praise.” He directs all our attention toward the praise of God; he leaves us nothing from which we may derive praise for ourselves. Let us glory in this all the more [Note: [Col. 0788] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “in God.”] and rejoice; let us cling to him; let us be praised in him.

You heard when the Apostle was read: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the base things of the world, and the things that are not, as though they were, in order to bring to nothing the things that are” (I Corinthians I, 26–28).

What did he wish to say? What did he wish to show? Our Lord Jesus Christ descended [Note: [Col. 0788] The editions read, “to restore in spirit”; the words “in spirit” are absent from most manuscripts.] to restore the human race and to give his grace to all who understand that it is his grace, not their merits. And so that no person might glory in the flesh, he chose the weak.

For this reason even Nathanael was not chosen at first. What do you think was the reason that he chose Matthew while he was sitting at the tax booth (Matthew IX, 9), and did not choose Nathanael, to whom the Lord himself bore witness, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit”?

It is therefore understood that this Nathanael had been learned in the Law. Not that he would not choose learned people; but if he had chosen them first, they would have thought that they had been chosen because of the merit of their learning. Thus their knowledge would have been praised, and the praise of Christ’s grace diminished.

He bore witness to him as to a good and faithful man, in whom there was no deceit; yet he did not take him among those disciples whom he first chose as uneducated. And from where do we understand that he was skilled in the Law? When he heard from one of those who had followed the Lord, who said, “We have found the Messiah,” which is translated “Christ,” he asked where. He was told, “From Nazareth,” and he replied, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

Without doubt, someone who understood that something good could come from Nazareth was skilled in the Law and had carefully examined the prophets.

I know that in those words there is another way of pronouncing the sentence, but it has not been approved by more discerning authorities: namely, that he seemed to despair when, hearing “From Nazareth,” he said, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”—that is, “Can anything possibly come from there?” Spoken in this way, it would express despair.

But the words that follow there are: “Come and see” (John I, 41–47). These words, “Come and see,” can follow either pronunciation. If you say, as one who does not believe, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” the reply is, “Come and see what you do not believe.” Again, if you say it affirmatively—“Something good can come from Nazareth”—the reply is, “Come and see how truly good is what I announce as coming from Nazareth; and since you believe rightly, come and experience it.”

Nevertheless, he is considered to have been learned in the Law because he was not chosen among the disciples by the one who first chose the foolish things of the world, although the Lord bore witness to him, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

The Lord therefore later chose speakers as well; but they would have been proud if he had not first chosen fishermen. He chose the rich; but they would have said that they had been chosen on account of their wealth if he had not first chosen the poor. He later chose rulers; but it is better that when an emperor comes to Rome he should lay aside his diadem and weep at the memorial of a fisherman than that a fisherman should weep at the memorial of an emperor.

“For God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and he chose the base things of the world, and the things that are not, as though they were, in order to bring to nothing the things that are.”

And what follows? The Apostle concluded: “So that no flesh may glory before God.” See how he took glory away from us in order to give glory: he took away ours to give his; he took away the empty to give the full; he took away the unstable to give the firm.

How much stronger and more secure our glory is because it is in God! You must not therefore glory in yourself; the truth has forbidden this. Rather, what the Apostle says, the truth has commanded: “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Corinthians I, 29, 31).

“Give glory, therefore, to his praise.”

Do not imitate the Jews, who wished, as though on the basis of their own merits, to attribute their justifications to themselves and begrudged the nations’ approach to evangelical grace, by which all sins were forgiven them—as though they themselves had nothing that needed to be forgiven, already awaiting their reward as good workers.

While they were still sick, they thought themselves healthy, and for that reason they were sick in a more dangerous way. For if they had been sick in a milder fashion, they would not have killed the physician like madmen.

“Give glory to his praise.”

5. [v. 3.] Say to God: “How fearsome are your works!” Why fearsome, and not lovable? Hear another voice of the psalm: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). What does this mean? Hear the voice of the Apostle: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” Why “with fear and trembling”? He added the reason: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13). If, then, God works in you, you work well by God’s grace, not by your own strength. Therefore, if you rejoice, also fear—lest what was given to the humble be taken away from the proud.

Now, so that you may know that this was done because of the very pride of the Jews, as though they were justifying themselves by works of the Law and therefore falling, another psalm says: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,” as though in certain means and instruments of their own for raising themselves; “but we,” he says, “will glory in the name of the Lord our God. Some trust in chariots and some in horses; but we will glory in the name of the Lord our God.” See how the former were lifted up in themselves; see how the latter gloried in God. What followed from this? “They were bound at the feet and fell, but we rose and stood upright” (Ps. 19:8–9).

Hear our Lord himself saying the same thing: “I came,” he says, “so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” See goodness on one side, and on the other something like evil. But what is better than he? What is more merciful? What is more just? Why, then, should those who do not see see? Because of goodness. And why should those who see become blind? Because of arrogance.

Did they really see and become blind? They did not see, but thought they saw. For see, brothers: when those Jews themselves said, “Surely we are not blind?” the Lord said to them: “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains in you” (John 9:39–41). You have come to the physician; do you claim that you see? The eye-salves will cease; you will remain blind forever. Confess that you are blind, so that you may deserve to be enlightened.

Consider the Jews; consider the Gentiles. “Those who do not see shall see,” he says; “for this I came, so that those who see may become blind.” The Jews saw our Lord Jesus Christ in the flesh; the Gentiles did not see him. See: those who saw him crucified him; those who did not see him believed.

What, then, did you do, O Christ, against the proud? What did you do? “We see,” because you deigned to grant us sight, and we are your members; we see. You concealed God; you set a human being before our eyes. Why did you do this? “So that a partial hardening might come upon Israel, and the fullness of the Gentiles might enter” (Rom. 11:25). For this you concealed God and set the human being before their eyes.

They saw, and did not see: they saw what you had received, and did not see what you were. They saw the form of a servant; they did not see the form of God (Phil. 2:6–7). They saw the form of a servant, in which the Father is greater (John 14:28); they did not see the form of God, on account of which you have just heard: “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 10:30). They seized what they saw; they crucified what they saw. They insulted the one whom they saw; they did not recognize the one who was hidden.

Hear the Apostle saying: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Therefore, O Gentiles who have been called, consider the branches cut off because of severity, while you have been grafted in because of goodness and made participants in the richness of the olive tree; do not be high-minded—that is, do not become proud. “For you do not support the root,” he says, “but the root supports you.”

Be even more afraid, because you see the natural branches cut off. For the Jews came through the Patriarchs; they were born from Abraham’s flesh. And what does the Apostle say? “But you will say, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Quite so: they were broken off because of unbelief. But you,” he says, “stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear; for if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.”

Consider, then, the branches that were broken off and yourself, who have been grafted in. Do not boast over the broken branches, but rather say to God: “How fearsome are your works!” Brothers, if we ought not to exalt ourselves against the Jews, once cut off from the root of the Patriarchs, but instead to fear and say to God, “How fearsome are your works!”, how much less ought we to exalt ourselves against more recent instances of being cut off?

The Jews were cut off first, and the Gentiles were grafted in; from this very grafting-in, heretics have been cut off. But neither should we exalt ourselves against them, lest the one who delights in insulting those who have been cut off deserve to be cut off himself.

My brothers, whatever voice of a bishop has sounded in your ears, we beg you to take care: whoever among you is in the Church, do not insult those who are not within; rather, pray that they too may be within. For God is able to graft them in again.

The Apostle said this concerning the Jews themselves, and it was fulfilled in them. The Lord rose, and many believed. They did not understand when they crucified him; nevertheless, afterward they believed in him, and so great a crime was forgiven them. The Lord’s blood, which had been poured out, was granted to murderers—not to call them “killers of God,” for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. Now the blood of the innocent, once poured out, was granted to murderers; and the very blood that they had poured out in their madness they drank by grace.

Say, therefore, to God: “How fearsome are your works!” Why fearsome? Because “a partial hardening has come upon Israel, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter” (Rom. 11:17–25). O fullness of the Gentiles, say to God: “How fearsome are your works!” Rejoice in such a way that you tremble; do not exalt yourself over the branches that were cut off. Say to God: “How fearsome are your works!”

6. “By the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you.” For this reason, he says, your enemies will lie to you, so that your power may be abundant. What does this mean? Listen more attentively.

The power of our Lord Jesus Christ appeared most especially in the resurrection, from which this psalm received its title. And when he rose, he appeared to his disciples. He did not appear to his enemies, but to his disciples (Acts 10:41). When crucified, he appeared to everyone; when risen, to believers—so that afterward anyone who wished might believe, and resurrection might be promised to the one who believed.

Many saints performed many miracles; none of them, after dying, rose again, since those whom they raised were raised to die again. Let Your Charity attend. Commending his works, the Lord said: “Believe the works, even if you do not wish to believe me” (John 10:38). The former works of the Prophets are also commended; and if not the very same works, nevertheless many works of the same kind and of the same power.

The Lord walked upon the sea and commanded Peter also to do so [Note: [Col. 0791] Some manuscripts read “led Peter.”] (Matt. 14:25, 29). Was the Lord himself not there when the sea parted so that Moses might cross with the people of Israel (Exod. 14:21)? The same Lord was doing those things. He who did these things through his own flesh was himself doing them through the flesh of his servants. Yet he did not do this through his servants—that is, that one of them should die and rise again to eternal life—for he himself was doing everything.

Since the Jews could say, when the Lord performed miracles, “Moses did these things too; Elijah did them; Elisha did them”—they could say this to themselves because those men had also raised the dead and performed many miracles—therefore, when a sign was demanded from him, he commended the distinctive sign that was to occur in him alone and said: “This perverse and embittering generation seeks a sign [Note: [Col. 0791] Most manuscripts read: ‘An evil and adulterous generation.’], and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:39–40).

How was Jonah in the belly of the sea-monster? Was it not so that he might afterward be vomited out alive? What the sea-monster was for Jonah, the underworld was for the Lord. He commended this as his distinctive sign; this is the most powerful sign.

[Col. 0792] It is more powerful to have come back to life after having died than never to have died. The greatness of the Lord’s power, insofar as he became human, appears in the power of the resurrection. The Apostle commends this when he says: “Not having my own righteousness, which comes from the Law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness that is from God based on faith, so as to know him and the power of his resurrection” (Phil. 3:9–10).

The same is also commended elsewhere: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4). Since, then, this great power of the Lord is understood in the resurrection, from which this psalm received its title, what does “By the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you” mean except that it should be understood in this way: your enemies will lie to you so that you may be crucified; you will be crucified so that you may rise? Their lie, therefore, will serve to commend the abundance of your power.

Why do enemies usually lie? So that they may diminish the power of the one about whom they lie. “In your case,” he says, “the opposite will happen.” For your power would appear less if they did not lie about you.

7. Consider also the lie of the false witnesses in the Gospel itself, and see that it concerns the resurrection. When the Lord was asked, “What sign do you show us, since you are doing these things?”—apart from what he had said about Jonah, he expressed the same thing by another comparison, so that you might know that this distinctive sign was especially commended—he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” And they said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” Then the Evangelist, explaining what this meant, says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:18–21).

Behold, he was saying that he would demonstrate this power of his to human beings, and for this reason he had given the comparison of the temple, on account of his flesh, which was the temple of the divinity hidden within. The Jews saw the temple outwardly; they did not see the deity dwelling within [Note: [Col. 0792] Some manuscripts read “dwelling within” with a different form of the verb].

From these words of the Lord the false witnesses constructed a lie that they could speak against him, taking them from the very passage in which he commended his future resurrection by speaking about the temple. For when they were questioned about what they had heard him say [Note: [Col. 0792] The manuscripts read as printed; the editions add “blasphemies”], the false witnesses testified against him: “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple and after three days I will raise it up’” (Matt. 26:61).

They had heard “After three days I will raise it up”; they had not heard “I will destroy,” but they had heard “Destroy.” They changed one word—and only a few letters—in order to fabricate false testimony.

But against whom are you changing the word, O human vanity, O human weakness? You change the word against the unchangeable Word! You change your own word; can you change the Word of God? Hence elsewhere it is said: “Iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12).

Why, then, did your enemies lie to you, O Lord, to whom the whole earth shouts for joy? “By the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you.” They will say, “I will destroy,” when you said, “Destroy.” Why did they say that you had said, “I will destroy,” and not report what you said, “Destroy”?

[Col. 0793] So that they might, as though without cause, defend themselves against the charge of destroying the temple. For Christ died because he wished to; and yet you killed him.

Behold, liars, we grant you this: he himself destroyed the temple. For it was said by the Apostle: “He loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. 2:20). It was said of the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

If, then, the Father gave up the Son, and the Son gave himself up, what did Judas do? The Father, in giving up the Son to death for us, acted well; Christ, in giving himself up for us, acted well; Judas, in handing over his Master because of his greed, acted wickedly.

The benefit granted to us through Christ’s passion will not be attributed to Judas’s wickedness. He will have the reward of wickedness; Christ will have the praise of grace. Certainly, he himself destroyed the temple—he himself who said: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:18).

He himself destroyed the temple by his grace [Note: [Col. 0793] The editions read: “not by your wickedness.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts], by your wickedness.

“By the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you.” Behold, they lie; behold, they are believed; behold, you are oppressed; behold, you are crucified; behold, you are mocked; behold, your head is shaken: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40).

Behold, when you wish, you lay down your life; a spear strikes your side (John 19:34), and the Sacraments flow forth from your side. You are taken down from the wood, wrapped in linen cloths, and placed in the tomb. Guards are added so that your disciples may not take you away. The hour of your resurrection comes: the earth is shaken, the tombs are split open; you rise while hidden, and appear openly.

Where, then, are those liars? Where is the false testimony of their malice? Did your enemies not lie to you “by the abundance of your power”?

8. Let those guards of the tomb also come forward; let them report what they saw. Let them receive money, and let them too lie. Let them too, perversely instructed by the perverse, speak; let them, corrupted by the Jews who refused to be upright in relation to Christ, speak and lie as well.

What will they say? Say it; let us see. You too will lie “by the abundance of the power of the Lord.” What will you say? “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him from the tomb” (Matt. 28:13).

O truly sleeping foolishness! Either you were awake, and you ought to have prevented it; or you were sleeping, and you did not know what happened. They too joined the lie of the enemies. The number of liars increased, so that the reward of believers might increase, because “by the abundance of your power your enemies will lie to you.”

Therefore they lied; they lied “by the abundance of your power.” You appeared against the liars to those who were truthful, and you appeared to those who were truthful whom you yourself had made truthful.

9. [v. 4.] Let the Jews remain in their lies. Since they lied to you “by the abundance of your power,” let what follows be fulfilled for you: “Let the whole earth worship you and sing praise to you; let it sing praise to your name, O Most High.”

A little earlier, you were most humble; now, Most High: most humble among the hands of lying enemies; Most High above the heads of praising angels.

“Let the whole earth worship you and sing praise to you; let it sing praise to your name, O Most High.”

10. [v. 5.] “Come and see the works of the Lord.” O Gentiles, O nations at the ends of the earth, leave the lying Jews and come confessing. “Come and see the works of the Lord, terrible in his counsels over the children of men.”

He too was called the Son of Man, and truly became the son of man: the true Son of God in the form of God; the true son of man in the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6). But do not measure this form of a servant by the condition of other human beings like him. He is “terrible in his counsels over the children of men.”

The children of men devised a plan to crucify Christ; once crucified, he blinded those who crucified him. What, then, did you do, O children of men, when you devised cunning plans against your Lord, in whom majesty was hidden and weakness appeared? You devised plans for destruction; he devised plans for blinding and saving—blinding the proud and saving the humble.

He blinded the proud for this purpose [Note: [Col. 0794] Two manuscripts read: “to blind the proud from among them”]: so that, having been blinded, they might be humbled; having been humbled, they might confess; having confessed, they might be enlightened. “Terrible in his counsels over the children of men.” Truly terrible!

Behold, a partial hardening has occurred in Israel. Behold, the Jews, from whom Christ was born, are outside. Behold, the Gentiles, who were once opposed to the Jews, are inside in Christ (Rom. 11:25). “Terrible in his counsels over the children of men.”

11. [v. 6.] What, then, did he do through the terror of his counsel? “He turned the sea into dry land.” For this follows: “He turned the sea into dry land.”

The sea was the world: bitter with salt, turbulent with storms, raging with the waves of persecutions—it was the sea. Certainly, the sea has been turned into dry land. Now the world, which was full of salt water, thirsts for fresh water.

Who did this? “He turned the sea into dry land.” What does the soul of all the Gentiles now say? “My soul is like land without water to you” (Ps. 142:6).

“He turned the sea into dry land. They shall cross the river on foot.” Those very people who have been turned into dry land, though previously they were a sea [Note: [Col. 0794] So some manuscripts. Others, with the editions, read “previously bitter”], will cross the river on foot.

What is the river? The river is all the mortality of this age. Consider the river: some things come and pass away; other things, destined to pass away, follow after them. Is this not what happens in the water of a river, which rises from the earth and flows onward? Everyone who has been born must yield to the one being born; and this whole order of passing things is a kind of river.

Let the desirous soul not throw itself into this river; let it not throw itself into it—let it stand firm. And how will it cross the pleasures of things that perish? Let it believe in Christ, and it will cross on foot. It crosses with him as guide; it crosses on foot.

What does “cross on foot” mean? It means to cross easily. It does not seek a horse in order to cross; it is not lifted up by pride to cross the river. The humble person crosses, and crosses more safely. “They shall cross the river on foot.”

12. “There we shall rejoice in him” [Note: [Col. 0794] In the editions the following was inserted here: “Rejoice in good works”; it is absent from most manuscripts].

O Jews, you glory in your works; put aside the pride of glorying in yourselves; receive the grace of rejoicing in Christ. For “there we shall rejoice,” but not in ourselves. There we shall rejoice in him.

When shall we rejoice? When we have crossed the river on foot. Eternal life is promised; resurrection is promised. There our flesh will no longer be a river, for it is a river now, when there is mortality.

See whether any age remains fixed. Children wish to grow, and they do not know that the span of their life is being diminished by the years that follow. Years are not added as they grow, but subtracted—just as the water of a river continually approaches, but recedes from its source.

Children wish to grow so that they may be free from the authority of their elders. Behold, they grow; time quickly passes; they reach youth. Those who have passed beyond childhood—if they can, let them hold on to youth. It too passes. Old age follows; or rather, let old age be eternal—it is taken away by death.

The river, therefore, is the flesh that is being born. The one who crosses this river of mortality easily—that is, on foot—passes through it without being overturned and swept away by desire for mortal things. He crosses humbly, with the guidance of the one who crossed first, who “drank from the stream on the way; therefore he lifted up his head” (Ps. 109:7).

Crossing this river on foot, that is, crossing this flowing mortality easily, “there we shall rejoice in him.” But now, in what do we rejoice except either in him or in the hope of him? Even if we rejoice now, we rejoice in hope; then we shall rejoice in him. Even now we rejoice in him, but through hope; then, face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

13. [v. 7.] “There we shall rejoice in him who rules by his power forever.” For what power do we possess, and is it eternal? If our power were eternal, we would not have fallen; we would not have fallen into sin; we would not have deserved punitive mortality.

He willingly assumed what our merit cast us down into: “he who rules by his power forever.” May we become participants in the one whose power will make us strong, while he is strong in his own power. We are enlightened; he is the light that enlightens. When we turn away from him, we are darkened; he cannot turn away from himself. We are kindled by his warmth; when we had grown cold by departing from him, we are kindled again by drawing near.

Let us therefore say to him that he preserve us in his power, because we shall rejoice in him who rules by his power forever.

14. But he does not grant this only to the Jews who believe. Because the Jews greatly exalted themselves, relying on their own power, they afterward learned in whose power they had been made strong for salvation, and some of them believed.

But this is not enough for Christ. What he gave is great; he gave a great price. What he gave ought not to benefit the Jews alone. “His eyes look upon the nations.”

Therefore: “His eyes look upon the nations.” What shall we do? The Jews will murmur; the Jews will say: “What they have, we have also. The Gospel is theirs as well as ours; the grace of the resurrection is theirs as well as ours. Nothing benefits us from having received the Law, having lived in the Law’s justifications, and having kept the commands of our fathers. None of this will count; they have what we have!”

Let them not quarrel; let them not contend. “Those who are bitter shall not exalt themselves.” Let them not exalt themselves in themselves.

O wretched and wasting flesh, are you not sinful? What does your tongue cry out? Let conscience be examined. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Recognize yourself, human weakness.

You received the Law so that you might also become a transgressor of the Law; for you did not keep and fulfill what you received. Through the Law there came to you not the justification that the Law commands, but the transgression that you committed.

If, then, sin abounded, why do you envy the grace that abounded still more? (Rom. 5:20). Do not be bitter, because “those who are bitter shall not exalt themselves.”

The words “Those who are bitter shall not exalt themselves” seem almost to be a curse. Rather, let them be exalted—but not in themselves. Let them be humbled in themselves and exalted in Christ. “For whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23:12). “Those who are bitter shall not exalt themselves in themselves.”

15. [vv. 8–9.] “Bless our God, O Gentiles.” Behold, those who are bitter have been rejected; the matter has been explained to them. Some have been converted; some have remained proud.

Do not let those who envy the Gentiles the grace of the Gospel frighten you. The seed of Abraham has already come, in whom all the Gentiles are blessed (Gen. 12:3). Bless him in whom you are blessed: “Bless our God, O Gentiles.”

And hear the voice of his praise. Do not praise yourselves; praise him. What is the voice of his praise? It is that by his grace we are whatever good we are.

“He placed my soul in life” [Note: [Col. 0796] The manuscripts consistently read “in life,” rather than “into life”]. Behold the voice of his praise: “He placed my soul in life.” Therefore it was in death; it was in death in you [Note: [Col. 0796] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “It was in death, because it was in you; hence it is…”].

Where will it be in life except in the one who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6)? How does the Apostle say to certain believers: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8)? Darkness, then, was in you; light is in the Lord. So death was in you; life is in the Lord.

“He placed my soul in life.” Behold, he placed our soul in life because we believe in him; he placed our soul in life [Note: [Col. 0796] The editions read “who is in life.” The word “who” is absent from the manuscripts]. But what is needed afterward except that we persevere to the end? And who will grant this except the one of whom it is consequently said: “And he did not give my feet over to slipping”?

He himself placed the soul in life; he himself guides the feet so that they do not waver, do not move, and do not slip. He himself makes us live; he himself makes us persevere to the end, so that we may live forever.

“And he did not give my feet over to slipping.”

16. [vv. 10–12.] Why did you say, “And he did not give my feet over to slipping”? What have you suffered, or what could you have suffered, so that your feet might slip?

What? Hear what follows. Why did I say, “He did not give my feet over to slipping”? Because we have suffered many things through which our feet would have been moved from the way unless he himself governed them and did not let them slip.

What things are these? “For you have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined.” You did not burn us as one burns hay, but as one refines silver: by applying fire to us, you did not turn us into ashes, but washed away our impurities. “You have refined us as silver is refined.”

And see how God rages against those whose soul he has placed in life. “You brought us into a snare,” not so that we might die after being captured, but so that, having been freed, we might be tested. “You laid afflictions on our back.”

For we had been standing wrongly, proud. Standing wrongly, we were bent down, so that, being bent down, we might be raised upright in the right way. “You laid afflictions on our back; you placed human beings over our heads.”

The Church has suffered all these things through various and diverse persecutions; it has suffered them individually, and it still suffers them. No one in this life can say that he is free from these temptations.

Therefore human beings are also placed over our heads. We tolerate those whom we do not wish to tolerate; at times we suffer as superiors those whom we know to be worse. When sins are absent, a human being is rightly superior; the more sins there are, the lower he is.

It is good for us to consider that we are sinners and thus to tolerate those placed over our heads, so that we may confess to God that we are suffering what we deserve. For what are you suffering undeservedly that the one who is just has done?

“You laid afflictions on our back; you placed human beings over our heads.”

God seems to rage when he does these things. Do not fear: since he is the Father, he never rages in such a way as to destroy. When you live badly, if he spares you, he is more angry. These afflictions are altogether the scourges of one who corrects, so that there may not be the sentence of one who punishes.

“You laid afflictions on our back; you placed human beings over our heads.”

17. “We passed through fire and water.” Fire and water are both dangerous in this life. Certainly, water seems to extinguish fire, and fire seems to dry up water. So too are the temptations with which this life abounds.

Fire burns; water corrupts. Both must be feared: the burning of tribulation and the water of corruption. When circumstances are difficult, and there is what is called misfortune in this world, it is like fire. When circumstances are prosperous and worldly abundance flows around us, it is like water.

Take care lest fire consume you; lest water corrupt you. Stand firm against the fire; you must be baked. You are placed like a clay vessel in a furnace of fire, so that what has been formed may be strengthened. A vessel already strengthened by fire does not fear water; but if a vessel has not been hardened by fire, it will dissolve in water like mud.

Do not hurry toward the water. Pass through fire to the water, so that you may also pass through the water. For this reason, in the Sacraments, in catechizing, and in exorcizing, fire is employed first. For where do unclean spirits so often cry out, “I am burning,” if that fire is not present?

After the fire of exorcism one comes to Baptism, so that one may pass from fire to water, and from water into refreshment. What occurs in the Sacraments [Note: [Col. 0797] The editions added here “the water of Baptism”; this is absent from the manuscripts] also occurs in the temptations of this age.

First comes the distress of fear, like fire; afterward, when fear has been removed, one must beware lest worldly prosperity corrupt. When the fire has not made you crack and you have not been submerged in the water but have swum across it, you pass through discipline into rest. Passing through fire and water, you are led out into refreshment.

For the realities whose signs are present in the Sacraments are themselves present in the perfection of eternal life. When we have crossed over into that refreshment, dearest brothers, we shall fear no enemy there, no tempter, no envious person, no fire, no water. There will be perpetual refreshment.

It is called refreshment because of rest. For if you say, “There is heat,” it is true; if you say, “There is refreshment,” it is true. If by “refreshment” you understand that we become sluggish there, that is not so: we do not become sluggish there, but rest. Nor, because heat is spoken of, will we burn there; rather, we will burn with the spirit.

Consider this very heat in another psalm: “There is nothing hidden from its heat” (Ps. 18:7). And what does the Apostle say? “Fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11).

Therefore: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.”

18. [v. 13.] Observe that he was silent neither about refreshment nor even about the fire itself, which is to be desired: “I will enter your house with burnt offerings.”

What is a burnt offering? Something wholly burned, but by divine fire. A burnt offering is so called when the whole sacrifice is set alight. There are other portions of sacrifices; a burnt offering is something else. When the whole thing burns and is entirely consumed by divine fire, it is called a burnt offering; when only a part burns, it is called a sacrifice.

Every burnt offering is a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a burnt offering. He therefore promises burnt offerings. The body of Christ speaks; the unity of Christ speaks: “I will enter your house with burnt offerings.”

Let your fire consume everything that is mine; let nothing of mine remain for me; let everything belong to you. This will occur in the resurrection of the righteous [Note: [Col. 0798] So the manuscripts. The editions read “of the dead”], when “this corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality.” Then what is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54).

Victory is like divine fire. When it swallows up our death, it is a burnt offering. Nothing mortal remains in the flesh; nothing culpable remains in the spirit. Everything from mortal life will be consumed, so that it may be brought to completion in eternal life [Note: [Col. 0798] The editions add here: “so that we may be saved from death into life”; this is absent from the superior manuscripts]. Those, then, will be the burnt offerings.

19. [v. 14.] And what will be in the burnt offerings? [Note: [Col. 0798] Some manuscripts of good standing read “what will they be?”] “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have distinguished.”

What is this distinction in vows? It is this: that you accuse yourself and praise him; that you understand yourself to be a creature and him to be the Creator; yourself to be darkness and him to be the one who enlightens, to whom you say: “You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:29).

For when you have said, O soul, that your light shines from yourself, you will not distinguish. If you do not distinguish, you will not pay distinct vows. Pay distinct vows. Confess that you are changeable and he unchangeable. Confess that without him you are nothing, while he is perfect without you; that you need him, while he does not need you.

Cry out to him: “I have said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Ps. 15:2).

When God takes you as a burnt offering, he does not grow, increase, become richer, or become better equipped. Whatever he does concerning you and for you benefits you, not the one who does it.

If you discern these things, you pay vows to your God—vows that your lips have distinguished.

“I will pay you my vows, which my lips have distinguished.”

[Col. 0799] 20. [v. 15.] “And my mouth spoke in my tribulation.” How often tribulation is sweet! How necessary it is! What did his mouth speak in his tribulation?

“I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings.” What does “marrow-filled” mean? Let me hold your love within; it will not be on the surface. What I love in you will be in my marrow.

Nothing is more inward than our marrow. The bones are within the flesh; the marrow is within the bones themselves. Therefore whoever worships God on the surface wishes rather to please human beings. If he thinks one thing inwardly, he does not offer burnt offerings filled with marrow. But the one who sees the marrow receives the whole person.

“I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings, with incense and rams.”

The rams are the leaders of the Church. The whole body of Christ speaks; this is what it offers to God. What is incense? Prayer. “With incense and rams”: for the rams especially pray for the flocks.

“I will offer you oxen with goats.”

We find oxen treading out grain, and they too are offered to God. The Apostle said that what is written, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain,” is to be understood of those who proclaim the Gospel. “Is it oxen that God is concerned about?” (1 Cor. 9:9). Therefore, those are great rams, great oxen.

What about the rest—those who perhaps are conscious of certain sins, who perhaps have fallen along the way itself and are healed through repentance? Will they remain behind and not belong to the burnt offerings?

So that they too may not be afraid, he added the goats: “I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings, with incense and rams; I will offer you oxen with goats.”

The goats are saved by this very association. By themselves they cannot be received; joined to the oxen, they are accepted. For they “made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they might receive them into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

These goats, therefore, will not be on the left, because they made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity. Which goats, then, are on the left? Those to whom it will be said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:42)—not those who redeemed their sins through almsgiving.

### 21. [vers. 16, 17.]

“Come, hear, and I will tell” all who fear God. Let us come and hear what he is going to tell. “Come, hear, and I will tell.” But whom does he mean by “Come and hear”? “All who fear God.” If you do not fear God, I will not tell you. There is no one to whom anything can be told where the fear of God is absent. Let the fear of God open the ears, so that there may be something to enter, and an entrance for what I am going to tell.

But what is he going to tell? “How great things he has done for my soul.” Behold, he wishes to tell; but what is he going to tell? Perhaps how far the earth extends, how widely the heavens are spread, how many stars there are, and what the courses of the sun and moon may be? This creation follows its appointed order; those who investigated it with great curiosity failed to know its Creator (Wis. 13:9).

Hear this; receive this, you who fear God: “How great things he has done for my soul”—and, if you wish, for yours also. [Note: [Col. 0799] Two manuscripts read, “receive this, all who,” etc.] “How great things he has done for my soul. To him I cried with my mouth.” He also declares that this itself was done for his soul: that he should cry to him with his mouth, he says was done for his soul.

Behold, brothers, we were Gentiles, even if not in ourselves, then in our ancestors. [Col. 0800] And what does the Apostle say? “You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led astray, carried away to voiceless idols” (1 Cor. 12:2). Let the Church now say, “How great things he has done for my soul. To him I cried with my mouth.”

I, a human being, was crying out to a stone; I was crying out to deaf wood; I was speaking to deaf and mute images. Now the image of God has turned toward its Creator. I who used to say to the wood, “You are my father,” and to the stone, “You gave me birth” (Jer. 2:27), now say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

“To him I cried with my mouth”—with my own mouth now, not with another’s. When I cried out to stones in the vain way of my ancestral tradition (1 Pet. 1:18), I was crying with another’s mouth. But when I cried out to the Lord—as he himself granted, as he himself inspired—I cried to him with my own mouth, “and exalted him beneath my tongue.”

What does “I cried with my mouth, and exalted him beneath my tongue” mean? I proclaimed him publicly; I confessed him in secret. It is not enough to exalt God with the tongue, but also beneath the tongue, so that what you speak with certainty you may silently ponder.

“To him I cried with my mouth, and exalted him beneath my tongue.” See how he wishes the one who offers a marrow-filled burnt offering to be wholly sound even in secret.

Do this, brothers; imitate this, so that you may say, “Come, hear how great things he has done for my soul.” For everything that he recounts is brought about in our soul by his grace. Consider the other things he says.

### 22. [vers. 18.]

“If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear.” [Note: [Col. 0800] So the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The editions instead read, “he will hear.”]

Consider now, brothers, how easily and how daily people, ashamed before other people, accuse iniquities: “He did evil; he acted ruinously; he is a criminal.” Perhaps he says this because of other people. See whether you do not regard iniquity in your own heart; perhaps what you censure in another you are thinking of doing yourself, and therefore you cry out against him not because he did it, but because he was found out.

Return to yourself; be your own judge within. Behold, in the hidden chamber of your heart, in that innermost vein where you alone are, together with the one who sees, let iniquity become displeasing to you, so that you may be pleasing to God.

Do not look back upon it—that is, do not love it—but rather look down upon it—that is, despise it and turn away from it. Whatever joyful thing it promises in order to entice you to sin, whatever sorrowful thing it threatens in order to drive you to wrongdoing: all of it is nothing; all of it passes away. It is worthy of being despised and trampled underfoot, not regarded so as to be accepted.

[For it sometimes makes suggestions through thoughts, or through the words of wicked people conversing. “Bad company corrupts good character”; do not regard such things (1 Cor. 15:33). But it is not enough merely in one’s expression, nor enough merely on the tongue: do not regard them in your heart—that is, do not love them, do not accept them. For it is common usage to take “regard” in the sense of “love.” First, because we say of God, “He regarded me.” What does “He regarded me” mean? Did he not see you before? Or was he looking upward, and, prompted by your prayers, was he persuaded to turn his eyes toward you? He saw you before as well; but when you say, “He regarded me,” you mean, “He loved me.” And to a person who sees you, when you ask him to have mercy on you, you say, “Regard me.” He sees you, and you say, “Regard me.” What does “Regard me” mean? “Love me, pay attention to me, have mercy on me.”

Therefore he did not say, “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart,” because absolutely no iniquity is ever suggested to the human heart. It is suggested there; the suggestion does not cease; but it must not become regard. For if you regard iniquity, you look backward and incur the sentence spoken by the Lord in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

What, then, should I do? What the Apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13). All the things behind us, which have passed away, are iniquitous. No one comes to Christ from righteousness: “All have sinned; they are justified by believing” (Rom. 3:22). Perfect righteousness will not exist except in that life; nevertheless, even progress and good conduct are inspired and granted by him.

Therefore do not reckon your merits—do not. And if iniquity makes a suggestion, do not consent. For what does he say?] [Note: [Col. 0801] Several numerous and reliable manuscripts lack all the verses enclosed in brackets.]

“If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear.”

### 23. [vers. 19.]

“Therefore God heard me,” because I did not regard iniquity in my heart. “And he attended to the voice of my prayer.”

### 24. [vers. 20.]

“Blessed be my God,” [Note: [Col. 0801] So the better manuscripts. The editions do not add “my” except in the final instance.] “who has not removed my prayer from me, nor his mercy from me.”

He maintains the sense from the place where he says, “Come, hear, and I will tell you, all who fear God, how great things he has done for my soul.” He has said what you have heard, and at the end he concludes in this way: “Blessed be my God, who has not removed my prayer from me, nor his mercy from me.”

For in this way the one who speaks reaches the resurrection, where we already are in hope—or rather, where we already are; and this is our voice. Therefore, as long as we are here, let us ask God not to remove our prayer from us or his mercy from us—that is, that we may pray perseveringly and that he may have mercy perseveringly.

For many grow weak in prayer. At the beginning of their conversion they pray fervently; afterward weakly, then coldly, then carelessly—as though they had become secure. The enemy is awake; are you asleep?

The Lord himself commanded in the Gospel that we ought always to pray and not grow weary. He gives the example of that unjust judge who neither feared God nor respected human beings. A widow appealed to him daily so that he would hear her; and he, who was not moved by mercy, yielded because of her persistence. The wicked judge said to himself: “Although I neither fear God nor respect human beings, nevertheless, because this widow troubles me every day, I will hear her case and vindicate her.” And the Lord said: “If the wicked judge did this, will your Father not vindicate his elect who cry out to him day and night? I tell you, he will vindicate them quickly” (Luke 18:1–8).

Therefore, let us not grow weary in prayer. What he is going to grant, even if he delays, he does not take away. Secure in his promise, let us not grow weary in praying; and even this is itself his gift.

Therefore he said: “Blessed be my God, who has not removed my prayer from me, nor his mercy from me.” When you see that your prayer has not been removed from you, be secure, because his mercy has not been removed from you.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 66. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [vers. 2.]

Your Charity remembers that, in the two psalms already discussed, we exhorted our soul to bless the Lord, and in devout song said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. 102:1; 103:1). If, then, in those psalms we exhorted our soul to bless the Lord, in this psalm it is rightly said: “May God have mercy on us and bless us.” May our soul bless the Lord, and may God bless us.

When God blesses us, we grow; and when we bless the Lord, we grow. Both are beneficial to us. He is not increased by our blessing, nor diminished by our cursing. Whoever curses the Lord is himself diminished; whoever blesses the Lord is himself increased.

The Lord’s blessing comes first in us, and it follows that we also bless the Lord. The former is the rain; the latter is the fruit. Thus the fruit is returned to God, the farmer who waters and cultivates us.

Let us sing these things with devotion—not with barren devotion or an empty voice, but with a true heart. For God the Father is most explicitly called a farmer. The Apostle says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building.” In the visible things of this world, a vineyard is not a building, and a building is not a vineyard. We, however, are the Lord’s vineyard, because he cultivates us for fruit; we are God’s building, because the one who cultivates us dwells in us.

And what does the same Apostle say? “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6–9). He, then, gives the growth.

Are perhaps these men farmers? A farmer is called one who plants and one who waters; yet the Apostle said, “I planted; Apollos watered.” We ask how he himself did this. The Apostle answers: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (ibid. 15:10).

Therefore, wherever you turn—whether through the angels, you will find God to be your farmer; whether through the prophets, he is your farmer; whether through the apostles, recognize that he himself is your farmer.

What, then, are we? Perhaps we are that farmer’s laborers, and even this is through strength imparted by him and grace granted by him. He, therefore, both cultivates and gives the growth.

A human farmer cultivates a vineyard only to the extent that he plows, prunes, and applies the other things belonging to a farmer’s diligence; he cannot make it rain upon his vineyard. If perhaps he can irrigate it, from whom does he have that power? He leads water into a channel, certainly, [Note: [Col. 0802] So Erasmus and several manuscripts. Lovanius reads, “he leads irrigation.”] but God fills the spring.

Finally, in his own vineyard he cannot give growth to the branches, form the fruits, fashion the seeds, or regulate the seasons of production. But God, who can do all things, is our farmer; we are secure.

Perhaps someone says: “You say that God is our farmer; rather, I call the apostles farmers, since they said, ‘I planted.’ ‘Apollos watered.’” If I say it, let no one believe; if Christ says it, woe to the one who does not believe. [Col. 0803]

What, then, does the Lord Christ say? “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer” (John 15:5, 1).

Let the earth, then, thirst and utter the cries of its thirst, since it is written: “My soul is like land without water for you” (Ps. 142:6). Let our earth, then—that is, ourselves—desiring God’s rain, say: “May God have mercy on us and bless us.”

### 2.

“May he illuminate his face upon us.”

Perhaps you were going to ask what “may he bless us” means. People wish to be blessed by God in many ways. One wants to be blessed so as to have a house full of the necessities of this life; another desires to be blessed so as to obtain bodily health without defect; another, if perhaps he is sick, wishes to be blessed so as to recover health; another, desiring children and perhaps saddened that they are not born, wishes to be blessed so as to have descendants.

And who could enumerate the various desires of people wishing to be blessed by the Lord God?

Who among us, moreover, would say that it is not God’s blessing if agriculture bears fruit for him, if someone’s house abounds in temporal goods, or if bodily health is either preserved so that it is not lost or restored after it has been lost? The fruitfulness of women also, and the chaste desires of those who wish for children—who could these belong to except the Lord God?

For the one who created what did not exist is himself the one who, through the succession of offspring, makes what he established endure. God does these things; God grants these things. It is not enough for us to say, “God does these things; God grants these things”; he alone does them, he alone grants them.

What if God does these things, but someone who is not God also does them? He does them, and he alone does them. In vain, then, are these things sought either from human beings or from demons. Whatever good things the enemies of God receive, they receive from him; and when they ask others for them, when they receive them, they receive them unknowingly from him.

Just as, when they are punished and think they are being punished by others, they are punished by him without knowing it, so also when they are invigorated, filled, saved, or delivered—even if in ignorance they attribute this to human beings, demons, or angels—they have it only from him, in whose power all things lie.

We have said these things, brothers, so that whoever desires even these earthly matters—whether for the necessities of life or because of some illness—may desire them from none other than him who is the fountain of all good things, the creator and re-creator of the universe.

### 3.

But there are other gifts that God gives to his enemies, and others that he preserves only for his friends.

What are the gifts he gives to his enemies? Those I have listed. For houses full of necessities do not belong only to the good; nor are only the good safe, or recover from illness; nor do only the good have children, money, and the other things suited to this temporal and passing life.

The wicked have these things as well, and sometimes the good lack them. But the wicked also lack them, and most often these things are more abundant among the wicked than among the good; at other times they abound more among the good than among the wicked.

God wished these temporal things to be distributed among both groups. For if he gave them only to the good, the wicked would think that God should be worshiped for the sake of these things. Conversely, if he gave them only to the wicked, the weak among the good would fear converting lest these things perhaps be lacking to them.

For a soul that is still weak is less capable of the kingdom of God; our farmer, God, must nourish it. Even a tree that now withstands storms with its strength was grass when it first emerged from the earth. That farmer therefore knows not only how to prune and cleanse strong trees, but also how to protect tender ones at their recent emergence.

Therefore, beloved, as I had begun to say, if these things were given only to the good, everyone would wish to convert to God in order to receive them. Conversely, if they were given only to the wicked, the weak would fear that, when they converted, they would lose what only the wicked possessed.

They are given indiscriminately to good and wicked alike. Again, if they were taken away only from the good, the same fear would arise among the weak, lest they convert to God and lose them; conversely, if they were taken away only from the wicked, that removal alone would be regarded as the punishment by which the wicked are chastised.

When he gives these things to the good, he consoles those making the journey; when he gives them also to the wicked, he admonishes the good to desire other things that they do not share with the wicked.

Again, he takes these things away from the good whenever he wishes, so that they may question their own strength and discover—those who perhaps were unaware of themselves—whether they can already say: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

For that soul also blessed the Lord and returned fruit, saturated by the rain of blessing. “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away”: he removed what had been given, but he did not remove the giver.

Every blessed soul is simple: it does not cling to earthly things, nor lie with its wings entangled in birdlime; Rather, with the brightness of its virtues spread out, it rejoices on the twin wings of twin love in the free air. It sees that what has been taken away from it was what it had trodden underfoot, not what it had rested upon; and it says confidently: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

He gave and took away; the one who gave remains, while what he gave has been taken away. Blessed be his name.

For this reason, then, these things are taken away from the good. But lest some weak person perhaps say, “When can I possess such strength as the holy Job?”—you marvel at the tree’s strength because you have only just been born. [Note: [Col. 0804] So the manuscripts, except that one has “you have only just been born” in the masculine. The editions read, “which has only just been born.”] This great tree that you marvel at, beneath whose branches and shade you find refreshment, was once a shoot. [Note: [Col. 0804] The manuscripts read, “you give refreshment.”]

But are you afraid that these things will be taken away from you when you have become such a tree? Observe that they are taken away from the wicked as well. Why, then, do you delay your conversion? What you, as a good person, fear losing, you may perhaps lose as a wicked person.

If you lose these things as a good person, the comforter who took them away is present. The chest is emptied of gold, but the heart is full of faith. Outwardly you are poor, but inwardly you are rich. You carry with you riches that you would not lose even if you emerged naked from a shipwreck.

If, then, you are perhaps going to lose these things as a wicked person, why should the loss not find you good, since you see that the wicked also suffer loss?

But they are struck by a greater loss: the house is empty, and the conscience is emptier. Whoever is wicked and has lost these things has nothing outside to hold on to, and nothing within in which to rest.

He flees from the place where he suffered loss, where he used to display himself before people’s eyes by flaunting his wealth; now he cannot display himself before people’s eyes. He does not return inward to himself, because he has nothing. He did not imitate the ant; he did not gather grain for himself while it was summer (Prov. 6:6; 30:25).

What did I say—“while it was summer”? When life was tranquil, when this world’s prosperity toward him prevailed, when he had leisure, when everyone called him fortunate—that was his summer.

He should have imitated the ant if he had listened to the word of God; he should have gathered grain and stored it within. The trial of tribulation came; the winter of torpor [Note: [Col. 0805] The word “of torpor” is absent from the manuscripts.] overtook him; the storm of fear, the chill of sorrow—whether there was loss, some danger to his health, the bereavement of someone dear, or some dishonor and humiliation—it was winter.

The ant returns to what it gathered in summer; and in its inner secrecy, where no one sees, it is refreshed by its summer labors. When it gathered these things for itself in summer, everyone saw; when it feeds on them in winter, no one sees.

What does this mean? Behold God’s ant. Every day it rises, runs to God’s church, prays, listens to the reading, sings a hymn, chews over what it has heard, reflects upon it within itself, and stores inside the grains gathered from the threshing floor.

Those who prudently listen to what is now being said do precisely this. They are seen by everyone going to church, returning from church, listening to the sermon, listening to the reading, finding a book, opening it, and reading. All these things are visible while they are being done.

That ant is crushing the path, carrying and storing things in the sight of those who observe. Winter comes sometime—for whom does it not come? Loss occurs; bereavement occurs. Others perhaps pity the person as miserable, not knowing what the ant has within itself to eat, and say, “Unhappy is the one to whom this has happened,” or “Unhappy is the one to whom that has happened. What do you think is going on in his mind? How devastated he is!”

They measure him by themselves; they sympathize according to their own strength, and therefore they are deceived, because they want to apply the measure by which they measure themselves to one whom they do not know.

You see him suffering loss, or humiliated, or struck by bereavement. What do you think? “This man must have done something evil for this to happen to him.” May my enemies have such a heart, such a mind!

You do not know, human being. Truly, you are your own enemy, because during summer you do not gather for yourself what this person gathered. Now, within, the ant is eating the labors of summer; you could see it gathering, but you cannot see it eating.

These things, brothers, insofar as the Lord has granted, insofar as he has deigned to suggest and instill into our weakness and humility, insofar as we comprehend according to our measure—we have explained why God gives all these things indiscriminately to good and wicked alike, and why he takes them away from both good and wicked.

He gave them to you; do not become proud. He took them from you; do not be broken. You fear that he may take them away; he can take them away from the good and from the wicked. It is better, then, that as a good person you lose what belongs to God, but retain God.

So we also exhort that wicked person: “You are going to suffer loss.” Who will not suffer bereavement? Some misfortune will burst upon you; some calamity will come from across your path. The world is full of examples from every direction; they do not cease.

I am speaking to you in summer. There is no lack of grain for you to gather. “Pay attention to the ant, you sluggard” (Prov. 6:6; 30:25); gather in summer while you can. Winter will not allow you to gather, but only to eat what you have gathered.

For how many suffer tribulation in such a way that they have no time either to read or to hear anything, and perhaps are not even admitted to those who might console them? The ant has remained in its cave; let it see whether it gathered anything in summer with which to occupy itself in winter.

### 4.

But now, since God will bless us, why will he bless us? What blessing does this voice ask for when it says, “May God bless us”?

It asks for the blessing that he preserves for his friends, which he gives only to the good. Do not desire as something great what the wicked also receive. For God is good; he does these things, making his sun rise upon good and evil and raining upon the just and unjust (Matt. 5:45).

What, then, does he give especially to the good? What especially to the just? “May he illuminate his face upon us.”

You illuminate the face of this sun upon good and evil; illuminate your face upon us. Both good and evil see this light together with the animals. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid. 5:8).

“May he illuminate his face upon us.” There is a twofold interpretation; both must be stated.

“Illuminate,” he says, “your face upon us”; show us your face. For God does not at some time illuminate your face, as though at some time he had been without light. Rather, “illuminate it upon us” means that what was hidden from us may be disclosed to us, and that what existed but was hidden from us may be revealed upon us—that is, illuminated.

Or certainly, illuminate your image upon us. In saying, “Illuminate your face upon us,” he may have meant: You impressed your face upon us; you made us according to your image and likeness (Gen. 1:26); you made us your coin. But your image ought not to remain in darkness. Send forth the ray of your wisdom; let it drive away our darkness, and let your image shine in us. Let us recognize that we are your image, and let us hear what is said in the Song of Songs: “Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women” (Song 1:7).

For it is said to the Church: “Unless you know yourself.” What does this mean? Unless you know that you were made according to the image of God.

O precious soul of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0806] Erasmus and two or three manuscripts read “precious” in the feminine form.] redeemed by the blood of the immaculate Lamb, consider how valuable you are; think about what was given for you.

Let us say, then, and let us desire: “May he illuminate his face upon us.” We bear his face. Just as the faces of emperors are spoken of, so truly there is a certain sacred face of God in his image. But the wicked do not recognize the image of God in themselves.

What should they say so that God’s face may be illuminated upon them? “You will illuminate my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will illuminate my darkness” (Ps. 17:29).

I am in the darkness of sins, but let my darkness be dispersed by the ray of your wisdom. Let your face appear; and if perhaps, through me, it has become somewhat disfigured, let what you formed be reformed by you.

“May he therefore illuminate his face upon us.”

### 5. [vers. 3.]

“So that we may know your way on earth.”

On earth—here, in this life—let us know your way. What is “your way”? The way that leads to you. Let us recognize where we should go; let us recognize by what way we should go. We cannot do both in darkness.

You are far from those making the pilgrimage, but you have extended to us a way by which we must return to you: “Let us know your way on earth.”

What is his way, since this is what we have desired—that we may know his way on earth? We will seek it, not learn it from ourselves. We can learn it from the Gospel: “I am the way,” the Lord says. Christ said, “I am the way.”

But are you afraid that you may go astray? He added, “and the truth.” Who goes astray in the truth? He goes astray who has departed from the truth. Christ is the truth; Christ is the way. Walk.

Are you afraid that you may die before you arrive? “I am the life.” “I am,” he says, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). It is as if he were saying: “What are you afraid of? You walk through me, you walk in me, you rest in me.”

What, then, does “Let us know your way on earth” mean except “Let us know your Christ on earth”?

But let the psalm itself answer, lest you think that testimony must be brought from other Scriptures because it is perhaps absent here. By repeating, it shows what he has said: “So that we may know your way on earth.” As though you were asking, “On what earth? Which way?”—“Among all nations is your salvation.”

On what earth are you asking? Listen: “Among all nations.” Which way are you asking for? Listen: “Your salvation.”

Or perhaps Christ is not his salvation? And what is it that the old man Simeon said—that old man, I say, preserved in the Gospel through his many years until the infancy of the Word? For that old man received the infant Word of God in his hands. Would the one who deigned to be in a virgin’s womb disdain to be in an old man’s hands?

He who was in the virgin’s womb was in the old man’s hands: a weak infant both within the womb and in the old man’s hands, to give us strength—he through whom all things were made; and if all things, then the mother herself as well. He came in humility; he came in weakness, but clothed in a weakness destined to be changed. For although he was crucified through weakness, he lives through the power of God (2 Cor. 13:4), as the Apostle says.

He was therefore in the old man’s hands. And what did that old man say? What did he say, rejoicing that he was now to be released from this life, seeing that the one by whom and in whom his salvation was contained was held in his own hands?

“Now you dismiss,” he said, “your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

Therefore: “May God bless us and have mercy on us; may he illuminate his face upon us, so that we may know your way on earth.” On what earth? “Among all nations.” Which way? “Your salvation.”

### 6. [vers. 4.]

What follows, since God’s way is known on earth and God’s salvation is known among all nations? “Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you,” he says.

A heretic appears and says, “I have peoples in Africa.” Another, from another region, says, “And I have peoples in Galatia.” You in Africa, he in Galatia—but I seek the one who has them everywhere.

Certainly you dared to rejoice at this voice, because you heard, “Let the peoples praise you, O God.” Hear the following verse, because it does not speak of a part: “Let all the peoples praise you.”

Walk on the way with all nations; walk on the way with all peoples, O children of peace, children of the one Catholic Church. Walk on the way; sing as you walk. Travelers do this for the relief of their labor.

Sing on this way; I beg you by the way itself, sing on this way. Sing a new song; let no one sing old songs there. Sing the songs of love for your homeland; let no one sing old songs. [Col. 0808] A new way, a new traveler, a new song.

Hear the Apostle exhorting you to a new song: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (2 Cor. 5:17).

Sing a new song on the way that you have come to know on earth. On what earth? “Among all nations.” Therefore the new song also does not belong to a part. Whoever sings in a faction sings an old song. Whatever he sings, he sings an old song; the old person sings; he is divided; he is carnal.

Certainly, insofar as he is carnal, he is old, and insofar as he is spiritual, he is new. See what the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal.” How does he prove them carnal? “When one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I belong to Apollos,’ are you not carnal?” (1 Cor. 3:1, 4).

Therefore sing a new song in the spirit, on the safe way. Travelers sing, and often they sing at night. Everything around them is frightening—or rather, not noisy but silent; and the more silent it is, the more frightening it is. Yet those who fear robbers still sing.

How much more safely do you sing in Christ! This way has no robber, provided that by abandoning the way you do not fall in with a robber.

Sing, I say, confidently, a new song on the way that you have come to know on earth—that is, among all nations. See that the one who chose to remain in a faction does not sing the new song with you.

“Sing to the Lord a new song,” he says, and he continues: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1).

“Let the peoples praise you, O God.” They have found your way; let them praise you. That singing itself is confession: confession of your sins and confession of God’s power. Confess your iniquity; confess God’s grace. Accuse yourself; glorify him. Rebuke yourself; praise him—so that, when he comes, he may find you as your own punisher and show himself to you as your savior.

What are you afraid to confess, since you have found this way among all nations? What are you afraid to confess and, in your confession, sing a new song with all the earth, throughout all the earth, in Catholic peace?

Are you afraid to confess to God lest he condemn you after you have confessed? If you hide without confessing, you will be condemned when you are confessed (i.e. exposed). [Note: [Col. 0808] The editions read, “if you do not confess, you will be condemned.” Delete “not,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]

You are afraid to confess, although by not confessing you cannot remain hidden. You will be condemned in silence, though by confessing you could be freed.

“Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you.”

### 7. [verse 8]

And because this confession does not lead to punishment, he continues and says: “Let the nations rejoice and exult.” If thieves weep after confessing before a human being, let the faithful rejoice after confessing before God. If a human being is the judge, the executioner and fear demand a confession from the thief; indeed, sometimes fear suppresses a confession, while pain exacts it. The man who weeps under torture, yet fears being killed after confessing, endures the torments as long as he can; and if pain conquers him, he utters his voice unto death.
