Nowhere, therefore, is he joyful, nowhere exultant: before he confesses, the claw tears him; after he has confessed, the executioner leads him away condemned: wretched everywhere.

[Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The editions read: “The executioner condemns him; the wretched man is led away everywhere.”]

“But let the nations rejoice and exult.” Why? Through that very confession. Why? Because the one to whom they confess is good: he demands confession for this purpose, that he may set the humble free; he condemns the one who does not confess for this purpose, that he may punish the proud. Therefore, be sad before you confess; after confessing, exult—you will already be healed.

Your conscience had gathered suppuration; the abscess had swollen and tormented you, allowing you no rest. The physician applies the soothing remedies of words, and at times he cuts; he applies the medicinal iron of corrective affliction. Recognize the physician’s hand; confess, and let all the suppuration come out and drain away in confession. Now exult, now rejoice; what remains will easily be healed.

“Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you.” And because they confess, “let the nations rejoice and exult,” because “you judge the peoples with equity.” No one deceives you: let the one who feared the judge rejoice, since he has feared the one who will judge. For he “[smiled beforehand; reading uncertain] and anticipated his face in confession” (Psalm 94:2); but when he comes, “he will judge the peoples with equity.”

What will the accuser’s cunning avail there, where conscience is the witness, where you will be present together with your case, where the judge does not seek a witness? He has sent you an advocate: on his account and through him, confess; plead your case. He is the defender of the penitent, the petitioner for pardon on behalf of the one who confesses, and the judge of the innocent. Can you truly fear your case, when your advocate will be your judge?

Let the nations, then, rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity. But they may fear that they will be judged badly. Let them submit themselves to correction and let themselves be directed by him who sees that they will be judged. Let them be corrected here, and not fear when they are judged.

See what he says in another psalm: “O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength” (Psalm 53:3). What does he say? If you do not first save me by your name, I ought to fear when you judge me by your strength. But if you first save me by your name, what shall I fear from the one judging by his strength, whose salvation has gone before me in his name?

So also here: “Let all the peoples confess to you.” And lest you think that anything in confession should be feared, he says: “Let the nations rejoice and exult.” Why should they rejoice and exult? “Because you judge the peoples with equity.” No one offers you a bribe against us, no one corrupts you, no one deceives you. Therefore, be secure.

But what of your case? It is clear that no one corrupts God. Perhaps, then, he should be feared all the more because he cannot be corrupted in any way. How, then, are you secure? According to what has already been said: “O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your strength.” So also here: “Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity.”

And lest the unrighteous be afraid, he added: “And you direct the nations upon the earth.”

[Note: Most manuscripts read *diriges*, “you will direct,” in the future tense, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint.]

The nations were crooked, the nations were twisted, the nations were perverse. Because of their crookedness, twisting, and perversity, they rightly feared the judge who was coming. His hand came; it was mercifully extended over the peoples. They are directed so that they may walk along the straight way. Why should they fear the coming judge, when they have first recognized the one who corrects them?

[Note: A few manuscripts read “the coming guide and judge”; perhaps this stands in place of “the judge of the upright.”]

Let them place themselves in his hands; he himself directs the nations upon the earth. Once directed, the nations walk in faith, exulting in him and doing good works. And if, since they are sailing across the sea, some water should enter through the tiniest openings and cracks into the bilge, they must drain it out through good works, lest, entering in greater quantity, it accumulate and sink the ship. Let them drain it out daily by fasting, praying, giving alms, and saying with a pure heart: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

By saying these things, walk securely and exult on the way; sing on the way. Do not fear the judge. Before you were faithful, you found a savior. Though you were impious, he sought you in order to redeem you; once redeemed, will he abandon you in order to destroy you? “And you direct the nations upon the earth.”

### 8. [verses 6–7]

He exults, rejoices, encourages, and repeats the same verses in exhortation: “Let the peoples confess to you, O God; let all the peoples confess to you: the earth has yielded its fruit.”

What fruit? “Let all the peoples confess to you.” The earth existed; it was full of thorns. The hand of the one who uproots them approached; the call of his majesty and mercy approached. The earth began to confess; now the earth yields its fruit.

Would it yield its fruit unless it were first drenched? Would the earth yield its fruit unless God’s mercy first came down from above? “Let them read to me,” you say, “that the drenched earth has yielded its fruit.”

Hear the Lord as he drenches it: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2). He rains, and that rain itself is thunder; it terrifies. Fear the one who thunders, and receive the one who rains.

Behold, after that voice of the thundering and raining God, let us look at something from the Gospel itself. Behold that sinful woman, notorious in the city. She burst into another person’s house, where she had not been invited by the host but had been summoned by the one who had been invited—not by the tongue, but by grace. In her sickness, she knew that she had a place there where she knew her physician was reclining.

She entered as a sinful woman; she does not dare approach except to his feet. She weeps at his feet, wets them with her tears, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them with ointment (Luke 7:37–38). Why are you surprised? “The earth has yielded its fruit.”

This, then, took place because the Lord was raining there through his mouth. The things we read in the Gospel came to pass. When he rained through his clouds—that is, through the Apostles sent out to preach the truth—the earth yielded its fruit even more abundantly; and this harvest has now filled the whole world.

### 9. [verse 8]

See what is said next: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.” May he bless us—as I have already said—may he bless us again and again, multiplying us through his blessing.

Let Your Charity observe that the fruit of the earth has already appeared in Jerusalem. For the Church began there. The Holy Spirit came there and filled the holy ones gathered together as one; miracles occurred, and they spoke in the languages of all peoples (Acts 2:1–4).

They were filled with the Spirit of God. Those who were there were converted; fearing and receiving the divine rain, they yielded such abundant fruit in confession that they brought all their possessions together, distributing them to the poor. No one called anything his own; rather, everything was held in common, and they had one soul and one heart toward God (Acts 4:32).

For the blood of the Lord which they had shed had been forgiven them; it had been forgiven through the Lord’s pardon, so that they might now learn even to drink what they had shed. Great was the fruit there: the earth yielded its fruit, a great fruit, an excellent fruit.

Was that earth alone supposed to yield its fruit? “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.” May he still bless us, for blessing is usually and properly understood as multiplication.

Let us prove this from Genesis. Observe the works of God. God made the light and divided the light from the darkness; he called the light “day” and the darkness “night.” It is not said, “He blessed the light,” for the same light returns and alternates through days and nights.

He called the firmament between the waters “heaven”; it is not said, “He blessed heaven.” He separated the sea from the dry land and named each: the dry land “earth,” and the gathering of waters “sea.” Here too it is not said, “God blessed.”

Then he came to those things that were to possess the seed of fertility and that were to come forth from the waters. These have the greatest abundance of multiplication, and the Lord blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.” Likewise, when he subjected all things to the human being whom he had made in his image, it is written: “And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the face of the earth” (Genesis 1).

Therefore, blessing properly signifies multiplication and the filling of the face of the earth. Hear it also in this psalm: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.” And to what end does this blessing serve? “And let all the ends of the earth fear him.”

Therefore, my brothers, God has blessed us abundantly in the name of Christ, so that he may fill the whole face of the earth with his sons, adopted into his kingdom as co-heirs with his Only-Begotten Son. He begot one, and did not wish him to remain alone. He begot one, I say, and did not wish him to remain one. He made brothers for him; though not by begetting, he made them his co-heirs by adoption. He first made him share in our mortality, so that we might believe that we could become participants in his divinity.

### 10.

Let us consider our price. Everything foretold has come to pass; everything is being displayed. The Gospel is going throughout the world. The whole labor of the human race in this present age bears witness to this; everything foretold in the Scriptures is being fulfilled.

Just as everything has happened up to the present day, so also what remains will happen. Let us fear the day of judgment; the Lord will come. He who came in humility will come in exaltation; he who came to be judged will come to judge. Let us recognize him in humility, so that we may not dread him in exaltation; let us embrace him in humility, so that we may desire him in exaltation. For he will come mercifully to those who desire him.

Those desire him who have kept his faith and done his commandments. For whether we wish it or not, he will come. Let us therefore wish that he may come—the one who will come even if we do not wish it.

How shall we wish him to come? By living well and acting well. Let past things not delight us; let present things not hold us captive. Let us not close our ear as though against a tail; let us not press our ear into the earth.

[Note: See *Expositions on the Psalms* 57, no. 7.]

Let us not be held back by past things from hearing; let us not be entangled in present things so as to be prevented from meditating on the future.

[Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The editions read: “Let us not be held back from obeying, nor be entangled in present things, but meditate on future things,” and so forth.]

Let us stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead and forget what is past (Philippians 3:13). And what we now labor over, what we now groan over, what we now sigh for, what we now speak of, what we now perceive in however small a part yet cannot comprehend—we shall comprehend and enjoy fully in the resurrection of the righteous.

“Our youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 102:5); only let us crush our old age against the rock, Christ (Psalm 136:9; 1 Corinthians 10:4).

Whether what is said about the serpent or what is said about the eagle is true, brothers, or whether it is rather human report than truth, the truth is nevertheless present in the Scriptures, and the Scriptures did not say this without reason. Let us do whatever that image signifies, and not trouble ourselves over whether the thing itself is true.

Be such that your youth may be renewed like the eagle’s. And know that it cannot be renewed unless your old age has been crushed against the rock; that is, unless by the help of the rock, by the help of Christ, you will not be able to be renewed.

Do not become deaf, through the sweetness of your former life, to the word of God. Do not cling so tightly to and become so hindered by present affairs that you say, “I have no time to read; I have no time to listen.” This is to press the ear into the earth.

Do not be such a person; rather, be such as you find described to the contrary: forget what is past, stretch yourself toward what lies ahead, and crush your old age against the rock.

And if certain comparisons are given to you, if you find them in the Scriptures, believe them. If you find that they are mentioned only as popular report, do not believe them too strongly. The matter may be so, or it may not be so. Make progress; let that comparison benefit you unto salvation.

If you do not wish to do so through this comparison, do it through another—provided that you do it. Then await the kingdom of God securely, lest your prayer quarrel with you.

For you, Christian, when you say, “Let your kingdom come,” how do you say, “Let your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10)? Examine your heart; look: “Let your kingdom come.” It cries out to you, “I am coming.” Are you not afraid?

We have often said to Your Charity: preaching the truth is nothing if the heart disagrees with the tongue; and hearing the truth is nothing if the fruit of hearing does not follow.

We speak to you from this place, as though from a loftier position. But how much we are in fear beneath your feet, God knows—the God who is gracious to the humble. For it is not so much the voices of those who praise us that delight us as the devotion of those who confess and the deeds of those who live rightly.

And how we delight only in your progress, yet how much we endanger ourselves through these praises—let him know who delivers us from every danger and deigns to recognize and crown us, together with you, as saved from every temptation in his kingdom.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 67

[Note: Dictated in the year of Christ 415, according to Letter 169 to Evodius, no. 1.]

### 1. [verse 1]

The title of this psalm does not seem to require elaborate discussion, for it appears simple and clear. It reads: “For the end; to David himself; a psalm of a song.”

In many psalms we have already explained what “for the end” means, since “Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4)—the end that brings to perfection, not the end that consumes or destroys.

Nevertheless, if anyone should try to investigate what is meant by “a psalm of a song”—why it is not either “a psalm” or “a song,” but both; or what difference there is between “a psalm of a song” and “a song of a psalm,” since the titles of certain psalms are also written in the latter form—he may perhaps discover something that we leave to those who are sharper and have more leisure.

Some before us distinguished between a song and a psalm.

[Note: Hilary, in the Prologue to the Psalms.]

Since a song is uttered by the mouth, whereas a psalm is sung with a visible instrument, namely, the psaltery, they held that “song” signifies the understanding of the mind, while “psalm” signifies the works of the body.

Thus, in this very Psalm 67, which we have now undertaken to expound, some have distinguished the words “Sing to God; play to his name” in such a way that “Sing to God” refers to the things the mind does within itself, which are known to God but not seen by human beings. Good works, however, are to be seen by human beings so that they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16); hence “play to his name,” that is, to his reputation, so that he may be named laudably.

As far as I recall, I myself once followed this distinction somewhere. Yet I remember that we have also read, “Play to God” (Psalm 46:7–8), because the things we visibly do well please not only human beings but also God. Not everything that pleases God, however, can please human beings, since they cannot see it.

Therefore, it is surprising if, just as both “Sing to God” and “Play to God” are read, “Sing to his name” can be read somewhere as well. If this too is found said in the holy Scriptures, this distinction has been worked out in vain.

I am also moved by the fact that, in general usage, the books are called “Psalms” rather than “Songs,” so that the Lord said: “The things written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44); and the book itself is called the Book of Psalms, not of Songs: “As it is written,” he says, “in the Book of Psalms” (Acts 1:20).

Yet according to this distinction they ought rather to have been called “Songs,” since a song can exist without a psalm, whereas a psalm cannot exist without a song. For there can be thoughts of the mind without bodily works; but there is no good work whose thought is not present in the mind.

Thus, in both cases there are songs, but not in both cases psalms. Nevertheless, as I said, they are generally called Psalms, not Songs; and the book is called the Book of Psalms, not of Songs.

And if the meanings of the words are understood and examined—where the title is simply “Psalm,” where it is simply “Song,” and where it is not “Psalm of a Song,” as here, but “Song of a Psalm”—I do not know whether this distinction can be demonstrated.

Therefore, as we had begun, leaving these matters to those who can and have the leisure to distinguish such things and define them according to a reliable principle, let us consider and expound the text of this psalm as far as the Lord enables us.

### 2. [verse 2]

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered.”

This has already happened. Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever, has arisen (Romans 9:5), and his enemies, the Jews, have been scattered among all nations. In the very place where they practiced their hostility, they have been defeated and from there scattered everywhere.

Even now they hate, but they fear; and in that very fear they do what follows: “Let those who hate him flee from his face.”

The flight of the soul is fear. For in bodily flight, where could they flee from his face, since he demonstrates everywhere the effect of his presence? “Where shall I go,” says one, “from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Psalm 138:7).

They flee in soul, then, not in body; by fearing, not by hiding. They flee not from a face they do not see, but from one they are compelled to see. His face is called his presence through his Church.

Hence, when they were hostile to him, he said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds” (Matthew 26:64). He comes in his Church, spreading it throughout the whole world, in which his enemies have been scattered.

He comes in such clouds as those of which he says: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6). “Let those who hate him flee from his face”: let them fear the presence of his holy and faithful people, of whom he says: “Whatever you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matthew 25:40).

### 3. [verse 3]

“As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish.”

They raised themselves from the fires of their hatred into the pride of arrogance. They set their mouths in heaven (Psalm 72:9), crying, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19:6); they mocked him after he had been seized and ridiculed him as he hung. From the very thing that made them swell with the appearance of victory, they soon vanished as the defeated.

“As wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God.”

Perhaps in this passage he signified those whose hardness is dissolved into tears of repentance. Yet it can also be understood as threatening future judgment: when in this world they have vanished by raising themselves like smoke—that is, by becoming proud—then at the end the final condemnation will come upon them, so that they may perish eternally from his face, when he is manifested in his glory, like fire, for the punishment of the ungodly and the light of the righteous.

### 4. [verse 4]

Finally, what follows is: “And let the righteous rejoice, and exult in the sight of God, and delight in gladness.”

Then they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:34). Let those who have labored rejoice, then, and exult in the sight of God.

Their exultation will not be like an empty boast before human beings, but will take place in the sight of the one who sees without error what he has given. “Let them delight in gladness”—no longer exulting with trembling (Psalm 2:11), as in this world, as long as “human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1).

### 5. [verses 5–6]

Then he turns to those to whom he has given such great hope, addressing and encouraging them while they live here: “Sing to God; play to his name.”

At the beginning, in explaining the title, we have already said what seemed necessary. He sings to God who lives for God; he plays to his name who works for his glory.

“Make a way for him,” he says, by singing and playing—that is, by living and acting in this way—“for the one who ascends above the setting.”

Make a way for Christ, so that through the beautiful feet of those who evangelize (Isaiah 52:7), the hearts of believers may be made passable for him.

For he is the one who “ascends above the setting”—either because the new life of one who turns to him does not receive him unless the old life of one who renounces this world has first died; or because he ascends above the setting when, by rising again, he conquers the falling of the body.

For “Lord” is his name. If they had known this, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8).

### 6.

“Exult in his sight.”

O you to whom it was said, “Sing to God; play to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the setting,” exult also in his sight, “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10).

While you make a way for him, while you prepare the path by which he may come and possess the nations, you will suffer much sorrow in the sight of human beings. But do not lose heart; exult also—not in the sight of human beings, but in the sight of God. “Rejoicing in hope, enduring in tribulation” (Romans 12:12).

“Exult in his sight.” For those who trouble you in the sight of human beings “will be troubled by his face,” the face of “the father of orphans and the judge of widows.”

They think those people deserted whom the sword of God’s word often separates from parents, and parents from children, and husbands from wives (Matthew 10:34–35). But the abandoned and widowed possess the consolation of the father of orphans and judge of widows.

They have the consolation of him to whom they say: “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Psalm 26:10). They have the consolation of those who have hoped in the Lord, persisting in prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5).

Those who trouble them will be troubled by his face when they see that they accomplish nothing, because “the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19).

### 7. [verse 7]

For from these orphans and widows—that is, from those deprived of the fellowship of worldly hope—the Lord builds a temple for himself. Concerning this he says next: “The Lord, in his holy place.”

He disclosed what his place is when he said: “God who makes those of one kind dwell in a house”—those who are of one mind and feel as one. This is the holy place of the Lord.

When he had said, “The Lord in his holy place,” we might ask in what place this is, since he is wholly everywhere and no place belonging to bodily space contains him. Immediately he added the answer, so that we should not seek him outside ourselves, but rather, by dwelling as those of one kind in a house, deserve that he himself also deign to dwell in us.

This is the holy place of the Lord—the place that many people seek so that they may have somewhere in which they will be heard when they pray. Let them themselves be what they seek. Let what they say in their hearts—that is, in such chambers of theirs—pierce them (Psalm 4:5). Let them dwell as those of one kind in a house, so that they may be inhabited by the Lord of the great house and may be heard within themselves.

For there is a great house in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also vessels of wood and clay; some are for honor, others for dishonor. If anyone cleanses himself from vessels of dishonor (2 Timothy 2:20), they will be those of one kind in the house and the holy place of the Lord.

Just as in a great human household its master does not rest in any place whatsoever within it, but in some more private and honorable place, so God does not dwell in everyone who is in his house—for he does not dwell in vessels of dishonor. His holy place consists of those whom he makes to dwell as people of one kind, or of one character, in the house.

For the Greek word *τρόποι* (*tropoi*) can be translated into Latin both as “ways” (*modi*) and as “characters” (*mores*). Nor does the Greek have “who makes them dwell,” but simply “makes dwell.”

“The Lord, then, is in his holy place.” What is this place? God himself makes it for himself. For God makes those of one character dwell in a house; this is his holy place.

### 8.

That he builds this place for himself by his grace, not on the basis of preceding merits in those from whom he builds it, see what follows: “He brings out the fettered in strength.”

For he loosens the heavy bonds of sins that prevented them from walking in the way of the commandments. He brings them out in the strength they did not possess before his grace.

Likewise, he brings out “those who are embittered, who dwell in tombs”—that is, those who are dead in every respect, occupied with dead works. They are embittered by resisting righteousness.

The fettered may perhaps wish to walk but be unable to do so; and they pray to God that they may be able, saying to him: “Bring me out of my necessities” (Psalm 24:17). When they are heard by him, they give thanks, saying: “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 115:17).

But those who are embittered and dwell in tombs belong to the class of which Scripture says elsewhere: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sirach 17:26). Hence the saying: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

It is one thing to desire; another to attack righteousness. It is one thing to wish to be freed from evil; another to defend one’s evils rather than confess them. Yet Christ’s grace brings both kinds out in strength.

In what strength, unless that they may fight against sin even to the shedding of blood? From both kinds are made those fit to become his holy place: the one group loosened, the other raised from the dead.

For by commanding, he loosed the bonds of the woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years (Luke 13:16), and by crying out overcame Lazarus’s death (John 11:43–44).

He who did these things in bodies can do more wonderful things in character and make those of one character dwell in a house: “bringing out the fettered in strength, likewise those who are embittered and dwell in tombs.”

### 9. [verses 8–10]

“O God, when you went out before your people.”

His going out is understood to occur when he appears in his works. He does not appear to everyone, but to those who know how to observe his works.

I am not now speaking of those works that are visible to everyone—heaven, earth, and sea, and everything that is in them—but of the works by which he brings out the fettered in strength, likewise those who are embittered and dwell in tombs, and makes them dwell as people of one character in a house.

Thus he goes out before his people, that is, before those who understand this grace of his. Hence what follows: “When you passed through the desert, the earth was shaken.”

The Gentiles were a desert, for they did not know God. It was a desert where no law had been given by God himself, where no prophets had dwelt and foretold that the Lord would come.

Therefore, when you passed through the desert, when you were preached among the Gentiles, “the earth was shaken”: earthly people were aroused to faith.

But from what was it shaken? “For the heavens distilled from the face of God.”

Perhaps someone here recalls the time when God passed through the desert before his people, before the children of Israel—by day in a pillar of cloud, by night in the brightness of fire (Exodus 13:21)—and understands “the heavens distilled from the face of God” to mean that manna rained upon his people (Exodus 16:13).

He may also understand what follows—“Mount Sinai, from the face of the God of Israel, separating the voluntary rain, God, for your inheritance”—to mean that God spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai when he gave the Law (Exodus 19:18 and following).

Thus manna would be the voluntary rain that God separated for his inheritance, that is, for his people, because he fed them in this way alone, and not the other nations. And when he then says, “And it was weakened,” the inheritance itself may be understood to have been weakened, because, grumbling and disgusted with manna, they rejected it, desiring meat and the foods they had been accustomed to eat in Egypt (Numbers 11:5–6).

But if, in these words, only the literal meaning is sought and no spiritual understanding, it must be shown, according to the bodily meaning, who at that time were the fettered and who were brought out in strength as those dwelling in tombs.

Moreover, if that people—that inheritance of God—was weakened by rejecting manna in disgust, it ought not to have followed: “But you perfected it”; rather, “But you struck it.” For after God was offended by those murmurings and that disgust, a great plague followed (Numbers 11:33).

Finally, they all fell in the wilderness, and none of them, except two, deserved to enter the promised land (Numbers 14:29–30).

Even if that inheritance is said to have been perfected in their children, we must hold more freely to the spiritual meaning. For all those things happened to them symbolically (1 Corinthians 10:11), until the day dawned and the shadows were removed (Song of Songs 2:17).

### 10.

Let the Lord, then, open to us as we knock, and let the secrets of his mysteries be disclosed to us insofar as he himself deigns.

For, so that the earth might be shaken to faith when the Gospel passed into the desert of the Gentiles, “the heavens distilled from the face of God.” These are the heavens of which another psalm sings: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

A little later in that psalm it says of them: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:2–5).

Yet such glory must not be attributed to these heavens as though grace had come from human beings into the desert of the Gentiles, so that the earth might be moved to faith. For the heavens did not distill from themselves, but “from the face of God”—that is, of the one who dwells in them and makes them dwell as people of one character in a house.

They are also the mountains of which it is said: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains; from there will my help come.” Yet, lest he appear to have placed his hope in human beings, he immediately added: “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 120:1–2).

To him it is said elsewhere: “You illuminate wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Psalm 75:5). Although it is “from the eternal mountains,” nevertheless, it is you who illuminate.

So here also: “The heavens distilled,” but “from the face of God.” For they too were saved through faith, and this was not from themselves; it is God’s gift, “not from works, lest anyone should boast.” For “we are his workmanship” (Ephesians 2:8–10), the one who makes those of one character dwell in a house.

### 11.

But what is meant by what follows: “Mount Sinai, from the face of the God of Israel”? Should “distilled” be understood here as implied, so that what he wished to be understood by the name “heavens” he also wished to be understood by the name “Mount Sinai,” just as we said that those called heavens are called mountains?

Nor should it disturb us in this interpretation that he says “mount,” not “mountains,” when in the earlier passage he said “heavens,” not “heaven.” For in another psalm, after it had said, “The heavens declare the glory of God,” Scripture, in its custom of repeating the same meaning in different words, goes on to say: “And the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.”

First it said “heavens,” not “heaven,” yet afterward it did not say “firmaments,” but “firmament.” For God called the firmament “heaven,” as it is written in Genesis (Genesis 1:8).

Thus “heavens” and “heaven,” “mountains” and “mount,” mean not something different but the same thing—just as many churches and one Church mean not something different but the same thing.

Why, then, is Mount Sinai said to “generate into slavery,” as the Apostle says (Galatians 4:24)? Perhaps the Law itself is to be understood as Mount Sinai, which the heavens distilled from the face of God so that the earth might be shaken. And is this the shaking of the earth, when people are disturbed because they cannot fulfill the Law?

If this is so, this too is the voluntary rain of which he says next: “God, separating the voluntary rain for your inheritance,” because he did not do this for any other nation and did not reveal his judgments to them (Psalm 147:20).

God therefore separated this voluntary rain for his inheritance when he gave the Law. “And it was weakened”—either the Law itself or the inheritance itself.

The Law can be understood to have been weakened because it was not fulfilled—not because it is itself weak, but because, by threatening punishment and not assisting through grace, it makes people weak.

The Apostle used the same word when he said: “What was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened through the flesh,” intending to signify that it is fulfilled through the Spirit. Yet he said that the Law itself was weakened, since it cannot be fulfilled by the weak.

That the inheritance itself was weakened—that is, that the people themselves were weakened when the Law was given—is understood without any ambiguity. For “the Law entered so that the offense might abound.”

What follows, “But you perfected it,” refers to the Law in this sense: it was perfected—that is, fulfilled—according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

Hence the Apostle, who had said that the Law was weakened through the flesh, because the flesh does not fulfill what is fulfilled through the Spirit—that is, through spiritual grace—also says: “That the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Romans 8:3–4).

This, then, is “But you perfected it,” because “the fullness of the Law is love” (Romans 13:10), and the love of God has been poured into our hearts—not by ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

This is “But you perfected it,” if “you perfected” is understood to refer to the Law. If it refers to the inheritance, the meaning is easier.

For if the inheritance of God was said to have been weakened—that is, if God’s people were weakened when the Law was given—because “the Law entered so that the offense might abound,” then what follows, “But you perfected it,” is understood from what the Apostle also says next: “Where the offense abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

For when offense abounded, their weaknesses multiplied; and afterward they hastened (Psalm 15:4), because they groaned and called upon God, so that, with his help, what had not been fulfilled at his command might be fulfilled through his assistance.

### 12

There is another sense in these words, which seems more probable to me. For it is understood much more suitably as the voluntary rain itself, because it is freely given without any preceding merits of works. “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6). “I am not worthy,” he says, “to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:9–10). This is the voluntary rain. For “of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth” (James 1:18). This is the voluntary rain. Hence elsewhere it is said: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Ps. 5:13).

When God passed through the desert—that is, when he was preached among the Gentiles—the heavens dripped this rain, yet not from themselves but from the face of God, since they too are what they are by the grace of God. And therefore Mount Sinai—because he too who labored more than all of them, yet “not he, but the grace of God with him” (1 Cor. 15:10)—might drip more abundantly among the Gentiles, that is, in the desert where Christ had not been proclaimed, lest he build upon another’s foundation (Rom. 15:20): he, I say, was an Israelite by race, of the tribe of Benjamin (Phil. 3:5). He too, therefore, had been born into slavery, from the earthly Jerusalem “which is in slavery with her children,” and for that reason he persecuted the Church. For, as he himself reminded us, “just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit, so also now” (Gal. 4:25, 29). But he obtained mercy because he acted ignorantly in unbelief (1 Tim. 1:13).

We are astonished, then, that the heavens dripped from the face of God; let us be still more astonished that Mount Sinai—that is, the one who had previously persecuted, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee according to the Law (Phil. 3:5)—did so. But why should we be astonished? For it was not from himself, but, as follows, from the face of the God of Israel. Of this God he himself says, “And upon the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16), of whom the Lord says, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

God therefore set apart this voluntary rain, without any preceding merits of good works, for his inheritance. “And it was weakened.” For it recognized that it was nothing through itself; it recognized that what it is must be attributed not to its own strength but to the grace of God. It recognized what is said: “I will glory in my weaknesses” (2 Cor. 12:9). It recognized what is said: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). It recognized what is said: “But he gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). “And it was weakened; but you perfected it,” because “power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Some manuscripts, both Latin and Greek, do not have “Mount Sinai,” but read: “From the face of God, Sinai; from the face of God, Israel.” That is: “The heavens dripped from the face of God”; and as though one asked, “From the face of which God?” he says, “From the face of God, Sinai; from the face of God, Israel”—that is, from the face of the God who gave the Law to the people of Israel.

Why, then, did the heavens drip from the face of God—from the face of this God—unless [Col. 0820] because what was foretold was fulfilled in this way: “He who gave the Law will give blessing” (Ps. 83:8)? He gave the Law to terrify the person who presumes upon human strength, and blessing to free the person who hopes in God. Therefore you, God, perfected your inheritance, because it was weakened in itself so that it might be perfected by you.

### 13. [verse 11]

“Your animals will dwell in it.” Yours, not their own; subject to you, not free for themselves; dependent upon you, not self-sufficient. Finally, what follows says: “You prepared it in your goodness for the needy, O God.” In your goodness, not in his own resources. For he is needy, since he was weakened in order to be perfected; he recognized himself as needy in order to be filled.

This is that goodness of which it is said elsewhere: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13), so that a good work may be done not from fear but from love; not from dread of punishment but from delight in righteousness. [Note: Col. 0820. Perhaps one should read: “from love of righteousness.”]

For this is true and sound freedom. But the Lord prepared this for the needy, not for the prosperous, to whom such poverty is a reproach. Of such people it is said elsewhere: “A reproach to those who abound, and contempt to the proud” (Ps. 123:4). For he called those proud whom he called prosperous.

### 14. [verse 12]

“The Lord will give the word”—namely, food to his animals that will dwell in it. But what will these animals do, to whom he will give the word? What else than what follows? “To those who evangelize with great power.”

With what power, unless with that strength by which he leads out those who are bound? Perhaps here he also calls “power” that by which those who evangelized performed wondrous signs.

### 15. [verse 13]

Who, then, will give the word to those who evangelize with great power? “The King,” he says, “of the powers of the Beloved.” The Father, therefore, is the King of the powers of the Son. For when “Beloved” is used without specifying whom is beloved, the only-begotten Son is understood by antonomasia.

Or is the Son himself the King of his powers—that is, of the powers serving him? For “the King of powers” will give the word to those who evangelize with great power; and of him it is said: “The Lord of powers, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23:10).

But the fact that he did not say, “King of his powers,” but “King of the powers of the Beloved,” is a form of speech extremely common in Scripture, if one pays attention. This is especially clear where a proper name is also expressed, so that there can be no doubt that the one who acts and the one to whom reference is made are the same. An example of this kind is found many times in the Pentateuch: “And Moses did this and that, as the Lord commanded Moses” (Num. 17:11, etc., according to the Septuagint). It does not say what is customary in our speech, “Moses did as the Lord commanded him,” but, “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses,” as though the Moses whom he commanded were one person and the Moses who acted another, although he is the very same person.

Such expressions are found only with great difficulty in the New Testament. Nevertheless, this is why the Apostle says: “Concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 1:3–4)—as though the Son of God who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh were one person, and Jesus Christ our Lord another, although he is one [Col. 0821] and the same.

In the ancient books this form of speech is frequent. Therefore, when it occurs somewhat obscurely, it should be understood from clear examples of the same kind, as it has been used somewhat obscurely here in the psalm we are explaining. For if it had said, “Jesus Christ, King of the powers of Jesus Christ,” it would have been as clear as “Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses.” But because it says, “King of the powers of the Beloved,” it is not easy for one to realize that the one who is King of the powers is himself also the Beloved.

“King of the powers of the Beloved,” therefore, can be understood as though it said, “King of his powers,” because Christ is both King of the powers and the Beloved—Christ himself. Although this interpretation is not so necessary that no other can be accepted. For the Father too may be understood as the King of the powers of his beloved Son, to whom the Beloved himself says: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John 17:10).

If someone asks whether the Father of God the Lord Jesus Christ may also be called King, I do not know whether anyone would dare to take this name away from him, when the Apostle says: “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God” (1 Tim. 1:17). Even if this is said of the Trinity itself, the God the Father is there also.

If we do not understand carnally the words, “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 72:2), I do not know whether anything other than “to your Son” has been said. The Father, then, is also King. Hence this verse of the psalm, “King of the powers of the Beloved,” can be understood in either way.

Since, therefore, he had said, “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power”—because that power itself is governed by him and serves him, from whom it is given—he says that the very Lord who will give the word to those who evangelize with great power is “King of the powers of the Beloved.”

### 16

Then follows: “Of the Beloved, and of the beauty of the house, to divide spoils.”

The repetition serves to emphasize the point, although not all manuscripts contain this repetition. More careful copies mark it beforehand with a star, the signs called asterisks, by which they indicate that these words are not in the translation of the Septuagint but are present in the Hebrew and are marked with such signs.

Whether the word “Beloved” is repeated or is understood as having been said only once, I think what follows—“and of the beauty of the house, to divide spoils”—should be understood as though it said: “Of the Beloved also, of the beauty of the house, to divide spoils,” that is, “of the Beloved also, for dividing spoils.”

For Christ made a beautiful house—that is, the Church—by dividing spoils among it, just as a body is beautiful through the distribution of its members. Spoils are called what is stripped from defeated enemies. The Gospel teaches us what this means, where we read: “No one enters the house of a strong man to plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12:29).

Christ therefore bound the devil with spiritual bonds by conquering death and ascending from the depths above the heavens. He bound him by the mystery of his incarnation: finding nothing in Christ deserving death, yet allowing him to be killed. Thus, having bound him, Christ took away his goods as spoils. For the devil was working in the sons of disobedience (Eph. 2:2), whose unbelief he used according to his own will.

The Lord cleansed these goods by the remission of sins and [Col. 0822] sanctified these spoils, taken from the enemy who had been defeated and bound. He divided them among the beauty of his house, appointing some apostles, some prophets, some pastors and teachers, “for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:11–12).

For just as the body is one and has many members, and although all the members of the body are many, the body is one, so also is Christ. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all powers? Do all possess gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one his own as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:12, 29–30, 11).

This is the beauty of the house to which the spoils are divided, so that its lover, inflamed by this beauty, may exclaim: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Ps. 26:8).

### 17. [verse 14]

In what follows he turns to address the very members from whom the beauty of the house is formed, saying: “If you sleep among the middle portions, wings of a silvered dove, and between her shoulders in the greenness of gold.”

First, one must determine the order of the words and where the sentence ends. It certainly remains incomplete when he says, “If you sleep.” Then, concerning “wings of a silvered dove,” it must be asked whether it is to be understood in the singular—“of this wing”—or in the plural—“these wings.” But the Greek excludes the singular, since the expression is clearly written in the plural there.

It still remains uncertain whether the reading is “these wings” or “O wings,” so that he appears to address the wings themselves. Does the sentence therefore end with the preceding words, so that the order is: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power, if you sleep among the middle portions, O wings of a silvered dove”? Or does it end with what follows, so that the order is: “If you sleep among the middle portions, the wings of a silvered dove will be whitened with snow on Salmon”—that is, the wings themselves will be whitened if you sleep among the middle portions?

On this interpretation he is understood to address those who are divided as spoils among the beauty of the house: “If you sleep among the middle portions, O you who are divided among the beauty of the house by the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good, so that to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith, to another kinds of healings in the same Spirit, and so forth” (1 Cor. 12:7, 9). If, then, you sleep among the middle portions, “the wings of a silvered dove will be whitened with snow on Salmon.”

It may also be understood in this way: “If you, wings of a silvered dove, sleep among the middle portions, you will be whitened with snow on Salmon,” with human beings understood as the subject—those who receive remission of sins through grace. Hence it is also said of the Church herself in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that ascends, whitened?” (Song 3:6, according to the Septuagint). For God’s promise is upheld through the Prophet’s words: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white like snow” (Isa. 1:18).

It may also be understood in this way: in the words “wings of a silvered dove,” one should supply “you will be,” so that the sense is: “O you who are divided like spoils of the beauty of the house, if you sleep among the middle portions, you will be wings of a silvered dove”—that is, you will be raised to higher [Col. 0823] things while remaining attached to the structure of the Church.

For I think no other dove can better be understood here as the silvered dove than the one of whom it is said: “My dove is one” (Song 6:8). It is silvered because it has been instructed in the divine utterances. For elsewhere the Lord’s utterances are called “silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12:7).

It is therefore a great good to sleep among the middle portions. Some have wished these to be the two Testaments: to sleep among the middle portions means to rest in the authority of those Testaments, that is, to assent to the testimony of both Testaments, so that whenever something is brought forward and proved from them, every dispute may be ended in peaceful quiet.

If this is so, what else do those who evangelize with great power seem to be admonished than that the Lord will then give them the word by which they can evangelize, if they sleep among the middle portions? For the word of truth is given to them when they do not abandon the authority of the two Testaments. Thus they themselves are the wings of the dove, silvered, by whose preaching the glory of the Church is carried into heaven.

### 18

“But between the shoulders”: this is certainly a part of the body. It is a part near the region of the heart, yet from behind, that is, from the back. He says that this part of the silvered dove is “in the greenness of gold,” that is, in the vigor of wisdom. I do not think this vigor can better be understood than as love. [Note: Col. 0823. Er. and several manuscripts read: “in the greenness (*virore*) of wisdom, which greenness …”]

But why from the back and not from the breast? I am nevertheless astonished at how this word has been placed in another psalm, where it says: “Between his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope” (Ps. 91:4), since one cannot be overshadowed under wings unless one is under what is from the breast.

In Latin, “between the shoulders” may perhaps be understood in some way as referring to both sides, front and back, if we take the shoulders to be those that have the head in the middle. The Hebrew may perhaps be ambiguous and permit this interpretation. But the Greek word μετάφρενα signifies only what is behind, namely, what is between the shoulders.

Is the greenness of gold there—that is, wisdom and love—because the roots of the wings are somehow located there? Or is it because that light burden is carried there? For what are the wings themselves except the two commandments of love, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40)? And what is the light burden except love itself, which is fulfilled in these two commandments?

Whatever is difficult in a commandment is light to the one who loves. For no other reason is the saying rightly understood, “My burden is light” (Matt. 11:30), except that he gives the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), so that by loving we may do freely what the person who does it from fear does slavishly. Nor is he a friend of what is right when he would prefer, if it were possible, that what is right not be commanded.

### 19

It may also be asked: since it does not say, “If you sleep in the portions,” but “among [Col. 0824] the middle portions,” what does “among the middle portions” mean?

If it were translated more explicitly from the Greek, it would say “among the midst of the portions,” a reading I have found in none of the translators. I therefore believe that what is said, “among the middle portions,” has the same meaning.

I shall explain what seems to me to be intended. This expression is often used to connect and reconcile things so that they do not disagree with one another. Thus, when God establishes a covenant between himself and the people, Scripture uses this expression. For where Latin has “between me and you,” Greek has “between my midst and your midst.”

So too, when God speaks to Abraham of the sign of circumcision, he says: “It shall be a covenant between me and you and all your seed” (Gen. 17:2, 7). Greek has: “between my midst and your midst, and between my midst and the midst of your seed.”

Likewise, when he spoke to Noah about the bow in the clouds, to establish it as a sign (Gen. 9:12), he repeats this expression very often. Where Latin manuscripts have “between me and you,” or “between me and every living soul,” and similar expressions, Greek has “between my midst and your midst,” which is ἀνὰ μέσον.

David and Jonathan also establish a sign between themselves, so that they may not disagree by forming different opinions (1 Sam. 20:20–23). Where Latin says “between the two,” Greek has “between the midst of the two,” using the same expression, ἀνὰ μέσον.

It was therefore very well done that in this passage the translators of our psalm did not say “among the portions,” which is customary in Latin speech, but “among the middle portions,” as though it said “among the midst of the portions,” which is more closely represented in the Greek and is customarily said of things that, as I have explained, ought to agree with one another.

Scripture therefore commands those who are either the wings of a silvered dove, or are enabled by this command to become such, to sleep among the middle portions.

But if these portions signify the two Testaments, what else are we admonished than not to oppose the Testaments when they agree with one another, but to assent by understanding them? [Note: Col. 0824. Nearly all manuscripts read: “than that we should not oppose those Testaments in their agreement with one another.” The Regius manuscript reads: “than that we should know those Testaments to agree with one another, not to be opposed.”] We are to be the sign and testimony of their harmony, recognizing that neither says anything against the other and displaying this with peaceful wonder, as though in the sleep of ecstasy.

Why, however, should the Testaments be understood by the word “portions,” when the term is Greek but is not the usual Greek word for “Testament”? The reason is that an inheritance is given through a testament, and inheritance is called κληρονομία in Greek, while an heir is called κληρονόμος. Κλῆρος, however, means “lot” in Greek, and lots are called the portions of the inheritance distributed to the people by God.

Hence the tribe of Levi was commanded not to have a lot among its brothers, because it was to be supported by their tithes (Num. 18:20). I also think that Clerus and Clerici derive their names from this, referring to those ordained in the grades of ecclesiastical ministry, because Matthias was chosen by lot; he was the first whom we read of as having been ordained by the Apostles (Acts 1:26).

Accordingly, because of the inheritance that is established by a testament, the Testaments themselves are signified by the name “portions,” as though that which is effected were named by the means that effects it.

### 20

Yet another sense occurs to me which, if I am not mistaken, ought to be preferred: that we should understand “portions” much more probably as the inheritances themselves. For the inheritance of the Old Testament, although it was a symbolic shadow [Col. 0825] of the future, is earthly happiness; whereas the inheritance of the New Testament is eternal immortality.

To sleep among the middle portions, then, is neither to seek that former inheritance eagerly nor yet to await the latter patiently. For those who serve God—or rather, who refuse to serve him for this reason—while seeking happiness in this life and on this earth have had sleep taken away from them and do not sleep. Driven by inflamed desires, they are thrust into shameful acts and crimes and find no rest at all, desiring to acquire and fearing to lose.

“But whoever listens to me,” Wisdom says, “will dwell in hope and rest without fear from every evil” (Prov. [lacuna], 33). This, as far as I understand it, is to sleep among the middle portions—that is, among the middle inheritances: to dwell, not yet in possession but nevertheless in hope, in the heavenly inheritance, and already to cease desiring earthly happiness.

When what we hope for has come, we will no longer rest between two inheritances; rather, we will reign in the new reality, the true reality, of which the old was a shadow.

Therefore, even if we understand the words “If you sleep among the middle portions” as though they said, “If you die among the middle portions,” with Scripture calling this death of the flesh “sleep” in its customary manner, this is the best kind of death: that a person should persevere to the end in restraining his desires from earthly things, in hope of the heavenly inheritance, and close the final day of this present life.

For those who sleep among the middle portions will be wings of a silvered dove, so that at the time when they rise again they may be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air and thereafter live forever with the Lord (1 Thess. 4:16). Or certainly, because through those who die in this way the Church is proclaimed more securely and therefore more exaltedly, she is raised aloft as though on wings of praise.

For it was not said without reason: “Before death, praise no one” (Sir. 11:30).

All the saints of God, therefore, from the beginning of the human race until the time of the Apostles—for they too knew how to say, “I have not desired the day of man; you know” (Jer. 17:16), and, “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. 27:4)—and from the time of the Apostles, when the distinction between the two Testaments was more clearly revealed, the Apostles themselves, the blessed martyrs, and the other righteous have slept among the middle portions like rams and sons of rams until the present time: already despising the happiness of an earthly kingdom, hoping for the eternity of the kingdom of heaven, but not yet possessing it.

And because they slept so well, the Church now flies, as it were, on their wings and is exalted by their praises—the silvered dove—so that, by this fame of theirs, posterity may be invited to imitate them. While the others also sleep in this way, wings are added by which she may be proclaimed in exaltation until the end of the age.

### 21. [verse 15]

“While the supercelestial one distinguishes kings over her, they will be whitened with snow on Salmon.”

The supercelestial one—the one who ascended above all the heavens in order to fulfill all things—distinguishes kings over her, that is, over the same silvered dove.

The Apostle continues and says: “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers.” For what [Col. 0826] else is it to distinguish kings over her than “for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. 4:10–12), since she herself is the body of Christ?

They are called kings from ruling. And what do they rule more than the desires of the flesh, so that sin may not reign in their mortal body to obey its desires, so that they may not present their members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but may present themselves to God as those alive from the dead, and their members as weapons of righteousness to God (Rom. 6:12–13)?

Thus they will first be kings distinguished from foreigners, because they do not enter into a common yoke with unbelievers; then they will be distinguished from one another harmoniously by their particular gifts. For not all are apostles, or all prophets, or all teachers; not all possess gifts of healings, not all speak in tongues, and not all interpret. “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one his own as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:29–30, 11). By giving this Spirit, the supercelestial one distinguishes kings over the silvered dove.

When the angel spoke of the Holy Spirit to the mother of Christ, who was full of grace, she asked how what had been announced—that she would give birth—could happen, since she did not know a man. He answered: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

What does “will overshadow you” mean except, “will make a shadow for you”? Hence these kings too, while they are distinguished by the grace of the Spirit of the Lord Christ over the silvered dove, “will be whitened with snow on Salmon.” For Salmon is interpreted as “Shadow.”

They are not distinguished by their merits or their own power. “For who distinguishes you?” he asks. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Therefore, to be distinguished from the impious, they receive remission of sins from the one who says: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. 1:18).

Behold how “they will be whitened with snow on Salmon”: in the grace of the Spirit of Christ, by which their particular gifts are also distinguished. Of this Spirit it was said, as I recalled above: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, will make a shadow for you—“therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

This shadow is understood as a shelter from the heat of carnal desires. Hence that virgin conceived Christ not by desiring him carnally but by believing spiritually.

A shadow consists of light and a body. Therefore, that which “was in the beginning the Word,” that true light, so that it might become a noonday shelter for us, “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14). God approached humanity as a body approaches light, and the shadow of protection covered those who believed in him.

This is not the kind of shadow of which it is said, “All those things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:9), nor the kind of shadow of which the Apostle says, “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17). It is the kind of shadow of which it is written: “Under the shadow of your wings protect me” (Ps. 17:8).

Therefore, while the supercelestial one distinguishes kings over the silvered dove, let them not exalt their own merits or trust in their own power. For “they will be whitened with snow on Salmon”: [Col. 0827] they will be made white by grace in the protection of the body of Christ.

### 22. [verse 16]

Next he calls this mountain the mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a mountain rich in cheese, or a fat mountain. What else could he call “fat” here than “fertile”? There is also a mountain called by this name, namely Salmon.

But what mountain should we understand as the mountain of God, the fertile mountain, the mountain rich in cheese, except the same Lord Christ, of whom another prophet also says: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2)?

He is the mountain rich in cheese because of the little ones who are to be nourished by grace as by milk; the fertile mountain, for strengthening and enriching them by the excellence of his gifts. For milk itself, from which cheese is made, wonderfully signifies grace: it flows from the abundance of a mother’s womb and is freely poured out in delightful mercy upon the little ones.

The case in Greek is ambiguous, whether nominative or accusative, since “mountain” is neuter in that language, not masculine. For this reason some Latin translators have not rendered it in the accusative, *montem Dei* (“the mountain of God”), but in the nominative, *mons Dei* (“mountain of God”).

I think it is better to understand it as: “In Salmon, the mountain of God”—that is, “in the mountain of God that is called Salmon”—according to the interpretation that we have explained above as best we could.

### 23. [verse 17]

Then, because he said “the mountain of God, the mountain rich in cheese, the fertile mountain,” lest anyone dare to compare the Lord Jesus Christ with the other saints, who themselves are also called mountains of God—for it is written, “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 36:7), whence the Apostle says, “So that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21)—and elsewhere it is said of these mountains, “You enlighten wonderfully from the eternal mountains” (Ps. 76:5), because eternal life has been given to them [Note: Col. 0827. The editions read, “he enlightening”; the manuscripts add, “through them,” in place of the Psalm’s “from the eternal mountains.”] and the most exalted authority of the holy Scriptures has been established through them, yet he enlightens through them who is addressed by the words, “You enlighten”—

for I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come; nevertheless my help is not properly from the mountains themselves, but “my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 121:1–2).

For one of those mountains, greatly excelling the others, when he had said that he had labored more than all of them, added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Lest anyone therefore dare to compare even “the beautiful mountain above the sons of men” (Ps. 45:3) with the mountains that are sons of men—for there were those who said that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt. 16:14)—he turned to them and said: “Why do you suspect the mountains rich in cheese? The mountain,” he says, “in which it pleased God to dwell.”

Why do you suspect them? Just as he is light, since it was also said to them, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14), yet another statement says, “the true light which enlightens every human being” (John 1:9), so too those are mountains, but this is a far different mountain, prepared on the summit of the mountains.

These mountains are glorious because they bear that mountain. One [Col. 0828] of them says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14), so that “whoever glories may glory not in himself but in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

Why, then, do you suspect the mountains rich in cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell? Not because he does not dwell in the others, but because he dwells in them through this one. For “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells” (Col. 2:9), not in shadow, as in the temple made by King Solomon, but bodily—that is, solidly and truly.

“For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). Whether we understand this as said of the Father, since he himself says, “The Father who remains in me, he does his works; I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10), or understand it in this way—“God was in Christ,” the Word was in the human being—it was certainly so that the Word was in the flesh, that the Word alone might properly be said to have become flesh, that is, that a human being might be joined to the Word in one person of Christ.

Why, then, do you suspect the mountains rich in cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell? He dwells in this mountain in a manner altogether different from that in the other mountains, one of which you also suspect this mountain to be.

For although those too are sons of God by the grace of adoption, none of them is therefore the Only-Begotten, to whom it was said: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. 110:1).

Indeed, the Lord will dwell in them to the end: that is, the Lord himself, who is the mountain prepared on the summit of the mountains, will dwell in those mountains—which are not to be compared with this mountain—in order to lead them to the end, that is, to himself, who is to be contemplated as God.

“For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

It therefore pleased God to dwell in this mountain, which is prepared on the summit of the mountains, to whom he says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). [Note: Col. 0828. Er. and Lov. read, “in whom I am”; “I am” is absent from Am. and the manuscripts, and is not found in the Greek Septuagint.]

This mountain itself is the Lord, who will dwell in the other mountains to the end, in whose summit he is prepared. For “there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5)—the mountain of mountains, just as the Holy of Holies.

Hence he says: “I in them, and you in me” (John 17:23).

Why, then, do you suspect the mountains rich in cheese, the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell? For this mountain rich in cheese, the Lord himself, will dwell in those mountains rich in cheese to the end, so that they may become something—those to whom he says: “For without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### 24. [verse 18]

Thus also comes what follows: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, manifold”; or, “ten-thousandfold manifold”; or, “myriad-fold manifold.” For the Latin translators each rendered in whatever way he could a single Greek word, μυριοπλάσιον. It could not be adequately expressed in Latin: for “thousand” is χίλια in Greek, while μυριάδες means many tens of thousands; a single μυριάς is ten thousand. By this term, therefore, he signified the immense multitude of saints and believers who, by bearing God, become in a certain sense the chariot of God. By dwelling in it and governing it, he brings it to the end as his chariot, as though to some appointed destination. [Col. 0829] “For Christ is the beginning, then those who are Christ’s at his coming, then the end” (1 Cor. 15:23–24).

This is the holy Church, which is what follows: “Thousands of rejoicing ones.” For they rejoice in hope until they are brought to the end that they now await through patience (Rom. 8:25). Remarkably, after saying, “Thousands of rejoicing ones,” he immediately added, “The Lord is among them.” Let us not be surprised that they rejoice: the Lord is among them. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21); but the Lord is among them. Therefore, although they are “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10), they do not yet rejoice in the end itself, which they have not reached, but rejoice in hope and are “patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12), because the Lord is among them—“in Sinai, in the holy place.”

In the interpretations of Hebrew names, we find that Sinai is interpreted as “Commandment”; it is also interpreted in certain other ways, but I think this meaning suits the present passage better. For, giving the reason why those thousands that constitute God’s chariot rejoice, he says: “The Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place”—that is, the Lord is among them, in the commandment; and the commandment is holy, as the Apostle says: “So then the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 7:12).

But what good would the commandment be if the Lord were not there, of whom it is said: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13)? For the commandment without the Lord’s assistance is “the letter that kills” (2 Cor. 3:6). “The Law came in besides, so that the trespass might increase” (Rom. 5:20). But since “the fulfillment of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10), the Law is fulfilled through love, not through fear. For “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This is why these thousands rejoice. For they accomplish the righteousness of the Law to the extent that they are assisted by the Spirit of grace, because the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place.

### 25. [verse 19]

Then, turning his speech toward the Lord himself, he says: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men.” The Apostle recalls and explains this in the following way when speaking of the Lord Christ: “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men.’ But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things” (Eph. 4:7–10).

Therefore, without doubt, this was said of Christ: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men.” Nor should it trouble us that, when recalling the same testimony, the Apostle does not say, “You received gifts among men,” but “He gave gifts to men.” For he spoke with apostolic authority in accordance with the fact that the Son is God with the Father [Note: [Col. 0829] Here the editions add, “made,” which is absent from the manuscripts.]. In accordance with this, he gave gifts to men, sending them the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

But in accordance with the fact that this same Christ is understood in his body, which is the Church—for this reason his members are his saints and faithful people; [Col. 0830] hence it is said to them, “You are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Cor. 12:27)—without doubt he also received gifts among men. For Christ ascended on high and sits at the right hand of the Father (Mark 16:19); but unless he were also here on earth, he would not have cried out from there: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Since, then, this same one says, “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40), why should we doubt that he receives in his members the gifts that his members receive?

### 26.

But what does “You led captivity captive” mean? Is it because he conquered death, which held captive those over whom it reigned? Or did he call the people themselves “captivity,” since they were held captive under the devil? The mystery of this is also contained in the title of that psalm: “When the house was being built after the captivity” (Ps. 95:1)—that is, the Church after paganism.

Calling those people who were held captive “captivity,” just as “army” can be used to mean those who serve in the army, he says that this same captivity was taken captive by Christ. For why should captivity not be blessed, if people can also be captured for the good? Hence it was said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching people” (Luke 5:10).

They were therefore taken captive because they were captured, and captured because they were subjected; they were placed under that gentle yoke (Matt. 11:30), freed from sin, of which they had been slaves, and made slaves of righteousness, from which they had been free (Rom. 6:18). Hence he himself is also in them—the one who gave gifts to men and received gifts among men. Therefore in this captivity, in this servitude, in this chariot, under this yoke, there are not thousands of weeping people but thousands of rejoicing people. For the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place.

Another interpretation also agrees with this meaning: Sinai is interpreted as “Measure.” For, speaking of these gifts of spiritual joy, the Apostle says what I quoted above: “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” Then what follows here also follows there: “Therefore he says: ‘He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men’”—which here is, “You received gifts among men.” What is more harmonious with this and that truth? What is clearer?

### 27.

But what does he add next? “For those who do not believe to inhabit”; or, as some manuscripts have it, “For those not believing to inhabit.” For what are those who do not believe other than those who do not believe? The meaning of what is said about them is not easy to understand.

For, as though an explanation were being given of the preceding words—when it had been said, “You led captivity captive, you received gifts among men”—there follows: “For those who do not believe to inhabit,” that is, “those not believing in order that they might inhabit.” What does this mean? Of whom does he say this? Does he show that this captivity, before it passed into a good captivity, had been an evil captivity? For by not believing they were possessed by the enemy, who works in the children of distrust, among whom, he says, “you once lived when you followed the course of this world” (Eph. 2:2–3).

By the gifts of his grace, therefore, the one who received gifts among men took this captivity captive. For they had been unbelieving in order that they might inhabit. Faith freed them from that condition [Note: [Col. 0830] Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. The Louvain edition has “will free.”], so that now, as believers, they might inhabit [Col. 0831] the house of God, themselves made the house of God and the chariot of God—“thousands of rejoicing people” [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition have “ten thousand.” “Ten thousand” is absent from the manuscripts.]

### 28. [verses 20–21]
