Therefore the one who sang these things, foreseeing them in the Spirit and himself filled with joy, burst forth in a hymn, saying: “The Lord God is blessed; blessed is the Lord God from day to day.” Some manuscripts have “day by day.” For the Greeks have ἡμέραν καθ’ ἡμέραν, which would more accurately be expressed as “day by day.” I think that expression signifies what is said here, “from day to day.” For every day he does this until the end: he leads captivity captive, receiving gifts among men.

### 29.

And since he leads that chariot to the end, he continues and says: “God, the God of our healings, will make a prosperous journey for us” [Note: [Col. 0831] Some manuscripts read salutarium (“of salvations”); others, sanitantium (“of healings”); most, anitatium (uncertain reading).], “our God, the God of saving.”

Grace is highly commended here. For who would be saved unless he himself healed? But lest the thought arise, “Why then do we die, if we have been saved by his grace?” he immediately added: “And the exits of the Lord are of death”—as though he were saying: “Why are you indignant that the human condition has an exit of death? The exit of your Lord was also one of death.” Therefore take comfort rather than becoming indignant; for the Lord’s exit too was one of death.

“For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25). Let us therefore also bear death itself patiently, following the example of the one who, although he was indebted to death through no sin and was Lord, so that no one could take his life from him, but he himself could lay it down of his own accord, nevertheless also had an exit of death.

### 30. [verse 22]

“Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the head of those who walk in their sins”—that is, of those who exalt themselves excessively and grow excessively proud in their sins, in which at least they ought to be humble, saying: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

But he will crush their heads, because “the one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:13–14). Accordingly, although the Lord’s exit too was one of death, nevertheless that same Lord, because he is God and died according to the flesh by his will, not by necessity, will crush the heads of his enemies—not only those who mocked the crucified one and, shaking their heads, said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross,” but also all who exalt themselves against his teaching and mock him as though he were merely a man’s death.

That same one of whom it was said, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:40, 42), is the God of our salvations and the God of saving. But, in order to provide an example of humility and patience, and to blot out with his blood the record of our sins, he also willed his own exit to be one of death, so that we would not fear this death but rather that other death from which he freed us through this one.

Nevertheless, though mocked and dead, he will crush the heads of his enemies, of whom he says, “Raise me up, and I will repay them” (Ps. 40:11): either good for evil, while he subjects the heads of believers to himself; or just punishment for the unjust, [Col. 0832] while he punishes the heads of the proud. In either manner the heads of his enemies are crushed and broken when they are cast down from pride, whether corrected by humility or dragged down into the depths of Tartarus.

### 31. [verses 23–24]

“The Lord said: ‘From Bashan I will return’”; or, as some manuscripts have it, “From Bashan I will cause to return.” For it is he who causes us to return so that we may be saved, of whom it was said above: “The God of our salvations, and the God of saving.” Elsewhere also it is said to him: “God of hosts, restore us; and show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:20). Again, elsewhere: “Restore us, O God of our salvations” (Ps. 84:5).

But he said: “From Bashan I will cause to return.” Bashan is interpreted as “Confusion.” What, then, is “I will cause to return from confusion” except that the person who prays for God’s mercy for the forgiveness of his sins is ashamed because of his sins? This is why that tax collector did not dare even to raise his eyes toward heaven: as he considered himself, he was ashamed; but he went down justified, because the Lord said, “From Bashan I will cause to return.”

Bashan is also interpreted as “Drought,” and it is rightly understood that the Lord causes a return from drought—that is, from poverty. For those who seem to themselves to be rich while they are starving, and full while they are utterly empty, do not return. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6). From this drought the Lord causes a return; for from a dry soul it is said to him: “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water before you” (Ps. 143:6).

It can also not improperly be understood in the form found in other manuscripts, “From Bashan I will return.” For he himself also returns to us who says, “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3)—and this not outside confusion, since our sin is always before us (Ps. 50:5), nor outside drought, by which we desire his rain, the one who has set apart a willing rain for his inheritance. For it had been weakened by drought; but when he himself returned, he perfected it, to whom it is said: “And when you have returned, you restored me to life” (Ps. 70:20).

Therefore the Lord said: “From Bashan I will cause to return; I will cause to return into the depth of the sea.” If he says, “I will cause to return,” why “into the depth of the sea”? When the Lord causes a person to return in a saving manner, he causes him to return to himself, and he is certainly not himself the depth of the sea.

Or perhaps Latin usage is misleading, and “into the depth” has been put for “deeply”? For he does not cause himself to return; rather, there he causes those to return who lie submerged in the depth of this age beneath the weight of their sins, where that person, when he has returned, says: “From the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. 129:1).

But if the reading is not “I will cause to return” but “I will return into the depth of the sea,” this is understood as our Lord’s saying that by his mercy he would return even into the depth of the sea, in order to free even those who were the most desperate sinners.

Although in a Greek manuscript I found not “into the depth” but “in the depths,” that is, ἐν βυθοῖς, which confirms the former interpretation: that even there God causes those crying from the depths to return to himself. And even if he is understood to return there himself in order to free such people, this is not incongruous.

Thus he causes them to return, or returns in this way to free them, so that his foot may be dipped in blood. The Prophet says to the Lord himself: “So that your foot may be dipped in blood”—that is, so that those who return to you, or to whose liberation you return, although they have been sunk into the depth of the sea under the burden of iniquity, may advance so far by your grace that, “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20).

They are to become your foot among your members, announcing your Gospel, and, bearing witness for your name for a long time, they are to contend even unto blood [Note: Most manuscripts omit “for a long time”; some have “speaking” instead of “bearing witness.”]. Thus, I think, it is more appropriately understood that his foot is dipped in blood.

### 32.

Finally he adds: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him”—calling those same people who were going to contend for the evangelical faith even unto blood “dogs,” as though they were barking for their Lord.

Not those dogs of whom the Apostle says, “Beware of dogs” (Phil. 3:2), but those who eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table. For this is what the Canaanite woman confessed and thereby deserved to hear: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish” (Matt. 15:28).

They are commendable dogs, not detestable ones: they keep faith with their master and bark against enemies on behalf of his household. For he did not merely say “of dogs,” but “of your dogs”; nor was it their teeth that were praised, but their tongue. For surely it was not without reason or without a great mystery that Gideon was ordered to take only those who lapped the water of the river like dogs; and no more than three hundred of this kind were found among so great a multitude (Judg. 7:5–6).

In this number there is the sign of the cross, because of the letter τ, which in the Greek notation of numbers signifies three hundred. Concerning such dogs it is also said in another psalm: “They will return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Ps. 58:15). For certain dogs were also reproved by the prophet Isaiah—not because they were dogs, but because they did not know how to bark and loved to sleep (Isa. 56:10). There he clearly showed that, if they were watchful and barked for their master, they would be commendable dogs, like those who are praised in the words, “The tongue of your dogs.”

Yet the Prophet foretold that these would come from the enemies, through that conversion of which he was speaking above. Hence that psalm also says: “They return at evening and growl like dogs.” Then, as though people were asking where they had received such a great good, that they should become dogs of the one whose enemies they had been, the response was added: “From him.” For it is read as follows: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” From his love, certainly; from his mercy; from his grace. For when could they have achieved this by themselves? “For while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). For this too was the Lord’s exit of death.

### 33. [verse 25]

“Your footsteps were seen, O God.” These are the footsteps by which you came through the world, as though you were going to traverse the whole earth in that chariot. The Gospel signifies his saints and faithful people by clouds when it says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in clouds” (Matt. 26:64; Mark 13:26).

Apart from that coming in which he will be judge of the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4:1), he says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in clouds.” “Your footsteps were seen,” that is, they were made manifest, when the grace of the New Testament was revealed. Hence it was said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Rom. 10:15)!

For this grace, and these footsteps, lay hidden in the Old Testament. But when the fullness of time came and it pleased God to reveal his Son, so that he might be proclaimed among the nations (Gal. 4:4), “your footsteps were seen, O God; the footsteps of my God, the King” [Note: The editions have “of my King.” The word “my” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek Septuagint], “who is in the holy place.” In what holy place, unless in his temple? For the Apostle says: “God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17).

### 34. [verse 26]

But in order that these footsteps might be seen: “The princes went before, joined with those who sing psalms, in the midst of young women playing tambourines.”

The princes are the Apostles. They went before so that the peoples might follow. They went before announcing the New Testament, joined with those who sing psalms, so that God might be glorified through their good works, including those visible works that are like instruments of praise.

The same princes are “in the midst of young women playing tambourines,” that is, in an honorable ministry. For this is how ministers appointed over the new Churches are in their midst. “Young women” signifies those who praise God after subduing the flesh; and “those playing tambourines” signifies this because tambourines are made from dried and stretched hide.

### 35. [verse 27]

Therefore, lest anyone receive these things carnally and form in his mind from these words certain lascivious dances, he continues and says: “In the Churches bless the Lord.” It is as though he were saying: “Why, when you hear of young women playing tambourines, do you imagine sensual pleasures? In the Churches bless the Lord.”

For the Churches are shown to you through this mystical meaning. The Churches are young women adorned with new grace; the Churches are those playing tambourines, spiritually resonant through disciplined flesh.

Therefore, “in the Churches bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel.” For from there he first chose those whom he would make fountains. From there the Apostles were chosen, and they first heard: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst; but the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

### 36. [verse 28]

“There is Benjamin, the younger, in ecstasy.” There is Paul, the last of the Apostles, who says: “For I too am an Israelite, from the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Phil. 3:5).

But certainly he was “in ecstasy,” since all were struck with awe at so great a miracle in his calling. For ecstasy is an excess or departure of the mind. Sometimes it occurs through fear; at other times through a kind of revelation, when the mind is separated from bodily senses so that what must be shown may be shown to the spirit.

Accordingly, “in ecstasy” here can also be understood in this way: when the persecutor was told from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” and the light of his bodily eyes was taken away, he answered the Lord whom he saw in the spirit. Those who were with him heard the voice of the one speaking, but they saw no one to whom he was speaking (Acts 9:4–7).

Here “ecstasy” can also be understood as that experience of his about which he himself says that he knows a man who was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or outside the body he does not know—but who was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words that a human being is not permitted to speak (2 Cor. 12:2–4).

“Princes of Judah, their leaders; princes of Zebulun, princes of Naphtali.”

Since he signifies the Apostles by “princes,” and since Benjamin the younger in ecstasy is also present—by which words no one doubts that Paul is signified—or since by the name “princes” all those in the Churches who excel and are most worthy of imitation may be signified, what do these names of the tribes of Israel mean?

If Judah alone were mentioned, because kings had come from that tribe, and from it also came the Lord Christ according to the flesh (Rom. 9:5), we might therefore suppose that the princes of the New Testament were represented by that tribe. But when he adds, “princes of Zebulun, princes of Naphtali,” someone might perhaps say that the Apostles came from these tribes and not from the others.

Although I do not see how this could be proved, nevertheless, since I also find no way to refute it, and since I see in this passage the princes and leaders of the Churches who bless the Lord being commended, I also approve this interpretation as not absurd [Note: [Col. 0835] Most manuscripts have “I bring forward” or “I put forward” instead of “I approve”]. But I am more pleased by what becomes clear from the interpretation of these names.

For they are Hebrew names. Judah is said to be interpreted as “Confession”; Zebulun as “Dwelling-place of strength”; Naphtali as “My enlargement.” All these meanings present to us true princes of the Churches, worthy of leadership, worthy of imitation, and worthy of honor.

For martyrs hold the highest place in the Churches and excel at the summit of holy dignity. In martyrdom, confession comes first; then, for the sake of that confession, the strength to endure whatever may happen is taken up; afterward, when everything has been endured and the hardships have ended, enlargement follows as the reward.

This can also be understood in such a way that, since the Apostle especially commends these three things—faith, hope, and love (2 Cor. 13:13)—confession is in faith, strength in hope, and enlargement in love.

For it belongs to faith that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). In the sufferings of tribulations, the situation is grievous, but hope is strong: “If we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:25).

Love provides enlargement through its diffusion in the heart. For “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), and fear brings torment through the narrowness of the soul.

Therefore: “Princes of Judah, their leaders, those who bless the Lord in the Churches. Princes of Zebulun, princes of Naphtali”—princes of confession, strength, and enlargement; princes of faith, hope, and love.

[Col. 0836] ### 37. [verse 29]

“Command your strength, O God.” For our one Lord is Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6), whom we read to be “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

But how does God command his Christ, unless by commending him? For God “shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8). How could he not also give us all things with him (Rom. 8:32)?

“Command your strength, O God; strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.” Command by teaching; strengthen by assisting.

### 38. [verses 30–31]

“From your temple in Jerusalem kings will offer gifts to you.” From your temple in Jerusalem, which is “our free mother” (Gal. 4:26), because it too is your holy temple—from that temple, therefore, kings will offer gifts to you.

Whatever kings are understood—whether the kings of the earth, or the kings whom he distinguishes above the silver-winged dove—kings will offer gifts to you. And what gifts are more pleasing than sacrifices of praise? [Note: The manuscripts have this wording. The editions instead read: “And what gifts? Pleasing ones. What sacrifices? Of praise.”]

But those who bear the Christian name while holding different opinions obstruct this praise. Therefore let what follows take place: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.” For they are beasts, since they do harm through lack of understanding; and they are beasts of the reed, since they distort the meaning of the Scriptures according to their own error.

The reed signifies the Scriptures as suitably as speech is signified by the tongue, according to the expressions “the Hebrew tongue,” “the Greek tongue,” “the Latin tongue,” or any other tongue—that is, by the instrument producing what is produced. It is customary in Latin speech for writing to be called a “stylus,” because it is made by a stylus; so too it is called a “reed,” because it is made by a reed.

The Apostle Peter says that the ignorant and unstable distort the Scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet. 3:16). These are the “beasts of the reed” of whom it is said here: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.”

### 39.

This is also the meaning of what he adds: “The assembly of bulls among the calves of the peoples, so that those who have been proved by silver may be excluded” [Note: On the same passage, verse 31, see *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 54, no. 22.].

Calling them “bulls” on account of the pride of their hard and untamed neck, he signifies heretics. By “the calves of the peoples,” I think easily seduced souls are to be understood, because they readily follow these bulls.

They do not seduce whole peoples, among whom there are serious and stable people—hence it is written, “Among a grave people I will praise you” (Ps. 34:18)—but only those among the peoples whom they find to be calves. For among these are those who enter houses and take captive little women burdened with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3:6–7).

When the same Apostle says, “There must also be factions among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19), this too follows here: “So that those who have been proved by silver may be excluded”—that is, that those who have been proved by the words of the Lord may appear.

For “the words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire on the ground” (Ps. 11:7). “May they be excluded” means “may they appear” or “may they stand out,” corresponding to the Apostle’s words, “may become manifest.”

Hence in the art of the silversmith, “excluders” are called those who know how to bring the shape of a vessel out of the confusion of a mass. For many meanings of the holy Scriptures lie hidden and are known to only a few who are more discerning. They are not brought forward more suitably or acceptably except when the need to answer heretics compels it.

Then even those who neglect the study of doctrine, once their slumber has been shaken off, are roused to listen attentively so that the adversaries may be refuted.

In the end, how many meanings of the holy Scriptures concerning Christ as God have been asserted against Photinus! How many concerning Christ as man against Mani! How many concerning the Trinity against Sabellius! How many concerning the unity of the Trinity against the Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians! How many concerning the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, and concerning the mingling of the wicked with the good until the end of the age—since this mingling does not harm the good in their fellowship in the sacraments of the Church—against the Donatists, the Luciferians, and others, if there are any who dissent from the truth through a similar error!

How many meanings have been asserted against the remaining heretics, whom it would be too long to enumerate or mention and unnecessary for the present work!

Yet the approved defenders of these meanings would either have remained completely hidden or would not have stood out so prominently, if the contradictions of the proud had not made them stand out. The Apostle mentions such people as bulls—that is, as not subjected to the peaceful and gentle yoke of discipline—when he says that one should be chosen for the episcopate who is able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict (Titus 1:9).

For there are many who are not subject. These are the bulls, impatient of the plow and the yoke because of the pride of their neck: “empty talkers and deceivers of minds.” This psalm signified these minds by the designation “calves.”

For this beneficial purpose divine Providence permits bulls to be gathered among the calves of the peoples, so that those who have been proved by silver may be excluded—that is, may stand out. For this reason heresies are permitted to exist: so that those who are approved may become manifest.

This can nevertheless also be understood in the following way: “The assembly of bulls among the calves of the peoples, so that those who have been proved by silver may be excluded by those calves.” For this is the intention of heretical teachers: to exclude from the ears of the souls whom they strive to seduce those who have been proved by silver—that is, to separate those who are able to teach the words of the Lord.

But whether the former or the latter is the meaning of this word, what follows is: “Scatter the peoples who desire wars.” For they are devoted not to correction but to contention. He therefore prophesies that those who refuse correction, who desire to scatter Christ’s flock, should themselves rather be scattered.

He called them “peoples” not because of family generations but because of the kinds of sects in which a succession of transmission confirms error.

### 40. [verses 32–34]

“Envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will forestall his hand.” By the names Egypt and Ethiopia he signified the faith of all nations, using a part for the whole, and he called the preachers of reconciliation “envoys.”

“For Christ,” he says, “we are ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5:20).

Thus it was mystically prophesied in this way that preachers of Christian peace would come not only from the Israelites, from whom the Apostles were chosen, but also from the other nations.

When he says, “Ethiopia will forestall his hand,” he means, “It will forestall his vengeance” [Col. 0838]—that is, by turning to him, so that sins may be forgiven and sinners not be punished by remaining sinners. The same is said in another psalm: “Let us come before his face with confession” (Ps. 94:2).

Just as “hands” signifies vengeance, so “face” signifies the revelation and presence that will occur in the judgment.

Therefore, since by Egypt and Ethiopia he signified the nations of the whole world, he immediately added: “To God, kingdoms of the earth.” Not to Sabellius, not to Arius, not to Donatus, not to the other stiff-necked bulls, but “to God, kingdoms of the earth.”

### 41.

Many Latin manuscripts, and especially the Greek ones, have the verses divided in such a way that “To God, kingdoms of the earth” is not a single verse. Rather, “to God” concludes the preceding verse, so that the wording is: “Ethiopia will forestall its hands to God”; and then the following verse begins: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, sing psalms to the Lord.”

This division, being supported by the agreement of many manuscripts of greater authority, should undoubtedly be preferred. It seems to me to commend the faith that precedes works, because the ungodly are justified through faith without the merits of good works, as the Apostle says: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5), so that afterward faith itself may begin to work through love.

For only those works should be called good that are done through the love of God. Faith must precede them, so that the works may begin from faith, not faith from the works, because no one works through the love of God unless he first believes in God.

This is the faith of which it is said: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6). This is the faith of which it is said to the Church herself in the Song of Songs: “You will come, and you will pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:8, according to the Septuagint).

For he came like the chariot of God among thousands of rejoicing people, having a prosperous journey, and passed from this world to the Father (John 13:1), so that what the bridegroom himself says might be fulfilled—he who passed from this world to the Father: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24)—but “from the beginning of faith.”

Therefore, since faith precedes so that good works may follow, and since there are no good works except those that follow preceding faith, “Ethiopia will hasten its hands to him, to God” seems to mean nothing other than: “Ethiopia will believe in God.” For in this way it will hasten its hands—that is, its works. Whose hands? Surely those of Ethiopia itself. For this is not ambiguous in Greek, where the pronoun is unmistakably feminine.

Accordingly, nothing else is said than: “Ethiopia will hasten its hands to God”—that is, by believing in God it will hasten its works.

“For we hold,” says the Apostle, “that one is justified by faith apart from works of the Law. Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles?” (Rom. 3:28–29).

Thus Ethiopia, which appears to be the farthest limit of the Gentiles, is justified by faith apart from works of the Law. In order to be justified, it does not glory in works of the Law; nor does it place its merits before faith, but by faith it hastens its works.

Certainly, many manuscripts do not have “hands” but “hand,” which amounts to the same thing, since it is used for “works” [Note: The editions have “Greek manuscripts do not have.” “Greek” is absent from the better manuscripts.].

I would prefer the Latin translators to have rendered it this way: “Ethiopia will hasten its hands,” or “its hand, to God” [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The editions instead have: “rather than, ‘its hands to God.’”]. For this would be clearer than the wording now used, “his”; and it could be done without compromising the truth, because in Greek the pronoun αὐτῆς can mean not only “his” or “its” but also “her own” or “its own.”

Thus “her own” is appropriate if the reading is “hand,” and “her own” in the plural if the reading is “hands.” For the Greek expression χεῖρα αὐτῆς, which many manuscripts have, can mean both “his hand” and “her own hand.” But the rarer expression in Greek manuscripts, χειρὰς αὐτῆς, can be rendered in Latin both as “his hands” and as “her own hands.”

42. Hence, as though all the events foretold through prophecy had now run their course—events which we already see fulfilled—he exhorts us to praise Christ, and then foretells his future coming. “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord; sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east”—or, as some manuscripts read, “who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east.” In these words, the person who does not believe in Christ’s resurrection and ascension does not understand him. By adding “toward the east,” did he not also indicate the very place, since it is in the eastern regions that he rose and from which he ascended? Therefore he sits above the heaven of heaven at the Father’s right hand. This is what the Apostle says: “He is the one who ascended above all the heavens” (Eph. IV, 10). For what heavens remain after the heaven of heaven? We can also call them “the heavens of heavens,” just as he called the firmament “heaven”; yet we read of that heaven also as “heavens,” where it is written: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII, 4).

And since he will come from there to judge the living and the dead, attend to what follows: “Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of power.” The one who, “like a lamb before its shearer, was without a voice” (Isa. LIII, 7)—behold, he will give his voice—not the voice of weakness, as one who is to be judged, but the voice of power, as one who is to judge. For he will not come as the hidden God, as before, not opening his mouth at the judgment of men; rather, “God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. XLIX, 3). What are you despairing of, unbelievers? Why do you mock? What does the wicked servant say? “My lord delays coming” (Luke XII, 45). Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of power.

43. [verse 35.] “Give glory to God: his magnificence is over Israel.” Of this the Apostle says: “Upon the Israel of God” (Gal. VI, 16). For “not all who are from Israel are Israelites” (Rom. IX, 6), since there is also an Israel according to the flesh. Hence he says: “See Israel according to the flesh” (I Cor. X, 18). “Nor are those who are children of the flesh children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as the offspring” (Rom. IX, 8).

Then, when his people will exist without any mixture of the wicked—like a mass cleansed by the winnowing fan (Matt. III, 12), like Israel in whom there is no deceit (John I, 47)—then his magnificence and his power in the clouds will be most eminent over Israel. For he will not come alone to judgment, but “with the elders of his people” (Isa. III, 14), to whom he promised that they would sit upon thrones judging (Matt. XIX, 28), and who will also judge angels (I Cor. VI, 3). These are the clouds.

44. [verse 36.] Finally, so that the clouds might not be understood as something else, he added what follows: “God is wonderful in his saints, the God of Israel.” Then that very name, Israel—“seeing God”—will be fulfilled most truly and completely, because “we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

“He himself will give strength and power to his people; blessed be God”—now they are fragile and weak.

[Note: Thus in the manuscripts. But the editions read: “now fragile and weak.”]

For “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 8). But then, also through the most glorious transformation of their bodies, he himself will give strength and power to his people. “This body is sown in weakness; it will rise in power” (I Cor. XV, 43). He will therefore give the power which he anticipated in his own flesh, concerning which the Apostle says: “The power of his resurrection” (Phil. III, 10). And he will give the strength by which death, the enemy, will be destroyed (I Cor. XV, 26).

Since, therefore, with his help we have at last brought to an end this lengthy and difficult Psalm, difficult to understand, blessed be God. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXVIII

## SERMON I. On the First Part of the Psalm

1. At the time when we arose in this world and were gathered into the people of God, that little plant from the mustard seed had already stretched out its branches; that leaven, which at first was contemptible, had already leavened the three measures (Matt. XIII, 31–33)—that is, the whole world restored from the three sons of Noah (Gen. IX, 19). For from east and west and north and south come those who will recline with the Patriarchs, while those who were born from their flesh but did not imitate their faith are cast outside (Matt. VIII, 11).

Thus we opened our eyes upon the glory of Christ’s Church, and we found that barren woman—to whom joy had been announced and foretold, because she would have more children than the woman who had a husband (Isa. LIV, 1; Gal. IV, 27)—already in such a condition that she had forgotten the reproaches and disgrace of her widowhood. Therefore, when we read in some prophecy words expressing the humility of Christ or of ourselves, we may perhaps be astonished. It may happen that we are less moved by them because we did not come at the time when such words were read with appreciation, while oppression abounded.

But again, if we consider the abundance of tribulations, and recognize the road on which we walk—if indeed we walk upon it—and how narrow it is (Matt. VII, 14), and how through oppressions and tribulations it leads to everlasting rest; and if we consider that what is called happiness in human affairs is more to be feared than misery, since misery commonly brings forth good fruit through tribulation, whereas happiness corrupts the soul through perverse security and gives place to the tempting devil—when, therefore, we have considered these things wisely and rightly,

[Col. 0841]

“like a salted sacrifice”—

[Note: Thus the Regius manuscript. But the editions read: “this sacrifice sings,” a reading incorrectly supported by most manuscripts.]

—and when we have remembered that human life upon earth is a temptation (Job VII, 1), and that no one at all is secure, nor ought anyone to be secure, until we come to that homeland from which no friend departs and into which no enemy is admitted, even now, amid the very glory of the Church, we recognize the voices of our tribulation. As members of Christ, joined to our head by the bond of charity and holding fast to one another, we will say from the Psalms what we find the martyrs who came before us saying here, because tribulation is common to all, from the beginning to the end.

Nevertheless, let us recognize in the mustard seed this Psalm which we have undertaken to explain, and concerning which we have proposed, in the Lord’s name, to speak to Your Charity. Let us draw our thoughts for a little while away from the height of the plant, the spreading of its branches, and that glory where the birds of heaven rest; and let us hear how this greatness which delights us in the plant arose from something small.

For Christ is speaking here—but we are saying this already to those who know it—Christ is speaking not only as the head but also as the body. We recognize this from the very words. Since Christ is speaking here, we are not permitted to doubt it at all. For here are clearly expressed the words fulfilled in his Passion: “They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” These words were fulfilled literally and exactly as they had been foretold. When Christ himself, hanging on the cross, said, “I thirst,” and vinegar was given to him in a sponge in response to this word, and when, after receiving it, he said, “It is finished,” and then, bowing his head, gave up his spirit (John XIX, 28–30), he showed that all these things foretold had then been completed in him. It is not permissible to understand anything else here.

The Apostles also, when speaking about Christ, gave testimonies from this Psalm. Who, then, would depart from their judgments? Or what lamb would not follow the rams? Therefore Christ is speaking here. Rather, we must demonstrate where his members are speaking, so that we may show that the whole Christ is speaking, than doubt that Christ is speaking.

2. [verse 1.] The title of the Psalm is: “For the end, for those who will be changed; for David.” Now hear of a change for the better, for change is either for the worse or for the better. Adam and Eve were changed for the worse; those who, from Adam and Eve, clung to Christ were changed for the better. “For as through one man came death, so also through one man comes the resurrection of the dead; and as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 21–22).

Adam was changed from what God had made him, but for the worse, through his iniquity. The faithful are changed from what iniquity had made them, but for the better, through the grace of God. Our iniquity brought about our change for the worse; our change for the better is accomplished not by our righteousness but by the grace of God. Therefore, let us attribute to ourselves the fact that we have been changed for the worse; but for the fact that we are changed for the better, let us praise God.

This Psalm is therefore “for those who will be changed.” But from where did this change occur, except through Christ’s Passion? Pascha itself is translated into Latin as “Passover” (*Transitus*). For “Pascha” is not a Greek name but a Hebrew one. It does sound like passion in the Greek language, because *paschein* (πάσχειν) means “to suffer”; but careful attention to the Hebrew expression indicates something else. “Pascha” signifies a passing over.

The evangelist John also made this clear. As the Passion approached, when the Lord came to the supper at which he commended the sacrament of his body and blood, he speaks as follows: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII, 1). Thus he expressed the Passover, the passing over. But unless he himself, who came for our sake, had passed from here to the Father, how could we pass from here, who did not descend for the sake of raising something up, but fell? He did not fall; rather, he descended in order to raise up the one who had fallen.

The passing over, therefore, both his and ours, is from here to the Father; from this world to the kingdom of heaven; from mortal life to eternal life; from earthly life to heavenly life; from corruptible life to incorruptible life; from a life of tribulations to perpetual security. Therefore the title of the Psalm is: “For those who will be changed.”

Let us therefore attend in the text of the Psalm to the cause of our change—that is, the Lord’s Passion itself—and to our voice amid tribulations; let us recognize it and groan together. And by hearing, recognizing, and groaning together, let us be changed, so that the title of the Psalm may be fulfilled in us: “For those who will be changed.”

3. [verse 2.] “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.” That little seed is despised for the moment; it appears to utter humble words. It is buried in the garden, while the world marvels at the greatness of the plant,

[Note: Erasmus and two manuscripts read: “despised by the world.” Shortly afterward, where the manuscripts have *obruitur* (“is buried”), the editions prefer *oritur* (“arises”). Finally, the Regius manuscript presents the passage as follows: “That little seed is despised. Now, what appears to utter humble words is buried in the garden. The world now marvels at the greatness of the plant,” and so forth.]

whose seed was despised by the Jews. Indeed, consider the tiny mustard seed: dark, utterly contemptible, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. LIII, 2).

He says that the waters have entered even to his soul, because those crowds, signified by the name of waters, were able to prevail to this point: to kill Christ. They prevailed in despising him, seizing him, binding him, insulting him, striking him with blows, and spitting upon him. How far, finally? As far as death. Therefore: “The waters have entered even to my soul.” For he called this life his soul, up to the point to which they were able to approach him in their fury.

But could they have done this unless he himself had permitted it? Why, then, does he cry out as though he were suffering something against his will, unless he was prefiguring his members in himself? He suffered because he willed to suffer; martyrs, even when they did not wish to suffer, suffered nevertheless. For he foretold his Passion to Peter in this way: “When you grow old,” he said, “another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go” (John XXI, 18).

Although we desire to cling to Christ, we do not wish to die; and therefore we suffer willingly—or rather, patiently—because no other passage is granted by which we may cling to Christ. For if we could reach Christ, that is, eternal life, by another way, who would wish to die?

Explaining our nature—that is, a certain fellowship of soul and body, and a kind of familiar bond and joining between these two—the Apostle says in one place that we have “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens”; that is, immortality prepared for us, with which we will be clothed at the end, when we have risen from the dead. And he says: “In this we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V, 1, 4).

If it were possible, he says, we would wish to become immortal in such a way that immortality itself would already come and transform us as we are, so that our mortality would be swallowed up by life, and the body would not be laid aside through death only to be received again at the end.

Although, therefore, we pass from evils to good things, the passage itself is nevertheless somewhat bitter and contains gall, which the Jews gave the Lord in his Passion; it contains something sharp that must be endured, by which those who gave him vinegar to drink are indicated (Matt. XXVII, 34).

Thus, prefiguring us and transforming us into himself, he says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.” Those who persecuted him were able even to kill him, but they will have no power to do anything more. For the Lord himself first offered this exhortation: “Do not fear those who kill the body and, after that, have nothing more that they can do; but fear him who has power to destroy both body and soul in the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

By a greater fear we despise lesser things; by a greater desire for eternity we disdain all temporal things. Here, temporal pleasures are sweet and temporal tribulations are bitter. But who would not drink the cup of temporal tribulation, fearing the fire of Gehenna? And who would not despise the world’s sweetness, longing for the sweetness of eternal life?

Therefore, so that we may be delivered, let us cry out, lest perhaps amid our pressures we consent to iniquity and truly be swallowed up irreparably: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.”

4. [verse 3.] “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.” What does he mean by “mud”? The very people who persecuted him? For man was made from mud (Gen. II, 7). But these people, by falling away from righteousness, became mud of the deep. When they persecuted and wished to drag someone into iniquity, anyone who did not consent to them made gold from their mud.

For that person’s mud will deserve to be changed into a heavenly condition and to become the companion of those concerning whom the title of the Psalm says: “For those who will be changed.”

[Note: The manuscripts read: “to become the companion of the title of the Psalm.”]

But when these people were mud of the deep, I was stuck in them—that is, they held me, prevailed over me, and killed me. Therefore: “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.”

What does “there is no substance” mean? Surely the mud itself is not a substance? Or, by clinging to it, have I become something that is not a substance? What, then, does “I am stuck” mean? Was Christ stuck in this way? Or was he stuck, and not, as it is written in the Book of Job, “The earth was handed over to the hands of the wicked” (Job IX, 24)?

Or was he stuck according to the body, because he could be seized, and because he underwent crucifixion itself?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “from him himself.”]

For unless he had been fastened with nails, he would not have been crucified. How, then, is there no substance? Or is that mud not a substance?

Let us therefore understand, if we can, what “there is no substance” means, provided that we first understand what “substance” means. Substance is also spoken of with reference to wealth. In this sense we say, “He has substance,” and, “He has lost his substance.” But shall we suppose that this is what is meant here—“there is no substance,” that is, “there is no wealth”—as though the subject now were some matter concerning wealth, or as though there were some question about riches?

Or perhaps because that very mud was poverty, and there will be riches only when we have become participants in eternity? For true riches exist when nothing will be lacking to us.

The meaning may also be understood according to this use of the word, so that the sense would be: “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance”—that is, “I have come into poverty.” For he says here: “I am poor and sorrowful”; and the Apostle says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that you might become rich through his poverty” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

Therefore, wishing to commend his poverty to us, the Lord may perhaps have said, “There is no substance.” He reached the greatest poverty when he assumed the form of a servant. What are his riches? Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized. These are great and incomparable riches.

From where, then, did this poverty come? Because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death,” so that he might say: “The waters have entered even to my soul.” Add “unto death”: what more could you add? The disgrace of death. Therefore it follows: “Even the death of the cross” (Phil. II, 6–8).

Great poverty! But from this there will be great riches, because just as his poverty was fulfilled, so our riches will also be fulfilled from his poverty. How great are the riches he possesses, since he made us rich from his poverty! What will he make us through his riches, those whom he made rich through his poverty?

5. “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.” “Substance” may be understood in another way: that which we are, whatever we are. This is somewhat more difficult to understand, although the matter itself is familiar. But because the word is unfamiliar, it requires a little explanation and exposition. If you pay attention, perhaps we will not labor over it.

A man is called a man; an animal, an animal; earth, earth; heaven, heaven; the sun, the moon, a stone, the sea, the air— all these are substances, precisely because they exist. The natures themselves are called substances. God is a certain substance, for whatever is no substance is altogether nothing. Substance, therefore, means being something.

Hence, in the Catholic faith, against the poisons of certain heretics, we are built up in such a way

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “we build up.”]

that we say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance. What does “of one substance” mean? For example, if the Father is gold, the Son is gold, and the Holy Spirit is gold.

Whatever the Father is insofar as he is God, the Son is this, and the Holy Spirit is this. But when the Father is Father, he is not what he is in himself. “Father” is said in relation to the Son; in relation to himself he is called God. Therefore, insofar as he is God, he is substance. And because the Son is of the same substance, without doubt the Son is also God.

But insofar as the Father is Father—because “Father” is not the name of a substance but is referred to the Son—we do not say that the Son is Father in the same way that we say that the Son is God. You ask what the Father is: the answer is, “God.” You ask what the Son is: the answer is, “God.” You ask what the Father and the Son are: the answer is, “God.”

Asked about the Father alone, answer “God.” Asked about the Son alone, answer “God.” Asked about both, do not answer “gods,” but “God.”

It is not so with human beings. You ask what Father Abraham is: the answer is, “A man”; his substance is given as the answer. You ask what his son Isaac is: the answer is, “A man”; Abraham and Isaac are of the same substance. You ask what Abraham and Isaac are: the answer is not “A man,” but “Men.”

It is not so in divine things. For there the fellowship of substance is so great that it admits equality but does not admit plurality. Therefore, if someone says to you, “When you say that the Son is what the Father is, then surely the Son is also the Father,” answer: “I told you that the Son is what the Father is according to substance, not according to that by which one is said in relation to another.”

God is said in relation to himself; the Son is said in relation to the Father. Again, the Father is said in relation to himself as God; in relation to the Son, as Father. What is said of the Father in relation to the Son is not the Son; what is said of the Son in relation to the Father is not the Father. But what is said of the Father in relation to himself, and of the Son in relation to himself, is what the Father and the Son are: namely, God.

What, then, does “there is no substance” mean? According to this understanding of substance, how can we understand this sentence of the Psalm: “I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance”?

God made man; he made a substance. If only man had remained in what God made! If man had remained in what God made, he would not have been stuck in the one whom God begot.

But because, through iniquity, man fell away from the substance in which he was made—for iniquity itself is not a substance; iniquity is not the nature which God formed, but a perversity which man made—the Son of God came to the mud of the deep and was stuck in it. Yet there was no substance in which he was stuck, because he was stuck in their iniquity.

“I am stuck in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.” “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3). All natures were made through him; iniquity was not made through him, because iniquity was not made.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit the words “because iniquity was not made”; in their place, some have: “because iniquity is not a substance.”]

Those substances were made through him which praise him. The entire creation praising God is commemorated by the three boys in the furnace; and from earthly things to heavenly things, or from heavenly things to earthly things, the hymn of those praising God proceeds (Dan. III, 24–90).

This does not mean that all these things possess the understanding necessary to praise; rather, everything rightly contemplated gives rise to praise, and the heart, through consideration of creation, is filled so as to pour forth a hymn to the Creator.

All things praise God—but the things God made. Did you notice in that hymn that greed praises God? The serpent praises God there; greed does not. For all creeping things are named there in the praise of God; all creeping things are named, but no vices are named there.

We possess vices from ourselves and from our own will, and vices are not substances. In these the Lord was stuck when he suffered persecution: in the vice of the Jews, not in the substance of human beings that was made through him.

“I am stuck,” he says, “in the mud of the deep, and there is no substance.” I am stuck, and I did not find what I made.

6. “I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me.” Thanks be to that mercy which came into the depth of the sea and deigned to be swallowed by the sea-monster; but he was vomited out on the third day (Matt. XII, 40).

He came into the depth of the sea, into the depth in which we had been sunk, in which we had suffered shipwreck. He himself came there, and the tempest overwhelmed him, because there he suffered the waves—that is, the very human beings—and the tempests, the voices of those saying, “Crucify, crucify!”

When Pilate said, “I find no cause in this man for which he should be killed,” the voices of those saying, “Crucify, crucify,” grew stronger (John XIX, 6). The tempest increased until the one who had come into the depth of the sea was overwhelmed.

And the Lord suffered at the hands of the Jews what he did not suffer when he walked upon the waters (Matt. XIV, 25)—something which not only he himself had not suffered, but which he had not permitted Peter to suffer either.

“I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me.”

7. [verse 4.] “I labored in crying out; my throat became hoarse.” Where did this happen? When did this happen? Let us question the Gospel. For in this Psalm we recognize our Lord’s Passion. We know that he suffered; we read and believe that the waters entered even to his soul, because the peoples prevailed against him even to his death; we recognize that he was overwhelmed by the tempest, because the uprising prevailed in order to kill him.

But we not only fail to read that he labored by crying out and that his throat became hoarse—we read the contrary. For he did not answer them a word, so that what was said in another Psalm might be fulfilled: “I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth” (Ps. XXXVII, 15); and what was prophesied in Isaiah: “He was led like a sheep to be sacrificed, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

If he became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth, how did he labor in crying out, and how did his throat become hoarse? Or was he already silent because he was hoarse, having cried out so much without cause?

We do know from a certain Psalm that his voice upon the cross was: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI, 2). But how great was that voice, or how long-lasting, for his throat to become hoarse through it?

For a long time he cried out: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. XXIII, 13–14). For a long time he cried out: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. XVIII, 7). And truly, how hoarsely he cried out—and therefore was not understood—when the Jews said: “What is this that he says? This saying is hard; who can hear it? We do not know what he is saying” (John VI, 61; XVI, 18).

He spoke every word, but his throat was hoarse to them, because they did not understand his voices.

“I labored in crying out; my throat became hoarse.”

8. “My eyes failed while hoping in my God.” Far be it from us to understand this as referring to the person of the head. Far be it from us to say that his eyes failed while hoping in his God—in him who was rather God reconciling the world to himself (II Cor. V, 19), and who was the Word made flesh and dwelling among us (John I, 14), so that God was not only in him but he himself was God.

It is not so, then. The eyes of our head himself did not fail while hoping in his God; rather, his eyes failed in his body, that is, in his members. This is the voice of the members; this is the voice of the body, not of the head.

How, then, do we find it in his body and members? What else shall I say? What else shall I recall? When he suffered and died, all the disciples despaired that he was the Christ. The Apostles were overcome by a thief, who believed at the moment when they had failed (Luke XXIII, 42).

See his despairing members; consider those two whom he found conversing with him on the road after the resurrection, one of whom was Cleopas, when their eyes were restrained from recognizing him. For how could they recognize with their eyes the one from whom they were wavering in their minds? Something had occurred in their eyes resembling their state of mind.

They were speaking with each other, and when he asked them what they were discussing, they answered: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem? Do you not know what has happened, how Jesus the Nazarene, powerful in deeds and words, was killed by the elders and chief priests? And we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 13–21).

They had hoped, and they did not hope. “Their eyes failed while hoping in their God.” Therefore he transformed them into himself when he said: “My eyes failed while hoping in my God.”

He restored this hope when he offered his scars to be touched. When Thomas touched them, he returned to the hope he had lost and exclaimed: “My Lord and my God.” Your eyes failed while hoping in your God: you touched the scars and found your God; you touched the form of a servant and recognized your Lord.

Yet the Lord himself said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” And, foretelling us with the voice of his mercy, he said: “Blessed are those who do not see and believe” (John XX, 28–29).

“My eyes failed while hoping in my God.”

9. [verse 5.] “Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head.” How numerous? So numerous that they added even one from the Twelve to themselves (Matt. XXVI, 14).

“Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head.” He compared his enemies to the hairs of his head. Deservedly were they shaved when he was crucified at the place of Calvary.

Let the members receive this voice; let them learn to be hated without cause. Now, Christian, if it is necessary for the world to hate you, why do you not ensure that it hates you without cause, so that in the body of your Lord, and in this Psalm spoken beforehand about him, you may recognize your own voice?

How will you make the world hate you without cause? If you do no harm to anyone and are nevertheless hated, that is “without cause.” Let it not be enough for you to be hated without cause; moreover, make it such that they repay you evil for good.

“My enemies have grown strong, those who persecute me unjustly.” What he said first—“Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head”—he later says as, “My enemies have grown strong”; and what he first called “those who hate me without cause,” he later calls “those who persecute me unjustly.” Thus “without cause” means “unjustly.”

This is the voice of the martyrs—not in the punishment but in the cause. To suffer persecution, to be seized, scourged, imprisoned, proscribed, or killed is not itself praise; rather, to suffer these things while having a good cause is praise. Praise lies in the goodness of the cause, not in the harshness of the punishment.

For however great the punishments of the martyrs may be, are they equal to the punishments of all robbers, all sacrilegious people, and all criminals? And does the world hate these people? It certainly does. For by the magnitude of their wickedness they exceed half the world, so to speak, and are alienated from the fellowship of worldly people, attacking even earthly peace. They suffer many evils, but not without cause.

Finally, consider the voice of the robber who hung with the Lord upon the cross. When one of the two robbers insulted the crucified Lord from the other side and said, “If you are the Son of God, save yourself,” the other restrained him and said: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for what we have done” (Luke XXIII, 39–41).

Behold, not without cause. But by his confession he poured out from himself his putrid discharge.

[Note: Thus two manuscripts. Others, together with the editions, read “blood.”]

and became fit for the Lord’s food. He cast out his iniquity, accused it, and was rid of it.

There were two robbers there, and the Lord also; they were crucified, and he was crucified. The world hated them, but not without cause; it hated him, but without cause.

“What I did not steal, then I paid back.” This is “without cause.” I did not steal, and I paid back; I did not sin, and I suffered punishment. For he alone was such a one; he alone truly stole nothing. Not only did he steal nothing, but even what he possessed not by theft he emptied himself of, so that he might come to us.

“For he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, yet he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6–7). He certainly did not steal.

But who did steal? Adam. Who stole first? The very one who deceived Adam. How did the devil steal? “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13). He arrogated to himself what he had not received: behold, theft.

The devil arrogated to himself what he had not received; he lost what he had received; and from the very cup of his pride he offered a drink to the one whom he wished to deceive: “Taste,” he said, “and you will be like gods” (Gen. III, 5). They wished to steal divinity and lost happiness.

Therefore he stole, and for that reason he paid back. “But I,” he says, “what I did not steal, then I paid back.”

The Lord himself, approaching his Passion, speaks in the Gospel as follows: “Behold, the prince of this world”—that is, the devil—“is coming, and he will find nothing in me”—that is, he will find no reason to kill me. “But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, arise, let us go” (John XIV, 30). And he went to his Passion, to pay back what he had not stolen.

What does “he will find nothing in me” mean? No guilt. Or did the devil lose something from his house? Let him search among the thieves:

[Note: Thus most manuscripts. Erasmus reads “the thief”; Lovaniensis reads “of the thief.”]

he will find nothing in me.

Yet he says that he stole nothing, considering sin—nothing that he had arrogated to himself which did not belong to him. For this is theft; this is iniquity. From the devil himself he extorted those whom the devil had stolen.

“No one enters the house of a strong man and plunders his vessels unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. XII, 29). He bound the strong man and plundered his vessels. Certainly he did not steal them; rather, he answers you: “These vessels had been lost from my great house. I did not commit theft; I recovered a theft.”

### 10. [verse 6]

“God, you knew my folly” [Note: [Col. 0849] So in manuscripts of good quality. But in the editions here: “you know”; and shortly afterward, “you knew.”] Again, this is spoken from the mouth of the body. For what folly is there in Christ? Is he not himself the Power of God and the Wisdom of God? Or does he call that his folly of which the Apostle says: “The foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25)? “My folly”: this very thing by which those who seem wise to themselves mocked me. You knew why it was happening; you knew my folly.

For what is so like folly as this: although he had it in his power, with a single word, to strike down his persecutors, he allowed himself to be seized, scourged, spat upon, struck with blows, crowned with thorns, and fastened to the wood? It is like folly; it seems foolish. Yet this foolishness surpasses all the wise. It is indeed foolishness; but a grain of wheat, when it falls into the earth, also seems foolish if no one knows the farmers’ custom. With great labor it is harvested, carried to the threshing floor, threshed, and winnowed. After so many dangers from the sky and storms, and after the labors of the peasants and the care of the owners, the cleaned grain is put into the granary. Winter comes; and what had been cleaned is brought out and scattered. It seems folly; but hope makes it not folly.

He therefore did not spare himself, because the Father also did not spare him, but “handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). And of him the Apostle says: “He loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. 2:20), because “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it will not yield fruit” (John 12:24–25). This is the folly; but you know it. Yet if they had understood, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

“God, you knew my folly, and my sins are not hidden from you.” This is plainly, clearly, and openly to be understood as spoken from the mouth of the body. Christ had no sins; he was the bearer of sins, but not their perpetrator. “And my sins are not hidden from you”: that is, I have confessed all my sins to you; and before my mouth, you saw them in my thought; you saw the wounds that you were to heal. But where? Certainly in the body, in its members—in those faithful people, from whom that member who was confessing his sins was already attached to him. “And my sins,” he says, “are not hidden from you.”

### 11. [verse 7]

“Let those who wait for you, Lord, Lord of hosts, not be put to shame because of me.” Again, this is the voice of the Head: “Let them not be put to shame because of me.” Let it not be said to them, “Where is the one in whom you trusted?” Let it not be said to them, “Where is the one who told you, ‘Believe in God, and believe in me’?” (John 14:1).

“Let those who wait for you, Lord, [Col. 0850] Lord of hosts, not be put to shame because of me. Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me.” This can also be understood as spoken by the body, provided that you do not take his body to mean one person. For his body is not truly one person: a single person is but a small member, whereas the body consists of members. His complete body, therefore, is the whole Church.

The Church rightly says: “Let those who wait for you, Lord, Lord of hosts, not be put to shame because of me. Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me.” Let me not be so afflicted by rebellious persecutors, so crushed by my envious enemies, by the heretics who went out from me because they were not of me; for if they had been of me, perhaps they would have remained with me (1 John 2:19). Let me not be so oppressed by their scandals that those who wait for you, Lord, Lord of hosts, are put to shame because of me. Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be confounded because of me.

### 12. [verse 8]

“For because of you I endured reproach; disgrace covered my face.” It is not a great thing merely to say, “I endured”; but what is said is, “because of you I endured.” For if you endure because you have sinned, you endure because of yourself, not because of God. “What glory is it,” Peter says, “if, when you sin and are punished, you endure?” (1 Pet. 2:20).

But if you endure because you have kept God’s commandment, then you truly endure because of God, and your reward remains forever, because you endured reproaches for God’s sake. He endured first for this reason: so that we might learn to endure. And if he endured, although he had nothing of what was charged against him, how much more should we, who—even if we do not have the sin that our enemy charges against us—nevertheless have something else in us that can deservedly be scourged?

Someone calls you a thief, although you are not a thief. You hear the reproach; nevertheless, you are not so free of being a thief that there is nothing in you displeasing to God. Moreover, if he who had stolen absolutely nothing, who had most truly said, “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30), was called a sinner (John 9:24), was called wicked, was called Beelzebul (Matt. 10:25), and was called insane, do you, servant, disdain to hear for your merits what the Lord heard without any merits of his own?

He came to provide you an example. As though he had done this gratuitously, you do not profit from it [Note: [Col. 0850] Er. and Lov. read “if”; Am. and the manuscripts, “thus.”]. Why did he hear these things, unless so that you would not fail when you heard them? Behold, you hear and fail; therefore he heard in vain—for he did not hear for himself, but for you.

“For because of you I endured reproach; disgrace covered my face.” “Disgrace,” he says, “covered my face.” What is disgrace? Not being confounded. Indeed, it seems like a vice when one says, “He is a shameless man.” It is a great disgrace in a person not to blush. Thus disgrace is a kind of shamelessness.

A Christian ought to possess this shamelessness when he comes among people who dislike Christ. If he is ashamed of Christ, he will be erased from the book of the living. You therefore need this shamelessness when Christ is insulted on your account, when someone says, “Worshiper of the crucified, adorer of one who died shamefully, venerator of the slain one.” If you are ashamed then, you are dead.

See the judgment of the one who deceives no one: “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, of him I too will be ashamed before the angels of God” (Luke 9:26). [Col. 0851] Take care, then; let there be shamelessness in you. Be bold when you hear reproach concerning Christ—be entirely bold. Why fear for your forehead, which you have armed with the sign of the cross?

This is what is meant by: “Because of you I endured reproach; disgrace covered my face.” Because of you I endured reproach; and because I was not ashamed of you when I was insulted on your account, disgrace covered my face.

### 13. [verses 9–10]

“I have become estranged from my brothers and a stranger to the sons of my mother.” He became a stranger to the sons of the Synagogue. For in his own homeland it was said: “Do we not know that he is the son of Mary and Joseph?” (Luke 4:22). And elsewhere: “But we do not know where he is from” (John 9:29).

“I have become a stranger to the sons of my mother.” They did not know from where I came, although my flesh was from them. They did not know that I was born from Abraham’s thigh—from which my flesh was hidden when the servant placed his hand under that thigh and swore by the God of heaven (Gen. 24:9).

“I have become a stranger to the sons of my mother.” Why this? Why did they not recognize him? Why did they call him a stranger? Why did they dare to say, “We do not know where he is from”? “Because zeal for your house consumed me”—that is, because I pursued their iniquities in them; because I did not patiently tolerate those whom I rebuked; because I sought your glory in your house; because I scourged those behaving improperly in the temple (John 2:15). There too it is written: “Zeal for your house consumed me.”

For this reason he was a stranger; for this reason a foreigner; for this reason they said, “We do not know where he is from.” They would have recognized where he was from if they had recognized what God commanded. For if I had found them keeping your commandments, zeal for your house would not have consumed me.

“And the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.” The Apostle Paul also used this testimony—indeed, the very reading has just been given—and said: “Whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction, so that through the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4).

He therefore said that this was Christ’s voice: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.” Why “of those reproaching you”? Is the Father reproached, and not Christ himself? Why did the reproaches of those reproaching the Father fall upon Christ? Because “whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); because no one reproached Christ without reproaching God; because “no one honors the Father except the one who also honors the Son” (John 5:23). “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me,” because they found me.

### 14. [verse 11]

“And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.” We have already commended Christ’s spiritual fasting to Your Charity in another psalm [Note: [Col. 0851] Above, in the Exposition of Psalm 34, sermon 2, no. 4.].

His fasting was taking place when all who had believed in him fell away; for his hunger was also that people should believe in him. His thirst too was present when he said to the woman, “I thirst; give me something to drink” (John 4:7); he thirsted for her faith. And when he said from the cross, “I thirst” (John 19:28), he was seeking the faith of those for whom he had said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

But what did those people offer him in his thirst? Vinegar. Old wine is also called vinegar [Note: [Col. 0851] So the manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “For vinegar is called old wine.”]. They rightly offered him something from the old person, because they did not wish to be new. Why did they not wish to be new? Because they did not belong to what is written in the title of this psalm: “For those who will be changed.” [Col. 0852]

“Therefore I covered my soul with fasting.” Finally, he also rejected the gall that they offered him: he chose to fast rather than receive bitterness. For embittered people do not enter into his body; of them the psalm says elsewhere: “Those who embitter should not exalt themselves” (Ps. 65:7).

“Therefore I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.” This very thing became a reproach to me: that I did not agree with them—that is, that I fasted from them. For one who does not consent to those giving evil advice fasts from them; and through this fasting he earns reproach, so that he is insulted precisely because he does not consent to evil.

### 15. [verse 12]

“And I made sackcloth my clothing.” We have already said something about sackcloth [Note: [Col. 0852] Exposition of Psalm 34, sermon 2, no. 3.], from which comes the passage: “But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting.”

“I made sackcloth my clothing”: that is, I set my flesh before them as something against which they could rage; I concealed my divinity. It was sackcloth because it was mortal flesh, so that “he might condemn sin in the flesh because of sin” (Rom. 8:3).

“And I made sackcloth my clothing, and I became a proverb to them”—that is, an object of mockery. A proverb is used when a likeness is offered concerning something, when something is spoken of maliciously. Thus, for example, “May he perish as that man did” is a proverb—that is, a comparison and likeness expressing a curse. “And I became a proverb to them.”

### 16. [verse 13]

“Those sitting at the gate insulted me.” “At the gate” means nothing other than in public. “And those who drank wine sang about me.”

Do you think, brothers, that this happened only to Christ? Every day it happens to him in his members. When it becomes necessary for a servant of God to forbid drunkenness and debauchery in some estate or town where the word of God has not been heard, it is not enough that they sing; they even begin to sing against the one by whom they are forbidden to sing.

Now compare Christ’s fasting with their wine. “And those who drank wine sang about me”: the wine of error, the wine of impiety, the wine of pride.

### 17. [verse 14]

“But I, in my prayer” [Note: [Col. 0852] The editions read, “my prayer.” But the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, read “in my prayer,” with “I was” understood, as Augustine immediately explains.] “to you, Lord.” But I was directed toward you. How? By praying to you.

For when you are cursed and have no means of knowing what to do; when reproaches are hurled at you and you cannot find a way to correct the one hurling them, nothing remains for you except to pray. But remember to pray for that person too.

“But I, in my prayer, was directed toward you, Lord.” “The time of your favor, O God.” For behold, the grain is buried; the fruit will rise. “The time of your favor, O God.” Concerning this time the Prophets also spoke, as the Apostle recalls: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

“The time of your favor, O God, in the abundance of your mercy.” This is the time of your favor: “in the abundance of your mercy.” For if there were not an abundance of your mercy, what would we do with the abundance [Col. 0853] of our iniquity?

“In the abundance of your mercy, hear me in the truth of your salvation.” Because he said “your mercy,” he added “the truth,” since “mercy and truth are all the ways of the Lord” (Ps. 24:10). Why mercy? Because he forgives sins. Why truth? Because he fulfills his promises. “Hear me in the truth of your salvation.”

### 18. [verse 15]

“Save me from the mud, so that I may not stick fast.” He had said above: “I am stuck in the deep mire, and there is no firm ground.” Since you received that passage well when it was explained, there is no need to hear it expressed more fully here. He says that he must be freed from the place where he previously said he was stuck: “Save me from the mud, so that I may not stick fast.”

He himself explains this: “I will be delivered from those who hate me.” They, then, are the mud in which I was stuck.

But perhaps someone will suggest this difficulty. Shortly before he said, “I am stuck”; now he says, “Save me from the mud, so that I may not stick fast,” whereas, according to the earlier statement, he ought to have said: “Save me from the mud in which I was stuck,” by delivering me, not by preventing me from sticking fast.

He was therefore stuck in the flesh, but he was not stuck in spirit. He says this from the weakness of his members. When you are perhaps seized by someone who presses you toward iniquity, your body is indeed held; according to the body, you are stuck in the deep mire. But as long as you do not consent, you have not stuck fast. If you consent, then you have stuck fast.

Let your prayer therefore be that, just as your body is now held, your soul may not also be held; that you may be free in your chains. “I will be delivered from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters.”

### 19. [verse 16]

“Let the storm of water not drown me.” But he had already been submerged: “I came into the depth of the sea,” you said; “and the storm submerged me,” you said. It submerged him according to the flesh; let it not drown him according to the spirit.
