To those who were told, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23), this was said so that they might be held neither in flesh nor in spirit. For we must not seek even to be held in the flesh; rather, as far as we can, we ought to avoid it.

But if we are held and fall into the hands of sinners, then we are held in the body; we are stuck in the deep mire. It remains to pray for the soul, so that we may not stick fast—that is, may not consent; so that the storm of water may not drown us and carry us into the depth of the mud.

“Nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me.”

What is this, brothers? What did he ask? The depth of human iniquity is a great pit; if anyone falls into it, he will fall into the depths. Yet if, while placed there, he confesses his sins to his God, the pit will not close its mouth over him. As it is written in another psalm: “From the depths I cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice” (Ps. 129:1–2).

But if what another sentence of Scripture says happens in him—“When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he will despise” (Prov. 18:3)—the pit has closed its mouth over him. Why has it closed its mouth? Because it has closed his mouth. He has lost confession; he is truly dead, and in him is fulfilled what is said elsewhere: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Sir. 17:26).

This is a matter to be greatly feared, brothers. If you see a person committing iniquity, [Col. 0854] he has sunk into the pit. But when you point out his iniquity to him and he says, “I have truly sinned; I confess it,” the pit has not closed its mouth over him. When, however, you see him say, “What evil have I done?” he has become the defender of his sin; the pit has closed its mouth over him, and he has no means of being rescued.

Once confession is lost, there will be no place for mercy. You have become the defender of your sin; how will God be your deliverer? Therefore, if he is to be your deliverer, you must be your own accuser.

## SERMON II. On the latter part of the same Psalm

### 1. [verses 16–17]

The latter part of the psalm about which we spoke to Your Charity yesterday remained for us to explain today. And I see that it is time to pay the debt, provided that its length does not leave us debtors today as well.

I therefore say this in advance, and I ask you not to expect a lengthy discourse on matters that are clear. In this way we can spend the necessary time on the more obscure passages and perhaps make up what we owe, so that on other days we may owe and repay other things.

Let us see, then, what follows. After he said, “Nor let the pit close its mouth over me”—a passage we commended to Your Charity yesterday, urging that we guard against this curse with complete attention of mind and faith—he explained that the pit closes its mouth over a person when the depth of iniquity not only has him lying submerged in sins, but also deprives him of access to confession.

When a person says, “I am a sinner,” some light shines even into the depth of the pit.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Head and the body, therefore continues, crying out amid his sufferings. As we have explained, in some passages you should recognize the words of the Head; but whatever is said in such a way that it cannot apply to the Head should be referred to the body. Christ speaks in this way as one, because he is truly one, of whom it is said: “The two will be one flesh” (Eph. 5:31). If they are one flesh, why are you surprised that they are also one voice?

He continues: “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is good.” He stated the reason why he should be heard: because God’s mercy is good. Would it not have been more logical for him to say, “Hear me, Lord, so that your mercy may be good to me”? Why, then, does he say, “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is good”?

He commended the goodness of the Lord’s mercy in his tribulation in other words when he said, “Hear me, Lord, for I am afflicted.” Indeed, the person who says, “Hear me, Lord, for I am afflicted,” gives the reason why he asks to be heard. But for a person placed in tribulation, God’s mercy must be good.

See what Scripture says elsewhere about this goodness of God’s mercy: “As rain in drought, so beautiful is God’s mercy in tribulation” (Sir. 35:26). What it calls “beautiful” there, it calls “good” here.

Bread would not be sweet unless hunger had preceded it. Therefore, even when the Lord permits or causes us to be in some tribulation, he is merciful then also. He does not remove nourishment; he arouses desire.

What, then, does he say now? “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is good.” Do not delay hearing me any longer. I am in such great tribulation that your mercy is good to me. You delayed coming to my aid so that what you gave me might be sweet; now there is no reason for you to delay any longer. My tribulation has reached the appointed measure of calamity; let your mercy come to perform its work of goodness.

“Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is good. According to the abundance of your compassion, look upon me”—not according to the abundance of my sins.

### 2. [verse 18]

“Do not turn your face away from your servant” [Note: [Col. 0855] The words “of humility” are absent from the manuscripts.]. This too is a commendation of humility: “from your servant,” that is, from one who is little, because through the discipline of tribulation I have now been stripped of pride.

“Do not turn your face away from your servant.” This is the beautiful mercy of God that he mentioned above. For in the following verse he explains what he said: “For I am afflicted; hear me quickly.”

What does “quickly” mean? There is no reason for you to delay any longer. I am afflicted; my distress has gone before you, and let your mercy follow.

### 3. [verse 19]

“Attend to my soul and redeem it.” This needs no explanation. Let us see, then, what follows: “Because of my enemies, deliver me.”

This is plainly a remarkable petition; it should neither be treated briefly nor passed over hurriedly. It is altogether remarkable: “Because of my enemies, deliver me.”

What does “Because of my enemies, deliver me” mean? So that they may be confounded, so that they may be tormented by my deliverance. What, then, if there were no enemies who would be tormented by my deliverance? Should I not be helped? Is your deliverance acceptable to you only when it involves another’s condemnation?

Suppose there are no enemies who will be either confounded or tormented by your deliverance. Will you remain as you are? Will you not be delivered? Or is the meaning that your enemies may benefit, so that they too may be converted through your deliverance?

But this too is remarkable, if it provides any reason for the petition. Is a servant of God delivered by the Lord his God so that others may profit? What if there were no one to profit? Was that servant of God then not to be delivered?

However I turn, whether toward the punishment or toward the deliverance of enemies, I do not see the reason for this petition, “Because of my enemies, deliver me”—unless we understand something which, with the Lord’s help, the one who dwells in you will judge when I have said it.

There is a hidden deliverance of the saints; this takes place for the saints themselves. There is also a public and manifest deliverance; this takes place because of their enemies, whether those enemies are to be punished or delivered [Note: [Col. 0855] At this point the editions inserted: “that God delivers his saints, some secretly and others publicly: secretly, as the Maccabees; publicly, as when he led the three boys out of the fiery furnace.” These words are not found in the better manuscripts.].

For God certainly did not deliver the Maccabean brothers from the fires of their persecutor. The raging Antiochus even brought in their mother, whose caresses were intended to turn them toward love of life, so that by loving life they would die to God. But that mother—now resembling not Eve but the mother Church—had borne them in sorrow so that she might recognize them alive; she saw them die with joy. She urged them to choose rather to die for the paternal laws of the Lord their God than to live against them.

What are we to believe here, brothers, except that they were delivered? Their deliverance, however, was hidden. [Col. 0856] Finally, Antiochus himself, by whom they were killed, seemed to himself to have done something dictated—or rather provoked—by his cruelty (2 Macc. 7).

But the three boys were openly delivered from the fiery furnace (Dan. 3:49), because their bodies were rescued and their salvation was public. They were therefore crowned secretly; the others were delivered openly. Yet all were saved.

What was the benefit of the deliverance of the three boys? Why was their crown made widely known? Nebuchadnezzar himself was converted to their God and proclaimed him, because he had delivered his servants—the God whom Nebuchadnezzar had despised when he sent them into the furnace.

There is therefore a hidden deliverance, and there is a manifest deliverance. Hidden deliverance concerns the soul; manifest deliverance concerns the body as well. In secret the soul is delivered; openly the body is delivered.

If this is so, let us recognize the Lord’s voice in this psalm. The hidden deliverance is meant by what he said above: “Attend to my soul and redeem it.” The deliverance of the body remains. When the body rose, ascended into heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit from above (Acts 1:9; 2:4), those who had raged against him in his death were converted to his faith; they became friends from enemies through his grace, not through their own righteousness.

Therefore he continues: “Because of my enemies, deliver me.” “Attend to my soul”—but this takes place secretly. “Because of my enemies, deliver me” [Note: [Col. 0856] Here Lov. and some manuscripts add “me.”]—and my body as well.

For it will profit my enemies nothing if you deliver only my soul: they will believe that they have accomplished something and brought something to completion. “What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?” (Ps. 29:10).

Therefore: “Attend to my soul and redeem it”—something known only to you. Then also, because of my enemies, deliver me, so that my flesh may not see corruption.

### 4. [verse 20]

“For you know my reproach, my confusion, and my shame.” What is reproach? What is confusion? What is shame?

Reproach is what the enemy charges against someone. Confusion is what gnaws at the conscience. Shame is what makes even an open and honorable face blush at the accusation of a false crime. [Note: [Col. 0856] So the manuscripts. After “blush at the accusation,” the editions continue: “Blushing indeed is not a crime; or, if it is a crime, it belongs not to the person against whom it is charged, but to the person who charges it. Yet the weakness,” etc.]

It is not a crime; or, even if it is a crime, it does not belong to the one against whom it is charged. Nevertheless, the weakness of the human spirit often feels shame even when a false charge is made—not because it has been charged, but because it has been believed.

All these things are found in the body of the Lord. For confusion could not exist in him, since no guilt was found in him. Christians were charged with the crime of being Christians. That was indeed a glory: the strong gladly accepted it, and accepted it in such a way that they were not ashamed at all of the name of their Lord.

For disgrace had covered the face of those who possessed the forehead of Paul, who said: “I am not ashamed [Col. 0857] of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Rom. 1:16).

O Paul, are you not a worshiper of the Crucified One? “It is too little,” he says, “for me not to be ashamed of it. Rather, I glory in the very thing of which the enemy thinks I should be ashamed.” “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Only reproach could therefore be charged against such a forehead. There could be no confusion in a conscience that had already been healed, nor shame on so free a face.

But when some were charged with having killed Christ, they were rightly pierced by an evil conscience, and were salutarily confounded and converted, so that they could say: “You have known my confusion.”

You, then, Lord, know not only my reproach but also my confusion. In some there is also shame: although they believe in me, they are nevertheless ashamed to confess me publicly before the ungodly, because human speech has more influence with them than the divine promise.

See them, then. Such people are commended to God—not so that he may leave them as they are, but so that by helping them he may bring them to perfection. For one man who believed yet wavered said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:23).

“In your sight are all those who trouble me.” You know why I suffer reproach; you know why there is confusion; you know why there is shame. Therefore, because of my enemies, deliver me, since you know these things about me, while they do not know them. And because they themselves are in your sight, they cannot be either confounded or corrected in their ignorance unless you openly deliver me because of my enemies.

### 5. [verse 21]

“My heart expected reproach and misery.” What does “expected” mean? He foresaw these future things and foretold them. For he did not come for anything else. If he did not wish to die, he would not have wished to be born. He did both for the sake of resurrection.

Two things were known to us in the human race, but one was unknown. We knew that human beings are born and die; we did not know that they rise again and live forever. To show us what we did not know, he took upon himself the two things we did know.

For this reason he came: “My heart expected reproach and misery.” But whose misery? He expected misery, especially the misery of those crucifying and persecuting him, so that misery might be in them and mercy in him. For, pitying their misery even while hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

“My heart expected reproach and misery; and I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none.” What benefit was there, then, in my expecting it—that is, in my foretelling it? What benefit was there in my saying that I had come for this? The time came when what I had said was fulfilled: “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for those who would comfort me, and I found none”—that is, there was none.

What he said in the preceding verse, “I looked for one who would grieve with me,” he says in the following verse as “and for those who would comfort me.” What he said in the preceding verse as “and there was none,” he says in the following verse as “and I found none.” Thus the later statement is not a different one added afterward, but a repetition of the preceding statement.

If we reconsider this statement, a certain question may arise. Were his disciples not grieved when he was led to his passion, when he was suspended on the wood, and when he died? They were so deeply grieved [Col. 0858] that Mary Magdalene, who saw him first, joyfully announced to those who were mourning what she had seen (John 20:18; Mark 16:9).

The Gospel speaks of this; it is not our presumption or suspicion. It is certain that the disciples grieved; it is certain that they mourned. Foreign women were weeping when he was led to his passion. He turned to them and said: “Weep—but not for me” (Luke 23:28).

How, then, did he look for one who would grieve with him, and there was none? We pay attention and find them grieving, mourning, and lamenting; therefore this statement seems astonishing to us: “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for those who would comfort me, and I found none.”

Let us look more carefully, and we shall see that he looked for one who would grieve with him, and there was none. They were grieving carnally over mortal life, which was to be changed through death and restored through resurrection. Their sadness arose from this.

The kind of companion he needed in his grief should have been found among those who, being blind, killed the physician; who, like lunatics suffering from a destructive fever, were doing injury to the one who had brought them healing. He wished to heal; they raged. This was the physician’s grief.

Ask whether he found anyone to share this grief. For he does not say, “I looked for one who would grieve, and there was none,” but “one who would grieve with me”—that is, who would grieve because of the very thing that grieved me—and I found none.

Peter certainly loved him greatly. Without hesitation he threw himself onto the waves and was rescued at the Lord’s voice (Matt. 14:29, 31). He followed him when he was led to his passion, with the boldness of love; yet, being troubled, he denied him three times.

Why, unless because it seemed evil to him that Christ should die? He was avoiding what he regarded as evil. Thus he too grieved in the Lord over what he himself was avoiding.

For this reason he had said earlier: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be favorable to you; this shall never happen”—for which he deserved to hear, “Satan,” after he had heard, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah” (Matt. 16:17, 22–23).

In the sadness that the Lord had over those for whom he prayed, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,” he found no companion. “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none.” There was absolutely none.

“And for those who would comfort me, and I found none.” Who are those who comfort? Those who make progress. They comfort us; they are a consolation to all preachers of the truth.

### 6. [verse 22]

“And they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

This did happen literally, and the Gospel tells us so. But we must understand, brothers, that the very fact that I found no one to comfort me, the very fact that I found no one who would grieve with me, was my gall, my bitterness, and my vinegar: bitterness because of their sorrow, vinegar because of their oldness.

For we read that gall was indeed offered to him, as the Gospel says (Matt. 27:34), but as a drink, not as food. Nevertheless, we must understand and recognize a mystery in the way this was both foretold and fulfilled: “They gave gall for my food.” In this very action—not only in the statement—we must seek the mystery, knock upon the hidden things, enter through the torn veil of the temple, and see the sacrament there, whether in what was said in this way or in what was done in this way.

“They gave,” he says, “gall for my food.” What they gave was not itself food, for it was a drink; but they gave it as food because the Lord [Col. 0859] had already received food, and the gall was injected into that food.

He had received sweet food when he ate the Passover with his disciples; there he displayed the sacrament of his body (Luke 22:19). Into this food, so sweet and pleasant—the unity of Christ, which the Apostle commends when he says, “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. 10:17)—who gives gall except those who contradict the Gospel, like those persecutors of Christ?

For the Jews who crucified him walking on earth sinned less than those who despise him sitting in heaven. What the Jews did, giving that bitter drink to be consumed with the food he had already received, is done by those whose evil lives bring scandal upon the Church. Heretics who embitter do this; but “they should not exalt themselves” (Ps. 65:7). They give gall upon such a pleasant food.

But what does the Lord do? He does not admit them to his body. Through this sacrament the Lord himself, when they offered him gall, tasted it and refused to drink (Matt. 27:34).

If we did not have to endure such people, we would not taste them at all. But since we must endure them, they must be tasted. Yet because such people cannot be members of Christ, they can be tasted, but they cannot be received into the body.

“And they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” I was thirsty, and I received vinegar: that is, I desired their faith and found their oldness.

### 7. [verses 23–24]

“Let their table before them become a snare.” Let the snare they presented to me by giving me such a drink become such a snare for them. Why, then, “before them”? It would have been enough to say, “Let their table become a snare.” There are people who know their iniquity and persist in it with the greatest stubbornness: their snare is made before them. They themselves are exceedingly pernicious, who “go down alive into hell” (Ps. 54:16). Finally, what was said about the persecutors? “If the Lord had not been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Ps. 123:2–3). What does “alive” mean? Consenting to them, and knowing that we ought not to consent to them. Therefore their snare is made before them, and they are not corrected.

Or does “because the snare is before them” mean that they should not fall into it? *[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “and they fall into it.”]* Behold, they know the snare, yet they put in their foot and submit their necks to be held. How much better it would have been to turn away from the snare: to recognize sin, condemn error, be free from bitterness, pass into the body of Christ, and seek the glory of the Lord! But the presumption of the mind is so powerful that, although the snare is before them, they still fall into it.

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see”—this follows here: since they saw without cause, let it also happen to them not to see. Therefore, “Let their table before them become a snare.” “Before them let it become a snare” is not the utterance of one wishing this, but of one prophesying it—not that it may happen, but because it will happen. We have often emphasized this, and you ought to remember it, lest what a prophetic mind speaks in the Spirit of God appear to be a malicious curse. Let it happen, then; nor can it happen otherwise, except that such things befall such people.

And since we see such things foretold by the Spirit of God as destined to happen to the wicked, let us understand them in them for this purpose: that we may avoid such things ourselves. *[Col. 0860]* For it benefits us to understand this and to profit from our enemies. Let it therefore happen to them both “for retribution” and “for a stumbling-block.” Is this unjust? It is just. Why? Because it is for retribution: nothing would happen to them that they had not deserved. It happens for retribution and for a stumbling-block, because they themselves are a stumbling-block to themselves.

### 8.

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and always bend their backs.” This follows naturally. For when their eyes have been darkened so that they do not see, it follows that their backs should be bent. Why is this? Because when they cease to perceive heavenly things, they must think about things below.

Whoever hears correctly, “Lift up your hearts,” does not have a bent back. Standing upright, he awaits the hope laid up for him in heaven, especially if he sends his treasure ahead, so that his heart may follow it (Matt. 6:21). But those who are already blinded and do not understand the hope of the future life think about things below; and this is to have a bent back. From this disease the Lord freed that woman. Satan had bound her for eighteen years; he raised her up when she was bent over *[Note: Almost all the manuscripts read “he healed her.”]*, and because he did this on the Sabbath the Jews were scandalized. They were rightly scandalized by her being upright, while they themselves were bent over (Luke 13:16). “And always bend their backs.”

### 9. [verse 25]

“Pour out your anger upon them, and may the indignation of your wrath overtake them.” These words are clear; yet when it says, “may it overtake them,” we recognize them as fugitives. But where will they flee? Into heaven? You are there. Into hell? You are present there also (Ps. 138:8). They do not wish to receive their wings, so that they might fly straight onward: “May the indignation of your wrath overtake them”; let it not permit them to escape.

### 10. [verse 26]

“Let their dwelling become desolate.” This is now evident. Just as he commended his deliverance not only as hidden, saying, “Attend to my soul and redeem it,” but also as manifest according to the body, adding, “For the sake of my enemies, rescue me,” so he also foretells certain future calamities for them, hidden calamities of which he had been speaking shortly before.

For how many are there who understand the misery of a person whose heart is already blind? Let the eyes of his body be taken away: everyone calls him miserable. Let him lose the eyes of his mind, yet abound in every abundance of worldly things: they call him happy—those who have likewise lost the eyes of their mind.

What, then, will be made manifest, so that it may appear to all that vengeance has been exacted upon them? The blindness of the Jews is hidden vengeance; but what is manifest? “Let their dwelling become desolate, and in their tents let there be none who inhabits them.”

This happened in the city of Jerusalem itself, in which they thought themselves powerful when they shouted against the Son of God, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6), and prevailed because they were able to kill him who raised the dead. How powerful, how great they seemed to themselves! Afterwards the Lord’s vengeance followed: the city was conquered, the Jews were defeated, and I do not know how many thousands of people were killed. No Jew is now permitted to approach there, where they were able to shout against the Lord; there they are not permitted by the Lord to dwell. They lost the place of their fury. Would that even now they might recognize the place of their peace!

What did Caiaphas gain by saying, “If we let this man go on in this way, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation” (John 11:48)? Behold, they did not let him remain alive, yet he lives; and the Romans came and took away from them both their place and their nation.

We heard just now, when the Gospel was being read: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:37–38). This too is said here: “Let their dwelling become desolate, and in their tents let there be none who inhabits them.”

Let there be none who inhabits them—but none from their number. For all those places are now full of people, yet empty of Jews.

### 11. [verse 27]

“Why this? Because they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds.”

What, then, was their sin, if they persecuted one who had been struck by God? What is charged to their account? Malice. For what ought to have happened was done to Christ. He had certainly come to suffer, and he punished the one through whom he suffered. Judas the betrayer was punished, and Christ was crucified; but he redeemed us by his blood, and punished Judas on account of his own price.

For Judas threw down the silver—the price for which the Lord had been sold by him—and did not recognize the price by which he himself had been redeemed *[Note: Two manuscripts read, “was to be redeemed.”]* (Matt. 27:5). This happened in Judas.

But when we see that there is a certain measure of retribution in everything, and that no one can be permitted to rage more than the power granted to him allows, how did they “add” to the Lord’s suffering, and what is this striking of the Lord?

He spoke, surely, from the person of the one from whom he had received his body and assumed flesh—that is, from the human race, from Adam himself, who was first struck by death on account of his sin (Gen. 3:19). Human beings, therefore, are born mortal and under punishment; and whoever persecutes human beings adds to this punishment.

This man would not already be dying unless God had struck him. Why, then, do you, a human being, rage further? Is it not enough for a human being that one day he will die? Each of us therefore bears his own punishment; those who persecute us wish to add to this punishment.

This punishment is the striking of the Lord. For the Lord struck humanity with a sentence: “On the day when you eat of it, you shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17). From this death he assumed flesh, and our old man was crucified together with him (Rom. 6:6). From the voice of that old man he said this: “The one whom you struck, they persecuted, and they added to the pain of my wounds.”

To what pain of wounds? They added to the pain of sins; for he called his sins his wounds. But do not look only to the head; attend to the body, according to whose voice he himself spoke in that psalm in which he manifested his voice, since he cried out its first verse from the cross: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” There he continued: “The words of my sins are far from my salvation” (Ps. 21:2).

These are the wounds inflicted by robbers along the road upon the man whom he lifted onto his own beast. The priest and the *[Col. 0862]* Levite had found him as they passed by and despised him; they could not heal him. But the Samaritan, as he passed by, had compassion on him, approached him, and lifted him onto his own beast (Luke 10:30–34).

“Samaritan” is interpreted in Latin as “Guardian” (*Custos*). And who is the guardian except our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior? Since he has risen from the dead and will die no more (Rom. 6:9), “he neither sleeps nor slumbers who guards Israel” (Ps. 120:4). “And they added to the pain of my wounds.”

### 12. [verse 28]

“Add iniquity upon their iniquity.” What does this mean? Who would not be terrified? God is told, “Add iniquity upon their iniquity.” From where would God add iniquity? Does he have iniquity to add? We know that what the apostle Paul said is true: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not!” (Rom. 9:14).

How, then, are we to understand, “Add iniquity upon their iniquity”? May the Lord assist us to speak, and enable us to speak briefly for the sake of your weariness.

Their iniquity was that they killed a righteous man; another was added because they crucified the Son of God. Their rage was directed against him as a man; but “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). In their iniquity they wished to kill him as a man; iniquity was added upon their iniquity, so that they crucified the Son of God.

Who added this iniquity? The one who said, “Perhaps they will respect my son; I will send him” (Matt. 21:37). They had been accustomed to kill the servants sent to them, the collectors of rent and payment. He sent his own Son, so that they might kill him too. He added iniquity upon their iniquity.

Did God do this by raging, or rather by justly repaying them? “Let it happen to them,” he says, “for retribution and for a stumbling-block.” They deserved to be blinded in such a way that they would not recognize the Son of God.

God did this by adding iniquity upon their iniquity—not by wounding them, but by not healing them. Just as one increases a fever or aggravates an illness not by administering the disease but by failing to give assistance, so, because they were such that they did not deserve to be healed, they somehow advanced in their very wickedness, as it is said: “But evil people and wrongdoers will advance toward worse” (2 Tim. 3:13). Thus iniquity was added upon their iniquity.

“And may they not enter into your righteousness.” This is clear.

### 13. [verse 29]

“Let them be blotted out of the book of the living.” Were they once written there? Brothers, we must not understand this as though God writes someone in the book of life and then erases him. If a human being said, “What I have written, I have written,” concerning the inscription on which was written “King of the Jews” (John 19:22), does God write someone and then erase him?

The matter is settled: he predestined before the foundation of the world all who would reign with his Son in eternal life (Rom. 8:29). He wrote these people into the book; the book of life contains them.

Finally, what does the Spirit of God say in the Apocalypse when that same Scripture speaks about the future tribulations under the Antichrist? “All who are not written in the book of life will consent to him” (Rev. 13:8). *[Col. 0863]* Therefore, without doubt, those who are written in it will not consent.

How, then, are these people erased from a place where they were never written? This was said according to their hope, because they thought themselves written there. What does “Let them be blotted out of the book of life” mean? Let it become clear even to them that they are not there.

The same manner of speaking occurs in another psalm: “A thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90:7). This means that many will be scandalized, both from the number of those who hoped that they would sit with you and from the number of those who hoped that they would stand at your right hand, separated from the goats on the left (Matt. 25:33). It does not mean that someone who has stood there will later fall, or that someone who has sat with him will be cast out; rather, many who thought themselves already there were destined to fall into scandal. That is, many who hoped to sit with you, and many who hoped to stand at your right hand, will themselves fall.

So here too, those who hoped that they had been written in God’s book on account of the merit of their righteousness—those to whom it is said, “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life” (John 5:39)—when their condemnation has also been brought to their knowledge, will be blotted out of the book of the living; that is, they will realize that they are not there.

For the following verse explains what was said: “And may they not be written with the righteous.” I said, “Let them be blotted out,” according to their hope; but according to your justice, what shall I say? “May they not be written.”

### 14. [verse 30]

“I am poor and sorrowful.” Why this? Is it so that we might recognize that this poor man curses them out of the bitterness of his soul? For he said many things that would befall them. And as though we were to say to him, “Why such things? Do not go so far,” he replies: “I am poor and sorrowful.” They reduced me to poverty and brought me down into this sorrow; therefore I say these things.

Yet this is not the irritation of one who curses, but the prediction of one who prophesies. For concerning his poverty and sorrow he will later commend certain things to us, so that we may learn to be poor and sorrowful. “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”; and, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:3, 5).

He first showed this to us in himself; therefore, “I am poor and sorrowful.” His whole body says this. The body of Christ is poor and sorrowful on this earth.

But let Christians be rich. Certainly, if they are Christians, they are poor: in comparison with the heavenly riches they hope for, they count all their gold as sand. “I am poor and sorrowful.”

### 15. [verse 31]

“And the salvation of your countenance, O God, has received me.” Is this poor man abandoned? When do you deign to bring a ragged poor man to your table?

Yet the salvation of God’s countenance received this poor man; in his countenance he hid his poverty. For it was said of them: “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your countenance” (Ps. 30:21).

Do you wish to know what riches are found in that countenance? These riches provide you with whatever you want, whenever you want it, for lunch; but those riches provide that you never hunger.

“I am poor and sorrowful; and the salvation of your countenance, O God, has received me.” For what purpose? So that I may no longer be poor, no longer sorrowful.

“I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with praise.” It has already been said: this poor man praises the name of God with a song and magnifies him with praise. How would *[Col. 0864]* he dare to sing unless he had been restored from hunger?

“I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with praise.” Great riches! What jewels of praise to God he has brought forth from his inner treasure! “I will magnify him with praise.” These are my riches. “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away.” Did misery remain? Certainly not. Behold the riches: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). “I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with praise.”

### 16. [verse 32]

“And it will please God”—this praise of mine will please him—“more than a young bull producing horns and hooves.” The sacrifice of praise will be more pleasing to him than the sacrifice of a bull.

“The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God. Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49:23, 14).

Therefore I will praise God, and my praise will please him more than a young bull producing horns and hooves. My praise proceeding from my mouth will please God more than a large victim brought to his altar.

Should something be said about the horns and hooves of this bull? Whoever is well instructed, rich in the praise of God, ought to have horns with which to drive away his adversary, and hooves with which to stir up the earth. For you know that young bulls do this as they mature and grow into the boldness of bulls.

It is called young because of the new life. If some heretic contradicts, let him be driven away by the horns. Another does not contradict but thinks in an abjectly earthly way; let him be stirred up by the hooves.

Therefore, “over this bull my praise will please you”—then, after poverty and sorrow, in the eternal fellowship of the angels, where there will be no adversary to drive away in combat and no sluggish person to stir up from the earth. *[Note: Thus the better manuscripts. Others read, “then that [praise] after,” etc.; the editions, “for that [praise] after,” etc. This is incorrect unless “that” is referred to “Let the poor see,” etc.]*

### 17. [verse 33]

“Let the poor see and rejoice.” Let them believe and rejoice in hope. Let them be poorer still, so that they may deserve to be filled; lest, while they belch up the fullness of pride, they be denied the bread by which they may live healthfully.

“Seek the Lord, you poor; hunger and thirst” (Matt. 5:6), for he is the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6:51). “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live.” You seek bread so that your flesh may live; seek the Lord so that your soul may live.

### 18. [verse 34]

“For the Lord has heard the poor.” He has heard the poor; nor would he hear the poor unless they were poor. Do you wish to be heard? Be poor: let sorrow cry out from you, not disdain.

“For the Lord has heard the poor, and he has not despised his prisoners.” Offended by his servants, he made them prisoners; but he did not despise them when they cried out from their chains.

What are these chains? Mortality and the corruptibility of the flesh are the chains by which we are bound. Do you wish to know the weight of these chains? It is said: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

When people wish to be rich in this world, they seek clothing for these chains. But let the clothing of the chains be sufficient; seek only *[Col. 0865]* as much as is enough to remove necessity. When you seek what is superfluous, you desire to load your chains.

In such a prison, then, let the chains alone remain. “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matt. 6:34). From this trouble we cry out to God: “For the Lord has heard the poor, and he has not despised his prisoners.”

### 19. [verse 35]

“Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and everything that creeps in them.” These are the true riches of this poor man: to contemplate creation and praise the Creator.

“Let heaven and earth praise him, the sea and everything that creeps in them.” And creation alone praises God when, having been contemplated, God is praised.

### 20. [verses 36–37]

Hear something else: “For God will save Zion.” He repairs his Church; he incorporates the faithful nations into his Only-Begotten Son; he does not defraud those who believe in him of the reward of his promise.

“For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built.” *[Note: Thus the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint; another reading is “the cities of Judah.”]* These are the Churches. Let no one say, “When will this happen, that the cities of Judah may be built?” If only you would recognize the structure and become a living stone, so that you might enter into it!

Even now the cities of Judah are being built. For “Judah” is interpreted as “Confession.” The cities of Judah are built from the confession of humility, so that the proud, who are ashamed to confess, may remain outside them.

“For God will save Zion.” Which Zion? Hear in what follows: “And the offspring of his servants shall possess it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.”

### 21.

The psalm has ended; but let us not leave these two verses without a brief discussion. They admonish us about something, lest through despair we fail to enter that structure.

“His servants’ offspring,” he says, “shall possess it.” Who, then, are the offspring of his servants? Perhaps you say: the Jews born from Abraham. But how shall we possess this city, since we were not born from Abraham?

Those Jews to whom it was said, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39), are not Abraham’s offspring. Therefore the offspring of his servants—the imitators of the faith of his servants—shall possess it.

Finally, the last verse explains the preceding one. As though someone were troubled, lest you think that this was said about the Jews—“His servants’ offspring shall possess it”—and were to say, “We are the offspring of nations that worshiped idols and served demons; what hope can we have in this city?” he immediately added something to encourage and give hope: “And those who love his name shall dwell in it.”

For this is the offspring of his servants: those who love his name. Since his servants loved his name, whoever does not love his name must not call himself the offspring of his servants; and those who love his name must not deny that they are the offspring of his servants.

## Exposition of Psalm 69. Sermon

*[Note: Delivered on the solemnity of the martyrs.]*

### 1. [verse 2]

Thanks be to the grain of wheat, because it was willing to die and multiply (John 12:25); thanks be to the only Son of God, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who did not disdain to undergo our *[Col. 0866]* death, so that he might make us worthy of his life.

Behold, he who was singular until he passed over, as he said in the psalm, “I am singular until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10). For he was a singular grain in such a way that he contained within himself the great fecundity of a multitude. In how many grains imitating his passion do we rejoice when we celebrate the anniversaries of the martyrs!

Many, therefore, are his members, joined under one head—our Savior himself—by the bond of charity and peace. As you know, since you have heard it very often, they are one man; and in the Psalms the voice of one man is often heard as theirs. Thus one cries out as though all were crying, because all are one in the One.

Let us hear, then, that the martyrs labored and were endangered amid the great storms of hatred in this world—not so much in body, which they would eventually lay down, but in faith itself, lest, failing and perhaps yielding to the bitter pains of persecution or to love of this life, they should lose what God had promised.

He had taken away every fear not only by word but also by example: by word, saying, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28); by example, doing what he commanded in words. He was unwilling to avoid the hands of those who beat him, the blows of those who struck him, the spittle of those who spat upon him, the crown of those who placed thorns upon him, or the cross of those who killed him.

He was unwilling to avoid any of these things, though he had no need of them, for the sake of those who did need them; he made medicine of himself for the sick.

The martyrs therefore labored; and unless he who said, “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20), were always present, they would certainly have failed.

### 2.

There is therefore in this psalm the voice of the afflicted, and consequently the voice of the martyrs endangered amid their sufferings, yet relying upon their head.

Let us hear them and speak with them from the feeling of our hearts, even if not in likeness of suffering. They have already been crowned; we are still in danger—not because persecutions of the kind that afflicted them press upon us, but perhaps because we face worse dangers in every kind of such great scandal.

Our times abound more greatly in that “Woe” which the Lord cried out: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18:7). “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

That holy man Lot, living in Sodom, was not suffering bodily persecution from anyone, nor had he been told not to live there; his persecution consisted in the evil deeds of the Sodomites (Gen. 19).

Now, therefore, with Christ already seated in heaven and glorified, with the necks of kings subjected to his yoke and their foreheads placed beneath his sign, with no one remaining who dares openly insult Christians, we still groan amid the musical instruments and symphonies. The enemies of the martyrs, since they cannot attack them with voice and sword, persecute them through their own lust.

Would that we had to grieve over pagans alone! *[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “endure.”]* It would be some consolation to await those who have not yet been marked with the cross of Christ, hoping that they will be marked and, once bound by his authority, cease to rage.

We see *[Col. 0867]* even those who bear his sign on their foreheads simultaneously bearing on those same foreheads the shamelessness of their lusts. On the days and solemnities of the martyrs they do not rejoice but insult.

Amid all this we groan; and this is our persecution, if we possess the charity that says, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

No servant of God, therefore, is without persecution. True is what the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). You may see from where it comes and in what manner; that devil is two-formed. He is a lion in his attack and a dragon in his ambush. Whether the lion threatens or the dragon lies in wait, he is an enemy.

When are we safe? Suppose all become Christians: will the devil also become a Christian? He does not cease to tempt; he does not cease to lie in wait. He is bridled and bound in the hearts of the impious, lest he rage against the Church and do as much as he wishes.

The teeth of the impious gnash against the dignity of the Church and the peace of Christians. Since they have nothing to accomplish by raging, by leaping, blaspheming, and indulging their lusts they do not strike the bodies of Christians but tear the souls of Christians.

Let us all cry out, then, with one voice, these words: “O God, attend to my help.” We need perpetual help in this world. When do we not? *[Note: Some manuscripts read, “When, however, not now? Yet,” etc.]* Yet now, placed in tribulation, let us say above all: “O God, attend to my help.”

### 3. [verse 3]

“Let them be confounded and fear who seek my soul.” Christ speaks—whether the head speaks or the body speaks. He speaks who said, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4); he speaks who said, “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40).

This is therefore the recognizable voice of this man, of the whole man, head and body; it need not often be emphasized, since it is familiar.

“Let them be confounded,” he says, “and ashamed who seek my soul.” In another psalm he says: “I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who recognized me; refuge failed me, and there was no one who sought my soul” (Ps. 141:5).

There he says of the persecutors that there was no one who sought his soul; here, however: “Let them be confounded and fear who seek my soul.” He grieved that no one sought him for imitation; he groaned because he was sought for oppression.

You seek the soul of a righteous person when you intend to imitate him; you seek the soul of a righteous person when you intend to kill him. Since the soul of a righteous person is sought in two ways, each is expressed in a different psalm.

There he grieves because no one seeks his soul in order to imitate his sufferings; here, however: “Let them be confounded and fear who seek my soul.” They seek his soul, not in order to possess two souls. They did not seek his soul as a robber seeks a traveler’s tunic: he kills in order to strip him and possess it. But one who persecutes in order to kill excludes the soul; he does not clothe himself with it.

“They seek my soul; they want to kill me.” What, then, do you wish for them? “Let them be confounded and fear.”

But what of what you heard from your Lord: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5:44)? Behold, you suffer persecution and curse those by whom you suffer. How do you *[Col. 0868]* imitate the preceding sufferings of your Lord, hanging on the cross and saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

The martyr responds to those who say such things and says: “You set before me the Lord saying, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’; recognize my voice also, so that it may be yours as well.”

What, then, did I say about my enemies? “Let them be confounded and ashamed.”

Such vengeance has already been carried out against the enemies of the martyrs. That Saul who persecuted Stephen was confounded and ashamed. He breathed out slaughter; he sought people whom he might drag away and kill. When he heard a voice from above, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” he was confounded and cast down, and he who had been inflamed to persecute was raised up to obey (Acts 7:57; 9:1, 4, 6).

This, then, is what the martyrs wish for their enemies: “Let them be confounded and fear.” For as long as they are not confounded and made to fear, they must defend their deeds. They seem glorious to themselves because they seize, bind, beat, kill, leap about, and insult. Let them at some point be confounded and made to fear on account of all these deeds.

For if they are confounded, they will be converted; and they cannot be converted unless they have been confounded and made to fear.

Let us therefore wish this for our enemies; let us wish it confidently. Behold, I have said it, and may I say it with you: let all who still leap about, sing, and insult the martyrs be confounded and fear; may they one day, confounded, beat their breasts against these walls.

### 4. [verse 4]

“Let them be turned backward and be ashamed who think evil against me.”

At first there was the onslaught of the persecutors; now the ill will of those who think evil remains. Distinct successive periods of persecution are certainly present in the Church. *[Note: Thus the better manuscripts; the editions read, “distinct in the persecution of the Church.” Continue with what follows.]*

The onslaught against the Church occurred when kings persecuted it. Since it had been foretold that kings would both persecute and believe, when one prediction was fulfilled the other necessarily followed.

That too occurred which followed: the kings believed, peace was given to the Church, and the Church began to stand at the height of dignity, even on this earth and in this life. Yet the roar of the persecutors is not absent; they have turned their attacks into thoughts.

In those thoughts, as in an abyss, the devil is bound. *[Note: The Louvain edition reads, “bound in birdlime”; “in birdlime” is absent from Erasmus and most manuscripts, though some read, “bound together.” This alludes to Revelation 20:2: “And he bound him for a thousand years and cast him into the abyss,” etc.]* He roars but does not break out. For it was said about these times of the Church: “The sinner will see and be angry.” And what will he do? Not what he did at first—“Drag, bind, strike.” He does not do this. What, then? “He will gnash with his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 111:10).

The martyr is, as it were, angry with these people, and yet the martyr prays for them. Just as he rightly wished for those of whom he said, “Let them be confounded and ashamed who seek my soul,” so now also: “Let them be turned backward and be ashamed who think evil against me.”

Why? So that they may not go before but follow. For whoever criticizes the Christian religion and wishes to live according to his own counsel wants, as it were, to go *[Col. 0869]* before Christ: as though Christ had been mistaken, and had been weak and powerless because he either wished to suffer at the hands of the Jews or was able to do so; while the critic himself seems wise and prudent because he avoids all these things—declining death, even lying unjustly so as not to die, and killing his soul in order to preserve his body.

The one who criticizes Christ goes before him, as though preceding Christ. Let him believe in Christ and follow Christ.

For what was now wished for the persecutors who thought evil, the Lord himself said to Peter. At one point Peter wished to go before the Lord. The Savior was speaking of his passion; if he had not accepted it, we would not have been saved. Peter, who shortly before had confessed him as the Son of God and, in that confession, had been called “Rock,” upon which the Church would be built, shortly afterward, when the Lord spoke of his future passion, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; be favorable to yourself; this shall never happen.”

A little earlier: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Now suddenly: “Get behind me, Satan.”

What does “Get behind me” mean? Follow me. You wish to go before me; you wish to give me counsel. It is better for you to follow my counsel. This means: “Go back; go behind me.”

He restrains the one who was going ahead, so that he may return behind him, and he calls him Satan because he wishes to go before the Lord. Shortly before, “Blessed”; now, “Satan.”

Why was he “Blessed” shortly before? “Because,” he says, “flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” Why now “Satan”? “Because,” he says, “you do not think the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matt. 16:16–23).

Therefore, if we wish to celebrate the anniversaries of the martyrs correctly, let us desire to imitate the martyrs, lest we wish to go before them and seem to ourselves to have better counsel because we avoid the sufferings for justice and faith that they did not avoid.

Therefore, let those who think evil and nourish their hearts in lust be “turned backward and ashamed.” Let them hear the Apostle saying afterward: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

### 5

What follows? “Let those who say to me, ‘Bravo, bravo,’ immediately turn back in shame.” There are two kinds of persecutors: those who insult and those who flatter. The tongue of the flatterer persecutes more than the hand of the killer; for Scripture has called that tongue a furnace as well. Certainly, when Scripture was speaking about persecution, it said: “As gold in a furnace he tested them,” speaking of the martyrs who were killed, “and like a sacrificial burnt offering he accepted them” (Wis. 3:6) [Note: [Col. 0869] Manuscripts of good quality read “a burnt offering, a sacrifice”; some others, “burnt offerings, a sacrifice.” Moreover, the Septuagint reads holokarpōma thysias, “a whole burnt offering of sacrifice.”]. Hear that the tongue of flatterers is like this too: “The fire tests silver and gold, but a person is tested by the mouth of those who praise him” (Prov. 27:21). That fire, and this fire also: you must come out safe from both.

The reprover broke you, and you were broken [Note: A number of manuscripts read “and you were made,” and a little farther below, “the fire comes near and strengthens.”] in the furnace like a clay vessel. The word formed you, and the trial of affliction came: what has been formed must be baked; if it has been well formed, the fire comes near to strengthen it. Hence he said in his passion: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16). For passion and the furnace of tribulation had made him stronger.

Again, if you are praised and flattered by flatterers, and you nod in agreement with them, like one buying oil but not carrying it with you, as did the five foolish virgins (Matt. 25:3), then the mouth of those who praise you will also be the furnace of your destruction. But we cannot do without these things; it is necessary both to enter into them and to come out from them. Let us enter into some reproach from evil and wicked people; let us also enter into some flattery from flatterers. But we must come out from it. Let us ask him of whom it was said, “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit” (Ps. 120:8), so that, entering whole, we may likewise leave whole.

For the Apostle also says: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear.” There you have the entrance. He did not say, “You will not be tested”; for whoever is not tested is not proved, and whoever is not proved does not advance. What, then, did he desire? “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear.” You have heard of the entrance; hear also of the exit: “But with the testing he will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

Therefore, let those also who say to me, “Bravo, bravo,” immediately turn back in shame. Why do they praise me? Let them praise God. For who am I, that I should be praised in myself? Or what have I done? What do I have that I have not received? “If you received it,” he says, “why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Let those, then, who say to me, “Bravo, bravo,” immediately turn back in shame.

By such oil the head of the heretics was made fat (Ps. 140:5), when they say, “I am, I am,” and it is said to them, “You, Lord.” They received “Bravo, bravo”; they followed “Bravo, bravo”; they became blind leaders of the blind who followed them (Matt. 15:14). In the clearest words these things are sung to Donatus [Note: [Col. 0870] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “songs.”]: “Bravo, bravo, good leader, excellent leader.” Yet he did not say, “Let those who say to me, ‘Bravo, bravo,’ immediately turn back in shame”; nor did he wish to correct them so that they would say of Christ, “Good leader, excellent leader.”

But the Apostle, fearing the “Bravo” of human beings, so that he might truly be praised in Christ, did not wish to be praised on Christ’s account. When some were saying, “I belong to Paul,” he replied in the freedom of the Lord: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13). Therefore, even amid the persecution of flatterers, let the martyrs say: “Let those who say to me, ‘Bravo, bravo,’ immediately turn back in shame.”

### 6. [verse 5]

And what happens when all those people turn away and are put to shame—whether those who seek my life, those who devise evil against me, or those who, with a perverse and feigned benevolence, wish by their tongue to soften what they strike? When they too have turned away and been confounded, what will happen?

“Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you”—not in me, not in this person or that, but in him in whom those who were darkness have become light. “Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you.” It is one thing to seek God, another to seek a human being. Let those who seek you rejoice. Then those who seek themselves will not rejoice, will they [Note: [Col. 0870] The Regius manuscript reads, “who seek not you.”]—the ones whom you sought first, before they sought you?

That sheep had not yet been seeking its shepherd; it had wandered from the flock. And he descended to it, sought it, and carried it back on his shoulders (Luke 15:4–5). Will you, O sheep, despise the one who seeks you—the one who first sought you when you were despising him and not seeking him? Begin, then, to seek the one who first sought you and carried you back on his shoulders. Do what he says [Note: [Col. 0871] Nearly all the manuscripts read: “Will you now despise the one seeking you? Begin, then, to seek the one who first sought you; do what he says,” etc.]:” “My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me” (John 10:3).

If, then, you seek the one who first sought you, and you have become his sheep, and you hear the voice of your shepherd and follow him, see what he has shown you about himself and what he has shown you about his body, lest you go astray concerning him or concerning the Church; lest someone say to you, “This is Christ,” when he is not Christ, or “This is the Church,” when it is not the Church.

For many have said that Christ did not have flesh and that Christ did not rise in his own body. Do not follow their voices. Hear the voice of the shepherd himself, who put on flesh in order to seek lost flesh. He rose again and said: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” He showed himself to you; follow his voice.

He also showed you the Church, so that no one might deceive you by the name of the Church: “It was necessary,” he says, “for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name throughout all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:39, 46–47). You have the voice of your shepherd; do not follow the voice of strangers (John 10:5), and you will not fear the thief [Note: The manuscripts, with great unanimity, read: “Do not follow the voice of robbers and thieves. You will be on your guard if you follow the shepherd’s voice,” and so forth.], if you have followed the shepherd’s voice.

But how will you follow him? If you have said to no human being, as though by that person’s merit, “Bravo, bravo,” and if you have not listened with rejoicing, lest your head be made fat with the oil of the sinner (Ps. 140:5).

“Let all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you,” and let them say. What should those who rejoice say? “May the Lord always be magnified.” Let all who rejoice and seek you say this. What? “May the Lord always be magnified, those who love your salvation.” Not merely “May the Lord be magnified,” but “always.”

Look: you were wandering and turned away from him. He called you; may the Lord be magnified. Look: he inspired you to confess your sins. You confessed; he forgave you; may the Lord be magnified. You have now begun to live justly; now, I suppose, since you are just, it is right that you too should be magnified. Indeed, when he called you while you were wandering, the Lord was to be magnified; when he forgave your sins after you confessed them, the Lord was to be magnified. Now, hearing his words, you have begun to advance, you have been justified, and you have reached a certain excellence of virtue; it is fitting that you too should at some time be magnified. Let them say: “May the Lord always be magnified.”

You are a sinner: may he be magnified so that he may call you. You confess: may he be magnified so that he may forgive. You now live justly: may he be magnified so that he may govern you. You persevere to the end: may he be magnified so that he may glorify you. Therefore, may the Lord always be magnified.

Let the righteous say this; let those who seek him say this. Whoever does not say it does not seek him. Look: “May the Lord be magnified.” Let all who seek him rejoice and be glad, and let them say, “May the Lord always be magnified, those who love your salvation.”

For their salvation comes from him, not from themselves. “The salvation of the Lord our God” is “the Lord our Savior Jesus Christ.” Whoever loves the Savior confesses that he has been healed; whoever confesses that he has been healed confesses himself to have been sick. Let them therefore say, “May the Lord always be magnified, those who love your salvation”—not their own salvation, as though they saved themselves; not human salvation, as though they were saved by that person.

“Do not,” he says, “put your trust in princes, or in human beings, in whom there is no salvation” (Ps. 145:2–3). Why is this? “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9). Therefore, “May the Lord always be magnified.” Who says this? Those who love your salvation.

### 7. [verse 6]

Look: may the Lord be magnified—but never you, nowhere you? If there is anything in him, there is nothing in me; and if there is anything in me, it is in him, not in me. What, then, are you? “But I am needy and poor.”

He is rich, he is abundant, he lacks nothing. Look: he is my light; from him I am illuminated, since I cry: “You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17:29). “The Lord releases those who are bound; the Lord raises up those who are cast down; the Lord makes the blind wise; the Lord watches over strangers” (Ps. 145:7).

What, then, are you? “But I am needy and poor.” I am like an orphan; my soul is like a widow, abandoned and desolate. I seek help; I always confess my weakness. “But I am needy and poor.”

My sins have been forgiven; I have now begun to follow God’s commandments. Yet I am still needy and poor. Why am I still needy and poor? Because “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23).

Why needy and poor? Because “blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6). I still hunger; I still thirst. My satisfaction has been postponed, not taken away. “But I am needy and poor; God, help me.”

This is why the words begin: “God, attend to my help; God, help me.” Lazarus too is most correctly said to be interpreted as “Helped”; he was that needy and poor man who was carried away into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22). And he represents the Church of God, which must always confess that it needs help. This is true; this is pious.

“I have said to the Lord: You are my God.” Why? “For you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). He has no need of us; we need him. Therefore he is truly Lord.

For you are not a very true lord of your servant: both of you are human beings, and both of you need God. But if you think that your servant needs you in order that you may give him bread, you too need your servant in order that he may help with your work. Each of you needs the other. Therefore neither of you is truly lord, and neither of you is truly servant.

Hear the true Lord, whose true servant you are: “I have said to the Lord: You are my God.” Why are you Lord? “For you have no need of my goods.” And what are you? “But I am needy and poor.”

Look: needy and poor. Let God feed me; let God lift me up; let God help me. “God,” he says, “help me.”

### 8

“You are my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay.”

You are my helper and my deliverer: I need assistance—help me; I am entangled—deliver me. For no one will deliver me from my entanglements except you.

The bonds of different concerns surround us; here and there we are torn apart as though by thorns and hedges. We walk along a narrow way; perhaps we have become caught in the hedges. Let us say to God: “You are my deliverer.”

He who showed the narrow way (Matt. 7:14) made us follow it. Let this cry persist in us, brothers. However long we live here, however much progress we make here, let no one say, “It is enough for me; I am righteous.” Whoever says this has remained on the road and does not know how to arrive. Where he says, “It is enough,” there he has become stuck.

Consider the Apostle, for whom it is not enough; see how he wishes to be helped until he arrives: “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider that I have apprehended it.” To those who thought that they had apprehended it, he says again: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2) [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “that he ought to know.” The manuscripts read, “as one ought to know.”]

What, then, does he say? “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it.” Above he had said, “Not that I have already received it or am already perfect”; and there follows: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it.” If he has not yet received it, he is needy and poor; if he is not yet perfect, he is needy and poor. He says well: “God, help me.”

But he understands something, and understands it in an exalted way. See, nevertheless, what he says: “To him who is able to do beyond all things, more abundantly than we ask or understand” (Eph. 3:20) [Note: [Col. 0873] Here the editions omit “beyond,” a word found in the manuscripts and in the Apostle’s Greek text.]. See, then, that he has not yet arrived, that he has not yet apprehended it.

What, then, does he say? “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it: but one thing I do—forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my purpose toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:12–14).

He is running, then, while you are stuck. He says that he is not yet perfect, while you are already boasting of perfection! Let those who say to you, “Bravo, bravo,” be confounded. And you too should be confounded among them, because you say to yourself, “Bravo, bravo.”

For whoever praises himself says to himself, “Bravo, bravo”; and whoever is praised by others and agrees with them does not carry oil with him. The lamps will fail, and he is about to close the door (Matt. 25:3, 10).

### 9

This, then, most beloved, is what this psalm has briefly taught us through the reminder of the martyrs’ solemnity: we understand that the martyrs suffered bodily tribulation here, while we, however much peace we may have here, must suffer spiritual tribulation. The Church and that whole mass must groan amid scandals, weeds, and chaff until the harvest comes, until the winnowing fan comes, until the final winnowing comes, so that the chaff may be separated from the grain and brought into the granary (Matt. 13:30; 3:12).

Until this happens, let us cry out: “But I am needy and poor; God, help me. You are my helper, O Lord; do not delay.”

What does “Do not delay” mean? Many say, “It is taking a long time for Christ to come.” What, then—because we say, “Do not delay,” will he come before the time he has appointed? What does this desire, “Do not delay,” mean? It means: May your coming not seem too delayed to me.

For it seems long to you; it does not seem long to God, for whom a thousand years are one day, or the three hours of a watch (Ps. 89:4). But if you do not have endurance, it will seem delayed to you. And when it seems delayed to you, you will turn away from him and become like those who grew weary in the wilderness and hastened to ask God for the pleasures he was reserving for them in their homeland.

When pleasures were not given to them on the journey—pleasures by which they might perhaps have been corrupted—they murmured against God and returned in their hearts to Egypt (Exod. 16:2; Acts 7:39). Although they had been separated from it in body, they returned to it in heart.

Do not be like that; do not be like that. Fear the word of the Lord who says, “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32). She too was on the way, already delivered from Sodom, but she looked back. Where she looked, there she remained; she became a pillar of salt (Gen. 19:29), so that she might season you.

She was given to you as an example, so that you might have a heart and not remain foolish on the way. Pay attention to the one who remained, and pass on. Pay attention to the one who looked back, and stretch forward yourself toward what lies ahead, like Paul.

What does it mean not to look back? “Forgetting what lies behind,” he says. That is why you follow, called toward the heavenly prize, about which you will later boast. For the same Apostle says: “There remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8).

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 70

### SERMON I. On the First Part of the Psalm

#### 1

In all the holy Scriptures, the grace of God that liberates us commends itself to us, so that it may have us as those who have been commended to it. This is what is sung in this psalm, about which we have undertaken to speak with Your Charity. May the Lord be present, so that I may conceive it in my heart as is fitting and bring it forth in the way that is useful to you.

For the love and fear of God move us greatly: the fear of God, because he is just; the love, because he is merciful. For who would say to him, “What have you done?” (Wis. 12:12), if he condemned the unjust [Note: The editions read “the just.” The more reliable Corbie manuscript reads “the unjust.” For Augustine repeats this later in section 15: “If you condemn all the wicked … if you condemn this mass of iniquity, will anyone say to you, ‘You have acted unjustly?’” Nor, surely, would anyone dare to say that someone just could by the judgment of God be made or declared worthy of punishment; this is precisely what the verb “to condemn” signifies. He seems to be referring to the words of Wisdom 12:12.]?

How great, then, is his mercy, that he justifies the unjust? From this passage read to us, we also heard the Apostle commending this same grace above all: because of his commendation of it he had the Jews as enemies, as people presuming upon the letter of the Law and loving and boasting of their own righteousness. Of them he says: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” And as though someone were saying to him, “What does it mean to have zeal for God not according to knowledge?” he immediately added: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:2–3).

Boasting, he says, as though on the basis of works, they exclude grace from themselves; and, falsely presuming upon their own health, they reject medicine. Against such people the Lord had also said: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance; it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:13, 12).

This, then, is the whole of the great knowledge: for a human being [Note: [Col. 0874] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and three manuscripts read “of a human being.”] to know that he is nothing by himself, and that whatever he is, he is from God and for God. “For what do you have,” he says, “that you did not receive? But if you received it [Note: [Col. 0874] The editions omit “also,” which is found in the manuscripts and in the Apostle’s Greek text.], why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

The Apostle commends this grace; because of it he merited the Jews as enemies, since they boasted of the letter of the Law and of their own righteousness. Commending this grace, then, in the reading that was read, he says: “For I am the least of the Apostles, unworthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

“But for this reason,” he says, “I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.” Then a little later: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world [Note: [Col. 0875] The editions read “into this world”; “this” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s Greek text.] to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:13, 15).

Were there no sinners before him? What, then, does “the first” mean? Not preceding all others in time, but in wickedness. “But for this reason,” he says, “I received mercy, so that in me Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example for those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:16).

That is, so that every sinner and wicked person, already despairing of himself and already possessing something like a gladiator’s spirit—so that he does whatever he wishes because he must necessarily be condemned—might nevertheless look toward the Apostle Paul, to whom such great cruelty and wickedness were forgiven by God; and, without despairing of himself, might turn to God.

God commends this grace to us also in this psalm. Let us look at it and see whether this is so, or whether perhaps I am imagining it differently. For I think that this is its disposition and that this is what nearly all its syllables resound with: namely, that it commends to us the free grace of God, which liberates us though we are unworthy—not for our sake, but for his own.

Even if I had not said this or introduced it beforehand, any person of moderate understanding, listening attentively to the words of this same psalm, would perceive it; and perhaps, if he had held something else in his heart, he would be changed by the very words and become what the psalm here proclaims.

What is this? That our entire hope should be in God and that we should presume nothing about ourselves as though it came from our own strength, lest, making our own what comes from him, we lose what we have received.

#### 2. [verse 1]

The title of this psalm, then, is—as a title customarily indicates at the threshold what is being done in the house—“For David himself, of the sons of Jonadab and of those who were first led into captivity.”

Jonadab was a certain man who is commended to us through the prophecy of Jeremiah. He had commanded his sons not to drink wine and not to live in houses, but in tents. His sons held and kept their father’s command, and because of this they merited being blessed by the Lord (Jer. 35:6–10).

The Lord, however, had not commanded this; their father had. Yet they received it as though it were a command from the Lord their God. For although the Lord had not commanded them not to drink wine and to live in tents, the Lord had nevertheless commanded that sons obey their father.

A son ought not to obey his father in that one matter if his father orders something against the son’s Lord God. Nor should a father become angry when God is placed before him. But when a father commands something that is not against God, he must be obeyed as God is, because God commanded obedience to one’s father.
