God therefore blessed the sons of Jonadab because of their obedience and set them before his disobedient people, reproaching them because, while the sons of Jonadab were obedient to their father, they were not obedient to their God.

When Jeremiah was doing these things, he was dealing with the people of Israel so that they might prepare themselves to be led into captivity to Babylon and not resist God’s will, nor hope for anything other than that they would become captives.

The title of this psalm therefore seems to have been given its coloring from that event: after saying “of the sons of Jonadab,” it adds, “and of those who were first led into captivity.” This is not because the sons of Jonadab were led into captivity, but because the sons of Jonadab were set before those who were to be led into captivity, since they were obedient to their father; so that the latter might understand that they were being made captives because they had not been obedient to God.

There is also the fact that Jonadab is interpreted as “the Spontaneous One of the Lord.” What does “the Spontaneous One of the Lord” mean? One who willingly serves God. What does “the Spontaneous One of the Lord” mean? “My vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them to you as praises” (Ps. 55:12). What does “the Spontaneous One of the Lord” mean? “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. 54:8).

If apostolic discipline admonishes a servant to serve his human master not as under compulsion but willingly, and by serving willingly to make himself free in heart, how much more must God be served with a whole, complete, and willing obedience, since he sees your very will?

For if a servant does not serve you from the heart, you can see his hands, his face, and his presence, but you cannot see his heart. Yet the Apostle says to them, “not serving for the eye.” And what does “not serving for the eye” mean? What, then, will my master see, how I serve him, so that you say to me, “not serving for the eye”? He added: “but as servants of Christ.” A human master does not see, but Christ the Lord does see. “From the heart,” he says, “with good will” (Eph. 6:6–7) [Note: [Col. 0876] Here the editions add: “Not because the sons of Jonadab were led into captivity”; and there follows, “Such was,” etc. But those words are absent from the better manuscripts.].

Such was Jonadab; that is, this is what his name means.

Who, then, are those who were first led into captivity? The sons of Israel were led into captivity first, second, and third. But when the psalm says “for them,” or speaks “about those who were first led into captivity,” this does not mean what it seems to say. The psalm itself, examined, searched out, and questioned in all its verses, tells you something else: it is not speaking about certain human beings, I do not know who or at what time, who, when enemies invaded, were led captive from Jerusalem into Babylon.

Rather, what does the psalm say? Nothing other than what you heard from the Apostle. It commends to us the grace of God; it commends to us that we are nothing by ourselves; it commends to us that whatever we are, we are by his mercy, while whatever we are from ourselves, we are evil.

Why, then, are we captives? And why is the very grace of the liberator commended under the name of captivity? The Apostle himself makes it clear: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members.” There you have being led captive.

What, then, does this psalm commend? What follows there in the Apostle: “Wretched human being that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:22–25).

Why, then, “first”? [Note: Several manuscripts read, “Are they commended? The grace of the liberator itself is revealed.”]

For it has been said why they are captives. As I understand it, this too is clear: because all disobedience was condemned in comparison with the sons of Jonadab. Through disobedience we became captives, because Adam himself sinned by not obeying.

The same Apostle said—and it is true—“all die in Adam, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). It is rightly said also, “they were first led into captivity,” because “the first human was from the earth, earthly; the second human was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.” The first human made us captives; the second human freed us from captivity.

“For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:47–49, 22). But they die in Adam through the birth of the flesh; they are freed in Christ through faith of the heart. It was not within your power not to be born from Adam; it is within your power to believe in Christ.

However much, then, you wish to belong to the first human, you will belong to captivity. And what does it mean, “you wish to belong”? Or what does it mean, “you will belong”? You already belong. Cry out: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). Let us therefore hear this man crying out in this way.

#### 3

“God [Note: [Col. 0877] One Pratellensis manuscript does not have “God.”], in you I have hoped; Lord, do not let me be confounded forever.”

I have already been confounded—only not forever! For how has one not been confounded to whom it is said: “What fruit did you have then from the things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6:21).

What, then, will happen so that we are not confounded forever? “Come to him, and be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:6). You were confounded in Adam; depart from Adam, come to Christ, and you will no longer be confounded.

“In you I have hoped, Lord; do not let me be confounded forever.” If I am confounded in myself, I will not be confounded forever in you.

#### 4. [verse 2]

“In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.” Not in mine, but in yours. For if in mine, I will be among those of whom he says: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

Therefore, in your righteousness, not in mine. For what is mine? Iniquity came first. And when I am righteous, it will be your righteousness, because I will be righteous through the righteousness given to me by you; and it will be mine in such a way that it is yours—that is, given to me by you.

For I believe in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that my faith may be reckoned as righteousness (Rom. 4:5). Thus it will also be my righteousness—but not as though it were my own, not as though it were given to me by myself, as those people thought who boasted through the letter and rejected grace.

For it is said elsewhere: “Judge me, Lord, according to my righteousness” (Ps. 7:9). Certainly he was not boasting in his own righteousness. But recall the Apostle to me: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). And so call it your righteousness while remembering that you received it, and do not begrudge it to those who receive it.

For that Pharisee also, as though he had received it from God, said: “I thank you, because I am not like the rest of humanity.” “I thank you”—good. “Because I am not like the rest of humanity”—why? Does the fact that another is bad delight you because you are good?

Finally, what did he add? “Unjust, robbers, adulterers, like this tax collector.” This is no longer rejoicing, but insulting. But the captive tax collector did not dare even to lift his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast, saying: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:11, 13).

It is therefore not enough for you to recognize that the good in you comes from God, unless you also refrain from exalting yourself over the one who does not yet possess it. For perhaps, when he receives it, he will surpass you.

When Saul was still stoning Stephen (Acts 7:59), how many Christians there were whom he was persecuting! Yet when he was converted, he surpassed all those who had preceded him.

Therefore say to God what you hear in the psalm: “In you I have hoped, Lord; do not let me be confounded forever. In your righteousness, not in mine, deliver me and rescue me.”

“Incline your ear to me.” This too is a confession of humility. Whoever says, “Incline to me,” confesses that he is lying prostrate like a sick person before a physician who is standing.

Finally, see that it is a sick person who speaks: “Incline your ear to me, and save me.”

#### 5. [verse 3]

“Be for me a protecting God.” May the darts of the enemy not reach me, for I cannot protect myself. And it is not enough to say “as a protector”; he added, “and as a fortified place, so that you may save me.”

Be a fortified place for me; you be my fortified place. Where is what you were fleeing from, Adam, when you hid yourself among the trees of paradise? Where is what made you fear his face, when you had been accustomed to rejoice before him (Gen. 3:8)?

You went away and perished. You were taken captive, and look: you are visited, and look: you are not abandoned. Look: the ninety-nine sheep are left on the mountains, and the lost sheep is sought. Look: it is said of the sheep that was found, “He was dead and came to life; he had perished and was found” (Luke 15:4, 24).

Look: God himself has become the place of refuge for you, though at first he was the object of your fear and flight. “Be for me,” he says, “as a fortified place, so that you may save me.” I will not be safe except in you. Unless you become my rest, my sickness cannot be healed.

Lift me from the earth; let me lie in you, so that I may rise into a fortified place. What is more fortified than this? When you have fled to that place, tell me what adversaries you will fear. Who will lie in wait and reach you?

Someone is said to have shouted from the summit of a mountain when an emperor was passing by, “I am not speaking about you.” The emperor is said to have looked back and replied, “Nor am I speaking about you.” He had despised the emperor with his military insignia and powerful army [Note: Erasmus and several manuscripts read this way. Lovaniensis reads “with power.”]—how? From a fortified place.

If that man was secure on high ground, how much more secure are you in him by whom heaven and earth were made?

“Be for me, then, as a protecting God and as a fortified place, so that you may save me.” If I choose another place for myself, I cannot be safe. Choose one, human being, if you find a place more fortified. There is therefore nowhere to flee from him except to him. If you wish to escape him when he is angry, flee to him when he is appeased.

“For you are my strength and my refuge.” What does “my strength” mean? Through you I am strong, and from you I am strong. “For you are my strength and my refuge”: so that I may become strong from you, if I should at some point become weak in myself, I will flee to you.

For the grace of Christ makes you strong and immovable against all the enemy’s temptations. But human frailty is also there; the first captivity is still there; the law in the members still wars against the law of the mind and wishes to lead you captive into the law of sin (Rom. 7:23). There is still “the body that is corrupted, weighing down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

However strong you may be through God’s grace, as long as you still carry an earthen vessel in which God’s treasure is contained, something must still be feared from the vessel itself, which is made of clay (2 Cor. 4:7).

You are therefore my strength, so that I may be strong in this world against all temptations. But if they are many and trouble me, you are my refuge. For this reason I will confess [Note: Lovaniensis reads “I confess.” The other books read “I will confess.”] my weakness, so that I may be timid like a hare, because I am full of thorns like a hedgehog.

And, as it is said in another psalm, “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares” (Ps. 103:18). “The rock,” however, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

### 6. [verse 4]

“My God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner.” In general [Col. 0879], “sinners”—among whom struggles this man who is now to be freed from captivity; this man who already cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25)? There is an enemy within: that law in the members. There are enemies also outside. To whom do you cry? To him to whom it was cried: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my secret faults; and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13–14).

Therefore, when it is said, “Save me,” it is said of your inward sickness, that is, of your iniquity: from that by which you are captive, from that by which you belong to the first man, so that you cry out among the first captives. Once you have been saved from your own iniquity, consider also the iniquities of others, among whom you must live until this life comes to an end.

And when will it end? Look: it comes to an end for you. Does it come to an end for the Church except at the end of the age? This one man, the unity of Christ, cries out these words. It is therefore necessary that many of the faithful who depart from this body should already be in that rest which God grants to the spirits of the faithful; but here they are still members of Christ—in those who live this life and in those who will be born afterward. Thus, until the end of the age, this one man will remain, crying out to be freed from his sins and from the law of his members that resists the law of his mind. Then he cries out amid the sins of others, among whom he must live until the end.

These sinners, however, belong to two classes: some have received the Law, others have not. All pagans have not received the Law; all Jews and Christians have received the Law. Thus “sinner” is the general designation: either a transgressor of the Law, if he has received the Law, or simply an unrighteous person without the Law, if he has not received it. The Apostle speaks of both classes and says: “Those who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law; and those who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Rom. 2:12).

But you, who groan amid both classes, say to God what you hear in the Psalm: “My God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner.” Of which sinner? “From the hand of the transgressor of the Law and of the unrighteous.” The transgressor of the Law is indeed also unrighteous—for one who transgresses the Law is not not unrighteous—but everyone who transgresses the Law is unrighteous, whereas not every unrighteous person transgresses the Law. [Col. 0880] “Where there is no Law,” the Apostle says, “neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). Those, therefore, who have not received the Law may be called unrighteous, but they cannot be called transgressors. Both are judged according to their merits.

But I, who desire to be freed from captivity by your grace, cry out to you: “Deliver me from the hand of the sinner.” What does “from his hand” mean? From his power: so that, when he rages, he does not bring me to agreement with him; so that, when he lies in wait, he does not persuade me to iniquity. “From the hand of the transgressor of the Law and of the unrighteous.”

He answers you: “Why do you seek to be delivered from the hand of the transgressor of the Law and of the unrighteous? Do not consent; but if he rages, be patient, endure.”

> **Note:** Most manuscripts read: “You who seek to be delivered from the hand of the transgressor of the Law and of the unrighteous, do not consent. But he rages: be patient,” and so forth.

But who endures, if he does not abandon the one who becomes a fortified place?

> **Note:** The editions read, “who endures you?” The word “you” is absent from most manuscripts. Why, then, do I say, “Deliver me from the hand of the transgressor of the Law and of the unrighteous”? Because it is not in me to be patient, but in you, who grant patience.

> **Note:** Thus the manuscripts. The editors read: “Understand generally: sinners”; and shortly afterward, the Lovaniensis edition has: “There are also enemies outside, on account of whom you cry out to him,” and so forth.

### 7. [verses 5–6]

Finally, what follows explains why I say this: “For you are my patience.” Now, if you are my patience, then what follows is also rightly said: “Lord, my hope from my youth.” Is it my patience because you are my hope—or rather, are you my hope because you are my patience? “Tribulation,” the Apostle says, “produces patience; patience, proven character; and proven character, hope; but hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:3, 5).

“Rightly have I hoped in you, Lord; I shall not be put to shame forever. Lord, my hope from my youth.” From your youth, is God your hope? Not also from your childhood and infancy? “Certainly,” he says. For see what follows, lest you think that I said, “My hope from my youth,” as though God had done nothing for my infancy or childhood. Hear what follows: “In you I have been established from the womb.” Hear still more: “From my mother’s womb you are my protector.”

Why, then, “from my youth,” unless it means from the time when I began to hope in you? Before that I did not hope in you, although you were my protector, who brought me safely to the time when I would learn to hope in you. But from my youth I began to hope in you, from the time when you armed me against the devil, so that, armed in the ranks of your army with faith, love, hope, and your other gifts, I might fight against your invisible enemies and hear from the Apostle: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this dark world, against spiritual wickedness” (Eph. 6:12).

The young man, then, is the one who fights against these things. Yet, although he is young, he falls unless the one to whom he cries is his hope: “Lord, my hope from my youth.”

### 8

“In you is my song always.” Does this mean from the time when I began to hope in you until now? No: “always.” What does “always” mean? Not only during the time of faith, but also during the time of vision. For now, as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6). The time will come when we shall see what we have believed without seeing; and when we see what we believe, we shall rejoice. But when the ungodly see what they did not believe, they will be put to shame.

Then the reality of which hope now consists will come. “For hope that is seen is not hope. [Col. 0881] But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8:24). Now, therefore, you groan; now you run to a place of refuge to be saved; now, placed in weakness, you ask the physician for help. But what when you have received perfect health as well? What when you have become equal to the angels of God (Matt. 22:30)? Will you perhaps then forget this grace by which you have been delivered? Far from it. “In you is my song always.”

### 9. [verse 7]

“I have become as a portent to many.” Here, in the time of hope, the time of groaning, the time of humility, the time of pain, the time of weakness, the time of a voice crying out from fetters—what is he here? “I have become as a portent to many.”

Why “as a portent”? Why do those who regard me as a portent insult me? Because I believe what I do not see. For they, blessed in the things they see, rejoice in drinking, luxury, fornication, avarice, riches, plunder, worldly honors, and the whitening of a muddy wall. In these things they rejoice. But I walk a different road, despising the things that are present and fearing even the prosperity of the world, secure nowhere except in God’s promises.

And they say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15:32). What do you say? Repeat it. “Let us eat and drink,” he says. Good; what did you say afterward? “For tomorrow we shall die.” You frightened me; you did not deceive me. By the very thing you said afterward, you struck fear into me, lest I agree with you. You said, “For tomorrow we shall die,” and before that came, “Let us eat and drink.” For when you had said, “Let us eat and drink,” you added, “For tomorrow we shall die.”

Hear my answer: “Rather, let us fast and pray, for tomorrow we shall die.”

Following this narrow and difficult way, I have become as a portent to many; “but you are a strong helper.” Be present, O Lord Jesus, who say to me: “Do not fail on the narrow way. I passed along it first; I am the way itself” (John 14:6). I lead; I lead in myself; I bring you to myself.

Therefore, although I have become as a portent to many, I shall not fear, because you are a strong helper.

### 10. [verse 8]

“Let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing your glory; all day long your magnificence.”

What does “all day long” mean? Without interruption. In prosperity, because you console me; in adversity, because you correct me; before I existed, because you made me; while I existed, because you granted me salvation; when I had sinned, because you forgave me; when I had turned back, because you helped me; when I had persevered, because you crowned me.

Yes, let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing your glory; all day long your magnificence.

### 11. [verse 9]

“Do not cast me away in the time of old age.”

> **Note:** Perhaps “into the time,” as in several places below, according to the Greek *eis kairon*.

“My hope from my youth: do not cast me away in the time of old age.”

What is this time of old age? When my strength fails, do not abandon me.

Here God answers you: “On the contrary, let your strength fail, so that mine may remain in you,” so that you may say with the Apostle: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). Do not fear being cast away in weakness, in this old age.

> **Note:** Several manuscripts read: “into weakness, into this old age.”

For was your Lord not weakened on the cross? Did not the strongest men, the fat bulls, shake their heads before him as before a powerless man, [Col. 0882] a captive and oppressed man, and say: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:39–40)? Was he abandoned because he was weak, although he preferred not to come down from the cross, lest he appear not to have displayed power but to have yielded to those who insulted him?

What did he teach you by hanging there, when he refused to come down, except patience among those who insulted him, and that you should be strong in your God?

Perhaps the words “I have become as a portent to many, but you are a strong helper” were also spoken from his person: from his person according to weakness, not according to power; according to what he had transformed us into in himself, not according to what he himself had descended to become. For he became a portent to many.

Perhaps that itself was his old age, because old age is not inappropriately called so from antiquity; and the Apostle says: “Our old man was crucified with him” (Rom. 6:6). If our old man was there, then old age was there, because what is old is old age.

Yet because it is true that “your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5), he rose on the third day and promised resurrection at the end of the age. The head has already gone before; the members will follow.

Why do you fear that he will abandon you, that he will cast you away in the time of old age, when your strength has failed? On the contrary, his strength will then be in you, when your strength has failed.

### 12. [verses 10–11]

Why do I say this? “For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watched over my soul took counsel together, saying: ‘God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him.’”

This was said of Christ. For he who, by the great power of his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father, had raised the dead, suddenly became weak among the hands of his enemies and was seized as though he were powerless.

When would he have been seized, unless they had first said in their hearts, “God has abandoned him”? Whence came that voice on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” (Ps. 21:2).

Did God, then, abandon Christ, when “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), and when Christ himself was God, who according to the flesh was from the Jews, “who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5)? Did God abandon him? Far from it.

But the voice was our voice in our old man, because our old man was crucified together with him. He had also received a body from that old man of ours, because Mary was descended from Adam.

Therefore, what they thought, he said from the cross: “Why have you abandoned me?” (Matt. 27:46)—that is, “Why do they, to their own harm, think that I have been abandoned?” What does “they think that I have been abandoned, to their own harm” mean? “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

“Pursue him and seize him.” Let us nevertheless understand this more familiarly, brothers, as spoken from the members of Christ, and recognize our own voice in these words. For he too uttered such words from our person, not from his own power and majesty, but from what he became for us, not according to what he was who made us.

### 13. [verse 12]

“Lord my God, do not be far from me.” It happens in this way, yet he is not far at all. “For the Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted” (Ps. 33:19). “My God, look to my aid.”

[Col. 0883]

### 14. [verse 13]

“Let those who attack my soul be confounded and fail.”

What did he desire? “Let them be confounded and fail.” Why did he desire this? “Those who attack my soul.”

What does “those who attack my soul” mean? Those who attack it as though for some quarrel. For those who are provoked to quarrel are said to be brought into conflict.

If this is so, let us beware of those who attack our souls. What does “those who attack our souls” mean? First, those who provoke us to resist God, so that God becomes displeasing to us in our troubles.

For when are you upright, so that the God of Israel is good to you? “God is good to the upright in heart” (Ps. 72:2). When are you upright? Do you wish to hear? When God pleases you in the good that you do, and does not displease you in the evil that you suffer.

See what I have said, brothers, and be on your guard against those who attack your souls. For all who deal with you in such a way that you grow weary amid sorrows and tribulations are seeking to make God displeasing to you in what you suffer, so that these words may come from your mouth: “What is this? What have I done?”

So now you have done no evil, and you are righteous while he is unrighteous? “I am a sinner,” you say; “I admit it. I do not call myself righteous. But what of it? A sinner—yes; but is it as much as the one who prospers? As much as Gaius or Seius? I know his evils; I know his iniquities, from which I, although a sinner, am far removed. Yet I see him flourishing in every good, while I suffer such things!”

Therefore you do not say, “God, what have I done to you?” because you have done absolutely no evil, but because you have not done enough to deserve suffering these things.

So again, you are righteous while he is unrighteous? Wake up, wretched man; your soul has been brought into conflict.

“No,” he says, “I did not call myself righteous.”

What, then, do you say?

“I am a sinner, but I have not committed such things that I deserve to suffer this.”

So you do not say to God, “I am righteous and you are unrighteous,” but, “I am unrighteous, yet you are more unrighteous.”

Behold, your soul has been brought into conflict; behold, your soul is already waging war. Against whom? Your soul against God—your soul, which was made against the one by whom it was made. Or rather, because you are one who cries out against him, you are ungrateful.

Return, then, to confession of your weakness; implore the hand of the physician. Let those who flourish for a time not appear happy to you. You are chastised; they are spared. Perhaps an inheritance is being reserved for you, a son chastised and corrected.

Return, then—return, transgressor, to your heart (Isa. 46:8); do not let your soul be brought into conflict. The one against whom you have declared war is far mightier. The larger the stones you hurl toward heaven, the stronger will be the ruin that crushes you.

Return instead; acknowledge yourself. It is God who displeases you: be ashamed; let yourself displease you. You would do no good if he were not good, and you would suffer nothing if he were not just.

Awaken, then, to this voice: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

The men who sat beside Job while he was rotting were unrighteous (Job 2:13); yet he, who was to be restored, was scourged, while they, who were to be punished, were spared.

Whatever tribulation may come upon you, whatever insult, do not let your soul be brought into conflict—not against God alone, but not even against those who do these things to you. For if you hate them as well, your soul has been brought into conflict against them.

Give thanks to them absolutely; pray for them. Perhaps this prayer you have heard is also for them: “Let those who attack my soul be confounded and fail.”

[Col. 0884] “Let them be confounded and fail”: for they presume greatly upon their own righteousness; therefore let them be confounded. It is beneficial for them to recognize their sins, for which they may be confounded and fail. For they presumed wickedly upon their own strength. Then, having failed, let them say: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10); and, having failed, let them say: “Do not cast me away in the time of old age.”

He therefore desired good for them: that they should be confounded by their evils and fail in their perverse strength; and then, having failed and been confounded, they should seek one who enlightens them from confusion and restores them from their failure.

Finally, see what follows: “Let those who devise evil against me be clothed with confusion and shame.” Confusion and shame: confusion because of a bad conscience, shame because of modesty. Let this happen in them, and they will be good.

Do not imagine that he is raging against them. Would that his prayer for them were heard! Stephen too seemed to rage when, with flaming mouth, he hurled those words: “You stiff-necked people and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist”—or, according to another reading, “resisted”—“the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51). What burning anger! How vehement he was against his enemies! It seems that his soul had been brought into conflict.

Far from it. He was seeking their salvation; he was binding madmen who were raging wickedly with his words. For see that his soul had not been brought into conflict, not only against God but not even against them: “Lord Jesus,” he said, “receive my spirit.”

Jesus did not displease him because he was suffering stoning on account of his word.

> **Note:** Thus the manuscripts. The editors read *passurus*, “about to suffer.”

Therefore his soul had not been brought into conflict against God. Likewise he said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). Therefore his soul had not been brought into conflict against his enemies either.

“Let those who devise evil against me be clothed with confusion and shame.” For all who trouble me seek this; they seek evil for me.

What evil did that woman seek when she suggested: “Say something against God and die” (Job 2:9)? And what evil did Tobit’s wife seek when she said to her husband: “Where are your acts of righteousness?” (Tob. 2:22)? She said this so that God, who had made him blind, would displease him; and when God displeased him, his soul would be brought into conflict.

### 15. [verse 14]

If no one, then, persuades you through tribulation, if no one forces you to let God displease you in the things you suffer, or to hate the people through whom you suffer, your soul has not been brought into conflict. Instead, you say securely what follows: “But I will always hope in you, and I will add to all your praise.”

What does this mean? “I will add to all your praise” ought to move us. Are you going to make God’s praise more perfect? Is there something that can be added to it? If all that praise already exists, what will you add?

God has been praised in all his good works, in all his creation, in the ordering of all things, in the governance and administration of the ages, in the order of times, in the height of heaven, in the fruitfulness of the earth, in the surrounding sea, in all the surpassing power of creation everywhere brought forth, in the sons of men themselves, in the giving of the Law, in freeing his people from captivity in Egypt, and in all his other wonders.

But he had not yet been praised in the fact that he raised flesh to eternal life. Let this praise, then, be added through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. In this way we rightly understand it as his voice “above all former praise.”

What of you, perhaps a sinner, who feared that your soul might be brought into conflict, who hoped in him alone so that you might be freed from that first captivity, who did not presume upon your own righteousness but upon his grace, which this Psalm commends? What of you—will you add something to all God’s praise?

“I will add,” he says. Let us see what he adds.

All your praise could have existed, and nothing at all would seem lacking to your praise, because nothing would be lacking if you condemned all the unrighteous. For the very justice by which the unrighteous are condemned would not fail to be great praise of God; it would be great praise.

You made man, gave him free choice, placed him in paradise, imposed a commandment, and announced the most just death if he violated the commandment. You did everything; no one can demand anything more from you.

He sinned. The human race became like a mass of sinners, flowing from sinners (Gen. 2–3). What, then? If you condemn this mass of iniquity, will anyone say to you, “You have acted unjustly”? You would indeed still be just in doing so, and all this would be your praise.

But because you also freed the sinner himself by justifying the ungodly, [Col. 0885] “I will add to all your praise.”

### 16. [verse 15]

“My mouth will declare your righteousness”—not mine. I will add to all your praise because, if I am righteous, even my being righteous is your righteousness in me, not mine; for you justify the ungodly (Rom. 4:5).

“My mouth will declare your righteousness; all day long your salvation.”

What does “your salvation” mean? “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3:9). Let no one claim for himself that he saves himself: salvation belongs to the Lord. No one saves himself by himself: “Salvation belongs to the Lord; human salvation is vain” (Ps. 59:13).

“All day long your salvation”: throughout all time. Something adverse occurs: proclaim the Lord’s salvation. Something prosperous occurs: proclaim the Lord’s salvation. Do not proclaim it in prosperity and fall silent in adversity; otherwise “all day long” will not be fulfilled.

For a whole day includes its night. When we say, for example, “Thirty days have passed,” do we not include the nights as well? Do we not include nights in the very designation “days”? What was said in Genesis? “There was evening and there was morning, one day” (Gen. 1:5).

Thus the whole day includes its night. For night serves the day, not the day the night. Whatever you do in mortal flesh ought to serve righteousness. Whatever you do according to God’s commandment must not be done for the profits of the flesh, lest the day serve the night.

Therefore praise God all day long—that is, in prosperity and in adversity: in prosperity as in daytime, in adversity as in nighttime. Nevertheless, praise God all day long, so that you have not sung in vain: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2).

When his sons, his livestock, his household, and all his possessions were safe, Job praised God; this was as daytime. Calamities came; bereavement came crashing down; what was kept perished, and those for whom it was kept died; this was as nighttime.

Yet see him praising throughout the whole day. When that daytime, in which he rejoiced because he had become as it were light—that is, prosperity—had set, did he cease praising God? Was there not day in his heart, [Col. 0886] from which this shone forth: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21)?

This was as yet evening. Then a thicker night came, deeper darkness: bodily pain and the decay of worms. Even in that decay he did not cease praising God outwardly in the night, while inwardly he rejoiced in the day.

When his wife urged him to blaspheme, bringing his soul into conflict and wickedly advising him, a miserable woman like a shadow of night, he said: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

Did we praise in the day and cease in the night? “All day long”—that is, together with its night—“your salvation.”

### 17

“For I have not known occupations in trade.”

“For this reason,” he says, “I proclaim your salvation all day long, because I have not known occupations in trade.”

What are these occupations in trade? Let merchants hear this and change their lives. If they have been merchants, let them be merchants no longer; let them not know what they were, but forget it. Finally, let them not approve or praise it; let them disapprove, condemn, and change, if trade is a sin.

For because of some insatiable desire to acquire, O merchant, when you suffer a loss you will blaspheme; and what is said, “All day long your praise,” will not be found in you. When, over the prices of the goods you sell, you not only lie but even swear falsely, how is God’s praise in your mouth all day long? When, if you are a Christian, the name of God is even blasphemed through your mouth (Rom. 2:24), so that people say, “See what Christians are like!”

Therefore, if this man praises God all day long because he has not known trade, let Christians correct themselves; let them not engage in trade.

But the merchant says to me: “I bring merchandise from far away to places where the things I bring are not available. I ask for a return for my labor, so that I may sell them for more than I paid. For how shall I live, when it is written, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wage’ (Luke 10:7)?”

But the issue is lying and perjury.

“This is my fault,” he says, “not the fault of trade. For if I wished, could I not conduct the business without this fault? Let me not therefore transfer my guilt to the occupation. If I lie, I lie; trade does not lie. For I could say, ‘I bought it for this much, but I will sell it for this much; if you wish, buy it.’ The buyer would not be driven away by hearing this truth; rather, everyone would come running, because they would value trustworthiness more than merchandise.

“Therefore warn me against lying and perjury, not against conducting the business by which I support myself.”

What do you call him to, then, when you call him away from this? Perhaps to some other craft? “I shall be a shoemaker; I shall make shoes for people.”

But are shoemakers not also liars? Are they not also perjurers? Do they not, after taking shoes to be made from one person and receiving payment from another, abandon what they were doing, undertake to make something for someone else, and deceive the person to whom they had promised to finish quickly? Do they not often say, “I will do it today; I will finish it today”?

Then, in the very sewing, do they not commit many frauds? They do these things and say these things; but the people themselves are bad, not the craft they profess.

Thus all craftsmen who do not fear God lie and swear falsely, whether for profit or through fear of loss or poverty; [Col. 0887] God’s praise is not continuous in them.

How, then, do you call me away from trade? Or should I become a farmer and murmur against God when he thunders? Should I consult a diviner when I fear hail? Should I ask what I can do against the sky? Should I wish the poor to go hungry so that I can sell what I have stored? Is this what you are leading me to?

“But good farmers do not do these things,” you say.

Neither do good merchants.

For is even having children an evil, because when their heads hurt, wicked and faithless mothers seek sacrilegious amulets and incantations? These are sins of people, not of things.

The merchant may say this to me: “Ask, then, Bishop, how you understand the occupations in trade that you have read in the Psalter, lest perhaps you do not understand them and prohibit me from trading. Advise me how to live. If I live well, it will go well with me. Nevertheless, I know one thing: if I am bad, it is not trade that makes me so, but my iniquity.”

When the truth is spoken, there is nothing to contradict.

> **Note:** Thus the manuscripts. The editors read *auctor*, “author,” instead of *actor*, “doer” or “agent.”

### 18

Let us therefore ask what occupations in trade he meant—occupations which the person who truly has not known them praises God all day long.

In Greek, *negotiatio* (“trade” or “business”) is said from activity; in Latin, from *negatum otium*, “leisure denied.” But whether it is derived from activity or from denied leisure, let us examine what it means.

> **Note:** Thus several manuscripts. The editions read: “and in Latin. Whether *negotiatio* is activity or business, let us examine what it is.”

Those who are active traders, as though they derive confidence from what they do, praise their own works and do not attain the grace of God. Thus “traders” stand opposed to that grace which this Psalm commends. For it commends grace so that no one may glory in his own works.

In one passage it is said: “Physicians will not raise the dead” (Ps. 87:11). Should people therefore abandon medicine? What does this mean? Under this designation are understood the proud, who promise salvation to human beings, although salvation belongs to the Lord.

Just as the saying “all day long your salvation” stands watch against physicians—that is, against proud people who promise salvation—so the saying “my mouth will declare your righteousness,” that is, not mine, [Col. 0888] stands watch against traders—that is, against those who rejoice in their activity and works.

Who are the traders, those who are pleased with themselves as though on account of their activity? Those “who, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

It is rightly called *negotium*, “business,” because it denies leisure. How great is the evil that denies leisure? The Lord rightly drove from the temple those to whom he said: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a house of trade” (Matt. 21:13).

That is, you glory in your works, seek no leisure, and do not hear Scripture speaking against your restlessness and business: “Be at leisure and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:11).

What does “Be at leisure and know that I am God” mean except that you should know that God is the one who works in you, and that you should not exalt yourselves on account of your works?

Do you not hear the voice of the one who says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29)?

This rest is proclaimed against traders; this rest is proclaimed against those who hate leisure, acting and boasting of their works so that they do not rest in God. And the more they exalt themselves over their own works, the farther they recoil from grace.

### 19

But in some copies we find: “For I did not know the *litteratura*.” Where other codices have *negotiationem*, some have *litteraturam*. How these readings agree is difficult to discover; nevertheless, the diversity among the translators may perhaps reveal the meaning rather than introduce an error. Let us therefore seek how we should understand *litteratura*, lest we offend grammarians as we did a little earlier, the negotiators; for a grammarian too can live honorably by his art—he need not swear falsely or lie.

Let us therefore seek the *litteratura* that this man did not know, in whose mouth the praise of God is all day long. There is a certain *litteratura* of the Jews; let us refer this matter to them also, and there we shall find what is meant. Just as, when we were asking about the negotiators, we found—because of their acts and works—that the negotiation meant here was one to be detested, as the Apostle indicated when he said: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3). Against this he says in the same way: “Not from works, lest anyone should boast.” How then? Shall we not do good? We shall do it—but with him working in us: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2:9–10).

How, then, do we find this directed against the negotiators—that is, against those who boast of their activity, who exalt themselves over their business, which denies leisure [*otium*] [note: Some manuscripts omit these words, “which denies leisure,” and some instead read: “which they transact”], and who are restless rather than good workers? For good workers are those in whom God works. In the same way, we find among the Jews a certain *litteratura*. May the Lord be present, so that I may explain in words what he has deigned to grant me to perceive in my heart.

The pride of the Jews, who presumed as though upon their own strength and the righteousness of their works, boasted in the Law: they themselves had received the Law, whereas the other nations had not received it. In that Law they did not boast of grace, but of the letter. For the Law without grace is the letter alone: it remains to convict iniquity, not to grant salvation.

What does the Apostle say? “For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22). Of this letter he says elsewhere: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

You possess the letter if you are a transgressor of the Law: “You who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the Law,” he says. Is it not rightly sung and said: “Deliver me from the hand of the one who passes beyond the law and of the wicked”? You possess the letter, but you do not fulfill the letter. Why do you not fulfill the letter? “Because you who preach against stealing, steal; you who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery; you who abhor idols, commit sacrilege. For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written” (Rom. 2:21–27).

What benefit, then, has the letter which you do not fulfill? And why do you not fulfill it? Because you presume upon yourself. Why do you not fulfill it? Because you are a negotiator: you exalt your works and do not know that the grace of the one who helps is necessary in order that the command of the one who orders may be fulfilled.

Behold, God has commanded; do what he has commanded. You begin to act as though by your own strength, and you fall; and the letter remains over you, punishing rather than saving. Rightly, then, “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Moses wrote five books; yet in the five porticoes surrounding the pool, the sick lay helpless and could not be healed (John 5:2). See how the letter remains, convicting the guilty but not saving the wicked. In those five porticoes, representing the five books, the sick were exposed rather than healed.

What, then, healed the sick man there? The movement of the water. When the pool had been stirred, the sick man descended into it, and one person was healed, because there is unity; whoever else descended at that same movement was not healed. [note: This is the reading of the better manuscripts; the editions read “before that same movement,” less well.]

How was the unity of the body that cries out from the ends of the earth commended? No other person was healed unless the pool was stirred again. The stirring of the pool therefore signified the disturbance of the Jewish people when the Lord Jesus Christ came. For the water in the pool was understood to be stirred by the arrival of an angel. The water, then, surrounded by five porticoes, was the Jewish people surrounded by the Law. The sick lay in the porticoes, and they were healed only in the water when it had been disturbed and stirred.

The Lord came; the water was disturbed; he was crucified. Let the sick man descend, so that he may be healed. What does “let him descend” mean? Let him humble himself.

Therefore, all of you who love the letter without grace will remain in the porticoes. You will be sick, lying there and not recovering, because you presume upon the letter. “For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly be from the law.” But the Law was given so that it might make you guilty; once made guilty, you would fear; fearing, you would ask for pardon; and then you would no longer presume upon your own strength or exalt yourselves through the letter.

The very same meaning is also represented by the fact that Elisha first sent his staff through a servant to raise a dead person. The son of the widow who had hosted him was dead. This was reported to him, and he gave his staff to his servant: “Go,” he said, “place it upon the dead man” (2 Kings 4:29).

Did the prophet not know what he was doing? The servant went ahead and placed the staff upon the dead man, but the dead man did not rise. “For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would truly be from the law.” The Law, sent through the servant, did not give life; nevertheless, the one who later followed and gave life sent his staff through the servant.

When the child had not risen, Elisha himself came, already bearing the figure of the Lord. He had sent his servant beforehand with the staff, as though with the Law. He came to the dead man lying there and placed his own limbs upon him. The child was small, whereas he was a grown man; he contracted and, so to speak, shortened the stature of his youth, making himself small so as to fit the dead child.

The dead man therefore rose when the living man adapted himself to the dead. The Lord did what the staff did not do; grace did what the letter did not do.

Those, then, who remained with the staff boast in the letter, and for that reason they are not given life. But I wish to boast of your grace. “But far be it from me,” says the Apostle, “to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14)—except in him who adapted himself, living, to me, who was dead, so that I might rise; “so that it might no longer be I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

Boasting in that very grace, “I did not know the *litteratura*”—that is, I utterly rejected those who presume upon the letter and recoil from grace.

### 20. [verse 16]

Rightly, then, what follows is: “I will enter into the power of the Lord”—not my own power, but the Lord’s. For they boasted in their own power, in the letter; therefore they did not recognize the grace joined to the letter.

For “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” He came to fulfill the Law when he gave charity, through which the Law could be fulfilled. “For the fullness of the Law is charity” (Rom. 13:10).

They did not have charity—that is, they did not have the Spirit of grace, since “God’s charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5)—and so they remained boasting in the letter. But because “the letter kills, while the Spirit gives life,” I did not know the *litteratura*, and I will enter into the power of the Lord.

Therefore the following verse confirms and completes the thought, fixing it in human hearts and allowing no other interpretation to intrude from any side:

“Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.”

O “alone”! What did he add by saying “alone”? I ask you. “I will remember your righteousness” would have been sufficient. “Alone,” he says—altogether alone. I do not consider my own righteousness there. “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Your righteousness alone sets me free; my own righteousness is nothing but sins. Let me not boast, then, of my strength; let me not remain in the letter. Let me reject the *litteratura*—that is, those who boast in the letter and perversely presume upon their own strength like madmen. Let me reject such people and enter into the power of the Lord, so that when I am weak, then I may be strong; so that you may be powerful in me, because I will remember your righteousness alone.

## SERMON II  
### On the Second Part of the Psalm

### 1

Yesterday we explained to Your Charity that the grace of God—by which we have been saved freely, without any preceding merits of ours except those deserving punishment—is commended in this psalm. Since we were unable to finish our treatment of it, we postponed its final part until today, promising in the name of the Lord that we would pay what we owed.

Since the time has come to pay it, be attentive in spirit, like fertile soil, where you may both multiply the seed and not be ungrateful for the rain. Yesterday we explained its title; but, in order to renew your attention and to make it known to those who were absent yesterday, we briefly recall it, so that those who heard may remember and those who did not know may hear.

It is the Psalm of the sons of Jonadab, a name interpreted as “Spontaneous of the Lord.” For the Lord must be served with a spontaneous—that is, good, pure, sincere, and perfect—will, not with a deceitful heart. This is also indicated where it is said: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. 53:8).

The Psalm is sung for his sons—that is, for the sons of obedience—and for those who were first led into captivity, so that our groaning may be recognized and “the evil of the day may be sufficient for it” (Matt. 6:34). For now, if we have deserted in pride, let us return, even if weary. And we cannot return except through grace.

Grace is given freely; for if it were not free, it would not be grace. Moreover, if it is grace because it is free, nothing of yours preceded, so that you might receive it. For if some good works of yours preceded, you received a payment, not a free gift. But the payment that was due to us is punishment.

Therefore, the fact that we are delivered is not due to our merits but to his grace. Let us therefore praise him; to him let us owe everything that we are and the fact that we are saved. This is what the psalmist concluded after saying many things: “Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.”

Yesterday’s exposition concluded with this verse.

The first captives—that is, those belonging to the first man—for this is why they are captives: because of the first man in whom we all die; “because the spiritual does not come first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46). Because of the first man there are first captives; because of the second man, second men are redeemed.

Indeed, redemption itself cries out about our captivity. For how could we be redeemed if we had not previously been captives? We indicated this captivity more explicitly from the Apostle’s letter, recalling some of his words, and we repeat them: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23).

This is our first captivity, in which “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17). This came as the punishment of sin: man was divided against himself because he had refused to be subject to one master. For nothing is so beneficial to the soul as obedience. And if it benefits the soul for a servant to obey his master, a son his father, and a wife her husband, how much more does it benefit a human being to obey God?

Adam therefore experienced the evil; every human being, however, is Adam. Likewise, among those who have believed, every human being is Christ, because they are members of Christ. Adam experienced an evil that he ought not to have experienced if he had believed the one who said, “Do not touch” (Gen. 2:17). Having experienced the evil, let him at least afterward obey the physician’s commands, so that he may rise—he who did not wish to believe the physician in order not to become sick.

A good and faithful physician gives a command even to a healthy person, so that the physician may not be necessary to him. “The healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). Good physicians are friends: they do not wish to sell their art, and they rejoice more over the healthy than over the sick. They give healthy people certain instructions, so that by observing them they may not fall into illness.

But if those people despise the instructions and fall ill, they beg the physician. Those who despised him when healthy now implore him when sick. If only they would at least implore him! Let them not, having lost their minds through fever, attack the physician as well.

You heard just now, when the Gospel was read, how the parable was spoken against them. Were those who said, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21:38), in their right minds? Certainly not. Imagine: they killed the son and were intending to kill the father also. That is not having a sound mind.

Finally, behold: because they killed the son, the son rose again, and “the stone rejected by the builders became the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22). They stumbled against him and were crushed; he will come upon them and grind them to pieces.

But this is not the case with the one who sings in the Psalm and says: “I will enter into the power of the Lord”—not my own, but the Lord’s. “Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.” I acknowledge none of my own; I will remember your righteousness alone. From you I have whatever good I have; whatever evil I have, I have from myself.

You did not repay me with punishment according to my merits; rather, you freely bestowed grace. Therefore I will remember your righteousness alone.

### 2. [verse 17]

“God, you have taught me from my youth.” What have you taught me? That I must remember your righteousness alone.

For, considering my past life, I see what was due to me and what I received in place of what was due to me. Punishment was due; grace was given. Gehenna was due; eternal life was given.

“God, you have taught me from my youth.” From the very beginning of my faith, by which you renewed me, you taught me that nothing had preceded in me from which I could say that what you gave was owed to me.

For who is converted to God except from iniquity? Who is redeemed except from captivity? And who can say that his captivity was unjust when he deserted his commander and defected to the deserter?

God is the commander; the devil is the deserter. The commander gave a command; the deserter suggested deception (Gen. 2:17; 3:1). Where were your ears between the command and the deception? Is the devil better than God? Is the one who defected better than the one who made you? [note: Two manuscripts read: “than the one who made you.”]

You believed what the devil promised and found what God threatened.

Now, therefore, having been freed from captivity, though still in hope and not yet in possession, walking by faith and not yet by sight [note: The manuscripts read “walking”; the editions, “you walk”], he says: “God, you have taught me from my youth.” From the time I turned to you, renewed by you—who had been made by you, restored who had been created, reformed who had been formed—from the time I turned, I learned that no merits of mine had preceded, but that your grace came to me freely, so that I might remember your righteousness alone.

### 3

What follows youth? For he says, “You have taught me from my youth.” What follows youth?

In your first conversion you learned that before conversion you were not righteous, but iniquity preceded, so that when iniquity was expelled, charity might take its place. Renewed into the new man in hope alone, not yet in reality [note: The manuscripts read “renewed”; the editions, “so that you may be renewed”], you learned that no good of yours had preceded, and by God’s grace you were converted to God.

Now perhaps, from the time you have been converted, you will have something of your own and ought to presume upon your strength? People commonly say: “Now let me go; it was necessary for you to show me the road, but that is enough. I shall walk along it.”

And the one who showed you the road says: “Perhaps you want me to lead you?” But if you grow proud: “No, enough; I shall walk along the road.” You are dismissed, and through weakness you will go astray again.

It was good for you that the one who first placed you on the road should lead you. Otherwise, unless he himself leads you, you will go astray again. Say to him, therefore: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Ps. 85:11).

That you have entered the road is youth itself: renewal and the beginning of faith. Previously you wandered along your own roads, straying through wooded and rugged places, lacerated in every limb. You were seeking your homeland—that is, a certain stability of spirit where you might say, “It is well,” and say it securely, at rest from every trouble, every temptation, and finally every captivity; but you did not find it.

What shall I say? Has the one who would show you the road come to you? The road itself came to you, and you were placed upon it without any merits of yours preceding, since you were certainly wandering.

What then? From the time you entered, do you now govern yourself? Does the one who taught you the road now abandon you? No, he says: “You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I will proclaim your wonders.”

It is wonderful that you still act, governing me—you who placed me on the road—and these are your wonders.

What, do you suppose, are God’s wonders? What is more wondrous among God’s wonders than to raise the dead?

“Am I dead?” you ask. If you were not dead, it would not be said to you: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

All unbelievers are dead; all the unrighteous are dead. They live in body, but in heart they are extinguished.

One who raises a dead body restores it to the light of this world and to the drawing of this air. But the one who raises it is not himself its light and air; the body begins to see as it saw before.

The soul is not raised in this way. The soul is raised by God—although the body too is raised by God. But when God raises the body, he restores it to the world; when he raises the soul, he restores it to himself.

If the air of this world departs, the body dies; if God departs, the soul dies. Therefore, when God raises the soul, unless the one who raised it remains present, the soul does not live once raised. He does not raise it and then abandon it to live by itself.

When Lazarus was raised, for example, after being dead four days, he was raised bodily through the bodily presence of the Lord. The Lord came bodily to the tomb and cried out, “Lazarus, come forth!” And Lazarus rose and came out of the tomb bound; afterward he was released and departed (John 11:41–44).

He was raised while the Lord was present, but he lived while the Lord was absent. Although the Lord raised him bodily, as far as visible things are concerned, it was the presence of his majesty that raised him—and by that presence he never departs.

For the time being, however, the Lord raised Lazarus through his visible presence. The Lord departed from that city, or from that place; did Lazarus therefore not continue to live?

The soul is not raised in this way. God raises it; it dies if God departs.

I shall speak boldly, brothers, but truthfully. There are two lives: one of the body and the other of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. Just as the body dies if the soul abandons it, so the soul dies if God abandons it.

This, then, is his grace: that he raises us and remains with us. Because he raises us from our former death and renews our life, so to speak, we say to him: “God, you have taught me from my youth.”

And because he does not depart from those whom he raises, lest they die when he has departed, we say to him: “And to this day I will proclaim your wonders.” For while you are with me, I live, and you are the life of my soul, which will die if it is left to itself.

Therefore, while my life—that is, my God—is present, “to this day.” What comes afterward?

### 4. [verse 18]

“And even into old age and gray hairs.”

These are two names for old age, and the Greeks distinguish between them. The maturity that follows youth has one name among the Greeks, and the final age that follows maturity has another. For *presbytēs* (πρεσβύτης) denotes an elder, while *gerōn* (γέρων) denotes an old man. Since Latin lacks a distinction between these two names, both are expressed in terms of old age: *senecta* and *senium*. You know, however, that there are two ages.

“You taught me your grace from my youth, and to this day, after my youth, I will proclaim your wonders,” because you are with me so that I may not die—you who came so that I might rise. “And even into old age and gray hairs,” that is, to my very end: unless you are with me, there will be no merit of mine. May your grace always remain with me.

One person might say this—you, he, or I. But because this voice belongs to a certain great person, that is, to unity itself, it is the voice of the Church. Let us seek the youth of the Church.

When Christ came, was crucified, died, rose again, and called the nations, they began to be converted. They became martyrs strong in Christ; faithful blood was poured out; the harvest of the Church sprang up. This was its youth.

As the times advance, however, let the Church confess and say: “To this day I will proclaim your wonders.” Not only in its youth, when Paul, Peter, and the first Apostles proclaimed them, but even as its age advances, I myself—that is, your unity, your members, your body—will proclaim your wonders.

What comes afterward? “And even into old age and gray hairs I will proclaim your wonders.” The Church will remain here until the end of the age. For if it will not be here until the end of the age, to whom did the Lord say: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20)?

Why was it necessary for these things to be said in the Scriptures? Because there would be enemies of the Christian faith who would say: “Christians exist only for a short time; afterward they will perish, and idols will return; what existed before will return” [note: See above, p. 454, note (a)].

How long will Christians exist? “Into old age and gray hairs”—that is, until the end of the age.

While you, wretched unbeliever, await the passing away of Christians, you yourself pass away without Christians. Christians will remain until the end of the age; and when, through your unbelief, you have ended your brief life, with what face will you go before the Judge whom, while you lived, you blasphemed?

Therefore: “From my youth, and to this day, and even into old age and gray hairs, Lord, do not abandon me.” Not as my enemies say, that it will last only for a time. “Do not abandon me until I proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come.”

“And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). The arm of the Lord is Christ.

Do not abandon me, therefore. Let not those who say, “Christians will exist only until a certain time,” rejoice. Let there be people who proclaim your arm. To whom? “To every generation that is to come.”

Therefore, if to every generation that is to come, then until the end of the age; for when the age has ended, no generation will come afterward.

### 5. [verse 19]

“Your power and your righteousness”—that is, that I may proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come.

And what did your arm provide? Our gratuitous deliverance. Let me proclaim this grace, then, to every generation that is to come. Let me say to every person who will be born: “You are nothing through yourself; call upon God. Your sins are yours; God’s merits are his. Punishment is owed to you, and when the reward comes, he will crown his own gifts, not your merits.”

I will say this to every generation that is to come: “You came from captivity; you belonged to Adam.”

I will say this to every generation that is to come—not my strength, not my righteousness, but your power and your righteousness, O God, reaching even to the highest things in which you have performed great deeds.

Your power and your righteousness—how far? Only to flesh and blood? No: “to the highest things in which you have performed great deeds.”

The heavens are in the heights; the angels are in the heights—Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers. They owe you that they are; they owe you that they live; they owe you that they live righteously; they owe you that they live blessedly.

“Your power and your righteousness”—how far? “To the highest things in which you have performed great deeds.”

Do not think that human beings alone belong to the grace of God. What was an angel before it was made? What is an angel if it abandons the one who created it?

Therefore: “Your power and your righteousness, reaching to the highest things in which you have performed great deeds.”

### 6

And human beings exalt themselves! And, so as to belong to the first captivity, they listen to the serpent suggesting: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5).

Human beings like gods! “God, who is like you?” Not in the abyss, not in hell, not on earth, not in heaven [note: The preposition “in” is absent from the manuscripts]—because you made everything.

What does the work contend with the craftsman? “God, who is like you?”

But Adam, wretched, says—and in Adam, every human being says: “When I perversely wish to be like you, behold what I have become, so that from captivity I cry out to you. I was well under a good king; I have become captive under my seducer; and I cry out to you because I fell away from you.”

And how did I fall away from you? By seeking to be perversely like you.

What then? Does God not call us to his likeness? Is it not he who says: “Love your enemies; pray for those who persecute you; do good to those who hate you”? In saying this, he urges us toward the likeness of God.

Finally, what does he add? “So that you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven.” What does he himself do? Certainly this: “He makes his sun rise over the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:44–45).

Whoever therefore wishes well to his enemy is like God. This is not pride but obedience. Why? Because we were made in the image of God: “Let us make man,” he said, “in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

It is therefore not something foreign if we bear God’s image within us. If only we would not lose it through pride!

But what is it to wish, through pride, to be like God? What do we suppose this perverse likeness is, that the captive might cry out: “Lord, who is like you?”

Listen and understand, if you can. We believe that the one who caused us to say these things to you will also grant you the ability both to understand and to comprehend them.

God needs no good; he himself is the supreme good, and every good comes from him. In order for us to be good, we need God. For God to be good, he does not need us—not merely us, but even the highest things in which he has performed great deeds. God does not need the heavenly beings, the superheavenly beings, or even what is called the heaven of heaven, in order to be better, more powerful, or more blessed.

For what would anything else be if he himself had not made it? What, then, does he need from you, who existed before you and was so powerful that, when you did not exist, he made you?

Do parents make children in the same way? Through a certain carnal desire they beget rather than create; for while these parents beget, God creates. If you create in this way, tell me what your wife will bear. Better still, let her say it herself, since she does not know what she carries.

Human beings nevertheless beget children both for their own consolation and as support in old age. Did God create all these things so that, when he grew old, they might assist him? God knows what he creates, what it is through his goodness, and what it will become through its own will. God knows and has ordered everything.

But for a human being to become something, he must turn toward the one by whom he was created. By withdrawing, he grows cold; by approaching, he grows fervent. By withdrawing, he grows dark; by approaching, he grows bright. From the one by whom he has being, he receives the means of being well.

Finally, the younger son, who wished to have his substance—which was best preserved for him with his father—in his own power, took control of himself, departed into a distant country, attached himself to an evil master, and fed pigs. Hunger corrected the one who had departed in pride because of his abundance (Luke 15:12–16).

Therefore, whoever wishes to be like God in such a way that he stands with him and keeps his strength for him, as it is written (Ps. 58:10), should not depart from him. By clinging to him, let him be sealed as wax is sealed from a ring; let him, fixed to God, bear his image, doing what has been said: “For me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). Thus he truly preserves the likeness and image in which he was made.

But if he perversely wishes to imitate God—so that, just as God has no one by whom he is formed and no one by whom he is ruled, he too wishes to use his own power, living as though no one formed or ruled him—what remains, brothers, except that, withdrawing from God’s warmth, he grows numb; withdrawing from the truth, he becomes empty; withdrawing from him who supremely and immutably is, he changes for the worse and perishes? [note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read “immutably”; the Lovaniensis edition reads “incomparably.”]

### 7

The devil did this. He wished to imitate God, but perversely—not to be under God’s power, but to have power against him.

Now man, placed under a command, heard from the Lord God: “Do not touch”—what? “This tree” (Gen. 2:17).

What is that tree? If it is good, why must I not touch it? If it is bad, what is it doing in paradise?

It is precisely because it is good that it is in paradise; but I do not want you to touch it.

Why must I not touch it? Because I want you to be obedient, not rebellious.

“Serve, servant, for this purpose, servant” [note: So some manuscripts. Others, more numerous, read: “Serve still, servant.” A smaller number, along with the printed editions, have: “not a rebellious servant; for this purpose, servant,” and so forth]; but do not be a bad servant.

Servant, first hear the command of the Lord, and then learn the purpose of the one who commands. The tree is good; I do not want you to touch it.

Why? Because I am the Lord and you are a servant. That is the whole reason.

If the matter is trivial, do you disdain being a servant? What is beneficial to you except to be under the Lord? How will you be under the Lord unless you are under a command?

Moreover, if it is beneficial for you to be under the Lord and under a command, what was God going to command you? Was he seeking something from you? Was he going to say, “Offer me a sacrifice”? Did he not himself make everything, including you?

Was he going to say, “Obey me,” whether at bed when I rest, at table when I refresh myself, or at the baths when I wash?

Since God needs nothing from you, should he therefore have commanded you nothing? But if he ought to command something so that you might recognize what benefits you—that you are under the Lord—you had to be prohibited from some thing, not because of the wickedness of that tree but because of your obedience.

God could not have demonstrated more perfectly how great the good of obedience is than by prohibiting something that was not evil. There, obedience alone holds the prize; disobedience alone finds punishment.

“It is good; I do not want you to touch it.” For you will not die merely by not touching it. Did the one who prohibited this withhold all the others? Is paradise not full of fruitful trees? What do you lack? “I do not want you to touch this; I do not want you to taste it.” It is good, but obedience is better.

Therefore, when you touched it, would that tree itself become evil, so that you would die? No: disobedience subjected you to death, because you touched what had been forbidden.

For this reason that tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:17)—not because such things hung from it as fruits, but because, whatever that tree was, whatever its apple or fruit may have been, it was so called because the human being who did not wish to distinguish good from evil through a command would distinguish them through experience. By touching what was forbidden, he would discover punishment.

Why did he touch it, my brothers? What did he lack? Let someone tell me what he lacked, placed in paradise, amid abundance and amid delights, for whom the very vision of God was a great delight, whose face he feared after sin as though he were an enemy.

What did he lack that he touched it, except that he wished to use his own power and took pleasure in breaking the command, so that, with no one ruling over him, he might become like God—for certainly no one rules over God?

Wandering badly, presuming badly, destined to die, withdrawing from the way of righteousness [note: Most manuscripts read “from the life of righteousness”]. Behold, he broke the command, shook the yoke of discipline from his neck, and in an outburst of pride tore apart the reins of government. Where is he now?

Certainly the captive cries out: “Lord, who is like you? I wished perversely to be like you, and I have become like a beast. Under your dominion, under your command, I was truly like you; but man, though placed in honor, did not understand. He was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Now, too late, cry out concerning the likeness of beasts and say: “God, who is like you?”

### 8. [verses 20–21]

“How many tribulations, great and evil, you have shown me!”
