Rightly so, proud servant. For you perversely wished to be like your Lord, whose image you had been made to bear. You wanted good for yourself after withdrawing from that good?

God says to you plainly: “If you withdraw from me and it is well with you, then I am not your good.”

Therefore, if he is good, supremely good, good in himself and for himself, good without any external good, and himself our supreme good, what will you be by withdrawing from him except evil?

Likewise, if he is our blessedness, what will be the condition of one who withdraws except misery?

Return, then, after misery, and say: “Lord, who is like you? How many tribulations, great and evil, you have shown me!”

9. But it was discipline: admonition, not abandonment. Finally, what does he say in thanksgiving? “And having turned, you gave me life, and again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.” When had this happened before? What does “again” mean here? You fell from the height, O man, a disobedient slave, proud against the Lord—you fell! In you was fulfilled: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled”; let this also be fulfilled in you: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Return from the depth. “I return,” he says; “I return, I acknowledge it: God, who is like you? How many and grievous tribulations you have shown me! And having turned, you gave me life, and again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.”

I understand; I hear. For you brought me up from the depths of the earth; you brought me up from the depth and submersion of sin. But why “again”? When had this already happened? Let us continue, lest perhaps the later portions of the psalm itself explain to us what we do not yet understand here—what he meant by “again.” Let us therefore listen:

“How many and grievous tribulations you have shown me! And having turned, you gave me life, and again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.” What follows? “You multiplied your righteousness; and having turned, you consoled me, and again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.” There is a second “again.” If we struggle to explain this “again” when it occurs once, who can explain it when it is doubled? The very doubling is already an “again,” and once more “again” is set down.

May he be present from whom grace comes; may the arm also be present that we proclaim to every generation yet to come. May he himself be present and, as with the key of his cross, open the mystery that has been closed [Note: [Col. 0898] A few manuscripts read *clavo*, “nail.”]. For it was not without reason that, when he was crucified, the veil of the temple was torn in two (Matthew 27:51): it was because through his passion the secrets of all mysteries were revealed. Let him therefore be present to those who are passing over to him; let the veil be taken away (2 Corinthians 3:16). Let our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ tell us why the Prophet’s utterance was prefaced in this way:

“You have shown me many and grievous tribulations; and having turned, you gave me life, and again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.”

Here “again” has been placed for the first time. Let us see what this means, and we shall discover why there is a second “again.”

10. What is Christ? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: he was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). Great is this! Mighty is this! And you—what are you, captive? Where do you lie? In the flesh, under death. Who, then, is he? Who are you? And what did he later become? For whose sake?

Who is he but the one called “the Word”? What Word? Lest perhaps it be a sound that comes and passes away: the Word, God with God; the Word through whom all things were made. What did he become for your sake? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

“He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all—how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Behold what he is, who he is, and for whose sake. The Son of God became flesh for the sinner, for the unrighteous, for the deserter, for the proud, for the perverse imitator of his God! He became what you are, son of man, so that we might become sons of God [Note: [Col. 0899] Most manuscripts omit *efficeremur*, “we might become.” Others read: “so that he might make us sons of God.”]

He became flesh. From where did he take flesh? From the Virgin Mary (Luke 2:7). Whence came the Virgin Mary? From Adam. Therefore, from that first captive; and Christ’s flesh came from the mass of captivity.

Why this? As an example. He took from you that in which he would die for you; he took from you what he would offer for you, by which example he might teach you. What would he teach you? That you will rise again. For how would you believe unless an example of flesh assumed from the mass of your death had gone before?

Therefore, in him we first rose again; for when Christ rose, we rose. It was not the Word that died and rose again; rather, in the Word, flesh died and rose again. Christ died where you are destined to die, and Christ rose where you are destined to rise. By his example he taught you what not to fear and what to hope for. You feared death: he died. You despaired of resurrection: he rose again.

But you say to me: “He rose again; surely not I?” Yet he rose in that which he received from you and for you. Therefore, your nature went before you in him; and what was taken from you ascended before you. Thus you too ascended there. He therefore ascended first, and in him we did also, because that flesh was from the human race.

Therefore, when he rose, we too were brought back from the depths of the earth. When Christ rose, you brought me back from the depths of the earth. But when we believe in Christ, you again brought me back from the depths of the earth. Here is one “again.”

Hear the Apostle fulfill this: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

He therefore went before us. We too have already risen, but still in hope. Hear the same Apostle Paul saying: “We ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body.” You still groan; you still await. What, then, has Christ granted you? Hear what follows: “For in hope we have been saved; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:23–25).

We have therefore again been brought up from the depths of the earth in hope. Why “again”? Because Christ had already gone before us. But because we shall rise in reality—for now we live in hope, now we walk according to faith—we have been brought up from the depths of the earth by believing in him who rose before us from the depths of the earth. Our soul has been raised from the iniquity of unbelief, and by faith a kind of first resurrection has taken place in us.

But if this alone will exist, what of the Apostle’s words: “Awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body”? What of what he said in that passage: “The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:10–11)?

Therefore, we have already risen in mind, faith, hope, and love; but it remains that we rise in the body. You have heard one “again”; you have heard a second “again”: one “again” because Christ went before us; and the other, still in hope, because what remains is yet to occur in reality [Note: [Col. 0900] The editions read *audi alterum*, “hear the second,” and below, after *praecedentem*, “the one who went before,” they had: “you have heard ‘again,’ but still in hope. What remains in reality?” These readings have been corrected in accordance with several manuscripts.]

“You multiplied your righteousness”: already in those who believe, already in those who first rose in hope. “You multiplied your righteousness.” The scourge also belongs to that righteousness, because “it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17), Peter says—that is, with his saints. “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3:12; Hebrews 12:6).

“You multiplied your righteousness”: for now you have not spared even your sons, but, for those for whom you were preserving an eternal inheritance, you did not abandon them in discipline. “You multiplied your righteousness; and having turned, you consoled me”—and because of the body that will rise at the end, “again you brought me up from the depths of the earth.”

11. [Verse 22.] “For I too will confess your truth with the vessels of the psalm.” The vessels of the psalm are the psaltery. But what is the psaltery? A wooden instrument with strings. What does it signify? There is a difference between it and the lyre, as those who know say: the hollow wood over which the strings are stretched so that they may resound has the psaltery above, whereas the lyre has it below. And because the spirit is from above and the flesh from the earth, the spirit seems to be signified by the psaltery and the flesh by the lyre.

And because he had spoken of our two restorations from the depths of the earth—one according to the spirit, in hope, and the other according to the body, in reality—hear of these two:

“For I too will confess your truth with the vessels of the psalm.” This concerns the spirit. What about the body? “I will sing to you with the lyre, Holy One of Israel.”

12. [Verses 23, 24.] Hear this again, because of the “again” and the “again.” “My lips will rejoice when I sing to you.” Since “lips” can refer both to the inner and to the outer person, it is uncertain in what sense “lips” has been used. What follows makes it clear: “And my soul, which you have redeemed.”

Therefore, saved in hope through the inner lips, brought up from the depths of the earth in faith and love, yet still awaiting the redemption of our body, what do we say? He has already said: “And my soul, which you have redeemed.” But lest you think that only the soul has been redeemed—the soul in which you have now heard one “again”—he continues: “But still”: what does “still” mean? “But still my tongue.” Therefore, already the tongue of the body:

“All day long it will meditate on your righteousness”—that is, throughout eternity without end. But when will this be? At the end of the age, in the resurrection of the body and its transformation into an angelic condition [Note: [Col. 0900] The editions read *in resurrectione*, “in the resurrection.” The manuscripts omit *in*.]

How is it proved that this refers to the end, when it says, “But still my tongue will meditate on your righteousness all day long”? “When those who seek evils for me have been confounded and put to shame.” When will they be confounded and put to shame, if not at the end of the age?

They will be confounded in two ways: either when they believe in Christ, or when Christ comes. For as long as the Church is here; as long as the wheat groans among the chaff; as long as the ears groan among the weeds (Matthew 3:12; 13:30); as long as the vessels of mercy groan among the vessels of wrath made for dishonor (2 Timothy 2:20); as long as the lily groans among the thorns—there will not be lacking enemies who say, “When will he die, and his name perish?” (Psalm 40:6). That is: “Behold, the time will come when they will come to an end, and there will be no Christians. Just as they began at some point, so they will last only until a definite time.”

But while they say these things, they die without end, and the Church remains, proclaiming the arm of the Lord to every generation yet to come [Note: [Col. 0901] Several manuscripts read *fide*, “in faith,” instead of *sine fine*, “without end.”]

He himself, the last one, will also come in his glory. All the dead will rise, each with his own case. The good will be separated to the right, but the wicked to the left (Matthew 25:33). Those who insulted will be confounded, and those who chattered will be put to shame. And so, after the resurrection, my tongue will meditate on your righteousness, all day long on your praise, “when those who seek evils for me have been confounded and put to shame.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 71

[Note: [Col. 0901] Dictated in the year of Christ 415, from Letter 169 to Evodius, section 1.]

1. [Verse 1.] The title of this psalm is prefaced “For Solomon”; yet it speaks of things that cannot suit that Solomon, king of Israel according to the flesh, in accordance with what holy Scripture says about him. They can, however, suit the Lord Christ most appropriately. Hence it is also understood that the name “Solomon” has been employed figuratively, so that Christ may be understood in it.

For *Solomon* is interpreted as “Peaceful” (*Pacificus*); and therefore this name most truly and fittingly belongs to the one through whom, as mediator, having received the forgiveness of sins, we are reconciled to God from a state of enmity [Note: [Col. 0901] Most manuscripts read *inimicitiis*, “from hostilities,” in place of *inimicis*, “from enemies.”]. “For while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10).

He is that Peaceful One who “made both one, and broke down the dividing wall of the fence, the enmity, in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, so that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, making peace; and coming, he preached peace to those who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:14–17).

He himself says in the Gospel: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14:27). And by many other testimonies the Lord Christ is shown to be the Peaceful One—not according to the peace that this world knows and seeks, but that peace of which it is said through the prophet: “I will give them true comfort, peace upon peace” (Isaiah 57:19, according to the Septuagint)—when the peace of reconciliation is joined to the peace of immortality.

For after all that God has promised has been restored, the same prophet shows that we ought to await the final peace, in which we shall live with God forever, when he says: “Lord our God, grant us peace; for you have given us everything” (Isaiah 26:12, according to the Septuagint).

That peace will plainly be perfect when the final enemy, death, has been destroyed. And in whom will this occur, if not in that Peaceful One who reconciles us? “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22); and “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Since, then, we have found the true Solomon—that is, the true Peaceful One—let us now attend to what the psalm itself teaches about him.

2. [Verse 2.] “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son.” The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). This, then, is: “O God, give your judgment to the king.”

He who is king is also the king’s son, because God the Father is certainly king as well. Thus it is written that “the king gave a wedding feast for his son” (Matthew 22:2).

According to the custom of Scripture, the same thing is repeated. For what he said, “your judgment,” he says in another way, “your righteousness”; and what he said, “to the king,” he says in another way, “to the king’s son.” So it is with the passage: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Psalm 2:4). What is “he who dwells in the heavens” is also “the Lord”; and what is “he will laugh at them” is also “he will mock them.”

Likewise: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands” (Psalm 18:2). “The heavens” is repeated under the name “firmament”; “the glory of God” is repeated as “the work of his hands”; and “declare” is repeated as “proclaims.”

These repetitions greatly commend the divine utterances, whether the same words are repeated or the same meaning is repeated in different words. They are found especially in the Psalms and in that mode of speech by which the emotions of the mind are stirred.

3. Next comes: “To judge your people in righteousness, and your poor in judgment.” The purpose for which the Father the King gave his judgment and righteousness to the King the Son is sufficiently shown when he says, “To judge your people in righteousness”—that is, for judging your people.

Such a mode of expression occurs in Solomon: “The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, to know wisdom and discipline” (Proverbs 1:1)—that is, “The proverbs of Solomon for knowing wisdom and discipline.” Thus, “Give your judgment, to judge your people” means, “Give your judgment for judging your people.”

What he first called “your people,” he later calls “your poor”; and what he first called “in righteousness,” he later calls “in judgment,” according to that mode of repetition.

Here he plainly shows that the people of God ought to be poor—that is, not proud but humble. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

In this poverty the blessed Job was also poor, even before he had lost those great earthly riches. I thought this should be mentioned because there are some who more readily distribute all their possessions to the poor than become themselves God’s poor. They are puffed up by the boastfulness with which they think that their good life should be attributed to them, not to the grace of God; and therefore they no longer live well, however many good works they may appear to perform.

They think they possess what they have as their own, and they glory as though they had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7): rich in themselves, not poor in God; self-sufficient, not needy before God.

But the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and deliver my body to be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing.” It is as though he said: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, but do not become God’s poor, it profits me nothing.”

For “love is not puffed up” (1 Corinthians 13:4); nor is the love of God true in one who is ungrateful to his Holy Spirit, through whom his love is poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5) [Note: [Col. 0903] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read *veritas*, “truth.”].

Therefore such people do not belong to the people of God, because they are not God’s poor. God’s poor say: “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things freely given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12).

For although in this psalm also, because of the mystery of the assumed man in which “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), it is said to God the Father, the King, “Give your righteousness to the king’s son,” these people do not want righteousness to be given to them; rather, they trust that they possess it from themselves. “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness” (Romans 10:3).

They are therefore, as I have said, not God’s poor but rich in themselves, because they are not humble but proud. He will come to judge God’s people in righteousness and God’s poor in judgment; and by that judgment he will distinguish his poor from their rich—but those whom he has made rich by their poverty.

For the poor people cry out to him: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm 42:1).

4. When, with the order of the words changed, he had first said, “O God, give your judgment to the king and your righteousness to the king’s son,” placing judgment first and righteousness afterward, he then placed righteousness first and judgment afterward, saying, “To judge your people in righteousness, and your poor in judgment.” This more clearly shows that he called judgment “righteousness,” demonstrating that it makes no difference in what order it is placed, since it signifies the same thing.

For it is customary to call a judgment “perverse” when it is unjust; but we do not ordinarily call righteousness “iniquitous” or “unjust.” If it is perverse and unjust, it cannot any longer be called righteousness.

Therefore, by placing judgment and repeating it under the name of righteousness, or by placing righteousness and repeating it under the name of judgment, he sufficiently teaches that he specifically calls “judgment” what is customarily designated by “righteousness”—that is, what cannot be understood as an evil judgment.

When the Lord says, “Do not judge according to appearances, but judge with righteous judgment” (John 7:24), he shows that judgment can be perverse, since he says, “Judge with righteous judgment”: he forbids the former and commands the latter.

But when he says “judgment” without any qualification, he immediately wants it understood as righteous, as in the words: “You leave the weightier matters of the Law—mercy and judgment” (Matthew 23:23).

So too in what Jeremiah says: “He who makes his riches not with judgment” (Jeremiah 17:11). He does not say, “He who makes his riches by perverse or unjust judgment,” or “not with right or just judgment,” but simply “not with judgment,” calling judgment nothing other than what is right and just.

5. [Verse 3.] “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.” Mountains are greater; hills are smaller. Surely these are the ones mentioned in another psalm: “Small and great together.” For these mountains “skipped like rams,” and these hills “like lambs of sheep,” at the exodus of Israel from Egypt (Psalm 113:13, 4, 1)—that is, in the liberation of God’s people from the servitude of this age.

Those who stand out in excellent holiness within the Church are mountains: they are capable of teaching others (2 Timothy 2:2), speaking in such a way that others may be faithfully instructed, and living in such a way that others may imitate them to their salvation. The hills are those who follow their excellence through obedience.

Why, then, do the mountains receive peace and the hills righteousness? Or perhaps it would make no difference if it were said: “Let the mountains receive righteousness for the people, and the hills peace.” Righteousness is necessary for both, and peace for both. It may be that peace has been called by another name—righteousness itself—for this is true peace, not the sort that the unjust establish among themselves.

Or should what he says—“the mountains peace, and the hills righteousness”—be understood with a significant distinction? Those who are eminent in the Church ought, with watchful attention, to safeguard peace, lest by acting proudly on account of their honors they create schisms and break apart the bond of unity.

The hills, however, should follow them through imitation and obedience in such a way that they place Christ before them, lest, seduced by the empty authority of evil mountains because they appear eminent, they break away from the unity of Christ.

Therefore it is said: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people.” Let them indeed say: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). But let them also say: “Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you something contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). Let them also say: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

Thus let them receive peace for the people of God—that is, for God’s poor—not wishing to reign over them, but with them. Let the others likewise not say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” or “I to Cephas,” but let all say, “I belong to Christ” (ibid., 1:12).

This is righteousness: not placing servants before the Lord or equating them with him; lifting one’s eyes to the mountains, from which help comes, yet not hoping for one’s help from the mountains, but from the Lord who made heaven and earth (Psalm 120:1–2).

6. It can also be understood most fittingly in this way: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people,” so that by peace we understand the reconciliation by which we are reconciled to God. The mountains receive this peace for his people.

The Apostle testifies to this as follows: “The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.” Behold how the mountains receive peace for his people.

“For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation.” In whom, if not in the mountains who receive peace for his people?

Therefore the ambassadors of peace add what follows and say: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:17–20).

The mountains receive this peace for his people—that is, the preaching and embassy of his peace. “And the hills righteousness”: that is, obedience, which is the origin and perfection of all righteousness in human beings and in every rational creature.

Thus the great distinction between the two men is commended: Adam, who was the head of our death, and Christ, who is the head of our salvation. “For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

Let the mountains therefore receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness, so that, with both agreeing in this way, what is written may come to pass: “Righteousness and peace have kissed each other” (Psalm 84:11).

As for what other manuscripts have: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills”—I think that both groups are to be understood as preachers of evangelical peace, whether those who precede or those who follow. In these manuscripts what follows is: “In righteousness he will judge the poor of the people.”

But those manuscripts are more approved which have what we explained above: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.” Some have “for your people”; others do not have “your,” but only “for the people.”

7. [Verse 4.] “He will judge the poor of the people, and save the children of the poor.” The poor and the children of the poor seem to me to be the same people, just as the same city is called Zion and the daughter of Zion.

But if the distinction is to be understood more precisely, we take the poor to be the mountains and the children of the poor to be the hills: the poor being the Prophets and Apostles, and their children—that is, those who make progress under their authority—being the children of the poor.

The fact that he first says “he will judge” and afterward “he will save” is a kind of explanation of how he will judge. For he will judge in order to save—that is, to distinguish from those being destroyed and condemned those to whom he grants the salvation prepared to be revealed in the last time (1 Peter 1:5).

It is from such people that the prayer is offered: “Do not destroy my soul with the wicked” (Psalm 26:9); and: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm 42:1).

It should also be considered that he does not say, “He will judge the poor people,” but “the poor of the people.” Above, when he said, “To judge your people in righteousness, and your poor in judgment,” he called the same people God’s people and God’s poor—that is, only the good, those who belong on the right.

But because in this age those on the right and those on the left are fed together—those who at the end will be separated like sheep and goats (Matthew 25:32)—he called the whole group, as it is mixed together, by the name “people” [Note: [Col. 0905] The manuscripts read *commixtus est*, “is mixed together.” The editions read *commixtum est*, “is mixed together,” neuter.]

And because here too he places judgment in a good sense—that is, for the purpose of saving—he says, “He will judge the poor of the people”: that is, he will distinguish for salvation those who among the people are poor.

We have already explained above who the poor are [Note: [Col. 0905] Above, section 3.]; let us understand these also as the needy.

“And he will humble the accuser.” No one is more appropriately recognized here as the accuser than the devil. His accusation is: “Does Job worship God for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

The Lord Jesus humbles him by assisting his own through his grace, so that they may worship God for nothing—that is, take delight in the Lord (Psalm 36:4).

He also humbled him in this way: when the devil, the prince of this world, found nothing in Christ (John 14:30), he killed him through the accusations of the Jews, whom the accuser used as his vessels, working in the sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2).

He was humbled because the one whom they had killed rose again and took away the kingdom of death, over which the devil exercised such power that, through one man whom he had deceived, he dragged all people through death into condemnation.

But he was humbled because, “if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:17). He humbled the accuser, who brought false charges, unjust judges, and false witnesses against him in order to destroy him.

8. [Verse 5.] “And he will remain for the sun,” or “he will remain with the sun.” Some of our writers thought that this should be interpreted better in this way, because the Greek has συμπαραμενεῖ (*symparameneî*). If it could be expressed in Latin by a single word, one would have to say *compermanebit*, “he will remain together with.” Since the verb cannot be expressed in Latin, the meaning was rendered at least by saying, “he will remain with the sun.”

For *compermanebit soli* means nothing other than *permanebit cum sole*, “he will remain with the sun.”

But what great thing is it for him through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3), to remain with the sun—unless this prophecy was uttered in advance because of those who think that the religion of the Christian name will last in this age only until a definite time and afterward will no longer exist?

He will therefore remain with the sun for as long as the sun rises and sets; that is, for as long as these times continue to revolve, the Church of God—the body of Christ on earth—will not cease to exist.

What follows, “And before the moon, generations of generations,” could have been said as “And before the sun,” that is, “both with the sun and before the sun.” This would be understood as “both with time and before time.”

That which precedes time is eternal. And that should truly be held eternal which is changed by no time, as in the words: “In the beginning was the Word.”

But he preferred to signify by the moon the increase and decrease of mortals. Accordingly, when he had said “before the moon,” wishing in a certain way to explain why he had mentioned the moon, he added, “generations of generations,” as though he were saying: “Before the moon”—that is, before the generations of generations that pass away through the departure and succession of mortals, like the waxing and waning of the moon.

Thus what is better understood by “remaining before the moon” than preceding all mortal things by immortality?

This can also be taken, without impropriety, to mean that what he does after the accuser has been humbled—namely, sits at the right hand of the Father—is what it means to remain with the sun. The Son is understood as “the radiance of eternal glory” (Hebrews 1:3), as though the Father were the sun and his Son were his radiance.

But these things can be said of the invisible substance of the Creator, not in the same way as of the visible creature in which the heavenly bodies exist, among which the sun shines more brightly and from which this comparison has been drawn—just as comparisons are also drawn from earthly things: a rock, a lion, a lamb, a man with two sons, and so forth.

After the accuser has been humbled, therefore, he remains with the sun, because, having conquered the devil through the resurrection, he sits at the right hand of the Father (Mark 16:19), where he no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Romans 6:9).

And this is “before the moon,” as the firstborn from the dead going before the Church, which passes away through the departure and succession of mortals. These are the generations of generations.

Or perhaps it is because there are generations by which we are generated mortally, but generations of generations by which we are regenerated immortally. This is the Church which he preceded, so that he might remain before the moon, the firstborn from the dead.

Certainly, as for the Greek expression γενεὰς γενεῶν (*geneas geneōn*), some have interpreted it not as “generations” but as “of the generation of generations,” because γενεὰς is an ambiguous Greek case: it is not evident whether it is the singular genitive τῆς γενεᾶς (*tēs geneās*), “of this generation,” or the plural accusative τὰς γενεάς (*tas geneas*), “these generations.” The latter meaning has rightly been preferred, since, as though explaining what he meant by “the moon,” he immediately added “generations of generations.”

9. [Verse 6.] “And he will descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.” He recalled and indicated that what happened through the judge Gideon finds its fulfillment in Christ.

Gideon asked the Lord for a sign: that the fleece placed on the threshing floor alone should be wet while the floor was dry; and again that the fleece alone should be dry while the floor was wet. And so it happened (Judges 6:36–40).

This signified that, as though on a threshing floor throughout the whole world, the former people, Israel, had been like dry fleece.

That same Christ, therefore, descended like rain upon the fleece while the threshing floor was still dry. Hence he also said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

There he chose the mother from whom he would receive the form of a servant, in which he would appear to human beings. There he chose the disciples to whom he gave this same command, saying: “Do not go among the Gentiles, and do not enter the towns of the Samaritans; go first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:5–6).

When he says, “Go first to them,” he shows that afterward, when the threshing floor was already to be wetted, they would also go to other sheep that were not from the former people of Israel. Of these he says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

Hence also the Apostle says: “For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers” (Romans 15:8). Thus the rain descended upon the fleece while the threshing floor was still dry.

But because what follows says, “and the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:9), so that, when the appointed time came, what the Prophet says might be fulfilled—“A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 17:45)—we now see that, by the grace of Christ, the Jewish people have remained dry, while the whole world, throughout all the Gentiles, has been drenched by the full clouds of Christian grace.

He signified the same rain by another expression when he said, “like drops dripping”—no longer upon fleece, but upon the earth. For what else is rain than drops dripping?

I think that people was signified by the name “fleece” either because it was to be stripped of the authority of its teaching, just as a sheep is stripped of its fleece, or because it held that same rain hidden within itself and did not wish it to be proclaimed to the uncircumcision—that is, revealed to the uncircumcised Gentiles.

10. [Verse 7.] “Righteousness will arise in his days, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away.” Some have interpreted what is said as “taken away” (*tollatur*) as “removed” (*auferatur*); others as “exalted” (*extollatur*), transferring the one Greek word ἀνταναιρεθῆ (*antanairethē*) according to each person’s judgment.

But those who said “taken away” and those who said “removed” do not differ greatly. For *tollatur* is more commonly used to mean “removed and no longer existing” than “raised higher”; whereas *auferatur* cannot be understood in any other way than as “destroyed,” that is, “no longer existing.” *Extollatur*, however, means nothing other than “raised higher.”

When used in a bad sense, this word ordinarily signifies pride, as in: “Do not be exalted in your wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 32:6). In a good sense, however, it refers to greater honor, as when something is raised up, as in: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord” (Psalm 133:2).

If here we understand *auferatur*, “be removed,” what will “until the moon is removed” mean except that it will be made not to exist?

Perhaps he wished this to be understood so that mortality would no longer exist when the final enemy, death, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26), and the abundance of peace would be extended to the point that nothing arising from the weakness of mortality would resist the blessed ones’ happiness [Note: [Col. 0908] Most manuscripts have *peccatorum*, “of sinners,” instead of *beatorum*, “of the blessed.” Two have *justorum*, “of the righteous.”]

This will occur in that age for which we hold God’s faithful promise through Jesus Christ our Lord, of whom it is said: “Righteousness will arise in his days, and an abundance of peace,” until, with death completely conquered and destroyed, all mortality is consumed.

But if by the term “moon” not the mortality of the flesh through which the Church now passes is signified, but the Church itself, which remains forever, freed from this mortality, then the passage should be understood in this way:

“Righteousness will arise in his days, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted,” as though it were saying: “Righteousness will arise in his days—a righteousness that conquers the contradiction and rebellion of the flesh—and peace will grow and abound until the moon is exalted,” that is, until the Church is raised up and will reign with him in the glory of the resurrection, with him who, as the firstborn from the dead, went before her in this glory so that he might sit at the right hand of the Father (Mark 16:19).

Thus he remains with the sun, before the moon, so that afterward the moon too might be exalted.

11. [verse 8.] “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” Of what, indeed, had he said this: “Justice shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted”? If the Church is rightly signified here by the word “moon,” he consequently shows how widely he was going to spread that same Church, when he adds: “And he shall rule from sea to sea.” For the earth is encircled by the great sea called the Ocean, from which a small portion flows into the midst of the lands and forms those seas familiar to us and frequented by ships. Therefore, by “from sea to sea” he said that he would rule from any extremity of the earth to any other extremity, he whose name and power were to be proclaimed throughout the whole world and to have great effect. Lest this be understood otherwise, after “from sea to sea” he immediately added, “and from the river to the ends of the earth.” Thus, what he says here, “to the ends of the earth,” he had said earlier as “from sea to sea.” But by saying now, “from the river,” he clearly expressed that Christ wished to commend his power from the place where he also began to choose his disciples: namely, from the river Jordan, where, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the baptized Lord, a voice sounded from heaven: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:17). From there, therefore, his teaching and the authority of his heavenly instruction, beginning, extends to the ends of the earth, when the gospel of the kingdom is preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come.

12. [verse 9.] “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0909] This is the reading generally found in Erasmus and the manuscripts; at the immediately following occurrence they have “shall prostrate themselves.”] By “the Ethiopians,” using a part for the whole, he signified all nations, choosing to name in particular the nation that lies at the ends of the earth. “They shall fall before him” means, they shall worship him. And because schisms were to arise in various regions of the earth, schisms that would envy the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world—and these schisms, divided according to the names of their human founders, would become hostile to the glory of Christ, which is spread through all lands, because they loved the men through whose agency they had been split—therefore, after saying, “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall,” he added, “and his enemies shall lick the earth.” That is, they will love men in such a way as to envy the glory of Christ, to whom it is said: “Exalt yourself above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. 107:6). For man deserved to hear: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). By licking this earth—that is, delighting in the empty talk of such men, loving them and holding them in the highest esteem—they contradict the divine utterances by which the Catholic Church was foretold, not as destined to exist in some one part of the earth, like the various schisms, but as reaching even to the Ethiopians, the farthest and darkest of human peoples, by bearing fruit and increasing throughout the whole world.

13. [verses 10, 11.] “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents. And all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him.” This passage now requires not an interpreter but a contemplator; indeed, it is presented not only to the sight of rejoicing believers but also to that of groaning unbelievers. Unless perhaps we should ask what is meant by “they shall bring presents.” For things that can walk are usually said to be brought. Could this, then, have been said of victims to be sacrificed? Far be it that such justice should arise in his days. These gifts, therefore, which are foretold as to be brought, seem to me to signify the people whom the authority of kings brings into the fellowship of Christ’s Church; although even persecuting kings brought gifts, without knowing what they were doing, when they sacrificed the holy martyrs.

14. [verse 12.] When he was explaining the reasons why such great honor would be paid him by kings and why he would be served by all nations, he says: “Because he has delivered the needy from the powerful, and the poor man who had no helper.” This needy and poor man is the people of those who believe in him. Among this people are also the kings who worship him. For they do not disdain to be needy and poor—that is, to confess their sins humbly and to lack the glory and grace of God—so that that King, the Son of the King, may deliver them from the powerful one.

The powerful one is the same person who above was called the accuser: his power to subject human beings to himself and keep them in captivity was not produced by his own strength, but by human sins. He himself is also called “the strong one,” and therefore here too “the powerful one.” But the one who humbled the accuser and entered the strong man’s house in order, after binding him, to plunder his vessels (Matt. 12:29)—he delivered the needy from the powerful and the poor man who had no helper. For neither anyone’s strength, nor any righteous human being, nor any angel could accomplish this. When, therefore, there was no helper, he himself came and saved them.

15. [verse 13.] It might be objected: If a person was held by the devil on account of his sins, did sins please Christ, who rescued the needy from the powerful? Far from it. Rather, “He will spare the needy and the poor”; that is, he will forgive the sins of the humble person who does not put confidence in his own merits or hope for salvation from his own strength, but is in need of the grace of his Savior.

When he added, “And he will save the souls of the poor,” he commended the twofold assistance of grace: both that which consists in the remission of sins, when he says, “He will spare the poor and needy,” and that which consists in participation in righteousness, when he adds, “And he will save the souls of the poor.” No one is sufficient for himself to attain salvation—which salvation is perfect righteousness—unless God’s grace assists him; for the fullness of the Law is nothing other than love, which does not arise from us within us, but is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

[Note: [Col. 0910] The editions read, “salvation is not perfect righteousness.” The word “not” is absent from the manuscripts.]

16. [verse 14.] “He will redeem their souls from usury and iniquity.” What are these usuries except sins, which are also called debts (Matt. 6:12)? I think they are called “usuries” because more evil is found in the punishments than was committed in the sins. For example, when a murderer destroys only a human body and can do no harm to the soul, both his soul and body are destroyed in Gehenna. With reference to such despisers of the present commandment and mockers of future punishment it was said: “I came, when I should collect with usury” (Matt. 25:27).

From these usuries the souls of the poor are redeemed by that blood which was poured out for the remission of sins. He will therefore redeem them from usuries by forgiving the sins that deserved greater punishments; and he will redeem them from iniquity by assisting them through grace even to perform righteousness. Thus the same two things are repeated here that were stated above. For what is said above, “He will spare the needy and the poor,” is understood here as “from usuries”; while what is said there, “And he will save the souls of the poor,” seems to be expressed here as “from iniquity,” with “he will redeem” understood in relation to both. For by sparing them he will redeem them from usuries; and by saving them he will redeem them from iniquity. Thus, when he spares the poor and needy and saves the souls of the poor, he will redeem their souls from usuries and iniquity.

“And his name will be honorable before them.” For in return for such great benefits, those who answer that it is fitting and right to give thanks to the Lord their God give honor to his name.

Alternatively, some manuscripts read: “And their name will be honorable before him.” For although Christians seem contemptible to this world, their name is honorable before him who gave them that name, no longer remembering the names by which they were previously called “with their lips” (Ps. 15:4), when they were bound to the superstitions of the Gentiles or marked by the names of their evil deeds and merits, before they became Christians. That name is honorable before him, even if it seems contemptible to his enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0910] More than one of the older manuscripts reads, “their majesty.”]

17. [verse 15.] “And he shall live, and there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia.” It would not be said, “And he shall live”—for of whom could this not be said, so long as he lived on this earth for however brief a period?—unless that life were being commended in which he no longer dies and death shall no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9). Therefore the one who was despised in dying shall also live, since, as another prophet says, “His life shall be taken from the earth” (Isa. 53:8; see Acts 8:33).

But what is meant by “and there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia”? For the fact that Solomon also received gold from there has, in this psalm, been figuratively transferred to another true Solomon, that is, the true peaceful one; for Solomon did not rule from the river to the ends of the earth. Thus it was prophesied that even the wise men of this world would come to believe in Christ.

By “Arabia” we understand the Gentiles; by “gold,” wisdom, which excels among all teachings as gold does among metals. Hence it is written: “Receive prudence as silver, and wisdom as tried gold” (Prov. 8:10–11).

“And they shall pray concerning him always.” Some have translated the Greek phrase περὶ αὐτοῦ (*peri autou*) as “concerning him”; others, “for him” or “on his behalf.” What is “concerning him,” unless perhaps it refers to our prayer when we say, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10)? For the coming of Christ will present the kingdom of God to the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 0911] So the manuscripts of good authority; the editions read, “has presented.”]

But how “for him” should be understood is more difficult, unless it is because when prayer is offered for the Church, it is offered for him, since the Church is his body. For the great mystery concerning Christ and the Church was stated earlier: “The two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5:31–32).

What follows, “All day long,” that is, throughout all time, “they shall bless him,” is sufficiently clear.

18. [verse 16.] “And there shall be firmament on the earth, on the summits of the mountains.” For all the promises of God are “Yes” in him (2 Cor. 1:20), that is, they are confirmed in him, because in him everything that was prophesied for our salvation has been fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0911] The Louvain edition reads, “that is, in Christ”; Erasmus omits this altogether. The manuscripts instead have, “that is, in him.” Thus Augustine is more readily understood here as interpreting the particle *etiam* (“yes”), for which the Vulgate now reads *est* (“is”) in 2 Cor. 1:20. The former corresponded to the Greek *to nai*, a word of affirmation among the Greeks, as *Amen* is among the Hebrews.]

By “the summits of the mountains” we should understand the authors of the divine Scriptures, that is, those through whom they were given. In them, certainly, he himself is the firmament, since everything divinely written is referred to him. He wished this to be on the earth because those Scriptures were written for the sake of those who are on earth. Hence he himself also came to earth in order to confirm all these things, that is, to show them fulfilled in himself. For he says: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44)—that is, “on the summits of the mountains.”

Thus he came “in the last days as the manifest mountain of the Lord, prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2)—which is expressed here as “on the summits of the mountains.”

“His fruit shall rise above Lebanon.” We usually understand Lebanon as representing the dignity of this world, since Lebanon is a mountain bearing lofty trees, and the name itself means “whiteness” or “whitening.” What wonder, then, if the fruit of Christ rises above every splendid height of this world, whose fruit has led those who love it to despise all worldly summits?

But if we understand Lebanon in a good sense, on account of the cedars of Lebanon that he planted (Ps. 103:16), what other fruit should be understood as exalted above this Lebanon except that of which the Apostle speaks when he is discussing love: “And I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31)? For this is also set forth first among the gifts of the Spirit, where he says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love,” and the other things that follow are woven together from it (Gal. 5:22).

“And they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.” Since the word “city” is placed ambiguously, and it is not added whose city it is—for it does not say, “from his city” or “from the city of God,” but simply “from the city”—it is understood in a good sense, so that they may flourish from the city of God, that is, from the Church, like grass; but fruitful grass, such as grain.

For this too is called “grass” in Holy Scripture. Thus, in Genesis, the earth was commanded to produce every tree and every grass (Gen. 1:11), and “every grain” was not added; this would certainly not have been omitted unless grain too were understood under the name “grass.” The same usage is found in many other passages of Scripture.

But if it is to be understood as “They shall flourish like the grass of the earth,” in the sense of the saying, “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass,” then that city too must surely be understood as signifying the society of this world. For it was not without purpose that Cain first founded a city (Gen. 4:17).

When, therefore, the fruit of Christ has been exalted above Lebanon—that is, above enduring trees and imperishable timbers, because his fruit is eternal—all human glory according to the temporal elevation of this world is compared with grass. For believers who already hope for eternal life despise temporal happiness, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh as the flower of grass. The grass withered, the flower fell; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6–8).

There is the fruit exalted above Lebanon. Flesh has always been grass, and the glory of flesh like the flower of grass; but because it was not shown which happiness ought to be chosen and preferred, the flower of grass was regarded as something great. It was not merely not despised; it was sought above all.

Thus, as though this had begun to happen only when everything that flourished in the world was rejected and despised, it was said: “His fruit shall rise above Lebanon, and they shall flourish from the city like the grass of the earth.” That is: what is promised for eternity will be proclaimed above all things, and everything regarded as great in this world will be compared with the grass of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0912] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *animadversum* (“noticed” or “observed”).]

19. [verse 17.] “Let his name be blessed forever; his name endures before the sun.” By “the sun,” times are signified. Therefore his name endures forever; for eternity precedes times and is not enclosed by time.

“And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him.” In him is fulfilled what was promised to Abraham. For he does not say, “In seeds,” as though in many, “but as in one: And to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. 3:16). To Abraham it was said: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). “It is not the children of the flesh who are counted as seed, but the children of the promise” (Rom. 9:8).

“All nations shall magnify him.” This is repeated as an explanation of what was said above. Because they shall be blessed in him, they shall magnify him—not by making him great, since he is great in himself, but by praising him and acknowledging him to be great. Thus we magnify God; thus also we say, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9), although it is always holy.

20. [verse 18.] “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders.” After considering all that was said above, the hymn bursts forth, and the Lord God of Israel is blessed. For what was said to that barren woman is fulfilled: “He who redeemed you, he himself shall be called the Lord, the God of Israel, of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:5). He alone does wonders, because whoever performs them, he himself works in them who alone does wonders.

21. [verse 19.] “And blessed is the name of his glory” [Note: [Col. 0913] More of the older manuscripts read, “of his majesty.”] “forever, and unto the age of the age.” What else could the Latin translators say, since they could not say, “forever, and forever of forever”? For it sounds as though one thing were said by “forever” and another by “unto the age,” whereas the Greek has: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος (*eis ton aiōna, kai eis ton aiōna tou aiōnos*). Perhaps it could more suitably be rendered, “unto the age, and unto the age of the age”: by “unto the age” understanding the duration of this present age, and by “unto the age of the age” what is promised to occur after the end of this age.

“And all the earth shall be filled with his glory: so be it, so be it.” You commanded it, Lord, and so it happens; so it happens until what began from the river reaches altogether to the ends of the earth.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 72. SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0913] A sermon delivered to the people, perhaps in 411, at the vigil of Saint Cyprian; see Letter 140 to Honoratus, chapter 5, section 13. The manuscripts of Audoen and Clermont add in the title that this sermon was delivered in the Basilica Restituta. M.]

1. [verse 1.] Listen, listen, most beloved members of the body of Christ, whose hope is the Lord your God, and who do not look toward vanities and lying madnesses (Ps. 39:5); and if you still do look toward them, listen so that you may not look.

This psalm has an inscription, that is, a title: “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have failed; a psalm for Asaph.” We have many psalms in whose titles the name David is written, but nowhere is “son of Jesse” added except in this one. We must believe that this was not done without purpose or to no effect. For everywhere God gives us hints and calls our loving devotion to understanding.

What is “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have failed”? Hymns are praises of God accompanied by song; hymns are songs containing praise of God. If there is praise but it is not praise of God, it is not a hymn. If there is praise of God but it is not sung, it is not a hymn. Therefore, if it is to be a hymn, it must have these three elements: praise, praise of God, and song.

What, then, is “The hymns have failed”? The praises that are sung to God have failed. He seems to announce something burdensome and almost mournful. For one who sings praise not only praises but praises cheerfully; one who sings praise not only sings but loves the one whom he sings. In praise there is the proclamation of one who confesses; in song, the affection of one who loves.

“Therefore the hymns of David have failed,” he says, and he adds, “son of Jesse.” David was king of Israel, son of Jesse (1 Kings 16:18), at a certain time of the Old Testament, when the New Testament was hidden there like fruit in a root. If you seek fruit in a root, you will not find it; yet you will not find fruit on the branches unless it has come forth from the root.

At that time, therefore, when the first people were coming physically from the seed of Abraham—for the second people too, belonging to the New Testament, belong to Abraham’s seed, but now spiritually—at that time, to that first people, still carnal, a few prophets foretold these future times and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. They understood both what God desired and when it would be publicly proclaimed.

And just as Christ himself, who was to be born according to the flesh, was hidden in the root, in the seed of the patriarchs, and was to be revealed at a certain time, appearing like fruit, as it is written, “A branch shall flower from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11:1), so also the New Testament itself, which is in Christ, was hidden in those earlier times. It was known only to the prophets and to a very few devout people—not through the manifestation of present realities but through the revelation of future ones.

For what does it mean, brothers, when we recall just one example: Abraham, sending his faithful servant to betroth a wife to his only son, makes him swear an oath and says to him, “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear” (Gen. 24:2)? What was in Abraham’s thigh, where he placed his hand while swearing? What was there except what had also been promised to him at that time: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18)? The flesh is signified by the name “thigh.” From Abraham’s flesh, through Isaac and Jacob, and—to pass over much—through Mary, came our Lord Jesus Christ.

2. But since the root was in the patriarchs, where shall we show this? Let us ask Paul. The Gentiles had already come to believe in Christ and, as though wishing to become proud against the Jews who crucified Christ—although from that same people another wall had come, meeting at the corner, that is, in Christ himself, the wall of circumcision coming from one direction and the wall of uncircumcision, that is, of the Gentiles, coming from another—when the Gentiles began to exalt themselves, he restrains them in this way:

“For if you,” he says, “having been cut from the naturally wild olive tree, were grafted into them, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you” (Rom. 11:17–18).

Thus he says that certain branches were broken off from the root of the patriarchs because of unbelief, and that a wild olive tree was grafted there so that it might share in the richness of the olive tree—that is, the Church coming from the Gentiles.

And who grafts a wild olive tree into an olive tree? Usually an olive is grafted into a wild olive; we have never seen a wild olive grafted into an olive. For whoever does this will find no berries except those of the wild olive. What is grafted is what grows, and the fruit of that thing is found: it is not the fruit of the root but of the shoot.

Showing that God, by his omnipotence, caused the wild olive to be grafted into the root of the olive tree and to produce not wild berries but olives, the Apostle refers this to God’s omnipotence and says: “If you were cut from the naturally wild olive and, contrary to nature, were grafted into the good olive tree” [Note: [Col. 0915] The word “good” is absent from the manuscripts.], “do not boast,” he says, “against the branches.”

“But you say,” he continues, “‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Very well: they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith; do not be high-minded, but fear.” What does “Do not be high-minded” mean? Do not become proud because you have been grafted in, but fear lest you be broken off through unbelief, just as they were broken off.

“They were broken off,” he says, “because of unbelief; but you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.”

[Note: [Col. 0915] One manuscript reads, “you stand by faith.”]

Then follows a good, necessary passage that must be heard in its entirety: “See, therefore,” he says, “the kindness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but kindness toward you who were grafted in, if you remain in his kindness; otherwise—that is, if you do not remain in his kindness—you too will be cut off. And they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in” (Rom. 11:17–24).

3. In the time of the Old Testament, therefore, brothers, the promises made by our God to that carnal people were earthly and temporal. An earthly kingdom was promised; that land was promised into which they were also led after being liberated from Egypt. Through Joshua son of Nun they were brought into the promised land, where earthly Jerusalem was also built and where David reigned.

They received the land after being liberated from Egypt and crossing the Red Sea. When the winding paths and wanderings of the deserts had ended [Note: [Col. 0915] So three manuscripts. Others, with the editions, read “and terrors.”], they received the land; they received the kingdom. Then, after receiving the kingdom, because they had received earthly things, they deservedly began to be attacked, defeated, and taken captive on account of their sins. Finally, the city itself was overthrown.

Such also were those promises, which were not to endure, but through which future promises that would endure were represented, so that the whole course of temporal promises might be a figure and a kind of prophecy of things to come.

Therefore, when that kingdom was failing—the kingdom in which David, son of Jesse, that is, a certain human being, reigned, although he was a prophet and a holy man because he saw and foresaw Christ who was to come, from whose seed he was also to be born according to the flesh—nevertheless a human being, not yet Christ, not yet our King, the Son of God, but David, son of Jesse—because, then, that kingdom was going to fail, the kingdom through which God was praised at that time by carnal people—for this alone they regarded as something great: that they had been liberated temporally from those who oppressed them, had escaped their pursuing enemies through the Red Sea, had been led through the desert, and had found a homeland and a kingdom; for these things alone they praised God, not yet understanding what God prefigured and promised in those figures—therefore, when the things for which the carnal people, over whom that David reigned, praised God were failing, “the hymns of David, son of Jesse, failed”: not of the Son of God, but of the son of Jesse.

We have passed over this dangerous point in the title of the present psalm as the Lord wished. You have received the explanation of why it was said, “The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have failed.”

4. Whose voice is this psalm? Asaph’s. What does “Asaph” mean? As we find in the interpretations translated from the Hebrew language into Greek and from Greek into Latin, “Asaph” is interpreted as “synagogue.” It is therefore the voice of the synagogue.

But when you hear “synagogue,” do not immediately detest it as though it were the slayer of the Lord. That synagogue was indeed the slayer of the Lord; no one doubts this. But remember that from the synagogue came the rams whose sons we are. Hence it is said in the psalm: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28:1).

Who were those rams? Peter, John, James, Andrew, Bartholomew, and the other Apostles. From there also came Saul himself, later Paul: at first proud, later humble. You know that Saul—the name from which Saul was called—was a proud and headstrong king.

The Apostle did not change his name out of any boastfulness; rather, Saul became Paul, the proud man became little. For *Paulus* means “little.”

Do you wish to know what Saul means? Listen to Paul himself now recalling what he had been through his wickedness and what he now was through God’s grace. Listen to how he had been Saul and how he was Paul: “I who was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Tim. 1:13).

You have heard Saul; hear Paul also: “For I am,” he says, “the least of the Apostles.” What does “the least” mean except “I am Paul”? And he continues: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle.” Why? Because I was Saul.

What does “I was Saul” mean? Let him say it himself: “Because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God,” he says, “I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:9–10). He removed all greatness from himself: now little in himself, great in Christ.

And what does this Paul say? “God has not rejected his people,” speaking of the people that came from the Jews, “the people whom he foreknew. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1–2).

Therefore Paul too is for us from the synagogue, and Peter and the other Apostles are from the synagogue. Thus, when you hear the voice of the synagogue, do not consider its merit; consider its offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0916] So the manuscripts; the editions read, “when you hear the voice of the old synagogue.”]

The synagogue therefore speaks in this psalm, while the hymns of David, son of Jesse, have failed—that is, while the temporal things through which God was accustomed to be praised by the carnal people have failed. But why did those things fail except so that other things might be sought?

What things were to be sought? Things that were not there? No; things that were concealed there under figures. Not things that were no longer there, but things hidden there, as in a root, in certain secret mysteries, which, as the Apostle himself says, “were our figures” (1 Cor. 10:6).

5. Now consider briefly that very figure of ours. The people of Israel were under the domination of Pharaoh and the Egyptians (Exod. 1:10). The Christian people, predestined for God before faith and already belonging to him, were nevertheless still serving demons and the devil, their prince. Behold the people subjected to the Egyptians, serving their own sins; for the devil can rule us only through our sins.

The people are liberated from the Egyptians through Moses; the people are liberated from their former life of sins through our Lord Jesus Christ. That people crosses the Red Sea; this people crosses through baptism. All the enemies of that people die in the Red Sea (Exod. 14:22–23); all our sins die in baptism.

Pay attention, brothers. After that Red Sea, the homeland is not immediately given, nor does one triumph securely as though enemies no longer existed. The solitude of the desert remains; enemies lying in ambush along the way remain. So too after baptism the Christian life remains amid temptations.

In that desert the promised homeland was longed for. What else do Christians who have already been washed in baptism long for? Do they already reign with Christ? We have not yet reached our promised land—but it will not fail, for there the hymns of David will not fail.

Let all the faithful hear this and know where they are: they are in the desert; they long for their homeland. The enemies died in baptism, but they still pursue from behind.

What does “pursue from behind” mean? Before our face we have future things; behind us, past things. All past sins have been erased in baptism. The sins by which we are now tested do not pursue us from behind; they lie in ambush along the way.

Thus the Apostle, still situated on the road through this desert, says: “Forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what is ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God” (Phil. 3:13–14)—as though he were saying, “Toward the homeland of God’s heavenly promise.”

And there, brothers, whatever that people suffered in the desert, and whatever God bestowed upon them—whatever those scourges and gifts were—are signs of the things that, in the solitude of this life, as we walk in Christ and seek our homeland, we both receive for consolation and endure for testing.

It is therefore no wonder that what prefigured the future failed. For that people was led into the promised homeland. But was it destined to stand forever? If it had been, it would not have been a figure but the reality itself. Since it was a figure, that people was led to something temporal. If it was led to something temporal, it had to fail, and by its failure it had to be compelled to seek what would never fail.

6. The synagogue, therefore—that is, those who worshiped God piously there, but nevertheless on account of earthly things, on account of present realities—for there are impious people who seek the goods of present things from demons—this people was better than the Gentiles in that, although it sought present and temporal goods, it sought them from the one God, who is the creator of all things, both spiritual and bodily.

When those pious people according to the flesh looked toward such things—that is, the synagogue that possessed good things for the time being [Note: [Col. 0918] The better manuscripts read “good things for the time being”; the editions, “temporal goods.”], not spiritual things, as were the prophets and the few who understood the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal—when, then, that synagogue considered what it had received from God and what God had promised to that people, namely an abundance of earthly things, a homeland, peace, and earthly happiness, it failed to understand that all these things were figures. Not understanding what lay hidden in the realities represented by those figures, it thought that God had given this as something great and that he had nothing better to give those who loved and served him.

It looked around and saw certain sinners, impious, blasphemous, servants of demons, children of the devil, living in great wickedness and pride, yet abounding in those earthly and temporal things for which it itself served God. And a most evil thought arose in its heart, one that would make its feet waver and almost cause it to fall away from God’s way.

Behold, this thought existed among the people of the Old Testament. Would that it not exist among our carnal brothers when the happiness of the New Testament is now preached openly!

What did that synagogue say then? What did that people say? “We serve God, and we are chastised and scourged. The things we love, and which we had received from God as something great, are taken away from us. But those wicked, utterly evil, proud, blasphemous, restless men abound in all the things for which we serve God. I think God is served without reason.”

This is the sense of the psalm: the people are failing and wavering as they consider that the earthly goods for which they served God abound among those who did not serve God. They waver and almost fall; and with those hymns they fail, because the hymns were failing in such hearts.

What does “the hymns were failing in such hearts” mean? It means that, because they were now thinking such things, they were not praising God. How could they praise God when he seemed perverse to them, giving such happiness to the impious and taking it away from those who served him?

God did not seem good to them; and those to whom God did not seem good certainly did not praise him. From those who did not praise God, the hymns failed.

Later, however, this people understood what God was admonishing it to seek when he took temporal things away from his servants and gave them to his blasphemous and impious enemies. It understood, once admonished, that above all the things God gives to both good and evil people, and sometimes takes away from both good and evil, he preserves something for the good.

What does “he preserves something for the good” mean? What does he preserve for them? Himself.

Now, as far as I judge, we are moving through the psalm; understanding has been attained in the name of the Lord. Listen to the one who recalls and repents, who had erred by thinking God not good because he gave earthly goods to the wicked and took them away from his servants. He understood what God preserved for his servants, and, reflecting and chastising himself, he burst forth in this way.

7. “How good is the God of Israel!” But to whom? “To those who are upright in heart.” What about the perverse? He seems perverse to them.

Thus he also says in another psalm: “With the holy man you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; and with the perverse man you will be perverse” (Ps. 18:25–26).

What does “you will be perverse with the perverse man” mean? The perverse man will think you perverse. It does not mean that God is in any way made perverse. Far from it: what he is, he is.

But just as the sun appears gentle to one who has pure, healthy, vigorous, and strong eyes, while to sore eyes it hurls something like rough darts—strengthening the one who gazes upon it and tormenting the other, not because it has changed, but because the observer has changed [Note: [Col. 0919] The manuscripts read, “not changing, but changing”]—so, when you begin to be perverse, God will seem perverse to you. You have changed, not he.

Therefore, what is joy to the good will be punishment to you. Recalling this, he says: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!”

### 8. [verse 2]

“But what of you?”—“But my feet were almost shaken.” When were my feet shaken, if not when my heart was not upright? Why was my heart not upright? Listen: “My steps were almost poured out.” What he said, “almost,” he also said, “just short of it”; and what he said, “my feet were almost moved,” he said, “my steps were poured out.” His feet were almost moved; his steps were almost poured out. His feet were moved—but moved where, and his steps poured out where? His feet were moved toward wandering; his steps were poured out toward falling—not completely, but almost. What does this mean? I was already going into error, but I had not gone; I was already falling, but I had not fallen.

### 9. [verse 3]

“But why this also?” [Note: Erasmus and the manuscripts read *Sed quare et hoc?*; Lovaniensis reads *Sed quare ad hoc?*—“But why for this?”] “Because,” he says, “I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.” I looked at sinners; I saw that they possessed peace. What peace? A temporal, fleeting, unstable, and earthly peace; yet it was the kind of peace that I too was desiring from God. I saw that those who did not serve God possessed what I desired in order to serve God; and my feet were moved, and my steps were almost poured out.

### 10. [verses 4–5]

Why sinners possess this, he states briefly: “For there is no turning aside from their death” [Note: Several manuscripts consistently prefer *morti*—“for their death”—rather than *mortis*—“of their death.”] “and there is strength in their scourging. They are not in the labors of men, and they will not be scourged with men.”

“I have now understood,” he says, “why they possess peace and flourish on earth: because there is no turning aside from their death”—that is, because a certain and eternal death awaits them, which neither turns aside from them nor allows them to turn aside from it. “For there is no turning aside from their death, and there is strength in their scourging.” There is strength in their scourging: for their scourging is not temporal, but firm forever.

Because of these evils, then, which will be eternal for them, what happens to them now? “They are not in the labors of men, and they will not be scourged with men.” Is the devil himself, then, not scourged with men, although eternal punishment has been prepared for him?

### 11. [verse 6]

What, then, has happened to these people while they are not scourged and do not labor with men? “Therefore,” he says, “pride took possession of them.” Look at them, proud and undisciplined; look at the bull devoted to sacrifice, permitted to wander freely and destroy whatever it can until the day of slaughter.

It is good, brothers, that we hear in the very words of the Prophet this bull of whom I have spoken. Scripture also mentions him elsewhere: it says that they are prepared as though for sacrifice and are spared for an evil freedom (Prov. 7:22). “Therefore,” he said, “pride took possession of them.”

What does “pride took possession of them” mean? “They are clothed all around with their iniquity and impiety.” He did not say “covered,” but “clothed all around”—covered on every side with their impiety [Col. 0920].
