Deservedly, the wretched neither see nor are seen, because they are clothed all around and their inner selves are not visible.

For if anyone could look into the interior of evil men who appear happy according to the present age; if anyone could see their savage consciences; if anyone could behold their souls being torn apart by such great disturbances of desires and fears, he would see them wretched even when they are called happy. But because they are clothed all around with their iniquity and impiety, they do not see—and neither are they seen.

The Spirit who says these things about them knew them; and we ought to look upon them with that eye by which we know that we can see, if the covering of impiety is removed from our eyes. Let us see such people; and when they are happy, let us flee them; and when they are happy, let us not imitate them. Nor should we desire from the Lord our God, as something of great value, such things as those who do not serve him have deserved to receive. He preserves something else; something else ought to be desired. But what that is, listen.

### 12. [verse 7]

First, let these people be described: “Their iniquity will go forth as if from fatness” [Note: The editions read *prodiit*—“went forth.” But most and better manuscripts read *prodiet*—“will go forth”—in accordance with the Greek Septuagint, *exeleusetai*—“will go forth.”]

See whether that bull has not been recognized. Listen, brothers: we must not pass casually over what he said, “Their iniquity will go forth as if from fatness.”

There are evil people who are evil because of leanness; that is, they are evil because they are thin, weak, and diminished, afflicted by a certain wasting of necessity [Note: Several manuscripts of good reputation read *tabe quadam*—“by a certain wasting.” The editions read *exiguitate quadam*—“by a certain smallness.”]—and they too are evil and deserving of condemnation. For every necessity is to be endured rather than any iniquity committed.

Yet it is one thing to sin from necessity and another to sin amid abundance. A poor beggar commits theft: his iniquity has proceeded from leanness. A rich man, abounding in such possessions—why does he seize what belongs to others? The iniquity of the former has proceeded from leanness; that of the latter from fatness.

Therefore, when you say to the lean man, “Why did you do this?” he replies humbly, afflicted and cast down: “Necessity compelled me.” “Why did you not fear God?” “Poverty forced me.”

Say to the rich man, “Why do you do these things and not fear God?”—if indeed you are someone who can say this. See whether he even deigns to listen; see whether his iniquity does not also go forth against you from his own fatness [Note: Perhaps *in te ipsum*—“against yourself”—rather than *in te ipso*—“against you yourself.”]

For they now declare hostility against their teachers and reprovers; they become enemies of those who speak the truth, having become accustomed to being flattered by the words of flatterers, with a soft ear but an unsound heart.

Who will say to a rich man, “You did wrong to seize what belongs to others”? Or perhaps, if someone dares to say this, and is such a person that the rich man cannot resist him, what does the rich man reply? He speaks everything in contempt of God.

Why? Because he is proud. Why? Because he is fat. Why? Because he is devoted to sacrifice. “Their iniquity will go forth as if from fatness.”

### 13

“They have passed into the disposition of the heart.” They have passed inwardly.

What does “they have passed” mean? They have gone beyond the road. What does “they have passed” mean? They have exceeded the boundaries of the human race; they do not consider themselves equal to the rest. They have passed, I say, beyond the boundaries of the human race.

When you say to such a man, “This poor man is your brother; you had the same parents, Adam and Eve,” do not pay attention to your swelling pride; do not pay attention to the arrogance into which you have been lifted. Even if a household surrounds you, even if abundant gold and silver are yours, even if a marble house contains you, even if coffered ceilings cover you, the roof of the world, the sky, covers both you and the poor man together. You differ from the poor man by possessions that are not yours, things added externally: see yourself in them, not them in yourself.

Consider yourself—what you are in relation to the poor man—not what you possess. Why do you despise your brother? Both of you were naked in your mothers’ wombs. Surely, even when you have departed this life and these fleshly bodies, after the soul has departed, have putrefied, can the bones of the rich man and the poor man be distinguished?

I am speaking of an equal condition, of that very lot of the human race in which all are born. The rich man, while he is rich here, will not always be here; and just as he did not come here rich, so he will not depart rich. The entrance of both is the same, and their departure is equal.

I add that perhaps you will exchange places. The Gospel is now preached everywhere. Consider a certain poor man covered with sores who lay before the rich man’s door and desired to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Consider also your equal [Note: Several manuscripts read *patrem*—“father”—rather than *parem*—“equal.”] who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day.

It happened, of course, that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried—for perhaps no one cared for his burial. And when that rich man was in torment among the dead, did he not lift up his eyes and see, in boundless joy, the one whom he had despised before his door? Did he not desire a drop of water from his finger, although the poor man had desired the crumbs falling from his table?

Brothers, how great was the poor man’s labor? How long did the rich man’s pleasures last? But what they exchanged is everlasting.

Therefore, because the rich man had no turning aside in death, and there was strength in his scourging, he was not in the labors of men and was not scourged among men. But the poor man, scourged here, rested there, because God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6).

But to whom are you saying these things? To one who feasted splendidly and clothed himself daily in purple and fine linen. To whom are you speaking? To one who “has passed into the disposition of the heart.”

Deservedly, he will say too late, “Send Lazarus; let him speak at least to my brothers” (Luke 16:19–31), when the fruit of repentance is not granted him. It is not that repentance is not given at all; rather, repentance will be eternal, and there will be no salvation after repentance. Therefore, these people have passed into the disposition of the heart.

### 14. [verse 8]

“They thought and spoke wickedness.” Men speak wickedness with fear; but how do these people speak? “They spoke iniquity on high.” They did not merely speak iniquity, but spoke it openly, before everyone, proudly: “I do this; I will show you. You will learn whom you are dealing with; I will not let you live” [Note: The editions insert *superbe*—“proudly”—at this point; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

You might think such things, but not pour them out; evil desire might be restrained within the enclosure of thought, or you might rein it in within your own thoughts. Why? Is he perhaps lean? “Their iniquity will go forth as if from fatness” [Col. 0922]. “They spoke iniquity on high.”

### 15. [verse 9]

“They set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth.” What does “passed over the earth” mean? It is explained by “They set their mouth against heaven.” For “passed over the earth” means that they pass beyond all earthly things.

What does it mean to pass beyond all earthly things? When he speaks, he does not consider that he may suddenly die; as though he would live forever, he threatens. His thought transcends earthly frailty. He does not know what sort of vessel covers him; he does not know what is written elsewhere concerning such people: “His spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth; on that day all his thoughts will perish” (Ps. 145:4).

But these people, who do not consider their final day, speak pride [Note: The manuscripts read *superba*—“proud things”; the editions read *superbiam*—“pride.”] They set their mouth in heaven and pass beyond the earth.

If he did not consider his final day—that is, the final day of his judgment—a robber sent to prison would be nothing more savage than he; and yet he might escape. Where will you flee so as not to die? That day will certainly come. What does “a long time” mean for which you will live? How long is any time that has an end, even if it were long? Besides, it is not long; and even the period called “long” is itself uncertain. Why does he not consider this? Because he has set his mouth against heaven, and his tongue has passed over the earth.

### 16. [verse 10]

“Therefore my people will return here.” Asaph himself now returns here. He saw these things abounding among the wicked; he saw them among the proud. He returns to God and begins to seek and discuss.

But when? “When the days are found to be fulfilled in them.” What are “fulfilled days”? “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4).

This is the fullness of time: when he came to teach that temporal things are to be despised, that nothing is to be considered great which evil men desire, and that whatever evil men fear must be endured. He became the way; he recalled us to our innermost thought and admonished us what should be sought from God.

And see how, from a thought struck back upon itself and somehow recalling the surge of its own impulse, one passes over to choosing true things. “Therefore my people will return here, and the days will be found to be fulfilled in them.”

### 17. [verse 11]

“And they said, ‘How has God known? And is there knowledge in the Most High?’”

See through what kind of thought they pass. “Behold, the wicked are happy; God does not care about human affairs. Does he really know what we are doing?”

Observe what is being said. We ask you, brothers: let Christians no longer say, “How has God known? And is there knowledge in the Most High?”

### 18. [verse 12]

For what makes it seem to you that God does not know and that there is no knowledge in the Most High? He replies: “Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have obtained riches.”

They are sinners, and, abounding in riches in the world, they have obtained them. He confessed that he did not wish to be a sinner only because he wanted to possess riches. A carnal soul had sold its justice for visible and earthly things.

What sort of justice is that which is maintained for the sake of gold—as though gold were more precious than justice itself, or as though, when someone withholds another’s property, the person from whom he withholds it suffers greater loss than the one who withholds it! One loses a garment; the other loses faith.

“Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have obtained riches.” Therefore God does not know; therefore there is no knowledge in the Most High [Col. 0923]!

### 19. [verse 13]

“And I said, ‘Therefore’” [Note: The word *ergo*—“therefore”—is absent here in Erasmus and in the manuscripts.] “I have justified my heart without cause.”

When I serve God and do not possess these things, while those who do not serve him abound in them, “therefore I have justified my heart without cause, and washed my hands among the innocent” [Note: The manuscripts read *in innocentibus*—“among the innocent”—in accordance with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read *inter innocentes*—“among innocent people.”]

I did this without cause. Where is the reward for my good life? Where is the prize of my service? I live well and am in need, while the wicked abounds. “And I washed my hands among the innocent.”

### 20. [verse 14]

“And I was scourged all day long.” God’s scourges do not depart from me. I serve well and am scourged; he does not serve, and he is adorned. He has raised a great question for himself.

The soul is shaken; the soul passes over, about to pass toward despising earthly things and desiring eternal ones. This is the soul’s passage in this thought: where it is tossed in a certain storm, it will reach the harbor.

And just as the sick who suffer a lingering illness commonly become more fevered when health is near, physicians call this a *cretic* crisis [Note: The editions read *criticam*. But in all the manuscripts it is written with *e*, *creticam*.], through which one passes to health: the fever is greater there, but it leads to healing; the burning is greater there, but recovery is near—so here too he burns.

For these are dangerous words, brothers, distressing and almost blasphemous: “How has God known?” Yet this is also “almost.” He did not say, “God did not know”; he did not say, “There is no knowledge in the Most High.” Rather, as if asking, hesitating, and doubting, he said this. This is what he said earlier: “My steps were almost poured out.” “How has God known? And is there knowledge in the Most High?” He does not affirm it; but the doubt itself is dangerous.

Through danger he passes toward health. Hear health now: “Therefore I have justified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent; and I was scourged all day long, and my correction was every morning.”

“Correction” means reproof; the one who is reproved is corrected. What does “every morning” mean? It is not postponed. The correction of the ungodly is postponed; mine is not postponed. Theirs is late—or nonexistent; mine is every morning. “And I was scourged all day long, and my correction was every morning.”

### 21. [verse 15]

“If I said, ‘I will speak thus’”—that is, “I will teach thus”—how would you teach? That there is no knowledge in the Most High? That God does not know? Do you wish to put forward the opinion that those who live justly live justly without cause; that the just man has lost the reward of his service; that God favors the wicked more, or that he cares for no one? Do you wish to say and teach this?

He restrains himself, checked by authority. By what authority? At times a man wishes to break out into this opinion, but he is recalled by the Scriptures, which say that one must always live well, that God cares for human affairs, and that he distinguishes between the godly and the ungodly.

Thus, wishing now to put forward this opinion, he recalls himself. And what does he say? “If I said, ‘I will speak thus,’ behold, I would reject the generation of your sons.” “I would reject the generation of your sons if I spoke thus”: I would reject the generation of the just.

Some copies also read: “Behold, to the generation of your sons to whom did I conform?” [Note: The better manuscripts read *generationi*—“to the generation.” Others read *generatio*—“the generation.” The editions read *generationem*—“the generation.”] That is, “To which of your sons did I conform?”—that is, “With whom did I agree? To whom did I accommodate myself?” I would be discordant with everyone if I taught thus.

For he who agrees is in harmony; he who does not agree is not in harmony. Am I going to say something different from what Abraham said, from what Isaac said, from what Jacob said, from what the Prophets said? All of them said that God cares for human affairs; am I going to say that he does not care? Is my wisdom greater than theirs? Is my understanding greater than theirs?

A most health-giving authority recalled his thought from impiety.

### 22. [verse 16]

And what follows? “If I said, ‘I will speak thus: behold, I would reject the generation of your sons’”—what did he do, then, so that he would not reject it? “And I undertook to understand.”

He undertook to understand. May God assist him so that he may understand. Meanwhile, brothers, he is recalled from a great fall when he no longer presumes to know already, but undertakes to understand what he did not know.

For he had wished to appear as though he knew and to proclaim that God had no care for human affairs. This became the most wicked and impious doctrine of the ungodly. Know, brothers, that many people argue and say that God does not care for human affairs, that everything is governed by chance, or that our wills are subject to the stars, because each person is not directed according to his merits but by the necessity of his stars. An evil doctrine, an impious doctrine!

This man was heading toward it—he whose feet were almost shaken and whose steps were almost poured out. He was heading toward this error. But because he did not agree with the generation of God’s sons, he undertook to understand; and he condemned the knowledge by which he did not agree with God’s righteous people.

Let us hear what he says, because he undertook to understand, was assisted, learned something, and made it known to us. “And I undertook,” he says, “to understand. This labor is before me.”

Truly, it is a great labor: to understand how God both cares for human affairs and yet the wicked prosper while the good labor. Great is the force of the question! Therefore he says, “This labor is before me.” It is as though a certain wall, impossible to unravel, stood before my face. Yet you have the Psalm’s voice: “In my God I will pass over a wall” (Ps. 17:30). “This labor is before me.”

### 23. [verse 17]

You speak truly: the labor is before you; but before God there is no labor. Place yourself before God, where there is no labor, and neither will there be labor for you.

And he did this, for he says how long the labor remained before him: “Until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand the final things.”

A great matter, brothers! “For a long time I have labored,” he says, “and before my face I see a certain almost inextricable labor: to understand how God is just, how he cares for human affairs, and how he is not unjust when sinners and criminals possess happiness on this earth, while the godly and those who serve God are often wearied by temptations and labors. It is a great difficulty to understand this; but it will remain so until I enter into the sanctuary of God.”

What is granted to you in God’s sanctuary so that you may resolve this question? “And I will understand,” he says, “the final things”—not the present.

“I direct my eyes from God’s sanctuary toward the end; I pass beyond the present.” All this which is called the human race, this entire mass of mortality, will come to judgment; it will come to the scales; human works will be weighed there. A cloud now envelops everything, but the merits of each person are known to God.

“And I will understand,” he says, “the final things”—but not by myself; for the labor is before me. From where will I understand the final things? Let me enter the sanctuary of God. There he understood, and understood why these people are happy for the present.

### 24. [verse 18]

“Nevertheless, because of their deceitfulness you set them.” Because they are deceitful—that is, fraudulent—they suffer fraud. What does it mean that because they are fraudulent they suffer fraud?

They wish to defraud the human race by all their wickedness; they themselves also suffer fraud, so that they choose earthly goods and abandon eternal ones. Therefore, brothers, in the very act by which they commit fraud, they suffer fraud.

I said this earlier, brothers: what sort of heart does the man have who, in order to gain a garment, loses faith? Is it the one from whom he took the garment who suffered fraud, or the one struck by so great a loss? If the garment is more precious than faith, the former suffers the greater loss. But if faith surpasses the whole world incomparably, the former will appear to suffer the loss of a garment; to the latter it is said, “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26).

What, then, happened to them? “Because of their deceitfulness you set them; you cast them down while they were exalting themselves.” He did not say, “You cast them down because they were lifted up,” as though he cast them down after they had been lifted up. Rather, in the very thing by which they were lifted up, they were cast down. For to be exalted is already to fall: “You cast them down while they were exalting themselves.”

### 25. [verse 19]

“How suddenly they have become desolation!” He marvels at them, understanding the final things.

“They failed.” Truly, like smoke which, while it rises, fails, so they failed. How does he mean “they failed”? As one who understands the final things: “They failed; they perished because of their iniquity.”

### 26. [verse 20]

“Like the dream of one awakening.” How did they fail? As the dream of one awakening fails.

Imagine a man dreaming that he has found treasures. He is rich—but only until he wakes. “Like the dream of one awakening”: so they failed, like the dream of one who wakes. One searches, and there is nothing: nothing in his hands, nothing in the bed.

A poor man had gone to sleep; in his dream he had become rich. If he had not awakened, he would have been rich. He awoke and found the misery he had left behind when he fell asleep. These people too [Note: The editions read “they will not find.” The word *non*—“not”—is absent from the manuscripts.] will find the misery they had acquired for themselves. When they awaken from this life, what they held as if in sleep will pass away: “like the dream of one awakening.”

And lest someone say, “What then? Does their splendor seem small to you? Does their pomp seem small to you? Do their titles, images, statues, praises, and retinues of clients seem small to you?”—“Lord,” he says, “in your city you will reduce their image to nothing” [Note: Erasmus and most manuscripts read *imagines*—“images”—only at this point.]

Therefore, my brothers, speaking freely on this subject, or at least where I am permitted—for when we mingle with you, we endure you more than we teach you—in the name of Christ and in fear of him I exhort you: whoever does not possess these things, do not desire them; whoever possesses them, do not place confidence in them.

Behold, I have told you: I do not say, “You are condemned because you possess them,” but “You are condemned if you place confidence in such things, if you are puffed up by such things, if you appear great to yourselves because of such things, if because of such things you fail to recognize the poor, if because of your outstanding vanity you forget the common condition of the human race.”

Then God must repay them at the end and reduce the image of such people to nothing in his city.

But let the rich man be rich in the way the Apostle commanded: “Command,” he says, “the rich of this world not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living God, who provides us richly with all things for enjoyment” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

He removes the pride of the rich and gives counsel. As though they were saying, “We are rich; you prohibit us from being proud and forbid us to display the pomp of our riches. What, then, are we to do with these riches? Is there really nothing for us to do with them?”—“Let them be rich,” he says, “in good works; let them give readily; let them share.”

And what does this profit? “Let them lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:18–19).

Where ought they to lay up treasure for themselves? Where this man directed his eyes when he entered the sanctuary of God.

Let all our rich brothers, abounding in money, gold, silver, household slaves, and honors, be filled with dread at what has just been said: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.”

Are they not worthy to suffer this, so that God may reduce their image to nothing in his city, because they themselves have reduced the image of God to nothing in their earthly city? “In your city you will reduce their image to nothing.”

### 27. [verse 21]

“Because my heart was delighted.” He indicates the things by which he is tempted: “Because my heart was delighted,” he says, “and my kidneys were changed.”

When these temporal things delighted me, my kidneys were changed.

This may also be understood in another way: “Because my heart was delighted”—in God—“and my kidneys were changed”; that is, my lusts were changed, and I became entirely chaste. “My kidneys were changed.” And hear how.

### 28. [verse 22]

“And I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know.”

I—the one who now says these things about the rich—once desired such things. Therefore I too was reduced to nothing when my steps were almost poured out.

“And I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know.” Therefore, there is no need to despair even of those about whom I was saying such things.

### 29. [verse 23]

What does “I did not know” mean? “I became like a beast before you, and yet I am always with you.”

There is a great difference between this man and the others. He became like a beast by desiring earthly things, when, reduced to nothing, he did not know eternal things. But he did not withdraw from his God, because he did not desire those things from demons or from the devil.

For I have already impressed this upon you: this is the voice of the Synagogue—that is, of the people who did not serve idols. I became like a beast, desiring earthly things from my God; but I never withdrew from that same God of mine.

### 30. [verse 24]

Therefore, although I became like a beast, I did not withdraw from my God; and what follows is: “You held the hand of my right hand.”

He did not say “my right hand,” but “the hand of my right hand.” If it is the right hand’s hand, then the hand has a hand: “You held the hand of my right hand, so that you might lead me.”

Why did he use “hand”? It can mean power. For we say that someone has in hand what he has in his power, just as the devil said to God concerning Job: “Stretch out your hand, and take away what he possesses” (Job 1:11). What does “stretch out your hand” mean? “Give power.”

He called the hand of God the power of God, just as it is written elsewhere: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). Does the tongue have hands? What, then, does “in the hands of the tongue” mean? In the power of the tongue. What is in the power of the tongue? “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. 12:37).

Therefore, “You held the hand of my right hand”: you held the power of my right hand. What was my right hand? “Because I am always with you.” I had the left hand because I had become like a beast—that is, because earthly desire was in me. But I had the right hand because I was always with you.

You held the hand of this right hand of mine; that is, you governed its power. What power? “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). He began already to be among God’s children, belonging to the New Testament. See how the hand of his right hand was held.

“In your will you led me.” What does “in your will” mean? Not according to my merits. What does “in your will” mean? Hear the Apostle, who was at first like a beast, desiring earthly things and living according to the Old Testament. What does he say? “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13).

What does “in your will” mean? “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). “And with glory you received me.” Where he has been received, and into what glory, who can explain? Who can say? Let us await this, because it will be in the resurrection; it will be at the end: “With glory you received me.”

### 31. [verse 25]

He began to contemplate that heavenly happiness itself and to reprove himself because he had been like a beast and had desired earthly things.

“For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?”

From your voice I see that you have understood. He compared the heavenly reward he is to receive with his earthly desire. He saw what was being kept for him there; and, thinking and burning in contemplation of a certain ineffable reality—which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9)—he did not say, “This or that is mine in heaven,” but “What is there for me in heaven?”

What is that which I have in heaven? What is it? How great is it? What is it like? And since what I have in heaven does not pass away, “what have I desired from you upon earth?”

You preserve something for me. Let me say it as I can, but forgive me; accept my effort, my devotion in striving, for there is no ability to explain it [Note: The manuscripts read *nullam facultatem*—“no ability”—rather than *nulla facultas*—“no ability.”]

“You,” he says, “preserve for me in heaven immortal riches—your very self. And I desired from you on earth what the ungodly possess, what evil men possess, what criminals possess: money, gold, silver, gems, households; what many wicked men possess, what many shameful women possess, what many shameful men possess. I desired these things as something great from my God upon earth, while my God is keeping himself for me in heaven.”

“For what is there for me in heaven?” He is going to show what that “what” is. “And what have I desired from you upon earth?”

[Col. 0928]

### 32. [verse 26]

“My heart and my flesh failed, O God of my heart.”

This, then, is what has been preserved for me in heaven: “God of my heart, and God my portion.”

What does this mean, brothers? Let us find our riches; let the human race choose its portions. Let us see men torn apart by the diversity of their desires. Let some choose military service, others advocacy, others various and diverse teachings, others commerce, others agriculture. Let them make these their portions from human affairs. Let the people of God cry out: “God my portion.”

“My portion” is not for a time; “God is my portion forever.” Even if I always possessed gold, what would I possess? If I did not always possess God, how great a good would I possess? Add to this that he promises himself to me, and promises that I will possess him forever. I possess so much—and I never fail to possess him! Great happiness: “God is my portion.”

For how long? Forever. For see how he loved him and made his heart pure: “God of my heart, and God is my portion forever.”

His heart became pure; now he loves God freely, and asks him for no other reward. Whoever asks God for another reward and therefore wishes to serve God makes what he wants to receive dearer than the one from whom he wants to receive it.

What then? Is there no reward from God? None apart from himself. God’s reward is God himself. This is what he loves; this is what he cherishes. If he loves something else, his love will not be pure. You withdraw from immortal fire; you will grow cold and decay. Do not withdraw; your withdrawal will be your corruption, your fornication.

Now this man returns; now he repents; now he chooses repentance; now he says, “God is my portion.” And how he delights in the one whom he has chosen as his portion!

### 33. [verse 27]

“Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish.”

This man, then, withdrew from God, but not far away, because he says, “I became like a beast, and yet I am always with you.” But those others withdrew far away, because they not only desired earthly things but asked for them from demons and from the devil.

“Those who distance themselves from you will perish.” And what does it mean to be far from God? “You have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you.”

The opposite of this fornication is pure love. What is pure love? The soul now loves its bridegroom. What does it seek from the bridegroom whom it loves? Perhaps it chooses for itself, as men choose sons-in-law or women choose husbands, wealth; it loves his gold, his estates, his silver, his money, his horses, his household, and the rest.

Far be it from us! This soul loves him alone; it loves him freely, because it possesses everything in him, because all things were made through him (John 1:3). “You have destroyed,” he says, “everyone who fornicates away from you.”

### 34. [verse 28]

But what do you do? “But for me it is good to cling to God.”

This is the whole good. Do you want more? I grieve for those who do. Brothers, what more do you want? Nothing is better than clinging to God, when we shall see him face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

What, then, for now? Because I am still speaking as a stranger: “It is good,” he says, “to cling to God,” but for now in pilgrimage, because the reality has not yet come. “To place my hope in God.”

As long as you have not yet clung to him, place your hope there. You are tossed about; send your anchor ahead to land. You do not yet cling through presence; cling through hope. “To place my hope in God” [Col. 0929].

And what will you do here, placing your hope in God? What will your work be except to praise the one whom you love and make fellow-lovers of him with you?

Suppose you loved a charioteer: would you not seize others so that they might love him with you? A lover of a charioteer speaks about him wherever he goes, so that the others may love him with him.

Wicked men are loved freely; yet a reward is sought from God in order that he may be loved! Love God freely; begrudge God to no one. Seize him, all of you who can, all of you who will be able to possess him. He does not become too small; you will set no limits in him. Each of you will possess the whole, and all of you will possess the whole.

Therefore, do this while you are here—that is, while you place your hope in God. What follows? “That I may proclaim all your praises in the courts of the daughter of Zion.”

“That I may proclaim all your praises”—but where? “In the courts of the daughter of Zion,” because preaching about God outside the Church is empty. It is not enough to praise God and proclaim all his praises: proclaim them “in the courts of the daughter of Zion.”

Strive toward unity [Note: The editions read *attende*—“pay attention.” The manuscripts read *tende*—“strive”; several of them shortly afterward read *rap[e] ad unum et fac unam*—“seize toward unity and make one.”] Do not divide the people, but seize them toward unity and make them one.

I have forgotten how long I have been speaking. Now that the Psalm is finished, and from this fragrance [Note: The Royal manuscript reads *ardore*—“ardor.” Other manuscripts, together with the editions, read *odore*—“fragrance”; perhaps it is instead for *sudore*—“sweat.”] I infer that I have delivered a lengthy sermon. But I cannot keep pace with your eagerness; you are far too forceful. Would that by this forcefulness you might seize the kingdom of heaven!

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 73: SERMON TO THE PEOPLE
### 1. [verse 1]

The title of this psalm is: “The Understanding of Asaph.” *Asaph* means “Assembly” in Latin and is called *Synagogue* in Greek. Let us see what this synagogue understood. But first let us understand the synagogue itself; then we shall understand what the synagogue understood.

Every assembly is called a synagogue in the general sense. One may speak of an assembly of animals or of human beings; but here it is not an assembly of animals, since we have heard that it possesses understanding. For when a human being neglects understanding within himself, though placed in honor, hear what is said of him: “Man, though placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13). Since, then, this is not an assembly of animals, there is no need for a lengthy discussion or a more careful exposition. But since it is an assembly of human beings, we must understand what kind of human beings they are.

Certainly it is not an assembly of those human beings who, placed in honor but lacking understanding, were compared with senseless beasts and became like them; it is an assembly of those who understand. For the title of the psalm establishes this, saying: “The Understanding of Asaph.” [Col. 0929] Thus an understanding assembly is one whose voice we are about to hear. But since the assembly of the people of Israel is properly called “Synagogue,” so that whenever we hear “Synagogue” we now customarily understand nothing other than the Jewish people, let us see whether perhaps it is their voice that is heard in this psalm.

But [Col. 0930] what kind of Jews, and what kind of people of Israel? Not the chaff, but perhaps the grain (Matthew 3:12); not broken-off branches (Romans 11:17), but perhaps those who have been strengthened. For “not all who are from Israel are Israelites”; rather, he says, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called”—that is, “not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Romans 9:6–8).

There are therefore certain Israelites, among whom was the one of whom it was said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47). I do not say this according to the sense in which we too are Israelites, since we too are Abraham’s offspring; for the Apostle was speaking to the Gentiles when he said: “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29). In this sense, then, all of us who follow the footsteps of our father Abraham’s faith are Israelites.

But here let us understand the voice of the Israelites in the way the Apostle said: “For I myself am an Israelite, from the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Romans 11:1). Here, then, let us understand what the Prophets said: “The remnant shall be saved” (Romans 9:27). Let us therefore hear the voice of the saved remnant: let the Synagogue speak, the people that had received the Old Testament and was intent upon carnal promises; and from this it came about that its feet tottered.

For in another psalm too, whose title also bears the name Asaph, what is said? “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved.” And as though we were to say, “Why were your feet moved?” he says: “My steps were almost poured out, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.” For while it was awaiting earthly happiness according to God’s promises belonging to the Old Testament, it noticed that such happiness abounded among the ungodly; it saw that those who did not worship God prospered in the very things it was expecting from God. And, as though it had served God without cause, its feet tottered.

There it says: “Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have obtained riches. Surely in vain have I justified my heart?” (Psalm 72:1–3, 12–13). See how its steps were almost poured out, so that the soul might now say to itself: “What benefit is there in serving God? Behold, that man does not serve Him, and he is happy; I serve Him, and I suffer.” Finally, suppose that I am happy; when the one who does not serve is also happy, why should I think myself happy for the reason that I serve? That psalm, whose testimony I have cited, precedes the one we now have in hand.

### 2.

It happened opportunely—not by our arrangement, but by God’s dispensation—that just now we heard from the Gospel: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

For if we distinguish the two Testaments, the Old and the New, their sacraments are not the same, nor are their promises the same; yet most of their commandments are the same. “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; honor your father and mother; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:12–17)—these commandments have also been given to us. Whoever does not observe them goes astray and is not at all worthy to deserve to receive [Note: Two manuscripts read “to ascend” in place of “to receive.”] God’s holy mountain, of which it is said: “Who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who [Col. 0931] shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm 14:1). “He who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart” (Psalm 23:4). [Note: In the printed editions the following passage was inserted here: “We say these things, dearly beloved brothers, so that you may all learn from the New Testament not to cling to earthly things but to attain heavenly things.” It is absent from the manuscripts.]

When the commandments are examined, then, either all of them are found to be the same, or scarcely any are found in the Gospel that were not spoken by the Prophets. The commandments are the same; the sacraments are not the same; the promises are not the same.

Let us see why the commandments are the same: because according to them we must serve God. The sacraments are not the same, because some sacraments give salvation, while others promise the Savior. The sacraments of the New Testament give salvation; the sacraments of the Old Testament promised the Savior.

Since, then, you now possess the Promised One, why do you seek the things that promise, when you already have the Savior? I say: possess the Promised One [Note: This is how it reads in manuscripts of good authority. Lovaniensis has: “having the Savior, now in this possess the promises.”], not because we have already received eternal life, but because Christ has already come—the one who was foretold through the Prophets.

The sacraments have been changed: they have become easier, fewer, more health-giving, and more blessed. Why are the promises not the same? Because the land of Canaan was promised—a rich and fruitful land, flowing with milk and honey; a temporal kingdom was promised; the happiness of this age was promised; fertility in children was promised; the subjection of enemies was promised (Exodus 3:8). All these things pertain to earthly happiness.

But why was it necessary that these things first be promised? Because “the spiritual was not first, but the natural, and afterward,” he says, “the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:46–49).

The Old Testament belongs to the image of the earthly; the New Testament belongs to the image of the heavenly. But lest anyone suppose that the earthly human being was made by one creator and the heavenly by another, God, showing Himself to be the creator of both, also willed to be acknowledged as the author of both Testaments: so that He might promise earthly things in the Old Testament and heavenly things in the New Testament.

But how long are you still an earthly human being? As long as you care for earthly things. When certain childish things and toys are given to a child to distract a childish mind, does it follow that, as the child grows, those things should not be taken from his hands so that he may now handle something more useful, something suitable for an adult? Yet you yourself gave your son both nuts when he was little and a book when he was grown. Therefore, because God through the New Testament took those things that were, as it were, children’s toys from the hands of His children, in order to give them something more useful as they grew, it does not follow that we should think that He Himself did not give the earlier things. He gave both.

“The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17): grace, because through love is fulfilled what was commanded through the letter; truth, because what was promised is bestowed.

This, then, is what this Asaph understood. Indeed, [Col. 0932] everything that had been promised to the Jews has been taken away. Where is their kingdom? Where is the temple? Where is the anointing? Where is the priest? Where are the Prophets now among them? Since the one who was proclaimed through the Prophets came, none of these things now remains among that people. They have now lost earthly things, and do not yet seek heavenly things.

### 3.

You ought not, therefore, to cling to earthly things, even though God gives them. Nevertheless, because we ought not to cling to them, we must not believe that anyone other than God gives them. He Himself gives them; but do not expect from Him as a great good what He gives even to the wicked. For if He gave these things as a great good, He would not give them to the wicked. But He wished to give them even to the wicked so that the good might learn to seek from Him another thing—something He does not give to the wicked.

Those who cling to earthly things are wretched and do not place their hope in the One who made heaven and earth, who gave them these earthly things themselves, who also freed them temporally from captivity in Egypt, who led them through the divided sea, and who overwhelmed their pursuing enemies in the waves (Exodus 14:22, 28). They did not place their hope in the One who would certainly give heavenly things to the mature, just as He gave earthly things to children. Fearing to lose what they had received, they killed the One who had given it.

We say these things, brothers, so that you may learn from the New Testament not to cling to earthly things. For if those people clung to earthly things inexcusably, although the New Testament itself had not yet been revealed to them, how much more inexcusably do those pursue earthly things to whom heavenly promises have already been revealed in the New Testament!

For recall, my brothers, what was said by those who persecuted Christ: “If we let Him go, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). See how, fearing to lose earthly things, they killed the King of heaven.

And what happened to them? They lost those earthly things as well. Where they killed Christ, they themselves were killed; and while unwilling to lose the land, they killed the giver of life, and, once killed, lost that same land. They killed Him at the very time when they were thereby to be warned why they would suffer these things.

For when the city of the Jews was destroyed, they were celebrating Passover, and the whole people had gathered in that place, in many thousands, for the celebration of that festival. There God—through wicked men indeed, but nevertheless being good; through unjust men, but being just and acting justly—took vengeance upon them in such a way that many thousands of people were destroyed and the city itself overthrown.

This is what the understanding of Asaph laments in this psalm. And in that lament, as understanding, he distinguishes earthly things from heavenly things and the Old Testament from the New Testament, so that you may see what you are to pass through, what you are to expect, what you are to leave behind, and to what you are to cling. Thus he began.

### 4.

“Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end?”

“You have rejected us to the end”—from the person of the Jewish people, and from the person of the assembly properly called Synagogue. “Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end?” He is not reproaching God, but asking: Why—on what account, for what reason—have you done this? What have you done? “You have rejected us to the end.”

What does “to the end” mean? Perhaps until the end of the age. Or have you rejected us toward Christ, who is the end for every believer (Romans 10:4)? “Why, then, have you rejected us, O God, to the end? Your anger is against the sheep of your flock.”

Why are you angry against the sheep of your flock, except because we clung to earthly things and did not recognize the shepherd?

### 5. [verse 2]

“Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning.”

Can this perhaps be the voice of the Gentiles? Did God possess the Gentiles from the beginning? Rather, He possessed the offspring of Abraham: the people of Israel, descended according to the flesh from the Patriarchs, our fathers. We have become their children, not by coming from their flesh, but by imitating their faith.

Those who were possessed by God from the beginning—what happened to them? [Col. 0933]

“Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning. You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.”

You redeemed that very congregation of yours, the rod of your inheritance. He called this congregation the rod of the inheritance.

Let us look back to the first event, when God wished to possess that congregation itself by freeing it from Egypt, and consider what sign He gave Moses when Moses said to Him: “What sign shall I give them, so that they may believe that You have sent me?” And God said to him: “What are you carrying in your hand?” “A rod.” “Throw it onto the ground.” He threw the rod onto the ground, and it became a serpent; and Moses was terrified and fled from it. And the Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it returned to its former state, becoming a rod, just as it had previously been a rod (Exodus 4:1–4).

What does this signify? It was not done without reason. Let us question God’s Scriptures. What did the serpent persuade the human being to do? To die (Genesis 3:4–5). Therefore, death came from the serpent. If death came from the serpent, the rod is in the serpent, and Christ is in death.

For this reason, also, when the Israelites were being bitten and killed by serpents in the desert, the Lord commanded Moses to raise up a bronze serpent in the wilderness and instruct the people that anyone who had been bitten by a serpent should look upon it and be healed (Numbers 21:8; John 3:14). And so it happened: people bitten by serpents were healed from the poison by looking upon the serpent.

To be healed by a serpent—a great sacrament! What does it mean to be healed by a serpent by looking upon a serpent? To be saved from death by believing in one who died.

And yet Moses was terrified and fled from that serpent. What does Moses’ flight from that serpent mean, brothers, except what we know happened in the Gospel? Christ died, and the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had been standing (Luke 24:21).

But what was said? “Take hold of its tail.” What is the tail? Grasp what comes afterward. This too was signified by the words: “You shall see my back” (Exodus 33:23). First the rod became a serpent, but, when the tail was held, it became a rod again; first He was killed, afterward He rose again.

There is also the end of the age in the serpent’s tail, because the Church now proceeds in mortality in this way: some depart and others come through death, as though through the serpent, because death was sown by the serpent. But at the end of the age, as the tail, we return to God’s hand and become the established kingdom of God, so that what is written may be fulfilled in us: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.”

But since this is the voice of the Synagogue, while the redeemed rod of God’s inheritance appears more clearly among the Gentiles, though the hope of the Jews is hidden—whether of those who were destined to believe, or of those who believed at the time when, after the Holy Spirit had been sent, the disciples spoke in the languages of all the nations (Acts 2:4)—for at that time several thousand of the Jews themselves, the crucifiers of Christ, believed. And because they were near, they believed in such a way that [Col. 0934] they sold everything they possessed and placed the prices of their goods at the feet of the Apostles (Acts 4:34).

Since this was hidden, and since the redemption of God’s rod was destined to become more manifest among the Gentiles, he explains from where he says what he has said: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance.”

He said this not about the Gentiles, among whom it is manifest. But from where? “Mount Zion.”

Even Mount Zion can still be understood in another way: “This mountain which you inhabited in it”—the place where the people formerly dwelt, where the temple was established, where sacrifices were celebrated, where all the things necessary at that time existed, things that promised Christ.

When the promise is fulfilled in reality, it becomes superfluous. For before what is promised is bestowed, the promise itself is necessary, lest the one to whom it is promised forget what was promised to him and die without waiting for it. He must therefore wait, so that when it comes he may receive it; for this reason he ought not to abandon the promise.

This is why the figures were not abandoned: so that, when the day came, the shadows might be removed. “This Mount Zion which you inhabited in it.”

### 6. [verse 3]

“Raise your hand against their pride to the end.”

Just as you rejected us to the end, so raise your hand against their pride to the end. Whose pride? The pride of those by whom Jerusalem was overthrown. And by whom was it overthrown, except by the kings of the Gentiles?

His hand was rightly raised against their pride forever, for they themselves have now come to know Christ. “For Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

How well he wishes this for them! He speaks as though angry and seems to curse; and may what he curses come to pass! Rather, let us already rejoice that it is coming to pass in the name of Christ. Those who already hold the scepter are subjected to the wood of the cross. What was foretold is now taking place: “All the kings of the earth shall worship Him; all nations shall serve Him” (Psalm 71:11). On the foreheads of kings, the sign of the cross is now more precious than the jewel of the diadem.

“Raise your hand against their pride forever. How much wickedness the enemy has committed against your holy things!”

Against those things that were holy to you—that is, in the temple, in the priesthood, and in all those sacraments that existed at that time—how much wickedness the enemy committed! Truly the enemy acted then. For the Gentiles who did this worshiped false gods, adored images, and served demons; yet they committed many evils against God’s holy things.

When could they have done this, unless they had been permitted? And when would they have been permitted, unless those holy things, which at first were things that promised, were no longer necessary, since the one who had promised was already being held?

“How much wickedness the enemy has committed against your holy things!” [Note: Several manuscripts read “necessary”; the editions have “first” and omit the word “necessary.”]

### 7. [verse 4]

“And all who hated you gloried.”

Consider the slaves of demons, the slaves of images—what the Gentiles were then, when they overthrew the temple and city of God—and they gloried.

“In the midst of your festival.”

Remember what I said: Jerusalem was overthrown while the festival itself was being celebrated, the festival during which they crucified the Lord. Gathered together, they raged; gathered together, they perished.

### 8. [verse 5]

[Col. 0935] “They set up their signs as signs, and they did not understand.”

They had signs to set up there: their standards, their eagles, their dragons—the Roman insignia; or perhaps their statues, which they first placed in the temple; or perhaps their signs, which they had heard from the prophets of their demons.

“And they did not understand.”

What did they not understand? “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). They did not understand that the honor had not been granted to them so that they might afflict, capture, or destroy the city; rather, their impiety became God’s axe. They became the instrument of one who was angry, not for the kingdom of one who had been appeased.

For God does what human beings often do. Sometimes an angry man takes up a rod lying in the middle—perhaps some sort of branch—and beats his son with it; then he throws the branch into the fire but preserves the inheritance for his son. In the same way, God sometimes instructs the good through the wicked and uses the temporal power of those destined for condemnation to discipline those destined for liberation.

What, then? Do you think, brothers, that discipline was given to that people in such a way that it was destined to perish entirely? How many believed afterward! How many will yet believe! Chaff is one thing, grain another; yet the threshing-floor comes upon both. Under the same threshing-sledge, one is crushed, the other cleansed.

What great good God has brought us from the evil of Judas the betrayer! From the very savagery of the Jews, what great good was provided for the faithful Gentiles! Christ was killed so that He might be on the cross for the one who had been struck by the serpent to look upon (Numbers 21:8).

Perhaps these people too had heard from their diviners that they ought to go to Jerusalem and capture it. And after they had captured and destroyed it, they said that this had been done by their demons:

“They set up their signs as signs, and they did not understand.”

What did they not understand? “As at a going forth from above” [Note: The editions read “at the going forth”; the manuscripts read “into the going forth.”]

For unless the command had come forth from above, the Gentiles, in their fury against the Jewish people, would never have been permitted to do such things. But it came forth from above, just as Daniel says: “From the beginning of your prayer the word went forth” (Daniel 9:23).

The Lord said this also to Pilate, who was puffing himself up, setting up his signs as signs, not understanding, and saying to Christ: “Do you not answer me? Do you not know that I have power to kill you and power to release you?” And the Lord, piercing the inflated man as one might puncture a bladder so that it could be deflated, said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:10–11).

So here also: “They set up their signs as signs, and they did not understand.” How did they not understand? “As at a going forth from above.” Could they possibly understand how that going forth had come from above so that this might be fulfilled?

### 9. [verse 6]

Let us now run through these verses concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, since they are clear and since I do not wish to linger over the punishment of the enemies.

“As in a forest of trees they cut down its doors with axes all together; with the axe and the hammer they brought it down”—that is, they brought it down conspiratorially and persistently, with the axe and the hammer.

### 10.

[Col. 0936] “They set fire to your sanctuary; they profaned on the earth the dwelling-place of your name.”

### 11. [verses 8–9]

“They said in their heart, their whole kindred together.”

What did they say? “Come, let us suppress all the festivals of the Lord from the earth.”

“Of the Lord” has been inserted from the person of Asaph. Those raging men would not call “Lord” the one whose temple they were overthrowing.

“Come, let us suppress all the festivals of the Lord from the earth.”

What does Asaph—the understanding of Asaph—say about these things? What? Does the discipline given produce no effect? Is the perversity of the mind not corrected? Everything that formerly existed has been overthrown: nowhere is there a priest, nowhere a Jewish altar, nowhere a victim, nowhere a temple.

Is nothing else, then, to be recognized as having succeeded what has departed? Or would this sign that promised have been removed unless what it promised had come? Let us therefore look here at the understanding of Asaph; let us see whether tribulation produces an effect.

Pay attention to what he says: “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet, and he does not yet recognize us.”

Behold these Jews, who say that they are still not recognized—that is, that they are still in captivity and have not yet been freed. They are still awaiting Christ. Christ will come, but He will come as judge: first as the one who calls, afterward as the one who separates. He will come, because He has come [Note: Several manuscripts read: “Afterward the one who separates will come. Because He will come.” Others read: “He will come who has already come.”], and it is clear that He will come; but He will now come from above.

He was before you, O Israel! You have been shaken because you stumbled against the one lying on the ground; lest you be crushed, look upon the one who comes from above. For it was foretold through the Prophet: “Whoever stumbles against that stone shall be shattered, and upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him” (Isaiah 8:14–15; see Luke 20:18).

The little one shatters; the great one will crush [Note: The editions read: “The little ones were shattered; the great ones he will crush.” The manuscripts, more correctly, have “little” and afterward “great.”].

You no longer see your signs; there is now no prophet; and you say: “He does not yet recognize us”—because you do not yet recognize Him. “There is now no prophet, and he does not yet recognize us.”

### 12. [verse 10]

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach us?”

Cry out [Note: This is the reading of Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis has “you cry out” here and in the immediately following passage.] as one abandoned, as one deserted; cry out like a sick man who preferred to strike the physician rather than be cured. He does not yet recognize you.

See what the one who does not yet recognize you has done. “For those to whom He was not announced shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isaiah 52:15; Romans 15:21). And you still cry out: “There is now no prophet, and he does not yet recognize us.”

Where is your understanding?

“The adversary provokes your name forever.”

The adversary provokes your name to the end so that, being angry, you may rebuke, and, in rebuking, may know to the end—or certainly, “to the end,” that is, until the end.

Until what end? Until you understand, until you cry out, until, having grasped the tail, you return to the kingdom.

### 13. [verse 11]

[Col. 0937] “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom forever?”

Here again there is another sign given to Moses. Just as the earlier sign concerned the rod, so this one concerns the right hand.

When that sign involving the rod had been performed, God gave another sign: “Put your hand,” He said, “into your bosom.” He put it in. “Bring it out.” He brought it out, and it was found to be white—that is, unclean. For whiteness on the skin is leprosy, not brightness (Leviticus 13:25).

God’s inheritance itself—that is, His people—sent forth from Him, became unclean. But what did He say to him? “Return it to your bosom.” He returned it, and it came back to its own color (Exodus 4:6–7).

When will you do this? asks this Asaph. How long will you estrange your right hand from your bosom, so that it remains unclean outside? Call it back; let it return to its color; let it recognize the Savior.

“Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom forever?”

The blind man cries out these things without understanding, and God does what He does [Note: The Regius manuscript reads “God did it.” The Corbeiensis reads “God did what,” and does not add “does.” The passage appears corrupt in both the printed editions and the manuscripts.].

Why did Christ come? “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

Therefore, Asaph, now recognize what came before, so that you may at least follow if you were unable to precede it. Christ did not come without reason, nor was Christ killed without reason, nor did the grain fall into the earth without reason, except so that it might rise in abundance (John 12:23).

The serpent was raised up in the wilderness so that it might heal the one struck by the poison (Numbers 21:9). Consider what has happened. Do not think that His coming was in vain, lest He find you evil when He comes again.

### 14. [verse 12]

Asaph understood, because the title of the psalm is “The Understanding of Asaph.” And what does he say?

“But God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

While we cry out, “There is now no prophet, and he will not recognize us any longer,” our God and King, who is before the ages—because He Himself is the Word in the beginning, through whom the ages were made—has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.

God, therefore, our King before the ages: what did He do? He worked salvation in the midst of the earth, while I still cry out as one deserted. He works salvation in the midst of the earth, while I have remained earth.

Asaph understood well, because he is called “The Understanding of Asaph.” Why did Christ work this salvation, and what kind of salvation did He work, except so that human beings might learn to desire eternal things and not always cling to temporal things?

“But God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

While we cry out, “How long, Lord, will the enemy reproach us forever? How long will the adversary provoke us? How long will you turn your hand away from your bosom?”—while we say these things, “God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth,” and we are asleep.

The Gentiles are already awake, while we snore and, as though God had deserted us, rave in our dreams.

“He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

### 15. [verse 13]

Now, then, Asaph, correct yourself toward understanding. Tell us what kind of salvation God worked in the midst of the earth.

When your earthly salvation was overthrown, what did He do? What did He promise?

“You established the sea by your power.”

As though the Jewish people were dry land separated from the waves, the Gentiles were the sea in its bitterness, washing around that land on every side. Behold, you established the sea by your power, and the land remained thirsting for your rain.

“You established the sea by your power; you crushed the heads of dragons in the waters.”

The heads of dragons—the prides of demons by whom the Gentiles were possessed—you [Col. 0938] crushed upon the water, because through Baptism you freed those whom they possessed.

### 16. [verse 14]

What follows the heads of the dragons? Those dragons have their prince, and he himself is the first and great dragon.

And what did the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth do to him? Listen:

“You crushed the head of the dragon.”

Whose dragon? We understand all the demons serving under the devil as dragons. Which individual dragon, then, whose head was crushed, should we understand except the devil himself?

What did He do to him?

“You crushed the head of the dragon.”

That is the beginning of sin. That is the head that received the curse, so that the seed of Eve might watch the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The Church was warned to avoid the beginning of sin.

What is the beginning of sin, as though it were the serpent’s head? “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sirach 10:15). Therefore the head of the dragon was crushed; diabolical pride was crushed.

And what did the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth do to him?

“You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.”

What does this mean? How am I to understand the peoples of Ethiopia? How except as all the Gentiles? And it is fitting that they are called dark-skinned, for Ethiopians are black.

Those who were black are called to the faith, so that it may be said to them: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). They are indeed called black, but so that they may not remain black. For from them the Church is made, to which it is said: “Who is this that comes up, made white?” (Song of Songs 8:5, according to the Septuagint).

What was made from the black woman except what is said: “I am black and beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:4)?

And how did these people receive this dragon as food? I think they rather received Christ as food: Christ by whom they would be completed, and the devil whom they would consume.

For this reason, too, there is that calf which the faithless, apostate people worshiped while seeking the gods of the Egyptians and abandoning the one who had freed them from Egyptian slavery. From this arose that great sacrament.

When Moses became angry with those who worshiped and adored the idol, and, inflamed by zeal for God, took temporal vengeance in order to terrify them away from the death that must be avoided forever, he nevertheless threw the calf’s head into the fire, destroyed it, crushed it to pieces, scattered it in water, and gave the people to drink (Exodus 32:1–20). Thus a great sacrament was enacted.

O prophetic anger, and a spirit not disturbed but enlightened! What did he do? Put it into the fire, so that its very form might first be disfigured; crush it into tiny pieces, so that it might gradually be consumed; put it into the water and give the people to drink.

What does this mean except that the worshipers of the devil had become his body? Just as those who recognize Christ become the body of Christ, so that it may be said to them: “You are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27), the body of the devil was to be consumed, and it was to be consumed by the Israelites.

For the Apostles came from that people; the first Church came from that people. And it was said to Peter concerning the Gentiles: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

What does “Kill and eat” mean? Kill what they are, and make them what you are. Here: “Kill and eat”; there: “Crush and drink.” Yet both belong to the same sacrament, because it was necessary—indeed, unquestionably necessary—that the body which had been the devil’s should pass through faith into the body of Christ.

Thus the devil [Col. 0939] is consumed as he loses his members.

This was also prefigured in Moses’ serpent. For the magicians did something similar: they threw down their rods and produced dragons, but Moses’ dragon swallowed all the rods of those magicians (Exodus 7:12).

Let the body of the devil, then, also be understood in the present case. This is what happens: it is devoured by the Gentiles who have believed; he has become food for the peoples of Ethiopia.

This too can be understood: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia,” because now everyone bites him.

What does “bites” mean? Rebuking, blaming, accusing. As it is said—in a prohibition, certainly, but nevertheless explicitly: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

What does “you bite and devour one another” mean? You quarrel with one another, slander one another, and hurl reproaches at one another.

Consider, then, that the devil is now being consumed by these bites. Who does not, even as a pagan, when angry with his servant, say to him: “Satan”? See that the devil has been given as food.

The Christian says this; the Jew says this; the pagan says this. He worships him, and curses him.

### 17. [verse 15]

Let us look at what follows. Brothers, I beg you, pay attention. These things are heard with great pleasure because, once heard, they are also recognized throughout the world.

When these words were being spoken, the things they described had not yet occurred, because they were then being promised and not yet bestowed. But now with what pleasure are we moved when we see being fulfilled in the world the things that we read were foretold in the book!

Let us see what the one whom Asaph now understands did—what the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth did.

“You split open springs and torrents.”

You split them open so that the liquid of wisdom might flow, so that the riches of faith might flow, so that they might water the saltiness of the Gentiles, so that through their irrigation all unbelievers might be changed into the sweetness of faith.

“You split open springs and torrents.”

Perhaps a distinction is intended; perhaps it is one thing, because the springs were so abundant that they formed rivers.

“You split open springs and torrents.”

But if a distinction is intended: in some people the word of God becomes “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14). Others hear the word and, although they do not possess it in such a way as to live well, nevertheless do not keep silent with their tongue; they become torrents.

For “torrents” properly means streams that are not perennial. Sometimes, however, the word is used figuratively for a river, as when it is said: “They shall be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Psalm 35:9). That torrent will not at some time dry up.

Properly speaking, torrents are streams that fail in summer but, swollen by winter waters, overflow and run.

You see, then, a person who is truly faithful, who will persevere to the end, who will not abandon God in any temptation, who endures every hardship for truth rather than for falsehood and error. From where does such a person derive this strength, except because the word has become in him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life”?

Another person receives the word, preaches it, does not remain silent, and runs; but summer tests whether it is a spring or a torrent.

Nevertheless, let the earth be watered by both—from the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Let the springs overflow; let the torrents run:

“You split open springs and torrents.”

### 18.

You dried up the rivers of Etham. Here he breaks open springs and torrents; there he dries up rivers, so that waters may flow from one side and waters dry up from the other. “The rivers,” he says, “of Etham.” What is Etham? It is a Hebrew word. What does Etham mean? “Strong,” “powerful.” Who is this strong and powerful one whose rivers God dries up? Who but that very dragon? For no one enters the house of a strong man to plunder his goods unless he has first bound the strong man (Matt. 12:29). He is the strong one, relying on his own power and abandoning God; he is the strong one who says, “I will set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

From the cup of this perverse strength he offered drink to humanity. They wanted to be strong, believing that by eating the forbidden food they would become gods. Adam became strong, so that he might be mocked [Note: [Col. 0940] The better manuscripts read this way. Others read, “when he was exalted.” But the editions read, “when he heard.”]: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Gen. 3:5, 6, 22). The Jews too were strong, presuming upon their own righteousness: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, as though strong, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

Observe a man who has dissipated his strength and remains weak, needy, standing far off, not daring to raise his eyes toward heaven, but beating his breast and saying, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). Now he is weak; now he confesses his weakness; he is not strong. The earth is dry; let it be watered by springs and torrents. Those who still presume upon their own strength are still strong. Let their rivers dry up: let the teachings of the nations, the arts of soothsayers, astrologers, and magicians make no progress, because the rivers of the Strong One have dried up [Note: [Col. 0940] The editions read, “the strong rivers.” The better manuscripts read, “of the strong one,” which is the interpretation of the name Etham.]: “You dried up the rivers of Etham.” Let that teaching wither; let the minds of people be flooded by the Gospel of truth.

### 19. [verse 16]

Yours is the day, and yours is the night. Who does not know this, since he himself made all these things, because all things were made through the Word (John 1:3)? To the very one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth it is said: Yours is the day, and yours is the night. Here we must understand something that pertains to the very salvation he worked in the midst of the earth.

Yours is the day. Who are these? The spiritual. And yours is the night. Who are these? The carnal. Yours is the day, and yours is the night. Let the spiritual speak spiritual things to the spiritual; for it is written: “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, we speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Cor. 2:13, 6). The carnal do not yet grasp this wisdom: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (ibid. 3:1).

Therefore, when the spiritual speak to the spiritual, “Day pours forth the word to day”; but when even the carnal do not keep silent about the faith of Christ crucified, which the little ones can grasp, “Night announces knowledge to night” (Ps. 18:3). Yours is the day, and yours is the night. The spiritual belong to you; the carnal belong to you. You illumine the former with unchangeable wisdom and truth; you console the latter by the manifestation of the flesh, as the moon consoles the night.

Yours is the day, and yours is the night. Do you wish to hear the day? See whether you can grasp it; raise your mind as far as you can. Let us see whether you belong to the day; let us now see whether your sight does not waver. Can you see what you have just heard from the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”? You do not know how to conceive of words except those that sound and pass away. Can you now grasp the Word—not a sound, but God? Did you not hear there, “And the Word was God”? Yet you think about these words: “All things were made through him”; and through him even those who make words were made. What, then, is that Word like? Do you grasp it, carnal person? Answer: do you grasp it? You do not grasp it; you still belong to the night. The moon is necessary for you, lest you die in darkness.

For certain sinners “bent their bow, to shoot at those upright in heart in the dark moon” (Ps. 10:3). The flesh of Christ, taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb, had indeed become darkened; and those who had killed him mocked him. He had not yet risen, and the disciples, upright in heart, were struck by arrows in the dark moon.

Therefore, so that not only “day may pour forth the word to day,” but also “night may announce knowledge to night”—because yours is the day and yours is the night—deign to descend, remaining with him from whom you descend, yet coming to those to whom you descend. Deign to descend, you who were in this world, and the world was made through you, and the world did not know you. Let the night also have its consolation; let it have, as it is written, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–14). Yours is the day, and yours is the night.

You made the sun and the moon: the sun, the spiritual; the moon, the carnal. The carnal person is still carnal; he must not be abandoned, but must himself also be perfected. You made the sun and the moon: the sun, like the wise person; the moon, like the foolish person; yet you did not abandon him. For thus it is written: “The wise person remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27:12).
