What, then? Since the sun remains—that is, since the wise person remains like the sun, while the fool changes like the moon—is the carnal person, still foolish, to be abandoned? And where is what the Apostle said: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1:14)? You made the sun and the moon.

### 20. [verse 17]

You made all the boundaries of the earth. Did you not do this earlier too, when he founded the earth? But how did the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth make the boundaries of the earth? How, unless in the manner the Apostle says: “By grace we have been saved, and this is not from ourselves, but is God’s gift; not from works, lest anyone should boast”? Therefore, there were no good works? There were. But how? By the grace of God. Continue; let us see: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. 2:8–10).

Behold how the one who worked salvation in the midst of the earth made the boundaries of the earth: “You made all the boundaries of the earth.” You made summer and spring. The summer is those who burn with the spirit. You, I say, made those who burn with the spirit; you also made those who are young in the faith: that is spring. You made summer and spring. Let them not boast as though they had not received them; you made them.

### 21. [verse 18]

Remember this creature of yours. What creature of yours? “The enemy reproached the Lord.” O Asaph, grieve in your understanding over your former blindness! “The enemy reproached the Lord.” It was said to Christ among his own people: “This man is a sinner; we do not know where he comes from. We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, he is a Samaritan” (John 9:24, 29; 8:48).

“The enemy reproached the Lord, and the foolish people provoked your name.” The people were foolish then, O Asaph; but Asaph did not then possess understanding. What is said in the preceding psalm? “I became like a beast before you; yet I am always with you,” because he did not go after the gods and idols of the nations. Although he did not know you as a beast, he nevertheless recognized you as a human being; for he said, “I am always with you,” like a beast.

And what follows in that very psalm, where Asaph speaks? “You held my right hand; you led me according to your will, and with glory you received me” (Ps. 72:23–24). According to your will, not according to my righteousness; by your gift, not by my work.

Thus here also: “The enemy reproached the Lord, and the foolish people provoked your name.” Did everyone, then, perish? Far from it. Although some branches were broken off, some nevertheless remain into which the wild olive might be grafted (Rom. 11:17); the root remains, and from those branches broken off through unbelief some were recalled through faith. For the Apostle Paul himself had been broken off through unbelief, and through faith was restored to the root.

Thus indeed the foolish people provoked your name when it was said: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40).

### 22. [verse 19]

But what of you now, O Asaph, with understanding? “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” I acknowledge it, says Asaph; for, as it is said in another psalm, “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not conceal my iniquity” (Ps. 31:5).

Why? Because Peter spoke while the Israelites marveled at the tongues, since they themselves had killed Christ, although Christ had been sent for their sake. When they heard this, they were pierced in heart and said to the Apostles, “What, then, shall we do? Tell us.” And the Apostles replied: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts 2:37–38).

Since, then, confession was made through repentance, “Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” Why “that confesses you”? Because “I turned into affliction when the thorn was fastened” (Ps. 31:4). They were pierced in heart; and through repentance they became afflicted, though previously they had been glorious in their savagery.

“Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you.” To what beasts, unless to those whose heads were crushed upon the waters? For the devil himself is called a beast, a lion, and a dragon. Do not, he says, give to the devil and his angels the soul that confesses you.

Let the serpent devour me if I still savor earthly things, if I still desire earthly things, if, now that the New Testament has been revealed, I still remain in the promises of the Old Testament. But once I have laid aside pride and no longer acknowledge my own righteousness but your grace, let the proud beasts have no power over me.

“Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses you. Do not forget forever the souls of your poor.” We were rich; we were strong. But you dried up the rivers of Etham. Now we do not establish our own righteousness, but acknowledge your grace; we are poor. Hear your beggars.

We no longer dare to raise our eyes toward heaven, but, beating our breast, we say: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). “Do not forget forever the souls of your poor.”

### 23. [verse 20]

Look upon your covenant. Give what you promised: we hold the tablets; we await the inheritance. Look upon your covenant—not that old one. I do not ask for the land of Canaan, nor for the temporal subjection of enemies, nor for the carnal fruitfulness of children, nor for earthly riches, nor for temporal safety. Look upon your covenant by which you promised the kingdom of heaven.

Now I understand your covenant; now Asaph possesses understanding; Asaph is no longer a beast. Now he sees what was said: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31–32).

“Look upon your covenant, because those who have been darkened by the earth of the houses of iniquity have been filled”—because they had iniquitous hearts. Our houses are our hearts; the blessed who are pure in heart gladly dwell there (Matt. 5:8).

Look, then, upon your covenant, “and let the remnant be saved” (Rom. 9:27), because many who pay attention to the earth have been darkened and have been filled with earth. Dust entered their eyes and blinded them, and they became like the dust that the wind drives away from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4).

Those who have been darkened by the earth of the houses of iniquity have been filled. By paying attention to the earth they were darkened; of them it is said in another psalm: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their backs forever” (Ps. 68:24).

They have been filled with earth, those who have been darkened by the earth of the houses of iniquity, because they had iniquitous hearts. For our houses, as we said above, are our hearts. We dwell there gladly if we cleanse them from iniquity.

There is an evil conscience, from which a person is driven to go where he is commanded, carrying his mat, once his sins have been forgiven, when the Lord says: “Take up your mat and go into your house” (John 5:8). Carry your flesh, and enter into your healed conscience.

“Because those who have been darkened by the earth of the houses of iniquity have been filled”: they have been darkened; they have been filled with earth. Who are those who have been darkened? Those who have iniquitous hearts. The Lord repays them according to their heart.

### 24. [verse 21]

Let the humble person who has been confounded not be turned away. Pride confounded them. “The needy and the poor will praise your name.” You see, brothers, how sweet poverty ought to be. You see that the poor and needy belong to God—but the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:3).

Who are the poor in spirit? The humble, those who tremble at the words of God and confess their sins, not presuming upon their merits or their own righteousness. Who are the poor in spirit? Those who, when they do something good, praise God; when they do something evil, accuse themselves.

“Upon whom will my Spirit rest,” says the prophet, “unless upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Now, then, Asaph has understood. He no longer clings to the earth; he no longer seeks the earthly promises of the Old Testament. He has become your beggar; he has become your poor man. He thirsts for your rivers, because his own have dried up.

Since he has become such a person, let him not be defrauded of hope: “He sought with his hands by night before you; let him not be deceived” (Ps. 76:3). “Let the humble person who has been confounded not be turned away; the needy and the poor will praise your name.”

Those who confess their sins will praise your name; those who desire your eternal promises will praise your name. Not those swollen with temporal things, not those lifted up and inflated in pride by their own righteousness—not they, but who? “The needy and the poor will praise your name.”

### 25. [verse 22]

“Rise up, Lord; judge my cause.” I seem abandoned, because I have not yet received what you promised. My tears have become my bread day and night, while I am told every day, “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41:4).

And because I cannot show my God, I am mocked as though I were pursuing something empty. It is not only the pagan, the Jew, or the heretic who does this; sometimes even a Catholic brother twists his mouth when God’s promises are proclaimed and the future resurrection is announced.

Even he, although already washed with the water of eternal salvation and carrying the sacrament of Christ, perhaps says: “And who has risen to this place?” and “I never heard my father speak from the grave in which I buried him.” God gave the law to his servants for a time, as a place to which they might withdraw; for who returns from the underworld?

And what shall I do with such people? Shall I show them what they do not see? I cannot. God need not become visible on their account. Let them act as they please; let them do this and attempt it, since they do not wish to be converted for the better but wish to convert God for the worse.

Let the one who can see, see; let the one who cannot, believe that God exists. Even if the one who can see sees, does he see with his eyes? He sees with understanding; he sees with the heart. For he did not wish to display the sun and the moon when he said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8).

But an impure heart is not even fit for faith, so that it may believe what it cannot see [Note: [Col. 0944] The particle “so that” is absent in Lov., but appears in the other books.]. “I do not see,” he says; “what am I to believe?” Your soul is visible, I suppose! Fool! Your body is visible; who sees your soul?

Since, then, only your body is seen, why are you not buried? He is astonished that I said, “If only your body is seen, why are you not buried?” And he replies—for he has some sense in this matter—“Because I am alive.”

How do I know that you are alive, when I do not see your soul? How do I know? You will reply: “Because I speak, because I walk, because I work.” Fool! From the works of the body I recognize that you are alive; from the works of creation you cannot recognize the Creator!

And perhaps the one who says, “Once I am dead, I shall no longer exist,” has learned letters and learned this from Epicurus, from some delirious philosopher—or rather, a lover of vanity, not of wisdom—whom even the philosophers themselves called a pig. Because he said that bodily pleasure was the highest good, they called that philosopher a pig, wallowing in the mire of the flesh.

Perhaps this educated man learned from him to say, “I shall not exist after I have died.” Let the rivers of Etham dry up; let these teachings of the nations perish; let the green growth of Jerusalem spring forth. Let them see what they can see; let them believe in their hearts what they cannot see.

Certainly all these things that are now seen throughout the world did not yet exist when God was working salvation in the midst of the earth, when these things were being foretold. And behold, they were then predicted; now they are shown fulfilled. Yet the fool still says in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13:1).

Woe to perverse hearts! For the things that remain will come just as those things came which at that time did not yet exist but were foretold as future. Or has God displayed to us everything that he promised, and deceived us only about the day of judgment?

Christ was not yet on earth: he promised it, and displayed it. A virgin had not yet given birth: he promised it, and displayed it. The precious blood had not yet been poured out by which the record of our death would be erased: he promised it, and displayed it. The flesh had not yet risen into eternal life: he promised it, and displayed it. The nations had not yet believed: he promised it, and displayed it.

Heretics armed with the name of Christ had not yet fought against Christ: he foretold it, and displayed it. The idols of the nations had not yet been removed from the earth [Note: [Col. 0945] Here the editions add “these things”; the word is absent from the manuscripts.]: he foretold it, and displayed it.

After he had foretold and displayed all these things, did he lie only about the day of judgment? It will certainly come, just as these things came. For these too were future before they came; they were first foretold as future, and afterward they came. It will come, my brothers.

Let no one say, “It will not come,” or, “It will come, but what will come is far off.” For you, it is near that you should depart from here. Let the first deception suffice. If we could not remain in the commandment at first, let us at least be corrected by the example.

There was not yet an example of human downfall when it was said to Adam: “You will surely die if you touch it.” Then the serpent came from the side and said: “You will certainly not die.” The serpent was believed; God was despised. The serpent was believed; the forbidden thing was touched; the human being died (Gen. 2:17; 3:4, 6, 19).

Was what God threatened not fulfilled rather than what the enemy promised? Certainly it was. We acknowledge this; from it we are all in death. Now, at least, having experienced it, let us be cautious.

For even now the serpent does not cease to whisper and say: “Surely God is not going to condemn such great crowds and save only a few?” What else is this than, “Act against the commandment; you will not die”? But as it was then, so it is now.

If you do what the devil suggests and despise what God commands, the day of judgment will come, and you will find that what God threatened was true and what the devil promised was false.

“Rise up, Lord; judge my cause.” You died and were despised, and I am told, “Where is your God?” (Ps. 41:11). Rise up; judge my cause. For the one who will come to judgment is none other than the one who rose from the dead.

He was foretold as coming; he came and was despised by the Jews while walking on earth; he is despised by false Christians while seated in heaven. “Rise up, Lord; judge my cause.”

Because I believed in you, let me not perish. Because I believed what I did not see, let my hope not deceive me; let me receive what you promised. “Judge my cause.”

“Remember your reproaches,” those which come from the foolish all day long. Christ is still mocked; nor will there be any lack, all day long—that is, until the end of the age—of vessels of wrath.

It is still said: “Christians proclaim empty things”; it is still said: “The resurrection of the dead is meaningless.” Judge my cause; remember your reproaches.

But whose reproaches, unless those which come from the foolish all day long? Surely a wise person does not say this. For “prudent” is derived from “seeing ahead” (*porro videns*). If the prudent person sees ahead, then he sees ahead by faith; for with the eyes one scarcely sees what lies before one’s feet all day long.

### 26. [verse 23]

Do not forget the voice [Note: [Col. 0945] The manuscripts read this way, in agreement with the Greek Septuagint. The editions read “voices.”] of those who entreat you—the voice of those who groan and already await what you promised in the New Testament, and who walk toward that very faith. Do not forget the voice of those who entreat you.

But they still say, “Where is your God?” Let the pride of those who hate you always rise up before you [Note: [Col. 0946] The editions read “rose up.” The better manuscripts read “let it rise up,” as does the Greek Septuagint, *anabaie*.]. Do not forget their pride either. And he does not forget it: he either punishes it outright or corrects it.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 74. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

### 1. [verse 1]

This psalm brings the medicine of humility to the swelling of pride, while it consoles the humble in hope. It works to ensure that no one presumptuously relies on himself, and that no humble person despairs of the Lord.

For God’s promise is valid, certain, established, firm and unshaken, faithful and free from every doubt; it consoles the afflicted. For the whole of human life upon earth, as it is written, is a trial (Job 7:1).

Nor should one choose what seems prosperous and avoid only what is adverse. Both must be guarded against: the former lest it corrupt, the latter lest it break. Thus, whatever the circumstances in which each person lives this life, he should have no refuge except God and no joy except in his promises.

For this life, overflowing with every kind of happiness, deceives many; God deceives no one. When anyone turns to God, his pleasure changes and his delights change—not because they are taken away, but because they are changed.

All our delights in this life are not yet present in reality; but hope itself is so certain that it should be preferred to all the delights of this age, as it is written: “Delight in the Lord.” And lest you think that you already possess what he promises, he immediately adds: “And he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. 36:4).

If, then, you do not yet possess the requests of your heart, from where do you delight in the Lord, unless because you hold fast to a trustworthy promiser who, by promising, has made himself your debtor?

The title of this psalm speaks of this prayer—that our hope may remain with us and that we may be brought into what God promised: “For the end; do not destroy.” What does “do not destroy” mean? “Fulfill what you promised.” But when? “At the end.”

Let the eye of the mind therefore be directed there, toward the end. Let everything encountered on the way be passed through, so that we may reach the end.

Let the proud rejoice in present happiness; let them swell with honors, shine with gold, overflow with households, and be crowded around by the services of clients. These things pass away; they go by like a shadow.

When that end comes, at which all who now hope in the Lord will rejoice, then unending sorrow will come upon them. When the humble receive what the proud mock, the swelling of the proud will be turned into mourning.

Then there will be that voice which we know from the Book of Wisdom. For then, seeing the glory of the saints—those who, when humbled here, endured, and those who, when exalted here, did not consent—the proud will say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision.” They also say: “What did our pride profit us? What did the boasting of riches bring us? All things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:3, 8–9).

Because they presumed upon corruptible things, their hope will be corrupted. But our hope will then be reality. We said that God’s promise should remain whole, firm, and certain toward us, and from the heart [Note: [Col. 0947] Four manuscripts read “from the mouth.”] of faith we said: “For the end; do not destroy.”

Therefore, do not fear that any of the powerful will corrupt God’s promises. He does not corrupt them, because he is truthful; he has no one more powerful by whom his promise could be corrupted.

Let us therefore be certain of God’s promises, and let us already sing the words with which the psalm begins.

### 2. [verse 2]

“We will confess to you, God; we will confess to you, and we will call upon your name.” Do not call upon him before you confess; confess, and call upon him. For the one whom you call upon, you call into yourself. What does it mean to call upon him, unless to call him into yourself? If he is called upon by you—that is, if he is called into you—to whom does he come?

He does not come to the proud. Certainly he is exalted; the elevated person does not reach him. Whenever we wish to touch lofty things, we lift ourselves up; and if we cannot reach them, we seek some machines or ladders so that, having been raised up, we may touch what is high.

But God is different: he is exalted, and yet he is touched by the humble. It is written: “The Lord is near to those who have crushed the heart” (Ps. 33:19). The crushing of the heart is piety and humility.

The one who crushes himself becomes angry with himself. Let him be angry with himself, so that God may be propitious toward him; let him make himself his judge, so that he may have God as defender.

Therefore, when called upon, God comes. To whom does he come? He does not come to the proud.

Hear another testimony: “The Lord is exalted, and he looks upon the lowly; but he recognizes the exalted from afar” (Ps. 137:6). “The Lord is exalted, and he looks upon the lowly,” not from afar; “but he recognizes the exalted from afar.”

And lest the proud, when it was said that he looks upon the lowly, rejoice in their impunity, as though he did not recognize the proud because he dwells in high places, they were terrified and told: “He sees you and knows you, but from afar.”

He makes those blessed to whom he draws near. But you, he says, O proud and exalted ones, will not be unpunished, because he recognizes you; you will not be blessed, because he recognizes you from afar.

See, then, what you are doing. For if he recognizes, he does not pardon. It is better, then, that he pardon than recognize. For what does it mean to pardon, unless not to recognize? What does “not to recognize” mean? Not to take notice; for the act of an avenger is also called taking notice.

Hear one praying that he may pardon: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11). What, then, will you do if he turns his face away from you? It is grievous, and to be feared, lest he abandon you.

But if he does not turn his face away, he takes notice. God knows this; God can both turn his face away from the sinner and not turn it away from the one who confesses.

Thus, elsewhere it is said to him: “Turn your face away from my sins”; and elsewhere it is said to him: “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 26:9). There: “Turn it away from my sins”; here: “Do not turn it away from me.”

Confess, then, and call upon him. By confessing, you cleanse the temple into which he comes when called upon. Confess, and call upon him.

May he turn his face away from your sins; may he not turn it away from you. May he turn his face away from what you have done; may he not turn it away from what he himself has made.

He made you a human being; you made your sins. Confess, then, and call upon him. Say: “We will confess to you, God; we will confess to you.”

### 3.

This repetition is a confirmation, so that you will not regret having confessed. For you have not confessed to some cruel person; not to an avenger, not to one who insults you. Confess without fear.

Hear another voice of the psalm exhorting us: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 105:1; 106:1). What does “for he is good” mean? What are you afraid to confess? He is good; he forgives the one who confesses.

Fear confessing to a human judge, lest perhaps he punish you after you have confessed; do not fear confessing to God. By confessing, make him merciful, whom by denying you do not make ignorant.

“We will confess to you, God; we will confess, and now without fear we will call upon your name.” We have emptied our hearts through confession; you have terrified us and cleansed us.

Confession makes us humble, and brings us near to the humble one, while you withdraw from the exalted. That repetition confirms a statement is taught to us in many passages of Scripture.

This is why the Lord says, “Amen, amen” (John 1:51). This is why in some psalms we find, “Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 71:19; 88:53). One “let it be” would suffice to signify the matter; a second “let it be” was added to signify firmness.

You know that Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, when Joseph was already imprisoned there because of his love of chastity, saw a dream familiar to all of us: seven fat cows consumed by seven lean cows, and again seven fruitful ears consumed by seven thin ears.

And what did Joseph interpret? If you remember, these are not two dreams but one vision. “Their interpretation is one,” he said; “but the fact that you saw it again,” he said, “serves for confirmation” (Gen. 41:1–32).

I have said this so that you will not think that repetition in the words of the sacred language is an appetite for excessive speech. Often repetition there has the force of confirmation.

“My heart is ready, O God,” he says; “my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8). Elsewhere he says: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14). There are countless examples of this throughout all the Scriptures.

It is enough that we have commended this manner of speech to you, so that you may observe it in all similar passages. Now attend to the matter itself.

“We will confess,” he says, “and we will call upon him.” I have explained why confession precedes invocation: because the one whom you call upon, you invite. But the one called upon does not wish to come if you are proud. If you are proud, you cannot confess; nor do you deny to God what he does not know.

Therefore, your confession does not teach him; it cleanses you.

### 4.

He has now confessed and called upon him—or rather, they have confessed and called upon him—and it is said in the person of one: “I will recount all your wonders.”

By confessing, he emptied himself of evils; by calling upon him, he filled himself with good things; by recounting them, he poured forth what had filled him.

And observe, brothers: when they were confessing, there were many: “We will confess to you, God; we will confess to you, and we will call upon your name.” For there are many hearts of those confessing, but one heart of those believing.

Why are there many hearts of those confessing, but one heart of those believing? People confess different sins; they believe one faith.

Once Christ has begun to dwell in the inner person through faith (Eph. 3:17), and once he has begun, when called upon, to possess the one who has confessed, the whole Christ comes to be—head and body—and from many there is made one.

Now hear the words of Christ. For they seemed not to be his words: “We will confess to you, God; we will confess to you, and we will call upon your name.”

Now speech begins in the person of the head. Whether the head speaks or the members speak, Christ speaks: he speaks in the person of the head; he speaks in the person of the body.

But what was said? “The two will be one flesh.” “This mystery is great; I am speaking,” he says, “of Christ and the Church” (Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:31–32). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matt. 19:6).

For, so that you may know that these are in a certain sense two persons and yet again one through the union of marriage, one person speaks through Isaiah and says: “As a bridegroom he bound a fillet around me, and as a bride he clothed me with an ornament” (Isa. 61:10). He called himself the bridegroom in reference to the head, and the bride in reference to the body.

One person therefore speaks. Let us hear him, and let us also speak in him. Let us be his members, so that this voice may also be ours.

“I will recount,” he says, “all your wonders.” Christ evangelizes himself; he evangelizes himself also in his members who already exist, so that he may bring in others, that those who were not present may approach, and that they may be joined to his members, through which members his Gospel was preached.

Thus one body may be formed under one head, in one Spirit, in one life.

### 5. [verse 3]

And what does he say? “When I receive the appointed time, I myself will judge righteous judgments.” When will he judge righteous judgments? When he receives the appointed time. The time itself has not yet come.

Thanks be to his mercy: first he proclaims righteous judgments, and then he judges righteous judgments [Note: [Col. 0949] Some manuscripts read this way. Er. reads: “Let him first proclaim righteousness, and then judge righteous judgments.” Lov. reads: “First righteousness proceeds,” and so forth.].

For if he wished to judge before proclaiming, who would be found to be set free? Who would come forward to be acquitted?

Now, therefore, is the time of proclamation: “I will recount,” he says, “all your wonders.” Hear the one who recounts; hear the one who proclaims. For if you despise him, he says, “When I receive the appointed time, I myself will judge righteous judgments.”

“I forgive sins now,” he says, “to the one who confesses; afterward I will not spare the one who despises me.”

“I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord,” it is said in the psalm (Ps. 100:1). Mercy and judgment: now mercy, afterward judgment; in mercy sins are forgiven, in judgment sins are punished.

Do you wish not to fear the one who punishes sins? Love the one who forgives. Do not reject him; do not exalt yourself; do not say, “I have nothing for him to forgive me.” Hear what follows: “When I receive the appointed time, I myself will judge righteous judgments.”

Did Christ receive a time? Did the Son of God receive a time? The Son of God did not receive a time; but the Son of Man received a time. The same one is both the Son of God, through whom we were made, and the Son of Man, through whom we were restored.

By assuming humanity, he himself was not assumed; by changing humanity for the better, he was in no way changed for the worse. He did not cease to be what he was, but received what he was not.

What was he? “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized”—these are the Apostle’s words. And what did he receive? “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7).

Just as he received the form of a servant, so he received a time. Was he therefore changed? Was he diminished? Made smaller? Did he fall into weakness? Far from it.

What, then, does it mean that he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”? He is said to have emptied himself by taking what was lower, not by degenerating from what was equal.

Therefore, brothers, what does this mean: “When I receive the appointed time, I myself will judge righteous judgments”? He received a time as the Son of Man; he governs times as the Son of God.

Hear how, as the Son of Man, he received a time for judging. He says in the Gospel: “He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).

As the Son of God, he never received authority to judge, because he was never without the authority to judge. As the Son of Man, he received a time, just as he received a time for being born and suffering, for dying and rising again and ascending, so also for coming and judging.

His body also says these things, for he will not judge without it. For he says in the Gospel: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Therefore the whole Christ speaks—that is, the head and the body in the saints: “When I receive the appointed time, I myself will judge righteous judgments.”

## 6. [verse 4]

[Col. 0950]

But now what? “The earth has melted away.” If the earth has melted away, from what did it melt away except from sins? For this reason they are also called *delicts* (*delicta*). To offend (*delinquere*) is, as it were, to flow away from some liquid substance [several manuscripts: “from a certain place”], away from the stability of the firmament of virtue and justice. Each person sins through desire for inferior things: just as one is strengthened by love of higher things, so one fails and, as it were, liquefies through desire for lower things.

The merciful Giver, the forgiver of sins and not yet the exactor of punishments, observing this flowing away of things in human sins, observed it and said: “The earth has melted away, and all who dwell in it.” The earth itself has melted away in those who dwell in it. This is an explanatory statement that follows, not an addition. It is as if you were to say: “How has the earth melted away? Have the foundations been removed, and has something in it been swallowed up by some fissure?” What I mean by “the earth” is “all who dwell in it.”

“I found,” he says, “the earth sinful; and what did I do? I established its pillars.” Which pillars did he establish? He calls the Apostles pillars. Thus the apostle Paul says of his fellow apostles, “Those who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. 2:9). And what would those pillars have been unless they had been strengthened by him? For in a kind of earthquake even the pillars themselves tottered: at the Lord’s Passion all the Apostles despaired. Therefore those pillars, which tottered at the Lord’s Passion, were strengthened by his resurrection.

The beginning of the building cried out through its pillars, and in all those pillars the architect himself cried out. The apostle Paul was one of those pillars when he said: “Or do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). Therefore, “I established its pillars,” he says: “I rose again; I showed that death is not to be feared; I showed those who feared that even the body itself does not perish in those who die.” The wounds terrified them; the scars strengthened them. The Lord Jesus Christ could have risen without any scar. For what was difficult for his power in restoring the structure of the body to such complete integrity that no trace whatsoever of the former wound appeared? He had the power to heal it even without a scar; but he wished to retain something by which he might strengthen the tottering pillars.

[Col. 0951]

## 7. [verse 5]

We have already heard, brothers, what is not silent every day; let us hear what he cried out through these pillars. It is time to listen because of that terror: “I will judge acts of justice when I receive the time.” He will receive the time to judge acts of justice; you already have the time to perform acts of justice. If he were silent, you would have nothing to do; but he cries out after strengthening the pillars.

What does he cry out?

“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly.”

He cries out, my brothers. Certainly you cry out too; it pleases you—listen to him crying out. I beseech you by him: let that voice terrify you. It is not so much your voices that ought to delight us as that voice ought to terrify you.

“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly.”

But they have already done so and are guilty; the earth has already melted away, and all who dwell in it. Those who crucified Christ were pierced to the heart; they acknowledged their sin and learned something from the Apostles, so that they would not despair of the preacher’s pardon (Acts 2:37–38) [several manuscripts: “sinners”].

For the physician had come, and for that reason he had not come to the healthy: “It is not the healthy who need a physician,” he says, “but those who are sick; I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:12–13).

Therefore: “I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly.” They did not listen. For it was said to us long ago; we did not listen, we fell, we became mortal, we were born mortal: the earth has melted away. Let them listen at least now, so that they may rise—the physician who came to the sick person. Those who were healthy did not wish to listen to him, so that they would not fall; let those who lie fallen listen, so that they may rise.

“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly. And to those who offend: Do not exalt your horn.” [The word “your” is absent here and below from most manuscripts.]

What does this mean? If you have done wrong through desire, do not defend it through arrogance; confess it, if you have done it. For whoever does not confess, while being wicked, exalts his horn. [The editions read: “and exalts his horn”; *and* is absent from the manuscripts.]

“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly; and to those who offend: Do not exalt your horn.”

The horn of Christ will be exalted in you if your horn is not exalted. Your horn comes from wickedness; Christ’s horn comes from majesty.

## 8. [verses 6–8]

“Therefore do not be lifted up; do not speak wickedness against God.”

Hear now the voices of many; let each person listen and be pierced. What do people usually say?

“Does God truly judge human affairs? And is there such a thing as God’s judgment? [The better manuscripts read: “Does God truly judge human affairs? And is there a judgment of God?”] Or does he really care what is done on earth? So many wicked people abound in prosperity, while the innocent are oppressed by hardships!”

But some evil befalls that person, with God chastising and warning him, and he knows his conscience; he knows that, in proportion to his sins, he may be suffering something deserved. Why does he argue against God? Since he cannot say, “I am righteous,” what do we suppose he says?

“There are worse wicked people, and yet they do not suffer these things.”

This is the wickedness that people speak against God. But see how wicked it is: while he wants to appear righteous, he makes God unjust. For whoever says, “I suffer unjustly what I suffer,” makes him unjust by whose judgment he suffers, while making himself righteous because he suffers unjustly.

I ask you, my brothers: is it right that God should be believed unjust and you righteous? But when you say these things, you speak wickedness against God.

## 9

What does he say in another psalm?

“You have done these things”—enumerating certain sins. “You have done these things,” he says, “and I was silent.”

What does “I was silent” mean? He never falls silent with respect to the commandment, but for a time he is silent with respect to punishment; he refrains from vengeance and does not pronounce sentence upon the condemned.

But that person says: “I did this and that, and God did not punish me; behold, I am well, nothing bad has happened to me.”

“You have done these things, and I was silent; you suspected wickedness, thinking that I would be like you.”

What does “that I would be like you” mean? Because you are wicked, you thought me wicked too—as though I approved your crimes rather than opposed and avenged them. [Most manuscripts read “rather than took notice of them,” not “rather than opposed them.”]

And what does he say to you afterward?

“I will rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:21).

What does this mean? Because now, by sinning, you place yourself behind your back: you do not see yourself, you do not examine yourself. I will set you before yourself and make you suffer punishment from yourself.

So also here:

“Do not speak wickedness against God.”

Pay attention. Many speak this wickedness, but they do not dare to do so openly, lest blasphemers be shunned by devout people. In their hearts they gnaw upon these things; inwardly they feed upon such wicked food. They delight in speaking against God, and if their tongue does not break out, their heart is not silent.

Hence it is said in another psalm:

“The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1).

The fool said it, but he feared human beings. He did not wish to say it where people would hear; he said it where the one of whom he spoke would hear it himself.

Therefore here too, in this psalm, beloved, pay attention. When he said, “Do not speak wickedness against God,” he saw many doing this in their hearts, and he added:

“For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the deserts of the mountains; for God is judge.”

God is the judge of your wickedness. If God is God, he is present everywhere. Where will you remove yourself from God’s eyes, so that you may say somewhere what he does not hear?

If God judges from the east, withdraw to the west and say whatever you wish against God. If he judges from the west, go to the east and speak there. If he judges from the deserts of the mountains, go into the midst of the peoples, where you may mutter to yourself.

He judges from no particular place, for he is hidden everywhere and public everywhere [Lov. reads: “He does not judge from any place”; *does not* is absent from Erasmus and the manuscripts]; no one is permitted to know him as he is, and no one is permitted to be ignorant of him.

See what you are doing. You speak wickedness against God.

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (another Scripture says this); and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice. For this reason the one who speaks wicked things cannot remain hidden (Wis. 1:7–8).

Do not therefore imagine God as confined to places. He is with you as you are.

What does “as you are” mean? He is good if you are good, and he will seem evil to you if you are evil—but he is a helper if you are good, an avenger if you are evil. There you have the judge in your secret place.

Wishing to do something evil, you withdraw from public view into your house, where none of your enemies can see you. From the open and exposed places of your house you remove yourself into a bedroom; fearing someone who might know even what happens in the bedroom, you withdraw into your heart and meditate there. He is more inward than your heart.

Therefore, wherever you flee, he is there. Where will you flee from yourself? Will you not follow yourself wherever you flee?

But since he is even more inward than you are, there is nowhere for you to flee from an angry God except to a reconciled God. There is absolutely nowhere else to flee.

Do you wish to flee from him? Flee to him.

Therefore, do not speak wickedness against God—not even there where you speak.

“He meditated wickedness upon his bed” (Ps. 35:5).

What did he meditate upon his bed? His bed is his heart. He says:

“Offer the sacrifice of justice and hope in the Lord.”

But above he said:

“Speak in your hearts, and be pierced upon your beds” (Ps. 4:6, 5).

As many goads of crimes as you have there, have just as many goads of confessions there.

Therefore, where you speak wickedness against God, there he judges you. He does not postpone judgment, but punishment. He already judges, already knows, already sees. Punishment remains. When it has been presented, you will also have punishment—when the face of that man appears who was mocked here, judged, crucified, and stood before a judge. When he appears judging in his own presence, then you will have punishment if you have not corrected yourself.

What shall we do now, then? Let us go before his face “in confession” (*ἐν ἐξομολογήσει*) (Ps. 94:2). Go before him in confession; the one whom you had made angry will come gentle.

“Neither from the deserts of the mountains; for God is judge”—not from the east, not from the west, not from the deserts of the mountains.

Why? Because God is judge.

If he were in some particular place, he would not be God. But because God is judge, not a human being, do not expect him from particular places. You will be his place if, being good and having confessed, you call upon him.

## 10

“He humbles this one and exalts that one.”

Whom does that judge humble, and whom does he exalt? Consider those two in the Temple, and you will see whom he humbles and whom he exalts.

“He went up into the Temple to pray,” it says: “one a Pharisee and the other a Publican.”

The Pharisee said:

“‘I give you thanks because I am not like the rest of humanity—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this Publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.’”

He had gone up to the physician and was displaying healthy limbs; he was concealing his wounds.

What, then, did the one who knew better where he was to be healed do? The Publican stood at a distance and was striking his breast. You see him standing at a distance; he was drawing near to the one whom he called upon.

“And he was striking his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you: that Publican went down justified rather than that Pharisee, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:10–14).

The verse of this psalm has been explained. What does God the judge do? He humbles this one and exalts that one; he humbles the proud and exalts the humble.

[Col. 0953]

## 11. [verse 9]

“For a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine with mixture.”

Deservedly. “And he inclined from this one to that one; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied: all the sinners of the earth will drink.”

Renew your attention for a little while; something obscure is involved. But, just as we have heard in the Gospel reading that has most recently been read:

“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7).

But you say: “Where am I to knock, so that it may be opened to me?”

“Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the deserts of the mountains; for God is judge.”

If he is present here and there, and absent nowhere, knock where you stand. Simply stand there, because one knocks by standing.

What, then, does this mean? The first question presents itself:

“It is full of unmixed wine with mixture.” How can it be unmixed if it has mixture?

In any case, when he says, “A cup is in the hand of the Lord”—I am speaking to those educated in the Church of Christ—you must not picture God in your heart as confined by a human form, lest, though your temples are closed, you construct idols in your hearts.

Therefore this cup signifies something. We shall discover what it is.

It is “in the hand of the Lord,” that is, in the power of the Lord. For God’s hand signifies the power of God. Indeed, it is often said of human beings, “He has this in his hand,” that is, “he has it in his power”; when he wishes, he does it.

“It is full of unmixed wine with mixture.” He himself then explains it:

“He inclined,” he says, “from this one to that one; nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied.”

There is the reason why it was full of wine with mixture. Therefore do not be frightened because it is both unmixed and mixed: unmixed because of its purity, mixed because of its dregs.

What, then, is the wine there, and what are the dregs? And what does it mean that “he inclined from this one to that one,” so that its dregs were not emptied?

## 12

Remember how he arrived at this point: “He humbles this one and exalts that one.” What was represented to us in the Gospel through two men, the Pharisee and the Publican, let us understand more broadly as referring to two peoples, the Jewish people and the Gentiles.

The Jewish people were that Pharisee; the Gentile people were that Publican. The Jewish people boasted of their merits; the Gentiles confessed their sins.

Anyone acquainted with the sacred writings, with the Apostolic Epistles and the Acts of the Apostles, sees there what I am saying. I shall not lengthen the discussion by explaining how the Apostles exhorted the Gentiles not to despair because they had lain in great sins, and restrained the Jews from exalting themselves as though they were justified by the Law, and therefore thought themselves righteous while the Gentiles were sinners—since the Jews had the Law, the Temple, and the priesthood (Rom. 3–4).

But the Gentiles were all worshippers of idols and venerators of demons, situated far away indeed, just as that Publican stood at a distance. Just as the former withdrew through pride, so the latter drew near through confession.

Therefore, the cup full of unmixed wine in the hand of the Lord—as far as the Lord grants me understanding—appears to me to be the Law given to the Jews, and all that Scripture called the Old Testament. Another may understand it better, for such is the obscurity of the Scriptures that it is difficult for them to produce a single interpretation. Whatever interpretation is offered, however, it must accord with the rule of faith: we neither envy our elders nor despair of the little ones [the editions read: “nor do we despair of the little ones”]. I state what seems to us to your Charity, not in order to close your ears to others who may perhaps say something better. There are contained in it the weights of all the sayings.

For the New Testament lies hidden there, as though in the dregs of bodily sacraments. Circumcision of the flesh is a matter of great sacramental significance, and from it circumcision of the heart is understood. That Temple in Jerusalem is a matter of great sacramental significance, and from it the body of the Lord is understood. The promised land signifies the kingdom of heaven.

The sacrifice of victims and animals possesses a great sacramental meaning; but in all those kinds of sacrifices the one sacrifice and the one victim on the cross—the Lord—is understood [the editions read “the Lord’s”; manuscripts of good authority read “the Lord”]. In place of all those sacrifices we have one, because they too prefigured these things—that is, these things were prefigured by them.

That people received the Law; it received just and good commandments. What is as just as:

“You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother. You shall not covet your neighbor’s property. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife. You shall worship one God and serve him alone” (Exod. 20:7–17; Deut. 5:6–21)?

All these things pertain to the wine. But those bodily things, as it were, settled to the bottom, so that all the spiritual meaning might be poured out from them.

The cup, therefore, is in the hand of the Lord—that is, in the power of the Lord. It is full of unmixed wine—that is, of the sincere Law—with mixture—that is, with the dregs of bodily sacraments.

And because he humbles this one, the proud Jew, and exalts that one, the confessing Gentile, “he inclined from this one to that one”—that is, from the Jewish people to the Gentile people.

What did he incline? The Law. Its spiritual meaning was filtered out. “Nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied,” because all the bodily sacraments remained among the Jews.

“All the sinners of the earth will drink.”

Who will drink? All the sinners of the earth. Who are the sinners of the earth? The Jews were indeed sinners, but proud; the Gentiles were sinners, but humble.

“All the sinners will drink”; but observe who drinks the dregs and who drinks the wine. For the former, by drinking the dregs, vanished away; the latter, by drinking the wine, were justified.

I dare to say that they were intoxicated, and I shall not be afraid. Would that you all might be intoxicated in this way! Remember:

“Your intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:5).

What then, my brothers? Do you suppose that all those who, by confessing Christ, even wished to die, were sober? They were so intoxicated that they did not recognize their own people. All their relatives who tried to turn them away from the hope of heavenly rewards through earthly blandishments were not recognized or heard by those intoxicated people.

Were they not intoxicated whose hearts had been changed? Were they not intoxicated whose minds had been estranged from this world?

“All the sinners of the earth will drink,” he says. But who will drink the wine? Sinners will drink, but so that they may no longer remain sinners; so that they may be justified, not punished.

## 13. [verse 10]

“But I”—for all drink, but I separately, that is, Christ with his body—“will rejoice forever; I will sing to the God of Jacob.”

This refers to that future promise at the end, concerning which it is said, “Do not destroy”:

“But I will rejoice forever.”

[Col. 0955]

## 14. [verse 11]

“And I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous will be exalted.”

This is: “He humbles this one and exalts that one.”

Sinners do not wish their horns to be broken [Gatian manuscript: “to break”], but they will undoubtedly be broken at the end. Do you not want him to break it then? Break it today yourself.

For you heard above—do not despise it:

“I said to the wicked: Do not act wickedly; and to those who offend: Do not exalt your horn.”

When you heard, “Do not exalt your horn,” you despised it and exalted your horn. You will come to the end, where this will take place:

“I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous will be exalted.”

The horns of sinners are the dignities of the proud; the horns of the righteous are the gifts of Christ. For by horns exalted positions are understood.

Hate earthly elevation on earth, so that you may be able to possess heavenly elevation. You love the earthly; it does not admit you to the heavenly. And it will belong to your disgrace that your horn is broken, just as it will belong to your glory if your horn is exalted.

Now, therefore, is the time for choosing; then it will not be. You will not say, “Let me be spared, and I will choose,” for the voices have gone before:

“I said to the wicked.”

If I did not say it, prepare an excuse, prepare a defense. But if I did say it, anticipate confession, lest you come to condemnation; for then confession will be too late, and there will be no defense.

[Col. 0956]

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 75. SERMON TO THE PEOPLE

## 1. [verse 2]

The enemies of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Jews known to everyone, are accustomed to boast in this psalm that we have sung, saying:

“God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel,”

and to insult the Gentiles, among whom God is not known, saying that God is known only to themselves, since the Prophet says, “God is known in Judea.” Therefore elsewhere he is unknown.

Yet God is truly known in Judea, if they understand what Judea is. For in truth God is not known except in Judea. Indeed, we too say this: unless each person is in Judea, God cannot be known to him.

But what does the Apostle say?

“He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter” (Rom. 2:29).

Therefore there are Jews in the circumcision of the flesh, and there are Jews in the circumcision of the heart. Many of our holy fathers possessed both circumcision of the flesh, because of the seal of faith, and circumcision of the heart, because of faith itself.

These people, degenerating from those fathers—people who now boast in the name but have lost the deeds—therefore, degenerating from those fathers, remained Jews in the flesh but pagans in the heart.

The Jews themselves are those descended from Abraham, from whom Isaac was born, and from Isaac Jacob, and from Jacob the twelve patriarchs, and from the twelve patriarchs the entire Jewish people.

But they were called Jews especially for this reason: Judas was one of the twelve sons of Jacob, a patriarch among the twelve, and the kingdom came to the Jews from his stock.

For that entire people had twelve tribes according to the number of Jacob’s twelve sons. Tribes are so called as distinct councils and gatherings of peoples.

That people therefore had twelve tribes. Among those twelve tribes was one tribe, Judah, from which the kings came; and there was another tribe, Levi, from which the priests came.

But because no land was assigned to the priests serving the Temple (Num. 18:20), while the entire region of promise had to be distributed among twelve tribes, once the one tribe of greater dignity, the tribe of Levi, which consisted of priests, was excepted, eleven would remain—unless the twelve were completed by the adoption of Joseph’s two sons.

Pay attention to what this means.

Joseph was one of Jacob’s twelve sons. This is the Joseph whom his brothers sold into Egypt, and who, on account of his chastity, was deservedly raised to a position of high dignity. God was with him in all his work. He received his brothers, by whom he had been sold, and his father, who were suffering from famine and had gone down to Egypt for bread.

This Joseph had two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. When Jacob was dying, as though by testament, he adopted those grandsons [the editions read “having taken them into his testament”; *having taken* is absent from several manuscripts] of his into the number of his sons and said to his son Joseph:

“Your other sons who are born to you shall be yours; but these shall be mine, and they shall divide the land with their brothers” (Gen. 48:5–6).

The promised land had not yet been given or divided, but he spoke prophetically in the Spirit.

When Joseph’s two sons were added, twelve tribes nevertheless came into being—indeed thirteen, since two were added in place of the one tribe of Joseph.

Therefore, when the tribe of Levi is excepted—that tribe of priests which served the Temple and lived from the tithes of all the others to whom the land was divided—twelve remain.

Among these twelve was the tribe of Judah, from which the kings came. For at first a king was given from another tribe, Saul (1 Sam. 9:1), but he was rejected as an evil king. Later David was given as king from the tribe of Judah, and after him the kings were from the tribe of Judah (ibid. 16:12).

Jacob had said this when he blessed his sons:

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom the promise was made” (Gen. 49:10).

From the tribe of Judah came our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as Scripture says and as you have just heard, he is from the seed of David, born of Mary.

As for the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which he is equal to the Father, he existed not only before the Jews but also before Abraham himself (John 8:58), and not only before Abraham but before Adam; not only before Adam but before heaven and earth and before the ages, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:3).

Therefore, since it was said in prophecy, “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom the promise was made,” the earlier times are considered, and it is found that the Jews always had kings from the tribe of Judah, from which they were called Jews. They had no foreign king before Herod, who existed when the Lord was born (Luke 3:1).

From Herod onward foreign kings began. Before Herod all were from the tribe of Judah—but only until he came to whom the promise was made.

Therefore, when the Lord himself had already come, the kingdom of the Jews was overturned and taken away from them. Now they have no kingdom because they do not wish to acknowledge the true king.

See now whether they should be called Jews. You already see that they should not be called Jews. By their own voice they renounced themselves from this name, so that they are not worthy to be called Jews except according to the flesh.

Where, then, did they separate themselves from this name? They were saying and raging against Christ—that is, against the tribe of Judah [the editions read “that is, against the tribe of Judah”; *against* is absent from the manuscripts]; they were raging against the seed of David.

Pilate said to them:

“Shall I crucify your king?”

And they replied:

“We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15).

O Jews, who are called so but are not Jews: if you have no king except Caesar, then the ruler has already failed from Judah. Therefore the one has come to whom the promise was made.

Those, then, are more truly Jews who, coming from the Jews, have become Christians. The other Jews, who did not believe in Christ, deserved to lose even the name itself.

True Judea, therefore, is the Church of Christ, believing in that king who came from the tribe of Judah through the virgin Mary; believing in him of whom the Apostle was speaking when he wrote to Timothy:

“Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (2 Tim. 2:8).

David was from Judah, and from David came the Lord Jesus Christ.

We who believe in Christ belong to Judah. We have come to know Christ, whom we have not seen with our eyes; we hold him by faith.

Therefore let the Jews not insult us, since they are no longer Jews. They themselves said:

“We have no king except Caesar.”

It would have been better for them if Christ had been their king, Christ from the seed of David and from the tribe of Judah.

Nevertheless, because Christ himself is from the seed of David according to the flesh, while God is blessed above all forever, he is our king and our God: our king according to the fact that he was born from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh—Christ the Lord and Savior; but our God as the one who existed before Judah, before heaven and earth, through whom all things were made, both spiritual and bodily.

For if all things were made through him, then Mary herself, from whom he was born, was made through him. How, then, could he be born like other human beings, when he himself made the mother from whom he was to be born?

Therefore he is the Lord. The Apostle, speaking about the Jews, says:

“Their are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

Therefore, because the Jews saw Christ and crucified him, they did not see God. But because the Gentiles did not see him and believed, they understood God.

Therefore, if God became known to them in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19), and if they crucified him because they did not understand God hidden in the flesh, let that which is called Judea, but is not Judea, withdraw, and let true Judea approach—the Judea to which it is said:

“Approach him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. 33:6).

The faces of true Judea will not be put to shame. For they heard and believed, and the true Judea became the Church, where Christ is known—the man from the seed of David, God above David.

## 2

“God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel.”

We must understand “Israel” in the same way as “Judea.” Just as those others are not true Jews, so neither are they true Israel.

For who is called Israel? “One who sees God.” And how did those among whom he walked in the flesh see God, when they thought him a human being and killed him?

After rising, he appeared as God to all to whom he wished to reveal himself. Those, therefore, deserve to be called Israel who were worthy to understand Christ as God placed in the flesh, so that they would not despise what they saw but worship what they did not see.

The Gentiles, with humble minds, received him whom they did not see with their eyes, and held him by faith. Therefore those who held him with their hands killed him; those who held him by faith worshipped him.

“His name is great in Israel.”

Do you wish to be Israel? Look to the one of whom the Lord says:

“Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

If the true Israelite is one in whom there is no deceit, then the deceitful and liars are not true Israelites.

Therefore let these people not say that God is among them and that his name is great in Israel. Let them prove themselves Israelites, and I will grant that his name is great in Israel.

## 3. [verse 3]

“And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.”

Again, Zion is regarded as the homeland of the Jews. True Zion is the Church of Christians.

The interpretation of the Hebrew names has been handed down to us in this way: Judea is interpreted as “Confession”; Israel as “Seeing God.”

After Judea comes Israel. Thus it is placed here:

“God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel.”

Do you wish to see God? First confess, and thus God’s place is made in you, because “his place was made in peace.”

As long, therefore, as you do not confess your sins, you are in a certain sense quarreling with God. For how are you not fighting with him when you praise what displeases him?

He punishes the thief, and you praise theft. He punishes the drunkard, and you praise drunkenness. You are fighting with God; you have not made a place for him in your heart, because “his place is in peace.”

And how do you begin to have peace with God? You begin with confession before him.

The voice of the psalm says:

“Begin for the Lord with confession” (Ps. 146:7).

What does “Begin for the Lord with confession” mean? Begin to be joined to God.

How? So that what displeases him may also displease you. Your evil life displeases him. If it pleases you, you are separated from him; if it displeases you, through confession you are joined to him.

See how unlike him you are in so great a part, since you displease him precisely because of that unlikeness. You were made, O human being, in the image of God; but through a perverse and evil life you have disturbed and destroyed within yourself the image of your Creator.

Having been made unlike him, you look upon yourself and displease yourself. You have already begun to become like him, because what displeases you also displeases God.

## 4

“But how am I like him,” you ask, “when I still displease myself?”

For this reason it was said, “Begin.” Begin for the Lord with confession; you will be perfected in peace.

For you still have a war against yourself. War is declared against you—not only against the suggestions of the devil, against the ruler of the power of the air, who works in the children of disobedience, against the devil and his angels, against the spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph. 6:12)—not only against them is war declared against you, but against yourself.

How against yourself? Against your evil habit, against the oldness of your evil life, which draws you toward what is customary and restrains you from what is new. [Lov. reads “draws you toward what is customary and is restrained by what is new”; the manuscripts read “draws you toward customary things and restrains you from what is new.”]

A certain new life is being announced to you, while you are old. You are suspended by the joy of novelty, but weighed down by the burden of oldness; a war against yourself begins for you.

But in that part of yourself in which you displease yourself, you are joined to God; and in that part in which you are already joined to God, you will be capable of conquering yourself, because the one who conquers all things is with you.

Pay attention to what the Apostle says:

“With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

Why with the mind? Because your evil life displeases you. Why with the flesh? Because evil suggestions and pleasures are not lacking. But because in your mind you are joined to God, you conquer what does not wish to follow in you.

You have advanced in one part and are delayed in another. Draw yourself toward the one who lifts you upward. You are weighed down by a certain burden of oldness; cry out and say:

[Col. 0960]

“Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? Who will free me from that by which I am weighed down? For the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

Who, then, will free you?

“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:25, 24).

But why does he allow you to quarrel against yourself for so long, until all evil desires are swallowed up? So that you may understand your punishment within yourself. Your scourge is in you and from yourself; let your quarrel be with yourself.

Thus the rebel against God is punished: the one who refused to have peace with God becomes his own war.

But hold your members back from your evil desires. Anger has risen; you hold back your hand, joined to God. It was able to rise, but it found no weapons.

There is force in your anger; the weapons are with you. Let the force be unarmed, and the one who rose up in vain will learn not to rise again.

### 5. [Verse 3]

But I say this, dearly beloved, lest, because we have said, “But with the flesh I serve the law of sin,” you should think that you ought to consent to your fleshly desires. Although for now they can be nothing other than fleshly desires, one must not consent to them. For this reason the Apostle did not say, “Let sin not be in your mortal body.” He knows that, as long as it is mortal, sin is there. Rather, what does he say? “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body.” What does “not reign” mean? He explained it himself: “so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). There are desires; they arise. You do not obey your desires, you do not follow those desires themselves, you do not consent to them. Sin is present in you, but it has lost its kingdom, since sin no longer reigns in you. Afterward, “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

For what is promised to us, since it is said, “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25)? Hear the promise: the unlawful desires will not always remain in the flesh. For it will rise again and be changed; and when this mortal flesh has been changed into a spiritual body, it will no longer tantalize the soul with any worldly desires or earthly pleasures, nor turn it away from the contemplation of God.

Thus what the Apostle says will take place in it: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, through his Spirit who dwells in you” (ibid. 8:10–11).

When, therefore, our bodies have been given life, there will be true peace, where God has his dwelling. But confession must come first. “God is known in Judah”: therefore confess first. “His name is great in Israel.” You do not yet see him in appearance; see him by faith, and what follows will come to pass in you: “And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” [Col. 0961].

Zion is interpreted as “Contemplation.” What is contemplation? [Note: [Col. 0961] Thus the editions. But the manuscripts read: “What contemplation is”; these words seem to have slipped in from the margin. Unless perhaps it should be read, as in the Pratellensis and Gemmeticensis codices: “we said yesterday already, and certain brothers heard what contemplation is—brothers whom we see present today also.”] “For we shall contemplate God face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). He is promised to us, in whom we now believe without seeing him. How shall we rejoice when we see him? Brothers, if the promise alone already produces such joy in us, how great will be the joy produced by its fulfillment? What he promised will indeed be given to us. And what did he promise? Himself, so that we may rejoice in his face and in the contemplation of him. Nothing else will delight us, because nothing is better than the one who made all the things that delight us.

“His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion”—that is, in a certain contemplation and vision, his dwelling was made in Zion.

### 6. [Verse 4]

“There he broke the strength of bows, and the shield, and the sword, and the battle.” Where did he break them? In that eternal peace, in that perfect peace.

And now, my brothers, those who have believed rightly see that they must not presume upon themselves. They break every power of their threats and whatever in them is sharp for doing harm [Note: [Col. 0961] The editions read this way; most manuscripts have *actum est* (“has been done”). Some have *aptum est* (“is suited”).]. They also break whatever they temporarily regard as a great means of protection [Note: [Col. 0961] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *protegant* (“may protect”). Ambrosianus and most manuscripts have *protegerent* (“would protect”). Others have *protegent* (“will protect”).], and the battle they waged against God while defending their sins. There he broke all these things.

### 7. [Verse 5]

“You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” What are the everlasting mountains? Those whom he himself made everlasting; those great mountains who are the preachers of truth.

You enlighten, but from the everlasting mountains. The first great mountains receive your light, and from the light which the mountains receive, the earth too is clothed. But those great mountains were the Apostles; the Apostles received the beginnings of the rising light.

Did they keep what they received for themselves? No; otherwise it would have been said to them: “Wicked and lazy servant, you ought to have put my money with the bankers” (Matt. 25:26–27). If, therefore, they did not keep for themselves what they received, but preached it throughout the whole world, then: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” Those whom you made everlasting—you promised eternal life to the others through them: “You enlighten wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.”

The word “you” is stated with great emphasis, so that no one may think that people are enlightened by the mountains themselves. For many, thinking that they were enlightened by those mountains, made parties for themselves out of the mountains; they cut down those very mountains [Note: [Col. 0961] The manuscripts, with great agreement, read: “and those mountains themselves were cut down.”]. Some made Donatus for themselves, some made Maximianus for themselves, some made this man or that man for themselves. Why do they reckon that their salvation lies in human beings and not in God?

O man, the light comes to you through the mountains; but God enlightens you, not the mountains. “You enlighten,” he says: you, not the mountains. You enlighten—from the everlasting mountains, indeed—but you enlighten.

And elsewhere what does the psalm say? “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me.” What then? Is your hope in the mountains, and will help come to you from there? Have you remained in the mountains? See what you are doing. There is something above the mountains; above the mountains is the one whom the mountains fear.

“I lifted up my eyes,” he says, “to the mountains, from where help will come to me.” But what follows? “My help,” he says, “is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:1–2). I lifted my eyes to the mountains because the Scriptures were shown to me through the mountains; but my heart is in the one who enlightens all the mountains.

### 8.

Therefore, brothers, this was said so that none of you may wish to place his hope in a human being. A human being is something only as long as he clings to the one by whom he was made human. But when he withdraws from him, a human being is nothing; and when he clings to them [Note: [Col. 0962] The editions read “when he clings to him.” The manuscripts have “to them,” with “the mountains” understood.].

Receive counsel through a human being in such a way that you consider the one who enlightens the human being. For you too can approach the one who speaks to you through a human being. He did not make that person approach him while driving you away.

And whoever has truly approached God so that God dwells in him is displeased with all who do not place their hope in God. For this reason an example was given when they divided the Apostles among themselves and entered into schisms, saying: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas”—that is, Peter. The Apostle mourns over them and says: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13).

See the good mountain seeking glory, not for itself, but from the one by whom the mountains are enlightened. He did not want people to presume upon him, but upon the one upon whom he himself had presumed. Therefore, whoever wishes to commend himself to the peoples in such a way that, if some disturbance should occur, he breaks the people behind him and divides the Catholic Church on his own account, does not belong to those mountains whom the Most High enlightens.

But who is this person? One darkened by himself, not enlightened by the Lord.

How are such mountains tested? If some disturbance should arise against the mountains in the Church, whether through popular uprisings of carnal people or through some false suspicions of human beings, a good mountain repels from itself all who wish to withdraw from unity on its account. For it will remain in unity only if that unity itself is not divided because of it.

But those men were divided: when the people withdrew from the whole world and followed their name, they rejoiced [Note: [Col. 0962] Four manuscripts read: “but they rejoiced.”]. They were lifted up, and they were cast down. They would have been humbled and exalted in the manner of the Apostle, who said: “Was Paul crucified for you?” And elsewhere: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid. 3:6–7).

Such mountains are humble in themselves and exalted in God. But those who are exalted in themselves are humbled by God: “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Therefore such men, who attend to their own pride, embitter the peaceful people in the Church [Col. 0963]. The peaceful wish to consolidate peace; these men mix dissension among themselves. And what does another psalm say about them? “Those who embitter, let them not be exalted in themselves” (Ps. 65:7).

“You enlighten”—pay attention here—“you wonderfully enlighten from the everlasting mountains.”

### 9. [Verse 6]

“All the foolish in heart were troubled.” The truth was preached; eternal life was proclaimed; another life, one that does not belong to this earth, was declared. Human beings despised the present life and loved the future life, enlightened through enlightened mountains.

But the foolish in heart were troubled. How were they troubled? When the Gospel is preached. And what is eternal life? And who is the one who rose from the dead? When the Apostle Paul spoke about the resurrection of the dead, the Athenians were astonished and thought that he was telling some kind of fable (Acts 17:18, 32).

But because he said that there is another life, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9), the foolish in heart were troubled.

But what happened to them? “They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands.” They loved present things and slept in those very present things; and so those present things became delightful to them, just as a person who dreams that he has found treasures is rich only so long as he does not wake up. The dream made him rich; waking makes him poor.

Perhaps sleep held him while he was lying on the ground, on something hard, poor and perhaps a beggar. In his dream he saw himself lying on an ivory or golden bed, on pillows built up higher [Note: [Col. 0963] The editions read “and on golden pillows.” The manuscripts do not add “golden.”].
