As long as he sleeps, he sleeps well; when he wakes, he finds himself on the hard surface where sleep had held him.

Such are these people. They came into this life and, through temporal desires, as though fell asleep here. Riches and fleeting empty displays received them and passed away; they did not understand how much good could have been done with them. For if they had known of another life, they would have stored up there what here was destined to perish.

Thus Zacchaeus, a chief of tax collectors, saw that good when he received the Lord Jesus as a guest. He said: “I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” He was not among those who dream in vanity, but among those who keep watch in faith [Note: [Col. 0963] The editions read *evigilantium* (“those who keep awake”). The manuscripts have *vigilantium* (“those who keep watch”).].

Therefore the Lord, because the physician had entered the sick man, pronounced his salvation and said: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:8–9). This was so that you might know that by imitating faith we are sons of Abraham, while the Jews who take pride in the flesh have fallen away from faith.

Therefore the men of wealth slept their sleep, and found nothing in their hands. They slept in their desires; these things delight them. This sleep passes; this life passes; and they find nothing in their hands, because they placed nothing in the hand of Christ.

Do you wish to find something in your hands afterward? Do not now despise the hand of the poor person; and look upon empty hands if you wish to have full hands.

For the Lord said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me,” and so forth. And they said to him: “When did we see you hungry, thirsty, or a stranger?” And he said to them: “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:35–40).

He who is rich in heaven wished to hunger in the poor, and you hesitate, human being, to give to a human being, when you know that what you give you give to Christ, from whom you received whatever you give!

But they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands.

### 10. [Verse 7]

“At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, all who mounted horses fell into slumber.” Who are those who mounted horses? Those who did not wish to be humble.

It is not a sin to sit on horses; rather, the sin is to raise the neck of one’s power against God and think oneself to possess some position of honor. Because you are rich, you mounted up; God rebukes you, and you sleep.

Great is the anger of the one who rebukes—great indeed! Let Your Charity attend to this fearful matter. A rebuke has a sound; sound usually causes people to wake up. Yet such is the weight of God’s rebuke that he said: “At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, all who mounted horses fell into slumber.”

See with what sleep that Pharaoh who mounted horses slept (Exod. 14:8). He was not awake in his heart, because his heart was hardened by the rebuke. Hardness of heart is a falling asleep.

I ask you, my brothers: see how those people sleep when, although the Gospel, “Amen,” and “Alleluia” resound throughout the whole world, they still refuse to condemn their old life and wake up to a new one.

The Scripture of God was in Judea; now it is sung throughout the whole world. In that one nation it was said that there is one God, who made all things, and that he must be worshiped and honored. Now, where is it silent: “Christ has risen” [Note: [Col. 0964] The reliable manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “there it is silent: Christ has risen. Christ has risen.”]? He was mocked on the cross, and now he has fixed the very cross on which he was mocked upon the foreheads of kings—and still people sleep!

Great is God’s anger, brothers! We have heard him better who says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). But who hears him? Those who do not mount horses.

Who are those who do not mount horses? Those who do not boast and exalt themselves as though in their honors and powers.

“At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell into slumber.”

### 11. [Verse 8]

“You are terrible, and who will resist you then, from your anger?” Now they sleep and do not feel that he is angry; but he was angry so that they would sleep. What they do not feel now, while sleeping, they will feel at the end.

For the judge of the living and the dead will appear. “And who will resist you then, from your anger?” Now they say whatever they wish, argue against God, and say: “Who are these Christians? Or who is Christ? Or how foolish are those who believe what they do not see, abandon the pleasures they do see, and follow faith in things that are not displayed to their eyes?”

You sleep and bray; speak against God as much as you can. “How long, sinners, O Lord, how long will sinners boast?” “They answer and speak iniquity” (Ps. 93:3, 4).

When does no one answer and no one speak, except when they turn back upon themselves? When will the teeth with which they now gnaw us and tear us apart by mocking Christians and criticizing the life of the saints turn back upon themselves?

They will turn back upon themselves when what is said in the Book of Wisdom happens to them: “They will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit,” when they see the glory of the saints. Then they will say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision.”

O you who slept so deeply! Surely you are awake now, and you find nothing in your hands. You see how full are the hands of the glory of God belonging to those whom you mocked as though they were poor.

Then say to yourselves, when you cannot resist the anger of God—not with hand, tongue, word, or thought—for the one whom you thought should be mocked will appear openly to you, when his coming to you had been announced.

And what will they say? “Therefore we wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us.” How could the sun of righteousness rise for those who were sleeping? But they sleep because of his anger and rebuke.

Perhaps someone will say, “I would not have mounted the horse.” Then they themselves will accuse their horses. Hear them accusing the horses on which they slept: “Therefore,” says Scripture, “we wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us. What did pride profit us? And what did the boasting of riches bring us? All things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:3, 6, 8–9).

Therefore, at some time you did keep watch. But it would have been better not to mount the horse, so that you would not then have fallen asleep, when you ought to have kept watch, and so that you would have heard the voice of Christ and Christ would have enlightened you.

“You are terrible, and who will resist you there then, from your anger?” For what will happen then?

### 12. [Verse 9]

“From heaven you shot judgment; the earth trembled and was still.” The earth that now agitates itself, that now speaks, will have cause at the end to fear and be still. It would be better for it to be still now, so that at the end it might rejoice.

### 13. [Verse 10]

“The earth trembled and was still.” When? “When God arose for judgment, to save all the meek of heart.”

Who are the meek of heart? Those who did not mount the neighing horses, but confessed their sins in humility.

“To save all the meek of heart.”

### 14. [Verse 11]

“For the thought of man will confess to you, and the remnants of thought will celebrate solemn rites for you.”

The first is “thought”; what comes afterward is “the remnants of thought.” What is the first thought? Where do we begin? It is that good thought from which you will begin to confess.

Confession joins us to Christ. Now confession itself—that is, the first thought—produces in us remnants of thought; and those remnants of thought will celebrate solemn rites for you.

“The thought of man will confess to you, and the remnants of thought will celebrate solemn rites for you.” What is the thought that will confess? The thought that condemns the former life, that is displeased with what it was so that it may become what it was not: that is the first thought.

But because you must withdraw from sins in such a way that, having confessed to God with the first thought, you do not let it depart from your memory that you were a sinner, through the fact that you were a sinner you celebrate solemn rites for God.

This must still be understood. The first thought contains confession and withdrawal from the old life. But if you have forgotten from what sins you were freed, you do not give thanks to the one who freed you, and you do not celebrate solemn rites for your God.

Consider the first thought of confession in the Apostle Saul, who afterward became Paul. When he heard the voice from heaven while persecuting Christ, raging against Christians, and wishing to bring them to execution wherever they were found, he heard the voice from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” And, surrounded by light and struck with blindness in his eyes so that he might see inwardly, he uttered the first thought of obedience. When he heard, “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting,” he said, “Lord, what do you command me to do?” (Acts 9:4–5).

This is the thought of one confessing: he already calls “Lord” the one whom he had been persecuting [Note: [Col. 0966] Some manuscripts read this way. The editions have: “And this is the thought of the one confessing.”].

You have heard how the remnants of thought celebrate solemn rites in Paul, when the Apostle himself was being read: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my gospel” (2 Tim. 2:8).

What does “remember” mean? Let the thought by which you first confessed not be erased from your memory; let the remnants of thought remain in your memory.

And observe how that same Apostle Paul repeats elsewhere what was forgiven him: “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Tim. 1:13). When he says, “I was formerly a blasphemer,” is he still a blasphemer? In order that he might not be a blasphemer, there was first the thought of one confessing. But in order that he might recall what had been forgiven him, there were the remnants of thought; through those remnants of thought he celebrated solemn rites.

### 15.

Indeed, my brothers, Christ has renewed us; he has forgiven all sins, and we have been converted. If we forget what has been forgiven us and by whom it was forgiven, we forget the gift of the Savior. But when we do not forget the gift of the Savior, is Christ not sacrificed for us daily?

Christ was sacrificed for us once, when we believed [Note: [Col. 0966] The editions read “for us”; “for” is absent from the manuscripts.]; that was the thought. But now there are remnants of thought, when we remember who came to us and what he gave us. From those remnants of thought—that is, from that very memory—he is sacrificed for us daily, as though he renewed us daily, the one who renewed us by his first grace.

For the Lord has already renewed us in Baptism, and we have become new people, rejoicing in hope so that we may be patient in tribulation (Rom. 12:12). Nevertheless, what has been bestowed upon us must not depart from our memory.

And if your thought now is not what it was—for the first thought was to withdraw from sin, whereas now you do not withdraw but withdrew then—let there be remnants of thought, so that the one who healed you may not fall from your memory.

If you forget that you had a wound, there will be no remnants of thought in you. What do you think David said? He speaks on behalf of everyone. The holy David sinned grievously. The prophet Nathan was sent to him and rebuked him. He confessed and said, “I have sinned” (2 Sam. 12:13). This was the first thought of one confessing: “The thought of man will confess to you.”

What were the remnants of thought? When he said: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). What, then, was the first thought? That he should withdraw from sin. And if he has already withdrawn from sin, how is his sin always before him, unless because that thought has passed but the remnants of thought celebrate solemn rites [Col. 0967]?

Let us therefore remember, dearly beloved brothers—we beg you: whoever has been freed from sin, let him remember what he was; let the remnants of thought be in him. For he carries another person who must be healed only if he remembers that he himself was healed.

Therefore let each person remember what he was, and whether he is no longer that. Then he will help the person who still is what he is no longer.

But if he boasts as though on the basis of his own merits, repels sinners as though they were unworthy, and rages without mercy, he has mounted the horse. Let him see to it that he does not sleep, for those who mounted horses fell into slumber.

He has already dismissed the horse and humbled himself; let him not mount it again—that is, let him not lift himself up again in pride.

How does this happen to him? If the remnants of thought celebrate solemn rites for God.

### 16. [Verse 12]

“Vow, and repay the Lord your God.” Let each person vow whatever he can, and repay it. Do not vow and fail to repay; rather, let each person vow whatever he can, and repay it.

Do not be slow to vow. You will not fulfill your vows by your own strength. You will fail if you presume upon yourselves. But if you vow with confidence in the one to whom you make your vow, you will repay it securely.

“Vow, and repay the Lord your God.”

What must we all vow together? To believe in him, to hope for eternal life from him, and to live well according to the common rule. There is indeed a common rule for everyone: not to steal is not prescribed only to a consecrated woman, nor only to a married woman; not to commit adultery is prescribed to everyone; not to love drunkenness, by which the soul is swallowed up and corrupts the temple of God within itself, is prescribed equally to everyone; likewise not to be proud, not to kill a human being, not to hate one’s brother, and not to hold destructive enmity against anyone. All this is prescribed equally to everyone.

All of us must vow these things.

There are also particular vows belonging to individuals. One person vows conjugal chastity to God, so that he will know no woman other than his wife; likewise a woman vows that she will know no man other than her husband.

Others, although they have experienced such a marriage, vow never again to undergo anything of that kind, never to desire or endure anything of that kind; they too have vowed something greater than the former.

Others vow virginity itself from an early age, so that they may not experience anything like what those others experienced and left behind; these have made a very great vow.

Others vow that their house will be hospitable to all holy travelers who arrive; they make a great vow.

Another vows to leave all his possessions to be distributed among the poor and to enter the common life, in the fellowship of the saints; he makes a great vow.

“Vow, and repay the Lord your God.” Let each person vow whatever he wishes to vow; let him take care that he repay what he has vowed.

Whatever a person vows to God, if he looks back, is evil.

Some consecrated woman wished to marry. What did she wish? What any virgin might wish. What did she wish? What her own mother had wished. Did she wish for something evil? Clearly, she wished for something evil. Why? Because she had already vowed to the Lord her God.

For what did the Apostle Paul say about such women? Although he says that young widows should marry if they wish (1 Tim. 5:14), he nevertheless says in another place: “But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice” (1 Cor. 7:40). He shows that she will be happier if she remains as she is, but he does not condemn her if she wishes to marry.

But what does he say about certain women who made vows and did not fulfill them? “They have condemnation,” he says, “because they have rejected their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:12). What does “they have rejected their first faith” mean? They vowed and did not repay.

Therefore, let no brother living in a monastery say: “I am leaving the monastery. Surely those who are in the monastery alone will reach the kingdom of heaven, and those who are not there do not belong to God.”

The answer is made to him: “But they did not vow; you vowed, and you looked back.”

When the Lord threatened the day of judgment, what did he say? “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32). He said this to everyone.

For what did Lot’s wife do? She was delivered from Sodom, and while on the way she looked back. Where she looked back, there she remained. She became a pillar of salt (Gen. 19:26), so that by her example people might be seasoned: let them have a heart, let them not be foolish, let them not look back, lest, by giving a bad example, they remain behind while seasoning others.

Even now we say this to certain brothers of ours whom we happen to see weakening in their good purpose: “Do you wish to be like that man?” We set before them certain people who looked back. Those people are foolish in themselves, but they season others when they are recalled, so that those who fear their example may not look back.

“Vow, and repay the Lord your God,” because Lot’s wife concerns everyone.

A married woman wished to commit adultery; she looked back from the place to which she had attained.

A widow who had vowed to remain as she was wished to marry; she wished for what was permitted to the woman who married. But it was not permitted to her, because she looked back from the place to which she had attained.

There is a chaste virgin, already dedicated to God. She possesses the other qualities that truly adorn virginity, without which virginity itself is shameful. For what if she is physically untouched but corrupt in mind?

What do I mean? What if no one has touched her body, but she is perhaps a drunkard, proud, quarrelsome, or foul-tongued? God condemns all these things.

If she had married before making her vow, she would not be condemned. She chose something better and surpassed what was permitted to her; yet she is proud and commits so many unlawful acts.

This is what I say: it is permitted to marry before making a vow; it is never permitted to be proud.

O virgin of God, you did not wish to marry, although it is permitted; you exalt yourself, although that is not permitted.

A humble virgin is better than a humble married woman; but a humble married woman is better than a proud virgin.

The woman who looked back toward marriage is not condemned because she wished to marry, but because she had already gone forward [Note: [Col. 0968] The manuscripts read this way. The editions have *ante recesserat* (“had previously withdrawn”).], and by looking back she became Lot’s wife.

Do not be slow—you who can, and to whom God gives assistance—to grasp the better steps. We do not say these things so that you will not vow, but so that you will vow and repay: “Vow, and repay the Lord your God.”

Now that we have discussed these matters, perhaps you intended to vow, but now you do not wish to vow. Pay attention to what the psalm says to you. It did not say, “Do not vow,” but “Vow, and repay.”

Because you have heard “repay,” do you not wish to vow? Then you wished to vow but not to repay? Rather, do both. One part will arise from your profession; the other will be accomplished through the help of God.

Look upon the one who leads you, and do not look back to the place from which he leads you out. The one who leads you walks before you; the place from which he leads you out is behind you. Love the one who leads you, and he does not condemn you for looking back.

“Vow, and repay the Lord your God.”

### 17.

“All who are around him will offer gifts.” Who are those who are around him? Where is he, that he should say, “All who are around him”?

If you think of God the Father, where is he not, since he is present everywhere? If you think of the Son according to the form of divinity, he too is everywhere with the Father, because he is the Wisdom of God, of which it is said: “But because of her purity she reaches everywhere” (Wis. 7:24).

But if you understand the Son according to what he assumed of flesh, and according to the fact that he was seen among human beings, was crucified, and rose again, we know that he ascended into heaven. Who are those around him? The angels.

Therefore, do we not offer gifts, since he said, “All who are around him will offer gifts”?

If our Lord were buried here on earth and his body lay here, as the body of some martyr or apostle does, we would look to those who were around it—whether peoples gathered from every direction around that place or those coming to the burial with gifts.

But now he has ascended; he is above. What does “All who are around him will offer gifts” mean?

For now I shall tell you what God has deigned to inspire in me through these words. If something better should later appear, that too belongs to you, because truth is common to everyone. It is neither mine nor yours; it belongs neither to this person nor that. It is common to all.

Perhaps for this reason it is in the middle, so that all who love the truth may be around him. For whatever is common to everyone is in the middle.

Why is it said to be in the middle? So that it may be equally distant from everyone and equally near to everyone. What is not in the middle becomes something private. What is public is placed in the middle so that all who come may receive it and be enlightened.

Let no one say, “It is mine,” lest he wish to make what is in the middle and common to all belong to his own faction.

What, then, does “All who are around him will offer gifts” mean? All who understand that truth is common to everyone, and who do not make it their own by taking pride in it—these will offer gifts, because they possess humility.

But those who make their own what is common to everyone, placed as it is in the middle, and try to draw it away into a faction, will not offer gifts. For “all who are around him will offer gifts to the Terrible One.”

Gifts will be offered to the Terrible One. Therefore let all who are around him fear. They will fear and praise with trembling because they are around him so that all may attain to him, and so that he may flow publicly to everyone and enlighten everyone publicly. This is what it means to tremble.

When you make him, as it were, your own rather than common to all, you are lifted up in pride, although it is written: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11).

Therefore those who are around him will offer gifts. They are humble, because they know that truth is common to everyone.

### 18. [Verse 13]

“To whom will they offer gifts?” To the Terrible One, “and to him who takes away the spirit [Note: [Col. 0969] Several manuscripts have *spiritus* (“spirits”) in this passage alone; this is also the reading in the Septuagint.] of princes.”

For the spirits of princes are proud spirits. Therefore they are not his spirits. Even if they know something, they want it to be their own, not public.

But the one who commends himself as equal to everyone, who places himself in the middle so that all may grasp as much as they can, whatever they can—not something belonging to any human being, but something belonging to God, and therefore his own, because they themselves have been made his—this one is different.

Therefore all such people must be humble. They have lost their own spirit and possess the Spirit of God.

From whom did they lose their own spirit? From the one who takes away the spirit of princes, since it is said to him elsewhere: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:29–30).

Someone has understood something; he wants it to be his own, and he still possesses his own spirit. It is good for him to lose his own spirit and possess the Spirit of God.

He still exalts himself among princes. It is good for him to return to his own dust and say: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102:14).

For if you confess yourself to be dust, God makes a human being from dust [Note: [Col. 0970] Three manuscripts read: “God makes you a human being from dust,” and so forth.].

“All who are around him offer gifts”: all the humble confess to him and worship him. They offer gifts to the Terrible One.

Why to the Terrible One? “Rejoice with trembling” (Ps. 2:11), and to the one who takes away the spirit of princes—that is, who removes the boldness of the proud.

“To the Terrible One among the kings of the earth.” The kings of the earth are terrible, but he is above them all, the one who terrifies the kings of the earth.

Be a king of the earth, and God will be terrible to you. “How,” you ask, “shall I be a king of the earth?” Rule the earth, and you will be a king of the earth.

Do not therefore place before your eyes, out of a desire to rule, vast provinces over which you may spread your kingdoms. Rule the earth that you carry.

Hear the Apostle ruling the earth: “I do not box as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:26–27).

Therefore, my brothers, be around him, so that whenever truth sounds forth for you through anyone, you do not attribute it to the person through whom it sounds. Let it be in the middle and common to all, because it is equally present to all.

And be humble, lest you yourselves claim for yourselves whatever good you may happen to understand of him. For what we understand better is yours, and what you understand better is ours, so that we may be around him and be humble.

And thus, losing our own spirit, we shall offer gifts to the Terrible One above all the kings of the earth—that is, above all who rule their flesh but are subject to their Creator.

## Exposition of Psalm 76. Sermon to the People.

1. [verse 1] The superscription of this psalm reads: “For the end, for Idithun, a psalm of Asaph.” You know what “for the end” means: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Idithun is interpreted as “transcending them”; Asaph is interpreted as “assembly.” Here, then, an assembly that transcends speaks, so that it may reach the end, which is Christ Jesus. What must be transcended in order that we may reach that end, where we shall no longer have anything to transcend [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read “we shall have”; Erasmus and Lovaniensis, “we have.”], the text of the psalm itself shows. For we must continue transcending whatever hinders us, whatever ensnares us, whatever binds us with some sort of glue and burdens our flight, until we reach that which is sufficient, beyond which there is nothing, beneath which are all things, and from which all things come.

Philip wanted to behold the Father himself, and he said to the Lord Jesus Christ, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”—as though he had to transcend whatever else existed until he reached the Father, where he could stand secure and have nothing further to seek; for this is what “It is enough” means. But he who had most truly said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), admonished Philip and taught every person who understood Christ that he too has his end in Christ, because he and the Father are one: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (ibid. 14:8–9).

Whoever, therefore, wishes to perceive, imitate, and retain the spirit of this psalm [Note: The manuscripts read “soul.”] should transcend all carnal desires, trample underfoot the pomp and allurements of this age, and set before himself no other place at which to stop than the one from whom all things come—while in all these matters he too labors until he reaches the end. What, then, does this one who transcends indicate to us?

2. “With my voice,” he says, “I cried to the Lord” [Note: Several manuscripts read “to God.”] But many cry to the Lord in order to acquire wealth and avoid losses, for the safety of their loved ones, for the stability of their household, for temporal happiness, for worldly rank, and finally even for the health of the body, which is the poor man’s patrimony. For these and similar things many cry to the Lord; scarcely anyone cries out on account of the Lord himself. It is easy enough for a person to desire anything whatsoever from the Lord without desiring the Lord himself—as though what he gives could be sweeter than the one who gives it.

Whoever, then, cries to the Lord for some other thing has not yet transcended. But what does this one who transcends say? “With my voice I cried to the Lord.” And lest you think that the voice with which he cried to the Lord was uttered for anything other than the Lord himself, he continues: “And my voice was to God.” A voice is uttered with which we cry to God, yet that very voice may be directed to something else and not to God. For a voice is directed to the purpose for which it is uttered. But this man, who loved God freely, who willingly sacrificed to God (Ps. 53:8), who had transcended everything below and had seen nothing above himself into which he might pour out his soul except the one from whom, through whom, and in whom he had been created, had directed his very voice to the one to whom he had cried: “My voice,” he says, “was to God.”

And was this without reason? See what follows: “And he attended to me.” He truly attends to you when you seek him himself, not when through him you seek something else. It was said of certain people: “They cried out, but there was no one who saved them, to the Lord, and he did not hear them” (Ps. 17:42). Why? Because their voice was not directed to the Lord. Scripture expresses this elsewhere, where it says of such people: “They did not call upon the Lord.” They did not cease crying out to him, and yet they did not call upon the Lord. What does “They did not call upon the Lord” mean? They did not call the Lord into themselves; they did not invite the Lord into their heart; they did not wish to be inhabited by the Lord.

And what happened to them? “There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). Therefore they trembled at the loss of present things, because they were not filled with the one whom they had not called upon. They did not love freely, so that, when temporal possessions were lost, they could say: “As it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Thus this man says, “My voice was to the Lord, and he attended to me.” Let him teach us how this happens.

3. [verse 3] “On the day of my tribulation I sought God.” Who are you, who do this? On the day of your tribulation, consider what you seek. If imprisonment causes the tribulation, you seek release from prison; if fever causes the tribulation, you seek health; if hunger causes the tribulation, you seek fullness; if losses cause the tribulation, you seek profit; if exile causes the tribulation, you seek the city of your flesh. And why should I enumerate everything, or when could I enumerate everything?

Do you wish to be one who transcends? On the day of your tribulation, seek God—not something else through God, but God himself out of the tribulation, so that God may remove the tribulation for this purpose: that you may cling securely to God. “On the day of my tribulation I sought God”: I sought not something else, but God. And how did you seek him? “With my hands, by night, before him.”

Say this again: let us see, understand, and imitate it, if we can. On the day of your tribulation, what did you seek? God. How did you seek him? With my hands. When did you seek him? By night. Where did you seek him? Before him. And with what result did you seek him? “And I was not deceived.” Let us therefore examine everything, brothers; let us consider everything and question everything: what is the tribulation in which this man sought God, what does it mean to seek God with the hands, what does “by night” mean, and what does “before him” mean? Then follows what everyone understands: “And I was not deceived.” For what does “I was not deceived” mean? I found what I was seeking.

4. Tribulation should not be understood as this or that particular thing. Indeed, every person who has not yet transcended does not think that anything is tribulation except what has happened in this life at some grievous moment. But the one who transcends counts this whole life as his tribulation. He loves his heavenly homeland so much that this earthly exile itself is his greatest tribulation.

For how could this life not be tribulation, I ask you? How could it not be tribulation when it has been called entirely a temptation? You have it written in the Book of Job: “Is not human life upon the earth a temptation?” (Job 7:1). Did he say, “Human life upon the earth is tempted”? No: life itself is a temptation. If it is a temptation, it is certainly tribulation.

In this tribulation, therefore—in this life—the one who transcends sought God. How? “With my hands,” he says. What does “with my hands” mean? With my deeds. He was not seeking something bodily that he might find by touching it, as though he were searching with his hands for a coin, gold, silver, clothing, or anything of that sort which can be held in the hands.

Yet our Lord Jesus Christ himself also wished to be sought with the hands when he showed his scars to the disciple who doubted. But when that man cried out as he touched the scars of his wounds, “My Lord and my God!”, did he not hear, “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:27–29)? If, then, the man who sought Christ with his hands deserved to hear this, so that having sought him in this way became a reproach to him, what of us, who are called blessed because we have not seen and yet believe? Does seeking with the hands not concern us?

It does, as I have said: it means seeking through deeds. When does this happen? “By night.” What does “by night” mean? In this age. For it is night before the day shines forth at the glorious coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Do you wish to see that it is night? Unless we had a lamp here, we would remain in darkness. For Peter says: “And we have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19). The day, then, will come after this night; meanwhile, in this night, let the lamp not be absent.

Perhaps this is what we are doing now: by explaining these Scriptures, we bring in a lamp, so that we may rejoice in this night. Indeed, it ought always to be lit in your homes. For people such as these are told: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19). And as though explaining what he meant, he adds: “Do not despise prophecies”—that is, let the lamp always shine within you.

This light [Note: The better manuscripts read “night.”] is called night in comparison with a certain ineffable day. For the life of the faithful itself is day in comparison with the life of unbelievers. How it is night, however, we have already stated and demonstrated by the testimony of the apostle Peter, who both mentioned the lamp and admonished us to pay attention to it—that is, to the prophetic word—until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.

But how the life of the faithful is already day in comparison with the life of the ungodly, Paul shows: “Let us cast off,” he says, “the works of darkness, and let us put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. 13:12). Thus, living honorably, we are in the day in comparison with the life of the ungodly.

But this day of the life of the faithful is not sufficient for this Idithun. He wishes to transcend even this day, until he comes to that day where he will no longer fear any temptation of the night. For although the life of the faithful is day, “human life upon the earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1).

Night and day: day in comparison with unbelievers, night in comparison with the angels. The angels possess a day that we do not yet possess. We already possess what unbelievers do not have; but the faithful do not yet possess what the angels have. They will possess it when they become equal to the angels of God, as was promised to them in the resurrection (Matt. 22:30).

In this present time, then, we are already in day and still in night: night in comparison with the future day that we desire, day in comparison with the former night that we have renounced. In this night, then, let us seek God with our hands. Let our deeds not cease; let us seek God, and let our desire not be empty. If we are on the way, let us spend what is needed so that we may arrive; let us seek God with our hands.

Even if we seek by night the one whom we seek with our hands, we are not deceived, because we seek “before him.” What does “before him” mean? “Do not practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven. Therefore, when you give alms”—those hands are seeking God—“do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do; but let your almsgiving be in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will repay you” (Matt. 6:1, 2, 4). Thus: “With my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived.”

5. Let us listen with the greatest attention to how much this Idithun endured on this earth and in this night, and how he had, so to speak, a necessity of transcending: tribulations struck and pricked him from below, so that he was compelled to transcend.

“My soul refused consolation” [Note: Thus the better manuscripts. The editors, however, read: “I refused to console my soul.”] So great a weariness seized me here that my soul closed itself against every consolation. What caused such weariness in him? Perhaps because hail had struck the vineyard, or because the olive crop had failed, or because rain had ruined the harvest. What caused his weariness? Hear this from another psalm. It is his voice there as well: “Weariness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law” (Ps. 118:53).

Thus this man says that he was affected by such weariness because of this evil that he refused to let his soul be consoled. Weariness had nearly swallowed him, and sorrow had completely overwhelmed him beyond recovery; he refused consolation. What, then, remained?

6. [verse 4] First consider from where he might receive consolation. Had he not waited for someone who would grieve together with him, and found none? (Ps. 68:21). Where could he turn for consolation when weariness over those who abandoned God’s law had seized him? Where could he turn? To some person of God? Perhaps by now this man had experienced great tribulation in many people, because he had presumed too much upon some pleasure found in them [Note: Most manuscripts read: “because he had presumed more upon some love for them.”]

For righteous people sometimes appear, and one rejoices in them; indeed, it is necessary to rejoice, because love cannot exist without joy. But if something perverse should happen to those in whom a person has rejoiced—as often happens—then, where there had been such great joy, how great a sorrow is added! A person afterward becomes afraid to loosen the reins of joy and afraid to entrust himself to happiness, lest, the more he had rejoiced, the more he should wither if something happens.

Struck, therefore, by abundant scandals, as though by many wounds, he closed himself against human consolation and refused to let his soul be consoled. From where, then, could life come? From where could relief come?

“I remembered God, and I rejoiced.” His hands had not labored in vain; they had found a great consoler. “I remembered God,” not while resting, “and I rejoiced.” God must therefore be proclaimed: this man remembered him, rejoiced, and was consoled in a certain sorrow, restored when salvation had in some sense been despaired of. God must be proclaimed.

Finally, after saying that he was consoled, he adds: “I chattered.” Having remembered God in that consolation, I rejoiced and chattered. What does “I chattered” mean? I rejoiced; I exulted in speaking. For those are properly called chatterers who are commonly called wordy, when joy has arisen and they are unable, or unwilling, to remain silent. This man became such a person.

And again what does he say? “And my spirit failed.”

7. [verse 5] He had withered from weariness, had rejoiced at remembering God, and had again failed through chattering. What follows? “All my enemies anticipated the watches.”

All my enemies kept watch over me; they watched more than I did; by keeping watch, they forestalled me. Where do they not set traps? “Have not all my enemies anticipated the watches?” [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. In the editions: “All my enemies have anticipated”; and in the Septuagint, *pantes* agrees in gender and case with *echthroi*, “enemies.”]

Who are these enemies except those of whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12)?

Thus we wage war against the devil and his angels. He called them “rulers of the world” because they rule the lovers of the world. For they do not rule the world as though they were rulers of heaven and earth; rather, he calls sinners “the world.” “And the world did not know him” (John 1:10): they rule such a world, which does not know Christ.

Against these we have perpetual enmity. Indeed, whatever enmity you may have against a human being, you consider ending it—whether by that person’s satisfaction, if he has injured you; by your own, if you have injured him; or by the satisfaction of either party, if you have injured one another. You labor to make satisfaction and restore peace. But with the devil and his angels there is no peace. They envy us the kingdom of heaven. They cannot become gentle toward us at all, because “all my enemies have anticipated the watches.”

They watched more carefully to deceive than I did to guard myself: “All my enemies have anticipated the watches.” For how could they not have anticipated the watches, when they have placed scandals everywhere and traps everywhere?

Weariness is in the heart; it must be feared lest sorrow swallow you. In joy it must be feared lest your spirit fail through chattering: “All my enemies have anticipated the watches.”

Finally, even in that very chattering, while you speak and speak securely, how often are things found that the enemies wish to seize upon and criticize, things from which they wish even to bring accusation and slander: “He said this; he meant that; he spoke in this way.” What can a person do except what follows?

“I was troubled, and I did not speak.” Troubled, then, lest the enemies who had anticipated the watches should seek and find grounds for slander in his chattering, he did not speak.

Yet this one who transcended would never cease working within himself. If he had perhaps ceased chattering—the chattering that had crept upon him because he took pleasure in pleasing people through his speech—he nevertheless did not stop; he did not cease trying to transcend this very thing. And what does he say?

8. [verse 6] “I considered the days of old.” Now, like someone who had been beaten outside, he withdrew within and conducted his business in the inner chamber of his mind. Let him tell us what he did there: “I considered the days of old.”

He is in a good place. Observe what he is considering, I ask you. He is within, considering the days of old in himself. No one says to him, “You spoke badly”; no one says, “You spoke too much”; no one says, “You thought perversely.” May he therefore be well with himself; may God help him. Let him consider the days of old, and let him tell us in that innermost chamber what he did, where he arrived, what he transcended, and where he remained:

“I considered the days of old, and I remembered the years of eternity.” What are the years of eternity? A great thought! See whether this thought does not require great silence. Whoever wishes to consider these eternal years must rest inwardly from every external noise and from all the turmoil of human affairs.

Are the years in which we live eternal, or those in which our ancestors lived, or those in which our descendants will live? Far be it from us to regard them as eternal. For what remains of these years? Behold, we say in speaking, “This year”; and what do we retain of this year except the one day in which we are? For the days of this year that have passed are already gone and cannot be held; those yet to come have not arrived.

We are in one day, and we say, “This year.” Rather, say, “Today,” if you wish to speak of something present. For what present thing do you hold from the whole year? Whatever of it is past is no longer; whatever of it is future is not yet. How, then, “This year”? Correct your speech: say, “Today.” You speak truly: “Today,” I will now say.

Again, consider that the morning hours of today have already passed, while the future hours have not yet arrived. Correct this as well: say, “At this hour.” And what do you hold of this hour? Some of its moments have already passed; those yet to come have not arrived. Say, “At this moment.”

Which moment? While I am speaking syllables, if I say two syllables, the second does not sound until the first has passed. Indeed, if a single syllable contains two letters, the second letter does not sound until the first has gone. What, then, do we retain of these years?

These years are changeable. We must consider the eternal years—the years that stand firm, which are not spent through days that come and go; the years of which Scripture says to God elsewhere: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

This one who transcended considered these years—not in external chattering, but in silence: “And I remembered the years of eternity.”

9. [verse 7] “And I meditated by night with my heart.” No slanderer is there seeking verbal traps [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “For he would not seek slanderous traps of words” (perhaps, “the slanderer would not seek…”).]; he meditated in his heart.

“I chattered.” There is that chattering again. Watch again, lest your spirit fail. “No,” he says; “I was not chattering in the same way as before, outwardly. Now it is different.” How different? “I chattered, and I examined my spirit.”

If this man were examining the earth in order to find veins of gold, no one would call him foolish; indeed, many would call him wise for wishing to reach gold. How much there is within a person, and yet he does not dig! This man was examining his spirit, speaking with his own spirit, and chattering in that very speech. He questioned himself; he examined himself; he was a judge within himself.

And it follows: “I examined my spirit.” It must be feared lest he remain within his spirit itself. He had chattered outwardly; and because all his enemies had anticipated their watches, he found sorrow there, and his spirit failed. The one who had chattered outwardly has now begun to chatter inwardly, securely, where he alone considers the eternal years in silence: “And I examined,” he says, “my spirit.”

Here too it must be feared lest he remain in his spirit and not be one who transcends. Yet he is already acting better than he acted outside. He has transcended something; let us see from here where he goes. For this one who transcends does not cease until he comes to the end for which the psalm bears its superscription: “I chattered,” he says, “and examined my spirit.”

10. [verse 8] And what did you find? “God will not reject forever.”

He had found weariness in this life, nowhere a trustworthy or secure consolation. Wherever he turned his attention among human beings, he found or feared scandal in them. Nowhere, therefore, was he secure. To remain silent was bad for him, lest he be silent about good things; to speak and chatter outwardly was burdensome, lest all his enemies, having anticipated their watches, seek grounds for accusation in his words.

Greatly constrained in this life, he thought much about another life, where there would be no such temptation. And when does one arrive there? For it is certain that what we suffer here is the wrath of God. This is said in Isaiah: “I will not be an avenger among you forever, nor will I be angry with you for all time.” And he says why: “For the spirit will go forth from me, and I made every breath. Because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him and turned my face away from him; and he went away sorrowful and walked in his own ways.”

Will this wrath of God, then, last forever? This is not what the man found in his silence. What does he say? “God will not reject forever; nor will he continue further to take pleasure in rejecting”—that is, he will not continue further to take pleasure in rejecting and rejecting forever.

He must call his servants back to himself; he must receive fugitives returning to the Lord; he must hear the voice of those in chains: “God will not reject forever; nor will he continue further to take pleasure in rejecting.”

11. [verses 9–10] “Or will he cut off mercy to the end, from generation to generation?” [Note: The editions read, “his mercy,” and in the following verse, “in his anger.” The better manuscripts, in agreement with the Septuagint, do not add “his” in either place.] “Or will God forget to show mercy?”

In you, from you, toward another, there is no mercy unless God grants it to you. And will God himself forget mercy? Does the stream run, while the very spring dries up? “Or will God forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in anger?” That is, will he be so angry that he does not show mercy?

He will more readily restrain anger than mercy. He had also said this through Isaiah: “I will not be an avenger among you forever, nor will I be angry with you for all time.” He said this after saying: “He went away sorrowful and walked in his own ways.” “I have seen his ways,” he says, “and I healed him” (Isa. 57:16–18).

When this man learned this, he transcended further, rejoicing in God, so that wherever he was, he might chatter more in God’s works—not in his own spirit, not in what he was, but in the one by whom he had been made. Thus, transcending, he went beyond even this. Observe the one who transcends; see whether he remains anywhere until he reaches God.

12. [verse 11] “And I said.” Having now transcended himself, what did he say? “Now I have begun”—when I had gone beyond even myself. “Now I have begun.” Here there is no danger. For remaining in myself was also a danger.

“And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” Now the Most High has begun to change me; now I have begun something in which I am secure; now I have entered a certain hall [Note: The better manuscripts read “breeze” (*auram*).] of joys, where no enemy is feared; now I have begun to be in that region where all my enemies do not anticipate the watches: “Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

13. [verse 12] “I remembered the works of the Lord.” Now observe him moving freely among the works of the Lord. He had chattered outside and, saddened by this, his spirit had failed; he chattered inwardly with his heart and with his spirit, and, examining that same spirit, remembered the eternal years and remembered the mercy of the Lord, because the Lord will not reject forever. Now he began to rejoice and exult securely in the Lord’s works.

Let us now hear the works themselves, and let us exult as well. But let us also transcend our affections, and let us not rejoice in temporal things. We too have our inner chamber. Why do we not enter there? Why do we not act in silence? Why do we not examine our spirit? Why do we not consider the eternal years? Why do we not rejoice in the works of God?

Let us hear now in this way and take pleasure in his speaking, so that, when we depart from here, we may do what we were doing while he was speaking—if indeed we do what he himself began when he said: “Now I have begun.”

To rejoice in the works of God is to forget even yourself, if you can take pleasure in him alone. For what is better than he? Do you not see that, when you return to yourself, you return to something worse?

“I remembered the works of the Lord; for I shall remember your wonders from the beginning.”

14. [verse 13] “And I shall meditate on all your works, and I shall chatter about your affections.” Here is the third chattering. He chattered outside when he failed; he chattered inwardly in his spirit when he made progress; he chattered in the works of God when he reached the place toward which he had advanced.

“And I shall chatter about your affections,” not about my own. Who lives without affections? Do you suppose, brothers, that those who fear God, worship God, and love God have no affections? Would you really suppose, and dare to suppose, that a picture, a theater, the chase, bird-catching, and fishing have affections, but the works of God do not? That meditation upon God does not possess its own inner affections when the world is contemplated, when the spectacle of nature is set before one’s eyes, when its craftsman is sought in these things, and when he is found to be displeasing nowhere and pleasing above all?

15. [verse 14] “God, your way is in the Holy One.” He now examines the works of God’s mercy toward us; from these he chatters, and in these affections he exults.

He began there: “Your way is in the Holy One.” What is your way in the Holy One? “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Return, then, you human beings, from your own affections. Where are you going? Where are you running? Where are you fleeing—not only from God, but also from yourselves? “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46:8). Examine your spirit; remember the eternal years; discover God’s mercy toward you; consider the works of his mercy: “His way is in the Holy One.”

Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? What are you seeking in your own affections? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? “And know that the Lord has magnified his Holy One” (Ps. 4:3–4): “Your way is in the Holy One.”

Let us therefore attend to him himself; let us attend to Christ. There is his way [Note: Thus most manuscripts. Some others read: “Let us therefore return to him, to Christ, and so forth.” The editions read: “Let us therefore attend to him, Christ; let us attend to his way there.”]: “God, your way is in the Holy One.”

“What god is great like our God?” The nations have affections concerning their gods; they worship idols. “They have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear; they have feet, but they do not walk” (Ps. 113:5–7). Why do you walk toward a god who does not walk?

“No,” he says, “I do not worship those things.” What, then, do you worship? The divinity that is there? Surely you worship what is said elsewhere: “For the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95:5). Either you worship idols or demons.

“Neither idols nor demons,” he says. What, then, do you worship? The stars, the sun, the moon—these heavenly bodies. How much better is the one who made both earthly and heavenly things! “What god is great like our God?”

16. [verse 15] “You are the God who alone performs wonders.” You truly are the great God, alone performing wonders in the body and in the soul.

The deaf heard, the blind saw, the sick recovered, the dead rose, the paralytics were strengthened. But these miracles occurred then in bodies; let us see them in the soul. People are sober who shortly before were drunk; they are faithful who shortly before worshiped images; they give their possessions to the poor who formerly seized the possessions of others: “What god is great like our God? You are the God who alone performs wonders.”

Moses also performed wonders, but not alone; Elijah performed them, Elisha performed them, and the apostles performed them—but none of them alone. When they performed them, you were with them; when you performed them, they were not with you. For they were not with you when you performed them, since you also made them.

“You are the God who alone performs wonders.” How alone? Is it perhaps the Father and not the Son? Or the Son and not the Father? No: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. “You are the God who alone performs wonders.”

For it is not three gods, but one God who alone performs wonders—and in the one who transcends. For even his transcending and reaching these things was a miracle of God. When he chattered inwardly with his spirit, so that he might transcend even his own spirit and rejoice in the works of God, God himself performed wonders there.

But what did God do? “You made your power known among the peoples.” Hence this assembly is Asaph, the one who transcends, because he made his power known among the peoples.

What power of his did he make known among the peoples? “But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

If Christ is therefore the Power of God, he made Christ known among the peoples. Or do we still not recognize this? Are we so foolish, lying so far below, transcending nothing so completely, that we do not see this? “You made your power known among the peoples.”

17. [verse 16] “You redeemed your people by your arm.” By your arm—that is, by your power. “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1).

“You redeemed your people by your arm, the children of Israel and Joseph.” How does he speak as though there were two peoples, the children of Israel and Joseph? Are not the children of Joseph among the children of Israel? Certainly they are. We know this, we read this, Scripture proclaims this, and truth indicates this: Israel, who is also Jacob, had twelve sons, among whom Joseph was one; and however many were born from the twelve sons of Israel belong to the people of Israel.

How, then, does he say, “The children of Israel and Joseph”? Here he has indicated that some distinction must be made. Let us examine our spirit. Perhaps God has placed something there that we ought to seek with our hands even by night, so that we may not be deceived. Perhaps we too shall find, in this distinction, the children of Israel and Joseph.

By Joseph he wished another people to be understood; he wished the people of the Gentiles to be understood. Why is the people of the Gentiles represented by Joseph? Because Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers (Gen. 37:28).

That Joseph whom his brothers envied and sold into Egypt, once sold into Egypt, labored and was humbled; once recognized, he was exalted, flourished, and ruled. What did all these things signify? What but Christ, sold by his brothers, expelled from his own land, as though into the Egypt of the Gentiles? There he was first humbled, when the martyrs endured persecutions; now he is exalted, as we see, because what was said about him has been fulfilled: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all the nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:11).

Joseph, therefore, represents the people from the Gentiles; Israel represents the people from the Hebrew nation. God redeemed his people, the children of Israel and Joseph. Through what? Through the cornerstone in which the two walls were joined together (Eph. 2:14).

18. [verse 17] He explains how: “The waters saw you, O God.” What are the waters? The peoples. What are these waters? It was stated in the Apocalypse and the answer was given: “The peoples.” There we find most clearly that the waters are figuratively set for the peoples (Rev. 17:15).

Above he had said: “You made your power known among the peoples.” Rightly, therefore: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they were afraid.” Therefore they were changed, because they were afraid.

“The waters saw you, O God, and they were afraid, and the abysses were troubled.” What are the abysses? The depths of the waters. Who is not troubled among the peoples when conscience is struck? You seek the depth of the sea—but what is deeper than the human conscience?

This depth was troubled when God redeemed his people by his arm. How were the abysses troubled? When all poured out their consciences by confessing: “And the abysses were troubled.”

19. [verse 18] “The multitude of the sound of the waters.” In praises of God, in confessions of sins, in hymns and songs, in prayers—there is a multitude of the sound of the waters.

“The clouds gave their voice.” From this comes the sound of the waters; from this comes the disturbance of the abysses, because “the clouds gave their voice.” What clouds? The preachers of the word of truth.

What clouds? Those concerning which God threatens a certain vineyard that produced thorns instead of grapes, saying: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

Finally, the apostles left the Jews and went to the Gentiles: among all the nations the clouds gave their voice; by preaching Christ, the clouds gave their voice.

### 20. [verse 19]

“For indeed your arrows passed through.” He again called the same voices of the clouds “arrows.” For the words of the Evangelists were arrows. These are comparisons, for properly speaking neither is rain an arrow nor an arrow rain; but the word of God is both an arrow, because it strikes, and rain, because it waters.

Let no one, then, be surprised at the disturbance of the abysses when your arrows passed through. What does “passed through” mean? They did not remain in the ears, but pierced the hearts.

“The voice of your thunder is in the wheel.” What does this mean? How are we to understand it? May the Lord help us. “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel.” When we were boys, we used to imagine, on hearing thunder from heaven, that wagons had somehow come out of a stable; for thunder has a certain crashing sound resembling wagons. Are we to return to such childish notions, understanding “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” as though God had some wagons in the clouds and the passage of the wagons stirred up that noise? Far from it. That is childish, empty, foolish.

What, then, is “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel”? Your voice is rolled onward. Yet I do not understand this either. What shall we do? Let us ask Idithun himself, lest he perhaps explain what he said: “The voice,” he says, “of your thunder is in the wheel.” I do not understand; let me hear what you say: “Your lightning flashes appeared to the world.”

Say, then: I had not understood. The world is the wheel; for the circuit of the world is rightly also called an orb, and hence a little wheel is called *orbiculus* [Note: [Col. 0981] The manuscripts have *orbicula*, that is, *orbiculus* is called.] “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel: your lightning flashes appeared to the world.”

Those clouds went around the world in the wheel; they went around it thundering and flashing, they stirred up the abyss, they thundered forth commands, they flashed with miracles. For “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5).

“The earth was shaken and became trembling”: that is, all those who dwell upon the earth. By a figure, however, the earth itself is meant. Why? Because all nations are designated by the name “sea,” since human life is bitter and subject to storms and tempests. Consider also that human beings devour one another like fish, when the greater swallows up the lesser: this, then, is the sea [Note: [Col. 0981] So several manuscripts. Others have: “therefore this is the earth, this the sea.” The printed editions, however, have: “therefore this is the sea.”]; it is there that the Evangelists went.

### 21. [verse 20]

“Your way is in the sea.” A little earlier, your way was in the holy place; now your way is in the sea, because the Holy One himself is in the sea, and rightly he also walked upon the waters of the sea (Matt. 14:25).

“Your way is in the sea”: that is, your Christ is preached among the Gentiles. For in another psalm it is said: “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us, that we may know your way on earth.” Where on earth? “Among all nations is your salvation” (Ps. 66:2–3). This is what is meant by “Your way is in the sea.”

“And your paths are in many waters”: that is, among many peoples. “And your footprints shall not be known.” I do not know whom he has touched; and it would be surprising if he did not mean the Jews themselves. Behold, the mercy of Christ has now been so openly revealed to the Gentiles that your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters; yet your footprints shall not be known.

By whom, then, shall they not be known, except by those who still say, “Christ has not yet come”? Why do they say, “Christ has not yet come”? Because they do not yet recognize him walking upon the sea.

### 22. [verse 21]

“You led your people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

It is somewhat difficult to investigate why he added this. Therefore help us by your attention, since after these two verses there will be an end both of the psalm and of the sermon. Perhaps, when you think that something still remains, you may pay less attention for the moment out of fear of the effort.

When he had said, “Your way is in the sea,” which we understand to mean among the Gentiles, and “your paths are in many waters,” which we understand to mean among many peoples, he added: “And your footprints shall not be known.” We were asking by whom they would not be known, and he immediately continued: “You led your people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” That is: your footprints shall not be known by this people of yours that was led by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

Why, then, was “Your way is in the sea” put here, unless for the purpose of rebuke and reproach? How is your way in the sea, except because it has been excluded from your land? They expelled Christ; the sick did not want him to be their Savior. But he began to be among the Gentiles, and among all nations, among many peoples.

Even remnants of that people were saved. An ungrateful multitude remained outside, and Jacob’s broad thigh became lame (Gen. 32:31). The breadth of the thigh is understood [Note: [Col. 0982] The printed editions have: “the breadth of the thigh is understood as the way,” and so forth. The word “way” is absent from the manuscripts.] in the multitude of the race; and among the greater part of the Israelites there arose a certain empty and foolish crowd that did not recognize the footprints of Christ in the waters.

“You led your people like sheep,” and they did not know you. You did so many good things for them! You divided the sea; you led them across dry land between the waters; you covered their pursuing enemies with the waves; in the desert you rained manna upon those in need, leading them by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Yet they expelled you from themselves, so that your way might be in the sea and they might not know your footprints.

## Exposition of Psalm 77

[Note: [Col. 0982] Dictated in the year of Christ 415, from Letter 169 to Evodius, section 1.]

### 1. [verse 1]

This psalm contains an account of events narrated as having taken place among the ancient people; but the more recent and later people are warned to beware lest they be ungrateful for God’s benefits and provoke the anger of the one whose grace they ought obediently and faithfully to receive:

“Lest they become,” he says, “like their fathers, a perverse and embittering generation; a generation that did not set its heart straight, and whose spirit was not held faithful with God.”

This, then, is the purpose of this psalm, its usefulness, and its most abundant fruit. Yet although everything appears to be said and narrated plainly and openly, its title first arouses and fixes our attention. For it is not without reason that it is entitled “Understanding of Asaph,” unless perhaps these words seek a reader who understands something deeper than what their surface suggests.

Then, as he is about to narrate and recall all these things—which seem to require an auditor rather than an expositor—he says: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning.”

Who would not be awakened from sleep at this? Who would dare to pass over in reading, as though they were obvious, the parables and propositions which, by their very names, indicate that they ought to be examined more deeply?

A parable presents the likeness of something; and although the word is Greek, it is now used as a Latin term as well. It is well known that in parables, which are called likenesses of things, the likenesses are compared with the things under discussion.

The propositions, however, which in Greek are called προβλήματα (*problēmata*), are questions containing something that must be resolved through discussion. Who, then, would read parables and propositions superficially? Who, on hearing these words, would not focus the vigilance of the mind, so as to arrive through understanding at their fruit?

### 2

“Attend,” he says, “my people, to my law.” Whom are we to believe speaking here except God? He himself gave the law to his people, whom he gathered after freeing them from Egypt; this gathering is properly called “Synagogue,” which is interpreted as “Asaph.”

Was it therefore said, “Understanding of Asaph,” because Asaph himself understood? Or should it be understood figuratively, as meaning that the same Synagogue—that is, the same people—understood, the people to whom it is said, “Attend, my people, to my law”?

What, then, is the meaning of the prophet’s rebuke to this same people: “But Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand” (Isa. 1:3)?

Certainly, however, there were also among that people some who understood, possessing the faith that was later revealed—not a faith belonging to the letter of the Law, but one belonging to the grace of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0983] The Regius manuscript has the plural *pertinentes* (“belonging”), agreeing with *sacramenta* (“sacraments”).].

For those who were able to foresee and proclaim that Christ would be revealed in the future did not exist without that faith, since those ancient sacraments too were signs of things to come. Or did only the Prophets have this faith, and not the people? Indeed, even those who faithfully listened to the Prophets were helped by the same grace to understand what they heard.

Yet the sacrament of the kingdom of heaven was veiled in the Old Testament, to be revealed in the fullness of time in the New. For the Apostle says:

> “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.”

Thus their food and drink were the same in mystery as ours; but they were the same in signification, not in outward form. For the very same Christ was prefigured for them in the rock and manifested for us in the flesh.

“But,” he says, “God was not well pleased with all of them” (1 Cor. 10:1–5). They all, indeed, “ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink,” that is, something signifying a spiritual reality; “but God was not well pleased with all of them.”

When he says, “not with most of them,” there were therefore some among them with whom God was well pleased. And although the sacraments were common to all, grace—the power of the sacraments—was not common to all.

So now also, when the faith that was then veiled has already been revealed, the bath of regeneration is common to all who are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19); but the grace of which these are the sacraments, by which the members of Christ’s body are regenerated together with their head, is not common to all.

For heretics possess the same Baptism, as do false brothers within the communion of the Catholic name. Therefore here too it is rightly said: “But God was not well pleased with most of them.”

### 3

Neither then nor now is the voice of the one saying, “Attend, my people, to my law,” fruitless. The wording is familiar throughout Scripture: he does not say, “Attend,” in the singular, but, “Attend,” in the plural. For a people consists of many, and what follows is likewise spoken to many in the plural:

“Incline your ear to the words of my mouth.”

This is what “Attend” means; that is, “Incline your ear.” And what he says there, “my law,” he says here, “the words of my mouth.”

For the person who piously attends to God’s law and the words of his mouth is the one whose ear is inclined in humility, not the one whose neck is stiffened by pride. What is poured in is received by the hollow of humility; the prominence of swelling pride drives it away.

Hence elsewhere he says: “Incline your ear and receive the words of understanding” (Prov. 22:17).

We have therefore been sufficiently warned to receive this psalm also—“the understanding of Asaph,” since the title has the genitive case, “of this understanding,” not “this understanding”—with an inclined ear, that is, with humble devotion.

Nor does it say “of Asaph himself,” but “for Asaph”; this is indicated by the Greek article and is found in certain Latin manuscripts. These words, then, are words of understanding: they are the words of the understanding given to Asaph himself. We understand this better not as referring to one man, but to the gathering of God’s people, from which we must by no means separate ourselves.

Although, properly speaking, the Jews’ gathering is called “Synagogue,” while the Christians’ is called “Church”—because a gathering is more commonly understood of animals, whereas an assembly is more commonly understood of human beings—we nevertheless find that the former too was called “Church.” Perhaps it is more fitting for us to say:

> “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may confess your holy name” (Ps. 105:47).

We ought not to disdain—in fact, we ought to give ineffable thanks—that we are the sheep of his hands, sheep he foresaw when he said:

> “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16),

namely, by joining the faithful people of the Gentiles to the faithful people of the Israelites, concerning whom he had previously said:

> “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

For “all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats” (Matt. 25:32).

Let us therefore hear what is said: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth,” not as though it were spoken to the Jews, but rather as spoken to us—or certainly as spoken also to us.

For when the Apostle had said, “But God was not well pleased with all of them,” thereby showing that there were also among them those with whom God was well pleased, he immediately added:

> “For they were struck down in the desert.”

Then he continued:

> “These things happened to them as figures for us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they desired them; nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Nor should we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Nor should we tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him, and perished by serpents. Nor should you murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer. All these things were happening to them figuratively; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:5–11).

These things, then, were sung especially for us. Hence in this psalm, among other things, it is said:

> “So that the generation to come might know, the children who will be born and rise up.”

Moreover, if that destruction by serpents, that ruin by the destroyer, and that slaughter by the sword were figures, as the Apostle clearly says—and it is evident that all those things actually happened, for he does not say, “They were spoken in a figure,” or, “They were written in a figure,” but, “They were happening to them figuratively”—with how much greater diligence of devotion must we avoid the punishments of which those things were figures!

Without doubt, just as in good things the reality signified by a figure is much greater than the figure itself, so in evil things the realities signified by the figures are far worse, since even the figures that signify them were so dreadful.

For just as the promised land to which that people was being led is nothing in comparison with the kingdom of heaven to which the Christian people are being led, so those punishments that were figures, although so atrocious, are nothing in comparison with the punishments they signify.

The figures that the Apostle mentioned are what this psalm, as far as we can judge, calls “parables” and “propositions.” They do not have their end in the events that happened, but in those realities to which they are referred by a rational comparison.

Let us therefore attend to the law of God, his people, and incline our ear to the words of his mouth.

### 4. [verse 2]

“I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning.”

From what beginning he speaks is sufficiently clear from what follows. He does not mean from the time when heaven and earth were made, or from the time when the human race was created in the first man, but from the time when the people gathered from Egypt were brought together, so that the meaning pertains to Asaph, which is interpreted as “Gathering.”

Would that the one who said, “I shall open my mouth in parables,” would also deign to open our understanding to them! For if, just as he opened his mouth in parables, he would also open the parables themselves, and just as he uttered propositions, he would also utter their explanations, we would not be struggling here.

But now everything is so covered and closed that, even if, with his help, we can reach something from which we may be healthfully nourished, nevertheless we eat our bread in the sweat of our face (Gen. 3:19), and pay the penalty of that ancient sentence by labor not only of the body but also of the heart.

Let him speak, then, and let us hear the parables and propositions.

### 5. [verse 3]
