“The things which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.”

The Lord was speaking above. For whose other words should we understand “Attend, my people, to my law” to be? What, then, does it mean that a human being suddenly speaks here? The words “How many things we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” are now plainly the words of a human being.

Certainly God was now going to speak through a human minister, just as the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). He first chose that the words should be spoken in his own person, so that the human being speaking his words would not be despised as merely human.

This is how God’s utterances are conveyed to us through the bodily senses. The Creator moves a submissive creature by an invisible operation; his substance is not converted into something bodily and temporal. Rather, through bodily and temporal signs—whether pertaining to the eyes or to the ears—he makes his will known insofar as human beings are able to receive it.

If an angel can use the ether, air, cloud, fire, and any other bodily nature or form; and if a human being uses his face, tongue, hand, pen, letters, or other signifying things to disclose the secrets of his mind; and finally, since he is human, sends human messengers and says to one, “Go,” and he goes, and to another, “Come,” and he comes, and to his servant, “Do this,” and he does it (Luke 7:8)—how much greater and more effective is the power of God, to whom all things are subject, when he uses both angel and human being to announce what pleases him!

Although, then, a human being now says, “The things which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us,” let us hear these words as God’s words, not as human fables.

For this reason it was said beforehand: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning.”

“The things which,” he says, “we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.”

It is like “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44:11). Things were heard in the Old Testament that are known in the New: heard when they were prophesied, known when they were fulfilled. When the promise is fulfilled, the hearing is not deceived. And our fathers—Moses and the Prophets—told us.

### 6. [verse 4]

“They were not hidden from their children, in the generation to come.”

This is our generation, in which regeneration has been granted to us.

“Announcing the praises of the Lord, and his powers, and his wonders that he did.”

The order of the words is: “Our fathers told us, announcing the praises of the Lord.”

The Lord is praised so that he may be loved; for what could be loved more healthfully?

### 7. [verses 5–8]

“And he raised up a Testimony in Jacob, and established a Law in Israel.”

This is the beginning of which it was said above: “I shall utter propositions from the beginning.” The beginning, therefore, is the Old Testament, and the end is the New.

For fear prevails in the Law, and “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). But “the end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). By his gift, love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5), and perfected love casts out fear (1 John 4:18), because now the righteousness of God has been manifested without the Law.

But since it has testimony from the Law and the Prophets (Rom. 3:21), “he raised up a Testimony in Jacob, and established a Law in Israel.”

For the tabernacle, which was constructed through such a notable work, full of so many signs, is also called the Tabernacle of Testimony (Exod. 40:2). In it there was a veil before the ark of the Law, just as there was a veil before the face of the minister of the Law; for in that dispensation there were parables and propositions.

The things that were preached and done were hidden under veiled signs, and were not perceived through unveiled manifestations. “But when you turn to Christ,” says the Apostle, “the veil will be taken away” (2 Cor. 3:13, 16).

“All the promises of God,” moreover, “are in him Yes, and in him Amen” [Note: [Col. 0987] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “in him they were,” followed by “Whatever.” See above, col. 911, no. 18.] (2 Cor. 1:20).

Whoever, therefore, clings to Christ possesses the whole good that he does not understand even in the letters of the Law. Whoever is alien from Christ neither understands nor possesses it.

“He raised up a Testimony in Jacob, and established a Law in Israel.” He repeats himself in his customary manner. For “he raised up a Testimony” means the same as “he established a Law”; and “in Jacob” means the same as “in Israel.”

Someone may say: there is a difference between “raised up” and “established.” Certainly there is, just as there is a difference between Jacob and Israel—not because they were two men, but because the same man received these two names for different reasons: Jacob because of supplanting, since at birth he held his brother’s heel; Israel because of the vision of God (Gen. 25:25; 32:28).

So also “raised up” means one thing and “established” another. For “he raised up a Testimony,” as I understand it, means that something was raised up by that Testimony.

“For without the Law,” says the Apostle, “sin was dead. I was once alive without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived.” This is what was raised up through the Testimony that is the Law: what had been hidden was brought to light, as he says shortly afterward: “But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Rom. 7:8–9, 13).

“Established a Law,” however, was said as though it were a yoke placed upon sinners. Hence it is said: “The law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1:9).

It is therefore a Testimony insofar as it proves something; but it is a Law insofar as it commands, although it is one and the same thing.

Accordingly, just as Christ is a stone—but for believers “the cornerstone” (Ps. 117:22), while for unbelievers “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense”—so the Testimony of the Law is a testimony to those who do not use the Law lawfully.

It is a testimony by which sinful people are convicted and condemned; but for those who use it lawfully, it is a testimony showing to whom sinners who are to be delivered must flee.

For the righteousness of God is in Christ’s grace, “having testimony from the Law and the Prophets,” by which the ungodly person is justified. Some, however, being ignorant of it and wishing to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

### 8

“The things which,” he says, “he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the generation to come might know, the children who will be born and rise up, and tell their children” [Note: [Col. 0988] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *narrabunt* (“they will tell”) only in this passage.], “so that they might place their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, and seek out his commandments.

“Lest they become like their fathers, a perverse and embittering generation; a generation that did not set its heart straight, and whose spirit was not held faithful with God.”

These words indicate, in a certain sense, two peoples: one belonging to the Old Testament and the other to the New.

For when he says, “How many things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children,” he says that they received commandments to make these things known to their children, but not that they themselves knew or fulfilled them. They received them for this purpose: so that the generation to come might know what that earlier generation did not know.

“The children who will be born and rise up.” Those who were born then did not rise up, because they had their hearts not above but rather upon the earth. For one rises with Christ. Hence it is said: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. 3:1).

“And tell,” he says, “their children, so that they might place their hope in God.” In this way the righteous do not wish to establish their own righteousness, but reveal their way to God and hope in him, so that he himself may act (Ps. 36:5).

“And not forget the works of God”: that is, by magnifying and boasting of their own works as though they themselves accomplished them, when it is God who works in those who do good both the willing and the doing, according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13).

“And seek out his commandments.” Once they have learned them, how are they still to seek them out? For he says: “The things which he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the generation to come might know.” What is it to know? Surely, the commandments that he commanded.

How, then, are they still to seek them out? Because, by placing their hope in God, they seek his commandments so that, with his help, they may fulfill them.

“Lest they become like their fathers, a perverse and embittering generation; a generation that did not set its heart straight.”

And he immediately explains why, adding: “And whose spirit was not held faithful with God.” That is, because it did not possess the faith that obtains what the Law commands.

For when the human spirit cooperates with the Spirit of God at work, then what God has commanded is fulfilled. This happens only by believing in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5).

That perverse and embittering generation did not possess this faith, and therefore it was said of it: “Its spirit was not held faithful with God.” This is expressed much more clearly to signify the grace of God, which not only works the remission of sins but also makes the human spirit cooperate with it in the work of good deeds—as though he were saying, “Its spirit did not believe God.”

For this is what it means to have one’s spirit held faithful with God: not to believe that one’s spirit can establish righteousness without God, but with God. This is also what it means to believe in God, which is certainly more than believing God.

For one ought often to believe any human being, although one ought not to believe in that person. To believe in God, then, is to cling to him through faith, so as to cooperate rightly with God, who works good in us:

> “For without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

What more could the Apostle say about this than: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17)?

Otherwise, the Law is a testimony by which the guilty are condemned, not by which they are acquitted. The letter is threatening: it convicts transgressors. It is not the assisting Spirit who frees and justifies sinners.

That generation, then, whose example must be avoided, was perverse and embittering because its spirit was not held faithful with God. For although it believed God in some matters, it did not believe in God; it did not cling to God through faith, so that, healed by God, it might cooperate rightly with God working within it.

### 9. [verse 9]

Finally:

> “The children of Ephraim, bending and shooting bows, turned back on the day of battle.”

“Pursuing the Law of righteousness, they did not attain to the Law of righteousness” (Rom. 9:31). Why? “Because it was not from faith.”

For it was a generation whose spirit was not held faithful with God. It was as though from works; for just as it bent and shot bows—something outwardly visible, as in the works of the Law—so it did not set its heart straight, where the righteous person lives by faith (Rom. 1:17), faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), by which one clings to God, who works in a human being both the willing and the doing according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13).

For what else does it mean to bend a bow, shoot, and turn back on the day of battle, except to attend and promise on the day of hearing, then abandon one’s promise on the day of temptation; to practice with weapons as though in play, and refuse to fight when the hour of combat arrives?

He says “bending and shooting bows,” although he appears to have needed to say “bending bows and shooting arrows.” For a bow is not shot; rather, something is shot from a bow.

Either this is the same expression discussed above, where it was said, “He raised up a Testimony,” because he raised something up through the Testimony; so here too, “shooting bows,” because they shot something with bows.

Or the order of the words is obscure, with a word omitted that must nevertheless be understood, so that the order is: “The children of Ephraim, bending bows and shooting”—with “arrows” understood—and the fuller expression would be: “Bending bows and shooting arrows.”

For even if he said, “Bending and shooting arrows,” we would not understand “bending arrows,” but, after hearing “bending,” we would rather supply “the bow,” although it had not been stated.

Some Greek manuscripts are said to read, “bending and shooting with bows,” so that we may without doubt supply “arrows.”

By wishing the children of Ephraim to be understood as the whole embittering generation, he uses an expression in which a part signifies the whole. Perhaps this particular tribe was chosen because something especially good might have been expected from it: because they were born from the one whom Jacob blessed—his own grandson, though that man’s father had placed him as the younger on the left—with his right hand, and set him before his older brother through a hidden blessing (Gen. 48:14).

Thus, when that tribe is blamed here and it is shown that what that blessing promised did not appear in it, we understand clearly that even then the words of the patriarch Jacob prefigured something far different from what the wisdom of the flesh expects.

For it was prefigured that those who were first would become last, and those who were last would become first (Matt. 20:16), through the coming of the Savior, of whom it was said:

> “The one who comes after me has been made before me” (John 1:27).

Thus righteous Abel was preferred to his older brother (Gen. 4:4–5); Isaac to Ishmael (Gen. 21:12); Jacob to Esau, his twin yet the one born first (Gen. 25:23); likewise Perez, himself a twin, surpassed the one who first thrust out his hand from the womb and had begun to be born, surpassing him even in birth (Gen. 38:27–29); and David was preferred to his older brothers (1 Sam. 16:12).

For this reason all these and other similar events—parables not only of words but also of deeds—went before. Thus the Christian people was preferred to the Jewish people; and for the redemption of the Christian people, Christ was killed by the Jews, just as Abel was killed by Cain (Gen. 4:8).

This too was prefigured when Jacob, stretching out his hands crosswise, touched Ephraim, who stood on the left, with his right hand, and set him before Manasseh, who stood on the right and whom he touched with his left.

For according to the flesh, “the children of Ephraim, bending and shooting bows, turned back on the day of battle.”

### 10. [verse 10]

But what it means that he says, “They turned back on the day of battle,” the following words make clear, in which he explained it most explicitly: “They did not keep,” he says, “the covenant of God, and they were unwilling to walk in his law.” This is what “They turned back on the day of battle” means: they did not observe God’s covenant. When, bending and shooting their bows, they also uttered the words of a most ready promise, saying, “Whatever the Lord our God has spoken, we will do and we will hear” (Exod. 19:8). [Note: [Col. 0990] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint. But the printed editions here read, “We will hear and we will do.”] “They turned back on the day of battle”: because the promise of obedience is tested not by hearing but by temptation.

But whoever has a spirit faithful with God holds God to be faithful: God will not permit him to be tempted beyond what he can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that he may be able to endure it (1 Cor. 10:13), and not turn back on the day of battle. Whoever, however, glories in himself and not in God (ibid. 1:31), no matter how much he boasts of his promise of virtue, like one bending and shooting his bow, turns back on the day of battle. For because his spirit was not faithful with God, the Spirit of God is not with him either; and, as it is written, “Because he did not believe, therefore he will not be protected” (Sir. 2:15).

But when he had said, “They did not observe God’s covenant,” he added, “And they were unwilling to walk in his law.” This is a repetition of the preceding statement, together with a certain explanation of it: for he called “his law” what above he had called “God’s covenant”; and what was said, “They did not keep,” is to be understood as repeated in the words “they were unwilling to walk.” Yet since it could have been said more briefly, “And they did not walk in his law,” it seems to me that in this word he wished us to seek something, since he preferred to say “they were unwilling to walk” rather than “they did not walk.”

For one might think that the law of works was sufficient for justification, when the things commanded are performed outwardly by people who would rather that what they do not do from the heart were not commanded, and yet they do them; and thus they seem, as it were, to walk in the law of God, but they are unwilling to walk: for they do not act from the heart. Yet what is done from the heart can in no way be done when it is motivated by fear of punishment and not by love of justice. [Col. 0991] For as far as outward actions are concerned, both those who fear punishment and those who love justice do not steal; and so they are alike in hand but unlike in heart, alike in deed but unlike in will.

Therefore they are marked in this way: “A generation,” he says, “that did not direct its heart.” He did not say “its works,” but “its heart.” When the heart is directed, the works are right; but when the heart is not directed, the works are not right, even if they appear right. And from what source this perverse generation did not direct its heart, he sufficiently revealed when he said, “And his spirit was not entrusted to God.” For God is upright; and therefore, by clinging to him as to an unchangeable rule, what in itself was a perverse human heart can become upright.

But for the heart to be with him, and thereby to be able to become upright, one approaches him not by foot but by faith. Therefore it is also said in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning that same perverse and embittering generation: “The word they heard did not profit them, since it was not united with the faith of those who obeyed” (Heb. 4:2). [Note: [Col. 0991] The editions read, “the word heard, not being united with their faith,” etc. But the manuscript reading restored here accords no less well with the Apostle’s Greek text.]

The will, therefore, which exists in an upright heart is prepared by the Lord, with faith preceding—the faith by which one approaches the upright God, so that the heart may become upright. This faith, through God’s mercy preceding and calling, is aroused by obedience; and it begins to draw the heart toward God, so that it may be directed. The more and more it is directed, the more it sees what it did not see, and is capable of what it was not capable of.

Simon had not done this. The apostle Peter said to him: “You have neither part nor lot in this faith, for your heart is not upright with God” (Acts 8:21). There he showed that the heart cannot be upright without God, so that people may begin to walk not like slaves, fearing under the law, but like sons, willingly in the law—in the law in which those people were unwilling to walk, and under which they remained guilty.

For this will is possessed not by fear but by love, which is poured into the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5). To them it is said:

> “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10).

Not as those people did, who were unwilling to walk in his law: they did not believe in him, nor reveal their way to him and hope in him, so that he himself might act.

### 11. [verses 11, 12]

“And they forgot his benefits and his wonders that he showed them, the wonders that he did before their fathers.” [Note: The particle *quae* (“which”) is absent from the printed editions, but is present in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.]

What this means is not a question to be neglected. Shortly before, he was speaking of those very fathers, saying that they had been a perverse and embittering generation. “Let them not become,” he says, “like their fathers, a perverse and embittering generation; a generation that did not direct its heart,” and the other things that are still said about that generation. He commands the other generation to avoid imitating it in this way: that they should place their hope in God, not forget the works of God, and seek his commandments. We have already discussed these matters sufficiently, insofar as seemed appropriate.

What, then, does he mean when, speaking of that same perverse generation, he says that they forgot God’s benefits and his wonders that he showed them, and adds: “The wonders that he did before their fathers”? Who were these fathers, when these very people themselves are the fathers whose descendants he does not want to be similar to them? If we take them to be those from whom these people were descended, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, they had long since fallen asleep when God showed the wonders in Egypt.

For what follows is: “In the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis,” where he says that God showed these people wonders before their fathers. Or were they present in spirit, because the Lord says of them in the Gospel, “For all live to him” (Luke 20:38)? Or should we more appropriately understand “fathers” as Moses, Aaron, and the other elders who are mentioned in the same Scripture as having received the spirit that Moses had received, so that they might help him govern and bear with that same people (Num. 11:16–17)?

Why should they not be called fathers? Not in the sense that God the Father alone regenerates by his Spirit those whom he makes sons for an eternal inheritance, but as a matter of honor, because of their age and their pious care. Thus Paul, as an elder, says: “I write these things not to shame you, but to admonish you as my dearest children,” although he certainly knew that the Lord had said, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, God” (Matt. 23:9). This was not said in order to remove the title of human honor from ordinary speech, but so that the grace of God by which we are regenerated for eternal life might not be attributed to the nature, power, or even holiness of any human being. Therefore, when he said, “I begot you,” he specified, “in Christ and through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:14–15), so that what belongs to God would not be thought to belong to him.

### 12

Therefore that perverse and embittering generation forgot God’s benefits and his wonders that he showed them—the wonders that he did before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis. And he begins, by recalling those same wonders, to unfold the account.

If these things are parables and propositions, they must certainly be referred to something by way of comparison. Nor should we turn the eye of our attention away from what the psalm itself intends to show: that this is the fruit of all that is being said, and the reason why we have been admonished to listen to these things with the greatest attention. God says:

> “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth,”

so that “we may place our hope in God, and not forget the works of God, and seek his commandments,” lest we become like those fathers, “a perverse and embittering generation; a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.”

Everything, therefore, must be referred to this; and consequently, whatever these figurative actions signify can take place spiritually in a person, either by God’s grace if the things are good, or by God’s judgment if they are evil, just as those good and evil things happened to the Israelites themselves and to their enemies.

If we do not forget these things, but place our hope in God and are not ungrateful toward his grace; if we fear him—not with slavish fear, by which only bodily evils are feared, but with the chaste fear that endures forever and ever, a fear that judges deprivation of the light of justice to be a great punishment—we shall not become, like those fathers, a perverse and embittering generation.

The land of Egypt, therefore, is to be understood figuratively as this present age. The plain of Tanis is the level ground of the humble commandment. For *Thanis* is interpreted as “humble commandment.” In this age, then, let us accept the commandment of humility, so that in the age to come we may be worthy to receive the exaltation promised by him who for our sake became humble here.

### 13. [verses 13–16]

For he who tore open the sea and led them across, who made the waters stand like waterskins, so that the wave stood as though it had been enclosed, can by his grace restrain the fluid and drifting movements of carnal desires when one renounces this age, so that, as though all sins had been destroyed as enemies, the people of the faithful may be led across through the sacrament of Baptism.

He who led them in a cloud by day and throughout the night in the illumination of fire can also direct the journey spiritually, if faith cries out to him: “Direct my paths according to your word” (Ps. 118:133). Elsewhere it is said of him: “For he himself will make your courses straight, and will bring your ways forward in peace” [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *perducet* (“will lead through”) instead.] (Prov. 4:27)—through Jesus Christ our Lord, whose sacrament in this age, as in the day, has been manifested in the flesh, as though in a cloud; but at the judgment, as in a terror of night, because then there will be a great tribulation of the age, like fire: it will shine upon the just and burn the unjust.

He who tore open the rock in the desert and watered them as though from a great abyss; who brought water out of the rock and led forth waters like rivers, can indeed pour into thirsty faith the gift of the Holy Spirit, which that event spiritually signified, from the spiritual rock that followed them, which is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). He stood and cried out:

> “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me”; and, “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

For, as the Gospel says, he was speaking of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive (John 7:37–39). To him, as to a rod, the wood of the Passion was applied, so that grace might flow out for believers.

### 14. [verse 17]

And yet those people, like a perverse and embittering generation, “continued still to sin against him”—that is, not to believe. For this is the sin concerning which the Spirit convicts the world, as the Lord says: “Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me” (John 16:9).

“And they embittered the Most High in dryness”—other manuscripts have “in the waterless place,” which expresses the Greek more precisely and signifies nothing other than dryness. Was this in the dryness of that wilderness, or rather in their own? For although they had drunk from the rock, they had not dry bellies but dry minds, bearing no green growth of righteousness. In that dryness they ought all the more faithfully to have besought God, so that he who had given satiety to their throats might also give justice to their conduct.

To him the faithful soul cries: “Let my eyes behold equity” (Ps. 16:2).

### 15. [verses 18–20]

“And they tempted God in their hearts, by asking for food for their souls.” To ask in faith is one thing; to ask while tempting is another. Accordingly, what follows says:

> “And they spoke against God, and said: ‘Can God prepare a table in the desert? Since he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed, can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?’”

They therefore asked for food for their souls without believing. The apostle James does not command the food of the mind to be sought in this way; rather, he teaches that it is to be requested by believers, not by those who tempt and speak against God:

> “If any of you lacks wisdom,” he says, “let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing” (James 1:5–6).

That faith was absent from the generation that had not directed its heart and whose spirit was not faithful with God.

### 16. [verse 21]

“Therefore the Lord heard, and delayed, and fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose up against Israel.” He explained what he meant by “fire.” For he called anger “fire,” although fire also literally consumed many of them.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “The Lord heard, and delayed”? Did he delay bringing them into the promised land, to which they were being led—a thing that could have happened within a few days—but because of their sins they had to be destroyed in the wilderness, where they were indeed crushed over forty years?

If this is the meaning, then he delayed the people, not those very individuals who were tempting and speaking against God; for all of them perished in the wilderness, and their children entered the promised land.

Or did he delay the punishment, first satisfying even their faithless desire, lest it be thought that he was angry because they were asking him—though while tempting and speaking against him—to do what he could not do? He therefore heard and delayed exacting vengeance; and after he had done what they had thought he could not do, then anger rose up against Israel.

### 17. [verses 22–31]

Finally, after briefly presenting both points, he proceeds to set out the order of the narrative openly:

> “Because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation.”

For after saying why fire was kindled in Jacob and anger rose up in Israel—that is, because they did not believe in God and did not hope in his salvation—he immediately adds how ungrateful they were for benefits so evident:

> “And he commanded the clouds above, and opened the doors of heaven. And he rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels” [Note: The same verse, 25, is explained above in Psalm 33, sermon 1, section 6.]; “he sent them food in abundance. He transferred the South Wind from heaven and brought in the southwest wind by his power. And he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents. And they ate and were filled exceedingly; and he brought them what they desired: they were not deprived of their desire.”

See why he had delayed. But what had he delayed? Let us hear:

> “The food was still in their mouths, and the anger of God rose up against them.”

This is what he had delayed. First he delayed; afterward “fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose up in Israel.” He had delayed, therefore, so that he might first do what they had believed he could not do, and then bring upon them what they had to suffer.

For if they had placed their hope in God, not only those desires of the flesh but also those of the spirit would have been fulfilled for them. He who commanded the clouds above, opened the doors of heaven, rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven, so that man might eat the bread of angels; he who sent them food in abundance in order to satisfy unbelievers—is not incapable of giving believers the true bread from heaven that the manna signified. This is truly the food of angels, whom the Word of God feeds incorruptibly as incorruptible beings [Note: The printed editions read, “which the Word of God feeds corruptible beings incorruptibly.” The *Regius* manuscript reads, “whom the incorruptible Word of God feeds incorruptibly.”]; and in order that man might eat it, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).

For this bread is rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds; and when the hearts of preachers have been opened like heavenly doors, it is proclaimed not to the murmuring and tempting Synagogue but to the believing Church that places its hope in him.

He who “transferred the South Wind from heaven, brought in the southwest wind by his power, and rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea; and they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents; and they ate and were filled exceedingly, and he brought them what they desired, nor were they deprived of their desire,” can also feed the small faith of believers—not of those who tempt him—with fleshly signs of words that pass through the air, like winged birds [Note: Several manuscripts have “of the little ones.”]

These do not come from the North, where cold and darkness prevail—that is, from eloquence that pleases this age [Note: The manuscripts have “that favors this age.”]—but from the transfer of the South Wind from heaven. Where else could it be transferred than to the earth? So that those who are small in faith may, by hearing earthly things, be nourished for the reception of heavenly things.

“For if I told you earthly things,” he says, “and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12). He had in a certain way been transferred from heaven, where he had been carried beyond himself in God, so that he might be measured in speaking to those to whom he said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1).

There he had heard unspeakable words (2 Cor. 12:4), which he was not permitted to speak on earth through sounding words, as though through winged birds. And by bringing in the southwest wind through his power—that is, through the fervent and shining spirits of preachers—and doing this by his power, he prevents the southwest wind from attributing to itself what it has from God.

These winds come willingly to human beings and bring them words sent from God, so that in their own dwellings and around their own tents they may gather such birds, and each person may worship the Lord from his own place—all the islands of the nations (Zeph. 2:11).

### 18

But for the unbelievers, like a perverse and embittering generation, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose up against them and killed many of them—that is, the greater number of them; or, as some manuscripts have it, “their fat ones.” We did not find this reading in the Greek copies available to us. But if it is the more accurate reading, what else should “their fat ones” be understood to mean but those prevailing in pride, of whom it is said: “Their iniquity will go forth as from fatness” (Ps. 72:7)?

“And it hindered the chosen of Israel.” There too were chosen people whose faith was not united with that of the perverse and embittering generation. But they were hindered from benefiting in any way those for whom they wished to care with paternal affection. For when God is angry, what does human mercy accomplish?

Or did he instead wish the chosen to be understood as shackled together with them, so that although they were distinguished by mind and life, they might endure hardships with them as an example not only of justice but also of patience? For perhaps we have learned that the saints were taken captive together with sinners for no other reason than this: in the Greek manuscripts we read not *ἐνεπόδισεν* (*enepodisen*), “he hindered,” but *συνεπόδισεν* (*synepodisen*), which more properly means “he shackled together.”

### 19. [verses 32, 33]

But “the perverse and embittering generation sinned still in all these things and did not believe in his wonders. And their days failed in vanity,” although, if they had believed, they could have had days without failing in truth with him to whom it was said: “Your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

Their days therefore failed in vanity, and their years with haste. For the whole life of mortals hastens, and what seems longer is merely a somewhat more prolonged vapor.

### 20. [verses 34, 35]

Nevertheless, when he was killing them, “they sought him”—not because of eternal life, but because they feared bringing the vapor to an end more quickly. Those who sought him were not, of course, the ones he had killed, but those who feared being killed by their example.

Scripture thus speaks of them as though those who were being killed were seeking God, because they were one people and the statement is made as of a single body:

> “And they turned back, and came early in the morning to God. And they remembered that God was their helper, and that God Most High was their redeemer.”

But all this was for the sake of acquiring temporal goods and avoiding temporal evils. For those who sought God because of earthly benefits were not really seeking God, but those benefits. And even now God is worshiped with slavish fear, not with free love. Thus God is not worshiped; for what is loved is what is worshiped. Since God is found to be greater and better than all things, he must be loved above all things in order to be worshiped.

### 21. [verses 36, 37]

Finally, let us consider what follows:

> “And they loved him with their mouth,” he says, “and with their tongue they lied to him. But their heart was not upright with him, nor were they regarded as faithful in his covenant.”

He, to whom the secrets of human beings are naked and who saw without any obstacle what they loved more, found one thing in their tongue and another in their heart.

The heart is upright with God when it seeks God for God’s sake. For one thing alone he desired from the Lord: this he will seek, that he may dwell in the house of the Lord forever and contemplate his delight (Ps. 26:4).

To him the heart of the faithful says:

> “I shall be satisfied,”

not with the pots of Egyptian meat, nor with melons, gourds, garlic, and onions, which the perverse and embittering generation preferred even to the bread of heaven (Exod. 16:3), nor with visible manna and those very winged birds; but:

> “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15).

For this is the inheritance of the New Testament, in which those people were not regarded as faithful. Yet even then, when it was veiled, its faith existed among the chosen; and now, when it has already been revealed, it is not present among many who are called: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16).

Such, therefore, was that perverse and embittering generation, even when it appeared to seek God: loving with its mouth and lying with its tongue, but not upright with God in its heart, where it loved instead those things for which it sought God’s help.

### 22. [verses 38, 39]

> “But he is merciful and will be propitious toward their sins, and will not destroy them. And he will abound in order to turn away his anger, and will not kindle all his anger. And he remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return.”

In these words many promise themselves impunity for their iniquity on the basis of divine mercy, even if they persist in being such as this generation is described: perverse and embittering, not directing its heart, and with its spirit not faithful with God. [Note: [Col. 0997] Thus the better manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions read in the past tense: “he abounded in order to turn away his anger, and did not kindle.”] It is not expedient to agree with them.

For if, to speak according to their own reasoning, God perhaps will not destroy the wicked, then without doubt he will not destroy the good. Why, therefore, do we not choose instead the position in which there is no uncertainty?

Those who lie to God with their tongue while their heart is otherwise disposed surely think and wish that, when he threatens such people with eternal punishment, God too is a liar. But since they do not deceive him by lying, he does not deceive them by speaking the truth.

Therefore let this generation not distort these words of the divine utterances, by which it flatters itself, as it distorted its own heart; for even when the heart is distorted, these words remain upright.

First, these words may be understood according to what is written in the Gospel:

> “So that you may be like your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45).

Who does not see how great is the patience of mercy with which he spares the wicked? But this is before judgment.

Thus he spared that nation, so that he would not kindle all his anger against it by uprooting and destroying it completely. [Note: The word “not” is absent from most manuscripts.] This is clearly evident in his words and in the intercession of Moses, his servant, for their sins, where God says: “I will destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32:10). Moses intercedes, more ready to be destroyed for their sake than to have them destroyed, knowing that he is dealing with the Merciful One, who, since he would in no way destroy Moses himself, would also spare them for his sake.

Let us see how much he has spared them, and continues to spare them. For he brought them into the promised land and preserved that nation until they bound themselves to the greatest of all crimes by killing Christ. And when he uprooted them from that kingdom and scattered them throughout all the kingdoms of the nations [Note: The word “kingdoms” is absent from the manuscripts.], he did not utterly destroy them. Rather, the same people remain, preserved through the succession of their descendants, like Cain, who received a sign so that no one would kill him—that is, destroy him completely (Gen. 4:15).

See how what was said is fulfilled:

> “But he is merciful, and will be propitious toward their sins, and will not destroy them; and he will abound in order to turn away his anger, and will not kindle all his anger.”

For if all his anger—that is, as much as they deserve—were kindled against them, no part of that nation would remain.

Thus God, of whom “mercy and judgment” are sung (Ps. 100:1), in this age makes his sun rise by mercy upon the good and the evil; and at the end of the age, by judgment, he punishes the wicked, separated from his eternal light, with eternal darkness.

### 23

Then, lest we seem to do violence to the divine words, and where it says, “He will not destroy them,” we should say, “But afterward he will destroy them,” let us observe in this very psalm a most customary scriptural manner of speaking, by which this question may be resolved much more carefully and truly.

Certainly, speaking of these same people a little later, after recalling what the Egyptians had suffered on their account, and recalling the final plague, he says:

> “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of their labor in the tents of Ham. And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the desert. And he led them in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies. And he brought them to the mountain of his holiness, the mountain that his right hand acquired. And he drove out the nations before them, and distributed the land to them by lot, by the measuring cord of distribution.”

If someone raises a question against these words and says, “How does he recall that all these things were bestowed upon them, when those who were freed from Egypt were not led into the promised land, since they died?” what shall we answer except that they are said to have been led there [Note: Thus Erasmus and the manuscripts. Lovaniensis has “led.”] because it was the same people through the succession of their children?

Thus, when we hear—especially since these are words of the future tense—

> “He will be propitious toward their sins, and will not destroy them; and he will abound in order to turn away his anger, and will not kindle all his anger,”

we should understand this as fulfilled in those of whom the Apostle says:

> “So therefore at the present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.”

Hence he also says:

> “Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews” (Rom. 11:5, 1; Phil. 3:5).

Scripture foresaw these people, who from that nation were going to believe in Christ and receive the remission of sins, even extending to that greatest crime in which, raging against him, they killed the physician himself.

This is the full meaning of the words:

> “But he is merciful, and will be propitious toward their sins, and will not destroy them; and he will abound in order to turn away his anger,”

because he also forgave that deed: that his only Son was killed by them. “And he will not kindle all his anger,” because a remnant has been saved.

### 24

“And he remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return.”

Therefore, by calling and showing mercy to them through his grace, he himself recalled them, because they could not return by their own power. For how does flesh return—a spirit that goes away and does not return—when the weight of its merits drives it downward into the depths and remoteness of evils, except through the election of grace?

Grace is not given as a reward according to merits, but freely as a gift, so that the ungodly may be justified and the lost sheep may return—not by its own strength, however, but carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders (Luke 15:5). It could lose itself while wandering of its own accord, but it could not find itself, nor would it be found at all, unless the shepherd’s mercy sought it.

Nor does that son fail to belong to this sheep, who, returning to himself, said: “I will arise and go to my father.” By a hidden calling and inspiration, he too was sought and raised up, by none other than him who gives life to all things. And when he was found, by whom was he found except by him who came to save and seek what had perished (Luke 19:10)? For he was dead and came to life; he had perished and was found (Luke 15:18, 24).

That other difficult question is also resolved in this way: in Proverbs, speaking of the way of iniquity, Scripture says, “All who walk in it will not return” (Prov. 2:19). This seems to have been said as though one should despair of all the wicked. But Scripture was commending grace: a person can walk in that way by himself, but cannot return by himself unless recalled by grace.

### 25. [verses 40–51]

These people, then, perverse and embittering:

> “How often they embittered him in the desert and provoked him to anger in the waterless place! And they turned back and tempted God, and embittered the Holy One of Israel.”

He repeats the same unbelief of theirs that he had already recalled above. But the reason for repeating it is that the plagues he inflicted upon the Egyptians on their account might also be remembered. They certainly ought to have remembered all these things and not proved ungrateful.

What follows, finally?

> “They did not remember his hand, on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor.”

And he begins to recount what he did to the Egyptians:

> “He set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis. And he turned their rivers into blood, and their rains, so that they could not drink them”—or rather, “the outpourings of their waters,” as some understand more accurately what is written in Greek, τὰ ὀμβρήματα, which in Latin we call *scaturigines*, waters bubbling up from below.

For the Egyptians dug and found blood instead of water.

> “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it consumed them; and the frog, and it destroyed them. And he gave their fruit to rust” [Note: The printed editions have *aerugini* (“mildew” or “rust”). But the more authoritative manuscripts have *rubigini* (“rust”); Augustine notes below, in this *Enarratio*, section 27, that some interpreted it as *aerugo*.], “and their labors to the locust. And he killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost. And he gave their cattle to hail, and their possessions to fire. He sent against them the anger of his indignation: indignation, anger, and tribulation, an immission through evil angels. He made a way for the path of his anger, and did not spare their souls from death, and enclosed their cattle in death. And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of their labors in the tents of Ham.”

### 26

All these punishments of the Egyptians can be explained by allegorical interpretation, according to how each person wishes to understand them and compare them with the matters to which they should be referred. We too shall attempt to do this; and we shall do it all the more appropriately insofar as we have been helped by God.

For this is required by those words of this psalm in which it was said:

> “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning.”

For this reason some things are also said here that we do not read as having happened to the Egyptians at all, although all their plagues are carefully woven together in order in Exodus. Since we are certain that what is not said there was not said without reason in the psalm, and since we can interpret it only figuratively, we should at the same time understand that the other things whose occurrence is established were either done or recorded for the sake of some figurative meaning.

Scripture does this in many passages of the prophetic utterances. It says something that is not found in the event it appears to recall, or is found to have happened otherwise, so that we may understand that it is not saying what one might suppose, but rather what ought more attentively to be understood.

An example is:

> “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8).

This was plainly not fulfilled in the kingdom of that Solomon, about which one might think that this psalm was speaking, since it was speaking of Christ the Lord.

In the plagues of the Egyptians, therefore, which are recorded in the book called Exodus—where Scripture took particular care to relate in order everything by which they were afflicted—we do not find the statement contained in this psalm:

> “And he gave their fruit to rust.”

Likewise, when it says, “And he gave their cattle to hail,” and adds, “And their possessions to fire,” we read in Exodus about cattle killed by hail (Exod. 9:25), but we do not read anywhere that their possessions were burned by fire. Although voices and fires occurred together with the hail, as thunder ordinarily accompanies lightning, it is nevertheless not written that anything was handed over to fire to be burned.

Finally, the tender things that hail could not damage are said not to have been struck—that is, injured by hard blows—and afterward the locust consumed them (Exod. 10:1–15).

Likewise, what is said here, “And their mulberry trees with frost,” is not found in Exodus. For frost differs greatly from hail: on clear winter nights the earth grows white with frost.

27. What these things signify, let the expositor explain as he can; let the reader and hearer judge as is right. The water turned into blood seems to me to signify thinking carnally about the causes of things. The dog-fly (*cynomyia*) signifies canine ways, which, when born, do not even see their parents. The frog is the most talkative vanity.

Blight secretly causes harm; some have also interpreted it as *aerugo* (“rust”), others as *canicula* (“little dog”) [Note: [Col. 1000] Several manuscripts read *caniculum*.]. To what vice is this evil more aptly compared than to excessive self-confidence, which appears only with the greatest difficulty? For there is a harmful vapor which works secretly in fruits, just as hidden pride does in one’s conduct, when someone thinks himself to be something although he is nothing (Gal. VI, 3).

The locust is malice that wounds with the mouth, namely through false testimony. Hail is iniquity that takes away what belongs to another, from which thefts, robberies, and acts of plunder arise; yet the plunderer himself is laid waste still more by his own vice. Frost signifies the vice by which love of one’s neighbor freezes in the darkness of folly, as though in the cold of night.

As for fire, if the fire mentioned here is not the fire that accompanied the hail from the flashing clouds—for here he said, “He delivered their possession to the fire,” thereby clearly signifying that it was burned, whereas that fire is not recorded as having done so—I think it signifies the monstrousness of anger, by which even homicide may be committed.

The death of the cattle, I think, figuratively represents the loss of chastity. For we share with cattle the desire from which offspring arises [Col. 1001]. To have this desire subdued and properly ordered is the virtue of chastity. The death of the firstborn signifies the loss of that very justice by which each person is social toward the human race.

But whether the figurative meanings of these things are as I have stated, or whether they are better understood in some other way, who would not be struck by the fact that the Egyptians are struck by ten plagues and that the tablets are written with ten commandments by which God’s people are governed? Since I have spoken elsewhere about comparing these things with one another—that is, the plagues and the commandments—there is no need to burden the exposition of this psalm with it here [Note: [Col. 1001] *Sermon on the Ten Plagues and the Commandments.*].

We merely point out that here too, although not in the same order, the ten plagues of the Egyptians are nevertheless recalled. For in place of the three found in Exodus but not here—gnats, boils, and darkness (Exod. VIII, 17; IX, 10; X, 22)—three others are recalled here that are not found there: blight, frost, and fire—not the fire of lightning, but the fire to which their possession was delivered, a fact not recorded there.

28. It is sufficiently clear here that, by God’s judgment, these things are carried out against them through evil angels, in this evil age, as though in Egypt and in the plain of Tanis, where we must remain humble until the age comes in which we may deserve to be exalted from this humility. For Egypt in the Hebrew language signifies “Darkness” or “Tribulations,” while in that language Tanis, as I mentioned, is understood to mean “Humble Command.”

Accordingly, when this psalm was speaking of the plagues themselves, it inserted the following statement about evil angels—something that must not be passed over casually: “He sent against them,” it says, “the anger of his indignation; indignation and anger and tribulation, a sending through evil angels.”

No believer is unaware that the devil and his angels are so evil that eternal fire has been prepared for them. But that a sending should be imposed through them upon those whom the Lord God judges worthy of such punishment seems harsh to those who are less able to consider how the supreme justice of God makes good use even of the wicked. For, insofar as concerns their substance, who else made them but God himself? Yet he did not make them wicked. Nevertheless, because he is good, he uses them well—that is, suitably and justly—just as, conversely, the wicked use his good creatures badly.

God therefore uses evil angels not only to punish the wicked, as in all the cases of which the Psalm speaks, and as in the case of King Ahab, whom a deceptive spirit, by God’s will, led astray so that he would fall in battle (III Kings XXII, 22), but also to test and reveal the good, as he did in Job.

As for the bodily matter of the visible elements, I think that both good and evil angels can use these things to the extent of the power granted to each, just as good and evil human beings use such things to the extent permitted by the measure of human weakness. We use earth, water, air, and fire not only for the necessities that sustain us, but also for many superfluous and playful purposes and for wonderfully artful works. The countless devices called *μηχανήματα* (“mechanisms” or “ contrivances”) are fashioned by skillful manipulation of these elements.

The angels, both good and evil, have far greater power over these things than we do, although the good certainly have greater power; nevertheless, they have only as much as God’s will and ordinance commands or permits, just as is the case with us. For we cannot do everything we wish with these things.

In the most trustworthy book we read that the devil was even able to bring fire down from heaven and consume, with a marvelous and dreadful assault, so great a number of the holy man’s animals. Perhaps no believer would dare attribute this to the devil if it were not read on the authority of holy Scripture. Yet that man, righteous, courageous, and devoutly wise by God’s gift, did not say, “The Lord gave, the devil took away,” but, “The Lord gave, the Lord took away” (Job I, 16, 21). He knew perfectly well that, although the devil had been able to do something through those elements, he would not have done it against God’s servant unless his Lord had willed and permitted it. He was confounding the devil’s malice [Note: [Col. 1002] Thus several manuscripts. Others have, “he despised the devil’s malice”; and some, “he confidently despised it.” But nearly all editions read: “he confidently believed that the devil’s malice had been carried out.”], since he knew who would use those things in testing him.

But the devil works in the children of disobedience as though in his own slaves (Eph. II, 2), just as human beings work with their own animals; even there, however, only to the extent permitted by God’s just judgment. There is a difference between a situation in which his power over his own subjects, whom he handles as he pleases, is restrained by a greater power, and one in which power is granted to him even over those who are alien to him. A person may do with his own animal, insofar as human capacity allows, what he wishes; yet he certainly does not do so if he is prevented by a greater power. With another person’s animal, however, he waits to be granted authority by its owner.

In the first case, therefore, a power that already existed is restrained; in the second, a power that did not exist is granted.

29. If this is so, and God inflicted those plagues upon the Egyptians through evil angels, shall we dare to say that the water was turned into blood by those same angels, and that the frogs were produced by those same angels—things similar to which Pharaoh’s magicians were also able to produce by their sorceries—so that the evil angels would stand on both sides, afflicting the Egyptians on the one hand and deceiving them on the other, according to the judgment and administration [Note: [Col. 1002] More manuscripts read “disposition.”] of the most just and almighty God, who justly makes use even of the malice of the wicked?

I do not dare say so. Why, then, were Pharaoh’s magicians entirely unable to produce gnats (Exod. VII, 20, 22; VIII, 6, 7, 17, 18)? Was it because those evil angels themselves were not permitted to do this [Note: [Col. 1002] Some manuscripts of good authority read, “are able”?]? Or is the cause hidden—and, as is more truly said, beyond the reach of our powers of inquiry?

For if we suppose that God did those things through evil angels because punishments were being inflicted rather than benefits bestowed, as though God inflicted punishments through no one but them, making them the executioners of the heavenly army, it would follow that we should also believe Sodom to have been overthrown through evil angels, and that evil angels were received as guests by Abraham and Lot. Far be it from us to think anything contrary to the clearest testimony of Scripture (Gen. XVIII and XIX).

It is therefore evident that such things can be done to human beings through both good and evil angels. What ought to be done, and when, is hidden from me; but it is not hidden from the one who does it, nor from the one to whom he chooses to reveal it. Nevertheless, insofar as divine Scripture guides our understanding, we read that punishments are inflicted upon the wicked both through good angels, as upon the people of Sodom, and through evil angels, as upon the Egyptians. But that the righteous are tested and proved through bodily punishments by good angels does not occur to me.

30. As for the present passage of this psalm: if we do not dare attribute to evil angels the marvelous things done with created beings, we have things that we can attribute to them without hesitation—the deaths of the cattle, the deaths of the firstborn, and especially that by which everything else is bound together, the hardening of their hearts, so that they would not be willing to let God’s people go.

When God is said to do this iniquitous and most wicked obstinacy (Exod. IV, 21), he does it not by instigating or inspiring them, but by abandoning them, so that those evil angels may work in the children of disobedience (Eph. II, 2) what God justly and rightly permits.

The statement of the prophet Isaiah is also understood in this way: “Lord, behold, you were angry, and we sinned; therefore we went astray, and we all became like the unclean” (Isa. LXIV, 5–6). For something had preceded, on account of which God, being most justly angry, would withdraw his light from them, so that the blindness of the human mind would stumble into sins that cannot be defended by any evasion as though they were not sins, by turning aside and wandering from the path of justice.

It is also written in another psalm concerning these same Egyptians that God turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants (Ps. CIV, 25). It is rightly believed that God did this through those evil angels, so that the diseased minds of the children of unbelief might be stirred by those angels, to whom the same vices are congenial, into hatred of God’s people, and so that those marvelous events might then follow for the frightening and correction of the good.

Those evils of conduct that we have said were signified by these bodily plagues—hence the statement, “I will open my mouth in parables”—are also most appropriately believed to be carried out by evil angels against those whom divine equity subjects to them.

For when what the Apostle says takes place, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. I, 24), are evil angels not there, as it were, handling the material of their own work and rejoicing in it? Human depravity has been most justly subjected to them, except in the case of those whom grace liberates.

“And who is sufficient for these things?” (II Cor. II, 16). Why, after saying, “He sent against them the anger of his indignation; indignation and anger and tribulation, a sending through evil angels,” did he add, “He made a path for his anger”? Whose insight is sufficient to penetrate and grasp the meaning hidden in such profound depths?

There was a path of God’s anger by which he would punish the impiety of the Egyptians according to a hidden justice. But he made a road for that path, bringing them, as it were, from hidden places through evil angels into manifest crimes, so that he might exact openly evident vengeance upon those who were openly impious [Note: [Col. 1003] The editions read “leading them through”; the manuscripts, “bringing them forth.”].

No one is freed from the power of evil angels except by the grace of God, of which the Apostle says: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” [Note: [Col. 1003] Thus the better manuscripts. Others, with the editions, read “of his brightness”] (Col. I, 13). This people prefigured that reality when it was rescued from the power of the Egyptians and transferred into the kingdom of the promised land flowing with milk and honey, which signifies the sweetness of grace.

31. [vv. 52–53.] After recalling the plagues of the Egyptians, the Psalm continues and says: “And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the wilderness. And he led them in hope, and they did not fear, and the sea covered their enemies.”

This is fulfilled in a far greater way when, inwardly rescued from the power of darkness, we are transferred in mind into the kingdom of God and are made sheep of God according to spiritual pastures, walking in this age as though in a wilderness, since our faith is visible to no one. Hence the Apostle says: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).

We are led in hope because we have been saved in hope; and we ought not to fear. For “if God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII, 24, 31). “And the sea covered our enemies”: in Baptism he abolished them through the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 1004] Most manuscripts read “remission.” The Regius manuscript reads “remission of sins.”].

32. [v. 54.] Then it continues: “And he brought them into the mountain of his sanctification.” How much better is this understood as the holy Church? “The mountain which his right hand acquired.” How much more exalted is the Church that Christ acquired, of whom it was said: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1).

“And he cast out the nations from before them”—and from before his faithful; for, in a certain sense, the nations are the evil spirits of pagan errors. “And he divided the land among them by lot, by the measuring-line of distribution.” In us also one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each person his own gifts as he wills (I Cor. XII, 11).

33. [vv. 55–58.] “And he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.” “In the tents,” he says, “of the nations he made the tribes of Israel dwell.” I think this should be explained spiritually in the following way: that through the grace of Christ we may be raised to the heavenly glory from which the sinning angels were cast out and thrown down.

That crooked and embittering generation, because it did not put off the garment of old age through these bodily benefits, nevertheless tested and provoked the Most High God, and did not keep his testimonies. “And they turned aside and did not keep the covenant, like their fathers.” For by a certain covenant and agreement they said, “Everything that the Lord our God has spoken, we will do and hear” (Exod. XIX, 8).

It should certainly be noted that he says, “like their fathers.” Although throughout the text of the Psalm he seemed to be speaking of the same human beings, it now becomes evident that he is speaking of those who were already in the promised land, while their fathers are called those who became embittered in the wilderness.

34. “They turned aside,” he says, “like a crooked bow”—or, as some manuscripts have it, “like a perverse bow.” What this means appears more clearly in what follows, where he says: “And they provoked him to anger on their hills.” He signifies that they rushed into idolatry.

A perverse bow, therefore, is one directed not for the name of the Lord but against the name of the Lord, who said to that same people: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. XX, 3). By the bow he signifies the intention of the mind.

Finally, expressing this same point more plainly, he says: “And with their carved images they provoked him to jealousy.”

35. [vv. 59–60.] “God heard and despised”—that is, he took notice and avenged. “And he reduced Israel to utter nothingness.” For when God despised them, what remained of those who had been what they were only with God’s help?

He is clearly recalling that event when they were defeated by the Philistines in the time of Eli the priest, the Ark of the Lord was captured, and they were devastated in a great slaughter (I Kings IV, 10–11).

This is what he means by: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle where he dwelt among human beings.” He elegantly explained why he rejected his tabernacle when he added, “where he dwelt among human beings.” Since they were not worthy to be those among whom he dwelt, why should he not reject the tabernacle, which he had established not for his own sake but for theirs—those whom he now judged unworthy to be his dwelling?

36. [v. 61.] “And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy.” He calls the Ark itself—the source from which they seemed invincible and in which they took pride—their strength and their beauty [Note: [Col. 1005] Most manuscripts read “in which they took pleasure.”].

Later, when they were living wickedly and boasting in the temple of the Lord, he frightens them through the prophet, saying: “See what I did to Shiloh, where my tabernacle was” (Jer. VII, 12).

37. [vv. 62–63.] “And he shut up his people under the sword, and despised his inheritance. Fire devoured their young men”—that is, anger. “And their maidens were not lamented,” because even this was impossible amid the fear of the enemy.

38. [v. 64.] “Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.” For the sons of Eli fell by the sword; one of their wives was widowed and soon died in childbirth, and because of the same disturbance she could not be mourned with the honor of a funeral (I Kings IV, 19–20).

39. [v. 65.] “And the Lord awoke as one sleeping.” He appears to sleep when he gives his people into the hands of those whom he hates, at which time they say to them: “Where is your God?” (Ps. XLI, 11).

He therefore awoke as one sleeping, as a powerful man overcome by wine. No one would dare say this of God unless his Spirit had said it. For he spoke as though in response to the insults of the impious, who imagine that he sleeps for a long time like a drunkard whenever he does not come to the aid of human beings as quickly as they think [Note: [Col. 1005] Two manuscripts read “as they demand.”].

40. [v. 66.] “And he struck his enemies in their hind parts”—those, certainly, who rejoiced that they had been able to capture his Ark; for they were struck in their seats (I Kings V, 6).

This seems to me to be a sign of the punishment by which anyone will be tormented if he looks back toward the things behind him, which, as the Apostle says, he ought to regard as refuse (Phil. III, 8). Those who receive God’s testament in such a way that they do not strip off their former vanity resemble the hostile peoples who placed the captured Ark of the Testament beside their idols.

And those former things indeed fall even against their will, because “all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell; but the Ark of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL, 6–7)—the hidden mystery of the Testament, the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal Word of God is.

But those who loved the things behind them will most justly be tormented by those very things: “For he gave them everlasting disgrace.”

41. [vv. 67–68.] “And he rejected,” he says, “the tabernacle of Joseph, and he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim. And he chose the tribe of Judah.”

He did not say, “He rejected the tabernacle of Reuben,” who was Jacob’s firstborn, nor those who followed Reuben and preceded Judah by birth, so that, with those rejected and not chosen, the tribe of Judah might be chosen.

It could reasonably have been said that those tribes were rejected, since even in Jacob’s blessing, when he blessed his sons, he gravely condemned and detested their sins (Gen. XLIX, 1–7), although the tribe of Levi deserved to be a priestly tribe among them, and Moses also came from it (Exod. II, 1).

Nor did he say, “He rejected the tabernacle of Benjamin,” or, “He did not choose the tribe of Benjamin,” from which a king had already begun to arise; for Saul had been chosen from it (I Kings IX, 1–2). Since this occurred so near in time to the rejection of Saul and the choice of David (ibid. XVI, 1, 13), the statement could appropriately have been made about Benjamin. Yet it was not made.

Instead, he named especially those who appeared to excel through more distinguished merits. Joseph had fed his father and brothers in Egypt; although wickedly sold, he was most justly exalted on account of his piety, chastity, and wisdom (Gen. XLI, 40). Ephraim was preferred to his elder brother by the blessing of his grandfather Jacob (Gen. XLVIII, 19). Yet God rejected the tabernacle of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.

What else, then, do we understand through these names of illustrious merit except that the whole people, in its ancient desire, seeking earthly rewards from the Lord, was rejected and condemned? The tribe of Judah, however, was chosen—not on account of Judah’s own merits. Joseph’s merits were far greater; but through the tribe of Judah, since Christ arose from it according to the flesh, Scripture testifies that the new people of Christ was preferred to that ancient people, as the Lord opened his mouth in parables.

From this point onward, too, we better understand “Mount Zion, which he loved” as the Church of Christ, which worships God not for the bodily benefits of the present age but looks far ahead with the eyes of faith toward future and eternal rewards. For Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation.”

42. [v. 69.] Finally it continues: “And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns”—or, as certain interpreters have rendered the unfamiliar word, “his sanctified place.”

The unicorns are rightly understood as those whose firm hope is raised toward that one thing of which another psalm says: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

The sanctified place of God is, according to the Apostle Peter, understood as the holy people and royal priesthood (I Pet. II, 9).

As for what follows, “On the earth which he founded forever”: the Greek manuscripts have *εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*. Whether we render this as “forever” or “for the age” lies within the discretion of the Latin translators, since the expression signifies both. Hence one form is found in some Latin manuscripts and the other in others. Some also have the plural, “for the ages”; we did not find this in the Greek manuscripts available to us [Col. 1007].

What believer, however, could doubt that the Church, even though some depart and others come, and though it passes from this mortal life, has nevertheless been founded forever?

43. [vv. 70–71.] “And he chose David his servant.” The tribe of Judah, then, on account of David; David, however, on account of Christ. The tribe of Judah, therefore, on account of Christ, when he passed by and the blind cried out, “Have mercy on us, son of David,” and immediately received the light of his mercy (Matt. XX, 30, 34), because what they cried out was true.

The Apostle does not mention this casually but commends it attentively when he writes to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my gospel, for which I suffer even to chains as a criminal; but the word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II, 8–9).

The Savior himself, therefore, made according to the flesh from the seed of David, is signified in this passage by the name David, as the Lord opens his mouth in parables.

Nor should it trouble us that, after saying, “And he chose David”—by which name he signified Christ—he added “his servant,” not “his son.” Rather, let us recognize from this that the reference is not to the substance of the Only-Begotten, coeternal with the Father, but to the form of a servant assumed from the seed of David.

44. “And he took him from the flocks of sheep; from behind the ewes giving birth he took him, to shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance.”

That David, from whose seed Christ’s flesh comes, was transferred from the pastoral care of animals to the rule of human beings. Our David, however—Jesus himself—was transferred from human beings to human beings, from the Jews to the Gentiles; nevertheless, according to the parable, he was taken and transferred from sheep to sheep.

For at present there are no churches of the Jews in that land belonging to Christ, as there were among the circumcised at the time of the recent passion and resurrection of our Lord. Concerning those churches the Apostle says: “I was personally unknown to the churches of Judaea that are in Christ; they heard only that he who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once devastated, and they glorified God in me” (Gal. I, 22–24).

Those churches have now passed from the circumcised peoples. Accordingly, in the Judaea that is now on earth, Christ is no longer present in this way; he has been taken away from there. Now he feeds the flocks of the Gentiles.

Certainly, he was taken from behind the ewes giving birth. For those earlier churches were of the kind described in the Song of Songs to the one Church composed of many—that is, to the one flock whose members are many flocks. Of such it is said: “Your teeth”—that is, those by which you speak, or by which you bring others into your body, as though by eating them—“are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song IV, 2).

At that time they laid aside, as it were, the fleeces that were the burdens of the world, when they placed the prices of the things they had sold at the feet of the Apostles (Acts II, 45; IV, 34). They were ascending from that washing of which the Apostle Peter reminds them, since they were troubled that they had shed Christ’s blood, saying: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts II, 38).

They bore twins through the twin works of the two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. Hence none among them was barren.

From behind these ewes giving birth our David was taken, and now he feeds other flocks among the Gentiles—both Jacob and Israel. For thus it was said: “To shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance.”

These sheep are not alienated from that seed which is Jacob and Israel merely because they come from the Gentiles. For they are the seed of Abraham, the seed of promise, concerning which the Lord said to him: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI, 12). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “It is not the children of the flesh who are counted as seed, but the children of the promise” (Rom. IX, 8).

The believers to whom he said, “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. III, 29), were from the Gentiles.

When he says, “Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance,” Scripture, according to its custom, repeats the same meaning.
