Unless perhaps someone wishes to distinguish the words in this way: that Jacob serves in the present age, while Israel is then the eternal inheritance of God, when he sees God face to face—from which he received the name Israel (Gen. XXXII, 28).

45. [v. 72.] “And he fed them,” he says, “in the innocence of his heart.” Who was more innocent than the one who possessed no sin—not merely one by which he could be conquered, but even one which he could conquer?

“And he led them by the understanding of his hands”—or, as some manuscripts have it, “by the understandings of his hands.”

Someone else might have thought it more fitting to say, “In the innocence of his hands and the understanding of his heart.” But the one who knew better than others what he was saying preferred to join innocence to the heart and understanding to the hands.

I think this was because many consider themselves innocent when they do not commit evil out of fear that they will suffer if they do so; yet they would wish to do it if they could do so with impunity. Such people may appear to possess innocence of the hands, but not of the heart.

And what sort or quality of innocence is this if it is not in the heart, where the human being was made in the image of God?

When he says, “In the understanding,” or “intelligence,” “of his hands he led them,” he seems to me to have called that intelligence the intelligence that he himself produces in believers. Hence the words “of his hands,” since making belongs to the hands. Yet the hands of God can be understood in this way [Note: [Col. 1008] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “but if they can thus be understood.”], because Christ is both human and God.

That David, from whose seed Christ came, could not have done this among the people over whom he ruled as a human being. But Christ does this, to whom the faithful soul can rightly say: “Give me understanding, and I will search out your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 34).

Therefore, lest we go astray from him while trusting in an understanding that seems to come from ourselves, let us submit ourselves in faith to his hands. Let him produce understanding in us, so that by the understanding of his hands he may lead us, rescued from error, and bring us to the place where we can no longer go astray.

This is the fruit of God’s people: attending to the law of God and inclining their ear to the words of his mouth, so that they may direct their heart toward him [Note: [Col. 1008] The editions read “their heart upward.” The manuscripts more correctly read “their heart,” a phrase taken from v. 8 of this Psalm.], and so that their spirit may be faithful with him [Col. 1009] and not be changed into a crooked and embittering generation [Note: [Col. 1009] Three manuscripts read “so that it may not imitate the generation,” and so forth.].

But when all these things have been announced to them—not only those belonging to the present life but also those belonging to eternal life, and not only for receiving the rewards of good works but also for performing good works themselves—let them place their hope in God.

## Exposition of Psalm 78

[Note: [Col. 1009] Delivered after the exposition of Psalm 77, concerning which see below, no. 3.]

1. [v. 1.] I do not think we need linger over the very brief and simple title of this psalm. But we plainly know that the prophecy placed here beforehand has been fulfilled.

For when these things were sung in the time of King David, nothing of this kind had yet happened through the hostility of the nations to the city of Jerusalem or to the temple of God, which had not yet been built. For who does not know that after David’s death his son Solomon built the temple for God?

What is therefore spoken of as past was seen in the spirit as still future: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance.” By the same manner of speaking the following was also prophesied concerning the Lord’s passion: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22), along with the other things in that psalm that are narrated as though they had already happened, although they were still to come.

Nor is it surprising that these things are said to God. They are not reported to one who is ignorant of them, since they are foreknown through his revelation. Rather, the soul speaks to God with the affection of devotion, which God knows [Note: [Col. 1009] Several manuscripts read, “for what does God not see?”].

Angels also announce to human beings things that human beings do not know; but what they announce to God, they announce to one who already knows, when they present our prayers to him and, in an ineffable manner, consult eternal truth concerning their actions, as though it were an immutable law.

This man of God, therefore, says to God what he learns from God, like a disciple speaking to a teacher who is not ignorant but judging: either approving what he has taught or reproving what he has not taught. This is especially so because, under the appearance of a person praying [Note: [Col. 1009] Thus several manuscripts. The editions read, “under the appearance of the present person.”], the Prophet transforms into himself those who would exist at the time when these things were to occur.

In prayer people commonly say to God what he has done in carrying out judgment, and add a request that he now show mercy and spare. In this way, too, the things foretold here are spoken by the one who foretells them as though they were spoken by those to whom they happened; and the very lamentation and prayer is prophecy.

## 2. [“God, the nations have come into your inheritance”]

“God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have reduced Jerusalem to a place for guarding fruit. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.”

If anyone among us thinks that in this prophecy we should understand the devastation of Jerusalem carried out by Titus, the Roman emperor, when the Lord Jesus Christ was already being proclaimed among the nations after his resurrection and ascension, I do not see how it could be said that that people were already God’s inheritance: they did not hold fast to Christ, and, having rejected and killed him, became rejected themselves because they refused to believe in him even after his resurrection and, in addition, killed his martyrs.

For from that people of Israel, all who believed in Christ—those to whom Christ was presented and, in a certain way, the promise was beneficially and fruitfully fulfilled—are the children of promise; they are reckoned as the offspring (Romans 9:8), and they belong to God’s inheritance. The Lord himself says of them: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

From there came Joseph, a righteous man, and the virgin Mary, who gave birth to Christ (Matthew 1:16); from there came John the Baptist, the friend of the bridegroom, and his parents Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:5); from there came the aged Simeon and the widow Anna, who heard Christ—not yet speaking—with the bodily sense, but knew him in the spirit while he was still an infant and unable to speak (Luke 2:25, 36); from there came the blessed Apostles; from there came Nathanael, in whom there was no deceit (John 1:47); from there came another Joseph, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God (John 19:38; Luke 23:51); from there came that great multitude which went before and followed his beast of burden, saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9). Among them was also the gathering of children in whom he declared fulfilled the words: “From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8:3).

From there also came those who, after his resurrection, were baptized—three thousand on one day and five thousand on another (Acts 2:41; 4:4)—fused by the fire of charity into one soul and one heart. No one called anything his own, but everything was held in common among them (Acts 4:32). From there came the holy deacons, among whom Stephen was crowned with martyrdom before the Apostles (Acts 7:58). From there came the many churches of Judea that were in Christ, to which Paul was unknown by face (Galatians 1:22), though famous for his savagery and even more renowned for Christ’s most merciful grace. From there also came he himself, according to the prophecy previously spoken about him: “A ravening wolf, in the morning seizing prey and in the evening dividing the spoil” (Genesis 49:27)—that is, first seizing people as a persecutor for death, and later feeding them as a preacher for life.

These were God’s inheritance from that people. Hence the least of the Apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), the teacher of the nations, himself says:

“I ask, then: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the offspring of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.”

This people, which came from that nation into Christ’s body, is God’s inheritance. For when the Apostle says, “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew,” he is certainly responding to that psalm where it is written, “For the Lord will not reject his people”; and there follows, “He will not abandon his inheritance” (Psalm 93:14). There it is clearly shown that such a people is God’s inheritance.

To make this point, the Apostle had first recalled the prophetic testimony about the future unbelief of the people of Israel: “All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Romans 10:21; Isaiah 65:2). Therefore, lest anyone misunderstand and think that the whole of that people had been condemned for the crime of unbelief and contradiction, he immediately added:

“I ask, then: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the offspring of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

Here he shows which people he meant: the people of earlier times. If God had rejected and condemned all of them, Paul himself could not be Christ’s apostle, an Israelite descended from Abraham and of the tribe of Benjamin.

He adds a very necessary testimony, saying:

“Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.’ But what does the divine reply say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.’ So also at the present time a remnant has been saved by the election of grace.”

These remnants are from that nation and constitute God’s inheritance—not those of whom he says shortly afterward, “But the rest were hardened.” For he says:

“What then? Israel did not obtain what it was seeking; but the election obtained it, while the rest were blinded” (Romans 11:1–7).

This election, these remnants, this people of God whom God has not rejected, is called his inheritance. But in that Israel which did not obtain this, in those who were hardened, there was no longer God’s inheritance—so that, after Christ’s glorification in heaven, in the time of the emperor Titus, one could say, “God, the nations have come into your inheritance,” and the rest of what appears in this psalm to have been foretold concerning the devastation of that people, temple, and city.

## 3.

Accordingly, we must either understand these things as having been done by other enemies before Christ came in the flesh—for at that time there was no other inheritance of God, when the holy Prophets were present, and when the people were led away into Babylonian captivity and that nation was grievously devastated (2 Kings 24:14); and under Antiochus the Maccabees also endured dreadful sufferings and were crowned most gloriously (2 Maccabees 7)—or, if the inheritance of God mentioned here is to be understood as occurring after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, we must understand those things as having been suffered by his Church from the worshipers of idols and the enemies of Christ’s name, amid the great multitude of martyrs.

Although Asaph is interpreted as “Synagogue,” which means “assembly,” and although that name became more customarily attached to the Jewish nation, we have already shown clearly enough in another psalm that this Church too can be called an assembly, and that the ancient people were called a church [Note: [Col. 1011] Above, in the exposition of Psalm 77, section 3.].

This Church, this inheritance of God, was gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision—that is, from the people of Israel and from the remaining nations—through the stone which the builders rejected, and which became the cornerstone (Psalm 117:22). In that corner, as it were, two walls coming from opposite directions would be joined together.

“For he is our peace, who made both one, in order to create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconciling both in one body to God” (Ephesians 2:14–16) [Note: [Col. 1011] Manuscripts: “transforming,” instead of “reconciling.”]. In that body we are children of God, crying, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6): “Abba” according to their language, “Father” according to ours; for *Abba* means the same as *Father*.

Therefore the Lord, who said, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24), showing that the promise of his presence had been returned to that nation, nevertheless says elsewhere:

“I have other sheep that are not from this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

He signifies the nations whom he was going to bring—not, indeed, through his bodily presence [Note: [Col. 1012] Several manuscripts: “through his bodily presence itself.”], so that the statement “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” might remain true, but through his Gospel, which they were going to spread:

“Beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Romans 10:15). For “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

Hence the Apostle also says:

“I say, then, that Christ Jesus became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.”

There is the meaning of “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel.” Then the Apostle continues:

“But the nations are to glorify God for his mercy.”

There is the meaning of “I have other sheep that are not from this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.”

Both statements are briefly expressed in the words the same Apostle recalls from the Prophet: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Romans 15:8–10).

This one flock under one shepherd is God’s inheritance—not only the Father’s but also the Son’s. For it is the Son’s voice that says, “The boundaries have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is glorious to me” (Psalm 15:6). And the voice of this inheritance is found in the Prophet: “Lord our God, possess us” (Isaiah 26:13, according to the Septuagint).

The Father did not leave this inheritance to the Son by dying; rather, the Son himself wonderfully acquired it through his death and possessed it through his resurrection.

## 4.

If, then, the words sung in the prophecy of this psalm—“God, the nations have come into your inheritance”—are to be understood of this inheritance, so that we take the nations to have come into the Church not by believing but by persecuting it, that is, as having invaded it with the intention of destroying and utterly wiping it out, as the examples of so many persecutions have shown, then what follows—“They have defiled your holy temple”—must be understood not of wood and stones but of the people themselves. The Apostle Peter says that God’s house is built from them as from living stones (1 Peter 2:5).

The Apostle Paul therefore says most plainly: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

The persecutors thus defiled this temple in those whom, by terrifying or torturing them, they forced to deny Christ, and whom they compelled with great insistence to supplicate idols. Many of these were restored through repentance and cleansed from that defilement. For the voice of one who repents is:

“Cleanse me from my guilt,” and, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Psalm 50:4, 12).

Now what follows—“They have reduced Jerusalem to a place for guarding fruit”—is also rightly understood of the Church under this name:

“Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother,” of whom it is written, “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Galatians 4:26; Isaiah 54:1).

By “a place for guarding fruit,” I think desertion is to be understood: the desolation produced by persecution—that is, something like a place for guarding fruit, since places where fruit is guarded are abandoned when the fruit has passed away.

And certainly, when the Church appeared deserted under the persecution of the nations, the spirits of the martyrs passed into the heavenly banquet, like many excellent and sweet fruits from the Lord’s garden [Note: [Col. 1013] Several manuscripts of good authority: “the Lord’s abundant fruit.”].

## 5. [Verse 2]

“He says: They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.”

What is said as “corpses” is repeated as “flesh,” and what is said as “your servants” is repeated as “your holy ones.” Only “to the birds of the sky” is varied into “to the beasts of the earth.”

Those who translated “corpses” certainly translated better than those who rendered it “mortal bodies.” For “corpses” refers only to the dead, whereas “mortal” can also describe living bodies.

Therefore, as I said, when the spirits of the martyrs had passed like fruits to their cultivator, their corpses and flesh were given to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth—as though anything of them could be lost to the resurrection, when the One who has numbered even our hairs (Matthew 10:30) will restore everything from the hidden recesses of nature.

## 6. [Verse 3]

“They have poured out their blood like water”—that is, abundantly and cheaply—“around Jerusalem.”

If we understand the earthly city of Jerusalem here, we understand their blood to have been poured out around it: the blood of those whom the enemies were able to find outside the walls.

But if we understand that Jerusalem of which it was said, “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” then its surrounding territory extends throughout the whole earth. For in that prophetic passage where it is written, “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband,” shortly afterward it is said to her: “He who redeemed you, the God of Israel, will be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:1, 5).

The surrounding territory of this Jerusalem must therefore be understood in this psalm as extending as far as the Church had then spread: flourishing and growing throughout the whole world, when persecution raged in every part of it and brought about the slaughter of the martyrs, whose blood was poured out like water, while producing great profits in the treasures of heaven.

As for what is added, “And there was no one to bury them”: either it should not seem incredible that in some places the terror was so great that there were absolutely no buriers of the holy bodies; or else, because unburied corpses could lie for a long time in many places, they were eventually buried as though stolen away by the devout.

## 7. [Verse 4]

“We have become,” he says, “a reproach to our neighbors.”

Therefore the death of the saints was precious, not in the sight of human beings, by whom this reproach was inflicted, but “in the sight of the Lord” (Psalm 115:15).

“Mockery and derision”—or, as some translated it, “insult”—“to those who are around us.”

This is a repetition of the preceding statement. What was earlier said as “reproach” is repeated here as “mockery and derision”; and what was earlier said as “our neighbors” is repeated as “those who are around us.”

Accordingly, in relation to the earthly Jerusalem, “neighbors” and “those around its nation” are understood as the other nations. In relation to Jerusalem, our free mother, its neighbors and those around it are the people among whom the Church dwells as it lives among its enemies throughout the whole world.

## 8. [Verse 5]

Then, already pouring out an explicit prayer, by which it can be understood that the preceding affliction was mentioned not as an accusation but as a lament, he says:

“How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?”

He is plainly asking that God not remain angry forever—that such great oppression, tribulation, and desolation should not continue forever, but that he moderate his correction, according to what is said in another psalm:

“You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure” (Psalm 79:6).

For “How long, Lord, will you be angry forever?” is equivalent to saying, “Lord, do not remain angry forever.”

In what follows—“Will your jealousy burn like fire?”—both expressions must be supplied: “how long” and “forever,” as though it said, “How long will your jealousy burn like fire forever?”

The same two expressions must be understood here as the one word “they gave” must be supplied above. The first statement reads, “They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky,” whereas the second does not repeat the verb when it says, “the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.” The verb “they have given” is obviously understood from the preceding line.

God’s anger and jealousy are not disturbances of God, as some people criticize the Scriptures they do not understand [Note: [Col. 1014] The Manichaeans.]. By “anger” is meant the punishment of wickedness; by “jealousy,” the exacting of chastity, so that the soul may not despise the law of its Lord and perish by committing fornication against its God.

Thus, by their actual effect, these things are turbulent in the affliction of human beings; but in God’s ordering they are tranquil. Of him it is said: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquillity” (Wisdom 12:18).

These words sufficiently show that such tribulations befall human beings because of sins, even when they are faithful—although from them the glory of the martyrs flourishes through the merit of patience and through discipline’s rule, when the Lord’s scourging is piously endured [Note: [Col. 1014] Several manuscripts of good authority: “when the Lord’s scourging is endured,” omitting “in.”].

The Maccabees testify to this amid savage torments (2 Maccabees 7), the three young men amid harmless flames (Daniel 3:21), and the holy Prophets in captivity. Although they bear their Father’s correction with the greatest courage and devotion, they do not keep silent about the fact that these sufferings arise from the merits of sinners. Their voice is also heard in the Psalms:

“The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not handed me over to death” (Psalm 117:18).

For “he scourges every son whom he receives”; and “what son is there whom his father does not discipline?” (Hebrews 12:6–7).

## 9. [Verse 6]

As for what he adds, “Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name,” this too is prophecy, not a wish.

These words are not spoken from a desire for harm; rather, what was foreseen in the spirit is proclaimed as coming to pass. So the evils that were going to befall Judas the betrayer in accordance with his merits were prophesied as though they had been wished for.

A Prophet does not command Christ, even though he expresses what he says in the imperative mood:

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one; in your appearance and your beauty, bend the bow, advance prosperously, and reign” (Psalm 44:4–5).

Likewise, the one who says, “Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you,” is not wishing for this but prophesying it.

In his customary manner he repeats the statement, saying, “And upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name.” The nations are repeated by “kingdoms,” and “they have not known you” is repeated by “they have not called upon his name.”

How, then, are we to understand what the Lord says in the Gospel:

“The servant who does not know his master’s will, and does things deserving of blows, will receive few blows; but the servant who knows his master’s will, and does things deserving of blows, will receive many” (Luke 12:48, 47),

if God’s anger is greater against the nations that did not know the Lord? By saying, “Pour out your anger,” he sufficiently indicated by that word that he intended a great amount of anger. Hence he later says, “Repay our neighbors sevenfold.”

Or is the reason that there is a great difference between servants who, although they do not know their master’s will, nevertheless call upon his name, and those who are strangers to the household of so great a master, who are so ignorant of God that they do not even call upon God?

For they call upon idols, demons, or some other creature in place of him—not the Creator, who is blessed forever. He does not mean that those of whom this is prophesied are ignorant of their Lord’s will while nevertheless fearing the Lord himself. Rather, they are so ignorant of the Lord himself that they do not call upon him and are enemies of his name.

There is therefore a great difference between servants who do not know their master’s will but nevertheless live in his household and family, and enemies who are unwilling not only to know the master himself but also to call upon his name, and who moreover attack his servants.

## 10. [Verse 7]

Finally, what follows is:

“Because they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place.”

Jacob represented the Church, just as Esau represented the ancient Synagogue. Hence it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23).

Under this name we can understand the inheritance of God about which we were speaking, into which the nations came after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension in order to invade and devastate it through persecution.

But we must consider how “Jacob’s place” is to be understood. It can more readily be taken as that city in which the temple also stood, where the Lord had commanded the whole nation to assemble for the purpose of sacrificing, worshiping, and celebrating the Passover.

For if the Prophet intended the gatherings of Christians, forbidden and suppressed by persecutors, to be understood, he would seem to have said “places laid waste,” not “place.”

We can, however, accept a singular number in place of a plural, as “garment” is used for “garments,” “soldier” for “soldiers,” and “cattle” for “herds.” It is customary to speak in many such ways, not only among ordinary speakers but also among the most eloquent authors.

This kind of expression is not foreign to divine Scripture itself. It uses “frog” for “frogs” and “locust” for “locusts” (Psalm 77:45), along with innumerable similar examples.

As for “They have devoured Jacob,” this is rightly understood to mean that they compelled many, by terror, to pass into their wicked body—that is, into their society.

## 11. [Verse 8]

He remembers, certainly, that although things deserved by their exceedingly evil will must be repaid to them out of God’s anger, they could not have prevailed against his inheritance unless he himself had wished to correct it by scourging it on account of its sins.

Hence he adds:

“Do not remember our ancient iniquities.”

He does not say “past,” which could include more recent sins, but “ancient”—that is, sins handed down from our parents. For such iniquities deserve condemnation, not correction.

“Let your mercies quickly anticipate us.”

They are to anticipate us, certainly, at your judgment. “Mercy triumphs over judgment”; but “judgment without mercy” belongs to the one “who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13) [Note: [Col. 1016] Several manuscripts: “mercy triumphs over judgment,” omitting “in.”].

When he adds, “For we have been made exceedingly poor,” he wants the anticipation of God’s mercies to be understood in this way: our poverty—that is, our weakness—must be helped by his mercy to fulfill his commandments, lest we come to his judgment to be condemned.

## 12. [Verse 9]

Therefore it follows:

“Help us, O God our Savior.”

By saying “our Savior,” he sufficiently explains what poverty he intended by the words, “For we have been made exceedingly poor.” It is precisely this weakness that requires a Savior.

When he wishes us to be helped, he neither shows ingratitude toward grace nor removes free choice. For the one who is helped also does something through himself.

He adds:

“For the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us,”

so that the one who boasts may boast not in himself but in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

“And be merciful,” he says, “to our sins for the sake of your name”—not for our sake. For what else do our sins deserve but due and fitting punishments? Yet he says, “Be merciful to our sins for the sake of your name.”

Thus you deliver us—that is, rescue us from evils—when you both help us to practice righteousness and show mercy to our sins, without which we do not live in this life:

“For no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

“Sin is lawlessness” (1 John 3:4); and “if you keep watch over iniquities, Lord, who will stand?” (Psalm 129:3).

## 13. [Verse 10]

As for what he adds, “Lest they say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”—this should rather be understood as concerning the nations themselves.

Those perish wickedly who despair of the true God, thinking either that he does not exist or that he does not help his own and is not merciful to them.

But what follows—“And let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been poured out become known among the nations before our eyes”—can be understood in this way: they come to believe in the true God, although they had persecuted his inheritance. For this too is vengeance: their savage wickedness is destroyed by the sword of God’s word, of which it is said, “Gird your sword” (Psalm 44:4).

Alternatively, it may refer to their being punished at the end while they remain enemies.

The bodily evils they suffer in this world can be shared by the good. There is also another kind of vengeance: in this world the sinner, the unbeliever, and the enemy sees and becomes angry at the Church’s expansion and fruitfulness after so many persecutions, when they had thought that it would perish utterly. “He gnashes his teeth and wastes away” (Psalm 111:10). Who would dare deny that this too is a very severe punishment?

But I do not know whether the phrase “before our eyes” is interpreted elegantly enough if we understand this kind of punishment as something occurring in the inner depths of the heart and tormenting even those who flatter us with smiles, while we cannot see what they suffer within.

The other interpretation—that either their wickedness is destroyed when they believe, or that final punishment is repaid to them when they persist in wickedness—can be understood without hesitation as the meaning of the words, “Let vengeance among the nations become known before our eyes.”

## 14.

This, as we have said, is prophecy, not a wish. But because it is written in the Apocalypse that the martyrs beneath God’s altar cry out to God, saying, “How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood?” (Revelation 6:9–10), we must not pass over the question of how this is to be understood, lest the saints be thought to desire vengeance in order to satisfy hatred—something far removed from their perfection.

And yet it is written:

“The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon the ungodly; he will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood” (Psalm 57:11).

The Apostle also says:

“Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath; for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

He therefore does not command them not to wish for vengeance, but not to avenge themselves and thereby prevent the wrath of God, who said, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay.”

In the Gospel the Lord also presents a widow as an example. Desiring to be avenged, she repeatedly appealed to an unjust judge, who eventually listened to her—not moved by justice but overcome by weariness (Luke 18:3–5). The Lord presented her in order to show that God, who is just, will much more quickly render judgment for his elect, who cry out to him day and night.

That is also the meaning of the cry of the martyrs beneath God’s altar: they ask to be avenged by God’s judgment.

What, then, of the command, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44)? What of, “Do not repay evil for evil or abuse for abuse” (1 Peter 3:9), and “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17)?

If evil must not be repaid to anyone, then not only must an evil deed not be repaid for an evil deed; neither must an evil wish be repaid for an evil deed or evil wish.

The person who wishes evil in return is the one who, even if he does not himself take vengeance, nevertheless waits and wishes for God to punish his enemy.

Therefore, when both a righteous person and a wicked person wish the Lord to avenge them upon their enemies, how can they be distinguished except by this: the righteous person desires that his enemy be corrected rather than punished; and when he sees the Lord taking vengeance upon him, he does not rejoice in the enemy’s punishment, because he does not hate him, but in divine justice, because he loves God?

Finally, if vengeance is taken upon the enemy in this world, the righteous person either rejoices on his behalf if he is corrected, or rejoices for the sake of others, so that they may fear to imitate him.

He too becomes better—not by feeding his hatred on the other’s punishment, but by correcting his own errors.

Accordingly, the righteous person rejoices when he sees vengeance and washes his hands—that is, makes his deeds purer—in the sinner’s blood, that is, in the sinner’s destruction, not taking joy in another’s evil but deriving from it an example of divine admonition.

If vengeance is taken in the future age, at God’s final judgment, what pleases him is what pleases God: that the wicked should not prosper, and that the impious should not share in the rewards of the godly—for that would certainly be unjust and contrary to the rule of truth, which the righteous person loves.

When the Lord urged us to love our enemies, he set before us the example of our Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). Does this mean, however, that he does not correct them through temporal discipline, or that at the end he does not condemn those who remain stubbornly hardened?

Thus let the enemy be loved in such a way that the Lord’s justice by which he is punished does not displease us; and let the justice by which he is punished please us in such a way that we rejoice not in his evil but in the good judge.

A malevolent spirit is saddened if its enemy escapes punishment through correction. When it sees him being punished, it rejoices as though it had been avenged, so that it delights not in the justice of God, whom it does not love, but in the misery of the person whom it hates.

When it leaves judgment to God, it wishes God to cause more harm than it itself could have caused. And when it gives food to a hungry enemy and drink to one who is thirsty, it maliciously understands the words:

“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head.”

It acts in order to increase his burden and stir up God’s indignation against him, thinking that this is signified by burning coals. It does not understand that the fire is the burning pain of repentance [Note: [Col. 1018] The editions read “pain”; several manuscripts read “the pain”], until the head raised up in pride is brought down by the enemy’s kindness to saving humility, and his evil is overcome by the other’s good.

Hence the Apostle added with watchful care:

“Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Romans 12:20–21).

But how can someone who is good on the surface and evil within conquer evil with good—someone who spares with his actions but rages in his heart, gentle in hand but cruel in will? [Note: [Col. 1018] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “evil in what is hidden.”]

Thus the future vengeance upon the wicked is prophesied in this psalm under the appearance of one who is asking for it, so that we may understand that God’s holy people loved their enemies and wished good for everyone: piety in this age and eternity in the future.

As for the punishments of the wicked, they rejoiced not in the wickedness of those people but in God’s good judgments. And wherever their hatred of human beings is read in the holy Scriptures, it was hatred of the vices that each person ought also to hate in himself if he loves himself.

## 15. [Verse 11]

As for what follows, “Let the groaning of the prisoners come before your sight”—or, as some manuscripts read, “in your sight”—it is not easy to find holy people thrown into chains by persecutors. Even if such a thing occurred amid the great and varied range of punishments, it happened so rarely that it cannot be believed that the Prophet chose to mention precisely this in the verse.

Rather, the chains are the weakness and corruptibility of the body, which weigh down the soul. Through the body’s fragility, as through the material of various pains and troubles, the persecutor could compel a person toward impiety.

The Apostle desired to be released from these chains and to be with Christ, but remaining in the flesh was necessary for the sake of those to whom he ministered the Gospel (Philippians 1:23).

Until this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53), weak flesh, as though bound in chains, impedes the spirit’s readiness.

Only those feel these chains who groan within themselves while burdened (2 Corinthians 5:4), desiring to be clothed over with the dwelling that comes from heaven—because death is dreadful and mortal life is sorrowful.

On behalf of these groaning people the Prophet himself groans, so that their groaning may come before God’s sight.

Those bound in chains may also be understood as those who are bound by the precepts of wisdom. When patiently endured, these chains are transformed into ornaments; hence it is written, “Put your foot into her chains” (Sirach 6:25).

“According to the greatness of your arm,” he says, “receive into adoption the children of those put to death”—or, as other manuscripts read, “possess the children of those killed” [Note: [Col. 1019] All our manuscripts read “those put to death.”].

Here Scripture seems to me to have shown sufficiently who the groaning of the prisoners was: those who endured the gravest persecutions for Christ’s name, which are most plainly prophesied in this psalm.

Placed amid various sufferings, they prayed for the Church, so that their blood might not be fruitless for those who came after them, and so that the Lord’s harvest—whose enemies thought it would perish—might spring up from that very place with greater fertility.

He calls them “the children of those put to death”: they were not frightened by the sufferings of those who preceded them, but, stirred by their glory to imitation, they believed in him for whose name they knew those people had suffered, in exceedingly great multitudes.

Therefore he said, “According to the greatness of your arm.” For such a great event followed among the Christian peoples that those who thought they were accomplishing something by persecuting the Christians could not possibly have believed it would occur.

## 16. [Verse 12]

“Repay,” he says, “our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom.”

He is not wishing evil but announcing what is just and prophesying what will come to pass [Note: [Col. 1019] The editions read “what will happen in the future.” Most manuscripts read “what is true.” Some read “what will come to pass.”].

By the number seven—that is, by a sevenfold repayment—he wants the completeness of punishment to be understood, because this number commonly signifies fullness.

Thus, among good things, we have the statement, “He will receive sevenfold in this age” (Mark 10:30), which is set down in place of “everything”: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10) [Note: [Col. 1019] Thus the better manuscripts. The editions read, “In good things it should be understood as ‘he will receive sevenfold.’ And in this…”].

He calls them “neighbors” because the Church lives among them until the day of separation; for bodily departure does not occur now.

He says “into their bosom” because he means what is hidden at present, so that the vengeance carried out secretly in this life may afterward become known among the nations before our eyes.

When a person is handed over to a depraved mind, he receives within his inward bosom the merit of future punishments.

“The reproach with which they reproached you, Lord”—repay this to them sevenfold in their bosom; that is, for this reproach, reject them completely in the hidden depths of themselves.

For there they reproached your name, thinking that they could wipe you out from the earth in your servants.

17. [verse 13.] “But we are your people”: this is to be understood generally of every class of devout and true Christians. We, therefore, whom they thought they could destroy—your people and the sheep of your flock, so that “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31)—“will give thanks to you forever.” Other manuscripts read, “We will give thanks to you eternally.” This difference arose from an ambiguity in the Greek: what the Greek has, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, can be translated either “forever” or “throughout the age”; but the better translation must be understood from the context. The sense of this passage seems to me rather to indicate that “throughout the age” should be said, that is, “until the end of the age.”

The following verse, in the manner of Scripture, and especially of the Psalms, repeats the preceding one with the order changed: it first has what was later there, and later what was first there. For what was said there, “we will give thanks to you,” is expressed here as “we will proclaim your praise.” What was said there, “throughout the age,” is expressed here as “from generation to generation.” This repetition of “generation” signifies perpetuity—or, as some understand it, because there are two generations, the old and the new. Yet both take place in this age, since “unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5); and, further, because God’s praise is proclaimed in this age. For in the age to come, when “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), there will be no one to whom it should thereafter be proclaimed.

We, therefore—your people and the sheep of your flock, whom those men thought they could consume by persecuting us—“will give thanks to you throughout the age,” since the Church, which they tried to destroy, will remain until the end. “From generation to generation we will proclaim your praise,” the praise which they tried to silence by putting an end to us. In many passages of the holy Scriptures we have already shown that “confession” is also used for “praise,” as in the passage: “You shall say this in confession: All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good” (Ecclus. 39:39); and especially in what the Savior himself said, although he had absolutely no sin that he might confess in repentance: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). I have said this so that it may be understood more clearly that what is repeated in the words “we will proclaim your praise” is what was previously said as “we will give thanks to you.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 79. SERMON

[Note: [Col. 1021] Delivered to the people after the exposition of Psalm 73, concerning which see below, no. 10.]

[Col. 1021]

1. [verse 1.] There are not so very many things in this psalm [Note: [Col. 1021] Most and better manuscripts read, “There are not so many things in this psalm,” omitting multa, “many.”] in which our discourse encounters difficulty, or which impede the understanding of the hearers. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, and with an eagerness to hear and see what has already been prophesied and foretold, we should run through what is clear, like pupils educated in Christ’s school. Thus, if perhaps obscure matters require the service of interpretation, the clear matters ought to demand from me the service of reading them.

Here the song concerns the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and his vineyard. But it is Asaph who sings—so far as appears, enlightened and corrected—whose name, as you know, signifies the synagogue. Finally, the title of the psalm is, “For the end, for those who will be changed”—certainly changed for the better, since Christ is “the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4), and he came for this purpose: to change it for the better. It adds, “a testimony to Asaph” [Note: [Col. 1021] The editions read, “his testimony,” referring to Asaph. The better manuscripts read, “a testimony to him,” in accordance with the Septuagint.]: a good testimony to the truth.

Finally, this testimony confesses both Christ and the vine: that is, the head and the body, the king and the people, the shepherd and the flock, and the entire mystery of all the Scriptures—Christ and the Church.

Finally, the title of the psalm concludes, “for the Assyrians.” “Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who direct.” Therefore, let there no longer be a generation “whose heart was not directed” (Ps. 77:8), but a generation that is now directing its heart. Let us therefore hear what he says in this testimony.

2. [verse 2.] “You who shepherd Israel, give heed.” What does “You who shepherd Israel, give heed, you who lead Joseph like sheep” mean? He is invoked to come, awaited to come, desired to come. Therefore, let him find those who direct: “You who lead,” he says, “Joseph like sheep”—Joseph himself like sheep.

Joseph himself consists of sheep, and Joseph himself is a sheep. When you hear “Joseph,” although the interpretation of his name also greatly assists us—for it means “Increase,” and he certainly came so that the grain that had died might rise in abundance (John 12:25), that is, so that God’s people might increase—nevertheless, from what you already know happened to Joseph, let the one sold by his brothers come to mind; let him who was dishonored by his own people and exalted among foreigners come to mind (Gen. 37:28; 41:40). Then you will understand in whose flock we ought to be, together with those who now direct their hearts, so that “the stone rejected by the builders” might become “the head of the corner” (Matt. 21:42; Ps. 117:22), holding together two walls coming from opposite directions but brought into harmony at the corner.

“You who sit upon the cherubim.” The cherubim are the seat of God’s glory, and the word is interpreted as “Fullness of knowledge.” There God sits in the fullness of knowledge. Although we may understand the cherubim to be the exalted powers and virtues of heaven, nevertheless, if you wish, you will be a cherub. For if the cherubim are God’s seat, hear what Scripture says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7).

“How,” you ask, “will I be fullness of knowledge? Who can fill this?” You have the means by which you may be filled: “The fullness of the Law is love” [Col. 1022] (Rom. 13:10). Do not go about among many things and become scattered. The spreading of the branches frightens you; hold fast to the root, and do not consider the tree’s size. Let love be in you, and the fullness of knowledge must follow. For what does one who knows love not know, since it has been said, “God is love” (1 John 4:8)?

3. [verse 3.] “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear.” For this reason we went astray, because you did not appear. “Before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.” Appear, I say, before the Jewish nation, before the people of Israel: there are Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin.

But let us examine the interpretation: Ephraim means “Fruitfulness”; Benjamin, “Son of the right hand”; Manasseh, “Forgotten.” Appear before the one made fruitful, before the son of the right hand; appear before the forgotten one, so that he may no longer be forgetful, but that he may remember you who delivered him.

For if “all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21:28), did that very people descended from Abraham not have its own wall to rejoice at the corner, when it is written, “The remnant will be saved” (Rom. 9:27)?

“Stir up your power.” For you appeared weak when it was said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:40). You seemed to be powerless: the persecutor prevailed over you. And you demonstrated this beforehand, because Jacob himself prevailed in wrestling—a man against an angel. When could this have happened unless the angel had willed it? The man prevailed, and the angel was defeated; and the victorious man held the angel and said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

A great mystery! The defeated one stands and blesses the victor: defeated because he willed it, weak in the flesh but strong in majesty. And he blessed him: “You will be called Israel,” he said. Yet he also touched the breadth of his thigh, and it withered, making that same man both blessed and lame (Gen. 32:26, 28, 25). You see that the Jewish people became lame; see there also the blessed lineage of the Apostles.

“Stir up your power, then. How long will you appear weak? Crucified in weakness, rise in power” (2 Cor. 13:4). “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us.”

4. [verse 4.] “God, restore us.” For we have turned away from you, and unless you restore us, we will not be restored. “And enlighten your face, and we shall be saved.”

Does he have a darkened face? He does not have a darkened face, but he placed upon it a cloud of flesh, as it were a veil of weakness, and he was not thought to be the same person when he hung upon the tree who was to be recognized when he sat in heaven. For this is what happened. Asaph did not recognize Christ present on earth and working miracles; yet after he had died, risen, and ascended into heaven, he recognized him and was pierced with remorse. He might have spoken this entire testimony concerning him, which we now recognize in this psalm: “Enlighten your face, and we shall be saved.” You concealed your face, and we grew sick; enlighten it, and we shall be saved.

5. [verse 5.] “Lord, God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?” Now your servant. You were angry at the prayer of your enemy; are you still angry at the prayer of your servant? You have restored us; we have recognized you; and are you still angry at the prayer of your servant?

Yes, you are angry—but as a father correcting, not as a judge condemning. Yes, you are angry, because it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). Do not think that God’s anger has already passed because you have been converted. It has passed, but so that it may not condemn you eternally.

Yet he scourges and does not spare, because he “scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). If you shrink from being scourged, why do you desire to be received? He “scourges every son whom he receives”: he scourges every one, since he did not spare even his Only-Begotten. Nevertheless, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant? No longer at the prayer of your enemy, but you are angry at the prayer of your servant. How long?

6. [verse 6.] It follows: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure.” What does “by measure” mean? Hear the Apostle: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Cor. 10:13). That is the measure, according to your strength; that is the measure, so that you may be instructed, not crushed.

7. [verse 7.] “You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors.” This certainly happened. For from Asaph’s people those were chosen who would go to the Gentiles and preach Christ, and it was said to them: “What is this announcer of new demons?” (Acts 17:18). “You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors.” They were preaching the one who was contradicted. Whom were they preaching? That the dead Christ had risen.

Who could hear this? Who could know it? It was a new thing! But signs followed, and miracles made an incredible event believable. He was contradicted, but the contradictor was conquered, and from a contradictor was made a believer.

There, nevertheless, was a great flame: there were martyrs fed with the bread of tears and given drink in tears—but by measure, not more than they could bear, so that after the measure of tears there might follow a crown of joys.

“And our enemies mocked us.” And where are those who mocked? For a long time it was said: “Who are these people worshiping a dead man and adoring one who was crucified?” It was said for a long time. Where is the nose of those who mocked? Do not those who now reproach us flee into caves so that they may not be seen? “And our enemies mocked us.”

8. [verses 8, 9.] But you see what follows: “Lord, God of hosts, restore us, and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.” We know this; it happened. How many nations were driven out—the Amorites, Hittites, Jebusites, Girgashites, and Hivites! After these had been expelled and conquered, the people delivered from Egypt were brought into the land of promise. We have heard from where the vine was transplanted and where it was planted. Let us see what happened next: how it believed, how greatly it grew, and what it occupied.

“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.”

9. [verses 10–12.] “You made a way before it, and planted its roots, and it filled the land.” Would it fill the land unless a way had been made before it? What way was made before it? “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). It rightly filled the land.

This has now been said about that vine as completed unto the end. Nevertheless, what came first? “Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. You extended its shoots to the sea, and its offshoots to the river.”

This requires the work of an expositor; it is not enough to be a reader and praiser. Help me by paying attention, for the mention of this vine in the psalm commonly creates obscurity for those who are not attentive.

The greatness of this vine has already been explained by us, and from what it was made [Note: [Col. 1024] These words, “and from what it was made,” are absent from some manuscripts.] and from what it became great has been foretold. “You made a way before it, and planted its roots, and it filled the land”: this was said of its perfection.

Yet the first nation was this Jewish vine. The Jewish nation ruled as far as the sea and as far as the river. “As far as the sea”: Scripture shows that the sea there was nearby (Num. 34:5). And as far as the river Jordan. For some Jews were settled beyond the Jordan; on this side of the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1024] Erasmus and the manuscripts read “below the Jordan.”], however, was the whole nation.

Thus the kingdom of the Jews, the kingdom of Israel, extended as far as the sea and as far as the river. But it was not from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. That is the perfected vine of which he foretold here: “You made a way before it, and planted its roots, and it filled the land.”

After foretelling the vine’s perfection, he returned to its beginning, from which that perfection came. Do you wish to hear its beginning? “As far as the sea and as far as the river.” Do you wish to hear its end? “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 61:8); that is, “it filled the land.”

Let us therefore examine Asaph’s testimony: what happened to the first vine, and what is to be expected of the second vine—or rather, of the same vine, for it is the same; it is not another. From there comes Christ, “salvation from the Jews” (John 4:22); from there come the Apostles; from there come the first believers, who laid the prices of their possessions at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 2:45; 4:35); from there comes all this.

And if some of the branches were broken off, they were broken off because of unbelief. But you, people of the Gentiles, stand fast through faith; do not be proud, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. But if you are proud, it is not you who bear the root, but the root that bears you (Rom. 11:18–21).

What, then, was the vine before which a way was made so that it might fill the land? Where was it first? “Its shadow covered the mountains.” Who are the mountains? The prophets. Why did its shadow cover them? Because they spoke obscurely of things that were foretold as future.

You hear from the prophets: “Observe the Sabbath”; “Circumcise the infant on the eighth day”; “Offer the sacrifice of a ram, a bull, a goat.” Do not be disturbed: it is its shadow covering the mountains of God. Manifestation will come after the shadow.

“And its branches the cedars of God”: that is, it covered the cedars of God, very lofty, but belonging to God [Note: [Col. 1024] Nearly all manuscripts read this way. The editions have “the seats of God.”]. For there are cedars signifying the proud, who are to be overthrown. “The cedars of Lebanon,” the heights of the world [Note: [Col. 1024] In the Remigius manuscript, “the cedars of God” is repeated here; this is absent from the other books. Perhaps one should read: “The cedars of Lebanon, the heights of the world,” with “signify” understood, so that what follows may be connected: “This vine, growing, covered the cedars of God,” etc.], this vine covered as it grew, as well as the mountains of God—all the holy prophets and patriarchs.

[Col. 1025]

10. [verse 13.] “But how far did you extend its shoots? As far as the sea, and as far as the river its offshoots.” What follows from this? “Why have you destroyed its hedge?”

You now see that nation of the Jews overthrown. From another psalm you have already heard: “With the axe and the hammer they cut it down” (Ps. 73:6). When would this have happened unless its hedge had been destroyed? What is its hedge? Its fortification.

For it became proud against its planter. The tenants scourged, struck, and killed the servants sent to them who asked for the rent. The only Son also came; they said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours”; and they killed him and threw him outside the vineyard (Matt. 21:34–39). Once thrown out, he possessed even more fully the place from which he had been expelled.

For through Isaiah he threatens it in this way: “I will destroy its hedge.” Why? “For I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns”; I expected fruit from it, and found sin. What, then, do you ask, O Asaph, “Why have you destroyed its hedge?” Do you not know why? “I expected it to execute judgment, but it committed iniquity” (Isa. 5:5, 2, 7). Was its hedge not to be destroyed?

And the Gentiles came. With the hedge destroyed, the vineyard was invaded, and the kingdom of the Jews was wiped out. This is lamented first, but not without hope. For the psalm now speaks of the direction of the heart—that is, it is “for the Assyrians,” for those who direct.

“Why have you destroyed its hedge, and all who pass along the road gather its grapes?” What does “those who pass along the road” mean? Those who rule for a time.

11. [verse 14.] “The boar from the forest ravaged it.” What are we to understand by the boar from the forest? To the Jews the pig is opposed, and in the pig they place the impurity of the Gentiles. The Jewish nation was indeed overthrown by the Gentiles; but the king who overthrew it was not merely an unclean pig—he was also a boar.

For what is a boar but a savage pig, a proud pig? “The boar from the forest ravaged it.” From the forest—from the Gentiles. For that vineyard was there, while the Gentiles were forests. But when the Gentiles believed, what was said? “Then all the trees of the forest will exult” (Ps. 95:12).

“The boar from the forest ravaged it, and a solitary wild beast devoured it.” What is “a solitary wild beast”? The very boar that ravaged it is the solitary wild beast. Solitary because proud. For this is what every proud person says: “I am; I am, and there is no one else.”

12. [verses 15, 16.] But what fruit comes of these things? “God of hosts, turn again indeed.” Although these things have happened, “turn again indeed. Look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine.” And perfect it, the vine which your right hand planted.”

Do not establish another one, but perfect this one. For it is the seed of Abraham, the seed in which all the nations are blessed (Gen. 22:18); there is the root that supports the grafted wild olive.

“Perfect this vine which your right hand planted.” But where does he perfect it? “And upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself.”

What could be clearer? What are you still waiting for us to explain to you through argument, rather than for us to cry out together with you in wonder: “Perfect this vine which your right hand planted, and perfect it upon the son of man”? Which son of man? “Whom you confirmed for yourself.”

A great foundation! Build as much as you can. “No one can lay any other foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11).

[Col. 1026]

13. [verse 17.] “Burned with fire and dug up, they will perish at the rebuke of your face.” What are “burned with fire and dug up,” which will perish at the rebuke of his face? Let us see and understand what has been burned with fire and dug up.

What did Christ rebuke? Sins. At the rebuke of his face, sins perished. Why, then, are sins burned with fire and dug up?

Two things produce all sins in a person: desire and fear. Think, examine, question your hearts, search your consciences; see whether sins can exist except through desiring or fearing.

A reward is offered so that you may sin—that is, something that delights you; you act because you desire it. But perhaps gifts do not persuade you; threats terrify you. You act because you fear.

Someone wants to corrupt you so that, for example, you may give false testimony. There are innumerable examples, but I shall offer clearer ones, from which you can infer the rest. You have considered God and said in your heart: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). I am not persuaded by a reward to destroy my soul for the sake of monetary gain.

Then that person turns to instill fear. He who could not corrupt you by a reward begins to threaten loss, expulsion, perhaps even slaughter and death. At that point, if desire has failed, fear may succeed in making you sin.

But if, from the Scriptures, the words “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” come to mind against desire, let these words also come to mind against fear: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28). Whoever wants to kill you has power over the body, but not over the soul. Your soul will not die unless you yourself wish to kill it.

Let another person’s iniquity destroy your flesh, while truth preserves your soul. But if you recoil from the truth, what more can your enemy do to you than you do to yourself? A raging enemy can kill your flesh; but by giving false testimony you kill your soul. Hear Scripture: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Therefore, my brothers, love and fear lead to every right action; love and fear lead to every sin. To do good, you love God and fear God; to do evil, you love the world and fear the world.

Let these two be turned toward what is good. You loved the earth; love eternal life. You feared death; fear hell. Whatever the world promises you when you act unjustly, can it give as much as God will give the righteous? Whatever the world threatens you when you act justly, can it do what God does to the wicked?

Do you wish to see what God will give if you live righteously? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Do you wish to see what he will do to the ungodly? “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

Certainly, you want nothing else except that things may go well for you. For in what you love, you want things to go well for you; and in what you fear, you do not want things to go badly for you. But you seek this in the wrong region, where it should not be sought.

You are in a hurry; you want to be free from want and free from trouble. What you want is good, but endure what you do not want so that you may attain what you want.

Therefore, when his face blots out sins, what will he do? What are the sins “burned with fire and dug up”? What had evil love done? It had kindled a fire, as it were. What had evil fear done? It had dug, as it were.

Love inflames; fear humbles. Therefore the sins of evil love are “burned with fire,” while the sins of evil fear are “dug up.” Good fear also humbles, and good love also kindles—but in one way and in another.

For the gardener, interceding for the tree that bore no fruit so that it might not be uprooted, says: “I dig around it and apply a basket of manure” (Luke 13:8). The digging signifies the devout humility of one who fears, and the basket of manure signifies the useful filth of the penitent.

Concerning the fire of good love, the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)—the fire with which those who are fervent in spirit and aflame with love of God and neighbor may burn.

Thus, just as all righteous works are done through good fear and good love, so all sins are committed through evil love and evil fear.

Therefore: “Burned with fire and dug up”—that is, all sins—“at the rebuke of your face they will perish.”

14. [verses 18–20.] “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you confirmed for yourself. And we will not depart from you.”

How long will there be a “perverse and provoking generation,” one “whose heart was not directed” (Ps. 77:8–9)? Let Asaph say: Let your mercy reveal itself; deal well with your vine; perfect it, since “a partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

When your face has been shown over the man of your right hand, whom you confirmed for yourself, “we will not depart from you.” How long will you rebuke us? How long will you accuse us? Do this, and we will not depart from you: “You will give us life, and we will call upon your name.”

You will be sweet to us; you will give us life. For previously we loved the earth, not you; but you “put to death our members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:5).

The Old Testament, having earthly promises, seems to persuade us not to worship God gratuitously, but to love him because he gives something on earth. What do you love, that you should not love God? Tell me. If you can, love something that he did not make.

Look around at the whole of creation. See whether you are held anywhere by the snare of desire and hindered from loving the Creator by anything except what he himself created—the very one whom you neglect. Why do you love these things except because they are beautiful? Can they be as beautiful as the one by whom they were made?

You marvel at these things because you do not see him. But through the things you marvel at, love the one whom you do not see. Question creation: if it exists of itself, remain in it; but if it exists from him, it is harmful to its lover for no other reason than that it is preferred to the Creator.

Why have I said this? Because of this verse, brothers. Those were dead who worshiped God for the reason that things might go well for them according to the flesh. For “to think according to the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6). And those are dead who do not worship God gratuitously—that is, because he himself is good, not because he gives the kinds of goods that he also gives to those who are not good.

Do you want money from God? A robber has that too. A wife, fertility of children, bodily health, worldly honor? Consider how many wicked people possess these things. Is this the whole reason you worship him? Your feet will totter; you will think that you worship him without cause when you see these things in those who do not worship him (Ps. 72:2).

Therefore he gives all these things even to the wicked; he reserves himself alone for the good.

“You will give us life”: for we were dead when we clung to earthly things; we were dead when we bore the image of the earthly man. “You will give us life”: you will renew us; you will give us the life of the inner person. “And we will call upon your name”: that is, we will love you.

You will be sweet to us, forgiving our sins; you will be the whole reward of the justified.

“Lord, God of hosts, restore us; and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

[Col. 1027]

**THE FIRST PART OF THE FOURTH VOLUME ENDS.**
